## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers Who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III

A chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition extant from the first twelve centuries of the Church, very carefully corrected by comparison of the most accurate editions with one another and with certain manuscripts; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the completion of the fullest editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on each text of each book of Scripture and in which places in their works.

A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the thoroughness of the correction, the variety and number of the *pecusorum* works [uncertain OCR], the very convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the course of the work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time brought together in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

### First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning. [Vrayet]

# In the Year of Our Lord 540. Dionysius Exiguus

[Col. 0009]

## Notice (from Cave)

[Col. 0009A] Dionysius Exiguus was a Scythian by nationality, a monk by profession, and a Roman abbot; he was a friend of Cassiodorus and his fellow student in the study of dialectic. He flourished in the year 533. He died before the year 556, in which Cassiodorus wrote his book On Divine Readings; in that book Cassiodorus praises Dionysius, already—as he says—departed from this life, with the greatest enthusiasm.

“The Catholic Church,” he says (chapter 23), “even today produces illustrious men, shining with the splendor of approved doctrines. For in our own times there was also the monk Dionysius—very learned in both languages—who rendered in his actions the justice he had read in the Lord’s books. He had examined and understood the divine Scriptures with such zeal that … In him great wisdom was joined to simplicity, humility to learning, and restraint in speech to eloquence. Entirely Catholic, entirely and steadfastly attached to the rules of the Fathers; whatever readers may seek by searching through various sources, they recognized as capable of shining in his knowledge.”

## Works

A collection, or Code of Ecclesiastical Canons, translated and arranged in Latin by Dionysius at the request of Stephen, bishop of Salona. It consists of the first fifty Apostolic Canons and the canons of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, Sardica, and certain African councils. It exists in all collections of the councils and was published by Justellus, Paris, 1628, in octavo, and in the Library of Canon Law, vol. I, p. 97.

A collection of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, from Siricius to Anastasius II, as many as could be found, together with a dedicatory letter to Julian, a Roman presbyter [Col. 0009C] who subscribed to the synods held at Rome in the years 488 and 499. It exists in every edition of the Councils and was published by Justellus together with the Code of Canons, Paris, 1628, in octavo, and in the Library of Canon Law, vol. I, p. 181.

[Col. 0010A] The synodical letter of Saint Cyril and the Council of Alexandria against Nestorius, translated into Latin. It exists elsewhere as well and was published by Justellus together with the earlier short works.

The Paschal Letter of Proterius to Leo, translated into Latin, together with two Paschal letters by Dionysius Exiguus himself to Petronius and Boniface. It is found in the appendix to Petavius’s work On Temporal Doctrine.

The Life of Saint Pachomius the Abbot, translated into Latin and published among the Lives of the Fathers by Heribert Rosweyde, Antwerp, 1615 and 1628, folio.

The Oration of Proclus On the Praises of the Mother of God—which Garnerius nevertheless argues was translated not by Exiguus but by Marius Mercator; accordingly, he published the translation among Mercator’s works, with the Greek text attached, part II, p. 19. Also Proclus’s letter On the Faith to the Armenians, and another [Col. 0010B] to Domnus on behalf of Athanasius, bishop of Perrha, translated into Latin. They are found in the edition of Proclus’s works prepared by Vincent Riccardi, Rome, 1630, in quarto.

Gregory of Nyssa’s book On the Making of Man, divided into two homilies and translated into Latin. The translation exists in Basel, 1562, and Cologne, 1573, but without Dionysius’s dedicatory letter to Eugyppius the presbyter and without Nyssa’s translated preface; Mabillon was the first to publish these in the Analecta, vol. II, p. 1.

The History of the Discovery of the Head of Saint John the Baptist, written in Greek by Marcellus the abbot and translated into Latin by Exiguus. It was published by the illustrious Du Fresne at the end of his historical treatise On the Head of Saint John the Baptist, Paris, 1665, in quarto.

The Paschal Cycle of ninety-seven years, beginning in the year 527; a fragment of it is found in Marianus Scotus’s Chronicle under the year 527. In this cycle Dionysius numbered the years from Christ’s Incarnation, and he was the first of all to employ this era in reckoning years.

# The Synodical Letter of Saint Cyril and the Council of Alexandria Against Nestorius, Translated into Latin by Dionysius Exiguus (G, S)*

## Preface to the Letter of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria

[Col. 0009D]

To the most blessed lord, Father Peter, bishop: Dionysius Exiguus sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0010D] Mindful of your benefits, venerable Father, and of the outstanding glory of Christ’s bishops, and always setting before the eyes of my mind the holy care with which you nourished me from my childhood—care which no distance of place or passage of time can erase—I seek to return thanks, although I know that I cannot adequately repay them.

But because what seems lacking in duty is often completed by a vow, I do not cease to reveal, with whatever diligence I can, the affection that I continually bear toward your fatherhood. For this reason I have sent you, through your reverend brother Sanctulus, the synodical letter of Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, addressed to Nestorius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople. Attached to it are twelve chapters condemning, under the threat of anathema, the blasphemies of that same Nestorius. I recently translated it from Greek into Latin and now send it to you.

I considered the present moment entirely suitable, so that the apostolic faith of so great a teacher—long well known to the Greeks but hitherto unknown to the Latins—might become known to them also. Thus the Nestorian stain may be clearly recognized by all and rightly rejected for its wickedness. Under the pretext of faith it never ceases to insinuate unbelief, and with both Jewish fury and error it strives to disturb the peace of the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world.

Although I know very well that wicked men listen to salutary instructions in a hostile spirit and persist in following their evil counsels, no instruction, however extensive, should therefore be omitted [Col. 0012A] on account of those who are deceived not through love of contention but through a certain simplicity. For it often happens, when God grants his help, that those who gave assent to falsehood turn their zeal toward the truth.

The present writings of the blessed Cyril therefore admonish Nestorius himself not to dare divide the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages and of the same essence as the Father, who descended for our salvation and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, into two; nor, with his accustomed craft, to try to assert some conjunction and association of God and man.

Those terms, as he uses them, do not signify the inseparable unity of both natures, nor the singularity of the person—or, more precisely, the subsistence—of the Son of God. Rather, by this pretext of such men they indicate two things, or indeed more than two, and display the criminal division of so wicked a doctrine. Its impious founder and his followers strive to join them by a certain dignity and authority, and also by relation, in the manner of their own folly.

But let these matters now be explained more fully through the assertion of the aforementioned Father. May God in his mercy restore the Catholic peace of your Beatitude and preserve us, through your prayers, among its members.

# Letter of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, Addressed to Nestorius, Formerly Bishop of the City of Constantinople, Containing Twelve Chapters of Anathemas

[Col. 0011]

[Col. 0011C] To the holy brother Nestorius, bishop: Cyril, bishop, and the synod assembled at Alexandria from the Egyptian diocese, send greetings in the Lord.

Since our Savior plainly declares, saying, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me,” what shall we suffer, who ask your Religion to love you more than Christ, the Savior of all? For who will be able to help us on the day of judgment, or what satisfaction shall we be able to offer, if we continue for so long to keep silent about the blasphemies you have uttered against him?

If you alone were being harmed by teaching or holding these opinions, our concern would be less. But you have scandalized the whole Church and introduced among the peoples—not only those present there but those established everywhere—the leaven of unprecedented depravity and a new heresy. Your books of exposition have been circulated everywhere. What further word of defense can suffice for our silence, or how can it not be necessary to remember Christ the Lord saying: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword; for I have come to separate a man from his father, and a daughter from her mother”?

When the faith is harmed, reverence for parents is despised as useless and dangerous, and love for children and brothers is avoided. Finally, devout men choose death rather than life itself, so that, as it is written, they may attain a better resurrection.

Behold, therefore, together with the holy synod assembled in the great city of Rome [Col. 0012C] under the presidency of our most holy brother and fellow priest, Coelestine, bishop, we have now for the third time addressed you in writing. We advise you to abstain from such depraved and distorted doctrines, which you are known both to hold and to teach.

Receive instead the true faith handed down from the beginning to the Churches through the most blessed apostles and evangelists, who are shown to have seen these things with their own eyes and to have been ministers of the Word.

If your Religion delays doing this, in accordance with the period fixed in the letter of our most holy and venerable fellow priest, Coelestine, bishop of the Roman Church, know that you have no share with us and that you will obtain neither a place nor an opportunity for conversation among priests and bishops.

For it is not lawful for us to disregard Churches so troubled, peoples so scandalized, and the most upright faith violated, or the flock dispersed which you ought to have guarded; nor is it lawful to disregard those who, together with us, should have been lovers of sound doctrine and should have followed devoutly in the footsteps of the holy Fathers.

Accordingly, all those whom your Religion removed from communion on account of the faith, or deposed from their order—laymen and clerics alike—we have received into our communion. It is not right that they should be oppressed by your decrees, since they know how to hold right opinions and, by doing what was good, wisely resisted you. You yourself took care to signify the same thing in the letter you sent to the holy bishop of the great city of Rome and our fellow bishop, Coelestine.

But it is not sufficient for your Religion merely to confess the creed set forth at that time, through the generosity of the Holy Spirit, by the venerable and great council assembled at Nicaea [Col. 0013A]. For you have neither understood nor correctly interpreted it. Indeed, although you have uttered the same words with the sound of your voice, perversely, it follows that you must also confess under oath that you anathematize your polluted faith and the profane teachings that you hold and teach—teachings contrary to what we all, whether bishops, teachers, or leaders of the peoples throughout East and West, believe and teach.

The letter sent from Alexandria to your Religion received the assent of the Church, both from the holy synod assembled at Rome and from all of us, since it was correctly and properly written.

We have appended to this letter what you ought to hold and teach and from what you ought to abstain. For this is the faith of the Catholic and apostolic Church, to which all orthodox bishops throughout East and West give their assent:

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty,” and the rest.

Following in every respect, therefore, the confessions of the holy martyrs, which they uttered while the Holy Spirit spoke through them, adhering with equal steps to the intention contained in their understanding, and walking along the royal road, we profess that the only-begotten Word of God himself, the Lord born from the very essence of the Father, true God from true God, light from light, through whom all things were made, whether in heaven or on earth, descended for our salvation and deigned to humble himself unto self-emptying.

Having become incarnate and man—that is, receiving flesh from the holy Virgin and making it his own—he endured our birth from the womb, proceeding as man from a woman, without casting away what he was. For although he came to be in the assumption of flesh and blood, nevertheless even so he remained what he was: God by nature and in truth.

We do not say that the flesh was converted into the nature of deity or changed into its substance. For deity is unconvertible and immutable, and, according to the Scriptures, he himself continually remains the same.

He was seen as an infant; yet, while still lying in swaddling clothes and held in the Virgin Mother’s arms, he filled the whole creation, existing as God undivided from his begetter. For what is divine is understood to be without quantity and without bulk, and is contained by no boundaries.

Therefore, confessing the Word of God united with flesh according to substance, we worship one Son and Lord Jesus Christ. We do not place and define man and God separately, as though they had been joined to one another by a unity of dignity and authority. For this is merely a novelty of expression and nothing more.

Nor, when we specifically call Christ God the Word who is from God, and separately call another Christ the one born from a woman, do we recognize two Christs. We recognize only one Christ, the Word of God the Father, together with his own flesh.

At that time he was also anointed according to our understanding, although he himself bestowed the Spirit upon those worthy, and not by measure, as the blessed evangelist John declares.

Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt as in an ordinary man born from the holy Virgin, lest Christ the man be believed to possess God as an indwelling inhabitant. Although it is said that the Word dwelt among us and that in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, we understand that, having become flesh, he did not dwell as he is said to dwell in the saints.

We have not tried to define his indwelling as such. Rather, united according to nature, without being wholly changed into flesh, he made for himself an indwelling of the kind that the soul of a man is also believed to have in its own body.

Therefore our one Christ, Son and Lord, is not united by some conjunction such as exists in the unity of dignity and authority between a man and God. For equality of dignity alone cannot unite natures.

Peter and John, for example, were equal in dignity to one another, and for that reason they are shown to be apostles and holy disciples. Nevertheless, the two are not one; nor, when we speak of comparison or connection, do we perceive a mode of conjunction [Col. 0014B]. For this is insufficient for natural unity, nor is such unity based on an affection of participation, as when we cling to the Lord and become one spirit with him.

Indeed, we avoid the name “conjunction” as unsuitable to signify the mystery of unity. Nor do we assert that God or Lord is the Word of God the Father’s Christ, lest we once more divide the one Christ, Son and Lord, more visibly into two and fall into the crime of sacrilege by making God and Lord for him.

For, as we said above, God the Word was united to the flesh according to subsistence. He is indeed God of all and rules the universe; nevertheless he is neither servant to himself nor lord over himself, since it is foolish, or rather impious, to think or say this.

Although he called God his Father, since he himself is also God by nature and from that essence, we nevertheless understand without any doubt that, remaining God, he also became man, existing under God according to the proper law of human nature. He himself, however, could not be God or Lord to himself.

Thus, just as a man, in a manner fitting the measure of his self-emptying, declared that he was with us under God, so also he was made subject to the law, although he himself had promulgated the law and existed as its divine Lawgiver.

We are careful not to say of Christ, “I venerate the assumed because of the one who assumed,” or, “I worship the visible because of the invisible.” It is horrifying to add even this: “The one who is assumed is called God together with the one who assumed him.” Whoever says such things again divides Christ into two, setting the man who is one apart in one part and God likewise apart in another.

For he plainly destroys the unity if one is not worshiped together with the other, or if one is called God. Rather, Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, is understood to be one, venerated with one worship together with his own flesh.

We also confess that the very same only-begotten Son who was born from God the Father, God by nature, although in his own nature he was without suffering, nevertheless suffered for us according to the Scriptures. With the body of his own flesh fixed on the cross, he impassibly referred its sufferings to himself.

By the grace of God he tasted death for all, handing over his own body to death, although he himself is naturally life and the resurrection of the dead.

In order by ineffable power to destroy death, to become in his own flesh the firstborn from the dead and the firstfruits of those who sleep, and to open the way for human nature to return from corruption, by the grace of God—as was said above—he tasted death for all, and, rising on the third day, stripped the underworld.

Therefore, although it is said that the resurrection of the dead was brought about through a man, we understand that the Word who is from God became man and that through him the dominion of death was destroyed.

At the appointed times he will come, as the one Son and Lord, in the glory of the Father, to judge the world in righteousness, as Scripture testifies.

We must necessarily add this as well. While announcing the death according to the flesh of the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the churches the unbloody service of sacrifice.

So also we approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all. We do not receive it as common flesh—God forbid—nor as the flesh of a man sanctified and joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or of one possessing divine indwelling, but as truly life-giving and made the proper flesh of the Word himself. For since he exists naturally as life, as God, and is united to his own flesh, he has confessed that flesh to be life-giving.

Therefore, although he says to us, “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” we must not regard it as the flesh of one ordinary man among us, since human flesh could in no way be life-giving according to its nature.

We must regard it as truly made the proper flesh of him who for us both became and was called the Son of Man.

We do not divide among two subsistences or persons the words spoken by our Savior in the Gospel. For the one and only Christ is not double, although he is understood to have come together from two different realities into an indivisible unity, just as a man, consisting of soul and body, is not rather two but one from both.

Therefore, discerning that human and divine words alike were spoken by the one Christ, we think correctly.

When he speaks in a manner wholly worthy of God about himself—“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” and “I and the Father are one”—we understand his divine and ineffable nature, according to which he is one with his Father because of one and the same substance, existing as his image and character and the radiance of his glory.

But when, without in any way dishonoring the measure of human nature, he addresses the Jews, saying, “Now you are seeking to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you,” we likewise recognize God the Word, who is in the likeness and equality of the Father, in the measures of his humanity.

If it is necessarily believed that the one who exists as God by nature became flesh, or rather a man endowed with a rational soul, why should anyone be ashamed of any of his words if he uttered words fitting for a man?

If he rejects speech appropriate to man, who compelled him, according to our confession, to become man? When he mercifully humbled himself voluntarily for our sake, why would he have avoided words appropriate to his self-emptying?

We therefore ascribe all his words in the Gospel to one person, to one subsistence: that of the Word incarnate, because there is one Lord Jesus Christ, as it is written.

He is called the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, as one who offers to God and Father the confession of our faith, which is continually offered by us to him and through him to God and Father.

[Note: [Col. 0015D] “Most worthy of God,” that is, “as befits God.” EDITOR.]

[Note: [Col. 0015D] The wording is altogether defective; perhaps it should be read: “He is called the apostle and high priest … as one who offers … that which is offered by us …” EDITOR.]

Again, when we say that he who is from God by nature is the only-begotten Son, we assign neither the name nor the office of priesthood to any man other than him.

For he became mediator between God and human beings and reconciler to peace, offering himself for us to God the Father as a fragrant offering:

“Therefore you did not desire sacrifice and offering; you did not delight in burnt offerings for sin. You fashioned a body for me. Then I said: Behold, I come. In the heading of the book it is written concerning me, to do your will.”

For he offered his body first, not for himself but for us, as a fragrant offering. What offering or sacrifice would he need for himself, since he existed as God free from every sin?

If all have sinned and lack the glory of God, since we are more readily inclined to depart into mutability and human nature has been weakened by sins, while he was not so; and if we are therefore overcome by his glory, what doubt can remain that the true Lamb was sacrificed for us and on our behalf?

But whoever says that he offered himself both for himself and for us will in no way escape the charge of impiety, since he committed absolutely no offense and made no sin whatsoever.

What offering, then, would he need when no crime of his own prompted it, for which it would be entirely appropriate to offer?

When he says of the Spirit, “He glorified me,” we rightly understand that Christ and the Son did not receive glory from the Holy Spirit as though they needed glory from another, since his Spirit is neither better nor superior to him.

Rather, because he performed wondrous works by the power of his own Spirit to demonstrate his deity, he is said to have been glorified by that Spirit.

It is as though someone said of human beings that his own strength or discipline glorifies each person. Although the Spirit exists in its own subsistence and its personal property is understood according to the fact that it is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless it is not alien.

For it was called by him the Spirit of truth, and Christ is truth; hence the Spirit proceeds from him in the same way as from God the Father.

Finally, this same Spirit, performing glorious miracles through the hands of the holy apostles, glorified the Lord Jesus Christ after he had ascended into heaven.

Christ was believed to exist as God by nature, working mighty deeds through his own Spirit. Therefore he said: “He will take from what is mine and announce it to you.”

The same Spirit is not said to be wise or powerful through participation in another, since it is perfect in every respect and entirely lacks nothing good.

It is believed to be the Spirit of the Father’s power and wisdom—that is, the Spirit of the Son—and therefore it is shown in reality and subsistence itself to be power and wisdom.

Since the holy Virgin therefore gave bodily birth bodily to God united with flesh according to subsistence, we confess that she is the Mother of God—not because the nature of the Word received from the flesh the beginning of its existence.

For “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God, and the Word was with God”; he himself is the creator of the ages, coeternal with the Father and creator of the universe.

Rather, as we said above, by uniting human nature to himself according to subsistence, he endured bodily birth from that womb—not because this birth, which took place at the end of the ages, was necessary for him or required by his nature, but so that he might bless the firstfruits of our nature.

When a woman gave birth to him united with flesh, the curse pronounced against the whole human race ceased, and our bodies were no longer destined for death.

He also dissolved what was said, “In sorrow you shall bear children,” and showed the truth of what the prophet had foretold: “Death has been swallowed up in victory,” and again, “God has taken away every tear from every face.”

For this reason we say that, in the economy of salvation, he blessed even the wedding feast when he graciously attended it in Cana of Galilee with the holy apostles who had been invited.

We have been taught to hold these things by the holy apostles and evangelists, by all divinely inspired Scripture, and also by the blessed confessions of the Fathers, which are supported by the truth.

It is fitting that your Religion should agree with all these things and consent without deceit or pretense. The matters that your Religion must anathematize are set forth below in this letter; if you do not do so, you will incur the judgment expressed in these articles.

## The Twelve Chapters

### I

If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and therefore that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God—for she gave birth bodily to the Word who is from God, according to what is written, “And the Word became flesh”—let him be anathema.

### II

If anyone does not confess that the Word of the Father is substantially one with the flesh, that Christ with his own flesh is likewise one, and that the same one is undoubtedly both God and man together, let him be anathema.

### III

If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, joining them only by an association that is according to dignity, authority, or power, and not rather by a coming together into natural unity, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0017D]

### IV

If anyone assigns to two persons or subsistences the words contained both in the Gospels and in the apostolic writings, or the words spoken about Christ by the saints or by Christ himself about himself, and believes that some of them are to be understood and applied specifically to the man apart from God the Word, while assigning others, as fitting for God, solely to the Word of God the Father, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0018A]

### V

If anyone dares to say that Christ is a man—ἄνθρωπον θεοφόρον, that is, “a man using God and carrying him” [sic]—and does not rather say that he is truly God, as the unique Son by nature, according to the statement “the Word became flesh,” and that he participated with us similarly in flesh and blood, let him be anathema.

### VI

If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ, and does not rather confess that the same one is both God and man together, because the Word became flesh according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.

### VII

If anyone says that God the Word worked in Jesus as in a man, and attributes the dignity of the Only-begotten to someone other than him, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0018B]

### VIII

If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be worshiped together with God the Word, and called God along with him, as one with another—the addition of a single syllable forcing this interpretation—and does not rather venerate Emmanuel with one reverence and offer him one glorification, according to the statement “the Word became flesh,” let him be anathema.

### IX

If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit as by an alien power, through which he worked and from which he received power against unclean spirits and through which he performed divine signs, and does not rather say that the Spirit was his own, just as it was the Father’s, through which he worked the signs, let him be anathema.

### X

Divine Scripture records that Christ became the High Priest and Apostle of our confession [Col. 0018C]. For he offered himself for us to God the Father as a fragrant offering.

Therefore, if anyone says that someone other than the very God the Word became our High Priest and Apostle when he became flesh and, according to our confession, man—if he says that a man born of a woman, as though someone other than the Word, became this in a particular sense—and if anyone says that he offered himself as an offering both for himself and for us, rather than for us alone—for he who knew no sin had no need of an offering—let him be anathema.

XI. If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving as belonging properly to God the Word himself, but regards it as belonging to someone else distinct from him, joined indeed according to dignity or according to the fact that it possessed only divine indwelling; and if he does not rather say that it is life-giving because it became the proper flesh of the Word of God, to whom it is possible to give life to all things, let him be anathema.

XII. If anyone does not confess that God the Word suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, insofar as he is both life and, as God, the giver of life, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0019]

# TWO LETTERS OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS ON THE COMPUTATION OF EASTER (C, S)

## FIRST LETTER. WRITTEN IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 525, DURING THE CONSULSHIP OF PROBUS, IN THE THIRD INDICTION

[Col. 0019A]

To the most blessed and greatly desired Father Petronius, bishop: Dionysius Exiguus.

We have now undertaken, aided by your prayers, to explain the computation of the paschal feast, which the persistent requests of many people have long and repeatedly demanded from us. In every respect we follow the venerable judgment, complete and true in this matter, of the three hundred and eighteen bishops who assembled at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia against the madness of Arius. They established the fourteenth moons of the paschal observance as fixed and unchanging within the nineteen-year cycle that continually returns upon itself. These moons pass through all ages with the same beginning at which they [Col. 0019B] recur (another reading: are restored), without varying in their course.

They established this rule of the aforesaid cycle not so much through individual expertise as through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and they are seen to have placed it like a firm and stable anchor in this reckoning of lunar measurement. Later, certain people, either scorning it through arrogance or transgressing it through ignorance, and led on by Jewish fables, handed down a different and contrary form of the single feast. Since no structure can stand without a solid foundation, they preferred to fix the Lord’s Pascha and the reckoning of the moon quite differently in certain years, arranging (another reading: beginning) disordered cycles. These cycles not only offer no stability of recurrence but also display a course conspicuously marked by error.

[Col. 0019C]

But the blessed Athanasius, archbishop of the city of Alexandria, who was himself also present at the Council of Nicaea as deacon of the holy bishop Alexander and assisted in everything; and afterward the venerable Theophilus and Cyril, did not in the least depart from this venerable decree of the synod. Rather, by carefully retaining the same nineteen-year cycle, which in Greek is called the *Enneacaidecaeteris*, they are shown not to have interrupted the paschal course with any variations.

Finally, Pope Theophilus, dedicating a hundred-year cycle to the emperor Theodosius the Elder, and Saint Cyril, composing a cycle of ninety-five years, observed in every respect this tradition of the holy council concerning the observance of the fourteenth paschal moons. Since the rule of this same cycle ought to adhere more firmly to those who are diligent and seek to know the truth, we have thought it right to set it down after our preface.

We have endeavored, to the best of our ability, to explain this cycle of ninety-five years. We have placed first in our work the last cycle of the blessed Cyril—that is, the fifth cycle—because six years still remained from it; and afterward we profess to have arranged five others according to the rule [Col. 0020A] of the same bishop, or rather of the often-mentioned Council of Nicaea.

Since Saint Cyril began his first cycle in the 153rd year of Diocletian and ended the last in the 247th, we, beginning with the 248th year of that tyrant rather than of a prince, did not wish to link the memory of an impious persecutor to our cycles. Instead, we chose to mark the times by the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be better known to us and the cause of the restoration of humankind—that is, the passion of our Redeemer—might shine forth more clearly.

We also thought the reader should be warned [Col. 0020B] that this ninety-five-year cycle which we have produced, when, after the completion of its period, it begins to return to the same point, does not retain its proposed exactness in every respect. Although the years of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve their order in continuous sequence, and the indictions proceed through their customary fifteen-year revolution; although you will also find the epacts, as the Greeks call them—that is, the annual lunar additions of eleven days, which return upon themselves at the end of thirty days—marked according to fixed rules; and although you will find the nineteen-year recurrence and the fourteenth paschal moons the same through the revolution of all ages, nevertheless the concurrent weekdays, the days of the Lord’s Pascha, and the dominical letters of that Sunday itself cannot preserve a similar constancy.

The reckoning of the coinciding weekdays [Col. 0020C] (another reading: of the seven days), which derives from the course of the sun, is completed in a continuous cycle of seven years. In calculating it, you will count one for each year; only in the year in which there is a leap day will you add two. This is also why the ninety-five-year cycle does not appear to correspond in every respect with its own recurrence. For although it does not disagree in the other years, in those alone in which the leap day intervenes the Lord’s Pascha, together with its moon, occurs according to a different reckoning.

But these matters, which proceed in fixed order through all times, can direct the shifting occurrences by their stable circuit without any difficulty. Therefore, after the completion of ninety-five years, when someone wishes diligently to return to the beginning of these matters, let him proceed attentively not to the fifth cycle [Col. 0020D] of Saint Cyril, which we were necessarily obliged to set before us, but to our first cycle; and, in the order we have described, let him support the progress of those cycles that appear to falter by means of those that retain a firm course.

We have judged that the following point must also be noted with no less care, lest we be deceived in recognizing the first month. Almost the whole error of paschal discrepancy arises from this, [Col. 0021A] when the beginning of the period is unknown. For when the almighty Lord commanded that this most sacred solemnity be celebrated by the children of Israel, who were being liberated from Egyptian slavery, he said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, in the book of Exodus: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year” (Exod. 12:2). Likewise, in the same place, he says: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening” (ibid., 18).

In Deuteronomy also the same lawgiver Moses admonishes the people concerning this matter, saying: “Observe the month of new fruits, and the first of springtime, so that you may celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God, because in this month the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt by night” (Deut. 16:1ff.). By such great divine authority it was made clear [Col. 0021B] that the paschal feast ought to be celebrated in the first month, from the evening of the fourteenth day through the twenty-first.

But since it is not clearly stated there where this month takes its beginning or where it ends, the aforesaid three hundred and eighteen bishops, diligently investigating the observance of ancient custom, handed down from Saint Moses—as is reported in the seventh book of the *Ecclesiastical History*—declared that the new moon occurring from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the Nones of April constituted the beginning of the first month; and that the fourteenth moon was to be carefully sought from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April through the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Since the moon does not revolve in equal measure with the course of the sun, it reaches the spring equinox after intervals of so many days. The equinox is specifically marked from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, according to the judgment of all Eastern peoples and especially of the Egyptians, who are more knowledgeable than anyone in calculation. In the event that the fourteenth moon should fall on a Saturday—which is clearly known to occur once in ninety-five years—the same holy synod established without ambiguity that Pascha should be celebrated on the following Sunday, that is, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, when the moon is fifteen days old.

It gave this warning in every possible way so that no one would seek the fourteenth moon of the paschal feast before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, since it is certain that such a moon belongs not to the first month but to the last.

We also thought that the following should not be omitted: those are greatly mistaken who suppose that the moon completes the course of its cycle in periods of thirty days, and therefore count twelve lunar [Col. 0021D] months as three hundred and sixty days, to which they add five days that antiquity called intercalary, so that they may appear to complete the solar year.

Careful investigation of the truth has shown that in two lunar cycles not sixty days but fifty-nine ought to be counted. Accordingly, in twelve lunar months the total is three hundred and fifty-four days. To this the Egyptians add the annual epacts, that is, eleven days, so that at last the lunar measurement (another reading: dimension) may be brought into equality with the reckoning of the sun.

That this is entirely true and certain is confirmed by the judgment of the Fathers mentioned above [Col. 0022A], who, according to this Egyptian calculation, handed down the fourteenth moons of the paschal observance. But some, ignorant of such great exactness—or rather of such an authoritative ruling—while seeking other methods of calculation, depart from the path of truth. Hence it often happens that when the aforesaid Fathers designate the fourteenth moon, these people suppose it to be the fifteenth; and when it is the twenty-first, they declare it to be the twenty-second.

But we, who love and care for the Christian religion, ought not to depart from it for any reason whatsoever. Rather, it is fitting that we preserve with the most sincere observance the paschal rule established by these men.

It is not difficult to show how greatly we rely upon the authority of these Fathers in the Churches spread throughout the whole world [Col. 0022B]. For the second council, assembled at Nicaea not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0021D] Another reading: “when the holy council had assembled at Antioch not long afterward,” etc.; this seems more correct, as appears from what follows], judged that their original definition concerning the computation of Pascha ought in no way to be violated.

Finally, in the holy canons, under title seventy-nine, which is the first of the Council of Antioch, the following is expressly stated:

“We decree that all who dare to dissolve the definition of the holy and great council assembled at Nicaea in the presence of the most devout and venerable prince Constantine concerning the saving solemnity of Pascha are to be excommunicated and expelled from the Church, provided that, being contentious, they persist against what has been rightly decreed.”

Let this be understood as referring to the laity. But if any of those who preside over the Church—whether a bishop, presbyter, or [Col. 0022C] deacon—after this definition should attempt, for the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the Churches, to gather people separately and celebrate Pascha with the Jews, the holy synod has from this point declared him alien from the Church, since he has become a cause of corruption and disturbance not only to himself but to many.

It not only removes such men from the ministry, but those also who afterward attempt to communicate with persons so condemned are themselves condemned and deprived of every external honor that the holy rule and the priesthood of God have bestowed.

The venerable Pope Leo, prelate of the apostolic see, pronounces similarly, saying:

“Against the statutes of the paternal canons, which many ages ago were founded in the city of Nicaea through spiritual decrees, no one is permitted to venture anything. Thus, if anyone wishes to decree something different, he diminishes himself rather than corrupting those statutes. If these are preserved inviolate by all bishops, as they ought to be, there will be peace and firm concord throughout all the Churches.”

And again:

“In all ecclesiastical cases we obey those laws which the Holy Spirit established, through the three hundred and eighteen bishops, for the peaceful observance of all priests. Thus, even if far more people should decree something different from what they established, whatever differs from the constitution of those men mentioned above is to be held in no regard.”

Sufficient warning, as we think, has been given to everyone that henceforth the most sacred Pascha is not to be celebrated otherwise than as the holy Fathers established [Col. 0023A]. If anyone should perhaps obstinately disregard the testimonies of so many priests, he will also find parallel statements briefly recorded in ecclesiastical history; and through the reports of many bishops, especially the blessed Athanasius, whom we mentioned above, he will learn that these same things were widely known.

The same is testified by the letter of Saint Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, addressed to the same Pope Leo concerning this same paschal question. We have translated it from Greek in recent years and have seen fit (another reading: have proposed) to append it to this work. We have also added the arguments discovered through Egyptian ingenuity, by which the paschal headings can easily be found if they should be unknown: namely, what year it is from the Incarnation of the Lord, what the indiction is, what lunar cycle or nineteen-year cycle is in progress, and the other matters similarly sought through a concise calculation.

May divine grace deign to preserve your Blessedness, who prays for us.

## SECOND LETTER. WRITTEN IN THE COMMON YEAR OF CHRIST 526

To my most revered lords Boniface, first secretary, and Bono, second secretary: Dionysius Exiguus sends greetings.

I had believed that, after being compelled by the repeated admonitions of the holy and venerable Bishop Petronius finally to commit the paschal rule to writing, every subsequent attack upon divergent practice would be removed [Col. 0023C], especially since I had earnestly endeavored to make known the authority of the three hundred and eighteen holy bishops who assembled at Nicaea. At that venerable council they regularly established the nineteen-year cycle and marked the fourteenth moons of the paschal observance as immutable throughout all the periods of its revolution.

But since, when this question arose, your Holiness has now produced writings from the archive of the Roman Church by the venerable Bishop Paschasinus—who is known to have presided at the holy Council of Chalcedon on behalf of the most blessed Pope Leo—and addressed to that same pope at the same time, writings that clearly agree with the holy Fathers, we have inserted them into this present work. In this way we may also rely upon the testimony of this man, who by an evident miracle confirms the paschal decrees of the venerable bishops.

Since the writings themselves mention common years and embolismic years, and since some people inquire at length about this computation, which is said to derive from the tradition of the Hebrews, wishing to know whether it appears to agree with the paternal rule (another reading: with the rule of the Fathers), we have judged it necessary to arrange this information also in a compressed form, lest it be shown to differ in any respect.

Let us therefore understand that the same nineteen-year cycle always revolves within an octad and a hendecad. The number itself is expressed by eight and eleven. The octad, which begins with the first nineteen-year cycle, namely the seventeenth lunar cycle, proceeds in this manner: the first and second years are common, that is, shorter; the third is embolismic, that is, longer; the fourth and fifth are again common; the sixth is embolismic; the seventh is common; and the eighth is embolismic.

Thus, five common years and three embolismic years are continually assigned to the octad. A common year contains twelve lunar months, comprising three hundred and fifty-four days. An embolismic year is shown to contain thirteen moons and three hundred and eighty-four days.

The hendecad likewise proceeds according to this rule. It begins in the ninth year of the nineteen-year cycle, which is the sixth lunar cycle. Its first and second years are common; the third is embolismic; the fourth and fifth are common; the sixth is embolismic; the seventh and eighth are common; the ninth is embolismic; the tenth is common; and the eleventh is embolismic.

Thus the hendecad ends with seven common years and four embolismic years. The reason for the existence of embolismic years is evident: they make up for the deficiency of the common years, so that the lunar course may be brought into equality with solar time.

Although the moon traverses the solar year in its individual months, it cannot complete it within its twelve months. In common years, therefore, the moon is seen to fall eleven days short of the reckoning of the solar year. In embolismic years, however, the moon appears to exceed the same solar year by nineteen days.

Accordingly, let us set forth the years of the octad and the hendecad according to the order of the aforesaid cycle, and we shall prove clearly that over eight and eleven years the course of the moon contends with the sun, when the moon gathers as many days as the sun has traversed.

We have said that the octad contains five common years and three embolismic years. Five times three hundred and fifty-four makes one thousand seven hundred and seventy; and three times three hundred and eighty-four makes one thousand one hundred and fifty-two. Thus together they make two thousand nine hundred and twenty-two.

Similarly, eight solar years, added together—that is, eight times three hundred and sixty-five and one quarter—make two thousand nine hundred and twenty-two. In the same way, if you add together the years of the hendecad, which are seven common years and four embolismic years, by the calculation we have described, you will find nearly the same total as that produced by eleven solar years: namely, four thousand [Col. 0024D] fourteen.

This, then, is the reason for the embolismic years, as we said above: by their additions they compensate for the losses of the common years.

But now I shall show you the most beautiful and excellent summary of the nineteen-year cycle itself, by which you may henceforth remove any ambiguity that may arise. No one should be so overwhelmed by astonishment that, once the light of truth has been shown to him, he does not rejoice and, abandoning the darkness of ignorance, immediately assent to so great a calculation.

From the fifteenth moon of the paschal feast of the preceding year, for example, to the fourteenth moon of the following year, which is the point we are investigating, there will be three hundred and fifty-four days if it is a common year, and three hundred and eighty-four if it is embolismic. If one day more or less should occur, there is clear error.

The first year of the aforesaid nineteen-year cycle is excepted. We count it from the fourteenth moon of Pascha in the last, that is, the nineteenth, year to the fourteenth moon of that same first year (another reading: “which we have assigned”). For this reason the last year, retaining eighteen epacts—that is, lunar additions—then assigns to the first year not eleven days, as normally happens in the other years, but twelve.

Since these revolve at the end of thirty days, no epact is placed at the beginning of the cycle itself. The second year, however, receives eleven epacts. Therefore, as we have said, from the fifteenth moon of Pascha in the first cycle to its end, there is no doubt that we find the prescribed number of days in both common and embolismic years. If the matter should at some time be presented differently through the incompetence of calculators, this method of reckoning will expose their falsehood [Col. 0025B].

And so that this may be understood more clearly, let us demonstrate it by the example of the present year. The indiction is the fourth, the lunar cycle the eleventh, and the nineteen-year cycle the fourteenth. Since it is the sixth year of the hendecad, it must be embolismic.

Let us therefore carefully inquire how many days there are from the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the fourteenth moon of the present one; and we shall undoubtedly discover when we ought to celebrate Pascha.

After the year had passed in the third indiction, who could doubt—if he has even a slight knowledge of the care required by this matter—that the fourteenth moon at Pascha occurred on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, that is, on the twenty-fourth of March? [Col. 0025C]

Therefore, let us take the eighth day before the Kalends of April as the beginning of our count. We have seven days of March, thirty of April, thirty-one of May, thirty of June, thirty-one of July, thirty-one of August, thirty of September, thirty-one of October, thirty of November, thirty-one of December, thirty-one of January, twenty-eight of February, thirty-one of March, and twelve days of April, which is the day before the Ides of April. Together these make three hundred and eighty-four.

But if, according to their definition [Note: [Col. 0025D] Here he denotes Victorinus’s lunar cycle V, which we have placed at 29 March, one day before the Alexandrian cycle’s fourteenth day, correctly according to Dionysius’s meaning]—those who calculate the moon differently from the truth—we suppose the fourteenth moon to occur not on the day before the Ides of April but on the third day before the Ides, we shall obtain three hundred and eighty-three days, with the total reduced by one. This is permitted in no way.

Thus, whenever such a doubt arises, let us always carefully count the days from the fifteenth moon of the past feast to the fourteenth moon of the Pascha we are investigating. If it is a common year, we shall find three hundred and fifty-four days; if it is embolismic, three hundred and eighty-four. No inequality will occur at all, because the rule of this cycle stands on this basis. We shall unfold its clarified formula in the description that follows.

In the first nineteen-year year, the seventeenth lunar year, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May to the Nones of April, since it is a common year, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the second nineteen-year year, the eighteenth lunar year, from the eighth day before the Ides of April to the eighth day before the Kalends of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the third nineteen-year year, the nineteenth lunar year, from the seventh day before the Kalends of April to the Ides of April, since it is embolismic, there are three hundred and eighty-four days.

In the fourth nineteen-year year, the first lunar year, from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May to the fourth day before the Nones of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the fifth nineteen-year year, the second lunar year, from the third day before the Nones of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the sixth nineteen-year year, the third lunar year, from the tenth day before the Kalends of April to the fourth day before the Ides of April, since it is embolismic, there are three hundred and eighty-four days.

In the seventh nineteen-year year, the fourth lunar year, from the third day before the Ides of April to the third day before the Kalends of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the eighth nineteen-year year, the fifth lunar year, from the day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, since it is embolismic, there are three hundred and eighty-four days.

[Col. 0026C]

In the ninth nineteen-year year, the sixth lunar year, from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May to the seventh day before the Ides of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the tenth nineteen-year year, the seventh lunar year, from the sixth day before the Ides of April to the sixth day before the Kalends of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the eleventh nineteen-year year, the eighth lunar year, from the fifth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, since it is embolismic, there are three hundred and eighty-four days.

In the twelfth nineteen-year year, the ninth lunar year, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May to the day before the Nones of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four [Col. 0026D] days.

In the thirteenth nineteen-year year, the tenth lunar year, from the Nones of April to the ninth day before the Kalends of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the fourteenth nineteen-year year, the eleventh lunar year, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April to the second day before the Ides of April, since it is embolismic, there are three hundred and eighty-four days.

In the fifteenth nineteen-year year, the twelfth lunar year, from the Ides of April to the Kalends of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the sixteenth nineteen-year year, the thirteenth lunar year, from the fourth day before the Nones of April to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the seventeenth nineteen-year year, the fourteenth lunar year, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the fifth day before the Ides of April, since it is embolismic, there are [Col. 0028A] three hundred and eighty-four days.

In the eighteenth nineteen-year year, the fifteenth lunar year, from the fourth day before the Ides of April to the fourth day before the Kalends of April, since it is common, there are three hundred and fifty-four days.

In the nineteenth nineteen-year year, the sixteenth lunar year, from the third day before the Kalends of April to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, since it is embolismic, there are three hundred and eighty-four days.

# [CODEX OF CANONS]

[Col. 0027]

# PREFACE OF CHRISTOPH JUSTELLUS TO THE CODEX OF THE CANONS OF THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH

[Col. 0027B]

In ancient times the primitive Christian Church was governed by a twofold law, divine and canonical. Divine law is contained in the codex of Sacred Scripture; canonical law, however, in the Codex of Canons.

Accordingly, at councils those two codices were customarily placed in the middle of the assembly, so that from their authority the bishops might examine doctrines of piety among themselves, refute heresies that had arisen, and settle controversies pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline and sacred *politeia* (πολιτεία, “constitution” or “order”).

The acts of the Council of Chalcedon indicate this custom, where these words are frequently found:

**προκειμένου ἐν τῷ μέσῳ τοῦ ἁγιωτάτου καὶ ἀχράντου Εὐαγγελίου** — “the most holy and undefiled Gospel having been placed in the midst.”

And Cyril of Alexandria, speaking of the Council of Ephesus in his *Apologeticus* addressed to the emperor Theodosius, says:

**Ἡ ἁγία σύνοδος σύνεδρον, ὥσπερ καὶ κεφαλὴν, ἐποιοῦτο Χριστὸν· ἔκειτο γὰρ ἐν ἁγίῳ θρόνῳ τὸ σεπτὸν Εὐαγγέλιον, ἐπιφωνοῦν τοῖς ἁγίοις ἱερουργοῖς, Κρῖμα δίκαιον κρίνατε.**

“The holy synod made Christ its fellow-seated assessor and, as it were, its head; for the venerable Gospel had been placed upon a holy throne, calling out to the holy ministers: ‘Judge a just judgment.’”

And so too the synodal letter of the Council of Aquileia, with the divine Scriptures placed in the middle (*Tomus I of the Councils*).

The Council of Chalcedon itself also mentions the Book of Canons and cites from it (Acts 4 and 11) canons 83, 84, 95, and 96—corresponding to canons 3, 4, 15, and 16 in the Council of Antioch—and pronounces judgment on ecclesiastical controversies according to their authority. The synodical letter of the bishops of the province of Pisidia, in the Asian diocese, to the emperor Leo (vol. II of the Councils, Roman edition) [Col. 0027D] cites canon 83, which is the fourth canon of the Council of Antioch. Dionysius Exiguus, in his first Easter letter to Bishop Petronius, cites canon 79 (80 in the Greek numbering), which is the first canon of that same Antiochene synod. And in the letter to Stephen, bishop of Salona, which he prefixed to his Latin translation of that old Book of Canons, he enumerates the canons from the First Council of Nicaea to the First Council of Constantinople—that is, from the first chapter through the one hundred and sixty-fifth—just as, he says, they had been arranged in the Greek original according to the order of the councils and the sequence of the numbers.

Pope Leo I and the Roman synod seem to have had this in mind in their letter to the emperor Theodosius on behalf of Flavian, patriarch of Constantinople (ibid.). They requested that he order a general synod to be held in Italy; the decrees of the Nicene canons, and the matters appended beneath them, testified that this was necessarily to be demanded after an appeal had been lodged [Col. 0028B]. By the expression “appended beneath,” it is reasonable to understand the canons of the councils which, from Nicaea to Constantinople, had been collected in one body according to numerical sequence and were found in the old Book of Canons.

Vigilius, too, in his letter to Rusticus and Sebastianus, deacons of the Roman Church, cites from that Book a canon approved and read at the Council of Chalcedon, which is numbered fifth in the Antiochene synod. Hence it is evident that the Fathers of the primitive Church, when compiling that old Book of Canons, according to which judgments concerning sacred matters were given, arranged the successive councils in a fixed order and numbered their canons in a definite and continuous sequence, without interruption in the numerical connection, so that nothing could be taken away from or added to this Book. For this reason the Ephesian and Chalcedonian Fathers, as well as other ecclesiastical writers, commonly call it the τάξις καὶ ἀκολουθία τῶν κανόνων—“the order and sequence of the canons”; ἀκολουθία ἐκκλησιαστική—“the ecclesiastical sequence”; and ἀκολουθία ἀριθμῶν—“the numerical sequence.” Accordingly, in the acts of the councils, the terms ἀκολούθως and κανονικῶς are used in the same sense.

The twenty canons of the Council of Nicaea were placed first, διὰ τὴν τῆς οἰκουμενικῆς συνόδου αὐθεντίαν—“because of the authority and prerogative of dignity belonging to that great council,” the first ecumenical council celebrated by the Christian Church. Its name was also prefixed, as some think, because this practice was not observed with the other canons that followed or were appended. From this, it seems, in the course of time, all of them came to be cited under the name of the Council of Nicaea.

This can be observed in Gregory, bishop of Tours (Book IX, chapter 33). There, citing from the decrees of the Nicene canons a canon that is actually canon 14 of the Council of Gangra, he says: “I reread the decrees of the Nicene canons, in which it is contained: ‘If any woman leaves her husband and rejects the marriage-bed in which she has lived well…’” There followed the twenty-five canons of the Council of Ancyra and canon 14 of Neocaesarea—these two councils having been celebrated before Nicaea and subsequently approved by it, as the acts of the Council of Florence testify—and then the canons later established: twenty-one of Gangra; twenty-five of Antioch (four of whose canons are cited from that Book at the Council of Chalcedon under numbers 93, 94, 95, and 96); fifty-nine of Laodicea; and four of the First Council of Constantinople [Col. 0029A] (in the Greek text [lacuna]). According to Dionysius Exiguus, these collected canons amount to 154.

From these canons the body of that ancient Book was originally composed. It is known to have been cited in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon and already to have possessed universal canonical force before that council. Eight canons of the Third Ecumenical Council, the Council of Ephesus, were later added to it, perhaps by Stephen, bishop of Ephesus. A collection of canons by him remains unpublished; it agrees entirely with the old Book of the Universal Church and presents the canons of the councils of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, and Constantinople in the same sequence and order, to which he added those of Ephesus. This collection is preserved in the Palatine Library among the heirs of Gelhart Ermenhorst at Hamburg, but so far we have not been able to obtain it [Col. 0029B]. Later, twenty-nine canons of the Council of Chalcedon, the Fourth Ecumenical Council, were added by another compiler.

Although these five councils were local, they acquired the authority of ecumenical councils, since the Fathers of the four earlier councils approved them and adopted them as their own. They were unanimously approved and confirmed by the whole Church, both Eastern and Western; they were received and inserted into the Book of Canons of the Universal Church in such an order and numerical sequence that they formed one and the same body. The Council of Chalcedon gave this body the force and authority of universal canonical law in canon 1, in these words:

Τοὺς παρὰ τῶν ἁγίων Πατέρων καθ’ ἑκάστην σύνοδον ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν ἐκτεθέντας κανόνας κρατεῖν ἐδικαιώσαμεν.

“We have judged it right that the canons issued by the holy Fathers at each council down to the present time should remain in force.”

Later, the emperor Justinian, in Novel 131, concerning ecclesiastical canons, stated:

Θεσπίζομεν τοίνυν τάξιν νόμιμον ἐπέχειν ἐκκλησιαστικοὺς κανόνας, τοὺς ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων τεσσάρων συνόδων ἐκτεθέντας, ἢ βεβαιωθέντας, τοῦτ’ ἐστὶ τῆς ἐν Νικαίᾳ, καὶ τῆς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει, καὶ τῆς ἐν Ἐφέσῳ πρώτης, καὶ τῆς ἐν Καλχηδόνι.

“We decree, therefore, that the ecclesiastical canons issued or confirmed by the four holy councils shall possess the force of law—that is, those of Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon.”

Here, by “those confirmed,” it is reasonable to understand the canons of the aforementioned diocesan councils—Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, and Laodicea—which had been received throughout the world, approved and confirmed by the four earlier ecumenical councils, and contained in the Book of Canons of the Universal Church [Col. 0029D]. Theodore Balsamon explicitly noted this in his commentary on the first title, chapter 2, of Photius’s Nomocanon:

Σημείωσαι τὴν παροῦσαν νεαράν (ρλαʹ) ὡς νόμους κρατεῖν, μὴ μόνον τοὺς παρὰ τῶν (τεσσάρων) ἁγίων συνόδων ἐκτεθέντας κανόνας, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς παρὰ τούτων βεβαιωθέντας, ἤγουν τοὺς κανόνας τῶν τοπικῶν συνόδων.

“Note that the present Novel (131) says that, as laws, not only the canons issued by the (four) holy councils ought to be observed, but also those confirmed by them—that is, the canons of the local councils.”

The Third Council of Constantinople, held at Trullo in the year 707 under Justinian II, likewise confirmed that ancient Book of the Universal Church in canon 11. It listed the councils of which it consisted—namely, the first four ecumenical councils and the five local councils—while also preserving the chronological order from the Council of Nicaea to that of Chalcedon. To these it added the eighty-five Apostolic Canons, the canons of Sardica and Carthage, the Trullan canons, and the canonical letters of the Greek Fathers, which had not previously been received or confirmed either by the ecumenical councils or by the emperors. Balsamon noted that by this canon the local councils were also confirmed: τὴν γενομένην διὰ τούτου ἐπικύρωσιν τῶν τοπικῶν συνόδων—“the confirmation of the local councils effected through this canon.”

The canons of the Second Council of Nicaea were added later. Finally, from all these canons and from the decrees of the Fathers, extending from the First Council of Nicaea to the Second Council of Nicaea, the Book of Canons of the Eastern Church was composed. Its title is Κανόνες τῶν ἀποστόλων, καὶ τῶν ἁγίων συνόδων—“Canons of the Apostles and of the Holy Councils.” It was first published in Greek at Paris by the distinguished John Tillius from the canonical library of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, and was later published by Elias Ehinger from the Augsburg Library at Wittenberg in 1614. Zonaras and Balsamon added their commentaries, which had already appeared in print [Col. 0030B].

The first, and by far the most ancient, collection of ecclesiastical canons is therefore rightly called the Book of Canons of the Universal Church, because the primitive Church, both in the East and in the West, once used it as a common and universal law when judging sacred controversies. Later, from that ancient Book—as from an established and common authority approved by the Universal Church, the body of the ancient ecclesiastical jurisprudence—all canonical law, both Greek and Latin, was transmitted throughout the dioceses and provinces of the entire Christian world [Col. 0030C].

There are also other ancient and more recent collections, or abridgments, of the canons—nomocanons as well, that is, compilations of concordant canons and laws—which gathered all the decisions of the canons under certain titles. These include the works of John Scholasticus, Photius and Arsenius, patriarchs of Constantinople; Alexius Aristenus; Symeon the Logothete; Constantine Harmenopulus; and other Greek compilers. They were written after the Council of Chalcedon and the time of the emperor Justinian as private works, without any public authority, and were confirmed neither by the ecumenical councils nor by the emperors. For that reason they have no force as universal canonical law, though they are nevertheless highly useful and necessary for interpreting the canons and for making them easier to learn [Col. 0030D].

As for the Western Church, it is certain that throughout the entire Western world, and in the dioceses and provinces of the Latin language, it too—like the Eastern Church—used, in ecclesiastical judgments, the ancient canons contained in the old Book of the Universal Church. This is demonstrated by the acts of the councils and the decrees of the popes, where frequent mention is made of the Book, the body of the canons, the ancient canons, and the Eastern canons. These expressions unquestionably refer to the Book of the Universal Church.

Various and differing Latin translations of these Greek canons are found. The ancient one is that used by the Latin compilers of councils under the name of Isidore Mercator, and which they joined with the Dionysian translation. Several copies of this ancient version exist in libraries. But there is another, still older version, not yet published, of which we possess a very ancient manuscript copy written in capital letters, revealing the character of its age.

The Latin translation of Dionysius Exiguus—which we published twenty years ago from an ancient manuscript in our library—was preferred to the others as purer and more elegant. It preserved the sequence and order of the councils, the succession of the canons, and the numerical connection found in the Greek exemplar that he used: from the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea to the First Council of Constantinople, that is, from the first chapter to the one hundred and sixty-fifth, as he himself says in the letter prefixed to his collection. He added to it—omitting the four later canons of Constantinople and the eight Ephesian canons, which are found in the Collection of Canons, in the Nomocanon of John Scholasticus, patriarch of Constantinople, and in all the other Greek collections of canons—the fifty canons called Apostolic, together with the Sardican and African canons, which had been published in Latin in the West. For that reason they were subsequently placed in all the collections, διὰ τὸ πολλὰ περὶ τίνων ἐπιχωρίων, ἤγουν τῶν δυτικῶν μερῶν διορίζεισθαι—“because they defined many matters pertaining to particular places and regions, that is, to the Western parts,” as Balsamon says in the manuscript prolegomena to his Nomocanon.

Dionysius Exiguus explains the arrangement of his collection of canons in these words:

“We translated from the Greek the canons called Apostolic, to which many have not readily given their assent, although subsequently certain decrees of the popes appear to have been taken from those canons. Next we set down the rules of the Council of Nicaea, and afterward those of all the councils, both those held before it and those held later, up to the synod of the 150 bishops who assembled at Constantinople. We arranged them according to the sequence of the numbers—that is, from the first chapter through the one hundred and sixty-fifth—as they are found in the Greek original. Then, adding the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon, we declare that here the Greek canons come to an end. The statutes of the Council of Sardica and of the African Council, which were issued in Latin, are also distinguished by their own numbers in our collection.”

This Dionysian collection was immediately received by the Roman Church, as Cassiodorus, his contemporary (Book on Institutions, chapter 23), testifies:

“In our time there was a monk named Dionysius, a Scythian by nation but entirely Roman in character, highly learned in both languages. At the request of Stephen, bishop of Salona, he compiled the ecclesiastical canons from Greek exemplars with the brilliance of great eloquence. The Roman Church now embraces them in most celebrated use.”

The canons sent by Pope John II in 533 concerning the case of Contumeliosus, bishop of Riez, are likewise found reproduced from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus (vol. I of the Councils of Gaul) [Col. 0031D].

Just as the canonical decrees, or letters, of the Greek Fathers were attached to the Book of Canons of the Eastern Church by the Council of Trullo, so Dionysius Exiguus, shortly after publishing the canons, collected into one body the decrees of the Roman pontiffs Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, and Anastasius—from the year 385 to the year 496—and divided them into an ordered arrangement under composed titles. He placed them in a single numerical sequence, in the same manner in which he had arranged the canons of the Fathers, as he himself states in the prefatory letter addressed to Julian, presbyter of the title of Saint Anastasia. We published this letter together with an index of the decrees in 1643 (in the Book of Canons of the Roman Church).

Julian is found among those who signed the synods held at Rome under Pope Symmachus, after the consulship of Paulinus—that is, in the year 499, on the first day of March—and under Flavius Avienus the Younger, on the eighth day before the Ides of November—that is, in the year 502. From this the date at which those Dionysian collections, both of the councils’ canons and of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, were written is clear [Col. 0032B].

This is the first and most ancient collection of papal decretals. Pope Zacharias called it the Book of Decrees in his letter to Pepin and the bishops of France, from which he cites certain chapters of Innocent, Leo, and Gelasius. Another compiler later added the decrees of the succeeding pontiffs—Hilary, Felix, Simplicius, Hormisdas, Symmachus, and Gregory the Younger.

From the canons of the councils and the decrees of the popes there was eventually compiled the Book of Canons of the Roman Church. It was first published at Mainz by John Wendelstinus from three manuscript copies in 1525, and dedicated to Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Angelo, under the title: “Canons of the Apostles, Constitutions of the Ancient Councils, and Earlier Decrees of the Pontiffs.” It was later published at Paris in 1609 under the title Book of Canons of the Roman Church [Col. 0032C].

This is the Book of Canons that Pope Hadrian I presented in Rome in 805 to King Charlemagne for the use of the Western Churches. It was prefixed by a letter, or acrostic in political verse, bearing the inscription: “To the excellent lord, his son, King Charles, Pope Hadrian.” This was published by the most learned Jacobus Sirmond. Several ancient manuscript copies of this Book are preserved in libraries, as well as an abridgment of it by Cresconius, an African bishop who lived around the year 690. In the abridgment, entire canons of councils and papal decrees are omitted, though they can easily be recovered from the collection itself.

These are the canons and decrees that the Roman Church used in ecclesiastical judgments, as Pope Leo IV testifies. He lists the councils themselves and the papal decrees contained in this Roman Book in these words:

“In all ecclesiastical judgments we use the following: the canons called those of the Apostles; those of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Laodicea, Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon, Sardica, Africa, and Carthage; and, together with them, the rules of the Roman bishops Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Simplicius, and Gregory the Younger. These are altogether the authorities by which bishops judge and by which clergy are judged together with them.”

Let us now consider the ecclesiastical law used by the African Church and by the other Western Churches [Col. 0033A].

First, it is certain that the Africans possessed the canons of the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, brought to them by Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, who had attended and subscribed to that council. The African Fathers themselves testify to this at the Council of Carthage held in 419, after the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius. The Nicene statutes were also sent to them by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, in the translation of Theilo and Tarasius preserved in the Cologne edition of the Councils.

They also used the other Greek canons contained in the old Book of Canons of the Universal Church—namely, those of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, and Constantinople. After peace had been restored to Africa, Fulgentius Ferrandus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, composed a Collection, or Abridgment, of the canons received in Africa before his time, in order to restore the discipline of the African Church. He did so at approximately the same time that Dionysius Exiguus published his Collection for the use of the Roman Church.
