Ferrandus omitted the Apostolic, Ephesian, and Chalcedonian canons, and added those of Sardica, certain decrees of Pope Siricius from his letter to the African bishops, and also the canons of the African and Carthaginian councils.

The African Church possessed a definite and received collection of its own synods, known as the African Canons. This collection had been approved by the universal Council of Carthage of the entire African diocese and inserted into its acts. We published it in Latin and Greek in 1615 under the title Book of Canons of the African Church, and now issue a new edition. Dionysius Exiguus included it in his Collection, and the Council of Trullo confirmed it.

The fact that the African Church itself later received the collection of canons and papal decrees arranged by Dionysius Exiguus is indicated by the Abridgment, or Concordance of Canons, of Cresconius, an African bishop. Written around the year 698, it is entirely reproduced from the Dionysian Collection. More will be said about these matters in the preface to the Book of Canons of the African Church [Col. 0033C].

The Gallican Church also used the ancient canonical law: namely, that of the first four ecumenical councils, together with the other canons confirmed by them and received by the Universal Church. It did not, however, use the Dionysian translation [Col. 0033D], but an older one—specifically, the version found in the collection bearing the name of Isidore Mercator, in the Cologne edition of the Councils.

The Book of Canons of the Gallican Church is mentioned by the Council of Paris in the case of Pretextatus, bishop of Rouen, as reported by Gregory of Tours (Book V, chapter 18). Gregory calls it the Book of Canons and says that Chilperic, king of the Franks, had attached to it a new canon, as though it were an Apostolic canon, which was not found in the old Book of Canons of the Universal Church:

“He himself”—that is, Chilperic—“departed, sending the Book of Canons, to which a new quire had been appended, containing canons that were apparently Apostolic and included the following: ‘A bishop found guilty of murder, adultery, or perjury shall be removed from the priesthood’ (Apostolic Canon 25).”

It is therefore clear that the canons called Apostolic had previously not been received by the Gauls and were unknown to them [Col. 0034A].

Sigebert, king of the Franks, in his letter to Desiderius, bishop of Cahors (vol. I of the Writers of Frankish History), declares that he wishes to preserve the Statutes of the Canons and the ecclesiastical rules as his ancestors had observed them. The bishops of Gaul under Childebert, king of the Austrasians, removed Egidius, bishop of Reims, from the priestly order after the canonical sanctions had been read at the Synod of Metz, as Gregory of Tours reports (Book X, chapter 19).

Under the same Childebert, in the case of Ingeltrudis, Gregory himself (Book IX, chapter 33) cites, under the name of the Nicene canons—which had been placed as the heading of the Book of Canons of the Universal Church used by the Gallican Church—canon 14 of the Council of Gangra:

“I reread the decrees of the Nicene canons, in which it is contained: ‘If any woman leaves her husband and rejects the marriage-bed in which she has lived well, saying that one who has been joined in marriage has no share in the glory of the heavenly kingdom, let her be anathema.’”

Certain Gallican synods as well—such as those of Valence, Riez, Arles II, Agde, and Epaon—cite the Nicene, Ancyrene, and Laodicean canons from the old translation then received among the Gauls and found in Isidore Mercator. They always used this version more freely than the Dionysian one, until the time of Charlemagne, to whom Pope Hadrian I presented a copy of it. Thereafter they continually used the Dionysian translation as their canonical corpus, together with the African canons and the decrees of the earlier Roman pontiffs collected by Dionysius Exiguus. This can be observed in the Gallican councils held under the emperor Louis the Pious and in those that followed [Col. 0034C].

This is clearly indicated by Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, who lived under the emperor Charles the Bald, in his work against Hincmar of Laon (chapter 43):

“Who are those whom both the Apostolic See, all the bishops throughout the world, and the whole Catholic Church call canons? They are those which, beginning with the Council of Nicaea—the first council in our books, which our ancestors received from the Apostolic See to be followed—we retain in order as canons to be received, venerated, and observed, down to the African Council.”

A little later, speaking of the decrees of the pontiffs, he says:

“Tell us, we ask, what you think of the decrees of those who, after the Council of Nicaea and the other Catholic councils, enacted and promulgated decretal constitutions concerning the same sacred canons to be observed, such as Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Symmachus, Gelasius, Hormisdas, Gregory, and all the others”—namely Anastasius and Simplicius, who are listed in the Dionysian collection—“whose decrees the Catholic Church, and our Fathers and predecessors, have regarded as binding and have venerated.”

From this it appears, as Baronius says, that the letters attributed to various Roman pontiffs before Silvester—read Siricius—which were collected by Isidore, had not previously been received in practice. The statement once made by the bishops of Gaul to Pope Nicholas I is to be understood in this sense: that the decretal letters of the ancient pontiffs were not found transcribed in the entire Book of Canons [Col. 0035A].

By the expression “Book of Canons” it is therefore reasonable to understand the Dionysian collection, composed of canons and papal decrees, which by that time had been generally received for ecclesiastical use in the Gallican Church. Hincmar frequently cites the decrees of the pontiffs from Siricius to Gregory the Younger, contained in the Roman Book, and expressly says that the letter of Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, was promulgated from the sacred canons.

He rejects the synodical decrees attributed to Silvester in these words:

“Since some people produce, as though with authority, certain things that Pope Silvester is said to have decreed, although the Catholic Church does not count them among its synodical decrees, which our ancestors left to us and to their successors as matters to be held, we have thought it necessary to set this down here. For it is written in a certain sermon, without the name of its excerptor, extracted from the Acts of Silvester—which Isidore of Seville collected together with the letters of the pontiffs of the Roman See from Clement to Blessed Gregory—that the same Silvester decreed that no layman should dare to bring a charge against a cleric, and so forth. No one can doubt how contrary these statements are to one another, and how different they are from the holy canons and sacred laws, if he considers these statements rationally and reads the sacred rules and laws with greater care.”

Hincmar wrongly attributes to Isidore, bishop of Seville, this collection of letters of the Roman pontiffs from Clement to Blessed Gregory. It must entirely be attributed to Isidore Mercator. Riculph, bishop of Mainz, brought it from Spain into Gaul and was the first to publish it, as Hincmar himself testifies in his letter against Hincmar, bishop of Laon.

Speaking there of decisions collected by Hadrian from Greek and Latin canons, synods, and papal decrees and given to Bishop Engelramnus, Hincmar says:

“This land is full of those decisions, just as it is full of the book of collected letters by Isidore, which Riculph, bishop of Mainz, brought from Spain and obtained in this form, being as curious about such matters as he was about royal capitularies, and caused these regions to be filled with it.”

Riculph lived in the time of Charlemagne and presided over the Council of Mainz held in 813 [Col. 0035C].

Besides the universal Book, the Gallican Church also possessed a collection of its own synods, received under the name of the Gallican Canons. Pope Hormisdas mentions these in Gratian in the following words:

“According to the titles of the ancient Fathers, written under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, and according to the decisions of the 318 bishops”—that is, the Nicene canons—“which the Gallican canons also appear to contain, clerics found in adultery, whether they have confessed it themselves or have been convicted by others, cannot return to their rank of honor” (canon “If Any Deacon,” distinction 50).

The Council of Tarragona, held in the time of the same Hormisdas in 517, canon 11, indicates that the Spaniards were diligent students of these Gallican canons and often proposed to follow their authority:

“Let no monk be an agent or executor in secular business, except in matters required by the needs of the monastery, while the abbot nevertheless commands him, with the provision of the Gallican canons concerning such matters observed above all.”

The Council of Lérida (524), canon 3; the Council of Valence (590), canon 2; and the First Council of Seville and the Twelfth Council of Toledo establish that the same provisions should be observed which had been enacted in the Gallican councils of Agde, Orléans, Riez, and Valence. They also append the wording of those provisions and pronounce judgments on ecclesiastical controversies from them. Such was the authority of the Gallican Church among the Spaniards at that time that they considered whatever had been enacted by it worthy of imitation and adoption.

Agobard, bishop of Lyon, who lived under Louis the Pious, also mentions the Gallican canons in these words (Book on Ecclesiastical Dispensation):

“There are those who think that the Gallican canons, or those of other regions, ought not to be received because the legates of Rome, or of the emperor, were not present at their enactment, and so forth.”

He says in a letter to the emperor:

“Moreover, there is something worthy of pious consideration concerning the Gallican canons, which some reject as superfluous or useless because the recent Romans have not commended them, although the ancients religiously venerated them. This is not said to imply that the sanctions of every episcopal assembly ought to be received with equal authority, like those of Nicaea, Chalcedon, and the other general councils assembled and received with the consent of the whole world. Rather, because of necessary matters whose definitions are not found in those general councils, faith should be given to them with the reverence that is their due.”

These words clearly demonstrate the distinction between the two collections used by the Gallican Church.

The same is also indicated by the Second Council of Vaison, held in 529, canon 1:

“And although both the ancient and the new canons are shown to contain everything that ought to be observed by holy priests and clerics…”

By this canon, as frequently in the councils of Gaul, there can be no doubt that the expression “the ancient canons” signifies the Book of Canons of the Universal Church.

I shall add that before the Dionysian collection was received by Charlemagne, the Gauls were accustomed to use the African canons, as the Second Council of Mâcon, held in 588, indicates in canon 6:

“This matter has already been decided in such a case by the African councils. We have judged it worthy to join that decision to our own decree and to place it alongside it, so that the sacraments of the altar may be celebrated only by those who are fasting.”

The Council of Agde also testifies that they inserted certain letters of the Roman pontiffs into their own Book, canon 9:

“The authority of Bishop Siricius, which is inserted in these canons, shall be preserved.”

This was taken from the letter of Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, which Dionysius Exiguus later inserted into his collection of papal decrees [Col. 0036D].

There are also certain other Gallican collections—namely, the ecclesiastical capitularies of the emperors Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and Lothair, collected by Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite. Almost all of them were taken from the Book of Canons of the Roman Church and from the collection of Isidore Mercator. At the Council of Meaux it was decided, canon 78:

“That the ecclesiastical capitularies promulgated by the lord emperor Charlemagne and by the lord Louis the Pious Augustus shall be strictly observed, just as it is known that the legal enactments must be observed.”

These capitularies frequently cite the canons and papal decrees contained in the Book of the Roman Church [Col. 0037A]. Hence it appears that the Book which, as we have said, was given by Hadrian I to Charlemagne was first received and approved by the Gallican Church around this time.

There also exist capitularies of Charles the Bald and of several subsequent kings of France, issued in various synods and collected into one body by Jacobus Sirmond, who illustrated them with highly learned notes in 1623. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, followed him; his collection, composed around the year 1102 under the title Decree, was published long ago.

It remains for us to say something about the Spanish and English Churches.

As for the Spaniards, there can be no doubt that from the beginning they rightly used the Book of the Universal Church containing the ancient canons. They were so devoted to and fond of them that, when subscribing to synods, they used the formula “saving the authority of the ancient canons,” as may be observed in the subscriptions to the Second Council of Toledo.

The Council of Braga, held in 563, expressly mentions the Book of Canons in these words:

Lucretius, bishop, said: “I consider it necessary, if it seems good to your fraternity, that the institutions of the holy Fathers should be made known by reviewing the ancient canons; and that, if not all, at least some of those pertaining to the instruction of clerical discipline should be reread.”

All the bishops said: “What has been said is pleasing, and it is appropriate that those who perhaps through negligence have allowed ecclesiastical constitutions to be abolished should hear the rule of the holy canons and observe it.”

The canons both of the general councils and of the local councils were reread from the Book of Canons before the council [Col. 0037C].

Later, canon 40 states:

“It has been resolved that no one dare to disregard the precepts of the ancient canons that have just been recited in the council.”

The Council of Toledo IV, held in 633, also mentions the Book of Canons in canons 3, 2, and 4:

“A deacon, bringing the Book of Canons into the middle, recites the chapters concerning the conduct of councils.”

The Spaniards, like the Africans and the Gauls, also appear to have possessed a special collection of their own synods, compiled from the councils of Spain. Pope Innocent III seems to imply this in his letter to Peter of Compostela, where he reports his words (vol. III of the Councils):

“You argued by many considerations that the Council of Elvira was authentic, both because it is contained with the other councils in the book called the Corpus of Canons, which Pope Alexander approved as authentic by a formal judicial declaration…”

It is easy to infer that some Gallican ecclesiastical constitutions and certain decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs had been inserted into this Spanish collection from what we said above concerning the Gallican canons and from canon 1 of the Third Council of Toledo (585) and canon 3 of the Council of Barcelona (599). These are the letters that were later inserted into the Book of Canons of the Roman Church.

What is said in canon 16 of the Fourth Council of Toledo—that the synodical decrees of the Roman bishops establish that the Apocalypse of John is to be received among the divine books—should unquestionably be understood as referring to the letter of Pope Innocent I to Exuperius of Toulouse. That letter discusses the books to be received into the canon, among which Innocent expressly lists the Apocalypse of John.

At the Sixth Council of Toledo, the opinion of Pope Leo I is praised; it was taken from his letter to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne. These letters of Innocent and Leo are found in the Book of Canons of the Roman Church [Col. 0038A].

In this very century, Martin, bishop of Braga, published a Latin translation of the Greek canons. It was addressed to Nitigesius, or to the entire council of the Church of Lugo, under the title *Collection of Eastern Canons*, and is preserved among the councils of Spain. He did not indicate from where the individual chapters were taken. But if we compare them with the Greek canons contained in the *Code of the Universal Church*, we shall find that they were taken from it almost entirely, except for a few items added—whether by Martin or someone else—from the councils of Toledo for the benefit of the churches of Spain. Nor did the Spaniards use the translation of Dionysius Exiguus, but the older one transmitted by Isidore; following its method, the councils of Spain, such as the Twelfth Council of Toledo, cite the Greek canons.

From this collection it is evident that Martin of Braga omitted the canons called Apostolic, since in his time they had not yet been received by the Spanish Church. Isidore, bishop of Seville, who subscribed the Fourth Council of Toledo, also reports the following about these canons:

> The canons called Apostolic—either because the Apostolic See does not receive them, nor did the holy Fathers give them their assent, or because they are recognized as having been composed by heretics under the name of the apostles—although useful provisions are found in them, are nevertheless plainly removed from canonical and apostolic authority in their proceedings and are reckoned among the apocrypha.

Another Isidore followed, also a Spaniard, who in many printed and manuscript codices is called Mercator. He enlarged the ancient codex by adding the Apostolic canons themselves, as well as those of Sardica and Africa, various councils of Gaul and Spain, and the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs from Clement through Gregory the Great. He himself attests this in the letter prefixed to his collection, which we possess in manuscript and which has also been incorporated into the *Corpus of Gratian* (*Canon Placuit*, Distinction 16):

> At the beginning of this volume we have set out how a council is celebrated among us, so that those who wish to follow our order may know how they ought to conduct it. Finally, because of their authority, we placed before the other councils the canons called Apostolic, although some call them apocryphal, since many receive them, and the holy Fathers confirmed their judgments by synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions. Next we inserted the decrees of certain letters of apostolic men—that is, Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, and the other apostolic men whose letters we have so far been able to find—down to Pope Sylvester. Afterward we placed the Nicene Synod, because of the authority of that great council. Thereafter we arranged, distinctly and in their own chapters, the councils of various Greek and Latin churches, whether held earlier or later, in the order of their numbers and dates. We also appended the remaining decrees of the Roman bishops down to Saint Gregory.

Isidore Mercator himself mentions the Eleventh Council of Toledo (675), and his collection extends from the Apostolic canons to the Twelfth Council of Toledo. It also contains the canons collected by Pope Hadrian I and delivered to Ingelramnus, bishop of the city of Metz. Hence it is clear that this collection is not by Isidore, bishop of Seville, as many, misled by the name, have wrongly supposed, but by that Isidore surnamed Mercator. Isidore of Seville, as Spanish writers testify, died in the year 635. From the foregoing, however, it is clear that Isidore Mercator lived around the time of Charlemagne and Pope Hadrian I; during their period his collection first became known in Gaul. Enlarged by the addition of many canons, it passed into the title by which it was also called the *Book* or *Corpus of Canons*. Thus its heading reads in my manuscript codex:

> Here begins the book called the **CORPUS OF CANONS**.

Some evidence for the *Code of Canons of the British or English Church* is found among historians of British affairs. We read that Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, wrote a book called the *Canons of the Fathers*, approved at the Council of Hereford (673), as its acts testify in Bede:

> In the third year of King Ecgfrith, Theodore summoned a council of bishops, together with those who selected and knew the canonical statutes of the Fathers.

A little later, Bede reports the words of Theodore himself, who presided over the council:

> I ask, dearest brothers, that whatever has been decreed and defined by the holy Fathers be preserved by all of us inviolate.

All his fellow priests replied:

> It pleases us all exceedingly that whatever the holy canons of the Fathers have decreed, we too should all preserve with eager and willing minds.

Then I immediately brought out the Book of Canons and showed them from it ten chapters which I had marked in various places because I knew them to be especially necessary for us.

Bede himself appends those chapters. Older and more recent canons of the synods of the British Church are also extant in the edition of the Councils of England by the distinguished H. Spelman. From them it is clear that the English made use of Greek, African, and Gallican canons.

There are also other Latin collections of canons, namely those of Burchard, bishop of Worms, and Ivo of Chartres, published under the title *Decrees*. Finally, Gratian, a Bolognese monk and the latest of all collectors of canons, composed under Pope Innocent II a decree compiled from Greek and African canons, decrees of the Roman pontiffs, and the opinions of the ancient Fathers. This work—absolutely called *canon law* or *pontifical law*—was approved and confirmed by the Roman Church, and by its authority all ecclesiastical disputes are judged today.

Let this suffice concerning the ancient *Code of Canons of the Universal Church*, its confirmation and authority, and the origin and development of canon law, both in the East and in the West, together with the ancient and recent Greek and Latin collectors and interpreters of the canons. What we have accomplished in this edition of the work will be made clear by the work itself. Certainly, we have faithfully transcribed the Greek text of the canons from the published codex of John Tilius. Since it was corrupt in many places, we carefully corrected it by comparing numerous printed and handwritten copies of the Greek canons, and we supplied the variant readings. We have used almost throughout the Latin translation of Dionysius Exiguus, and finally have added certain notes and observations.

[Col. 0039]

# CODE OF THE CANONS OF THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH

## Twenty Canons of the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea (A.D. 325)

[Note: [Col. 0039] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### 1

If anyone has undergone surgery while ill at the hands of physicians, or has been castrated by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone, while healthy, has castrated himself, he ought, even if he is found to be in the clergy, to cease from the clergy, and thereafter no such person is to be promoted. Just as it is clear that this has been said concerning those who deliberately undertake the act and dare to castrate themselves, so, if some have been made eunuchs by barbarians or by masters, and are otherwise found worthy, the canon admits such persons into the clergy.

### 2

Since many things have occurred contrary to ecclesiastical canon, either through necessity or because people were otherwise compelled by circumstances—so that persons newly coming from pagan life to the faith, and instructed for only a short time, were immediately led to the spiritual bath, and as soon as they had been baptized were promoted to the episcopate or the presbyterate—it has rightly seemed good that nothing of this kind should happen in the future. The catechumen requires time, and after baptism greater testing is necessary. For the apostolic writing clearly says: “Not a recent convert, lest, being puffed up, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil.” But if, as time passes, some sin of the soul is found in the person and he is convicted by two or three witnesses, let such a man cease from the clergy. Whoever acts contrary to this, as though boldly opposing the great council, will himself be in danger concerning his clerical office.

### 3

The great council altogether forbade a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all among the clergy to keep a subintroduced woman, unless she is perhaps his mother, sister, aunt, or one of those persons alone who are beyond every suspicion.

### 4

A bishop ought, preferably, to be appointed by all the bishops in the province. If this is difficult, either because of urgent necessity or because of the length of the journey, at least three bishops should assemble for this purpose, provided that those absent give their consent and approve the matter in writing; then the ordination is to be performed. Confirmation of what is done in each province is to be entrusted to the metropolitan.

### 5

Concerning those deprived of communion, whether they are among the clergy or belong to the lay order, the judgment of the bishops of each province shall prevail according to the canon which declares that those rejected by some are not to be received by others. It must also be investigated whether they have been excommunicated because of the bishop’s pettiness, contentiousness, or some other such displeasure.

For this to receive proper examination, it has rightly seemed good that synods be held twice each year in every province, so that all the bishops of the province may assemble together and examine such matters. Thus those who have plainly offended the bishop may rightly appear excommunicated by all until the body of bishops decides to issue a more humane judgment on their behalf.

One synod is to be held before Lent, so that every grievance being removed, a pure offering may be presented to God; the second is to be held around the time of autumn.

### 6

Let the ancient customs prevail in Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these regions, since the Roman bishop also has this customary authority. Likewise, in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to the churches be preserved.

The following is altogether clear: if anyone becomes a bishop without the metropolitan’s judgment, the great council has determined that he ought not to be a bishop. If, however, two or three oppose an appointment approved by the common vote of all, a vote consistent with reason and with ecclesiastical canon, merely because of their own contentiousness, the decision of the majority shall prevail.

### 7

Since custom and ancient tradition have prevailed that the bishop of Aelia should be honored, let him retain the rank appropriate to that honor, while the proper dignity of the metropolitan see is preserved.

### 8

Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, “Pure,” and come over to the catholic and apostolic Church, the holy and great council has determined that, after receiving the laying-on of hands, they may remain in the clergy.

Above all, they must profess in writing that they will agree with and follow the doctrines of the catholic and apostolic Church—that is, that they will communicate with those who have married a second time and with those who fell during the persecution, for whom a period and a fixed time have also been established—and that in all things they will follow the doctrines of the catholic Church.

Wherever they alone are found ordained, whether in villages or cities, those found among the clergy shall remain in the same order. But if they come to a place where there is a bishop or presbyter of the catholic Church, it is clear that the bishop of the Church shall possess the dignity of bishop, while the one called a bishop among the so-called Cathars shall have the honor of a presbyter, unless the bishop should decide that he may share the honor of the title.

If this does not please the bishop, he shall devise for him a place as chorepiscopus or presbyter, so that he may appear to belong entirely to the clergy, and so that there may not be two bishops in the city.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] It would be better to read: “Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, but at some time …,” as the Latin reading seems to require. EDIT.]

### 9

If some men have been advanced to the presbyterate without examination, or, when examined, have confessed their sins, and after their confession people, acting contrary to the canon, have laid hands upon them, the canon does not admit such persons. For the catholic Church vindicates what is free from reproach.

### 10

All those who were ordained from among the fallen through the ignorance, or even the foreknowledge, of those who ordained them do not thereby prejudice the ecclesiastical canon; once they are known, they are deposed.

### 11

Concerning those who transgressed without necessity, without confiscation of their property, without danger, or without some such circumstance as occurred under the tyranny of Licinius: although they were unworthy of mercy, the council decided nevertheless to treat them kindly.

Those who genuinely repent shall spend three years among the hearers, and shall lie prostrate for seven years. For two further years, without an offering, they shall join the people in prayers.

### 12

Those who were called by grace, displayed their first zeal, and laid aside the military belt, but afterward returned like dogs to their own vomit—some even giving money and securing restoration to military service by benefits—shall lie prostrate for ten years after the period of three years among the hearers.

In all these cases, the intention and character of the repentance must be examined. Those who demonstrate their return in deed and not merely in appearance, through fear, tears, endurance, and good works, shall, after completing the prescribed period among the hearers, reasonably be admitted to the prayers. The bishop may afterward decide to deal with them more humanely.

Those who bore their discipline indifferently and thought that merely appearing to enter the Church was sufficient for their return must complete the entire prescribed period.

### 13

Concerning those who are dying, the ancient and canonical law shall still be observed: if anyone is at the point of death, he must not be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum. If someone who had been despaired of, after receiving communion, should recover and again be numbered among the living, he shall remain only among those who share in the communion of prayer.

In general, whenever anyone at the point of death asks to receive the Eucharist, the bishop shall impart the offering after examination.

### 14

Concerning catechumens who have fallen, the holy and great council has determined that they shall be hearers only for three years; afterward they shall pray with the catechumens.

### 15

Because of the great disturbances and seditions that occur, it has been decided that the custom found in certain places contrary to the canon should be entirely abolished, so that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon may transfer from one city to another.

If anyone, after the decree of the holy and great council, undertakes anything of this kind or gives himself to such an action, the undertaking shall be entirely annulled, and the bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall be restored to the Church in which he had been ordained.

### 16

All presbyters, deacons, or anyone at all who is numbered among the clergy, who rashly and recklessly depart from the Church without keeping the fear of God before their eyes and without recognizing the ecclesiastical canon, must not be received in any other Church. They must be compelled by every means to return to their own parishes; if they persist, they ought to be deprived of communion.

If anyone dares to seize a person belonging to another church and ordain him in his own church without the consent of the person’s own bishop, from whom the cleric under examination has departed, the ordination shall be invalid.

### 17

Since many among the clergy, pursuing greed and shameful profit, have forgotten the divine Scripture which says, “He has not given his money at interest” (Psalm 14:5), and, lending money, demand centesimal interest, the holy and great council has rightly decreed that if anyone is found after this definition taking interest on a loan, or pursuing the matter in some other way, or demanding one and a half times the principal, or devising anything whatever for the sake of shameful profit, he shall be deposed from the clergy and shall be excluded from the canon.

### 18

It has come to the holy and great council’s attention that in certain places and cities deacons give the Eucharist to presbyters. Neither canon nor custom has handed down that those who do not have authority to offer should give the body of Christ to those who offer it.

It has also become known that some deacons even touch the Eucharist before the bishops. Let all these practices therefore be abolished. Let deacons remain within their proper limits, knowing that they are ministers of the bishops and inferior to presbyters.

They shall receive the Eucharist in their proper order, after the presbyters, either from the bishop or from the presbyter. Deacons may not sit among the presbyters, for this is contrary to canon and order. If anyone refuses to obey after these definitions, he shall cease to be a deacon.

### 19

Concerning the Paulianists: if they come over to the catholic Church, it has been decreed that they must be rebaptized without exception.

If some of them were formerly in the clergy and are found blameless and irreproachable, they are to be ordained after rebaptism by the bishop of the catholic Church. If examination finds them unsuitable, they ought to be deposed.

The same procedure shall be observed concerning deaconesses and, in general, concerning all who are examined as belonging to the clergy. We have mentioned deaconesses who are enrolled in the habit, although they have received no laying-on of hands; they are therefore to be counted altogether among the laity.

### 20

Since there are some who kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, so that everything may be observed alike in every parish, the holy council has determined that prayers should be offered to God standing.

## Twenty-five Canons of the Council of Ancyra (A.D. 314)

These canons are earlier than those of Nicaea, but have been placed afterward because of the authority of the ecumenical council.

[Note: [Col. 0047] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### 1

Presbyters who sacrificed and afterward resisted—not by some pretense, but sincerely, and without having previously contrived or deliberately planned the matter—and who gave the impression of being subjected to tortures, although these were inflicted only in appearance and by pretence: it has been decided that they may retain the honor of their seat, but may not offer, preach, or perform any priestly ministry at all.

### 2

Deacons who likewise sacrificed and afterward resisted shall retain the same honor, but shall cease from every sacred ministry, whether offering bread or the cup, or preaching.

If some bishops are aware of their labor, humility, or gentleness and wish to grant them something more or to take something away, this shall be within their authority.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] Understand “the honor.” EDIT.]

### 3

Those who fled but were captured, or were handed over by their own household, or otherwise deprived of their possessions, or endured tortures, or were thrown into prison, crying out that they were Christians; those who were so restrained that their persecutors forcibly thrust something into their hands, or compelled them by necessity to eat some polluted food; those who continually confessed that they were Christians and always displayed grief over what had happened through their clothing, appearance, and humility of life—such people, as being free from sin, are not to be barred from communion.

If they have been barred by some persons because of excessive strictness or through ignorance, they are to be received immediately. The same shall apply to those from the clergy and to other laypeople.

It was also investigated whether laypeople who had fallen into the same necessity could be promoted to an order. It was decided that they too should be promoted as having committed no sin, provided that their previous manner of life is found to have been upright.

### 4

Concerning those who sacrificed under compulsion and also dined at the idols: those who, when taken away, approached in a cheerful appearance, wore more expensive clothing, and partook without concern of the prepared banquet shall spend one year among the hearers, lie prostrate for three years, and share in prayer alone for two years; then they may approach perfection.

### 5

Those who came wearing mourning clothes, sat down and ate while shedding tears throughout the entire meal, if they have completed the three-year period of prostration, may be received without an offering.

If they did not eat, after lying prostrate for two years they shall communicate in the third year without an offering, so that they may attain perfection in the fourth year.

The bishops shall have authority, after examining the manner of their conversion, either to deal with them more humanely or to add further time. Above all, both their former life and their subsequent life must be examined; only then is mercy to be measured out to them.

### 6

Concerning those who yielded only to threats of punishment, confiscation of property, or deportation, and sacrificed, but until the present time have neither repented nor returned, and who now, around the time of the council, have presented themselves and begun to consider returning: it has been decided that they should be admitted among the hearers until the great day, and after the great day should lie prostrate for three years. Afterward they shall communicate for two years without an offering, and thus, after completing six years, come to perfection.

If some were admitted to repentance before this council, their six-year period shall be reckoned from that time. But if danger and expectation of death arise through illness or some other circumstance, they shall be received according to the canon.

### 7

Concerning those who feasted at a pagan festival in a place assigned to pagans, bringing and eating their own food: it has been decided that, after lying prostrate for two years, they may be received.

Whether they should be received with an offering is to be examined by each bishop, who must also investigate each person’s other manner of life.

### 8

Those who sacrificed twice or three times under compulsion shall lie prostrate for four years; for two years they shall communicate without an offering, and in the seventh year they shall be fully received.

### 9

Those who not only defected but also rebelled, compelled their brothers, and were responsible for others being compelled shall spend three years in the place of the hearers, and another six years in prostration. For one further year they shall communicate without an offering, so that after completing ten years they may attain perfection.

During this period their other manner of life must also be watched.

### 10

Deacons who are ordained and, at the very time of their ordination, declared that they ought to marry because they could not remain otherwise, may remain in the ministry if they later marry, since the bishop granted them permission.

But if some remained silent and accepted ordination on the understanding that they would remain as they were, and afterward married, they must cease from the diaconate.

### 11

Betrothed girls who were afterward carried off by others are to be restored to those to whom they had been betrothed, even if they suffered violence at their hands.

### 12

Those who sacrificed before baptism and were afterward baptized may be promoted to an order, since they have been cleansed.

### 13

Chorepiscopi may not ordain presbyters or deacons. Nor may city presbyters, without letters from the bishop, perform any act in another parish.

[Note: [Col. 0051D] This canon appears to be seriously corrupt. If the Latin version is trusted, it should be corrected in this way or in something similar: “… nor may presbyters … perform anything in another parish …” EDIT.]

### 14

Presbyters or deacons among the clergy who abstain from meat shall be required to touch it and then, if they wish, abstain from it. But if they refuse to eat vegetables cooked with meat and do not yield to the canon, they shall cease from their order.

### 15

Concerning property belonging to the Lord: whatever presbyters sold while no bishop was present is to be restored to the Lord. It shall be for the bishop to judge whether the price ought to be recovered or not, since the proceeds of things sold have often yielded them a greater value.

[Note: “Of things sold” should be read as derived from *to sell*, not “of things that have been done.” EDIT.]

### 16

Concerning those who have behaved irrationally or are behaving irrationally: those who sinned before reaching the age of twenty shall, after fifteen years of prostration, obtain communion in prayer. Then, after persevering for five years in that communion, they may also approach the offering.

Their life during the period of prostration must be examined, and mercy is to be granted accordingly. If some have clung excessively to these sins, they shall undergo a longer period of prostration.

Those who have passed this age and, while having wives, fell into this sin shall lie prostrate for twenty-five years and obtain communion in prayer. Then, after completing five years in the communion of prayer, they may receive the offering.

If those who have wives and are over fifty years old have sinned, they shall receive communion at the end of life.

### 17

The holy council commanded that those who have behaved irrationally, and those who are lepers or have become lepers, should pray among the afflicted.

### 18

If certain bishops have been appointed but not accepted by the parish to which they were assigned, and wish to invade other parishes, use force against those already appointed, and stir up seditions against them, they are to be rejected.

If, however, they wish to sit in the presbyterate in which they were formerly presbyters, they are not to be deprived of their honor. But if they stir up seditions against those who have been appointed there, they are to be deprived even of the honor of the presbyterate and publicly expelled.

### 19

Those who promise virginity but violate their promise shall fulfill the definition concerning those who marry a second time. We forbid virgins who live with certain men as sisters.

### 20

If someone’s wife commits adultery, or if a man himself commits adultery, he is to attain perfection in seven years, according to the stages that lead to it.

### 21

Concerning women who prostitute themselves, destroy their offspring, and diligently seek to procure abortions: the earlier definition prohibited them until death, and some agree with it. But, having found something more humane, we have prescribed a period of ten years according to the established stages.

### 22

Concerning voluntary murderers: they shall undergo prostration, but at the end of life they shall be deemed worthy of perfection.

[Note: The Greek has *φόνων* (“murders”), apparently for *φονέων* (“murderers”). EDIT.]

### 23

Concerning involuntary murders: the earlier definition commands that they receive perfection in seven years, according to the prescribed stages. The second [definition commands them] to complete a period of five years.

### 24

Those who practice divination, follow the customs of the pagans, or bring people into their houses to search for sorceries or perform purification rites shall fall under the five-year canon according to the prescribed stages: three years of prostration and two years of prayer without an offering.

### 25

If someone betrothed a girl, corrupted her sister, and afterward married his betrothed, while the corrupted sister hanged herself, those who were privy to the matter are to be admitted among those standing according to the prescribed stages over a period of ten years.

[Note: The Greek reading is corrupt and has been emended in the supplied text.]

## Canons 21–36

### 21

Presbyters who sacrificed and afterward resisted—not by some pretense, but sincerely, and without having previously contrived or deliberately planned it, though they gave the appearance of being subjected to tortures when these were inflicted only in appearance—may retain the honor of their seat. They may not offer, preach, or perform any sacred ministry.

### 22

Deacons who likewise sacrificed and afterward resisted may retain that honor, but must cease from every sacred ministry, whether offering bread or the cup, or preaching.

If some bishops are aware of their labor, humility, and gentleness and wish to grant or remove something more, this shall be within their authority.

### 23

Those who fled but were captured, were handed over by their own people, were otherwise deprived of their possessions, endured tortures, or were thrown into prison, crying out that they were Christians; those who were so constrained that their persecutors forcibly thrust something into their hands or compelled them to eat polluted food; those who continually confessed that they were Christians and displayed their grief over what had happened through their clothing, appearance, and humility of life—such people, as blameless, are not to be excluded from communion.

If they have been excluded by anyone for the sake of greater caution or through ignorance, they are to be received immediately. The same applies to clergy and to other laypeople.

It was also investigated whether laypeople who had fallen into the same necessity could be promoted to an order. It was decided that they too should be promoted as having committed no sin, provided that their preceding manner of life is found to have been upright.

### 24

Concerning those who sacrificed under compulsion and also dined at idols: those who were taken away and approached in a cheerful appearance, wore more expensive clothing, and carelessly shared in the prepared banquet shall be placed among the hearers for one year, lie prostrate for three years, and share in prayer alone for two years; then they may approach perfection.

### 25

Those who came in mourning clothes and ate while seated at the table, shedding tears throughout the meal, if they have completed the three-year period of prostration, shall be received without an offering.

If they did not eat, after lying prostrate for two years they shall communicate in the third year without an offering, so that they may attain perfection in the fourth year.

The bishops shall have authority, after examining the manner of their return, either to deal with them more humanely or to add more time. Above all, their former life and their subsequent life must be examined, and mercy granted accordingly.

### 26

Concerning those who yielded only to threats of punishment, confiscation of property, or deportation, and sacrificed, but until the present time have not repented or returned, and who now, around the time of the council, have presented themselves and begun to consider returning: they shall be admitted among the hearers until the great day, and after the great day shall lie prostrate for three years. They shall then communicate for two years without an offering and, after completing six years, come to perfection.

If some were admitted to repentance before this council, their six years shall be reckoned from that time. If danger and expectation of death arise through illness or another circumstance, they shall be received according to the canon.

### 27

Those who feasted at a pagan festival in a place assigned to pagans, bringing and eating their own food, shall, after lying prostrate for two years, be received.

Whether they should be received with an offering is to be examined by each bishop, who must also investigate each person’s other manner of life.

### 28

Those who sacrificed twice or three times under compulsion shall lie prostrate for four years; for two years they shall communicate without an offering, and in the seventh year they shall be fully received.

### 29

Those who not only defected but also rebelled, compelled their brothers, and caused others to be compelled shall spend three years among the hearers, six further years in prostration, and one additional year communicating without an offering. After completing ten years they may attain perfection.

During that period their other manner of life must also be observed.

### 30

Deacons who, at the time of their ordination, declared that they ought to marry because they could not remain otherwise may, if they later marry, remain in the ministry, since the bishop permitted it.

Those who remained silent and accepted ordination on the understanding that they would remain as they were, but afterward married, must cease from the diaconate.

### 31

Betrothed girls who were later carried off by others are to be restored to those to whom they had been betrothed, even if they suffered violence at their hands.

### 32

Those who sacrificed before baptism and were afterward baptized may be promoted to an order, as having been cleansed.

### 33

Chorepiscopi may not ordain presbyters or deacons. Nor may city presbyters, without letters from the bishop, perform any act in another parish.

### 34

Presbyters or deacons among the clergy who abstain from meat shall be required to touch it and then, if they wish, abstain from it. But if they refuse to eat vegetables cooked with meat and do not yield to the canon, they shall cease from their order.

### 35

Concerning property belonging to the Lord: whatever presbyters sold while there was no bishop is to be restored to the Lord. It belongs to the bishop to judge whether the price ought to be recovered or not, since the proceeds from things sold have often returned a greater value to those very men.

### 36

Concerning those who have behaved irrationally or are behaving irrationally: those who sinned before reaching the age of twenty shall, after fifteen years of prostration, obtain communion in prayer. Then, after persevering for five years in that communion, they may also approach the offering.

Their life during the period of prostration must be examined, and mercy granted accordingly. If some have persisted excessively in these sins, they shall undergo a longer period of prostration.

Those who have passed this age and, while having wives, fell into this sin shall lie prostrate for twenty-five years and obtain communion in prayer. Then, after completing five years in the communion of prayer, they may receive the offering.

If those who have wives and are over fifty years old have sinned, they shall receive communion at the end of life.

### 37

The holy synod commanded that those who have behaved irrationally, and those who are lepers or have become lepers, should pray among the afflicted.

### 38

If certain bishops have been appointed but not accepted by the parish to which they were assigned, and wish to invade other parishes, use force against those already appointed, and stir up seditions against them, they are to be rejected.

If they wish to sit in the presbyterate in which they were formerly presbyters, they are not to be deprived of their honor. But if they stir up seditions against those who have been appointed there, they are to be deprived even of the honor of the presbyterate and publicly expelled.

### 39

Those who promise virginity but violate their promise shall fulfill the definition concerning those who marry a second time. We forbid virgins who live together with certain men as sisters.

### 40

If someone’s wife commits adultery, or if a man himself commits adultery, he is to attain perfection in seven years, according to the stages that lead to it.

### 41

Concerning women who prostitute themselves, destroy their offspring, and diligently seek to procure abortions: the earlier definition prohibited them until death, and some agree with it. But, having found something more humane, we have prescribed a period of ten years according to the established stages.

### 42

Concerning voluntary murderers: they shall undergo prostration, but at the end of life they shall be deemed worthy of perfection.

### 43

Concerning involuntary murderers: the earlier definition commands that they receive perfection in seven years, according to the prescribed stages. The second commands them to complete five years.

### 44

Those who practice divination and follow pagan customs, or bring people into their houses to search for sorceries or perform purification, shall fall under the five-year canon according to the prescribed stages: three years of prostration and two years of prayer without an offering.

### 45

If a man betrothed a girl, corrupted her sister, and afterward married his betrothed, while the corrupted sister hanged herself, those who knew of the matter are to be admitted among those standing for ten years according to the prescribed stages.

XXXVII.—17. The holy synod decreed that those who have behaved irrationally, and those who are or have been lepers, should pray among those endangered by an unclean spirit.

[Col. 0052D] XXXVIII.—18. If certain bishops, having been appointed but not received by the parish for which they were designated, should wish to invade other parishes, use force against those who have been appointed there, and stir up seditions against them, it has been resolved that they be rejected. If, however, they wish to remain in the presbytery in which they had previously been presbyters, they are not to be deprived of their honor. But if they should also stir up seditions against those appointed there, they are to be deprived even of the honor of the presbyterate and deposed.

XXXIX.—19. Whoever, while promising virginity, makes the promise void shall fulfill the definition concerning digamists. We prohibit virgins who live with certain men as though they were sisters.

XL.—20. If someone’s wife has committed adultery, or he himself has committed adultery, he must attain perfection over seven years, according to the stages that lead him to it.

XLI.—21. Concerning women who fornicate, kill their children, and devote themselves to producing abortions by drugs: the earlier definition indeed prohibited them until the end of life, and some agree with it; but, acting more humanely, we define that they fulfill ten years according to the prescribed stages.

XLII.—22. Those who have committed voluntary homicide are to be placed among the penitents; but at the end of life they are to be deemed worthy of perfection.

[Col. 0054B] XLIII.—23. Those who have committed homicide neither deliberately nor voluntarily: the earlier definition commands that they attain perfection after seven years, according to the prescribed stages; the second, that they complete a period of five years.

XLIV.—24. Those who seek divination, follow pagan customs, or bring such people into their houses to inquire by magical art or for the purpose of purification, shall fall under the five-year canon, according to the defined stages: they shall lie prostrate for three years and communicate in prayer for two years without offering.

XLV.—25. A certain man, having a fiancée, corrupted her sister, so that she conceived, and afterward married the fiancée; the woman who had been corrupted then took her own life. Those who were aware of this were ordered to be received for ten years [Col. 0054C] among those who stand, according to the prescribed stages.

## Canons of the Council of Neocaesarea, fourteen  
*(A.D. 314.)* These are later than the Ancyran canons but earlier than the Nicene canons.

[Note: [Col. 0053] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0053]

μϛ'. If a presbyter marries, he is to be removed from his rank. But if he fornicates or commits adultery, he is to be expelled completely and brought to repentance.

μζ'. If a woman marries two brothers, she is to be expelled until death. Nevertheless, at the point of death, if she says that, should she recover, she will dissolve the marriage, she shall receive repentance because of humanity. But if a woman dies while in such a marriage—or if the husband dies—repentance will be difficult for the survivor.

μη'. Concerning those who enter into many marriages: the prescribed period is clear, but their conduct and faith shorten the period.

μθ'. If someone, desiring a woman, proposes to sleep with her, but his intention does not come to fulfillment, it appears that he has been rescued by grace.

ν'. If a catechumen, entering the church and standing in the order of the catechumens, sins, then, if he kneels, let him hear the word while no longer sinning. But if, even while hearing, he continues to sin, let him be expelled.

[Col. 0055A] να'. Concerning a pregnant woman: she is to be baptized whenever she wishes. For the one who gives birth shares nothing in this matter with the one being born, since each person’s own intention is shown in the confession.

νβ'. A presbyter must not feast at the marriage of a digamist. Since the digamist seeks repentance, who will the presbyter be who, by participating in the feast, approves that marriage?

νγ'. If a certain layman’s wife is proved openly to have committed adultery, such a man cannot enter the ministry. But if she commits adultery after his ordination, he ought to dismiss her. If he lives with her, he cannot retain the ministry entrusted to him.

νδ'. If a presbyter who previously sinned bodily is promoted [Col. 0055B] and confesses that he sinned before ordination, he must not offer, but may remain in the other respects, because of his diligence in the rest of his life. For many have said that other sins are remitted through the laying on of hands. But if he does not confess and cannot be openly convicted, the authority to decide is to be left to him.

νε'. Likewise, if a deacon falls into the same sin, he shall retain the rank of a minister.

νϛ'. A presbyter must not be ordained before the age of thirty, even if he is a very worthy man; he must wait. For the Lord Jesus Christ was baptized [was enlightened] in his thirtieth year and began to teach.

νζ'. If someone is baptized while ill, he cannot be advanced to the presbyterate [presbytery], for his faith is not a matter of free choice but of necessity—unless perhaps his subsequent diligence and faith, and the scarcity of men, should warrant it.

νη'. Local presbyters cannot offer in the church of the city when the bishop or the city’s presbyters are present, nor may they give bread in prayer or the cup. But if they are absent and he alone is summoned to prayer, he may give them. Chorepiscopi are indeed in the pattern of the Seventy; but, as fellow ministers, because of their diligence toward the poor, they offer, being honored.

νθ'. There ought to be seven deacons according to the canon, even if the city is very large; this is confirmed by the Book of Acts.

[Note: [Col. 0055C] I do not see how the phrase can stand with this feminine participle. Perhaps πεισθήσῃ should be read. EDIT.]

[Col. 0054C] XLVI. If a presbyter marries, he is to be removed from his rank; but if he fornicates or commits adultery, he is to be expelled entirely and reduced to penance.

XLVII. If a woman marries two brothers, she is to be expelled [Col. 0054D] until death. Nevertheless, at death, if she promises that, once she recovers, she will dissolve the marriage, she shall have repentance because of humanity. But if the woman dies while in such a marriage, or her husband dies, repentance will be difficult for the survivor.

XLVIII. Concerning those who enter into many marriages: the defined period is clear, but their conversion and faith shorten the period.

XLIX. If someone, desiring a woman, proposes to lie with her, but his desire does not come to fulfillment, he appears to have been saved by grace.

L. If a catechumen, entering the church and standing in the order of catechumens, sins, then, if he kneels, let him hear while no longer sinning; but if, even while hearing, he sins, let him be expelled.

[Col. 0056A] LI. Concerning a woman who carries a child: she is to be baptized whenever she wishes. For the woman who gives birth communicates nothing in this matter to the one born, since each person’s own intention is shown in the confession.

LII. A presbyter must not feast at the marriage of a digamist. Since the digamist seeks repentance, who will the presbyter be who approves that marriage by feasting at it?

LIII. If it is clearly established that someone’s wife committed adultery while he was a layman, such a man cannot enter the ministry. But if she commits adultery after his ordination, he ought to dismiss her. If he lives with her, he cannot retain the ministry entrusted to him.

LIV. If a presbyter who has committed a bodily sin is promoted [Col. 0056B] and confesses that he sinned before ordination, he must not offer, but may remain in the other respects, because of his diligence in the rest of his life. For many have said that the remaining sins are removed through the laying on of hands. But if he does not confess and cannot be openly convicted, the matter is to be left to his own judgment.

LV. Likewise, if a deacon falls into the same sin, he shall retain the rank of a minister.

LVI. A presbyter must not be ordained before the age of thirty, even if he is very worthy, but must observe this period. For the Lord Jesus Christ was baptized in his thirtieth year and began to teach.

LVII. If someone is baptized while ill, he cannot be promoted to the honor of the presbyterate, for his faith is not from free choice but from necessity [Col. 0056C]—unless perhaps his subsequent diligence and faith, and the scarcity of men, should warrant it.

LVIII. Regional presbyters cannot offer in the church of the city when the bishop or the city’s presbyters are present; nor can they give bread in prayer or the cup. But if they are absent and he alone has been summoned to prayer, he may give them. Chorepiscopi are indeed in the pattern of the Seventy; but, as fellow ministers, because of their diligence toward the poor, they offer, being honored.

LIX. There ought to be seven deacons according to the canon, even if the city is large; the Book of Acts confirms this (Acts 6).

## Canons of the Council of Gangra, twenty  
*(A.D. 325.)*

[Note: [Col. 0055] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0055]

[Col. 0055D] ξ'. If anyone condemns marriage, and detests or reproaches a woman who sleeps with her husband, although she is faithful, pious, and devout, as though she could not enter the kingdom, let him be anathema.

ξα'. If anyone condemns one who eats meat without blood, or meat sacrificed to idols or strangled, with piety and faith, as though, because he partakes of such food, he had no hope, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0057A] ξβ'. If anyone, under the pretext of devotion to God, teaches a slave to despise his master, withdraw from his service, and not serve him with goodwill and every honor, let him be anathema.

ξγ'. If anyone separates himself from a married presbyter, on the ground that one ought not to partake of the offering when that presbyter has ministered, let him be anathema.

ξδ'. If anyone teaches that the house of God and the assemblies held in it are to be despised, let him be anathema.

ξε'. If anyone holds assemblies privately apart from the church, and, despising the church, wishes to perform the things belonging to the church without the presbyter’s presence and the bishop’s consent, let him be anathema.

ξϛ'. If anyone wishes to receive or give the fruits or offerings of the church outside the church, contrary to the judgment of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such matters, and wishes to act without his consent, let him be anathema.

ξζ'. If anyone gives or receives an offering of fruits apart from the bishop or the person appointed to administer benevolence, both the giver and the receiver shall be anathema.

ξη'. If anyone practices virginity or ascetic continence as though detesting marriage and withdrawing from it, not because of the goodness and holiness of virginity itself, let him be anathema.

ξθ'. If anyone among those who practice virginity for the Lord exalts himself over married people, let him be anathema.

ο'. If anyone despises those who, in faith, hold agapē-feasts and, for the honor of the Lord, invite the brothers, and refuses to participate in their invitations because he disparages what is being done, let him be anathema.

οα'. If any man, on account of a supposedly religious ascetic practice, uses a cloak, and, as though possessing righteousness by this fact, condemns those who, with reverence, wear the ordinary and customary garments, let him be anathema.

οβ'. If any woman, on account of a supposedly religious ascetic practice, changes her clothing and takes up a man’s garment [masculine garment] instead of the customary woman’s clothing, let her be anathema.

ογ'. If any woman leaves her husband and wishes to withdraw, detesting marriage, let her be anathema.

οδ'. If anyone abandons his own children and does not raise them, and does not, so far as he is able, lead them toward the proper devotion to God, but neglects them under the pretext of asceticism, let him be anathema.

οε'. If any children withdraw from their parents, especially believing parents, under the pretext of devotion to God, and do not render their parents the honor that is due, devotion to God evidently being preferred among them, let them be anathema.

οϛ'. If any woman, on account of a supposedly religious ascetic practice, cuts off the hair God has given her as a reminder of submission, thereby undoing the command of submission, let her be anathema.

οζ'. If anyone fasts on the Lord’s day on account of a supposedly religious ascetic practice, let him be anathema.

οη'. If anyone among those practicing asceticism, without bodily necessity, becomes arrogant and abolishes the fasts traditionally observed in common and maintained by the church, with a perfect judgment within him rejecting them, let him be anathema.

οθ'. If anyone, acting with a proud disposition, accuses or detests the assemblies of the martyrs, the services celebrated in them, or their commemorations, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0056D] LX.—1. If anyone condemns marriage, and detests or reproaches a woman who sleeps with her husband, although she is faithful, pious, and devout, as though she could not enter the kingdom of God, let him be anathema.

LXI.—2. If anyone condemns one who eats meat without blood, or meat sacrificed to idols or strangled, with piety and faith, as though he had no hope because of such participation, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0058A] LXII.—3. If anyone, under the pretext of divine worship, teaches a slave to despise his master, withdraw from his service, and not serve him faithfully and with every honor, let him be anathema.

LXIII.—4. If anyone rejects a married presbyter, as though one ought not to share in his offering when he ministers, let him be anathema.

LXIV.—5. If anyone teaches that the house of God and the assemblies held in it are to be despised, let him be anathema.

LXV.—6. If anyone holds private assemblies outside the church, and, despising the church, wishes to perform the things belonging to the church without the presbyter’s presence and the bishop’s consent, let him be anathema.

LXVI.—7. If anyone wishes to receive or give the church’s offerings of fruits outside the church, contrary to the consent of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such offices, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.

LXVII.—8. If anyone gives or receives an offering of fruits apart from the bishop or the person appointed to administer benevolence, both the giver and the receiver shall be anathema.

LXVIII.—9. If anyone, preserving virginity or practicing continence, withdraws as though abhorring marriage—not because virginity is holy, nor for the goodness of virginity itself—let him be anathema.

LXIX.—10. If anyone who preserves virginity for the Lord exalts himself over married people, let him be anathema.

LXX.—11. If anyone despises those who hold agapē-feasts in faith and, for the honor of the Lord, invite the brothers, and refuses to participate in such invitations because he disparages what is being done, let him be anathema.

LXXI.—12. If any man, on account of a supposedly religious ascetic practice, uses a cloak, that is, a covering mantle, and, as though establishing righteousness in this, condemns those who, with reverence, wear *beroi* and other ordinary, customary clothing, let him be anathema.

LXXII.—13. If any woman, on account of a supposedly religious ascetic practice, changes her dress and takes a man’s garment instead of the customary woman’s clothing, let her be anathema.

LXXIII.—14. If any woman leaves her husband and wishes to withdraw, abhorring marriage, let her be anathema.

LXXIV.—15. If anyone abandons his children, does not feed them, and does not, so far as he is able, train them in devotion and the worship due to God, but neglects them under the pretext of asceticism, let him be anathema.

LXXV.—16. If children withdraw from their parents, especially believing parents, under the pretext of divine worship, and do not show their parents the honor due, divine worship evidently being preferred among them, let them be anathema.

LXXVI.—17. If any woman, on account of a supposedly religious ascetic practice, cuts off the hair God gave her as a reminder of submission, thereby dissolving the command of submission, let her be anathema.

LXXVII.—18. If anyone fasts on the Lord’s day on account of a supposedly religious ascetic practice, let him be anathema.

LXXVIII.—19. If anyone among those devoted to ascetic practice, without bodily necessity, becomes arrogant and abolishes the fasts handed down in common and observed by the church, that perfect reasoning within him evidently rejecting them, let him be anathema.

LXXIX.—20. If anyone, using a proud disposition, detests the assemblies of the martyrs, the sacred rites celebrated in them, and their commemorations, let him be anathema.

## Canons of the Council of Antioch, twenty-five  
*(A.D. 341.)*

[Note: [Col. 0059] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0059]

[Col. 0059A] π'. We decree that all who dare to set aside [transgress] the definition of the holy and great synod assembled at Nicaea in the presence of the pious and God-beloved Emperor Constantine concerning the holy feast of the saving Pascha shall be excluded from communion and expelled from the church, if they persist contentiously in opposition to what has been rightly decreed. This has been said concerning laypeople. But if any of the leaders of the church—a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—after this definition should dare, for the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the churches, to act separately and celebrate Pascha with the Jews, the holy synod has from this point judged him alien from the church, since he becomes the cause not only of sin for himself but of destruction and subversion for many. It not only deposes such persons from the ministry, but also those who dare to communicate with them after their deposition. [Col. 0059C] Those who have been deposed are also to be deprived of the external honor which the holy canon and the priesthood of God have received.

πα'. All who enter the church of God and hear the holy Scriptures, but do not join in prayer with the people, or reject participation in the Eucharist through some disorder, are to be expelled from the church until, after confessing, showing fruits of repentance, and making supplication, they are able to obtain forgiveness. It is not permitted to communicate with the excommunicated, to assemble in houses and pray with those who do not pray with the church, or to receive in one church those who do not assemble in another church. If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone else in the canon is found communicating with the excommunicated, he too shall be excommunicated, as one who confuses the canon of the church.

πβ'. If a presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all from the priestly order leaves his own parish and goes to another, then, having completely transferred himself, attempts to remain for a long time in another parish, he is no longer to minister—especially if he does not obey when his own bishop calls him and advises him to return to his own parish—then, if he persists in this disorder, he is to be completely deposed from the ministry, with no possibility of restoration. If another bishop receives one deposed for this reason, he too shall be subject to a penalty from the common synod, as one who abolishes the ecclesiastical ordinances.

[Col. 0061A] πγ'. If a bishop deposed by a synod, or a presbyter or deacon deposed by his own bishop, dares to perform any ministerial act—whether the bishop according to the former custom, or the presbyter, or the deacon—he is no longer to have any hope of restoration or opportunity for defense in another synod. All who communicate with him are also to be expelled from the church, especially if, knowing the sentence issued against those named above, they dare to communicate with them.

πδ'. If a presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the church, holds an assembly privately, sets up an altar, and refuses to obey when the bishop summons him—neither obeying nor submitting when summoned once and then twice—he is to be completely deposed, receive no further remedy, and be unable to recover his honor. If he persists in causing disturbances and upheaval in the church, he is to be brought back by external authority as a seditious person.

πε'. If anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop, he is not to be received by others before being received by his own bishop, unless, when a synod has assembled, he appears, gives his defense, persuades the synod, and obtains another decision. The same rule applies to laypeople, presbyters, deacons, and all who are subject to the canon.

πϛ'. No stranger is to be received without letters of peace.

πζ'. Presbyters in the countryside are not to issue canonical letters, nor even send letters to neighboring bishops; unimpeachable chorepiscopi, however, may issue letters of peace.

πη'. The bishops in each province ought to know that the bishop presiding in the metropolis assumes responsibility for the whole province, because all who have business come together from every direction in the metropolis. Therefore it has seemed good that he should also precede them in honor, while the other bishops should do nothing extraordinary without him, according to the ancient canon of our fathers that has prevailed, but only what belongs to each one’s parish and to the districts subject to it. For each bishop has authority over his own parish, to administer it according to the piety incumbent on him and to care for the entire district subject to his city, including ordaining presbyters and deacons and deciding each matter with judgment. He must not attempt anything beyond this without the metropolitan bishop, nor may the metropolitan act without the judgment of the others.

πθ'. Concerning those in villages or rural districts who are called chorepiscopi: even if they have received the laying-on of hands of bishops, the holy synod has decreed that they must know their own limits, administer the churches subject to them, and be content with their care and oversight. They may appoint readers, subdeacons, and exorcists, and be content with these promotions; but they must not dare to ordain a presbyter or deacon without the bishop of the city to whom both they and the district are subject. If anyone dares to transgress what has been defined, he is to be deposed from the honor he holds. A chorepiscopus is to be appointed by the bishop of the city to whom he is subject.

90ζ'. If any bishop, presbyter, or anyone at all subject to the canon undertakes to go to the emperor without the consent and letters of the bishops of the province, especially the metropolitan, he is to be repudiated and expelled not only from communion but also from the dignity of which he is a participant, as one who dares to trouble the ears of our most God-beloved emperor contrary to the ordinance of the church. But if urgent necessity calls him to go to the emperor, he is to do so after deliberation with, and by the judgment of, the metropolitan bishop of the province or the bishops in it, and he is to be equipped with their letters.

[Col. 0063B] 90α'. If a presbyter or deacon deposed by his own bishop, or a bishop deposed by a synod, dares to trouble the emperor’s ears, he ought instead to turn to a greater synod, refer what he believes to be just to a larger number of bishops, and await their examination and judgment. If, disregarding these provisions, he troubles the emperor, he is worthy of no forgiveness, has no opportunity for defense, and must not expect any hope of future restoration.

90β'. No bishop may dare to move from one province to another and ordain people in a church for advancement in the ministry, nor bring others with him, unless he has been summoned by letters from the metropolitan and the bishops with him, in whose district he is entering. If he goes without anyone calling him, in disorder, to ordain someone or arrange ecclesiastical matters that do not belong to him, what he has done is invalid; he himself shall suffer the penalty due for his disorder and irrational undertaking, being from this point deposed by the holy synod.

90γ'. If a bishop is being judged on certain charges and the bishops of the province happen to disagree about him, some declaring the accused innocent and others guilty, then, to remove all dispute, the holy synod has decreed that the metropolitan bishop summon certain judges from the neighboring province to settle the dispute and, together with the bishops of the province, confirm what has been established.

[Col. 0063D] 90δ'. If a bishop accused of certain charges is judged by all the bishops of the province, and all unanimously issue one verdict against him, he is not to be judged again by others; the unanimous decision of the provincial bishops is to remain firm.
