90ε'. If a bishop who is at leisure thrusts himself upon a vacant church and seizes its see without a complete synod, he is to be expelled, even if all the people whom he has seized choose him. A complete synod is one in which the metropolitan is also present.

90ϛ'. If a bishop, having received the laying-on of hands from a bishop and been appointed to preside over a people, refuses to accept the ministry or to go to the church entrusted to him, he is to be excommunicated until he is compelled to accept it, or until the complete synod of the provincial bishops makes some decision concerning him.

90ζ'. If a bishop ordained for a parish does not go to the parish for which he was ordained, not through his own fault but because of the people’s refusal or another cause not arising from him, he is to share in the honor and ministry, provided that he does not interfere with the affairs of the church in which he assembles. He is to await whatever the complete synod of the province, after judging the matter, determines.

90η'. A bishop must not be ordained without a synod and the presence of the metropolitan of the province. When the metropolitan is present, it is best that all the fellow ministers in the province be present with him, and he ought to summon them by letter. If all attend, so much the better; but if this is difficult, the majority must certainly be present, or must join in the vote by letter, and the appointment must then be made with the presence or vote of the majority. If it is done otherwise, contrary to what has been defined, the ordination is invalid. But if the appointment has been made according to the prescribed canon and some object through personal contentiousness, the vote of the majority shall prevail.

90θ'. For ecclesiastical needs and the resolution of disputes, it has seemed good that synods of bishops be held twice each year in every province: once after the third week of the feast of Pascha, so that the synod may be held in the fourth week of Pentecost, the metropolitan reminding the provincial bishops; and the second synod on the Ides of October, which is the fifteenth of Hyperberetaeus. At these synods presbyters, deacons, and all who believe they have been wronged are to appear and receive judgment from the synod. No one may hold synods privately without those to whom the metropolises have been entrusted.

ρ'. A bishop must not move from one parish to another, neither thrusting himself forward of his own accord, nor being compelled by peoples through force, nor being forced by bishops. He must remain in the church which he received by lot from God at the beginning and must not leave it, according to the definition previously issued on this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0065D] “μὴ μεθίστασθαι” [“must not move”] should be read, so that the sense is coherent. EDIT.]

ρα'. A bishop must not enter a foreign city that is not subject to him, or a district that does not belong to him, to ordain anyone; nor may he appoint presbyters or deacons in places subject to another bishop, unless perhaps he acts with the judgment of the bishop who properly governs that district. If anyone dares to do such a thing, the ordination is invalid, and he himself shall receive a penalty from the synod.

ρβ'. A bishop may not appoint another as his successor in his place, even if he is at the point of death. If such a thing occurs, the appointment is invalid. The ecclesiastical ordinance is to be preserved, which declares that a bishop may be appointed only with a synod and the judgment of bishops who, after the death of the departed bishop, have authority to advance the one who is worthy.

ργ'. The church’s possessions ought properly to be preserved for the church with every diligence, a good conscience, and faith in God, the overseer and judge of all. They ought also to be administered with judgment and by the authority of the bishop entrusted with the whole people and the souls of those who assemble. The things belonging to the church must be manifest, with the knowledge of the presbyters and deacons around him, so that they know and are not ignorant of what belongs to the church and nothing is hidden from them. Thus, if the bishop should die, the things belonging to the church, being known, will neither be lost nor perish, and the bishop’s personal property will not be disturbed under the pretext of ecclesiastical affairs. For it is just and pleasing to God and human beings [Note: The conjunction should be suppressed. EDIT.] that the bishop’s personal property be left to whomever he wishes, while the church’s property is preserved for the church. In this way neither will the church suffer loss, nor will the bishop be confiscated under the pretext of the church, nor will those connected with him fall into lawsuits, so that he himself is burdened with slander after death.

ρδ'. A bishop has authority over the affairs of the church, so that he may distribute them to all who are in need, with complete reverence and fear of God. He himself may also receive what he needs, if indeed he needs it, for his necessary uses and for the brothers who are entertained by him, so that they are in no way deprived, according to the divine Apostle’s words: “Having food and coverings, with these we shall be content” [1 Tim. 6:8]. But if he is not content with these and turns the church’s property to his own household needs, handling the church’s revenues or the produce of the fields without the judgment of the presbyters or deacons, and grants authority over them to his household, relatives, brothers, or sons, thereby secretly damaging the church’s accounts, he must render an account of his administration to the provincial synod. If the bishop, or the presbyters with him, are otherwise accused of taking for themselves what belongs to the church, whether from the fields or from any other ecclesiastical source, so that the poor are oppressed and accusation and disgrace attach both to the church’s administration and to those who administer it in this way, they too shall receive correction, with the holy synod determining what is proper.

[Col. 0056D] LXXX.—1. We decree that all who dare to dissolve the definition of the holy and great synod assembled at Nicaea in the presence of the most religious Emperor Constantine concerning the holy feast of the saving Pascha shall be excommunicated and expelled from the church, if they persist contentiously against what has been rightly decreed. Let this be said concerning laypeople. But if any of those who preside over the church—a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—after this definition dares, for the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the churches, to act separately and celebrate Pascha with the Jews, the holy synod has judged him from this point to be alien from the church, since he becomes the cause not only of sin for himself but of destruction and subversion for many. It not only deposes such persons from the ministry, but also those who dare to communicate with them after their deposition. [Col. 0060C] Those who have been deposed are also to be deprived of every external honor which the holy canon and the priesthood of God have obtained.

LXXXI.—2. All who enter the church of God and hear the holy Scriptures, but do not join in prayer with the people or, through some perversity, reject participation in the holy Eucharist, are to be expelled from the church until, after confessing, showing fruits of repentance, and imploring forgiveness, they are able to obtain pardon. It is not permitted to communicate with the excommunicated, to pray with those who assemble in houses but do not join in the prayers of the church, or to receive in one church those who do not assemble in another. If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone else in the canon is found communicating with the excommunicated, he too shall be excommunicated, as one who confounds the canon of the church.

LXXXII.—3. If a presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all from the priestly order leaves his own parish and goes to another, then, after completely transferring himself, attempts to remain for a long time in another parish, he is no longer to minister—especially if he does not obey when his bishop calls him, advises him, and exhorts him to return to his own parish—then, if he persists in his perversity, he is to be completely deposed from the ministry, with no possibility whatever of restoration. If another bishop receives one who was deposed for this reason, he too shall be restrained by the common synod, as one who abolishes the ecclesiastical statutes.

[Col. 0062A] LXXXIII.—4. If a bishop deposed by a synod, or a presbyter or deacon deposed by his own bishop, dares to perform any ministerial act—whether the bishop according to the former custom, or the presbyter, or the deacon—he is no longer to have any hope of restoration or opportunity for defense in another synod. All who communicate with him are also to be expelled from the church, especially if, after learning of the sentence issued against those named above, they dare to communicate with them.

LXXXIV.—5. If a presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the church, holds a private assembly, establishes an altar, and refuses to obey when the bishop summons him, neither obeying nor submitting when summoned once and twice, he is to be completely deposed, receive no further remedy, and be unable to recover his honor. If he persists in making disturbances and seditions in the church, he is to be restrained by external, that is, secular, authority as a seditious person.

LXXXV.—6. If anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop, he is not to be received by others before being reconciled with his own bishop, unless he appears before an assembled synod, defends himself, persuades the synod, and obtains another decision. This definition is to be observed concerning laypeople, presbyters, deacons, and all who are subject to the canon.

LXXXVI.—7. No stranger is to be received without letters of peace.

LXXXVII.—8. Presbyters in the districts must not issue canonical letters, nor even send letters to neighboring bishops. Unimpeachable chorepiscopi, however, may issue letters of peace.

LXXXVIII.—9. The bishops in every province ought to know that the bishop presiding in the metropolis assumes the care and oversight of the whole province, because all who have business come together from every direction in the metropolis. Therefore it has seemed good that he should also precede them in honor; while the other bishops, according to the ancient canon of our fathers that has prevailed until now, should do nothing extraordinary or beyond their boundaries, but only what belongs to each one’s parish and the regions subject to it. Each bishop has authority over his own parish, administering it according to his own zeal and piety and caring for the entire region subject to his city. Thus he may ordain presbyters and deacons and arrange each matter with judgment, but must not attempt anything beyond this without the metropolitan bishop, nor may the metropolitan act without the judgment of the others.

LXXXIX.—10. Concerning those in villages and districts who are called chorepiscopi: even if they have received the laying-on of hands of bishops, the holy synod has decreed that they know their own limits, administer the churches subject to them, and be content with their care and oversight. They may appoint readers, subdeacons, and exorcists, and regard their advancement as sufficient; but they must not dare to ordain a presbyter or deacon without the bishop of the city to whom both they and the district are subject. If anyone dares to transgress what has been defined, he too is to be deprived of the honor he holds. A chorepiscopus is to be appointed by the bishop of the city to whom he is subject.

XC.—11. If a bishop, presbyter, or anyone at all in the canon undertakes to go to the emperor without the consent and letters of the bishops of the province, especially the metropolitan, he is to be deposed and expelled not only from communion but also from the dignity of which he appears to be a participant, as one who dares to trouble the ears of our most religious emperor contrary to the church’s ordinance. If necessary cause requires him to approach the emperor, he is to do so after deliberation with, and by the judgment of, the metropolitan bishop of the province or the bishops in that province, and he is to depart equipped with their letters.

[Col. 0064B] XCI.—12. If a presbyter or deacon deposed by his own bishop, or a bishop deposed by a synod, dares to trouble the emperor’s ears, when he ought to turn to a greater synod and refer the right he believes himself to possess to a larger number of bishops, receiving their examination and judgment, then, if he disregards these provisions and troubles the emperor, he is worthy of no pardon, has no opportunity to defend himself, and must not expect hope of restoration.

XCII.—13. No bishop may dare to move from one province to another and ordain people in a church for advancement in the ministry, nor bring others with him, unless he has been summoned by letters from the metropolitan and the bishops with him, in whose region he is entering. If he comes without anyone calling him, in disorder, to ordain someone or arrange ecclesiastical affairs that do not belong to him, what he does is invalid; he himself shall pay the penalty due for his perversity and irrational undertaking, being from that point deposed by the holy synod.

XCIII.—14. If a bishop is judged concerning certain crimes and the bishops of the province happen to disagree about him—some declaring the accused innocent and others guilty—the holy synod has decreed, for the complete settlement of the dispute, that the metropolitan bishop summon other judges from the neighboring province to remove the dispute and confirm, together with the provincial bishops, what has been established.

[Col. 0064D] XCIV.—15. If a bishop accused of certain crimes is condemned by all the bishops of the province, and all issue one unanimous verdict against him, he is not to be judged again by others; the firm decision of the provincial bishops is to remain.

XCV.—16. If a bishop who is at leisure thrusts himself upon a vacant church and seizes its see without a complete synod, he is to be expelled, even if the entire people whom he has seized should choose him. A complete synod is one in which the metropolitan bishop also participates.

XCVI.—17. If a bishop, having received the laying-on of hands from a bishop and been ordered to preside over a people, does not accept the ministry or agree to go to the church entrusted to him, he is to be excommunicated until he is compelled to accept it, or until the complete synod of the provincial bishops makes some determination concerning him.

XCVII.—18. If a bishop who has been ordained does not go to the parish for which he was ordained—not through his own fault, but because of the people’s opposition or another cause not arising from him—he is to share in the honor and ministry, provided that he causes no disturbance to the affairs of the church in which he assembles. He is to accept whatever the complete synod of the province determines after judging the matter.

XCVIII.—19. A bishop must not be ordained without a synod and the presence of the metropolitan of the province. When the metropolitan is present, it is altogether better that all the fellow ministers in the province be present with him, and the metropolitan ought to summon them by letter. If all attend, so much the better; but if this is difficult, the majority must certainly be present, or must join in the vote by letter, and the ordination is then to take place with the presence or vote of the majority. If it occurs otherwise, contrary to what has been defined, the ordination is invalid. But if the ordination has taken place according to the prescribed canon and some oppose it through contentiousness, the decision of the majority shall prevail.

XCIX.—20. For ecclesiastical needs and the resolution of disputes, it has seemed right that synods of bishops be held twice each year in every province. The first is to be held after the third week of the feast of Pascha, so that the synod may be completed in the fourth week of Pentecost, with the metropolitan reminding the provincial bishops. The second synod is to be held on the Ides of October, which is the fifteenth of Hyperberetaeus. At these synods presbyters, deacons, and all who believe themselves wronged are to appear and receive judgment from the synod. No one may hold synods privately without those to whom the metropolises have been entrusted.

C.—21. A bishop must not move from one parish to another, neither thrusting himself forward of his own accord, nor being forced by peoples through violence, nor compelled by bishops. He must remain in the church which he received by lot from God at the beginning and must not leave it, according to the definition previously issued concerning this matter.

CI.—22. A bishop must not enter a foreign city that is not subject to him, or a region that does not belong to him, to ordain anyone; nor may he appoint presbyters or deacons in places subject to another bishop, unless perhaps he acts with the judgment of the proper bishop of that region. If anyone dares to do such a thing, his ordination is invalid, and he himself shall be punished by the synod.

CII.—23. A bishop may not appoint another as his successor, even if he is at the end of his life. If such a thing occurs, the appointment is invalid. The ecclesiastical ordinance is to be preserved, which declares that a bishop may be appointed only with a synod and the judgment of the bishops who, after the death of the bishop who has rested, have authority to advance the one who is worthy.

CIII.—24. It is right that the things belonging to the church be preserved for the church with every diligence, a good conscience, and faith in God, who sees and judges all things. They ought also to be administered with judgment and by the authority of the bishop entrusted with the whole people and the souls of those who assemble in the church. The things belonging to the church must be manifest, with the knowledge of the presbyters and deacons around him, so that they know what belongs to the church and nothing is hidden from them. Thus, if the bishop should die, the things belonging to the church, being known, will neither be lost nor perish; nor will the bishop’s personal property be disturbed under the pretext of ecclesiastical affairs. For it is just and pleasing to God and human beings that the bishop’s personal possessions be left to whomever he wishes, while the church’s possessions are preserved for the church, so that neither the church suffers any loss nor the bishop is confiscated under the pretext of the church, nor those connected with him fall into lawsuits, with the result that he himself is burdened with reproach after death.

CIV.—25. A bishop has authority over the affairs of the church, so that he may distribute them to all who are in need, with complete reverence and fear of God. He himself may also receive what he needs, if indeed he needs it, for his necessary uses and for the brothers who are entertained by him, so that they are in no way deprived, according to the divine Apostle’s words: “Having food and coverings, with these we shall be content” [1 Tim. 6:8]. But if he is not content with these and turns the church’s property to his own household needs, handling its revenues or the produce of the fields without the judgment of the presbyters or deacons, and grants authority over them to his household, relatives, brothers, or sons, so that the church’s accounts are secretly damaged in this way, he must render an account of his administration to the provincial synod. If the bishop, or the presbyters with him, are otherwise accused of taking for themselves what belongs to the church, whether from the fields or from any other ecclesiastical source, so that the poor are oppressed and accusation and disgrace attach both to the church’s administration and to those who administer it in this way, they too shall receive correction, with the holy synod examining what is proper.

## Canons of the Council of Laodicea, fifty-nine  
*(A.D. 364.)*

[Note: [Col. 0067] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0067]

[Col. 0067D] ρε'. Concerning those who have freely and lawfully entered into a second marriage, without contracting a clandestine marriage: we have decreed that, after a short time has passed and they have devoted themselves to prayers and fasts, communion is to be restored to them by way of indulgence.

ρϛ'. Concerning those who sin in various offenses, persevere in the prayer of confession and repentance, and make a complete renunciation of evils: after a period of repentance has been granted to such persons in proportion to their offense, they are to be admitted to communion because of the mercies and goodness of God.

ρζ'. Concerning the prohibition against those recently baptized being admitted to the priestly order.

ρη'. Concerning the prohibition against members of the clergy lending money, taking interest, and receiving the so-called one-and-a-half-fold returns.

ρθ'. Concerning the prohibition against ordinations taking place in the presence of hearers.

ρι'. Concerning the prohibition against allowing heretics to enter the house of God while they persist in heresy.

ρια'. Concerning those returning from the heresies—that is, the Novatians, Photinians, or Quartodecimans—and the faithful who are among them: they are not to be received before they anathematize every heresy, especially the one in which they were held. Thereafter, those called faithful among them, after learning the articles of the faith and being anointed with the holy chrism, are thus to participate in the holy mystery.

ριβ'. Concerning those returning from the sect of the so-called Phrygians [the Montanists from the sect], even if they happen to belong to the clergy they recognize among themselves, and even if they are said to be very great: such persons are to be carefully instructed and baptized by the bishops and presbyters of the church.

ριγ'. Concerning the prohibition against permitting members of the church to go to the cemeteries or to the so-called martyr-shrines of any heretics for the sake of prayer or healing; such persons, if they are believers, are to be excommunicated for a time, but, if they repent and confess that they have erred, are to be received.

ριδ'. Concerning the prohibition against members of the church indiscriminately joining their children in marriage to heretics.

ριε'. Concerning the prohibition against appointing the so-called presbytides, or women presiding, in the church.

ριϛ'. Concerning the appointment of bishops to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and the neighboring bishops, after they have long been tested both in the doctrine of the faith and in an upright manner of life.

## Greek recension — Laodicea (continuation)

[Col. 0069D] 137. Concerning the prohibition against allowing the crowds to conduct the elections of those who are to be appointed to the priesthood.

138. Concerning the prohibition against sending the holy gifts, as tokens of blessing, to other parishes during the feast of Easter.

139. Concerning the prohibition against anyone besides the canonical singers—who ascend the ambo and sing from a parchment—singing in the church.

140. Concerning the reading of the Gospels together with the other Scriptures on Saturday.

141. Concerning the prohibition against joining the psalms together in the assemblies; rather, an interval is to be made after each psalm for a reading.

[Col. 0071A] 142. Concerning the obligation that the same order of prayers always be observed both at the ninth hour and at evening.

143. Concerning the obligation that, first and separately, after the bishops’ addresses, a prayer for the catechumens be offered; and after the catechumens have departed, that the prayer for those under penance be offered; and after these have approached, received the laying on of hands, and withdrawn, that three prayers of the faithful then be offered: the first in silence, while the second and third are completed by spoken responses. Thereafter peace is to be given. After the presbyters have given peace to the bishop, the laypeople are then to give peace. Thus the holy offering is to be celebrated. Only those in the priestly order are permitted to enter the sanctuary and receive communion.

[Col. 0071B] 144. A deacon must not sit before a presbyter, but must sit only at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, deacons are to be honored by assistants and by all the clergy.

145. Assistants must not have a place in the diaconicon, nor touch the vessels belonging to the Lord.

146. An assistant must not wear an orarion, nor leave the doors unattended.

147. Readers or singers must not wear an orarion and then read or sing.

148. Those in the priestly order, from presbyters down to deacons, and thereafter anyone in the ecclesiastical order, down to assistants, readers, singers, exorcists, or doorkeepers, as well as those belonging to the order of ascetics, must not enter a tavern.

[Greek variant: *ἐπορκιστῶν* and *ἐφορκιστῶν*, variant spellings of “exorcists.”]

[Col. 0071C] 149. Assistants must not distribute bread or bless the cup.

150. No one who has not been advanced by bishops may perform exorcisms, either in churches or in houses.

[Greek variant: *ἐπορκίζειν* and *ἐφορκίζειν*, variant spellings of “to perform exorcisms.”]

151. Priests, clergy, or laypeople invited to a communal meal must not take away portions, since this brings reproach upon the ecclesiastical order.

[Greek variant: *τῇ ἐκκλησιαστικῇ* (“the ecclesiastical order”) or *τῇ ἱερατικῇ* (“the priestly order”).]

152. The so-called communal meals must not be held on the Lord’s days or in churches, nor may people eat in the house of God or spread couches there.

[Col. 0071D] 153. Christians must not Judaize or keep idle on the Sabbath, but must work on that same day. Preferring the Lord’s Day, they should, if they are able, keep it idle as Christians. If they are found to be Judaizers, let them be anathema from Christ [from God].

[Greek variant: “let them be anathema before Christ” (*παρὰ Χριστῷ*) or “before God” (*τῷ Θεῷ*).]

154. Priests or ascetics must not bathe with women in a bathhouse, nor indeed any Christian or layperson. For this is the first accusation made by the pagans.

155. One must not contract marriages with any heretics, nor give sons or daughters to them; rather, one should receive them if they promise to become Christians.

[Greek variant: *ἐπαγγέλοιντο* (“if they should promise”) or *ἐπαγγέλλονται* (“they promise”).]

156. One must not receive blessings from heretics, since some such things are rather irrationalities (*alogiai*) than blessings.

[Col. 0073A] 157. One must not pray with heretics or schismatics.

158. No Christian must abandon the martyrs of Christ and go to false martyrs—that is, heretics—or to those who have become heretics. For these are alien to God. Therefore let those who go to them be anathema.

[Greek variant: *πρὸς* or *εἰς*, both construing movement “toward/to” the aforesaid heretics.]

159. Christians must not abandon the Church of God, depart, name angels, or hold assemblies, since these practices are forbidden. If anyone is found devoting himself to this hidden idolatry, let him be anathema, because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and approached idolatry.

[Col. 0073B] 160. Priests or clergy must not be magicians, enchanters, mathematicians, or astrologers, nor make what are called amulets, which are in fact bonds imprisoning their own souls. We have commanded that those who wear them be expelled from the church.

161. One must not accept the festival gifts sent by Jews or heretics, nor celebrate festivals with them.

162. One must not accept unleavened bread from Jews or share in their impieties.

163. One must not celebrate festivals with the pagans or share in their godlessness.

164. Bishops summoned to a synod must not show contempt, but must attend and teach or be taught, for the correction of the Church and of the others. If such a man shows contempt, he will condemn himself, unless he is absent because of illness.

[Col. 0073C] 165. A priest or cleric must not travel without canonical letters.

166. A priest or cleric must not travel without the bishop’s command.

167. Assistants must not leave the doors, even briefly, but must devote themselves to prayer.

168. Women must not enter the sanctuary.

169. No one is to be admitted to illumination [baptism] after the second week of Lent.

[Greek textual variants in canon 6: *βουλόμενοι* (“wishing”) or *πειρώμενοι* (“attempting”); *ἤρεσεν* (“it pleased [the synod]”) or *ὥρισε* (“[the synod] decreed”); active *ἐπιτρέπειν* (“to permit”) or passive *ἐπιτρέπεσθαι* (“to be permitted”); *ἰδιωτικήν* (“private”) or *ἤγουν χρηματικήν* (“that is, financial”); *τοῦ κατηγόρου* (“of the accuser”) or *τοῦ κατηγορουμένου* (“of the accused”); *ἀποσχήσαντας* (“having separated themselves”) or *ἀποσχισθέντας* (“having split off”); *ἀντισυνάγοντας* (“holding counter-assemblies”) or *ἀντισυναγαγόντας* (“having gathered counter-assemblies”); *πρῶτον* (“first”) or *πρότερον* (“previously”); *ὑποτιμήσασθαι* (“to subject themselves to”) or *ἐπιτιμήσασθαι* (“to impose upon themselves”) the same peril; *τάξει* (“order/sequence”) or *ἐξετάξει* (“examination”) of the proceedings; and the case variants *βασιλικάς/βασιλικαῖς* (“imperial”) and *ἀκοάς/ἀκοαῖς* (“ears/audiences”).]

170. Those receiving illumination must learn the faith by heart and recite it to the bishop or [Col. 0073D] presbyters on Thursday.

[Greek textual variants in canon 7: *ἀριστερούς* (“left-handed”) or *ἀρίστους* (“excellent/best”); *εἴτουν* or *ἤγουν* (“or, that is”); *διδάσκοντας* (“teaching”) or *δοξάζοντας* (“holding the belief”); “all the other heresies” (*τὰς ἄλλας πάσας αἱρέσεις*) or “all the other heretics” (*τοὺς ἄλλους πάντας αἱρετικοὺς*); and those “coming” (*ἐρχόμενοι*) or “originating” (*ὀρμώμενοι*) from the Galatian region.]

171. Those who receive illumination while ill and afterward recover must learn the faith by heart and understand that they have been deemed worthy of a divine gift.

172. Those being illuminated must, after baptism, be anointed with heavenly chrism and become participants in the kingdom of Christ [of God].

[Greek variant: “the kingdom of Christ” (*τοῦ Χριστοῦ*) or “the kingdom of God” (*τοῦ Θεοῦ*).]

173. Bread must not be offered during Lent except on Saturday and Sunday alone.

[Greek variant: *ἐκπίπτοντας* or *ἀποπίπτοντας*, both expressing falling or being cast from their rank.]

174. During the final week of Lent one must not break the fast on Thursday and thus dishonor the whole of Lent; rather, the whole of Lent must be fasted, eating dry food.

[Greek variant: “all Lent” or “all Lent itself” (*αὐτὴν*).]

[Col. 0075A] 175. During Lent the birthdays [feast-days] of martyrs must not be celebrated; rather, a commemoration [memorials] of the holy martyrs is to be made on Saturdays and Sundays.

[Greek variant: singular *μνείαν* (“commemoration”) or plural *μνήμας* (“memorial observances”).]

176. Weddings or birthday celebrations must not be held during Lent.

[Greek variant: laypeople are to *ὑπάρχειν* (“be”) or *τυγχάνειν* (“be found/remain”) excommunicate.]

177. Christians who go to weddings must not dance or leap about, but must dine or take their midday meal modestly, as is fitting for Christians.

[Greek variants: the fathers were *συναχθέντων* (“assembled”) or *συνελθόντων* (“come together”); persons *θέλουσιν* or *ἐθέλουσιν* (“wishing”) to turn to knowledge of the truth; and Nestorius’s doctrines are *πικρά* (“bitter”) or *μιαρά* (“impure/defiled”).]

178. Priests or clergy must not watch entertainments at weddings or banquets; rather, before the performers enter, they must rise and depart.

179. Priests or clergy—and likewise laypeople—must not hold banquets by mutual contribution.

[Col. 0075B] 180. Presbyters must not enter before the bishop’s arrival and sit in the sanctuary, but must enter with the bishop, unless the bishop is ill or away from home.

[Greek variant: *ἐκπορίαν* (“sale/export for profit”) or *ἐμπορίαν* (“commerce/trade”) in describing the venal ordination.]

181. Bishops must not be appointed in villages and districts, but circuit-visitors are to be appointed. Those already appointed must do nothing without the consent of the bishop of the city. Likewise, presbyters must do nothing without the bishop’s consent.

[Greek variants: clerics *ἀνεχόμενοι* (“undertaking/enduring”) or *ἀναδεχόμενοι* (“taking upon themselves”) the management of estates; involving themselves in secular administration of *πραγμάτων* (“affairs”) or *κτημάτων* (“estates/possessions”); and acting from fear of *τοῦ Θεοῦ* (“God”) or *κυρίου* (“the Lord”).]

182. Offerings must not be made in houses by bishops or presbyters.

183. Private psalms must not be recited in the church, nor noncanonical books, but only the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments.

[Col. 0075C] These are the books of the Old Testament that are to be read: 1. Genesis, “Creation of the World”; 2. Exodus, “Departure from Egypt”; 3. Leviticus; 4. Numbers; 5. Deuteronomy; 6. Joshua son of Nun; 7. Judges and Ruth; 8. Esther; 9. First and Second Kingdoms; 10. Third and Fourth Kingdoms; 11. First and Second Chronicles; 12. First and Second Esdras; 13. the Book of the 150 Psalms; 14. Proverbs of Solomon; 15. Ecclesiastes; 16. Song of Songs; 17. Job; 18. the Twelve Prophets; 19. Isaiah; 20. Jeremiah and Baruch, Lamentations and Epistles; 21. Ezekiel; 22. Daniel.

The books of the New Testament are these: the four Gospels, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John; the Acts of the Apostles; seven Catholic Epistles, as follows: one of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude; fourteen Epistles of Paul: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, [Col. 0075D] one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.

## Latin recension — Laodicea

[Col. 0068D] 105. That, according to the ecclesiastical canon, those who have freely and lawfully entered into a second marriage, and have not contracted a clandestine marriage, are to be restored to communion after a short period has elapsed, once they have devoted themselves to prayers and fasts, according to the measure of indulgence.

106. That those who have sinned in various ways, [Col. 0070A] and persevere in the prayer of confession and repentance, demonstrating a complete conversion from their evils, are to be granted communion, out of the mercy and goodness of God, after a period of penance proportionate to the character of their offense has been assigned to them.

107. That those recently baptized must not be promoted to the priestly order.

108. That priests must not lend money at interest or accept the interest called “the hundredth.”

109. That elections must not be held in the presence of hearers.

110. That heretics must not be permitted to enter the house of God if they persist in heresy.

[Col. 0070B] 111. That those who turn from heresies—that is, from the Novatians, Photinians, or Quartodecimans—or those who are called faithful among them, must not be admitted until they have anathematized every heresy, especially the one in which they were held; and thereafter those called faithful among them, having learned the symbols of the faith and having been anointed with holy chrism, are to participate in the holy mystery in this manner.

112. That those who turn from the heresy of those called Phrygians, even if they are in the clergy as they are reputed to be among them, or are called their highest officials, must be carefully catechized and baptized by the bishops and presbyters of the Church.

[Col. 0070C] 113. It must not be permitted for members of the Church to go to the cemeteries or to what are called martyria of any heretics for the sake of prayer or healing. If such persons are faithful, they are to be deprived of communion for a time; but if they repent and confess that they have done wrong, they are to be received.

114. That members of the Church must not indiscriminately join their children in marriage to heretics.

115. That those called senior widows, or presiding women, must not be appointed in the church.

116. That bishops are to be appointed to ecclesiastical office by the judgment of the metropolitans and neighboring bishops, after having been tested for a long period both in the word of faith and in the administration of right doctrine.

[Col. 0070D] 117. It must not be permitted for the crowds to conduct the elections of those who are to be appointed to the priesthood.

118. That holy gifts, as tokens of blessing, must not be sent to other parishes during the feast of Easter.

119. That no one besides the canonical singers, who ascend the ambo and sing from a parchment, should sing in the church.

120. That the Gospels are to be read together with the other Scriptures on Saturday.

121. That psalms must not be joined together in the assemblies, but that a reading should take place with an interval after each psalm.

[Col. 0072A] 122. That the same order of prayers ought to be observed both at the ninth hour and at evening.

123. That, first and separately, after the bishops’ sermons, the prayer for the catechumens should be offered; and after the catechumens have departed, the prayer for those under penance should take place. After these have approached, received the laying on of hands, and withdrawn, three prayers of the faithful should then be offered: the first in silence, while the second and third are completed by spoken responses. Thereafter peace is to be given. After the presbyters have given peace to the bishop, the laypeople are then to give peace. Thus the holy offering is to be celebrated. Only priests are permitted to approach the altar and receive communion.

[Col. 0072B] 124. A deacon must not sit before a presbyter, but must sit at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, deacons ought to be honored by assistants and by all the clergy.

125. Assistants must not have a place in the diaconicon, nor touch the vessels belonging to the Lord.

126. An assistant must not wear an orarion, nor leave the doors unattended.

127. Readers or singers must not wear an orarion and then read or sing.

128. Priests—from presbyters down to deacons—and thereafter anyone in the ecclesiastical order, down to assistants, readers, singers, exorcists, doorkeepers, or members of the order of monks, must not enter a tavern.

[Col. 0072C] 129. Assistants must not distribute bread or bless the cup.

130. Those who have not been advanced by a bishop must not perform exorcisms, either in churches or in houses.

131. Priests, clergy, or laypeople invited to a communal meal must not take away portions, since this brands the ecclesiastical order with disgrace.

132. Communal meals must not be held on the Lord’s days or in churches, nor may people eat in the house of God or spread couches there.

[Col. 0072D] 133. Christians must not Judaize or keep idle on the Sabbath, but must work on that day. Preferring the Lord’s Day, they should, if they are able, keep it idle as Christians. If they are found to be Judaizers, let them be anathema from Christ.

134. Priests, clergy, or monks must not bathe with women in a bathhouse, nor indeed any Christian or layperson. For this is the first accusation made by the pagans.

135. One must not contract marriages with any heretics, nor give sons or daughters to them; rather, one should receive them if they promise to become Christians.

136. One must not receive blessings from heretics, since they are rather curses than blessings.

[Col. 0074A] 137. One must not pray with heretics or schismatics.

138. No Christian must abandon the martyrs of Christ and go to false martyrs—that is, heretics—or to those who have become heretics. For these are alien to God. Let those who go to them be anathema.

139. Christians must not abandon the Church of God, depart, name angels, or hold assemblies, since this is forbidden. If anyone is found serving this hidden idolatry, let him be anathema, because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and approached idolatry.

[Col. 0074B] 140. Priests or clergy must not be magicians or enchanters, mathematicians or astrologers, nor make what are called amulets, which are in fact bonds of their own souls. We command that those who wear them be expelled from the church.

141. One must not accept the festival gifts sent by Jews or heretics, nor celebrate festivals with them.

142. One must not accept unleavened bread from Jews or share in their impieties.

143. One must not celebrate festivals with the pagans or share in their godlessness.

144. Bishops summoned to a synod must not show contempt, but must attend and teach or be taught, for the correction of the Church and of the others. If anyone shows contempt, he will condemn himself, unless he is unable to attend because of illness.

[Col. 0074C] 145. A priest or cleric must not travel without canonical letters.

146. A priest or cleric must not travel without the bishop’s command.

147. Assistants must not leave the doors, even briefly, but must devote themselves to prayer.

148. Women must not enter the altar area.

149. No one is to be admitted to baptism after the second week of Lent.

150. Those who are to be baptized must learn the faith by heart and recite it to the bishop or presbyters on Thursday.

[Col. 0074D] 151. Those who receive baptism while ill and afterward recover must learn the faith by heart and understand that they have been deemed worthy of a divine gift.

152. Those who are baptized must, after baptism, be anointed with heavenly chrism and become participants in the kingdom of Christ.

153. Bread must not be offered during Lent except on Saturday and Sunday alone.

154. During Lent, on the Thursday of the final week, one must not break the fast and thus dishonor the whole of Lent; rather, the whole of Lent must be fasted, eating dry food.

[Col. 0076A] 155. During Lent the birthdays [feast-days] of martyrs must not be celebrated, but a commemoration of the holy martyrs is to be made on Saturdays and Sundays.

156. Weddings or birthday celebrations must not be held during Lent.

157. Christians attending weddings must not dance or leap about, but must dine or take their midday meal chastely, as is fitting for Christians.

158. Priests or clergy must not watch entertainments at weddings or banquets; rather, before the performers enter, they must rise and depart.

159. Priests or clergy—and likewise laypeople—must not hold banquets by mutual contribution.

[Col. 0076B] 160. Presbyters must not enter before the bishop’s arrival and sit in the sanctuary, but must enter with the bishop, unless the bishop is detained by illness or has gone abroad.

161. Bishops must not be appointed in villages and districts, but administrators or circuit-visitors are to be appointed. Those already appointed must do nothing without the consent of the bishop of the city. Likewise, presbyters must do nothing without the bishop’s consent.

162. Offerings must not be made in houses by bishops or presbyters.

163. Private psalms must not be recited in the church, nor noncanonical books, but only the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments.

[Col. 0076C] These are the books of the Old Testament that ought to be read: 1. Genesis; 2. Exodus, that is, the departure from Egypt; 3. Leviticus; 4. Numbers; 5. Deuteronomy; 6. Joshua son of Nun; 7. Judges and Ruth; 8. Esther; 9. First and Second Kingdoms; 10. Third and Fourth Kingdoms; 11. First and Second Chronicles; 12. First and Second Esdras; 13. the Book of the 150 Psalms; 14. Proverbs of Solomon; 15. Ecclesiastes; 16. Song of Songs; 17. Job; 18. the Twelve Prophets; 19. Isaiah; 20. Jeremiah and Baruch, Lamentations and Epistles; 21. Ezekiel; 22. Daniel.

The books of the New Testament are these: the four Gospels, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John; the Acts of the Apostles; seven Catholic Epistles, namely, one of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude; fourteen Epistles of Paul: one to the Romans, [Col. 0076D] two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Hebrews, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.

# The Canons of the Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, Seven Canons (A.D. 381)

[Note: [Col. 0075] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## Greek recension — Constantinople

[Col. 0075D] 164. The faith of the three hundred and eighteen fathers who assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia must not be abolished. Rather, it must remain authoritative, and every heresy must be anathematized, specifically that of the Eunomians, or Anomoeans; that of the Arians, or Eudoxians; [Col. 0077A] that of the Semi-Arians, or Pneumatomachi; that of the Sabellians; that of the Marcellians; that of the Photinians; and that of the Apollinarists.

165. Bishops who are over a diocese must not enter churches outside their boundaries or confuse the churches. Rather, in accordance with the canons, the bishop of Alexandria is to administer only what belongs to Egypt; the bishops of the East are to govern only the East, while the privileges granted by the Nicene canons to the Church of Antioch are preserved; the bishops of the Asian diocese are to administer only what belongs to Asia; those of Pontus only what belongs to Pontus; and those of Thrace only what belongs to Thrace. Bishops from outside a diocese, when not summoned, must not intervene in ordinations or in other ecclesiastical administrations.

[Col. 0077B] When the foregoing canon concerning the dioceses is preserved, it is clear that the provincial synod is to administer what belongs to each province, according to the decisions made at Nicaea. The churches of God among the barbarian peoples must be administered according to the custom established by the fathers.

166. The bishop of Constantinople is to have the privileges of honor after the bishop of Rome, because Constantinople is New Rome.

167. Concerning Maximus the Cynic and the disorderly appointment made by him in Constantinople: Maximus must neither become nor be a bishop, nor may those ordained by him in any rank of the clergy be recognized; all that was done by him, by those associated with him, and by those ordained by him is annulled.

[Col. 0077C] 168. Concerning the document of the Westerners: we have also accepted those in Antioch who confess one divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

169. Since many people, wishing to confuse and overthrow ecclesiastical order, maliciously and slanderously fabricate accusations [Col. 0077D] against the orthodox bishops who administer the churches, attempting nothing other than to stain the reputation of the priests and create disturbances among peoples living in peace, for this reason the holy synod of the bishops assembled at Constantinople has decreed that accusers must not be admitted without examination, nor must everyone be permitted to bring accusations against those who administer the churches; yet neither are all to be excluded.

If someone brings a personal complaint—that is, a private [or financial] complaint—against a bishop, as one who has been defrauded or otherwise wronged by him, such accusations are not to be examined with regard either to the accuser’s person [or the accused person] or to his religion. For in every way the bishop’s conscience ought to remain free, and the person who says he has been wronged, whatever his religion, ought to obtain justice.

But if the charge brought against the bishop is ecclesiastical, then the persons of the accusers must be examined, so that, first of all, heretics may not be permitted to bring ecclesiastical accusations against orthodox bishops. By “heretics” we mean those who were formerly expelled [Col. 0079A] from the Church and those later anathematized by us; in addition, those who pretend to profess the sound faith but have separated themselves and hold counter-assemblies against our canonical bishops.

Further, if some people have previously been condemned and expelled from the Church for certain offenses, or are excommunicated, whether they belong to the clergy or to the laity, they too must not be permitted to accuse a bishop until they have first cleared themselves of their own charge. Likewise, those who are already under accusation must not be admitted to accuse a bishop or other clergy until they have shown themselves innocent of the charges brought against them.

If, however, certain people are neither heretics nor excommunicated, neither previously condemned nor previously accused of offenses, but [Col. 0079B] say that they have an ecclesiastical accusation against a bishop, the holy synod commands them first to bring their accusations before all the bishops of the province and to prove before them the charges against the bishop under accusation.

If the provincial bishops prove unable to correct the charges brought against the bishop, then the accusers are to approach the greater synod of the bishops of that diocese, who are to be summoned for this reason. They must not bring the accusation before first submitting themselves in writing to the same danger, should they be found, in the examination of the proceedings, to have slanderously accused the bishop.

If anyone, despising the decisions previously stated, dares either to assail imperial [Col. 0079C] ears, or to trouble the tribunals of secular authorities, or to disturb an ecumenical council, having disregarded all the bishops of the diocese, such a person must not be admitted to an accusation at all, as one who has insulted the canons and harmed ecclesiastical order.

170. We receive those who come over from the heretics and wish to join the orthodox faith and the portion of those who are being saved, according to the following order and custom.

We receive Arians, Macedonians, Sabbatians, Novatians—who call themselves “pure” and “left-handed” [variant: “excellent”]—Quartodecimans, or Tetradites, and Apollinarists when they present written statements and anathematize every heresy that does not think as the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God thinks. They are first sealed, or anointed, with the holy oil on the forehead, eyes, nostrils, [Col. 0079D] mouth, and ears; and as we seal them we say: “The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

But Eunomians, who are baptized by a single immersion; Montanists, who here are called Phrygians; Sabellians, who teach the doctrine of the Father-Son identity [who hold that the Father and Son are the same], and commit certain other grave offenses; and all the other heresies—for there are many here, especially those who come from the region of the Galatians—we receive all who wish to come over from them to orthodoxy as pagans. On the first day we designate them Christians, on the second catechumens; then on the third day we exorcize them, while also blowing three times into their faces and ears. Thus we catechize and instruct them, arrange that they remain in the church for a long period and listen to the Scriptures, and then we baptize them.

# The Canons of the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, Eight Canons (A.D. 431)

## Greek recension — Ephesus

[Note: [Col. 0081] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0081A] 171. If any metropolitan of a province, having withdrawn from the holy and ecumenical synod, joins the council of the secessionists, or later joins it, or has adopted or should adopt the opinions of Celestius, he is utterly unable to do anything against the rulers and bishops of the province, since from that point he has been excluded by the synod from all ecclesiastical communion and is without authority to exercise any office. He shall also be entirely subject to the bishops of his province and to the neighboring metropolitans who hold the orthodox faith, and shall be expelled from the rank of the episcopate. [F. reads “entirely” for “into the whole.”]

172. If any provincial bishops were absent from the holy synod and joined the council of the secessionists, or attempted to join it, or, after signing the deposition of Nestorius, returned to the council of the secessionists, they are, according to the decision of the holy synod, to be entirely excluded from the priesthood and to fall from their rank.

[Greek variant: *ὑπογράψαντες* (“after signing”) or *ὑποστρέψαντες* (“having turned back”); the clause then says they returned to the secessionists’ council.]

[Col. 0081B] 173. If any clergy in any city or district were expelled from the priesthood by Nestorius and those with him because they thought rightly, we have judged it right that they should also recover their own rank. We command generally that clergy who agree with the orthodox and ecumenical synod in no way be subject to bishops who have seceded or are seceding.

174. If any clergy have seceded and dared, privately or publicly, to hold the opinions of Nestorius or Celestius, the holy synod has judged that they too are deposed.

[Col. 0081C] 175. Those who were condemned by the holy synod or by their own bishops for disgraceful acts, and whom Nestorius, acting with complete disregard for due order, or those who share his opinions, have attempted or may attempt unlawfully to restore to communion or to office, are to remain without benefit from such restoration; we have judged that they remain no less deposed.

176. Likewise, if anyone should wish in any way to undermine what was done concerning any matter at the holy synod in Ephesus, the holy synod has decreed that, if they are bishops or clergy, they shall utterly fall from their rank; if they are laypeople, they shall be excommunicated.

177. The holy synod has decreed that no one may present, write, or compose another faith besides that defined by the holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea together with the Holy Spirit. Those who dare to compose, introduce, or present another faith to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of the truth from paganism, Judaism, or any heresy whatsoever—if they are bishops or clergy, the bishops shall be alienated from their episcopate and the clergy from the clergy; if they are laypeople, they shall be anathematized.

[Col. 0083A] In the same way, if any bishops, clergy, or laypeople are discovered either to hold or to teach the doctrines contained in the exposition presented by the presbyter Charisius concerning the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, or the bitter [impure] and distorted doctrines of Nestorius appended to it, they shall be subject to the judgment of this holy and ecumenical synod. Thus the bishop shall be deprived of his episcopate and deposed, while the cleric shall likewise fall from the clergy. If the person is a layman, let him also be anathematized, as has been said.

[Col. 0081D] 178. Our most devout fellow bishop Reginus, together with the most reverent bishops [Col. 0083B] of the province of Cyprus, Zeno and Evagrius, reported a practice introduced contrary to ecclesiastical institutions and the canons of the holy fathers, and affecting the liberty of all.

Since common illnesses require a greater remedy because they cause greater harm, and since no ancient custom has established that the bishop of Antioch should perform ordinations in Cyprus, as the most reverent men who came before the holy synod demonstrated in written statements and in their own words, the leaders of the holy churches of Cyprus shall retain their right inviolate, according to the canons of the holy fathers and ancient custom, performing the ordinations of their most reverent bishops by themselves.

The same rule shall also be preserved in the other dioceses and provinces everywhere: no most reverent bishop is to seize another province [Col. 0083C] that from the beginning was not under his authority or that of his predecessors. If anyone has seized such a province and forcibly made it his own, he must restore it, so that the canons of the fathers are not violated, nor the arrogance of secular power secretly introduced under the pretext of administering sacred affairs, nor we gradually and unknowingly lose the liberty that our Lord Jesus Christ, the liberator of all human beings, bestowed on us by his own blood.

Therefore the holy and ecumenical synod has decreed that every province retain pure and inviolate the rights that belonged to it from the beginning, according to ancient custom; and that each metropolitan have the freedom to obtain copies of the proceedings for his own security. If anyone produces a decree contrary to what has now been defined, the entire holy and ecumenical synod has decreed that it be invalid.
