# The Canons of the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, Eight Canons (A.D. 431)

## Latin recension — Ephesus

[Note: [Col. 0081] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0082A] 171. If any metropolitan of a province, having withdrawn from the holy and ecumenical synod, joins the council of the secessionists, or later joins it, or has held or should hold the views of Celestius, he can do absolutely nothing against the presidents and bishops of the province, since from that point he has been excluded by the synod from all ecclesiastical communion and is unfit to exercise any office or duty. He shall also be entirely subject to the bishops of the province and to the neighboring metropolitans who profess the orthodox faith, and shall be removed from the episcopal rank.

172. If any provincial bishops did not attend the holy synod and joined the council of the secessionists, or tried to join it, or, after signing the deposition of Nestorius, fell back into the council of the secessionists, they are, as seemed right to the holy synod, to be excluded entirely from the priesthood and to fall from their rank.

[Col. 0082B] 173. If any clergy in any city or district were expelled from the priesthood under Nestorius and those with him because they thought rightly, we judged it right that they too should recover their rank. We command all clergy who agree with the orthodox and universal synod not to be subject in any way to bishops who have seceded or are seceding.

174. If any clergy have seceded and dared, privately or publicly, to hold the opinions of Nestorius or Celestius, it seemed right that they too should be deposed by the holy synod.

[Col. 0082C] 175. Whoever was condemned for wicked acts by the holy synod or by his own bishops, and whom Nestorius, acting without discrimination in everything, or those who share his opinions, restored or attempted to restore unlawfully to communion or office, has gained nothing from such restoration; we have judged that such persons remain deposed nevertheless.

176. Likewise, if anyone wishes in any way to weaken what was done concerning any matter at the holy synod of Ephesus, the holy synod decrees that, if they are bishops or clergy, they shall utterly fall from their rank; if they are laypeople, they shall be excommunicated.

[Col. 0082D] 177. The holy synod has decreed that no one may bring forward, write, or compose another faith besides that defined by the holy fathers assembled at Nicaea in the Holy Spirit. Those who dare to compose, introduce, or present another faith to those wishing to return to the knowledge of truth from paganism, Judaism, or any heresy—if they are bishops or clergy, the bishops shall be alienated from their episcopate and the clergy from the clergy; if they are laypeople, they shall be anathematized.

In the same manner, if any bishops, clergy, or laypeople are found either holding or teaching the doctrines in the exposition presented by the presbyter Charisius concerning the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, or the impious [impure] and perverse doctrines of Nestorius inserted therein, they shall be subject to the sentence of this holy and universal synod: the bishop shall be deprived of his episcopate and deposed, and the cleric shall likewise fall from the clergy. If the person is a layman, he too shall be anathematized, as stated above.

[Col. 0084A] 178. Our most devout fellow bishop Reginus, together with the most reverent bishops [Col. 0084B] of the province of Cyprus, Zeno and Evagrius, reported a practice innovated contrary to ecclesiastical constitutions and the canons of the holy fathers, and affecting the liberty of all.

Since common diseases require a greater remedy, as they also cause greater harm, and since no ancient custom has prevailed by which the bishop of Antioch performs ordinations in Cyprus, as the most reverent men who came before the holy synod demonstrated in written statements and in their own words, the leaders of the holy churches in Cyprus shall retain their right inviolate, according to the canons of the holy fathers and ancient custom, themselves performing the ordinations of their most reverent bishops.

This shall likewise be preserved in the other dioceses and provinces everywhere, so that none of the most God-loving bishops may invade another province that from the beginning was not under his authority or that of his predecessors. If anyone has invaded such a province and forcibly made it his own, [Col. 0084C] he must restore it, so that the canons of the fathers are not violated, nor the arrogance of secular power creep in under the guise of sacred administration, nor we gradually and unwittingly lose the liberty that our Lord Jesus Christ, the liberator of all human beings, bestowed on us by his own blood.

Therefore the holy and universal synod has decreed that each province retain pure and inviolate the rights that belonged to it from the beginning, according to ancient custom, and that every metropolitan be free to obtain copies of the proceedings for his own security. If anyone brings forward a decree that conflicts with what has now been defined, the entire holy and universal synod has decreed that it be void.

# The Canons of the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, Twenty-Nine Canons (A.D. 450)

## Greek recension — Chalcedon

[Note: [Col. 0083] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0083D] 179. We have judged that the canons issued by the holy fathers at each synod down to the present must remain in force.

180. If any bishop performs an ordination for money and brings the grace that cannot be bought into commerce, and for money ordains a bishop, a chorepiscopus, presbyters, deacons, or any other person enrolled among the clergy, or for money appoints an administrator, advocate, sacristan, or anyone whatsoever belonging to the canon, for his own disgraceful profit, the person who attempts this and is convicted shall risk his own rank.

The person ordained shall gain nothing from the ordination or appointment made for money; rather, he shall be deprived of the dignity or office that he obtained for money. If anyone is found acting as an intermediary in such disgraceful and unlawful transactions, he too, if he is a cleric, shall fall from his rank; if he is a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized.

[Col. 0085A] 181. A matter was brought before the holy synod: some persons enrolled among the clergy, out of disgraceful greed, become tenants of other people’s estates and undertake secular business contracts, neglecting the service of God, frequenting [Col. 0085B] the houses of secular persons, and, out of love of money, accepting the management of property.

Therefore the holy and great synod has decreed that henceforth no one—not a bishop, cleric, or monk—may rent estates or involve himself in secular administrations of affairs, except when he is summoned by law to an unavoidable guardianship of minors, or when the bishop of the city entrusts him with the care of ecclesiastical affairs, or of orphans and unprotected widows, or of persons who especially require the Church’s assistance, for fear of God [the Lord].

If anyone henceforth attempts to transgress these decrees, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical penalties.

## Canons: Translation of the Greek Text

### 182

Those who truly and sincerely pursue the monastic life shall be deemed worthy of the honor due to them. But since [Col. 0085C] some, using the monastic guise as a pretext [*προσχήματι*, “pretext/guise”; variant *σχήματι*, “habit/appearance”], disturb both the churches and civil affairs, wandering indiscriminately through the cities and also undertaking to establish monasteries for themselves, it has been decreed that no one anywhere may build or establish a monastery or house of prayer without the consent of the bishop of the city. Monks in each city and region shall be subject to the bishop, embrace quietness, and devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer, persevering in the places where they renounced the world. They shall neither interfere in nor participate in ecclesiastical or secular affairs by abandoning their own monasteries, unless the bishop of the city should permit this on some necessary occasion. [Note: Variants: *μηδαμοῦ*, “nowhere,” / *μηδαμῶς*, “in no way”; *ἐπικοινωνεῖν* / *κοινωνεῖν*, both “participate,” the variant omitting the prefix.]

No one shall receive a slave into a monastery for the purpose of making him a monk without the consent of his own master. We decree that anyone who transgresses [Col. 0085D] this rule of ours shall be excommunicated, lest the name of God be blasphemed. The bishop of the city, for his part, must exercise the proper care over the monasteries.

### 183

Concerning bishops or clerics who migrate from one city to another, it has been decreed that the canons enacted concerning them by the holy Fathers shall retain their force.

### 184

No one shall be ordained without a specific title—not a presbyter, not a deacon, nor anyone at all among those in the ecclesiastical order—unless the person to be ordained is expressly assigned to a church of a city or village, a martyr-shrine, or a monastery. The holy synod has decreed that those ordained without such a title have [Col. 0087A] such an ordination declared invalid and shall nowhere be able to exercise their ministry, to the disgrace of the one who ordained them.

### 185

Those who have once been enrolled among the clergy, and monks, shall not enter military service or a secular dignity. Those who dare to do so and do not repent, so as to return to that which they previously chose for God’s sake, shall be anathematized.

### 186

The clerics of charitable institutions, monasteries, and martyr-shrines shall remain under the authority of the bishops in each city, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, and shall not presumptuously withdraw from their own bishop. Those who dare in any way to overturn this arrangement and do not submit to their own bishop shall, if they are clerics, be [Col. 0087B] subjected to the penalties of the canons; if they are monks or laypeople, they shall be deprived of communion. [Note: Variant: *τῶν ἐν ἑκάστῃ πόλει*, “those in each city,” / *ἑκάστης πόλεως*, “of each city,” a genitive construction describing the bishops.]

### 187

If a cleric has a dispute with another cleric, he shall not abandon his own bishop and rush to secular courts. Rather, he shall first pursue the case before his own bishop, or, with that bishop’s agreement, let the case be heard before those whom both parties may choose. Whoever acts otherwise shall be subjected to canonical penalties. [Note: Variant: *συγκροτεῖσθαι*, “for the proceedings to be conducted,” / *συγκροτείσθω*, “let the proceedings be conducted,” changing infinitive to imperative.]

If a cleric has a dispute with his own bishop or with another bishop, he shall be judged by the synod of the province. If a bishop or cleric has a dispute with the metropolitan of that same province, he shall approach either the exarch of the diocese or the see of imperial Constantinople, and shall be judged there.

[Col. 0087C]

### 188

A cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities: both in the city in which he was originally ordained and in the city to which, supposedly because it is greater, he has fled through desire for empty glory. Those who do this shall be restored to their own church, in which they were ordained from the beginning, and shall minister there alone.

If someone has already been transferred from one church to another, he shall have no involvement in the affairs of his former church or of the martyr-shrines, charitable institutions, or hostels belonging to it. Those who, after the definition of this great and universal synod, dare to do any of the things now forbidden shall, the holy synod has decreed, be expelled from their own rank.

### 189

We decree that all poor persons and those in need of assistance shall travel, [Col. 0087D] after examination, only with ecclesiastical letters of peace, and not with letters of commendation, since letters of commendation ought to be given only to persons held in esteem [*ἐν ὑπολήψει*].

### 190

It has come to our attention that certain persons, seeking power contrary to the ecclesiastical regulations, have divided one province into two by means of official documents, so that there would consequently be two metropolitans in the same province. The holy synod therefore decrees that henceforth no bishop shall dare anything of this kind; otherwise, the one who undertakes it shall be expelled from his rank.

Those cities which have already been honored with the title of metropolis by imperial letters, and the bishop who administers [Col. 0089A] the church of each, shall enjoy only the honor, with the proper rights of the true metropolis preserved.

### 191

Foreign and unknown clerics shall not minister anywhere, in any manner, in another city without letters of commendation from their own bishop.

### 192

Since in some provinces readers and singers have been permitted to marry, the holy synod decrees that none of them may take a wife belonging to another religious confession.

Those who have already fathered children from such a marriage shall, if they have had the children baptized by heretics, bring them into communion with the catholic Church. The variant *ἑαυτῶν τέκνα*, “their own children,” replaces *τὰ ἐξ αὐτῶν τεχθέντα*, “those born from them.” If the children have not been baptized, they may no longer have them baptized by heretics. Nor may they marry them to a heretic, a Jew, or a Greek [Ἕλληνι, here “pagan”], unless the person being joined to the Orthodox Christian declares that he or she will convert to the Orthodox [Col. 0089B] faith. [Note: Variant: *παρὰ* / *ἐπὶ* with “the heretics,” alternative prepositions for baptism among/by them.]

Whoever transgresses this definition of the holy synod shall be subjected to canonical punishment.

### 193

A woman shall not be ordained deaconess before the age of forty, and then only after careful examination. If, after receiving the laying on of hands [*χειροθεσίαν*, “laying on of hands”; variant *χειροτονίαν*, “ordination”] and remaining for some time in the ministry, she gives herself to marriage, dishonoring the grace of God, she shall be anathematized together with the man joined to her.

### 194

A virgin who has dedicated herself to the Lord God, and likewise monks, may not enter into marriage. If they are found to have done so, they shall be excommunicated. We decree, however, that the local bishop shall have authority to show them [Col. 0089C] leniency.

### 195

The rural or local parishes belonging to each church shall remain undisturbed in the possession of the bishops who hold them, especially when those bishops have administered them without coercion for thirty years. [Note: Variant: *ἐκκλησίαν*, “church,” / *ἐπαρχίαν*, “province.”]

If, within the thirty years, a dispute has arisen or arises concerning them, those who claim to have been wronged may bring an action concerning them before the synod of the province. If anyone is wronged by his own bishop or metropolitan, he shall litigate before the exarch of the diocese or before the see of Constantinople, as stated above. [Note: Variants: *ἐτῶν γεγένηταί τις, ἢ γένοιτο*, “years, a [dispute] has arisen or might arise,” / *ἐνιαυτῶν ἐγένετό τις ἢ γένηται*, “years, a [dispute] arose or may arise,” with a different word for years and different verb forms; *περὶ* / *ὑπέρ*, “concerning”; *καθὰ* / *καθώς*, “as [stated above].”]

If a city has been newly established by imperial authority, or is newly established in the future, the arrangement of its ecclesiastical parishes shall follow the civil and public arrangements.

[Col. 0089D]

### 196

The crime of conspiracy or factional association is altogether prohibited even by external laws; much more, therefore, must it be forbidden to occur in the Church of God.

If any clerics or monks are found either swearing conspiratorial oaths, forming factions, or plotting against bishops or fellow clerics, they shall be entirely expelled from their own rank.

### 197

It has come to our ears that in the provinces the synods of bishops established by the canons are not being held, and that consequently many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are neglected.

The holy synod therefore decrees, in accordance with the canons of the holy Fathers, that the bishops of each province shall assemble twice a year at a place [Col. 0091A] approved by the metropolitan bishop, and shall correct each matter that arises. Bishops who do not attend, although residing in their own cities, enjoying good health, and free from every unavoidable and necessary occupation, shall be admonished fraternally.

### 198

As we have already decreed, clerics serving in a church may not be appointed to the church of another city. They shall remain content with the church in which they were originally deemed worthy to minister, except those who, having lost their native country through necessity, have transferred to another church. [Note: Variant: *ἀπὸ* / *ὑπὸ* with “necessity,” “from/under necessity,” alternative prepositions.]

If, after this definition, a bishop receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, it has been decreed that both the one received and the one who received him shall be excommunicated until the cleric who transferred has returned to his own church.

[Col. 0091B]

### 199

Clerics or laypeople who accuse bishops or clerics indiscriminately and without examination shall not be admitted to make an accusation unless their own reputation has first been investigated.

### 200

Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, plunder the property belonging to him, as this was also forbidden by the ancient canons. Those who do so shall place their own rank in jeopardy. [Note: Variants: *κληρικοὺς*, “clerics” (accusative), / *κληρικοῖς*, “for clerics” (dative); *διαρπάζειν*, “plunder,” / *ἁρπάζειν*, “seize”; *ἰδίους* / *οἰκείους*, “their own,” alternative adjectives modifying ranks.]

### 201

It has come to the ears of the holy synod that certain clerics and monks, to whom nothing has been entrusted by their own bishop—and who sometimes have even been excluded from communion by him—reach imperial Constantinople and remain there for a long time, causing disturbances, throwing the ecclesiastical order into confusion, and [Col. 0091C] even overthrowing the households of certain persons.

The holy synod therefore decrees that such persons shall first be warned by the defensor of the most holy Church of Constantinople to leave the imperial city. If they persist shamelessly in the same conduct, the same defensor shall expel them even against their will, so that they may return to their own places. [Note: Variant: *κατὰ Κωνσταντινούπολιν*, “at Constantinople,” / *Κωνσταντινουπόλεως*, “of Constantinople,” describing the church.]

### 202

Monasteries once consecrated with the consent of the bishop shall remain monasteries perpetually. Their property shall be preserved for the monastery, and it shall no longer be possible for them to become secular dwellings. Those who permit this to happen shall be subjected to the penalties prescribed by the canons.

### 203

Since, as we have learned, certain metropolitans [Col. 0091D] neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay the ordinations of bishops, it has seemed good to the holy synod that the ordinations of bishops take place within three months, unless unavoidable necessity should compel the period of delay to be extended.

If they fail to do this, they shall be subjected to ecclesiastical punishment. The income of the vacant church, however, shall be preserved intact by the steward of that same church.

### 204

Since, as we have learned, in certain churches bishops administer ecclesiastical affairs without stewards, it has seemed good that every church which has a bishop should also have a steward from its own clergy, who shall administer the ecclesiastical property according to the judgment of his own bishop.

This is so that the administration of the church may not be without witnesses, so that its property may not thereby be scattered, and so that [Col. 0093A] reproach and disgrace may not be brought upon the priesthood. If he fails to do this, he shall be subjected to the divine canons.

### 205

The holy synod has decreed that those who abduct women under the pretext of marriage, or who assist or cooperate with the abductors, shall, if they are clerics, be expelled from their own rank; if they are laypeople, they shall be anathematized. [Note: Variant: *ἰδίου* / *οἰκείου*, “his own,” alternative adjectives modifying rank.]

### 206

Following everywhere the definitions of the holy Fathers, and recognizing the canon recently read of the one hundred and fifty most beloved of God bishops assembled under the pious-memory Emperor Theodosius the Great in the imperial city of Constantinople, New Rome, we likewise define and decree the same concerning the privileges of the most holy [Col. 0093B] Church of Constantinople, New Rome.

The Fathers rightly granted privileges to the see of elder Rome because that city was the imperial city. Moved by the same consideration, the one hundred and fifty most beloved of God bishops granted equal privileges to the most holy see of New Rome, reasonably judging that the city honored by empire and senate, and enjoying privileges equal to those of elder imperial Rome, should likewise be exalted and magnified in ecclesiastical affairs, standing second after it.

Accordingly, only the metropolitans of the Pontic, Asian, and Thracian dioceses, as well as the bishops in the barbarian regions of those dioceses, shall be ordained by the aforementioned most holy see of the most holy Church of Constantinople.

[Col. 0093C] That is, each metropolitan of the aforementioned dioceses shall ordain the bishops of his province together with the bishops of that province, as the divine canons prescribe. The metropolitans of those dioceses, however, shall, as stated, be ordained by the archbishop of Constantinople, after elections have been conducted according to custom and reported to him. [Note: Variant: *προειρημένων*, “previously mentioned,” / *εἰρημένων*, “mentioned,” describing the dioceses.]

### 207

Those who are said to have descended from episcopal dignity into the order of presbyters, if they were condemned for just causes, are reasonably not even worthy of the honor of the presbyterate. But if they were lowered to the lesser rank without any reasonable cause, then, provided they are found free from blame, they are entitled to recover both the dignity of the episcopate and the priesthood.

[Col. 0084D] **1.** We have judged it right that the canons hitherto established by the holy Fathers in each synod should be observed.

### 180

**2.** If any bishop performs an ordination for money, reduces priceless grace to a price, and for money ordains a bishop, chorepiscopus, presbyters, deacons, or any of those numbered among the clergy; or, for the sake of shameful gain, promotes a steward, [Col. 0086A] defensor, mansionarius, or indeed anyone whatsoever under the canon: whoever is convicted of having attempted this shall forfeit his rank. The person ordained shall derive no benefit from an ordination or promotion obtained by gain or trafficking, but shall be deprived of the dignity and office which he acquired for money. If anyone is found to have acted as intermediary in such shameful and impious profits, he too, if a cleric, shall lose his own rank; but if a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized.

### 181

**3.** It has come to the holy synod’s attention that some of those admitted to the clergy, for shameful gain, become lessees of other persons’ estates and conduct secular business, neglecting the service of God while running about the [Col. 0086B] houses of secular persons and, through greed, undertaking the management of their property. The holy and great synod therefore decrees that henceforth no one—bishop, cleric, or monk—shall lease estates or involve himself in the administration of secular affairs, unless perhaps he is called by law to the unavoidable guardianship of minors, or the bishop of the city permits him to undertake the care of ecclesiastical property, or he acts, from fear of God, on behalf of orphans, undefended widows, and persons especially in need of the Church’s assistance. Whoever henceforth transgresses these decrees shall be subject to ecclesiastical penalties.

## Notes of Christopher Justellus on the Code of the Canons of the Universal Church

[Col. 0093D] **“If anyone is in illness” — *εἴ τις ἐν νόσῳ***

This canon, which is the first canon of the Council of Nicaea, excludes eunuchs, or those who have voluntarily castrated themselves, from the priesthood. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* II.21, reports that Leontius was deprived of the presbyterate for this reason:

> *Λεόντιος, ἡνίκα πρεσβύτερος ἦν, ἀφῃρέθη τῆς ἀξίας, ὅτι τῶν γενητικῶν ἐξέτεμεν ἑαυτόν.*  
> “When Leontius was a presbyter, he was deprived of his dignity because he had cut off his genitals.”

Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* II.24, speaking of the same Leontius, who was later made bishop of Antioch by the Arians, writes:

> *Ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ δὲ, κατὰ Στέφανον Λεόντιος τὴν προεδρίαν ἐδέξατο, παρὰ τοὺς ἐν Νικαίᾳ γραφέντας ὅρους ταύτην λαβών. Ἐντομίας γὰρ ἦν αὐτουργὸς γενόμενος τῆς τόλμης.*  
> “At Antioch, after Stephen, Leontius assumed the presidency of the Church, obtaining it contrary to the decrees written at Nicaea; for he had himself cut off his genitals with his own hand.”

Origen also at one time interpreted rather literally the statement in Matthew 19:12, “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,” and voluntarily castrated himself. For this reason his ordination was condemned by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, as Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.8, and Epiphanius, *Against Origen*, *Heresy* 64, report.

There were also heretics called eunuchs who, perhaps following Origen’s example, castrated themselves out of zeal for piety. Augustine, *Heresy* 27; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 58; and Nicetas, *Treasury of Orthodox Faith* IV.30, discuss them.

This canon, however, makes an exception for those who were not castrated voluntarily or by their own choice, but by force and necessity at the hands of barbarians or masters. Thus a certain Tigrius, a barbarian by birth and a eunuch but not so from birth, obtained his freedom and was advanced to the dignity of the presbyterate, as Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.15 and VIII.24, reports:

> *Καὶ Τίγριος οὗτος βάρβαρος τὸ γένος, οὐκ ἐκ γενετῆς εὐνοῦχος μετέσχεν ἐλευθερίας, εἰς πρεσβυτέρου ἀξίαν προελθών.*  
> “This Tigrius, a barbarian by race and not a eunuch from birth, obtained freedom and advanced to the dignity of a presbyter.”

The same must be said of those who are eunuchs by birth:

> *οἵ τινες ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς ἐγενήθησαν οὕτω*  
> “who were born thus from their mother’s womb.”

This is the first of the three kinds of eunuchs mentioned in Matthew 19:12. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.32, reports that Dorotheus, bishop of Antioch, belonged to this category:

> *Δωρόθεον πρεσβείου τοῦ κατὰ Ἀντιόχειαν ἠξιωμένον ἔγνωμεν. Ἦν δὲ τὴν φύσιν εὐνοῦχος, οὕτω πεφυκὼς ἐξ αὐτῆς γενέσεως.*  
> “We know Dorotheus as one honored with the primacy of the Antiochene Church. He was by nature a eunuch, formed in this way from birth itself.”

Castration was prohibited not only by the sacred canons but also by civil laws. Under Hadrian’s edict, the physician who performed it incurred a capital penalty, as did the person who voluntarily submitted to being castrated: *Digest* IV, §2, *On the Cornelian Law concerning Assassins*. Hence the man mentioned by Justin Martyr in his *Apology to Antoninus Pius*, who wished to castrate himself, first sought permission for the edict from the prefect of Egypt. He presented a petition to Felix, prefect of Alexandria, asking that he permit a physician to remove his testicles:

> *Βιβλίδιον ἀνέδωκεν ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ Φήλικι ἡγεμονεύοντι, ἀξιῶν ἐπιτρέψαι ἰατρῷ τοὺς διδύμους αὐτοῦ ἀφελεῖν. Ἄνευ γὰρ τῆς τοῦ ἡγεμόνος ἐπιτροπῆς τοῦτο πράττειν ἀπειρῆσθαι οἱ ἐκεῖ ἰατροὶ ἔλεγον.*  
> “He presented a petition to Felix, prefect of Alexandria, asking that he permit a physician to remove his testicles; for the physicians there asserted that it was forbidden to do this without the prefect’s permission.”

See also *Digest* I, *On Eunuchs*; Justinian’s Novel 142, *On Those Who Castrate*; Evagrius IV.22; Leo’s Novel 60; and Zonaras on Apostolic Canon 21.

**“A neophyte” — *νεόφυτον***

Suidas interprets *νεόφυτον* as “one newly planted,” that is, someone who has recently embraced the Christian religion from paganism, has been planted into the Church of God through baptism, is not yet sufficiently established in doctrine, and has not yet been adequately tested in life.

This canon prohibits such a person from immediately becoming a bishop, and Justinian likewise prohibits it in Novel 123, chapter 1, lest someone object with the words of Gregory Nazianzen in his funeral oration for Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria:

> *Ὁμοῦ τε μαθηταὶ καὶ διδάσκαλοι τῆς εὐσεβείας, χθὲς ἱερόσυλοι, καὶ σήμερον ἱερεῖς· χθὲς τῶν ἁγίων ἔξω, καὶ μυσταγωγοὶ σήμερον.*  
> “At once disciples and teachers of piety; yesterday sacrilegious, today priests; yesterday outside the sacred things, today ministers of the mysteries.”

So too Jerome says: “Yesterday a catechumen, today a bishop.”

Nevertheless, the blessed Ambrose, not merely a neophyte or one not yet initiated through baptism, but still a catechumen, was elected from a secular prefecture to the episcopate by the common vote of the people of Milan. His election, although contrary to the Nicene canon, was approved by the judgment of the whole Church and with the consent of the Emperor Valentinian, as Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* II.11, and Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.6, report.

Ambrose’s election, however, should be attributed to divine rather than human command, as Nicholas I, pope of Rome, testifies in his letter to Photius of Constantinople, preserved among the Acts of the Eighth Ecumenical Council:

> *Ἀμβρόσιον, inquit, τὸν ἐκ κατηχουμένου θείᾳ ἀποκαλύψει πρὸς ἐπισκοπὴν ἀναχθέντα οὐ χρὴ προσφέρειν ὑμᾶς. Ἀρκεῖ γὰρ ἐκεῖ ἡ θεία, καὶ οὐκ ἀνθρωπίνη κέλευσις.*  
> “You ought not to cite Ambrose, who was advanced from the catechumenate to the episcopate by divine revelation. For there the divine command, not the human, is sufficient.”

Thus, when Emperor Valentinian confirmed this election, he said, according to Rufinus, that it was God’s work that had suddenly brought the discordant faith and divided minds of the people back into one consent and one judgment. Or, as Theodoret reports:

> *παντὸς κανόνος ἀκριβεστέραι τὰς ψήφους, καὶ θείαν εἶναι τὴν ψῆφον ἐκ τῆς τῶν τἀναντία φρονούντων συμφωνίας*  
> “The votes were more certain than any canon, and the vote was divine, arising from the agreement of those who had held contrary opinions.”

Likewise Synesius writes in Letter 67:

> *Χάριτος θείας ἐστὶν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐξομιλῆσαι.*  
> “It belongs to divine grace to draw human beings into the same judgment.”

This is precisely what is stated in Apostolic Canon 80:

> *Τὸν ἐξ ἐθνικοῦ βίου προσελθόντα καὶ βαπτισθέντα, οὐ δίκαιόν ἐστι παραυτὰ προχειρίζεσθαι ἐπίσκοπον, εἰ μή που κατὰ θείαν χάριν τοῦτο γένοιτο.*  
> “It is not right for one who has come from a pagan life and been baptized to be immediately appointed bishop, unless this should happen by divine grace.”

**“By two or three witnesses” — *ὑπὸ δύο ἢ τριῶν μαρτύρων***

Paul, First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 5:

> *Κατὰ πρεσβυτέρου κατηγορίαν μὴ παραδέχου, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ δύο ἢ τριῶν μαρτύρων.*  
> “Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.”

**“A woman introduced from outside” — *συνείσακτον γυναῖκα***

I translated *συνείσακτον* into Latin as *extraneam mulierem*, “an outsider woman.” So did Rufinus of Aquileia in Book I, chapter 6, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, in his account of the Nicene canons, as well as the old translator of the Council of Nicaea, followed by Fulgentius Ferrandus, chapter 122, and Isidore Mercator.

The Fourth Synod of Toledo, canon 43, likewise says:

> “Women from outside shall in no way dwell with clerics, for this too was decreed by the constitution of the ancient Fathers.”

And canon 42:

> “Certain clerics, not having a lawful marriage, seek the forbidden companionship of women from outside.”

The same usage is found in the First Synod of Carthage, canon 3; the Synod of Lérida, canon 15; the First Synod of Seville, canon 3; the Third Synod of Braga, canon 5; and in the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, *Code*, Book XIX, *On Bishops and Clerics*:

> “Let all who are supported by the priesthood, whatever their rank, or who are reckoned among the honor of the clergy, understand that the forbidden companionship of women from outside is prohibited to them.”

Others prefer to interpret *συνείσακτον* as *subintroductam*, “a woman introduced into the household.” This is the interpretation found in the translations of Teilo and Tharistus inserted into the Acts of the Sixth Council of Carthage, and in Dionysius Exiguus’s *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church*, followed by Burchard, Book II, chapter 109; Ivo, Book VI, chapter 186; and Gratian, canon *Interdixit*, Distinction 32.

Nicholas and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, likewise say in the same distinction, canons 5 and 6:

> “Let no one hear the Mass of a presbyter whom he knows to have a concubine or an introduced woman.”

Justinian also confirmed this definition of the Council of Nicaea concerning women from outside or women introduced into the household, in Novel 123, chapter 29:

> *Τοῖς δὲ πρεσβυτέροις, καὶ διακόνοις καὶ ὑποδιακόνοις, καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἄλλοις τοῖς ἐν κλήρῳ τεταγμένοις ἀπαγορεύομεν κατὰ τὴν τῶν ἁγίων κανόνων δύναμιν γυναῖκά τινα ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ οἴκῳ ἐπείσακτον ἔχειν.*  
> “We forbid presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and all others enrolled in the clergy, according to the force of the holy canons, to have in their own house any woman from outside or introduced into the household.”

In Novel 137, chapter 1, he also cites the canon of the Council of Nicaea itself. Basil of Caesarea does the same in his seventeenth letter to the presbyter Gregory, which is also preserved by Balsamon and Zonaras:

> “Read the canon established by our holy Fathers at the Council of Nicaea, which expressly forbade anyone to have an introduced woman.”

The term *συνείσακτοι* is also frequently mentioned by ecclesiastical writers. The synodical letter of the Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata, preserved by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.24, says:

> *τὰς δὲ συνεισάκτους αὐτοῦ γυναῖκας, ὡς Ἀντιοχεῖς ὀνομάζουσι, καὶ τῶν περὶ αὐτὸν πρεσβυτέρων καὶ διακόνων, οἷς καὶ τοῦτο καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἁμαρτήματα ἀνίατα ὄντα συγκρύπτει.*  
> “As for his introduced women, as the Antiochenes call them, and the presbyters and deacons around him, with whom he conceals this and his other incurable sins.”

Epiphanius reports in *Heresy* 67 that the Hieracites were mocked because they had *συνείσακτοι* women:

> *Χλευάζονται δὲ δι᾿ ἃς κέκτηνται ἕκαστος συνείσακτους γυναῖκας, δι᾿ ἃς εἰώθασι φιλοτιμεῖσθαι ἔχειν εἰς ὑπηρεσίαν.*  
> “They are mocked because each of them has introduced women, whom they are accustomed to boast of having for service.”

Speaking of the Origenists in *Heresy* 63, he says:

> *Κατηγοροῦσι δὲ τῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τὰς ἀγαπητὰς λεγομένας συνείσακτους γυναῖκας κεκτημένων, ὡς καὶ αὐτῶν τοῦτο ἐπιτελούντων κρυφῇ διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων αἰδῶ, ἵνα μὲν τῇ πονηρίᾳ συνθάπτωνται, τῷ δὲ προσχήματι, τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἕνεκα τὸ ὄνομα σεμνύωνται.*  
> “They accuse those in the Church who possess women called beloved and introduced into the household, as though they too secretly do this out of respect for human beings, so that they may be buried together with their wickedness while, under the pretext, they glorify the name for the sake of men.”

A little later, speaking of a certain bishop of Palestine, he says:

> *Ἐσχηκότος δὲ τοιαύτας ἐξυπηρετουμένας αὐτῷ, φημὶ δὲ συνεισάκτους.*  
> “He had such women serving him—introduced women, I mean.”

In *Heresy* 78, Epiphanius shows from where the most impure persons attempted to justify from Scripture the terms *συνείσακτοι* and *ἀγαπηταί*. What sort of women the *συνείσακτοι* were, however, is not sufficiently clear. Rufinus, Eusebius’s translator, left the Greek term untranslated in the passage cited. Suidas merely noted it and did not explain it.

They were neither wives nor concubines, but women of a third kind, whom clerics kept with them—not for the sake of children or sexual desire, but out of zeal for piety, or at least under that pretext. Chrysostom testifies to this in his sermon *To Those Who Have Introduced Women*, a fragment of which Rhenanus cites in a note on the foregoing passage of Eusebius:

> *Εἰσὶν γάρ τινες οἳ γάμου καὶ συνουσίας χωρὶς κόρας ἀπειρογάμους ἀγόμενοι καθίζουσιν οἴκοι διαπαντὸς, καὶ εἰς ἔσχατον γῆρας ἑαυτοῖς συγκατακλείουσιν, οὔτε ἐπὶ παιδοποιΐᾳ, οὔ γάρ φασιν αὐταῖς συγγενέσθαι, οὔτε ἐξ ἀκολασίας, λέγουσι γὰρ αὐτὰς ἀκεραίους διατηρεῖν.*  
> “There are some who take unmarried girls and, without marriage or intercourse, keep them permanently in their houses and shut them up with themselves until extreme old age—not for the sake of producing children, for they say that they have no intercourse with them, nor out of licentiousness, since they say that they preserve them undefiled.”

[Note: [Col. 0097D] The Greek phrase *οὔ γάρ φασιν αὐταῖς συγγενέσθαι* [Col. 0098D] would be more correctly translated: “For they say that they do not have intercourse with them.” — EDITOR.]

This is relevant to what Gregory of Nyssa records in his work *On Virginity*, chapter 23:

> *Οἱ μέχρι ὀνόματος τὴν ἀγαμίαν ἐπιτηδεύσαντες, οὐδὲν διαφέρουσι τοῦ κοινοῦ βίου· οὐ μόνον τῇ γαστρὶ τὰ πρὸς ἡδονὴν χαριζόμενοι, ἀλλὰ γυναιξὶ κατὰ τὸ φανερὸν συνοικοῦντες, καὶ ἀδελφότητα τὴν τοιαύτην συμβίωσιν ὀνομάζοντες, ὡς δὴ τὴν πρὸς τὸ χεῖρον ὑπόνοιαν ὀνόματι σεμνοτέρῳ περικαλύπτοντες.*  
> “Those who pursue celibacy in name only differ in no way from ordinary life. They not only indulge the belly in pleasures, but openly live with women and call such cohabitation brotherhood, as though concealing the suspicion of something worse beneath a more honorable name.”

It must not be omitted that the highly learned G. Budaeus once noted that *συνείσακτον* means a companion of celibacy, whether a virgin has a male companion or a monk a female companion. This practice was once customary among Christians, but was disapproved because of the suspicion of sexual misconduct. Gregory Nazianzen writes:

> *Τοὺς δὲ συνεισάκτους, ὡς δὴ φάσκουσιν ἅπαντες,*  
> *Οὐκ οἶδ᾿ εἴτε γάμῳ δώσομεν, εἴτ᾿ ἀγάμους*  
> *Θήσομεν, εἴτε μέσον τι φυλάξομεν. Οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγε*  
> *Κᾂν με λέγητε κακῶς τὸ πρᾶγμ᾿ ἐπαινέσομαι.*

> “As for the introduced companions, as everyone says,  
> I do not know whether we shall give them to marriage,  
> or keep them unmarried, or preserve some middle course.  
> For my part, even if you speak ill of me, I shall not praise the practice.”

The printed note adds: “Perhaps the reading should be *πρᾶγμα τόδ᾿ αἰνέσομαι*: ‘I shall praise this practice.’” [This replaces the final phrase only; the preceding *οὐ*, “not,” still negates the complete sentence.]

The same author writes:

> *Ἄρσενα πάντ᾿ ἀλέεινε, συνείσακτον δὲ μάλιστα.*  
> “Avoid every male, and especially an introduced companion.”

**“By all those in the province” — *ὑπὸ πάντων τῶν ἐν τῇ ἐπαρχίᾳ***

Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History* V.9:

> *Παλαιός τε θεσμὸς κεκράτηκε καὶ τῶν ἁγίων ἐν Νικαίᾳ πατέρων ὅρος, καθ᾿ ἑκάστην ἐπαρχίαν τοὺς τῆς ἐπαρχίας, καὶ εἴπερ ἐκεῖνοι βούλοιντο σὺν αὐτοῖς τοὺς ὁμόρους πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον ποιεῖσθαι τὰς χειροτονίας.*  
> “An ancient custom has prevailed, as has the definition of the holy Fathers at Nicaea: in each province, the bishops of that province, together with neighboring bishops if they so wish, conduct ordinations for the common good.”

And chapter 23:

> *Κανόνες πάντας συγκαλεῖσθαι τῆς ἐπαρχίας τοὺς ἐπισκόπους κελεύουσι· καὶ αὖ πάλιν δίχα τριῶν ἐπισκόπων ἐπισκόπῳ χειροτονίαν ἀπαγορεύουσι γίνεσθαι.*  
> “The canons command all the bishops of the province to be summoned, and again forbid a bishop’s ordination from taking place without three bishops present.”

Synesius, Letter 67, concerning a certain Siderius, bishop of Palebisca:

> *Οὐδὲ τοῦτον ἐνθέσμως, ἐκθέσμως μὲν οὖν, ὅσα γε τῶν γερόντων ἠκούσαμεν, εἰ μήτε ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ κατέστη, μήτε παρὰ τριῶν ἐνθάδε.*  
> “He was not appointed lawfully—or rather unlawfully, as far as we have heard from the elders—if he was established neither at Alexandria nor here by three bishops.”

**“By letters” — *διὰ γραμμάτων***

Cyprian, Book IV, Letter 8:

> “It was decided, for the confirmation of your ordination, that letters should be sent throughout all those located in this province.”

**“Those rejected by others” — *τοὺς ὑφ᾿ ἑτέρων ἀποβληθέντας***

The synodical letter of the African Council to Celestine, pope of Rome, preserved in the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church* and in the Greek collection of the canons of the African Church, says:

> *Ἱκετεύομεν, ἵνα τοῦ λοιποῦ, πρὸς τὰς ὑμετέρας ἀκοὰς, τοὺς ἐντεῦθεν παραγινομένους, εὐχερῶς μὴ προσδέχησθε· μηδὲ τοὺς παρ᾿ ἡμῶν ἀποκοινωνήτους, εἰς κοινωνίαν τοῦ λοιποῦ θελήσητε δέξασθαι. Ἐπειδὴ τοῦτο καὶ τῇ ἐν Νικαίᾳ συνόδῳ ὁρισθὲν εὐχερῶς εὕροι ἡ σὴ σεβασμιότης.*  
> “We beseech you henceforth not readily to admit to your hearing those who come from here, nor to receive into communion those whom we have excommunicated. For your reverence will easily recognize that this too was defined by the Council of Nicaea.”

**“Authority” — *ἐξουσία***

This *ἐξουσία* is the authority of the metropolitan, which the Fathers of Nicaea decree in this canon to belong to him in the three provinces named here—Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis—which together formed the entire diocese of Egypt, both in civil and ecclesiastical matters.

**“The privileges shall be preserved for Antioch” — *κατὰ τὴν Ἀντιόχειαν τὰ πρεσβεῖα σώζεσθαι***

Thus canon 165 of this code says:

> *Φυλαττομένων τῶν ἐν τοῖς κανόσι τοῖς κατὰ Νικαίαν πρεσβείων τῇ Ἀντιοχέων ἐκκλησίᾳ.*  
> “While preserving the privileges granted to the Church of Antioch by the Nicene canons.”

The *πρεσβεῖα*, or privileges, which these canons command to be preserved for the Church of Antioch concern the precedence of the bishop of Antioch over all the metropolitans in the eastern diocese. They assign him no jurisdiction over the other metropolitans beyond the honor of precedence. They do not mean that all the metropolitans of the eastern diocese were to be ordained by him through a special right, as the letter of Innocent I to Alexander of Antioch seems to assert, contrary to the intention of the Council of Nicaea.

### “The bishop in Aelia”

After Jerusalem had been destroyed by Titus and Vespasian, and rebuilt by Aelius Hadrian, it was called Aelia. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.6, speaking of it, says:

> “The Roman city that was subsequently established, having changed its name, was called Aelia in honor of its ruler, Aelius Hadrian.”

When Jerusalem had been occupied by the Romans, it changed its name and was called Aelia in honor of the emperor Aelius Hadrian. Cedrenus, concerning Hadrian, says:

> “He founded a new Jerusalem, which he also called Aelia.”

Dio likewise relates this in his account of Hadrian; so do Zonaras, volume II, and Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople, in his *Chronography*. Jerome, in his commentary on Acts, says:

> “Jerusalem, formerly the metropolis of all [Col. 0098D] Judaea, is now called Aelia after the emperor Aelius Hadrian, because he restored it on a more extensive site after it had been destroyed by Titus.”

Hence the name Aelia is frequently used for Jerusalem in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* II.12, VI.21, and VIII.21; in Theodoretus I.31; in Basil of Seleucia, Sermon 38, *Against the Jews*; and in book I, §6, of the *Digest*, *On the Census*.

### “Those being received by the laying-on of hands”

Formerly, in the Church, hands were laid upon heretics who were returning to their right mind; after confession, peace was granted to them. Dionysius of Alexandria also attests this, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.2:

> “Since an ancient custom has prevailed in the case of such persons, to use only the prayer given through the laying-on of hands.”

Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, likewise says in the Greek collection of the canons of the African Church, canon 57, when the Donatists were being discussed: [Col. 0099A]

> “After the name of the error has been anathematized, let them be received into the one Church through the laying-on of the hand.”

Add the decree of Siricius, chapter 1, and that of Innocent, chapter 15.

### “To remain thus in the clergy”

Heretics, or persons ordained by heretics, who acknowledged their error, were received by the laying-on of hands when they came to the Church, and were confirmed in the priesthood. Thus the Council of Nicaea decreed concerning those ordained by Meletius:

> “Those who were appointed by him and confirmed by a more mystical ordination shall retain their honor and ministry,”

as Gelasius of Cyzicus reports from the synodical letter of the same council, *Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, book I, and as Theodoretus reports in book I, chapter 9. Nevertheless, the leaders of the heresies were excepted.

Athanasius, in his *Apology II*, says:

> “Alexander received into the Church the presbyters appointed by Meletius.”

The same author, in his letter to Rufinianus, says:

> “It was decided by common decree that, if any who had fallen away on their own initiative and had been leaders of impiety should come to their senses, they should indeed be forgiven, [Col. 0099B] but should not be restored to the number of the clergy. Those, however, who had not been authors of the error but had been compelled by necessity and violence were judged worthy both of forgiveness and of restoration to the clerical order.”

Ruffinus reports that this had formerly been decided at the Alexandrian synod, *Ecclesiastical History* I.28:

> “After the authors of the perfidy had been removed, the remaining priests were to be given the choice—if they should wish, after renouncing the error of their perfidy, to return to the faith and the decrees of the Fathers—and the way was not to be denied to those returning.”

The synodical letter of the Council of Nicaea, in Theodoretus at the place cited, says:

> “Therefore the synod decided that Meletius should remain in his own city, but should have no authority either to ordain or to lay hands upon anyone; he was merely to retain the name of honor.”

The synod decided that Meletius should remain in his own city, but should possess no authority either to ordain anyone or to lay hands upon anyone; he was to retain only the name of honor. Meletius, moreover, was “the leader of the heresy of those called Meletians after him,” as Socrates writes in books I.3 and I.6. Add the first session of the Second Council of Nicaea, volume III of the councils.

[Col. 0099C]

### “To confess them in writing”

Canon 170 of this collection.

Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.11, reports that Liberius, bishop of Rome, before receiving the repentant Macedonians into communion, asked them to put their profession of faith in writing, and that they presented him with a written statement:

> “Liberius demanded a written confession of their belief; and they offered him a book.”

And in chapter 12:

> “Having secured the envoys by this book as by a pledge, Liberius received them into communion.”

Thus, having bound the envoys by that document as by their pledge, Liberius received them into communion. Likewise Valens and Ursacius submitted their profession in writing to Julius, bishop of Rome, in these words, reported by Sozomenus, *Ecclesiastical History* III.22:

> “Having written these things with our own hand, we confess again that we have condemned forever the Arian heresy and its authors, as we stated above.”

Basil, in his letter 72 to the inhabitants of Emesa, says:

> “If they say that they have repented, let them demonstrate their repentance by their own written statement, together with their rejection of the [Col. 0099D] faith which they embraced.”

The Sixth Council, in Trullo, canon 96, says:

> “The Nestorians must draw up written statements and anathematize the heresy.”

The Eighth Ecumenical Council, session 6, says:

> “The ordinances of the Church decree that bishops returning from heresy are to be received when they give a written statement and anathematize their own heresy.”

Ecclesiastical laws decree that bishops brought back from heresy are to be received when, by a written statement, they renounce their heresy.

### “Digamists”

Who the *digami* are in this canon and in canons 39, 52, and 105 of this collection may be seen in the annotation on canon 105 below.

### “The honor of the name”

Thus the Fathers of Ephesus decreed that a certain Eustathius should possess the name and honor of bishop without the actual office or power, in the synodical letter to the synod of Pamphylia, which is found among the acts of the Council of Ephesus, volume II, appendix I, chapter 1, and in Zonaras and Balsamon:

> “We have determined that he should possess both the name and the honor of the episcopate, but in such a way that he himself should not ordain.”

We have determined that he should possess the name and [Col. 0100A] honor of the episcopate, but should not himself ordain. The same is attested concerning Meletius by the synodical letter of the Council of Nicaea in Theodoretus I.9, whose words we quoted above. Sozomenus, *Ecclesiastical History* I.33, speaking of the same man, says:

> “The synod condemned him to remain in Lycus, possessing only the name of bishop; and thereafter he was not to ordain either in a city or in a village.”

The synod pronounced sentence against him: he was to live in Lycus and retain only the name of bishop; thereafter he was not to ordain either in a city or in a village.

### “There should not be two bishops in the city”

Hence Sozomenus, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.15, says that it is contrary to ecclesiastical laws for one Church to be governed by two bishops:

> “The throne of Peter should not be thought to be directed by two leaders, which is a sign of dissension and foreign to ecclesiastical order.”

Augustine, letter 110, says:

> “I occupied the see with my aged father and bishop, Valerius, something which I did not know had been prohibited by the Council of Nicaea.”

Pacianus, in his letter to Sympronianus, says:

> “Neither law nor right permits the office of a single priesthood [Col. 0100B] to have two bishops of the same Church at one and the same time.”

Ado of Vienne, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 810, says:

> “Canonical authority declares that there should not be two bishops in one city.”

Thus Cornelius, bishop of the Roman Church and contemporary with Cyprian, writes in his letter to Fabius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, concerning Novatus, the founder of the Cathar heresy:

> “That defender of the Gospel did not know that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church.”

Cornelius clearly says that there was, or ought to have been, one bishop in one city. Cyprian likewise says of the same schismatic, in letter 32:

> “Since a second cannot exist after the first, whoever has been made after the one who ought to be alone is no longer a second, but is nothing.”

See Bils., p. 392.

### “Those among the fallen who have been previously ordained”

Formerly, fallen bishops and presbyters were indeed received into penance, but were prohibited from ordination and priestly honor. Cyprian, book I, letters 4 and 7, urges the people of Assuras not to admit Fortunianus, [Col. 0100C] who had sacrificed to idols, to the episcopate. In book IV, letter 2, he indicates that Trophimus, while doing penance, had been admitted to communion as a layman, not so that he might usurp the place of a priest. Add canon 21 of this collection.

### “Having laid aside their belts”

Pagan rulers were accustomed to remove the military belt from those who refused to deny the faith. Eusebius attests this in *Ecclesiastical History* VII.15, speaking of a certain Christian soldier named Marinus. When, after following the order of his rank, he had attained the honor of a military office, the man immediately below him cried out that the office could not lawfully be assigned to him because he was a Christian and had not sacrificed to the emperors:

> “It is not lawful for him, being a Christian and not sacrificing to the emperors, to share in the Roman rank according to the ancient laws.”

Eusebius says similarly in book X.8 and in *The Life of Constantine* I.47, concerning Licinius:

> “He ordered that the soldiers in each city be selected from the rest and deprived of the rank of honor unless they chose to sacrifice to the demons.”

[Col. 0100D] He ordered that the soldiers in each city be removed from the ranks of the others and deprived of their rank of honor unless they were willing to sacrifice to the demons. Ruffinus, *Ecclesiastical History* I.32, says of Julian:

> “He ordered that the military belt should not be given except to those who sacrificed.”

Hence the words of Marcellus the centurion, whose acts are found in Baronius under the year 298:

> “If the condition of military service is that soldiers are compelled to perform sacred rites to the gods and emperors, behold, I throw down the vine-staff and the belt; I renounce the standards and refuse military service.”

### “To have successfully resumed military service”

This canon does not speak of those who, during a persecution, had thrown away the military belt for the sake of the faith and afterward, having renounced the faith, had recovered their former military service through money and gifts, and then returned to the Church. Rather, it concerns those who, inspired by divine grace, laid aside the military belt in order to undertake a better, more perfect, and more Christian way of life, but later resumed it and again bound themselves by the military oath. For these, a period of penance was rightly prescribed.

For it must not be thought that this canon prohibited military service to Christians [Col. 0101A] except insofar as it was a sign of idolatry, and insofar as it could be practiced only at the expense of the Christian faith, since soldiers were compelled to sacrifice to the gods. Otherwise it is clear that Christians were accustomed to serve under pagan rulers, from Dio’s account of Marcus Antoninus, Eusebius V.5, Tertullian’s *Apology* 42, and his *On the Crown of the Soldier* 1. There he speaks of a Christian soldier who refused to place the military laurel upon his head, but remained alone among his fellow soldiers with his head uncovered and the crown hanging uselessly in his hand.

Vegetius also mentions the military oath customarily taken by Christian soldiers, and gives its formula in these words:

> “They swear by God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit, and by the majesty of the emperor, which, after God, ought to be loved and honored by the human race.”

A little later he says:

> “The soldiers swear that they will diligently do everything which the emperor commands, that they will never desert military service, and that they will not refuse death for the Roman commonwealth.”

### “The final provision for the journey”

[Col. 0101B] The Eucharist is called *viaticum*—provision for the journey—in the case of the dying, because it is given to those departing from this life, thinking of God and, as it were, undertaking a journey, as assistance for the road. Thus in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 78, and in letter 3 of Sixtus, bishop of Rome, volume III of the councils:

> “Bassus was condemned by the synod, but in such a way that the viaticum was not to be denied him on his final day.”

Synesius, in letter 67 to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, speaking of a certain excommunicated Lamponianus, says:

> “I have referred the authority to release him to the sacred see. I have allowed myself this much: if death should approach Lamponianus, and the decisive day should appear to be present, I have permitted all the [Col. 0101C] presbyters who are then present to give him communion; for let no one die bound by an anathema imposed by me. When he has recovered, however, let him again be liable to punishment on the same charges, and let him await from your divine and humane soul the signal of forgiveness.”

Add canon 26 of this collection.

### “Those hearing”

Formerly, the people in the Church were divided into three classes: the *catechumeni*, the *credentes*, and the *paenitentes*—catechumens, believers, and penitents. This canon shows that there were two classes of catechumens. One consisted of those who heard the word of God and wished to become Christians but had not yet requested baptism. They were called *audientes*, or hearers. The others had already approached, had been properly instructed in the faith, and were requesting baptism; they were called *competentes*.

Tertullian mentions the *audientes*, or hearers, in *On Repentance*:

> “Let no one flatter himself because he is counted among the first exercises of the hearers, as though he might still be permitted to sin; or is Christ one for those who have been baptized and another for those who are hearing?”

Likewise:

> “Hearers ought to desire baptism, [Col. 0101D] not presume upon it.”

And in *On the Prescription against Heretics* 41:

> “Who is a catechumen and who is a believer is uncertain; they approach together, hear together, and pray together.”

Cyprian, book III, letter 17, says:

> “If any of the hearers should be overtaken by danger, or should be at the point of death, let your vigilance not be lacking. When they implore divine grace, let the Lord’s mercy not be denied them.”

Augustine mentions the *competentes* in *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead* 12:

> “As Easter approached, he enrolled his name among the other competentes.”

And in homily 49:

> “Let the penitents hear what I say to the competentes and the faithful.”

Jerome also mentions them in his letter to Pammachius. The Council of Agde, canon 13, says:

> “It was also decided that the Creed should be publicly preached in the Church to the competentes.”

Leo I, bishop of Rome, in his decrees, chapters 2 and 12, calls them the elect:

> “We inform your charity that, in the case of those elected for baptism in the Church, the two periods of which we have spoken are legitimate.”

### “A bishop is not to transfer from city to city”

[Col. 0102A] Jerome, in his letter to Oceanus, says:

> “At the Council of Nicaea the Fathers decreed that a bishop should not be transferred from one Church to another.”

By this canon, the centesimal rate of interest and *hemioliai* are forbidden to clerics, so that the Nicene Fathers might impose a limit upon clerical greed for dishonest gain.

### “Pursuing dishonest gain”

Paul, First Letter to Timothy 3:3:

> “The bishop must be blameless, not desirous of dishonest gain, but free from avarice.”

And Peter, First Letter 5:2:

> “Feed the flock of God which is among you, not seeking dishonest gain.”

Jerome, book II, letter 12, says:

> “It is a disgrace to a priest to be concerned with his own riches.”

This is relevant to what Sozomenus reports in book IV, chapter 23, and Nicephorus in book IX, chapter 45: a certain Sophronius was deposed because, driven by avarice, he had pursued profit from the Church’s money.

### “Hemioliai”

The Council of Laodicea, canon 4, says:

> “Concerning the fact that priests [Col. 0102B] must not lend money, take interest, or receive the so-called hemioliai.”

*Hemioliai* are interest payments in which one third of the principal is added under the name of interest. Suidas defines *hemiolia* as “half of the principal,” and again says:

> “A hemiolios is a number which contains the whole and half of it.”

Thus *hemiolismos* is used by Harpocration and Suidas. Gellius, book XVIII, chapter 14, says:

> “A hemiolius is one which contains the whole number and half of it: for example, three to two, fifteen to ten, thirty to twenty.”

A *hemiolion* is half of each thing. Suidas also says:

> “A payment is to be given to those who choose to serve in the army with him, one and a half times what is now being given.”

See below, on canon 108. Add Jerome’s passage:

> “Moneylenders are accustomed to argue and say: ‘I gave one measure, which produced ten measures. Is it not just that I should receive half a measure more of what is mine, since from my generosity he has nine and a half of my measures?’”

Constantine, in book I of the Theodosian Code, *On Interest*, regulated *hemioliai* on grain. Yet the interest on grain lent to farmers was reduced to the [Col. 0102C] centesimal rate by Justinian, in the law *Eos qui*, 26 of the Code, *On Interest*, and in Novels 32, 33, and 34, chapter 1. From these the *Authentic* appended to the law *Cum non frumentum*, 16 of the Code, *On Interest*, was taken.

Jerome calls interest on commodities *specierum usurae*, that is, interest on produce, or *karpōn*, as the Greeks correctly call it in the *Synopsis of the Basilics*, book XXIII, title III, *On Interest*, chapter 66. See the scholion and the law *Frumenti*, 12 of the Code, *On Interest*.

### “Centesimal interest”

Hemioliai, or interest on grain, are different from the centesimal interest on money. It is well known that the centesimal rate was formerly the lawful rate of monetary interest. See Brissonius, *Selecta*, and law I, §2, of the Theodosian Code, *On Interest*; Dositheus, book III; Volusius Maecianus; Chrysostom, homily 56 on Matthew, p. 362; and Sidonius, book IV, letter 24.

The centesimal rate was the interest that paid one coin each month for every hundred coins lent. For interest was formerly monthly among the Greeks as among the Romans. Hence, as Basil elegantly says in his homily on Psalm 14, p. 159:

> “The months were the fathers of interest.”

If one calculates by years, as today, the centesimal rate is that which yields twelve coins in a year. [Col. 0102D] Pliny, in book X, letter 62, likewise calls this interest *tokos epi drachmē*, “interest on a drachma,” because a drachma was one hundredth of a mina.

Constantine, in the aforementioned law I of the Theodosian Code, *On Interest*, restored monetary interest to the old centesimal standard; but he imposed a limit on interest in grain, for which no sufficiently definite limit had previously been established. The centesimal rate increased under Valentinian the Elder, under whom the valuation of gold was also increased. See the sole law *De oblatione votorum* of the Theodosian Code, and law XIII, *On Receivers*, and law II of the Code, *On the Value of Old Coinage*.

It should be noted that the first law mentioned was enacted only one month before the Council of Nicaea, whose canon 17 likewise forbids centesimal interest and *hemioliai* to clerics, so that the Nicene Fathers might impose a limit upon clerical greed for dishonest gain. The law *De usuris* I was enacted in the year 325, on 17 April, during the consulship of Paulinus and Julian.

Firmicus, book II, chapter 41, says:

> “Never practice lending at interest, nor let a wretched increase of money be brought to you from the needs of others.”

See Chrysostom, homilies on Matthew [Col. 0103A] VI, pp. 35 and 56, and p. 362; Basil, homily on Psalm 14, p. 158; and Justinian’s Novels 32, 33, and 34.

### “Not to sit in the midst of the presbyters”

Thus canon 424 says:

> “A deacon must not sit before a presbyter.”

Jerome, letter 85, says:

> “I hear that someone has burst into such great folly that he places deacons before presbyters, that is, before bishops. What has the minister of tables and widows to do, that he should proudly exalt himself above those at whose prayers the body and blood of Christ are made?”

### “They are to be rebaptized”

Augustine, *On Heresies* 44, says:

> “The Council of Nicaea established that the Paulianists were to be baptized in the Catholic Church. From this it must be believed that they did not possess the rule of baptism, which many heretics took away with them when they departed from the Catholic Church and have preserved.”

It is certain that the Paulianists, or Paulianians, did not baptize in the name of the Trinity, because they believed Christ to be merely human and openly denied the Trinity. Hence they were also called “second Jews.”

Epiphanius, *On Heresies* 65, says:

> “These people [Col. 0103B], corrupting Judaism and possessing nothing more than the Jews, were called second Jews and Samosatans.”

Nicetas, *Treasury of the Orthodox Faith* IV.32, says that when Paul wished to comply with Zenobia, who ruled Syria and Phoenicia and professed Judaism, he too taught that there is one God, who is called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one and the same:

> “For there is one God and his Son in him, just as speech is in a human being.”

Epiphanius, speaking of the same heresy at the place cited, likewise says:

> “This man asserts that God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God; and that his Word and his Spirit are always in God, just as a person’s own word is in a human heart.”

[Col. 0103C] The Paulianists, or Paulianians, were also called Samosatans after Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, as Suidas states under the entry “Manes”:

> “There was a certain Paul, his contemporary, bishop of great Antioch; from him came the Paulianians.”

There was also another Paul of Samosata, a renovator of the Manichaean heresy, from whom came the Paulicians, whom Balsamon incorrectly confuses with the Paulianists. Cedrenus is correct:

> “The Paulicians, who are also Manichaeans.”

He adds:

> “They were renamed Paulicians instead of Manichaeans after a certain Paul of Samosata, the son of a Manichaean woman named Callinice.”

Matthew Blastares conveys the same account in his *Synopsis*, where he clearly distinguishes the Paulianists from the Paulicians.

The *Miscellaneous History*, in Nicephorus, book XXIV, says:

> “He was a friend of the Manichaeans who are now called Paulicians.”

Theophanes states that the heresy of the Paulicians was spread through Thrace under Constantine Copronymus. The same *Miscellaneous History*, in the life of Michael, testifies that it was condemned by the emperor:

> “Moved by divine zeal against the Manichaeans, who are now called Paulicians, the most pious emperor promulgated a [Col. 0103D] capital punishment.”

The Montanists, too, are ordered to be baptized in canon 112.

### “They are to be ordained blameless and irreprehensible”

Paul, First Letter to Timothy 3:2:

> “The bishop must be irreprehensible.”

Irenaeus, book III, *Against Heresies*, chapter 3, says:

> “Bishops were established in the Churches by the apostles.”

A little later he adds:

> “They wished those whom they left as successors, handing over to them their own place of teaching, to be exceedingly perfect and irreprehensible in all things, so that their upright conduct might bring great benefit, while their falling away would bring the greatest calamity.”

Justinian, book XLI of the Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*, says:

> “Following also the teaching of the holy apostles concerning the fact that priests ought to be ordained irreproachable.”

We likewise follow the teaching of the holy apostles concerning the appointment of irreprehensible priests. And Novel 6, chapter 1, says:

> “We decree, following in all things the divine canons, that whenever anyone is brought forward for episcopal ordination, his life must first be examined, according to the holy apostle, to determine whether he is respectable, blameless, [Col. 0104A] and irreprehensible in every respect.”

We decree, following in all things the sacred canons, that when someone is brought forward for episcopal ordination, his life must first be examined, according to the holy Apostle, to determine whether he is honorable, blameless, and irreprehensible in every respect.

### “Deaconesses”

Deaconesses are frequently mentioned by writers on ecclesiastical affairs. Paul, in his Letter to the Romans 16:1, commends Phoebe, who was a deaconess of the Church of Cenchreae:

> “Who is a deacon of the Church at Cenchreae.”

Ignatius, in his letter to the Antiochenes, salutes “the deaconesses.”

Pliny the Younger, writing to Trajan about the Christians, calls them *ministrae*, or female ministers, in book X, letter 97:

> “For this reason I considered it even more necessary to discover the truth by torture from two female slaves who were called ministers.”

Theodoretus, book III, chapter 14, says:

> “There was a certain distinguished woman in piety who had been deemed worthy of the gift of the diaconate.”

Sozomenus, book IV, chapter 24, writes that Elpidius was deposed from the episcopate because he had admitted a certain Nectaria to the dignity of deaconess before she had completed her penance, although she had [Col. 0104B] been excluded from communion because she had violated an oath:

> “He deemed Nectaria worthy of the diaconate, although she had been excluded from communion on account of violations of agreements and oaths.”

The reading should be *diakonias*, as is clear from Nicephorus, book II, chapter 45, not *dianoias*, as the commonly circulated Greek manuscript mistakenly has it.

Epiphanius calls deaconesses *presbytides* in heresy 79, as does the Council of Laodicea, canon 115 of this collection. Concerning the ministry of deaconesses, see the annotation on canon 193 of this collection.

### “Laying-on of hands”

Here *cheirothesia* is understood as ordination or consecration, not as a blessing. So also in canon 193 of this collection and elsewhere. For formerly there were two kinds of *cheirothesia*: that of blessing and that of ordination, as Tharasius, patriarch of Constantinople, says in the first session of the Second Council of Nicaea, volume III of the councils.

Nor was *cheirothesia* always a sign of consecration; it could also be a prayer over a person upon whom hands were laid. [Col. 0104C] Paul mentions the laying-on of hands connected with the ordination of bishops and presbyters in First Timothy 4:14 and 5:22. Optatus of Milevis, book I, says:

> “These judgments were pronounced against Donatus: that he had confessed to rebaptizing and to laying hands upon fallen bishops, something foreign to the Church.”

Here the laying-on of hands is understood as ordination, which the ancients judged should not be repeated. Thus, if peace was later granted through the laying-on of hands to bishops who had fallen into heresy or had been ordained by heretics, and they remained in their own rank, they were not to be ordained again. See what we noted above on canon 8.

The laying-on of hands as a blessing, however, was customarily used for penitents who had fallen and for those returning from heretics to the true Church. Cyprian, book III, letter 14, says:

> “For when sinners do penance for lesser sins at the proper time, and according to the order of discipline come to confession, they receive the right of communion through the laying-on of the hands of the bishop and clergy.”

The same was done for those who had been baptized. Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, says:

> “Do you not know that this too is the custom of the Churches: that hands are afterward [Col. 0104D] laid upon those who have been baptized, and the Holy Spirit is invoked in this way?”

Cyprian, letter 73 to Jubaianus, says:

> “What is now also done among us is that those who are baptized in the Church are presented by the leaders of the Church and receive the Holy Spirit through our prayer and the laying-on of hands.”

Finally, there is no doubt that every election of any ecclesiastical minister was formerly carried out through this kind of laying-on of hands. Deaconesses, subdeacons, readers, and the other ministers were not ordained; rather, a blessing was poured out over them through prayer and the laying-on of hands. See the annotation on canon 115 below.

### “Bending the knee on the Lord’s Day,” etc.

It was an ancient custom of Christians to worship kneeling, or on bent knees, as Tertullian says. Eusebius, book V, chapter 5, speaking of Christians who served in the Roman legions under Marcus Aurelius, writes:

> “When they had placed a knee upon the ground in the battle formation against their enemies, according to the custom of prayer proper to us, they turned to supplications addressed to [Col. 0105A] God.”

This canon makes an exception for Sunday and for the intervening period between Easter and Pentecost, during which the ancients worshiped standing, in remembrance of the Lord’s resurrection. The author of the *Questions to the Orthodox*, attributed to Justin, attests this in question 115:

> “Not bending the knee on Sunday is a symbol of the resurrection, through which, by the grace of Christ, we have been freed both from sins and from the death that was slain by him.”

Concerning Pentecost he says:

> “During it we do not bend the knee, because it is to be regarded as equivalent to the day of the Lord.”

Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier* 3, says:

> “On Sunday we consider it unlawful to fast or to worship on our knees; we enjoy the same freedom from Easter Day until [Col. 0105B] Pentecost.”

Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, says:

> “On Sunday and throughout Pentecost, the practice of not worshiping on one’s knees, of ending the fast, and of many things not written in Scripture has claimed for itself a reasonable observance.”

Nevertheless, we read that Paul worshiped on bent knees at Tyre during the very period extending from Easter to Pentecost, Acts 21:5.

### “To bring forward bread or a cup”

Formerly the deacons served bread and the cup to the people. Justin Martyr, *Apology* II, says:

> “Those who are called deacons among us give each of those present a share of the bread, wine, and water over which thanks have been given, and carry them to those who are absent.”

Cyprian, *Sermon on the Fallen* 5, says:

> “When the solemn rites had been completed, the deacon began to offer the cup to those present.”

### “To proclaim”

[Col. 0105C] Socrates, book VI, chapter 11, speaking of Athanasius, says:

> “He ordered a deacon to proclaim the prayer.”

Hence the frequent acclamations of deacons in the Greek liturgies:

> “Pray, you catechumens.”
>
> “You faithful, let us pray for the catechumens.”
>
> “All you catechumens, depart.”
>
> “The holy things for the holy.”

Chrysostom, homily 17 on Hebrews 9, says:

> “The deacon, standing in an elevated place, with a loud voice and terrifying cry, like a herald raising his hand aloft, calls some, forbids others, drives some out, and brings others in.”

It is therefore clear that the word *kēryssein*, “to proclaim,” which when applied to priests signifies *homilein* and *euangelizesthai*, “to preach” and “to proclaim the Gospel,” indicates in the case of deacons the ministry by which, after the signal had been given with the *orarion*, they regulated the rites and order of the sacred actions.

[Col. 0105D] Matthew Blastares attests this in his still unpublished *Synopsis of the Greek Councils*, in these words:

> “The deacons who wear the orarion, standing beside the priests as they perform the sacred rites and observing the prayers of the sacred service, signal by the orarion to the deacons who are in the ambo when the proper proclamation should be made to the catechumens and to the faithful.”

Similarly, in the synagogues of the Jews, someone stood beside the person reciting the law from the pulpit, holding a handkerchief, and gave the people the signal to say “Amen,” as the learned Casaubon observed in his notes on Vopiscus. Concerning the *orarion*, see the annotation on canon 126 below.

### “Having taken some food under compulsion”

[Col. 0106A] Gregory Thaumaturgus, bishop of Neocaesarea, in his canonical letter preserved by Zonaras and Balsamon, says:

> “Food does not burden us if captives have eaten what those who exercise dominion over them set before them.”

### “Having fallen into the lower posture”

Formerly, there were several degrees of ecclesiastical discipline: *prosklausis*, *akroasis*, *hypoptosis*, and *systasis*. Gregory Thaumaturgus mentions all of them in canonical letter 11, as does Basil in canonical letter 3 to Amphilochius, canon 5:

> “The adulterer is to spend fifteen years: four years weeping, five years hearing, four years fallen down, and one year standing.”

*Prosklausis* occurs when someone who has committed a sin stands outside the church and, with mourning and tears, asks those entering to obtain God’s mercy for him. The Greek scholiast of Harmenopulus, *Epitome of the Canons*, section 5, title 3, says:

> “Weeping: that is, standing outside the church and asking those entering to pray for him.”

[Col. 0106B] Hence Tertullian elegantly said that the penitent “entrusts to the brethren the embassy of his supplication.” Cyprian, book IV, letter 2, speaks of confessing one’s former error through penitential supplication.

An example of *prosklausis* occurs in Eusebius, book V, chapter 28, where a certain Natalis is discussed:

> “With great earnestness and many tears he fell before the bishop Zephyrinus, rolling beneath the feet not only of those in the clergy but also of the laity, and by his tears overwhelmed the compassionate Church of merciful Christ.”

Ruffinus translates this as follows:

> “With many tears, lamenting his error, he prostrated himself before the feet of the bishop Zephyrinus. Falling at the feet of all, not only the clergy but also the laity, with much lamentation, I moved the whole Church to tears and compassion, so that they might implore pardon for him from Christ by continuous and unceasing prayers.”

Synesius, letter 67 to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, says:

> “Jason brought an accusation of injustice against Lamponianus. But he, anticipating the proof by confession, is undergoing punishment, excluded from ecclesiastical assemblies, although he has shed [Col. 0106C] tears in repentance and the people have supplicated on his behalf. I nevertheless persisted in what had been decreed; but I referred the authority to release him to the sacred see.”

*Akroasis* occurs when someone stands outside the church and hears the divine Scriptures up to the reading of the holy Gospel. The Greek scholiast at the place cited says:

> “Those who were hearers stood outside the church until the reading of the holy Gospel.”

Likewise:

> “A hearer—that is, one standing outside in the narthex.”

That is, in the vestibule or portico of the temple. See the annotation on canon 50 below.

[Col. 0106D] *Hypoptosis* occurs when someone stands inside the church enclosure behind the ambo and leaves with the catechumens. The same scholiast says:

> “One who has fallen down—that is, standing inside the church behind the ambo and going out with the catechumens.”
