Canon 45 of this collection mentions *systasis*. This occurs when someone prays with the faithful but has not yet been admitted to the sacraments. The same scholiast says:

> “One who stands with them—that is, praying together with the faithful, but not yet deemed worthy of the sacred mysteries.”

### “Chorepiscopi may not,” etc.

This is confirmed by canon 98 of this collection and by Damasus, bishop of Rome, in his letter to the bishops of Numidia, volume I of the councils:

> “Let chorepiscopi not be permitted to consecrate priests or deacons.”

Leo I, bishop of Rome, in letter 88 to the bishops of Gaul and Germany, speaking of chorepiscopi, says:

> “Although they share with bishops in the administration of many ministries, let them nevertheless recognize that certain things are forbidden to them by ecclesiastical regulations, such as the consecration of presbyters and deacons.”

[Col. 0107A] Chorepiscopi are those who, placed over regions, rural districts, or villages, performed the office of bishop as episcopal deputies. They are frequently mentioned by ecclesiastical writers and in the subscriptions of councils.

### “Lord’s house”

Here *kyriakon*, “the Lord’s [house],” is understood as a temple or church. So in canons 50, 58, and 132 of this collection, and in Maximinus’s edict on behalf of the Christians, an example of which is found in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.10:

> “They are also permitted to build their own houses of the Lord.”

The same usage occurs in the *Life of Constantine*:

> “The temples that had been consecrated to God received the name of the Lord’s houses; this name was imposed upon them not by human beings but by the Lord of all, and for this reason they were called the Lord’s houses.”

The same usage appears in Ruffinus, *Ecclesiastical History* I.3. Cyprian likewise uses *dominicum* in the sense of the Lord’s house, in his sermon *On Almsgiving*:

> “Do you, though wealthy and rich, think that you are celebrating the Lord’s house, when you pay no attention at all to the collection and come to the Lord’s house without a sacrifice?”

[Col. 0107B] ### “Presbyterium” (πρεσβυτέριον)

Here *presbyterium* is understood as the assembly of presbyters over which the bishop presided. Thus, in the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 4, verse 14: “Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterium.”

Ignatius, in his Letter to the Antiochenes, greets “the holy presbyterium” (τὸ ἅγιον πρεσβυτέριον) and “the sacred body” (ἱερὸν σύστημα); and in his Letter to the Trallians he indicates what the presbyterium is in these words: “What, then, is the presbyterium except a sacred body, the counselors and fellow-seated assessors of the bishop?”

Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, says in Cyprian, Book 3, Letter 11: “When every matter had been reported to me, it seemed good to convene the presbyterium.”

Pius I, Roman Pontiff, expressing this term in Latin, called it a senate. In his letter to Justus, bishop of Vienne, in volume 1 of the Councils, he says: “The senate of Christ’s poor established at Rome greets you.” And Jerome, in his Letter to Rusticus, says: “The Church has a senate, a council of presbyters.”

[Col. 0107C] ### “As sisters” (ὡς ἀδελφάς)

The emperors Honorius and Theodosius say in Book 19 of the Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*: “One who leads a life commendable according to the discipline of the age ought not to be disfigured by association under the name of sisterhood.”

Thus certain clerics used to call their immoral companions “sisters” and conceal their vices under this appearance of piety; and Martial’s verse was not inappropriately thrown at them:

> You ask why Fabulla has no wife,  
> Themison? She has sisters.

The word “brothers” was used in the same sense. The interpreter of Lycophron says: “They make strangers into brothers for erotic purposes; for lovers, when caught, say, ‘He is my brother, or my kinsman.’”

Martial likewise writes:

> O how fondly you speak, Ammianus, of your mother!  
> How fond your mother is of you, Ammianus!  
> She calls you brother, and she is called sister.  
> Why do more shameful names touch you?  
> You think this merely a game and joke.

[Col. 0107D] The emperor Justinian, *Novel* 6, chapter 6, says:

> “We also wish the deaconesses who are brought to ordination, whether from widowhood or virginity, not to have any companions living with them under the supposed designation of brothers, relatives, or those called ‘beloved’—for by using such names they fill their lives with every evil suspicion—but either to live alone, or only with their parents and children, or with true brothers or uncles.”

Such women were the *syneisaktoi* (συνείσακτοι) and *agapetai* (ἀγαπηταί), that is, virgins who, as Jerome says in his Letter to Oceanus, derived their name from charity and were said to be joined by a kind of spiritual love to the ecclesiastics in whose households they lived. Without marriage, under another name, they were their wives, concubines, and prostitutes. See the note on canon 3 above.

### “Destroying what is generated” (ἀναιρουσῶν τὰ γεννώμενα)

Tertullian says in the *Apology*: “Since homicide has once and for all been forbidden to us, it is not permissible for us even to dissolve a fetus in the womb while the blood is still being transformed into a human being. To prevent birth is an anticipatory homicide; nor does it matter whether someone snatches away a soul already born or disturbs one that is being born. The one who is to be a human being is already a human being; and the whole fruit of the human being is already present in the seed.”

### “Abortifacients” (φθόρια)

These are medicines producing abortion, or abortifacient drugs. Minucius says in the *Octavius*: “There are women who, by drinking medicines in their very wombs, extinguish the beginning of the future human being and commit parricide before they give birth.”

Athenagoras calls them *amblōthridia* (ἀμβλωθρίδια) in his *Apology for the Christians*: “We say that women who use abortifacient medicines commit homicide; on what principle, then, do we ourselves murder human beings”—that is, human beings already born and fully formed?

The Sixth Synod in Trullo, canon 91, likewise says: “We subject to the penalty of homicide those who give abortifacient medicines and those who receive poisons that kill the fetus.”

Suidas calls an *amblōtridion* (ἀμβλωτρίδιον) a “destructive medicine” (φθόριον φάρμακον).

### “Those who are established” (συνεστῶτας)

See the note on canon 25 above.

### “Was rescued by grace” (ὑπὸ τῆς χάριτος ἐῤῥύσθη)

“Saved by grace,” that is, by divine favor rather than by intention and deliberate purpose. Profane writers also used this expression concerning fate and the power of the gods.

Thus Plato, in Book 9 of the *Laws*, considers that the punishment of a man who, wishing to kill another, merely wounded him ought to be mitigated on the ground that thanks should be given rather to the favor of the deity, who had freed the one from the danger of death and the other from the severity of the impending punishment.

Likewise the jurist says in Book 32 of the *Digest*, *On the Julian Law concerning Adultery*: “Although, the adulterer having been killed, the woman survived after such severe wounds as her father had inflicted upon her, she was preserved more by fate than by his intention.”

See Fornerius, Book 6, *Miscellaneous Matters*, chapter 9.

[Col. 0108C] ### “If, bending the knee” (ἐὰν γόνυ κλίνων)

Balsamon and the Greek scholiast of Harmenopulus explain this canon in the *Epitome of the Canons*, section 5, title 3, in these words:

> “There were two orders of catechumens: one, that of those who bent the knee, the more advanced; the other, that of those who listened, the less advanced. He therefore says: if someone belongs to the order of those who bend the knee and commits sin, then, once he has ceased sinning, he should be placed among those who listen; but if he belongs to those who listen, let him stand outside the church.”

For those who listened also stood inside the church only until the reading of the holy Gospel. See the notes on canons 14 and 25 above.

### Council of Eliberis

Tertullian, Book 4 *Against Marcion*: “What does the husband do in your community if his wife has committed adultery? Will he keep her? Christ forbids neither marriage nor separation: by forbidding repudiation, he does not wish marriage to be dissolved; yet by permitting divorce, he does not allow a woman to be retained with her stain.”

Chrysostom says: “Just as the man who dismisses a chaste wife is cruel and unjust, so the man who retains a prostitute is foolish and impious.”

Innocent III, chapter *Qui vir*, *On Adultery*.

### “A presbyter before the age of thirty” (πρεσβύτερος πρὸ τῶν τριάκοντα ἐτῶν)

This is confirmed by the Sixth Synod in Trullo, canon 14, and by the Council of Agde, canon 17: “Let no one presume to ordain a presbyter or bishop before his thirtieth year, that is, before he has reached the age of a fully mature man.”

Justinian’s *Novel* 123, chapter 13, requires thirty-five years. Among the Jews, thirty years was prescribed for the ordination or initiation of priests. Thus 1 Numbers, chapter 4, verse 3, and 1 Chronicles, chapter 23, verse 3: “From thirty years of age and upward, even to fifty years of age.” So the Hebrew edition and the Chaldaic paraphrase read.

The Greek edition of the Seventy, however, followed by Philo the Hellenistic Jew of Alexandria in the book entitled *That the Worse Commonly Plots against the Better*, and by Theodoret in question 13 on Numbers, reads: “From twenty-five years of age and upward, even to fifty years of age.”

But that passage has been corrupted, and instead of “twenty-five” (εἴκοσι πέντε), one must certainly read “thirty” (τριάκοντα), as learned men have already observed.

Jerome, in his Letter to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, against the error of John of Jerusalem, says: “Let him remember the ancient law, and he will see that after twenty-five years a man from the tribe of Levi was chosen for the priesthood; or, if in this one passage he follows the Hebrew truth, let him know that a priest became such at thirty years.”

Later David prescribed the number of twenty years. For when he observed that the sons of Levi, both priests and Levites, because of the multitude of sacrifices that was increasing daily, could not fulfill the duties of the temple if their thirtieth year had to be awaited—since many of them were below that age—he contracted the annual term of the priests into a shorter period and fixed it at the twentieth year, as 1 Chronicles, chapter 23, verse 27, testifies: “According to the last words of David, the number of the Levites was counted from twenty years of age and upward.”

Likewise 1 Chronicles, chapter 31, verse 17, and Ezra, chapter 3, verse 8: “They appointed the Levites from twenty years of age and upward to preside over the work of the house of God.”

It may also be inferred from this that the apostles were not extremely concerned about age, provided that the other qualifications were present, since Timothy was young and the Apostle Paul did not wish his youth to be despised. In 1 Timothy, chapter 4, verse 12: “Let no one despise your youth.”

Ignatius likewise says in his Letter to the Magnesians: “It is also fitting for you not to despise the age of the bishop.”

Thus Eleutherius, because of his outstanding virtue and piety, was ordained bishop of Illyricum when only twenty years old, as Nicephorus reports in Book 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 29.

### “Christ in his thirtieth year” (Χριστὸς ἐν τῷ τριακοστῷ ἔτει)

Saint Luke, chapter 3, verse 23, speaking of Christ’s baptism, says: “And Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began.”

The expression “about” (ὡσεί) has two senses, and the Greeks use it sometimes affirmatively and sometimes doubtfully. It must be taken in the former sense in this passage and in John, chapter 1, verse 14: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.” There he calls him “only-begotten” affirmatively, so that there can be no doubt about it.

Ignatius supports this interpretation in his Letter to the Trallians: “And having lived thirty years, he was baptized by John.”

Chrysostom and Euthymius state the same in their commentaries on Matthew, chapter 3. The author of the sermon *On Fasting*, attributed to Cyprian, says: “When the Lord had assumed flesh and was baptized in his thirtieth year.”

Jerome, in his Letter to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, against the error of John of Jerusalem, speaking of the age required for a presbyter, says: “When it has reached the span of thirty years, I think that it ought not to be reproached in this respect, since according to the mystery of the humanity assumed in Christ it is perfect.”

Bernard, sermon 4 *On Epiphany*, likewise says: “When he was already thirty years old, he himself went to baptism.”

Irenaeus differs from this in Book 2, chapter 39: “He came to baptism,” he says, “before completing thirty years, but when he was beginning to be as though thirty years old.”

Epiphanius says in heresy 51: “For he was in fact twenty-nine years and ten months old when he came to baptism—thirty years old, indeed, but not fully so.”

Add what the most distinguished Scaliger formerly observed on this matter in Book 6 of *On the Correction of the Chronology*.

Certainly the age of thirty years is an age of solid and mature judgment, endowed with greater strength both of mind and body. Euthymius gives this as the reason, in the passage cited, why Christ came to baptism after his thirtieth year.

Thus canon 17 of the Council of Agde calls it the age of a mature man. It is also called the perfect age in Book 10, title 2, of the Visigothic laws, and the lawful age in Theophilus, Book 1, title *On Liberty*, section 4: “The lawful age,” he says, “is that which exceeds thirty years,” because the Aelia Sentia law formerly required this age for a manumitted slave. Ulpian reports this provision in the *Fragments*, title 1: “So that it was not permitted to manumit a slave under thirty years of age.”

### “If someone sick receives illumination” (ἐὰν νοσῶν τις φωτισθῇ)

Cornelius, bishop of Rome, in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius in Book 6, chapter 43, speaks of Novatian:

> “For he abandoned the Church of God, in which, after receiving the faith, he had been deemed worthy of the honor of the presbyterium through the favor of the bishop who had laid hands upon him for the rank of the presbyterium. That bishop, although prevented by the entire clergy and also by many of the laity—for it was not permitted that one who, like him, had been baptized by affusion while lying in bed because of illness should be admitted into the clergy—requested that he alone be permitted to ordain this man.””

The subject was one who had been baptized while ill. This is also mentioned in canon 151 of this collection and canon 48 of the African collection. Cyprian, Book 4, Letter 7, reports that such persons were called *clinics*.

There were two kinds of clinics. Some had embraced the Christian faith but had not yet been baptized; if they fell ill, they were baptized during the illness while lying in bed—“and in the bed” (καὶ ἐν τῇ κλίνῃ).

Epiphanius mentions them in heresy 28: “Those who are about to die, if they are catechumens, are deemed worthy of the bath before death.”

Basil likewise records in Letter 5 that the praetorian prefect Arinthaeus received the bath of regeneration at the very end of his life.

Others, however, were Christians by profession and instructed in the teaching of piety, but deliberately postponed baptism until the very end of life, wishing to be baptized and die at the same time, so that after receiving baptism they might not sin again. Deceived by an error widely prevalent in those times, they believed that baptism required a life free from every subsequent fall and that no further expiation remained for those who sinned.

This opinion was occasioned by a mistaken understanding of Saint Paul’s passage in Hebrews, chapter 6; the Novatians also abused it by altogether denying pardon to the fallen.

Thus the emperor Constantine was baptized at the end of his life by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, as Eusebius reports in Book 4 of his *Life of Constantine*, chapter 62, and as other ecclesiastical writers also relate: Socrates, Book 1, chapter 26; Theodoret, Book 1, chapter 32; Sozomen, Book 2, chapter 34; Jerome in his *Chronicle*; and Nicephorus, Book 8, chapter 54.

Constantius also wished to be baptized while dying: “As he was dying, he decided to be baptized” (ἀποθνήσκων ἔδοξε βαπτίζεσθαι), as Athanasius teaches in *On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*.

Ambrose relates the same of Theodosius the Great in his funeral oration for him, as does Socrates, Book 5, chapter 6.

The orthodox Fathers sharply reproved both this practice of the clinics and the delay in receiving baptism.

Tertullian says in his book *On Repentance*: “Moreover, every fault of delay and evasion with respect to repentance implies presumption regarding the washing. For, confident of the certainty of the forgiveness of sins, they steal the intervening time and make for themselves an opportunity for sinning.”

Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 3, *On Holy Baptism*: “Let us be baptized today, lest tomorrow we be compelled by some greater force; let us not prolong the benefit as though it were an injury, nor wait until we have accumulated more sins so that more may be forgiven us; nor let us be weighed down by a heavier burden than our strength can bear, lest we be overwhelmed with the ship by the waters and lose the grace of baptism in shipwreck; and, while conceiving more things in hope and intention, lose everything,” and so forth.

Some also understand Saint Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians, chapter 15, verse 29, as referring to the clinics: “What will those do who are baptized for the dead?” That is, as they suppose, those who are baptized as though dead or dying.

For my part, without prejudice to a better judgment, I think that this refers to those who, following the perverse custom of certain heretics, were baptized in place of the dead. Epiphanius indicates this custom when speaking of the Cerinthians in heresy 28:

> “A matter of tradition has come down to us: among them some died, overtaken by death without baptism; but others were baptized in their place, in their name, so that when they had risen in the resurrection, they would not have to suffer punishment because they had not received baptism.”

The Marcionites later practiced the same thing, perhaps borrowing the example from the Cerinthians. Chrysostom describes them in his fortieth homily on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 15:

> “When one of their catechumens dies, they conceal a living person beneath the bed of the deceased. They approach the dead man, speak to him, and ask whether he wishes to receive baptism. Then, when he gives no answer, the person hidden below answers in his place that he wishes to be baptized; and thus they baptize him in place of the one who has died.”

Tertullian calls this baptism of the Marcionites “vicarious baptism” in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*:

> “If some are also baptized for the dead, you will see whether it is not with sound reasoning that this presumption has established among them that baptism might benefit the flesh as a vicarious baptism, for the hope of resurrection—a resurrection which, unless it were bodily, would not otherwise be bound by bodily baptism.”

He says the same in Book 5, chapter 10, *Against Marcion*.

Ambrose, explaining Paul’s passage in 1 Corinthians, chapter 15, says:

> “He introduces the example of those who were so confident about the future resurrection that they even baptized themselves for the dead, if someone had perhaps been overtaken by death, fearing that the one who had not been baptized might either not rise or rise improperly; the living person was immersed under the name of the dead.”

### “Seven deacons” (διάκονοι ἑπτά)

See Acts of the Apostles, chapter 6, verse 3, and chapter 20, verse 8; the Sixth Synod in Trullo, canon 16; and Sozomen, Book 7 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 19:

> “Among the Romans there are still no more than seven deacons, in imitation of those who were ordained by the apostles; among the others, however, their number varies.”

### “Apart from blood, things sacrificed to idols, and what has been strangled” (χωρὶς αἵματος καὶ εἰδωλοθύτου καὶ πνικτοῦ)

We read that this very rule was established in the first apostolic synod, Acts of the Apostles, chapter 15, verse 28, and chapter 21, verse 25; and ancient writers on ecclesiastical affairs testify that it was long observed in the Church.

Tertullian says in the *Apology*, chapter 9: “Let your error blush before Christians, who do not even have the blood of animals among our edible foods and who therefore also abstain from things strangled and from animals that have died, lest we be contaminated by some blood, even blood buried within the entrails.”

Minucius says in the *Octavius*: “For us it is not lawful either to see or hear of homicide, and we are so careful to avoid human blood that we do not even know the blood of cattle as food.”

Eusebius, Book 5 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1, and Nicephorus, Book 4, chapter 17, report the same answer given long ago by Biblys in the midst of torture. While she was being pressed under torment, because of her confession of Christ, to reveal something against the Christians by force—as though they ate human flesh—she replied:

> “How could such people eat children, when they are not even permitted to eat the blood of irrational animals?”

Lucian appears to allude to this Christian practice in the *Peregrinus*: “Having committed some offense against them, since he had apparently, as I think, eaten something forbidden to them,” and so forth.

Add Clement of Alexandria, Book 3 of the *Pedagogue*, chapter 3, and the emperor Leo, *Novel* 58: “That no one should make food from blood.”

### “A married presbyter” (πρεσβυτέρου γεγαμηκότος)

That is, married presbyters.

Socrates, Book 2 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 33, speaking of Eustathius, who was condemned at the Council of Gangra, says:

> “He forbade prayers to be held in the houses of married people and ordered that the blessing and communion of a presbyter who had a wife—whom he had married lawfully while still a layman—be avoided as a pollution.”

Balsamon says concerning this canon: “The present canon anathematizes those who do not partake without hesitation from priests who have wives.” Gentianus Hervetus translates it: “The present canon anathematizes those who do not communicate without distinction from the sacred ministers who have wives.”

Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, in his *Breviary of the Canons*, chapter 89, recently edited from the Corbie manuscript by the learned Franciscus Chiffletius, says: “No one should dare to refuse communion from the offering of a married presbyter,” according to title 4 of the Council of Gangra.

The old version used by Isidore Mercator in his collection of the Canons reads: “Concerning the offering of a married presbyter. If anyone distinguishes a married presbyter, as though on account of his marriage he ought not to offer, and for that reason abstains from his offering, let him be anathema.”

The ancient translator in the manuscript of the Thuana Library likewise renders the phrase as “married presbyter.” Dionysius Exiguus translated it incorrectly as “one who had a wife,” which does not at all correspond to the expression *gegamēkotos* (γεγαμηκότος), but rather to *having a wife* (γυναῖκα ἔχοντος), as Socrates and Balsamon correctly interpreted it.

### “The house of God” (οἶκον τοῦ Θεοῦ)

Here, and in canon 106 of this collection, “the house of God” means the church. The expression is frequently used in this sense by ecclesiastical writers.

Zeno of Verona, sermon on Psalm 126: “Our custom is to call the assemblies of the churches, enclosed by the walls of buildings for the secret worship of the sacraments, the house of God.”

See the observations of the most learned D. Heraldus on Arnobius, Book 6.

### “Agapes” (ἀγάπας)

The Lord’s Supper formerly had three parts. The first was the “breaking of bread” (ἄρτου κλάσις), mentioned by Saint Luke in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 2, verse 42, and chapter 20, verse 7. The Syriac interpreter there translates the Greek expression *breaking of bread* with the Greek-derived word “Eucharist.”

The second part was the “cup of blessing” (ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας), mentioned by Saint Paul in 1 Corinthians, chapter 10, verse 16.

The third part was the *agape* (ἀγάπη), that is, a sober communal meal, ordinarily celebrated by Christians in the church after the Eucharist and instituted chiefly for the refreshment of the poor. Numerous testimonies to it are found among the ancient writers on ecclesiastical affairs.

The same must certainly be understood in the Letter of the Apostle Jude, chapter 1, verse 12, where he reproves the impiety of certain people in these words:

> “These are blemishes at your agapes, feasting together with you and fearlessly feeding themselves.”

The old translator has “blemishes at your feasts.”

Oecumenius says concerning this passage: “At that time there were tables that were prepared, of the kind of which Paul also speaks in his Letter to the Corinthians; these they also called *agapes*.”

Tertullian elegantly describes this public banquet of the Church in the *Apology*, chapter 39:

> “Our supper shows its reason for existing by its name. It is called *agape*, which among the Greeks means ‘love.’ However much it costs, it is a gain to spend in the name of piety. For by this refreshment we assist the needy. If the cause of the feast is honorable, judge the remainder of its order from that cause, which proceeds from religious duty: nothing of vulgarity or immodesty is admitted. No one reclines before prayer to God has been offered as a foretaste. People eat as much as the hungry desire and drink as much as is useful to the temperate,” and so forth.

In his book *To the Martyrs*, he calls it “the agape of the brethren.”

Cyprian, Book 3 *Against Quirinum*, chapter 3, speaks of “the agape and love of the brethren.”

Minucius says in the *Octavius*: “We practice banquets that are not only chaste but also sober; for we do not indulge in feasts or prolong the banquet with unmixed wine, but temper cheerfulness with seriousness.”

The agape is also undoubtedly meant by what Pliny the Younger wrote to Trajan about the Christians in Book 10, Letter 97:

> “They affirmed that this was the whole of their guilt or error: that they were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn and sing a hymn to Christ as to a god among themselves; and that they bound themselves by an oath not to commit any crime, but not to commit theft, robbery, or adultery, not to break faith, and not to deny a deposit when called upon to return it. After these things had been completed, they said that it was their custom to depart and meet again to take food, ordinary and harmless food.”

That this custom of dining together in the Church was still observed in the time of Chrysostom is clear from his twenty-seventh homily on chapter 11 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “On appointed days they made the tables common, as was natural; and when the assembly had been completed, after participation in the mysteries, everyone went to a common feast. The wealthy brought the food, while the poor, who had nothing, were also invited by them, and all feasted together.”

At those banquets everyone reclined indiscriminately, with no distinction observed; the equality of all the diners was the same, so that neither did the rich recline first nor the poor later. Because the Corinthians failed to observe this, Saint Paul reproves them in the same chapter, verse 21.

Augustine also refers to them in *Against Faustus*, Book 20, chapter 20: “Our agapes feed the poor, whether with grain or with meat”; and shortly afterward: “Since meat is often distributed to the poor even at agapes, you say that the mercy of Christians is like the sacrifices of the pagans.”

This most ancient custom of dining together in the Church gradually fell into abuse, partly through the ambition of the wealthy and partly through the insolence of the multitude. We read that such banquets were prohibited in churches by canon 132 of this collection and by canon 30 of the Third Council of Carthage.

The name nevertheless remained in ecclesiastical usage, so that banquets prepared for the refreshment of the poor and of guests were called *agapes* and “charities”; and they began to be separated from the Lord’s Supper, which it was lawful to administer only in the church.

The Greeks are said even today to preserve traces of the ancient custom. On the sacred day of the Lord’s Resurrection, after communion in the holy mysteries, they bring food into the church and feast together; they also sing a solemn hymn consisting of these words:

> “Christ has risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and granting life to those in the tombs.”

So formerly observed the most learned student of ecclesiastical antiquity, G. Cassander, in his *Liturgics*.

Moreover, the Christian agape does not differ greatly from the sacred banquets of the Romans, which were called *charistia*. At these, disputes among relatives and friends were settled. The poet mentions them in Book 2 of the *Fasti*:

> “Dear kinsmen called the next [day] *charistia*.”

Valerius Maximus describes them in Book 2, chapter 17, in these words:

> “Our ancestors established a solemn banquet and called it a *charistia*. No one except relatives and in-laws was admitted, so that if any quarrel had arisen between close persons, it might be removed at the sacred table and amid the cheerfulness of their spirits, with advocates of concord brought in.”

I omit the *syssitia* of the Cretans and the *phiditia* of the Lacedaemonians; on these see N. Cragius, Book 1 *On the Lacedaemonian Republic*, chapter 9.

### “Outer garment” (περιβολαίῳ)

Suidas says: “A *peribolaion* is a garment,” that is, clothing.

Pollux, in Book 7, chapter 13 of the *Onomasticon*: “The outer garments and those worn over other clothing may be called *peribolaia*.”

Balsamon and Zonaras here call a *peribolaion* “the covering placed over the others,” that is, a cloak or garment worn over other clothing.

The Seventy Interpreters also used this word in Psalms 101 and 103, as did Saint Paul in the Letter to the Hebrews, chapter 1, and in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11.

[Col. 0114A] ### “Beroi” (βήρους)

Zonaras here calls *beroi* (βήρους) “silken woven fabrics,” that is, garments woven of silk; these belonged to persons of higher rank.

There was also a *burrus* or *byrrus*, a kind of garment somewhat less expensive. See P. Pithoeus, Book 2 *Adversaria*, chapter 16.

### “Should change attire” (μεταβάλλοιτο ἀμφίασμα)

The promiscuous use of garments is condemned in Deuteronomy, chapter 22: “A woman shall not wear a man’s garment, nor shall a man use a woman’s garment.”

Philo the Jew mentions this law in *On Courage*. Josephus does so in Book 4 of the *Antiquities*, at the end of the book; and Cyprian in Letter 37 to Encratius.

### “Should cut off her hair” (ἀποκείροιτο τὰς κόμας)

Saint Paul says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11, verse 6: “It is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved.”

Sozomen, Book 7 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 16, reports that the emperor Theodosius decreed that women who shaved their heads were to be expelled from the churches, and that bishops who admitted them were to be deprived of their episcopal offices.

[Col. 0114B] ### “The decree of the Council of Nicaea concerning the feast of Easter” (ὅρον τῆς ἐν Νικαίᾳ συνόδου περὶ ἑορτῆς τοῦ πάσχα)

Epiphanius, speaking of the Fathers of Nicaea in heresy 69, says:

> “At the same time, in that same synod, they established certain ecclesiastical canons, and at the same time concerning Easter they decreed that there should be one unity and concord, so that the holy and all-virtuous day of God might be celebrated.”

Sozomen, Book 1, chapter 21, says:

> “When the controversy concerning the doctrine had ceased, the synod decided that all should celebrate the feast of Easter at one and the same time.”

### “Canonical letters” (κανονικὰς ἐπιστολάς)

These are the *canonical letters* (κανονικὰ γράμματα) mentioned in canon 145 of this collection.

The use of canonical, or ecclesiastical, letters was most ancient in the Church. Orthodox bishops sent them to one another as tokens of their faith, so that through this exchange they might show their fellowship in the same religion and, as Tertullian says in chapter 20 of *On the Prescription against Heretics*, “the communion of peace and the mutual recognition of hospitality.”

This is confirmed by the synodical letter of the Council of Antioch to Dionysius of Rome and Maximus, bishop of Alexandria, preserved in Eusebius, Book 7 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 30. It concerns the deposition of Paul of Samosata and the substitution of Domnus in his place:

> “We have indicated to you that you should write to Domnus and receive from him letters of communion.”

Optatus of Milevis accordingly reports in Book 2 that the unity of the Church was customarily demonstrated in this way: “The entire world agrees with us through the exchange of *formatae*, in the fellowship of one communion.”

Augustine says in Letter 162: “Thus it happened that we also wrote to certain leading Donatists—not letters of communion, which they no longer accept because of their perversity, having been separated from the Catholic unity spread throughout the whole world, but merely private letters.”

In Letter 163, speaking of Eleusius and his associates, he says: “At first he attempted to assert that his communion existed throughout the world. I asked whether they could give the letters of communion, which we call *formatae*, wherever they wished,” and so forth.

There were various and distinct kinds of canonical or *formatae* letters, with different names, as can be observed throughout the Acts of the Councils and ecclesiastical history. Generally, however, by the expression “canonical letters” (κανονικῶν ἐπιστολῶν), peaceful and commendatory letters—*eirenic* (εἰρηνικαί) and *commendatory* (συστατικαί)—are meant.

Zonaras here calls canonical letters “commendatory and peaceful letters.” In canon 22 of the Council of Laodicea he says:

> “The letters that are peaceful and commendatory he called canonical documents here, as being issued according to a rule.”

### “Peaceful letters” (εἰρηνικάς)

The *eirenic* letters are also mentioned in canon 189 of this collection. There are two kinds.

Some are also called letters of dismissal. They are given to bishops by metropolitans and to metropolitans by patriarchs when, as circumstances require, they travel to the emperor.

Others are given by bishops to clerics who wish to travel to another city and be received into its clergy. They are called “peaceful” because they are, as it were, arbiters of peace.

Zonaras says in canon 11 of the Council of Chalcedon:

> “Peaceful letters are those called letters of dismissal. Such are those given to bishops by the metropolitans under whom they serve, and to metropolitans by the patriarchs by whom they are appointed, when they depart for the emperor because of some necessary matter; and such are those given to clerics by their own bishops when they wish to go to another city and be enrolled in that church. They are called peaceful because they establish peace.”

The Greek scholiast of Harmenopulus gives the same account of the *eirenic* letters in the *Synopsis of the Canons*, section 3, title 2.

### “The territory under a city” (χώρας τῆς ὑπὸ πόλιν)

The word “city” signifies not only a town enclosed by walls but also the region or territory assigned to the city.

Thus Dio Chrysostom, Oration 34, among the things he says Caesar granted to the people of Tarsus, mentions a *chora*: “He granted you a territory, laws, honor, authority,” and so forth.

Xiphilinus, speaking of Byzantium after it had been destroyed by the emperor Severus and reduced to the form of a village, says:

> “He granted the city and all its territory to the Perinthians, and they used it as though it were a single village.”

The jurists call this the territory of a city. Pomponius says: “Territory is the totality of the fields within the boundaries of each city, within which, as Siculus Flaccus says, there was jurisdiction.”

Hence the expression “the territory of the judge” in the final law, *On Jurisdiction*.

Nor did cities have regions and territories only in civil government; they had them also in the Church. These are frequently designated in councils and ecclesiastical history by the name *paroikiai*.

Justinian, Book 26 of the Code, *On Bishops Hearing Cases*: “In that city or *paroikia,” that is, in the city or its vicinity.

And Book 35 of the Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*: “If anyone dares to deprive a city of its own bishop or of its surrounding territory, he is rendered infamous.”

Thus the territory of a bishop is mentioned in canon 19 of the First Council of Orléans, canon 18 of the Third Council of Orléans, canon 3 of the Council of Vaison, canon 60 of Worms, and in the acts of the Council of Constantinople under Menas, where the territory of Apamea is mentioned.

### “Exorcists” (ἐπορκιστάς)

The *exorcists* (ἐπορκισταί), or *ephorcists* (ἐφορκισταί), are also mentioned in canons 128 and 130 of this collection.

At the beginning of the emerging Church, the gift of expelling demons seems to have been common even to laypeople who had embraced the faith of Christ. The expulsion of demons is numbered among the signs said to follow believers in Mark, chapter 16, verse 17:

> “These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons.”

Tertullian, Book *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 20, testifies that unclean spirits were expelled by soldiers: “Those whom he drove away by exorcisms during the day, he will defend at night.”

In *On Idolatry*, chapter 11, he teaches that parents were accustomed to exorcize their own children: “With what confidence will he exorcize his foster children, to whom he provides his house as a cellar? If he has indeed expelled the demon, let him not pride himself on his faith; he has not expelled his enemy.”

Later, exorcism became a particular and distinct office in the Church.

The Greek scholiast of Harmenopulus, in the *Epitome of the Canons*, section 1, title 9, interprets *exorcists* as “catechists.”

Theodore Balsamon likewise says concerning canon 26 of the Council of Laodicea: “To exorcize means to catechize unbelievers.”

Thus: “To exorcize, that is, to catechize unbelievers.”

### “A greater synod of bishops”

That is, **a synod of the bishops of the diocese** (*σύνοδον ἐπισκόπων τῆς διοικήσεως*), as in canon 169 of this codex.

### “To appoint another successor”

Formerly, while a bishop was still living, he was permitted to ordain his successor. Eusebius, book VII, chapter 32, speaking of Anatolius, says:

> “The first to lay hands upon him for the episcopate was Theotecnus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, intending to designate him as his own successor after his death for the administration of his own parish.”

Theotecnus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, first ordained him bishop by the laying-on of hands, and arranged that after his death he should be chosen as his successor for the administration of his parish. This was later prohibited, as is clear from this canon.

Ado of Vienne, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 810, writes:

> “Bernard was bishop of Vienne, and Leidrad was bishop of Lyons. At the beginning of the reign of the emperor Louis, Leidrad requested the position at the monastery of Soissons; and in his place Agobard, chorepiscopus of the same Church, was substituted as bishop, with the consent of the emperor and of the entire synod of the bishops of Gaul.”

Some who wished to defend this action said that the venerable Agobard had been ordained at the see of Lyons by three bishops at the command of Leidrad. But canonical authority declares that there must not be two bishops in one city, nor may a bishop, while still living, appoint his own successor.

### “To render an account” (*εὐθύνας παρέχειν*)

This is translated into Latin as **to render an account of one’s administration**. Thus, among Greek writers, *εὐθύνεσθαι* and *εὐθύνας διδόναι* commonly mean to render an account of the administration of the state—or, as Cicero says, to explain what each person has done in public office, as was formerly done before the censors.

Hence, in Demosthenes, *εὐθύναι τῶν πεπολιτευμένων* means “accounts of one’s public acts”; likewise *εὐθύναι τῆς πρεσβείας*, “accounts of one’s embassy”; and *εὐθύναι βίου*, the censures by which someone is compelled to render an account of his past life. In Plutarch’s *Life of Pericles*, *περὶ τὰς εὐθύνας ἀπαραίτητος* means “inexorable in demanding accounts.”

Thus, in Aristophanes, *ὑπεύθυνοι* are those liable to render accounts, or those who have not yet reported an account of their conduct in office.

Some also interpret *εὐθύνας διδόναι* as being subjected to a prosecution for extortion, just as *εὐθύνας ὀφλεῖν* or *ὠφληκέναι* means to be condemned for extortion. See Budaeus, notes on the *Digest*.

The meaning of this canon, therefore, is that bishops entrusted with authority over ecclesiastical property, if they convert any of it to their own use or give it to their relatives, are liable to the synod of the province for the rendering of accounts, and are, as it were, subjected to a prosecution for extortion.

Alexius, patriarch of Constantinople, explains it similarly in his synodical letter preserved in book II of the *Sentences of the Synod*, in these words:

> “Let stewards likewise be appointed by the metropolitans, who are to provide, together with the bishops, for all the churches with the greatest care, and to demand accounts of the annual administration. That the things we have determined are consonant with the exact meaning of the canons is demonstrated by the divine canons themselves. For the fifth and twentieth canons of the synod of Antioch, while entrusting bishops with authority over ecclesiastical affairs, forbid them to convert these things to private uses or give them to their own relatives, lest the accounts of the churches be secretly harmed. Therefore, by making them accountable to the provincial synods, they permit those synods to examine what is fitting. The accompanying Latin rendering then says: “For canon XXV of the synod of Antioch, while granting bishops authority over ecclesiastical property, forbids them to convert it to their own uses or give it to their relatives, so that the accounts of the churches may not secretly suffer loss; therefore, by making them accountable to provincial synods, it enjoins upon them the duty of investigating what is proper.””

### “Those lawfully joined in second marriages”

There is also mention of **digamists** in canons 8, 39, and 52 of this codex. From these it is clear that digamists were formerly condemned by the Church and that a definite period of penance was prescribed for them. Who these people were, however, is generally little known.

To make this clear, it should be observed that there are three kinds of digamy.

The first occurs when someone has two wives simultaneously: *δύο ἔχει κατὰ ταυτὸν γυναῖκας*. Such was the digamy of the barbarians and the Jews, among whom it is well known that a plurality of wives was permitted.

Josephus, book XVII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 2, testifies concerning the Jews:

> “It was our ancestral custom to have several wives at the same time.”

Justin Martyr, in his dialogue with Trypho, says:

> “Your teachers, even to the present time, permit each of you to have four or five wives.”

This license of pagans and Jews was prohibited by Roman law: book II of the *Code*, *On Incestuous Marriages*; book XVIII of the *Code*, *On the Julian Law concerning Adultery*; and book VIII of the *Code*, *On the Jews*.

Theophilus, *On Marriage*, sections 6 and 7, says:

> “A capital punishment has been established against those who contract a double marriage.”

Theodoret, commenting on the First Epistle to Timothy, writes:

> “Formerly the Greeks and the Jews were accustomed to be joined in marriage to two, three, or even more wives at the same time. Even now, although the imperial laws prohibit taking two wives simultaneously, they maintain relations with concubines and prostitutes.”

The second kind of digamy occurs when, after the previous marriage has been dissolved by the death of one’s spouse, someone contracts a second marriage. There is no uncertainty about this kind.

The third kind, however, is commonly unknown and must be discussed briefly.

Some traces of it appear in the edict of the praetor. Anyone who has established two betrothals or two marriages at the same time is marked with infamy: book I of the *Digest*, *On Those Noted with Infamy*. And book XII, section 2, of the same title says:

> “What the praetor says—‘at the same time’—is not to be understood as referring to the beginnings of betrothals made at the same time, but to their continuing into the same period.”

By Roman law, marriages were indeed dissolved by divorce. Yet, so that this might not be done rashly and without legal procedure, the repudiation had to be made in certain prescribed and solemn words, with seven adult Roman citizens present as witnesses. This was required by the Julian law, which imposed limits on divorces and decreed that a divorce made outside the prescribed formula was to be regarded as legally nonexistent.

Pomponius the jurist also notes this, book XXXV of the *Digest*, *On Gifts between Husband and Wife*:

> “If the divorce was not made according to the legally prescribed procedure, the marriage is not considered dissolved.”

Gaius, book XLIII of the *Digest*, *On Adultery*, says:

> “If repudiation has not been sent in accordance with the law, the woman is still considered married.”

The emperors Constantine and Theodosius also decreed that marriages could be dissolved only after a repudiation had been sent, and not without legitimate cause: book I of the Theodosian *Code*, *On Repudiation*, and book VIII of the same title. There they designate the causes for which a husband may repudiate his wife and a wife her husband.

Such repudiation consisted in the husband releasing the wife from the marriage, or the wife releasing the husband. Accordingly, whoever, without cause and without a legitimate repudiation, takes another woman—or whoever marries another man—has established two marriages at the same time.

For the same reason, ecclesiastical writers call those persons digamists who, after dismissing a first spouse without legitimate repudiation—that is, without the cause of adultery—bring in another spouse.

It is entirely clear that the causes of divorce accepted by secular laws and devised by the emperors, with the exception of adultery, were never accepted by the Church. Therefore, those who divorced lawfully—that is, in accordance with the permission granted by human law—and passed to another marriage were judged by the Church to have established two marriages at the same time. Consequently, canonical punishment was rightly imposed upon them.

Chrysostom clearly indicates this kind of digamy in his tenth homily on the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3:

> “Among the Jews it was permitted both to associate with a second marriage and to have two wives at the same time.”

Justin Martyr, in the *Second Apology*, says:

> “Those who contract a double marriage under human law are sinners in the judgment of our Teacher.”

By these words he alludes to Christ’s saying in Matthew, chapter 19, verse 9:

> “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of adultery, and marries another, commits adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

Justin likewise calls a second marriage “respectable adultery” (*δεύτερος γάμος εὐπρεπὴς μοιχεία*).

Those whom Justin calls “persons contracting a double marriage under human law,” this canon calls “those lawfully joined in second marriages” (*νομίμως δευτέροις γάμοις συναφθέντας*).

The Greek scholiast of Harmenopulus, in the *Epitome of the Canons*, section 3, title 1, says:

> “A digamist is one who has betrothed one woman and married another according to the laws, and also one who marries a woman betrothed to another.”

John Xiphilinus, patriarch of Constantinople, says in his synodical letter on betrothals, book I of the *Synodical Sentences*:

> “He who has contracted a betrothal, dissolved it according to the laws, and then married another woman is a digamist.”

The foregoing canons—8, 39, 52, and 105 of this codex—must therefore be understood of such digamists.

Opposed to these are those whom Saint Paul calls “husbands of one wife” (*ἄνδρες μιᾶς γυναικός*) in the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3, verses 2 and 12, and in the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, verse 6:

> “A bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife”;  
> “Let deacons be husbands of one wife.”

By these words the Apostle, following the footsteps of Christ, commands that no one be admitted to the office of bishop or deacon who, after rashly repudiating his wife, has brought in another according to the laws.

Oecumenius, commenting on chapter 3, says:

> “If he comes from the worldly, let him at least not be a second-marrier.”

Chrysostom, explaining these words of Saint Paul in his second homily on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, says:

> “ ‘The husband of one wife’: he also restrains the licentious and does not allow one who has contracted a second marriage to be entrusted with this leadership. For he who showed no affection toward the woman who had departed—how could he become a good ruler? What accusation would he not incur? You all know, you know that even if the laws do not prohibit association with a second marriage, the matter nevertheless exposes a person to many accusations. He therefore wishes the ruler to provide those under him with no occasion for accusation.”

Theophylact, in the same place, says:

> “To restrain the licentious, he says, ‘the husband of one wife.’ For he who showed no affection toward the woman who departed—how will he govern the Church well? A bishop must be blameless. A digamist, however, is not blameless, even if this is acceptable to secular laws.”

Theodoret, in the passage cited, says:

> “For if he himself, having driven away his first wife, had been joined to another, he would have been worthy of reproach and rightly liable to accusation.”

With the same phrase and meaning, Saint Paul said in the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 5, verse 9:

> “Let a widow be enrolled who has been the wife of one man.”

This kind of digamy was common both to men and to women, since among the Greeks and Romans women were equally permitted to divorce. Even distinct names for the act had been handed down: if a husband separated from his wife, it was called *ἀποπεμπή*; if a wife separated from her husband, *ἀπόλειψις*.

It is generally known that men were permitted by law to divorce and to bring in other wives even while the repudiated wives were still alive. There is also abundant testimony, among both pagan and sacred writers, that a wife was permitted to divorce her husband.

Solon, according to Plutarch, required a woman to place the document of her divorce before the archon, not through another person but in person. Thus the wife of Alcibiades deposited her writ of divorce before the archon, as Plutarch records in his *Life of Alcibiades*.

Andocides, in his speech *For Nicostratus*, says:

> “Let him say before which archon the wife whom he had promised repudiated him.”

Among the Romans, Martial indicates that such scandalous conduct was common. In book VIII he writes:

> “Not yet has the thirtieth day dawned,  
> And Thelesina is already marrying her tenth husband.”

And in book XII:

> “You abandon, Proculeia, your old husband,  
> And order him to keep his own belongings.”

Juvenal writes:

> “Thus there will be eight husbands—  
> Five within five autumns.”

Caelius, in Cicero’s eighth letter of book VIII of the *Letters to Friends*, says:

> “The sister of Triarius divorced without cause on the very day her husband was expected to return from the province; she is going to marry Decimus Brutus.”

Seneca, book III of *On Benefits*, chapter 16, says:

> “Does any woman now blush at divorce, since certain distinguished and noble women count their years not by the number of consuls but by the number of husbands, and leave marriage for the sake of marrying, and marry for the sake of divorcing? This was feared so long as it was rare. But since now no life is conducted without divorce, they have learned to do what they often heard others doing.”

Tertullian, in the *Apology*, chapter 6, says:

> “Where is that happiness of marriages which, for nearly six hundred years from the founding of the City, saw no household write a divorce? But now, among women, divorce is already a vow, as though it were the fruit of marriage.”

Ambrose, in *On Abraham*, says:

> “Let no one flatter himself on the basis of human laws. What is not permitted to the wife is not permitted to the husband; the same chastity is owed by the husband as by the wife.”

Justin Martyr also testifies, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 17, that a certain Christian woman, having given her husband a writ of divorce, separated from him because of his licentious conduct:

> “She gave what is called among us a *repudium* and separated from him.”

We likewise read that Fabiola separated from her husband and later married another, and that public penance was imposed upon her for this reason, as Jerome relates in the *Epitaph of Fabiola*.

Add Christ’s saying in Mark, chapter 10, verse 12:

> “If a woman divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.”

The Council of Elvira, canon 8, says:

> “Women who, without any preceding cause, have abandoned their husbands and joined themselves to other men are not to receive communion even at the end of life.”

And canon 72 says:

> “If a widow has committed adultery and afterward has the same man as her husband, it has been decided that, after five years, once the prescribed penance has been completed, she is to be reconciled to communion. But if, after leaving that man, she takes another, communion is not to be given even at the end of life. Or, if the man whom she has taken is a believer, she is not to receive communion until she has completed ten years of prescribed penance.”

See also the jurist J. Leschassier, in his observation written in French, *On Digamy*.

### “Hundredths”

This is an error by the translator, who translated *ἡμιολίας* as “hundredths.” Zonaras and Balsamon likewise erred by taking the term in canon 17 to mean half-percent interest, as though *τὸ ἥμισυ τοῦ ὅλου τόκου*—“half of the entire interest”—were what is called “half a hundredth” in the final law of the *Code*, *On Fiscal Interest*.

Cujas, in his commentary on book XX of the *Code*, *On Interest*, understood *ἡμιολίας* as “bessal interest,” which was itself forbidden to clerics. Nor is the interpretation of Scaliger and others on monetary matters, page 95, any better, when they interpret *ἡμιολίας* as sesquialteral interest—that is, when eighteen are paid annually on one hundred, and therefore one and a half hundredths.

Interest was not called *ἡμιολίαι* in relation to the hundredth, but in relation to the principal, which is properly the *whole* (*ὅλον*), the capital (*κεφάλαιον* or *ἀρχαῖον*), or, in Tertullian’s expression, the entirety. When the interest amounts to half of the whole—that is, of the principal—it is *ἡμιόλιον*. It is not half-interest, bessal interest, hundredth interest, or sesquihundredth interest.

Jerome accurately describes it in book VI of his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 18, folio 206:

> “It is customary for interest to be demanded in grain, millet, wine, oil, and other commodities. For example, one gives ten measures in winter and receives fifteen at harvest—that is, an additional half.”

Constantine prescribed the measure of interest in book I of the Theodosian *Code*, *On Interest*: grain might bear *ἡμιολίαι*, while money might bear only hundredth interest. Whatever is added to the grain, and whatever exceeds or is added to the principal, is interest.

Sidonius, book IV, letter 24, elegantly calls it “the superimposed half,” when the interest equals the principal.

See above, the note on canon 17.

### “Elections in the presence of hearers” (*χειροτονίας ἐπὶ παρουσίᾳ ἀκροωμένων*)

Here *χειροτονία* means election, or the form of voting that the ancient Church observed in choosing bishops and presbyters.

The word was transferred into the Church from secular usage. Among the Athenians there were two methods of appointing magistrates. Some were chosen by lot, whence came *κληρωταὶ ἀρχαί*, “magistracies chosen by lot,” and the place where they were selected was called a *κληρωτήριον*. Others were chosen by *χειροτονία*, that is, by the extension of hands, which the people raised when approving someone; those so chosen were called *χειροτονηταί*.

Demosthenes, in *Against Neaera*, and Aeschines, in *Against Ctesiphon*, teach this in the following words:

> “They will say that magistrates are those whom the Thesmothetae select by lot in the temple of Theseus, and those whom the people customarily declare by *χειροτονία*, the extension of hands.”

Cicero likewise testifies that this method of voting was customary among the Romans, in his speech *For Flaccus*:

> “Thus those famous decrees that are recited were established—not declared by opinions or authorities, nor secured by an oath, but by the extending of hands and the outcry of an excited multitude.”

In the course of time, therefore, the civic term was transferred to sacred usage. We read that the apostle Paul and Barnabas, at the beginning of the emerging Church, appointed presbyters in each city or Church by *χειροτονία*, that is, by the vote and consent of the people.

Saint Luke testifies to this in Acts, chapter 14, verse 23:

> “Having chosen presbyters by vote in every church.”

For this reason Luke himself is said to have been *χειροτονηθείς ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν*, “chosen by the votes of the Churches,” in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 8, verse 19.

*Χειροτονία* is used in this same sense in the present canon, namely, for the election and vote of the people, as Balsamon and Zonaras explain in their commentary on canon 1 of the Apostles. I shall set down Zonaras’s words from a manuscript of the Royal Library:

> “At present *χειροτονία* is called the completion of the prayers and the invocation of the Holy Spirit when the person chosen for the priesthood is initiated and consecrated. The name comes from the fact that the high priest extends his hand while blessing the man being ordained. Formerly, however, the vote itself was also called *χειροτονία*. For when the peoples of the cities were permitted to choose the chief priests, the crowds assembled, and some chose one man while others chose another. In order that the vote of the majority might prevail, those making the choice were said to extend their hands; by these extended hands the number of those voting for each candidate was counted, and the one chosen by the majority was preferred for the high priesthood. From this the name *χειροτονία* was derived. The fathers of the synods are likewise found to have used it in this way, calling the vote *χειροτονία*. For the synod at Laodicea says in its fifth canon that *χειροτονίαι* must not take place in the presence of hearers. They called the votes *χειροτονίαι*. At the actual liturgical consecration by the high priest, it was more customary for many people to assemble; but at the voting, because certain accusations concerning the men being voted upon might be introduced, no one is permitted to be present and hear them.”

Concerning the hearers, or catechumens, see the notes above on canons 14, 25, and 50.

### “To the cemeteries” (*εἰς τὰ κοιμητήρια*)

Athenaeus, book IV, chapter 5, quoting Dosiadas’s book IV of *Cretan Matters*, reports that among the Cretans there were public buildings in each city where strangers used to sleep; hence they were called *κοιμητήρια*:

> “Throughout Crete there are everywhere two houses. One they call the men’s house; the other, in which they lodge strangers, they call a *coimeterion*.”

Christians adopted this word. Since faith taught that the dead would rise again, they said that the dead were meanwhile sleeping, and they called their tombs *κοιμητήρια*, as though they were dormitories or places prepared for rest and sleep.

They were accustomed especially to assemble at the tombs of their martyrs, whose memory was sacred, and to celebrate the sacred rites there.

Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book V, chapter 3, writes:

> “The fasting people went out to the cemetery for the sake of prayer.”

Hence *κοιμητήρια* are frequently mentioned by the early writers of ecclesiastical history.

Aemilianus, governor of Egypt, addresses the Christian bishops in Eusebius, book VII, chapter 10:

> “It will by no means be permitted either to you or to anyone else to hold assemblies or to enter the places called *cemeteries*.”

Eusebius, book IX, records that Maximinus at one time attempted to deprive Christians of this privilege when he wished to scatter and destroy them:

> “First he tried to prevent us, under one pretext or another, from assembling in the cemeteries.”

Pontius Paulinus, in the account of the martyrdom of Cyprian, speaking of Valerian’s edict against Christians, says:

> “It was ordered that they hold no assemblies and enter no cemeteries.”

Thus these cemeteries were for Christians something like temples. Learned men have also observed that the cemeteries themselves gave rise to temples. The ancient Fathers trace the origin of pagan temples to tombs, and state that their most celebrated temples were burials of dead bodies and monuments of the deceased: Arnobius, book VI; Cyril, book I *Against Julian*; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*; and Theodoret, *Sermon on the Martyrs*.

### “Elder women, or women presiding” (*πρεσβύτιδας ἤτοι προκαθημένας*)

It is established that in the ancient Church there were matrons who exhorted other women to live honorably. They were called *πρεσβύτιδες*, “elder women,” and, because they sat above the other women in the churches, *προκαθήμεναι*, “women presiding.”

This canon, which is canon 11 of the synod of Laodicea, abolishes them.

Perhaps Saint Paul is referring to these women when he wishes the *πρεσβύτιδες* to be holy in conduct, not slanderers, not enslaved to wine, and teachers of good things, so that [they may instruct] younger women; *πρεσβύτιδες* is to be rendered “elder widows.” The old translator correctly rendered the term as “elder widows,” and Fulgentius Ferrandus followed him in chapter 221 of his *Brief Summary of the Canons*.

Epiphanius, heresy 79, says:

> “It should be observed that, up to the order of deaconesses, the ecclesiastical order required women whom it also called widows, and the older among these it called *πρεσβύτιδες*, elder widows.”

This canon also calls them *προκαθήμεναι*, “women presiding,” because they had a fixed seat in the church.

Concerning the age and ministry of such widows or deaconesses, see below the note on canon 193 of this codex; Grotius, *On the Authority of the Supreme Powers in Sacred Matters*, pages 403–404; and Chifflet, notes on the *Brief Summary of the Canons* of Ferrandus, pages 306–307.

### “To be established in the church” (*ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ καθίστασθαι*)

This canon prohibits elder widows, or deaconesses, from being ordained in the Church.

The old translator expresses its meaning as follows:

> “Women who among the Greeks are called presbyteresses, but among us elder widows, one-husband women, and enrolled widows, are not to be established in the Church as though they had been ordained.”

For this reason they are also said not to possess a *χειροθεσία*, that is, an ordination, and are counted among the laity, canon 19 of this codex.

The Council of Epaon, canon 21, says:

> “We completely abolish throughout our entire region the consecration of widows whom they call deaconesses, imposing upon them only the blessing of penance.”

Thus the Cataphrygians are condemned, since they believed that women could be ordained deacons. Marianus Scotus and Sigebert, in their *Chronicle* under the year 525 or 526, attribute the same error to the Acephali.

Ambrose, commenting on the third chapter of the First Epistle to Timothy, says:

> “The Cataphrygians, seizing upon the occasion of the error because Paul addresses women as deacons, defend with empty presumption that women ought themselves to be ordained deacons. But, so that heretics may seem to establish their view by the words rather than the meaning of the law, they contend against the Apostle’s meaning by using the Apostle’s words. For when he commands that a woman should remain silent in the church, they, on the contrary, claim for her authority in the church and the exercise of ministry.”

### “That the holy things be sent to other parishes” (*τὰ ἅγια εἰς ἑτέρας παροικίας διαπέμπεσθαι*)

“Holy things” means the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ.

Thus Curopalates, in his book *On the Offices of Constantinople*, says:

> “He then comes to the place called the *prothesis*, where the holy things lie.”

Shortly afterward he adds:

> “The deacons and priests come, holding other sacred vessels, and also the holy things themselves.”

Likewise, in the Greek collection of the canons of the African Church, canon 37 says:

> “In the holy offerings nothing more is to be presented than the body and blood of the Lord, as the Lord himself delivered it—that is, bread and wine mixed with water.”

This is what the Council of Carthage III, canon 24, says:

> “In the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord, nothing more is to be offered than what the Lord himself delivered: bread and wine mixed with water.”

And throughout the Greek liturgies one finds:

> “The holy things for the holy.”

This canon, therefore, prohibits the holy things—that is, the sacraments of the body and blood—from being sent to other parishes as tokens of blessing.

Theodore Balsamon explains this in a manuscript commended to us by the distinguished and learned J. Casaubon:

> “This is what is done today by the Latins at the feast of Easter: after the unleavened breads have been sanctified, they distribute them to the laity as though they were ordinary things. Apparently this was formerly also done by our people with the holy mysteries. The canon therefore prohibits this and determines that the most holy things are not to be carried here and there as though they were ordinary and commonplace.”

Zonaras likewise explains the same canon in a manuscript of the Royal Library:

> “This was an ancient custom. After Easter, the holy things—that is, portions of the holy body and blood of Christ—were sent from one parish to another as a blessing for those to whom they were sent. This canon prohibited it. For it was rightly and piously judged improper and unbecoming to carry the divine mysteries on long journeys and to transport the most sacred things as circumstances happened to dictate.”

Pope Innocent, in his letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, preserved among his decrees in chapter 5 of the *Canons of the Roman Church*, says concerning the *fermentum*:

> “You wished to consult us unnecessarily concerning the consecrated bread that we send on Sunday through the titular churches. All our churches within the city are established together; yet, since their presbyters cannot meet with us on that day because of the people entrusted to them, they receive from us through acolytes the consecrated bread, so that on that greatest day they may not consider themselves separated from our communion. I do not think this should be done through distant parishes, because the sacraments ought not to be carried over long distances. Nor do we send them through different cemeteries where presbyters are established, since their presbyters possess both the right and the authority to consecrate them.”

### “The prayer of the catechumens” (*κατηχουμένων εὐχήν*)

Here “the prayer of the catechumens” means the sacred service of readings, prayers, and other things of that kind, which is celebrated in the Church before the dismissal of the catechumens.

The Latins called it the “Mass of the catechumens.” The Council of Valence, canon 1, says:

> “We have judged that this must be observed: the sacred Gospels are to be read after the order of the readings in the Mass of the catechumens, before the offering of the gifts.”

Ivo, letter 219, says:

> “The person who heard the Mass of the catechumens withdrew from the Mass of the sacraments.”

### “For the catechumens to go out” (*ἐξελθεῖν κατηχουμένους*)

Formerly, after the reading of the sacred books had been completed and the sacrament of the Eucharist was about to be celebrated, the catechumens, the possessed, and the penitents were dismissed.

Dionysius testifies to this in the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*:

> “After this, the catechumens go outside the sacred enclosure, and with them those possessed and those who are engaged in penance; but those who are worthy of the contemplation and communion of divine things remain.”

Maximus, in the *Mystagogy*, chapter 14, says:

> “After the divine reading of the holy Gospel, the dismissal and expulsion of the catechumens and of the others who are unworthy of contemplating the divine mysteries about to be revealed are carried out by the sacred ministers.”

The Latins also called this dismissal a *missa*, using *remissa* in the sense of “dismissal.”

Hincmar of Reims, in an as-yet unpublished letter to Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, says:

> “Some are ordered to remain in the church until the Mass of the catechumens; others are joined to the celebration of the sacred mysteries only in the prayer of the faithful within the church, but are excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table.”

Augustine, sermon 237 *On Time*, says:

> “Behold, after the sermon the dismissal is made for the catechumens; the faithful will remain, and we shall proceed to prayer.”

### 127. “Three prayers of the faithful” (*εὐχὰς πιστῶν τρεῖς*)

Hence, throughout the Greek liturgies, one finds:

> “The first prayer of the faithful,”  
> “The second prayer of the faithful,”  
> “The third prayer of the faithful.”

### “To wear the *orarion*” (*ὠράριον φορεῖν*)

This canon prohibits ministers—that is, subdeacons—from wearing the *orarion*. Balsamon states that it was the distinctive vestment of deacons. I shall give his words from a Greek manuscript:

> “To wear the *orarion* belongs only to deacons. For, standing beside those who celebrate and observing the rites of the sacred prayers and the proclamations of the presbyters, they give notice by means of the *orarion* to the deacons in the ambo when the proclamation of the petitions for the catechumens and the others is to be made—that is, when the time has come for the extended litany [the manuscript reads *ἐκτενοῦς*; perhaps read *ἐκτενείας*]. It was called *orarion* from *ὠρῶ*, ‘I observe’ or ‘I watch over.’”

Matthew Blastares gives almost the same account in his *Synopsis of the Greek Canons*. I quoted his words above, from a Greek manuscript belonging to the illustrious president Jacques-Auguste de Thou, in the note on canon 22.

The *orarion* is also mentioned by Curopalates in his book *On the Offices of Constantinople*:

> “The archdeacon, wearing his customary maniple (*sticharion*), and over it also a cloak (*phelonion*), but not a collar (*epitrachelion*), rather an *orarion*.”

Agmonius incorrectly explains *ὠράριον εὐκτικὸν μέλος* as “a prayerful psalm.”

The origin of this word is wholly Roman; it was transferred into the Church from secular usage. Balsamon’s etymology is therefore false, as the very learned Casaubon correctly observed in his notes on Vopiscus, where he explains with great learning what the *orarion* means among secular and sacred Latin, Greek, and Syriac writers.

See also what Lipsius formerly observed concerning the *orarion* in book II of his *Select Essays*, chapter 10.

### “To take portions” (*μέρη αἴρειν*)

Among the gentiles, portions of sacrificial dishes were set out for each person; these portions were called *μερίδες* by Athenaeus, and the banqueters took them for themselves.

This canon prohibits Christians from doing the same at the *agapae*, or banquets, that were prepared in the church. It is easy to infer from what we noted above on canon 70 that at those meals everyone was supposed to eat together indiscriminately from the food that had been set out.

### “Agapae must not be held in the churches” (*οὐ δεῖ ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ἀγάπας ποιεῖν*)

Chrysostom testifies, in his sermon on Paul’s saying “There must be heresies” (First Corinthians, chapter 11), that agapae were formerly held in the church after the sacred assembly.

He says:

> “After all the faithful had gathered, heard the teachings, prayed, and shared in the mysteries, they did not immediately go home when the assembly was dismissed. Rather, the wealthy brought food and provisions from their houses, invited the poor, and made the tables common—common meals and common banquets in the church itself. Thus, from sharing the table and from reverence for the place, they were stimulated on every side to reverence for God.”

### “That Christians must not Judaize” (*ὅτι οὐ δεῖ χριστιανοὺς ἰουδαΐζειν*)

This part of the canon is missing from Tilius’s published codex. We have restored it from an unpublished Greek text of the Royal Library, inserted in the commentaries of Theodore Balsamon and John Zonaras.

### “To keep the Lord’s Day, if they are able” (*κυριακὴν εἴγε δύναιντο σχολάζειν*)

Theodore Balsamon writes concerning this canon:

> “The fathers did not command that people abstain from work on the day named after the Lord as an absolute obligation; rather, they added, ‘if the faithful are able.’ For if someone works on the Lord’s Day because of poverty or some other necessity, he is not to be prejudiced on that account.”

Constantine likewise says in law III, *On Holidays*, where he orders everyone to rest on the day of the sun, but prudently exempts agricultural work in which delay or postponement would cause great danger:

> “Those living in the countryside may freely and lawfully devote themselves to cultivating the fields, since it frequently happens that grain cannot be committed to the furrows, or vines to their trenches, more suitably on another day.”

Harmenopulus, in the *Handbook*, says:

> “On Sunday and on the other feast days, judges and everyone else are to rest, except farmers.”

The emperor Leo, however, issued a law ordering that farmers too should rest on Sunday.

### “To bathe in a bathhouse with women” (*ἐν βαλανείῳ μετὰ γυναικῶν ἀπολούεσθαι*)

Hesiod, book II of *Works and Days*, commands that men should not wash their bodies in a women’s bath:

> “Nor should a man cleanse his body in a woman’s bath.”

Aelius Spartianus relates in the *Life of Hadrian* that the emperor Hadrian constructed bathhouses separately for the sexes.

Clement of Alexandria, book III of the *Paedagogue*, chapter 5, censures the lack of restraint of those women who use the common bath with men.

Cyprian, in his treatise *On the Dress of Virgins*, prohibits virgins from attending mixed baths:

> “What of those women who enter mixed baths, who expose bodies dedicated to modesty and chastity to curious eyes for the sake of lust, who shamefully see naked men and are themselves seen naked by men? Do they not themselves offer enticement to vice?”

The emperor Justinian also counts among the legitimate grounds for divorce the case in which a woman dares to bathe together with men—*ἀνδράσι συλλούεσθαι*, “to share a bath with men”—in Novel 22, chapter 16, and law 11 of the *Code*, *On Repudiations*.

### To call angels

This kind of superstition was already prevalent in the time of Saint Paul at Colossae, a city of Phrygia under the metropolitan see of Laodicea, as he himself testifies in his Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2, verse 18: “Let no one disqualify you through the worship of angels.” Explaining this passage, Theodoret refers to the meaning of this canon in these words:

“Those who defended the Law,” he says, “also led people to worship angels, saying that the Law had been given through them. This vice, however, remained for a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. Accordingly, the synod also which assembled at Laodicea, the metropolis of Phrygia, prohibited by law that they should pray to angels and abandon our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 58:

“The Church,” he says, “receiving various benefits from God throughout the whole world, accomplishes them in the name of Christ—not by angelic invocations, but directing her prayers purely, clearly, and openly to the Lord who made all things, and to the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Origen, *Against Celsus*, book 8:

“We find that, having learned to call these angels by their office, they are sometimes called gods in the sacred Scriptures because of a certain divinity. But this is not so that we should be commanded to worship or honor with divine honors those who minister and bring us the things of God, instead of God. For every petition, prayer, intercession, and thanksgiving must be sent up to the God who is over all, through the living Word and God, the High Priest over all angels.”

Augustine, *On Heresies*, 39, relates that there were ancient heretics who were also called Angelics. “The Angelics,” he says, “inclined toward the worship of angels.” Epiphanius also mentions the *Angelici* in *Against Heresies*, 60.

He further testifies that the Essenes, Jewish heretics, rendered worship to angels. This is shown by the formula of the oath required of them, “to preserve the names of the angels,” as Josephus reports in book 2 of *The Jewish War*, chapter 7.

### Astrologers

Sozomen, book 3, chapter 5, writes that a certain Eusebius of Emesa was accused because he professed that branch of astronomy which predicts the outcomes of events:

“He was accused,” he says, “of practicing that part of astronomy which they call *apotelesmatic*”—that is, astrology concerned with determining effects or outcomes.

For this reason Aquila, a Jewish Christian, was expelled from the Church, as Epiphanius reports in *On Weights and Measures*:

“Aquila,” he says, “believed in Christianity. But he did not abandon his former disposition—namely, his belief in vain astrology, which he had studied thoroughly. Instead, he examined every day the horoscope of his birth. Though reproved by the teachers and reprimanded for this, he did not correct himself; rather, he opposed them even more obstinately.
