He was therefore expelled from the Church again as useless for salvation.”

### Wearing phylacteries

This canon commands that those who make phylacteries and those who use phylacteries be expelled from the Church.

Nicholas I, pope of Rome, in his response to the Bulgarians, chapter 79:

“You report that it is customary among you for sick persons to receive and wear a certain pendant binding beneath the throat in order to obtain health, and you ask whether we should henceforth order this to be done. We not only do not order it to be done, but forbid by every means that it should occur. Such bindings are phylacteries invented by demonic cunning and are proved to be bonds of human souls. Therefore, those who use them are struck by apostolic decrees with an anathema and are commanded to be driven from the Church.”

Saint Basil, in his homily on Psalm 45, condemns amulets marked with characters. Chrysostom, in Homily 43 on Matthew, chapter 23, attacks those who in his own time wished to appear holier by means of phylacteries hung around the neck.

“Priests,” he says, “because they wish to appear righteous before men, tie phylacteries around their necks; some even attach a portion of the Gospel in writing. Tell me, foolish priest: is the Gospel not read daily in the church and heard by the people? If the Gospels are of no benefit to him in their hearing, how can they save him when hung around his neck? Furthermore, where is the power of the Gospel—in the shapes of the letters or in the understanding of their meaning? If in the shapes, then you do well to hang it around your neck; but if in the understanding, then it is more beneficial when placed in the heart than when hung around the neck,” and so forth.

### He shall accuse himself

Saint Paul uses this formula of speech in his Epistle to Titus, chapter 3, verse 11:

“Reject a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned.”

Jerome, commenting on that passage of the Apostle, says:

“For this reason he is called self-condemned: for a fornicator, adulterer, murderer, and those guilty of other vices are expelled from the Church by priests; but heretics pronounce judgment upon themselves, withdrawing from the Church of their own will. Their withdrawal appears to be a condemnation imposed by their own conscience.”

Eusebius of Emesa, in his homily *On the Repentance of the Ninevites*:

“He who is destined to please God is displeasing to himself; in a certain sense, under the judgment of his private knowledge, he is both witness and accuser against himself.”

So also canon 29 of the sixth Council of Carthage:

“If anyone who has been excommunicated presumes to receive communion before being heard, he shall be judged to have pronounced upon himself the sentence of condemnation.”

See also what the learned R. Fornerius observed on this subject in book 6 of *Daily Matters*, chapter 21.

### Those who eat dry food

Epiphanius also mentions *xerophagy* in his *Summary of Catholic Doctrine*:

“For the six days of Passover all the people continue in the eating of dry foods—that is, at that time they use bread, salt, and water until evening.”

A little later:

“And thus they remain in the same eating of dry foods.”

Socrates, book 5, chapter 22, where he discusses the various and differing observances of fasts:

“Some partake only of dry bread.”

Tertullian, *To Scapula*:

“When have even our kneelings and fasts failed to drive away droughts?”

And in *Against the Psychics*, chapter 13:

“It is well, then, that bishops also customarily impose fasts upon the whole people—not, I say, deliberately for the collection of contributions, as your own greed demands, but sometimes for some reason arising from ecclesiastical concern. Therefore, if by a human edict you all practice humility together, how can you reproach in us the very unity of fasts, dry-eating, and stations?”

The Greek scholiast on Harmenopulus, section 5, title 3:

“The faster condemns the fornicator to two years, if he fasts only until evening each day and eats dry foods.”

### Canon 158 [ρνηʹ]

We restored this canon, which is lacking in the commonly circulated manuscript of Tillet, from the manuscript copies of Balsamon and Zonaras. It is also found in all the Latin editions of the Council of Laodicea.

### The thymelic performers

Isidore interprets *thymelici* as stage musicians who played before others on organs, lyres, and citharas. They were so called because in ancient times they stood in the orchestra and sang upon the platform called the *thymele*.

Julius Pollux, *Onomasticon*, book 4:

“The stage belongs particularly to the actors, but the orchestra belongs to the chorus; in it is also the *thymele*, whether it is a kind of tribunal or an altar”—that is, an elevated place where the actors danced.

Phrynichus, in his *Selection of Attic Words*, says that *thymele* was the name for “a place in the theater from which flute-players, cithara-players, and certain others competed.”

Vitruvius, book 5, chapter 8:

“Among the Greeks, tragic and comic actors perform their parts on the stage; the other performers carry out their activities throughout the orchestra. Hence, in Greek, the performers are separately called *scenici* and *thymelici*.”

The *thymelici* are also mentioned in book 10 of the Digest, *On Promises*; book 4 of the Digest, *On Those Notorious for Infamy*; and the final title of the Theodosian Code, *On Spectacles*. They are called *thymelitae* in book 21, *On Bakers*, and book 5, *On Stage Performers*, of the Theodosian Code.

### But periodeutae

We have corrected this passage from the manuscript copies of the Royal Library. The commonly circulated manuscript of Tillet reads incorrectly, “or periodeutae.”

Balsamon explains this canon in these words:

“Other canons have determined that village bishops and presbyters should be established in villages and rural districts. The present canon, however, orders that *periodeutae* be appointed, and not bishops, so that the dignity of the episcopate may not become cheap and despised. The *periodeutae* are those who today are appointed by bishops as exarchs. For they travel about, supervise spiritual faults, and perfect the faithful.”

Zonaras says:

“They are called *periodeutae* because they go about and perfect the faithful who do not possess a proper see.”

Justinian also mentions the *periodeutae* after the Council of Chalcedon, in book 42 of the Code, *On Bishops and Clergy*:

“We decree, as has been established by the divine canons, that neither a bishop, nor a village bishop, nor a periodeutes, nor a presbyter, nor any other cleric of whatever rank may be ordained in exchange for a payment.”

They are mentioned in the Council of Laodicea and in other ancient synods. It is therefore clear that *periodeutae* must be distinguished from village bishops, with whom some commonly confuse them.

Thus *periodeutae* in the Church are circuit-riders or visitors who, as vicars of bishops, visit and travel through the regions subject to the cities, while possessing no proper see, as Zonaras says.

Physicians are likewise called *periodeutae*, “circuit-riders,” as the old translator renders the term in book 6, section 1, of the Digest, *On Excusing Guardians*: they go around the city to restore people to health and practice the art of medicine.

Among the Latins, Gregory I mentions visitors in letter 2 of book 3, addressed to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse:

“Let the visitors of the churches,” he says, “and their clergy, who are worn out with them through the parishes not belonging to their own city, receive from you some assistance for their labor.”

John II, pope of Rome, also mentions them in letter 3 to the bishops of Gaul, which appears in volume 2 of the Councils.

### Private psalms must not be recited

Eusebius, book 2 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17, testifies that the early Christians, in addition to the divine Scriptures, used to compose and sing certain psalms and hymns to God:

“They compose songs and hymns to God, shaping them in every kind of meter and melody with rhythms of a more solemn character.”

And in book 5, chapter 28:

“How many psalms and hymns, written from ancient times by faithful brothers, hymn Christ, the Word of God, confessing him as God?”

The same author, book 7, chapter 30, speaking of Paul of Samosata:

“He abolished the psalms which were sung in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, as though they were recent compositions and the work of recent men.”

Eusebius also reports, in book 3, chapter 16, and book 4, chapter 23, that the letter of Clement, pope of Rome, written to the Corinthians, was formerly customarily read in the Church.

But once writings other than the sacred Scriptures had been admitted into the Church, many things gradually entered—some corrupted by the ignorant, others perverted and falsely fabricated by heretics—as those experienced in ecclesiastical history know. This canon therefore prohibits such writings and decrees that none should be read in the Church except the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments.

### One to Philemon

These words, which are omitted from the manuscript of Tillet, have been restored from the manuscript copies of Balsamon and Zonaras. Otherwise, the number of Paul’s epistles included in this canon would not be complete.

They are also found in the old Latin edition of the Council of Laodicea, in the first volume of the Councils, and in the collection of Isidore Mercator.

### The seven canons of the council held at Constantinople

These seven canons of the First Council of Constantinople are found in the commonly circulated manuscript of Tillet, in the manuscript copies of Balsamon and Zonaras, and in the first volume of the Greek and Latin editions of the Ecumenical Councils published at Rome in 1608 by the authority of Pope Paul V.

### Administration

The word *diocese* means nothing other than administration. In ancient usage the Greeks called by this name any territory or province in which a governor or praetor customarily administered justice and held assizes.

Strabo demonstrates this in book 13, when speaking of Phrygia and other regions of Asia:

“The Romans did not divide these places according to tribes, but arranged the administrative districts in another way, in which they held markets and administered justice.”

[Note: Perhaps read *ἀγορὰς* (“markets”).]

In the same sense he reports that the Cibyratic diocese was counted among the largest dioceses of Asia:

“The Cibyratic is reckoned among the greatest administrative districts of Asia.”

Cicero uses the word in this sense in his letter to Thermus:

“If Genucilius has any dispute with some inhabitant of the Hellespont, I ask that you refer it to that diocese.”

And in his letter to Publius Servilius, concerning himself as proconsul:

“From my province of Cilicia, which you know was assigned three Asian dioceses.”

After Constantine divided the empire, the designation *diocese* acquired a broader meaning. It then referred to the administration of several provinces together.

Theodore Balsamon says in his commentary on canon 9 of the Council of Chalcedon:

“A diocese is one that contains many provinces within itself.”

In this sense dioceses are frequently mentioned in the *Notitia Dignitatum* and in the imperial constitutions, where dioceses and provinces are repeatedly distinguished. Theodosius clearly indicates this in book 14 of the Code, *On Patrimonial Estates*:

“We order that all those who, in any diocese, province, or city, have possessed property for forty years under any title or without title need fear no action.”

This political division of the Roman world was transferred by a kind of imitation from the state to the Church. Hence dioceses are frequently mentioned by writers on ecclesiastical affairs and throughout this code, in canons 169, 178, 187, 195, and 206, as well as in the acts of the Council of Ephesus:

“Bishops gathered from different dioceses and provinces.”

We shall discuss these matters more fully in our *Sacred and Political Geography*, which, God willing, we shall soon publish.

### To have the bishop of Constantinople possess the privileges of honor

See above, canon 6: “the order of honor.”

Justinian, imperial novella 131, chapter 2:

“We decree, in accordance with the definitions of the ecclesiastical canons, that the most holy pope of elder Rome be first among all priests; that the most blessed archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, hold second place after the holy apostolic see of elder Rome; and that he be honored above all the other sees.”

### The volume of the Westerners

By “the volume of the Westerners” he means the exposition of the faith sent to Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, and to the other bishops of the West from the synod held at Antioch under Meletius in the year 378.

### Heretics may not bring accusations

Justinian issued a law that heretics should not be allowed to give testimony against the orthodox, book 21 of the Code, *On Heretics*:

“We decree that, in litigation against the orthodox, testimony may not be admitted from a person bearing the name of heretic, nor from those who practice Jewish superstition—whether both parties are orthodox or only one of them is.”

Athanasius, *Apology 2*:

“They are Meletians, of course, who present themselves as accusers—men wholly unworthy of belief, being both schismatics and enemies of the Church.”

### At a greater synod of the bishops of the diocese

Canon 91 of this code says “a greater synod of bishops,” that is, a synod of the diocese.

Thus in the acts of the Council of Ephesus:

“The synod assembled at Alexandria from the Egyptian diocese.”

Likewise:

“The holy synod of the Eastern diocese.”

A synod of a diocese is also mentioned in book 23 of the Theodosian Code, *On Bishops and Clergy*:

“If there are matters arising from certain minor disagreements and lesser offenses that pertain to religious observance, let them be heard in their proper places and by the synods of their own diocese.”

That the Council of Aquileia, presided over by Ambrose of Milan, was of this kind is clear from the letter of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, in which they order the bishops of the diocese of Italy to assemble for a council in the city of Aquileia.

### The eight canons of the council held at Ephesus

These eight canons of the Council of Ephesus are found in the manuscript of Tillet, in the manuscript copies of Balsamon and Zonaras, and in the acts of the Council of Ephesus in volume 1 of the Ecumenical Councils published at Rome in 1608—namely, the first six on page 499, and the final two on pages 442 and 497.

They are entirely absent from the Latin manuscript of the Canons of the Roman Church. Therefore, in order to fill this gap, John Wendelstinus, who first arranged for the Roman manuscript to be printed at Mainz in 1525, writes that he added to it the synodical letter of the Council of Ephesus together with the twelve chapters against Nestorius. But he did not notice that this synodical letter and the twelve anathemas appended to it do not belong to the Council of Ephesus, but only to Cyril and the synod of the diocese of Egypt. This is shown by the superscription of that letter, which is found in Greek and Latin among the acts of the Council of Ephesus published at Rome in 1608 and in the manuscript of the distinguished gentleman Peter Stella, in these words:

“To the most reverent and God-beloved fellow-minister Nestorius, Cyril and the synod assembled at Alexandria from the Egyptian diocese send greetings in the Lord.”

That is, as the old manuscript written in capital letters in the library of the distinguished gentleman John Bochard, lord of Champigny, who now serves as ambassador at Venice for the Most Christian King, has it:

“Cyril, bishop, to the holy brother Nestorius, bishop, and the synod assembled at Alexandria from the Egyptian diocese: greetings in the Lord.”

### The arrogance of secular authority

So the African Fathers wrote in their synodical letter to Boniface, pope of Rome, when the question concerned appeals from across the sea:

“We trust, with the assistance of the mercy of the Lord our God, that under your holiness presiding over the Roman Church we shall no longer have to endure this arrogance.”

And in the letter to Celestine, pope of Rome, which is found in the same place:

“Do not send your clerical agents to everyone who asks; do not grant them this power, lest we appear to introduce into the Church of Christ the smoky arrogance of the world. The Church presents the light and day of simplicity and humility to those who desire to see God.”

These synodical letters are found in the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church* and in volume 1 of the Councils.

Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, repeats the same words in his apologetic rescript to Hadrian II, pope of Rome, chapter 10, in the first volume of the *Imperial Constitutions* recently published by Melchior Goldast. The issue there concerned Hincmar of Laon and appeals from beyond the Alps:

“It is also written,” he says, “in the aforesaid letter sent to us in your name concerning Hincmar, as follows: ‘We wish and, by apostolic authority, command that Hincmar, bishop of Laon, relying upon your power, come to the threshold of the saints and to our clemency,’ and so forth.

“When we reread these words, although we find that they were spoken contrary to the custom of your predecessors and forebears—namely, that they introduce the shadowy arrogance of the world into their Church, which offers the light and day of simplicity and humility to those who desire to see the Lord—we nevertheless did not doubt your intention, since what is appropriate after deliberation can easily be stolen from the human mind.”

Saint Augustine also uses the word *arrogance* in book 2 of *On Baptism*, chapter 3, where he writes that earlier councils may be corrected by later ones:

“When experience of matters reveals what had been closed and knowledge discloses what had remained hidden, without any arrogance of sacrilegious pride, without any swollen-necked haughtiness, and without any contention born of envious ill will, but with holy humility, Catholic peace, and Christian charity.”

### Freedom

Saint Paul, Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 5, verse 1:

“Stand fast in the freedom with which Christ has set us free, and do not again become entangled in the yoke of slavery.”

### Paramonarius

*Mansionarius* is correctly translated in this way by Dionysius Exiguus in the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church*.

Justinian, book 46 of the Code, *On Bishops and Clergy*, also lists *paramonarii* among those who administer ecclesiastical property.

The *paramonarii* are stewards or managers of estates, as the learned jurist Jacques Cujas writes in his commentary on title 5 of the Code, *On Bishops and Clergy*.

A *villicus*, according to Isidore, book 9 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4, is properly the governor of a country estate; hence the name *villicus* derives from *villa*. Sometimes, however, *villicus* signifies not the governor of an estate but, in Cicero’s usage, the steward of an entire household—that is, the administrator of all estates and villas.

Varro, book 1 of *On Agriculture*, chapter 2, calls a *villicus* the person who is in charge of a rural district and responsible for the whole agricultural operation.

The *paramonarii*, therefore, or *mansionarii*, receive their name from *mansio*. A *mansio* is a dwelling, an abode, a place of residence.

In legal texts and in Symmachus, Sidonius, Cassiodorus, and Lampridius, *mansiones* are “changes” or establishments, which are called *mansionatica*—that is, lodgings to which travelers withdraw for the night.

Gregory, in the *Dialogues*, book 3, *On the Lives of the Saints*:

“The apostle then appeared to her in a dream and said to her: ‘Go to the church’s *pro-mansionarius*, called Sabundius, the *mansionarius*, and he himself will give you health.’”

Apuleius, book 4:

“We were to have a lodging very near at hand, and the end of the entire journey was to be rest.”

These lodgings are separate from cities and towns. Hence the words *mansion*, *mansuarii*, and *massarii* also occur in the laws and histories of the Franks and Germans.

### For the guardianship of minors

Justinian, novella 123, chapter 5, prohibits bishops and monks from becoming guardians or curators of any person under any law.

He permits presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons, however, by right of agnation or cognation, to undertake lawful guardianship and any care which they may wish to assume voluntarily and of their own accord. They therefore undertake no guardianship or curatorship unwillingly, lest they be drawn away from prayers and sacred duties.

Cyprian, book 1, letter 9:

“It was established long ago in a council of bishops that no one should appoint any member of the clergy or minister of God as guardian or curator in his will, since each person honored with the divine priesthood, and all who are appointed to clerical ministry, ought to serve only at the altar and in sacrifices and devote themselves to prayers and supplications.”

Emperor Leo, novella 68:

“The ancient legislators decided that neither monks nor those whom the sacred order claims for itself should participate in such affairs. For they understood that those devoted to divine service ought to be free from external occupations and distractions. No one is unaware how much the upbringing of children and the management of other affairs possess the power to distract and draw away those who are occupied with them from the service owed to God. For, generally speaking, those who undertake this guardianship are bound for their whole lives to these burdensome cares.”

[Note: The construction of the phrase is unclear if the reading is *οὐ πόνῳ*. Perhaps *δυσπόνῳ* should be read.]

It is nevertheless possible, according to the aforementioned novella 68 of Leo the Wise, for bishops and monks to be executors of wills; he says that these are also called *epitropoi*, that is, guardians of last wills. They are merely administrators and in no way ought to be guardians or curators of persons or property.

### The person being ordained shall be publicly announced

“Let the person who is to be ordained be announced in the Church.”

That is, after being publicly announced or named, as canon 38 of this code says, he is to be assigned to the ministry of this or that Church. Later authorities expressed the same idea by saying that no one should be ordained without a title.

Lampridius uses *announced* in the same sense in his life of Alexander Severus:

“When someone wished either to appoint governors for the provinces, or to make prefects or procurators—that is, financial administrators—he published their names, urging the people that if anyone knew of any crime, he should establish it by clear evidence; if he did not prove it, he would incur the death penalty. He also said that, since Christians and Jews did this in publicly announcing priests who were to be ordained, it was a serious matter that it was not done with governors of provinces, to whom both the fortunes and the lives of men would be entrusted.”

Such was the ancient custom of the Church in the ordination of bishops: the votes were requested not only from the clergy but also from the people. In order to inquire into everyone’s judgment concerning the person who was to be ordained, his name was publicly announced to the people, with everyone granted the opportunity to bring against him whatever charges they wished.

This is what Balsamon writes in his commentary on canon 5 of the Council of Laodicea:

“In the votes, matters are often mentioned which are unworthy, for the sake of those who are casting the votes.”

And Zonaras says the same in his commentary on canon 1 of the Apostles, whose words we quoted above in the note on canon 109.

Traces of this ancient custom also remain in Cyprian, book 1, letter 4. After recounting how Eleazar, son of Aaron, had been made priest, he says:

“Before the whole assembly God commands the priest to be appointed; that is, he teaches and shows that priestly ordinations ought to take place only with the knowledge of the assembled people, so that, in the presence of the people, the crimes of the wicked may be exposed or the merits of the good proclaimed, and so that the ordination may be just and lawful when it has been examined by the vote and judgment of all.”

A little later he says:

“Let the bishop be chosen in the presence of the people, who know the life of each person most fully and have observed the conduct of every individual.”

In book 5, letter 5, he addresses the presbyters, deacons, and the entire people in these words:

“In ordaining clergy, dearest brothers, we customarily consult you beforehand and weigh the character and merits of each person by common deliberation.”

Among the ancient Romans there was a similar law, the Domitian law concerning priesthoods, proposed by the tribune of the people, Domitius Ahenobarbus:

“Let it not be the priestly colleges that co-opt whomever they wish; rather, let this privilege belong to the people.”

There was also the Licinian law, proposed by Quintus Licinius:

“Let the co-optation of priests be transferred from their own college to the people.”

### The exarch of the diocese

There were formerly three grades of bishops: bishops of cities, metropolitans of provinces, and exarchs of dioceses, as is clear from this canon and from canon 195 of this code.

Thus, in the Second Council of Antioch, preserved among the acts of the Council of Chalcedon in volume 2 of the Councils, the bishop of Antioch is called “exarch of the Eastern diocese.”

The exarchs of dioceses are patriarchs, to whom entire dioceses were assigned. Zonaras confirms this in his commentary on the present canon:

“They say that the exarchs of the dioceses are the patriarchs.”

But, I hope, there will be another occasion for discussing these matters.

Furthermore, Justinian confirms this canon’s definition concerning the order of judicial proceedings in book 46 of the Code, *On Bishops and Clergy*; book 30 of the Code, *On the Hearing of Bishops*; and novella 123, chapter 22.

### The poor are to travel with letters of peace

*Letters of peace* are also mentioned in canons 86 and 87 of this code above.

Gregory Nazianzen, book 1 *Against Julian*, testifies to the frequent use of such letters among Christians:

“He also established inns and guesthouses, and added humanity toward those in need—not only that which consists in other forms of assistance, but also that which is contained in epistolary tokens, by which we send those who are in need from one nation to another.”

Sozomen, speaking of the same Julian, book 5, chapter 16:

“He is said especially to have imitated the tokens of episcopal letters, by which travelers customarily receive one another, wherever they go and from whatever place they come, as guests, and are deemed worthy of assistance, as acquaintances and dear friends because of the testimony of the sign.”

*Epistolary tokens* and *tokens of letters* were certain signs, symbols, marks, or tokens used by bishops in composing ecclesiastical letters so that fraud might not enter.

Thus Procopius uses *to write symbolically*:

“They sent to the Achaean letters written in cipher.”

Latin ecclesiastical writers call such letters *formatae*, because they were composed according to a fixed form and with fixed marks.

Accordingly, travelers who carried such epistolary tokens, or *formatae* letters, were received as guests wherever they went, and these letters served them as provisions for their journey.

Lucian, in *The Peregrine*:

“He therefore set out on a second journey, intending to wander, believing that he had sufficient provisions stored up in the Christians. Escorted by them wherever he went, he lived in complete abundance and was supported in this way for some time.”

Hence Tertullian called the reciprocal token of hospitality “the hospitality token,” borrowing the term from the Greeks.

Among the ancient pagans it was customary for the bond of hospitality to be contracted not only between private persons but also between peoples and cities. This kind of friendship was called *proxeny* or *private proxeny*. Among the Greeks this kind of friendship was called *proxeny* or *private proxeny*; among the Latins, public and private hospitality. Its sign and pledge was the token of hospitality. Through this covenant, mutual friendships were cultivated among them and were transmitted even to their descendants.

Plautus, in *The Carthaginian*:

> If that is so, if you wish to exchange  
> A token and establish hospitality, here—I have brought one.  
> Come, show it here; it matches perfectly, for I have one at home.  
> Welcome, guest! A thousand greetings, for your father—  
> Your father, then, Antidamas, was my guest;  
> This was once my token of hospitality with him.

A token was given to guests so that the guest might be recognized. Hence one who violated the right of hospitality was said to have broken the token.

The same author, in *The Cistellaria*:

> Go and seek where your oath will find sufficient assistance;  
> Here among us, Alcesimarchus, you have already broken the token.

### Commendatory letters

*Commendatory writings* are mentioned in canon 191 of this code.

Saint Paul refers to such letters in his Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 3, verse 1:

“Do we need, as some do, commendatory letters to you or commendatory letters from you?”

They are called *commendatory*, that is, letters of recommendation, because they are given to clerics or laypersons who have been separated from communion, or to unknown persons departing for another city, recommending them to the bishop of that place as persons released from censures or as faithful Christians.

Zonaras, here and in his commentary on canon 13 of the Apostles:

“Commendatory letters are those handed to clerics or laypersons who have been separated from communion, or to unknown persons departing for another city, and which recommend these men to the bishop in that city as having been released from penalties or as being faithful.”

The Greek scholiast on Harmenopulus, in the *Epitome of the Canons*, section 2, title 3, and section 3, title 1, says:

“Commendatory letters are those given to persons subject to a penalty for their acquittal, by which they are recommended to another bishop for communion.”

See also what the very learned C. Labbaeus inserted from Matthew Blastares into his observations on the *Synopsis of the Basilics*.

It should moreover be observed that the ancient Christians exercised careful examination when receiving commendatory letters, so that fraud might not enter, testing the faith of those who carried them.

Canon 3 of what are called the Apostolic Canons deals with this matter. Lucian indicates this custom in *The Peregrine*, speaking of the Christians:

“They despise everything equally, and regard as common property whatever they receive for common use from anyone who brings such things without any careful examination of his credentials.”

The Council of Elvira likewise establishes this in canon 58:

“It has been decided that everywhere, and especially in the place where the bishop presides over the chief see, those who present letters of communion should be questioned whether everything is in good order, and should confirm it by their own testimony.”

### Unknown persons

We have corrected this passage from the manuscript of Zonaras in the Royal Library.

Matthew Blastares also confirms this correction when he gives the meaning of this canon in the manuscript of the distinguished President August Thuanus:

“The seventh canon of Antioch commands that foreign and unknown clerics must not minister without commendatory letters from their own bishop.”

The commonly circulated manuscript of Tillet and the manuscript of Balsamon read incorrectly, “readers.”

### A woman deacon of forty years

Saint Paul, in the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 5, verse 9, establishes the age of widows or deaconesses as sixty years:

“Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years old.”

Following the same principle, Emperor Theodosius established:

“Women are not to be entrusted with the ministry unless they have passed their sixtieth year, according to the explicit command of the Apostle Paul.”

[Note: The printed Greek reads *τὰς γυναῖκας ὑπὲρ ἑξήκοντα ἔτη γένοιτο*, but the editor thinks it should read *εἰ μὴ ὑπὲρ ἑξήκοντα ἔτη γίνοιντο* (“unless they attain more than sixty years”).]

Valentinian, book 1, title 27 of the Theodosian Code, *On Bishops and Clergy*:

“No woman is to be admitted to the company of deaconesses before completing sixty years, in accordance with the Apostle’s command.”

Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, speaking of widows:

“To this office, besides those over sixty years of age, only women who have had one husband—that is, who have been married once—are chosen, and also mothers and certain nurses of children.”

Jerome, book 2 of his commentary on Isaiah:

“A widow is not supported by the provisions of the Church unless she is sixty years old and possesses maturity both of conduct and of age.”

Later, permission was granted for them to be chosen at fifty years, in novella 6, chapter 6; also at forty years, both in this canon and in novella 123, chapter 13.
δεξαμένη τὴν χειροθεσίαν] “Having received the laying-on-of-hands.” Here χειροθεσία is understood as the laying on of hands for blessing, not ordination. See the note on canon 19 and 115 above.

τῇ λειτουργίᾳ] “Concerning the ministry.” The author of the Apostolic Constitutions discusses the ministry of deaconesses in book III, chapter 15 [Col. 0133B]:

“Choose a faithful and holy deaconess for the ministry to women, for it sometimes happens that you cannot send a deacon to women in certain households because of unbelievers. You shall therefore send a female deacon, because of the thoughts of evil men; for we need a deaconess for many purposes, and first of all when women are being enlightened.”

And Epiphanius, *Against the Collyridians*, heresy 79:

“Καὶ ὅτι μὲν διακονισσῶν τάγμα ἐστὶν εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, ἀλλ` οὐχὶ εἰς τὸ ἱερατεύειν, οὐδέ τι ἐπιχείρειν ἐπιτρέπειν· ἕνεκεν δὲ σεμνότητος τοῦ γυναικείου γένους, ἢ δι` ὥραν λούτρου, ἢ ἐπισκέψεως πάθους, ἢ πόνου, καὶ ὅτε γυμνωθείη σῶμα γυναίου, ἵνα μὴ ὑπὸ ἀνδρῶν ἱερουργούντων θεαθείη, ἀλλ` ὑπὸ τῆς διακονούσης.”

“The order of deaconesses does indeed exist in the Church, but not so that they may offer sacrifice, nor may they be permitted to undertake anything of that kind; rather, for the sake of the dignity of the female sex, or for the time of bathing, or for visiting sickness or suffering, and when a woman’s body has been stripped, so that it may not be seen by men performing sacred rites, but by the woman serving.” [Col. 0133C]

And in the summary of the whole work, where he describes the Church of his own time, p. 465:

“Καὶ διακόνισσαι δὲ καθίστανται εἰς ὑπηρεσίαν γυναικῶν μόνον διὰ τὴν σεμνότητα, ἂν χρεία κατασταίη λούτρου ἕνεκα, ἢ ἐπισκέψεως σωμάτων.”

“Deaconesses are appointed solely for the service of women, because of dignity, reverence, or modesty, and charity, if there should be need on account of baptism or for the examination of bodies.”

Jerome, in his letter to Nepotianus, says: “The Church supports many old women who perform service for the sick and receive a benefit by ministering.”

Add Justinian’s Novel 6, chapter 6, where he states that deaconesses minister at baptism. What, however, the ministry of deaconesses at baptism consisted of is indicated by the Fourth Synod of Carthage, canon 12:

“Widows or religious women who are chosen for the ministry of baptizing women are to be so instructed in their office that they can teach ignorant and rustic women in suitable, clear, and intelligible speech when they are to be baptized, how they should answer the baptizer, and how they should live after receiving baptism.” [Col. 0133D]

They also cared for the poor and those bound in prison, and many other works of piety were entrusted to them. That office of deaconesses, however, has now been removed from the Church.

ἐκδίκου] “Concerning the defender.” In former times, the emperors appointed to churches that requested them ἔκδικοι, or defenders, who were laymen. Their office was to ward off every act of violence and disturbance from the church and its pastors, and to ensure that nothing was done in the church by force or through sordid means. See Novel 56. The *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, canon 75:

“It has seemed necessary to ask the emperors, on account of the distress of the poor, whose troubles continually weary the churches, that defenders be assigned to them, with the provision of the bishops, against the power of the wealthy.”

This canon 206, and the one immediately following it, 207, are found in the Codex of Tilius and in Balsamon and Zonaras.

ἐν τοῖς βαρβαρικοῖς] “In barbarian territory.” *In Barbarico*, that is, in the land of the Barbarians. The expression is understood in this way in the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, canon 52:

“We make no regulation concerning the province of Mauretania, because it lies at the boundaries of Africa and borders on the Barbaricum.”

So too in Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVIII: “A soldier was seen in the Barbaricum”; and in book 2 of the *Code*, *On Commerce*. The word *Barbaria* is repeatedly found in this sense in writers of Roman history. Lampridius, speaking of the frontier commanders in his *Alexander Severus*, says:

“He also added animals and slaves to these things, so that they could cultivate what they had received, lest the neighboring fields be abandoned through lack of people or because of the old age of their possessors, since they bordered on Barbaria.”

Rufus Festus, in his *Breviary*: “Trajan made Dacia beyond the Danube into a province, in the land of Barbaria.”

Gellius, book IX, chapter 12: “A Thracian man from the farthest Barbaria.”

Paulinus, letter 26 to Victricius, bishop of Rouen: “Where formerly there were wildernesses of forests and shores alike throughout the whole Barbaria of the newcomers,” and so forth.

Synesius used τὴν βάρβαρον in letter 101, where the Latin translator correctly rendered it *Barbaria*. Augustine, letter 178: “For not in Africa, nor throughout all Barbaria, but in Syria or Greece,” and so forth.

Roman writers therefore called whatever lay beyond the boundaries of the world or of the Roman Empire *Barbaricum* and *Barbaria*; they called the Roman world itself *Romania*, as the most learned Casaubon has already observed from Epiphanius in his notes on Lampridius at the passage cited. I shall add several other testimonies.

Athanasius, *To All Those Living the Solitary Life*: “μητρόπολις ἡ Ῥώμη τῆς Ῥωμανίας ἐστί”—“Rome is the metropolis of Romania.”

Epiphanius, heresy 66: “ὅρμοι τῆς ἐρυθρᾶς θαλάσσης διάφοροι, ἐπὶ τὰ στόμια τῆς Ῥωμανίας”—“The various harbors of the Red Sea lie toward the mouths of Romania.”

Likewise: “Εἰς τὰς ἄλλας πατρίδας διὰ θαλάσσης διερχόμενοι, οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰνδικῆς ἐπὶ τὴν Ῥωμανίαν ἐμπορεύονται”—“Passing by sea into other regions, those who come from India trade with Romania.”

In Constantine Porphyrogenitus, chapter 47 of *On the Administration of the Empire*: “τοὺς ἐν Ῥωμανίᾳ οἰκήσαντας”—“those who dwell in Romania”; and chapter 46. The word *Romania* is understood in this sense in Evagrius, book VI, chapter 20, and Nicephorus, book XVIII, chapter 21.

Add Orosius, book VII, [Col. 0134C] chapter 43, who, speaking of Ataulf, king of the Goths, says:

“He especially desired and ardently strove that, after the Roman name had been obliterated, he might make and call all Roman soil the empire of the Goths, and that Gothia might become what Romania had been.”

Hence Romans are everywhere contrasted with Barbarians. In the edict of Theodoric, king of Italy, chapter 43:

“Let no one transfer his own claims under any title to a powerful Roman or Barbarian”; and chapter 44: “Let no powerful Roman or Barbarian involve himself in a matter as defender or patron.”

The Romans are the ancient inhabitants; the Barbarians are the victorious newcomers. Thus in the laws of the Visigoths, book I, title 1:

“Let it be lawful for a Goth to join a Roman woman in marriage, and for a Roman to join a Gothic woman”; and book X, title 2, concerning Gothic and Roman allotments; and in the confession of the bishops, presbyters, and leading men of the Gothic people, which appears among the acts of the Third Council of Toledo:

“Whoever accepts as true the detestable document issued by us in the twelfth year of King Leovigild, in which the conversion of the Romans to the Arian heresy is contained, let him be anathema.”

And the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 13: [Col. 0134D]

“By general judgment all freedmen of the churches are forbidden henceforth, for the sake of marriage, to be joined either to freeborn Romans or to Goths.”

In these passages the name “Romans” denotes the ancient inhabitants of Spain, who before the Goths’ invasion of Spain were subject to the Roman Empire. Thus in Victor of Vita, book I of *The Vandal Persecution*, the ancient inhabitants of Africa, conquered by the Vandals, are called Romans.

So too the Gauls who were subject to the Roman Empire before the arrival of the Franks, Burgundians, and other Barbarians, as may be observed in the Salic Law, title 15: “If a Roman has despoiled a Frank,” and in King Gundobad’s preface to the Burgundian laws: “Burgundians and Romans as counts of cities or districts”; and in the Second Council of Tours, chapter 9:

“Let no one presume to ordain a Briton or a Roman as bishop in Armorica without the consent or letters of the metropolitan or the neighboring bishops.”

[Col. 0135]

# CODE OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL CANONS OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, or THE ANCIENT CODE OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

From volume II of the *Councils of Gaul* by Jacob Sirmond of the Society of Jesus, priest, p. 117.

Concerning the *Code of Canons* which was presented to King Charlemagne by Pope Hadrian when he was at Rome, in the year of Christ, as is conjectured, 787.

## [NOTE.]

[Col. 0135A] In earlier years there was first published at Ingolstadt, in volume VI of the *Ancient Reading*, and then at Cologne, in volume III of the *Councils*, an epitome of the Eastern and African canons, with a title indicating that it had been offered by Pope Hadrian to King Charlemagne, when he was at Rome, for the use of the Western Churches.

Yet it is clear that what was offered to Charlemagne was not an epitome but a complete collection: both the canons from which that epitome was subsequently compiled and the decrees of the pontiffs from Siricius to the younger Gregory. Finally, it was that very book given to Charlemagne which Pope Nicholas calls the *Code of Canons* in 519, under the heading “If of the Romans”; and which, first printed at Mainz in 1525, was later entitled in the Paris edition *The Ancient Code of the Roman Church*.

This is demonstrated by the many copies of this collection seen in the libraries of Gaul. At their beginning, as a dedication of the gift presented, there is prefixed Hadrian’s letter to Charlemagne, whose initial letters of the individual lines produce this title:

**DOMINO EXCELL. FILIO CARULO REGI HADRIANUS PAPA**  
“Pope Hadrian to his excellent lord, his son, King Charles.”

The letter itself reads as follows, both in the numerous copies I have mentioned and in the most ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain, from the time of Charlemagne himself, in the thirty-seventh year of his reign, that is, in the year of Christ 805.

## LETTER OF POPE HADRIAN TO KING CHARLEMAGNE

Prefixed in ancient copies to his *Code of Canons*.

The scepter shines with divine teaching and surpasses the glory of kingship;

Happy origin of kings, ever-blessed begetting;

[Col. 0135C] We see the mass of the law possessing the grace of praise;

From a just king is born a defender of the nourishing Church;

For heavenly discipline can never be conquered;

Already once receiving the example of his paternal kingdom,

[Col. 0136A] He triumphs, by which devoted faith rejoices in victory,

With Christ’s help and blessed Peter, the key-bearer,

He subjects all hostile peoples beneath his royal feet.

Behold, the blessed root has bestowed an equal offspring.

Gladly to worship God, ever to love the divine law,

To preserve praiseworthy faith and defend holy life,

Having as his patron the gatekeeper in the triumphs of heaven.

Trusting in his victorious power, he always perseveres.

Following the light of the teaching of the faith of the apostolic see,

The great King Charles shines in this holy see.

Enriched through him with every good, it triumphs everywhere;

He has deserved always to possess a heavenly kingdom in these things.

Taking up divine weapons, he has trampled proud nations.

[Col. 0136B] He restored the ancient gifts to his mother, the Church,

And great cities, boundaries, and various fortresses as well.

By divine power he struck down the Lombard and Herulian peoples.

Rejoicing, he embraces the faith which he received from his ancestors.

This great lineage shines throughout the whole world:

Lofty, noble, radiant, he rules diverse kingdoms.

Rejoicing and swift, he came safely to the threshold of the apostles,

And is celebrated by the entire people with abundant praises and hymns.

He earnestly asks the supreme bishop to pray for him,

That the offenses committed in his youth may be redeemed for him.

Stripped of blessed intercessions, he promised with his tongue to the Master

To preserve forever the spirit of the holy Roman Church,

[Col. 0136C] To protect the laws of his blessed protector Peter,

So that, as a suitable benefactor, he might pour out a gift at his confession.

Moreover, Bishop Hadrian of Christ foretold triumphs,

[Col. 0137A] That he would long be protected by the divine right hand, with Peter and Paul accompanying him,

They granting the sword of victory and fighting for you.

You will remain unharmed and victorious with your people; through them

You will seek entrance to the city of Pavia and enter it as a victor.

You will trample the wicked neck of the faithless King Desiderius,

Overthrowing his forces and plunging him into the abyss of the deep.

Surrounded by the kingdom of the Lombards, you will repay your gift,

The sacred gifts promised to the key-bearer of Peter’s palace,

Giving you still greater victory and honor,

To reign through the ages here with your people and with your future offspring.

Never depart from the law, observing these statutes.

[Col. 0138A] Thus far Hadrian’s letter, as it could be extracted from corrupt copies.

As for the date: since Charles came to Rome three times while Hadrian was still alive—namely, in 774, when he was besieging Pavia; again in 781, when Hadrian anointed his sons Pepin, king of Italy, and Louis, king of Aquitaine; and finally in 787, when he proceeded from there also to Capua and Benevento against the duke Grimoald—we, although the matter is uncertain, have judged that Hadrian’s code should rather be referred to the last expedition than, as others preferred, to the first, to which many things read in his letter can scarcely be made to apply.

# TO THE READER

[Col. 0137]

[Col. 0137B] We now give you in full the *Code* or *Collection of Ecclesiastical Canons* of Dionysius Exiguus, whose index alone was first published in 1609 from the manuscript codex of the most learned Nicolas Fabri. We have taken it from another ancient manuscript codex of the library of the distinguished Christoph Justel. It is the oldest monument of canon law that exists in Latin; indeed, no one can doubt that it was drawn from this source.

This collection contains almost the same canons of the councils as the Greek *Code of the Universal Church*, published by the same Justel in 1610. In addition, it contains the fifty canons called Apostolic, twenty-one of Sardica, and 138 chapters of the African, or Carthaginian, synods.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, makes an unmistakable reference to it in his *Opusculum* 55, *Capitula against Hincmar, bishop of Laon*, chapter 43, in these words:

“Who are those,” he says, “whom both the apostolic see, all the bishops throughout the world, and the entire Catholic Church call canons, and whom, from the Council of Nicaea—which is first in our codices, which our ancestors received from the apostolic see to be followed—in due order through the African Council, they retain as canons to be received, venerated, and observed?”

This was Dionysius Exiguus, who, abandoning the profane reckoning of years by Olympiads, consuls, or indictions, was the first to begin marking the dates from the Incarnation of Christ, and who composed a paschal cycle of ninety-five years. He did so under the consulship not of Flavius Mavortius, as Marianus Scotus writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 527, but of Flavius Philoxenus and Anicius Probus the younger, in indiction 3, that is, in the year of Christ 525, as Dionysius himself testifies [Col. 0137D] in his first paschal letter to Bishop Petronius, recently first published by the learned Petavius from a manuscript.

In that letter he also cites, from the sacred canons—that is, from the ancient *Code of Canons* which we now publish—and from his own translation, canon 79, which proves to be the first canon of the Council of Antioch. From these facts the order and number of the canons preserved in that code are confirmed, and it may be inferred that Dionysius had already translated these ecclesiastical canons from Greek copies.

Who, however, was the author of that ancient Greek collection of canons, which extends from Nicaea to the Council of Constantinople and whose translation Dionysius himself undertook, is unknown.

[Col. 0138B] Nevertheless, it is plainly established that the collection was older than the Council of Chalcedon. In its fourth, eleventh, and thirteenth sessions, five canons were read and cited from the collection already made and approved by the common authority of the ancestors: namely, canons 4, 83, 84, 95, and 96, which prove to be 4 of Nicaea and 4, 5, 16, and 17 of the Council of Antioch.

These canons occur in the same order and in a continuous, uninterrupted numerical sequence—which the ancients call *regular succession*—in the Greek *Code of the Canons of the Universal Church* and in this Latin collection of Dionysius Exiguus.

It is also clear from a letter prefixed by Dionysius himself to this code that the Greek collection was made before the Council of Ephesus. In it he enumerates the canons of Nicaea and of the other councils that followed, whether held before or afterward, up to the Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, in the same numerical order, that is, from the first chapter through the 165th.

It is easy for anyone to determine which those 165 canons are from the order of the councils and the succession of the canons that constituted that ancient code. For the 20 canons of the Council of Nicaea, 24 of Ancyra, 14 of Neocaesarea, 20 of Gangra, 25 of Antioch, 59 of Laodicea, and 3 of Constantinople produce, when gathered together, a total of 165.

From this we also learn that the ancients did not use the same method in numbering the canons of the councils. For from the words of the Council of Chalcedon it may be inferred that the canons cited above—1, 4, 5, 16, [Col. 0138D] and 17 of the Council of Antioch—were numbered 80, 83, 84, 95, and 96 in the ancient Greek code, whereas in the Latin collection of Dionysius Exiguus they are numbered 79, 84, 85, 96, and 97.

This difference appears to have arisen because the Council of Ancyra consists of twenty-five canons in the Greek code and the Council of Neocaesarea of fifteen, whereas in the Latin collection of Dionysius there are only fourteen and twenty-four respectively. The fourth and fifth canons of the Council of Ancyra, and likewise the thirteenth and fourteenth of Neocaesarea, are treated as one canon, as can easily be observed by comparing the two codes.

We have also appended from a very ancient manuscript codex of the same Justel the synodical letter of Saint Cyril and the council of the diocese of Egypt, assembled at Alexandria in the year 430, together with the twelve anathemas against Nestorius, from the Latin translation of Dionysius Exiguus. He prefixed to it a letter addressed to a certain Bishop Peter.

This synodical letter is attributed by Isidore and by the other Latin collectors of councils who followed him to the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, contrary to the testimony of all the ancient Greek and Latin codices. That council is known to have been held only in the following year, under the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus.

This letter exists in Greek and Latin, though in another translation, among the acts of the Council of Ephesus, session 1, and of the Fifth Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, collation 6, Roman and Cologne editions, with this heading:

[Col. 0140A] “Τῶ εὐλαβεστάτῳ, καὶ θεοφιλεστάτῳ συλλειτουργῷ Νεστορίῳ Κύριλλος, καὶ ἡ συνελθοῦσα σύνοδος ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τῆς Αἰγμπτιακῆς διοικήσεως ἐν Κυρίῳ χαίρειν.”

“Cyril and the synod assembled at Alexandria of the Egyptian diocese send greetings in the Lord to the most reverend and most God-beloved fellow minister Nestorius.”

Liberatus, archdeacon of Carthage, also mentions it in his *Breviary*, book IV:

“Cyril,” he says, “sent a synodical letter to Nestorius, in which he composed and inserted twelve chapters against his doctrine; and it begins: ‘When the Lord says, “Whoever loves his father and mother more than me is not worthy of me.”’”

Since these matters contribute to preserving the memory of canonical and ecclesiastical antiquity, reader, regard our work favorably and enjoy the benefit it provides.

# SOME TESTIMONIES CONCERNING DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS AND HIS LATIN TRANSLATION OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL CANONS

[Col. 0139]

[Col. 0139B] Cassiodorus, chapter 23 of *Divine Readings*:

“Even today the Catholic Church produces illustrious men, shining with the beauty of commendable doctrines. In our own time there was Dionysius the monk, Scythian by nation but wholly Roman in character, highly learned in both languages, who rendered into his actions the equity he had read in the books of the Lord. He had examined and understood the divine Scriptures with such carefulness that, whenever he was questioned about anything, he had a suitable answer ready without any delay.

“In him great simplicity was joined with wisdom, humility with learning, and restraint in speech with eloquence, so that he preferred himself to no one, not even to the lowest servants, although he was unquestionably worthy of conversations with kings. When requested by Stephen, bishop of Salona, he composed the ecclesiastical canons from Greek copies, in keeping with his character, which was straightforward and eloquent, with the light of great eloquence. The Roman Church now embraces these canons with the highest esteem. You too ought to read them constantly, lest you appear culpably ignorant of rules of the Church so conducive to salvation. He also translated many other works from Greek into Latin that could serve the Church’s benefit.”

Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45:

“The order of the passage of time is set out by the course of the first ten-year cycle, which Greek calculators observed from the years of the emperor Diocletian. But Dionysius, the venerable abbot of the city of Rome, endowed with no ordinary knowledge of both languages, Greek and Latin, when writing the paschal cycles, did not wish, as he himself testifies, to attach to them the memory of the impious persecutor. Rather, he chose to mark the dates from the Incarnation of our Lord [Col. 0139D] Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be more clearly known to us.”

The same author, in his *Chronicle*, or book *On the Six Ages*, under the year of the world 4480:

“Dionysius writes the paschal cycles beginning with the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 532, which is [Col. 0140B] the 248th year of Diocletian, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes.”

John Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“Dionysius, Roman abbot, surnamed Exiguus, a man great and most renowned in talent and knowledge, learned in the Holy Scriptures and nobly trained in secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin speech, an excellent computist and calculator of times, wrote several small works in Latin. Of these I have found only the following: the great paschal cycle of 532 years; he translated from Greek into Latin the life of Saint Pachomius the abbot, a book of Gregory of Emesa *On the Nature of Man*, and the writings of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo, together with certain other works. He began his cycle in the year of the Lord 531, and so forth. [Col. 0140C] He flourished under the great Justinian in the year 540.”

From the *Ecclesiastical Annals* of Cardinal Caesar Baronius, year 325, no. 123:

“If the greatest possible fidelity and skill in translating, and the utmost sincerity in publishing, are required, no edition can be demanded that is more exact and faithful than the one prepared by that great man—though surnamed Exiguus—Dionysius, whose exceptional proficiency in both languages and outstanding moral integrity Cassiodorus praises with worthy commendation.”

Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, year 525:

“Dionysius Exiguus, Scythian by nation but Roman in character, just as he was Exiguus by name but greatest in learning and holiness, lived in the time of Theodoric, king of Italy, and his successors. For in the year 527 he wrote the paschal cycle, and, abandoning the profane reckoning of years from the reign of Diocletian, the impious persecutor, he began to count from the Incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ. He also wrote a collection of the sacred canons from the councils of the Catholic Church; Martin of Braga and Cresconius later imitated him.”

# PREFACE TO THE CODE OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL CANONS OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS

[Col. 0139]

[Col. 0139D] Dionysius Exiguus sends greetings in the Lord to my venerable lord and father, Bishop Stephen.

[Col. 0140D] Although our very dear brother Laurence, through his constant and familiar exhortation, urged our smallness [Col. 0141A] to translate the ecclesiastical rules from Greek, being, I believe, offended by the confusion of the earlier translation, nevertheless I undertook the imposed labor out of consideration for your blessedness. Almighty God Christ, who in his customary mercy looks after the peoples, has bestowed upon you the dignity of the highest priesthood.

Thus, among the many ornaments of virtue with which you adorn the Church of the Lord through the holiness of your conduct, preserving inviolate the most sacred laws arranged by God’s grace in pontifical assemblies, you may govern clergy and people with perfect direction. May you not be content with the practice of our age, by which we desire more readily to know what is right than to do it; rather, joined to divine assistance, may you first accomplish what you command to be done, so that you may benefit the faithful by the most effective example.

Great indeed is the authority of one who commands, and of one who first fulfills what he has commanded, so that the discipline of the ecclesiastical order may remain unshaken and inviolable and provide all Christians access to the everlasting reward. Through it holy bishops may be fortified by the rules of their fathers, and obedient peoples imbued with spiritual examples.

At the beginning, therefore, we translated from Greek the canons called Apostolic. [Col. 0141B] Since very many have not readily assented to them, we did not wish to leave this unknown to your holiness, although certain regulations of the pontiffs afterward appear to have been taken from those canons.

Next we arranged the rules of the Council of Nicaea, and afterward those of all the councils, whether held before it or later, up to the synod of the 150 bishops who assembled at Constantinople, in numerical order, that is, from the first chapter through the 165th, as they are found in the Greek authority.

Then, adding the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon, we declare that the Greek canons end there. Moreover, so that I might not seem to withhold anything from your knowledge, the statutes of the Council of Sardica and of the African council, which have been published in Latin, are seen to be distinguished by us with their own numbers. Finally, arranging the titles of all the definitions more concisely after this preface, we have placed together, at a single glance, what was promulgated separately in the individual councils, so that we may appear to have provided some aid for investigating each matter.

# ECCLESIASTICAL RULES OF THE HOLY APOSTLES, DELIVERED THROUGH CLEMENT, PONTIFF OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0141]

## On the ordination of a bishop

### I

A bishop is to be ordained by two or three bishops.

## On the ordination of a presbyter, a deacon, and the others

[Col. 0141C]

### II

A presbyter is to be ordained by one bishop, and likewise a deacon and the other clerics.

## Nothing besides what the Lord prescribed is to be offered in the sacrifice

### III

If any bishop or presbyter, contrary to the Lord’s ordinance, offers anything else upon the altar in the sacrifice—that is, honey, or milk, or beer instead of wine, or prepared foods, or birds, or any animals, or vegetables—he is acting against the Lord’s constitution and is to be deposed at the proper time.

## Which things are to be brought to the altar not for sacrifice but for a simple blessing

### IV

Nothing may be offered at the altar except new ears of grain and grapes; and oil for the lamps and incense, that is, frankincense, at the time when the holy offering is celebrated. [Col. 0141D]

## Things that cannot be offered in churches are to be brought by the faithful to the houses of the priests

### V

All other fruits are to be sent to the bishop’s and presbyters’ house as firstfruits, and are not to be offered on the altar. It is understood, however, that they are to be divided among the bishops and presbyters, and also among the deacons and the other clerics.

## A bishop or presbyter is not to leave his wife, whom he ought to govern chastely

### VI

A bishop or presbyter must in no way cast away his own wife under the pretext of religion. If he does cast her away, he is to be excommunicated; and if he persists, he is also to be deposed.

## Priests and ministers of the altar are to abstain from worldly concerns

[Col. 0142B]

### VII

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon must in no way undertake worldly concerns; otherwise, they are to be deposed. [Col. 0142C]

## When Easter is to be celebrated

### VIII

If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon celebrates the holy day of Easter before the spring equinox with the Jews, he is to be deposed.

## Ministers of the altar are to communicate after the offering has been celebrated

### IX

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone listed in the priestly order, after the offering has been made, does not communicate, he must either state the reason, so that, if it is reasonable, he may obtain pardon; or, if he does not state it, he is to be deprived of communion, as one who has become a cause of injury to the people, giving rise to suspicion concerning the one who offered the sacrifice—that he did not offer it rightly.

## Faithful laypeople who enter the church are to communicate

[Col. 0142D]

### X

All the faithful who enter the church and hear the Scriptures, but do not remain in prayer and do not receive holy communion, are appropriately to be deprived of communion, as those who stir up disturbances in the Church.

## One is not to pray with the excommunicated

### XI

If anyone prays together with an excommunicated person, even in the same house, that person is to be deprived of communion.

## One is not to pray with condemned clerics

### XII

If anyone prays together with a condemned cleric, as though he were a cleric, that person is to be condemned.

## No member of the faithful is to be received without letters of commendation

[Col. 0143A]

### XIII

If any cleric or layperson suspended from communion, or one who is in communion, goes to another city and is received without letters of commendation, both those who received him and the one received are to be deprived of communion. In the case of the excommunicated person, however, the excommunication itself is to be prolonged, since he has lied and deceived the Church of God.

## Bishops are not to invade another’s parish

### XIV

A bishop may not invade another’s parish, leaving his own, even if he is compelled by many people. Unless perhaps a reasonable cause compels him, on the grounds that he could bring greater benefit to those established there and provide some definite advantage in the matter of religion. Even then he must not attempt this on his own, but must accomplish it by the judgment and earnest entreaty of many bishops. [Col. 0143B]

## Clerics are not to leave their own churches

### XV

If any presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the number of clerics, leaving his own parish, goes to another and, having entirely migrated, remains in a foreign parish without the knowledge of his bishop, we do not permit him to minister any longer—especially if, summoned by his bishop, he has refused to return, persisting in his disorder. Nevertheless, he is to communicate there as a layman.

## A bishop who receives another’s clerics is to be deprived of communion

### XVI

If the bishop with whom it has been established that the persons mentioned are staying, disregarding as worthless the cessation decreed against them and receiving them as clerics, is to be deprived of communion as a teacher of disorder.

## Bigamists are not to be admitted to the clergy

### XVII

If anyone, after baptism, has entered into a second marriage or has kept a concubine, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor at all one of the number of those who serve in the sacred ministry.

## One who has taken a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute is not to be admitted to the clergy

### XVIII

If anyone has taken a widow, a divorced woman, a prostitute, a female slave, or any woman from those who are devoted to public spectacles, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor belong to the number of those who serve in the sacred ministry.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] “Eorum” should be read, as in the preceding canon. EDITOR.]

## One who has married two sisters is not to be admitted to the clergy

[Col. 0143D]

### XIX

A man who has taken two sisters in marriage, or the daughter of his brother, cannot be a cleric.

## A cleric cannot act as a surety

### XX

A cleric who engages in suretyships is to be deposed.

## Those who were not voluntarily made eunuchs are to be received into the clergy

### XXI

A eunuch who was made so through human treachery, or whose genitals were cut off during persecution, or who was born so, is to become a bishop if he is worthy.

## One who has made himself a eunuch is not to become a cleric

[Col. 0144A]

### XXII

If anyone has castrated himself—that is, if anyone has cut off his own genitals—he is not to become a cleric, because he is his own murderer and an enemy of God’s creation.

## A cleric who has made himself a eunuch is to be removed from the clergy

### XXIII

If anyone, while he is a cleric, castrates himself, he is absolutely to be condemned, because he is his own murderer.

## A layman who has made himself a eunuch is to be deprived of communion for three years

### XXIV

A layman who castrates himself is to be deprived of communion for three years, because he has proved an assailant of his own life.

## A bishop, presbyter, or deacon condemned for crimes is nevertheless not to be deprived of communion

[Col. 0144B]

### XXV

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed; nevertheless, he is not to be deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord will not exact vengeance twice for the same thing.”

## Likewise the other ministers of the Church

### XXVI

Likewise, the other clerics are to be subject to this condition.

## Which clerics may be joined to wives

### XXVII

To those who are unmarried and have been advanced to the clergy, we prescribe that, if they wish, they may take wives—but only readers and singers.

## A bishop, presbyter, or deacon ought not to beat sinful believers

### XXVIII

We command that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who strikes faithful people committing offenses, or unbelievers acting wickedly, and who wishes to inspire fear through such conduct, be deposed from his office, because the Lord nowhere taught us this. On the contrary, when he himself was struck, he did not strike back; when he was cursed, he did not curse in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten.

## Those condemned for crimes are not to assume again the office they formerly held

### XXIX

If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been justly deposed for specified crimes dares to take up again the ministry formerly entrusted to him, he is to be completely cut off from the Church.

## Ecclesiastical offices are not to be obtained with money

[Col. 0144D]

### XXX

If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, both he and the one who ordained him are to be deposed and in every way cut off from communion, as Simon Magus was by Peter.

## The Church is not to be invaded by secular power

### XXXI

If any bishop, using the powers of the world, obtains the Church through them, he is to be deposed, and all who communicate with him are to be separated.

## Concerning a presbyter who attempts to gather a separate assembly against his bishop

### XXXII

If any presbyter, despising his bishop, gathers an assembly separately and erects another altar, having no valid complaint against the bishop in a matter of piety and justice, he is to be deposed as one who loves preeminence—for he is a tyrant. The other clerics who agree with him are likewise to be deposed, while laypeople are to be separated. This is to be done after the bishop’s first, second, and third admonition.

## Condemned clerics are not to be received by others

### XXXIII

If any presbyter or deacon is separated by his bishop, it is not lawful for him to be received by another, but only by the one who separated him—unless perhaps the bishop himself, who is known to have separated him, has died.

## No bishop, presbyter, or deacon is to be received without letters of commendation
[Col. 0145B] **XXXIV.** No foreign bishop, presbyter, or deacon is to be received without letters of commendation. When they bring written documents, they are to be examined most carefully and then received, if they prove themselves preachers of piety; otherwise, the necessities are not to be supplied to them, and they are in no way to be admitted to communion, because many things arise through surreptitious intrusion.

### On the Primacy of Bishops

**XXXV.** The bishops of each nation ought to know who among them is regarded as first, whom they should consider as a head, and without whose knowledge they should undertake nothing beyond those matters alone that individually concern their own parish and the villages belonging to it. [Col. 0145C] But neither should that bishop do anything without the knowledge of all; for thus unanimity will exist, and God will be glorified through Christ in the Holy Spirit.

### That a Bishop May Not Ordain Clerics in Another Province

**XXXVI.** A bishop must not dare to perform ordinations outside his own boundaries, in cities and villages that are subject to him by no right. If he is convicted of having done this without the knowledge of those who hold authority over the cities and villages themselves, both he and those ordained by him are to be deposed.

### On Bishops Who Have Been Ordained but Not Received

**XXXVII.** If a bishop does not accept the office and care of the people entrusted to him, he is to be deprived of communion until he consents and offers obedience; the same applies to a presbyter and a deacon. If he proceeds but is not received—not because of his own decision, but because of the people’s malice—he is nevertheless to remain bishop; but the clerics of that city are to be deprived of communion, because they did not instruct the disobedient people.

### That Councils Be Held Twice Each Year

**XXXVIII.** Councils of bishops are to be held twice each year, so that they may examine one another’s doctrines of piety and remove emerging ecclesiastical disputes: once in the fourth week after Pentecost, and a second time on the twelfth day of the month Hyperberetaeus, that is, according to the Romans, on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

### That the Bishop Alone Have Charge of Ecclesiastical Affairs

[Col. 0146A]

**XXXIX.** The bishop is to have charge of all ecclesiastical affairs and administer them as though God were observing him. He may not take anything at all from them or give what belongs to God as a gift to his own relatives. If they are poor, he is to provide for them as for the poor, and the affairs of the Church are not to be plundered on their account.

### On the Bishop’s Dignity and His Authority over His Own Property

**XL.** Presbyters and deacons must not attempt to do anything without the bishop. The Lord’s people have been entrusted to him, and he will render an account for their souls. The bishop’s own possessions [Col. 0146B]—if indeed he has any—are to be clearly distinguished from the Lord’s possessions, so that, when dying, the bishop may have authority to leave his own property, as he wishes and to whom he wishes. Nor should these possessions be lost under the pretext of ecclesiastical property, since he may perhaps have a wife, children, relatives, or servants. This is just before God and human beings: the Church must not suffer loss through ignorance of the bishop’s property, nor should the bishop or his relatives be proscribed under the pretext of the Church and those belonging to him be brought into lawsuits, so that his death is subjected to injury and bad reputation.

### That the Bishop Have Authority over Ecclesiastical Property for the Provision of the Poor

**XLI.** We command that the bishop have ecclesiastical property under his authority. For if human souls have been entrusted to him as precious, much more ought he to administer the funds, so that everything may be distributed by his authority to those in need and supplied with fear and complete diligence. From these resources he himself may receive what he needs—if indeed he needs anything—for his own necessities and for the use of visiting brothers, so that they may lack nothing at all. For the law of God commands that those who serve the altar be fed from the altar, since a soldier does not take up arms against his enemies at his own expense.

### That a Bishop, Presbyter, or Deacon Must Not Be a Gambler or Drunkard

**XLII.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who devotes himself to gambling and drunkenness must either desist or certainly be condemned.

Clerics and laypeople likewise, if they persist in gambling, are to be deprived of communion.

**XLIII.** A subdeacon, lector, or cantor who does similar things must either desist or be deprived of communion; the same applies also to laypeople.

### That a Bishop, Presbyter, or Deacon Must Not Receive Interest

**XLIV.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who exacts interest from debtors must either desist or certainly be condemned.

### That a Bishop, Presbyter, or Deacon Must Not Pray with Heretics

**XLV.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has prayed with heretics is to be deprived of communion alone; but if he has encouraged them to act or pray as though they were clerics, he is to be condemned.

### That the Baptisms of Heretics Must Not Be Approved

**XLVI.** We command that a bishop or presbyter who accepts the baptism of heretics be condemned. For what agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever?

### That One Baptized with the Church’s Baptism Must Not Be Baptized Again, and That One Not So Baptized Must Be Baptized

**XLVII.** If a bishop or presbyter baptizes again someone who possesses baptism according to the truth, [Col. 0147B] or fails to baptize someone polluted by the impious, he is to be deposed, as one mocking the cross and death of the Lord and failing rightly to distinguish priests from false priests.

### A Layman Who Casts Out His Wife Is to Be Deprived of Communion

[Col. 0148A]

**XLVIII.** If a layman casts out his own wife and takes another, or takes a woman dismissed by another man, he is to be deprived of communion.

### That Baptism Must Be Administered in the Name of the Trinity

**XLIX.** If a bishop or presbyter does not baptize according to the Lord’s command in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but in three principles without beginning, or in three Sons, or in three Paracletes, he is to be expelled.

### That a Single Immersion Must Not Occur in Baptism as Though It Were in the Lord’s Death

**L.** If a bishop or presbyter does not celebrate the triple immersion of the one mystery, but immerses once in baptism, which is understood to be given in the Lord’s death, [Col. 0148B] he is to be deposed. For the Lord did not say to us, “Baptize in my death,” but, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

## TWENTY CANONS OF THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA

[Col. 0147]

### On Eunuchs and Those Who Have Castrated Themselves

[Col. 0147B]

**I.** If someone has been mutilated by physicians because of illness, or castrated by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy. But if someone has castrated himself while in good health, he should be excluded even if he has been established in the clergy, and thereafter no one of this kind is to be promoted. Just as it is clear that this statement concerns those who deliberately seek or dare to castrate themselves, so the rule permits those who have been castrated by barbarians or by their masters, but who are otherwise entirely worthy, to be received into the clergy.

### On Those Who, Having Come from Paganism, Are Promoted to the Clerical Order after Baptism

**II.** Since many things have been done contrary to ecclesiastical rule, either from necessity or because people were compelled by other persons—namely, that men recently coming from pagan life to the faith, and instructed for only a short time, were immediately brought to the spiritual washing and, as soon as they had been baptized, promoted even to the episcopate or presbyterate—it has seemed entirely right that nothing of this kind be done hereafter. For time is needed by one who is being catechized, and after baptism there must be extensive testing. The apostolic Scripture is clear when it says: [Col. 0147D] “Not a novice, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil.” If, as time goes on, some offense against the soul is discovered in such a person and he is accused by two or three witnesses, he is to be excluded from the clergy.
