But if anyone acts contrary to this, as though setting himself against the great council, he will himself be in danger of losing the honor of the clergy.

### On Women Introduced into the Household

**III.** The great synod has altogether forbidden a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all in the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household, unless she is his mother, sister, aunt, or one of those persons alone who are beyond suspicion.

### On Those Promoted to the Episcopate in the Provinces

[Col. 0148B]

**IV.** A bishop ought above all to be ordained by all the bishops in the province. If this is difficult, either because of pressing necessity or because of the length of the journey, three bishops must nevertheless assemble for this purpose, while those absent likewise make their decision and give their consent in writing; then the ordination may be celebrated. The confirmation of what is done in each province is to be assigned to the metropolitan bishop.

### On Those Excommunicated

**V.** Concerning those deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the lay order, the bishops in each province are to maintain the canonical judgment, so that those rejected by some are not received by others. It must also be investigated lest someone appear to have been excluded from the congregation through the bishop’s faintheartedness, contentiousness, or any other fault. In order that this may be investigated more appropriately, it has seemed good that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that, when all the bishops of the province have assembled together, such questions may be examined communally. Thus those who have plainly sinned against their own bishop are to be reasonably regarded as excommunicated by all, until either the common body or that bishop himself is pleased to issue a more humane judgment concerning them. The councils are to be held once before the Lenten season of Easter, so that, after every disagreement has been removed, the offering may be presented to God in complete purity; and a second time around the season of autumn.

### On the Privileges Belonging to Certain Cities

**VI.** Let the ancient custom be preserved throughout Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these regions. For a similar custom also belongs to the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in Antioch and the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their Churches be preserved. This, however, is generally clear: if anyone has been made bishop contrary to the judgment of the metropolitan, the great synod has determined that he ought not to be considered a bishop. But if, after a reasonable decision common to all and approved according to ecclesiastical rule, two or three oppose it on account of their own disputes, the judgment of the majority is to prevail.

### On the Bishop of Aelia, That Is, Jerusalem

**VII.** Since custom and ancient tradition have prevailed that the bishop of Aelia be honored, let him have the corresponding honor, while the dignity of his own metropolitan see remains intact.

### On Those Called Cathari, That Is, the “Pure”

**VIII.** Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, “pure,” if they ever come to the Catholic Church, it has seemed good to the holy and great council that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they remain in the clergy. Before all else, however, they must profess in writing that they accept and follow the doctrines of the Catholic and apostolic Church: that is, that they communicate with those who have married twice and with those who fell during persecution, for whom periods and appointed times have also been established, so that in every respect they follow the decisions of the Catholic and apostolic Church.

Wherever, whether in towns or cities, they alone are found ordained, those who are found in the clergy may remain in the same status. But when some of them come to a place where a bishop or presbyter of the Catholic Church has been established, it is certain that the bishop of the Church will possess the dignity of bishop. The one called a bishop among them will possess the honor of the presbyterate, [Col. 0149C] unless it should please the bishop to allow him to retain the honor of the title. If this does not please him, he will provide him either the place of chorepiscopus or that of presbyter, so that he may plainly remain in the clergy, lest two bishops appear to exist in one city.

### On Those Who Have Been Promoted to the Honor of the Presbyterate without Examination

**IX.** If any presbyters have been promoted without examination, or, when examined, have confessed their sins, and people, moved contrary to the canons, have attempted to lay hands upon those who confessed, the rule does not admit such persons, because the Catholic Church defends what is irreproachable.

### On Those Who Denied the Faith during Persecutions and Were Later Promoted in the Clergy

[Col. 0149D]

**X.** Whoever, through ignorance or through the concealment of those ordaining them, has been promoted from among the fallen to the clerical order has not thereby prejudiced the ecclesiastical rule; once recognized, such persons are to be deposed.

### On Laypeople Who Denied the Faith

**XI.** Concerning those who transgressed without necessity, without the confiscation of their property, without danger, or without something of this kind that occurred under the tyranny of Licinius, the synod has decided that, although they are evidently unworthy of kindness, benevolence should nevertheless be extended to them. Therefore, whoever truly repent is to be counted among the faithful hearers for three years; for six years they are to humble themselves in complete contrition; and for two years they are to join the people in prayer without an offering.

### On Those Who Renounced the World and Subsequently Returned to It

**XII.** Whoever, called by grace, first displayed an initial impulse by laying down his military belt, but afterward returned to his own vomit, so that some even gave money and used privileges to re-enter military service, must remain in affliction for ten years after the three-year period during which they will be among the hearers.

In all these cases, however, their disposition and the form of their repentance must be examined. For all who demonstrate their conversion by the facts themselves—not by pretense—through fear, tears, repentance, or good works: after completing the appointed period among the hearers, let them then join the faithful in prayer; afterward, the bishop may consider showing them some greater humanity. But those who have borne the matter indifferently and have thought that merely securing an entrance into the Church would suffice for their conversion must complete the appointed period in every respect.

### On Those Who Request Communion at the Time of Death

**XIII.** Concerning those who are approaching the end, the ancient and canonical law is still to be observed, so that, if someone is departing from the body, he is not to be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum. But if someone who had been despaired of, after receiving communion and becoming a participant in the offering, should recover, he is to remain among those who receive only communion in prayer. In general, whenever anyone at the point of death asks that the grace of communion be granted to him, the bishop ought reasonably to give it from the offering.

### On Catechumens Who Have Fallen

**XIV.** Concerning catechumens, the holy and great council has decided that they are to remain for three years among the hearers alone, and afterward pray with the catechumens.

### That There Must Be No Transfer

**XV.** Because of the great disorder and seditions that occur, it has seemed good to abolish entirely a custom that appears to have been admitted in certain places contrary to the rule, namely, that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon be transferred from city to city. If anyone, after the decision of the holy and great council, attempts to do such a thing and commits himself to such an undertaking, the act is entirely invalid, and he is to be restored to the Church in which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

### On Those Who Did Not Remain in the Churches in Which They Were Promoted

**XVI.** All presbyters, deacons, or anyone else who exists entirely under the rule, who leave the Church rashly and dangerously, without the fear of God before their eyes and without recognizing ecclesiastical rule, must not be received in any way into another Church. Every necessity should be imposed upon them so that they return to their own parishes; if they do not, they ought to be deprived of communion.

If anyone attempts boldly to invade another’s jurisdiction and ordain someone in his own Church without the consent of the bishop from whom the person subject to the rule has departed, such an ordination is to be declared invalid.

### On Clerics Who Receive Interest

**XVII.** Since many who have been established under the rule pursue greed and shameful profits, forgetting the divine Scripture that says, “He who has not given his money at interest,” and, when lending money, demand hundredfold returns, the holy and great synod has rightly judged that, if anyone after this decision is found receiving interest, or conducting business by any device or in any manner, or demanding *hemiolia*, that is, one-and-a-half times the amount, or devising anything of this kind for the sake of shameful profit, he is to be removed from the clergy and be a stranger to the rule.

### On the Privileges of Presbyters

**XVIII.** It has come to the attention of the holy and great council [Col. 0151B] that in certain places and cities deacons distribute the grace of sacred communion to presbyters. Neither rule nor custom has handed this down: those who offer the body of Christ should receive it from those who lack the authority to offer. It has also become known that certain deacons touch the sacred offerings before the bishops.

Let all these practices therefore be abolished, and let deacons remain within their proper measure, knowing that they are ministers of the bishops but are lower than presbyters in rank. Therefore they are to receive the grace of sacred communion after the presbyters, with either the bishop or the presbyter distributing it to them. Nor is it lawful for deacons to sit among the presbyters, for if this is done, it is shown to be contrary to rule and order. If anyone, even after these decisions, refuses to obey, he must cease from the ministry.

### On Those Who Come to the Church from Paul of Samosata

**XIX.** Concerning the Paulianists who flee to the Catholic Church, a decision has been issued that they must be baptized in every respect. If any of them formerly belonged to the clergy, then, provided they appear blameless and irreproachable, they are to be ordained after baptism by the bishop of the Catholic Church; but if examination finds them unsuitable, they ought to be expelled. The same rule is to be observed concerning deaconesses and, in general, concerning all who are subject to the rule.

With regard to deaconesses who are found to remain in the same status, we remember that they have received no laying on of hands; therefore they are to be counted entirely among the laity.

### On Bending the Knee

**XX.** Since there are some who bend the knee on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, so that everything may be observed harmoniously in all places, the holy council has decided that we should fulfill our vows to the Lord while standing.

## RULES OF THE COUNCIL OF ANCYRA

[Col. 0151]

[Col. 0151C] These rules are indeed earlier than those of Nicaea; but the Nicene rules were written first because of the authority of that great and holy council assembled at Nicaea.

### On Presbyters Who Sacrificed during the Persecution

**XXI.** Concerning presbyters who sacrificed and afterward entered the struggle again: if they did this not through some deception but in truth, and did not, through relatives seeking and urging, arrange to be thought subjected to torments while being subjected to them only in appearance and outward bearing, it has seemed good that they retain the honor of their own seat, but that they may neither offer, nor address the people, nor perform any priestly functions at all.

### On Deacons Who Sacrificed

[Col. 0151D]

**XXII.** Deacons who likewise sacrificed are to retain their honor, but must cease from every sacred ministry, whether offering bread or the cup, or preaching. If some bishops are aware of their labor, humility, and gentleness and wish to grant or remove something further from them, the authority belongs to those bishops.

### On Those Who Were Seized While Fleeing and Were Forced to Endure Something of the Pagan Rites

**XXIII.** Those who were seized while fleeing, or handed over by members of their household, or who endured torture after their property had been taken away, or who, thrust into custody, proclaimed that they were Christians, and were so tightly restrained that those grasping their hands forcibly dragged them and brought them to unholy sacrifices, or forced them by necessity to consume some polluted food—while continually confessing that they were Christians and unceasingly displaying grief over what had occurred through every form of abasement, conduct, and humility of life—such people, as having been placed outside the offense, are not to be barred from the grace of communion.

If they have been prohibited by some for the sake of greater caution or because of someone’s ignorance, they are to be received immediately. The same is to be observed concerning clerics and the other laity. It was also investigated whether laypeople who fell into these straits of necessity could be promoted to the clerical order. It has therefore seemed good that these too, as having committed no sin, be promoted to this office, provided their previous life is also found worthy of approval.

### On Those Who, for Various Reasons, Performed Something of the Pagan Rites

[Col. 0152D]

**XXIV.** Concerning those who were forced to sacrifice and also dined in an idol’s temple: if, when they were being led there, they appeared cheerful, wore more expensive clothing, and participated without concern in the prepared dinner, it has seemed good that they be placed among the hearers for one year, submit for three years, join in prayer for two years, and then attain the grace of full restoration.

But all who entered the temples in mournful dress and wept throughout the entire meal while reclining, if they have completed three years of repentance, are to be received without an offering. If they did not eat, they are to undergo two years of repentance and, in the third year, join in communion without an offering, so that they may attain full restoration after four years.

The authority belongs to the bishops, after examining the manner of their conversion, either to treat them more humanely or to assign a longer period. Above all, their former and later life is to be investigated, and humanity is to be extended to them accordingly.

### On Those Who Performed Pagan Rites through Fear

**XXV.** Concerning those who yielded only to threats of punishments, or, terrified by the loss of their property or by exile, sacrificed, and who, having until then neglected repentance and not been converted, offered themselves at the time of this council and formed plans for their conversion, it has seemed good that they be received among the hearers until the Great Day, and after the Great Day perform repentance for three years, then join in communion for two years without an offering, and only then, after six years have been completed, attain the grace of full restoration.

If some were admitted to repentance before this synod, their six-year period is to be counted from that time. But if any danger, expectation of death, illness, or some other circumstance occurs, communion is not to be denied to them under the established decision.

### On Those Who Ate in the Places of Idols

**XXVI.** Concerning those who, on the feast days of the pagans, held banquets in their remote places and brought their own food and ate there, it has seemed good that they be received after two years of repentance; whether they are to be received with an offering is to be examined individually by the bishops, who are to assess their lives and their individual acts.

### On Those Who Frequently Sacrificed to Idols

**XXVII.** Those who sacrificed a second and third time under compulsion are to undergo four years of repentance; for two years they are to join in communion without an offering, and in the seventh year they are to be fully received.

### On Those Who Gave Others Reasons to Sacrifice

**XXVIII.** Those who not only went astray themselves but also rose up, compelled their brothers, and provided reasons for their being compelled are to receive a place among the hearers for three years, undergo more severe repentance for another six years, and in the following year receive communion without an offering, so that they may attain full restoration after ten years. [Col. 0153D] During this period their manner of life is also to be weighed.

### On Deacons Who, at the Time of Their Ordination, Gave Notice Concerning Marriage

**XXIX.** Any deacons who, at the very time of their ordination, protested and said that they wished to marry because they could not remain as they were: if they afterward take wives, they are to remain in the ministry, because the bishop gave them permission. But those who kept silent, accepted the laying on of hands, professed continence, and afterward became bound by marriage must cease from the ministry.

### On Betrothed Girls Who Were Violated by Others

**XXX.** Concerning betrothed girls who were afterward seized by others, it has seemed good that they be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence was inflicted upon them by their abductors.

### On Those Who Sacrificed to Idols While They Were Catechumens

**XXXI.** Concerning those who sacrificed to idols before baptism and afterward received baptism, it has seemed good that they be promoted to the clerical order, since they are considered cleansed.

### That Chorepiscopi Must Not Ordain Clerics Except in the Countryside and Small Villages

**XXXII.** Chorepiscopi are not permitted to ordain presbyters or deacons, nor are the presbyters of a city permitted to do so in any parish without the bishop’s command or letters.

### On Those in the Clergy Who Avoid Eating Meat

[Col. 0154B]

**XXXIII.** Concerning presbyters and deacons who are in the clergy and abstain from meat, it has seemed good that they should partake of it and then abstain, if they wish. But if they abominate meat to such an extent that they do not consider even vegetables cooked with it fit to eat, they must cease from the order as people who do not consent to the rule.

### On Ecclesiastical Property Sold while the Churches Themselves Were without Bishops

**XXXIV.** Concerning property belonging to the Church, whatever presbyters sold while there was no bishop: it has seemed good that, after the contract has been rescinded, the property be restored to ecclesiastical ownership. It will be for the bishop to decide whether the price should be recovered, since often the return from the property sold will have yielded a greater sum than the price that was paid.

### On Those Who Commit Unnatural Fornication, That Is, Who Have Intercourse with Animals or Are Defiled with Males

[Col. 0154C]

**XXXV.** Concerning those who have acted unnaturally, or are acting so: all who committed such a crime before the age of twenty are to receive communion in prayer after completing fifteen years of repentance; then, after remaining in this communion for five years, they may finally partake of the sacraments of the offering. Their life during the period of repentance is also to be examined, and they are to obtain mercy accordingly. If they cling to these crimes insatiably, they are to spend a longer period in repentance.

Those who, after reaching the age of twenty and while having wives, have fallen into this sin are to be received into communion in prayer after twenty-five years of repentance; [Col. 0154D] after remaining in it for five years, they may finally receive the sacraments of the offering. But if some, while having wives and having passed their fiftieth year of age, have committed such an offense, they are to receive the grace of communion only at the end of life.

### On Those Who Have Been Defiled by Animals or Males, Whether Formerly or Who Continue to Waste Away in This Vice

**XXXVI.** Those who have lived unnaturally and polluted others with the leprosy of an unjust crime: the holy synod has commanded that they pray among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit.

### On Those Promoted to the Episcopate but Not Received

**XXXVII.** If bishops have been ordained but not received by the parish for which they had been designated, and wish to occupy other parishes and use force against their bishops by stirring up seditions against them, it has seemed good that they be expelled. But if they wish to remain as presbyters in the order of presbyterate in which they had previously been, they are not to be deprived of their proper dignity. If they stir up seditions against the bishops established there, the honor of the presbyterate is also to be taken away from them, and they are to become marked by condemnation.

### On Those Who Profess Virginity and on Women Who Live with Men under the Appearance of Sisterhood

**XXXVIII.** All who promise virginity but invalidate their pledge are to be counted among those married twice. We prohibit virgins from living with certain men as though they were sisters.

### On Those Who Have Adulterous Wives or Who Are Themselves Found to Be Adulterers

[Col. 0155B]

**XXXIX.** If someone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he ought to attain full restoration through seven years of repentance, according to the established stages.

### On Those Who Kill Their Offspring Conceived through Fornication in Various Ways

**XL.** Concerning women who commit fornication and kill their offspring, or who act against themselves so as to expel what has been conceived in the womb: the ancient decision removes them from the Church until the end of life. But now we define more humanely that we grant them a period of ten years according to the prescribed stages of repentance.

### On Murderers

**XLI.** Those who have committed voluntary murder are to submit themselves continually to repentance, but they are to attain full restoration around the end of life.

### On Those Who Committed Murder Unintentionally

**XLII.** Concerning unintentional murders, the earlier decision commands that full restoration be attained after seven years of repentance; the second commands completion of a five-year period.

### On Those Who Seek Divinations

**XLIII.** Those who seek divinations and follow pagan custom, or introduce such people into their homes to make inquiries by magical art or for the purpose of purification, are to remain under the rule for five years, according to the prescribed stages of repentance.

### On Those Who Are Accomplices in the Violation of Virgins

**XLIV.** A certain man, having a fiancée, violated her sister and made her pregnant; afterward he took as his wife the woman betrothed to him, while the woman who had been violated killed herself with a noose. Those who were accomplices were ordered to be received after ten years of satisfaction, according to the established stages of repentance.

## FOURTEEN RULES ISSUED IN THE SYNOD OF NEOCAESAREA

[Col. 0155]

[Col. 0155C] These rules are recognized as having been issued after those promulgated at Ancyra; but they are found to be earlier than the Nicene rules.

### On Presbyters Who Have Taken Wives or Committed Fornication

**XLV.** If a presbyter takes a wife, he is to be deposed from the order. If he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled still more severely and reduced to repentance.

### On Women Who Marry Two Brothers, or Men Who Take Two Sisters as Wives

**XLVI.** If a woman marries two brothers, she is to be expelled until death. Nevertheless, at the end of life, out of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, she may obtain the fruit of repentance. But if a woman [Col. 0155D] or a man dies while involved in such a marriage, repentance will be difficult during the remaining life.

### On Those Who Have Married Many Times

**XLVII.** Concerning those who have entered into many marriages, the appointed period is indeed clear, but their manner of life and faith shorten the period.

### On Those Who Resolve to Commit Fornication but Are Prevented

**XLVIII.** If someone, desiring a woman, intends to lie with her, but his thought does not reach fulfillment, it is evident that he has been freed by the grace of God.

### On Sinning Catechumens

**XLIX.** If a catechumen enters the church and takes his place among those being instructed, but is found committing sin: if he kneels, let him listen, so that he may not sin further; but if, while listening, he sins again, let him be expelled.

### On a Pregnant Catechumen

**L.** A pregnant woman is to be baptized whenever she wishes, for the one who gives birth communicates nothing of herself to the one being born. Each person’s own intention is declared in confession.

### That a Presbyter Must Not Pray at the Marriage of One Married Twice

**LI.** A presbyter ought not dine at the wedding of one married twice, because, since such a person requires repentance, what presbyter could, on account of a banquet, give consent to such a marriage?

### On Those Joined to Adulterous Women

[Col. 0156D]

**LII.** If the wife of a layman is clearly proved to have committed adultery, he cannot enter the ministry of the clergy. If she commits adultery after his ordination, he ought to dismiss her; but if he lives with her, he cannot retain the ministry entrusted to him.

### On Those Promoted to the Presbyterate Who Are Conscious of Sins Committed before Ordination

**LIII.** If a presbyter is promoted while burdened by bodily sin and confesses concerning himself that he sinned before ordination, he must not consecrate the offerings, but may remain in the other duties because of his good zeal. For many have said that other sins can be remitted through the laying on of hands. But if he has not confessed concerning himself and cannot be openly accused, he is to be left to the judgment of his own authority.

### Likewise Concerning Deacons

**LIV.** In the same way, if a deacon has fallen into the same sin, he is to be removed from the order of the ministry.

### At What Time a Presbyter Should Be Ordained

**LV.** A presbyter must in no way be ordained before his thirtieth year, even if he is exceedingly worthy; he must observe this age. For our Lord was baptized in the thirtieth year of his age, and thus began to teach.

### On Those Who Receive Baptism in Illness

**LVI.** If someone was baptized while ill, he cannot be promoted to the honor of the presbyterate, because his faith arose not from intention but from necessity, [Col. 0158A] unless perhaps, because of his subsequent zeal, faith, and the scarcity of suitable men, such a person may be admitted.

### On Rural Presbyters
LVII. Rural presbyters may not offer in the church of the city when the bishop is present, or when the presbyters of that city are present; nor may they give the consecrated bread or hand around the chalice. If, however, these men are absent and the rural presbyters are summoned to give the prayer, they alone shall perform these functions. Chorepiscopi also appear to number seventy, after the model and pattern of the seventy; but as fellow ministers they are to be honored because of the devotion they show toward the poor.

### On the prescribed number of deacons

LVIII. There shall be seven deacons, according to the rule, even if the city is very large. The Book of the Acts of the Apostles also indicates the same thing.

## TWENTY RULES OF GANGRA, SET FORTH AFTER THE COUNCIL OF NICAEA

[Col. 0157]

### On those who condemn marriage

[Col. 0157B]

LIX. If anyone condemns marriage and detests a faithful and religious woman who sleeps with her husband, or judges such women blameworthy, as though they could not enter the kingdom of God: let him be anathema.

### On those who abominate those who eat meat

LX. If anyone condemns a person who eats meat—apart from blood, meat sacrificed to idols, and strangled meat—when it is eaten with religion and faith, as though such a person had no hope because of this consumption: let him be anathema.

### On slaves who cast off the yoke of service under the pretext of Christianity

LXI. If anyone, under the pretext of divine worship, teaches a slave to despise his own master, to leave his service, and not to serve him with goodwill and every mark of honor: let him be anathema.

### On presbyters who have had a wife

LXII. Whoever distinguishes against a presbyter who has had a wife, saying that one ought not, while he is ministering, to receive from the offering: let him be anathema.

### On those who consider the assemblies of the Church contemptible

LXIII. If anyone teaches that the house of God is contemptible, and that the assemblies held in it are contemptible: let him be anathema.

### On those who perform ecclesiastical ministries outside the Church

LXIV. If anyone holds an assembly separately outside the Church and, despising the Church, wishes to usurp the things belonging to the Church, without the presbyter being present according to the bishop’s decree: let him be anathema.

### On offerings of produce that are given to the ministers of the Church

LXV. If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and does not wish to act with his counsel: let him be anathema.

### On those things that are contributed for the use of the poor

[Col. 0158B]

LXVI. If anyone gives or receives offerings, apart from the bishop or the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor: both the giver and the receiver shall be anathema.

### On those who persist in virginity and continence

LXVII. Whoever maintains virginity or practices continence, yet disparages marriage as though horrified by it, and does not take on the name of virginity because it is good and holy: let him be anathema.

### On those who are proud because of virginity

LXVIII. If anyone among those who preserve virginity for the Lord exalts himself against married people: let him be anathema.

### On those who make agapae—that is, meals for the poor—a subject of ridicule

[Col. 0158C]

LXIX. If anyone despises those who faithfully provide agapae, that is, meals, for the poor, and summon the brethren for the honor of the Lord, and refuses to participate in such invitations, making light of what is being done: let him be anathema.

### On those who wear cloaks and become proud on that account

LXX. If any man, because of his supposed continence, wears a cloak as a garment, believing that by this he possesses righteousness, and despises those who reverently wear *birri* and other ordinary and customary garments: let him be anathema.

### On women who wear men’s clothing

[Col. 0158D]

LXXI. If any woman, because of her supposed continence, changes her dress and, instead of the customary feminine garment, assumes a man’s clothing: let her be anathema.

### On those who abandon marital intercourse as though it were sinful

LXXII. If any woman leaves her own husband and wishes to depart, condemning marriage: let her be anathema.

### On those who despise their children under the pretext of Christianity

LXXIII. If anyone, abandoning his children, does not nourish them and does not instruct them, so far as pertains to him, in the piety of divine worship, but neglects them under the pretext of continence: let him be anathema.

### On those who despise their parents on the occasion of Christianity

[Col. 0159A]

LXXIV. Whoever, under the pretext of divine worship, withdraws from his parents and does not render them their due reverence, although they unquestionably prefer divine worship to themselves: let him be anathema.

### On women who cut their hair under the pretext of Christianity

LXXV. If any woman, for the sake of divine worship, as she supposes, cuts the hair that God gave her as a reminder of subjection, thereby setting aside the commandment of obedience: let her be anathema.

### On those who fast on the Lord’s day as though it differed in no way from the other days

[Col. 0160A]

LXXVI. If anyone, because of supposed continence or out of stubbornness, fasts on the Lord’s day: let him be anathema.

### On those who dissolve the ecclesiastical fasts without necessity

LXXVII. If anyone among those who practice continence, without bodily necessity, proudly abandons the fasts established in common and observed by the Church, driven by the impulse of his own thinking: let him be anathema.

### On those who condemn the assemblies held in commemoration of the martyrs

LXXVIII. If anyone, moved by a proud disposition, abominates the assemblies held at the memorials of the martyrs, and condemns the ministries performed there together with their commemorations: let him be anathema.

## TWENTY-FIVE RULES SET FORTH AT ANTIOCH AT THE DEDICATION

[Col. 0159]

### On those who act contrary to what was regularly established concerning Easter at the Council of Nicaea

[Col. 0159B]

LXXIX. We decree that all who dare to dissolve the definition of the holy and great council assembled at Nicaea in the presence of the most devout and venerable emperor Constantine concerning the saving and most sacred solemnity of Easter are to be excommunicated and expelled from the Church, provided that they persist contentiously against what has been rightly decreed. This has been said concerning laypeople.

But if any of those known to preside over the Church—whether bishop, presbyter, or deacon—after this definition attempts, for the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the Churches, to assemble separately and celebrate Easter with the Jews, the holy synod has already judged him to be alien from the Church, since he has become a cause of corruption and disturbance not only to himself but also to many others. It removes such persons not only from the ministry but also those who afterward attempt to communicate with them after their condemnation. Moreover, the condemned are to be deprived of every external honor that the holy rule and the priesthood of God have allowed them to attain.

### On those who withdraw from receiving holy communion, and those who communicate with excommunicated persons in private houses

XXC. All who enter the Church of God and hear the holy Scriptures but do not communicate in prayer with the people, and through a kind of intemperance turn away from receiving holy communion, are to be removed from the Church until they show the fruits of repentance through confession and obtain forgiveness by prayers.

It is not permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons. Nor is it permitted to pray together with those who assemble in private houses while avoiding the prayers of the Church. A person who does not assemble in one Church is not to be received by another Church. But if any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone whatever from the clergy is discovered communicating with excommunicated persons, he too shall be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rule of the Church.

### On those who remain in other parishes without the knowledge of their own bishops

[Col. 0160B]

XXCI. If any presbyter, deacon, or absolutely anyone from the clergy leaves his own parish and hastens to another, then, abandoning it altogether, strives to remain for a long time in another parish, he shall no longer minister there—especially if he has contemptuously refused to obey his own bishop when summoned and admonished to return to his own parish.

If he persists in this indiscipline, he shall be removed from the ministry in every way, so that he may find no possibility of restoration. But if another bishop receives a person condemned for this reason, that bishop too shall be restrained by the common synod, as one who dissolves the ecclesiastical constitutions.

### On the condemned who attempt to minister

[Col. 0160C]

XXCII. If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, dares to undertake anything belonging to the sacred ministry—whether the bishop according to the preceding custom, or the presbyter or deacon—he shall in no way be permitted, even in another synod, to have hope of restoration or an opportunity for making satisfaction. All who communicate with him shall also be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against those mentioned, they have attempted to communicate with them.

### On those who withdraw from ecclesiastical ministry and assemble separately

XXCIII. If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the Church, establishes an altar by assembling separately, and refuses to accept the admonition of his bishop or to consent and obey when summoned once and again, let him be condemned in every way and receive no further remedy, since he cannot recover his dignity.

If he persists in disturbing and troubling the Church, let him, as a seditious person, be suppressed by the civil authorities.

### On excommunicated clerics and laypeople

XXCIV. If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, he shall not be received by others until he has been reconciled with his own bishop, or has at least appeared before the synod that is being convened, made satisfaction on his own behalf, and persuaded the council to accept another judgment.

This definition shall also apply to laypeople, presbyters, deacons, and all who are shown to be subject to the rule.

### On receiving travelers

XXCV. No traveler shall be received without peace letters—that is, letters of recommendation.

### On the peace letters of travelers, that is, letters of recommendation

XXCVI. Presbyters who are in the countryside cannot issue canonical letters; they shall send letters only to neighboring bishops. Chorepiscopi who are irreproachable may issue peace letters, that is, general letters.

### On the metropolitans of the individual provinces

[Col. 0161B]

XXCVII. In each region it is fitting to know that the metropolitan bishop bears responsibility for the whole province; for this reason all who appear to have business come from everywhere to the metropolis. Therefore it has seemed right that he should excel in honor, and that the other bishops should do nothing beyond him, according to the ancient rule established by our fathers, except those things that pertain to their own diocese and to the properties subject to them.

Each bishop shall have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern according to the reverence due to each person and oversee every property situated under his city. Thus he shall ordain presbyters and deacons and settle each matter by his own judgment. He shall attempt nothing further apart from the metropolitan bishop, and the metropolitan shall act only with the counsel of the other bishops.

### On those who are called chorepiscopi

XXCVIII. Those who are called chorepiscopi in villages or on estates, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decided that they should recognize their proper limits: they are to govern the Churches subject to them and be content with their administration and care.

They may also ordain readers, subdeacons, and exorcists; these promotions shall suffice for them. But they shall not dare to ordain either a presbyter or a deacon without the city bishop to whom they themselves and the estate are subject. If anyone attempts to transgress these statutes, he shall be deposed and deprived of the honor he had been using. The city bishop to whom the chorepiscopus is subject shall ordain the chorepiscopus.

### On bishops and clerics who approach the emperor

XXCIX. If any bishop, presbyter, or anyone subject to the rule of the Church approaches the emperor without the counsel and letters of the bishops of the province, especially the metropolitan, he ought to be rejected and expelled, not only from communion but also from the honor of which he appears to be a participant. For he has attempted to bring annoyance to the ears of the venerable emperor, contrary to the laws of the Church.

If, therefore, necessity requires someone to approach the emperor, this shall be done with the deliberation and counsel of the metropolitan and the other bishops who reside in the same province; they too shall accompany the one departing with their letters.

### On condemned bishops or clerics who approach the emperor

XC. If a presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, or a bishop perhaps condemned by a synod, becomes troublesome to the emperor, he ought to appeal to the greater council of bishops and present to many bishops whatever he thinks he has that is just, and await their investigations and judgments.

But if, disregarding these things, they trouble the emperor, they are worthy of no pardon, shall have no opportunity to make satisfaction, and shall have absolutely no hope of future restoration.

### On those who, although from another province, dare to perform ordinations in other provinces

[Col. 0162B]

XCI. No bishop from another province shall dare to cross into another province and ordain persons to ecclesiastical ministry in its Churches, even if some appear to give their consent, unless he comes when summoned by letters from both the metropolitan and the other bishops who are with him, and then proceeds to carry out the ordination.

But if, with no one summoning him, he hastens in an irregular manner to settle certain ordinations or ecclesiastical affairs that do not concern him, the acts performed by him shall be invalid; and he himself shall suffer punishment for his disorderly movement and irrational boldness, having thereby already been condemned by the holy council.

### On disagreement concerning the judgment of bishops, when provincial bishops appeal

[Col. 0162C]

XCII. If a bishop is judged for definite crimes and the bishops of the province happen to disagree about him, with some believing him innocent after judgment and others guilty, the holy synod has decided, for the removal of all uncertainty, that the metropolitan bishop should summon other judges from a neighboring province to resolve the dispute, so that through them and through the provincial bishops alike whatever appears just may be approved.

### On bishops unanimously excluded by the priests of the same province

XCIII. If a bishop accused of definite crimes is condemned by all the bishops of the same province, and all unanimously issue the same form of decree against him, he shall in no way be judged by others; the sentence of the bishops of the province who agreed together shall remain firm.

### On vacant sees

XCIV. If a bishop who is without a see rushes into a vacant Church and seizes the see without a full and complete council, he must be expelled, even if the entire people whom he has seized chose to have him.

A complete council is one at which the metropolitan bishop has been present.

### On those who avoid being appointed to the episcopate

XCV. If any bishop has received the laying on of hands for the episcopate and, having been appointed to preside over a people, neglects to undertake the ministry and refuses to go to the Church entrusted to him, he ought to be deprived of communion until he accepts the office under compulsion, or until the synod of the priests of that province, in a complete session, makes some decision concerning him.

### On those who are promoted to the episcopate but are not received

XCVI. If a bishop ordained for a parish does not reach the parish to which he was elected, not through his own fault but because the people avoid him or for some other reason not caused by his fault, he shall retain both his honor and his share in the ministry, provided that he causes no trouble to the affairs of the Church in which he is known to minister.

He shall also observe whatever the complete synod of the province decides and decrees in judgment.

### On episcopal ordinations in the provinces

[Col. 0163B]

XCVII. No bishop shall be ordained without the synod and the presence of the metropolitan. Once this has been established in every way, it is best that all the priests of the same province be present together; the metropolitan bishop must summon them.

If all attend, so much the better. But if this proves difficult, at least the greater number must be present; or else the same judgment must be confirmed in writing, and the ordination must be celebrated in the presence of, or according to the decree of, the majority.

If anything is done otherwise, contrary to the definitions, the ordination shall have no force. But if it is carried out according to the established rule and some oppose it out of personal contentiousness, the judgment of the majority shall prevail.

### On the synods that bishops must celebrate in the province at their appointed times

[Col. 0163C]

XCVIII. For ecclesiastical necessities and for resolving matters that admit of doubt and controversy, it has seemed most fitting that councils of bishops be held twice each year in every province.

The first shall be held after the third week of the feast of Easter, so that the synod may meet in the fourth week of Pentecost, with the metropolitan admonishing the provincial bishops. The second synod shall be held on the ides of October—that is, on the fifteenth day of October, which the Greeks call *Hyperberetaeon*.

At these councils presbyters, deacons, and all who consider themselves wronged shall be present, and they shall submit themselves to the examination of the synod. No one may hold councils on his own, except those to whom the metropolitans appear to have entrusted such authority.

### That a bishop must in no way pass from one parish to another

XCIX. A bishop shall in no way move from one parish to another, neither rushing there of his own accord, nor compelled by force by the peoples, nor driven by necessity by another bishop. He shall remain in the Church that he first received by lot from God and shall not move from it, according to the earlier determination established on this matter.

### That the bishop of one parish must in no way ordain clerics belonging to another parish

C. A bishop shall not approach another city that is not subject to him, nor enter an estate that does not belong to him for the purpose of ordaining anyone; nor shall he appoint presbyters or deacons subject to another bishop, except perhaps with the counsel and consent of the bishop of the region.

If anyone attempts to do such a thing, his ordination shall be invalid, and he himself shall be disciplined by the synod. For if he is unable to ordain, he shall in no way judge.

### That no one may designate a successor for himself to be promoted to the episcopate

CI. A bishop may not designate another person as his successor, even if he has reached the end of his life. If anything of this kind is done, the appointment shall be invalid.

The ecclesiastical right shall be observed, which requires that the one who proves worthy be promoted only by the synod and by the judgment of the bishops who, after the death of the bishop who has completed his life, possess the authority to do so.

### On matters belonging to the Church and those recognized as the bishop’s own property

CII. The things belonging to the Church shall be preserved with every care, a good conscience, and faith in God, who observes and judges all things. They are to be administered according to the judgment and authority of the bishop to whom the people and the souls gathered within the Church have been entrusted.

The things that appear to belong to the Church must be made known, with the presbyters and deacons who are around the bishop informed, so that they recognize and do not fail to know what belongs specifically to the Church and so that nothing is hidden from them.

If it should happen that the bishop departs from this world, the Church’s possessions being clearly identified, these must not collapse and perish, nor may what is proved to be the bishop’s own be seized under the pretext of dealing with the Church’s property.

For it is just and pleasing before God and human beings that a bishop leave his own possessions to whomever he wishes, while what belongs to the Church is preserved for that same Church, so that neither the Church suffers any loss nor the bishop is proscribed under the pretext of the Church’s property, causing those connected with him to fall into legal proceedings and bringing curses upon himself after death.

### That the bishop has authority to administer ecclesiastical property

CIII. The bishop shall have authority over ecclesiastical property, in order to distribute it to all who are in need, with the greatest reverence and fear of God.

He too may share in whatever he needs—if indeed he is in need—for the necessary support of himself and of the brethren received by him, so that they may not be defrauded on any occasion, according to the holy Apostle’s saying: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content.”

But if he is not content with these things, and converts the Church’s property to his domestic uses, or handles its revenues or the produce of its estates without the knowledge of the presbyters and deacons, but entrusts control of these matters to his household, relatives, brothers, or sons, so that through such persons the rest of the Church’s property is secretly harmed, he shall pay the penalty to the synod of the province.

If, moreover, a bishop or the presbyters who are with him is accused on another count—that they appropriate to themselves what belongs to the Church, whether from its estates or from any other ecclesiastical resource, so that the poor are afflicted and both the preaching of the word and those who administer it are thereby exposed to accusation and blasphemy—then these persons must be corrected, with the holy synod approving what is appropriate.

## FIFTY-NINE RULES SET FORTH AT LAODICEA

[Col. 0165]

The holy synod that assembled at Laodicea of Phrygia Pacatiana from various regions of Asia set forth the ecclesiastical definitions appended below.

### On bigamists

CIV. Concerning those who, according to the ecclesiastical rule, have freely and legitimately entered into a second marriage and have not secretly contracted the marriage union: after a short period has passed, they ought to devote themselves to prayers and fasts; in accordance with indulgence, we have also decreed that communion be restored to them.

### On those who have more fervently required repentance for various offenses

CV. Concerning those who have sinned through various crimes and, persevering in the prayer of confession and repentance, have achieved a complete conversion from their evils: after the period of repentance appropriate to the character of the offense has been completed, communion shall be granted to such persons because of the clemency and goodness of God.

### That no one should be promoted to the clergy immediately after baptism

CVI. Concerning those who have recently been enlightened by baptism: it is not fitting that they be promoted to the priestly order.

### On the time of ordinations

[Col. 0165C]

CVII. Ordinations ought not to be celebrated in the presence of those who are still hearers.

### That those who serve in the sacristy must not exact interest

CVIII. Priests and clerics who lend at interest ought not to receive interest, or what is called *sescuplus*—that is, both the principal sum and half of the principal sum.

### On heretics entering churches or the basilicas of martyrs

CIX. Heretics who remain in heresy must not be permitted to enter the house of God.

### On those who come to the churches from the heretics

CX. Those who convert from heretics—that is, from the Novatians, Photinians, or Quartodecimans—whether they have been baptized or are catechumens, must not be received until they anathematize all heresies, and especially the one by which they were held.

Only then shall those who were called faithful among them be taught our symbol of faith, anointed with holy chrism, and admitted to the sacred mysteries.

### On those who come from the heresy of the Cataphrygians

CXI. Those who convert from the heresy called that of the Cataphrygians—even if they are believed to have been members of the clergy among them, and even if they are called eminent—must be instructed and baptized with every care by the bishops or presbyters of the Church.

### On those who go to the caves of heretics for prayer

[Col. 0166A]

CXII. Ecclesiastical persons must not be permitted to go for prayer or healing to the cemeteries of heretics or to places they call *martyria*. If such persons are faithful, they shall be deprived of communion for a specified time; but those who repent and confess that they have sinned ought to be received.

### On those who enter into marriage with heretics

[Col. 0166B]

CXIII. Ecclesiastical persons ought not indiscriminately to join their sons and daughters to heretics in the bond of marriage.

### That those called presbyterae must not be ordained among women

CXIV. Those called *presbyterae* or women presiding in churches ought not to be ordained.

### On episcopal ordinations

CXV. Bishops are to be advanced to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and of the bishops who are in the surrounding region—namely, those who have been tested for a long time both in the word of faith and in the example of upright conduct.

### That ordinations must not be made by the judgment of the multitude

CXVI. The crowds must not be permitted to make the elections of those who are to be promoted to the priesthood.

### That eulogiae offered in one parish must not be sent to other parishes

[Col. 0166C]

CXVII. Holy offerings must in no way be sent to other parishes as *eulogiae* during the season of the Easter feast.

### On those who should sing on the ambo, that is, the pulpit

CXVIII. No one other than those who are regularly singers, and who sing from the book, ought to ascend the pulpit and sing in the church.

### On the readings that should be recited on Saturdays

CXIX. On Saturdays the Gospels should be read together with the other Scriptures.

### That there should be an interval between the psalms in the assemblies

CXX. In the gathering of the faithful it is in no way fitting to continue the psalms without interruption; rather, the readings should be recited at intervals, that is, between individual psalms.

### On prayers to be celebrated at the ninth hour and in the evening

CXXI. The same office of prayer must always be performed at the ninth hour and in the evening.

### On prayers to be offered after homilies, that is, after sermons delivered to the people, and on those who may communicate within the sacristy

CXXII. First, after the bishops’ addresses, a prayer should be celebrated separately over the catechumens. After the catechumens have gone out, a prayer should be made over those who are doing penance.

When these people approach the priest’s hand and depart, three prayers for the faithful shall be completed: the first in silence, while the second and third are completed with the customary acclamations. Only then shall they give one another the peace.

After the bishop has given the kiss of peace to the presbyters, the laypeople shall give it to one another. Thus the holy offering shall be celebrated. Only those devoted to the sacred ministry may enter the altar area and communicate there.

### On the honor that deacons under the presbyters owe to presbyters

CXXIII. A deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a presbyter; he shall sit only at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, honor shall be shown to deacons by those who serve under them, that is, by subdeacons and all clerics.

### That subdeacons must be kept away from the diaconicon, that is, the secretary

CXXIV. Subdeacons ought not to have a place in the diaconicon or to touch the Lord’s vessels.

### That subdeacons must not assist wearing oraria

CXXV. A subdeacon ought not to use an *orarium* or leave the doors.

### That readers and singers must not perform their office wearing oraria

CXXVI. Readers and singers ought not to use *oraria* when reading or singing.

### That no ecclesiastical person should eat in taverns

[Col. 0167C]

CXXVII. Those devoted to the sacred ministry, from presbyters through deacons, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order—that is, through subdeacons, readers, singers, exorcists, and doorkeepers—as well as those numbered among the continent and monks, ought not to enter taverns.

### That subdeacons must not bless or give a blessing

CXXVIII. Subdeacons ought not to give bread or bless the chalice.

### On exorcists who have not been ordained by bishops

CXXIX. Those who have not been ordained by bishops may not perform exorcisms either in churches or in houses.

### That portions of food from banquets held as agapae must not be taken

[Col. 0167D]

CXXX. Clerics or laypeople devoted to the sacred ministry who are invited to an agape ought not to take portions of the food, because this causes an affront to the ecclesiastical order.

### That meals must not be held in churches

CXXXI. Banquets called agapae ought not to be held in divine dwellings, that is, in churches; nor should anyone eat or spread couches within the house of God.

### On Christians who are known to keep the Sabbath, or in some manner to Judaize

CXXXII. Christians ought not to Judaize or be idle on the Sabbath, but should work on that day. If they wish to rest, they should honor the Lord’s day above all and rest on it as Christians. If they are found to be Judaizing, let them be anathema from Christ.

### On men who bathe with women

CXXXIII. Those devoted to sacred offices, whether clerics, continent persons, or any Christian layman, ought not to bathe with women, since this is the first reproach among the nations.

### On those who contract marriage alliances with heretics

CXXXIV. Marriage alliances must not be made with heretics of any kind, nor should sons or daughters be given to them; rather, sons or daughters may be taken from them, provided that they promise to become Christians.

### That eulogiae must not be received from heretics

[Col. 0168B]

CXXXV. *Eulogiae* must not be received from heretics, since they are curses rather than blessings.

### On schismatics

CXXXVI. One must not pray together with heretics or schismatics.

### On the martyrs of heretics

CXXXVII. No Christian ought to abandon the martyrs of Christ and go to false martyrs, that is, those of heretics. Those who are clearly themselves heretics are alien from God. Therefore let those who approach such persons be anathema.

### On those who worship angels

[Col. 0168C]

CXXXVIII. Christians ought not to leave the Church of God and go to invoke angels and hold assemblies, practices known to be forbidden. If anyone is found serving this hidden idolatry, let him be anathema, because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and surrendered himself to idolatry.

### On those who use incantations and amulets

CXXXIX. Those devoted to sacred offices and clerics ought not to be magicians or enchanters, or make amulets, which are proved to be bonds for their souls. We command that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.

### On those who receive festival gifts from heretics or Jews

[Col. 0168D]

CXL. Festival gifts sent by Jews or heretics ought not to be received, nor should anyone celebrate their festivals with them.

### On Christians who eat the unleavened bread of the Jews

CXLI. One ought not to receive unleavened bread from the Jews or share in their impieties.

### On Christians who celebrate pagan festivals

CXLII. One ought not to celebrate festivals with the pagans or share in the depravity of those who are without God.

### On bishops who avoid the summonses issued for a synod

CXLIII. Bishops summoned to a synod ought not to disregard the summons completely, but should go at once and teach or learn those things that concern the correction of the Church and of its other affairs. The person who disregards the summons will accuse himself, unless he is unable to go because of illness.

### That those serving the sacred ministry must not travel without letters

CXLIV. A priest or cleric ought not to travel without canonical letters.

### That a cleric must not travel without the bishop

CXLV. A priest or cleric ought not to travel without the command of his own bishop.

### That subdeacons should remain at the doors

CXLVI. Subdeacons ought not to leave the doors, even for a short time, and devote themselves to prayer.

### That women must not enter the sacristy

[Col. 0169B]

CXLVII. Women ought not to enter the altar area.

### On those who come for baptism around the middle of the week

CXLVIII. No one ought to be admitted to baptism after the second week of Lent.

### On the recitation of the faith by those to be baptized

CXLIX. Those who come for baptism ought to learn the faith and recite it to the bishop or presbyters on Thursday of Holy Week.

### On those baptized in illness

CL. Those who receive baptism in illness ought, after recovering, to learn the faith thoroughly and understand of what gift they have been made participants.

### That chrism should be given after baptism

[Col. 0169C]

CLI. Those who are baptized ought, after the washing, to receive heavenly chrism and be found participants in the kingdom of Christ.

### That offerings must not be made in Lent

CLII. During Lent, the bread of blessing ought not to be offered on Saturday or Sunday.

### That the fast must not be broken on Thursday of Holy Week
### Canon CLIII

That during Lent one ought not to break the fast on the Thursday of the final week [Note: [Col. 0169D] It should read: “on the Thursday of the final week.” In any case, the text of this manuscript often suffers from considerable obscurity. **Ed.**], and thus pass through the whole of Lent without reverence; rather, it is more fitting to observe the whole of Lent with a strict fast.

### Commemorations of martyrs are not to be held on fast days

[Col. 0170A]

### Canon CLIV

That during Lent the festivals of the martyrs’ births [i.e., their heavenly birthdays] ought not to be celebrated, but that their holy commemoration should fittingly be held on Saturdays and Sundays.

### Festivals and weddings are not to be held during Lent

### Canon CLV

That during Lent one ought not to celebrate either weddings or festivals.

### Christians are not to dance at weddings

### Canon CLVI

That Christians attending weddings ought not to applaud or dance, but should dine or lunch reverently, as is fitting for Christians.

### Clerics are not permitted to attend theatrical entertainments

[Col. 0170B]

### Canon CLVII

That priests or clerics ought not to attend any kind of spectacle, whether at banquets or at weddings; rather, before the theatrical performers enter, they should rise and depart.

### It is wholly unfitting for Christians to attend revelries

### Canon CLVIII

That priests or clerics ought not to hold banquets from collections or drinking parties; indeed, this is not fitting even for laypeople.

### Priests may not enter the altar area before the bishop enters

### Canon CLIX

That priests ought not to enter the sacristy and sit down before the bishop’s procession, but should enter with the bishop or sit on the benches, unless perhaps he is prevented by illness or the bishop is away [Col. 0170C].

### Who should be ordained in villages or estates

### Canon CLX

That bishops ought not to be established in small villages or rural districts, but visitors should be appointed there. Nevertheless, those already established should do nothing without the knowledge of the bishop of the city; likewise, priests should do nothing without the bishop’s advice.

### Offerings are not to be celebrated in private houses

### Canon CLXI

That bishops or priests ought not to celebrate offerings in private houses.

### What it is fitting to sing or read in churches

### Canon CLXII

That privately composed psalms ought not to be sung in church, nor should books other than the canonical ones be read; only the sacred volumes of the New or Old Testament should be read.

## THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN RULES

[Col. 0169]

[Col. 0169D] Under the most pious Emperor Theodosius, three canons were promulgated at Constantinople. These decrees were issued by 150 bishops who had assembled there at Constantinople when blessed Nectarius was ordained bishop.

### That the decrees established at Nicaea should remain unaltered; and concerning the anathema of the Arians, Eunomians, Macedonians, Sabellians, Photinians, Marcellians, and Apollinarians

### Canon CLXIII

The faith of the 318 Fathers who assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia must not be violated, but must remain firm and stable [Col. 0170D]. Every heresy must be anathematized, especially that of the Eunomians or Anomians; the Arians or Eudoxians; the Macedonians, or those who resist the Holy Spirit; the Sabellians; the Marcellians; the Photinians; and the Apollinarians.

### Concerning the order of the individual dioceses, and the privileges owed to the Egyptians, Antiochenes, and Constantinopolitans

### Canon CLXIV

The bishops who preside over dioceses must in no way [Col. 0171A] enter churches outside the boundaries assigned to them, nor disturb them by such presumption. Rather, in accordance with the canons, the bishop of Alexandria shall govern only the churches in Egypt, and the bishops of the East shall govern only the East, while preserving the privileges granted by the Nicene canons to the Church of Antioch. The bishops of the Asian diocese likewise shall administer only what belongs to the Asian diocese. Similarly, the bishops of Pontus shall govern only what is in Pontus, and those of Thrace only what is in Thrace. Bishops who have not been summoned shall not go beyond their own diocese for the purpose of ordinations or any other ecclesiastical administration.

Once the rule written concerning these jurisdictions has been preserved, it is clear that the matters in each province [Col. 0172A] should be administered by the synod of that province itself, as the Council of Nicaea is known to have decreed. The churches of God established among barbarian peoples should be governed according to the custom observed by the Fathers. Nevertheless, the bishop of Constantinople shall have the primacy of honor after the bishop of Rome, because that city is younger than Rome [Col. 0171A].

### Concerning the unlawful ordination of Maximus

### Canon CLXV

Concerning Maximus the Cynic and his irregular installation, which took place at Constantinople, it was decided that Maximus neither is nor was a bishop, and that those whom he ordained as clerics in any rank are not clerics, since everything perpetrated by him is regarded as null and void.

## THE TWENTY-SEVEN ECCLESIASTICAL RULES PROMULGATED BY THE HOLY COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON

[Col. 0171]

### Concerning the canons of each council

[Col. 0171B]

### I

We have decreed that the rules of the holy Fathers, established in each council up to the present, shall retain their proper force.

### Bishops and all clergy are not to be ordained for money

### II

If any bishop performs an ordination for money, or places under a price a favor that cannot be sold, and ordains for money a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone numbered among the clergy, or promotes for money a steward, defender, or anyone subject to the rule, for the sake of his most shameful profit, the person proved to have attempted this shall incur the penalty of losing his own rank.

The one who has been ordained or promoted through such a commercial transaction shall derive no benefit from that ordination or promotion, but shall be excluded from the dignity or responsibility that he acquired with money. If someone has acted as an intermediary in such shameful and ungodly gifts or payments, then, if he is a cleric, he shall fall from his own rank; if he is a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized [Col. 0171C].

### Bishops, clerics, and monks are not to lease other people’s estates

### III

It has come to the holy synod’s attention that certain persons who appear to have been enrolled among the clergy, for the sake of shameful profits, become lessees of other people’s estates and undertake secular business under their own management. They disregard the service of God while running about secular households and, out of greed, assuming responsibility for patrimonies [Col. 0171D].

Therefore this holy and great council has decreed that henceforth no one—neither bishop, cleric, nor monk—may lease estates or involve himself in secular business, except for the unavoidable care of orphans where the laws impose it; or where the bishop of the city orders him to oversee ecclesiastical property; or where the fear of the Lord requires care for orphans, widows, and persons without any provision, who especially need ecclesiastical assistance [Col. 0172B]. Whoever thereafter attempts to transgress these statutes shall be subject to ecclesiastical reproof.

### Concerning the honor due to monks, and that none of them should disturb ecclesiastical or secular affairs or receive another’s slave without his master’s knowledge

### IV

Those who truly and sincerely pursue the solitary life should be honored appropriately. Since, however, certain persons, wearing the monastic habit, disturb ecclesiastical and civil affairs, wandering indiscriminately through the cities and also attempting to establish monasteries for themselves, it was decided that no one may build or establish a monastery or house of prayer anywhere without the knowledge of the bishop of the city.

Monks in each city or region are to be subject to the bishop, love quiet, and devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer, remaining in the places where they renounced the world. They are not to participate in ecclesiastical or secular business, nor cause trouble in any way by abandoning their own monasteries, unless the bishop of the city orders them to do so for some necessary work.

No one is to receive a slave into a monastery under the pretext of making him a monk without the knowledge of his master. We have decreed that anyone who transgresses this definition is excommunicated, lest the name of God be blasphemed. Nevertheless, the bishop of the city ought to exercise appropriate oversight of the monasteries [Col. 0172C].

### No transfer from one city to another

[Col. 0172D]

### V

Concerning bishops or clerics who transfer from one city to another: it was decided that the canons established on this matter by the holy Fathers shall retain their proper force.

### No one is to be ordained without a specified appointment

### VI

No one should be ordained absolutely as a priest or deacon, or to any ecclesiastical rank, unless it is expressly declared that he is being ordained for a particular church of a city, estate, martyr-shrine, or monastery. With regard to those who are ordained without such an appointment, the holy synod has decreed that this laying-on of hands is invalid and that they may nowhere minister, to the injury of the one who ordained them [Col. 0173A].

### Concerning clerics and monks who do not remain in their chosen state

### VII

We decree that those who have once been assigned to the clergy or have chosen the monastic life are not to enter military service or any worldly dignity. Those who attempt this and do not repent, so as to return to what they originally chose for God’s sake, are to be anathematized.

### Concerning clerics in orphanages, monasteries, and martyr-shrines under the authority of the bishops of the respective cities

### VIII

Clerics placed in charge of orphanages, or ordained in monasteries and basilicas of martyrs, are to remain under the authority of the bishops of the respective cities, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers [Col. 0173B]. They must not rebelliously separate themselves from their bishop. Those who dare to overturn this arrangement in any way and do not submit to their own bishop shall, if they are clerics, be subject to canonical correction; if they are laymen or monks, they shall be deprived of communion.

### Clerics who have disputes with one another must not leave their own bishop and resort to secular courts

### IX

If one cleric has a dispute with another cleric, he must not abandon his own bishop and hasten to secular courts. Rather, the case must first be heard before his own bishop, or, with that bishop’s advice, judgment may be conducted before judges chosen by both parties [Col. 0173C]. Whoever acts otherwise shall be subject to canonical correction.

If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or against another bishop, he shall be judged by the synod of the province. If a bishop or cleric has a grievance against the metropolitan of that province, he shall appeal to the primate of the diocese or to the see of the royal city of Constantinople, and shall be judged before him.

### A cleric may not minister in the churches of two cities

### X

A cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities: both in the church in which he was first ordained and in the one to which he has fled as though it were superior, out of a desire for empty glory. Those who do this must be recalled to the church in which they were first ordained and minister there alone [Col. 0173D].

If anyone has already been transferred from one church to another, he must have no involvement in the property of the former church, or of the martyr-shrines, orphanages, or hostels belonging to it. The holy synod has decreed that those who, after the definition of this great and universal synod, dare to perpetrate anything forbidden here must withdraw from their own rank.

### The poor are not to be given commendatory letters; persons of higher standing are to be approved by letters of recommendation

### XI

We have decreed that all poor people and those in need of assistance, when they travel after having been examined, are to be commended only by letters of passage or ecclesiastical letters of peace, and not by letters of recommendation [Col. 0174A], since commendatory letters should properly be granted only to persons of higher standing.

### A province is not to be divided between two metropolitans

### XII

It has come to our attention that certain persons, acting contrary to ecclesiastical statutes, have fled to secular authorities and, through an imperial administrative arrangement, divided one province into two, so that as a result two metropolitans appear to exist in one province.

Therefore the holy synod decrees that henceforth no bishop should attempt anything of this kind. Whoever undertakes it shall incur the loss of his own rank. Whatever cities have been supported by imperial letters with the honor of the metropolitan title shall enjoy that title only, while the bishop who governs its church shall retain it, without prejudice, of course, to the privileges of the true metropolis [Col. 0174B].

### Foreign clerics may not minister without letters of recommendation

### XIII

Foreign clerics and readers must nowhere minister in another city without letters of recommendation from their own bishop.

### A cleric may not marry a woman of another faith

### XIV

Since in certain provinces readers and psalmists have been permitted to marry, the holy synod decrees that none of them may take a wife of another faith. If they have already had children from such a marriage, and those children were baptized by heretics, they should offer them to communion with the Catholic Church; but those not yet baptized may not thereafter be baptized among heretics [Col. 0174C].

Nor should a woman who is about to marry be joined to a heretic, Jew, or pagan, unless he promises that he will transfer himself to orthodox faith and be joined to an orthodox person. Whoever transgresses this definition of the holy synod shall be subject to canonical correction.

### Concerning women deacons

### XV

A woman is not to be ordained as a deacon before the age of forty, and even then only with the greatest scrutiny. If, after receiving the laying-on of hands and remaining for some time in the ministry, she gives herself to marriage, thereby insulting the grace of God, she and the man joined to her are to be anathematized.

### Concerning virgins

[Col. 0174D]

### XVI

A virgin who has consecrated herself to the Lord God, and likewise a monk, may not enter into the rights of marriage. If they are found to have done so, they shall be excommunicated. In the case of those who confess their fault, we have decreed that the bishop of the place may extend mercy and humane treatment.

### Concerning parishes

### XVII

The rural parishes or estates of individual churches are to remain undisturbed under the bishops known to retain them, especially if they have governed them under their administration for thirty years while holding them without force. If, however, a dispute concerning them arose or arises within the thirty-year period, those who claim to have been wronged may bring the matter before the holy synod of the province [Col. 0175A].

If anyone is wronged by the metropolitan, he shall be judged by the primate of the diocese or by the see of Constantinople, as stated above. If a city is reorganized by imperial authority, or is subsequently reorganized, the ecclesiastical order of its parishes should follow the civil arrangements and public administration.

### Concerning conspiracy or collusion

### XVIII

The crime of conspiracy or collusion is wholly prohibited even by secular laws; much more, therefore, must it be forbidden in the Church of God. If any clerics or monks are found conspiring, colluding, or laying plots against bishops or clerics, they shall be completely deposed from their own rank.

### Councils are to be held twice a year in each province

[Col. 0175B]

### XIX

It has come to our ears that the episcopal councils prescribed in the provinces are scarcely being held, and that as a result many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are being neglected.

Therefore the holy synod has decreed that, according to the canons of the Fathers, the bishops are to assemble twice a year in each province, at a place approved by the metropolitan bishop, so that each matter that may have arisen can be corrected.
