Any bishops who do not attend, while remaining in their own cities and being in good health and free from every unavoidable and necessary occupation, are to be corrected in a spirit of brotherly affection [Col. 0175C].

### Clerics should not be transferred

### XX

As we have already established, clerics ministering in one church ought not to be appointed to the church of another city. They should remain content in the churches in which they were first found worthy to minister, except for those who, having lost their own provinces, have necessarily transferred to another church.

If, after this definition, any bishop receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, it was decided that both the cleric received and the bishop receiving him are to be deprived of communion until the cleric who transferred has returned to his own church.

### Concerning accusers of bishops or clerics

[Col. 0175D]

### XXI

Clerics or laypeople who accuse bishops or clerics indiscriminately and without proof are not to be admitted to an accusation unless their reputation and standing have first been examined.

### Clerics may not seize property belonging to their bishop after his death

### XXII

Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, seize property belonging to him, as was also established by the ancient canons. If they attempt to do so, they shall incur the penalty of losing their ranks [Col. 0176A].

### Concerning clerics and monks who come to the royal city of Constantinople against the will of their bishop

### XXIII

It has come to the ears of the holy council that certain clerics and monks, to whom their bishop has entrusted nothing—and from whom he sometimes even withholds communion—come to the royal city of Constantinople and remain there for a long time, stirring up disturbances, disrupting ecclesiastical order, and even overthrowing the households of certain people.

The holy synod has decreed that such persons should first be warned by the defender of the holy Church of Constantinople to leave the royal city. If they persist shamelessly in the same activities, the defender is to expel them even against their will, so that they may return to their own places [Col. 0176B].

### Consecrated monasteries may not be turned into secular lodging houses

### XXIV

Monasteries once dedicated are to remain monasteries forever, by decision of the bishops, and the property belonging to them is to be reserved for the monasteries. They may not thereafter be converted into secular dwellings. Those who permit this shall be subject to the judgments of the canons.

### Episcopal ordinations are not to be long delayed

### XXV

Since, as we have learned, certain metropolitans neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay the ordination of bishops, it was decided by the synod that episcopal ordinations should be conducted within three months [Col. 0176C], unless some unavoidable necessity requires the period of delay to be extended. If anyone fails to do this, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction. Nevertheless, the revenues of the widowed church are to be kept intact by its steward.

### Concerning the stewards of individual churches

### XXVI

Since, as we have learned by report, in certain churches the bishops themselves administer ecclesiastical resources in addition to the stewards, it was decided that every church having a bishop must have a steward from its own clergy to administer ecclesiastical property according to the judgment of its own bishop.

This is so that the administration of the church may not be without witnesses, ecclesiastical resources may not consequently be scattered, and reproach may not be brought upon the priesthood [Col. 0176D]. Whoever fails to do this shall be subject to the divine constitutions.

### Concerning those who abduct girls

### XXVII

The holy synod has decreed that those who abduct women under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or connive at the abductors, are to be punished as follows: if they are clerics, they shall fall from their own rank; if they are laypeople, they shall be anathematized.

## TWENTY-ONE CANONS OF THE SYNOD OF SARDICA

[Col. 0175]

### Concerning bishops who have changed cities and are also to be deprived of lay communion

[Col. 0175D]

### I

Bishop Hosius said:

A bad custom no less than a pernicious corruption [Col. 0176D] must be eradicated completely, so that no bishop may be permitted to transfer from his own city to another. The reason [Col. 0177A] why he attempts this is obvious, since no bishop has yet been found in this matter who transferred from a larger city to a smaller one. Hence it is evident that they are inflamed by the heat of greed, serve ambition, and seek to exercise domination.

If this is acceptable to all, let such wickedness be punished more severely and more strictly, so that a person of this kind may not even have lay communion.

They all replied: “It is acceptable.”

### Again concerning the same bishops: if they change their see through ambition, they are not to receive even lay communion at the end of life

### II

Bishop Hosius said:

Even if some such rash person should arise and perhaps assert, by way of excuse, that he received letters from the people, it is obvious that many people without sincere faith could have been [Col. 0177B] corrupted by reward and payment so that they would shout in the church and appear to request him as bishop. I judge that such frauds must be condemned altogether, so that such a person may not receive even lay communion at the end of life.

If this is acceptable to all of you, establish it.

The synod replied: “It is acceptable.”

### Provincial bishops are to hear disputes between bishops; if the condemned party appeals to the Roman bishop, his decision is to be observed

### III

Bishop Hosius said:

This too must necessarily be added: bishops are not to pass from their own province into another province in which there are bishops, unless perhaps they have been invited by their brothers, lest they appear to close the door of charity.

If, in any province, one bishop has a dispute with another bishop, one of the two should summon a bishop from another province as judge [Col. 0177C].

If a bishop has been judged in some case and believes that he has a good cause for the council to be convened again, then, if it is acceptable to you, let us honor the memory of the holy Apostle Peter. Let those who examined the case write to Julius, bishop of Rome; and if he judges that the case should be reheard, let it be reheard, and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that what has been done should not be reopened, his decision shall be confirmed.

If this is acceptable to all.

The synod replied: “It is acceptable.”

### No one is to usurp the see of an accused bishop

### IV

Bishop Gaudentius said:

If it is acceptable, let this be added to the judgment you have pronounced with complete holiness: when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of bishops residing in neighboring places, and has appealed for his case to be heard in the city of Rome, no other bishop is to be ordained in his chair after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has first been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop [Col. 0177D].

### When a bishop should be ordained by bishops of neighboring provinces

### V

Bishop Hosius said:

If it should happen in a province containing many bishops that only one bishop remains, and he, through negligence, is unwilling to ordain a bishop, while the people assemble, the bishops of the neighboring province must first approach the bishop residing in that province and show him that the people are requesting a ruler for themselves. It is just that they themselves should come and ordain the bishop together with him [Col. 0178A].

If, after being approached by letter, he remains silent, dissimulates, and sends no reply, the needs of the people are to be met: the bishops of the neighboring province should come and ordain a bishop.

### Bishops are not to be ordained in villages or small cities

### VI

Permission must not be granted to ordain a bishop in any village or in a small city for which one priest is sufficient, since it is unnecessary to establish a bishop there, lest the name and authority of a bishop be cheapened.

Those invited from another province ought not to ordain a bishop there unless it is in cities that have had bishops, or in a city that is of such a kind or so populous [Col. 0178B] that it deserves to have a bishop.

If this is acceptable to all.

The synod replied: “It is acceptable.”

### A provincial synod may be reconsidered through representatives of the bishop of Rome if he so decides

### VII

Bishop Hosius said:

It was decided that if a bishop is accused, and the bishops of that region assemble, judge him, and depose him from his rank, then, if the deposed man appeals and takes refuge with the bishop of the Roman Church, wishing to be heard, the Roman bishop, if he considers it just that the examination be renewed, should write to the bishops in the neighboring and adjoining province, so that they may investigate the matter thoroughly and decide according to the truth of the faith [Col. 0178C].

If the person requesting that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his petition to send a priest from his own side, it shall be within the bishop’s power to determine what he wishes and considers appropriate. If he decides that men should be sent to sit in judgment with the bishops present, possessing the authority of the one who sent them, that shall be at his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the case to an end, he shall do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.

### When, and in what cases, bishops should go to the imperial court

### VIII

Bishop Hosius said:

The pressure, excessive frequency, and unjust petitions of certain people have caused us not to enjoy as much favor or confidence as we should, since some bishops do not cease going to the imperial court. This is especially true of the Africans, who, as we have learned, disregard and despise the salutary counsels of our most holy brother and fellow bishop, Gratian [Col. 0178D].

They bring to the imperial court not only many different cases that will not benefit the Church, rather than seeking, as is customary and proper, assistance for the poor, widows, or orphans, but also request secular dignities and administrative offices for certain people. This depravity has long stirred up not only murmuring but also scandals.

It is honorable for bishops to offer intercession to those who are oppressed by unjust force, or when a widow is afflicted or an orphan despoiled, provided that these persons have a just case or petition. If this is acceptable to you, dearest brothers, decree that bishops may not go to the imperial court unless they have been invited or summoned by letters from the religious emperor.

Since, however, it often happens that those who suffer injustice, or those who are condemned to exile or to the islands because of their offenses, or who receive any other sentence, take refuge in the mercy of the Church [Col. 0179A], assistance must be given to them and pardon must unquestionably be requested. Establish this, if it is acceptable to you.

They all said: “It is acceptable, and let it be enacted.”

### Deacons are to be sent to the imperial court

### IX

Bishop Hosius said:

Your Prudence should also consider this matter, since you have decreed that bishops must not, through misconduct, seek to go to the imperial court. Therefore, whoever has or receives petitions of the kind mentioned above should send them through his deacon, since the person of a minister is not subject to envy, and he will be able to report more quickly what he has obtained.

It also seems appropriate that, from each province, the bishops should send petitions to that brother and fellow bishop of ours who resides in the metropolis, so that he may send both his deacon and the petitions, supplying letters of recommendation in the same manner to our brothers and fellow bishops who at that time reside in the regions and cities in which the fortunate and blessed Augustus governs the state [Col. 0179B].

If a bishop has friends at court and wishes to obtain something that is nevertheless honorable, he is not forbidden to make the request through his deacon and to inform those whom he knows can offer a kindly intercession on behalf of an absent person, provided that the occasion is appropriate.

### The imperial court should be approached for orphans, widows, and those suffering necessity

### X

Those who have come to Rome, as stated, should deliver the petitions they have to our most holy brother and fellow bishop of the Roman Church [Col. 0179C], so that he himself may first examine whether they are honorable and just, and may take care and responsibility for having them brought to the imperial court.

They all said that this pleased them and was an honorable policy.

Bishop Alypius said:

If people undertake the hardships of travel for the sake of orphans, widows, or persons in distress who suffer unjust wrongs, they will have some justification. But when they chiefly seek things that cannot be obtained without provoking people’s envy and criticism, it is not necessary for the bishop himself to go to the imperial court.

### Bishops who are on the route to the imperial court are to be carefully examined

### XI

Bishop Gaudentius said:

The salutary measures you have wisely adopted, which are agreeable to everyone’s judgment and pleasing to God, can retain their force if fear is joined to this decision. We know that, very often, because of the shamelessness of a few, the honorable name of the priesthood has itself been criticized.

Therefore, if anyone, contrary to the judgment of all, attempts to please ambition more than God, he must understand that, after giving an account of his actions, he will lose his honor and dignity. This can be carried out only if each one of us who is stationed along the route, whenever he sees a bishop traveling, investigates his passage, examines his reasons, and learns where he is going [Col. 0179D].

If he finds that the bishop is going to the imperial court, he must also inquire into the matter stated above, lest perhaps the bishop has been invited and is therefore permitted to go. But if, as your Holiness stated above, he is going to the imperial court out of desire and ambition, his letters must not be signed, nor is he to be admitted to communion.

If this is acceptable to you, it should be confirmed by the judgment of all.

They all said that this enactment was honorable and pleased them.

### Concerning those who do not know what has been established in the synod

### XII

Bishop Hosius said:

Moderation is also necessary, dearest brothers, lest some people who do not yet know what has been decreed in the synod suddenly come to the cities that lie along the route. The bishop of that city must therefore warn and instruct him, and from that place send his own deacon [Col. 0180A]. Once warned, he himself must nevertheless return to his own parish.

### Laymen are not to be made bishops rashly

[Col. 0180B]

### XIII

Bishop Hosius said:

I also consider it necessary that you examine this matter most carefully: if perhaps a wealthy man, a legal scholar from the marketplace, or someone from an administrative office is requested as bishop, he must not be ordained until he has fulfilled the office of reader and the ministry of deacon or priest, so that, if he is worthy, he may ascend through each rank to the summit of the episcopate.

Through these promotions, which will necessarily take a considerable amount of time, it can be tested with what faith, modesty, seriousness, and reverence he lives. If he is found worthy, let him be honored with the divine priesthood. For it is neither fitting nor permitted by reason or discipline that a bishop, priest, or deacon should be ordained rashly and lightly, especially since the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, appears to have warned and forbidden that this be done. Rather, those should be ordained whose lives have been examined over a long period and whose merits have been proven [Col. 0180C].

### How long a bishop may remain in another city

### XIV

Bishop Hosius said:

You must also establish this: if a bishop comes from one city to another, or from his own province to another province, and, serving ambition more than devotion, wishes to remain for a long time in another city, a situation may arise in which the bishop of the place is not so well instructed or learned. The newcomer may then begin to despise him and frequently deliver sermons that dishonor and weaken his reputation, so that on this pretext he does not hesitate to abandon the Church assigned to him and transfer to another [Col. 0180D].

Therefore, set a limit of time. It is inhuman not to receive a bishop, but it is harmful for him to remain too long. Provision must therefore be made to prevent this.

I remember that at the previous council our brothers established that if a layman did not hold an assembly for three Sundays—that is, for three weeks—in the city where he resides, he would be deprived of communion. If this was established for laypeople, much less is it permitted or fitting for a bishop to remain away from his own Church beyond the stated period, unless some very serious necessity keeps him there.

They all said that this pleased them.

### A bishop may not be absent from his Church for more than three weeks
### XV

**Bishop Hosius said:** Since nothing ought to be omitted, there are certain of our brothers and fellow bishops who are not established as bishops in the city in which they appear to hold office, or who at least possess only a small property there, while they are known to have suitable estates elsewhere, or relatives toward whom they show indulgence. They ought to be permitted, therefore, to go to their properties and arrange or manage the produce of their labor, so that, after three Sundays—that is, after three weeks—if it is necessary for them to remain, they may stay rather on their own estates.

Or, if there is a nearby city in which there is a presbyter, let him go there, so that he may not appear to spend the Lord’s Day without a church. In this way, neither will his household affairs suffer loss through his absence, nor will he, by frequently coming to the city in which the bishop resides, incur suspicion of ostentation and ambition.

All said that this pleased them.

### Clerics removed from communion by one bishop are not to be received by another bishop

[Col. 0181B]

### XVI

**Bishop Hosius said:** This also pleases everyone: if a deacon, presbyter, or any other cleric has been deprived of communion by his own bishop and has gone to another bishop, and the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was rejected by his own bishop, he ought not to grant him communion. If he does so, he must know that, when the bishops are convened, he will have to give an account of the matter.

All said: This statute will preserve peace and maintain concord.

### Excommunicated persons are to be heard by neighboring bishops

### XVII

**Bishop Hosius said:** I must not remain silent about what still troubles me. If a bishop—who perhaps is angry, although he ought not to be—becomes quickly and harshly stirred against his presbyter or deacon and wishes to drive him from the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. Therefore, let the man who has been rejected have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined more carefully, for it is not right to deny a hearing to one who asks for it. Let the bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that his judgment may either be approved by many or corrected.

Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no one ought to presume to unite to communion the person who has been separated from communion, before the case has been investigated.

If those who assemble to hear the case see that the cleric is acting contentiously and arrogantly—for it is not fitting that a bishop should suffer injury or insult—let them rebuke the clerics in sterner words, so that they obey the honorable bishop who gives the command. Just as that bishop ought to show the clerics sincere charitable love, so likewise the ministers ought to show their bishop unfeigned obedience.

### Clerics belonging to another bishop are not to be enticed away

### XVIII

**Bishop Januarius said:** Let your holiness also decree that no bishop may entice away an ecclesiastical minister belonging to another bishop’s city and appoint him in his own parishes.

All said: It pleases us, because discord commonly arises from such disputes; therefore, by the judgment of all, let no one dare to do this.

### Clerics belonging to another bishop are not to be ordained without that bishop’s consent

[Col. 0182B]

### XIX

**Bishop Hosius said:** We unanimously establish this also: if anyone from another parish wishes to ordain someone else’s minister without the consent and will of that minister’s bishop, his ordination shall not be valid. Whoever usurps this power ought to be admonished and corrected by our brothers and fellow bishops.

### Concerning the length of time presbyters and deacons who come to Thessalonica may remain there

### XX

**Bishop Aetius said:** You are not unaware how great and important the city of the Thessalonians is. Presbyters and deacons frequently come to it from other regions, and they are not content to remain for a short time; rather, they either settle there or are scarcely able to return to their own churches except after long intervals.

All said: The periods established for bishops ought also to be observed with regard to these persons.

### Concerning the reception of those who suffer persecution

### XXI

**Bishop Hosius said:** At the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Olympius, this also has pleased us: if someone has suffered violence and been unjustly expelled on account of discipline, the catholic confession, or the defense of the truth, and, fleeing danger, has come innocent and devout to another city, he must not be forbidden to remain there for as long as he is either able to return or receives a remedy for his wrong. For it is harsh not to receive one who is suffering persecution; generous goodwill and humane treatment must also be shown to him.

The canons, or decrees, of the Council of Sardica end here. All the bishops signed as follows: “I, that bishop of that city and that province, believe thus, as it is written above.”

# Synod at Carthage of the Africans, which established 138 canons

[Col. 0181]

[Col. 0181D] After the consulship of the most glorious emperors, Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augusti, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the basilica of Faustus, when Aurelius the pope, together with Valentinus of the first see of the province of Numidia, Faustinus of the Church of Potentia in the province of Italia Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, and also the legates of the various African provinces—namely, the two Numidias, Byzacena, Mauretania Caesariensis, and Tripolitana—and Vincentius of Colossae, Fortunatianus, and the other bishops of the proconsular province, 217 in number, were in session, along with Philip and Asellus, presbyters and legates of the Roman Church, the deacons standing by, Bishop Aurelius said:

After the appointed day of the council, as you remember, most blessed brothers, many matters were requested while we awaited our brothers who have now arrived as legates at the present synod; these matters must be joined to the acts. For this, we give thanks to our Lord God for the gathering of so great an assembly.

It remains that both the copies of the Nicene Council that we now possess, and the decrees established by the Fathers, as well as the material brought forward here by our predecessors in confirmation of that same synod, and whatever has been beneficially ordered according to its pattern through all the clerical grades, from the highest to the lowest, should be presented.

The entire council said: Let them be presented.

The notary Daniel read:

The profession of faith of the Nicene Council and its decrees are as follows. As he was saying this, Bishop Faustinus of the congregation of Potentia, in the province of Italia Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, said:

Some matters have been entrusted to us by the apostolic see in writing, and some orally, to be discussed with your blessedness, as we recalled in the earlier acts. These concern the Nicene canons: that they, their decrees, and their custom be preserved, since some matters are maintained by established procedure and canon, while others have been confirmed by custom.

Let us therefore first discuss these matters, if it pleases your blessedness, and afterward let the other matters that have been enacted or begun be inserted and confirmed, so that you may also inform the venerable see by your replies, and it may clearly appear that we have been instructed by the venerable pope, although the chapters of the proceedings have already been inserted in the acts.

As I said above, we must deal with these matters according to what pleases your blessedness. Let the memorandum therefore be brought forward, so that your blessedness may know what it contains and replies may be given to each point.

**Bishop Aurelius said:** Let the memorandum be presented, which our brothers and fellow priests recently cited in the acts; the other matters that have been enacted or are to be enacted will follow.

The notary Daniel read:

**Memorandum to Brother Faustinus and to the presbyters Philip and Asellus, his sons, from Bishop Zosimus.**

The affairs entrusted to you are not unknown to you. Carry them all out as though they were ours—indeed, because our presence there is in you—especially since you may also have this as our mandate, together with the words of the canons that we have inserted into this memorandum for fuller confirmation.

For this is what the brothers said at the Nicene Council when they were deciding about the appeal of bishops:

“It was decreed that if a bishop has been accused, and the bishops of that region have assembled, judged him, and deposed him from his rank, and he appears to have appealed and has fled to the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and wishes to be heard, and the bishop of Rome judges it right that the examination be renewed, let him write to the bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the truth.

“If anyone asks that his case be heard again and by his entreaty moves the Roman bishop to send a presbyter from his side, it shall be within the bishop’s power to decide what he wishes and what he judges appropriate. If he decides that persons should be sent who, being present, may judge together with the bishops, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, this shall be at his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.”

As this was being read, Alypius, bishop of the Church of Tagaste and legate of the province of Numidia, said:

We have already replied concerning this in earlier letters of our council, and we profess that we shall observe what was established at the Nicene Council. Yet I am still troubled by the fact that, when we examined the Greek copies of this Nicene synod, we did not find this passage there at all, for whatever reason. We therefore ask your reverence, holy Pope Aurelius: since this authentic Nicene Council is said to be in the city of Constantinople, may you deign to send certain persons with letters from your holiness, not only to our holy brother the bishop of Constantinople, but also to the venerable priests, the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, so that they may send us this council under the attestation of their letters and all later uncertainty may be removed. For we did not find these things as Brother Faustinus presented them.

Nevertheless, as I said earlier, we profess that we shall observe them for a short time, until complete copies arrive. Our letters should also request the venerable bishop of the Roman Church, Boniface, to deign to send persons to the aforesaid Churches who may bring back the same copies in accordance with his letters. For the present, we attach to these proceedings the copies of the aforesaid Nicene Council that we possess.

**Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, said:** Nor does your holiness prejudice the Roman Church, whether concerning this chapter or others, by saying—as our brother and fellow bishop Alypius has done—that the canons are doubtful. But deign to write these very matters to our holy and most blessed pope, so that he too, seeking the complete canons, may discuss all the decrees together with your holiness.

It is sufficient that the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome, just as your holiness is discussing the matter among yourselves, should likewise investigate it, lest contention appear to arise between the Churches. Rather, you may deliberate in fraternal charity, with him writing back concerning what ought best to be observed.

[Col. 0184D] **Bishop Aurelius said:** Besides the matters that we have brought forth in the acts, it is necessary that we also communicate fully, in a letter from our humble selves, each matter we are discussing to our holy brother and fellow priest Boniface. Therefore, if our proposal pleases everyone, let us learn this from the voice of all.

The entire council said: It pleases us.

**Bishop Novatus, legate of Mauretania Sitifensis, said:** We now remember that this memorandum also contains provisions concerning presbyters and deacons—how they ought to be heard by their own bishops or by neighboring bishops. We have not read this at all in the Nicene Council; therefore, let your holiness order this very passage to be read.

**Bishop Aurelius said:** Let what is requested also be read at its place.

The notary Daniel read:

Concerning appeals by clerics—that is, those of a lower rank—the synod itself gave a definite answer. We believe that what you are to do in this matter should be inserted. It was said as follows:

**Bishop Hosius said:** I must not remain silent about what still troubles me. If a bishop—who perhaps is angry, although he ought not to be—becomes quickly or harshly stirred against his presbyter or deacon and wishes to drive him from the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. Let the man who has been expelled have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined more carefully, for it is not right to deny a hearing to one who asks for it. Let the bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that his judgment may either be approved or corrected, and so forth.

[Col. 0185B] As these matters were being read, Augustine, bishop of the Church of Hippo in the province of Numidia, said:

We also profess that we shall observe this, subject to a more careful investigation of the Nicene Council.

**Bishop Aurelius said:** If this also pleases all your charity, confirm it by your response.

The entire council said: Everything established at the Nicene Council pleases us all.

Jocundus, bishop of the Church of Suffetula, legate of the province of Byzacena, said: Whatever was established at the Nicene Council can in no way be violated by anyone.

**Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, said:** According to the profession of your holiness, both that of the holy Alypius and that of our brother Jocundus, I believe that some matters are being weakened and others confirmed, although they ought not to be, since the canons themselves have now become doubtful.

Therefore, as it pleases both us and your blessedness, may your holiness refer the matter to the holy and venerable bishop of the Roman Church, so that he too may deliberate about what the holy Augustine has deigned to establish—whether this also ought to be granted or kept silent, namely, the matter of an appeal by one of lower rank.

If this matter has therefore again become doubtful, and if it is right that the bishop of the most blessed see be informed about this chapter, that should be done—provided that this can be found in the approved canons.

**Bishop Aurelius said:** Further, permit the copies of the decrees of the Nicene Council, which we formerly communicated to your charity, to be read now, as well as the matters beneficially established here by our predecessors according to the pattern of that same council, and those now ordered by us; let all these be inserted in the acts.

The entire council said:

The copies of the faith and the decrees of the Nicene synod that were brought to our council by Caecilian, bishop and predecessor of your holiness, now blessed in memory, who was present there, as well as what the Fathers established here by following those copies, and what we now establish by common deliberation, shall remain inserted in these ecclesiastical acts.

Accordingly, as was said above, may your blessedness write to the venerable bishops of the Churches of Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople, so that they may send the most authentic copies of the Nicene Council under the attestation of their letters. When the truth has been made clear, the chapters that our present brother and fellow bishop Faustinus, together with his fellow presbyters Philip and Asellus, brought with them in the memorandum—or that are found there—will either be confirmed by us; or, if they are not found, we shall assemble a synod and discuss the matter at a later time.

The notary Daniel read the profession of faith and the decrees of the Nicene Council in the African council.

## Profession of faith of the Nicene Council

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of visible and invisible things; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father as the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion*, through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth.

For us human beings and for our salvation he descended, was incarnate and made human, suffered, and rose again on the third day. He ascended into the heavens, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead; and we believe in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and “Before he was begotten he did not exist,” and who say that he was made from things that did not exist, or from another substance, calling the Son of God mutable and changeable—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

The decrees of the Nicene Council were likewise read in twenty chapters, as they are found written above. Then the matters promulgated in the African councils are known to have been inserted in the present acts.

### That the decrees established at the Nicene Council be preserved in every respect

[Col. 0186C]

### I

**Bishop Aurelius said:** These are the copies of the decrees that our Fathers then brought back with them from the Nicene Council. Preserving its form, we shall maintain and guard the following decrees, confirmed by us.

### Concerning the preaching of the Trinity

### II

The entire council said:

By God’s favor, the ecclesiastical faith, which we transmit in this glorious assembly with a common confession, must first be professed; only then is the ecclesiastical order of each person to be preserved with the agreement of all.

For strengthening the minds of our brothers and fellow bishops recently promoted, we must set forth what we received from the Fathers by a definite arrangement, so that we may instruct God’s peoples as we speak concerning the unity of the Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which we retain as consecrated in our understanding and which is known to have no distinction.

All the bishops recently promoted likewise said: We have plainly received it thus, hold it thus, and teach it thus, following the evangelical faith together with your teaching.

### Concerning continence

### III

**Bishop Aurelius said:** When the matter of continence and the discipline of chastity was treated in the previous council, it pleased us that these three orders, which are joined by a certain bond of chastity through their consecrations—namely, bishops, presbyters, and deacons—should be continent in all things, as is fitting for holy overseers and priests of God, as well as for Levites and those who serve the divine sacraments.

Thus they may be able in simplicity to obtain from the Lord what they ask, so that we too may preserve what the apostles taught and antiquity itself maintained.

### Concerning abstinence from wives by the various orders

### IV

**Bishop Faustinus of the Church of Potentia, in the province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, said:** Let it please us that the bishop, presbyter, and deacon, and those who handle the sacraments, as guardians of chastity, abstain from their wives.

All the bishops said: Let chastity be preserved in all who serve at the altar.

### Concerning avarice

### V

**Bishop Aurelius said:** The desire for avarice, which no one doubts to be the mother of all evils, must accordingly be restrained, lest anyone usurp another’s boundaries or cross, for payment, the limits established by the Fathers. Nor may any cleric at all receive interest on any matter.

Although recent proposals, whether obscure or concealed under some category, will receive a rule when we have examined them, no judgment should be tolerated concerning matters expressly decreed by divine Scripture; rather, it must be carried out.

Therefore, what is condemned in laymen ought much more to be condemned in advance among clerics.

The entire council said: No one acts against the Prophets or against the Gospels without danger.

### That chrism is not to be made by presbyters

### VI

**Bishop Fortunatus said:** We remember that previous councils established that chrism, the reconciliation of penitents, and the consecration of virgins are not to be performed by presbyters. If someone should be found doing this, what ought to be decreed concerning him?

**Bishop Aurelius said:** Your dignity has heard the proposal of our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus. What do you say about this?

All the bishops said: Let the making of chrism and the consecration of virgins not be performed by presbyters; nor is it lawful for a presbyter to reconcile anyone at a public Mass. This pleases us all.

### Concerning those who are reconciled when placed in danger

### VII

**Bishop Aurelius said:** If anyone has been placed in danger and has asked to be reconciled to the divine altars, and the bishop is absent, the presbyter must certainly consult the bishop and, at his command, reconcile the person in danger. We ought to confirm this matter by a salutary decision.

All the bishops said: What your holiness has rightly deigned to teach us pleases us.

### Concerning those who bring accusations against their superiors, and that no one guilty of crimes may accuse a bishop

### VIII

**Bishop Numidius of Maxula said:** Furthermore, there are very many persons of poor conduct who think that their elders or bishops may be summoned indiscriminately and recklessly to accusation. Should such persons be admitted so easily or not?

**Bishop Aurelius said:** Does it therefore please your charity that a person entangled in certain crimes should not have a voice to accuse his superior?

All the bishops said: If he is a criminal, let him not be admitted. It pleases us.

### Concerning those who are expelled from the Church’s assembly on account of their crimes

[Col. 0188A]

### IX

**Bishop Augustine, legate of the province of Numidia, said:** Deign to establish that if anyone has been expelled from the Church on account of his crimes, and has been received into communion by some bishop or presbyter, that person too shall be held liable with them to an equal crime, because they have avoided the regular judgment of their own bishop.

All the bishops said: It pleases everyone.

### Concerning presbyters who are corrected by their own bishops

### X

**Bishop Alypius, legate of the province of Numidia, said:** Nor should this be omitted: if a presbyter, having been corrected by his bishop, should, inflated by arrogance or pride, suppose that sacrifices ought to be offered to God separately, or should believe that another altar ought to be erected against ecclesiastical faith or discipline, he must not escape unpunished.

**Valentinus of the first see of the province of Numidia said:** What our brother Alypius has set forth is necessarily consistent with ecclesiastical discipline and faith. Therefore, declare what appears right to your affection.

### If a presbyter, inflated against his bishop, creates a schism, let him be anathema

### XI

All the bishops said:

If a presbyter has been corrected by his superior, he must certainly bring his complaint before neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and he may be reconciled through them to his bishop. But if he does not do this and, inflated by pride—which God forbid, he should be—judges that he ought to separate himself from communion with his bishop, and, creating a schism with certain persons, offers sacrifice to God separately, let him be held anathema and lose his position. But if he has no just complaint against his bishop, an inquiry must be made.

### If a bishop is detained under accusation outside the time of a synod, let him be heard by twelve bishops

### XII

**Bishop Felix said:** I propose, in accordance with the decrees of the ancient councils, that if a bishop—which we do not wish—has incurred some charge and there is an extreme necessity preventing the gathering of many bishops, so that he does not remain under accusation, he should be heard by twelve bishops; a presbyter by six bishops together with his own bishop; and a deacon by three.

### That a bishop may not be ordained except by many bishops; but if necessity requires, let three bishops ordain him

[Col. 0188D]

### XIII

**Bishop Aurelius said:** What does your holiness say to this?

All the bishops said:

The decrees of the ancient councils must be preserved. Nor should a group of bishops too readily presume to ordain a bishop without consulting the primate of the province. But if there is necessity, three bishops, wherever they may be, must ordain a bishop at the primate’s command. If anyone acts in any matter contrary to his own profession or subscription, he shall deprive himself of his honor.

### That one bishop from Tripoli should come as legate, and that a presbyter there should be heard by five bishops

### XIV

It was also decreed concerning Tripoli that, because of the poverty of the province, one bishop should come as legate, and that a presbyter there should be heard by five bishops and a deacon by three, as mentioned above, with his own bishop presiding.

### Concerning the various orders serving the Church: that if anyone incurs a criminal charge and rejects ecclesiastical judgment, he must suffer the consequences; and that the sons of priests must not attend secular spectacles

### XV

It was also decreed that if any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric has been charged with a crime in the Church, or a civil action has been brought against him, and, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, he wishes to be cleared in public courts, then—even if a judgment has been pronounced in his favor—he shall lose his position in a criminal case; in a civil case, he shall lose what he won, if he prefers to retain his position.

It was also decreed that if an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, this shall not prejudice those whose judgment was overturned, unless they can be convicted of having judged with an inimical spirit or of having been corrupted by some form of greed or favor.

But if the judges were chosen by agreement of the parties, even if they were fewer in number than has been established, no appeal may be made.

The sons of priests must not put on secular spectacles or even watch them, although this has always been forbidden to all Christians; and they must not attend places where blasphemies occur.

### That no bishop, presbyter, or deacon may be a contractor; that readers should take wives; that clerics abstain from usury; and at what age they and consecrated virgins may be ordained

### XVI

It was also decreed that bishops, presbyters, and deacons must not be contractors or agents, nor seek a livelihood through any shameful or dishonorable business, since they ought to remember that it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.”

It was also decreed that readers, when they reach the age of puberty, must be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.

It was also decreed that if a cleric lends money, he may receive money back; if he lends a commodity, he must receive back the same commodity, in the quantity that he gave.

No deacons may be ordained, nor virgins consecrated, before the age of twenty-five years. Readers must not greet the people.

### That each province, because of distance, should have its own primate

### XVII

It was decreed that Mauretania Sitifensis, as it requested, should have its own primate, being separated from the assembly of the province of Numidia. With the consent of all the primates of the African provinces, or of all the bishops, it was permitted to have its own primate because of the distance.

### If a cleric is ordained, he must be warned to observe the decrees; the Eucharist and baptism must not be given to the bodies of the dead; and the metropolitans must assemble in council every year from all the provinces

### XVIII

It was also decreed that when bishops or clerics have been ordained, their ordainers must first impress upon their ears the decrees approved by the councils, lest they later regret having done anything contrary to the council’s statutes.

It was also decreed that the Eucharist must not be given to the bodies of the dead. For it is written: “Take and eat,” but corpses can neither take nor eat. Nor should the negligence of presbyters cause dead persons to be baptized.

For this reason, it must be confirmed in this holy synod that, in accordance with the Nicene decrees, a council shall be convened every year because ecclesiastical matters, which often grow old to the ruin of the congregations, remain unresolved. To it, all provinces that possess primatial sees shall send from their councils two bishops as legates, or as many as they choose, so that, once the assembly has been gathered, it may possess full authority.

### That if a bishop is accused, the case should be brought before the primate of his province

### XIX

**Bishop Aurelius said:** Whoever accuses a bishop must bring the case before the primates of that province. The person accused must not be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned by letter to state his case before the chosen judges on the appointed day, he entirely fails to appear—that is, within one month from the day on which it is established that he received the letter.

If he proves that he was unable to appear because of genuine and compelling necessities, he shall have full opportunity to state his case within another month. Nevertheless, after the second month he shall not communicate until he has cleared himself.

If he refuses to appear at the universal annual council, so that his case may be concluded there, he shall be judged to have pronounced sentence of condemnation against himself. During this period of non-communion, he shall not communicate either in his own Church or in his parish.

But if his accuser has never been absent on the days appointed for stating the case, he shall not be removed from communion. If, however, he has at any time been absent, withdrawing himself, then, once the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser himself shall be removed from communion—yet in such a way that he too is not deprived of the opportunity to pursue the case, if he proves that he did not wish to appear on the appointed day but was unable to do so.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Certainly *noluisse* (“did not wish”) should be read, so that the sense may stand.]

When he begins to act before the bishops’ court, if the accuser is a culpable person, he must not be admitted to bring an accusation unless he wishes to assert his own cases, but not ecclesiastical ones.

### Concerning accused presbyters and clerics

### XX

If presbyters or deacons have been accused, they shall be joined by the proper number of colleagues from neighboring places, together with their own bishop, whom the accused themselves shall request from that bishop. That is, six in the case of a presbyter and three in that of a deacon shall examine their case, preserving the same procedure concerning days, postponements, removal from communion, and the examination of persons, both for the accusers and for those accused. [Note: [Col. 0189D] Below, where there is a double asterisk, *discussionis* (“of the examination”) appears to be the reading. Ed.]

The cases of the remaining clerics may be heard and concluded by the bishop of the place alone.

### That the sons of clerics must not marry heretics

### XXI

It was again decreed that the sons of clerics must not be joined in marriage to pagans or heretics.

### That bishops and clerics must give nothing to those who are not catholic

### XXII

It was also decreed that bishops and clerics must not give anything from their possessions by donation to those who are not catholic Christians, even if they are their relatives.

### That bishops must not travel overseas

### XXIII

It was also decreed that bishops must not travel overseas without consulting the bishop of the first see of their respective province, so that they may especially obtain from him a *forma* or letter of recommendation.

### That nothing except the canonical Scriptures may be read in the Church

### XXIV

It was also decreed that nothing should be read in the Church under the name of divine Scripture except the canonical Scriptures.

The canonical Scriptures are these: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, four books of Kings, two books of Chronicles, Job, the Psalter, five books of Solomon, twelve books of the Prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Tobit, Judith, Esther, two books of Ezra, and two books of Maccabees.

Of the New Testament: four books of the Gospels, one book of the Acts of the Apostles, fourteen Epistles of Paul, two of the apostle Peter, three of the apostle John, one of the apostle James, one of the apostle Jude, and one book of the Apocalypse of John.

This should also be made known to our brother and fellow priest Boniface, and to the other bishops of those regions, in order to confirm this canon, because we received from the Fathers that these books are to be read in the Church.

### Concerning bishops and the following orders who handle the sacred mysteries: they are to abstain from wives

### XXV

**Bishop Aurelius said:** We add this, dearest brothers. Since a report has been made concerning the lack of continence of certain clerics, even readers, toward their own wives, it has pleased us—as has also been confirmed in various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, as well as deacons, presbyters, and bishops, in accordance with their own statutes, should also abstain from their wives, so that they may appear to be as though they had none. If they do not do this, they shall be removed from ecclesiastical office.

The other clerics are not to be compelled to this except at a more mature age.

The entire council said: We confirm what your holiness has rightly and reverently regulated, and what is pleasing to God.

### That no one may alienate Church property

### XXVI

It was also decreed that no one may sell Church property. If it produces no income and some extreme necessity compels a sale, the matter must be reported to the primate of that province, so that he may decide, together with the established number of bishops, whether it ought to be done.

If such a great necessity presses upon the Church that prior consultation is impossible, he should at least summon neighboring bishops as witnesses, taking care to report all the needs of his Church to the council.

If he fails to do this, he shall be held liable before God and the council as the seller, and shall lose his honor.

### Presbyters and deacons convicted of a serious offense must by no means receive the laying on of hands as laymen

### XXVII

It was also confirmed that if presbyters or deacons are ever convicted of some serious offense for which it is necessary to remove them from the ministry, hands must not be laid upon them as though they were penitents or faithful laymen. Nor may persons who have been rebaptized be permitted to advance to the clerical rank.

Presbyters, deacons, or clerics who think they should appeal their case overseas are not to be received into communion.

**XXVIII.** It was also decided that presbyters, deacons, or other lower-ranking clerics, in cases they have, if they complain of the judgments of their bishops, are to be heard by neighboring bishops with the consent of their own bishop, and that the bishops appointed by them are to settle the matter between them. But if they think they should appeal from these bishops as well, they are not to appeal to overseas tribunals, but to the primates of their provinces, as has often been established concerning bishops. Anyone who thinks he should appeal overseas is not to be received into communion by anyone within Africa. [Col. 0192B]

If an excommunicated person presumes to receive communion before a hearing, he has pronounced judgment of condemnation upon himself.

**XXIX.** It was also decided by the entire council that whoever has been excommunicated for his own neglect—whether a bishop or any cleric—and, during his excommunication, presumes to receive communion before a hearing, is to be judged to have pronounced upon himself the sentence of condemnation.

**Concerning the accused or the accuser.**

**XXX.** It was also decided that the accused or the accuser, if he fears some violence from a rash crowd, should choose for himself a place near the location of the person accused, so that it will not be difficult to bring the witnesses there and conclude the case.

If any clerics promoted by their bishops refuse, they are not to remain where they have been unwilling to leave.

[Col. 0192C]

**XXXI.** It was also decided that whatever clerics or deacons, for the needs of the Churches, do not obey their bishops when the bishops wish to promote them to greater honor in their own Church, are not to minister in their own rank where they have been unwilling to depart.

If any poor cleric promoted within the order later acquires property, it is to be subject to the authority of the Church.

**XXXII.** It was also decided that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained possessing nothing, and who during their episcopate or clerical office acquire fields or any estates in their own name, are to be held guilty of invading the Lord’s property, unless, after being admonished, they transfer those very things to the Church. But if something personally comes to them through someone’s generosity or through inheritance from their family, let them do with it what accords with their profession. If, however, they deviate backward from their profession, they are to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, like reprobates.

**That presbyters must not sell the property of the Church in which they have been appointed, and that no bishop may usurp the property of the titular mother Church.**

**XXXIII.** It was also decided that presbyters must not sell the property of the Church in which they have been appointed without the knowledge of their bishops, just as bishops are not permitted to sell Church estates without the knowledge of the council or of their presbyters. Therefore, if there is no necessity [F. “if there is necessity”], neither may a bishop usurp the property of the mother Church, nor a presbyter the property of his own titular Church. [Col. 0193A]

Various councils of the whole province of Africa, held in earlier times during the episcopate of Aurelius of Carthage, were also read out at this synod.

**Concerning the council held at Hippo Regius.**

Under the most glorious emperor Theodosius Augustus for the third time consul, and Abundantius, vir clarissimus, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, at Hippo Regius, in the secretariat of the Basilica of Peace, and so forth. The proceedings of this council have not been transcribed because the matters established there are shown to have been inserted above.

**Concerning the Council of Carthage, where proconsular bishops are sent as legates to the Council of Adrumetum.**

Under the most glorious emperors Arcadius Augustus for the third time consul and Honorius Augustus for the second time consul, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage. At this council proconsular bishops were selected as legates to the Council of Adrumetum. [Col. 0193B]

**Concerning the Council of Carthage, where many matters were established.**

Under the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, men of clarissimus rank, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the restored basilica, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat together with the bishops, with deacons also standing by, and with Victor the elder of Puppiana, Tuto of Migirpa, and Evangelus of Assuras arriving.

**Address of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, to the bishops.**

Bishop Aurelius said:

“After the appointed day of the council we have taken our seats, as you remember, most blessed brothers, and we had supposed that legations from all the provinces throughout Africa had assembled for the appointed day, as I said, of our deliberations. But after the letter of our Byzacene priests had been read, and after what those same men who had anticipated the time and day of the council had discussed with me had been read to your Charity, a legation sent from the province of Sitifis was also read by Brothers Honoratus and Urbanus, who are taking part with us in the council today.

“Brother Reginus also sent to my lowliness a letter of the Church of Vegei Selita [Note: [Col. 0193D] The phrase lacks a verb governing the word *litteras*; perhaps *legit* should be substituted. EDIT.] from Crescentianus of the principal see, as he himself indicates, of Numidia, and from Aurelius, our fellow bishops. In these writings your Charity recognizes with me that they had promised either that they themselves would be pleased to come or that they would, as customary, send legates to this council. But since this appears not to have happened at all, the legates coming from far away in Mauretania Sitifensis testify that they cannot be detained for long. Therefore, brothers, if it seems good to your Charity, let the letter of our Byzacene brothers, together with the summary that they appended to the same letter, be read to this assembly gathered here, so that, if anything there should perhaps move the heart of your Charity, whatever has been more carefully observed in the summary may be amended for the better.

“For this is what our brother and fellow bishop of the principal see, Mizonius, a man distinguished by the merit of his seriousness and prudence, requested when writing to my lowliness. Therefore, if it pleases you, let the matters discussed be read, and let each be considered by your Charity.”

**That nothing is to be amended in the Council of Hippo.**

**XXXIV.** Bishop Epigonius said:

“In this summary, [Col. 0194A] which has been excerpted from the Council of Hippo, we think nothing needs to be amended or added, except that the date of Holy Easter should be made known at the time of the council.”

**That bishops and clerics should not easily emancipate their children.**

**XXXV.** Bishops and clerics are not to allow their children to leave their authority through emancipation unless they are secure concerning their character and age, so that their children can now be responsible for their own sins.

**That bishops and clerics are not to be ordained unless they have made all their household members Christians.**

**XXXVI.** Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are not to be ordained before they have made all who are in their household Catholic Christians.

**That nothing except bread and wine mixed with water should be offered in the sacraments.**

[Col. 0194B]

**XXXVII.** In the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood nothing more is to be offered than what the Lord himself handed down, namely bread and wine mixed with water. The firstfruits—or honey and milk—which on one most solemn day are customarily offered in the mystery concerning infants, although they are offered on the altar, are nevertheless to have their own proper blessing, so that they are distinguished from the Lord’s sacrament of the body and blood. Nor is anything more to be offered among the firstfruits than produce from grapes and grain.

**That clerics and persons practicing continence should not visit virgins or widows.**

**XXXVIII.** Clerics or persons practicing continence are not to visit widows or virgins except by order or permission of the bishops [Col. 0194C] or presbyters. They are not to do this alone, but with fellow clerics or with those whom the bishop or presbyter has ordered to accompany them. Nor are the bishops and presbyters themselves to visit such women alone, but only where either clerics are present or certain respected Christians.

**That the chief priest should not be called bishop.**

**XXXIX.** The bishop of the principal see is not to be called “chief priest,” “high priest,” or anything of this kind, but only “bishop of the principal see.”

**That clerics should not enter taverns except while traveling.**

**XL.** Clerics are not to enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking, except when compelled by the necessity of travel. [Col. 0194D]

**That sacrifices should be celebrated by those who are fasting.**

**XLI.** The sacraments of the altar are to be celebrated only by people who are fasting, except on the one anniversary day when the Lord’s Supper is celebrated. If a commemoration is to be made in the afternoon for some of the dead, whether bishops or others, it is to be done by prayers alone, if those who conduct it are found already to have eaten.

**That banquets should by no means be held in churches.**

**XLII.** No bishops or clerics are to hold banquets in a church, unless perhaps, while passing through, they refresh themselves there because of the necessity of lodging. The people, too, are to be prevented from such banquets as far as possible.

**Concerning penitents.**

[Col. 0195A]

**XLIII.** For penitents, the bishops are to determine periods of penance according to the difference among sins. A presbyter is not to reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when necessity caused by the bishop’s absence compels it. If any penitent has a public and notorious crime that has disturbed the whole Church, hands are to be imposed upon him before the apse.

**Concerning virgins.**

**XLIV.** When consecrated virgins have been deprived of the parents by whom they were guarded, they are, through the care of the bishops—or, when the bishop is absent, of the presbyters—to be entrusted to more serious women; or women living together are to guard one another, lest, wandering about indiscriminately, they damage the reputation of the Church. [Col. 0195B]

**Concerning the sick who cannot answer for themselves.**

**XLV.** The sick who cannot answer for themselves are to be baptized when those responsible for them have given testimony to their wishes, at their own risk.

Grace or reconciliation is not to be denied to actors, performers, and other persons of this kind, or to apostates who have converted or returned to God.

**Concerning the passions of the martyrs.**

**XLVI.** It is also permitted to read the passions of the martyrs when their anniversaries are celebrated.

**Concerning infants baptized among the Donatists.**

**XLVII.** Concerning the Donatists, it was decided that we should consult our brothers and fellow priests Siricius and Simplicianus concerning only the infants who are baptized among them, lest, when they have been converted to the Church of God with a salutary purpose, the error of their parents prevent those whom they did not make responsible by their own judgment from being promoted as ministers of the sacred altar.

When these matters had been inserted, Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus, legates of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis, said:

“Some time ago, when we were presenting writings before your Holiness, we were delayed in consideration of the possibility that our brothers, the legates from Numidia, might arrive. But since they have not come after being awaited for many days, we ought no longer to postpone the matters entrusted to us by our fellow bishops. Therefore, brothers, receive our petition willingly.

“We have heard concerning the faith of the Nicene discussion. Concerning the prohibition of sacrifices after a meal, so that they may be offered by those who are fasting, as is fitting, this was confirmed then and is confirmed now.” [Col. 0195D]

**Concerning rebaptisms, reordinations, and transfers of bishops.**

**XLVIII.** We also present what has been entrusted to us and what appears to have been established in the plenary Synod of Capua: that rebaptisms, reordinations, or transfers of bishops must not be permitted.

For Cresconius, bishop of Villa-Rhegia, abandoned his own people and invaded the Church of Tubuna. Although admonished to this day, in accordance with what had been established, to leave the people whom he had invaded, he has refused. We have heard that the pronouncements made against him were indeed confirmed. But we ask, in accordance with what has been entrusted to us, that you deign to give us assurance that, now that necessity itself compels it, we may freely approach the governor of the province against him, according to the statutes of the most glorious rulers, so that the man who refused to comply with your Holiness’s mild admonition and to correct what was unlawful may immediately be excluded by judicial authority. [Col. 0196A]

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Provided the form of discipline is preserved, it will not be considered an act of aggression if he refuses to withdraw after being moderately summoned by your Charity, once he has been summoned because of his contempt and defiance, with judicial authority also taking effect.”

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“Does this therefore please everyone?”

All the bishops said:

“It is just; it pleases us.”

**How many bishops should ordain a bishop?**

**XLIX.** Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“We have also been instructed to ask that, since recently two of our brothers from Numidia presumed to ordain a bishop, you decree that episcopal ordinations be celebrated only by twelve bishops.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“The ancient form shall be preserved: no fewer than three who have been appointed to ordain a bishop shall suffice.

“For in Tripoli and perhaps in Arzuges barbarian peoples appear to lie between the communities. In Tripoli, as is reported, there are only five bishops, and perhaps two of that number may be occupied by some necessity. It is difficult for all the bishops of any number to be able to attend. Should this itself be an impediment to ecclesiastical usefulness?

“In this Church also, to which your Holiness has deigned to come, we frequently have men to be ordained, almost on every Sunday. Will I often be able to summon twelve bishops, or ten, or even somewhat fewer? But it is easy for me to add two bishops who are near my lowliness. Therefore your Charity sees with me that this cannot be observed.”

**How many additional bishops should be added to the number of those ordaining when there is an objection concerning the bishop to be ordained?**

**L.** But this must be established: when we have gathered to choose a bishop, if any objection arises—for such matters have been discussed among us—the three who are already present must not presume to clear the man who is to be ordained. Instead, one or two should be added to the number mentioned above, and first the persons making the objections should be examined in the very community for which he is to be ordained. Finally, the charges brought should also be investigated. Once he has been cleared in the presence of the people, he is then to be ordained. If this accords with the mind of your Holiness, let it be confirmed by the response of your graciousness.

All the bishops said:

“It pleases us sufficiently.”

**That the date of Easter should be announced from the Church of Carthage.**

**LI.** Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“Since all the matters in our memorandum are known to have been discussed, we add that we have also been instructed concerning the date of Easter: we should always be informed by the Church of Carthage, as is customary, and not within an excessively short period of time.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“If it seems good to your Holiness, since we remember having promised long ago that we would gather each year for deliberation, then, when we have assembled together, the holy day of Easter will be announced through the legates who are present at the council.” [Col. 0197A]

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“From this present assembly we ask that you deign to inform our province by letter concerning this date.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“It must be done.”

**Concerning the visitation of the provinces.**

**LII.** Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“We have also been instructed orally that, since it was established at the Council of Hippo that each province should be visited at the time of the council, you should deign to visit the province of Mauretania either this year, which you postponed according to the order, or in another year.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“We made no provision concerning the province of Mauretania because it lies on the borders of Africa and is near barbarian territory. But may God grant that, without making extravagant promises, we may come to your province. You must consider, brothers, that the brothers of Tripolitania and Arzuges could make the same demand if circumstances permitted.” [Col. 0197B]

**That dioceses should not receive a bishop without the consent of their own bishop.**

**LIII.** Bishop Epigonius said:

“At many councils this has been established by the priestly assembly: communities held within dioceses by bishops, which have never had bishops of their own, are not to receive their own rulers—that is, bishops—unless with the consent of the bishop under whom they are held.

“But because some, after gaining a certain domination, shun the communion of their brothers, or, once corrupted, claim domination for themselves as though in a tyrannical fortress—and because many proud and foolish presbyters raise their necks against the bishop, either winning over the people for themselves by banquets or, through evil persuasion, seeking by unlawful favor to have such rulers installed for themselves—I say this because of their evil thoughts and perversely contrived plans.

“We retain as a distinguished expression of your mind, religious brother Aurelius, the fact that you have often suppressed such petitioners by refusing to attend to them. The community that has always been subject to a diocese and has never had its own bishop must not receive a ruler.

“Therefore, if what I have set forth pleases the entire most holy assembly, let it be confirmed.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“I do not oppose the proposal of our brother and fellow priest. I declare that I have both done and will continue to do this concerning those who are in agreement—not only concerning the Church of Carthage but concerning the entire priestly fellowship.

“For there are many who conspire with their own communities, which they deceive, as has been said, scratching their ears, men of corrupt life who are smooth in order to seduce, or at any rate inflated and separated from this fellowship. They think they should cling to their own community and sometimes, when summoned, refuse to come to the council, perhaps fearing that their crimes will be exposed.

“I say that, if it pleases you, concerning such men not only are their dioceses not to be preserved, but every effort must also be made against the Church of their own that has wickedly favored them, so that they may even be rejected by public authority and removed from those very principal sees. [Col. 0198A]

“For the man who remains attached to all his brothers and to the entire council ought to possess not only his own see with full right, but also the dioceses. But those who think their own communities are sufficient for them, despising brotherly love, should lose not only the dioceses but, as I have said, also their own sees through public authority, as rebels.”

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“Your Holiness’s supreme provision has united the minds of all, and I think that what you have deigned to set forth should be confirmed by the response of everyone.”

All the bishops said:

“It pleases us; it pleases us.”

**That one bishop should not receive another’s cleric.**

**LIV.** Bishop Epigonius said:

“At many councils this has been established, and now it has also been confirmed by your prudence, most blessed brothers: no bishop is to seize for himself another’s cleric against the will of the bishop to whom the cleric belongs.

“I speak of Julianus, who is ungrateful for the benefits of God bestowed upon him through my lowliness. He has proved so reckless and audacious that he seized a man whom I baptized when he was an extremely needy boy, who had been commended to me by that same Julianus, and whom I supported and raised for many years. As I said, it is established that he was baptized in my Church through the hand of my lowliness.

“He then began to be a reader in the diocese of Mappalia, indeed had served as a reader for nearly two years. Julianus, I do not know from what contempt for my humility, seized him, claiming that he was practically a citizen of his own place, Vazarum, and usurped him without consulting me. He even ordained him a deacon.

“If this is permitted, let this permission be open to us, most blessed brothers. If it is not, let such shamelessness be restrained, lest he interfere with anyone’s communion.”

Bishop Numidius said:

“If Julianus appears to have done this without asking or consulting your graciousness, we all judge that it was done unjustly and unworthily. Therefore, unless Julianus corrects his error and, with satisfaction, restores to your people the same cleric whom he had dared to ordain, he will receive judgment, separated from us because of his obstinacy in acting contrary to the statutes of the council.”

Bishop Epigonius said:

“Our brother and colleague Victor, a father by age and most senior in promotion itself, wishes this petition to be made general for everyone.”

**That the bishop of Carthage may ordain a cleric from wherever he wishes.**

[Col. 0198D]

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Listen to my speech, brothers. It sometimes happens that Churches lacking overseers request either presbyters or bishops. Nevertheless, mindful of the statutes, I follow this procedure: I approach the bishop concerned and impress upon him that his cleric has been requested by some Church. Perhaps today they have not resisted; but, in case they should ever resist when I have requested them in this matter—for you know that I bear responsibility for many Churches and for those who are to be ordained—is it just that I approach any fellow priest with two or three witnesses from our fellowship?

“But if he should prove unwilling, what does your Charity think should be done? For, as you know, brothers, by God’s graciousness I bear responsibility for all the Churches.” [Col. 0199A]

Bishop Numidius said:

“This see has always had the permission to ordain a bishop wherever it wished and from whichever person it had summoned, according to the desire of each Church.”

Bishop Epigonius said:

“Goodness separates you from the possibility of abuse. You presume less, brother, when you present yourself as good and merciful to everyone. You do have this authority, but it is far from possible to satisfy every individual bishop at merely the first summons.

“If this see considers that what it is permitted to do must be claimed for itself, you must support all the Churches. We do not give you this authority, but assign it to you, so that you may have the freedom of your will and always retain whoever you wish, and so that you may not appoint as overseers of communities or Churches those who have been requested from wherever you wish.”

Bishop Posthumianus said:

“Then, if someone has only one cleric, should that one presbyter be taken away from him?” [Col. 0199B]

Bishop Aurelius said:

“There can be one bishop through whom, by divine graciousness, many presbyters can be appointed; but it is difficult to find one bishop who can be appointed. Therefore, if someone has a presbyter necessary for the episcopate and, as you said, brother, has only one, he must give even that man for promotion.”

Bishop Posthumianus said:

“Then, if someone else has an abundance of clerics, should another community come to my aid?”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Certainly. When you have aided another Church, the one who has more clerics will be persuaded to give you one to be ordained.”

**That bishops ordained in dioceses should claim no diocese for themselves.**

[Col. 0199C]

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“We have heard that it was established that dioceses should not be permitted to receive bishops except with the consent of the bishop under whom they had been constituted. But in our province, when certain men have perhaps been ordained as bishops in a diocese with the permission of the bishop under whose authority they had been constituted, they also claim the dioceses for themselves. This must be corrected by the judgment of your Charity and prohibited in the future.”

Bishop Epigonius said:

“What was fitting has been preserved for each bishop: no community was taken from the body of dioceses as having its own bishop unless the bishop himself had given his consent to its being granted. It is enough, if he has granted it, that the diocese assigned to him have only its own bishop.
