They must not claim the other dioceses for themselves, since, removed from the bundle of many, that single one alone deserved to receive the honor of an episcopate.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“I do not doubt that it pleases all your Charity that the man who, with the permission of the bishop who held the mother Church, was ordained in a diocese should retain only that same community in which he was ordained.

“Since, therefore, I think that everything has been discussed, if all this accords with your mind, strengthen everything by your response.”

All the bishops said:

“All these things have pleased us, and we have confirmed them with our subscription.”

And they subscribed.

“I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and subscribed after it was read aloud.”

Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

**At this council it was established that bishops should not sail without a *formata*.**

Under the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, men of clarissimus rank, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, it was decided that no bishop should sail without a *formata* from the primate. Whoever seeks the proceedings in the authentic records will find them.

**The bishops who were sent as legates to the emperor from this council are written below.**

After the consulship of the most glorious emperor Honorius Augustus for the fourth time and Eutychianus, vir clarissimus, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the restored basilica. At this council Bishops Epigonius and Vincentius undertook a legation, so that, concerning those fleeing to the Church, whatever their offenses, they might obtain a law from the most glorious rulers preventing anyone from daring to drag them away.

**At this council a legation was sent to the bishops of Rome and Milan concerning infants baptized among heretics, and to the emperor concerning the removal of the remains of idols and many other matters.**

[Col. 0200B]

After the consulship of Flavius Stilicho, vir clarissimus, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the restored basilica. When Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat with his fellow bishops, with deacons standing by, Bishop Aurelius said:

“Your Charity knows very well with me, most holy brothers, the needs of the Churches established throughout Africa. Since the Lord has granted that the presence of your holy assembly has been gathered here in part, it seems to me that we should bring forward the same needs that, in our concern, we have been able to investigate. Once your sincerity has approved them, it follows that one of our number should be chosen as a fellow priest who, with the help of the Lord and your prayers, can undertake these needs and energetically carry them through to completion.

“He will travel to the regions of Italy across the sea, so that he may make known this need, grief, and poverty of ours both to our holy brothers and fellow priests—to the venerable holy brother Anastasius, bishop of the apostolic see, and also to the holy brother Venerius, priest of the Church of Milan.

“For I know that this matter had been prohibited by those sees, and that it must be provided for as a danger shared by all, especially since there is such a shortage of clerics and so many Churches are so deserted that they are found to have not even a single deacon, however unlearned.

“I think it unnecessary to speak of the higher ranks and offices, because, as I said, if the ministry of a deacon is not easily found, it is entirely certain that those of higher honors cannot be found either. We can no longer endure the daily lamentations of nearly lifeless communities throughout the various regions. Unless help is given to them at some point, a grave and inexcusable charge concerning countless souls who are perishing will remain against us before God.” [Col. 0200D]

**That infants baptized among the Donatists should be ordained as clerics in the Catholic Church.**

**LVII.** Your unanimity recognizes with me that it was established at the preceding council that those who were baptized as infants among the Donatists, while not yet able to understand the destruction involved in their error, and who later, after reaching an age capable of reason, recognized the truth, rejected their falsehood, and were received into the Catholic Church of God, spread throughout the world, according to the ancient order through the imposition of hands, should not be prevented by the name of their former error from receiving the office of the clergy.

They considered the Church of those people to be the true Church when they came to the faith, believed in Christ there, and received the sacraments of the Trinity—all of which are certainly true, holy, and divine, and in which the whole hope of the soul is established.

Although the presumptuous audacity of heretics, cloaked in the name of truth, dares to hand these things on, nevertheless, because they are simple, as the blessed Apostle declares when he says, “One God, one faith, one baptism,” and because what ought to be given once may not be repeated, let them, after the name of their error has been anathematized, be received through the imposition of hands into the one Church, the dove, as it is called, and the one mother of all Christians, where all those sacraments are received in a saving, eternal, and life-giving manner. [Col. 0201B]

For those who persevere in heresy acquire a great punishment of condemnation, so that what would have been more luminous for them in the truth, for attaining eternal life, becomes darker and more destructive in error.

Some flee this and recognize the breasts of the Catholic mother Church. Having believed and received all those holy mysteries out of love for the truth, when uprightness of good life is added to their reception of the sacraments, no one can deny that such persons should without doubt be assigned to the clerical office, especially in so great a need.

Although some clerics of the same sect wish to come over to us together with their communities and honors—men who, out of love of honor, either persuade others toward life or retain them for salvation—I think this should be left to the greater consideration of the brothers mentioned above. When they have weighed the substance of our petition with their more prudent judgment, may they deign to inform us what they think about this matter.

We are concerned only with those who were baptized as infants, so that, if it pleases them, they may agree with our will concerning the ordination of such persons.

Therefore, let your honorable fraternity consider with me that all the matters we have set forth above are to be dealt with by the holy bishops.

**Concerning the removal of the remains of idols and the temples to be abolished by the emperors.**

**LVIII.** Other needs also press upon us, to be requested from the religious emperors: that they order the remains of idols throughout Africa to be utterly removed. For in many maritime places and on various estates the wickedness of this error still flourishes. They should order that these remains themselves be destroyed and that their temples, established in the fields or in hidden places and possessing no adornment, be entirely demolished. [Col. 0201D]

**That clerics should not be compelled to give public testimony concerning matters they have judged.**

**LIX.** It should also be requested that they deign to establish the following: if they should wish to conduct in the Church any case under the apostolic jurisdiction imposed upon the Churches, and if perhaps the clerics’ decision displeases one party, it must not be permitted that the cleric who was the judge or was present be summoned to court as a witness. No ecclesiastical person should be pressed to give testimony.

**Concerning the removal of pagan banquets.**

[Col. 0202A]

**LX.** It should also be requested that they prohibit the banquets held in many places contrary to the divine commandments, which have been drawn from pagan error, so that Christians are now compelled by pagans to celebrate them. From this it appears that, in the times of Christian emperors, a second persecution is secretly being carried out. Let them order such practices to be prohibited in cities and on estates under an imposed penalty [Note: [Col. 0201D] It seems that *imposita poena* should be read, in the ablative case. EDIT.].

This is especially necessary because in some cities they do not shrink from committing such acts even at the birthdays of the martyrs and in the sacred places themselves. On those days, too—shameful as it is to say—they perform the most criminal dances through the alleys and streets, so that the honor of matrons and the modesty of countless women who come devoutly to the most sacred day are assaulted by wanton outrages, and access to the holy religion itself is almost avoided. [Col. 0202B]

**Concerning spectacles, which should by no means be held on Sunday or on the other festivals of the saints.**

**LXI.** It should also be requested that theatrical spectacles and other games be removed from Sunday and from the other most solemn days of the Christian religion. This is especially necessary because on the day of the octave of Holy Easter the people gather at the circus more than at the church. If such days happen to coincide, their days of devotion should be transferred, and no Christian ought to be compelled to attend these spectacles.

There is especially no necessity of persecution by anyone in carrying out practices contrary to the commandments of God. Rather, as is fitting, a person should remain with the free will divinely granted to him. For the danger faced especially by those who are compelled by great terror to attend the spectacles contrary to God’s commandments must be considered. [Col. 0202C]

**Concerning condemned clerics.**

**LXII.** It should also be requested that they deign to establish the following: if a cleric of any rank has been condemned by the judgment of the bishops for any offense, he may not be defended either by the Churches over which he presided or by any individual. A penalty involving loss of money and honor is to be imposed, and they are to order that neither age nor sex be accepted as an excuse.

**Concerning Christians who have been actors.**

**LXIII.** It should also be requested concerning such persons that, if anyone wishes to come from any theatrical profession to the grace of Christianity and remain free from that stain, no one may lead or compel him to return to the same activities. [Col. 0202D]

**Concerning manumissions celebrated in the church, to be requested from the emperor.**
LXIV. Concerning manumissions to be performed in the church: if our fellow priests in Italy are found carrying them out, we too shall confidently follow their procedure. Let permission plainly be granted to the envoy sent, so that whatever he may be able to do in good faith for the condition of the Church and the salvation of souls, we shall gladly accept as approved in the sight of the Lord. If all this pleases Your Holiness, declare it, so that they may understand that my proposal has your approval and that their sincerity may gladly receive the agreement of all of us.

All the bishops said: “We approve everything that has been assigned for execution and that has been prudently set forth by Your Holiness.”

### Concerning Equitius, the condemned bishop

LXV. Bishop Aurelius said: “The matter of the legation concerning Equitius, formerly justly condemned by episcopal judgment on account of his own conduct, must not, I think, be passed over. Thus, if the envoy should happen to find him in those regions, let it be his concern, for the condition of the Church, to do what ought to be done against him, wherever this may be permitted.”

All the bishops said: “This action also greatly pleases us, especially since Equitius was formerly condemned and since his shameless disturbance must everywhere be increasingly rejected for the condition and salvation of the Church.”

And they subscribed. “I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was read aloud, have subscribed.” Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

### In this council a letter of Anastasius, bishop of the Roman Church, admonishing the Catholic bishops concerning the Donatists, is read

Under the consulship of Vincentius and Fravitus, men of clarissimus rank, on the Ides of September at Carthage, in the secretariat of the restored basilica, when we bishops from all the African provinces had assembled and were seated in council in the Church of Carthage—that is, Aurelius, bishop of that see, together with his colleagues, as their subscriptions make clear—the letters of our most blessed brother and fellow priest Anastasius, bishop of the Roman Church, were read aloud. In them, with the solicitude and sincerity of paternal and fraternal charity, he exhorted us not to disregard in any way the snares and wickedness of the heretical and schismatic Donatists, by which they gravely harass the Catholic Church in Africa.

We give thanks to our Lord, who has deigned to inspire that excellent and holy bishop with such pious care for the members of Christ, although separated by the diversity of lands but joined in the one structure of the body.

### That the Donatists be treated more leniently

LXVI. After everything that seemed conducive to the benefit of the Church had been examined and considered, with the Spirit of God assenting and admonishing us, we chose to deal gently and peacefully with the aforementioned people, although they have been cut off by restless dissension from the unity of the Lord’s body. Thus, so far as lies within us, it may become thoroughly known throughout all the African provinces to all who are entangled in their communion and association by what pitiable error they are bound.

Perhaps, as the Apostle says, while we correct those who think differently with gentleness, God may grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth, and they may recover from the snares of the devil, having been captured by him for his will.

### Concerning letters to be sent to the judges, so that what was done between the Donatists and the Maximianists may become known

LXVII. Accordingly, it was decided that letters should be sent from our council to the African judges, from whom it would seem appropriate to request that they assist the common mother, the Catholic Church, in this matter: namely, that where episcopal authority can be strengthened in the cities, they should investigate—by judicial power and diligence, in accordance with the Christian faith—what was done in all the places where the Maximianists obtained basilicas, having separated from them in schism, and should have these matters entered into the public records, for the sake of firm and necessary knowledge for everyone.

### That the clergy of the Donatists be received into the Catholic Church’s clergy

LXVIII. Then it was decided that letters should be sent to our brothers and fellow bishops, and especially to the apostolic see, over which our aforementioned venerable brother and colleague Anastasius presides, so that he might know that Africa has a great need, for the sake of the peace and benefit of the Church.

If any clergy from among the Donatists should wish, after correcting their judgment, to pass over to Catholic unity, they should, according to the will and counsel of each Catholic bishop who governs the Church in that place, be received in their offices, if this should seem beneficial to Christian peace, just as it is manifestly shown to have been done in earlier periods of this same division.

The examples of many, indeed nearly all, of the African Churches in which such an error arose bear witness to this. This is not so that the council held in the transmarine regions concerning this matter should be annulled, but so that its provision may remain in force concerning those who pass over to the Catholic Church in such a way that no compensation for unity is thereby procured through them.

But wherever Catholic unity may be seen to be either entirely advanced or assisted by them, through the evident gain of their brothers’ souls, it should not harm them that the transmarine council established a rule against their holding office, although salvation has been closed to no one. That rule was this: those ordained in the party of Donatus, if they wished, after correction, to pass over to the Catholic Church, were not to be received in their offices according to the transmarine council—except for those through whom provision is made for Catholic unity.

### That an envoy be sent to the Donatists for the sake of establishing peace

LXIX. Then it was decided that, after these matters had been completed, envoys should also be sent from our number to the Donatists themselves—both to those whom they have as bishops and to the peoples—for the purpose of proclaiming the peace and unity [Note: [Col. 0203D] It seems that *gratia* or *causa* should be supplied, in the ablative case. EDIT.], without which Christian salvation cannot be attained. Through these envoys it should be made known to everyone that they have nothing which they can justly say against the Catholic Church.

Above all, it should become clear to everyone, also through the municipal records, for the sake of the reliability of the documents, what they themselves did against their own schismatic Maximianists. There, if they are willing to pay attention, God shows them how unjustly those men were then cut off from the unity of the Church, just as unjustly as they now shout that the Maximianists have created a schism from them.

Yet from the number of those whom they had already condemned by the authority of their plenary council, they again received some into their offices; and they accepted the baptism given by those whom they had condemned and excluded. Let them see how foolishly they resist the peace of the Church spread throughout the whole world, when they do such things on behalf of the party of Donatus. They do not say that they themselves are contaminated by the communion of those whom they received in this manner, out of regard for peace; yet they condemn us—that is, the Catholic Church, established even in the furthest regions of the earth—as polluted through communion with those whom, when accusing them, they were unable to convict.

### Which clergy must abstain from their wives

LXX. Furthermore, when a report was made concerning the incontinence of certain clergy, even with respect to their own wives, it was decided that bishops, presbyters, and deacons, in accordance with the earlier statutes, must also practice continence from their wives. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.

The other clergy, however, are not to be compelled to this, but the matter must be observed according to the custom of each Church.

### Concerning those who abandon their own communities

[Col. 0205B]

LXXI. Again it was decided that no one should have the power, after abandoning his principal see, to transfer himself to a Church established in the diocese, or, while remaining in his own affairs longer than is proper, to neglect the care or regular attendance of his own see.

### Concerning the baptism of infants when there is doubt whether they have been baptized

LXXII. It was likewise decided concerning infants that whenever no completely reliable witnesses are found who can testify without doubt that they have been baptized, and when, because of their age, they are not capable of answering concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, they are to be baptized without any scruple, lest this hesitation cause them to be deprived of the cleansing of the sacraments.

For this reason the envoys of the Moors, our brothers, consulted us, since they redeem many such children from the barbarians.

### The day of Easter to be announced on the day of the council

[Col. 0205C]

LXXIII. It was likewise decided that the venerable day of Easter be announced to everyone by a signed formal letter; but that the day of the council remain the same as was established in the Council of Hippo, namely, the tenth day before the Kalends of September. Letters are also to be written to the primates of each individual province, so that whenever they assemble a council in their own regions, they do not interfere with this date.

### That an intervening bishop should not occupy the see where he is serving as administrator

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Perhaps one should read *in cathedra* (“in the see”). EDIT.]

LXXIV. It was likewise established that no administrator may retain the see to which he has been appointed as administrator, whatever the enthusiasm or seditions of the people may be; rather, he must take care to provide them with a bishop within one year. If he neglects this, after the year has elapsed another administrator is to be appointed.

### Concerning defenders of the Churches to be requested from the emperor

LXXV. It was unanimously judged that the emperors should be asked, on account of the distress of the poor, by whose troubles the Church is ceaselessly wearied, to assign them defenders against the power of the rich, with provision made by the bishops.

### Concerning bishops who do not attend councils

LXXVI. It was likewise decided that whenever a council is to be assembled, bishops who are prevented neither by age, nor illness, nor any more serious necessity should attend in due measure. The primates of each province are to be notified so that, from all the bishops, two or three groups may be formed and, from each group in turn, as many as have been chosen should attend the day of the council with the utmost urgency.

If they cannot attend, they must record their excuses in the official reply; or, if some necessity should suddenly arise after the dispatch of that reply, unless they render an account of the impediment to their own primate, they must be content with communion in their own Church.

### Concerning Cresconius

LXXVII. Concerning Cresconius of Villa Regensis, it was unanimously judged that the matter should also be reported from here to the primate of Numidia, so that he may know that the aforementioned Cresconius must be summoned by written notice, in order that he not delay presenting himself at the next universal African council. If he refuses to come, let him understand that a sentence will be pronounced against him.

### Concerning the Church of Hippo Diarrhytus

LXXVIII. Again it was decided that, since the abandonment of the Church of Hippo Diarrhytus must no longer be neglected, and since the Churches there are being held by those who withdrew from the criminal communion of Equitius, bishops should be sent from the present council: Reginus, Alypius, Augustine, Maternus, Thasius, Evodius, Placidus, Urbanus, Valerius, Ambivius, Fortunatus, Quodvultdeus, Honoratus, Januarius, Aptus, Honoratus, Ampelius, Victorianus, Evangelus, and Rogatianus.

After those who, with culpable obstinacy, thought that the flight of Equitius himself should be awaited have been summoned and corrected, let a bishop be ordained for them with the consent of all. But if they do not wish to consider peace, they must not obstruct the welfare of the Church, which has been without a bishop for so long, in choosing and ordaining a superior.

### Concerning clergy who do not arrange to conduct their case within a year

LXXIX. It was again established that whenever clergy have been convicted and confessed in some crime, whether for the sake of sparing the shame of those involved, or because of the disgrace to the Church, or because of the insolent attacks of heretics and pagans, if they should wish to appear on behalf of their case and assert their innocence, they must do so within one year of their excommunication.

If, however, they refuse to clear themselves within a year, no statement from them is thereafter to be heard at all.

### That those received from another monastery may not be ordained either as monastery superiors or as clergy

[Col. 0206D]

LXXX. It was likewise decided that if anyone wishes either to promote to the clergy someone found in another monastery or to appoint him as superior of the monastery in his own monastery, the bishop who does this is to be separated from communion with the others and remain content with communion only with his own people; and that man is not to continue either as a cleric or as a superior.

### Concerning bishops who appoint heretics or pagans as heirs

LXXXI. It was likewise established that if any bishop prefers to the Church heirs who are unrelated to him by blood, or even heretics related to him by blood, or pagans, at least after his death an anathema is to be pronounced against him, and his name is in no way to be recited among the priests of God.

Nor can he be excused if he dies intestate, since, having been made a bishop, he certainly ought not to have delayed arranging his property in a manner appropriate to his profession.

### Concerning manumissions

LXXXII. It was likewise decided that the emperor should be petitioned concerning manumissions performed in the church.

### Concerning false memorials of martyrs

LXXXIII. It was likewise decided that altars established here and there through the fields and along the roads as though they were memorials of martyrs, where no body or relics of martyrs are proved to have been buried, should be overturned by the bishops who preside over those places, if this can be done.

If popular disturbances prevent this, the communities should nevertheless be warned not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held there by any superstition. In general, no memorial of martyrs is to be accepted as credible except where there is a body or some relics, or where the origin of some habitation, possession, or martyrdom is handed down with the most reliable provenance.

For altars established anywhere on the basis of dreams and the empty revelations, so to speak, of various people are to be rejected in every way.

### Concerning the eradication of the remains of idols

LXXXIV. It was likewise decided that the most glorious emperors should be asked to destroy completely the remnants of idolatry, not only in images but in every place, grove, and tree.

### That letters be dictated and subscribed in the name of all the bishops by the bishop of Carthage whenever necessary

[Col. 0207C]

LXXXV. All the bishops likewise said that, if any letters should be judged necessary to dictate in the council, the venerable bishop who presides over this see should deign to dictate and subscribe them in the name of all.

It was also decided that letters should be given to the bishops who are to be sent through the African provinces in the case of the Donatists, containing the terms of their mandate, which they must not exceed.

And they subscribed: “I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was read aloud, have subscribed.” Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

### In this council earlier decrees are confirmed

Under the consulship of the fifth-time consuls Arcadius and Honorius Augusti, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the city of Milevis, in the secretariat of the basilica, when Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, was seated in the universal council, with deacons standing by, Bishop Aurelius said:

“Since the holy Churches have one body and the head of all the members is one, it has come about, by God’s will and with his help for our weakness, that we have come to this Church, invited in the spirit of love and brotherhood. Therefore I ask your charity—since this must be believed, since our approach to you is neither superfluous nor unwelcome to all—that the agreement of all of you may be made manifest. May you be pleased to have the decrees that were long ago either confirmed in the Council of Hippo or later defined in a better council at Carthage now recited to us in due order.

“Then the concord of your brotherhood will shine more brightly than light, if you manifest that what we know to have been legally defined by the earlier councils is shown not only by your agreement in these proceedings but also by your subscriptions.”

Xantippus, bishop of the chief see of Numidia, said: “I believe that what pleased the whole brotherhood and that they confirmed by their own hand, by subscribing, may also be confirmed by our assent as pleasing to us; and we confirm it by our subscription.”

Nicetius, bishop of the chief see of Mauritania Sitifensis, said: “Since the decrees that have been read lack nothing in reason and have been approved by everyone, these matters also please my small self, and I shall confirm them by my own subscription.”

### Concerning the order of bishops: those ordained later must not dare to place themselves before those ordained earlier

[Col. 0208B]

LXXXVI. Bishop Valentinus said:

“If your good patience permits, I shall pursue what was done in former times in the Church of Carthage and made clear by the subscriptions of the brothers. I also declare that we shall observe this. But we know that ecclesiastical discipline has always remained inviolate, so that none of the brothers has ever dared to place himself before those who preceded him. Rather, what was always shown to those earlier in office through the duties of charity was gratefully received by those who came later.

“May Your Holiness strengthen this order more firmly through your decisions.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“It would not have been proper for us to repeat these matters, unless perhaps there were thoughtless minds among some people that sharpened our judgment to establish them. But this is a common matter, which our brother and fellow priest has brought forward: each of us must recognize the order assigned to him by God, and those who came later must defer to those who came earlier and presume to do nothing without consulting them.

“Concerning this, I say, as far as my understanding retains it, that those who think they may presume to do anything while despising their elders must rightly be restrained by the whole council.”

Xantippus, bishop of the chief see of Numidia, said:

“The presence of all the brothers has heard the statement of our brother and fellow priest Aurelius. What do they reply to this?”

Bishop Datianus said:

“What the judgment of our elders has decreed shall be committed to our assent, so that what is contained in the records of the earlier councils of the Church of Carthage may be held fully confirmed among everyone by our agreement.”

All the bishops said:

“This order has been observed by our fathers and elders, and, with God’s favor, it will be observed by us, while the right of primacy of Numidia and Mauritania is also preserved.”

### Concerning the archives and register of Numidia

Then all the bishops who subscribed in this council decided that the register and archive of Numidia should be kept both at the chief see and in the metropolis, that is, Constantina.

### Concerning Bishop Quodvultdeus

LXXXVII. Concerning Quodvultdeus of Centuriae: since his adversary, after requesting to be admitted to our council, was asked whether he wished to pursue the case with him before the bishops, and had first promised to do so, but on the following day replied that this did not please him and departed, all the bishops decided that no one should communicate with Quodvultdeus until his case had reached whatever conclusion it could.

For no Christian could rightly have thought that his episcopate should be taken from him before the outcome of his case had become clear.

### Concerning Bishop Maximianus

LXXXVIII. Concerning Maximianus of Bagai, it was decided that letters should be sent from the council both to him and to the people themselves, so that he might withdraw from the episcopate and they might seek another bishop for themselves.

### That bishops who are ordained receive from their ordainers letters bearing the day and consul

LXXXIX. Then it was decided that, in the future, whoever is ordained by bishops throughout the African provinces should receive from his ordainers letters subscribed by their own hand, stating the consul and the day, so that no dispute might arise concerning those ordained later or earlier.

### Concerning those who have read in the Church even once, who may not be promoted by another Church

XC. It was likewise decided that whoever has read in the Church even once may not be taken by another Church into the clergy.

And they subscribed: “I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was read aloud, have subscribed.” Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

### In this council it is reported what the bishops sent as envoys overseas accomplished

Under the consulship of the most glorious Emperor Theodosius Augustus and Rumoridus, man of clarissimus rank, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district, when Aurelius was seated in the universal council, with deacons standing by, Bishop Aurelius said:

“Your brotherhood has been assembled at this council by compelling reason. For some time ago, as Your Holiness remembers, after holding a council we sent our brothers as envoys overseas. They ought to report in the assembly of Your Holiness how they fulfilled the course of their embassy. Although yesterday, when we were seated, we carefully discussed what they had done in this matter, apart from the ecclesiastical records, today it is nevertheless necessary that yesterday’s discussion be confirmed by the ecclesiastical proceedings.”

### Concerning the bishops of the African provinces who were not present at this council

[Col. 0209D]

“The order of events therefore requires that we first inquire concerning our brothers and fellow priests who came to this council either from Byzacena or from Mauritania, and ask how they decided to take part in this council.”

When the bishops Philologius, Gesta, Venustianus, and Felicianus of the province of Byzacena presented the letters of their embassy and these were read aloud, and when Lucianus and Sylvanus, envoys of the province of Mauritania Sitifensis, likewise presented and had read aloud the letters of their embassy, Bishop Aurelius said:

“The text of these documents shall be joined to the records.”

### Concerning the bishops of Byzacena

Bishop Numidius said:

“We have observed that our brothers and fellow bishops of the province of Byzacena and of Mauritania Sitifensis have sent envoys to the council. Let us now inquire whether the envoys of Numidia have arrived, or those of the province of Tripolitana, or of Mauritania Caesariensis.”

### Concerning the bishops of Mauritania Sitifensis

The bishops Lucianus and Sylvanus, envoys of the province of Mauritania Sitifensis, said:

“The official summons reached our Caesarean brothers late, for they would already have come. Nevertheless, they must come, and we trust their disposition, because, if anything has been done in this council, they too will doubtless give their agreement.”

### Concerning the bishops of Numidia

Bishop Alypius of the Church of Tagaste said:

“We have indeed come from Numidia—I and the holy brothers Augustine and Possidius—but an embassy could not be sent from Numidia, because, owing to the disturbance of the recruits, the bishops are still either prevented or occupied in their cities by their own necessities.

“For when I was delivering Your Holiness’s official summons to the holy old man Xantippus, it had seemed appropriate in the present discussion that a council be announced to which an organized embassy could be sent. But when I later informed him by letter of the impediment caused by the recruits, as I have said above, he excused himself in his own reply.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“There is no doubt that the aforementioned brothers and fellow bishops of Numidia, when they receive the records of the council, will give their agreement and hasten to put into effect whatever has been approved. Therefore, the care of this see must necessarily see to it that this is reported to them.”

### Concerning the bishops of Tripolitana

[Col. 0210C]

“Concerning our brothers from Tripolitana, I was able to learn that they had sent our brother Dulcitius as envoy. But because he was unable to attend, certain of our sons who came from the aforesaid province asserted that the aforementioned man had entrusted himself to a ship, and it is credible that some delay caused by storms occurred and held back his arrival.

“Nevertheless, concerning them also, if this pleases your charity, the following procedure will be observed: the decisions of the council will be transmitted to them.”

All the bishops said:

“What Your Holiness has established pleases everyone.”

### Concerning summoning the Donatists

XCI. Bishop Aurelius said:

“What has come into the discussion of your charity, I think, must be confirmed by ecclesiastical records. For your statement has made this clear to everyone: each of us must personally summon the leaders of the Donatists in his own city, or join himself to a neighboring colleague, so that together they may summon them in each individual city or place through the magistrates or local elders.

“If this pleases everyone, let it be declared.”

All the bishops said:

“It pleases everyone, and we have all confirmed it by this subscription of ours. We also request that, in the letters to the judges to be sent from the council, Your Holiness subscribe on behalf of everyone.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“If this pleases your charity, let the form of their summons be read aloud, so that, if it is approved, we may all follow this wording in our statement.”

All the bishops said:

“Let it be read.”

The notary Laetus read it aloud.

### Form of the summons to the Donatists

[Col. 0211A]

XCII. That bishop of that Church said:

“We ask you to recite what we have obtained from the authority of that most eminent see, to attach it to the records, and to order that it be put into effect.”

After the order had been read and attached to the records, that bishop of that Church said:

“Therefore, what mandate from the council of the Catholic Church is to be conveyed to the Donatists through your authority, deign to let us hear it, insert it into the records, and convey it to them; and then make their reply known to us again through your records.

“We have come to you, sent with the Catholic authority of our council, desiring to rejoice in your correction and considering the charity of the Lord, who said: ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.’ Through the Prophet he also commanded us, even concerning those who say that they are not our brothers, to say: ‘You are our brothers.’

“Therefore, you ought not to despise this peaceful admonition of ours, which comes from charity. If you think that you possess any truth, do not hesitate to assert it. That is, assemble your council and choose from among yourselves those to whom you may entrust the defense of your claim. We too may do this, so that from our council those may be chosen who, together with those whom you have chosen, at an appointed place and time may discuss peacefully whatever question separates your communion from ours.

“Then at last, with the help of the Lord our God, this long-standing error may reach an end, lest, on account of human hostility, weak souls and ignorant peoples perish in sacrilegious dissension.

“If you receive this fraternally, the truth will easily come to light; but if you refuse to do this, your distrust will easily become known.”

When this had been read aloud, all the bishops said:

“This is entirely pleasing; let it be done.”

And they subscribed: “I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was read aloud, have subscribed.” Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

### This synod sends an embassy to the emperors against the Donatists

Under the consulship of the most glorious Emperor Honorius Augustus for the sixth time, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district, Theasius and Evodius undertook an embassy against the Donatists. In this council a memorandum was inserted, as follows.

### What memorandum the envoys received against the Donatists

[Col. 0211D]

XCIII. Memorandum for the brothers Theasius and Evodius, envoys sent from the Council of Carthage to the most glorious and most devout emperors, when, with the Lord’s help, they approach the most pious emperors, so that they may inform them as follows:

In accordance with the council of the previous year, the leaders of the Donatists were summoned through the municipal records, with full confidence that, if they trusted their own assertions, they would choose from their number suitable representatives to confer peacefully with us and, with Christian gentleness, not hesitate to demonstrate whatever truth they held. In this way the Catholic sincerity that had already long been evident in earlier times might now also become known to those resisting through ignorance or obstinacy.

But because they were oppressed by distrust, they scarcely dared to give any reply. Since the episcopal and peaceful duty toward them has therefore been fulfilled, and those who were unable to answer the truth have turned to savage violence, they have attacked many bishops and many clergy by ambush, to say nothing of the laity. They have also invaded some Churches and attempted to invade others.

It is now the responsibility of their Clemencies to provide for the security of the Catholic Church, which religiously bore them in Christ in her womb and nourished them in the firmness of faith, so that it may also be protected by their foresight and so that reckless men may not prevail, in these religious times, by terrifying the weaker peoples, since they cannot corrupt them by deception.

The detestable hand of the Circumcellions, in whose frenzy they rage, is well known and has often been denounced by the laws. It has also been condemned by the frequent enactments of those most devout emperors. Against their fury we may obtain defenses that are neither unusual nor alien to the Holy Scriptures, since the Apostle Paul, as is known to the faithful from the Acts of the Apostles, suppressed the conspiracy of factional men even with military assistance.

But we ask that protection be provided without any concealment for the ranks of the Catholic Churches in each city and for the neighboring landowners in their various localities.

It must also be requested that they order the law promulgated by their father of revered memory, Theodosius, imposing a fine of ten pounds of gold upon those who ordain or are ordained as heretics, and also upon owners where their assembly is discovered, to be confirmed henceforth in such a way that it may apply to those against whom Catholics, provoked by their snares, have lodged a formal complaint. At least by this terror let those desist from schismatic or heretical depravity who refuse to be corrected and reformed by consideration of eternal punishment.

It must also be requested that the law which denies heretics the power to receive or leave anything by gift or testament be renewed by their piety to this extent: that it deprive of the right to leave or receive property those who, blinded by the fury of obstinacy, wish to persist in the error of the Donatists.

For those, however, who wish to correct themselves out of consideration for unity and peace, the way to receive an inheritance should remain open without the prohibition of this law, even if something had come to them earlier by gift or inheritance while they were still in heretical error.

Those must certainly be excepted who, when sued in litigation, thought they should pass over to the Catholic Church, since it is credible of such people that they preferred Catholic unity not so much through fear of heavenly judgment as out of desire for earthly advantage.

For all these matters the support of the authorities of the various provinces is necessary. We therefore decree that the envoys have free authority to do and command whatever they understand to be beneficial for the interests of the Church.

Moreover, we were all pleased that letters should be sent from our assembly to the most glorious emperors and the most eminent authorities, informing them, with the agreement of all, that envoys have been sent by us to the most blessed imperial court.

But since it is extremely slow for all to subscribe to the same letters, unless those letters are burdened with the subscriptions of each individual, we ask you, brother Aurelius, that your charity deign to subscribe to them in the name of us all.

And they subscribed: “I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and have subscribed.” Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

Letters must also be sent to the judges, so that, until the Lord permits the envoys to return to us, they may provide protection for the Catholic Church through the municipal authorities and the possessors of estates.

Something must also be added concerning Equitius: his wickedness, by which he most shamelessly claims for himself the right of the priesthood, is to be driven from the diocese of Hippo Diarrhytus in accordance with the imperial statutes.

Letters must also be sent to the bishop of the Roman Church commending the envoys, and to others wherever the emperor may be. And they subscribed.

Likewise, I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was read aloud, have subscribed. Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

### In this synod an appended summary briefly explains what was established

Under the consulship of Stilicho for the second time and Arthemius, men of clarissimus rank, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district.

I have not set down the proceedings of this council in full, because matters that were necessary at the time were established rather than any general provisions; but, for the instruction of diligent readers, I have arranged a brief account of that council.

### Brief account of the cases

XCIV. That a free embassy be sent to the council from all the provinces: envoys and letters were ordered to be sent to Mizo, for the purpose of sending a free embassy.

Since unity had been achieved only at Carthage, letters were also to be given to the judges, so that they might order efforts to be made for unity in the other provinces and cities as well. Letters of thanks concerning the Church of Carthage, on behalf of all Africa, for the exclusion of the Donatists, were to be sent to the imperial court together with the bishops’ letters.

The letters of Pope Innocent were read aloud, stating that bishops should not easily travel overseas, and this was confirmed by the judgment of the bishops themselves: for the sake of giving thanks and excluding the Donatists, two clergy of the Church of Carthage were to be sent to the imperial court.

### In this council certain earlier enactments are corrected
[Col. 0213D] In the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius, for the seventh time, and Theodosius, for the second time, Augusti, on the Ides of June, at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district. When Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat together with his bishops, with the deacons standing by, since it had been decreed at the Council of Hippo that a plenary council of Africa should be convened every year—not only here at Carthage, but also in the various provinces in their proper order—and since it had been reserved that we should convene sometimes in Numidia and sometimes in Byzacena, this seemed burdensome to all the brethren.

### A Universal Council Should Be Held Only When Necessity Requires It

**XCV.** It was decided that there should no longer be an annual obligation that would weary the brethren, but that whenever the common cause—that is, the cause of all Africa—demanded it, wherever letters concerning this matter had been sent to this see, a synod should be convened in the province where practical necessity indicated. Causes that are not common, however, should be judged in their own provinces.

### That It Be Unlawful to Appeal from Judges Chosen by the Parties

**XCVI.** If an appeal should nevertheless be made, let the appellant choose the judges, together with the person against whom he has appealed, so that thereafter it be unlawful for either party to appeal from those judges.

### Concerning the Legations of the Various Provinces

When the legations of the various provinces were presented, they were received with the greatest gratitude: those of the Numidians, the Byzacenians, the Mauri Sitifenses, [Col. 0214B] likewise those of the Caesareans, and also those of the Tripolitanians.

### Concerning Ecclesiastical Agents

It was further decided that five agents should be requested for all the needs that the Church has, to be distributed among the various provinces.

### That the Emperors Be Asked for the Defense of Advocates in Ecclesiastical Cases

**XCVII.** It was also decided that the legates who were to proceed in the name of all the provinces, Vincentius and Fortunatianus, should ask the most glorious emperors to grant the power of appointing advocates from among trained legal scholars who are active in practice or in the office of defending cases, so that, in accordance with the custom of the priests of the province, those very men who have undertaken the defense of the Churches should have the authority, whenever necessity demands, to enter the secretariats of the judges, [Col. 0214C] either to resist those who creep in by stealth or to present what is necessary.

### That the Legation Be Free

It was decided that the chosen legates sent to the imperial court should have a free legation.

### Protest of the Mauri Bishops Concerning Primosus

It is further established that the Mauri Caesarienses protested that Primosus had been summoned by their letters through the leading men of the city of Thigana, so that, in accordance with the decisions of the leading men, he might present himself at the plenary council; and, when properly sought, Primosus was not found, as the deacons reported. But since those same Mauri requested that letters ought to be sent concerning the plenary council to the venerable old man, our brother Innocentius, it was decided that they should be sent, so that he might know that Primosus had been sought at the council [Col. 0214D] and had by no means been found.

### Concerning Communities That Have Never Had Bishops

**XCVIII.** It was also decided that communities which have never had their own bishops should not receive one unless this has been decreed by the plenary council of each province and by its primate, with the consent of the bishop to whose diocese that Church belonged.

### Concerning Communities Converted from the Donatists

**XCIX.** It was decided, certainly, that those communities which have been converted from the Donatists and unquestionably had bishops should be allowed to retain them without consulting the council. But if communities had a bishop and, after his death, wished not to have their own bishop but to belong to the diocese of some other bishop, this should not be denied them.

It was also reported that, before the emperor’s law concerning unity was enacted, whichever bishops converted to the Catholic Church should retain the communities they had brought over. But from the law of unity onward, all the Churches should claim for themselves the Catholic bishops of those places to which those Churches had belonged under the heretics, whether the places had been converted to the Catholic faith or had remained with the heretics; likewise their dioceses and, if there happened to be any, the Church’s documents or property belonging to its rights. Those who have usurped anything shall restore whatever they usurped after the law, once formally summoned to do so.

### Concerning the Petition of Bishop Maurentius

**C.** At the petition or request of Bishop [Col. 0215B] Maurentius, when the document presented by Bishop Placentinus, who was acting as legate of Numidia, had been read, the judgment of that same Placentinus was recited in the presence of the bishops. When the deacons sought at the doors for those whom he had wished to be present—namely, the elders from New Germania—and they were not found, although they were sought a second and a third time, the holy council therefore decreed that a letter should be sent to that same elder Xantippus, so that he might know that the will of the aforesaid community should in no way be allowed to succumb to the injury inflicted by a bishop.

Bishop Maurentius said:

“Since the elders from New Germania were sought a second and a third time and were not found, although the primate had ordered them to come to the venerable council now being held on the Ides of June, they have brought about their own absence. [Col. 0215C] Therefore let Your Holiness determine something concerning this matter, lest I appear to be suffering innocently under the burden of their accusation.”

The holy council decreed:

“Certainly, according to priestly discipline, a judgment ought to have been issued by this council against the contumacious. But since ecclesiastical gentleness must be preserved in all cases, letters have been promised to the elder Xantippus, so that the judges chosen by the council may know that they must without delay examine the matter in the city of Thubursicum, in order that an examination appropriate to the case may be applied.”

Bishop Maurentius said:

“I ask that you order these judges to be appointed for me: the holy elder Xantippus, Saint Augustine, Florentius, Theasius, Sansucius, Secundus, and Possidius.”

The holy council granted the judges requested. The remaining judges necessary to complete [Col. 0215D] the number were appointed by the elder Xantippus, with the elders from New Germania themselves choosing them.

### Concerning the Pacification of the Roman and Alexandrian Churches

**CI.** It was also decided that the holy pope Innocentius should be written to concerning the disagreement between the Roman and Alexandrian Churches, so that both Churches might maintain among themselves the peace which the Lord commanded.

### Concerning Those Who Abandon Their Wives or Husbands and Remain Thus

**CII.** It was decided that, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man abandoned by his wife nor a woman abandoned by her husband should join themselves to another, but should remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. If they should despise this rule, they are to be reduced to penance; and in this matter it should be requested that an imperial law be promulgated.

### Concerning Prayers to Be Said at the Altar

**CIII.** It was also decided that the prayers which have been approved in the council—whether prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands—should be celebrated by all, and that no others at all should be put forward against the faith; but whatever prayers have been collected by the more prudent should be recited.

### Concerning Those Who Have Asked the Emperor to Hear Public Judicial Cases

**CIV.** It was decided that whoever has asked the emperor to hear a public judicial case should be deprived of his proper rank. If, however, he has requested an episcopal judgment from the emperor, this shall not harm him.

### Concerning Those Who, While Not in Communion in Africa, Attempt to Slip Across the Sea

**CV.** Whoever, while not in communion in Africa, attempts to enter communion overseas shall suffer the loss of his clerical office.

### That Those Proceeding to the Imperial Court Should Endeavor to Make Their Case Known to the Bishop of Carthage or to the Roman Pontiff

**CVI.** It was decided that whoever wishes to go to the imperial court should be identified in the *formata* that is sent to the Church of the city of Rome, so that from there he may also receive a *formata* for the imperial court. If, however, after receiving only a *formata* for Rome and concealing the necessity that requires him to proceed to the imperial court, he should wish also to proceed to the imperial court, he shall be removed from communion. If, while there at Rome, an unexpected necessity should arise for him to proceed to the imperial court, he shall lay that necessity before the bishop of the city of Rome and carry with him a written statement from that Roman bishop concerning it.

The *formatae* given by primates or by any bishops to their own clergy shall bear the date of Easter. If the date of Easter in that same year is still uncertain, the date of the preceding Easter shall be added, just as it is customary for the year after the consulship to be entered in public records.

It was also decided that the legates sent from this glorious council against the Donatists and the pagans, or against their superstitions, should obtain from the most glorious princes whatever they might see to be useful.

It was also decided, at the request of all the bishops, that Your Holiness alone should subscribe all letters issued by the council.

And they subscribed.

I, Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was read aloud, have subscribed. The other bishops likewise subscribed.

### Council Against the Pagans and Heretics

In the consulship of Bassus and Philippus, most illustrious men, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the Restored Basilica. At this council Bishop Fortunatianus again undertook a legation against the pagans and heretics.

### Another Council Against the Pagans and Heretics

In the consulship of Bassus and Philippus, most illustrious men, on the third day before the Ides of October, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the Restored Basilica. At this council Bishops Restitutus and Florentius undertook a legation against the pagans and heretics, at the time when Severus and Macarius were killed; and on their account Bishops Evodius, Theasius, and Victor were also slain.

### Council Concerning the Hearing of a Bishop’s Case

**CVII.** In the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius, for the seventh time, and Theodosius, for the third time, Augusti, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district. At this council it was decided that one bishop should not claim jurisdiction for himself alone. I have therefore not recorded the acts of this council, since it was a provincial, not a universal, council.

### Council Against the Donatists

After the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius, for the eighth time, and Theodosius, for the third time, Augusti, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district. At this council Bishops Florentius, [Col. 0217B] Possidius, Praesidius, and Benenatus undertook a legation against the Donatists, at the time when the law was issued allowing anyone, by free choice, to embrace Christian worship.

### Council Against the Heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius

**CVIII.** In the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius, for the twelfth time, and Theodosius, for the ninth time, Augusti, on the Kalends of May, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the Basilica of Faustus. When Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat with the universal council, with the deacons standing by, all the bishops whose names and subscriptions are included approved the following, having been assembled in the holy synod of the Church of Carthage.

### That Adam Was Not Made Mortal by God

**CIX.** If anyone says that the first man Adam was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die bodily—that is, depart from the body—not on account of the merit of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.

### That Infants Are Baptized for the Remission of Sins

**CX.** It was likewise decided that if anyone denies that newborn infants should be baptized, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but that they derive no original sin from Adam which is cleansed by the bath of regeneration—so that it follows that in them the form of baptism “for the remission of sins” is understood not truly but falsely—let him be anathema.

For the Apostle’s statement, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned,” must not be understood in any other way than the Catholic Church, spread everywhere, has always understood it. For on account of this rule of faith even infants, who as yet could not have committed any sins themselves, are truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that what they have drawn from generation may be cleansed in them through regeneration.

### That the Grace of God Grants Not Only the Remission of Sins but Also Assistance So That We Do Not Sin

**CXI.** It was likewise decided that if anyone says that the grace of God, by which a person is justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also as assistance so that sins may not be committed, let him be anathema.

### That the Grace of Christ Grants Not Only Knowledge of What We Should Do but Also Inspires Love So That We May Fulfill What We Know

[Col. 0217D]

[Col. 0218A] **CXII.** If anyone says that the same grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us in not sinning only because through it the commandments are revealed and understanding is opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not granted the ability and love to do what we have learned ought to be done, let him be anathema.

For when the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up,” it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have the grace of Christ for that which puffs us up, but not for that which builds us up, since both are gifts of God: both knowing what we ought to do and loving so that we may do it, so that, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. Just as it is written concerning God, “He teaches human beings knowledge,” so it is also written, “Love is from God.”

### That Without the Grace of God We Can Fulfill No Good Thing

**CXIII.** It was likewise decided that if anyone says that the grace of justification is given to us so that, while we are commanded to do something by free choice, we may fulfill it more easily through grace—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema.

For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do it with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing.”

### That This Is Not Only a Humble but Also a Truthful Saying of the Saints: “If We Say That We Have No Sin, We Deceive Ourselves”

[Col. 0218C] **CXIV.** It was likewise decided that whoever thinks that what the holy Apostle John said—“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”—should be understood to mean that we ought to say, out of humility, that we have no sin, not because this is truly so, let him be anathema.

For the Apostle continues and adds: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, so that he may forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.” Here it is sufficiently clear that this is to be said not only humbly but also truthfully. The Apostle could have said, “If we say, ‘We have no sin,’ we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.” But when he says, “We deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” he clearly shows that the person who says that he has no sin is not speaking the truth but falsely.

### That the Saints Say in the Lord’s Prayer for Themselves, “Forgive Us Our Debts”

**CXV.** It was likewise decided that if anyone says that the saints say “Forgive us our debts” in the Lord’s Prayer not for themselves, because they no longer need this petition, but for others in their people who are sinners—and that therefore each saint does not say, “Forgive me my debts,” but “Forgive us our debts,” so that the righteous person is understood to ask this for others rather than for himself—let him be anathema.

For the Apostle James was holy and righteous when he said, “For we all offend in many things.” Why was “all” added, unless so that this statement might also agree with the Psalm, where we read, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight”; and with the prayer of the wisest Solomon, “There is no one who has not sinned”; and with the Book of the holy Job, “In the hand of every human being he marks [this], so that every person may know his weakness”?

For this reason the holy and righteous Daniel also, when he said in his prayer in the plural, “We have sinned, we have acted wickedly,” and the rest of what he confesses there truthfully and humbly, did not wish it to be thought—as some understand it—that he was speaking not of his own sins but rather of the sins of his people. He later said: “When I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God,” he did not say “our sins,” but spoke of the sins of his people and of his own, because, like a prophet, he foresaw those future people [Col. 0219B] who would understand this so wrongly.

### That the Saints Truly Say, “Forgive Us Our Debts”

**CXVI.** It was likewise decided that if anyone wishes the very words of the Lord’s Prayer, where we say, “Forgive us our debts,” to be said by the saints in such a way that they are said humbly but not truthfully, let him be anathema.

Who could tolerate someone praying and lying not to human beings but to the Lord himself, saying with his lips that he wishes his debts to be forgiven while saying in his heart that he has no debts requiring forgiveness?

### Concerning Communities Converted from the Donatists

**CXVII.** It was likewise decided that, although several years ago a plenary council decreed in the Church that all Churches established in a diocese which had become Catholic before the laws concerning the Donatists were enacted should belong to those episcopal sees through whose bishops they had been brought into communion with Catholic unity, while after the laws all those that entered into communion should belong to the places to which they had belonged when they were in the Donatist party, nevertheless, because many disputes have subsequently arisen and are still arising among bishops concerning the dioceses, and because insufficient provision appears to have been made for them at that time, the holy council now decided as follows:

Wherever both the Catholic Church and the Donatist party existed, and belonged to different episcopal sees, whenever unity was established or shall be established there—whether before or after the laws—the community shall belong to the episcopal see to which the Catholic community that was already there belonged.

### Concerning Dioceses: How Catholic Bishops and Those Converted from the Donatist Party Shall Divide Them Among Themselves

[Col. 0219D]

**CXVIII.** In such a way, certainly, that if a bishop has been converted from the Donatists to Catholic unity, they shall divide equally among themselves those places in which both parties are found. That is, some places shall belong to one and some to the other, with the bishop who has spent the longer time in the episcopate making the division, and the junior choosing.

If there should happen to be one place, it shall belong to the bishop to whose see it is found to be nearer. If it is equally near to both sees, it shall belong to the one whom the community chooses.

If the ancient Catholics wish to have their own bishop, and those who have been converted from the Donatist party wish to have theirs, the preference shall be given to the will of the greater number over that of the fewer. If the parties are equal, it shall be assigned to the bishop of longer standing.

If so many places are found in which both parties existed that they cannot be divided equally—for example, if their number is odd—after the places whose number is even have been distributed, the remaining place shall be handled according to what was stated above concerning the case of a single place.

### That If a Bishop Has Possessed for Three Years a Diocese Freed from Heresy, No One Shall Reclaim It

**CXIX.** It was likewise decided that even if someone has converted a place to Catholic unity after the laws, if he has retained it for three years without anyone reclaiming it, it shall no longer be reclaimed from him.

If, however, during those three years there was a bishop who could have reclaimed it but remained silent, he shall suffer prejudice. If there was no such bishop, the parent see shall not suffer prejudice; rather, when the place receives a bishop although it previously had none, it shall be permitted to reclaim it within three years from that very day.

Likewise, if a bishop has been converted to Catholicism from the Donatist party, the prescribed period shall not prejudice him; from the day of his conversion he shall have three years in which to reclaim the places that belonged to that episcopal see.

### Concerning Those Who Force Their Way into Communities They Think Belong to Them Without Summoning Those Who Hold Them

**CXX.** It was likewise decided that any bishops who think that communities belong to their episcopal see must not reclaim them by forcing their way in while another bishop retains them, without bringing their cases before bishops acting as judges, whether the communities wish this or not. They shall suffer loss in their case.

If any have already done this, and the dispute among the bishops has not yet been concluded but is still being contested on that account, the person who is shown to have forced his way in while disregarding ecclesiastical judgments shall withdraw.

No one should flatter himself because he has obtained letters from a primate allowing him to retain the community. Whether he has such letters or not, he must summon the person who holds it and receive his letters, so that it may become evident that he has held peacefully the Church belonging to him.

If he raises any question, the case shall be concluded by episcopal judges, whether judges appointed for them by the primates or judges whom they themselves have chosen from among their neighbors by common agreement.

### Concerning Those Who Neglect Communities Belonging to Them

**CXXI.** It was likewise decided that whoever neglects to win over to Catholic unity places belonging to his episcopal see shall be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, so that he does not delay in doing this.

If they have not accomplished it within six months from the day of the summons, the places shall belong to whoever is able to win them over.

This shall be understood in such a way that, if the person to whom the places appeared to belong can prove that his apparent negligence was more likely chosen by the heretics so that they might remain there with impunity, and that his diligence was forestalled, so that his more attentive care might be prevented, then, when the episcopal judges have learned this, they shall restore the places to his see.

If the bishops among whom the case is being disputed belong to different provinces, the primate in whose province the disputed place lies shall appoint the judges. If by common agreement they choose neighboring judges, they shall choose either one or three; if they choose three, they shall follow either the judgment of all or that of two.

### That the Judgment of Judges Chosen by Common Agreement Must Not Be Disregarded

[Col. 0221A]

**CXXII.** It shall not be lawful to appeal from judges chosen by common agreement. Whoever, having been summoned, is found through contumacy to refuse obedience to the judges, once this has been proved to the bishop of the first see, that bishop shall issue letters ordering that none of the bishops communicate with him until he obeys.

### That if a Bishop Neglects His Diocese, He Shall Be Deprived of Communion

**CXXIII.** If a bishop in the parent sees is negligent toward the heretics, he shall be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, and his negligence shall be demonstrated to him, so that he cannot excuse himself.

If, within six months from the day on which he is summoned, there is an agent in his province and he has not taken care to convert them to Catholic unity, no one shall communicate with him until he fulfills his duty.

If the agent has not come to the places, this shall not be charged against the bishop.

### Concerning Bishops Who Falsely Claim to Have Received Donatists into Communion

**CXXIV.** If it is proved that he lied concerning their communion, saying that people had entered communion whom it is established, with his knowledge, had not entered communion, he shall also lose his episcopate.

### Concerning Presbyters and Clerics: That They Appeal Only to African Councils

**CXXV.** It was likewise decided that presbyters, deacons, and other lower clerics who have cases and complain about the judgments of their own bishops shall be heard by neighboring bishops, who shall conclude whatever matter there is between them, having been called in by agreement with their own bishops.

If they should think that an appeal ought also to be made from those bishops, they shall appeal only to African councils or to the primates of their own provinces. Anyone who thinks he should appeal overseas shall be received into communion by no one within Africa.

### Concerning the Veiling of Even Younger Virgins

**CXXVI.** It was likewise decided that if any bishop, because of the danger threatening a virgin’s chastity—when either a powerful suitor or a ravisher is feared, or when she has been troubled by some dangerous fear of death lest she die unveiled—or at the insistence of her parents or of those responsible for her care, veils or has veiled a virgin before she reaches twenty-five years of age, the council’s decree concerning that number of years shall not prejudice him.

### That Bishops Should Not Be Held Too Long at the Council, but Should Choose Three Judges from Each Province

**CXXVII.** It was likewise decided, so that all the bishops gathered for the council should not be detained longer, that three judges should be chosen from each province by the entire council.

The following were chosen: from the province of Carthage, Vincentius, Fortunatianus, and Clarus; from the province of Numidia, Alypius, Augustine, and Restitutus; from the province of Byzacena, together with the holy elder Donatianus, the primate, Cresconius, Jocundus, and Aemilianus; from Mauritania Sitifensis, Severianus, Asiaticus, and Donatus; from the province of Tripolitana, Plautius, who, according to custom, was sent as the sole legate.

All of these, together with the holy elder Aurelius, shall hear all the cases. The entire council requested that he himself subscribe all the acts already completed and all the letters.

And they subscribed.

I, Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have consented to this decree and, after it was read aloud, have subscribed. The others likewise subscribed.

### The Legation of the Roman Church Also Took Part in This Council

After the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius, for the twelfth time, and Theodosius, for the eighth time, Augusti, on the third day before the Kalends of June, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the Restored Basilica.

When Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat together with Faustinus of the Church of Potentia in the Italian province of Picenum, the legate of the Roman Church, Vincentius of Culosita, Fortunatianus of Neapolis, Marianus of Uzippara, Adeodatus of Simidicum, Pentadius of Carpis, Rufinianus of Muzuba, Praetextatus [Col. 0222B] of Sicilibba, Quodvultdeus of Veres, Candidus of Abbir, and Gallonianus of Utica, legates of the province of Proconsularis; Alypius of Thagaste, Augustine of Hippo Regius, and Possidius of Calama, legates of the province of Numidia; Maximianus of Aquae, Jocundus of Suffetula, and Hilarianus of Horreocella, legates of the province of Byzacena; Novatus of Sitifis and Leo of Mocta, legates of the province of Mauritania Sitifensis; Ninellus of Rusurrus, Laurentius of Icosium, and Numerianus of Rusgunia, legates of the province of Mauritania Caesariensis, chosen as judges by the universal council, with the deacons standing by, and when certain matters had been completed, many bishops complained that they could not endure the delay while the others’ remaining business was being conducted and were hurrying to their own Churches, the entire council decided that from each province judges should be chosen by all who would remain to attend to the other matters.

And it happened that those were present whose subscriptions testify to their presence.

### That Excommunicated Persons Should Not Be Admitted to Bring an Accusation

**CXXVIII.** It was decided by all that, although earlier councils had already established which persons should be admitted to accuse clerics, and had not specified which persons should not be admitted, we therefore define that no one is properly to be admitted to bring an accusation who, after having been excommunicated, wishes to accuse someone while still remaining under that excommunication, whether he is a cleric or a layman.

### That Slaves, Freedmen, and All Infamous Persons Should Not Bring Accusations

[Col. 0222D]

**CXXIX.** It was likewise decided that no slaves or personal freedmen should be admitted to bring an accusation, nor anyone whom the public laws do not admit to the accusation of public crimes.

Nor should anyone stained by the marks of infamy be admitted—that is, actors and persons subject to disgraceful occupations, as well as heretics, pagans, and Jews. Nevertheless, all those to whom the right of accusation is denied must not be denied the right to bring an accusation in their own cases.

### That Anyone Who Has Failed to Prove One Crime Should Not Be Admitted to Bring Another

**CXXX.** It was likewise decided that whenever accusers charge clerics with many crimes, and are unable to prove one of those charges, the one with which they first proceeded, they shall not thereafter be admitted to bring the remaining charges.

### Who Should Be Admitted as Witnesses

**CXXXI.** Those witnesses shall not be admitted to testify who have been ordered not to be admitted as accusers, nor those whom the accuser himself has produced from his own household. No one under fourteen years of age shall be admitted to testify.

### Concerning a Bishop Who Excommunicates Someone Who Says He Confessed a Crime to the Bishop Alone

**CXXXII.** It was likewise decided that if a bishop says that someone confessed a personal crime to him alone, and that person denies it, the bishop should not consider it an insult to himself that he is not believed on his testimony alone. This applies even if the bishop says that, because of the scruple of his own conscience, he does not wish to communicate with the person who denies it.
