### That a Bishop Should Not Rashly Deprive Anyone of Communion

**CXXXIII.** As long as his bishop does not communicate with an excommunicated person, no other bishops shall communicate with that bishop, so that the bishop may take greater care not to make an accusation against anyone that he will be unable to establish by other evidence.

Bishop Aurelius said:

“In accordance with the decrees of the entire council assembled and with the judgment of my own insignificance, it is fitting to bring all matters to a conclusion. Let the titles designated and arranged in the proceedings of this day be received as ecclesiastical acts. Whatever has not yet been set forth we shall, on the following day, communicate in writing through our brethren Faustinus [Col. 0223C] the bishop, Philippus and Asellus the presbyters, to our venerable brother and fellow bishop Bonifatius.”

And they subscribed.

I, Aurelius, bishop, have subscribed these proceedings containing the decrees enacted among us.

Valentinus, bishop of the first see of the province of Numidia, have subscribed these proceedings.

Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Potentia in the province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, have subscribed these proceedings.

Augustine, bishop of Hippo, legate of the province of Numidia, have subscribed these proceedings.

Possidius, bishop of Calama, legate of the province of Numidia, have subscribed these proceedings.

Vincentius of Culosita have subscribed these proceedings.

[Col. 0223D] Fortunatianus of Neapolis have subscribed these proceedings.

Pentadius of Carpis have subscribed these proceedings.

Rufianus of Maxula have subscribed these proceedings.

Praetextatus of Sicilibba have subscribed these proceedings.

Quodvultdeus of Veres have subscribed these proceedings.

Candidus of Germania have subscribed these proceedings.

Maximianus of Aquae have subscribed these proceedings.

Jocundus of Suffetula, legate of the province of Byzacena, have subscribed these proceedings.

Maximinus, legate of the province of Byzacena, have subscribed these proceedings.

Hilarianus of Horreocella, legate of the province of Byzacena, have subscribed these proceedings.

Novatus of Sitifis, legate of that same province, have subscribed these proceedings.

[Col. 0224A] Ninellus of Rusurrus, legate of the province of Caesariensis, have subscribed these proceedings.

Laurentius of Icosium, legate of the province of Caesariensis, have subscribed these proceedings.

Numerianus of Rusgunia, legate of the province of Caesariensis, have subscribed these proceedings.

Leo of Mocta, legate of the province of Caesariensis, have subscribed these proceedings.

The other Leo, legate of the province of Sitifensis, have subscribed these proceedings.

And the remaining 227 bishops likewise subscribed.

I, Philippus the presbyter, legate of the Roman Church, have subscribed these proceedings as they were recalled by us.

I, Asellus the presbyter, legate of the Roman Church, have subscribed these proceedings, which have been sent by us.

## Here Begins the Letter Sent by the Entire African Council to Bonifatius, Bishop of the City of Rome, Through Faustinus the Bishop and Philippus and Asellus the Presbyters, Legates of the Roman Church

[Col. 0224B]

**CXXXIV.** To the most blessed and honorable lord and brother Bonifatius: Aurelius; Valentinus, of the first see of the province of Numidia; and the rest of us who were present, 217 in number, from the entire council of Africa.

Since it pleased the Lord that our humility should reply not to the bishop of blessed memory Zosimus, from whom our holy brothers, the fellow-bishop Faustinus and the fellow-presbyters Philip and Asellus, brought us instructions and letters, but to your Veneration, who by divine appointment have been established in his place, we ought briefly to make known what was settled by the agreement of both parties, and not those matters contained in the lengthy volumes of the proceedings, over which—without indeed abandoning charity—we lingered, though not without some effort of dispute, deliberating in the proceedings upon what now pertains to the case. Although he too, if he were still alive, would more gladly accept this, Lord Brother, seeing that it had been brought to a peaceful conclusion.

The presbyter Apiarius, concerning whose ordination, excommunication, and appeal there had arisen no slight scandal—not only for the Church of Sicca but also for the whole African Church—was restored to communion after asking forgiveness for all his errors. Our former fellow-bishop Urban of Sicca, for his part, corrected without hesitation whatever in him seemed to require correction. But since provision had to be made for the peace and tranquility of the Church not only at present but also in the future, because many such events had preceded this one and it was necessary thereafter to guard against similar or even more serious occurrences, it pleased us that the presbyter Apiarius should be removed from the Church of Sicca, while retaining the honor of his rank, and that, having received a letter of release, he should exercise the office of presbyter wherever else he wished and was able. We granted this to him without difficulty when he himself requested it by letter.

Before this case was brought to its conclusion, however, among the other matters with which we were occupied in prolonged disputations, reason itself required us to ask, in the ecclesiastical proceedings, our brothers the fellow-bishop Faustinus and the fellow-presbyters Philip and Asellus to declare whatever had been instructed to them for them to undertake with us. They did indeed present some matters verbally, without any written document, but when we insisted rather on what they had been carrying in their letters, they produced a memorandum of instructions. After it was read to us, it was also cited in the proceedings which they are carrying with them to you.

In it, four matters were entrusted to them to deal with us: first, appeals by bishops to the bishop of the Roman Church; second, that bishops should not sail importunately to the imperial court; third, the handling of the cases of presbyters and deacons before neighboring bishops if they had been unjustly excommunicated by their own bishops; fourth, the excommunication of Bishop Urban, or even his summons to Rome, unless he corrected what appeared to require correction.

Concerning the first and third of these matters—that is, that bishops should be permitted to appeal to Rome, and that clerics’ cases should be concluded before the bishops of their own provinces—we had already taken care in the previous year to indicate our position in letters sent to the same bishop Zosimus, of venerable memory. We asked that these arrangements be allowed to stand for a little while without any injury to him, until the statutes of the Council of Nicaea could be investigated.

Now also we ask your Holiness that, just as these matters were handled or established by the Fathers at Nicaea, so you may permit what has been done by us to be preserved, and may have those provisions which they brought in the memorandum put into effect there among you. That is: if a bishop has been accused, and the bishops assembled from his region have judged and deposed him from his rank, and he appears to have appealed and has taken refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, and wishes to be heard, and he has judged that the examination should be renewed, let him write to those bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the truth.

But if the person who asks for his case to be heard again has moved the Roman bishop by his petition to send a presbyter from his own side, it shall be in the bishop’s power to do what he wishes and judges appropriate. If he decides that persons should be sent who will sit in judgment with the bishops present, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, the matter shall remain within his discretion. If, however, he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the affair to an end, he shall do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.

The same applies to presbyters and deacons. If some bishop, being irascible—which he ought not to be—should quickly or harshly become angry with his presbyter or deacon and wish to expel him from the Church, care must be taken lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. The expelled man shall have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, and his case shall be heard and more carefully examined, because a hearing ought not to be denied to one who asks for it. The bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, must patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that either his judgment may be proved right or corrected.

These provisions were inserted into the proceedings pending the arrival of the most accurate copies of the Council of Nicaea; they are contained in the memorandum, just as our brothers from the apostolic see themselves alleged it here among us. If this order were also preserved by you in Italy, we would in no way wish—or be compelled—to tolerate such things as those already mentioned. Rather, with the help of the mercy of the Lord our God, we believe that, with your Holiness presiding over the Roman Church, we shall no longer have to endure this arrogance. And what ought to be preserved toward us will be preserved, even without our arguing the matter, in fraternal charity, which according to the wisdom and justice bestowed upon you by the Most High you yourself also see must be maintained—unless the canons of the Council of Nicaea happen to have a different wording.

Although we have read very many copies, nowhere in the Latin copies did we read in the Council of Nicaea what is said to have been sent from there in the aforementioned memorandum. Moreover, we were unable to find these provisions in any Greek copy. For this reason, since the same decrees are said to be available in authentic form in the Eastern Churches, we desire all the more that they be brought to us. We therefore beseech your Veneration also to write to the bishops of those regions, namely, of the Churches of Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople.

And if it should also please your Holiness that the same canons established by the Fathers at the city of Nicaea be sent to us from elsewhere, may you, above all, confer this benefit upon all the Western Churches with the Lord’s assistance. For who could doubt that the copies of the Council of Nicaea, assembled in Greece, are the most accurate when copies brought from and compared with such diverse places and noble Greek Churches agree?

Until this is done, we profess that we shall preserve, pending verification, the provisions alleged to us in the aforementioned memorandum concerning appeals by bishops to the bishop of the Roman Church and concerning the conclusion of clerics’ cases before the bishops of their own provinces; and we trust that your Blessedness, in accordance with God’s will, will assist us in this.

As for the remaining matters enacted or confirmed in our synod, since our aforementioned brothers—the fellow-bishop Faustinus and the presbyters Philip and Asellus—are carrying them with them, they will make them known to your Holiness, if you deign to receive them.

In another hand: May our Lord preserve you for us for many years, most blessed brother.

Alipius, Augustine, Possidius, Marinus, and the other bishops also signed.

## Responses to the African Council from Cyril, bishop of Alexandria

Here begin the replies to the African Council from Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, in which they transmitted authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea, translated from Greek by the presbyter Innocent. These letters, together with the same Council of Nicaea, were sent through the aforementioned presbyter Innocent and Marcellus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage, to the holy bishop Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

### CXXXV

To the honorable lords and holy fellow-bishops, Aurelius and Valentinus, and to the entire holy assembly gathered in the synod at Carthage, Cyril sends greetings in God to your Charity.

I received with complete joy the letter of your Veneration, full of complaint, conveyed by our son the presbyter Innocent. In it you ask us to present to your Love, under our profession of faith, the most accurate copies from the archive of our Church, from the authentic synod established and confirmed by the holy Fathers at the city of Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia.

Therefore, honorable lords and brothers, with the Lord granting safety, I considered it necessary to send to your Charity, through the bearer of this letter, our son the presbyter Innocent, the most trustworthy copies from the authentic synod held in the Bithynian city of Nicaea. You will also find this information when you consult ecclesiastical history.

Regarding Easter, as you wrote, we inform you that in the coming indiction we shall celebrate it on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May.

In another hand: May our God and Lord preserve your holy assembly, which is our desire, dearest brothers.

## Letter of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, to the same persons

### CXXXVI

To the holy and deservedly most blessed lords and brothers, fellow-bishops Aurelius and Valentinus, and the other beloved men established in the synod held at Carthage, Atticus, bishop.

Through our son Marcellus, your subdeacon, I received the letter of your Love with complete thanksgiving, giving thanks to the Lord that I have been found worthy to enjoy the blessing of such great brothers.

Most blessed lords and brothers, you wrote asking me to send, under the attestation of the faith, the most accurate canons established by the Fathers at the city of Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia. Who is there who would deny the common faith, or the statutes confirmed by the Fathers, to his brothers?

Therefore, through that same son of mine, Marcellus, your subdeacon, who was making great haste, I have sent in full, as you ordered, the canons established by the Fathers in the city of Nicaea. I ask that your holy assembly order abundant prayers to be offered for me.

In another hand: May our God preserve your Holiness, which is our desire, holy brothers.

## Copies of the Council of Nicaea

Sent on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, after the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augusti, to Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome.

### CXXXVII

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, creator of things visible and also invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of the same substance as the Father, through whom all things were made, both in heaven and on earth.

For us human beings and for our salvation he descended, was incarnate, and became human; he suffered. And he rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead.

And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and those who say that he was made from nothing, or from another substance or essence, or who say that the Son of God is mutable or changeable, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

Copies of the statutes of that same Council of Nicaea were also appended to this creed by the aforementioned bishops, as everything is set out above. We have judged it unnecessary to write them out here again.

## Letter of the African Council to Pope Celestine, bishop of the city of Rome

### CXXXVIII

To the beloved and honorable lord and brother Celestine, Aurelius, Palatinus, Antonius, Tutus, Servusdei, Terentius, Fortunatus, Martinus, Januarius, Optatus, Ceticius, Donatus, Theasius, Vincentius, Fortunatianus, and the others who were present at the universal African Council of Carthage.

We would have wished that, just as your Holiness informed us by letters sent through our fellow-presbyter Leo that you had rejoiced at the arrival of Apiarius, so we too might send this letter with joy concerning his clearing of the charges. Then certainly both our eagerness and yours would now be more assured, and would not appear premature, since the eagerness concerning his hearing had preceded the hearing itself.

When our holy brother and fellow-bishop Faustinus came to us, we convened a council. We believed that he had been sent with Apiarius for this reason: just as through his efforts Apiarius had previously been restored to the presbyterate, so now, through Faustinus’s exertions, he might be acquitted of the many crimes charged against him by the people of Thabraca.

But the examination conducted by our council discovered crimes in him so numerous, so great, and so monstrous that they surpassed the advocacy rather than the judgment of the aforementioned man, and the exertion of a defender rather than the justice of an examiner. For, first, consider how much he obstructed the whole assembly by inflicting various injuries, as though claiming the privileges of the Roman Church and wishing to receive Apiarius into communion with us. Your Holiness, believing that Apiarius had appealed—something he was unable to prove—had restored him to communion. Yet this was entirely impermissible, as you will learn more clearly from reading the proceedings.

After a most laborious three-day trial, while in great distress we were investigating the various charges brought against him, God, the just, strong, and long-suffering judge, brought a swift end to the delays of our fellow-bishop Faustinus and the evasions of Apiarius himself, by which he was trying to conceal his abominable acts.

The obstinacy, darker and fouler still, by which he sought through the shamelessness of denial to bury so great a mass of filthy mire was suppressed. When our God constrained his conscience and made public to human beings the hidden things that he had already condemned in his heart, as in a swamp of crimes, the deceitful denier suddenly broke into a confession of all the crimes alleged against him.

Finally, he voluntarily convicted himself of all his unbelievable disgraces and turned even our own hope—by which we had believed and wished that he might be cleansed of such shameful stains—into lamentation. Our sorrow was mitigated by only one consolation: his confession both freed us from the labor of a prolonged inquiry and provided some kind of remedy for his wounds, despite his reluctant confession, made against the resistance of his own conscience, Lord Brother.

After offering the greeting due to you, we earnestly beseech you henceforth not to admit so readily those who come from here to your ears, and no longer to wish to receive into communion those whom we have excommunicated. Your Veneration will easily recognize that this too was defined by the Council of Nicaea.

For if the Council appears there to have taken precautions concerning lower clerics or laypeople, how much more did it wish this to be observed concerning bishops, so that those suspended from communion in their own province should not appear to be restored prematurely or improperly to communion by your Holiness.

Your Holiness should also reject, as befits you, the improper refuges of presbyters and lesser clerics, since no definition of the Fathers has taken this away from the African Church. The decrees of Nicaea, whether concerning clerics of lower rank or the bishops themselves, most clearly entrusted them to their own metropolitans. With the greatest prudence and justice, they provided that whatever cases arise should be concluded in the places where they originated.

Nor will the grace of the Holy Spirit be lacking to the province of each, so that equity may be perceived wisely and held most firmly by Christ’s priests. Above all, each person has been granted the right, if he has been offended by the judgment of those who examined him, to appeal to the councils of his own province or even to a universal council.

Unless perhaps someone believes that justice can be inspired into the judgment of any single person while being denied to innumerable priests assembled in council. Or how will an overseas judgment be valid when the necessary witnesses cannot be brought, whether because of their sex, the frailty of old age, or many other impediments?

For we have found no provision established by any synod of the Fathers that persons should be sent as though from the side of your Holiness. The material which you previously sent through our fellow-bishop Faustinus, as though from the Council of Nicaea, was not something we were able to find in the more accurate councils accepted as Nicaean, which were sent from an authentic source by our fellow-bishop Cyril of the Alexandrian Church and by the venerable bishop Atticus of Constantinople.

These documents had already previously been sent by us to your predecessor, the bishop Boniface, of venerable memory, through the presbyter Innocent and the subdeacon Marcellus, by whom they had been sent to us from those bishops. In them we could find nothing of this kind.

Do not send your clerical agents to anyone who asks for them; do not grant them permission, lest we appear to introduce into Christ’s Church the smoky arrogance of the world—a Church that offers the light of simplicity and humility to those who long to see God.

As for our brother Faustinus, since Apiarius has now, regrettably, been removed from Christ’s Church for his abominable crimes, we are confident that, through the integrity and moderation of your Holiness, and without prejudice to fraternal charity, Africa will no longer have to endure him.

In another hand: May our Lord preserve your Holiness, praying for us for a long age, Lord Brother.

# Collections of Decrees

## Collection of the Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs, by Dionysius Exiguus

### To the Reader

[Note: This Preface was prefixed by C. Justel to the Collection of the Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs, by Dionysius Exiguus, published in 1643.]

To this new edition of Dionysius Exiguus’s Collection of Ecclesiastical Canons, so that nothing belonging to the old canonical jurisprudence might appear to be lacking, we have appended a letter of that same Dionysius Exiguus to Julian, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Anastasia. It serves as a preface to his Collection of the Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs. We now restore it for the first time to its author, from an old manuscript belonging to the highly learned man Jacob Sirmond, presbyter of the Society of Jesus, to whom we acknowledge our debt. We provide it for you together with an index of the chapters only, omitting the complete chapters of the Decrees, which anyone can easily recover from the old codex of the Canons of the Roman Church, first printed at Mainz in 1525 and later at Paris in 1619.

This Julian is the presbyter who signed the synods held at Rome under Pope Felix, in the consulship of Dinamius and Siphidius—that is, in the year of Christ 488—and under Symmachus, after the consulship of Paulinus—that is, in the year 499. This indicates that the Dionysian collection was made around this period, after the translation of the Greek canons.

It contains the decretal letters of Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, and Anastasius, from the year 385 to the year 486. Cresconius also lists them in his *Canonical Breviary*, as does Pope Leo IV in Gratian, canon “On Petitions,” distinction 20, and Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, against Hincmar, bishop of Laon, chapter 43.

This is also the collection which Pope Zachary, in his letter to Pippin, mayor of the palace, and to all the bishops established in the kingdom of France, calls the *Book of Decrees*, citing from it certain chapters of Siricius, Innocent, Leo, and Gelasius. Since we are preparing a fuller treatment of this matter, we have thought it worthwhile to give here a brief notice concerning the first collection of the decretals of the Roman pontiffs.

|---|---:|

## Preface of Dionysius Exiguus

To my venerable lord Julian, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Anastasia, Dionysius Exiguus.

Stirred by the pious zeal of your Holiness—a zeal which in its inquiries omits absolutely nothing pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline—I have collected, with as much care and diligence as I could, the decrees of the former pontiffs of the apostolic see. I have brought them into a certain order and distinguished them with arranged titles, so that I might conclude, in a single numbered sequence, all the decrees of the individual pontiffs that I found, and append all the titles to this preface, in the same manner in which I formerly arranged the canons while translating them from the Greek language of the Fathers—a method which I learned had pleased you greatly.

You love God with the most sincere affection and therefore sustain his servants with praiseworthy solicitude. For what pilgrim serving Christ is not cherished by your hospitality? I considered it right to serve you in this matter, so that your industry, which you devote to heavenly regulations, might be imitated by the present age and admired by posterity.

For, because of your love of virtue, you desire to learn all useful things, although you fulfill in your conduct every observance of the venerable law. And how great is the blessed Pope Gelasius in merit before God, we, who did not see him bodily in his lifetime, more easily judge through you, his disciples.

Formed by his teaching, you adorn the rank of presbyter through holy conduct, so that in the manifest service of your character his activity seems in some way to shine forth. As we have learned from your account, we rejoice that he was a man of such good will that, with the Lord’s approval, when he assumed primacy in the Church for the salvation of many, he raised it up by serving rather than ruling, and enlarged the purity of his life through the merits of his teaching.

Indeed, all his activity is said to have consisted either in prayer or in reading. At times he also undertook the work of writing, as the occasion or reason required, and he rejoiced in the companionship and fellowship of the greatest servants of God.

Through their spiritual conversation he was nourished by such devotion to divine love and such meditation on the word of God that the saying of the Psalmist could also be applied to him:

> Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and whom you teach from your law, that you may give him relief from the days of evil.

For he passed through the evil days of this age in such a way, with the Lord mitigating and governing them, that he endured every temptation with remarkable prudence and patience. He rejected pleasures through fasts, trampled pride under humility, and shone with such mercy and joyful generosity of spirit that he deserved to satisfy nearly all the poor while himself remaining needy.

Truly blessed was he in this poverty, through which he always clung to divine praises, as the prophet says to the Lord:

> The poor and needy will praise your name.

He was a man brilliant in intellect, outstanding in life, and worthy of reverence in authority. Therefore, adorned with so many insignia of virtue, he did not approach so lofty an office unworthily. He considered the honor of the highest dignity an exceedingly heavy burden and maintained that even a small negligence in a pontiff was a great danger to souls.

For this reason he surrendered himself neither to idle leisure nor to luxurious and extravagant banquets. From such things arise diseases of the soul as well as of the body.

This pastor, an excellent imitator of the supreme and good Shepherd, was therefore a distinguished prelate of the apostolic see, who both did and taught the divine commandments. For this reason we are confident that he is great among the saints, according to the promise of Christ the Lord:

> Whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

# Decretal Letter of Pope Siricius

## Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, greetings

The report of your Brotherhood, sent to our predecessor Damasus, of holy memory, found me already established in his seat, as the Lord had ordained. When we read it more carefully in the gathering of the brothers, we found as many matters deserving rebuke and correction as we would have wished to find worthy of praise.

And because it was necessary for us to take up the labors and concerns of the man whom, by God’s grace, we succeeded in honor, after first giving, as was proper, an indication of my advancement, we do not refuse to give an appropriate answer to each point of your consultation, insofar as the Lord has deigned to assist us.

In view of our office, we have no freedom to dissemble or to remain silent. The zeal of Christian religion, which rests upon us more than upon all others, requires us to bear the burdens of all who are burdened. Indeed, blessed Peter the Apostle bears these burdens in us; as we trust, he protects and guards us as heirs of his administration in all things.

## On not rebaptizing Arians

### I

At the very beginning of your letter you indicated that many baptized by the impious Arians are hastening to the catholic faith, and that some of our brothers wish to baptize them a second time. This is not permitted, since the Apostle forbids it (Ephesians IV), the canons oppose it, and the general decrees sent to the provinces after the Council of Ariminum had been annulled by my predecessor Liberius, of venerable memory, prohibit it.

We associate them with the assembly of Catholics, together with the Novatians and other heretics, as was established in the synod (Council of Nicaea, canon 8), through the sole invocation of the sevenfold Spirit and the laying on of the bishop’s hand. The entire East and West also observes this practice. You too must not henceforth deviate from this path, if you do not wish to be separated from our synodal college by a sentence of the synod.

## That baptism should not be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost

### II

There follows the matter of the various times for baptizing, according to each person’s preference—a disorder that must be rejected and corrected. Our fellow priests, as we say with indignation, presume this not on the basis of any authoritative reason but through sheer rashness, so that innumerable crowds, as you report, freely and indiscriminately receive the mystery of baptism on the festivals of Christ’s birth, of his manifestation, and also of the Apostles and Martyrs.

Yet this privilege is claimed especially by Easter, together with its Pentecost, both among us and among all Churches. Only on these days of the year is it fitting that the general sacraments of baptism be administered to those coming to the faith.

This applies to the elect who have enrolled their names forty days or more beforehand and have been purified by exorcisms, daily prayers, and fasts, so that the apostolic injunction may be fulfilled:

> When the old leaven has been cleansed out, a new dough may begin to be.
> (1 Corinthians V)

Just as we say that reverence for Easter must in no respect be diminished, so we wish infants, who because of their age are not yet able to speak, and those who in any necessity require the sacred water of baptism, to be aided with all speed. It must not work toward the destruction of our souls if, when they desire it, the saving font is denied and each person departing from this world loses both the kingdom and life.

Whoever encounters the danger of shipwreck, an enemy attack, the uncertainty of a siege, or the despair of any bodily illness, and asks to be aided by the single support of faith, must receive, at the very moment of asking, the reward of the regeneration he desires.

Let the error in this matter now be sufficient. From this point onward let all priests observe the rule stated above, if they do not wish to be torn away from the solidity of the apostolic rock upon which Christ built the universal Church (Matthew X).

## On apostates

### III

It has also been reported that certain Christians have passed into apostasy—which is an unspeakable thing—and have been polluted by the worship of idols and the contamination of sacrifices. We order that they be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, by which they were formerly redeemed through rebirth.

If at some point they repent and turn to lamentation, they must perform penance for as long as they live, and at the end of their life the grace of reconciliation must be granted to them, because, as the Lord teaches, we do not desire the death of a sinner, but only that he should turn and live (Ezekiel XVIII).

## That no one may take another man’s betrothed as his wife

### IV

You have inquired concerning the violation of marriage: may one man take as his wife a girl betrothed to another? We prohibit this in every way, because among the faithful the blessing which a priest bestows upon a woman who is about to marry is comparable to a sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

## On those who have not observed their penance

### V

Your Love was right to consult the apostolic see concerning those who, after performing penance, have returned like dogs and pigs to their former vomit and wallowing. They have again sought military service, theatrical pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden sexual relations. Children born after their absolution have exposed their professed incontinence.

Since such persons now have no further refuge in penance, we have decided that they are to be joined to the faithful within the church only in prayer. They may attend the celebration of the sacred mysteries, although they do not deserve to do so, but they must be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table.

Thus at least corrected by this destruction, they may both punish their own errors within themselves and provide an example to others, so that they may be drawn away from shameful desires.

Nevertheless, since they fell through the weakness of the flesh, when they begin to depart to the Lord we wish them to be assisted by the grace of communion as viaticum. We judge that the same rule must be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves to such defilements.

## On monks and virgins who do not preserve their profession

### VI

Furthermore, we have learned that certain monks and nuns, having cast aside their profession of holiness, have sunk into such an excess of license that at first, secretly and as though under the pretext of monasteries, they joined themselves in illicit and sacrilegious contamination. Later, driven into the abyss by despair of conscience, they freely fathered or bore children from their illicit embraces. Both the public laws and ecclesiastical regulations condemn this.

We therefore order that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the community of monasteries and from the assemblies of the churches. Shut up in their own prisons, they are to lament such a great crime continually and, through the purifying fire of repentance, to refine themselves, so that at least at death, out of regard for mercy alone, forgiveness may be able to assist them through the grace of communion.

## On incontinent clerics
VII. Let us now come to the most sacred orders of the clergy. We have learned, through your charity’s report, that throughout your provinces they have been trampled upon and confused in such a way as to do injury to venerable religion that we must say with the voice of Jeremiah: “Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep for this people day and night?” (Jer. IX). If the blessed prophet therefore says that, for lamenting the sins of the people, his tears would not suffice, how greatly must we be struck with grief when we are compelled to mourn the crimes of those who are members of our own body, for whom, according to blessed Paul, the daily burden of earnest care and concern for all the churches rests continually upon us (II Cor. XI)? “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?”

For we have learned that many priests and Levites of Christ, even after long periods following their consecration, have fathered offspring both from their own wives and from shameful intercourse, and that they defend their crime by this pretext: that in the Old Testament the power of begetting is said to have been granted to priests and ministers. Let that follower of lust and teacher of vices now tell me, whoever he may be, whether he thinks that in the law of Moses the reins of lust were everywhere loosened by our Lord for the sacred orders. Why, then, does He warn those to whom the Holy of Holies was entrusted, saying: “Be holy, because I also, the Lord your God, am holy” [Col. 0235A] (Lev. XX)? Why, moreover, were the priests ordered to dwell in the temple, far from their homes, during the year of their service (Luke I)? Clearly this was so that they could not even then engage in carnal relations with their wives, and, shining with integrity of conscience, might offer God an acceptable gift. After their period of service had been completed, marital relations were relaxed solely for the sake of producing offspring, because no one from any tribe other than Levi was commanded to be admitted to God’s ministry (Num. XVIII).

Accordingly, when the Lord Jesus had enlightened us by His coming, He declares in the Gospel that He came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it (Matt. IX). For this reason He willed the Church—whose bridegroom is “beautiful in form” (Eph. V)—to shine with the splendor of chastity, so that on the day of judgment, when He comes again, He might find her without stain or wrinkle, as He established through His apostle [Col. 0235B].

By an unbreakable law all priests and Levites are bound by these decrees, so that from the day of our ordination we dedicate both our hearts and our bodies to sobriety and chastity, provided that in all things we please our God by the sacrifices we offer daily. “Those who are in the flesh,” says the chosen Vessel [i.e. Paul] (Rom. VIII), “cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit—if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” And where could the Spirit of God dwell, unless in bodies, as we read (Wis. I), holy to God?

Since, as your holiness has reported, some of those about whom we speak lament that they fell through ignorance, we declare that mercy must not be denied them on this condition: that, without any increase in honor, they remain for as long as they live in the office in which they were discovered, provided that thereafter they strive to show themselves continent. But those who rely on the excuse of an illicit privilege and assert that this was granted to them by the ancient law should know that, by the authority of the apostolic see, they have been cast out of every ecclesiastical honor which they unworthily held, and that they can never again touch the venerable mysteries from which they deprived themselves while they indulged in obscene desires.

And because present examples warn us to take precautions for the future, let every bishop, presbyter, and deacon—though we do not wish it—who henceforth is found to be such, understand that every avenue of indulgence is now closed to him by us. For wounds that have not felt the healing of remedies must necessarily be cut away with the knife [Col. 0235D].

### Concerning the clergy: who ought to be promoted

VIII. We have also learned that men of unexamined lives, some of whom have even had numerous marriages, are freely and unrestrainedly aspiring to the aforementioned dignities, as each person chooses. We attribute this not so much to those who reach them through immoderate ambition as specifically to the metropolitan bishops, who, by conniving at forbidden attempts, disregard, insofar as it lies with them, the commands of our God.

To pass over what we suspect of still graver matters, where is that which our God established in the law given through Moses, saying, “My priests shall marry only once” (Lev. XXI)? And elsewhere: “The priest shall take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been repudiated, [Col. 0236A] not a prostitute” (Ezek. XLIV). Following this, the Apostle, who had been transformed from persecutor into preacher (II Tim. III), commanded that both priest and deacon must be the husband of one wife.

All these provisions are so despised by the bishops of your regions as though they had actually been established to the contrary. Since we must not neglect such usurpations, lest the just voice of the indignant Lord rebuke us, saying, “You saw a thief and ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Ps. XLIX), we decree by a general pronouncement what all the churches must henceforth follow and what they must avoid.

### Concerning the conduct of the clergy

IX. Whoever, therefore, has vowed himself to the service of the Church ought, from infancy and before the years of puberty, to be baptized and associated with the ministry of the lector. From the beginning of adolescence until his thirtieth year, if he has lived commendably, he must be content with one wife only—the woman whom, as a virgin, he received through the common blessing of a priest—and must serve as acolyte and subdeacon. After this, he may approach the rank of deacon if he has first proved himself worthy, with continence leading the way. If he has served there commendably for more than five years, he shall suitably attain the presbyterate; thereafter, after ten years, he may obtain the episcopal chair, provided that during these periods the integrity of his life and faith has been approved.

### Concerning the elderly

X. Whoever, already advanced in age and moved by a life of better purpose, hastens from the lay state to enter the sacred service shall obtain the fruit of his desire only if, at the time of his baptism, he is immediately associated with the number of lectors or exorcists—provided it is established that he has had, or has, only one wife, and that he took her as a virgin.

Once he has been initiated, after completing two years he shall serve for another five years as acolyte and subdeacon. Then, if during these periods he has been judged worthy, he shall be advanced to the diaconate. Thereafter, with the passage of time, he shall not undeservedly receive the presbyterate or episcopate if the election of the clergy and people calls him to it.

### That a cleric who has taken a second wife is to be deposed

XI. Any cleric who has married either a widow or, certainly, a second wife shall immediately be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical dignity, with only lay communion granted to him. He will be able to retain this only if he thereafter commits nothing that would cause him to lose it.

### Which women may live with clerics

XII. We permit no women to live in the houses of clerics except those whom the Synod of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely because of the necessities of family relationships.

### Concerning the promotion of monks

XIII. We both desire and decree that monks—whose seriousness of conduct and holy discipline of life and faith commend them—be associated with the offices of the clergy. Those who are under thirty years of age are to be promoted through the individual minor grades as time advances, and thus, with the consecration of mature age, are to reach the insignia of the diaconate or presbyterate. They must not ascend immediately, by a leap, to the summit of the episcopate unless the periods which we established above for each dignity have likewise been observed [Col. 0237A].

### That a penitent is not to become a cleric

XIV. It was also fitting for us to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman may ever attain clerical honor. Although they may have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, those who were formerly vessels of vices ought not to receive the instruments for administering the sacraments.

### That if, through ignorance, a penitent, a bigamist, or the husband of a widow has become a cleric, he is not to be promoted

[Col. 0237B]

XV. Since the sole excuse offered for all these matters that incur reproach is ignorance—and, out of regard for piety alone, we must meanwhile forgive this mercifully—any penitent, any bigamist, or any husband of a widow who has improperly and incompetently slipped into the sacred service should understand that forgiveness has been granted him by us on this condition: he must regard it as a great favor if, deprived of every hope of promotion, he remains permanently in the order in which he is found.

Henceforth the chief bishops of all the provinces are to know that if they believe they may admit any such person to the sacred orders, an appropriate judgment will be issued by the apostolic see both against them and against the status of those whom they have promoted contrary to the canons and our prohibitions [Col. 0237C–0238A].

We have explained, as I think, dearest brother, all the matters set forth in the complaints, and we have given, as far as I judge, sufficient answers to each of the cases which you reported to the Roman Church through our son Bassianus the presbyter—as to the head of your body. Now we urge your fraternal spirit more and more to preserve the canons and uphold the decretal decisions.

See to it that what we have written in reply to your inquiries is brought to the attention of all our fellow bishops, not only those established in your diocese, but also all the Carthaginians, Baeticans, Lusitanians, and Gauls, as well as those who border on your neighboring provinces on every side. Let what we have established in salutary order be sent to them through your letters.

Although no priest of the Lord is free to be ignorant of the statutes of the apostolic see or the venerable definitions of the canons, it may nevertheless be highly glorious to your affection, both because of the antiquity of your priesthood and for that reason, if what has been written generally to you in a special way is conveyed, through your united diligence, to the knowledge of all our brethren. Thus what we have established, not rashly but prudently, with the utmost caution and deliberation, and for the sake of salvation, may remain inviolate, and access may be closed to every excuse in the future—an access which, among us, can now be open to no one.

Given on the third day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto, illustrious men (A.D. 385).

# Decrees of Pope Innocent

[Col. 0237]

[Col. 0237C] Innocent to Decentius, bishop of Eugubium, greetings.

If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, intact, there would be no diversity or variation in the orders and consecrations themselves. But while each person considers that what he himself thinks—not what has been handed down—is what must be observed, the result is that different practices appear to be held or celebrated in different places and churches, and scandal arises among the people. Not knowing that ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, they think that these practices do not suit them or the churches, or that contradiction has been introduced by the apostles or by apostolic men [Col. 0237D].

Who could fail to know or notice that what was handed down by the chief of the apostles, Peter, to the Roman Church and is preserved to this day ought to be observed by all, and that nothing should be imposed or introduced which either lacks authority or appears to have taken its example from elsewhere?

This is especially clear because throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one is known to have established churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read, if another apostle is found or read to have taught in those provinces. If they do not read this, because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves, since there is no doubt that they received their beginning from it. Otherwise, while pursuing foreign assertions, they may appear to omit the source of their institutions [Col. 0238C].

There is no doubt that your affection has often come to the city and assembled with us in the Church, and that you have learned what custom is observed in the consecration of the mysteries and in the other sacred rites. I would have considered this sufficient instruction for your church, or sufficient reformation if your predecessors had held anything less or differently, had you not thought it necessary to consult us about certain matters.

We therefore reply—not because we believe that you are ignorant of anything, but so that you may instruct your own people with greater authority, and, if any have departed from the institutions of the Roman Church, admonish them or not delay to identify them, so that we may know who introduces innovations or thinks that the custom of any church other than the Roman Church ought to be observed [Col. 0238D].

### Concerning giving the peace after the mysteries have been completed

I. You state that some command the people to exchange the peace before the mysteries have been completed, or exchange it among the priests themselves, whereas the peace must necessarily be announced after everything which I ought not to disclose. Through it, it is made clear that the people have given their assent to everything that is performed in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and the conclusion of all things is shown by the seal of the peace that follows.

### Concerning not reciting names before the priest’s prayer

II. As for reciting the names before the priest offers the prayer and commends in his prayer the offerings of those whose names are to be recited, you yourself, in your prudence, recognize how superfluous this is: before offering a person’s sacrifice to God, to mention that person’s name, although nothing is unknown to Him.

The offerings, therefore, must first be commended, and then the names of those to whom they belong must be announced, so that they may be named during the sacred mysteries, not among the other matters which we introduce beforehand in order to open the way for the prayers that will follow in the mysteries themselves.

### That the baptized should be confirmed only by bishops

[Col. 0239B]

III. Regarding the confirmation of infants, it is clear that this may be performed by no one other than a bishop. For although presbyters are priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. That this belongs solely to bishops—that they may either confirm or confer the Paraclete Spirit—is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles which says that Peter and John were sent to confer the Holy Spirit upon those who had already been baptized.

When presbyters baptize, whether without a bishop or in the presence of a bishop, they may anoint the baptized with chrism; but they may not sign the forehead with that same oil, which belongs solely to bishops when they confer the Paraclete Spirit. I cannot state the words, lest I appear to betray more than to answer a consultation [Col. 0239C].

### That fasting should properly be observed every Saturday

IV. The clearest reasoning demonstrates that one must fast on Saturday. For if we celebrate the Lord’s Day, on account of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, not only at Easter but also in every weekly cycle, repeatedly commemorating the image of that day; and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s passion, we must not pass over Saturday, which appears to lie between the sorrow and joy of that period.

It is certainly established that the apostles spent those two days in sadness and mourning and hid themselves out of fear of the Jews. There is no doubt that they fasted so intensely during those two days that the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments were not celebrated at all during them [Col. 0239D].

This practice must certainly be maintained every week, because the commemoration of that day must always be celebrated. If they think that one should fast only once, on a single Saturday, then the Lord’s Day and Friday ought likewise to be celebrated only once, at Easter. But if the image of the Lord’s Day and Friday is renewed every week, it is madness to observe the custom of the two days while omitting Saturday, since it has the same reason as Friday: on Friday the Lord suffered and descended to the underworld, so that, rising on the third day, He might restore joy after the preceding two-day sorrow.

We do not, therefore, deny that one must fast on Friday, [Col. 0240A] but we say that this must also be done on Saturday, because both days brought sorrow to the apostles and to those who followed Christ. On the Lord’s Day they were made joyful and not only wished that day itself to be most festive, but also considered that it should be observed throughout all the weeks.

### Concerning sending the fermentum to the presbyters of the city

V. Regarding the fermentum which we send on the Lord’s Day to the titular churches, you wished to consult us about something unnecessary. All our churches are located within the city, and their presbyters cannot meet with us on that day because of the people entrusted to them. Therefore they receive from the acolytes the fermentum prepared by us, so that, especially on that day, they may not consider themselves separated from our communion.

I do not think this ought to be done in the rural parishes, because the sacraments do not have to be carried far, nor do we send them to presbyters established in different cemeteries, since their presbyters possess both the right and the permission to consecrate them [Col. 0240B].

### Concerning baptized persons possessed by a demon

VI. Your affection asked about baptized persons who are later seized by a demon, some illness, or the intervention of sin, whether they may or ought to be confirmed by a presbyter or deacon. This is not permitted unless the bishop has ordered it. Hands must not be laid upon such a person at all unless the bishop has granted authority for it to be done.

For it to be done, it belongs to the bishop to command that hands be laid upon the person by a presbyter or by other clerics. For how could this be accomplished without great difficulty, if a possessed person living far away had to be brought to the bishop? If such a case occurred during the journey, it would not be easy either to bring the person to the bishop or to return him to his own home [Col. 0240C].

### Concerning penitents

VII. Regarding penitents who are performing penance, whether for more serious or for lesser offenses, the custom of the Roman Church shows that, if no illness intervenes, they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter.

As for determining the weight of sins, it is the priest’s responsibility to judge: he must attend to the penitent’s confession and to the weeping and tears of the one who is correcting himself, and then order him to be released when he has seen that adequate satisfaction has been made.

If someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he must be released before the time of Easter, lest he depart from the world without communion [Col. 0240D].

### Concerning the epistle of the holy apostle James, in which prayer for the sick is commanded

VIII. Since your affection wished to consult us about this matter as about the others, my son the deacon Coelestinus also added in his letter that you had cited what is written in the epistle of the blessed apostle James:

“Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.”

There is no doubt that this must be understood of faithful Christians who are sick. They may be anointed with the holy oil of chrism, which, having been prepared by the bishop, may be used not only by priests but by all Christians, for anointing themselves or their own dependents in time of need [Col. 0241A].

We regard as superfluous the added suggestion that there should be doubt concerning the bishop in a matter which it is beyond doubt that presbyters may perform. The reason presbyters are mentioned is that bishops, occupied with other responsibilities, cannot visit all the sick.

But if a bishop either can or considers it worthy to visit someone personally, he may without hesitation bless and touch him with chrism, since he is the one who prepares the chrism itself. This cannot, however, be poured upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For those to whom the other sacraments are denied, how could one kind be thought capable of being granted?

To all these matters, therefore, dearest brother, which your affection wished us to explain, we have taken care to respond as best we could, so that your Church may be able to preserve and maintain the Roman custom from which it derives its origin. The remaining matters, which it was not lawful to write, we shall be able to state when you are present, if questioned.

It will also belong to the power of the Lord to arrange that you may properly instruct both your Church and our clerics who, under your episcopate, serve in the divine offices, and that you may offer others a model which they ought to imitate.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and Palladius, illustrious man (A.D. 416).

Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, greetings.

Although, dearest brother, because of the rank and honor of the priesthood in which you are especially eminent, all matters concerning living and teaching according to ecclesiastical regulations are known to you, and although there is nothing in the sacred readings which seems to have escaped your grasp, nevertheless, since you earnestly requested the norm and authority of the Roman Church, I have readily complied with your wish and sent with my letter the ordered disciplines of life and commendable conduct. Through them, the peoples of the churches in your region may learn by what matters and regulations Christian life ought to be governed in each person’s calling, and what discipline is maintained in the churches of the city of Rome.

It will be your responsibility diligently to commend this book of regulations, as a kind of teaching manual and admonition, to the neighboring peoples and to our fellow priests who preside over their own churches in those regions. Thus they may learn our practices and, through the diligence of their instruction, form the conduct of those who come together in the faith [Col. 0241D].

For either they will learn their own purpose from this appropriate instruction of ours, or, if anything is still lacking, they will easily be able to supply it through good imitation.

Let us begin, therefore, with the help of the holy apostle Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ received their beginning. Since many causes have often emerged which, in some cases, were not merely causes but crimes, let every priest henceforth be concerned to maintain such care in his own church as the apostle Paul teaches: a Church is to be presented to God without stain or wrinkle (Eph. V), lest our conscience be defiled and violated by the breath of any diseased sheep.

You rightly requested that in those regions the form maintained by the Roman Church should be observed, for the sake of those who, through ignorance or negligence, do not maintain ecclesiastical discipline and presume to do many things that ought not to be presumed [Col. 0242A]. We are not imposing any new commands, but we wish those things which the negligence of some has caused to be neglected to be observed by all. These things, nevertheless, were established by apostolic and patristic tradition.

For Paul, in his admonition to the Thessalonians, writes: “Stand firm and hold to our traditions, whether by word or by letter” (II Thess. II, 14).

That should certainly stir your mind more powerfully: you must be found secure and free from every stain of this world before the sight of God, for from the one to whom much has been entrusted, more is required in the form of punishment.

Since we are compelled to render an account not only for ourselves but also for the people of Christ, we must instruct the people in divine discipline [Cod. ms., “sanctified discipline”]. For some have arisen who, failing to maintain the statutes of their predecessors, violated the Church’s chastity through their own presumption, following the favor of the people and not fearing God’s judgment.

Therefore, lest by our silence we seem to give them consent, as the Lord says, “You saw a thief and ran with him” (Ps. XLIX, 18), these are the matters which, in view of divine judgment, every catholic bishop must henceforth take care to observe.

### That no bishop may be ordained without the knowledge of the metropolitan

IX. First, no one is to presume to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop. A judgment is sound when it is confirmed by the opinions of many, and no single bishop should presume to ordain, lest the benefit conferred appear furtive. This was established and defined by the Synod of Nicaea.

### Who may not be admitted to the clergy, and that clerical cases are to be settled by their own bishops

[Col. 0242C]

X. Likewise, if anyone, after the remission of sins, has borne the belt of secular military service, he must not be admitted to the clergy at all.

If any cases or disputes arise among clerics, whether of the higher or lower order, the quarrel is to be settled, in accordance with the Synod of Nicaea, by assembling the bishops of the same province. No one may, without prejudice to the Roman Church, abandon the priests who by divine will govern the Church of God in that province and hasten to other provinces.

If anyone should presume to do so, let him be judged by all both removed from the clerical office and guilty of injury [Col. 0242D]. If more serious cases have arisen, they are to be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, as the synod established.

### That a cleric must not marry a widow

XI. A cleric must not marry a widow, because it is written: “The priest shall take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been cast out” (Lev. XXI, 13). Anyone who strives to attain the priesthood through his own labor and uprightness of life must beware lest, impeded by this disqualification, he be unable to attain it.

### That if a layman has married a widow, he must not become a cleric

XII. A man who, even as a layman, has married a widow—whether before baptism or after baptism—is not to be admitted to the clergy, because he appears to be excluded by the same fault [Col. 0243A]. In baptism sins are forgiven; the relationship with a wife already taken is not annulled.

### That one who has had a second wife must not be a cleric

XIII. A man who has married a second wife must not become a cleric, because it is written: “The husband of one wife” (I Tim. III); and again: “My priests shall marry only once” (Lev. XXI); and elsewhere: “My priests shall not marry again” (Ezek. XLIV).

If some think that, when a man married before baptism and, after that wife departed from the world, married another, the matter was forgiven in baptism, they are seriously mistaken about the rule. In baptism sins are forgiven; the number of wives taken is not abolished. A wife is, of course, taken according to the precept of the law, so much so that even in paradise, when the parents of the human race were joined together (Gen. II), they were blessed by the Lord Himself. Solomon also says, “A wife will be prepared for a man by God” (Prov. XIX).

The Church’s practice itself demonstrates that all priests must preserve this form. It is most absurd to believe that a wife taken before baptism is not counted after baptism, when the blessing imposed by the priest upon those marrying is taught to have given not the substance of wrongdoing but the form of the law established by God from ancient times.

If a wife taken before baptism is not thought to count, then children begotten before baptism likewise ought not to be regarded as children.

### That no bishop may usurp the right to ordain clerics belonging to another church

XIV. No one is to presume to ordain a cleric from another church unless that cleric’s bishop, entreated by prayers, is willing to grant permission. The Synod of Nicaea also established this: one church must not receive a cleric rejected by another.

### That those who come to the Church from the Novatians or Montenses are not to be rebaptized

XV. Those who come from the Novatians or Montenses are to be received by the laying on of hands alone, because, although baptized by heretics, they were nevertheless baptized in the name of Christ. The exception is those who, after passing from us to them, were perhaps rebaptized by them. If such people repent and, considering their fall, prefer to return, they are to be admitted only after a prolonged penance and satisfaction.

### That priests and Levites must not have intercourse with women

[Col. 0243D]

XVI. Moreover, the Church must uphold in every way what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry.

For it is written: “Be holy, because I also, the Lord your God, am holy.” If in ancient times the priests did not leave the temple of God during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah (Lev. XXI), and did not touch their homes at all—although marital relations had been relaxed for them on account of the succession of offspring, since no one from another tribe, or except from the seed of Aaron, had been commanded to approach the priesthood (Num. XVIII)—how much more ought these priests and Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry exists without succession, and no day passes when they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the ministry of baptism?

For if Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (I Cor. VII), and gave this command even to laymen, how much more must priests, whose constant duty is both to pray and to sacrifice, always abstain from such relations?

If they have been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will they perhaps presume to sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit will they believe themselves heard, when it is said: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus I)?

Perhaps someone thinks this is permitted because it is written, “The husband of one wife” (I Tim. III). But Paul did not say that he should remain in the desire to beget children; he said this on account of future conscience. He did not exclude those who were physically intact, for he says: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (I Cor. VII). And he declares still more openly: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. VIII).

### That if a monk becomes a cleric, he must preserve his way of life

XVII. Monks who, after remaining for a long time in monasteries, later attain the clerical order must not depart from their former way of life.

Either he must remain as he was in the monastery, and, having preserved that way for a long time, must not abandon it when placed in a higher rank; or, if he was corrupted and then baptized while residing in a monastery and wishes to enter the clerical order, he may not have a wife at all, because, having already been corrupted, he cannot be blessed with a bride.

This rule is observed especially among clerics, since the ancient regulation provides that whoever, having been corrupted, was baptized and wished to become a cleric must promise that he would never take a wife.

### That a cleric must not be made from the curiales, because of the entertainments which he is compelled to provide, invented by the devil

XVIII. Moreover, some of our brethren frequently attempt to make clerics of curiales or of men occupied with public functions. Later, when the emperor orders them to be recalled, greater grief arises for them than gratitude for those who were admitted.

It is clear that such men, in the very performance of their offices, provide entertainments which there is no doubt were invented by the devil, and either preside over or perhaps participate in the arrangements of games and public spectacles [Col. 0244D].

Let the concern and grief of our brethren serve as an example. We have often endured these troubles in the presence of the emperor, when we repeatedly pleaded on behalf of such men—as you yourself learned when you were present with us. Not only lower-ranking clerics drawn from the curiales, but even men already established in the priesthood, were subjected to great pressure that they be returned.

### Concerning veiled virgins who have gone astray

XIX. Women who have spiritually married Christ and have been veiled by a priest, if they later either marry publicly or secretly corrupt themselves, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they joined themselves has departed from the world.

If this principle is observed among human beings—that any woman who marries another while her husband is alive is considered an adulteress and is not granted permission to perform penance unless one of the two has died—how much more must it be observed in the case of a woman who had previously joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward passed over to human marriage?

### Concerning un veiled virgins who have gone astray

XX. Those who have not yet been covered with the sacred veil but have always pretended to remain in the purpose of virginity, even though they were not veiled, if they should happen to marry must perform penance for a certain period, because their pledge was held by the Lord.

If among human beings a good-faith contract is ordinarily dissolved for no reason at all, how much more can this promise, which they made with God, not be dissolved without punishment? For if the apostle Paul says that women who departed from their purpose of widowhood have condemnation because they made their first faith void (I Tim. V), how much more do virgins deserve it when they have tried to break faith with their earlier promise?

If this rule, dearest brother, is observed with full vigilance by all the priests of God, ambition will cease, dissension will fall silent, heresies and schisms will not arise, the devil will find no place to rage, unanimity will remain, iniquity will be trampled down after its defeat, truth will burn with spiritual fervor, and the peace preached by the lips will agree with the will of the soul.

The saying of the Apostle will be fulfilled: that we remain of one mind, thinking one thing, in Christ (Phil. II), claiming nothing for ourselves through contention or empty glory, but pleasing not human beings but our God and Savior—to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time and Aristonetus, illustrious man (A.D. 404).

Innocent to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, greeting.

When you consulted me, dearest brother, about what I thought concerning each of the matters proposed, I replied, to the extent of my understanding, with what seemed appropriate: what should be followed, whether reason, receptive to instruction, persuaded it, or the authority of reading demonstrated it, or the continuous sequence of events made clear. Indeed, your affection, following the practice of prudent men, preferred to refer to the apostolic see what ought to be observed in doubtful matters, rather than, by presumed usurpation, to obtain for yourself what seemed right in each individual case. For why should we consider it more shameful to learn something [Col. 0245D] than to be wholly ignorant? Even for me, teachability comes through discussion, so that, after examining the reasons, I am compelled to respond to the matters proposed; and thus it happens that the one asked to teach is always learning something himself. I shall therefore set out each matter and append the answer.

## On the incontinence of priests or Levites

### XXI

You proposed the question of what ought to be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministry of the diaconate or in the office of the presbyterate, have been shown by the children born to them to be or to have been incontinent. Concerning such men, the discipline of the divine laws is clear, and the evident admonitions of Siricius, bishop of blessed memory, have been transmitted: those placed in such offices who are incontinent are to be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor [Col. 0246A] and are not to be admitted to such a ministry, which ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.

For there is a very ancient authority of sacred law (I Chronicles XXV; Luke I), observed from the beginning: priests were commanded to dwell in the temple during the year of their turn, so that, serving the sacred offerings, they might claim the divine mysteries for themselves as pure and cleansed from every stain. Nor is it lawful for those to be admitted to the sacrifices who engage in carnal intercourse even with their wives, since it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Leviticus XX).

Marital intercourse had indeed been relaxed for them because of the succession of offspring, since no one from another tribe had been commanded to approach the priesthood. How much more, then, ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, for whom [Col. 0246B] there is either priesthood or ministry without succession, and no day passes on which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the duty of baptism?

For if Paul writes to the Corinthians: “Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (II Corinthians VII)—and this he certainly commanded the laity—how much more ought priests, whose constant duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, always to abstain from such intercourse? If one has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit believe that he will be heard, when it is said: “All things are pure for the pure, but for the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus I)?

Perhaps he thinks this is permitted because it is written: “The husband of one wife” (I Timothy III). He did not say this of one who remained in the desire to beget children, but with future continence in mind. For he did not exclude those who were physically whole when he said: “I wish that all were as I myself am” (I Corinthians VII); and he declares it more openly, saying: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Romans VIII). He said “having children” (I Timothy III), not “begetting them.”

But the judgment is plainly distinct and divided. If that form of ecclesiastical life and discipline which was transmitted by Bishop Siricius to the provinces is not shown to have reached certain men, they shall be granted pardon for their ignorance, provided that from now on they begin entirely to abstain, and retain the ranks in which they are found, so that they may not be permitted to advance to higher ones. It should count as a benefit for them that they do not lose even the position they retain.

But if any are discovered to have known the manner of life transmitted by Siricius and nevertheless not to have immediately cast off the desires of lust, they must by every means be removed: after learning the admonition, they judged pleasure preferable.

## On final penance

### XXII

It was also asked what ought to be observed concerning those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves throughout their lives to the pleasures of incontinence and, at the very end of life, request both penance and restoration to communion.

With regard to such persons, the earlier practice was harsher, while the later practice, through the intervention of mercy, is more lenient. For the earlier custom persisted that penance should be granted to them but communion denied. Since persecutions were frequent in those times, it was feared that the easy granting of communion might prevent people from being recalled from their fall by making them secure in reconciliation. Communion was therefore rightly denied while penance was granted. Thus nothing was wholly refused, but the circumstances of the time made the remission more severe.

After our Lord restored peace to his Churches, however, once terror had been removed, it was decided that communion should be given to those departing this life, out of regard for the Lord’s mercy, as viaticum for those about to set out, lest we seem to follow the harshness and severity of the Novatian heretics, who deny forgiveness. Communion, therefore, is to be granted together with final penance, so that such persons, even at their last hour, may, with the permission of our Savior, be rescued from everlasting destruction.

## On public administration

[Col. 0247B]

### XXIII

A question was also raised concerning those who, after baptism, have held public office and have either exercised only punishments or also pronounced a capital sentence. Concerning these matters, we read that nothing was defined by our predecessors (Romans XIII). For they remembered that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that the minister of God had been appointed as an avenger in such matters. How, then, could they have condemned an act which they saw had been permitted by God as its author?

Therefore, concerning such persons, we maintain the practice preserved until now, lest we seem either to overthrow discipline or to act contrary to the Lord’s authority. In the rendering of their account, however, all their deeds will be retained.

## Why men do not remain with adulterous wives

[Col. 0247C]

### XXIV

It was also desired to know why husbands who remain in communion do not associate with adulterous wives, whereas wives seem to remain in the company of adulterous husbands.

In this matter the Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and their hidden sins do not incur punishment; husbands, on the other hand, more freely bring adulterous wives before the priests. Therefore communion is denied to women once their crime has been exposed, whereas, when the offense of men remains hidden, no one is readily excluded on the basis of suspicions; nevertheless, he too will be removed if his scandalous conduct is exposed.
