Since the case is therefore equal, sometimes, when proof is lacking, the application of punishment is suspended.

## That those who dictate petitions or criminal charges are to be regarded as exempt

[Col. 0247D]

### XXV

You also wished to inquire whether those who dictate petitions are to be granted freedom, after the regeneration of baptism, to ask princes for someone’s death or for blood as a penalty for guilt. Princes never grant such a request without investigation; rather, they always refer the matters or crimes committed to judges, so that punishment may follow after the case has been examined. Once the matter has been assigned to the investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the case. While the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the one who dictated the petition will remain exempt.

## That those who, after a divorce, have contracted another marriage are shown to be adulterers

### XXVI

Your affection also inquired about those who, after a divorce has intervened, have joined themselves to another marriage. It is clear that such persons are adulterers on both sides.

Those who, while their wife is still alive, even though the marriage may appear to have been dissolved, hasten to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers. Indeed, even the persons joined to them appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery; likewise, whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery” (Matthew XIX). Therefore all such persons are to be excluded from the communion of the faithful.

Concerning their parents or relatives, nothing of this kind can be decreed unless they are discovered to have encouraged the illicit union.

## Which books are to be received into the canon

[Col. 0248B]

### XXVII

A brief list shows which books are to be received into the canon of Scripture. These are the books about which you wished to be instructed orally:

The five books of Moses—that is, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy—as well as one book of Joshua son of Nun, one of Judges, and four books of Kingdoms, together with Ruth.

Sixteen books of the Prophets; five books of Solomon; and the Psalter.

Among the historical books: one book of Job, one of Tobit, one of Esther, one of Judith, two of Maccabees, two of Ezra, and two of Chronicles.

Likewise, in the New Testament: four books of the Gospels; fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul; three Epistles of John; two Epistles of Peter; the Epistle of Jude; the Epistle of James; the Acts of the Apostles; and the Apocalypse of John.

But the other writings, whether under the name of Matthias, or of James the Less, or of Peter and John—written by a certain Leucius—or under the name of Andrew—written by the philosophers Nexocharides and Leonides—or under the name of Thomas, and any others of this kind, you should know are not only to be rejected but also condemned.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of March; in the consulship of Stilicho for the second time and Anthemius. (Year of Christ 405.)

Innocent to Felix, bishop of Nocera, greeting.

We cannot be surprised that your affection follows the practice of our predecessors by referring to us, as to the head and summit of the episcopate, every matter that can admit any doubt, so that the apostolic see, having been consulted, may pronounce from the doubtful circumstances themselves what must be done. We gladly accept this, and commend your affection for remembering the canons.

You have written that, through the fervor of faith with which you are endowed and your love for the holy people, you have either restored the Churches of God or built new ones. But you do not have clerics to appoint in these Churches; some are mutilated and some have been married twice. We were astonished that a prudent man wished to consult us about matters which are known with complete certainty to all. Thus we do not speak to you as though you were ignorant, but we say that perhaps, being occupied with other matters, you have forgotten this.

## If anyone voluntarily amputates part of his body, he cannot be a cleric; if involuntarily, he can

### XXVIII

If anyone voluntarily cuts off part of any finger from himself, the canons do not admit him to the clergy. But if this happens to someone by accident, while he is attending to agricultural work or, while doing something else, strikes himself unintentionally, the canons command that such men both be made clerics and, if they are found already in the clergy, not be expelled.

In the former, the will is judged: he dared to apply iron to himself, something which others, clearly, would not hesitate to do. In the latter, accident has merited pardon.

## That men married twice cannot be admitted to the clergy

### XXIX

There should have been no need to consult about men married twice, since the apostle’s clear teaching says that the husband of one wife is to be admitted to the priesthood or the clergy (I Timothy III).

This applies only if he took her as a virgin. For if she had previously had a husband, even if he has died, and was afterward joined to a cleric, the cleric who took her cannot himself be a cleric, because the law has decreed that a priest may not have as his wife “a widow or a rejected woman.”

## Which laymen ought not to be promoted to the clergy

[Col. 0249B]

### XXX

Your religious authority also consulted us concerning laymen whom the canons prohibit from being ordained. It is certain that ecclesiastical rules contain this provision, but it has not been defined in such a way that it applies to every layman.

For men cannot be born clerics rather than made clerics; rather, categories have been designated of those who cannot attain the clergy. These include anyone among the faithful who has served in the army; anyone among the faithful who has prosecuted cases—that is, acted as an accuser; and anyone among the faithful who has held public office.

Concerning members of the municipal councils, the reason is clear: although men of this sort may be found who ought to become clerics, they are nevertheless frequently reclaimed for municipal service. They must therefore be avoided because of the troubles that often arise for the Church from such men.

## Which laymen may become clerics; concubinage is expressly prohibited here

[Col. 0249C]

### XXXI

Laymen who were baptized while having wives, and who afterward conducted themselves in such a way that their reputation never wavered—so that either they were attached to clerics or, from the time of their baptism, remained connected with monasteries—are not prohibited from being admitted to the clerical order, provided that they have known neither a concubine nor a paramour and have kept watch in every good work.

## The length of time to be spent in the clergy

### XXXII

This must be done in such a way that the periods of service established by our predecessors are observed: no one should quickly become a lector, quickly an acolyte, quickly a deacon, or quickly a priest.

For if they remain for a long time in the lesser offices, and both their life and their service are approved, they may afterward rise to the priesthood with the merits of their service, and may not seize what an approved life deserves to receive.

Since it has therefore been shown by a definite rule who ought to be admitted and who rejected, from among all those whom your Dignity sees cannot be rejected, you must choose those whom you will make clerics. For if we wish to show no favor or benefit to anyone, we can find men whose appointment will bring us neither guilt nor shame.

Innocent to Maximus and Severus, bishops in Bruttium.

The rule of the ecclesiastical canons ought to be unknown to no priest, because it is sufficiently disgraceful for a bishop not to know these things—especially when religious laymen both know them and consider them necessary to observe. The attached text of the petition shows what sort of complaint Maximilian, our son, an agent in public affairs, recently brought forward.

## That those who have begotten children while in the presbyterate ought to be removed from office

### XXXIII

Moved by zeal for the faith and discipline, he does not tolerate the Church’s being polluted by unworthy presbyters whom he asserts to have begotten children while in the presbyterate. I would explain that this is not permitted, unless I knew that your Prudence possessed knowledge of the whole law.

Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the contents of the attached petition, you will order those who are said to have committed such acts to be brought forward publicly. After the accusations made against those presbyters have been investigated, if they can be convicted, they are to be removed from the priestly office. For those who are not holy cannot handle holy things, and they must be made strangers to the ministry which they polluted by living unlawfully.

We are astonished that bishops conceal such matters, so that they may be judged either to tolerate or to be unaware that such conduct is unlawful.

## That no one can be admitted to the clergy after penance

### XXXIV  
**Innocent to Agapitus, Macedonius, and Marianus, bishops in Apulia.**

Many reports from different persons and highly trustworthy representations have disclosed that, in your province, numerous practices contrary to the ecclesiastical canons and the decrees of our predecessors are being usurped. These could easily be cut away if bishops were not found to be responsible for them.

While trying to show favor either to friends or to those who serve them, they violate religion and corrupt the orders. Thus it happens that certain unworthy men receive ecclesiastical honors [Col. 0250C] and are admitted to the clergy who would not deserve to hold an honorable place even among the laity.

As has now been demonstrated to us by a petition, a certain Modestus, entangled in many crimes—and said on account of them to have performed penance—not only has been made a cleric, which is not permitted, but is also seeking the summit of the episcopate, although the canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest clerical offices.

Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the contents of the petition, you will order him to be presented. If it is truly established that he is as the petition asserts, he must be removed not only from his ambition for the episcopate but also from the clerical office.

## Concerning Bubalius and Taurianus, condemned by the provincial bishops, whose sentence the apostolic see undertook to reconsider

[Col. 0250D]

### XXXV  
**Innocent to Rufus, Gerontius, Sophronius, Flavianus, Macedonius, Prosdotius, and Aristeas, bishops established in Macedonia.**

The delay of our co-bishops Maximianus and Eumenes—or rather the pressures of the times—caused you to repeat your complaint about Bubalius and Taurianus and caused us once again to rise against those utterly depraved men. But, since I can imitate the brevity of so many evils in fewer words, I shall briefly review what I have observed in the volume of your letter.

It could not seem burdensome to your most devout minds that any judgment should be reconsidered, because truth, when repeatedly tested, shines more brightly in the light, and destruction, recalled for judgment, is condemned more gravely and without reprieve. For it is a divine fruit, dearest brothers, to examine justice repeatedly.

But I see what has disturbed your minds: Bubalius, often detected in many deceits, produced what he claimed were copies of letters forged as though they had come from us. Since nothing he produced could now seem trustworthy, given the man’s usual conduct, let every complaint about such a matter now be silenced, and let the very breathings of the convicted devil be suppressed.

We have appended to this the earlier letters which I sent through the bishops mentioned above. In them the full judgment of our mind has been set out so clearly that, when you reread them, you will not afterward repeat anything ambiguous or in need of further inquiry in this case.

Send this little letter of ours to the bishops who believe more carefully, so that they may reread it and know most fully what is to be observed concerning Bubalius and Taurianus and the others in the provinces. Those who deserve admonition should learn to beware of such men, lest they encounter similar things.

## That boundaries are not to be transferred

### XXXVI  
**Innocent to Florentius, bishop of Tibur.**

Divine Scripture cries out not once but repeatedly (Deuteronomy XIX and XXVII; Proverbs XXII) that the boundaries established by our fathers ought not to be moved. It is wrong for one person to invade what another has always possessed. Our brother and co-bishop Ursus asserts that you have done this.

He has complained with sorrow that you invaded the Nomentan or Felician parish, which had belonged by ancestral right to his diocese, and celebrated the divine mysteries there without consulting him or his knowledge.

If this is true, you must know that you have incurred no light offense. Therefore, if you wish to avoid the ill repute of so great a usurpation, it is fitting that, admonished by our letter, you abstain. Certainly, if you believe that justice supports your position, with everything intact and remaining in its former condition, you must appear after the days of venerable Easter, so that you may answer the claims mentioned above and, with the parties brought before us, we may investigate what antiquity or truth establishes.

## If someone’s wife has been carried into captivity and the husband has taken another, when the first returns the second woman must be excluded

### XXXVII  
**Innocent to Probus.**

The upheaval caused by the storm of the barbarians brought calamity upon the operation of the laws. A well-established marriage between Fortunius and Ursa would have suffered a blemish through the incursion of captivity, unless the holy statutes of religion had provided for the matter.

For while the woman Ursa was being held in the captivity mentioned above, the said Fortunius is known to have entered another marriage with Restituta. But, by the favor of the Lord, Ursa returned, approached us, and proved without anyone denying it that she was the wife of the man mentioned.

Therefore, lord and deservedly illustrious son, with the Catholic faith supporting us, we have decreed that the marriage first founded and joined by divine grace was the true marriage. The union with the second woman, while the first survived and had not been cast out by divorce, could in no way be legitimate.

## A letter of greeting, full of charity, to Aurelius of Carthage and Augustine of Hippo, bishops

### XXXVIII  
**Innocent to the bishops Aurelius and Augustine.**

The return of Germanus, my most welcome fellow presbyter, ought not to have gone without a response from our office. For it seems natural and fitting to us that beloved men should greet those dearest to us.

We therefore wish your brotherhood, whom we love most dearly, to rejoice in the Lord, and we ask you to offer to God prayers equal to ours on our behalf. For, as you know well, through common and reciprocal prayers we accomplish more than through prayers that are individual or private.

## An exhortatory letter written by the same pope to Juliana, a noblewoman

### XXXIX

It is sufficiently evident to all that you are a singular member of the Church and that the greatness of your religious devotion is held by us in the highest reverence. At the very summit of nobility, you offer the Church a devotion far nobler; you obey its commandments with the joyful recognition of Christ; and you exult more in faith than you boast in the splendor of so great a lineage.

It is the mark of the highest virtue to overcome the glory of the flesh, and of great grace in Christ to surpass nobility by one’s conduct, lady and deservedly illustrious daughter.

Therefore, dearest daughter, being certain of this, strive to illuminate whatever spans of this life there may be with eternal and divine duties, so that he who has made you distinguished may render you more glorious to himself throughout the ages.

## To Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, concerning Easter

### XL  
**Innocent to Aurelius.**

The duty of our charity is severed by no interval, even if no written page carries any letters. For spiritual grace lives reciprocally in our hearts, and the priestly fellowship itself nourishes our love.

Since it is unworthy that the unity of the Church should not be preserved, and since we all equally think and declare the same thing, dearest brother, I have written this letter concerning the calculation of Easter for another year, that is, the coming year.

Since on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April the moon will be almost sixteen days old—for it is a little short of that—and on the fourth day before those same Kalends it will reach its twenty-third day, I have judged that the Easter festival should be celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends mentioned, since we know that no Easter has ever previously been celebrated before the twenty-third day of the moon.

I have set out and declared the substance of my opinion. It will now be your responsibility, my brother and partner, to reconsider this very matter in a most devout synod with your unanimous fellow bishops and fellow priests. If nothing results against our arrangement, write back to us fully and openly, so that we may prescribe in advance, as is customary, the Easter day that has been determined, to be observed in writing at the proper time.

As for the fellow presbyter Archidamus, although I know that you will receive him most willingly and according to your usual custom, I nevertheless ask, in addition, that you deign to have him among your own.

## Concerning the Church of Antioch

### XLI  
**Innocent to Boniface, presbyter.**

The Church of Antioch, which the blessed apostle Peter illumined by his presence before he came to the city of Rome, like a sister of the Roman Church, did not permit itself for long to remain separated from it. For it sent envoys and requested and obtained peace in such a way that it received the Evagrians into their orders and places, without disturbing the ordination they had received from the man mentioned, and gathered together the clergy and laity of John of holy memory.

The bishop of that city, my brother Alexander, promised that, even if someone should come to them from us or from elsewhere with a later ordination, he would receive him without dispute and recite the name of the bishop mentioned among the bishops who were at rest.

Let him know that, in this matter, we have given our hands, dearest brother, and have received them into our very heart, so that the members who had sought healing would not long be regarded as alien from the unity of the body.

My son, the deacon Paul, the bearer of this letter, will be able to recount to your affection everything that was done in due order, so that you may share our common joy and inform those who are accustomed to intervene on behalf of Atticus.

## To Alexander, bishop of Antioch, concerning peace

[Col. 0253B]

### XLII  
**Innocent to Bishop Alexander.**

How welcome, how devout, and how necessary was the embassy sent to us by your Holiness, dearest brother, you will learn from a repetition of the events themselves.

For our fellow presbyter Cassianus wished this little record of our friendship to be composed by our fellow presbyter Paul, the deacon Nicolaus, and the subdeacon Peter, our sons, as the first fruits of our peace.

I therefore greet both your brotherhood in Christ, which is most dear to me, and the whole Church which shares your good judgment. I ask you to address us, as you do, more frequently by letter and to gladden us more often with news of your well-being. For, as I trust, the Lord will grant us to make up for all the losses of the past through the most loving conversation of our letters.

## Concerning Atticus, bishop of Constantinople

### XLIII  
**Innocent to Bishop Maximianus.**

We are astonished that your Prudence asks us to write to Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople, both through our own representation and by means of the petition appended below. You have brought us no letters at all from him, not even a single one, either to us or to your synod, and yet you think that this should be granted to one who has made no request.

You ought to understand that communion, once suspended, is restored to one who demonstrates, after his case has been examined, that the causes which brought about the suspension have now been removed and that he has fulfilled the conditions of peace.

But, as I have said, Atticus has neither wished to state nor to demonstrate, by sending any of his representatives either to you or to us, that these conditions have been fulfilled.

You have learned how Alexander, our brother and co-bishop of the Church of Antioch, both advanced and proved his case through a worthy embassy. You were pleased to be present at all these matters, and you learned how I examined one by one all the documents we had previously issued concerning this cause of the most blessed John, formerly our co-bishop, and how they showed with complete clarity that everything which ought to have been done at Antioch had been completed.

By embracing their peace, we gave it our assurance and showed a great path to all who would seek the same peace: provided that they themselves at some time demonstrate that they have done or completed, in their own place, what has been examined and fulfilled, and request that communion be restored to them, as these men have solemnly requested it through an embassy sent for that purpose.

We therefore await the statement of the person mentioned concerning the fulfillment of all the conditions which we have set out at various times, as well as his request for communion, so that we may rightly restore it to one who both requests it and proves himself worthy of it, dearest brother. For you received long ago a full letter concerning all these matters addressed to the holy synod of our brothers.

## Likewise to Alexander, bishop of Antioch, concerning peace

### XLIV

The grace of apostolic favor has shone upon us with the great splendor of peace, and so much light of joy has dawned upon the faithful that, while giving the greatest thanks to God, we confess that we owe him still greater thanks. We have been made more joyful by God because, after all the aspects of the actions of your brotherhood had been examined, we learned that everything had been conducted with such piety and patience that we praised the Lord in every respect.

We see that this success was granted to your labors because, being a lover of peace with all your strength, you sought the peace that was sought, found it, and preserved it with the greatest charity—toward everyone, but especially toward those who had once been counted under the name of the bishops Paulinus and Evagrius.

I regard the fulfillment of my wishes as complete, since the cleansing of the ancient stain has been prolonged through your time and your merits. I have also judged that those of the same name who had received the rank of clerics in Italy should retain, for the sake of peace, the favor they had obtained.

And because our fellow presbyter Cassianus said that it would be pleasing to your Dignity if, by my advice, they were considered worthy to hold the clerical order in your city, I have decided, out of regard for your benevolence and in view of the promise of the man mentioned, that they should be numbered among the other priests and ministers who are in the city, dearest brother.

Moreover, I was glad to learn concerning the bishops Elpidius and Pappus that they had recovered their Churches without dispute. I carefully investigated the acts, as the attached documents show, to determine whether all the conditions had been satisfied in the case of the blessed and truly God-worthy priest John.

When, in each detail, the envoys’ assertion declared that everything had been completed as desired, I gave thanks to the Lord and received your Church into communion in such a way that I publicly acknowledge that the fellow disciples of the apostolic see were the first to show the others the way of peace. In this peace, once you and we have been established, the kindness of the Lord Christ will embrace us in such a way that communion will not afterward be shaken by any irritation or touched by the slightest shame of anyone’s dispute.

We have also received the writings of Bishop Acacius, since they were submitted together with yours, so that he, who had formerly been suspended by us, would not be rejected through an injury to you. Nevertheless, we have laid down fully in the acts—as you will kindly undertake to reread—what must be observed concerning his person: if he should ask to be joined in every respect to your holy counsels and actions, communion is to be granted to the old man through your favor and our judgment, together with the favor of the letter extended to him by us.

Twenty bishops of Italy subscribed.

## Likewise to Alexander, bishop of Antioch: that it is remembered that the first see of the blessed Peter was at Antioch

### XLV

Both the burden and the honor imposed upon us by your brotherhood have introduced the reasons for an important discussion, so that we may respond to your letter or memorandum, as the grace of the Holy Spirit grants.

Accordingly, we have reviewed the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which expresses the one mind of all the priests throughout the world. What it decreed concerning the Church of Antioch, all the faithful—not to say all priests—must preserve. We recognize that the aforementioned Church was established over its diocese, not over some province.

From this we understand that this distinction was attributed to it not so much because of the magnificence of the city as because it is shown to be the first see of the first apostle. There the Christian religion received its name; there the most renowned gathering of the apostles deserved to take place; and it would not yield to the see of the city of Rome, except that Rome received what Antioch merited in passing, while Antioch rejoices that what it received was completed in its midst.

Therefore, dearest brother, we think that, just as you appoint metropolitans by your singular authority, so you should not allow the other bishops to be created without your permission and knowledge.

You will properly observe this arrangement: those who live far away you should decree are to be ordained, on letters issued by you, by those who now ordain them solely at their own discretion; but those who are nearby, if you think fit, you should arrange to come for the laying on of hands by your grace. For those whose greatest care is entrusted to you ought especially to merit your judgment.

## That, according to imperial arrangements, there ought not to be two metropolitan bishops

### XLVI

You ask whether, when provinces are divided by imperial judgment so that two metropolitan cities come into being, two metropolitan bishops ought likewise to be named.

It has not seemed right, then, for the Church of God to be altered according to the shifting needs of worldly affairs, or to undergo honors or divisions which the emperor may decide should be made for his own purposes. Therefore metropolitan bishops ought to be counted according to the former custom of the provinces.

You also assert that the Cypriots, once harassed by the power of Arian impiety, did not preserve the Nicene canons in the ordination of their bishops and still presume to ordain according to their own discretion, consulting no one. We therefore persuade them to take care to hold Catholic judgment according to the faith of the canons and to agree with the other provinces, so that it may be evident that they too, like all the Churches, are governed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## That Arian clerics are not to be received in their offices, although the Church confirms their baptism, which is acknowledged to be Catholic

### XLVII

Moreover, concerning the Arians and the other plagues of the same kind: since we receive their laypeople who have converted to the Lord under the appearance of penance and through the laying on of hands for the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, it does not seem right to receive their clerics with the dignity of the priesthood or of any ministry.

For we allow only their baptism to be valid, since it is performed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. We do not think that they possess the Holy Spirit through that baptism or through those mysteries. When the founders of their sect departed from the Catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit which they had received, and they cannot give the fullness of that Spirit. That fullness operates especially in ordinations, and they lost it through the perfidy of their impiety rather than, I should say, through faith.

How could we consider the profane priests of such men worthy of the honors of Christ, when we receive their laypeople as imperfect—as I have said—to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit under the appearance of penance?

Your Gravity should therefore bring this to the knowledge of your co-bishops, either through a synod, if possible, or through the reading of these letters, so that what you yourself have inquired about so necessarily, and what we have answered with due precision, may be preserved by the common consent and zeal of all.

## Concerning John, bishop of Constantinople

### XLVIII  
**Innocent to Acacius, bishop of Beroea.**
[Col. 0256B] We have reviewed with joy your Fraternity’s letters concerning the reception of the clerics and peoples of the bishops Paulinus and Evagrius, and concerning the restoration of our fellow bishops Elpidius and Pappus; and we have clearly perceived that, even if late, you have chosen to cherish the grace of restored peace, setting aside every contention. Therefore we have sent these letters to your unanimity, to be delivered to our most distinguished brother and fellow bishop Alexander—namely, so that, if every hostility and every rivalry concerning both the name of the holy and admirable bishop John and all the participants in the same communion has departed from your animosity, you may receive these letters of our fellowship, dearest brother, provided that you personally acknowledge before our beloved mediator Alexander, as is fitting for one who shares our communion, everything that has been confirmed here by the proceedings. For just as the cause of unanimity and charity is venerable to us, so our concern clings to it, lest anything distorted or superfluous be known to remain in anyone.

## Concerning the Bonosians, and that they are to be compared with the Jews

### XLIX. Innocent to Laurentius, bishop of Siena

We were long amazed, after reading the letters of your Dilection, that in your territory there are not only heretics who follow the poisons of Photinus, but that they also publicly prepare meeting places for themselves on the estates of certain people, although almost nowhere in the whole world have so many of them chosen to live as among you. Marcus, the author of their wicked teaching, long ago expelled from the city, has been driven by such great audacity that he claims the first place among them. But so that they may no longer have the opportunity to revel, and may not drag simple and rustic people with them into the Gehenna to which they have been destined, action has been taken against them by defenders of our Church so that they may expel them. For they deny that Christ God was begotten before the ages from the substance of the Father; therefore they are to share the condemnation of the Jews, who denied the deity and continue to deny it to this day.

It is your duty, dearest brother, to carry out without slackness what has been commanded, lest through dissimulation you lose the people entrusted to you and begin to render an account to God for those who have been lost.

## The same pope concerning the reception of clerics whom Bonosus is known to have ordained before his condemnation

### L. Innocent to Martianus, bishop of Naissus

[Col. 0257A] In an earlier period, if I remember correctly, I recall sending letters of this kind both to your Dilection and to our brothers and fellow bishops Rufus, Eusebius, and the others, concerning the clerics of Naissus—namely, those who claimed that, before Bonosus’s condemnation, they had been ordained by him as both priests and deacons. I wrote that, if they wished to abandon and condemn his error and be joined to the Church, they should gladly be received, lest those who might be worthy of recovering salvation perish in the same error.

But now, while I was staying in the city of Ravenna on account of the frequent needs of the Roman people, Germanio, who claims to be a priest, and Lupentius, who says that he is a deacon, came to me, as though undertaking an embassy on behalf of many such men. With earnest supplication they sought to express their own distress, asserting that they still retained the churches situated in the parishes of your Dilection, but that they had not been able to obtain your communion. They alleged that this was because a certain man named Rustitius had received the presbyterate through a repeated ordination.

This creates a serious impediment: either they grieve that such a man is retained in the Church, or he thinks that he ought to sin in the case of others who recognizes that there is sin in his own case. Although my letters on this matter contain a fuller statement, the ones I mentioned above, we have nevertheless now thought it necessary again to admonish your Fraternity: if it is truly established that certain men ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation afterwards wished, or now wish, to return, we judge that they should be received. The men mentioned above particularly assert that they were ordained so long ago that Cornelius, a man of holy memory and bishop of Sirmium, as well as our brother Nicetas and several others, were present when they were advanced to the honors which they say they possess. Therefore, dearest brother, if their assertion receives the credibility of truth, you must not hesitate to receive those whom you have allowed for so long to retain the churches entrusted to them.

## Innocent sends greetings in the Lord to Rufus, Eusebius, and the other bishops and deacons in Macedonia

I was filled with great joy when, after so many dangers of the whole world, so to speak, Vitalis the archdeacon, carrying your letters, arrived from those regions all the way to us. As soon as we saw him, we asked him, as was proper, about your situation. When we learned that you were living according to your desire, we gave abundant thanks to our Lord God, who deigns both to protect you, his servants serving at his altars, in adversity and to govern you in prosperity.

When he had delivered the letters, I immediately ordered them to be read. I saw that many things had been set down in them that would produce astonishment in our minds and cause us considerable doubt as to whether we had understood matters differently or whether they had been written as they sounded. Having had them read repeatedly, I noticed that some injury was being done to the apostolic see, to which your report had been sent as to the head of the Churches, since its judgment was still being brought into question. Therefore, concerning matters about which I remember having written long ago, your repeated inquiry now compels me to restate the position of your report with clearer arguments.

## If a priest or any member of the clergy marries a widow or a divorced woman, he is to lose his office

[Col. 0258A]

### LI. I have learned that those who are said to have taken widows as wives were not merely made clerics but even attained the insignia of the highest priesthood. No one is unaware that this is contrary to the commands of the Law. For when Moses the lawgiver loudly declares, “Let the priest take a virgin as his wife,” and so that this command might not be thought ambiguous he adds, “Not a widow, nor one who has been cast out.” Against this command, supported by divine authority, no defense based on another ordinance may be advanced—unless it be your custom, which, as you yourselves admit, was established through ignorance, or, to put it more modestly, not through apostolic tradition and sound reason.

Your Dilection should know that we, and all the Churches throughout the East and West, entirely reject this practice. We do not admit such men even to the lowest place in the ecclesiastical order; and if they are found, we remove them.

## If a catechumen has had a wife and, after her death, has taken another after baptism, he cannot be a cleric

### LII. Next it is argued that a man who had a wife while a catechumen and lost her should not be called a bigamist if, after baptism, he took another; the latter, they say, should be regarded as his first wife, because that former marriage was removed, along with the other sins, through the sacrament of baptism. If this is said of one wife, then certainly, if he had three wives while he was in the old man, the fourth, taken after baptism, will—according to this interpretation—be regarded as his first, and will likewise receive the designation “virgin,” although she was taken as his fourth wife.

Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, which says that a bishop must be “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3)? But it is objected that in baptism everything done in the old man has been dissolved.

Tell me—I speak with your indulgence—are only sins forgiven in baptism, or also those things that are fulfilled according to the Lord’s commands and God’s institutions? Is taking a wife a sin, or is it not a sin? If it is a sin, then, with the preceding pardon, I should say that the author is at fault who, in order that sins might be committed in paradise, blessed them when he himself joined them together (Genesis 2). But if it is not a sin, since what God has joined it would be impious to call a sin, and Solomon added, “For a wife is prepared for a man by God” (Proverbs 19), how can we believe that what is read as having been completed by God’s authority was forgiven among sins?

What is judged concerning the children of such unions? Surely those who were born from a woman who was a wife before baptism are not to be excluded from sharing in the inheritance; yet will they be called either natural children or bastards because there is no legitimate marriage except, as you think, the one entered into after baptism? When the Lord was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife, and explained that this ought not to be done, he added: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19). And lest anyone think that he was speaking only of unions contracted after baptism, let them remember that this question was asked by Jews and answered for Jews.

I ask, and I ask anxiously: if the wife of a man who was first a catechumen and afterwards became a believer is one and the same, and if he had children by her while he was a catechumen and later had others while he was a believer, are they to be called brothers or not? After their father’s death, are they to share in the division of the inheritance, although spiritual rebirth is believed to have taken away from some of them the name of children?

Since it is absurd to think and judge in this way, what reason—indeed, what evil reason—is there for defending this position and proclaiming it on the strength of an empty opinion rather than supporting it by some authority, when what the Law commands and God joins cannot be counted among sins?

Suppose a catechumen devoted himself to virtue, pursued humility, maintained patience, gave alms, rescued people condemned to death by whatever means, detested adultery, and preserved chastity. I ask whether, when he became a believer, he lost these things because through baptism everything done by the old man is thought to be taken away.

Let us look at the Gentile Cornelius, occupied with prayers and almsgiving, who saw an angel through a revelation and Peter himself. Were these things taken away from him through baptism—the very things on account of which baptism appears to have been granted to him? If this is believed, trust me, there is considerable error. For whatever has been done well and preserved according to the commands of the Law cannot perish for those who have done it.

Therefore the marital union, because it is completed by God’s command, cannot be called a sin; and what is not a sin must absolutely not be believed to be dissolved among sins. It will consequently remain proper to judge that the designation “former wife” cannot be erased, since it was not forgiven as sin, because it was completed according to God’s will.

## Clerics ordained by heretics are not to be admitted

[Col. 0259C]

### LIII. We have come to the third question, which because of its difficulty requires a longer discussion. We say that those ordained by heretics have their head wounded by that laying on of hands. Where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied so that health may be restored. But the health that follows a wound cannot be without a scar; and where the remedy of penance is necessary, there the honor of ordination cannot have a place.

For if, as we read, “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Leviticus 11; Numbers 19), how can that be granted to him which purity and cleanliness customarily receive? Yet we agree with the assertion that one who has lost an honor cannot give honor, and that the other received nothing because there was nothing in the giver that he could receive. This is certainly true: he could not give what he did not possess.

He gave the condemnation that he had through a perverse laying on of hands; and I cannot discover how one who has become a partner of the condemned should receive honor. But it is said that the true and just blessing of a legitimate priest removes every defect that had been introduced by a defective one.

## Crimes and defects are not rightly believed to be removed through ordinations

### LIV. If this is so, then let sacrilegious persons, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be brought to ordination, since through the blessing of ordination crimes and defects are thought to be removed. Let there be no place for penance, since ordination can provide what prolonged satisfaction customarily provides.

But this is the law of our Church: to those coming from heretics who have nevertheless been baptized there, we grant only lay communion through the laying on of hands, and we do not appoint any of them, even to the slightest degree, to the honor of the clergy.

## Those ordained by the heretic Bonosus were received so that scandal might not remain in the Church

### LV. Yet those who passed from the Catholic Church to heresy—whom it is proper to receive only through penance—not only do not perform penance among you, but are even heaped with honor.

But this was the considered decision of our former brother Anysius and the other fellow priests: that those whom Bonosus had ordained should be received, lest they remain with him and no small scandal arise. Thus, I think, we overcame the ambiguous cases.

It is therefore established that what was decided as a remedy and necessity of the time did not exist at first, and that there were ancient rules, handed down by the apostles or apostolic men, which the Roman Church observes and commands those accustomed to listen to her to observe. But the necessity of the time urgently demanded that this be done.

Therefore, what necessity devised as a remedy must also cease when the necessity has ceased, because lawful order is one thing, and an usurpation compelled by the exigency of the present time another.

But since the canons established at Nicaea permitted this to be done in the case of the Novatians, the earlier canon instituted by the Fathers must first be set forth, so that we may understand what was meant or commanded by them and in what manner. “Concerning those,” it says, “who call themselves Cathari, that is, Pure Ones, and who at some time come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy.”

Can we say that this command concerns only the Novatians and does not apply to clerics of other heresies? For if they had defined it concerning all, they would have added that those returning from the Novatians and other heretics should be restored to their own order. If that were so, then especially what was said concerning the Paulianists could confirm it, since those coming from them are also commanded to be baptized.

When they command this concerning the Paulianists, are all who return from heretics to be baptized according to this example? Since no one dares to do this, reason itself demonstrates that the command concerns only those people.

Finally, those who were rightly baptized by Philip the evangelist are perfected by Peter and John through the laying on of hands alone (Acts 8). But those whom the Apostle Paul found baptized with John’s baptism (Acts 19), and whom he asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit, when they admitted that they had not even heard the name, he ordered to be baptized.

You see, therefore, that those who have been rightly baptized cannot have that gift repeated for them, while it is found necessary that those washed only with water be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Thus it is read with clear evidence that the command was given only concerning the Novatians. The clear reason why this was distinguished between the two heresies is that the Paulianists do not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The Novatians, however, baptize with these same awe-inspiring and venerable names; and among them no question has ever been raised concerning the unity of the divine power—that is, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, among all those separated from the Church, this one group alone was selected as the group to which this concession might be granted, because they committed no offense against the sacrament of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

But if someone who passed from the Catholic Church to heresy, or who returned from faith to apostasy, should repent and wish to return, could he be permitted to the clergy by the same reasoning? Their offense can be erased only through prolonged penance, and even after penance the canons do not permit them to become clerics by their own authority.

It is therefore clear that those who passed from the Catholic Church to the condemned Bonosus, and who allowed or desired themselves to be ordained by him, ought not to have received the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination. They abandoned the common judgment of all the Churches and decided that the peculiar vanity of Bonosus alone should be followed.

Yet it is clear that many suffered force and were ordained by him unwillingly and against their resistance. Let anyone who believes this answer me: if he was not present after Bonosus’s ordination, if he did not participate in his communion, if he immediately returned to the Church after leaving his most wicked assembly, then such a man may have some form of excuse.

As for the others, who returned to the Church either after a year or after a month, it is understood that those who knew they could not be admitted to ordination in the Catholic Church because of their own vices went to the man who performed illicit ordinations indiscriminately and without any examination, believing that through this institution they could find a place in the Catholic Church from which they had previously despaired.

Now I ask about what remains: the man who returned after a month or more, confident that he had been ordained a priest by Bonosus—if he did not perform the sacraments, if he did not distribute them to the people, if he did not complete the Masses according to custom—what is your judgment concerning such men? Please state it more openly.

In summary, those who received nothing from Bonosus are guilty of usurping a dignity: whether they claimed for themselves the authority to perform the sacraments or did not claim it, they thought themselves to be what had not been granted to them by any regular procedure.

## The sin of the people in the Church is ordinarily allowed to pass unpunished

[Col. 0261D]

### LVI. Let your Dilection therefore understand that such matters have continued up to this point, and observe that, as you say, necessity dictated that one must not presume to disturb Churches already established in peace. But, as often happens, whenever a people or crowd commits a sin, because punishment cannot be imposed on everyone on account of their multitude, the matter ordinarily passes unpunished. I say, therefore, that the earlier matters should be left to God’s judgment; in future, the greatest care must be taken to prevent them.

## What was taken from the apostolic see, and how it changed its judgment for the better when it rescinded Photinus’s condemnation

I now come to the great matter of Photinus, as it were a principal theme, and I shall review the judgments of my predecessors concerning something that is anxious and most difficult for me.

Something more serious had been decided concerning him in some fashion, as you yourselves also remember. But since you assert and demonstrate that this was extracted from this see through a false rumor and obtained by deception, because the matter has returned to the path of salvation, after his condemnation we now grant you this pardon in the apostolic manner, especially because you have pressed us so strongly. We judge that it would be harsher than any hardship not to consent to such assertions of yours and to men so good and so dear.

Therefore, dearest brothers, according to your judgment, sentence, and request, consider it permissible to establish the matter concerning Bishop Photinus as you ask, and receive our judgment, changed for the better, as the fulfillment of your desire through your labor or testimony.

Likewise, do not expect Eustathius, whom I have very often approved, to be stripped of the grace of the diaconate. I gladly hear that you are concerned for his salvation, but I do not willingly accept anything directed against his head. To him to whom you extend your hand, I extend mine together with you; to him to whom I extend mine, extend yours together with me.

For this apostolic kindness was declared to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 1), so that good people may always follow without distinction a judgment led and led back in one spirit.

I confess that this first commends Eustathius the deacon to me: he has never said anything against the faith, has not admitted anyone who spoke against it, and I have never learned that any capital charge was either alleged or fabricated against him. Whoever is safe in these respects, even if he does not possess attractive ways of life in every regard, should be regarded as less beloved for the time being, not as an enemy handed over eternally to the devil.

I know that amid those rivalries and storms, against the efforts of many—I will not say of what kind—he held a different opinion. Although the circumstances and misfortunes on this side have been corrected, the correction concerning the subdeacons Dizonianus and Cyriacus has still not been able to revive among you.

I ask you to restrain from him and from those men the minds of all whom you see to be moved by unjust rivalries, so that he may be found unimpaired among us and, together with his companions, restored among you, deserving of peace and recognizing a charity that is not feigned.

Therefore let charity meet all of you, individually and collectively, and, joined with you forever by bonds that Christ can in no way dissolve, let it rejoice in the Lord.

# Decrees of Pope Zosimus

## Monks or laymen should not reach the highest priesthood except through the ecclesiastical ranks

### I. Zosimus, bishop of the city of Rome, to Hesychius, bishop of Salona

Your Dilection has demanded a command of the apostolic see, in which the decrees of the Fathers agree, and you report that certain men from the company of monks—whose solitude, although greater than their numbers, is nevertheless widespread—and also certain laymen are hastening to the priesthood.

It is established that this was specifically forbidden both under our predecessors and recently by us, in letters sent to Gaul and Spain, regions in which this presumption is common. Nor is Africa exempt from this warning of ours: no one who has not been instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines in due order, and trained through the testing of time in divine service, should presume to aspire to the highest priesthood of the Church contrary to the commands of the Fathers.

Such ambition should not merely be considered ineffective in the candidate; the men who ordain him should also be deprived of the rank which they presumed, contrary to the commands of the Fathers, to confer without due order.

We are therefore surprised that the statutes of the apostolic see were not conveyed to your Dilection. We praise the purpose of your steadfastness, dearest brother. Nothing else was to be expected from the judgment of the ancient authority of the episcopate than that, standing in the battle line of faith, you should confront such ambitions in accordance with the commands of the Fathers.

Therefore, if you think that anything has been lacking in your authority—which we do not believe—we supply it. Resist such ordinations; resist the approaching pride and arrogance. The commands of the Fathers are with you; the authority of the apostolic see is with you.

If secular offices confer the highest position only after a person has entered not the vestibule of public service but has been examined through many ranks and periods of service, who is so arrogant and shameless as to desire immediately to become a commander in the heavenly army—a service that must be weighed with even greater care and tested like gold through repeated fires—when he has not first been a recruit and wishes to speak before learning?

Let him become accustomed to the Lord’s camp, beginning in the rank of lector, to the rudiments of divine service. Let it not seem beneath him to become, in due order, an exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon—not by a leap, but at the times established by the ordination of the ancestors.

Then let such a man approach the height of the presbyterate, so that his age fulfills the title and his previously completed service bears witness to the merit of his character. From there he ought rightly to hope for the position of highest pontiff.

The excessive leniency of our fellow priests causes this practice. They seek the pomp of a multitude and think that some dignity is acquired for themselves from this crowd. Hence, everywhere, a numerous popular following is found even in places where there is solitude, while they desire to extend parishes or confer sacred orders on those to whom they can provide nothing else. This ought always to be a matter of strict judgment, for whatever is great is rare.

## Whoever disregards these prohibitions will endanger his rank

[Col. 0263D]

### II. Accordingly, so that we may not detract from the merits of your Dilection, we have directed this letter especially to you, so that it may be brought to the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow bishops—not only those who are in that province, but also those who are joined to the provinces neighboring your Dilection.

Anyone who, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and the apostolic see, neglects this shall know that we will punish it with the greatest severity. Let him have no doubt that his position will not remain secure if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, this may be attempted with impunity. Whatever is repeatedly usurped despite repeated prohibition is done out of a desire to insult.

## What periods are prescribed for each rank of the clergy

### III. The following periods are to be observed for each rank.

If someone has given his name to ecclesiastical service from childhood, he is to remain continuously among the lectors until his twentieth year. If he has come to it when already older and advanced in age, yet wishes immediately after baptism to devote himself to divine service, he is to remain either among the lectors or among the exorcists for five years. Thereafter he is to serve as acolyte or subdeacon for four years, and then, if he deserves it, advance to the blessing of the diaconate. He must remain in that rank for five years, provided that he has conducted himself without fault.

After this, with the service rendered through all these ranks supporting him, and with proofs of his own faith given, he may earn the priesthood of the presbyterate. If a more exacting life directed toward good morals leads him from that rank, he ought to hope for the highest pontificate, provided that this rule is observed: neither a bigamist nor a penitent may be admitted to these ranks.

It is also right that defenders of the Church who come from the laity should be bound by the foregoing observance if they deserve to belong to the clerical order.

Issued on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of our lords Honorius Augustus for the twelfth time and Theodosius Augustus for the eighth time.

## To the priests of Ravenna

### IV. A reminder of Bishop Zosimus to the priests and deacons who are in Ravenna

From the report of our brother Archidamus the priest we have learned how you were received and what you did, as well as how those men were received who, contrary to the canons and daring with I know not what presumption, wished to go to the imperial court against us.

To them we had previously sent the letters which we have now dispatched, replying to the letters they had sent us in an insulting manner. But since they were unable to remain in their own church—that is, in our Roman Church—with our fellow priests, we have sent these letters to you to be delivered to them.

In them, by our decree, we have established that the troublemakers mentioned above were alienated from the communion of our apostolic see and had received, by our signature, the sentence that was issued against them. As for those who wished to lend their assent to this act and plan with unrestrained counsel, it is for your Charity to judge how they should be regarded.

You must charge them with this: in accordance with the commands of the canons, they attempted to incur a serious offense and, in a manner unbecoming to priests, tried to become rebels.

You, however, must remember that you should be watchful, lest any audacity of those whom the holy and apostolic Church knows to have been anathematized break forth.

As for those who joined themselves to their association, when you have returned we shall consider with better counsel what we ought to do concerning them.

And in another hand:

Issued on the fifth day before the Nones of October, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the twelfth time and Theodosius Augustus for the eighth time. (In the year of Christ 418.)

# Decrees of Pope Boniface

## Petition of Pope Boniface that the emperor establish that no bishop should ever be ordained in the city of Rome through canvassing or faction

[Col. 0263D]

### I. Boniface, bishop, to Honorius Augustus

[Col. 0264D] Concern for my Church, to which our God has assigned my priesthood while you govern human affairs, compels me not to fail in presenting its causes before the ears of the most Christian emperor, although I am still detained by bodily weakness, on account of the assemblies stirred up by all the priests, clerics, and disturbances of the Christian people.

For if matters turn out otherwise than they ought, it will not be you who do this—you who arrange everything with equitable moderation—but through our silent negligence we shall appear to have lost what could overturn the city’s tranquility and the Church’s peace.

Since, by the favor of the Lord, you preside over human affairs as a worshiper of the divine religion, it will be our fault if, under your glory—which is certainly always more ready in spirit to favor divine matters—what has been preserved through so many years and under emperors who were not constrained by any concern for our religion is not guarded by firm and stable right. That is, what is lawful should be preserved, and under the rule of your Clemency what is unlawful should by no means be feared.

[Col. 0265B] The Church itself, most Christian emperor, calls upon your devotion—indeed, through my speech but with the venerable affection that belongs to her. Christ our God, the faithful ruler and governor of your empire, keeps her betrothed to himself alone and as an undefiled virgin. Do not allow the waves of plotting storms to strike her, or her peaceful face to be disturbed by the swelling of an unfamiliar tempest, most glorious and most tranquil Emperor Augustus.

The Church herself, betrothed to one alone yet also your mother, calls upon your piety through this embassy which she has entrusted to her priests; she recalls past and present events and says:

“While you rule religiously, the people are now safe—faithful to God as well as to you, who are a Christian ruler. For amid the very mysteries and prayers that she offers for the prosperity of your empire, with holy Peter as witness, before whom and concerning whose see the matter is being conducted, she cries out with anxious words for the observance of religion. Prayer is mingled with earnest petition that, once torn away, we may not be scattered into various affairs from our accustomed worship while the tempter provokes discord.”

She would say more, most Christian prince, if her causes were not secure with you; and she would not speak if, in the suppression of idols and the correction of heretics, your faith—flourishing equally in divine worship and in imperial power—had not always prevailed.

She has a refuge in the devout spirit of your Clemency, joined to reverence for her religion. Since you do whatever benefits her, grant to my brothers and fellow priests—men of proven character, envoys from me and from all who make up this Church, pursuing the cause of sacred religion—that, in the city of your Clemency, you may provide permanently for the universal Church with the same spirit in which you assent to their request.

Issued on the Kalends of July.

## Rescript of Honorius Augustus to Boniface, Roman pope: he establishes that if two bishops are again ordained at Rome, both are to be expelled from the city

### II. Victor Honorius, illustrious victor, ever Augustus, to the holy and venerable Boniface, pope of the eternal city

We received the writings of Your Blessedness with the congratulation due to reverence. After reading them, we gave the greatest thanks to almighty God, because we learned that after a long illness your holiness had been restored to the health you desired.

Therefore, as the venerable men return, we mark our joy with the testimony of sacred letters and ask that your apostolate deign to offer, in daily prayers, its devotion and its prayer for the safety and empire of us.

Know that this has been especially pleasing to our piety: your holiness is concerned about disturbance among the Churches or the people. Our Clemency has believed that sufficient provision has been made so that this may not arise in any way.

Finally, because Your Blessedness has proclaimed it, we have wished this to reach the knowledge of all the clergy, so that if something should happen to your religious office by human chance—which we do not desire—all may know that they must abstain from ambitions.

But if two men, contending rashly and unlawfully, should be ordained, neither of them will be a priest at all. Only the man whom divine judgment and the consensus of the whole community choose from among the clergy through a new ordination will remain in the apostolic see.

Therefore, all must observe this: on the warning of our serenity, they are to preserve a tranquil mind and peaceful dispositions, and must not attempt anything through seditious conspiracies, since it is certain that the efforts of neither party will benefit it.

## Letter of Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome, to the bishops of Gaul concerning Bishop Maximus, accused of various crimes

### III. Boniface, bishop, to Patroclus, Remigius, Maximus, Hilary, Severus, Valerius, Julianus, Castorius, Leontius, Constantinus, John, Montanus, Marinus Mauricius, and the other bishops established throughout Gaul and its seven provinces.

The clerics of the city of Valentina approached us, presenting in a written petition [Col. 0266C] the charges which, with the whole province as witness, they assert that Maximus committed: although the investigation had repeatedly been delegated and tribunals established, they say that he continually evaded judgment nor, confident in his conscience, hasten to have everything examined so that, if innocent, he might be cleared. We have learned of these matters repeatedly, also from the evidence of our own records. By his contrary conduct he proved those allegations true, since, in order to refute them—though they were innumerable—the provincial investigation was delegated by my predecessors.

He is also said to have avoided the assembly and to have been entirely unwilling to attend. No one doubts that a guilty man evades judgment in this way, whereas an innocent man seeks to be acquitted. But the cunning sophistry of those who think matters must be handled by crafty schemes will never acquire the name of innocence. Anyone who thinks he can evade judgment [Col. 0266D] by delays thereby confesses everything. Yet eventually the man so described will appear in public; it will not benefit him that he has so often hidden and so often evaded judgment. Wherever he flees, his own actions and offenses pursue him, and, if the charges brought against him are true, they will pursue him as crimes.

Indeed, I ought even now to have delivered a sentence worthy of the acts of which he is accused before our tribunal, since by repeatedly avoiding the investigation and the decision of the judges he thought he could make a mockery of them. But lest anyone judge me premature, or say that nothing had been reserved for him who is absent, although we had summoned him, we preferred to postpone the matter by allowing an interval of time, especially since his accusers themselves made this request.

The more slowly Maximus presents himself before the tribunal that has been constituted, the more securely, they assert, he is committing acts deserving condemnation [Col. 0267A]. They accuse him of being enveloped in the darkness of the Manichaeans, a disgraceful sect to which he formerly belonged—so that, they say, his mind cannot be cleansed from the imputed charge by a sordid repudiation of it. They produce the records of the synod and declare that he is everywhere entangled in crimes. They assert that he showed no regard for soundness of mind, and that, driven by his madness and insane recklessness even before the tribunals of secular judges, he reached the point of being subjected to examination—a disgraceful thing even in the case of a lowly person—and was condemned for murder, as the records brought forward publicly attest.

They lament with the deepest grief that, after committing such and so many offenses, this man still claims for himself the name of bishop in his hiding places, to the disgrace of his own city, and wishes to pollute the sacred name by claiming it for himself. Therefore, dearest brothers [Col. 0267B], since he refused to present himself to be heard, lest perhaps, after being convicted by the clerics accusing him, he might at last, when he appeared, receive from an episcopal tribunal the sentence appropriate to the judgment, we granted him a delay and decreed that judgment should take place within your province. A synod is to be assembled before the Kalends of November, so that, if he wishes to attend, he may answer the charges in person, provided that he has confidence; but if he neglects to attend, he must not gain a postponement of the sentence by his absence. For it is manifest that a man confesses his crime when, after a judgment has been indulgently granted and repeatedly delegated [Col. 0267C], he makes no use of the opportunity to clear himself.

It makes no difference whether everything alleged is proved in a hearing at which he is present, since his repeated absence, deliberately arranged, is itself established by his confession. We shall send letters throughout all the provinces, so that he may not plead ignorance as an excuse, and so that he may be compelled to come to the province and present himself there before the constituted tribunal. Whatever your charity decides should be done in this matter, once it has been reported to us, must necessarily be confirmed by our authority, as is fitting.

Given on the day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Monaxius, vir clarissimus. (A.D. 419.)

## Let no one be ordained bishop in any province in contempt of the metropolitan

### IV. Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome, to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne [Col. 0268A]

We lend difficult credence to complaints that disturb the priests of the Lord, especially when they say that those priests have attempted something contrary to the statutes of the Fathers. Yet, as now, a multitude of complainants frequently makes such allegations.

For behold, as your charity recognizes from what follows, the clerical order of the Lutubensian Church, or the people, have sent their petitions and tears to us, as far as can be understood, with great grief. They say that our fellow bishop Patroclus, despite the absence of their request, ordained someone—I do not know whom—in the place of a deceased bishop, in another province and with the metropolitan passed over, contrary to the rules of the Fathers. We certainly cannot endure this patiently, since it is fitting that we should be diligent guardians of the sanctions of our fathers.

No one, it seems, is unaware of the decree of the Nicene synod [Col. 0268B], which prescribes the following; let us set down its very words: throughout each province, the metropolitan bishops are individually to possess their proper authority, and no one province is to be subject to two metropolitans. Since it is impossible to believe otherwise, they judged that this must be observed, with the Holy Spirit suggesting it to them.

Therefore, dearest brother, if matters are as stated, and the territory of your province includes the Church mentioned above, proceed there fortified by our authority—which you ought indeed to do voluntarily—having regard for the wishes of those who petition. Go to the place where such an ordination is said to have taken place, armed with metropolitan authority and relying upon our instructions. Understand that we have granted you discretion, according to the rules of the Fathers, to do whatever must be done, so that, once everything has been completed, whatever you decide may become known to the apostolic see through your report, since it is clear that the administration of the entire province has been entrusted to you [Col. 0268C].

Let none of them, therefore, boldly and presumptuously cross their boundaries, nor, in their own territories, maintain anything not seen to have been granted to them, to the injury of the others. Let the presumption of those who extend the limits of their dignity beyond what is permitted cease, restrained by our authority.

We say this so that your charity may understand how faithfully we observe the commands of the canons: our own decree likewise determines that each province must always await the governance of its own metropolitan in all matters.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of February, in the consulships of our lords Honorius Augustus, for the thirteenth time, and Theodosius Augustus, for the tenth time. (A.D. 422.)

# Decrees of Pope Celestine

[Col. 0267]

## On Prosper and Hilary, who accuse certain priests of Gaul of being followers of Pelagius

[Col. 0267D]

### I. Celestine, bishop, to his dearest brothers Venerius, Marinus, Leontius, Auxonius, Arcadius, Filtanius, and the other bishops established throughout Gaul

The words of the apostolic commandment are that we must be without offense among Jews and Gentiles (II Peter II). Every Christian guards this with the whole strength of his soul (Romans XIV). Since this is so, great danger may await before God the person who refuses to display it even toward the faithful (I Corinthians VIII).

For how deeply these things distress us—things that strike Christian minds when Christian men are responsible for them—the Lord’s word in the Gospel bears witness. The Savior himself says that it is better for one who scandalizes one of the little ones to be plunged into the depths of the sea (Matthew XVIII). Let us therefore ask what punishment awaits the one for whom we read that such a penalty is better.

Our sons Prosper and Hilary, whose concern for our God is worthy of praise, have reported to us that certain priests there, I know not by what authority, are permitted such license as to labor for dissension in the Churches. They say that these men stubbornly bring undisciplined questions before the public and preach things opposed to the truth [Col. 0269A]. But we more justly attribute the matter to your affection, since those men have the opportunity to dispute above you.

We read that a disciple is not above his teacher (Matthew X); that is, no one ought to claim a doctrine for himself as an insult to his teachers. We know that you yourselves were appointed by our God to teach, since, as the Apostle says (I Corinthians XII), the third place within the Church is assigned to them.

What hope is there where these men speak while their teachers are silent, if indeed they were not their disciples? I fear that this silence is connivance; I fear that those who allow them to speak in such a manner are themselves speaking through them. In matters of this kind, silence is not free from suspicion, because truth would intervene if falsehood were displeasing [Col. 0269B]. The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence.

Therefore such men must be corrected. They must not be free to speak according to their own will. If matters are as stated, novelty must cease its attack upon antiquity, and disturbance must cease troubling the peace of the Churches. They often strive to drown in shipwreck those whom a secure station keeps safe while they stand within the harbor. Secure indeed is the station of all whose footprints do not move from the path of perfection.

The men mentioned above have appealed to the apostolic see, complaining to us of this very disturbance which assails them. Hold this deliberation, dearest brothers, to be undertaken for the peace of the Catholic people. Let them know—if indeed they are counted worthy of the dignity of the presbyterate—that they are subject to you. Let them know that all who teach badly ought rather to learn more and more than to teach.

For what are you doing in the Churches if they hold the supreme authority to preach? Unless perhaps this obstacle stands in the way—an obstacle supported neither by authority nor yet by reason—that some of the brethren, recently admitted from the company of the laity into our college, perhaps do not know what they ought to claim for themselves.

Much has already been said about these matters at the time when we sent a written reply to our brother Tuentius. Yet now, repeating our admonition again and again, we urge that such men be avoided—men who strive throughout the lands to sow something other than what our husbandman commanded. Nor can we be surprised that they now dare to attempt such things against the living, since they also strive to scatter the memory of our brothers who have fallen asleep.

## II. A remarkable declaration of praise concerning the holy bishop Augustine

[Col. 0269D]

We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion on account of his life and merits. No rumor of sinister suspicion ever touched him, even slightly. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that my predecessors always counted him among the best teachers.

All therefore rightly formed a common judgment concerning him, since he was everywhere both loved and honored by all. Accordingly, such men must be resisted—men whom we see growing wickedly. It is an offense against God for religious souls to endure these things; and since they are our members, their affliction ought also to make us suffer, although the blessedness promised by the Lord remains for all who are proved to endure persecution for righteousness’ sake (Matthew V).

What the Lord promises them in the future is declared by the following passage. This is not merely the cause of those who are acting: the universal Church is shaken by whatever novelty arises. Let us understand that the very things displeasing to us are displeasing to you. We shall be able to prove this only if, after silence has been imposed upon the wicked, complaint about such a matter ceases in the future.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers.

## Authorities of the bishops of the apostolic see in former times concerning the grace of God

### III

Since some who glory in the Catholic name remain fixed in the condemned opinions or depravity of heretics, whether through perversity or ignorance, and presume to oppose devout disputants; and although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Celestius, they nevertheless revile our teachers as though they had exceeded what was necessary, claiming that they follow and approve only what the most sacred see of blessed Peter, through the ministry of its bishops, established and taught against the enemies of God’s grace, it was necessary to inquire carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church judged concerning the heresy that arose in their time, and what they determined should be held concerning the grace of God against the most harmful defenders of free will.

We have therefore also joined certain statements of the African councils, which the apostolic bishops made their own when they approved them. Thus, so that those who doubt in any respect may be more fully instructed, we set forth in a concise catalogue the constitutions of the holy Fathers. If anyone is not excessively contentious, he will recognize that the coherence of all the disputations depends upon the brevity of the authorities set out below, and that no grounds for contradiction remain if he believes and speaks with Catholics.

## That Adam injured all human beings, and that no one can be saved except by the grace of Christ

### IV
