Pope Innocent, of blessed memory, pronounced that, through Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost natural ability and innocence, and that no one can rise from the depth of that ruin through free will unless the grace of the merciful God raises him. In his letter to the council of Carthage he says:

“For when that man suffered the loss of free will while using his own goods too thoughtlessly, he fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression, and found no way by which he could thereafter rise. Deceived forever in his freedom, he would have remained hidden beneath the oppression of this ruin, unless the coming of Christ, in accordance with his grace, had afterward raised him up. Through the purification of the new birth, Christ cleansed every former fault by the washing of his baptism.”

## That no one is good by his own powers, except through participation in the One who alone is good

### V

No one is good by himself unless the One who alone is good grants participation in himself (Matthew XIX). The judgment of the same pontiff, expressed in the same writings, bears witness to this, saying:

“Can we thereafter judge the minds of those people to be upright who think that they themselves are responsible for being good, and do not consider the One whose grace they receive daily, while they confidently believe that they can attain so much without him?”

## That unless we are continually helped by the grace of God, we cannot overcome the devil’s snares

### VI

Not even one renewed by the grace of baptism is capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and defeating the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he receives perseverance in a good way of life. The teaching of the same bishop confirms this in the same pages, saying:

“For although he redeemed human beings from their former sins, he nevertheless knew that they could sin again; therefore he preserved many remedies by which he could restore them after those sins. He provides daily remedies. Unless we rely upon and trust in them, we can in no way overcome human errors. For it is necessary that, by the aid of the One through whom we conquer, we should again be conquered if he does not help us.”

## That through Christ we make good use of free will

### VII

That no one makes good use of free will except through Christ is proclaimed by the same teacher in a letter sent to the council of Milevis, where he says:

“Recognize at last, O perverse doctrine of most foolish minds, that the first human being was so deceived by freedom itself that, while using its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from this unless the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored the state of his former freedom.”

## That all the merits of the saints are gifts of God

### VIII

All the endeavors, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one is pleasing to him for any reason other than what he himself has granted.

The authoritative rule of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us toward this judgment. Writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

“We, however, by the prompting of God—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—have reported everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.”

The African bishops venerated this speech, radiant with the light of the most sincere truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man:

“But what you placed in the letter which you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, when you said, ‘Yet we acted by the prompting of God,’ and so forth, we have understood as meaning that, with the sword of truth, you cut down in passing those who exalt the freedom of human will against the help of God.

“For what did you do with such free will as when you referred everything to the conscience of our humility? Yet you faithfully and wisely saw, and truthfully and confidently said, that this had been done by the prompting of God. This is because the will is prepared by the Lord, and he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations so that they may do something good.

“For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. Thus we do not perceive that our will is absent, and yet we do not doubt that his help is more powerful in each movement of the human will toward good.”

## That every holy thought and movement of a pious will is from God

### IX

God works in human hearts and in free will itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will are from God, because through him we can do something good, and without him we can do nothing.

The same teacher trained us for this confession when, speaking to the bishops of the whole world about the assistance of divine grace, he said:

“What time, then, intervenes when we do not need his help? In all actions, circumstances, thoughts, and movements, we must pray to him as helper and protector. For it is arrogant for human nature to presume anything for itself, while the Apostle cries out (Ephesians VI): ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.’

“And as he says again (Romans VII): ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.’

“And again (II Corinthians XV): ‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain; rather, I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me.’”

## That the grace of God not only forgives sins but also helps prevent their commission, and enables the law to be fulfilled—not, as Pelagius says, easily, as though without grace the law could be fulfilled only with greater difficulty

### X

We also embrace as belonging properly to the apostolic see what was established in the decrees of the council of Carthage. Its third chapter defined:

“Whoever says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the forgiveness of sins already committed, and not also as assistance so that sins may not be committed, let him be anathema.”

And again, the fourth chapter says:

“Whoever says that the grace of God through Jesus Christ helps us not to sin only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to desire and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not enabled to love and to be capable of doing what we have recognized must be done, let him be anathema.”

For when the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (I Corinthians VIII), it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have the grace of Christ for that which puffs up, but not for that which builds up, since both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do, and loving it so that we may do it. Thus, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up.

As it is written of God, “He teaches human beings knowledge” (Psalm XCIII), so it is also written, “Love is from God” (I John IV).

Likewise, the fifth chapter says:

“Whoever says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason only: that what we are commanded to do by free will we may more easily fulfill through grace—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema.”

For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do it only with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing.”

## That, apart from the statutes of the apostolic see, all prayers resound with the grace of Christ, by which the human race is restored from eternal damnation

### XI

Moreover, let us consider the inviolable sanctions of the most blessed apostolic see. By overthrowing the arrogance of destructive novelty, our most devout Fathers taught us to refer to the grace of Christ the beginnings of good will, the growth of worthy endeavors, and perseverance in them to the end.

Let us also consider the sacred rites of priestly supplication, handed down by the apostles and celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in the whole Catholic Church, so that the law of praying may establish the law of believing.

For when the bishops of the holy peoples perform the embassy entrusted to them, they plead the cause of the human race before the divine mercy. With the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, once the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may come to their senses through acceptance of the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and finally that, when catechumens have been brought to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them [Col. 0273B].

The results of these prayers show that they are not requested from the Lord superficially or in vain. For God deigns to draw many from every kind of error, transferring them, once rescued from the power of darkness, into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Colossians I), and making them vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath (Romans IX). This is so entirely understood to be the work of God that, for the illumination or correction of such people, thanksgiving and confession of praise are always rendered to God who accomplishes it [Col. 0273C].

## That the grace of God is also attested by the established purification of those who are to be baptized, since unclean spirits are driven from them by exorcisms and exsufflations

### XII

We do not contemplate without careful attention what the holy Church uniformly does throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized.

When infants or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not approach the fountain of life before the unclean spirit has been driven from them by the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy. Thus it may truly appear how the prince of this world is cast out, how the strong man is first bound (John XII; Matthew XII; Mark III), and how afterward his vessels are plundered and transferred into the possession of the victor, who leads captivity captive and gives gifts to human beings (Ephesians IV).

Accordingly, shaped by these ecclesiastical rules and by teachings drawn from divine authority, with the Lord’s help we have professed God to be the author of all good affections, works, endeavors, and virtues by which one turns toward God from the beginning of faith. We do not doubt that all human merit is preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

This help and gift of God does not take away free will but frees it, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes sound, and what was imprudent becomes prudent.

The goodness of God toward all human beings is so great that he wishes our merits to be what are in fact his gifts, and for the things he has bestowed he will grant eternal rewards. He acts within us so that we both will and do what he wills, and he does not permit the gifts he has granted for exercise, rather than neglect, to be idle within us.

Thus we may be fellow workers with the grace of God (I Corinthians III), and if we see something in us growing weak through our own negligence, we should hasten anxiously back to him who heals all our weaknesses (Psalm CI), redeems our life from destruction, and to whom we say daily: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew VI).

## That deeper questions are neither to be despised nor asserted absolutely

### XIII

As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise—questions treated at greater length by those who resisted the heretics—we neither dare to despise them nor consider it necessary to establish them. For confessing the grace of God, from whose work and favor nothing at all must be taken away, we believe that it is sufficient to accept whatever the writings of the apostolic see have taught us according to the rules stated above. We therefore should not regard as Catholic anything that appears contrary to the judgments laid down.

## Celestine sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne

We would certainly wish to rejoice in the administration of your Churches in such a way that we might congratulate you on your progress rather than grieve over anything done contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. For both good deeds reach us as a source of joy, and the deeds that have been done badly prick us with the goads of sorrow.

Nor can we remain silent when the impulse of our office urges us to recall some people from unlawful actions. We have been placed by God on the watchtowers, so that, proving the diligence of our vigilance, we may cut away what must be restrained and establish what must be observed.

Although spiritual concern does not fail even with regard to distant places, but extends everywhere that the name of God is proclaimed, nothing attempted through the authority of novel presumption for the overthrow of the rules escapes our knowledge.

## That priests or clerics should not minister in the church wearing cloaks and girding their loins

### XIV

We have learned that certain priests of the Lord serve a superstitious form of worship rather than the purity of mind or faith [Col. 0274D]. It is not surprising that they act contrary to ecclesiastical custom, since they did not grow up in the Church. Coming by another path, they brought into the Church practices that they had observed in another way of life. Wearing cloaks and girding their loins, they think that they fulfill the teaching of Holy Scripture not spiritually but literally.

For if these commandments were given so that they might be observed in this manner, why are the things that follow not done as well—why are burning lamps not held together with a staff? These things have their own mystery, and to those who understand, their meaning is so clear that they should be observed according to the symbolism appropriate to them.

The girding of the loins signifies chastity; the staff, pastoral governance; and the burning lamps, the radiance of good works, concerning which it is said, “Let your works shine” [Col. 0275A].

Yet perhaps those who live in more remote places and dwell far from others follow this dress as a custom rather than as a matter of reason. But why should this attire be introduced into the Gallican Churches, so that the custom of so many years and of so many bishops should be changed into another form of dress?

We must be distinguished from the people and from others by teaching, not by clothing; by conduct, not by appearance; by purity of mind, not by ornament. For if we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by the Fathers and make room for unnecessary superstitions.

We must not therefore lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful into such practices. They must be taught rather than entertained. Precepts must not be imposed upon their eyes but poured into their minds. There are indeed many things we could say concerning ecclesiastical discipline or the rationale of the matter itself, but we are drawn away from these to other subjects [Col. 0275B].

## That final repentance must be denied to no one

### XV

We have learned that repentance is being denied to the dying, and that the wishes of those who desire this remedy for their souls at the time of death are being rejected.

I confess that we shudder to find anyone so impious as to despair of the mercy of God—as though he could not come to the aid of one who hastens to him at any time, and as though he wished to destroy a person endangered beneath the burden of sins, when that person desires to be freed and delivered from it.

What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and by one’s cruelty to kill his soul so that it cannot be absolved, when God is fully prepared to help, invites the sinner to repentance, and promises him in these words:

“On whatever day he turns, his sins will not be counted against him” (Ezekiel XVIII).

And again:

“I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (ibid.).

Whoever denies repentance at the hour of death therefore takes salvation away from a person and despairs of the mercy of God, since he does not believe that God can suffice to help the dying even in a moment.

The thief hanging on the cross at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the repentance of a single hour had not helped him. Though he was undergoing punishment, he repented and, through the promise of a single utterance, earned a dwelling in paradise by God’s promise (Luke XXIII).

True conversion to God among those placed at the end of life must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by the length of time, as the Prophet declares:

“When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved” (Ezekiel III and XXXIII).

Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart (I Kings XVI; Jeremiah XVII), repentance must not be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since the person binds himself to that Judge who knows that all hidden things will be revealed.

## That the office of the episcopate must be reached through the ecclesiastical orders

### XVI

We have learned, dearest brothers, that certain men have been ordained bishops who had not been formed through any ecclesiastical orders before attaining the summit of such dignity. This was done in violation of the decrees of the Fathers, through the usurpation of one who acknowledges that he committed this act.

For the episcopate must be reached through those stages by which provision has most often been made, so that those initiated into lesser offices may be strengthened for greater ones. Anyone who wishes to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may teach what he has learned.

Every institution of life confirms itself by this principle in relation to the goal toward which it strives. One who has given no attention to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. One who has not advanced through each stage of service cannot reach the rank of an accomplished servant.

Is the priesthood, I ask, the only thing made cheaper than these, since it is more easily bestowed even though it is more difficult to fulfill?

But it is no longer enough to ordain laymen, whom no ecclesiastical order permits to become priests; men whose crimes are widely known throughout almost every province are also being ordained.

For recently, in a report sent to us from the regions of the East, Daniel was accused by the entire monastery of virgins over which he had presided, through abominable charges and many offenses brought against him. He was sought throughout the land, so that, if he trusted in his innocence, he would not avoid a judgment requested against him. We sent instructions through our subdeacon Fortunatus to the bishop of Arles that Daniel should be brought before an episcopal tribunal [Col. 0276B].

Burdened by such weighty testimony and assailed by accusations of so many crimes, he is said to have been ordained bishop despite being defiled by incest with sacred virgins, as the charge runs. The documents are contained in our archives of petitions, and we have also sent copies of them to you.

At this time, when he was being summoned by letters sent from us to answer the case, he insinuated himself into the dignity of the episcopate. Far be it from the sacred name to suffer insult: in granting such dignity to such a man, the ordainer himself has more likely forfeited it than the ordained obtained it. The one who believed that he should be joined to a convicted man by bestowing the episcopate upon him will share his condemnation; for whoever ordains such men shows what kind of person he himself is [Col. 0276C].

Since these matters have now been brought into the open, and many among you have spent some time with us and know the statutes of the apostolic see, let your brotherhood hasten to bring everything into conformity with the rule of discipline, in accordance with the exhortations we have delivered.

## That each province must be content with its own metropolitan

### XVII

First, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, each province must be content with its own metropolitan, as the constitutions contained in the letter of our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne establish. No opportunity for usurpation is to be granted to any priest to the injury of another.

Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him. Let no one presume anything in another’s province. In their own Churches, let foreign and unknown clerics, and those previously unheard of, not be placed over distinguished clerics to the exclusion of those who have earned the good testimony of their fellow citizens, lest some new institution or college for making bishops appear to have been established [Col. 0276D].

## That no one should be ordained bishop against the wishes of the clergy or people

### XVIII

Let no bishop be given to unwilling people. The consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order must be sought.

Someone from another Church may then be chosen if no worthy person can be found among the clergy of the city for which the bishop is to be ordained—something we do not believe can happen. For the local clergy must first be rejected before anyone from another Church is rightly preferred.

Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has spent his life through all the offices. Let no one intrude upon another’s service, and let no one dare claim for himself the reward due to another.

Let the clergy have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being oppressed, and let them not be afraid to reject those whom they recognize as being thrust upon them from outside. If they are not to receive the reward that is due, they should at least have free judgment concerning the man who is to govern them.

## That unlawful ordinations must be avoided
### XIX. That unlawful ordinations must also be avoided

Unlawful ordinations must also be avoided: no layman, no man married twice, and no man who is or has been the husband of a widow is to be ordained; rather, the candidate must be irreproachable and of the kind chosen by the Apostle (I Tim. III; Lev. XXI; II Tim. III). Through Moses the Lord commanded that a priest should take a virgin as his wife; the Apostle, speaking in the same Spirit, follows and adds that a bishop must be consecrated as the husband of one wife. Let priests therefore be chosen according to this standard; and if any unlawful ordinations have been made, let them be removed, since they cannot stand and will not be able to evade our investigation—however much they may think they can conceal how they came to office—so that no reverence due to religion may be darkened by obscurity.

Let there be no vain boasting among those who wear the pallium; let those who are bishops follow episcopal practice. Daniel, as we have said, who thought he could escape accusation by episcopal rank and reached such eminence only by concealing himself from his accusers, is to know that for the present he is separated from the assembly of your holiness. He ought to cast himself out by our judgment if he knows that he possesses confidence in his own conscience.

As for the priest of the Church of Massilia, who is said—an abominable thing to say—to have rejoiced in such a manner at the death of his brother that he went to meet the man who had arrived stained with his brother’s blood, intending to share a portion with him, we delegate him to be heard by your council.

Issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Felix and Taurus.

### That no priest may be ignorant of the canons

XX. Celestine to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria.

No priest may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could conflict with the regulations of the Fathers. For what worthy thing will be preserved by us if the standard of the decretal constitutions is broken at someone’s whim, with license granted to the populace? [Col. 0278A]

### That bishops should not be ordained from among the laity, with the clergy of the Churches disregarded

XXI. We have heard that certain cities, deprived of their proper rulers, wish to seek bishops from among the laity, and consider so lofty an office so cheap that they think we can confer it upon men who have served not God but the world. In doing this they judge ill not only of their own clergy, whom they hold in contempt, but also of us, since they believe that we are capable of doing such a thing.

They would never dare this if the agreeing judgment of certain people there did not wink at it. Thus the decrees issued so frequently accomplish nothing: as though nothing had ever been written on this matter, it is disregarded. What benefit was there in clerics having served through the successive grades of office and having spent their whole lives in the Lord’s camp, if those who are to rule over them are sought from among the laity—men free from secular occupations, ignorant of the entire ecclesiastical order, and seeking, with immoderate desire, to cross by an excessively rash leap into another person’s honor, passing into another way of life while trampling on the reverence owed to ecclesiastical discipline?

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we guard the helm of our law—that is, of the canons—we must oppose such men. By this letter we admonish your fraternity that no one is to admit a layman to the episcopal order or allow something to be done that will both deceive that man and create for himself grounds on which he will become liable under the established decretals.

### That the people are to be taught, not followed

[Col. 0278C] XXII. The people are to be taught, not followed; and if they do not know what is permitted and what is not permitted, we must admonish them, not give them our consent. Whoever attempts to try what has been forbidden will find that the censure of the apostolic see will in no way be lacking. For what we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone, we must punish with severity appropriate to the regulations.

We therefore wish this to be made known throughout all the Churches that lack their proper rulers, so that no one, perhaps flattering himself with some hope, may deceive himself.

Issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius. (In the year of Christ 429.)

## DECRETALS OF POPE LEO

[Col. 0277]

[Col. 0277D] Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, and throughout all [Note: [Col. 0277D] “provinces or Churches” is missing. EDIT.]

Just as the condition of the Churches, arranged by a salutary disposition, gives us cause for rejoicing, so we are troubled by no slight grief whenever we learn that something has been attempted or committed contrary to the established canons and ecclesiastical discipline. If we do not cut away such things with the vigilance we ought to exercise, we cannot excuse ourselves before the One who wished us to be watchmen (Ezek. III and XXXIII), allowing the untainted body of the Church—which we ought to guard pure from every stain—to be defiled by the wicked contagion of ambitious persons, while the very structure of its members fails to cohere through dissimulation. [Col. 0278D]

### That no bishop should presume to promote another’s slave to clerical office

I. Men are freely admitted to the sacred order who possess no dignity of birth and no dignity of character to support them; men who have not been able to obtain freedom from their masters are promoted to the height of the priesthood, as though servile lowliness could receive this honor and as though a man could be believed capable of pleasing God who has not yet been able to prove himself to his own master.

There is therefore a twofold guilt in this matter: the sacred ministry is polluted by association with such a person, and the rights of masters are violated insofar as this involves the rashness of unlawful usurpation. Therefore, dearest brothers, let all the priests of your province abstain from such men; and not only from them, but also from others who are bound by their origin or by any other status. We wish restraint to be observed unless perhaps the request or consent of those who claim some authority over them has been given.

For the man who is to be enrolled in divine service must be free from the control of others, so that he may not be withdrawn by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s camp, in which his name is inscribed.

### That those promoted to the priesthood who are husbands of widows or have contracted numerous marriages are to be excluded from all ecclesiastical offices

II. We have learned both from the Apostle’s teaching, from divine command, and from the regulations of the canons what the honesty of birth and the character of each person joined to the ministry of the sacred altar ought to be. Yet we find that many of our brothers have departed from these rules and entirely gone astray.

For it is established that husbands of widows have reached the priesthood, and that some who have contracted numerous marriages have likewise been admitted, with a freer way of life and unrestricted access to the sacred order, contrary to the blessed Apostle’s declaration concerning such men: “the husband of one wife”; and contrary to the command of the ancient law, which says and prescribes: “Let the priest take a virgin as his wife, not a widow, not a divorced woman” (I Tim. III; Lev. XXI).

Therefore, by the authority of the apostolic see, we order that all such men who have been admitted be excluded from ecclesiastical offices and from the name of priest. They cannot claim a capacity of which they were not made capable precisely because this impediment stood in their way.

We claim for ourselves the special responsibility of investigating this matter, so that if anything of this sort has perhaps been committed, it may be corrected and no further such act may be permitted. And so that no excuse may arise from ignorance—although it has never been permissible for a priest to be ignorant of what has been defined by the rules of the canons—we have sent these instructions concerning your provinces through our brothers and fellow bishops Innocentius, Legitimus, and Segetius. What is known to have grown up wrongly must be torn out by the roots, so that no weeds may corrupt the Lord’s harvest. For the things that are sound will produce abundant fruit only if those things that customarily destroy the growing crop are cut away with the greatest care.

### That not only clerics but Christian laymen also must not exact interest

[Col. 0279D]

III. We have also judged that this must not be passed over: certain men, seized by a shameful desire for profit, practice usury and seek to grow rich through interest. We grieve that this occurs not only among those established in clerical office, but also among laymen who wish to be called Christians. We decree that those who are convicted of this are to be punished more severely, so that every opportunity for sinning may be removed.

### That a cleric must not practice usury either in his own name or in another’s

IV. We have also judged it necessary to give this warning: just as no cleric may practice usury in his own name, so no one may attempt to do so in another’s name. It is disgraceful to devote one’s own crime to another’s advantage.

We ought to regard and practice only that kind of interest by which we may receive from the Lord what we mercifully give here—receiving it from Him who will repay it many times over and preserve it forever. [Col. 0280A]

### That if any priest acts contrary to these prohibitions, he is to be removed from office

V. Our admonition therefore declares that if any of our brothers attempts to act contrary to these regulations and dares to admit what has been forbidden, he is to know that he will be removed from his office and will not share in our communion, since he refused to be a partner in discipline.

Lest anything be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions of the blessed Innocentius, of revered memory, and of all our predecessors—those promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons—be guarded by your affection in such a way that whoever violates them may know that forgiveness will henceforth be denied him. [Col. 0280B]

Issued on the sixth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Maximus for the second time and Paternus. (In the year of Christ 443.)

Leo, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy.

We call you into partnership in our concern, so that with pastoral vigilance you may take more diligent care of the flocks entrusted to you, lest the devil’s cunning be able to do anything. The disease that, by the mercy of the Lord revealing it, is being driven from our sheep through our care must not proceed through the Churches of your sees while you have not yet been warned and remain unaware of what is happening, nor must it find hidden tunnels in which to conceal itself. What is extinguished by us in the city must not be sown among you with roots hidden in darkness. [Col. 0280C]

### That very many Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome through the vigilance of Pope Leo

VI. Our investigation discovered very many followers and teachers of Manichaean impiety in the city; vigilance exposed them, and authority and discipline restrained them. Those whom we were able to correct, we corrected. We compelled them, by a public profession in the Church and by the subscription of their own hands, to condemn Manichaeus together with his preaching and doctrines. After they had confessed the depths of their impiety, we relieved them by granting them penance.

But certain others had sunk so deeply that no remedy capable of assisting them could reach them. They were therefore subjected to the laws, according to the constitutions of the Christian emperors, and were condemned by public judges to perpetual exile, lest they pollute the holy flock with their contagion. [Col. 0280D]

Everything profane or shameful that they possess both in the Scriptures and in their secret traditions we exposed clearly before the eyes of the Christian people, so that the people might know what to reject and avoid. Indeed, the man who was said to be their bishop, when held by us, disclosed the disgraceful things he retained in his mysteries, as the sequence of the proceedings will be able to inform you. We have also sent those proceedings to you for your instruction; when you read them, you will be able to know everything we discovered.

Since we have learned that some of those whom a more severe guilt had bound, so that they could not be released, have fled, we have sent this letter to your affection so that your holiness, having been made more fully informed, may act with greater care and caution, lest men of Manichaean perversity find anywhere the opportunity to injure your peoples or discover teachers of this sacrilege. [Col. 0281A]

For we cannot rule those entrusted to us in any other way than by pursuing with zeal for the Lord’s faith those who are both destroyers and destroyed, and cutting them away from sound minds with whatever severity we can, lest this plague spread more widely.

Therefore I exhort, implore, and admonish your affection to keep watch with the concern that you ought to exercise and are able to exercise, seeking them out lest they find an opportunity to conceal themselves. Just as the person who diligently carries out whatever may benefit the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God the reward of a worthy recompense, so whoever refuses to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will not be able to excuse himself before the Lord’s tribunal for the guilt of negligence. [Col. 0281B]

Issued on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Theodosius XVIII and Albinus, illustrious men. (In the year of Christ 444.)

Leo, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.

We are urged by divine commands and apostolic admonitions to watch diligently and tirelessly for the condition of all the Churches, and if anything anywhere is found liable to blame, to recall it—through the concern of the clergy—from ignorance and incompetence or from presumptuous usurpation.

Since the command of the Lord’s voice remains, by which the most blessed apostle Peter is instructed through a threefold repetition of the mystical sanction to feed Christ’s sheep, because he loves Christ (John XXI), we are constrained by reverence for that very see over which we preside through the abundance of divine grace, so that we may avoid, as far as we can, the danger of negligence. Otherwise the profession of the chief Apostle, by which he testified that he loved the Lord, might not be found in us, since anyone who negligently feeds the flock entrusted to him so many times is proved not to love the chief Shepherd. [Col. 0281C]

### That the celebration of baptism on the day of Epiphany is forbidden

VII. Since, while I am concerned with fraternal affection for the acts of your charity, reliable indications have made known to me that you differ from the custom of apostolic institution concerning that which is principal among the sacraments of the Church—so that the sacrament of baptism is celebrated more frequently on the day of Epiphany than during the Paschal season—I am astonished that you or your predecessors could have adopted so irrational an innovation.

By confusing the mysteries of the two seasons, you have apparently believed that there is no difference between the day on which Christ was adored by the Magi and the day on which Christ rose from the dead. You could never have fallen into this fault if you had taken the law of the entire observance from the source from which you receive the consecration of your honor, and if the see of the blessed apostle Peter, which is the mother of your priestly dignity, had been the teacher of ecclesiastical reason. A departure from its regulations could have been tolerated with less equanimity if some admonition from us had preceded it.

But now, because correction is not despaired of, the custom must be preserved. Although it is scarcely tolerable for priests to plead ignorance, we nevertheless prefer to temper the necessary censure and instruct you by the clearest reasoning of truth.

### That all the mysteries of our salvation were arranged in due order through the incarnation of our Lord

[Col. 0282A]

VIII. The restoration of the human race, immutably preordained, always remained in God’s eternal plan. But the temporal order of events to be accomplished through Jesus Christ our Lord began with the incarnation of the Word.

Accordingly, one is the time when, at the announcement of the angel, the blessed Virgin Mary believed that she would conceive through the Holy Spirit and conceived; another when, the integrity of her virginity preserved, the child was born and, amid the joy of the heavenly ministers, was announced to the shepherds; another when the infant was circumcised; another when the legal offering was presented for him; and another when the three Magi, stirred by the brightness of the new star, came from the East to Bethlehem and adored the little child, honoring him with the mystical offering of gifts (Matt. II).

Nor are the days the same on which he was taken away from the impious Herod through his divinely ordered transfer to Egypt, and on which, after the persecutor’s death, he was recalled from Egypt to Galilee.

Amid these varying dispensations, his bodily growth proceeded. The Lord grew, as the Evangelist testifies (Luke II), in the advances of age and grace. During the days of Passover he came with his parents to the temple at Jerusalem; and when he was absent from the company of those returning, he was found sitting among the elders and disputing with the teachers who marveled at him. Giving the reason for his remaining there, he said: “Why is it that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in those things which are my Father’s?” (Matt. III; Luke III). He thereby indicated that he was the son of the one whose temple it was.

Then, when in more mature years he sought the baptism of his forerunner John in order to manifest himself more openly, what uncertainty about his divinity remained when, after the Lord Jesus had been baptized, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained, and the Father’s voice was heard from heaven saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased”?

We have touched upon all these matters as briefly as we could so that your affection may know that all the days of Christ were consecrated by countless acts of power and that the mysteries of the sacraments shone forth in all his actions. Yet what he announced in signs was fulfilled in another manner through events, and not everything that is numbered among the works of the Savior can be assigned to the time of baptism.

For if we were also to honor indiscriminately those things that we know were done by the Lord after the washing of blessed John, all seasons would have to be counted as continuous festivals, since all are filled with miracles.

But because the Spirit of wisdom and understanding instructed the Apostles and the teachers of the whole Church in such a way that Christian observance would tolerate nothing disordered and nothing confused, the reasons for the solemnities must be distinguished, and in all the institutions of our Fathers and rulers a rational distinction must be preserved. For we are one flock and one shepherd only if, as the Apostle teaches (II Cor. II), we all say the same thing: “Let us be perfect in the same understanding and in the same wisdom.”

### That in baptism death comes through the killing of sin, the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial, and the lifting from the waters is like resurrection from the tomb

[Col. 0282D]

[Col. 0283A] Although both the things pertaining to Christ’s humility and those pertaining to his glory converge in one person, and everything in him—both divine power and human weakness—tends toward our restoration, nevertheless it is properly through the death of the crucified one and the resurrection of the dead one that the power of baptism creates a new creature from the old. Thus, in those who are reborn, both the death of Christ and his life are operative, as the blessed apostle Paul says: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” (Rom. VI).

“We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection,” and so forth—the other matters that the teacher of the nations discussed at greater length in order to commend the mystery of baptism.

Thus it became evident, through the spirit of this teaching, that for the rebirth of the sons of men and their adoption as sons of God, that day and that time were chosen in which, through the likeness and form of the mystery, the things enacted in the members—which are enacted in the head itself—might correspond: for in the rule of baptism death intervenes through the killing of sin, the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial, and the lifting from the waters is like the rising from the tomb. [Col. 0283B]

The very character of the act therefore teaches that the proper day for the universal celebration of grace is the day on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose. For confirmation of this, it is of the greatest importance that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, after he had risen from the dead, gave his disciples—in whom all the rulers of the Churches were being instructed—both the form and the power of baptizing, saying: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

He could certainly have instructed them about this before his Passion, unless he had specifically wished it to be understood that the grace of regeneration began with his resurrection.

The solemnity of Pentecost, consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit, is also added to this observance; it depends upon the Paschal festival. Although other festivals belong to other days, Pentecost always occurs on the day distinguished by the Lord’s resurrection, extending, as it were, the hand of assisting grace to those whom illness, the length of a journey, or the difficulty of navigation has prevented from coming since Easter. It invites them, although hindered by whatever necessities, to obtain through the gift of the Holy Spirit the fulfillment of their desire.

The only-begotten Son of God himself, in the faith of believers and in the power of works, did not wish there to be any separation between himself and the Holy Spirit, because there is no diversity in nature. He said: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John XIV). And again: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom my Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything I have said to you” (ibid.). And again: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth” (John XVI).

Since Christ is the truth (John XIV), and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth, and the name Paraclete belongs properly to both, the festival is not different where the sacrament is one.

### That the blessed apostle Peter baptized three thousand men on the day of Pentecost

X. We prove that we should preserve this not on the basis of our own persuasion but by the very suitable example of apostolic authority. We follow the blessed apostle Peter, who on the very day when the promised coming of the Holy Spirit filled the whole number of believers consecrated by the washing of baptism the people of three thousand whom his preaching had converted.

Holy Scripture, which contains the Acts of the Apostles, teaches this in faithful narrative, saying: “When they heard these things, they were pierced in heart, and they said to Peter and the other apostles, ‘What shall we do, men and brothers?’” (Acts II).

But Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you and to your children and to all who are far away, whoever the Lord our God will call.” He testified and exhorted them with many other words, saying: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.”

Therefore those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added on that day.

### That these two seasons, Easter and Pentecost, were lawfully appointed by the Roman pontiff for baptism

[Col. 0284C] XI. Since it is most clearly evident that the two seasons of which we have spoken are the lawful times for those chosen in the Church to be baptized, we admonish your affection not to mix any other days into this observance.

### That at all times those pressed by the necessity of death—that is, illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck—must be baptized

XII. Although there are other festivals to which much reverence is owed in honor of God, the mystical and rational pattern of the principal and greatest sacrament must nevertheless be preserved. This does not prohibit the permission by which assistance is given through baptism at any time to those in danger.

Thus we defer the free wishes of those who are safe and living in the security of peace to these two festivals, joined and related to each other, so that in the danger of death, in the peril of siege, in the distress of persecution, and in the fear of shipwreck, we may at no time deny anyone this unique safeguard of true salvation.

But if anyone thinks that the festival of Epiphany, which is to be venerated with due honor in its proper order, possesses the privilege of baptism because some believe that on that same day the Lord approached the baptism of Saint John, let him know that the grace and purpose of that baptism were different, and that it did not belong to the same power by which those who are born through the Holy Spirit are regenerated. Of them it is said: “who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John I).

The Lord, needing no remission of sin and seeking no remedy of rebirth, wished to be baptized just as he also wished to be circumcised and to have an offering of purification made for him: so that he who had been made from a woman might, as the Apostle says, also be made under the law—which he had not come to abolish but to fulfill and bring to completion (Rom. X). And as the blessed Apostle proclaims: “The end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

He established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding primacy in all things, he taught that he was the beginning. He then confirmed the power of regeneration when blood for redemption and water for baptism flowed from his side.

Just as the Old Testament was a testimony to the New, and the law was given through Moses while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, so different sacrifices prefigured one offering, and the slaughter of many lambs ended in the immolation of him of whom it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world.”

So too John—not Christ, but Christ’s forerunner; not the bridegroom, but the bridegroom’s friend—was so faithful, seeking not his own things but those of Jesus Christ, that he confessed himself unworthy to loose the sandals of his feet (John III; Matt. III; Luke III). For John was indeed to baptize in water for repentance, whereas Christ was to baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire; by a twofold power he would both restore life and consume sins.

Therefore, dearest brothers, with so many and such great proofs before you, you clearly recognize, once every ambiguity has been removed, that for those chosen to be baptized—those who, according to apostolic rule, are to be examined by exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preaching—only two seasons are to be observed: Easter and Pentecost. We announce this to your charity so that you may not thereafter depart from apostolic institutions through any excess. For henceforth it cannot go unpunished if anyone believes that the apostolic rules may be neglected in any respect.

### That three bishops from Sicily must unfailingly come to Rome each year on the third day before the Kalends of October to join the synod

XIII. As the first measure required for the preservation of the most harmonious unity, we demand this: since the holy Fathers most salutarily established that there should be two assemblies each year, three of you must unfailingly come to Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October, to be joined to the fraternal council.

With the grace of God assisting, it will more easily be possible to provide that no scandals and no errors arise in the Churches of Christ, when everything must always be discussed collectively in the presence of the most blessed apostle Peter, so that all his constitutions and the decrees of the canons may remain inviolate among all the Lord’s priests.

We wish these matters, which we have believed should be brought to your attention under the inspiration of the Lord, to reach your knowledge through our brothers and fellow bishops Vaccillus and Paschasinus. Through their report we shall learn with what reverence the institutions of the apostolic see are observed by you.

Issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Calopodius and Ardabur. (In the year of Christ 447.)

### That a cleric of any order who abandons the Catholic faith and joins heretical communion, if he returns to the Church, must remain in the grade he held, without promotion

[Col. 0286D]

[Col. 0286A] XIV. Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia.

After reading the letters of your fraternity, we recognized the strength of your faith, which we had known in former times. We congratulate you because you vigilantly carry out pastoral care for the protection of Christ’s flock, lest wolves who have entered under the appearance of sheep tear the simple apart with beastlike savagery, and lest they not only make no progress themselves through correction but also corrupt what is sound.

To prevent viperous deceit from succeeding, we have judged that your affection must be admonished. We point out that it endangers the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics and schismatics, and has in any way stained himself with the contagion of heretical communion, is received into Catholic communion after repentance without the proper profession of satisfaction.

For it is most salutary and wholly beneficial as spiritual medicine that priests, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected and seek to return to the Catholic faith, which they formerly abandoned, should first confess without ambiguity that they condemn both their own errors and the authors of those errors. Thus, once their perverse opinions have also been destroyed, no opportunity for hope will remain, nor can any part of the Church be violated by association with such persons, since their own profession will in every respect begin to stand against them.

Concerning such men, we also command that the following constitutional rule of the canons be observed: they should regard it as a great benefit if, with every hope of promotion taken away, they remain permanently in the order in which they are found—provided they have not been defiled by a repeated baptism.

He incurs no slight guilt before the Lord who judges that men of this kind should be promoted to the sacred orders. If promotion is granted to those without guilt only after a rigorous examination, it must much less be permitted to those who are suspect.

Therefore let your affection, whose devotion gives us joy, join its care to our regulations and ensure that the measures so laudably proposed and so salutarily ordered for the safety of the whole Church are carried out carefully and promptly.

Your affection should not doubt that, if—as we do not believe—what we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith is neglected, we shall be moved to even greater severity. For the faults of subordinates are attributable to no one more than to rulers who are idle and negligent; such rulers often nourish extensive disease while refusing to apply the necessary medicine. [Col. 0286D]

Issued on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Alypius and Ardabur.

Leo to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne: with responses submitted and rescripts issued in reply to his inquiries.

I gladly received the letters of your Fraternity, which the archdeacon Hermes delivered. They concern a variety of matters, linked together and numerous, but not so burdensome to the reader’s patience that anything in them was overlooked amid the concerns pressing in from every side. Thus, having grasped the substance of your entire address and reviewed the proceedings drawn up before the examination of bishops and distinguished persons, we understood that Sabinianus and Leo, the presbyters involved in your case, lacked confidence, [Col. 0287A] and that those who voluntarily withdrew from the discussions they had begun had no just grievance remaining. In their case, I leave it to your moderation to determine what form and measure of justice you ought to maintain.

Nevertheless, I urge you, in the spirit of charity, to apply spiritual medicine to the sick for their healing, and, as Scripture says, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7), to deal more gently with those who seem, out of zeal for chastity, to have exceeded the proper measure of punishment, lest the devil, who deceived the adulterers, rejoice over those who avenge adultery.

I am astonished that your Fraternity should be so shaken by the adversity of scandals arising on every occasion that you say you would prefer release from the labors of the episcopate and would rather spend your life in silence and leisure than remain in the duties entrusted to you. Yet the Lord truly says: “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end” (Matthew 10). And whence does blessed perseverance come, if not from the virtue of patience? For according to apostolic teaching, “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3). This persecution is not to be reckoned only as what is inflicted against Christian devotion by sword, fire, or whatever punishments; the savagery of persecutions is also supplied by differences of character, the obstinacy of the disobedient, and the weapons of malicious tongues.

Since all the members of the body are always struck by these conflicts, and no portion of the devout is free from struggle—so that even leisure is not without dangers, nor labor without them—who will guide a ship through the waves of the sea if the helmsman withdraws? Who will guard the sheep from the wolves’ ambushes if the shepherd’s care does not remain watchful (John 10)? Finally, who will resist robbers and thieves if love of repose draws the watchman, stationed at his lookout for surveillance, away from his vigilant purpose (Ezekiel 3)?

We must therefore remain at the work entrusted to us and in the labor undertaken. Justice must be held firmly, and mercy must be offered kindly. Let sins be hated, not people. Let the proud be corrected, the weak be tolerated; and whatever must be punished more severely should be punished not with the spirit of one who rages, but of one who heals.

But if a more violent tribulation should weigh upon us, let us not be so terrified as though we were resisting that adversity by our own strength, since Christ is both our counsel and our strength. Without him we can do nothing, but through him we can do all things. He strengthens the preachers of the Gospel and ministers of the sacraments, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew, final chapter). And again: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me. In this world you will have tribulation, but take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16).

Since these promises are undoubtedly clear, we must not be weakened by any scandals, lest we appear ungrateful toward God’s election, whose aids are as evident as his promises are true.

As for the questions of your Fraternity, which your archdeacon delivered separately in writing, it would be more appropriate to inquire in person what ought to be thought of them, if we had the opportunity to see you. For since some of the questions seem to exceed the proper limits of inquiry, I understand that they are better suited to conversation than to writing. Just as some matters cannot be compelled by any reasoning, so there are many that ought to be moderated in view either of people’s ages or of the circumstances of the cases. This condition must always be preserved: in matters that are doubtful or obscure, we must recognize that we should follow what is found to be contrary neither to the commands of the Gospel nor to the decrees of the saints.

## The answers given below to the inquiries of the same bishop begin here.

### XV. Bishops are not to be recognized whom neither the clergy elected, nor the people sought, nor the provincial bishops consecrated; nevertheless, if clerics are ordained by such pseudo-bishops, the ordination may be valid.

No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were elected neither by the clergy, nor requested by the people, nor consecrated by the neighboring bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan. Since a question often arises concerning an honor wrongly received, who could doubt that it must by no means be granted by those who are not shown to have received it?

If, however, some clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches belonging to their proper bishops, and their ordination was carried out with the consent and judgment of the presiding bishops, it may be held valid, provided that they remain in those churches. Otherwise, the consecration must be considered void: it is founded neither upon the proper place nor supported by authority.

### XVI. If presbyters or deacons have fallen into some crime, they cannot obtain the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands.

It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those consecrated to the dignity of the presbyterate or to the rank of the diaconate should receive, for some crime of their own, the remedy of repentance through the laying on of hands. This undoubtedly derives from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest should sin, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2).

Therefore, for such fallen persons to obtain God’s mercy, private withdrawal must be sought, where, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.

### XVII. Deacons, like bishops and presbyters, must cease from conjugal relations, but they must not repudiate their marriages.

The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. When they were laymen or readers, they were lawfully able both to marry wives and to beget children; but when they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been lawful for them began no longer to be permitted. Therefore, so that a carnal marriage may become a spiritual one, they ought neither to dismiss their wives nor, as though they did not have them, to possess them in such a way that the affection of marriage remains intact while the practice of marital intercourse ceases.

### XVIII. A wife is one thing and a concubine another; and no one should be considered to have erred if he gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine.

Not every woman joined to a man is his wife, just as not every son is an heir to his father. The agreements of marriage are legitimate among freeborn persons and among equals; indeed, the Lord established this much earlier than the beginning of Roman law. Thus a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another.

For this reason the Apostle too, in order to make clear the distinction between these persons, adduces testimony from Genesis (chapter 21), where it is said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Galatians 4).

Since the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning so that, beyond the union of the sexes, it might bear the sacramental meaning of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage if she is taught not to have possessed the nuptial mystery.

Therefore, if a cleric of any place gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as though he had given her to a married man, unless that woman is shown to have become freeborn, to have been lawfully endowed, and to have been honored by a public wedding. Women joined to men by paternal decision are free from guilt if the women whom the men kept were not in marriage, because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another.

### XIX. It is not a duplication of marriage when, after dismissing a slave woman, a wife is taken.

To cast a slave woman away from one’s bed and take a wife of certain freeborn status is not a duplication of marriage but an advance in honorability. The negligence of such men is certainly blameworthy, but they must not be wholly abandoned, so that, stirred by frequent exhortations, they may faithfully carry out what they necessarily sought.

For no one is to be despaired of while he remains in this body, since what is sometimes postponed through distrust of one’s age may be accomplished through more mature counsel.

### XX. Concerning those who were deprived of communion and died in that condition.

The case of such people must be reserved for God’s judgment. It was in his hand that their death should not be delayed until the remedy of communion. But those to whom we did not give communion while they were alive, we cannot give communion when they are dead.

### XXI. Concerning those who postpone doing penance.

This hesitation may arise not from contempt for the remedy but from fear of committing a more serious offense. Therefore, when the penance that was postponed is sought with greater earnestness, it must not be denied, so that the wounded soul may in some manner reach the medicine of pardon.

### XXII. One who asks pardon for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from many lawful things.

It is one thing to demand back what is justly owed; it is another to renounce one’s own possessions out of love for perfection. But one who asks pardon for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from lawful things, as the Apostle says: “All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Corinthians 6).

Therefore, if penitents have a case that perhaps they ought not to neglect, it is better for someone to seek an ecclesiastical judgment than a civil one.

### XXIII. A penitent ought not to engage in profitable commercial business.

The character of profit either excuses or condemns the merchant, for there is honorable gain and there is disgraceful gain. Nevertheless, it is more beneficial for a penitent to suffer loss than to be entangled in the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the transactions of buying and selling.

### XXIV. After penance, one ought not to return to secular military service.

It is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical rules to return to secular military service after performing penance, since the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2). Therefore, the person who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the devil’s snares.

### XXV. If a young man undertook penance under the pressure of some danger but does not remain continent, he may be supported by the remedy of a wife.

If, while still in adolescence, someone undertook penance under the pressure either of fear of death or of the danger of captivity, and afterward, fearing a lapse into incontinence, chose the pardonable union of a wife so as not to incur the sin of fornication, he seems to have done something pardonable, provided that he had known no woman at all outside marriage.

Nevertheless, we are not establishing a rule in this matter; we are judging what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more fitting for one who has done penance than persevering chastity of both mind and body.

### XXVI. If anyone abandons his monastic purpose, he must be cleansed through the satisfaction of public penance.

A monastic purpose undertaken by one’s own judgment and will cannot be abandoned without sin. For what someone has vowed to God, he ought also to repay. Therefore, one who, having abandoned his profession of solitude, turns to military service or to marriage must be cleansed through the satisfaction of public penance. For although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, abandoning the better choice is a transgression.

### XXVII. Girls who, not under compulsion but by their own will, undertake the purpose of virginity commit an offense when they marry, even if they have not yet been consecrated.

Girls who, not compelled by their parents’ authority but by their spontaneous judgment, have undertaken the purpose and habit of virginity, if afterward they choose marriage, act faithlessly, even if the grace of consecration has not yet been bestowed upon them. They would certainly not have been deprived of that gift if they had remained in their purpose.

### XXVIII. Those concerning whom it is doubtful whether they received baptism must be reborn through baptism.

If there are no indications among relatives or household members, nor among clerics or neighbors, by which the persons in question can be shown to have been baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn, lest those perish manifestly for whom reason does not permit us to regard as repeated what is not shown to have been done.

Those who can remember that they came to church with their parents may recall whether they received what was given to their parents. But if this too is foreign to their memory, it seems that what is not known to have been given should be conferred upon them, because there is no rash presumption where there is careful devotion.

### XXIX. Those who recognize that they were baptized but do not know in what faith should be received through the laying on of hands.

As for those about whom you wrote, who know that they were baptized but profess that they do not know what faith was held by those who baptized them: since in some manner they received the form of baptism, they must not be baptized again. Rather, through the laying on of hands, they must be joined to the Catholics and receive the power of the Holy Spirit, which they could not receive from heretics.

### XXX. Concerning those who took part in the banquets of the pagans and ate sacrificial foods.

If they merely took part in pagan banquets and ate sacrificial foods, they can be cleansed through fasting and the laying on of hands, so that thereafter, by abstaining from food sacrificed to idols, they may participate in the sacraments of Christ.

But if they either worshiped idols or were polluted by murder or fornication, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.

### XXXI. The bishop of Thessalonica has always fulfilled the functions of the Apostolic See.

**Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.**

If you were to perceive with sound judgment and weigh with proper examination how much has been entrusted to your Fraternity by the authority of the most blessed apostle Peter, and what responsibilities have also been committed to you through our favor, we could greatly rejoice in your devotion to the solicitude imposed upon you.

For just as my predecessors delegated authority to your predecessors, so I too, following the example of those before me, have delegated to your Fraternity the functions of my oversight. In this way you were to assist, as an imitator of our gentleness, in the care that by divine institution we owe principally to all the churches; you were to extend, in a sense, the presence of our visitation to provinces distant from us; and, through continual and timely supervision, you were to be able readily to recognize what you should settle by your own diligence in each matter and what you should reserve for our judgment.

Since it was open to you to suspend greater affairs and more difficult outcomes of cases while awaiting our decision, you had neither reason nor necessity to deviate into what exceeded your measure. For you have an abundance of letters containing our admonitions, by which we have often instructed you concerning moderation in all your actions, so that through an exhortation of charity you might summon the churches of Christ entrusted to you to the health-giving benefit of obedience.

For although among negligent or careless brothers there are often matters that ought to be corrected with greater authority, correction must nevertheless be applied in such a way that charity is always preserved. Thus the blessed apostle Paul, instructing Timothy in ecclesiastical governance, says: “Do not rebuke an elder, but appeal to him as to a father; younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all chastity” (1 Timothy 5).

If this moderation is owed, by apostolic institution, to whatever lower members there are, how much more must it be rendered without offense to our brothers and fellow bishops? Even if things sometimes occur in priestly persons that deserve reproach, benevolence should accomplish more toward correcting them than severity, exhortation more than agitation, and charity more than power.

But those who seek what is their own and not what is Christ Jesus’ (Philippians 2) easily depart from this law. When they prefer to dominate their subjects rather than care for them, honor inflates pride; and what was provided for concord turns toward wrongdoing. This, as we must say, does not arise without great pain of heart.

I feel myself, in a certain sense, drawn into guilt when I learn that you have departed immoderately from the rules handed down to you. If you were insufficiently attentive to your own reputation, you ought at least to have spared mine, lest actions arising solely from your own mind appear to have been carried out by our judgment.

Let your Fraternity reread our pages and go through all the letters sent to your predecessors by the bishops of the Apostolic See. You will find that either I or my predecessors ordered what we have learned that you presumed to do.

For our brother Atticus, metropolitan bishop of Old Epirus, came to us with the bishops of his province and complained in a tearful appeal of the utterly undeserved affliction he had suffered, in the presence of your attending deacons. By offering nothing in response to his tearful complaints, they showed that the matters brought before us were not without credibility.

It was also read in your letters, which those same deacons delivered, that Brother Atticus had come to Thessalonica and had confirmed his consent by a written declaration. Thus nothing else could be understood by us than that his coming and the document he had written promising obedience had proceeded from his own will and spontaneous devotion. Yet the very mention of that document revealed the mark of an injury.

It was not necessary for the man who had already demonstrated his obedience by the service of his voluntary arrival to be bound by a written document. Thus your letter gave testimony to the complaints mentioned above, and, through what was not concealed, it laid bare what had been covered by silence: namely, that the prefecture of Illyricum had been approached and that the highest secular authority had been stirred up to compel the appearance of an innocent bishop.

A terrible execution was sent out, one that united all public offices in order to carry out the command, so that a priest accused of no crime—or falsely accused—might be dragged from the sacred inner chambers of the Church. No respite was granted him on account of the hardship of his illness or the severity of winter. Instead, he was compelled to travel by a difficult road, full of dangers and blocked by impassable snows; the labor and peril were so great that some of those who accompanied the bishop are said to have collapsed.

I am deeply astonished, dearest brother, and also exceedingly grieved, that you could be moved so atrociously and violently against a man about whom you had indicated nothing beyond the fact that, when summoned, he delayed appearing and offered illness as an excuse. This is especially so since, even if he had deserved such treatment, you ought to have awaited what I would write in response to your questions.

But, as I see it, you held a good opinion of my character and most accurately anticipated how civilly I would respond in order to preserve priestly concord. For that reason you hastened, without concealment, to carry out your impulses, lest, once you had received letters from us ordering something different in accordance with our moderation, you should no longer have the license to do what was done.

Or perhaps some crime had become known to you, and the metropolitan bishop was weighed down by the burden of a new offense in his own province? Yet you yourself confirm that this was foreign to him by bringing no accusation against him. But even if he had committed something grave and intolerable, our decision ought to have been awaited, so that you yourself would decree nothing before learning what pleased us.

For we entrusted our functions to your Fraternity in such a way that you were called to share in the solicitude, not to possess the fullness of power. Therefore, just as the things you have piously managed greatly rejoice us, so the things wrongly done distress us exceedingly. After the experience of many cases, it is necessary to look ahead more carefully and take precautions more diligently, so that through the spirit of charity and peace every source of scandal may be removed from the churches of the Lord that we have entrusted to you. The dignity of your episcopate may indeed take precedence in those provinces, but every excess of usurpation must be cut away.

### XXXII. The rights of metropolitans are to be preserved.

Therefore, in accordance with the canons of the holy Fathers—established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world—we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, whose care is extended through our delegation by your Fraternity, shall retain unimpaired the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor through presumption.

### XXXIII. Metropolitans must ordain as bishops neither laymen, nor bigamists, nor husbands of widows, but men who are irreproachable.

In cities whose bishops have died, the following procedure must be observed for appointing their successors: the man to be ordained, even if supported by the testimony of a good life, must not be a layman, a recent convert, or the husband of a second wife, nor one who has or has had one wife whom he married as a widow.

The choice of priests is so eminent that matters which are not counted as faults in other members of the Church are nevertheless considered unlawful in them.

### XXXIV. Carnal marriage is to be denied to subdeacons.

Although those outside the clerical order possess free choice to devote themselves to marriage and the begetting of children, nevertheless, in order to display the purity of perfect continence, carnal marriage is not permitted even to subdeacons. Thus those who have wives should be as though they did not have them (1 Corinthians 7), while those who do not have wives should remain unmarried.
