If this is rightly preserved in the order that is fourth from the head, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, and third orders, so that no one may be judged suitable for Levitical dignity, presbyteral honor, or episcopal excellence if it is discovered that he has not yet restrained himself from the pleasure of a wife?

### XXXV. No bishop is to be ordained against the will of the people.

When the election of the chief priest is under consideration, the man who has been unanimously requested by the agreement of the clergy and the people is to be preferred above all others. If the votes of the parties should perhaps be divided in favor of another person, the metropolitan’s judgment shall prefer the candidate who is supported by greater zeal and merits.

This condition must be maintained: no one is to be ordained against the will of those who neither desire nor request him, lest the city despise or hate a bishop it did not want and become less devout than is fitting because it was not permitted to have the one it chose.

### XXXVI. The metropolitan of Epirus must report to the bishop of Thessalonica concerning the candidate whom he is going to ordain as bishop; similarly, the provincial bishops must report concerning the elected metropolitan.

Concerning the person to be consecrated as bishop and the agreement of the clergy and people, the metropolitan bishop must report to your Fraternity and inform you of what has been approved in the province, so that your authority too may confirm the ordination as properly celebrated. That authority must create neither delay nor difficulty for rightly ordered arrangements, lest the Lord’s flocks be deprived of the care of shepherds for too long.

When a metropolitan has died and another must be substituted in his place, the provincial bishops must assemble in the metropolitan city. After examining the will of all the clergy and all the citizens, they must choose the best man from among the presbyters or deacons of that church.

The provincial priests must report his name to your knowledge and fulfill the wishes of those who make the request once they know that what pleased them has also pleased you. For just as we do not want just elections to be wearied by delays, so we permit nothing to be presumed without your knowledge.

### XXXVII. Two provincial councils of bishops are to be held each year; if a difficult matter arises and is not resolved by the judgment of the bishop of Thessalonica, it is to be referred to the bishop of Rome.

Concerning councils of bishops, we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers beneficially ordained: namely, that two assemblies be held each year, in which judgment is given on all the complaints that ordinarily arise among the various orders of the Church.

If a case should arise among those who preside concerning more serious sins—which God forbid—and it cannot be settled by provincial examination, the metropolitan must instruct your Fraternity concerning the entire matter. If, after the parties have been brought before you, the matter is not quieted by your judgment, whatever it may be must be transferred to our consideration.

### XXXVIII. If a bishop abandons his own city and seeks a greater see out of ambition, he may obtain neither that see nor retain his own.

If a bishop, despising the modesty of his own city, seeks the administration of a more famous place and by any means transfers himself to a larger community, he must indeed be expelled from the foreign cathedra, but he must also lose his own. Thus he will preside neither over those whom he coveted through avarice nor over those whom he despised through pride.

Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries and not desire to be enlarged beyond the measure of his lawful jurisdiction.

### XXXIX. No one may solicit or retain another bishop’s cleric without that bishop’s consent.

No one may receive or solicit another bishop’s cleric against the will of his own bishop, unless, by an agreement made in charity, this has been settled between the one who gives and the one who receives.

For the person who dares either to cast away or to retain what is more useful or more valuable from a brother’s church is guilty of a more serious injury. Therefore, if the matter occurs within the province, the metropolitan will compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own church. If he has gone farther away, he will be recalled by the authority of your command, so that neither greed nor ambition may find an opportunity.

### XL. Moderation must be maintained by the bishop of Thessalonica when summoning provincial bishops, so that priestly honor is not subjected to insult under this pretext; no more than two bishops from each province, approved by their metropolitans, are to be sent.

When summoning bishops to you, we want you to be most moderate, lest you appear to glory in injuries inflicted upon your brothers under the pretext of greater diligence. Therefore, if there is some greater matter for which it is reasonable and necessary to summon a fraternal assembly, it is sufficient for two bishops from each province, whom the metropolitans judge should be sent, to come to your Fraternity.

### XLI. Bishops are not to remain longer than fifteen days beyond the time established for the council; if a dispute arises among them, everything must be reported to the Roman pontiff through a record of the proceedings, so that he may order whatever pleases God.

Those who have assembled must not be delayed beyond fifteen days after the appointed time. If, in the matter that you believe must be discussed or decided with the brothers, their judgment should differ from your will, everything must be brought to us with the proceedings as evidence, so that, once ambiguities have been removed, what pleases God may be decreed.

To this end we direct all our concern and care: that whatever pertains to the unity of concord and whatever pertains to the preservation of discipline may be violated by no disagreement and neglected by no indolence.

Therefore, dearest brother, I exhort and admonish both you and those of our brothers who are offended by your excesses—although the grounds of their complaints are not all alike—not to disturb through contention what has been piously ordered and beneficially arranged. Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another (1 Corinthians 10). As the Apostle says, “Let each of you please his neighbor for his good, for his edification” (Romans 15).

For the structure of our unity cannot be firm unless the bond of charity binds us into inseparable solidity. Just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. The connection of the whole body creates one health and one beauty.

This connection of the whole body requires unanimity, but it especially demands concord among priests. Although their dignity is not equal, their general order is one. For even among the most blessed apostles there was, despite their likeness of honor, a certain distinction of power; and although all were chosen equally, one was nevertheless given precedence over the others. From this pattern the distinction among bishops also arose.

By a great ordering it was provided that no one should claim everything for himself. Rather, there should be in each province one person whose judgment held first place among the brothers; and again, there should be certain men established in the greater cities who would assume a broader solicitude, through whom the care of the universal Church would converge upon the one See of Peter, and nothing anywhere would disagree with its head.

Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over some people should not be troubled that someone has been placed over him. Let him also render the obedience that he demands; and just as he does not wish to bear the burden of a heavy load, so let him not dare to impose an unbearable weight upon another.

For we are disciples of a teacher who is humble and gentle, who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11). How will we experience this unless we also observe what the same Lord says: “The greater among you will be your servant” (Matthew 20; Luke 22); and, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14)?

**Leo, to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia: greetings.**

My son Adeodatus, a deacon of our See, returned to us and reported that your Fraternity had asked to receive the authority of the Apostolic See concerning matters that seem to present considerable difficulty for judgment. In view, however, of the circumstances of the present necessities, care must be applied so that wounds inflicted by the adversity of hostility may be healed chiefly through the means of religion.

### XLII. Women who had married other men while their husbands were captive must be joined to their former husbands when those husbands return from captivity, so that each person may recover what is his own.

You say that, through the devastation of war and the gravest incursions of hostility, certain marriages were so divided that, when their husbands had been led into captivity, the women were left without them. They thought their own husbands had either been killed or would never be freed from their captors’ domination, and, compelled by their solitude, they entered into marriage with other men.

Now, with the situation changed for the better by the Lord’s assistance, some of those who were thought to have perished have returned. Your Fraternity understandably seems uncertain what we should decree concerning the women who have been joined to other men.

But because we know that it is written that a woman is joined to a man by God, and because we recognize the command that “what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19), we must believe that the bonds of legitimate marriage are to be restored. Once the evils brought about by hostility have been removed, each person must be restored to what he or she lawfully possessed. Every effort must be made so that each person receives what is his or her own.

### XLIII. The man who appears to have taken a captive’s wife in marriage is not to be judged culpable.

Nor is the man to be judged culpable or regarded as an invader of another’s legal right who took the place of a husband who was thought no longer to exist. For many things belonging to those who had been led into captivity could pass into another’s legal possession, and yet it is entirely just that, when they return, their own property be restored to them.

If this is rightly observed with regard to slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be done in the restoration of marriages, so that what was disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored through the remedy of peace!

### XLIV. If husbands returning from captivity are not offended by their wives’ conduct and wish to receive them back in marriage, they are to have full freedom to do so.

Therefore, if husbands return after a long captivity and remain so devoted to their wives that they wish them to return to their marital partnership, what necessity brought about must be set aside and judged blameless, and what fidelity demands must be restored.

### XLV. If women refuse to return to their former husbands, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion as impious.

But if some women are so captivated by love for their later husbands that they prefer to remain with them rather than return to a legitimate marriage, they are rightly to be censured. They are even to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion because they chose the contamination of guilt over an excusable situation, showing that, through their incontinence, they preferred what a just release could have forgiven.

Let marriages return to their proper condition through voluntary restoration, and let no one turn into a reproach of evil will what the necessity of circumstances forced. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands must be regarded as impious, so those who return to the affection established by God deserve praise.

### XLVI. Penitence is to be granted to captives who were compelled by error or hunger, not by religious veneration, to eat sacrificial foods.

Concerning those Christians who are said to have been polluted by sacrificial foods among those by whom they had been held captive, we have thought that this too must be answered to your charitable inquiry: they are to be cleansed through the satisfaction of penance, which must be measured not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart.

Whether error extorted this act or hunger compelled it, there must be no doubt that it is to be wiped away, since such food was consumed out of fear or need, not out of religious veneration.

### That those who, compelled either by force or fear to submit to a repetition of baptism, are to be relieved by the remedy of penance, with careful consideration also given to old age, childhood, illnesses, and other necessities

**XLVII.** Concerning those about whom your affection likewise judged that we should be consulted—those who, compelled either by fear or led astray by error, underwent baptism a second time, and now recognize that they acted against the sacrament of the catholic faith—the following moderation must be observed: they are not to be received into our fellowship and restored to the unity of communion except through the remedy of penance and the laying on of the bishop’s hand. The periods of penance are to be determined by your judgment, with due moderation, according as you observe the devotion of those who have turned back; and consideration is likewise to be given to advanced age and to the necessities arising from any dangers or illnesses. If anyone is so severely afflicted that, while still doing penance, his salvation is feared to be in danger, he must be assisted through priestly concern by the grace of communion.

### That those who were baptized by heretics are to be strengthened solely by invocation of the Holy Spirit

**XLVIII.** Those who received baptism from heretics, since they had not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed solely by invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, because they received only the form of baptism, without the power of sanctification. As you know, we proclaim that this rule is to be observed in all Churches: the washing once begun must not be violated by repetition. The Apostle says: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians IV). Its cleansing must not be profaned by repetition; rather, as we have said, only the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is to be invoked, so that they may receive from catholic priests what no one receives from heretics.

You shall cause this letter of ours, which we have sent in response to the consultation of your brotherhood, to reach all the brethren and your fellow bishops of the province, so that the authority thus given may benefit the observance of all.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the Emperor Majorian.

## In the case of Bishop Lupicinus: Leo to all the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauretania

**[Col. 0298B]**

**XLIX.** Since the frequent reports of those coming to us conveyed that certain unlawful practices concerning the ordination of priests had been usurped among you, the demands of piety required us, out of the concern which by divine institution we owe to the universal Church, to make every effort to learn the truth of these matters. We therefore entrusted the task of our care to our departing brother and fellow priest, Potentius, who, in accordance with the letters which we sent to you through him, was to investigate what truth there was concerning the bishops whose election was reported to be blameworthy and to report everything faithfully to us.

Since he has now disclosed everything fully to our knowledge and has sincerely made clear to us under what kind and sort of rulers certain peoples of Christ are held in the regions of the province of Caesarea, it was necessary that, by letters now also addressed to your affection, we should express the grief of our heart with which we burn on account of the dangers threatening the Lord’s flocks. We are astonished that, under the pretext of troubled times, either the presumption of ambitious men or popular tumult has had such power among you that the pastoral dignity and government of the Church have been given to persons unworthy and far removed from priestly merit.

This is not to govern peoples but to harm them; it is not to provide leadership but to increase danger. The integrity of those who preside is the salvation of those subject to them; and where obedience is secure, there the form of doctrine is sound. A principate conferred by sedition or seized by ambition is pernicious because of the example of its very beginning, even if the person’s morals and conduct do not give offense; and it is difficult for things to end well which began with an evil beginning.

If care must be taken prudently and intelligently in every grade of the Church, so that nothing disordered or perverse may exist in the house of the Lord, how much more must we labor to avoid error in the election of him who is placed above all the grades? For the condition and order of the whole household of the Lord will waver if what is required in the body is not found in the head.

Where is that command of the blessed Apostle Paul, uttered through the Spirit of God, by which the whole number of Christ’s priests is instructed in the person of Timothy, and each of us is told: “Lay hands quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (II Timothy V)? What does it mean to lay hands quickly except to confer priestly honor on those not yet tested—before the maturity of age, before the time of examination, before the merit of obedience and labor, before experience in discipline? And what does it mean to share in the sins of others except to become an ordainer of the sort of man who is himself unworthy of ordination?

For just as the man who exercises sound judgment in choosing a priest gains the fruit of a good work for himself, so the man who admits an unworthy person into his fellowship afflicts himself with serious loss. Therefore, what is contained in the general statutes must not be disregarded in anyone’s case, nor should that honor be considered legitimate which has been conferred contrary to the commands of divine law.

The Apostle says, among the other rules governing election, that the bishop must be one who is known to have been or to be “the husband of one wife” (I Timothy III). This command has always been held so sacred that the same condition was understood to apply even to the wife of the priest to be chosen: she must not, before marrying the man who had had no other wife, have experienced marriage with another husband.

Who, then, would dare to tolerate the violation of so great a sacrament, when even the statutes of divine law have not been lacking for this great and venerable mystery? They clearly determine that a priest is to take a virgin as his wife (Leviticus XXI; Ezekiel XLIV), and that the woman who is to become a priest’s wife must know no other husband’s bed.

Already then the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church was being represented in priests, so that, since the man is the head of the woman, the bride of the Word might learn to know no other man than Christ (Ephesians V; I Corinthians XI). He rightly chose one, loves one, and joins no other to his fellowship besides her.

If, therefore, this form of priestly marriages was observed even in the Old Testament, how much more, established under the grace of the Gospel, must we serve the apostolic commands? However good a man’s morals may be, and however adorned he may be with holy works, he must in no way ascend to the rank of deacon, the honor of the presbyterate, or the summit of the episcopate if it is established either that he himself is not the husband of one wife, or that his wife has not been the wife of one man.

The Apostle warns and says: “And let these also first be tested, and so let them minister” (I Timothy III). What else are we to understand by this except that in these advancements we must consider not only the chastity of marriages but also the merits of labors, lest pastoral office be entrusted either to newcomers from baptism or to those suddenly converted from secular life?

Since, throughout all the grades of Christian service, advancement ought to be judged by growth in achievement—whether greater responsibilities can be entrusted to anyone—the venerable decrees of the blessed Fathers rightly judged, when speaking of the election of priests, that those were fit for sacred administrations who had advanced for a long time through the individual grades of office and had given credible proof of themselves, so that the account of their conduct might bear witness to each person’s life.

If it is unworthy to reach worldly honors without the support of time and without the merit of labor, and if those whose proofs of integrity do not assist them are customarily marked as ambitious, how careful and prudent must be the administration of divine gifts and heavenly dignities? The apostolic and canonical decrees must not be violated in any respect, nor must the Church of the Lord be entrusted to those ignorant of legitimate institutions and wholly unfamiliar with humility—those who do not wish to rise from the lowest positions but want to begin at the highest. For it is extremely unjust and absurd that the inexperienced should be preferred to teachers, the new to the old, and the untrained to those proven by service.

In a great house, as the Apostle explains, there must be vessels of different kinds: some of gold and silver, others of wood and clay. Their service is distinguished according to the quality of their material, and the use of precious vessels is not the same as that of cheap ones. Everything will be disordered if clay vessels are preferred to golden ones, and wooden vessels to silver ones.

Just as the kinds of men who do not yet shine with any virtues are represented by the wooden and clay vessels, so without doubt those who, through the fire of long instruction and the furnace of prolonged labor, have been refined into tested gold and pure silver are represented by the golden and silver vessels. If reward is not given to such men for their devotion, the whole discipline of the Church is dissolved; the entire order is thrown into confusion when, in the Church, those who have undergone no ministry obtain, through the perverse judgment of the electors, a principate to which they have no right.

Since, therefore, among you either popular favor or the ambition of the proud has had such power that we learn that not only laymen but also men with second wives, or husbands of widows, have been advanced to pastoral office, do not the clearest reasons require that the Churches in which these things have been committed be cleansed by a more severe judgment, and that appropriate punishment be inflicted not only on such prelates but also on their ordainers?

Yet we are surrounded on one side by the gentleness of mercy and on the other by the rigor of justice. Since the piety of the universal apostolic See compels us to temper our judgment in such a way that the weight of offenses is carefully assessed—and these offenses are certainly not all of one measure—we believe that some may somehow be tolerated, while others must be completely cut away.

Neither apostolic nor legal authority permits those who have entered a second marriage or joined themselves in marriage to widows to claim the priesthood. Still more must we reject the man who, if disproved in your judgment, is reported to be simultaneously the husband of two wives, or the man who, after being dismissed by his wife, is said to have married another.

As for the others, whose advancement incurs only this criticism, that they were chosen from among laymen for episcopal office, and who cannot be held culpable merely because they have wives, we permit them to retain the priesthood they have received. We do not thereby prejudice the statutes of the apostolic See or annul the rules of the blessed Fathers, by which it was salutarily established that no layman, however much supported by popular votes, should ascend to the first, second, or third grade in the Church before reaching that merit through legitimate advancement.

What we now tolerate to some extent as venial cannot afterward remain unpunished if anyone usurps what we altogether forbid. The remission of sin does not grant permission to sin, nor will what could be conceded for some reason be lawful to commit with impunity thereafter.

Since, concerning almost everything contained in the report of our brother Potentius, you have now seen the fullest account through our brother and fellow bishop David—who has been approved by us both for the merit of his priesthood and for his training in conduct—it remains, brothers, that you receive these salutary exhortations in harmony, doing nothing through contention, but united in every effort of devotion obeying the divine and apostolic constitutions, and permitting the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated in nothing.

What we have remitted after consideration of particular cases must henceforth be guarded according to the ancient rules, lest what we have conceded for a time in merciful leniency be punished by just enforcement. We must be especially and more vigorously moved against those who, in ordaining bishops, neglected the statutes of the holy Fathers and consecrated men whom they ought to have rejected.

Therefore, if any bishops have consecrated a priest of a kind that may not be permitted, even if they have in some way escaped loss of their own honor, they shall no longer possess the right of ordination, nor shall they ever participate in that sacrament which, through disregard of divine judgment, they conferred undeservedly.

We particularly wish this statute concerning priestly dignity to be observed among all the canons: no one is to be consecrated in just any place, in any fort, or in locations where there had previously been no bishops. Where the peoples are smaller and the assemblies smaller, the care of priests is sufficient; episcopal government ought to preside only over larger peoples and more populous cities. Otherwise the priestly dignity, which the divinely inspired decrees of the holy Fathers forbade to be bestowed on villages, estates, obscure places, and solitary townships, will be granted there, and the honor which ought to be entrusted to those of greater distinction will be cheapened by its very proliferation.

Bishop Restitutus has now complained that this has been done in his diocese, and he has reasonably requested that, if the bishops of those places in which they ought not to have been ordained should have died by ordinary human fate, those places should return to the jurisdiction of the bishop to whose authority they had previously belonged. It is useless for priestly dignity to be diminished through the careless ordination of men and its needless multiplication.

Concerning those established in the sacred profession of virginity who suffered barbarous violence and lost the integrity of their chastity not in mind but in body, we think that the following moderation should be observed: they are not to be cast down to the rank of widows, nor are they to be counted among sacred and persevering virgins. Yet, if they persevere in every respect in their virginal commitment and preserve the firmness of chastity in their minds, communion in the sacraments is not to be denied them, because it is unjust to accuse or mark them for what they did not lose by their will but had taken from them by hostile force.

We also order that the case of Bishop Lupicinus be heard there. To him, who has requested communion and an accounting repeatedly and at length, we have restored communion and granted redress, since he had appealed to our judgment, we saw that he had been unjustly suspended from communion while the matter was pending.

It is also reported that another man was rashly set over him, although he ought not to have been ordained before Lupicinus, who is present, had either been disproved or at least confessed his guilt and could justly be subjected to a sentence, so that the vacant place might be occupied by the man being consecrated, as ecclesiastical discipline requires.

If any other cases arise that concern the condition of the Churches and the harmony of the priests, we wish them to be examined there under the fear of the Lord, and a full report of everything resolved and settled to be sent to us, so that whatever has been determined justly and reasonably according to ecclesiastical custom may also be strengthened by our judgment.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of August.

# Decrees of Pope Gelasius

### On moderating ecclesiastical regulations according to the circumstances of the times

**[Col. 0301]**

**[Col. 0301C]**

**1.** Gelasius to all the brethren, the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily.

The necessary administration of affairs constrains us, and the governance of the apostolic See obliges us, to weigh the decrees of the Fathers’ canons and measure the commands of our predecessors, the bishops who have gone before us, in such a way that, after careful consideration, we moderate as far as possible whatever the necessity of the present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the Churches. We must do this so that we may not appear wholly to exceed the form of the ancient rules, while restoring the offices of the clerical service which the incursions of war and famine have so consumed throughout various parts of Italy that, in many Churches—as we have learned from the frequent report of our brother and fellow bishop John, priest of the Church of Ravenna—the service of ministers has been almost entirely exhausted.

Unless the intervals anciently prescribed for ecclesiastical promotions are for a short time relaxed, the Churches will remain utterly deprived of the sacred orders without which they cannot be administered; and in very many places, because of the lack of suitable assistance, the saving support of redeeming souls will be absent. We would incur great guilt if, while such danger presses upon us, we did not provide some remedy.

### That where no urgent necessity exists, the decrees of the Fathers are to be preserved inviolate, and, when clerics are lacking, they may be chosen from monks

**[Col. 0302D]**

**II.** Since the ancient regulations are to remain in force out of reverence for them, and ought to be observed according to the rule wherever no difficulty arising from circumstances or times presses upon us, we grant that the periods for instituting and promoting clerical office may be administered in this way for Churches that are either entirely deprived of ministers or so stripped of adequate service that they cannot provide the divine gifts to the peoples belonging to them.

If someone comes to clerical office from a religious vocation and has been trained in monastic disciplines, his life in past times must first be investigated. It must be determined whether he is not proved to be stained by any serious crime; whether he has perhaps not had a second wife, nor is shown to have taken as his wife a woman abandoned by her husband; whether he has not performed public penance; whether no part of his body appears impaired; whether he is not subject to servile or hereditary status; whether he is already shown to have been released from the bonds of municipal service; and whether he has acquired literacy, without which he could scarcely fulfill even the ministry of doorkeeper.

If he is supported by all the qualifications just mentioned, he may immediately become a lector, notary, or defensor, and after three months become an acolyte—especially if his age also supports this advancement. In the sixth month he may receive the name of subdeacon; if he proves to be of modest conduct and honorable intention, in the ninth month he may be a deacon; and when the year is complete, he may be a presbyter. The devotion voluntarily undertaken through a holy vocation must nevertheless be shown to have supplied what the intervals of years would have contributed.

### That if any laymen are chosen for the clergy, the matters stated concerning monks are to be investigated in them with much greater care

**III.** If, however, some layman is to be added to ecclesiastical offices, his person ought to be examined with proportionately greater care in each of the matters listed above, to the extent that there is known to be a difference between worldly and religious life. Ecclesiastical ministries suited to the Church must not be imposed upon men whose merits are unsuitable.

The qualities that can make someone fit for sacred service must be sought in their formation all the more carefully because time is being taken away from the period in which these qualifications would ordinarily be acquired. He must be shown to possess in character the integrity which a longer habit of life has not provided, lest we be judged, under the pretext of supplying the shortage of clerics, to have introduced vices into divine worship rather than to have secured the advantages of a legitimate household. For such promotions we likewise substitute six months beyond the prescribed annual intervals.

As has been said, there ought to be a distinction between a person devoted to divine worship and one coming from lay conduct. Yet we believe this concession may be granted only to those Churches in which the attacks of war have left either no ministries at all or only a very small number. Once these have been restored, by God’s favor, and persons are again being appointed to the ecclesiastical grades, the ancient form of the Fathers’ canons must be observed. No one should use against them what is provided as a remedy for the deficiency of those entering office; it is not proposed as a new law against the decrees of the elders.

Other Churches, which have not been devastated by a similar calamity, must refrain from this opportunity and retain the former practice in making ordinations. Thus, warned by this occasion, we may devote ourselves more earnestly to observing the venerable canons and admonish the consciences of those in each grade not to attempt unlawful excesses.

Let no bishop presume that he may attach to divine service bigamists, men who have taken women abandoned by other husbands, or persons who have performed penance, or who are without literacy, physically impaired, subject to servile or hereditary status, entangled in municipal or public obligations, or examined without the observance of a suitable period of time. Nor should they presume, according to their own inclination, to invade another’s rights without a just disposition and command of the apostolic See.

### That new basilicas are to be dedicated by bishops in accordance with the pope’s command

**IV.** They must not dare to dedicate newly established basilicas without first seeking the customary commands; nor should they attempt to claim for themselves clerics belonging to another’s authority.

### That no fees are to be demanded for baptizing and confirming the faithful; those who do so will risk their honor

**V.** They must set no fees for baptizing and confirming the faithful, nor seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any exactions, since we are commanded to give freely what we receive freely (Matthew X).

Therefore, they must not attempt to demand anything at all from the persons mentioned above, lest, deterred by poverty or turned back in indignation, they disdain to approach the means of their redemption. They must be certain that those discovered to have committed what is forbidden, or who do not correct their offenses of their own accord, will incur the danger of losing their own honor.

### That presbyters observe the proper measure of their office, not make chrism, not confirm, not presume to pray or sit in the presence of a bishop unless ordered by him, and not make acolytes or subdeacons

**VI.** We likewise forbid presbyters to extend themselves beyond their proper measure or boldly assume for themselves what belongs to episcopal dignity. They must not seize the authority to make chrism or to perform episcopal confirmation; nor, in the presence of any bishop, unless perhaps ordered, presume to claim the right either to pray or to conduct a sacred action; nor, in his presence, unless ordered, presume to sit or handle the venerable mysteries.

They must remember that they are in no way granted the right, without the chief pontiff, to make a subdeacon or an acolyte. They must not doubt that, if they undertake on their own initiative anything specifically belonging to episcopal ministry, they will immediately be deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate and of sacred communion.

We judge that this must occur if such transgression is proved when their bishop brings it forward. Nor will that bishop himself be free from the guilt of connivance and from punishment if he neglects to punish those acting immoderately.

### Likewise, that deacons keep their proper measure according to the decrees of the Fathers

**[Col. 0304D]**

**VII.** We likewise establish that deacons are to keep their proper measure and do not permit them to attempt anything beyond what the paternal canons assign to them. They must not take upon themselves any of those duties which antiquity has assigned specifically to the higher orders. They must not dare to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless extreme necessity should compel them to perform these duties because the persons mentioned above are absent for a considerable distance; even Christian laymen are often permitted to do this.

### That deacons may not sit in the presbyterium, nor exercise precedence over the sacred body when an ecclesiastical proceeding is being held, in the presence of presbyters

**VIII.** Deacons have no right to sit in the presbyterium while divine rites are being celebrated or any ecclesiastical proceeding is being held, nor to exercise precedence over the sacred body in the presence of a bishop or presbyter, except when these are absent.

Since we too strive with the greatest care to preserve the decrees of venerable sanctions, we believe that even those matters which might perhaps appear relaxable for the sake of some useful advantage must not be relaxed at the cost of those decrees.

### That the apostolic See preserves the canons of the Fathers with pious and devoted care

**IX.** Since we wish to presume that nothing is permitted to us contrary to the reverence due to salutary rules, and since, with the Lord’s favor, the apostolic See diligently strives with pious and devoted purpose to maintain all that has been established in the paternal canons, it is wholly unworthy for any bishop or member of the lower orders to reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both follow and teach.

It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance, which it sees flourishing where the Lord has established the principate of the whole Church.

Scripture says: “Set charity in order among me,” and again, “Let all things be done in order” (I Corinthians XIV). The Psalmist likewise proclaims: “Encircle Zion and embrace her; recount her in her towers; set your hearts upon her strength; distribute her ranks, so that you may tell it to another generation. For this is God, our God forever and ever, and he will rule us for ages” (Psalm XLVII).

Here, without doubt, God our God and ruler is to be proclaimed among Christian peoples: in the height of ecclesiastical dignities he is recounted, and in whose strength hearts are to be set, with all the ranks distributed. No one should think that anything has been diminished for him, since nothing is lost from the perfection of each grade; and, by retaining appropriately what has been conferred through heavenly administration, we are enabled both to know God and to acknowledge him as our ruler.

If something is granted concerning the length of time, it is compensated by energetic diligence added to conduct. If what ought to have been accomplished through extended age is already contained in a life devoted to its purpose, this may be acceptable—provided that none of those impediments secretly creep in. If any one of them is shown to be present, it rightly proves the person unfit for clerical insignia.

Although matters which, if the integrity of the others is established, cannot by themselves cause harm may sometimes be allowed, those things must nevertheless be guarded against with the greatest care which cannot be admitted without manifest disfigurement.

If the pressure of circumstances or times, or the need for accelerated provision, excuses even those matters which are sometimes thought permissible without detriment, how much more must those matters not be curtailed which neither necessity nor any ecclesiastical advantage at all demands that we curtail?

### That, apart from the time of Easter and Pentecost, no one may presume to baptize, except those whom extreme illness compels

**X.** No one should think that he possesses unrestricted confidence to baptize at any time whatever, except during the solemn sacrament of the Easter feast and Pentecost, with the sole exception of an attack of the gravest illness. In that case it must be feared that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may perhaps depart overtaken by death without the saving remedy.

### That the ordinations of presbyters and deacons may be celebrated at specified times

**XI.** The ordinations of presbyters and deacons must not be carried out except at fixed times and on appointed days: during the fast of the first and fourth months, the seventh and tenth months, and also at the beginning of Lent and on the midpoint day of Lent; they are to be known as celebrated toward evening on the Saturday fast.

No one, for the sake of any advantage, is to prefer either a presbyter or a deacon to those who were ordained before them.

### That sacred virgins are to be veiled on the appointed days

**XII.** A sacred veil is not to be placed upon dedicated virgins except on the Epiphany, during the white days of Easter, or on the feasts of the Apostles. Nevertheless, as was said concerning baptism, it should not be denied to those seized by severe illness who request it, lest they depart from this world without receiving the gift.

### That widows are not to be veiled

**XIII.** No bishop is to presume to veil widows, since neither divine authority delegates this practice nor the form of the canons establishes it. It is therefore not to be usurped at all; ecclesiastical assistance is to be brought to them in such a way that nothing unlawful is committed.

### That no bishop may defend, under the religious pretext, a slave or hereditary dependent of a Church or monastery against the will of the owners; anyone attempting this will risk his honor and communion

**XIV.** We must also avoid the presumption that has occasioned a general complaint, by which virtually everyone alleges that slaves and hereditary dependents, fleeing the rights and property of their owners, are indiscriminately received—under the pretext of religious conduct—either into monasteries or into ecclesiastical service, with bishops themselves sheltering them.

This evil must be removed by every means, lest, under the institution of the Christian name, another’s property appear to be invaded or public discipline to be overturned. This is especially so because the dignity of clerical ministry itself ought not to be stained by such an obligation, nor be forced to quarrel about the status and condition of those serving it, or to appear—as God forbid—to be subject to persons whom careful and appropriate prohibition has forbidden.

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or person known to preside over monasteries keeps such persons with him and thinks they should not be restored to their patrons, or thereafter thinks they should be assigned either to ecclesiastical service or to religious communities, unless perhaps they have first been released by the will of their owners, as attested in a written document, or have been granted by a lawful settlement, let them not doubt that they will incur the danger of losing their honor and communion if anyone’s truthful complaint brings the matter before us.

For, according to the blessed Apostle, we must take great care lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed (Romans XIV; I Timothy VI).

### That clerics pursue no dishonorable business or shameful profits

**XV.** It was consequently necessary that we should not pass over what a report recently sent to us from the region of Picenum announced: namely, that very many clerics were engaged in dishonorable business and shameful profits, observing without any sense of shame the evangelical reading in which the Lord himself is said to have driven the merchants from the temple with whips (Matthew XXII; John II).

They also disregard the Apostle’s words: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business” (II Timothy II). They likewise close their deaf ears to the Psalmist David singing: “Because I have not known commerce, I will enter into the powers of the Lord” (Psalm LXX).

Therefore, let them know that they must henceforth abstain from such dishonorable gains and cease from every device and desire of business; otherwise, whatever grade they occupy, they must immediately be compelled to withdraw from clerical offices. The house of God must be, and must be called, a house of prayer, lest it instead become a workshop of commerce and a den of thieves (Luke X; Isaiah LVI).

### That no one ignorant of letters or impaired in any part of the body is to be promoted to the clergy

**XVI.** We have also learned that illiterate men and those impaired in some part of the body are being admitted indiscriminately to ecclesiastical service. Ancient tradition and the established practice of the apostolic See do not accept this, because a man without literacy cannot be fit for sacred offices, and the legal commands have decreed that nothing defective is to be offered at all to God (Leviticus XXI).

Accordingly, such practices must henceforth be avoided in every way, and no such person is to be admitted to the clergy. If any such men have already been admitted, whether through their own rashness or through the negligence of those presiding, let them remain in the positions to which they have been appointed, but let them never seize any further promotion. They should consider it sufficient that, out of excessive compassion, even this has been permitted to them.

### Concerning those who castrate themselves

**XVII.** Concerning those who have castrated themselves, the canons of the Fathers have clearly set down what must be followed; it is sufficient to insert their provision. They say that those who commit such acts, as soon as they are recognized, must be excluded from clerical office. We must observe this in every respect, since no one is authorized to judge otherwise than the memorable rule has decreed.

### That criminals cannot be promoted to the clergy, and that those already in the clergy, if found guilty of crimes, are to be excluded from their offices

**[Col. 0307D]**

**XVIII.** We have discovered that certain men involved in appalling crimes, with all discernment set aside, are not only without the necessary repentance for their atrocious deeds, but are also striving for the honor of divine ministry without any correction having followed.

Others, already established in the orders, are not being rejected when they commit serious crimes, even though the Apostle cries out: “Let hands be laid quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (I Timothy V). The venerable constitutions of the Fathers likewise declare that both those who sinned before ordination, if detected even after they have slipped into office, must be expelled, and those who have forgotten their sacred profession and violated their holy vocation must undoubtedly be removed.

### That those entangled in demons and other afflictions may not handle the sacred ministries

**XIX.** We have discovered that unlawful practices have advanced to such an extent that those entangled in demons and similar afflictions are being entrusted with handling the most sacred ministries. If, while engaged in this work, some personal necessity should arise for them, who could have confidence concerning the salvation of the faithful when he sees the ministers themselves afflicted by such a calamity requiring human healing?

They must therefore necessarily be removed, lest scandal be generated among the weak, for whom Christ died. Finally, if divine law did not permit a person wounded or disabled in body to touch holy things (Romans XIV; I Corinthians VIII; Leviticus XXII), how much less is it fitting that those struck down in mind should be dispensers of the heavenly gift?

## That those who join themselves to sacred virgins and enter into incestuous unions may not receive communion unless they have perhaps performed public penance

### XX

We have learned that certain men rashly join themselves to sacred virgins and, after the dedication of their purpose to God, enter into incestuous and sacrilegious unions. It is immediately just that such men be driven from sacred communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance; or at least, if they have repented, viaticum should not be denied them as they depart from this world.

## That widows, as stated above, are not to be veiled, and that if, after changing their purpose, they trample upon the continence they have professed, they themselves must render an account to God for their own deeds

[Col. 0308C]

### XXI

For concerning the veiling of widows under no blessing whatsoever, we have already discussed the matter at length above. If, by their own will, they trample with changeable minds upon the chastity they professed from their former marriage, it will be their concern with what satisfaction they ought to appease God for their danger. For just as, if they were perhaps unable to remain continent, they were in no way forbidden to marry, according to the Apostle (I Tim. V), so, after deliberating with themselves, they ought to have kept the pledge of chastity promised to God.

We, however, ought to impose no snare upon such women, but set before them only exhortations concerning eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may render an account to God on their own behalf. For one must beware of what blessed Paul the Apostle testifies concerning their morals and actions (in the same place). We refrain from explaining it more plainly, lest the unstable sex should seem to be not so much deterred as admonished.

## That second marriages are not denied to secular persons, but that, on account of this deed, they are by no means permitted to enter the clergy

[Col. 0308D]

### XXII

Just as secular persons are permitted to enter into a second marriage, so after it no one is permitted to enter the clerical fellowship. For one permission is that generally granted to human frailty; another ought to be the life dedicated to the service of divine things (I Cor. VII).

## That if anyone receives a deserter from his own Church and advances him to some dignity, both are to be subject to the sentence established by the canons

### XXIII

Whoever, having deserted his own Church without any [Col. 0309A] existing cause, thinks he ought to transfer to another, and whoever has rashly received and promoted him, whether the deserter himself or his receiver and promoter, will not escape the regulations established by the venerable canons concerning presumptuous persons of this kind.

## That if any of the monks and laymen mentioned above are chosen for the clergy, the ancient regulations concerning them must be observed when no necessity compels otherwise; but if they are proved to have purchased sacred dignity for a price, they are to be deposed from office, for the crime of Simon Magus implicates both giver and receiver

### XXIV

Concerning monks and laymen, we dealt more fully in the first part of this injunction with what concessions have been made according to the necessity of circumstances and times, and with how, wherever no necessity arising from any deed is shown to exist, the ancient institution alone ought to be [Col. 0309B] observed. But those who are clearly shown to have purchased sacred dignity for a price, unworthy as they are of it, must be barred once convicted; those who commit such a crime do so at their peril, because condemnation by Simon Magus, as Holy Scripture bears witness (Acts VIII), involves giver and receiver alike.

## Concerning newly established sacred places: although this was said above, it is now added that no basilica is to be dedicated under the name of the dead

### XXV

Although the consecration of holy places was briefly included above, it has also become clear to us that some presume to consecrate churches or oratories constructed without the command of the apostolic see. We have nevertheless been moved by this still more detestable report: they are said boldly to establish for sacred functions buildings constructed under the name of any deceased persons—and, as is reported, persons who are not even among the faithful. [Col. 0309C] Since these practices are so bitter and harsh that our hearing can scarcely endure them, if the Christian devotion in those regions is truly firm and established, let these matters be investigated with greater strictness and let those by whom they were done be disclosed.

For just as, while the names remain hidden in this atrocity, there is no one against whom the deserved sentence may be pronounced, so, when the matter has been exposed by clear evidence, the enormity of so great a crime will in no way escape the vengeance it requires.

## That it is unlawful for women to minister at the sacred altars or to presume to undertake any of those offices assigned to men

[Col. 0309D]

### XXVI

Nevertheless, we have heard with indignation that such contempt for divine things has arisen that women are affirmed to minister at the sacred altars and to perform for a sex to which it does not belong everything assigned solely to the service of men. Yet the guilt and crime of all the offenders in each of the transgressions we have touched upon fall upon those priests who either commit these acts or, by failing to make public those who commit them, show that they favor such wicked excesses—if indeed those who strive so to overthrow the religious office entrusted to them that, without any regard for Christian discipline, they eagerly pursue every perverse and profane precipice are still to be called priests.

Since it is written (Ecclus. XIX), “Whoever despises what is least falls little by little,” what should be thought of such men, [Col. 0310A] who, overwhelmed by immense and manifold masses of depravity, have brought about a great ruin through assaults of many kinds—a ruin that seems not only to bury them themselves but, unless they are healed, to inflict deadly destruction upon all the Churches?

Let those who have dared to practice these things, and also those who have hitherto kept silent about what they knew, have no doubt that they lie under the loss of their own honor, unless they hasten with all possible speed so that these lethal wounds may be cured by suitable treatment. For by what manner do they uphold the rights of bishops, when they conceal the duties imposed upon episcopal vigilance to such an extent that they instead commit acts contrary to the house of God over which they preside?

Let them consider how much they might merit before God if they pursued only what is fitting, and how much they deserve when, with detestable zeal, they pursue the opposite, and [Col. 0310B] when, as though this were rather the rule by which the Church ought to be governed, everything hostile to ecclesiastical regulations is perpetrated. For even if each bishop knew the canons, he ought to have maintained them with unbroken vigilance; and if perhaps he did not know them, he ought confidently to have consulted someone who did. Thus no excuse comes to the aid of those who err: one who did not know set out to preserve what he knew, and one who was not ignorant took care to know what he was doing.

## That in each Church presided over by a bishop, four portions are to be made both from revenue and from the offerings of the faithful: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the Church buildings

### XXVII

Four portions ought to be made both from revenue and from the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each Church permit [Col. 0310C] (as was reasonably decreed long ago): one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the buildings.

Concerning these portions, just as it will be the priest’s responsibility to pay the entire amount mentioned to the ministers of the Church, so the clergy must understand that they may insolently demand nothing beyond the sum assigned to them. The amount allotted to ecclesiastical buildings, truly devoted to this work, must be shown by the evident restoration of the holy places. For it is unlawful that, when sacred buildings are left without resources, a bishop should divert to his own profit the expenses designated for them.

Likewise, although he may appear to have distributed the portion assigned to the poor according to divine accounting, it must nevertheless, in accordance with what is written, “that they may see your good works and glorify your Father [Col. 0310D]” (Matt. I), also be proclaimed through present testimony and not be concealed from the praises of good reputation.

## That if a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is truthfully accused by any cleric of acting against these regulations, he may without hesitation be struck by judgment; and that a bishop will also endanger his own honor if he keeps silent about these matters, which the whole Church ought to know

### XXVIII

Therefore, let no cleric suppose that he will be immune from this offense if, when he sees either a bishop, presbyter, or deacon transgressing in the matters we have set forth for salutary observance, he does not immediately take care to report it to our ears, provided that suitable proofs are duly presented, so that vengeance may fall upon the transgressor and prohibition [Col. 0311A] upon the others against offending.

Each bishop, however, will in every way be the destroyer of his own rank and honor if he thinks these matters [Col. 0312A] ought to be suppressed from the hearing of any cleric or of the entire Church.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, most illustrious men. (A.D. 494.)

# DECREES OF POPE ANASTASIUS

[Col. 0311]

[Col. 0311A] To the most glorious and merciful son, Anastasius Augustus: Anastasius, bishop.

At the beginning of my pontificate, I first proclaim the peace bestowed upon the peoples; thereafter, for the sake of the Catholic faith, I approach your humble piety as a suppliant. In the first of these matters I trust that I have drawn near to divine favor, since the harmony between myself and your most august name plainly provides assistance, so that, just as the exalted title of your piety shines throughout all nations across the whole world, so through the ministry of my humility the see of the most blessed Peter may hold in the universal Church—as it has always done—the primacy assigned to it by the Lord God, and may not, on account of one dead man, allow that saving garment, woven from above throughout its whole length (John XIX), to suffer the uncertainty of an evil lot; for it alone could not be brought into division because of its firmness.

Even in private life he showed such devotion to the pursuit of sincere religion that, as the most certain report has proclaimed, no one, even among the foremost priests, is said to have guarded the rules of the Church established by the holy Fathers more faithfully. We trust that this holy zeal has increased together with the majesty of imperial power.

## That he acts as Christ’s ambassador while pleading for the peace of the Church

[Col. 0311C]

### I

We therefore act as ambassadors for Christ, so that you may not allow those persons to be publicly named on account of offense or scandal whose merits and deeds cannot be hidden from that Judge before whose judgment they already stand. Nor can rash presumption, still in a mortal body, intrude there, where not only open confession reveals the merits of each person, but even the secret of silence itself cannot remain hidden.

For our predecessor, Pope Felix, and also Acacius are unquestionably there, where no one, under so great a Judge, can lose the quality of his own merit.

## That judgment must not be rashly passed upon those who have already departed to God

### II

Therefore, since blessed Paul the Apostle warns us that this must be observed lest there be an occasion of offense in the Church, when we attempt to judge those who have already departed—something we cannot do—let your tranquility know this.

For he says concerning those who presume to judge matters belonging to God alone (Rom. XIV):

“No one among us lives for himself, and no one dies for himself. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For Christ rose from the dead for this purpose, that he might rule over both the living and the dead. But you, why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God.”

For it is written (Isa. XLV): “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.” Therefore, each of us will render an account to God for himself. Let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling block or an occasion of scandal before your brother.

The blessed Apostle therefore warns that no one should presumptuously usurp judgment in this matter, daring to judge those concerning whom no one can judge more truly or better than God, and that, on this account, the peace and unity of the Church should not be shattered.

For it is also said in the Book of Kings (II Kings XVI): “God does not see as man sees, because man sees the face, but God sees the heart.” Likewise, in the First Book of Chronicles (I Chron. XXVIII): “And now, Solomon, know the God of your fathers, and serve him with a perfect heart and willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts and knows every thought.” Likewise, in Ezekiel the Lord says this (Ezek. XI): “Thus you have said, house of Israel, and I know the thoughts of your spirit.” Hence it is also said of the Lord as Judge in the Gospel: “But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said: Why do you think evil in your hearts?”

## That the name of Acacius is to be silenced specifically in the Church

### III

We therefore ask your clemency that, in particular, the name which for many reasons has stirred scandal and offense in the Church be silenced by special designation. As we have said, in the general company of priests the merit of each person cannot be hidden from that Judge, who alone knows what ought to be assigned to each according to the considered distribution of merits, since even their thoughts are manifest to him.

As for the many excesses and presumptions of Acacius, lest it perhaps seem burdensome to your clemency for us to report them one by one, we have given Cresconius and Germanus, my brothers and fellow bishops, whom we have sent to your serenity, a complete account of the individual matters concerning Acacius and of what sort of man he was. If it should please your piety to investigate more carefully, this account may be reviewed in particular by your clemency, so that the truth of our representation may not appear in any respect to have been lacking.

Thus, in accordance with your divine wisdom, you may clearly see that the sentence against Acacius did not proceed from pride or exaltation of the apostolic see, but from certain crimes—as far as we can judge outside that judgment which alone cannot err—and arose rather from zeal for divinity.

## That contention must be avoided with the greatest care

### IV

We, however, humbly supplicating, do not wish controversy to remain in the Church, since contention must be avoided above all, as it is said in Proverbs (chap. X): “Contention stirs up hatred.” Friendship protects all who do not contend.

For the Apostle also says to the Corinthians (I Cor. III): “Since there are jealousies and contentions among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” Likewise, to the Philippians (chap. II): “If, therefore, there is any consolation in Christ, any encouragement of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tenderness and compassion, complete my joy by saying the same thing, having the same love, doing nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility of mind considering one another superior to yourselves, each looking not to his own interests but to those of others.”

## That he should admonish the Alexandrians to return to sincere faith and Catholic peace

### V

This above all I bring to the attention of your serenity, most glorious and merciful son Augustus: when the case of the Alexandrians has been laid open to your most pious ears, compel them by your authority, wisdom, and divine admonitions to return to sincere and Catholic faith.

If you also command it, we shall renew what is to be held in the Catholic religion according to the definitions of the Fathers and the teaching of all the priests who have flourished in the Church, handing it down to the memory of those who know it and offering it for learning, as our duty of instruction requires, to those who are ignorant, so that no boastfulness or depravity of human ingenuity may be heard outside these things.

## The emperor is admonished to obey the regulations of the apostolic see

### VI

For the love of your empire and for the blessedness that the kingdom may attain, we proclaim this especially in accordance with our apostolic office: as is fitting and as the Holy Spirit dictates, obedience should be given to our admonitions, so that all good things may attend your commonwealth, as is promised in Exodus (Exod. XV):

“If you will hear the voice of the Lord your God and do what is pleasing [Col. 0313C] before him, obey his commandments, and keep all his justice, I will not bring upon you any of the sicknesses that I brought upon the Egyptians; for I am the Lord who saves you.”

And there again the most powerful trumpet is sounded:

“And now, Israel, what else does the Lord your God require of you except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, love him, and serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul?” (Deut. X).

“Keep the commandments of the Lord your God and his ordinances, which I command you.”

Let your piety not repeatedly despise me when I bring these things to your attention, keeping before your eyes the words of the Lord in the Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me, and whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke X).

The Apostle, agreeing with our Savior, also says: “Therefore, whoever despises these things despises not man but God, who has given his Holy Spirit in us” (I Thess. IV).

The breast of your clemency is the sanctuary of public happiness, so that through your perseverance—since he commanded you to preside on earth as his representative—there may be no resistance to evangelical and apostolic commands through harsh pride, but that what brings salvation may be fulfilled through obedience.

## That no injury is to touch those whom Acacius baptized or ordained after his condemnation

### VII

In accordance with the custom of the Catholic Church, let your most sacred serenity recognize that no portion of injury on account of Acacius is to touch any of those whom Acacius baptized or whom he ordained as priests or levites according to the canons, so that the grace of the sacrament bestowed through him should not perhaps appear less firm because it was delivered through an unrighteous man. [Col. 0314A]

For even baptism—although it be far from the Church, or be given by an adulterer or a thief—reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift, because that voice which sounded through the dove excludes every stain of human pollution. This is made clear when it is said (John I): “This is he who baptizes with the Spirit and with fire.”

If the rays of this visible sun, when they pass through exceedingly foul places, are not stained by any pollution from contact, how much more is the power of the one who made this visible sun constrained by no unworthiness of a minister?

Judas too, although he was sacrilegious and a thief, whatever he did among the apostles in accordance with the dignity entrusted to him, caused no loss to the benefits bestowed through an unworthy person. The Lord declares this in the clearest voice [Col. 0314B] (Matt. XIII): “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon the chair of Moses. Do whatever they say, but do not do what they do; for they speak and do not act.”

Therefore, whatever any minister in the Church appears to perform for the advancement of human beings in accordance with his office is wholly contained within the effect of fulfilling divinity. Thus Paul, through whom Christ speaks, affirms (I Cor. III): “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

God does not ask who or what sort of person preaches, but whom he preaches, so that he confirms that even the envious preach Christ well. The devil himself was cast down because of this evil, yet by that very means he does not cease to preach.

## That wicked men harm only themselves when ministering good things and do not stain the sacraments of the Church

[Col. 0314C]

### VIII

Therefore this man, whose name we say ought to be withheld, harmed only himself by ministering good things wickedly. The inviolable sacrament, however, which was given through him, obtained for others the perfection of its power.

Since this is so, the curious suspicion of certain people has extended so far that, after Pope Felix pronounced his judgment, it imagines that Acacius subsequently acted ineffectively in the sacraments which he usurped. Accordingly, those who received the mysteries delivered either in consecrations or in baptism fear that the divine benefits may appear void.

Let them remember that the foregoing treatment prevails equally in this matter, since the one who was condemned did this not without usurping the priesthood. While the mysteries retain their power, the person guilty before himself did not harm others in this matter either. For what concerned him is expressed in the trumpet of David:

“Yet God has shattered the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins” (Ps. X).

Pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon another, as the entire authority of the heavenly Scriptures bears witness. Thus it is also said through the Holy Spirit in the prophet: “The one who practices pride has not dwelt in the midst of my house” (Ezek. XVIII).

Therefore, since he claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head in condemnation. The people, who thirsted for his gift in the mysteries, were not excluded; only that sinful soul, which had offended, was properly subject to a just judgment. The abundant teaching of the Scriptures everywhere bears witness to this.

Therefore, with the interests and stratagems of human beings who are still placed in this present frailty removed, in accordance with our prayers, may you by imperial effort and authority offer to our God one Catholic and apostolic Church. [Col. 0315A] For this alone is that in which [Col. 0316A] you may triumph forever not only on earth but also in heaven.

**Subscription:** May almighty God preserve your kingdom and salvation with perpetual protection, most glorious, most merciful, and forever Augustus.

# APPENDIX TO THE DIONYSIAN COLLECTION

[Col. 0315]

## CATALOGUE OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS WHOSE DECREES ARE INCLUDED IN THIS COLLECTION

| HILARY | 461 |
