# REGULATIONS OF HILARY, IN THE CONSULSHIP OF FLAVIUS BASILICUS AND HERMINERICUS, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MEN

[Col. 0315]

[Col. 0315B]

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, when the venerable man Pope Hilary was presiding in the basilica of Saint Mary, and Maximus of the city of Turin in the province of Gaul; Ingenuus of the province of Embrun; the holy men of the province of Milan; Saturninus of Avignon;

Peter of Porto; Primus of Atella; Gaudentius of Abitina; Paulinus of Aquaebia; Palladius of Salapia; Soter of Naples; Tiburtius of Capua; Felix of Luna; Eusebius of Siena; Justus of Falerii; Concordius of Bari; Caprarius of Casinum; Constantius of Aquino; Praetextatus of Interamna; Claudius of Pausula;

[Col. 0315C]

Adeodatus of Velletri; Crispianus of Subaugusta; Servodeus of Nomentum; Hilary of Ameria; Paul of Forum Novum; Apuleius of Tarquinii; Asterius of Gabii; Asterius of Forojulium; Gaudentius of Vecconia; Gaudentius of Scyllacium; Eubodius of Trapezus; Majorianus of Asti; Felix of Sipontum; Uranus; Januarius of Praeneste; Adeodatus of Como; Tiberius of Cures in the Sabine territory; Gerontius of Camerinum; Lucifer of Tifernum Metaurense; Romanus of Alba; Florentius of Talesia;

[Col. 0316B]

Candidus of Tibur; Eusebius of Sutrium; Gaudentius of Antium; Projectus of Nepi; Philippus of Nomentum; Restitutus and Octavius of Africa.

With all the presbyters also present, and the deacons standing by, Hilary, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome and presiding over the synod, said:

Since this religious assembly, gathered by the Holy Spirit, urges us to deal with all matters necessary for ecclesiastical discipline with more diligent care, if it pleases you, brothers, let us, with the Lord’s assistance, establish for all ages those matters that pertain to the order of ordinations, in accordance with the precepts of divine law and the regulations of the Nicene canons. Let us establish them so firmly that no one may rashly violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see without endangering his own status.

For we, who administer the duties of the highest priesthood, will be answerable for the guilt of such transgressions if we are found negligent in the matters of God. We remember how the Lord threatens the negligence of priests, since the one who enjoys greater honor commits a greater offense, and the height of dignities makes the vices of sinners more serious.

Above all, therefore, care must be taken that, as was previously prescribed in the earlier records, no one who has married a woman who was not a virgin should aspire to the sacred ranks. Anyone who has entered into a second marriage contrary to the apostolic precepts must likewise be rejected. Those ignorant of letters, those who have suffered the loss of any limb, and those who are penitents must not dare to aspire to the sacred orders.

Whoever has consecrated such a person will himself undo what he has done. If he wishes to avoid his own danger, he will condemn what he has unlawfully committed or what he has found admitted by his predecessors. For we do not wish to exercise the severity of vengeance in any matter. But whoever has offended in the matters of God through obstinacy or negligence, or has been unwilling to abolish what he wrongly did, will find in himself whatever he has not cut off from another.

So that this may henceforth be guarded more firmly, if it pleases you, submit all the matters and your own subscriptions, so that access to unlawful acts may be closed by synodal judgment.

The bishops and presbyters all acclaimed:

“Hear us, O Christ”; “May Hilary live”—said six times.

“We confirm these things; we teach these things”—said eight times.

“These things must be held; these things must be observed”—said five times.

“We give thanks for your teachings”—said ten times.

“We ask that these things be observed forever”—said fifteen times.

“Through the lord Peter, we ask that they be observed forever”—said eight times.

“May such presumption never occur”—said ten times.

“Whoever violates these things will find it in himself”—said seven times.

After silence had been made, Hilary the bishop said:

Moreover, brothers, as has reached us through letters sent from Spain in a definite report, new and unheard-of seeds of depravity are continually arising in certain places. Some people, finally, regard the episcopate—which is granted only on the basis of preceding merits—not as a divine gift but as an inherited advantage, and believe that the priesthood, like perishable and mortal possessions, can be transferred by legal or testamentary right.

For many priests, placed at the threshold of death, are said to designate others by name to be substituted in their place, so that a legitimate election is not awaited, but the favor of the deceased is counted as the consent of the people. Consider how serious this is. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us also remove this permission generally from the Churches, lest—shameful though it is to say so—anyone should think that he ought to claim as his own what belongs to God.

But so that what has been reported to us may also come to your knowledge, let the writings of our Spanish brothers and fellow bishops be read.

Paul the notary recited them.

To the most blessed Pope Hilary, honored by us in Christ with apostolic reverence: Ascanias and all the bishops of the province of Tarragona.

Your apostolic concern for the priests of your provinces, we have learned from our illustrious son Vincentius, governor of our province, whose prompting caused our wish to rise, with willing devotion, to the boldness of writing. Therefore, rendering to your crown the due services in a letter from the province, we ask that, with the same condescension by which you deign to keep the others in mind in your prayers, you also deign to remember our humility; and, most blessed father, revered by us with apostolic reverence in Christ, we especially beseech you to strengthen by carefully considered assertions what we have done, which is brought to your knowledge both by the wish of almost the entire province and by the example of antiquity.

As he read, all the bishops and presbyters acclaimed:

“Hear us, O Christ; Hilarus, may you live,” was said ten times.

“Let this presumption never occur,” was said six times.

“What belongs to God cannot be given by man,” was said six times.

“Through the lord Peter, may these things be preserved forever,” was said six times.

“We ask that these things be reserved.”

Bishop Hilarus said: “Read.”

The notary Paulus read:

“The holy Nundinatius, bishop of the city of Barcino, fulfilled the lot of human condition. To our venerable brother, Bishop Irenaeus, whom he himself had previously established in his diocese with our consent, he left whatever supreme poverty could possess according to the freedom of his will, and he wished that Irenaeus be substituted in his place. But the judgment of the deceased does not waver regarding his merit.

“As this was being read, Bishop Probus rose from his seat and said: ‘That was permitted; this was not permitted. God gives successors. Resist this matter by your apostolic authority.’

“Bishop Hilarus said: ‘Continue what you began.’

“The notary Paulus read:

“Indeed, all the clergy and people of the same city, together with the leading men and the greater number of the provincials, hoped from us, once our consent had been given, that he might occupy the same position. We considered the judgment of the deceased, approved his life, and considered the nobility and number of those who were making the request, as well as the advantage to the aforesaid Church. We therefore judged it best that a bishop of no lesser merit should be substituted for so great a priest who had departed to the divine realm, especially since it is clear that the Church of that municipality, in which he had previously been ordained, had always been a diocese of the Church of this city.

“Therefore we humbly beseech your apostolic office to confirm by your authority what appears to have been justly done by our humility. Some time ago we had also complained in our letters about the presumption of Bishop Sylvanus, and we are astonished that we have received no reply from your apostolic office. Now, bringing the same matters to your attention, we ask that you deign to instruct us by apostolic pronouncements concerning what must be observed in these matters. And lest perhaps, through the negligence of the bearer or the difficulty of the long journey, our letter concerning this affair should not have reached you, we have preferred to repeat our petition.”

And the subscription:

“May the divine eternity preserve your holy apostolic office, which prays for us, throughout perpetual ages, for all of us and for His Church, truly our lord and apostolic pope.”

Bishop Hilarus said: “Let another letter be read.”

The notary Paulus read:

“To the most blessed lord and pope Hilarus, revered by us with apostolic reverence in Christ, Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarraconensis.

“Even if no necessity of ecclesiastical discipline existed, we truly ought to have sought that privilege of your see by which, after receiving the keys of the kingdom, the unique preaching of the most blessed Peter, following the Savior’s resurrection, provided illumination for the whole world. The primacy of his vicar, just as it is preeminent, is likewise to be feared and loved by all.

“Accordingly, worshiping God first of all in you, whom you serve without complaint, we return to the faith praised by the apostolic mouth (Romans I), seeking answers from the place where nothing is commanded through error, nothing through presumption, but everything through pontifical deliberation.

“Although matters stand thus, there is nevertheless among us a false brother. Just as his presumption did not permit us to remain silent any longer, so the necessity of the future judgment compelled us to speak. Sylvanus, bishop of Calagurris, established in the farthest part of our province, by usurping ordinations not due to him has driven our humility to the point that, against his utterly empty superstition, we demand the unique remedy of your see.

“For already seven or eight years or more, setting aside the regulations of the Fathers and disregarding your institutions, he ordained a bishop when no people had asked for one. We thought that his rash action could be healed by fraternal and peaceful admonition, but he advanced to worse. Finally, against the antiquity of the canons and against the decrees of the synod, inflamed only by the spirit of presumption, in the same place that had been assigned to another of our brothers, he made him a bishop—he had imposed hands upon that man unwillingly and against his resistance, even though he had already been incorporated into our assembly.

“Thus it happened that our brother, the bishop of the city of Caesaraugusta, reported the whole matter to us concerning his most wretched rashness; his diligence and concern had taken great care to prevent this, if only it had been of any help. Indeed, he repeatedly warned all the bishops situated in the neighboring region not to join themselves to a schismatic. Yet, with damnable obstinacy, that man alone did not blush to commit everything that was illicit—and what we are ashamed to say—everything that is shameful to utter.

“Therefore, since these presumptions, which divide unity and create schism, must be confronted swiftly, we ask your see to instruct us through apostolic utterances concerning what you wish to be observed in this matter. Thus, with the brotherhood gathered and the decrees of the venerable synod brought forward, supported by your authority against the spirit of rebellion, we may, with God’s help, understand what ought to be done both concerning the ordination and concerning the man who was ordained.

“Your triumph will surely be complete if, during the time of your apostolic office, the Catholic Church hears what the chair of Saint Peter possesses, and if the new seeds of the weeds are uprooted.”

And the subscription:

“May the divine eternity preserve your holy apostolic office, which prays for us, throughout perpetual ages.”

All the bishops and presbyters acclaimed:

“We ask that these things be corrected,” was said six times.

“We ask that these things be cut away,” was said seven times.

“We ask that discipline be preserved,” was said eight times.

“We ask that antiquity be preserved,” was said seven times.

“We ask that discipline [sic] be preserved,” was said five times.

“We ask that the canons be guarded,” was said seven times.

“We ask that punishment be imposed upon the presumptuous,” was said seven times.

“Let the apostolic ordination be preserved inviolate,” was said eight times.

“Hear us, O Christ; Hilarus, may you live,” was said five times.

“A worthy pope, a worthy teacher,” was said eight times.

Bishop Hilarus said:

“Having heard what has been read concerning all these matters, now, brothers, bring forward your particular judgments, with God inspiring us.”

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Taurina, said:

“In guarding all the disciplines pertaining to sacred ordinations, I declare more effectively through the profession of my judgment that I shall never do any of what is forbidden. Concerning the rest, I judge that whoever does such things, or refuses to cut away what has been detected in the Churches, should know that he will have to render a grave account before the judgment of the apostolic see, where he will necessarily undergo its sentence.”

Ingenuus, bishop of Ebrodunum, said:

“My judgment concerning all these matters is likewise the same, by which I bind myself lest I ever attempt anything forbidden in these matters, because I know my status and profession. Concerning the rest also I judge that whoever proves to be a transgressor of the statutes should know that he is bound by the snares of ecclesiastical rule and incurs the guilt of the apostolic see.”

Paulus, bishop of Aquaeviva, said:

“I too bind myself by a similar law, and concerning the others who may be transgressors I judge likewise, so that they may not dare to attempt anything of this kind without danger to themselves, when it ought rightly to be punished.”

Primus, bishop of the Church of Atella, said:

“I too judge that this must be observed.”

Palladius, bishop of the Church of Salapia, said:

“I promise that I shall do nothing against ecclesiastical discipline or the statutes of the holy canons.”

Tiberius, bishop of the Church of Sabina, said:

“I profess that I shall observe the statutes of the apostolic see in all things. If in my Church I discover any cleric who, contrary to the commands of the holy canons, has taken a woman or has two wives, he shall be separated from ecclesiastical office.”

All the bishops said:

“We all follow the judgments of the brothers; we all confirm them, and we decree that they must be observed.”

“Hear us, O Christ; Hilarus, may you live,” was said seven times.

“May what has been wrongly admitted be corrected through you,” was said eight times.

“Let what is not permitted not be done,” was said eight times.

Hilarus, bishop of the Church of the city of Rome and presiding over the synod, said:

“Since we decree that the form of the present decision, established according to the judgment of the holy Fathers, must reach the knowledge of all the Churches, the diligence of the notaries shall take care to publish the acts, so that no one may claim that what is not permitted is permitted because of ignorance.”

Hilarus to Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarraconensis.

“After receiving the letters of your affection, in which you requested that the presumptions of Sylvanus, bishop of the Church of Calagurris, be restrained, and again asked that the excessively illicit wishes of the people of Barcino be confirmed, we have learned that letters from the leading men and landowners of the cities of Turiasso, Ascantum, Calagurris, Varegia, Tritium, Leviana, and Veroviscum, together with the subscriptions of various persons, were sent to us. Through these letters they excused what your complaint had brought forward concerning Sylvanus.

“Yet their most just reproof was not lacking a correspondingly just allegation, because it became clear that priests had been ordained in certain cities without the knowledge of the metropolitan, our brother and fellow bishop Ascanius. Therefore, since we see that whatever has been reported by either side is thoroughly confused by perversity, having considered the necessity of the times, we decree by this reasoning that what has been done pertains to pardon, provided that henceforth nothing is attempted against the commands of the blessed Apostle or against the decrees of the canons of Nicaea.

“I. First, according to the regulations of those same Fathers, we wish this to be guarded: no bishop is to be consecrated in any way without the knowledge and consent of our brother Ascanius, the metropolitan. The ancient order has maintained this, and the authority of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers has defined it. Whoever stretches out his hands against this confesses himself unworthy of the fellowship of those whose commands he has resisted.

“II. In insult to these Fathers, that other provision is also despised through a proud spirit, by which it is forbidden for anyone to presume to leave his own Church and pass to another. Bishop Irenaeus is attempting to commit this, while you most improperly connive at it and, more grievously still, maintain it. Yet you desire to be strengthened by our authority, though you profess yourselves especially inflamed with great indignation over unlawful matters.

“Therefore, after your letters had been read in the assembly of the brothers whom the celebration of my birthday had gathered—letters in which you set forth what concerns the ordination of bishops according to the statutes of the canons and the decrees of my predecessors—you will learn the decision from the tenor of the acts that we have likewise sent.

“III. Therefore, once Bishop Irenaeus has been removed from the Church of Barcino and sent back to his own, and once the desires that, through ignorance of ecclesiastical laws, seek to obtain what is not permitted have been calmed through priestly modesty, a bishop is immediately to be ordained for the people of Barcino from their own clergy, such as you, brother Ascanius, ought especially to choose and would properly consecrate. Otherwise, if something similar should have been done, our command will rebuke it—not without reproach directed chiefly at your name—because we have learned that something has been admitted to the injury of God, from whom alone the grace of priestly dignities comes. Nor must episcopal honor be considered a hereditary right, since it is bestowed upon us solely by the kindness of our God, Christ.

“IV. We nevertheless confirm the bishops who have now been ordained—although they were advanced without your knowledge and deserved to be removed together with those responsible for them—provided that none of them has been the husband of a widow and that he has entered into the marriage and vows of one virgin, as the legal statutes also command when they say: ‘A priest shall take a virgin as his wife, not a widow, not one who has been repudiated’ (Leviticus XXI; Ezekiel XLIV). In accordance with this, blessed Paul the Apostle, teacher of the nations, also did not remain silent in his own instruction concerning those who desire to become priests, saying (1 Timothy III): ‘The husband of one wife.’ You ought to be instructed by the force of this judgment so that, among the other things that must be avoided, you take special care to preserve what you know is commanded above all else.

“V. Among these matters it must also be ensured that there are not two priests in one Church, that no one ignorant of letters or lacking any part of his limbs, and that no one from among the penitents, is ever permitted to approach the sacred ministry. Nor should you think that the petitions of the people have such force that, when you wish to comply with them, you abandon the will of our Lord, which forbids us to sin. His indignation is stirred more gravely by this, because his kindness is offended when illicit acts are committed by those who are interpreters of reconciliation.

“VI. So that all things may be corrected according to what we have written, we have sent this letter with the arrival of our subdeacon Trajanus. But if Bishop Irenaeus neglects, after laying aside the ambitious wrongdoing, to return to his own Church—a concession granted to him not as a matter of judgment but of humanity—let him know that he must be removed from the fellowship of bishops.

“Given on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Basilicus and Herminericus, illustrious men. (A.D. 465.)”

# DECREES OF POPE SIMPLICIUS

I. Simplicius, bishop, to Joannes, bishop of Ravenna.

“If you had any regard for ecclesiastical discipline, or if any priestly modesty were maintained by you, punishable excesses would never have been committed. If you were unable to restrain yourself from them by any command of the rules of the Fathers, at least you ought to have been recalled by the example of your predecessor of holy memory, who, though he had erred less in making an unwilling man a presbyter, nevertheless understood that a judgment worthy of such usurpation awaited him.

“Where did you learn these actions, which you committed against our brother and fellow bishop Gregory—not through election, but through envy? You allowed him to be dragged to you and harassed by an inexcusable violence, so that you might confer honor upon him not through tranquility of mind but, as must be said, through madness. Such things could not have been done with sound judgment. We do not wish to exaggerate what was done, lest we be compelled to pronounce the judgment it deserves. For he deserves to lose his privilege who abuses the power entrusted to him.

“But one consideration makes us give a milder judgment, which we preferred to have you learn from the report of our brother and fellow bishop Projectus rather than publish it in our letters, for the sake of avoiding public disgrace. Our moderation restrained the scandal whose author you are recognized to be in such a way that my brother and fellow bishop Gregory, who is clearly not one who was advanced but one who was driven out, will govern the Church of Mutina, as he requested, without having any case to pursue against you; and he will not refuse to embrace the spiritual fellowship which he ought not to have been compelled to accept against his will. If any dispute should perhaps arise concerning him, let an examination by us be sought either from him or against him.

“We shall also provide by this decision for the necessities that he is compelled to endure because of you: once the estate which, as he states, was given to him a year ago has been restored to the Church of Ravenna, let possession in the territory of Bononia, yielding thirty solidi of free annual revenue, be handed over to him without hesitation, for the duration of his life, while the ownership rights of the Church of Ravenna remain intact. After his death it shall return to that Church.

“If our decrees are not obeyed, you yourself understand what awaits the obstinate after transgression. We declare, moreover, that if hereafter you presume to do anything of this sort and should attempt to make anyone—whether bishop, presbyter, or deacon—against his will, you shall know that the ordinations of the Church of Ravenna and of Aemilia will be taken away from you.

“Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Severinus, an illustrious man. (A.D. 481.)”

II. Simplicius, bishop, to Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, bishops.

“Your report instructed us, and the sequence of the acts informed us more fully, that Gaudentius, priest of the Church of Aufinum, committed illicit ordinations contrary to the statutes of the canons and our commands. We order that all authority over these be taken away from him completely.

“For we have written to our brother and fellow bishop Severus. If necessary, he himself is to perform this office in the aforesaid Church, after considering the regulations of the Fathers, in which Gaudentius has been proved to have abused his office. Those who were advanced illicitly by him are to be removed from ecclesiastical ministries.

“Likewise, let him presume that nothing is permitted him concerning the revenues of the Church or the offerings of the faithful, since he does not know what is proper; only a fourth portion of these is to be remitted to him. Two portions are to be administered by the presbyter Onager, under penalty to his order, for the Church buildings, the distribution of aid to pilgrims, and the poor. The final portion is to be divided among the clergy according to the merits of each.

“Moreover, let the usurper be compelled, through the persistent action of the aforesaid brother, to restore the Church ministries that we have found to have been alienated. We have specially commanded that he also be required to return the three portions that he is said to have claimed exclusively for himself for three years.

“Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, after the consulship of Leo Augustus. (A.D. 475.)”

# DECREES OF POPE FELIX

*(Roman Synod. A.D. 487.)*

In the consulship of Flavius Boethius, an illustrious man, on the third day before the Ides of March, in the Constantinian basilica, with the venerable Pope Felix presiding, together with:

Candidus of Tibur; Paschasius of Centumcellae; Equitius of Matelica; Epiphanius of Spello; Herennius of Portus; Agnellus of Telesia; Urbanus of Fulginia; Martinianus of Formiae; Cresconius of Tuder; Basilius of Tolentinum; Constantius of Aquino; Philippus of Nomentum; Bonus of Ostia; Constantius of Trebia; Constantinus of Capua; Severus of Cassinum; Martianus of Ameria; Herculius of Otricoli; Maximus of Blera; Projectitius of Tarquinii; Maximinus of Ferentium; Felix of Antium; Felix of Anagni; Andreas of Gabi; Cyprianus of Nomentum; Vitalis of Fundi; Constantius of Sutrium; Gaudentius of Forum Clodii; Asterius of Forum Novum; Victor …; Rusticus and Pardalius of Africa; Petrus of Subaugusta; Bassus of Ferentinum; Innocentius of Mibana; Benignus of Aquaeviva; Decius of the Three Taverns; Athanasius of Alba; Petrus of Lorium; Felicissimus of Sabina; Bonifacius of Velitrae; Romulus of Praeneste; Donatus—bishops;

and the presbyters:

Rusticus, Laurentius, Cassius, Januarius, Lepidus, Asterius, Alexander, Laurentius, Servus Dei, Petrus, Petrus, Soranus, Asterius, Smaragdus, Paschasius, Fulgentius, Valentinus, Andreas, Romanus, Castinus, Laurentius, Leo, Gordianus, Epiphanius, Justinus, Projectitius, Epiphanius, Servandus, Urbicus, Petrus, Paschasius Firminus, Vincomalus, Petrus, Martianus, Maxentius, Petrus, Redemptus, Jovinus, Petrus, Julianus, Valens, Valentinus, Asellus, Bonifacius, Felix, Callistus, Sebastianus, Petrus, Dominus, Simplicius, Canusius, Eugenius, Petrus, Epiphanius, Felix, Bonifacius, Bonus, Marcellinus, Paulinus, Asterius, Asterius, Bonifacius, Sixtus, Petronius, Romanus, Martinianus, Opilio, Agapetus, Petrus, Petrus, Laurentius, Joannes, Epiphanius, Sebastianus, and Abundantius;

with the deacons also present, Felix, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome and presiding over the synod, said:

“It is a common grief and a general lament that we have learned that in Africa even bishops, presbyters, and deacons have been rebaptized. Without doubt this matter has also come to the knowledge of your holiness. It is fitting that we determine what must be observed concerning it. Therefore, so that our judgment on this matter may be clear, let what has seemed right to us be read.”

The deacon Anastasius read:

“To all the beloved brothers in Christ Jesus who are bishops established throughout the various provinces.

“No part of the world has failed to groan, and no land has been unaware, of how the devil’s cunning raged in the African regions against the Christian people and burst forth through manifold deception, so that it plunged not only the unwary multitude but even priests themselves into the depths of death. Therefore, placed in great sorrow, we cannot conceal the peril of those souls that are perishing and will be demanded from us. Consequently, a suitable remedy must be applied to such wounds, lest an untimely readiness to treat do no good to those seized by a deadly plague, while a calamity handled too slowly envelops both the wounded and the physicians in the guilt of an illegitimate cure.

“First, the confession and person of anyone who comes to you seeking a remedy must be carefully examined, so that an appropriate cure may be supplied. In the case of one who, wishing to satisfy God through repentance, grieves that he was rebaptized, it must be investigated whether he rushed into this crime or approached it under compulsion. Let him know that the one who deceives is himself deceived, and that nothing is taken away through our leniency from the judgment of the supreme tribunal, for that tribunal regards as valid what is pious, true, and just. The matter of intention must be handled differently according to necessity.

“The case of one who was perhaps enticed by payment into destruction is worse. The enemy left nothing unattempted. To prevent him from rejoicing in his capture, those who have been ensnared must be helped, and the hunter’s snare must be crushed, so that those lamenting their fall [the printed *in fugatim* is uncertain] may return to the court they had abandoned, through both the moderation of justice and the compunction of piety. Let them not perhaps be ashamed or reluctant to obey the prescribed periods of fasting and lamentation or to comply with other commands of salutary observance, because grace is given to the humble, not to the proud (James IV).

“Let anyone who seeks to be raised up in Christ be cast down by grief over his fall. Through the ministry of our administration—which ought to follow your charity, and which no one has the right either to wish or to be able to surpass—let us handle with priestly vigor and humanity the case of one who, against apostolic teaching, gave himself over to the repetition of a most unhappy baptism, or of one who cleverly judged that his own consent should be excused by some arguments. Thus, with the Lord the judge assisting, faith—which, unless it is one, is already no faith at all—may be restored to salvation without offense caused by our haste. For when a sinner’s satisfaction is prolonged by us, his mind is found purer for pardon, not without our praise and joy.

“Therefore remember that our judgment concerning these matters is this: while preserving discrimination among sinners, not all who have fallen are to be weighed on the same scale, since a greater penalty must be exacted from the one to whom the discipline of the Lord’s house has been entrusted.

“Let us begin, then, from the heights of the Church. Those who are shown to have been bishops, presbyters, or deacons, and who are found, whether willingly or under compulsion, to have suffered the loss of that one and saving washing, and to have stripped off Christ, whom they had put on not only through the gift of regeneration but also through the grace of the honor they had received—for it is clear that no one could come to a second baptism unless he had openly denied that he was a Christian and professed himself to be a pagan—must be treated as follows. Although this is generally to be execrated in everyone, it is proved horrifying even to hear or mention it in bishops, presbyters, and deacons.

“Yet because the same Lord and Savior is most merciful and wishes no one to perish, they should be placed in penance until the day of their death, if they repent. They are not to participate at all in the prayer, not of the faithful and not even of the catechumens. At death, however, lay communion is to be restored to them. The care of a most proven priest must investigate and carry this out diligently.

“Concerning clerics, monks, maidens of God, and secular persons, we command that the following rule be observed, which the Council of Nicaea established for those who have fallen or shall fall: those who, without necessity, fear, or danger of any kind, impiously surrendered themselves to heretics to be rebaptized, if they nevertheless repent from the heart, are to remain for three years among the hearers; for seven years they are to submit themselves among the penitents under the hands of priests; and for two years they are not to be admitted to the offerings in any manner, but are merely to join the people in prayer. Let them not be ashamed to bow their necks before God, since they did not fear to deny him.

“If, however, as mortals, the end of life begins to press upon them within the limits of the prescribed period, aid must be given to the one who implores it. Whether from the bishop who imposed the penance, or from another who confirms that it was imposed, or similarly from a presbyter, the viaticum must not be denied to one departing from the world.

“Concerning children, who, because they are still immature, are designated by the term ‘underage,’ whether clerics or laypersons, and likewise concerning girls of similar age, whose ignorance is supported by their years, communion is to be restored after they have been held for a time under the laying on of hands. Their penance is not to be awaited. The severity that exempts them from punishment excuses them, as we have prudently established, lest those who still have more or less of the contamination of earthly corruption remaining to them should, while still undergoing penance, perhaps commit further acts requiring penance.

“If, before the appointed period of penance, someone recovers after having been despaired of by physicians or oppressed by clear signs of death, once the grace of communion has been received, let us observe what the canons of Nicaea ordained: he is to be counted among those who communicate only in prayer until the period of time prescribed for him has been completed.

“Nor do we pass over our catechumens who were baptized under such a profession, because the case is not different—as the same holy canons ordained—from that of one who in any manner renounces Christ, whom he had once confessed. Let them remain for three years among the hearers; afterward let them be permitted to pray with the catechumens, and let them receive the grace of Catholic communion through the laying on of hands.

“Excepting only bishops, presbyters, and deacons, whom we have already said are to be reconciled only at the time of their death, we decree that all the others—whether clerics, monks or nuns, or laypersons of either sex—who are shown to have undergone a repetition of baptism under compulsion and danger, or who say through some evasion that they are not held by the guilt of this crime, are to remain in penance for three years and to be received into the fellowship of the sacrament through the laying on of hands.

“In all things the following must be guarded: no one of these persons, at whatever age, who has been baptized or rebaptized anywhere other than in the Catholic Church, is ever to be permitted to enter the ecclesiastical service. It must be enough for them that they have been received among the number of Catholics. Whoever violates this rule among the bishops, or whoever fails to remove someone whom he knows to have slipped into the clerical ministry from among such persons, will be judged concerning his own order and communion.

“Above all, care must be taken and every precaution provided so that none of our brothers and fellow bishops, or even of the presbyters, receives in another’s city or diocese a penitent, one placed under a priest’s hand, or someone who says that he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or presbyter. A presbyter must not receive such a person in a parish, nor a bishop in a city, without this documentation. Neglect through any concealment touches with guilt even the clerics who reside in places where this matter has been less carefully attended to.

“Once these matters have been properly arranged and brought to the knowledge of your Churches through our deliberation, it is fitting that you obey. Although nothing may seem to be lacking for the restoration of souls, nevertheless, if anything new should be revealed to anyone—something that escaped us—let him confidently make it known, according to the blessed Apostle Paul (1 Corinthians XIV), while the one who spoke first remains silent. For the Holy Spirit inspires where he wills, especially when his own cause is being handled. We shall not be reluctant to listen, nor shall we arrogantly reject anything omitted; rather, we shall arrange it reasonably.

“Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of Dinamius and Siphidius, illustrious men. (A.D. 488.)”

# DECREES OF POPE SYMMACHUS

*(Roman Synod. A.D. 499.)*

After the consulship of Paulinus, an illustrious man, on the Kalends of March, in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, with the most blessed Pope Symmachus presiding over the synod, the archdeacon Fulgentius said:

“Your Beatitude has frequently summoned synods of the priests of Italy by authorities previously sent throughout the provinces. Their presence now seems to stand before your eyes. Now may your Beatitude deign to arrange through practical deliberation whatever pertains to ecclesiastical security and to the peace or harmony of the whole Church.”

All the bishops and presbyters acclaimed:

“Hear us, O Christ; Symmachus, may you live,” was said ten times.

“May his see and years endure,” was said eight times.

“We ask that you do this,” was said ten times.

Bishop Symmachus of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome said:

“Our concern for ecclesiastical security has gathered this council of your affection, despite the harshness of winter, especially so that, through shared deliberation, we may firmly and vigorously cut away in the future the episcopal ambition, the uncertainty of confusion, and the popular tumult which is known to have arisen through underhanded seizure. Therefore let us take care in the future that no overthrow of discipline or audacity of the presumptuous may desire to attempt similar things, and let us settle the matter by a common enactment, expressly sanctioning through decisions what must be observed concerning the ordination of the Roman bishop.”

All the bishops and presbyters said:

“We ask that it be done,” was said ten times.

“We ask that scandals be cut away,” was said nine times.

“We ask that ambition be extinguished,” was said twelve times.

“Hear us, O Christ; Symmachus, may you live,” was said six times.

“May his see and years endure,” was said five times.

“Let it be done in the presence of the assembly,” was said ten times.

Bishop Symmachus said:

“Since your brotherhood has stirred our concern for provision by its exhortations and offers a similar disposition concerning the tranquility of the Church, in contemplation of our God, as we have already said, now that deliberation has been held, inform us through all your judgments what pleases you, so that they may be read in this venerable council through the ecclesiastical offices.”

When they had risen and shortly afterward sat down again, Aemilianus, the notary of the synod, published the following from the tablet:

“I. Because of the frequent ambitions of certain persons, the stripping bare of the Church, and the clash among the people, which the greedy desire of those improperly seeking the episcopate has generated, the holy synod has decreed that, in order to extinguish such a pernicious presumption for future times, if any presbyter, deacon, or cleric, while the pope is alive and without consulting him, should attempt either to lend his subscription for the Roman pontificate, or to make a promise by a written note, or to give an oath, or certainly to promise any support, or to deliberate and decide on this matter in private gatherings, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his position or of communion.

“The entire synod rose and acclaimed:

‘Hear us, O Christ; Symmachus, may you live,’ was said ten times.

‘Here there is peace with Symmachus,’ was said fifteen times.

‘May his see and years endure,’ was said eight times.

“The same severity is to strike anyone who, while this pontiff is alive—as was said—is convicted of having sought the office by any means or of having attempted to do so; all those guilty of this offense are to be punished by the penalty of anathema.”

Bishop Symmachus said:

“Therefore, does this judgment please the whole assembly, and is it acknowledged and approved by all?”

The entire synod said:

“It pleases us; and what pleases all shall be done.”

“II. If, God forbid, the pope’s death should occur unexpectedly, so that he cannot previously decide concerning the election of his successor, as was agreed above, then, if the election of the entire ecclesiastical order inclines unanimously toward one person, the elected man shall be consecrated bishop.

“If, as usually happens, the preferences of those among whom the contest has arisen should begin to differ, the judgment of the majority shall prevail, provided that the man who, having been won over by a promise, makes his decision concerning the election without sound judgment shall be deprived of the priesthood.”

The synod said:

“It pleases us,” was said ten times.

“III. Because of hidden frauds and the secret plots of conspiracies to which this severe decision applies, if anyone brings to the knowledge of the Church the plans of those who have engaged in ambition for the pontificate contrary to this synod, and proves them by reasonable evidence, he shall be a participant in the action of this kind, not only purified from every guilt but also raised up by a reward that is not unworthy.”

The entire synod rose and acclaimed:

“All these things please us.”

And it added:

“Hear us, O Christ; Symmachus, may you live,” was said thirteen times.

“We ask that they be preserved in this manner,” was said ten times.

“We beseech that no one henceforth come to the Roman episcopate by any other means,” was said ten times.

“We ask that you confirm our decrees,” was said ten times.

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said: “Your acclamations and the judgment of the synod will be received by the present record. And he added: Those provisions which he established in accordance with religion and peace, to quiet the errors of long-standing presumption and the hostile maladies of affliction by which the deliberation of the universal Church was troubled, shall receive perpetual firmness, with God granting this—God whom we know to be the guardian of good things—so that the synodal ordinance may prevail. And all who thereafter dare, without distinction of any person, shall be punished by the strict penalty imposed above.” And seventy-three bishops subscribed.

Caelius Symmachus, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, consenting to these synodal enactments, approved and confirmed by me, have subscribed.

Caelius Rusticus, bishop of the city of Minturnae, have subscribed and consented to the synodal enactments, and declare that I remain in this judgment.

Caelius Boniface, bishop of the Church of Velitrae, have subscribed and consented to the synodal enactments, and declare that I remain in this judgment.

Missenus of Cumae; Cresconius of Tuder; Basilius of Tullia; Decius of the Three Taverns; Valentinus of Amiternum; Vitalis of Fanum; Maximus of Blera; Benignus of Aqua Viva; Palladius of Sulmo; Constantius of Otriculum; Germanus of Pisaurum; Candidus of Tibur; Vitalianus of Narnia; Justus of Acherontia; Stephanus of Nursia; Fortunatus of Anagni; Clarus of Alife; [Col. 0327A] Rufinus of Canusium; Vitalis of Fundi; Innocentius of Mibanatis; Bassus of Ferentinum; Vitalianus of Rosella; Constantinus of Capua; Fortunatus of Suessa; Vindemius of Antium; Joannes of Ariminum; Martyrius of Terracina; Laurentius of Trebia; Serenus of Nomentum; Adeodatus of Caere; Dulcitius of Sabina; Paschasius of Volturnum; Fortunatus, bishop of the Church of Anagni, for Sanctulus, bishop of the city of Signia, because he could not subscribe, have subscribed for him; Valerius of Calenotum; Felicissimus of Forum Sempronii; [Col. 0327B] Valentinus of Amiternum, for Romanus, bishop of the Church of Pitinum, have subscribed; Colonius of Forum Clodii; Joannes of Spoleto; Maximianus of Perusia; Lucianus of Tarquinii; Florentius of Paestum; Fortunatus of Fulgentia; Gaudentius of Tadinum; Felix of Nepi; Aucupius of Puteoli; Rosarius of Surrentum; Epiphanius of Beneventum; Constantius of Venafrum; Salustius of Ameria; Malensis of Centumcellae; Maximianus of Subaugusta; Joannes of Vibo; Mercurius of Sutrium; [Col. 0327C] Serenus of Nola; Timotheus of Abellinum; Stephanus of Naples; Rosarius, bishop, for my brother Ursus, bishop, have subscribed; Gaudentius of Volsinii; likewise Gaudentius, bishop of Volsinii, for Projectitius, bishop of Forum Novum; Quintus of Teanum; Bellator of Ostia; Lampadius of the city of Alba; Ursus of Stabiae; Gaudentius of Salernum; Marius of Tifernum; Adeodatus of Forbia; Saturninus of Herdonia.

Sixty-seven presbyters subscribed. Caelius Laurentius, archpresbyter of the titular church of Praxedes, have subscribed here and consented to the synodal enactments, and declare that I remain in this judgment.

[Col. 0327D] Januarius, presbyter of the titular church of Vestina; Martianus, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Caecilia; Gordianus, presbyter of the titular church of Pammachius; Petrus, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Clement; Urbicus, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Clement; Paulinus, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Julius; Valens, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Sabina; Petrus, presbyter of the titular church of Chrysogonus; ### Subscription of the deacons

Cyprianus, deacon of the holy Roman Church, of the seventh region, have subscribed these proceedings and consented to the synodal enactments, and declare that I remain in this judgment.

## OTHER DECREES OF POPE SYMMACHUS

[Col. 0328D]

### Roman Synod, A.D. 502

In the consulship of Flavius Avienus, the younger, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, with the venerable man Pope Symmachus presiding, together with the venerable bishops

Laurentius, Aemilianus, Cresconius, Innocentius, Joannes, Fortunatus, Mercurius, Asellus, Paschasius, Hilarus, Colonicus, [Col. 0329A] Fortunatus, Stephanus, Memor, Innocentius, Maximilianus, Martyrius, Vindemius, Dulcitius, Servusdei, Felix, Chrysogonus, Maximus, Tigridius, Pacatianus, Joannes, Serenus, Laurentius, Candidus, Elpidius, Hilarus, [Col. 0329B] Innocentius, Vitalis, Veneriosus, Silvanus, Propinquus, Romanus, Bassianus, Rufentius, Stephanus, [Col. 0328D] Jocundus, Eutychius, Severinus, Sebastianus, Felix, Benignus, Maximus, Eulalius, Eustachius, Fortunatus Aprilius, [Col. 0329A] Proculeianus, Martianus, Felix, Innocentius, Gerontius, Severinus, Castus, Aresto, Valentinus, Victor, Adeodatus, Eusebius, Venantius, Probus, Mercurius, Asterius, Augustus, Rusticus, Basilius, Ursus, [Col. 0329B] Petrus, Laurentius, Asellus, Concordius, Amadus, Martinianus, Projectitius, Sallustius, and Florentius.

The following presbyters were also present:

Projectitius, Servusdei, Abundantius, Marcellus, Paschasius, Adeodatus, Hilarus, Venantius, Litorius, and Chrysogonus, [Col. 0329C] Fortunatus, Epiphanius, Octavianus, Paulinus, Benedictus, Severus, Timotheus, Marcus, Petrus, Fortunatus; Tinulus or Maximinus; Martinus, Epiphanius, Vicomalus, Agatho, Julianus, Joannes, Adeodatus, Petrus, Sebastianus, Anastasius, Julianus, Crescentianus, Paulinus, Laurentius, Stephanus, Chrysogonus.

The following deacons were also standing by: Anastasius, Hormisdas, Joannes, and Agapetus.

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

**I.** Your Fraternity has indeed obeyed the ecclesiastical laws and, in fear of the divine judgment, has determined what had to be established; it has reached the summit of justice by embracing everything sufficiently, and its fullness requires no addition—especially concerning the clerics whom love of domination has invaded and caused to reject the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline. It has become clear among you that these men therefore created a schism. Nevertheless, you did not deny them the mercy which God commands to be extended to all, as was fitting, provided that the hardness of their hearts does not bring punishment upon them by despising the remedies offered, although it would be difficult to recount their offenses.

Yet I do not delay in bringing one matter that has arisen to the attention of your venerable order. Among other things, they said that a document had been written by Basil of illustrious memory, supposedly out of love for the substance of the Church, in which no bishop of the Roman Church either took part or subscribed, through whom it could have acquired legitimate force. Therefore, so that I may not dispute a matter which your council can judge, let it be sought and brought forward, so that by reading it you may recognize what sort of substance it possesses.

The holy synod replied: “Let it be brought forward, so that its nature may be recognized.” And as it was being said, the deacon Hormisdas read:

**II.** When the sublime and most eminent man, the praetorian prefect and patrician, also acting as deputy of the most excellent King Odoacer, Basil, had sat together with them at the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he said:

“Although it is principally in the interest of our zeal and religion that concord be preserved in the Church in the election of a bishop, lest, through the opportunity of sedition, the condition of the city be thrown into doubt, nevertheless you remember that the admonition of our most blessed father Pope Simplicius—which we ought always to keep before our eyes—was expressly entrusted to us: because of that disturbance and the injury to the venerable Church, if it should happen that he passed from this life, no election of anyone should be celebrated without consultation with us.”

And as he was reading, Cresconius, bishop of the Church of the city of Tuder, rose from the assembly and said:

“Here let the holy synod consider how, setting aside religious persons who are especially concerned for so great a pontiff, they might bring the matter under their own control. This is plainly contrary to the canons.”

The deacon Hormisdas likewise read:

“Lest the venerable Church suffer any confusion or loss, we are astonished that anything was attempted without us, since nothing ought to have been undertaken while our priest was still alive. Therefore, if it pleases your Excellency or Holiness, let us preserve intact, with religious care, everything that concerns the election of the future bishop, placing before it especially this law, which, in Christian devotion, we enact for ourselves and our heirs.

“Let it be judged ineffective and void for anyone who is now to be appointed bishop by common election, and for those who will follow in future ages, to alienate under any title or pretext any rural or urban estate, ornaments, or furnishings of the Churches that now exist, or that have come to the rights of the Churches under any title. Let anathema rest upon the one who does this, consents to it, or accepts it.”

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Blera, said:

“Now may the holy synod deign to declare: Was it lawful for a layman to pronounce an anathema against an ecclesiastical order? Or, if a layman could pronounce an anathema against a priest and establish something contrary to the canons—which was not within his competence—tell me what you think. Was it lawful for a layman to give a law?”

The holy synod said: “It was not lawful.” And it added: “Read what follows.”

The deacon Hormisdas read:

“And whoever has acquired a rural or urban estate belonging to ecclesiastical property should know that he is protected by no law or prescription. But whether the one who alienated it, or someone who follows him, should attempt to reclaim by contrary will such an alienated estate, let the person who acquired it restore it together with its fruits.”

As he was reading, Stephanus, bishop of the Church of Venusia, rose from the assembly and said: “Let it be read through.”

The deacon Hormisdas read:

“It has also pleased us that the heirs and their successors should be subject to this penalty. In this matter, every cleric shall have the freedom to object. For it is unjust, and akin to sacrilege, that what anyone has contributed to the venerable Church for the salvation or repose of his soul, or has certainly left to it for the sake of the poor, should be transferred to high-ranking persons by those who above all ought to have preserved it.

“Clearly, whatever in gems, gold, silver, or clothing appears less suitable for the Church’s use or adornment, or cannot be preserved and kept for long, shall be sold at a just valuation, and the expenditure shall be devoted to a religious purpose.”

When this had been read, Laurentius of the Church of Milan said:

“This document could bind no bishop of the Roman Church, because it was not lawful for a layman to possess any authority in the Church for establishing anything apart from the Roman pope, whom there remains an obligation to obey but no authority to command—especially since neither the Roman pope subscribed, nor is the assent of any metropolitan, according to the canons, read there.”

Petrus, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, said:

“It is clear that the document circulated in our assembly cannot stand by any force, because it agrees neither with the canons and appears to have been composed by a lay person, especially since no bishop of the Apostolic See is shown to have taken part in it or confirmed it by his own subscription.”

Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, said:

“The document that was read in the priestly council is demonstrably invalid. First, it appears to have been produced contrary to the rules of the Fathers by laymen, even though they were religious men, to whom no power to dispose of ecclesiastical resources is ever recorded as having been granted. Second, it is shown not to have been confirmed by the subscription of any bishop of the Apostolic See.

“And if the holy Fathers decreed that whatever priests of any province attempt within their own boundaries in a council held without the authority of their metropolitan bishop must be void, how much more must it be acknowledged that what was presumed by laymen—even with the consent of certain bishops, who nevertheless could not prejudice the Pontiff by whom they are known to have been consecrated—while no bishop was present at the Apostolic See, lacks force. The bishop of that See, who, possessing throughout the world the primacy of priesthood through the prerogative of the blessed apostle Peter’s merit, is accustomed to confer firmness upon synodal enactments, was absent. Such a thing cannot in any way be counted among ecclesiastical statutes.”

[Col. 0331B]

**III.** The holy synod said:

“Although, in accordance with the statements of our venerable brothers Laurentius, Petrus, Eulalius, Cresconius, Maximus, and Stephanus, it is not uncertain to us that this document is wholly without force, nevertheless—even if it could in any way be sustained—it was appropriate that it be weakened and annulled in every respect by the prudent judgment of Your Blessedness in the synodal assembly, lest it remain as an example of presumption, allowing any laymen, however religious or powerful, in any city and by any method, to decide anything concerning ecclesiastical resources. For the care of disposing of these is taught to have been entrusted by God indisputably to priests alone.”

Symmachus, bishop, said:

“Now, because God has granted me your desired presence on this occasion, I wish, if it pleases you, to make firm a matter which I believe accords with ecclesiastical resources, so that all whom empty fury has stirred against me may recognize that I seek nothing more earnestly than that what has been entrusted to me by God under stewardship may remain secure. It ought also to be pleasing to any successors who fear God, and it belongs to the safeguarding of the Church’s patrimony.”

The holy synod said:

“We know that your foresight is devoted to necessary matters, and therefore it is in your power to arrange what must be followed.”

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

“Great reverence is indeed owed to a venerable and priestly purpose, which is concerned to arrange what is right out of diligence, not out of necessity. But since, when certain persons request what belongs to others, avarice—the mother of vices—after rejecting the barriers of honesty thinks that everything permissible is expedient, and, while it gapes after plunder, abuses the patience of heavenly mercy, they await correction under the governance of heaven and suppose that they are not held accountable by judgment. It is clear that, among some people, the delay of the divine sentence becomes an opportunity for seizure.

“But for us, whom pastoral care binds, and to whom an account must be rendered for the stewardship entrusted to us of the substance, it is necessary to extend our concern not only to the present but also to succeeding ages, lest it bring harm to our souls if those who have power should transgress through presumption of innocence against the statutes, when both we and our successors can be supported by religious authority while serving the ecclesiastical laws.

**IV.** Therefore, having weighed these matters, and with this decree to remain in force under the consideration of our God, we enact that from this day onward no bishop of the Apostolic See, so long as the saving doctrine of the Catholic faith remains by the Lord’s arrangement, shall be permitted to transfer to anyone’s ownership any rural estate, whatever its size or smallness, by perpetual alienation or exchange. Nor shall any such act be excused on the pretext of necessity.

“For what we are saying is not personal, nor may any cleric or layman use this occasion to protect himself. Nor shall it be lawful for rights to be granted to anyone in usufruct, or for rights already granted to be retained, except for clerics, captives, and travelers, lest an opportunity for bad treatment be provided, since other avenues remain open for generosity.

“Only houses established in any cities, whose condition necessarily requires support through substantial expenditure, may be exchanged, provided that, if they must be taken away, revenues are received at a just valuation and in fear of the divine judgment.”

**V.** We also wish the custodians of the Churches throughout all the titular churches of the city of Rome—whether they are presbyters or whoever they may be—to be bound by an equal law. For it is wicked to say that a person of the second order in the Church is not held by the obligation through which the supreme pontiff binds himself by the charity of Christ.

“Whoever, however, forgetful of God and heedless of this decree by which we wish the priests of the city of Rome to be bound by religious ties, should, in violation of the present enactment, attempt by any means to alienate any property belonging to the titular churches or to the Church mentioned above—apart from gold, silver, gems, clothing, if there are any, or movable objects that may have been added and do not pertain at all to divine adornment, under perpetual title, with the sole exception of the houses under the condition stated above—shall be punished by the loss of his honor, whether he is the donor, alienator, or seller.”

**VI.** Moreover, whoever has requested or accepted such property, or whoever among the presbyters, deacons, or defenders has subscribed to the donor’s act, shall be struck with anathema, by which God strikes souls in anger. The recipient or subscriber, concerning the persons included above—that is, those whom we have decreed should be struck with anathema—shall also incur association in the established penalty, while the punishment previously prescribed for the alienator remains in force. Unless, perhaps, the alienator, when reclaiming the property, and the one who accepted it, should provide for themselves by prompt restoration.

**VII.** But if anyone, with insufficient concern for his soul, should perhaps neglect the remedy offered, then, beyond the classes of penalties written above, any instrument composed contrary to right shall be enforced with every force, even though it possessed no force from the beginning.

“It shall also be lawful for any ecclesiastical persons to raise a voice of objection and to be supported by ecclesiastical authority, so that they may reclaim the alienated property together with its fruits. Let no one fortify himself with any obstacle before the tribunal of Christ, because he has dispersed, contrary to right and without any consideration of mercy, what was left by religious souls for the substance of the poor.

“We wish the law of this constitution to be observed only in the Apostolic See. For all the Churches throughout the provinces, let their rulers preserve the custom that they judge to accord with the purpose of religion, according to their consideration of souls.”

And they subscribed.

Caelius Symmachus, bishop of the Roman Church, have subscribed this enactment made by us.

Caelius Laurentius, bishop of the holy Church of Milan, have subscribed this enactment made by the venerable Pope Symmachus.

Petrus, bishop of the Catholic Church of Ravenna, have subscribed this enactment made by the venerable Pope Symmachus.

Eulalius, bishop of the holy Church of Syracuse, have subscribed this enactment made by the venerable Pope Symmachus.

[Col. 0332D] Felix of Interamna; Aemilianus of Velletri; Tigridius of Turin; Bassus of Mutina; Maximus of Blera; Rufentius of Agnatum; Martinianus of Ostia; Fortunatus of Vessa; Eucarpus of Messana; Stephanus of Venusia; Romulus of Praeneste; Vindemius of Antium; Fortunatus of Fulgentia; Martianus of Aecae; Chrysogonus of Alba; Laurentius of Bovianum; Paschasius of Volturnum; Aprilis of Nuceria; [Col. 0333A] Innocentius of Forum Sempronii; Felix of Nepi; Amandus of Potentia; Colonius of Forum Clodii; Projectus of Forum Novum; Bonifacius of Forum Flaminii; Rusticus of Bursentum; Victor of Duna; Sylvimus of Velletri; Aresto of Ostia; Felix of Nepi; Asterius of Aquino; Eusebius of Fanum; Cresconius of Tuder; Jocundus of Augusta; Vitalis of Fundi; Pacatianus of Coanilium; Martyrius of Terracina; Basilius of Tullia; Benignus of Aqua Viva; [Col. 0333B] Severinus of Tundar; Joannes of Spoleto; Valentinus of Amiternum; Probus of Carmejanum; Candidus of Tibur; Proculeianus of Sepinum; Maximianus of Perusia; Eutychius of Trani; Fortunatus of Anagni; Marcus of Samnium; Memor of Canusium; Florentius of Blestina; Concordius of Messana; Asellus of Populonia; Elpidius of Velletri; Veneriosus of Pellena; Sebastianus of Sura; Venantius of Senigallia; Innocentius of Tifernum; [Col. 0333C] Justus of Signia; Augustus of Lipara, for Ursus; Propinquus of Trebia; Romanus of Nomentum.

### Roman Synod, A.D. 501

In the consulship of Rufus Magnus and Faustus Avienus, men of illustrious rank, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, the holy synod, assembled in the city of Rome by command of the most glorious King Theoderic from various regions, said in the name of Christ:

“When royal authority had commanded priests to come to the city of Rome from various provinces, so that the holy council might judge the accusations which the adversaries of the venerable Pope Symmachus, bishop of the Apostolic See, were said to be bringing against him, the bishops of Liguria, Aemilia, and Venetia—whom the journey itself had drawn to the presence of the prince—were necessarily compelled to consult the king, who had wished these men, broken by age and weakened by bodily infirmity, to assemble for this purpose.

“The aforesaid most pious king replied that many dreadful reports concerning the acts of Pope Symmachus had been brought to him, and that it was proper for the synod to consider whether the accusations of his enemies were true, once the matter had been examined.

“The bishops mentioned above, who were about to have the opportunity to present their case, suggested that the man who was said to have been attacked ought himself to have convened the synod. They knew that, first, the merit and primacy of the apostle Peter’s See, and then, by the Lord’s command, the authority of venerable councils, had conferred upon it a unique power in the Churches. Nor, in a similar case, would it easily be possible to establish any precedent by which the aforementioned bishop of the See had been subjected to the judgment of inferiors.

“But the most powerful prince indicated that the pope himself had also shown by letters his willingness to assemble the synod. His letters were requested from his clemency, and, since it was known that they had been sent by him, he ordered them to be given without delay to the priests, together with whatever had been done in the same matter and had reached Rome in writing from different parts of the lands and regions through God’s providence.

“And while the venerable assembly was considering the beginning of the case, as the matter under discussion required, the holy Pope Symmachus quickly entered the basilica of Julius, where the bishops had assembled, as his care directed him. He gave thanks to the most merciful king for convening the synod and testified that the object of his desire had come to pass.

“Thus the cause of the priests’ distress, which had produced sadness concerning the council not yet confirmed, was removed. He declared himself ready to submit his authority to the assembled order, in the presence of all the bishops who had gathered there, as the ecclesiastical statutes required. He hoped that the visitor—whose appointment had been sought by a party of the clergy or by certain laymen contrary to religion, contrary to the statutes of the ancients, and contrary to the rules of our predecessors—would, by the decision of the bishops and as befitted a holy purpose, yield at the outset; that everything he had lost through the representations of his enemies would be restored to his authority by the honorable council; that the bishop of so great a See would first be legally restored to his former status; and that he would then come to the case and, if it seemed right, answer the accusations of his accusers.

“This seemed a worthy course to the greatest number of the priests, and it was carried out as deserved. Nevertheless, the synod did not presume to decide anything without the king’s knowledge. A just representation, because of the negligence of the envoys, did not receive a response according to their wishes.

“By the king’s commands, Pope Symmachus was ordered to contend in debate with his opponents before receiving back the patrimony or the Churches that he had lost. He had submitted the privileges of his authority and what he had offered for the correction of his conscience, as we rightly judge it, and on this occasion he did not wish to resume them.

“But while the synod was established in the Basilica of Jerusalem in the Sessorian Palace, certain priests thought that the written indictment prepared by the accusers, who were daily appealing through seditions, should be received by the synod. In that indictment were two points either hostile to truth or, as the assembly showed, wholly opposed to its ecclesiastical purpose.

“One was that they said the crimes of the aforementioned Pope Symmachus had been established before the royal court. This was shown to be false. For he would not have entrusted himself to a new hearing of the case if his conscience had known that he had been convicted of error and was merely awaiting sentence.

“The other was that he could be convicted through slaves concerning the matters they alleged against him. They added that he himself should surrender the slaves by whom, as they asserted, he could be overcome in the judgment. This was contrary both to the canons and to the public laws themselves, since the statutes of the Fathers had decreed that those whom the laws of the world do not admit to accusation should not be granted permission either to speak in an inquiry or to accuse anyone.

“While these matters were being discussed—what ought to be done—the aforesaid pope was approaching in order to plead his case. When he arrived, he was treated by the attacking mobs of his rivals in such a way that the slaughter itself would have caused the death of many presbyters who were with him. The illustrious Count Aligernus and the eminent men Gudila and Vedeulfus, stewards of the royal household, saw the fresh traces of the wounds and saw that he had taken refuge within the enclosure of the blessed apostle Peter, from which he had departed.

“After these events, and with affairs thrown into varied confusion, we again turned to the sovereign’s justice, knowing that the Lord’s divinity itself governs what it has provided for the direction of Italy. We reported everything to his clemency in an orderly account, as the situation required.

“We also informed him that the pope mentioned above had been admonished, after the slaughter he and his companions had suffered, to go out again to the judgment if he were willing. But he alleged through the bishops who had been sent to him that, although the canonical mandates had granted him the right of purging himself, he had humbled the summit of his dignity through devotion and had nearly been overwhelmed by so many dangers.

“He said that the lord king had the power to do whatever he wished, but that he could not meanwhile be compelled, against the resistance of justice, by canonical statutes.”

To this the most serene king replied, with God’s help:

“It belongs to the synod to prescribe what should be followed in so great a matter. Nothing concerning ecclesiastical affairs pertains to me beyond reverence. I entrust it also to the authority of the bishops to deliberate whether they wish to hear the case proposed or not, and what they consider more useful—provided that, through the venerable council’s foresight, peace may exist in the city of Rome for all Christians. When it is offered justly, God’s commands are fulfilled.

“Recognizing that he has given a ruler to his Italy, we understand that no other labor remains for us except to exhort those who disagree, with humility of purpose, toward concord. For only one thing remains in such a great matter by which we may obey God: in accordance with the holy prince’s will, we invite the most illustrious Senate, sending an embassy as was fitting, and admonishing and instructing them to commit the causes of God to God’s own judgment—he who can kill the body and cast the soul into Gehenna (Matthew X), who says, ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay’ (Ezekiel IX), and before whom conscience is naked (Romans XII), and from whom hidden things are not concealed.

“They ought to consider, as prudent men, how many things had occurred at the beginning of this affair improperly and prejudicially, and we ought not to open a way for sins through what they themselves called remission, but to close it. We must instruct them that Christ became known to them through us (John X), and that it is not the part of sheep to foresee the ambushes of wolves, but of the shepherd—especially since, in the case mentioned above, many of them acknowledged that they were involved in error and had to give satisfaction to God.

“And because, on this occasion, the members of the Church could not be scattered further but rather had to be sustained through gentleness, as the teacher Paul instructed us in good works (II Timothy IV), saying that many must be healed through patience and teaching; and since all who are thought guilty and entangled in serious sins—although no one is without offense, as the apostle John testifies (I John I): ‘If I say that I have no sin, I am a liar’—ought nevertheless to be supported amid human pressures, those passions restrained, and divine judgments suspended; especially since the matters we mentioned above concerning the authority of the See stood in the way.

“For what the blessed Peter, once its possessor, merited has increased the nobility of its possession and gives you its ancient glory. Let him give the rulers the gift of Christ. Let us cry out that it is written by the prophet in the person of God (Isaiah L): ‘Is my hand not strong enough to consume those who have gone astray?’

“Let us repeatedly admonish them, as was proper, so that, having taken our intention into account, they might depart and neither examine what we had done—what God had inspired—in accordance with the prince’s command, nor dispute it, but follow it as sons of the Church ought to do, and not, under this suspension, contend and increase the Church’s losses.

“The situation demanded that help be brought with haste, and necessity imposed this speed upon us and obedience upon them—especially since we see that almost the entire people has clung inseparably to his communion. A not insignificant concern for us urged that it not slip into any error.

“After these statements, calling upon our God, we decree, bound by consideration of these necessities and religious duties and having weighed everything in the heavenly inspiration concerning the matter, that Pope Symmachus, bishop of the Apostolic See, attacked by accusations of this kind, is, so far as human beings are concerned, immune and free. Since, because of all the obstacles to the case described above, the matter has plainly been left to divine judgment, he shall be free of these accusations and, without any presentation of the charges against him to the Christian people, shall exercise his office in all his Churches belonging to the right of his See and administer the divine mysteries. For we have recognized that, because of the attacks of his opponents and the causes stated above, he could not be bound.

“Therefore, in accordance with the imperial commands which assign this to our authority, we restore to him whatever ecclesiastical property belongs within the sacred city of Rome or outside it, reserving the entire matter for God’s judgment. We exhort everyone to receive holy communion from him as the situation requires and to remember God and their own souls, because he is both a lover of peace and peace itself. He says: ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you’ (John XIV; [Col. 0336A] Matthew X). And affirming that peace must be established in every city, he calls the peacemakers blessed (the same passage, chapter V).

“Whoever, instructed by us—which we do not expect—either does not accept this or believes that it can be reconsidered should understand that, in divine judgment, he will render an account for his contempt, as we trust in God.

“Concerning the clerics of the aforementioned pope who departed from their bishop some time ago contrary to the rules and created a schism, we have decreed that, once they have given satisfaction to their bishop, mercy should follow them and they should rejoice at being restored to their ecclesiastical offices. For our Lord and Redeemer rejoices when he finds the lost sheep recovered from error, and the heavenly healer grants paternal freedom to the prodigal son (Luke XV).

“But whoever among the clerics, after this form approved by us, should presume to celebrate Mass in any consecrated place of God within the Roman Church without the knowledge of Pope Symmachus, shall, while Symmachus lives, be struck as a schismatic according to the canonical statutes.

“Let it suffice that we have sincerely stated these matters with God as our witness.”

And they subscribed.

[Col. 0336B] Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan, have subscribed this statute of ours, in which we have committed the entire matter to God’s judgment.

I, Peter, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, have subscribed to this statute of ours, in which we have entrusted the whole matter to God’s judgment.
