# Decrees of Pope Hormisdas

## [Letter]

### Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas

[Col. 0337A] We have made publicly known the zeal that we have always had, and still have, for reconciling the opinions of those who cultivate the Catholic faith, so that all may venerate with one mind the undivided light of the Trinity. For this very purpose we are now voluntarily sending to Your Beatitude the distinguished Gratus, master of the imperial chancery, so that a remedy may at last be found for the disagreements of those who contend with one another in opposing ways. We are now also receiving with willing and humble affection the most religious men whom your apostolic see has judged should be sent as mediators of unity.

Indeed, we have looked upon them with joyful eyes, as though upon peace itself, and have led them to our embrace with outstretched hands. Moreover, with every intention we shall arrange that the venerable Church of Constantinople, as well as many other churches, receive your wishes—not only in other matters, but also in removing from the sacred diptychs the names whose removal you especially requested.

Yet there were certain cities and churches, both Pontic and Asian, and especially Eastern ones, whose clergy or peoples, though assailed by every kind of threat and persuasion, were nevertheless in no way moved to remove or reject the names of bishops whose reputation flourished among them. They consider death harsher than life if they should condemn the dead whose life, while they lived, they gloried in. What, then, are we to do with such obstinacy, which neither obeys commands nor fears tortures, to such an extent that it would consider it a great and festive occasion if it should give up its body before giving up its religious resolve?

It seems to us that we must act more gently and mercifully—qualities which, if they cannot now be found in Your Holiness, will not be found elsewhere. For we have not accepted a petition out of desire for blood and punishments—something painful even to say—nor have we done so so that the hopes of concord might remain incomplete through a slight peril. Rather, we seek to extend, by whatever means we can, the union of the members of the Church.

Which, then, will be more advantageous: for the sake of lesser matters to become wholly opposed to such great multitudes, or, by granting and relaxing small points, to correct greater matters that must be sought by every means, so that what could not be achieved in every respect may at least be secured in the necessary parts? [Col. 0337D]

We therefore ask that the names be spared—not that of Acacius, nor those of either Peter, nor those of Dioscorus or Timothy, whose names were contained in the letter sent to us by Your Holiness—but the names whom episcopal reverence has honored in other cities, excepting those cities where the petition of Your Beatitude has already been fully accepted, unless Your Benevolence should also decide that this part ought to be corrected more gently.

Nor is the matter without the judgment of the apostolic see, so that it should be called pardon rather than a definition already deliberated and examined. For Anastasius, of most religious memory, had publicly and openly established the summit of your Church when he wrote concerning this same matter to our predecessor: it was enough for those seeking peace if Acacius’s name alone were kept silent.

Thus he follows the earlier constitutions of your see, which do not judge all memories of the dead deserving of contempt. It would be unworthy and inappropriate if your gentleness, made known throughout the ends of the earth, were not more gracious toward all—not only the dead but also the living. We shall not doubt that this will be so pleasing to you that, as soon as you give a peaceful reply, the world will become more joyful. [Col. 0338A]

Let Your Holiness retain what we wrote some time ago: that petitions from the East have been sent to us, containing their will and decision, in which they show that they will remain firm and from which they consider that they must not withdraw for any reason. We have therefore rightly judged that this document should now be sent to you, in accordance with our promises, through John, a most reverend bishop, so that, once its tenor has also been accepted by your see, it may contribute to gathering and uniting the venerable churches everywhere, and especially the Church of Jerusalem. Everyone shows such favor toward it, as though toward the mother of the Christian name, that no one dares separate himself from it.

It is therefore fitting that Your Holiness should declare your own agreement also in an epistolary document, so that, once the tenor of this document has been known and made public, the world may rejoice that it is also praised and steadfastly preserved by you.

Given at Chalcedon on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of Rusticius; received on the day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of the same. (A.D. 520.)

## Copy of the Petition

### II. Petition and supplication to the God-beloved and most pious emperor, the Augustus Justin, most Christian ruler, from the clergy, abbots, and landholders of the province of Syria, from Jerusalem, Antioch, and Second Syria

[Col. 0338C] “Draw water with joy from the fountains of salvation,” cries and proclaims the prophet Isaiah (Isa. XII), clearly indicating the fountains of salvation—the evangelical truths and proclamations—from which the blessed apostles, their disciples in succession, and the wise teachers of the Church drew the saving water of faith and watered the entire holy Church of God. Founded upon the rock of the chief of the apostles, preserving a right and unshakable confession, it cries out confidently with him at all times to the only-begotten Son of God, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI).

Receiving this saving confession from the four holy synods honored by the evangelical commandments, we have never, by Christ’s grace, departed from the sound doctrines handed down to us, as the proof of events bears witness [Col. 0338D] and steadfastness in the time of faith’s necessity demonstrates.

If, therefore, as Christians, most pious lord, we share in the reason of faith and hasten toward common peace and unity, we make known to Your Piety through this declaration of ours the faith that we received from the beginning, so that it may be known that we join in peace and, with God’s help, do not turn away from the right faith. Rather, we execrate every heresy equally: not only the Eutychianists and Acephali, but also the Nestorians; and we hate and anathematize with all our heart those who worship a mere human being.

We, most Christian lord emperor, as was said above, having been baptized and believing from the beginning in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, worship one essence of God in three subsistences, according to the teaching and creed of the holy Fathers. We believe in one God the Father almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God the Word, and likewise in one Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, we also understand and accept the definition promulgated by the holy Council of Chalcedon, according to this divine teaching, [Col. 0339A] confessing and believing that there is one substance, or person—which the same holy synod proclaimed in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity, indivisibly and without confusion. God the Word and our Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy Trinity and is of one essence with it.

For if we accept one God in three subsistences, as has been said, and the Father was not incarnate, nor the Holy Spirit, but God the Word was incarnate and became human, then he is one of the holy Trinity and of one essence with it, according to the property of sonship.

Thus, believing according to the aforementioned four holy synods, and according to God’s Word, we do not refuse to confess the birth according to the flesh. Hence the holy Virgin is properly believed to be the Mother of God, since she bore as human the Son of the Father, God the Word, who by nature is unchangeable and of one essence with the Father, having become human from her. We confess that the two natures in Christ are united in essence or substance, as in one person or substance. After the union, we neither remove their distinction or proper character, nor have we been taught by the union to divide them into two persons and substances.

We know the same only-begotten Son of God, both before his incarnation and afterward, to be simultaneously God and human: passible in the flesh, impassible in divinity; circumscribed by the body, uncircumscribed in spirit; earthly and heavenly; one whom the world received as human but could not contain as God; mortal and immortal. Nowhere has the distinction of the natures been abolished, nor do we divide the union in essence.

For this truly is the great mystery of piety: that one of the holy Trinity, and one of its one essence, God the Word, was incarnate and became human, and is known and worshiped in both natures, divinity and humanity, indivisibly and without confusion. He did not undergo conversion or change, but preserved within himself the proper character of each nature in one person.

Therefore, accepting and preserving the aforementioned holy synods on account of this faith, we anathematize all who at any time or in any manner have written anything against them, especially John Egota [reading uncertain], who, like a Nestorian, poured forth many blasphemies against the aforesaid holy Council of Chalcedon. We likewise condemn Timothy surnamed Aelurus, who, like an Eutychianist, barked against it with his followers.

Thus, with God’s help, we have always thought, and we think now also. For this reason we have offered this declaration to Your Piety. You were pleased to command us to set forth our own understanding and how we think concerning the sound faith, because certain heretics, while hastening to conceal their evil faith, try to disparage our freedom in Christ and our right faith.

We therefore beseech Your Clemency to take care for the perfect unification of the holy churches, so that, once unity has been established with God’s help, peace may remain undisturbed thereafter by any reasonable or unreasonable fuel of occasion. May the God of all fulfill your pious desire for his glory and for the ordering of the commonwealth. [Col. 0339D]

### Hormisdas to Justin Augustus

### III

Among the matters that you committed to writing concerning the unity of the Church, for whose sake God chose Your Clemency’s imperial rule, you also added this, most venerable emperor, out of your concern for the faith—a concern that you make evident in many ways: that certain petitions should be delivered to my humility, so that I might learn what question arose from them, or give a reply suited to religious knowledge in order to remove the uncertainty of the consultation that had been proposed.

I read everything with the care that was appropriate. Although it might have been sufficient for a complete reply if I had written back only those things that had been defined by the ancients, nevertheless, so that I might reward the devotion of your religious purpose, I did not think I should withhold the service of my own discourse as well. For what paternal instruction omitted concerning the emerging poisons of Nestorius and Eutyches, synodical decrees, united in one judgment, had already anticipated: nearly all impieties together with the inventors of such nefarious doctrines.

Once such seeds of perfidy have been cut away, there is no further room either to believe that Christ our Lord existed without the reality of flesh, or to deny that the same one emerged as human from the inviolate fecundity of his mother’s womb. One of them, by denying the dispensation through which we were saved, would, so far as lay in him, make it void; the other, with an opposing opinion but similar impiety, would exclude divine power from true humility in the same Lord Jesus Christ. The former did not remember that Christ showed his flesh to be touched (Luke XXIV); the latter did not remember the Gospel’s saying that the Word became flesh (John I). The voice of the Lord should have sounded unceasingly in his ears, the voice by which he said and taught (John III): “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

These matters have often been contained in the judgments of many predecessors. Yet Your Clemency, venerable emperor, even though they have been said before, will not disdain to hear them repeated; nor are we ashamed to review what our predecessors proclaimed. For there can be no diversity in proclamation where there is one form of truth, and it will rightly be judged no aberration if, in faith, we agree with those with whom we are united, and likewise agree in doctrine.

Let the synodical decrees and the constitutions of blessed Pope Leo, consonant with the sacred faith, be recalled to the pious ears of Your Gentleness. You will find in them the same things that you review in ours. What, then, after that fountain of faithful statutes, can an inquisitive investigator seek further—provided that he preserves the boundaries of faith? There is no need either for an addition by the populace or for an institution for things already perfected, unless someone prefers to doubt rather than believe, to contend rather than know, and to follow uncertainties rather than preserve decrees.

For if God is Trinity—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and God is one, as the lawgiver expressly says (Deut. VI), “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one,” how could it be necessary either to divide the divinity into many parts or to inflict suffering specifically upon the very essence of the Trinity? And—far be this from the minds of the faithful—this would mean either introducing several gods in the manner of profane paganism or transferring sensible pain to a nature that is alien to every kind of suffering.

The holy Trinity is one. It is not multiplied by number, does not increase by addition, and cannot either be comprehended by the intellect or be separated by distinction in what God is. Who, then, would attempt to force a profane division into the secret, eternal, and impenetrable substance which not even the nature of any invisible creature has been able to investigate, and reduce divine and hidden mysteries to the reckoning of human custom?

Let us worship the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the distinct yet undifferentiated, incomprehensible, and ineffable substance of the Trinity. Although reason permits the number of persons, the unity of essence does not permit singularity to be divided. Yet let us preserve what belongs to the divine nature and what belongs to each person, so that neither a singularity of divinity is generated among the persons nor what is proper to the names is transferred to the essence.

Great and incomprehensible is the mystery of the holy Trinity. God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit: an undivided Trinity. Yet it is known that it belongs properly to the Father to generate the Son; it belongs properly to the Son of God to be born from the Father, equal to the Father; and it is also known what belongs properly to the Holy Spirit: to proceed from the Father and the Son under one substance of divinity.

It belongs properly to the Son of God that, according to what is written, in the last times the Word should become flesh and dwell among us (1 Pet. I; John I). Thus, within the womb of the holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, the two natures were united without any confusion, so that he who was the Son of God before the ages might become the son of man and be born in time in the manner of human birth, opening his mother’s womb when born, yet not destroying his mother’s virginity through the power of divinity.

It was entirely fitting to the mystery of God’s birth that he should preserve childbirth without corruption, who caused conception to be without seed, preserving what he was from the Father and displaying what he received from his mother.

For how else could he who was seen lying in a manger be in heaven, wrapped in swaddling clothes and worshiped by the Magi, born among animals and announced by angels, scarcely beyond infancy yet proclaiming mystical teachings without a teacher, and, amid the beginnings of childhood, displaying heavenly signs of power?

He is the same God and human being—not, as unbelievers say, under a fourth introduction of a person, but himself the Son of God, God and human; the same power and weakness, humility and majesty, redeeming and sold, placed upon the cross and bestowing the kingdoms of heaven.

In the weakness of our condition, so that he could be killed, yet in the innate power by which he could not be destroyed by death, he was buried according to the fact that he willed to be born as a human being, and according to the fact that he was like the Father, he rose again: suffering wounds and saving the sick, one of the dead and the giver of life to those who die.

Descending to the underworld, yet not departing from the Father’s bosom, he therefore soon reclaimed the soul that he had surrendered according to the common condition, according to his singular virtue and wondrous power.

To show that these things are so and that no doubt ought to be admitted—namely, that our Lord Jesus Christ should not be believed to be God amid the sufferings of the body, nor merely God and not also human amid the works of wondrous powers—he instructed us by the example of two apostles, declaring Christ our Lord to be God through Peter’s faith and human through Thomas’s doubt.

For what purpose would he have wished his disciples to inquire whom people said he was, unless, when Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he wished to make known that this had not been revealed by flesh and blood but by God the Father’s inspiration, and that through the testimony of the praised answer the faith of the truth might be revealed?

Why would he have arranged that, when the Lord appeared after the resurrection, Thomas alone should either be absent from the others or doubt by himself, unless so that the world might believe what the doubting disciple had investigated, and so that, while he allowed himself to be touched by the hands of one man, it might be recognized by the whole body of the faithful what he was?

The doubt, therefore, was not introduced to condemn the disciple, but to instruct posterity.

Or does he expect anything else from the fact that the same Lord, while Cleopas and another disciple were traveling toward Emmaus and speaking about him, joined them in the conversation (Luke XXIV)? Although they had learned of the Lord’s resurrection from the women who had first come to the tomb, nevertheless, in order through their doubt to give firmness to those who would believe in future ages, he began with Moses and all the prophets and explained that the Christ had to suffer and thus enter into his glory. In this way he showed through the human suffering that he had a human nature, and through the glory that he had a divine nature. [Col. 0342A]

These things are suggested by many examples in the holy Scriptures. They are not spoken to Your Religious Conscience, venerable emperor, as though they were unknown. For the faith that you steadfastly assert itself gives you this gift: it implants in your understanding devotion to itself and pours into you the knowledge by which it may be asserted more diligently.

Nevertheless, it belongs to the dispensation entrusted to me that I should not remain silent even about matters known to the learned, so that, as the Catholic proclamation succeeds itself through the changing succession of times, what is unceasingly asserted may gradually be believed without end.

I could discuss at greater length the matters that concern the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the union in him of two natures without confusion, according to the definitions of the ancients, if I had to argue against those who disagree with them. But since both the synodical constitutions and the doctrines of blessed Pope Leo are in everyone’s hands, I have judged it more appropriate to touch briefly upon a few points rather than unfold everything.

For now it is enough to recognize and guard this: that the proper character and essence must be understood in such a way that one knows what must be attributed to the person and what to the substance. Those who improperly fail to understand this, or conceal it through cunning impiety, while omitting what belongs properly to the Son within the Trinity, lay snares for unity.

But if what has been stated is held firmly with deep roots, neither will one depart from the paternal tradition nor fail to meet questions steadfastly.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valerius and Victor. (A.D. 521.)

### Hormisdas to the presbyters, deacons, and archimandrites of Second Syria

### IV

[Col. 0342B] When I read the letter of your affection, in which the madness of God’s enemies was exposed and the stubborn fury of the unbelievers was sorrowfully set forth—those who, hating God with a revived spirit, wickedly persecute his members—as far as concerns my recognition of your steadfastness, I blessed God, who preserves the faith of his soldiers amid adversity. But again, considering the upheaval of the churches and the troubles and labors of God’s servants, I, like the prophet, … [lacuna]

# Decrees of Pope Gregory the Younger

[Col. 0341]

[Col. 0341C] In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, during the reign of our lord, the most pious Augustus Leo, crowned by God, great emperor, in the sixth year after his consulship, in his sixth year, and also in the second year of Constantine, his son and the new emperor, in the month of April, in the fourth indiction.

With the most holy and thrice-blessed Gregory, apostolic pope, presiding in the basilica of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and with the most holy bishops also seated before the confession:

Agnellus of Ferentinum, Vitalis of Alatri, Martianus of Gabii, Tiberius of Silva Candida, Georgius of Nepi, Andreas of Alba, Tribunatius of Falerii, Joannes of Blera, Sergius of Praeneste, Synderedus, archbishop of Spain, Sedulius, bishop of Britain, Fergustus, bishop of Scotland, Majorinus of Polimartium, [Col. 0341C] Joannes of Beliternum [reading uncertain], Opportunus of Maturum, Georgius of Portus, Gregorius of Anagni, Joannes of Signia, Agnellus of Sutrium, Anastasius of Tibur, Vuillari of Narni, Petrus of Amelia,

and the venerable presbyters:

Sisinnius, Joannes, [Col. 0342D] Marinus, Epiphanius, Sisinnius, Georgius, Gregorius, [Col. 0342C] Joannes, Joannes, Eustratius, Constantinus, Marinus, Joannes, Thalassius, Joannes,

with the deacons also standing by:

Petrus the archdeacon, Gregorius Maeoseus, and Benedictus, deacons, and all the clergy,

the most holy and blessed Pope Gregory said:

Since by the heavenly mercy of the Lord we are rulers of the Christian people, we ought to think with special diligence, relying upon God’s protection, about their salvation, lest—God forbid—we be found to have disappointed the souls entrusted to us and be compelled, before the supreme Shepherd, to render a strict account if correction does not come beforehand to ward off offenses.

When I consider, or bring back to mind, how carefully we ought, in our vigilance, to oppose the wickedness of each person’s crime, and whenever it attacks in order to disturb the minds of the faithful, to resist its assault with heavenly assistance, I am greatly shaken and waste away with anxiety, lest, through the serpent’s cunning—God forbid—it deceive even the more careless.

With God truly favoring us, we must, in great concern and with a tranquil mind, relying upon divine help, strive for the salvation of all, so that we may deserve to stand before the eternal Judge with an unconfounded face, not stricken by anyone’s deceit, and hear the voice saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV; Luke XIX).

For this reason I say with a groan that I hear that some Christians living throughout the province of Italy hold opinions contrary to the Catholic faith and the statutes of the Fathers, to such an extent that they dare to take women consecrated to God as wives and join female relatives to themselves in marriage. This must be cut away with a spiritual sword and, if it pleases Your Holiness, uprooted from the roots, lest the crop of the good farmer become filthy with horrid fruits, mixed with weeds (Matt. XIII). [Col. 0343B]

The most holy bishops and venerable presbyters answered:

We truly recognize that, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the heart of Your Apostolate burns so that the squalor of such great misery may be wiped away from the minds of the faithful, and that, like a wound fixed in the body, this misery may be healed by a saving antidote once access to it has been blocked. As has rightly been foreseen through the prohibition of anathema, no one—whether Roman, Lombard, or of whatever nation, and washed in the waters of sacred baptism—should attempt this again, lest, oppressed by the weight of so great a sacrilege, he fall headlong or be swallowed up in the abyss of iniquity. It must be avoided and uprooted from the roots.

After this unanimous response, the apostolic Pope Gregory, before the body of the aforementioned venerable chief of Christ’s apostles, delivered the judgment and said:

I. If anyone takes a presbyteress in marriage, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

II. If anyone takes a deaconess in marriage, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

III. If anyone takes a nun, whom they call a servant of God, in marriage, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

IV. If anyone takes his spiritual co-mother in marriage, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

V. If anyone takes his brother’s wife in marriage, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

VI. If anyone takes his niece or granddaughter in marriage, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

VII. If anyone takes his stepmother or his daughter-in-law in marriage, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

VIII. If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

IX. If anyone takes as wife a woman from his own kin, or one whom a kinsman has had, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

X. If anyone abducts a widow as his wife, or anyone consents to him, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

XI. If anyone abducts a virgin as his wife unless he has betrothed her, or anyone consents to him, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

XII. If anyone observes omens through diviners, haruspices, or enchanters, or uses an amulet, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

XIII. If anyone in any respect violates the previously issued apostolic commands concerning olive groves and various properties, and does not observe them in every particular, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

XIV. Let Hadrian, son of Exhilaratus, who, after having sworn an oath in the apostolic confession, unlawfully keeps Epiphania the deaconess as his wife, be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

XV. Let Epiphania the deaconess, who, after having sworn an oath, fled and became the wife of Hadrian, son of Exhilaratus, be anathema. And all answered three times: Let her be anathema.

XVI. If anyone gives his assent to them in so cruel a matter, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

XVII. If anyone among the clergy lets his hair grow long, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: Let him be anathema.

# The Second Part of the Works of Dionysius Exiguus: Ascetic and Paraenetic Treatises

## [On the Creation of Man]

### Letter to the presbyter Eugipius, concerning his translation of Gregory of Nyssa’s book *On the Constitution or Making of Man*

[Col. 0345C] To my most holy lord and greatly revered sacred presbyter Eugipius, Dionysius Exiguus.

In obedience to the sacred devotion of Your Veneration, to the best of my ability I have translated from the Greek the book of Blessed Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, *On the Formation of Man*, explained by him in thirty-one chapters. How much difficulty I encountered in this work will be evident from the reading itself. For, dwelling at length on many matters in accordance with the opinions of the philosophers, he displayed such an abundance of learning that he omitted scarcely anything of those questions which learned and leisurely minds have arranged here through their intricate investigations. He also demolished some of their follies in such a way as almost to suggest to us that saying of the Apostle by which he instructs the faithful: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition [Col. 0345D] of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8). For just as he wisely approves certain sound teachings that God has revealed to them, so he either corrects their errors himself or points them out so that others may avoid them—except, naturally, for a few cases in which, while vigorously attacking vices, he himself also uttered certain faulty expressions, as commonly happens.

Accordingly, while emulating the eloquence of so great a teacher, I did indeed strive to follow his expressiveness, although I was entirely unequal to attaining it with my very limited ability. Nevertheless, as far as my mediocrity allowed, I preserved the fidelity of his arguments, knowing that nothing is more excellent than truth. And since, as I have said, there are certain passages that may reasonably be criticized, let no reader suppose that I am bound to agree with them; for I have explained them in the capacity of a translator, not approved them in the judgment of a critic.

Therefore, with humble devotion I beg that Your Holiness may receive with a most grateful mind the fulfillment of my promise, and may mercifully grant pardon wherever I seem to have expressed myself less elegantly. For, being withdrawn by the pressures of time from the company of the most learned men, I did not arrange this book with the polish that I ought to have given it. Just as it is judged to abound in many virtues, so, as I have often stated, it seems to be sprinkled with certain blemishes. May your dignity therefore pray for me, so that, pressed by such great hardships, I may at least rejoice in the breadth of spiritual pursuits; and may present sorrows never be permitted to draw us away from the purpose of future delight. For we take the greatest consolation in this misery if, through unbroken meditation, we dwell upon the glory that is to come. Although a person may, through love of heavenly things, suffer the hardships of this pilgrimage and cry out sorrowfully with the prophet, “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Psalm 119:5), and may confidently affirm with the blessed Apostle, “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23), nevertheless he is not considered to be exiled far from his homeland if he continually reaches his homeland through desire.

[Col. 0347]

## Saint Gregory the Bishop to His Brother Peter the Presbyter, on the Image—that Is, on the Formation of Man—which Had Been Omitted by Their Brother, Saint Basil the Bishop, in the *Hexaemeron*

[Col. 0347A] If it were necessary to honor those who excel in virtues with the price of money, the whole world would seem poor in riches, as Solomon says (*Proverbs*, post. verse 40 according to the Septuagint), if it could be made equal to your virtues. But since the grace owed to your Veneration is far better than an abundance of riches, and since holy Easter also demands its customary generosity of affection, we offer to your excellent prudence, O man of God, a gift that is indeed small, although it may seem worthy of being presented to you, and is not regarded as beyond the strength of us who offer it. This gift is a discourse, like a most impoverished garment, woven with no little labor from our destitute understanding. The subject of the discourse, however, may perhaps seem excessively daring to many; nevertheless, it is judged neither absurd nor improper. The one who was created according to God alone considered God’s creation worthily. And truly Basil, our common father and teacher, was fashioned and formed according to the image of God. Through his contemplation he made the highest ornament of the whole creation intelligible to many, and he established the world, formed in the true wisdom of God, as well known to those who, through his prudence, are equipped for this contemplation.

Although we are quite unable to admire him as he deserves, we nevertheless thought that what is lacking in what this teacher has perceived ought to be added—not in any way diminishing his diligence by the present undertaking (for it would not be lawful for his sublime eloquence to be overshadowed by our discourses), but lest the glory that appears to be lacking in the teacher be imputed to his disciples. For since his exposition in the *Hexaemeron* [Col. 0347C] on the formation of man is absent, if none of his hearers were to contribute some effort to complete what was lacking, an opportunity for criticism might perhaps be furnished against his great glory, as though he had neglected to train the minds of his disciples in a certain habit of perceptive understanding.

Now, therefore, having undertaken to expound, according to our abilities, what is lacking, if anything is found in our work that is not unworthy of his teaching, let it rightly be attributed to the teacher. But if our discourse does not attain the magnificence of his contemplation, he will remain beyond accusation, escaping the charge that he supposedly did not wish to communicate to his disciples the fruit of a more accomplished result. We, however, shall consequently be exposed to those who delight in criticism, as though, through the smallness of our heart, we were unable to grasp the wisdom of so great a teacher.

The subject proposed for our contemplation is no small one, nor is it to be ranked below any of the wonders that exist in the world; perhaps it should even be preferred to everything subject to our knowledge. For none of the things that are seen is like God, as the formation of man is. Accordingly, we must now ask the goodwill of our hearers’ forgiveness for whatever we are about to say, if our discourse should appear inferior to the dignity of its subject. I think that we ought to leave entirely undiscussed none of the things believed to have been accomplished concerning man in the past, nor those hoped to be completed in the future, nor those now visible in the present. Otherwise, if anything shown to belong to the subject were omitted while man is placed before our contemplation, this exposition might be accused of falling short of its promise.

Moreover, the things that appear to have happened to him contrary to expectation, and why those things which were made in the beginning are not found in his nature, are explained more suitably through a certain necessary sequence, gathered both from the authority of Scripture and from the exercise of reason. Thus the whole subject coheres with itself, since the order and sequence that seem contrary converge upon one and the same end, divine power and strength granting us hope against hope and ability out of difficulty. For the sake of clarity, I thought it best to set out the present discourse for you in chapters, so that in a short space you may recognize the result of the entire work through the individual arguments we have undertaken.

[Col. 0347]

## Book of Gregory of Nyssa, On the Creation of Man: A Supplement to the *Hexaemeron* of His Brother Basil the Great, Translated by Dionysius the Roman, the Exiguus

### Chapter I. A Particular Account of the World, a Natural Discussion, and a Clearer Exposition of What Is Shown to Have Been Previously Settled in the Formation of Man

[Col. 0347D] “This is the book,” Scripture says, “of the generation of heaven and earth,” when all visible things had been completed, each had been separated and assigned to its proper place, when this revolving body of heaven had established all things, while the heavy bodies tending downward—earth, namely, and water, mutually containing one another—had received the central place of the whole creation.

The bond and foundation, as it were, of the things that have been made is the divine and eternal power, implanted in the natures of existing things and governing the whole through twofold effects. For in both stability and motion it contrived not only the generation of things from what did not exist, but also their continued existence once they had subsisted. Around the most weighty and unchangeable immobility of nature, like a stable and exceedingly firm axis, it continually carries the swiftest revolution of heaven in the manner of a wheel, preserving the indissoluble substance of both through one another.

For revolving matter, by its extremely rapid motion, driven around the solidity of the earth, compresses it; and the stability of the earth, through its immovable firmness, is continually extended by the circuit of revolving things. An equal magnitude has been compacted in accordance with each of the things whose operation differs—that is, both of the nature that is stable and of that which is carried along in unceasing rotation. For neither can the earth be moved from its own solidity, nor can heaven ever be loosened from the swiftest circuit of its motion.

These things are shown to have been constructed first, according to the wisdom of the Creator, as a kind of beginning of the whole structure. The magnificent Moses declares this when he records that in the beginning God made heaven and earth, and that from the motion and rest visible in this creation all things were produced according to the divine plan.

When, therefore, heaven and earth had been separated from one another in equal proportions according to their contrary operation, the creation situated between these contraries, participating in some measure in things that are joined together, connects the divided extremities through its own mediation. Thus the union of the contraries with one another through this interposition is evident.

For air in some measure imitates the substance of ever-moving and most subtle fire, both in the lightness of its nature and in the suitability of its motion. Yet it is not of such a kind that it appears unrelated to the kinship of the most solid elements: it neither remains always immobile nor continually flows away and diminishes. Rather, through the property of both, it becomes adjacent to the effects of the contraries, simultaneously mingling and separating within itself things that are distinct by nature.

According to this reasoning, the liquid substance too, supported by a twofold affinity, is fitted to both contraries. Insofar as it is heavy and inclined downward, it is bound to earthly nature by much kinship; but insofar as it possesses the efficacy of something fluid and flowing, it is recognized as not entirely lacking the nature of motion. Thus a certain mixture and convergence of opposites comes about through it: gravity passes into motion, while motion in turn is not impeded by gravity. Things that are naturally divided at their extremities come together while being joined to one another through a certain mediation—or rather, even the substance of the contraries itself does not exist without the intermingling of the other’s property.

Furthermore, as I believe, all things seen in the world agree with one another through mutual association, and the whole of creation is recognized as conspiring toward unity, since it is found in the properties of opposites. For since motion occurs not only through local transfer but also through alteration and change, while stable nature in no way admits motion occurring through change, the wisdom of God, exchanging the properties of each, made the immobile nature changeable and the mobile nature unchangeable. He ordered these things through a certain providence so that what is unique and proper to the divine nature—namely, immobility and unchangeability—would not cause anyone to judge God to be present in some creature.

For the soul could not appear to possess an opinion of divinity if the divine were mobile or changeable. Therefore the earth is stable but changeable, whereas heaven, conversely, although it is not changeable, is likewise not stable. Thus, by attaching changeability to stable substance and mobility to unchangeable substance, and joining each to the other through their contrary properties, divine power removed both from any conception of divinity; for whatever is found changeable and unstable cannot be judged to belong to the divine nature.

All things, therefore, have been fittingly adapted to their own end. For heaven and earth, as Moses says, and everything that lies between them, have been perfected with marvelous beauty, each thing being appropriately adorned. Heaven shines with the lights of the stars; the sea and air rejoice wonderfully with living creatures, both swimming and flying; and the earth, with its many kinds of grasses and its diversity of shrubs, seems in a fashion to exult. It produced, through divine command, the vegetation that preserves all things, and was filled with every species, producing fruits together with flowers, full and prepared for the things that customarily arise in them.

All the ridges and summits of the mountains, whatever was convex and elevated, and whatever was level and spread out in the valleys, were crowned with the fresh appearance of grasses and the varied beauty of trees. Some things rose from the earth, while all hastened toward their perfection and soon rejoiced in their beauty, everything being given life according to its nature by the divine command.

The beasts remained in the forest, moving about in herds according to their kinds; and all the woods resounded in harmony with the measured songs of the birds. The surface of the sea, as one may judge, was then established in the greatest calm and tranquility among its deepest gatherings. Along its shores, stations and harbors, fashioned by divine will like certain inlets, joined the seas to the lands. The very gentle movements of the waves quivered like green meadows, their surfaces lightly ruffled by the gentlest and harmless breezes. The whole world stood ready, according to its creation, on land and sea. But as yet there was no one to use these things.

### Chapter II. Why Man Was Made Last, After the Creation

For the great and precious being, man, the lord of the world, was not yet present; nor was it fitting that the ruler should exist before the things over which he would exercise rule. But once everything had been prepared to be subjected to him, it was now fitting that the ruler should appear.

Since the Creator of the universe had made a kind of royal dwelling for the future king, and since that dwelling was the earth, the islands, the seas, and above these the heaven curved like a vaulted roof; and since he had stored up the kingdom’s manifold riches—by riches I mean the whole of creation, whatever exists in grasses, plants, and trees, whatever exists among spiritual, perceptible, and living things, and, if it is fitting to count metals among these riches, those too, which appeared precious to human eyes because of the beauty of their colors, such as gold, silver, and the stones that human beings value—after concealing an abundance of all these things within the boundaries of the earth like royal treasures, he immediately introduced man into this world.

He did so so that man might be a spectator of certain wonders and might exercise principal dominion over others, in order that through the things he used he might recognize the giver, and through the beautiful things he contemplated he might be able to investigate the ineffable power of his Maker.

For this reason man was introduced into the world last, after creation—not as something most contemptible, cast out into the final place, but as one whom it was fitting to be born immediately as ruler. For just as a good host does not bring a diner into the house before preparing the meal, but first arranges everything, suitably adorns the house, prepares the couch, the table, and the rest, and then invites his guest to the delights already prepared, so in this manner the rich and generous Creator and nourisher of our substance, filling the dwelling of this world with all good things and arranging this great and varied banquet, introduced man and entrusted to him the distinguished task of guarding it, so that he might rejoice not in the possession of things that did not exist but in the enjoyment of things already present.

Therefore he also wove into him the causes of a twofold composition, mingling the spiritual with the earthly, so that through the kinship of both he might possess the properties of both: enjoying God spiritually, and receiving earthly goods through bodily use.

### Chapter III. That the Human Condition Is More Precious Than Every Visible Creature

It is also fitting that this matter not pass without contemplation: the construction of this whole great world and the entire arrangement of its parts contained within the elements were immediately accomplished by divine power, subsisting together with the command. But in the formation of man, the counsel of so great an artificer preceded it. Through the description of the word, what was to come was first marked out: what man ought to be, whose original form he should resemble, for what reason he should be made, what he would accomplish when completed, and over what things he would exercise dominion. Everything was first considered in action, so that even before his generation man might in some sense receive an older dignity, possessing the lordship of all things before he subsisted.

For God said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea, the beasts of the earth, the birds of heaven, and the cattle of the whole earth.”

O what a wonder! The sun is made, and no counsel precedes it. Heaven too, to which nothing in visible creation can be compared, is perfected by a word alone; and concerning so marvelous a work neither from what it is made nor how it is made is anything disclosed. In the same way each individual creature—the ether, the stars, the air that occupies the middle place, the sea, the earth, the animals, and all things that spring forth—is brought into existence by a word alone.

But in the formation of man alone the Creator of the universe approaches with something like deliberation. He prepares the material necessary for his construction, adapts it to the likeness of the original and principal beauty, indicates the purpose for which he is made, and establishes for him a nature suited to its effects, which proves most appropriate to the intended purpose.

### Chapter IV. Why the Human Construction Signifies in Every Respect a Certain Sovereign Power

[Col. 0352B] For just as, in this life, instruments are suitably adapted by craftsmen for any use, so our nature is constructed by the best craftsman as something suited to the work of ruling. Whether in respect of the soul’s prerogative or the body’s constitution, it exists in such a way as to appear especially suited for command.

Finally, the soul’s royal and most exalted character, separated far from private lowliness, is clearly declared by the fact that it is subject to no dominion, possessing freedom of choice and ordering itself according to its own will and direction. For whose characteristic is this, if not that of one who rules?

Moreover, since man has been made in the image of his Creator, the Lord of all creation, this indicates nothing other than that royal nature was immediately formed in him. For just as, according to human custom, those who fashion an image of a ruler imitate not only the impression of his form but also depict his royal dignity with a purple garment, and the image itself is already customarily called “the emperor,” so the human substance, because it was created for the governance of others in imitation of the King of all, is composed as a kind of living image. It shares in the original form both in name and in honor—not by being wrapped in purple clothing, nor by implying the glory of its dignity through a scepter or diadem, for the principal form is not seen to consist in these things. Instead of a purple robe, it is clothed with virtue, which is proved more precious than all royal ornaments; instead of a scepter, it is exalted by blessedness and immortality; and it is crowned with the royal wreath of justice. Thus, through all these things, it is shown that the beauty born for royal dignity carefully expresses within itself the likeness of the original form.

### Chapter V. That Man Is Shown to Be the Likeness of Sovereignty

It is clear that divine beauty is advanced not by some bodily appearance or outward form, nor by the brightness of any color, but by the ineffable honor of blessedness. For just as painters transfer human forms onto panels through certain colors, mixing their own appropriate tints so that the beauty of the original form may pass into a likeness through the most careful adaptation, so I understand the maker of our substance to have bestowed marvelous beauty upon his image through certain colors of the virtues, expressing in us his own sovereignty.

The colors of this image are multiple and manifold, through which the likeness of the true form is painted. It is not white lead or vermilion, nor a quality produced by mixing one of these with the other, nor some application of blackness that darkens the eyebrows and eyes and, through a certain blending, makes them resemble a depressed and hollow character, or any of the similar forms that the skill of painters’ hands has composed. Instead of these there are purity, freedom from suffering, blessedness, aversion to every evil, and all things of this kind, through which the divine likeness is impressed upon human beings.

With such flowers the wondrous Creator adorned his own image—that is, the nature of our formation. If you also examine the other things through which divine beauty shines forth, you will find these preserved in the image according to its likeness. For the highest Divinity is mind and word. “In the beginning was the Word,” and those who, according to Paul, make progress profess that they possess the mind of Christ, who speaks in them.

Do not, therefore, consider these things far removed from human nature. For in you there are both word and understanding, which imitate the divine Word and mind. Likewise there is love, and the source of love; for that great John says that “love is from God.” Christ, the former of our substance, bestowing this upon us as a kind of personal likeness, says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” But if this love is absent from us, the appearance and form of the whole image will be destroyed.

The Divinity also sees and hears all things and searches out everything. You too recognize that through your eyes and ears you possess the living efficacy of this faculty and an understanding capable of searching out what exists.

### Chapter VI. An Investigation into the Relation of the Mind to Nature; in Which the Doctrine of the Eunomians Is Incidentally Refuted

Let no one suppose that I am saying that divine power embraces all things through diverse effects in imitation of human operation. For it is not lawful to discern in that divine simplicity a varied and manifold power of operation. Nor are there many effective powers of causes and things within us, although the things pertaining to life appear to occur through manifold operations.

There is one particular power implanted in us—the mind—which extends through each of the senses and embraces the things presented to it. Through the eyes it sees what is to be seen; through the ears it hears what is said; it rejoices in things that are desired and turns away from those judged unpleasant. Through the hands it accomplishes whatever it wishes, holding things with them and again casting them away, and using the effects of these instruments as it judges expedient.

If, therefore, in man, whose different bodily functions were formed by the Creator, there is one and the same entity that operates through all the senses, using each appropriately as the circumstance requires, and does not change the power and force of its nature through differences of operation, how much more, in the case of God, although the effects of his powers are various, should no one suspect that his essence is multiple?

“Does he who planted the ear not hear? Or does he who formed the eye not perceive?” As the prophet testifies, through these examples he introduces such operations as certain very familiar impressions of human nature, saying: “For God said, ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness.’”

But where, then, will the impious heresy of the Eunomians find a foothold? What will they say against this declaration? How will they defend the novelty of their doctrine by these words? “Is it possible,” they will say, “for one image to represent a likeness of dissimilar forms? For if, according to their opinion, the Son is unequal in nature to the Father, how did God make one image of different natures?”

For he who said, “Let us make man according to our image,” revealing the holy Trinity to us through the plural expression, would certainly not have testified to his image in the singular if the original forms had been unlike one another. For it is impossible for one likeness to be displayed among those who do not at all correspond to one another. But if their natures were different, he would certainly have created different images corresponding individually to each of them.

Or is it because there is one image but not one form of the image? Who is so deprived of understanding that he could fail to know that things shown to be similar to one are also without doubt mutually similar to one another? Perhaps for this reason the divine word, foreseeing this wickedness in the formation of human life and cutting off the perversity of the Eunomians, says: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.”

### Chapter VII. Why Man Is Found Naked, Without Natural Weapons or Coverings

But what is the meaning of the uprightness of his bodily form? And why are the means of strength not congenitally joined to the body for the sake of life? Instead, man is brought into this life naked, without natural coverings, unarmed, and lacking all necessary things—so that, according to what is seen, he appears worthy of pity rather than happiness.

He is not armed at birth with horns, nor protected by the defense of claws or teeth, nor furnished with some stinger that pours deadly poison—things with which most wild beasts and serpents are naturally equipped for their own defense. Nor is his body covered with hair, although one who was destined to rule over others ought, by natural provision, to be enclosed in his own weapons, so that he would not need the assistance of others for his protection.

Yet the lion, boar, tiger, leopard, and anything similar naturally possess sufficient strength for their safety. The bull has horns; the hare has speed; the stag has leaping ability and keen sight; other animals have size; and the remaining creatures have the prominent function of the mouth that common usage calls the trunk. Birds have the use of wings, bees have a stinger, and every creature without exception has been given some natural defense.

Man alone, however, is believed to have been deprived of these things above all others. He is recognized as slower than those distinguished by speed of running, slighter than those outstanding in bodily mass, and more contemptible than those excelling in natural weapons.

“And how,” someone may say, “has the lord of all received such a dominion?” I think it is not difficult to demonstrate the answer through the very thing that is believed to be lacking in our nature. This provides the definite occasion by which he obtains dominion over all his subjects.

For if man possessed such power that he surpassed a horse in speed, if his foot were not worn down but rested upon the firm strength of a hoof, and if he bore horns, stingers, or some hooked weapons of vengeance, then first he would be like the beasts and would appear difficult to approach because of the bodily aids naturally attributed to him. Next, he would disdain exercising dominion over others whose assistance he in no way needed.

But now the use of life is distributed among the individual things made subject to us, so that we may clearly see that necessary dominion is exercised over them. The slowness of our body and its difficulty in rapid movement led us to employ horses; and, providing through the annual yield of wool the supplements lacking to nature, it is likewise evident that other necessities of life are supplied from other sources.

Beasts of burden have been subjected to us for carrying heavy loads. And because we cannot graze on grasses like animals, we have taken care to make oxen subject to our use, so that by their labor we may obtain food more easily.

Because we needed teeth and biting power to restrain such beasts in self-defense, what was lacking in us was supplied by the nature of dogs. Through their innate speed, they have also been assigned to our uses like a kind of living sword.

Instead of horns or claws, human beings invented iron, stronger and more penetrating. Unlike those defenses, which remain naturally attached to irrational beasts, iron does not always remain with us; the sword provides protection in wartime and afterward remains idle in peace.

The same iron is also used in place of the crocodile’s scales. Sometimes even the hide of the beast itself provides protection in battle; otherwise, as has been said, iron is fashioned by the craftsman in its likeness. Serving necessity, it protects the one whom it arms in wartime, and abandons him in peace.

Flying creatures too have been adapted to our uses, and reason has not overlooked even their speed. Some of them, once tamed, appear to cooperate with us; others, by their presence, provide a means of capturing others that can be applied to our advantage.

Art has also fashioned feathered missiles for us. Stretched upon a bow, they display a birdlike flight for human purposes. And because the traces of our feet are more easily worn down when completing a journey, the necessary aids provided by those subject to us indicate the materials from which suitable footwear may be fashioned.

### Chapter VIII. Why Man Has an Upright Form, and for What Reason Hands Were Given to Him; Including a Discussion of Certain Differences among Souls Introduced into the Argument Concerning Nature
What is certain is that the human posture is upright and raises itself toward heaven, looking upward; these are principal gifts, demonstrating royal power. Indeed, the fact that he alone is formed in this way, while the bodies of all the others are prone and inclined more readily downward, clearly displays the difference in his honor: it is evident that they are subject to his power, whereas he possesses a dignity that surpasses theirs. For in all the others the forward limbs of the body are the feet, since what is inclined forward evidently needed the support of firmness. In the constitution of the human being, however, these limbs were made hands, because, given his upright posture, a single step seemed sufficient—cautiously supported by the provision of two feet—to secure stability in standing.

The hands were also adapted for the service of reason, and anyone who said that the hands are the proper instrument of rational nature would not be mistaken. I am not referring only to what is common and readily apparent to our understanding—namely, that we mark words with letters through the agency of our hands. Even this gift is not unworthy of rational dignity, since we can also speak through letters and, in a certain way, converse with our hands by depositing our speech in the forms of the alphabet. But, directing my attention to something quite different, I affirm that the hands, through a kind of cooperation, obey the command of reason.

Before we examine this point, however, let us investigate more fully the reasoning that we have passed over. For almost the entire order and purpose of created things has escaped us: why do they come first? Let the earth bring forth vegetation; then let irrational animals follow; and after their creation, in the third place, let the human being be formed. Perhaps through this sequence we perceive not merely what is obvious—that the Creator of the universe established the nature of plants chiefly for the sake of animals, and created animals for the sake of human beings. Hence he produced pasture before the herds, but before the human being those things that could provide aids for human life.

It seems to me, however, that the succession of this discourse intimates some doctrine concerning hidden matters. Thus Moses left as a secret reserved for philosophical inquiry the condition of the soul under divine command. On this subject, indeed, external learning also imagined something for itself, but did not clearly perceive what was to be seen. Through these things, therefore, reason itself, as I understand it, teaches that this vital and animal power is declared in three distinctions.

The nature of plants is suited only to growth and nourishment, providing a fitting increase for those nourished by it. It is therefore also called “germinal,” and the same substance is clearly seen in shrubs and trees. In these growing things there is a certain vital power, but it is deprived of animation by sense. Beyond this there is another kind of life, to which the Creator both granted growth and commanded that it be administered through the senses. We readily observe it in the nature of irrational creatures: they are nourished and nourish others as grass grows, but they are also recognized as possessing sensory power.

The third and perfected life of the body is constituted in the rational essence of the human being. It is nourished and nourishes, senses, and, participating in reason, is animated by the mind.

We must also know that there is a certain division of existing things, so that one thing is intellectual and another corporeal. But let the division of intellectual essence according to its proper character be omitted for now; we have no occasion to speak about it here. Of corporeal substance, one kind is entirely without life, while another participates in life. Again, among living bodies, some are endowed with sense and others lack sense, as do our hair and fingernails. Sensible things, in turn, are divided into rational and irrational natures.

For this reason, after lifeless matter, the lawgiver first set forth this germinal substance as a kind of foundation; thereafter he disclosed the generation of things that are confined merely to the senses. And because, according to this sequence, those things that have received life in the flesh appear able to subsist by themselves as sensible things without intelligibles, while rational substance cannot be contemplated apart from a sensible body, the human being was made after the plants and animals: nature progressing consequentially by a certain path toward perfection.

For the human being, this rational animal, participates in all the species: in the growing plant and in the sentient living creature. He is nourished according to the natural substance of the soul; but he receives the power of growth through sensory provision. This, in its own way, is placed midway between intellectual and material substance: as much coarser in comparison with the former, so much purer in relation to the latter. Then the most subtle and luminous aspect of sensible reality, joined to the intellectual, becomes a fitting mixture of nature, so that the human being appears to subsist in these three elements.

We know that the Apostle intimates something of this kind when, praying for the Thessalonians, he says: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you entirely, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ”—placing the body for the nutritive part, the soul for the sensible part, and the spirit for the intellectual part.

Similarly, when instructing the scribe in the Gospel, the Lord places love of the Lord above every commandment; it is accomplished “with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the intellect.” The present discourse also seems to offer me an interpretation of the same distinction. By “heart” it indicates the more corporeal efficacy; by “soul” it signifies the middle position; and by “intellect” it suggests the higher substance of rational and perceptible power.

The Apostle therefore also recognizes three distinctions of wills: the carnal, which obeys only vicious pleasures connected with the belly and lower parts; the animal, which moves midway between virtue and wickedness, rising above the latter but in no way possessing the purity of the former; and the spiritual, which attains a manner of life pleasing to God.

Thus, writing to the Corinthians, he reproves them for their devotion to a pleasure-loving and passive life, saying: “Are you not carnal, and walking according to the human being?” That is, you are shown to be incapable of more perfect teachings. Elsewhere, making a comparison between this middle condition and that higher and more perfect one, he says: “The animal human being does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually examined; but the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one.”

Thus, just as the animal surpasses the carnal, so, by the same measure, the spiritual surpasses the animal.

The fact, therefore, that Scripture records the human being as having been made last, after all things, secretly instructs us that we ought to philosophize about the condition of the soul. It indicates, through a necessary sequence of things, that what is perfect is manifested at the end. For rational nature also contains the other things: the growth of plants and the sensation of living creatures. Sensible nature likewise unquestionably embraces the germinal species. But, because it is immaterial, it contains itself alone. Consequently, nature ascends as though by certain steps—from lower to more perfect forms of life, I mean.

## CHAPTER IX. That the human constitution was constructed most suitably for the work of reason

Since the human being is a rational animal, it was necessary that the instrument of the body be fashioned in accordance with the demands of reason. Just as we see the most skilled musicians practice their art of melody according to the nature of their instruments—trumpeters do not play the barbiton with its strings, nor harpists the trumpet—so the construction of the instruments had to correspond to reason, so that it might most appropriately resound for the use of speech, which is formed through the functions of the vocal organs.

For this reason the hands were fitted to the body. It would be easy to enumerate the thousand advantages of this life that these convenient and durable instruments, the hands, diligently provide, fulfilling every art and every activity appropriately in war and in peace. Yet above all other reasons, nature joined the hands to the body suitably for the sake of reason.

For if the human being had existed without hands, then, because of the necessity of receiving food, the members of his face would certainly have been formed like those of quadrupeds. His face would have been elongated and narrowed, with the nose projecting at the front; the lips of his mouth would have been calloused, thicker, and exceedingly firm, suitably adapted for plucking grasses. His tongue too would have been larger, harder, and rougher, cooperating with the teeth in receiving and processing what had to be chewed; it would have extended more broadly on either side, as in dogs and other flesh-eating animals, moving through the rough intervals between the teeth.

If, then, the body had no hands, how could articulate speech have been formed for it, when such a configuration of the mouth would be wholly unsuitable for the use of language? The human being would necessarily have emitted bleatings or barks, or neighed like a horse, or produced a voice like that of oxen and asses, or uttered some bestial roar.

But now the hands have been adapted to the body so that the mouth may remain free for the service of speech. It is therefore proper to rational nature to have hands in the body, so that, with the Creator of all things granting the capacity, speech may be produced through them.

When God bestowed a certain divine principle of grace, or of the image, and granted the rational creature the gifts of his goodness, he bestowed the other goods upon human nature in pious generosity. But of mind and understanding it is not strictly correct to say that he “gave” them; rather, he bestowed upon nature its proper beauty, assigning it to the image.

Since the mind is an intelligible and incorporeal thing, it would possess grace in a certain incommunicable manner unless it revealed the movement of its activity through certain devices. For this reason it needed this construction of limbs: by touching the instruments capable of producing sound as though with a plectrum, it could interpret its inward movement through the qualities of sounds.

Just as someone trained in the art of music, if he lacked a voice suited to a particular emotion but wished to display his skill, might imitate other voices and publish his art through a lyre or flute, so the human mind, which is shown to be the inventor of every kind of understanding, cannot reveal the impulses of its intelligence to the bare soul through the senses of the body. Instead, touching these skillfully animated instruments as though in a kind of modulation, it makes its hidden understanding manifest through their sounds.

We may contemplate this mingled and varied music in the instruments of the human limbs, which, like lyre and flute, resound to one another in a certain harmony. When the vessel that receives the breath is struck by the speaker’s impulse and forms into voice the part resounded by the inward passages, those rounded structures made in the likeness of flutes certainly imitate the sound produced by flutes, which projecting membranes arranged in a circle set in motion.

The upper part, gradually hollowed out, receives the sound from below and, extending by twin tubes as far as the nostrils, breaks the voice toward the region of the sieve and produces greater sounds. The marvelous formation of the cheeks, tongue, and throat likewise contributes; along these the chin, drawn down in a gentle curve, is sharpened into a rounded form.

All these structures appear to imitate the movement of strings. The mind, touching them in place of a plectrum—as has often been said—composes, according to the demands of the moment and the need at hand, melodies with great speed, in various ways and through many combinations. The opening and closing of the lips does the same thing as the fingers that admit the breath of the flute according to the harmony of the melody. Through these instruments of the limbs, the skilled mind modulates reason within us; through this we are also shown to have become rational, possessing, as I think, the gift of reason.

Without this arrangement, we would be compelled to acquire the serious and laborious service of the body merely through the use of the lips. But now the hands have taken this function upon themselves and left the mouth free for the service of speech.

## CHAPTER X. That the mind operates through the senses

The effect of this instrument should be considered twofold. One of its functions produces speech; another remains available for receiving the intelligible impressions that come from outside. Neither function is mixed with the other, but each fulfills the operation established by nature without causing any disturbance to its neighbor. Hearing does not speak, nor does the voice hear. The voice always offers something, whereas hearing, continually receiving, is never filled.

Solomon testified in a certain passage to something that also seems to me especially worthy of admiration above all else within us: the breadth of that inner capacity into which everything poured through hearing flows; the memorial records that inscribe the impressions of the senses entering within; the spacious receptacles of understanding in which things conveyed through the ears are stored inwardly; and how, although the things deposited are numerous and follow one another, confusion and error do not arise at all in relation to the proper placement of what is introduced.

Who could likewise estimate the efficacy of sight? Through the eyes the mind apprehends what lies outside the body and draws into itself the likenesses of what appears, itself tracing the forms of things resembling one another.

Suppose there were a city capable of receiving a multitude of people who converge upon it through different entrances. They would not all assemble in one place of the city: some would hasten to the marketplace, others to their dwellings, others to the churches and streets, each according to his purpose. In a similar way I contemplate within us a kind of city constituted in the mind. Although our senses fill it through different entrances, the mind, judging and distinguishing each kind of thing that enters, arranges everything in places appropriate to understanding.

As in the example of a city, we see people of one nation and kinship enter not through the same gates, but each through a different entrance, as circumstance may offer. Nevertheless, once within the walls, those joined by mutual familiarity are again together. Conversely, those who are strangers or unknown to one another may often use the same entrance to the city, but they are not joined by their entering together; once inside, they can be separated in their dwellings.

I observe that something similar can occur in the breadth of our mind. Frequently one body of knowledge is gathered for us from different senses, each distributing the same object through a variety of sensory channels. The opposite also occurs: from one particular sense we learn and retain many varied things that, according to their nature, do not harmonize or correspond with one another.

For example—and examples make the meaning clearer—let us suppose that some characteristic of tastes is being investigated: what is pleasant to the senses and what should be avoided by those tasting. Experience itself discovers the bitterness of gall and the exceedingly pleasant quality of honey.

Although these things are certain, the same object, investigated in many ways—that is, through taste, sight, hearing, smell, and often touch—contributes one item of knowledge. Someone who sees honey, hears its name, tastes it, perceives its odor, and verifies it by touch recognizes one thing through all the senses.

In the same way, we also apprehend and retain varied and multiform things through a single one of the senses. Hearing receives voices of many kinds, and the sight of the eyes has an undifferentiated and manifold power for observing things that differ in kind. It likewise contemplates white and black and everything distinguished from them by opposition of color; and smell, taste, and touch are similarly shown, through their own effects, to grasp knowledge of things of every variety.

## CHAPTER XI. Why the human being is shown to be naked of natural weapons and coverings

What, then, is the mind according to its own nature, distributing itself among the sensory powers and suitably acquiring through each of them knowledge of existing things? I do not think that any prudent person would doubt that it is something other than sense.

For if the mind were itself the same thing as sense, it would necessarily possess only one property corresponding to the efficacy of sense, because the mind itself would be simple, and nothing diverse can be observed in what is simple. But now, since everyone agrees that touch is one thing, smell another, and that the other senses are likewise distinct, unchanging, and unmixed with one another, while the mind is equally present to each of them, it must be defined as something other than the sensory substance, lest any variety be attributed to the intelligible reality.

“Who has known the mind of the Lord?” the Apostle says. I, however, ask: Who has been able to consider his own mind? Let those who think they can comprehend the nature of God say whether they have considered themselves, whether they know the substance of their own mind. If it is something manifold and of varied composition, how does it enter into multiple senses? How is what is diverse found in unity, and what is singular in diversity?

But I have found a solution to this most difficult question by returning to the divine utterance itself: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.”

An image is properly recognized as an image so long as it differs in nothing from the original form in which it subsists. If it departs from the likeness of the form, then, to that extent, it is no longer an image. Since, therefore, incomprehensibility of essence is also contemplated in the divine nature, the image must necessarily imitate the substance of the original form.

If the nature of the image can be comprehended while the original form remains in its incomprehensibility, then by this very contrast—namely, that it is comprehended—the image is shown to be unlike it. Since, then, the nature of our mind, which has been made according to the image, escapes human knowledge, it expresses the omnipotence of the incomprehensible nature through its own incomprehensibility.

## CHAPTER XII. An inquiry into where the principal element of the human being appears to reside, and concerning tears and laughter

Let all conjectural and vain speech be silent—speech that encloses the power of intellectual activity within various bodily organs. Some locate the principal element of the human being in the heart; others suspect that it subsists in the brain, strengthening their opinion through a certain superficial plausibility.
