The person who defines the heart as the human principal element attempts to add arguments for his reasoning from its position, because the heart appears to occupy the central place of the entire body, so that spontaneous movement, more readily extending from the center through the whole body, may break forth into whatever effects it wishes. As witnesses for this reasoning they seem to bring forward the sorrowful and irascible affections of the human being, since such passions appear to move this part toward sympathetic response.

Those who believe that the brain is the dwelling place of intelligence assert that the head was constructed by nature as a kind of citadel of the whole body. They declare that the mind inhabits it like a queen, surrounded on every side by the senses as by messengers or guards.

They too offer signs suggesting this suspicion: the mind is led away from sound judgment and from what is fitting whenever the brain’s membrane is disturbed, and those whom drunkenness weighs down live in ignorance of what is honorable.

To these arguments they add certain natural causes, by which they appear to confirm the opinions they maintain concerning the principal part of the human being. One of them affirms a kinship between the movements of the mind and the fiery nature of the heart, because both mind and fire are shown to be wakeful in substance. Since he admits that the mind flows into the region of the heart, he therefore argues that the movement of the mind is regulated by the mobility of its heat, and declares the heart to be the receptacle of intelligible nature, in which warmth overflows.

The other bears witness that the membrane of the brain is, as it were, the principle and root of all the senses. He confirms his reasoning by asserting that the effect of intelligence is situated nowhere else than in that part where the ears are fitted to receive incoming sounds, where sight, concentrated in the very depths of the eyes, transmits inward to the pupils the forms of images that come before them, and where the qualities of various odors are distinguished after being drawn in.

The sense completed through taste is likewise approved by an indication of the brain’s membrane, as was said above. From it certain small branches of nerves, perceptible in themselves through their knots, extend nearby down through the neck and interlace with those regions that function like a sieve and with the surrounding muscles.

I, however, since the mind’s understanding is often disturbed by the approach of passion, and since the effect of thought is dulled alongside the body’s natural vigor, affirm that this too is truly caused by a bodily illness. I do not deny that the heart is a certain source of bodily heat, since it is easily stirred toward irascible impulses.

Nevertheless, I accept that the membrane of the brain presides over sensible things, in accordance with the reasoning of those who investigate these matters by natural argument. It encompasses the brain beneath it, and, having heard from those who have occupied themselves with anatomical examinations that it is also warmed by the vapor of fat, I do not entirely reject what is reported. But I will not attempt to prove from these facts that an incorporeal substance is confined within certain local boundaries.

We have learned that irrational excesses do not arise from heaviness of the head. The most skilled physicians, when either side containing the membranes of the brain is disturbed by some disorder, define our rational faculty as diseased, calling the condition “phrenic,” because those same membranes are called *phrenes*.

Those who suspect likewise that the heart is affected by sadness are certainly mistaken. When it is not the heart but the mouth of the stomach that is disturbed by grief, they incompetently transfer the disorder of this disease to the heart.

Those who have taken care to investigate the causes of the passions explain the matter as follows. In grief, the channels through which the vapors of the entire body naturally pass are compressed and closed. Whatever is prevented from leaving through these breathing passages is driven into the deepest regions within. Hence sadness is kindled when the viscera are constricted, and the breath is often drawn violently from the depths so that what has contracted may be expanded.

We call this breath expelled by grief a groan—that is, an indication of excessive pain. But those who think that this same passion affects a portion of the heart, as I said, are mistaken. The discomfort belongs not to the heart but to the mouth of the stomach, for the reason we have mentioned: when the passages of the vapors are compressed, the constricted gallbladder pours its harsh and biting fluid into the mouth of the stomach.

This is proved by the fact that, when the surface of the complexion is depressed, it appears stained as though by jaundice, while the gall’s fluid is diffused through the veins by excessive constriction.

This explanation is also especially confirmed by the disease that seems contrary to this one—namely, the condition arising from joy and laughter. Through the perception of some exceedingly pleasant experience, the vapors of the entire body are in a certain way expanded and released.

Just as in grief the thin and uncertain breaths are again compressed, and, constricting the inner organs, suppress toward the head and the membrane of the brain the moist vapor that flows abundantly through the hollows left beneath the passages of evaporation and runs toward the eyes, from which it is expelled drop by drop through the compression of the eyelids—and this drop is called a tear—so we should understand the contrary condition arising from distress’s opposite.

When the pathways of breathing are stretched more than usual, the breath enters their deep recesses and is immediately driven outward through the opening of the mouth by nature. All the viscera, and especially the liver—as those experienced in such matters say—by a kind of agitation and extremely vigorous movement, drive outward the breath thus gathered.

Accordingly, nature, devising a certain ease of exit for this breath, opens the mouth transversely, stretching both cheeks; and what is produced in this way has received the name “laughter.”

The principal element of the human being should therefore not be thought to reside in the liver, nor because of the heat of the blood, which is abundant around the region of the heart, nor on account of irascible affections should the dwelling place of the mind be judged to be in the heart. These matters are to be referred to bodily qualities.

We must believe that the mind touches each limb equally, according to the ineffable balance of reason. If some people bring Scripture forward to assert that the principal element is in the human heart, we should not accept this without examination. For the one who mentioned the heart also asserted the kidneys, saying: “God searches hearts and kidneys.” Thus either both or neither may be regarded as containing the intellectual element of the human being.

Although I have learned that these intellectual powers may be dulled, or even exist entirely without effect, through the condition of bodily affections, I do not regard this as a sufficient argument for asserting that the power of the mind is contained in particular locations, as though it could be driven out of its proper breadth by swellings occupying certain parts.

That is a bodily conception: a vessel already occupied by other things cannot receive anything else. The intellectual substance, however, neither dwells in the empty and convex parts of the body, nor is it expelled by the size or manner of flesh.

Since it is clear that the whole human body has been constructed as a kind of musical instrument, it often happens that those skilled in music cannot display their art because of the mutilation of the instrument, which resists the effectiveness of their skill—whether it has been damaged by time, broken by some accident, or worn away by rust or moisture. Thus it remains without the effects of sound, although it is breathed into by someone skilled in playing the flute.

In the same way, the mind, passing through the entire instrument of the body, appropriately touches the parts that possess intellectual functions, according as nature has fitted them.* In those that remain sound according to their substance, it exerts the power of its operation; in those that, through some defect, cannot admit its skillful movement, it exists apart from the effect of its operation.

Naturally, in a certain way the mind is fitted to reside properly and suitably in those limbs that are invigorated by their sound condition; from those afflicted by some weakness, it is wholly alienated.

## CHAPTER XIII. A certain natural contemplation concerning matter, nature, and the examination of the mind

It seems to me that the contemplation in this passage is more than merely natural, and that through it we can be instructed in certain more useful doctrines.

Since the Divinity itself is the best, highest, and pre-eminent good above all things, toward which all things that are held by desire for the good return, we therefore also confess that the mind, having been made according to the image of the most beautiful Creator, preserves a certain likeness of the original form and itself exists among the highest things. If it departs from that form, it is at the same time stripped of the beauty in which it existed.

Just as we say that the mind is adorned by likeness to the beauty of the principal form, like a certain mirror shining through the impression of what surpasses it, so, according to the same reasoning, we believe that the nature governed and directed by the mind is itself contained by the mind and adorned by its form, made as it were a mirror of a mirror.

We also acknowledge that this material element of our substance is sustained by nature, around which that same nature is seen to operate. Since one thing is contained by another, through all these levels the participation of that highest and true reality proceeds fittingly, with what is lower being adorned through what is higher.

But whenever there is a separation of this good communion, and, conversely, the higher pursues the lower, then the deformity of matter itself appears, when it is abandoned by nature. Matter in itself is an amorphous and disordered thing; when this formlessness of matter is present, the beauty of nature, which is adorned by the vitality of the mind, is also seized. Thus, through the defect of nature, the deformity of matter extends even to the mind itself, so that the image of God can no longer be seen in this impression of the creature.

Like a mirror—that is, the form of goodness and virtue—it turns its back and casts away the brilliance of its surpassing splendor; instead, it takes into itself the formlessness of matter. In this way the birth of evil occurs, creeping in through the deprivation of good.

Whatever is joined to the highest good is good. But if something lies outside the likeness of this making, it will undoubtedly remain without good. Since, according to the reasoning under consideration, the highest good is what is truly good, and since the mind was made according to the image of the highest good and received the capacity to be well, the nature contained by the mind is shown to be a kind of image of the image.

From this it is shown that our material substance subsists and is contained rightly when it is governed and directed by nature. Again, it is dissolved and cast down when it is deprived of nature’s providence and at the same time excluded from union with the good. This happens only when it has turned toward nature’s contrary, and its desire no longer advances toward the highest good but declines from it, appearing always to lack beauty.

What attains its likeness must necessarily be conformed to the most despised and foul deformity of matter. But these things have been said by us as a consequence, introduced through the contemplation proposed.

The question, however, was whether intellectual power is located in some part of the limbs or moves equally through all the members. To those who, as was said above, confine the mind within particular locations and bring forward as proof of their opinion the fact that the understanding of those whose brain membrane is disturbed contrary to nature does not function properly, reason shows that the mind naturally operates through all the parts of the human constitution, each member according to its fitness.

Similarly, the power of the soul exists apart from its efficacy when some part of the body no longer remains in its natural condition. For this reason the contemplation proposed has been introduced into our discourse: so that we may learn that, in the construction of the human being, the mind is governed by God, while our material life is contained by the mind so long as it persists in its natural condition. If it departs from nature, it must also be deprived of the mind’s cooperation.

Let us return again to the point from which we digressed. If, in those things that have entirely deviated from their natural constitution through some disorder, the mind preserves its proper effect, remaining sound in those that are vigorous but becoming powerless in those that cannot receive the force of its operation, then it is proper to confirm the meaning of this doctrine from other matters as well.

And if it is not burdensome or troublesome, I shall explain as well as I can, despite the fatigue of the present discourse, a few of these matters.

## CHAPTER XIV. A discussion of sleep and yawning, and a consideration of dreams
Source/review notes: The draft reversed the sense of the bodily nutritive power’s presence during waking activity.; Several phrases were substantively mistranslated or obscured, including the threefold vital powers, the relation of sensory and rational substances, and nature following the mind.

This material and fluid life of the body, always proceeding in motion, has this power and capacity of existing: that it never ceases altogether from motion, but, like a river flowing according to its own current, displays a full channel through which it descends. Yet the same water does not appear to remain around the same place; one part of it passes on, while another comes in. So too this material life of the present, through a certain motion of opposites, proceeds by their frequent succession in itself; it cannot come entirely to rest from its change, but, impatient of repose, possesses a continual transformation of things in like manner.

If it ever ceases from motion, it will likewise cease to exist. Thus emptiness relaxes fullness, and fullness in turn succeeds emptiness; sleep sustains the continual labor of wakefulness. Wakefulness likewise consolidates what seemed to have been dissolved. Neither of these remains in the same condition, but each succeeds the other through their mutual presence. Nature therefore renews itself through alternating changes, receiving a portion of each and moving from one to the other. For if the animal were always engaged in activity, exertion would produce the rupture and separation of the parts that are stretched; while continual rest of the bodies would bring about a kind of collapse and dissolution of their condition. But when each is received in due measure over time, it contributes strength toward the preservation of substance, which is restored on both sides through continual passage to opposites and their alternating succession.

Thus, having obtained an opportunity for repose, nature devises how to come to the aid of the body, strained by wakefulness, through sleep. It removes the senses from activity for a time, grants them leisure, and, as though restraining horses after contests and sweat, brings them to a halt. Rest is necessary for the body so that food may be diffused without impediment through all the limbs by hidden channels belonging to it, no obstacle of tension blocking its traversable passage. For just as, from earth soaked by rains when it has been warmed by the sun’s rays, certain dark vapors are drawn from its deepest regions, so it also happens in our “earth.” When food is cooked within by its innate heat, a certain vapor, naturally airy, strives upward; and, like smoke penetrating through cracks in a wall, it reaches the region of the head. From there it is exhaled through the aforesaid connections with the senses.

It is therefore necessary that, at that time, the senses should be at leisure, detained by the passage of the vapors. The eyes are put to sleep and, by the covering of the eyelids, are enclosed as though beneath the even weight of some mechanical device. Hearing too is obstructed by these vapors and, as though a kind of door had been placed over the ears, is struck from its natural activity. This condition is called sleep: the three bodily senses being vacant and, according to their natural motion, doing nothing at all, so that the digestion of food may take place with easier passage and may traverse its channels through the exhalation itself.

Consequently, if the regions around the senses are constricted by these exhalations and sleep is delayed by a kind of obstruction, they become filled with vapor. Since they are composed of nerves, they are naturally stretched of themselves, like the neck and throat, so that by this extension those parts which had been compressed by the vapors are thinned—just as happens when people wring garments soaked with water by excessive pressure and strive to squeeze out all their moisture. Since the parts around the throat appear more rounded and, as has been said, abound in nerves, whenever the thickness of the vapors must be dispersed from them—for it is impossible for an extended roundness to be displayed unless it accomplishes this according to its own configuration—the spirit released in yawning draws the chin downward toward the face by a certain concavity. When all the inner parts have thus been opened into a circle, that watery thickness which had settled in those places is driven onward by the advancing spirit.

The same thing often happens to us even after sleep, when something undigested has been left behind from those vapors. From these causes, then, the mind is clearly shown to be one, and to be in accord and agreement with nature: while the latter is awake, the mind likewise exercises its effects; when it has been dissolved into sleep, the mind nevertheless remains motionless. Unless, perhaps, someone should judge the images of dreams to be movements of the mind and suppose that it is active through sleep by means of its own motions.

We, however, firmly maintain that only that activity should be referred to the mind which is accomplished through wisdom and deliberation. The delirious fantasies that arise during sleep we regard as certain images produced by the mind’s activity, which the irrational part of the soul constructs through various accidents. Since the soul is called away from the senses in sleep, it must also be deprived of the mind’s activity. For it is through the senses that the mind, in a certain way, returns to the human being; when they are vacant, the understanding too must be at rest. The proof of this is that we are frequently mocked while asleep by the most foolish and empty forms. This would never happen if the soul were then governed by deliberation and reason.

It seems to me, however, that when the soul’s more immediate power—that is, the activity of the mind—and the senses are at rest, only that part of it operates in dreams which distributes nourishment and growth. If this is so, the dreams that occur, and the images corresponding to the senses and understanding, arise for the following reason. Whatever has been impressed upon us through that part of the soul in which memory is active is formed, as chance determines, into images, as though by the work of a painter, with a certain figure continually clinging to that aspect of the soul in which memory is contained.

Through these fantasies a person is deceived—not led by any orderly path toward conversation with the vision of things that appear, but misled by confused and inconsequential errors. For just as, in bodily activity, when each limb performs what properly belongs to it according to the power naturally implanted in it, a certain cooperation from a resting limb also contributes its agreement, so the same line of reasoning must be applied to the soul. When one part of it rests while another moves, the whole necessarily agrees with the part, because it is impossible for natural unity to be divided, even if some of its powers continue in activity.

Just as, when we are awake and occupied, the mind exercises authority and the senses obey it, yet that administering power of the body is not thereby shown to be absent—since the mind provides food for the needs of the body, while the senses take what has been provided, and the bodily power that attends to nourishment acquires for itself what is given—so in sleep, when the use of these powers is in a certain way removed, their roles in us are changed, and that which is proved to be more irrational exercises authority. The activity of the others comes to rest, but is not wholly restrained. For then the power of the soul that attends to nourishment, although through sleep it presses on toward the task of digestion and allows the whole of nature to be at leisure for itself, does not withdraw the sensory power from its activity. Nor is it lawful that what has once been naturally united should be torn apart. Yet its effect cannot shine forth, impeded as it is by the leisure of sleep.

For this reason, when the mind turns toward the form of the sensory soul, it follows that, when the latter moves, we should say that the mind likewise moves, and when it rests, that it similarly rests. It is natural for something of this sort to happen around a fire: when it is covered on every side with straw and stirred by no opening through which it might be kindled, it neither spreads around the covering nor is completely extinguished, but smoke rises in place of flame. If it is moved even slightly, the smoke immediately becomes flame.

Likewise, when the mind is covered by the leisure of the senses during sleep, it can neither shine forth through them nor be entirely intercepted, but seems to operate like smoke: in one respect lacking, in another prevailing. And just as a musician, when the strings of a lyre have been loosened, may strike the strings with the plectrum, but no proper melody answers him—for what is not stretched cannot resonate suitably—although his hand often moves skillfully, guiding the plectrum to the proper positions of the accents, while no sound is produced except an unordered noise from the movement of the strings, which the Greeks call Βόμβον (*bómbon*, “a buzzing or booming sound”); so in sleep, when the natural organs of the senses have been loosened, either the mind as craftsman rests entirely, if the body is weighed down by excessive fullness, or else it operates more weakly and obscurely, when this sensory instrument is unable to receive its art with sufficient precision.

Consequently, in dreams memory is confused and foreknowledge buried beneath certain veils. Against desire and intention, it contemplates certain images and sometimes foretells something of what is to come. For through the subtlety of its nature it possesses more than the density of the body for contemplating what approaches and appears; yet it cannot disclose the future in proper order, because what is discerned in dreams is not presented with clear and manifest instruction. Whatever it may be, then, it is an ambiguous announcement of the future—an “enigma,” as those who seem able to discern such things call it—because it presents one thing in words while conveying another in its meanings.

Thus Pharaoh’s cupbearer imagines himself pressing a bunch of grapes into a cup, while the baker imagines himself carrying loaves in a basket; each sees himself in sleep according to the occupation he practiced. For the likenesses of their accustomed arts, impressed upon the mind’s foreknowledge, provided through the whole prophetic vision an indication of what was to come.

But the fact that Daniel and Joseph, and others like them, were instructed by divine power in knowledge of future things without being disturbed in their senses, has no bearing on the present question. For no wise person ought to attribute such things to the category of dreams; otherwise he would also think that visions occurring by divine agency to those who are awake could come about not through a heavenly visitation but spontaneously, as a consequence of nature operating by itself.

Just as, among all people who govern themselves according to their own mind, there are some who deserve to be illumined by divine converse, so, in accordance with nature and in the common occurrence of dream-images among us, some during sleep become participants in a certain divine revelation. For everyone else, if foreknowledge is generated through a dream, it is generated in the manner described above.

But if that Egyptian or Assyrian tyrant was divinely instructed through dreams in knowledge of future things, something else was being accomplished through them by a wondrous dispensation. The wisdom of the saints, which appeared to be hidden, had to be made manifest, lest it pass through ordinary life without benefit or advantage. For how would Daniel have been recognized as such if the efforts of the enchanters and magicians had not failed to obtain the meaning of the dream? And how would Egypt have been saved while Joseph remained in prison, unless the interpretation of dreams had brought him forth into the public eye?

Therefore, whatever else these things signify, they must not be judged entirely according to ordinary fantasies. The customary appearance of dreams is the same for everyone, presenting itself in many forms through a certain mode of imagination. Either, as has been said, the likenesses of daytime occupations remain in that part of the soul in which memory is contained, or the expression of dreams is very often prefigured according to the qualities of bodily conditions.

Thus a thirsty person is astonished to find himself at fountains; one who needs food delights in feasting; and a young man vigorous in age is deceived by the allurements of images corresponding to his passions. I know also another cause of dreams that are enigmas and that provide relief. One of my acquaintances, seized by delirium and greatly burdened by it, had been given more food than his strength required. He imagined that several intestines filled with excrement had been placed upon him. When his exhausted body was already close to being relieved by sweat, he earnestly begged those present, while he lay there, to bring him water with which he could be drenched. He did not stop demanding this with cries until the outcome of the matter disclosed the cause of such complaints.

For at the same time a great quantity of sweat burst from his body, and his loosened belly explained the imagined weight of the intestines. What nature, impaired by illness, endured at that time was responding to the body’s imbalance: it felt distress but could not clearly express it because of the disease. As can be understood, if this had not resulted from physical discomfort while the mind remained sound in its natural sleep, a dream would certainly have arisen for someone in such a condition: water signifying sweat, the evacuation of the intestines signifying heaviness, and food indicating the weight and pressure that had caused it.

Many experienced physicians appear to hold the same view: that, according to the differences among illnesses, different forms of dreams occur to the sick—some to those whose stomachs are weakened, others to those afflicted by a disorder of the brain; still others to those suffering from fever, and others to those endangered by choler or phlegm. They likewise differ in those who lie sick from fullness and those suffering from emptiness.

From these observations it is possible to recognize that the power of the soul through which nourishment and growth come to us possesses some portion of intellectual capacity, joined to it by a kind of fellowship. While the quality of the bodily condition in some way presents a likeness, this power produces an imagination corresponding to the prevailing disorder.

Dream-images are likewise formed in many people according to differences of character. Some belong to the brave, others to the fearful, others to the lustful, and others to the self-controlled. One person is deceived by generous images, another by avaricious ones. Yet in none of these cases does the intelligence of the mind operate; rather, the more irrational part of the soul, as we have often said, produces these fantasies and, whatever pursuits it becomes accustomed to while awake, prefigures for itself their likenesses in sleep.

## CHAPTER XV. That there is only one soul in the human body, consisting of three powers

But we have been led far from our subject. Our discussion had promised to demonstrate that the mind is not enclosed in some particular part of the body, but is equally dispersed and spread throughout it, producing the movement of the part subject to it according to the likeness of nature.

There are occasions, moreover, when the mind itself follows nature’s impulses and, in a certain way, renders the service of a servant. Nature frequently precedes the body and conveys either opportunities for joy or causes of sorrow, so that it itself provides the beginning either of desiring food or of fulfilling some other pleasure. The mind, receiving such movements of the flesh, prepares the effects of considered things through the efforts of its deliberation.

This does not happen in everyone, but only in those who are shamefully disposed, subjecting the dominion of reason to the signals of nature and servilely obeying the pleasures of the senses at the bidding of that same mind. It is certain, however, that this does not happen among the more perfect, in whom the mind precedes in all things. They carry out what is fitting by reason rather than passion, and nature follows straight in the footsteps of what goes before.

Since reason discerns three differences in vital power—namely, the nutritive, which receives increase through certain senses; the sensory, which is nourished in such a way as to perceive; and the rational, which is perfect and extends through all of these—it must therefore be noted that one is merely vital, another sensory, and a third, above the rest, rational as well.

Yet no one should infer from this that there are three souls in the constitution of the human being, confined within separate boundaries, or imagine that the soul is compounded from several parts. The true and perfect soul is one, naturally spiritual and intelligible, and through the senses it is mingled with material substance.

Everything material and corporeal that is subject to transformation and change, if it participates in vital power, receives movement through growth. But if it withdraws from vital activity, it will testify to its movement through corruption. Thus neither the senses operate on account of material substance, nor does the intellectual power in us operate on account of the senses.

## CHAPTER XVI. That the soul of the human being is and is properly called rational, and that the soul, spread throughout the whole body, has nowhere a fixed seat

Since some creatures rely only on the power by which they are nourished and grow, while others prevail through sensory power, and since the former are shown not to participate in sensitive substance and the latter not in rational substance, why should anyone suspect a plurality of souls rather than define their differences by an appropriate account?

For everything that exists in the world, if it is called perfectly and integrally by its name, properly is what it is called. But if it does not exist in every respect as it is named, the name assigned to it is considered empty, as though it did not demonstrate the power of the thing. We say that a name is properly imposed upon its subject.

Suppose someone displays a likeness of real bread fashioned from stone. It has the same form, appears equal in size, and bears the same resemblance of color, so that it might be judged real by many indications. But since it lacks the capacity to be food, we say that it is properly and naturally a stone, and has received the name “bread” only abusively.

The same applies to all other things which are not in every respect what they are called: they possess their name by an abuse of language. Thus, although the soul possesses perfection in reason and understanding, whatever is not this may indeed be called “soul” equivocally, but is not truly called soul. Rather, it is a certain vital activity which, by an abuse of language, is named soul.

For this reason God gave the natures of irrational creatures, as not far removed from vegetative or seed-bearing life, for human use, assigning a measure of His law to each of them, so that those who eat their flesh might regard them as vegetables:

> “You shall eat all flesh as you eat the grass of the field.”

They seem to possess only a little more through the growth that comes by the senses than do the things by which they are nourished and through which they receive growth. This should teach lovers of flesh not to bind their soul to many sensory things, but rather to occupy themselves with spiritual privileges, in which the effects of the soul are truly seen. For in carnal things the irrational creatures are our companions and equals.

But somehow the sequence of the discussion has been bent toward another subject. The purpose was not to inquire what is more excellent in the human being, the activity of the mind or material substance, but to show that the mind is not attached to some one part of the things within us. Rather, it spreads itself equally through all things and in all things, neither contained externally nor contained internally.

This form of containment is clearly seen in jars, buckets, and other similar vessels and bodies, which properly contain themselves by their capacity. The mind’s communion with the body, however, is understood to possess a certain ineffable and incomprehensible bond. The mind is not within the body, since an incorporeal thing cannot be contained by a body; nor is it spread around or surrounding it externally. Rather, by an invisible and unexplored mode of nature, it is joined and connected to the body, and is seen in and around it in the manner I have described—so that it cannot altogether be conceived or expressed, except that, according to its proper order, the mind also exercises its effects through the same operative nature.

But if nature should falter through some defect, the mind’s movements must also falter.

## CHAPTER XVII. An exposition of the divine utterance, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness”; in which it is investigated in what respect, and according to what principle, our passible and mortal nature is like the blessed and impassible nature, and how male and female are approved in the image, although they do not appear to exist in the primordial form

Let us again take up the oracle of the divine voice:

> “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.”

Some outsiders have entertained small and unworthy notions about the grandeur of the human being, thinking to exalt him by comparing him with this world. They have said that the human being is a small world, composed from the universal elements themselves.

But what did such boastful talk about this name contribute to human substance? They entirely forgot themselves while foolishly constructing praises of the human being from the properties of the mouse and the gnat. Nature too is composed of four elements in those creatures, and in all living things some portion, greater or smaller, of these elements is observable, without which beings that use the senses cannot subsist at all.

What, then, is so remarkable if the human being is thought to be preferred to the form or likeness of the world—to the air, the heaven that passes away, the earth that changes, and all that is contained in them and passes away under the same condition?

But according to ecclesiastical reasoning, the greatness of the human being consists not in having been made in the likeness of the world, but in having been made in the image of the Creator.

Perhaps you will ask what the principle of the image is: how the corporeal can be like the incorporeal; what is temporal like the eternal; what is changed by continual motions like the unchangeable; what is subject to passion and corruption like the impassible and incorruptible; and what is constantly involved in wickedness and failure like Him who is without any wickedness.

There is a great difference between the primordial form and that which has been made in its likeness. For an image, if it preserves the likeness of the original form, is truly and properly called an image. But if it departs from its imitation, it is shown to be something else.

How, then, will mortal humanity be proved to be the image of that pure, immortal, and ever-subsisting nature? The truth itself alone clearly recognizes the true account of these matters. We, however, investigating the truth diligently, as far as we can grasp it, through certain conjectures and inferences, think that this is what is being sought. Neither is the divine utterance misleading, which relates that the human being was made in the image of God, nor is the misery of human nature something to be lamented, since it bears the likeness of that blessed and impassible life.

It is necessary to confess one of two alternatives: either, if someone compares what is ours with God, he must suppose the divine substance passible or the human substance impassible, so that a likeness of substance may be observed in both through these equalities; or, if the Divinity is not subject to passion and our nature is not shown to be exempt from passions, what other account remains according to which we can declare the divine utterance truthful when it testifies that the human being is the image of God?

Let us therefore take up the whole passage of Scripture, to see whether through it some clarification of the matter under investigation may shine forth for us. After saying, “Let us make the human being,” and indicating for what purpose he was made, Scripture adds:

> “God made [him] in [the] image; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them.”

It has already been said above that this statement was advanced for the destruction of heretical impiety. We are properly instructed by it that the only-begotten God made the human being in the image of God, so that we may not attempt in any way to distinguish the divinity of the Father and the Son, since divine Scripture equally confesses both to be God: both the one who made the human being and the one in whose image he was made.

But let this assertion be set aside for the present. Let us turn to the question proposed: how can the divine nature be blessed while Scripture describes the nature resembling it as miserable? Let us therefore examine the very words more carefully, and we shall find that one thing was made in the image of God, while something else is now seen in misery.

“God made the human being,” it says; “in the image of God he made him.” The condition of the one made in the image of God is complete. Then, as though speaking of that same condition, it adds:

> “Male and female he made them.”

But I think it is well known to everyone that this is understood to be alien to the primordial form. For, as the Apostle says, in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female. Since the divine word has divided humanity by these distinctions, it is shown that there is a twofold formation of our nature: one that reflects the divine likeness, and another that is shown to differ from it.

The sequence of the passage suggests something of this kind. First it says:

> “God made the human being; in the image of God he made him.”

Then it adds:

> “Male and female he made them.”

The latter is plainly foreign to what is understood of God. Yet I think that through these words of Holy Scripture a great and sublime doctrine is declared, which I understand as follows: the human substance stands midway between two realities separated from one another at their extremes—between the divine and incorporeal nature, on the one hand, and the irrational and brutish nature, on the other.

The principle of each is seen in the constitution of the human being. The divine is represented by the fact that the human being is rational and intellectual, and that this aspect rejects the distinction between male and female. The irrational is represented by the fact that the human being bears a corporeal constitution divided into male and female. In these two aspects are contained all the elements through which human substance exists.

We have learned from the very order of creation that what is intellectual in us was set above that which serves human generation. For in the effect of generation there is an innate connection between the human being and irrational creatures.

First, therefore, Scripture says:

> “God made the human being; in the image of God he made him.”

By this it shows what we said above that the Apostle defined: “In Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female.” Then it adds what expresses the distinctive properties of human nature:

> “Male and female he made them.”

Let no one blame me for seeming to derive the interpretation of the proposed argument from too great a height. God, who exists naturally and is superior to whatever good we embrace in thought—indeed, superior to every good that can be conceived or grasped—created the human being for no other reason than that He is good.

Since He is such, and therefore became the creator of a nature endowed with such form, He did not display the imperfect power of His goodness by giving some of what He possessed while withholding other things under the compulsion of envy. Rather, the mark of perfect goodness is that He brought what did not exist into generation and made it a participant in good things.

Since it is evident that good things are gathered together in great number, too great to be easily comprehended, Scripture wished to signify them all at once through a general expression when it related that the human being had been made in the image of God. This is equivalent to saying that human nature was made a participant in every good. For if divinity is the fullness of goodness, and the human being is its image, then this image too must possess the fullness of every good, since it bears the likeness of the primordial form.

Thus the condition of every good, every virtue and wisdom, and whatever else can be understood as best, exists in us. Above all, we are free from every necessity and are not subjected to some natural power, but incline by our own choice toward whatever counsel pleases us. For virtue is something voluntary and is subject to the dominion of no one. What is compelled by necessity can no longer be virtue.

Since an image displays the beauty and form of the primordial form in almost every respect, unless it differs from it in some respect it will no longer be a likeness, but will be shown to be identical and equal to it in all things—which is proved to be unchangeable in all respects.

Where, then, do we see the difference between the Divinity and its likeness? Clearly, in this: the Divinity is uncreated, whereas the likeness subsists as a creation. This difference in property produced, in turn, a corresponding sequence of other properties.

Everyone encounters the unquestionable confession that the uncreated nature is unchangeable and always remains in the same condition, while a creature cannot persist without change. Indeed, the very passage from nothing into existence was a kind of movement and transformation, when what did not exist was changed into being by divine counsel.

Just as the holy Gospel calls the figure impressed upon bronze an image of Caesar, through which we learn that the likeness of Caesar appears according to the figure, while a difference from him appears in the underlying material, so in the matters mentioned above the things observed in contemplation of the divine and human natures function as figures. In the things that share the same likeness, we discover an essential difference in the underlying subject, which the mind’s contemplation perceives as the difference between the uncreated and the created nature.

Since the Divinity itself always is, while the human being began to exist through creation and from change, and appears to have a certain kinship with mutable nature, He who knows all things before they come to be, as the prophet promised, foresaw and anticipated through the power of His foreknowledge toward what the movement of the human will would incline according to its voluntary choice.

He saw what would come to pass and assigned to the image the distinction of male and female, which would no longer look toward the divine and principal form but, as has been said, would appear to approach irrational nature.

Only those who behold the truth with their own eyes and are ministers of the Word understand the cause of so great an act of craftsmanship. We, however, pursuing the traces of truth through certain conjectures and indications as far as possible, communicate what has occurred to our mind to devout hearers, not as an absolute pronouncement but as an exercise.

What, then, have we been able to devise concerning these matters? When divine Scripture says, “God made the human being,” its indefinite expression signifies the whole human race. Adam is not named here in the account of creation, as the subsequent history also makes clear; rather, the name “human being” is a general name for the created human being, not for any particular person.

From this general designation of nature we are compelled to conceive something like the following: the divine power and foreknowledge seem to have embraced the whole of human nature in its first creation. For we must not suppose that anything created by God is indefinite, but that the wisdom of the Creator has established a most definite measure for each existing thing.

Just as each individual human being here is bounded by the quantity of his body, and the measure of his substance is its quality, which unfolds together with the surface of the body, so I think that the Creator of the universe, through the power of foreknowledge, embraced the whole fullness of humanity as though in a single body. Scripture intimates this when it says:

> “And God made the human being; in the image of God he made him.”

This image is not limited to one part of nature, nor is this grace confined to some individual person seen in his own singularity. Rather, this great and powerful capacity extends equally through the entire race.

The sign of this is that the mind is equally implanted in all. All are acknowledged to possess the capacity for thought and reflection, together with everything else through which the likeness of the divine nature is revealed in the recognition that the human being was made in the image of God.

Whether the one formed at the beginning of the world or the one who will exist after the completion of the whole world, each is shown equally to bear the divine image within himself. For this reason the one human being has been called the universe: the divine power, which contains all things, beholds neither something past nor something future, but also what is awaited, as though it were already present.

The whole of nature, extending from the first to the last, is therefore one image of substance. The distinction between male and female was subsequently carried out in the formation for the following reason, as I understand it.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What answer should be given to those who inquire, in doubt, whether the procreation of children is sin
Better, before the proposition is aired, I think we should seek the solution to the question advanced by our opponents. For they say that before sin there was neither childbirth nor labor nor the desire that serves the propagation of offspring; but after they had been driven from paradise because of their transgression, and the woman had been condemned to the punishment of childbirth, Adam then came together with his wife in lawful intercourse, and thus the beginning of procreation came into being.

If, therefore, marriage did not exist in paradise, nor labor there, nor childbirth, they say that it must consequently be judged that human beings would never have multiplied unless immortality had fallen into mortality, and unless nature had preserved itself through marriage by its own arrangement, continually restoring through those born from them those who had died. Thus sin appears in a certain manner to have been introduced usefully for the human race. Otherwise, the human race would have remained in those two who were first formed, since nature would not have been moved toward succession by any fear of death.

Yet in these matters, whatever the true explanation may be, it is known only to those who, according to Paul, are proved to have been instructed in the ineffable words of paradise. Our own assertion, however, is shown to be as follows.

When the Sadducees resisted the truth of the resurrection and brought forward the woman who had married seven brothers, to confirm their wicked doctrine, and then asked whose wife she would be after the resurrection, the Lord answered—not merely instructing the Sadducees, but revealing to all the mysteries of the life that would follow the resurrection:

“In the resurrection,” he said, “they neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they can no longer die, since they are equal to the angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection.”

The grace of the resurrection promises us nothing other than that we shall be renewed from our falls into our original condition. For a certain return to the former life is the grace for which we wait, by which the human being driven from paradise is once again happily introduced there.

If, then, the fellowship of those who have been restored will be joined to the angels in intimacy and number, it is clear that before his fall the human being was regarded as a kind of angel. Therefore, when our life has recovered its former state, it will unquestionably be made equal to the angels.

But although, as has been said, there is no marriage among them, there are nevertheless countless thousands in the angelic host, as the prophet Daniel makes known in his visions. Thus, in the same way, if no transgression of sin had drawn us away from that angelic dignity, marriage would certainly not have been necessary for the multiplication of the race.

Whatever that movement of nature may be by which angels are multiplied, it is most perfect, although human conjecture cannot devise it. Nevertheless, this mode certainly exists, and it has displayed the effect of its operation also in those who have been honored only a little less than the angels, multiplying the human race by the Creator’s will until the predetermined number is reached.

If someone should perhaps press us, asking by what means souls could have come into being if human beings had not sought marriage, let us in turn ask what the mode of angelic constitution is—how they are shown to subsist in one essence while existing in countless thousands, that is, in such great number.

This, then, is the more fitting answer to one who asks how a human being could persist without marriage: that it would occur in the same way in which angels are known to exist without marriage. For the fact that the human being was like them before the transgression is again shown by his restoration to the same likeness.

With these matters thus disclosed, let the discourse return to the question proposed: whether, after creating the image, God deemed it fitting to devise the distinction between male and female as a firm feature of humanity.

For this reason I acknowledge that the foregoing examination, which we have brought forth, is useful. He who brought all things into being, and who formed the whole human being according to the divine image by his own ordering, would not have allowed the number of souls to appear less complete through small and limited additions. Rather, he simultaneously bestowed the whole fullness of human nature through the effect of his foreknowledge. He also adorned it with the most exalted end, one not unlike that of the angels.

Since he knew, through his all-powerful providence, that the judgment of the human will would not move rightly, and that for this reason humanity would depart from the angelic fellowship, he arranged that the multitude of human souls should not thereby be diminished. Since humanity had fallen away from the mode by which the angels were multiplied, he therefore fashioned for our nature a mode of multiplication suitable and fitting for those who would fall into sin. In place of the angelic sublimity, he inserted into human substance the manner of beasts and irrational creatures, by which living things succeed one another through generation.

This is why it seems to me that the great David, compassionating human misery, lamented our nature in such words:

“Humanity, when it was in honor, did not understand”—calling “honor” the fact that it had been made like the holy angels. “Therefore it was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.”

For he truly became like a beast who received this animal generation into his nature, because of the fall attendant upon the transformation that befell him through material composition.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### That irrational passions in us are shown to have their occasions from kinship with nature itself

For I think that from this beginning all vices as well, flowing forth as from a certain spring, poured into the wretched conduct of human life. The present assertion is strengthened by this argument: a certain kinship between our passions and those of irrational creatures appears to be equal in us.

For it is not permissible to ascribe the beginnings of passible affection to human nature, insofar as it was formed according to the divine likeness. But because the life of irrational animals preceded humanity in this world, and because, for the reasons already stated, the human being also received something from the same formation with regard to the adornment of generation, he consequently became a participant in the other effects observable in nature.

For humanity is not like God through rage, nor is that transcendent nature represented through passible pleasure. Fear and boldness, the desire for greater possessions and hatred of diminution, and things similar to these, are far removed from the form in which divinity is expressed.

Human substance, then, derived these things from its rational part. Those features by which the life of brute creatures is equipped for its preservation, when transferred to the preservation of humanity, became the beginnings of the passions.

Beasts that feed on flesh are preserved by rage. Whatever creatures are lustful multiply their kind through propagation. Flight protects the weak, and fear guards the one who is more easily seized by stronger creatures. Gluttony preserves the corpulent, and if one fails to attain what pleasure seeks, this becomes an occasion of irrational grief.

There is no doubt that all these things, and whatever resembles them, came to human generation from the animal and brute formation. But grant me leave to describe the human form in speech by means of a certain imaginative comparison.

Just as we see sculpted images made from imagined subjects, which turn the minds of those who behold them toward astonishment, and those recognized as skilled in this art sometimes carve a single head with two faces, so a certain double and contradictory likeness seems to exist in the human being. Through the mind, by which humanity is worthy of God, it was formed according to divine beauty; but through the passions by which it is driven, it is joined by a certain affinity to brute animals.

Often its movement becomes almost brutish whenever it inclines wholly toward irrational impulses, obscuring what is better in it through attachment to what is worse. For as soon as someone bends the power of the mind toward the corruption of passion and compels his counsels to serve it, a certain distortion of the good formation is revealed. Thus the whole nature is changed into wickedness, when reason entirely cultivates the beginnings of the passions and multiplies the causes of vices in order to increase evil.

For when the mind offers its cooperation to the passions, it gives birth to a many-branched and dense abundance of evils. Thus sexual desire had its beginning from a likeness to irrational nature, but it grew exceedingly among human beings through excess, producing from the will itself such varieties of offspring as one could not find among irrational creatures.

Thus the disturbance of rage is indeed akin to something irrational, but it grows through the addition of thought. From this arise the memory of evil, envy, lying, ambushes, and pretenses. All these things proceed from the cultivation of an unjust mind.

For if the impulse of passion is not raised up by the assistance of thought, it soon grows weary, and violent rage is shown to be weak; as soon as it has arisen, it is extinguished. Thus the greedy eating of swine supplied occasions for avarice; thus the horse’s charging became the beginning of pride; and all the conditions found among irrational creatures became, through the practice of an evil mind, the beginnings of such things among rational mortals.

Conversely, when thought restrains and curbs these impulses, they are immediately transformed into the likeness of virtue. From rage comes courage; from fear, caution. Fear produces submission, while hatred incites the rejection of wickedness. The virtue of love also brings about desire for the true good. Exaltation likewise lifts character away from the passions and preserves free judgment from slavery to shamefulness.

The blessed Apostle also praises the appearance of this subtle transformation when he repeatedly commands us to set our minds on the things above. Thus one will find that every such movement which raises the mind to what is high is conformed to the beauty of the divine image.

But because there is a certain heavy and downward-turning quality in sins, and because the irrational nature prevails over the better part, the governing principle of the soul is depressed by its weight—for what is heavy and earthly is lifted up only with difficulty by the loftiness of the mind—it often happens that our misery fails to recognize the divine gifts, covering the most beautiful image with the ugliest face of passion.

Therefore those who observe such things are justified in not readily conceding that the divine form exists in such people; rather, they should behold the divine image in human beings who shine through a life of upright conduct.

For if someone vicious or devoted to the flesh does not allow us to believe that the human being is adorned with divine beauty, let the one who is perfect in virtue and completely pure from every contamination confirm that judgment which rests upon the better part of humanity. For what is said is proved better by example: the beauty of nature is diminished by contact with wickedness, especially in the one who is known to be most conspicuous in sins, such as Jeconiah or some other person remembered as renowned for wickedness.

But in Moses and those like him the beauty of the image is seen in perfection. In those whose beauty is not defiled by any obscurity, the truth of what is said shines clearly, since the human being is shown to be an imitator of divine goodness.

Perhaps someone is ashamed that, because we consume food, the likeness of irrational life constrains us, and therefore considers it unworthy of the human being who was made according to the image of God. But let us hope that nature will one day be granted immunity from this function in the life that is to come.

“For,” as the Apostle says, “the kingdom of God is not food and drink.” The Lord also testified that human beings live not by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. He likewise affirmed the glory of the resurrection when he showed that our life will be made equal to that of the angels.

Among the angels there is no food. It is therefore entirely fitting to believe that the human being who was made in the likeness of the angels will be freed from this function.

## CHAPTER XX  
### The mystical interpretation of the statement that the human being was permitted to eat from every tree that was in paradise

But perhaps someone will say that the human being is not returning again to the same kind of life, since at first we lived by eating. Yet, listening to holy Scripture, I do not understand bodily food, nor joy that comes only from the flesh. I recognize another food altogether, which bears a certain likeness, proportionate to the food of the body, but whose pleasure and sweetness pass only into the soul.

Thus Wisdom exhorts the hungry and says: “Eat of my breads.” And the Lord declares blessed those who hunger for such food. He also says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.”

The great Isaiah likewise says: “Drink joy,” giving this command to those who are able to hear his magnificence.

There is also a certain prophetic threat against those who deserve such punishment, namely, that they should be punished as though by hunger. Hunger, however, is not lack of bread or water, but lack of the word:

“Not a hunger for bread, nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of God.”

As for that planting which was made by God in Edom, pleasure—for *Edom* is interpreted as “pleasure”—compels us to conceive of a worthy fruit by which human substance was undoubtedly nourished. It is certainly not fitting to understand this pleasure as the pleasure that passes away and flows off in the life of paradise.

“You shall eat,” he says, “from every tree that is in paradise.”

Who will give to one who hungers healthfully that tree which is in paradise, which embraces every good, whose name is “all,” and to which the law grants participation? For by this general and transcendent word the whole form of goods is understood as one’s own, and all of it is one.

But who will remove me from the taste of that tree which is mixed and inclines in both directions? For it is not at all uncertain, among those whom the grace of contemplation enlightens, what the tree is whose fruit is life, and again what that mixed and confused thing is whose contact produces death.

He who granted every delight with abundant generosity evidently prohibited human beings, by some reason and providence, from partaking of what is common.

It seems to me that we ought not to bring forward the most magnificent David and the wisest Solomon as deserters of this law. Both professed the living grace of this food. For what truly is good is altogether good.

David says: “Delight, or take your pleasure, in the Lord.” Solomon calls Wisdom itself, which is the Lord, the tree of life.

Therefore the tree of life is the same as the tree “all,” whose food the divine law granted to the one who was created according to God.

Conversely, another tree is distinguished from this tree: its food is the knowledge of good and evil. It does not produce each of the two separately, each bearing fruit in its own portion according to the significance of their opposition; rather, it brings forth a certain confused and mixed fruit, compounded from contrary qualities. From partaking of it the Author of life prohibits us.

The serpent, however, persuades us to eat, so that through this he may contrive the entrance of death. When the persuasion prevailed, it offered a deadly counsel and sprinkled the same fruit of pleasures with a deceptive color, making it appear exceedingly sweet and causing desire to be kindled by its taste.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### What the life in paradise was, and what that tree was which was forbidden

What, then, is that tree which contains the knowledge of good and evil and appears most pleasing through the pleasure of the senses? I think that, by applying myself to conjectures, I do not depart far from the truth, using my understanding of knowledge to attain this contemplation.

For I think that the knowledge perceived by those whose senses have been trained is not, in the present case, a discipline. Rather, I find that the customary usage of the divine Scriptures distinguishes between knowledge and discernment.

According to discipline, the Apostle says that distinguishing good from evil belongs to a more perfect state, namely, to those whose senses have been trained. For this reason he also taught us to test all things and said that it is characteristic of the spiritual person to be able to judge and discern everything.

“Knowledge,” however, does not everywhere signify discipline and acquaintance according to its ordinary meaning. It is also used in a good sense according to the effect of grace, as in the statement: “The Lord knows those who are his.” And God says to Moses: “I have known you above all.” But concerning those who are condemned for their evils, the one who knows all things testifies and says: “I never knew you.”

Therefore that tree which produces a mixed and confused knowledge belongs among the things forbidden to us by the Lord.

Its fruit appears joined from contrary qualities, and it is also proved to have the serpent as its advocate. Perhaps the reason is that evil is not presented naked and uncovered, so that it could be seen by itself according to its nature. Otherwise evil would remain ineffective, since it would not be colored by any imitation of good through which the deceived might be drawn into desiring it.

Now the nature of evil is mixed in a certain way: it contains ruin at its core, like an ambush laid openly. But in the seduction that is not apparent, it displays before itself a certain image of good.

Gold appears good to the greedy and covetous as the material of their desire, but avarice is the root of all evils. Who would plunge into the filth of the most hideous and shameful lust unless he considered pleasure something good and acceptable, drawn toward the disease of passion by a certain enticement?

So too, all the other sins have a thoroughly mixed character: at first sight they seem most acceptable, and through the coloring of seduction they are sought as goods by the thoughtless and imprudent.

Since many people consider whatever delights the senses to be good, and since there is a certain kinship of name between the truly existing good and what is thought to be good but is not, Scripture therefore calls that desire which draws one toward evil as though toward good “the knowledge of good and evil.”

This knowledge indicates a certain affection: it is neither absolutely evil, because it is colored by the surface of good, nor genuinely good, because the destruction of evil lies hidden within it. Rather, it is mixed—that is, perplexed from both—and Scripture declares that the fruit of the forbidden tree was of this kind, saying that its taste draws those who touch it toward death.

It proclaims this almost openly, both in doctrine and in language: what truly is good is simple and one, alien to every form of evil; but evil is various and disguised. It is thought to be one thing, while experience proves it to be another. The knowledge of it—that is, the effect of its operation—is the cause of death and the beginning of corruption.

Therefore, when the serpent displayed the most wicked fruit of sin, it did not openly reveal evil as it exists by nature—for no one would have been seduced by manifest wickedness. Instead, it illuminated what appeared through a certain form, insinuating pleasure through the senses and conveying it to the taste. In this way it persuaded the woman to transgress, as Scripture says:

“And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, pleasing to the eyes, and beautiful to behold; and she took of its fruit and ate.”

That food became the mother of death for human beings.

There is therefore a mixed production of fruit. For the statement clearly disclosed the meaning: it showed how that tree appeared to be called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

It is like poison coated with honey: because the sweetness scattered over it pleases the senses, it is believed to be good; but because it seizes and destroys those who take it, it becomes worse than every evil.

When deadly poisons had thus prevailed against human life, the human being—great in reality, great in name, and formed according to the divine nature—became, as the prophet says, like vanity.

The image of God, therefore, is properly seen in those things that are understood to be best in us. Whatever in our life appears wretched and grievous is shown to be entirely alien to the divine likeness.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### That the resurrection must be upheld not only from the preaching of Scripture but also from the very necessity of things

Evil is not so strong that it can prevail against divine power, nor is the instability of our nature better or more enduring than the wisdom of God. For it is impossible that what is mutable and changeable should exist more tenaciously and firmly than that which remains continually and endures in goodness without any change.

The divine purpose, therefore, is wholly immutable; but the mutability of our substance does not retain even evil in permanence.

Whatever is always in motion—if its advance tends toward the good, because it approaches an infinite reality which it reaches by progressing—will never bring that progress forward to an end, since it cannot find any limit to the one it seeks at which its motion ought finally to cease.

But if its intention turns toward the opposite, once it has completed its course in wickedness and reached the highest summit of evil, then the impulse of its continual movement, finding no stable condition in its own nature, will necessarily turn its motion toward the best things when it has run through the allotted extent of wickedness.

For since wickedness cannot advance without limit but is enclosed within necessary boundaries, the succession of good will consequently be the end of evil. Thus, as has been said, our nature—which is always unmoved—will afterward pursue the course of good through a certain return, instructed by the memory of the evils with which it has been afflicted, so that it may not again turn back toward similar things.

Our course, then, will once more be among good things. This is why, as I said, nature is proved to have had necessary limits imposed upon the realm of wickedness.

Those who discuss lofty matters say that the whole world is filled with light in its upper regions, while darkness is generated from the shadow of the earthly body and its obstruction—this according to the figure of a body gathered into the form of a sphere, with the rays of the sun extending behind it and excluding the light like a cone.

They say that the sun, being much larger than the earth, surrounds it on every side with its encircling rays, removing the projections of light according to the limit of the cone. If someone were granted the power to pass beyond the measure to which the shadow extends, he would certainly always be in the light, with no darkness confronting him.

So, I think, we should also conceive of ourselves: when we have passed beyond the limits of wickedness and have been placed in the deepest darkness of sins, after the ages we shall again dwell in the light, whose bounds cannot be contained, as though the substance of good surpassed the measure of the shadow.

Paradise, then, once again; every tree, once again—that tree which is also the good of life; once again, the grace of the image and the dignity of rule.

Nor does it seem to me that these things refer to what God has now given human beings for the necessities of life. Rather, the hope of another reality is promised, whose meaning is shown to be ineffable.

But let us pursue the consequences of what we are examining.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Against those who say: If the resurrection of the dead is good and excellent, why did it not take place long ago, but is delayed through certain cycles of time?

Perhaps someone, inflamed by thought of so sweet a hope, considers it a heavy burden and a great loss that he does not arrive more quickly at those good things that transcend human sense and knowledge, and is distressed by the interval of time, which through its delay stretches out what is desired.

But let him not be troubled like a child impatiently awaiting a brief delay in pleasure. Since all things are administered with reason and wisdom, whatever takes place must necessarily be governed by reason and wisdom.

You say to me: What is the reason why one is not immediately allowed to reach from this most troublesome life the object of one’s desire? Why is this grave and temporal existence, fixed for definite periods, made to await the end of the whole consummation, so that then human life, as though released from certain barriers, may again proceed in peace and freedom toward the blessed and impassible state of future contemplation?

Whether this explanation comes close to the truth, the Truth itself knows clearly concerning the matters under investigation. But what enters into our understanding is as follows.

I take up again the first statement in which God said: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.” The perfect image of God achieved the measure of perfection in the whole of human nature.

Adam, however, had not yet been formed. The earthly condition, according to a certain expression of its name, is called *Adam*, as those skilled in the Hebrew language assert. Therefore the Apostle, sufficiently instructed in the ancestral language—that is, the language of the Israelites—calls the human being “earthly,” transferring the name Adam into a Greek sound.

The universal human being was therefore made according to the image, since nature is most like God. And by omnipotent Wisdom he was made not as a part of the whole but as the fullness of the entire nature at once.

He saw, as Scripture recalls, that all the ends of the earth are in his hand. He who knows all things before they come to be, comprehending everything by divine knowledge, saw how great humanity would be in each individual according to its number.

And because he likewise saw beforehand that the creature would be more inclined toward evil, and that, freely falling away from angelic dignity, it would be joined in the utmost humility to the common nature, he mingled something from irrational creatures with his image.

For in that divine and blessed nature there is no distinction between male and female. But he transferred to the human being a certain characteristic of irrational formation, as I have said, and did not establish the multiplication of our generation according to that most exalted creation.

For it was not when he made humanity according to the image of God that he commanded human beings to increase and multiply. Rather, when he made the distinction between male and female, he then said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” This is not a characteristic of divine nature but of irrational nature, as the text of the history shows, indicating that this was first spoken by God concerning irrational creatures.

If he had first made the distinction between male and female in us, and through the word “Increase” had bestowed on humanity the power of multiplication, we would not have needed this mode of generation by which irrational creatures are reproduced.

Since God had therefore already contemplated through his foreknowledge that the fullness of human beings would come into life through animal procreation, he who disposes all things in order and with reason established this mode of generation as necessary for humanity. It would be more inclined toward the humility of our nature, which he saw before it came to be—for he beholds future things as though they were present.

Therefore, in creating humanity, he also established beforehand the measure of time, so that, in accordance with the dwelling of the souls predestined for this world, both their sojourn and the delay of time might extend together. Then the flowing movement of time itself would at last come to rest, when the human race could no longer arise within it.

When human generation has been completed, time also will fail, and thus the restoration of all things will take place. In this universal transformation the human race will be changed, passing from a corruptible and earthly condition to one that is impassible and eternal.

It seems to me that the holy Apostle also foretold this sudden halting of time and, conversely, the dissolution of mutable things when he said to the Corinthians:

“Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.”

For when, as I think, the fullness of human nature has reached its limits according to the measure foreknown by God, when nothing further is lacking for the increase of the number of souls, he taught that the change of existing things would take place in a moment of time. By “moment” and “twinkling of an eye” he named that indivisible time and terminus without any interval, so that nothing could possibly be added in speed beyond the last and highest point.

For this reason, a large part of humanity will remain at the end to possess this change in death. But as soon as the trumpet sounds—the trumpet that will then awaken the dead—those who are found alive will also be changed, in likeness to those who have risen from the dead, and will come together with them to incorruption.

Then they will no longer be pressed downward by bodily weight, nor will an earthly mass hold them back; rather, they will be carried aloft into the air.

“For,” the Apostle says, “we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we shall always be with the Lord.”

We therefore await that time, which is now necessarily extended by the increase of humanity.

Abraham and the patriarchs who were with him indeed desired to see the good things of the Lord, but they were not able to attain the heavenly homeland, as the same Apostle says. They remain still in the grace of hope, because God has provided something better for us, according to the word of the blessed Paul, so that they should not be made perfect without us.
