If they bore this delay with equanimity—those who, seeing the good things of the Lord from afar by hope and faith alone and greeting them, as the Apostle testifies, placed the sure delight of things hoped for solely in their trust in the faithful Promiser—what ought we to think, who perhaps cannot even maintain hope for something better on account of the quality of our life?

The prophet’s soul also failed from longing; through his psalmody he confessed the greatness of his love and said:

“My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord.”

And if he happened to be cast among the lowest, he asked that it be better and more excellent to be among the last in those courts than to be first in the tents of sinners.

Nevertheless, he was most patient concerning the delay, blessing that fellowship and preferring even a brief participation in it to thousands of days in the present age:

“For one day in your courts is better than thousands.”

Yet he did not bear with resentment the necessary ordering of the things that take place. It is certainly a fitting condition for blessedness that human beings do not cease to hope for good things. Therefore the same prophet places this at the end of the psalm and says:

“Lord God of hosts, blessed is the person who hopes in you.”

It is not fitting, then, to confine concern for the things that are to come within a narrow heart. Rather, lest we fall away from the promises, we ought to devote ourselves to them.

Suppose someone inexperienced and unskilled were warned that in summer there would be an abundant gathering of fruits, that the granaries would be filled with crops, and that the table would be laden with the many foods produced by such plenty. He would plainly be foolish if he hastened to anticipate the arrival of that season, since he must first scatter the seeds and prepare the fruits for himself through diligence, whether he wishes to or not.

For the appointed season will come, but it will not receive equally those who have prepared an abundance of crops and those who, empty of every provision, are overtaken at that very hour.

So, I think, it is also expedient for us. Divine preaching has made clear to all that we should press on toward the future time of our transformation, not investigate the times that are to come, since Scripture says that it is not ours to know the times or the moments, nor should we seek out speculations by which the soul might be weakened and wearied of the hope of resurrection.

But if we possess any faith in the things that are promised, we ought to cling to the pursuits of the best way of life and patiently await the venerable antiquity of the future grace itself.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### That whoever acknowledges the beginning of the world’s constitution must necessarily also concede its end
If, however, someone, observing the course of the present world moving according to a certain law, by which the span of time flows onward, should in no way say that the cessation of motion, which has been foretold, can take place, it is clear that such a person does not acknowledge that heaven and earth were made by God in the beginning either. For whoever believes in a beginning of motion has no doubt at all about its end; but whoever does not admit an end plainly has not admitted a beginning. Yet just as we understand through faith that the ages were established by the word of God, as the Apostle says, so that visible things might come into being from invisible things, by that same faith let this be believed concerning the Word of God, who foretold that a necessary transformation of existing things would occur.

But in what manner this will happen belongs to the curious to investigate. For there too we perceive through faith in invisible things that the visible things are complete, passing beyond the investigation of what cannot be comprehended. Indeed, since the teaching reminds us that we are ignorant of many things, it has granted no small consolation concerning the uncertainty of matters that must be believed. For contentious people could there too, by certain arguments, consistently overturn the faith, lest the statement pronounced by Holy Scripture—that everything that exists is from God—be thought true with regard to material creation.

[Col. 0386B] Those who strive by the contrary argument say that matter is coeternal with God, constructing their doctrine with arguments of this kind: “If God is of a simple nature, he is certainly without matter, without quantity, without mass, and without composition, existing apart from the defining characteristics of every figure. But all matter is perceived in the extension of dimensions, and it entirely fails to escape the grasp of the senses. It is recognized in color and shape, in mass and quality, in impression or hardness, and in other similar properties; yet none of these can be found at all in the divine nature. What, then, is the device by which a nature contained within dimensions proceeds from that which is defined by no distance? For if these things are believed to exist from that source, it is certain that they must be thought to adhere to it and, according to an ineffable principle, to have thus entered into the order of generation. But if there is something material in it, how is he himself not material, who contains matter within himself? Likewise, if everything by which material nature is formed is in him, and quantity is therefore believed to exist for that reason, how is God without quantity? If he is in that which is composite, how is he himself simple and without composition?”

Thus it is necessary either to regard him as material, since reason itself compels us to conclude that matter subsists from him, or, if anyone shrinks from this, he will nevertheless judge that matter was introduced from outside for the constitution of the universe. If, therefore, it was extraneous, it will be clear that there existed something other than the Lord, which must also be understood to have subsisted eternally alongside the Unbegotten. Thus reason would bring together two equally unbegotten principles: namely, the one who works with greater skill, and the one that receives the disciplined form of this workmanship.

[Col. 0386D] But if anyone, compelled as it were by necessity, posits eternal matter for all created things, what support and defense for his doctrines will Mani find, when he strives to make a material cause equal to the good nature in its unbegotten and ungenerated existence?

We, however, hearing Scripture say that everything is from God, retain this belief; and, since how things are from God is beyond our understanding, we do not investigate it curiously. We believe the divine nature to be the creator of all things, since it both established what existed as reason and, once what had been established was in being, brought it by wondrous transformation into whatever magnitude it wished. Accordingly, we judge that existing things can subsist by the will of divine power for that state of establishment which does not yet exist. And if, referring the consummation of things to his power, we were in no respect to take up a rational explanation within our discipline on account of what we profess to believe, we might nevertheless, by a certain invention of words, persuade those who dispute contentiously about matter not to dare thereafter readily to oppose our argument.

## CHAPTER: On the nature of heaven, and that according to Aristotle it is not composed of the four elements

*(The following chapter does not belong to this book, but seems perhaps to have slipped here from the book On the Elements because of the similarity of its subject; in that work it is the fourth chapter.)*

Aristotle, however, introduces a fifth body, the ethereal body, I mean, which is carried around in a circle, refusing to say that heaven was generated from the four elements. He says that this fifth body is carried in a circle because it moves in a circular revolution. Plato, on the other hand, clearly argues that it consists of fire and earth, saying as follows:

“A corporeal form must be both visible and tangible. Yet nothing will ever become visible without fire, nor tangible without something solid; and the solid cannot exist without earth. Therefore God, beginning the body of this universe from fire and earth, made it. But two things cannot properly subsist without a third, for a bond is needed to join the two together. The best bond is that which makes both itself and the things joined as fully one as possible. The most suitable way to accomplish this is proportionality; by ‘bond’ I mean the two intermediate elements assumed according to such a proportion.”

[Col. 0387C] Those who follow Hebrew teaching, however, differ concerning heaven and earth. Nearly all of them say that heaven and earth were generated from no pre-existing matter, because Moses says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Apollinarius, however, wishes God to have made heaven and earth from the abyss. Yet Moses does not mention the generation of heaven in connection with the abyss as something generated. In Job, however, it is said that he made the abyss. From this Apollinarius judges that all other things were generated. He does not, however, wish the abyss to be ungenerated; rather, he says that it was produced before all bodies and that it received from the Creator a prior role in bringing the others into existence. Hence the abyss is matter (*hylē*, ὕλης); but however this may be, it makes no difference. For in this way too God is shown to be the creator of all things, having made everything from things that did not exist.

[Col. 0387D] Against those who assert that there is only one element—earth, fire, air, or water—the statements attributed to Hippocrates are sufficient. If there were only one element, a human being would never suffer pain, for there would be nothing from which pain could arise if only one thing existed. And if he did suffer pain, from where would there be something to heal him? The sick person must, however, be transformed with awareness. But if there were only one element, there would be nothing into which it could be transformed. If it were not transformed but remained in itself, it would not suffer pain at all, even if it were capable of sensation. Yet whatever suffers must necessarily suffer from something.

If, therefore, there were only one element, apart from its quality there would be no other quality from which the living creature could suffer. And if it could neither be transformed nor suffer, how could it feel pain? Demonstrating that this is impossible, Hippocrates adds, as a matter of course: “But if it did suffer pain, from where would there be something to heal it?” In fact, however, the thing that heals is not one but many; therefore the human being is not constituted from one element.

Moreover, the very grounds by which each of these thinkers attempts to reinforce his own doctrine most clearly demonstrate that there are four elements. Thales, saying that water alone is the element, attempts to show that the other three are generated from it: its sediment becomes earth; what is finer (*λεπτομερέστερον*) becomes air; and what is thinner than air becomes fire. Anaximenes, positing air alone, likewise attempts to show that the other elements are produced from air. Heraclitus and Hipparchus of Pontus, in turn, putting forward fire, employ the same demonstrations.

Since, then, these thinkers say that fire generates the other elements, while one says the same of air and another of water, it is plainly evident that all the elements are mutually transformed and turned into one another; consequently, each of them must necessarily be an element. For whichever of the four elements you take away, it will be found to be produced from another.

## CHAPTER XXV. Against those who dare to assert that matter is coeternal with God

The opinion concerning matter that is found by inference is not consistent with the assertion that matter, too, exists without matter on the basis of the intellectual nature. For we find that every kind of matter subsists through certain qualities; if it were deprived of these, it could in no way be grasped.

Yet each species of quality is divided by reason as an underlying subject. Intellectual reason is not corporeal inspection. Suppose, for example, that some animal, or a piece of wood, or anything else that subsists through material constitution, is placed before our contemplation. By the discernment of thought we consider many features belonging to the same underlying subject; each of them, although observed together with the others, is contained separately according to reason and order, without any commingling.

The account of color is one thing, and the account of weight and quantity another. The account of quality is likewise one thing, and that of touch another. For softness, being two cubits long, and the other properties just mentioned agree neither with one another nor with the body by any likeness of nature. Each has its own particular account attached as its interpreter, sharing in none of the qualities perceived in its underlying subject.

If, therefore, color is intelligible, and shape is intelligible, and quantity and the other properties of this kind are likewise intelligible, while, if each of these is removed from the underlying subject, the entire account of the body is dissolved, it follows that we must judge the coming together and concurrence of those things whose absence we recognize as causing the dissolution of the body to constitute material nature.

For just as the body is not color, shape, distance, weight, or any of the other properties in which it participates—and since each of these, as we have said, is present in something, none of them can be the body, but is shown according to its own property to be something other than the body—so, conversely, wherever the things mentioned come together, they complete a corporeal substance.

Indeed, if the intellectual apprehension of these things is established, and the divine nature is intellectual, there is nothing incongruous in supposing that from the incorporeal, intelligible nature these principles of corporeal generation can subsist. For the intellectual nature produces intelligible powers, while their coming together with one another consequently brings forth material nature and generation.

But these matters have been discussed only in passing. We must once more refer the whole argument to faith, through which we have learned that everything was established from things that did not exist, and, having been taught by the venerable Scriptures, we have no doubt that everything will again be transformed into another state.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How even someone from outside the faith may be led to believe the Scripture teaching concerning the resurrection

Perhaps, however, someone, observing bodies already dissolved and assessing divine power according to the measure of his own abilities, will acknowledge that dissolution is impossible and declare that what is in motion cannot stand still, and, indeed, that what is not now in motion cannot rise.

But whoever he may be, let him first accept this as the chief and greatest argument for the truth of the resurrection: its preacher is shown to be entirely worthy of faith, while the credibility of what is said retains its firmness from the things that were foretold and have been fulfilled.

Since the authority of divine Scripture has commended many different statements to us, I think it easy to determine from what has already been fulfilled whether the things that were said are false or true, and through those things to examine this doctrine of the resurrection as well. For if its other statements are shown to be false and far from the truth, this too is recognized as lying outside truth. But if everything else is true, as experience itself testifies, it follows that through these things the preaching of the resurrection is also true.

Let us therefore recall one or two of the things that were foretold and at the same time set forth their outcome, so that we may recognize whether our statement corresponds to the truth.

Who, then, is unaware of how the Israelite people flourished in ancient times, exalting themselves over nearly all the powers of the world? What were their kingdoms in the city of Jerusalem; what were its walls and towers; how great was the magnificence of the temple, so that even Christ’s disciples regarded it with wonder and begged the Lord to take notice of it? They were so overwhelmed with amazement at what they saw that, as the history of the holy Gospel declares, they said: “What works these are, and what buildings!”

The Lord, however, disclosed to those who were then admiring it excessively the future desolation of the place and the destruction of its beauty, saying that shortly none of the things they saw would remain.

At the time of his Passion as well, when women followed him weeping and lamenting because he had been condemned by an unjust sentence—for they could not yet understand the dispensation of what was taking place—he offered them counsel and told them to cease weeping for what concerned him, since those things were not worthy of tears. Rather, they should reserve their lamentations and mourning for the time when they would express genuine grief: when their city would be pressed by besiegers and they would come into such distress and calamity that they would declare blessed the one who had not been born in that time.

Among these events he also foretold the crime in which they would devour their own children because of famine, saying that in those days the barren woman who had not given birth would be fortunate.

Where, then, is that kingdom? Where is the temple? Where is the height of the walls and towers? Where is that power of the Israelites? Do they not appear to be scattered, one here and another there, throughout nearly all the lands, and has not the kingdom too been destroyed together with their overthrow?

It seems to me that the Lord foretold these things and others like them not for the sake of the events themselves—for what benefit would knowledge of future events bring to his hearers, when, even if they did not know them beforehand, experience itself would teach them?—but so that through them faith might now consequently be established concerning greater matters. For the testimony established in these events is shown to be an indication of truth in those other matters as well.

Just as, when a farmer tells someone inexperienced about the power of seeds, and that person does not believe him, it is enough for the farmer, as proof of the truth, to demonstrate their power in one seed, so that his assertion concerning the rest may be firmly established: once someone has seen a single grain—for example, wheat, barley, or any of the others that may be used in medicinal measure—rise into an ear after being placed in the earth’s womb, he can no longer doubt the others.

So it seems to me that the truth itself, foretold and fulfilled in events, or rather the experience of the resurrection itself, which we have learned not so much through words as through things, provides suitable testimony concerning the mystery of the resurrection.

Since the miracle of the resurrection was something great and beyond belief, the Lord, beginning with a lesser sign of power, gradually accustoms our faith to greater things by successive stages. Just as a mother appropriately nursing a little child first puts her breast to its tender lips, but when it begins to grow teeth offers it bread—not hard or stiff as it is, lest its solidity irritate the softness of the gums, but chewing it with her own teeth and preparing food suited to the child’s strength—and then, in proportion to its growth, prepares stronger food for one who has become accustomed to softer nourishment, so the Lord, feeding and guiding human weakness as though it were an immature infancy, through such mighty miracles and through the illness that lay seemingly beyond hope, instructs it in the power of the resurrection.

That event was indeed pitiable in its completion, but not such that it could be believed wholly impossible. For by commanding the fever that was violently consuming Simon’s mother-in-law, he immediately removed the cause of the illness, so that she rose without delay and was able to serve those present, although it had been expected that she would die at once.

After adding a small increase of power, he healed the ruler’s son, who was lying ill in acknowledged danger. The Gospel narrative relates it thus: “He was beginning to die,” while the father cried out and said, “Come down, Lord, before my child dies.” Then the worker of resurrection, performing with greater power the miracle of the one who was believed to be dying, did not even come to the place, but, while remaining at a distance, transmitted life to the child through the power of his command.

Next, instructing us step by step, he leads us to higher manifestations of power. For he went of his own accord to the daughter of the ruler and provided the occasion for the journey, so that both her health—she was suffering from a flow of blood—might become known and enough time might pass for death to overcome the sick girl.

[Col. 0391A] But when the soul had already departed from the body, and those who were proclaiming the event with troubled and mournful cries were raising lamentation, he restored the girl to life by a commanding word, as though awakening her from sleep.

Raising human frailty by a kind of progression and sequence toward greater things, and again surpassing these miracles customary to him by a higher power, he prepared a path by which human beings might accept faith in the resurrection.

Holy Scripture records that there was a certain city in Judaea called Nain. In it was the only son of a certain widow—not a boy who would be counted among little children, but one who had already advanced from boyhood almost into young manhood. Hence the heavenly discourse calls him a young man, suggesting much in a few words.

The account itself is a great lamentation: “The mother of the dead man,” it says, “was a widow.” You perceive the weight of the calamity and how briefly it expressed her suffering. For what is implied? That she had no other hope by which she might restore children to herself and receive relief from such bereavement. She was a widow and had no other child whom she could see in place of the dead one. Her offspring had been a single one.

Everyone who knows the laws of nature easily understands how great this evil was. She had known only this child in her labor pains, had nursed only him at her breasts; he alone brightened her table. He alone was the cause of all her sorrow and joy—when he played or did anything, when he was taught or adorned, when he joined his peers in processions, athletic grounds, or gatherings. Whatever sweet and precious thing lay before his mother’s eyes, he alone, her only child, provided.

Now the time for marriage had arrived. He seemed to be the stock of the family, the branch of succession, the staff of old age, and the increase of her years.

There was also another cause for lamentation. In reporting that he was a young man, the account at the same time indicated a flower that had withered, whose face was still covered with down and whose cheeks shone with a pleasing radiance.

What, then, did his mother endure over his death? With what fire were her entrails burned? How abundant and bitter were the tears she poured over him? Wasting away, as it were, and embracing his corpse, wishing that its burial might be delayed and longing to be satisfied by such a catastrophe, she wanted to utter long cries of grief for a considerable time, so that all who heard her would be moved to mourning.

The sacred account did not omit this either. “When the Lord saw her,” it says, “he was moved with compassion, and he approached and touched the bier; those who were carrying it stopped. And he said to the dead man: ‘Young man, I say to you, arise.’” Immediately he presented him alive to his mother.

Here there was no long delay or great distance. Although he had not yet been buried, he was nevertheless near burial; by the Lord’s command the dead man’s life was a resurrection. The miracle was greater, but the command was precisely the same.

Still more magnificent signs of power are now brought forth, so that we may draw ever nearer to the event concerning which there seems to be doubt—the resurrection of the dead.

One of Christ’s familiars, Lazarus by name, became ill. Although the Lord loved him, he delayed visiting him and remained away from the sick man so that, while life was absent, death might find an opportunity and accomplish through the illness what belonged to it.

He told the disciples what had happened to Lazarus in Galilee and that he needed to hasten there to raise him from the dead. But they avoided the places mentioned because of the Jews’ hostility, considering it fatal and dangerous to go again into Judaea and to live among murderers and impious people. Thus they delayed and postponed their return, prolonging the time lest they go back there.

The Lord’s command prevailed, and as he departed the disciples followed, so that in Bethany they might behold, as it were, the first fruits of the universal resurrection.

It was already the fourth day after his burial, and everything seemed to have been done that was customary concerning the dead. The body had been placed in the tomb, and, as was to be expected, corruption had already begun to dissolve it under the pressure of death. For the bodily fluids were necessarily flowing into the earth; and, without doubt, an extremely foul odor was exhaled as nature compelled what had been dissolved to decay.

This happened so that the work of the general resurrection, which unbelievers find difficult to believe, might be proved by the manifestation of an evident miracle. This was not someone recovering from illness, nor someone lying at the point of death and being kept alive, nor a little girl who had recently died and was raised, nor a young man near the tomb who abandoned his own bier. It was a man of mature age, already putrefying and dissolving, so that even his sisters could not bear the Lord’s approaching the tomb because of the offensive condition of the corpse, which had already decomposed.

Yet, brought to life by a single word, he provides the preacher with evidence that confirms the hope of the resurrection.

This is what we should believe concerning all people in general, since experience itself has taught us the matter in particular cases. For just as the Apostle says that, at the universal resurrection, the Lord himself will descend from heaven “with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God,” in order to raise the dead to incorruption, so now he who was in the tomb, dispersing death as though it were sleep by the command of the Lord’s voice and driving far from himself the corruption that had come from death, leaps forth from the grave whole and complete, not prevented from walking even by the bonds with which he had been fastened.

Do you regard these things as small evidence for believing that we expect the resurrection of the dead? Or do you ask that this conviction be confirmed for you by other examples as well?

It does not seem to me that the Lord spoke without purpose, as though in the person of the inhabitants of Capernaum: “Surely you will say to me this proverb: Physician, heal yourself.” For it was fitting that the miracle of resurrection which he had performed in the bodies of others should, when made known, be confirmed in himself according to the fact that he had deigned to become human. By many kinds of evidence he also confirmed his preaching through his own death.

You have seen a girl who had just ceased to live, a young man already approaching the grave, and Lazarus almost completely dissolved; all were summoned equally to life by a single command. Do you also seek those who came to death through blood and wounds, lest perhaps there be some deficiency here, and the grace of him who gives life to all fail to appear?

See the Lord’s hands pierced by nails. See his side pierced by a spearpoint. Run your fingers through the openings of the nails; put your hand into the wound made by the spear. Perhaps you can infer how far inward the spear’s point penetrated from the breadth of the scar. You may even measure its depth, for the wound itself, made by the thrust of a man’s hand, clearly shows how far it descended.

[Col. 0393A] If, therefore, he rose from the dead in this condition, we appropriately bring forward the Apostle’s words: “How do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?”

Since every pronouncement of the Lord is shown to be true by the testimony of events—for we have learned this not merely through words but through the work itself, and we rejoice that through those who have already come from resurrection to life we have received the manifest hope of his promise—what opportunity for unbelievers can remain?

Shall we not, renouncing those who attempt through philosophy and empty deceit to despise the simplicity of faith, retain the purest confession of our hope, saying in the manner of the prophet, in the words he addresses to the Lord: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust; send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth”? He also affirms that the Lord rejoices in his works, when sinners fail from the earth.

For how will anyone be called a sinner any longer, when sin can no longer exist?

## CHAPTER XXVII. That the resurrection of the dead is not contrary to what is fitting

There are some, however, who, through the weakness of human thoughts, judge divine power according to our measure and affirm that what they themselves cannot comprehend cannot be possible for God either.

They point out to us the remains of ancient dead people that have been wholly consumed, those that fire has reduced to ashes, and, in addition, animals that feed on flesh. They bring forward the fish that transfers into its own body the flesh of a human being who has perished in a shipwreck, and then the fact that this fish becomes food for a human being and is converted through digestion into the substance of the one who eats it. They produce many other exceedingly foolish examples, utterly unworthy of the power and majesty of the great God, to overturn the true doctrine—as though God could not once more, through these same processes, restore from the completed dissolution what properly belongs to the human being.

But let us cut short, in brief, their lengthy excursions of most empty reasoning. We confess that the dissolution of the body occurs into the elements from which it is known to have been constituted: not only does earth, according to the authority of the divine word, return to earth, but air and moisture are also restored to portions most like themselves, and each of the things within us migrates back to its proper origin.

Even if a human body is handed over as food to birds that feed on flesh or to wild beasts that feed on flesh, and is mingled with them through these events; even if it enters the teeth of fish, and through fire is converted into vapors and dust, wherever someone may have carried the human being according to the underlying order of things, he must necessarily remain within this world, which the divinely inspired voice teaches to be held in God’s hand when it says: “In his hand are all the ends of the earth.”

If you cannot be unaware of what you contain within your own palm, do you suppose that God’s knowledge—which surpasses your power—can fail to investigate what is contained by divine power in his hand?

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That, once human bodies have been dissolved into all the elements, what belongs to each can again be restored from the common elements to the individual

Perhaps, however, looking at the elements of the whole world, you think it difficult for our constitution, drawn into its kindred element of air, which is hot and moist, and for the earthly part of our substance, similarly mingled with its proper components, to be restored again from the common elements to each individual according to what belongs to that individual.

For this reason, even from human examples, you do not consider that this too lies within the limits of divine power. You have surely seen somewhere, in human settlements, a common flock feeding together as one body; but when the flock is again divided among its respective owners, whether by local custom or by marks placed on the animals, what belongs to each is restored to each.

If you reflect on something similar in your own case, you will not depart from what is fitting. Since the soul is held to the body it inhabited by a natural bond and affection, there is within it a certain hidden mixture of the mutual affection and recognition that now exist between them, as though nature had placed certain marks upon them, by which their commonality remains undivided while the properties of each remain distinguishable.

When, therefore, the soul again draws to itself the kindred and proper thing, what difficulty, I ask, can there be—especially when nature does not prevent divine power—from their coming together again in themselves and, through an ineffable concurrence of nature, each hastening toward what properly belongs to it?

That certain marks of our form remain even after bodily dissolution is shown by the discourse that took place in Hades, when, although their bodies had already been committed to burial, a certain bodily knowledge remained attached to their souls, through which Lazarus could be recognized and the rich man could not remain unknown.

There is therefore nothing contrary to reason in believing that bodies, when they rise, recover their properties from the common elements. This is especially perceived by one who has taken pains to investigate nature more diligently.

For not everything that belongs to us flows away and changes in every respect; otherwise such things would be wholly incomprehensible, possessing no stability by nature. But when the matter is examined with greater care, it appears that some things within us remain fixed, while others flow away through change.

The body changes through increase and diminution, as though putting on successive garments through successive ages. Yet throughout all these changes the form remains unaltered, never abandoning the marks once impressed upon it by nature; through all the body’s transformations it retains its own identity by means of them.

The transformation that becomes joined to the form on some occasion must, however, be excluded from this account. For the form takes on a certain foreign appearance through illness, which it endures amid the troubles of sickness. When that condition is removed—as happened with Naaman the Syrian or with those whom the Gospels recount—the form that had been hidden beneath the affliction returns again to its proper appearance through health.

Thus, insofar as it is like God, the form neither flows away nor is transformed by any change; it remains fixed, always existing as the same. According to this permanence, our restoration contains the divine likeness.

Since differences of form are produced by the qualities of mixtures, while a mixture is nothing other than the condition of the elements, and since we call elements those things subject to the constitution of the universe, from which we confess that the human body too subsists, the form, as though impressed with a seal, necessarily remains with the soul and in no way fails to recognize the very shape it has received through its imprint.

Therefore, at the time of the resurrection, it receives again into itself whatever corresponds to that form. What corresponds to it is whatever is shown to have been implanted in the form from the beginning. Thus it appears entirely reasonable that what belongs to each should once more return from the common elements to the individual.

There is also something called *hydrargyrum* (*ὑδραργύριον*), which ordinary people call “living silver,” or mercury. If it is poured over sloping and dusty ground, it separates through the earth into very small globules, and even when these come together they cannot mingle with one another. But if someone gathers again into one mass what has been scattered in many directions, it joins its source and proper kind, hindered by no intervening obstacles from reuniting.

I think something similar should be recognized in the composition of the human being. As soon as power has been granted by God, like parts will of their own accord be mingled with their proper parts, without any difficulty for him who deigns to restore nature.

We observe the same in things that grow from the earth: we see no labor imposed upon nature when it transforms wheat, millet, or any other seed of grain or legume into a stalk, ears, and spikes. For food that corresponds to each seed passes spontaneously from the common substance to the property of each individual seed.

If, therefore, moisture is commonly supplied to all shoots arising from the earth, and each is nourished by it and draws toward its own growth what is suited to it, what is new or surprising if the same occurs in the restoration of our restoration [sic], when each of those who rise draws to itself what properly belongs to it, just as happens with seeds?

From all these examples, then, it is possible to learn that the preaching of the resurrection is nothing beyond what experience itself has made known to us.

Indeed, concerning what belongs to us, I had almost passed over in silence the most familiar example of all: the beginning of our formation itself. For who does not know the wonder of nature—what the mother’s womb receives and what it brings to completion?

You see how simple and, in a certain sense, small is what is deposited in the womb as the beginning of the formation of our body. Yet who could explain in words the variety of the completed substance?

And whoever recognizes that this is a work of common nature, who would not think that what takes place is possible? If that small thing, which is almost counted as nothing, is known to be the beginning of so great a work—and by “great” I mean not only with reference to the formation of the body, but I first declare the soul itself to be wholly worthy of wonder, together with what is perceived concerning the mind—

## CHAPTER XXIX. Against those who say that souls exist before their bodies, or, conversely, that bodies are formed before souls; concerning a certain fabulous opinion about souls
I think it is beyond the present purpose for us to investigate [Col. 0396A] the question disputed in the churches concerning the origin of the soul or of the body. For some who before us discussed the principles of things and brought forward what was almost a kind of plague have thought that souls subsist beforehand in a life proper to themselves. They suppose that examples of both vice and virtue are set before them there: that a soul persevering in good perceives none of the experiences of bodily union; but that, if it should fall away from participation in the good, it then withdraws into this life and dwells in a body.

Others, observing the order handed down by Moses concerning the creation of humanity, maintain that the soul comes second, that is, after the body, according to the sequence of events: first, they say, God took clay from the earth and formed the human being, and afterward animated it by breathing into it. By this reasoning [Col. 0396B] they show the body to be more excellent than the soul joined to it, on the ground that the body was formed first. They say that the soul was made for the sake of the body, so that the formation might not remain motionless without spirit. But everything that is made for the sake of something else is evidently inferior to that for whose sake it is made, as the Gospels declare when they say that the soul is more than food and the body more than clothing, because these things have been granted for their sake. The soul was not made for food, nor is it the case that bodies were formed for the sake of clothing; rather, once the former exist, the latter are provided as necessities for their use.

Since, therefore, the assertion of neither opinion is free from blame—whether that of those who think that souls live beforehand in some state and order of their own, or that of those who suppose that they were created after bodies—I think it necessary [Col. 0396C] to examine to some extent what is asserted in their doctrines. For if we wished to investigate more carefully the arguments of both sides and expose all the absurdities that are approved and attached to their opinions, we should need a long period of time. Therefore, examining briefly, as far as possible, what they have said, let us not delay refuting it.

Those who support the first position and assert that souls have an earlier existence on account of this bodily life do not seem to me to be free from the errors of pagan doctrines. The pagans have invented many fabulous stories about the transformation of souls into bodies. If anyone examines their assertions carefully, he will discover that necessity itself drives their reasoning toward this conclusion.

It has been reported [Col. 0396D] that one whom they regarded as wise said that he had been both man and woman, had then flown away into birds, had at another time blossomed, and had finally received life in the form of moisture. This is not far from the truth—indeed, it accords with the judgment of one who was not ashamed to utter such things. For these doctrines of theirs, which affirm that one soul passes through so many forms, are truly worthy of the chatter of frogs and crows, of the irrationality of fish, and of the insensibility of trees.

The cause of this absurdity is that they believe souls to subsist beforehand. For when the principle of their doctrine advances and presses forward into what precedes, it necessarily descends as far as these monstrosities. If, as they assert, a soul falls from a higher state because of some wickedness and becomes a human being, while bodily life is plainly more vicious than intellectual life, then it is altogether necessary that, once placed in such a life—one in which there can be no shortage of occasions for sin—it should be afflicted by still greater evils and prove more vicious than before.

The wickedness of a human soul is comparable to that of an irrational creature; when it is familiarly joined to such a nature, it in a certain sense falls back into the condition of animals [Col. 0397A]. For once it has rushed into wickedness, even after it has become irrational, it ceases, as it were, from the pursuit of greater things. For a halt in evil is the beginning of virtue, whereas there is no virtue among irrational creatures. Thus, by sheer necessity, it will continually be changed for the worse, becoming what is more degraded and base, and reaching by unceasing change whatever is most extreme.

As rational nature transcends the sensible, so the fall from the sensible is into the insensible [Col. 0397B]. Yet, although their argument proceeds beyond the truth, it nevertheless follows a certain sequence, so that absurdity produces absurdity. From this, through incongruous and impossible consequences, their fabulous doctrine also generates the complete destruction of the soul.

For once a soul has fallen away from its higher mode of life, it can no longer remain within any measure of wickedness. Entangled in the affections of the passions, it passes from the rational to the irrational, and from the irrational it is transferred into insensible plants. The insensible and the lifeless are close to one another in a certain respect; and what is lifeless is followed by what does not exist. Thus, by the full logic of their argument, the soul will be dissolved into nonexistence, since it was impossible for it, by necessity, to advance toward better things.

Yet they lead the soul from the thickets to humanity [Col. 0397C]; therefore, by this reasoning, they demonstrate that the life in the thickets is superior to the mode of incorporeal life. For it has been shown that the soul’s progress, when it strives toward evil, consequently rolls down to the lowest things, and that lifeless nature is inferior to the insensible nature, to which the beginning of their doctrine necessarily brings the soul.

But since they do not wish to accept this conclusion, they either confine the soul within the realm of sensible things, or, if they bring it back from there once more to humanity, they show the wooden life to be better, as has been said, than that first mode of existence, since the fall into wickedness occurred from it; whereas from the wooden life progress toward virtue was assigned.

This assertion, therefore, is proved [Col. 0397D] to be without beginning and without end: it declares that souls live among themselves before bodily life and that, because of wickedness, they are bound to bodies.

But the inconsistency of those who contend that the soul is younger than the body will be destroyed by what is explained in what follows. For this reason, the argument advanced by both sides must be rejected; instead, I think that our doctrine ought to direct itself toward the truth by taking a middle course between their opinions.

Our position is this: we do not suppose, in accordance with pagan delusion, that souls have been depressed by some wickedness—souls which, as the pagans say, are unable, because of weakness, to keep pace with the rotation of the entire celestial sphere as it is carried along with immense speed, and therefore fall back to earth. Nor, again, do we say that a human being is first formed in some manner [the source reads *instantiam*], and that the soul is subsequently supplied to it for this reason. Otherwise, intelligible nature would be shown to be inferior to the formation of clay.

### CHAPTER XXX. Assertion that the same and common cause of subsistence appears to belong both to the soul and to the body

Since there is one human being, consisting of soul and body, we must assign to it one common beginning of formation, lest it appear to be earlier and later than itself, so that the formation of one part in it is first and that of the other second.

At present, in accordance with the reasoning set out shortly before, we profess that the whole fullness of human nature subsists beforehand in the divine power, as the prophet testifies to us when he says that the Lord knows all things before they come to be. But in the formation of the individual parts we do not give precedence to either over the other. We do not say that the soul comes before the body, nor the body before the soul, lest the human being, divided according to temporal difference, depart from himself [Col. 0398B].

For, according to the Apostle’s teaching, our nature is understood to be twofold: the visible human being and the hidden one. If one part subsisted beforehand and the other came afterward, the creator’s power would appear imperfect, as though it were not sufficient for both at once but occupied itself separately with the halves of each through a divided work.

Just as in wheat or in any other seed we see the whole form of the ear contained potentially—that is, the grass, the stalk, the joints, the grain, and the awns—and do not say that any of these subsists beforehand according to the order of nature or comes afterward, but recognize that the power implanted in the seed is revealed by a natural sequence, with no other nature superimposed upon it, so we think that the cause of the human seed exists according to the same principle.

At the first beginning of formation [Col. 0398C] it is sown all at once, according to the power of nature; but by a certain natural sequence it is extended and revealed, advancing toward what is perfect and taking nothing from outside for the occasion of its perfection. For it extends itself successively toward perfection, so that it cannot truthfully be affirmed either that the soul subsists before the body or that the body subsists for the sake of the soul. Rather, whether either is the principle of the other is, according to the higher account, disposed in the first will of God, but according to the other account established in the occasions of generation.

For just as the distinction of the limbs cannot be observed before formation in what is cast down as the beginning of bodily conception, so it is impossible to contemplate the properties of the soul before they emerge into acts of operation [Col. 0398D]. And just as no one doubts, in the case of the differences among limbs and internal organs, that what has been deposited is shaped not by some other power entering from outside but by the power implanted in nature applying itself to this operation, so they likewise judge proportionately concerning the soul by rational reasoning.

Even if it is not yet recognized through any visible operations, nevertheless nothing belonging to a single reality is seen to be absent from it. For just as the form of the future human being is present in it through a certain power and potentiality, but remains hidden because it cannot yet appear until the necessary sequence permits and allows it, so the soul is indeed present in it, although it does not yet appear. Its proper and natural operative effect will appear, advancing together with bodily growth [Col. 0399A].

Since the power of conception is exercised not by a dead body but by a living and breathing one, we therefore say that it is reasonable not to regard as dead and lifeless what is directed by a living being toward the beginning of life. For lifeless flesh is certainly dead; death occurs through the deprivation of the soul. But no one could claim that deprivation is prior to possession, unless someone should assert that what is lifeless and dead is older than the soul.

If anyone demands clearer proof that the part which becomes the beginning of the formation of the living creature is alive, it is possible to observe this also from the other signs by which the living is distinguished and separated from the dead. We take as signs of life in human beings the fact that someone is warm, that he moves, and that he acts; whereas coldness and immobility in bodies are nothing other than mortality itself.

Since, therefore, we have seen that what we are discussing is warm and active, we gather from this also arguments that it is not lifeless. Yet just as, with respect to the body, we do not say that it is already flesh, bones, hair, or whatever else we observe in a human being, but that each of these exists in power and potentiality without yet appearing visibly, so likewise with respect to the soul we affirm that its rational and irascible faculties, and whatever else is considered in the soul, do not yet have their place in it.

Rather, we say that the soul’s operations are proportionate to the formed body and reach completion together as the underlying subject advances. Thus the perfected human being displays, among the greater operations of the soul, an effect that is already appropriate and fitting to him; and, at the beginning of his formation, he demonstrates within himself efforts suited and adapted to the soul’s present use, so that through the infused material he may form for himself a most fitting dwelling [Col. 0399C].

For we do not believe that the soul can suitably be inserted into structures belonging to another, just as a seal impressed in wax cannot be made to correspond properly to a completely different engraving. And just as the body proceeds from a small beginning toward perfection, so the operations of the soul joined to the underlying subject likewise grow and advance.

At the first formation the soul advances like a hidden root, concerned only with the cavities assigned to nourishment and growth—for the smallness of what receives cannot take in anything more. Then, when what has been planted has come forth into the light and produced a shoot, the faculty of sensation blossoms in it. As it grows together and extends suitably into greater dimensions, a certain rational power, like a fruit, begins to shine forth [Col. 0399D].

For it does not appear all at once. Rather, it grows carefully together with the perfection of its instrument and continually bears as much fruit as the potentiality of its subject can contain.

If, however, you are seeking the operation of the soul in this formation of the body, pay attention to yourself, as Moses says, and, as though in a book, read the history of the soul’s activity. Nature itself will in a certain sense speak to you, more effectively than any use of language, displaying the soul’s various activities in the body and in the soul, in both its universal and particular constitution.

But I think it superfluous to speak about ourselves and, as though recounting matters distant and outside our bounds, to describe familiar wonders [Col. 0400A]. For who, by looking at himself, needs words in order to understand the laws of nature? It is very easy for someone, by considering the manner of his life and examining how he possesses a body suited to every effect of vital activity, to notice the end for which the seed of the primordial—or rather, germinal—soul, drawn from a living body, is committed to nature’s craftsmanship.

For the interior parts of fruits and the shoots of roots, although not yet deprived of the exceedingly vigorous force implanted in them by nature, preserve, when committed to the earth, a hidden yet pure quality. But the earth that contains them does not impart such force and potentiality, as though giving it from outside itself; otherwise it would also make dead wood germinate. Rather, it brings into the light what has been implanted, through its own nurturing care, like a nurse, perfecting what has been planted in the root into marrow, bark, and branches [Col. 0400B]. This could not happen unless some natural power were joined to it, drawing from what lies near an aliment that is kindred and suitable, and producing a shrub, a tree, an ear of grain, or something else of this kind.

### CHAPTER XXXI. A certain medical contemplation—or rather, an account of the construction of bodies—is briefly set forth.

Yet although each person is taught by the most certain formation of his own body, from which he understands, lives, and senses, having his own nature as teacher, nevertheless it is also lawful to learn diligently from the books of wise men who have investigated these matters more carefully. For some have described the position of each of the things that are in us through what physicians call anatomy—that is, the incision of individual joints and veins—and, having contemplated the functions of all the members of the body, internally and externally, have reported them to others, so that a sufficient knowledge for human instruction might be established through diligent study. If anyone asks us about these matters, the Church will certainly provide him with instruction. For this is the spiritual law of the sheep, as the Lord says: that they do not listen to the voice of strangers.

Let us therefore set forth the matter briefly. We have understood three things concerning the nature of the body, on account of which each of the things in us is seen to have been constituted. Some have been formed for life, others for living well, and others suitably for the succession of offspring. Whatever, then, is granted to us without which human life could not subsist, we perceive to exist likewise in three parts: in the brain, the heart, and the liver. Whatever, however, nature has bestowed upon human beings for the increase of their goods and for living well is declared to be the instrument of the senses. Such things do not contain our life, since even when some of them are lacking, the human being nevertheless continues to exist; but without them it is impossible for life to be maintained in its fullest pleasantness.

The third purpose of the division likewise concerns the duties of succession. There are also certain other things besides these, assigned commonly to all the members for the body’s endurance, bringing forth from themselves appropriate operations, such as the stomach and the lung: the latter, by the breath which it takes in and gives back to the heart, breathing through it as through a seal; the former, receiving food into the internal organs for common use.

Since, then, our formation is divided in this way, we must observe more carefully that the power belonging to our life is not accomplished simply through one particular member, but that nature distributes among many parts the means necessary for our preservation, so that whatever nature has fashioned for the protection and beauty of life appears to be very numerous and to possess an altogether considerable mutual difference. But I think it necessary first to divide briefly the primary principles that are shown to pertain to the constitution of our life. The matter of the whole body, however, which commonly underlies each of the members, must now be passed over by us, since a discussion of universal nature does not seem at present to belong to the particular contemplation proposed.

Since everyone therefore acknowledges that a portion of all the elements existing in this world is present in us—namely, the hot and the cold, as well as the other pair consisting in moisture and dryness—we must discuss each of them. We accordingly perceive three powers that administer life. One of them warms the whole world with its own heat; another, being moistened with moisture, restores what has been consumed by heat, so that the animal is preserved midway between contrary qualities in an equal balance: neither does an excess of heat dry up the moisture, nor does an abundance of moisture extinguish the heat.

The third power, by itself, according to a certain harmony and modulation, holds together the members that have been separated, fitting them together by its own bonds. It grants to all, of itself, a power of movement and spontaneous activity. If this is absent, the body exists loose and immobile, deprived of the voluntary vitality and efficacy of the spirit. We ought rather to contemplate the earlier art and workmanship of our nature in the very condition of the body.

For since nothing hard receives sensible functions at all—as we see in our bones and in shrubs and trees, in which a certain form of life is indeed discerned in the fact that they are nourished and grow, yet whose hardness does not admit any of the senses—it was necessary for a certain formation, like soft wax, to be placed beneath the operation of sensation, so that it could be impressed by forms meeting it and yet not be dissolved by excessive moisture. What is impressed cannot endure in something wet, nor can excessive rigidity receive an image by impression, because what does not know how to yield cannot receive an image. Between these two, therefore, a certain intermediate substance was placed, between the witheringly soft and the rigid, lest the animal be deprived of the finest movements of its power, namely, its sensations.

Since what is soft and yielding is altogether immobile and indistinct unless it is strengthened through the cooperation of solid things, for this reason nature mingled the strength of bones into the body. Joining them to one another through harmonious coordination, she thoroughly bound their structures and joints with the links of the nerves, and thus mingled with them a measure of sensible vigor, enveloping the surface with flesh somewhat harder, capable of bearing affections.

Upon this exceedingly solid nature of the bones, as upon columns supporting a massive structure, she imposed the burden of the entire body. Nor did she join the bones as undivided or undifferentiated; otherwise the body would have remained immobile and without function. Had the human being been formed in that way, he would have remained like a tree standing in one place, since he could neither move forward by the alternating motion of his legs nor display the conveniences of life through the service of his hands.

Now, however, through this provision, the instrument of walking and acting has been formed, so that spontaneous bodily movements are produced by the voluntary spirit inserted into the nerves. Hence the hands’ varied, manifold, and most adaptable service for every task devised by thought; hence the bending of the neck, the inclination and elevation of the head, and a certain activity around the chin; hence also the gathering of the eyelids, together with the other functions that arise along with understanding.

For the movement itself of the members operates through the nerves, which extend and relax, like certain machines by which an impulse is set in motion. The power, however, pressing upon these with its own force, exercises voluntary command and, through a voluntary spirit according to a certain dispensation of nature, displays its proper effect in each part.

It has therefore become perfectly clear that the root and beginning of all the movements believed to be produced through the nerves is that membrane by which the brain is enclosed, compacted with nerves. We therefore do not think that we need now inquire more curiously into the function of the animal’s members, since the nature of such movement has been made clear in the formation of the brain.

That the greatest strength for preserving life is conferred upon us by the brain is clearly recognized from the contrary event. For if that membrane suffers any wound or incision, death immediately follows. Nature cannot resist the affliction caused by the wound even for a moment; rather, as when a foundation has been undermined, the whole building collapses together with the part. Thus the manifest destruction of the whole body follows the injury to that membrane. In it, therefore, the cause of our own life must in no way be denied to reside.

When, moreover, the innate heat of those who cease to live is contracted, and what is dead consequently grows cold, it is necessary for us also to recognize such a cause in heat: when it is absent, death certainly follows, and therefore we must confess that the animal lives through the presence of heat.

We have perceived the heart to be the source and beginning, as it were, of this power and energy. From it, like tubes, numerous veins diffuse warm and burning spirit throughout the whole body. And since nature also had to provide the heat continually with some nourishment—for it is not lawful for fire to endure by itself unless it is fed with suitable sustenance—for this reason the streams of blood, as though from a certain fountain, are aroused by the heat of the liver, and flow everywhere throughout the body at once, lest one part become desolate of another and nature be corrupted at its origin.

Let this very fact also teach those who abstain from material things, formed according to the equality of that material, that avarice is a corrupting passion, and that Divinity alone is without any need; for human poverty needs those things that seem to contain its substance.

Therefore, through these three powers which we have said govern the whole body, nature, supplying material from outside, administers it by different channels, providing what is appropriate to each. To the fountain of blood, which is the liver, she entrusted the distribution of food. Whatever, through this provision, it continually introduces to the liver’s fountains, she likewise prepares to be conveyed from the liver. Just as snow in the mountains, through its moisture, enlarges the springs beneath it and sends its own liquid down from above into the lower channels, so the ventilation of the heart is supplied by the function of a neighboring member called the lung. It is a receptacle of air through the artery inherent in it, which reaches as far as the mouth and draws breath from outside.

The heart, situated in the middle like a fire that is in motion and continuous operation, itself moves and works without cessation. Just as the bellows of smiths do, it draws into itself from the surrounding spirit a series of compressions, filling itself by expansions, and warming with what is fiery in it the neighboring arteries. It does not cease doing this: it draws to itself what is external by rising and breathing, while by compression inserting into the surrounding arteries what is around it. It seems to me that this is also the cause that continually maintains such spontaneous breathing.

Indeed, the mind is often occupied with other things and comes entirely to rest while the body is dissolved in sleep; nevertheless, the breath drawn from the air cannot rest, not even for a little, with the spontaneous decision of the will cooperating in this. For I think that the heart, wrapped and surrounded by the lung, moves the member from its posterior part through its own respirations and compressions, and contrives for the lung the drawing in and sending out of air.

The lung, being extremely porous and full of cavities, keeps all its openings, like apertures, open toward the base and summit of the artery. When compressed, it necessarily expels the spirit residing in its extremities; when it yields and expands, and again draws in air, it is moved through separation. The cause of this involuntary respiration is that what is fiery and fervid in us cannot remain at rest. Since activity through movement is proper to heat, and we have perceived its beginning to be in the heart, whatever continual agitation exists in the heart produces, through the office of the lung, the unceasing drawing in and sending out of air.

Consequently, whenever heat grows beyond nature, the breathing of those with fevers becomes frequent, as though the heart, hastening, were trying to restrain the flame placed above it by the continual supply of new spirit.

But since our nature is exceedingly poor and in need of everything pertaining to its constitution, it suffers not only from a lack of its own air and spirit—for the breath that nourishes the internal heat continually flows in from outside for the preservation of the animal—but also procures from outside, with provident adaptation, the supports of food that lighten the body’s burden. Therefore it strives to supply its need through foods and drinks, inserting into the bodies a certain appetitive power for what is lacking and an expulsive power for what is excessive, and through this providing no small cooperation of nature for nourishing the heart’s fire.

Since we have reported that the heart is especially proper to such members, according to the explanation given above, because it warms each of them with the heat of its own spirit, our creator therefore made it most effective in every respect, so that no part might be judged idle or vacant in the administration of the entire body. Drawing the lung behind it toward itself through continuous movement, it expands its passages for the reception of air; then, pressing it down again, it prepares what has been received to be breathed out. In front of itself, however, it lies directly above the stomach, warming it and making it suitable for its proper operations—not arousing it to resume the spirit, but impelling it to receive the food appropriate to it.

The entrances of food and spirit are joined close together; they extend lengthwise toward one another and are separated by an equal measure at their upper end, yet in such a way that they are joined together and closed by a single mouth of access. Thus one becomes the entrance of food and the other of spirit; but this occurs in the deeper recesses of the internal organs. The entrance of this union does not remain joined throughout, for the heart is placed in the middle between the end of each. From one side it gives breath, while from the other it provides the capacity to receive food. Nature, suitably fiery, seeks material to consume, and this also necessarily produces the stomach, which receives food.

To the extent that it becomes fiery through the nearness of heat, to that extent it continually demands more food to nourish the heat. We more appropriately call this desire “appetite.” But even if the stomach receives a sufficient quantity of material, the operation of the fire does not thereby cease.

For just as in a smelting furnace it brings about a certain gathering together of all the material, dissolving and mixing everything and pouring it, as though through a refining vessel, into the passages that follow, so it then separates the coarser part from the purer. It conveys the thinner substance through certain channels to the entrances of the liver, while it delivers the muddy and feculent matter to the wider passages of the intestines. Turning it through many coils, it retains the food in the internal organs for no short time, so that, if it were expelled more easily in a straight course, it would immediately arouse in the animal the appetite for eating, and, following the nature of irrational creatures, a human being would never cease from this occupation.

And since the cooperation of heat is especially necessary to the liver, so that moisture may be converted into blood, while this member is separated from the heart by a considerable distance according to its position—for I do not think it was possible for one principle and root of vital power to be cramped by the proximity of another principle—nevertheless, lest the distance of the hot substance cause any failure in the body’s administration, the nervous channel which those skilled in these matters call an artery receives the fervent spirit from the heart and conveys it to the liver. There it is joined to the passage through which moist substances are received, and, warming that same moist substance, inserts into it something of the fiery vigor of its continuous heat.

Hence the appearance of the blood is sprinkled with ruddy heat. From there, two connected streams each receive their own substance like tubes: one the spirit, the other the blood. Through their easy flow, the moist substance moves onward through the action of heat. Thus, when the body has been refreshed throughout, it is distributed in many ways into the several beginnings of streams that are spread through the whole body. The two beginnings of the vital powers, mingled together—one diffusing heat and the other moisture everywhere through the body—provide, as it were, a necessary contribution from their own resources and preside over it as the principal power in the vital yoke.

This power is seen to reside in the membranes of the brain. From it, the movement of all the joints, the cohesion of the whole body, and the vigor of the voluntary spirit infused into each member demonstrate our earthly statue to be effective and self-moving through a certain mechanism.

For the purest part of the heat and the thinnest part of the moisture, united through both powers by a certain mixture and tempering, nourish and warm the brain through vapors. From this, a rarified exhalation again reaches the purer substance and penetrates the members. That membrane is contained in the brain; reaching from the upper regions into the depths like a tube, and extending wholly through the joining of the successive parts and the marrow inserted into it, it ends at the extremity of the spinal column. Thereafter, presiding like a charioteer over the bones and nerves, as well as over the beginnings of joints and marrows, they bestow upon each part the power, impulse, and force for remaining in place or moving.

For this reason, it seems to me that it has also received more certain protection. In the head, it is evidently surrounded by double bones; in the joints, however, and in the projections of the ribs, as well as in the numerous and scarcely describable structures, it is preserved with every stability by the same protection that encloses and secures what occupies the third place.

In the same way, one may infer this also concerning the heart: just as a house is strengthened by a solid mass, so the heart is fortified all around by the defenses of bones. At its rear it is enclosed on both sides by the spine and the shoulder blades; along both sides it is bound by the belt of the ribs, which surrounds its middle and protects it from every injury. In front, the chest and the lowered junction of the neck gently provide it with protection on every side against whatever might inflict harm from outside.

Just as we observe in agriculture that either rains from the clouds or streams from rivulets moisten what lies beneath, and suppose, for the sake of comparison, that a certain source is placed at the origin of our account, nourishing a thousand varieties of trees and the many kinds of things that the earth produces, whose form, quality, and color are shown to differ greatly in each case: although one moisture nourishes all the things in a single field, so that this power, moistening and nourishing each thing, is, as I have said, one and simple in its nature, nevertheless the character of the things nourished by it is changed into different species and qualities.

The same moisture becomes bitter in wormwood; in hemlock it is changed into a deadly juice; and in another plant it produces something else—whether in balsam, saffron, or poppy. One of these is hot, another cold, and another possesses a certain intermediate quality. In laurel, mastic, and similar plants it is fragrant. In figs and pears it conveys sweetness; through the vine it produces a cluster, from which wine flows; and it produces the juice of the apple, the redness of the rose, the whiteness of the lily, the blue of the violet, and the purple of the hyacinth and of dyes. Everything that we see arising from one and the same moisture out of the earth is transformed into such different forms according to its shape, appearance, and quality.

Something of this kind has also been wonderfully accomplished by nature in this living field of ours—or rather by the Lord, the fashioner of our nature. Bones, cartilage, veins, arteries, nerves, joints, flesh, skin, fat, muscles, hair, nails, eyes, nostrils, ears, and all the other things distinguished from one another through these by a thousand different properties are produced from one kind of nourishment, according to the likeness of their own nature. Thus, as the nourishment approaches each individual member, it is changed according to the member it reaches and imparts to it its own integrated power of vigor.

If it reaches the region of the eyes, it is tempered for their use and divided among the membranes of the pupils and the eyelids. If it flows into the organ of hearing, it is mingled with the nature of the ears according to their quality. When it comes to the lips, it becomes a lip; in the bone it is compacted; in the marrow it becomes soft; in the nerves it is strengthened; on the surface of the skin it is extended; it passes into the nails; and it completes the extremely fine growth of the hair through vapors most suitably exhaled. If these vapors emerge through winding passages, they produce curling and twisted hair; but if their progress through the vaporous channels is straight, straight and elongated hairs are born.

Our discourse has been led far from its purpose while we pursued more deeply the works of nature, attempting to describe how and from what each of the things in us is constituted, whether those that belong to living well or whatever other things, together with these, we have seen to exist according to the first sequence of our division.

Our purpose was to show that this seed-like material of our constitution is neither an incorporeal soul nor a lifeless body, but that, in the first formation, something living and animated is deposited from living and animated bodies. Human nature receives this as a kind of nourishment and preserves it through its own sustaining forces and nutriments. It is suitably directed toward both aspects and receives the growth of each.

Through this skillful and teachable formation, the effect of the soul is shown to have been joined to it, at first appearing more obscurely and then shining forth with the perfection of the instrument. We see something similar among sculptors of stone. An artist sets out to preform the shape of some animal in stone. First he cuts the stone from its related material; then, cutting away what is superfluous, he sketches what he has proposed by altering its original shape, so that an experienced observer may infer the artist’s intention without difficulty from what appears.

Again, as he explains and brings it closer to the likeness of the thing whose form he is pursuing, he then carefully and completely reveals the figure in the material and brings his art to completion. It becomes a lion, a human being, or something else made by the artist—something that a little earlier was unformed stone. The material has not been obliterated by the form; rather, the form is shown to have been impressed upon the material through art.

In this way, anyone thinking about the soul will not deviate at all from the path of reason. The one who works all nature with consummate artistry, taking material of the same kind, formed a living statue from a portion of the human being. For just as form follows the working of stone, at first more obscure and afterward more perfect when the work has been completed, so too in the sculpting of this instrument the form of the soul is revealed: in the imperfect it is proportionately imperfect, while in the perfect it exists whole and perfected.

Yet it was perfect in the beginning, had nature not been corrupted through wickedness. Therefore the communion that came to us in passible and animal generation does not immediately make the divine image shine forth in our constitution. Rather, by a certain successive progression, the human being is led to perfection and completion through the material properties of the soul.

The blessed Apostle also intimates this kind of doctrine in his Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; when I became a man, I put away the things of a child.” This does not mean that something other than what was understood in the child enters into the perfected man, so that the childish mind is removed and a manly one inserted. Rather, the very same thing is imperfect in the former and demonstrates the effect of its perfection in the latter.

For just as we acknowledge that everything which is born and grows lives, and no one would say that everything which participates in life and is invigorated by natural movement is entirely lifeless, nevertheless we do not say that such life participates in a perfect soul. Thus, in shrubs, a certain vital operation is carried as far as sensible movement but cannot reach it. Likewise, through the growth of the animal, a certain power comes to irrational creatures, but it too does not attain the perfection of reason and receives none of the grace of understanding.

For this reason we define the true and perfect human soul as that which is recognized to flourish through every function.
