If anything else participates in life, we confess, by a certain abuse of customary language, that it is animated—not because a perfect soul exists in it, but because certain parts of animal operation exist in it. We recognize that these parts have also come to us, according to the mystical account of the lawgiver Moses concerning the generation of the human being, because of our participation in passibility.

Therefore the blessed Paul, offering counsel to those who were able to hear him, urges them to seize perfection and sets forth the way by which the proposed goal may be attained, saying: “Putting off the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him.”

But let us return again to that divine grace by which God created the human being in the beginning, when he said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

The end of the book of Saint Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, concerning the Image, containing what follows from the things left by his brother, the blessed Basil, in the Hexameron.

[Col. 0407]

THE LIFE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS, RENDERED IN LATIN BY DIONYSIUS.

(This Life, together with Rosweyde’s Lives of the Fathers, will be published at the end of the sixth century.)

[Col. 0407]

TRANSLATION OF PROCLUS’S PRAYER CONCERNING THE MOTHER OF GOD.

(Which you may read among the works of Marius Mercator, Patrologia, vol. XLVIII, col. 775.)

[Col. 0407]

[THE LETTER OF PROCLUS OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO THE ARMENIANS CONCERNING THE FAITH.]

PREFACE OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS TO THE LETTER OF SAINT PROCLUS, TRANSLATED BY HIMSELF INTO LATIN.

[Col. 0407C] Dionysius Exiguus the Roman, to Felicianus the Pastor.

Reminded by the command of your Veneration, I have taken care to present in Latin expression to your ears the letter addressed to the Armenians by the blessed Proclus, bishop of the city of Constantinople. I judge that it will be of no little benefit to those presently concerned, since that question which was then rejected by temerity is now troubling the Churches—an issue that seeks, under the guise of religion, to overturn it.

In the time of the aforesaid bishop, while the emperor Theodosius was governing the state in Syria and Armenia, the disciples of Theodore, bishop of the city of Mopsuestia, began to proclaim a perverse faith to the uneducated peoples by corrupting the creed. With the utmost subtlety they preached the blessed Trinity as being of one essence, yet absolutely refused to acknowledge Christ our Lord, the creator of the universe, as one of the Trinity. From this followed the foolish absurdity of their temerity: since Christ is demonstrably true God and Lord, they asserted four persons in three and undoubtedly proclaimed two Sons of God.

But the aforesaid pontiff wonderfully resisted this impiety. He taught that Christ our Lord, who in the beginning was the Word with God, the Word who is God, is one of the Trinity; through him all things were made, as the blessed Paul testifies: “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” For our salvation, he taught, the same one became truly human and remained one Son; nor did a fourth person arise in the Trinity.

And because, owing to a scruple introduced by certain persons, there is now hesitation concerning the true faith, they avoid declaring any one of the blessed Trinity. Lest they seem to introduce division into the Trinity, however, after the apostolic authority that sets forth the same teaching, it has been confirmed in many ways by the testimonies of the venerable Fathers that, for the distinction of persons, whenever reason demands it, one of the three may faithfully be proclaimed.

This is especially directed against Sabellius, who believes the holy Trinity to be one person and admits it to exist only in names, not in realities. We, while venerating it as one essence, distinguish it solely by the knowledge of its persons.

We also oppose the followers of Nestorius with this saving faith. They do not confess Christ our Lord as one of the Trinity, since they deny that the Word of God was born according to the flesh from the blessed Virgin and that he endured the other things for the redemption of the human race.

He also refutes by paternal authority the opinion of certain others who, while asserting one of the three, refuse for no reason to say “one of the Trinity.” They suspect that the word “Trinity” signifies not persons but substance. Although, for instruction in the truth, the designation itself ought to have sufficed—since, by sounding in the plural number, it unquestionably expresses not essence but persons—nevertheless, lest contention among Catholics continue to grow, he has attached to this preface, out of love for holy religion, one of the many testimonies of the blessed Augustine. In the eleventh book of *The City of God* he speaks briefly of this matter as follows:

“We believe and hold, and faithfully proclaim, that the Father begot the Word, that is, Wisdom, through whom all things were made; the only-begotten Son, one producing one, coeternal with the coeternal, supremely good and equally good. And that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son, himself also consubstantial and coeternal with both; and that this whole is the Trinity, on account of the distinctiveness of the persons, and one God, on account of the inseparable divinity.”

Behold the most excellent and truthful teacher, openly distinguishing the matter under discussion: he confidently explained that it is called “Trinity” not on account of substance but on account of persons.

This confession distinguishes us from the heretical Jews and the gentiles. We proclaim one essence in the Trinity, whereas all of them, or nearly all, admit that they worship one God, but either do not rightly pronounce the mystery of the Trinity or altogether ignore it.

If, then, “Trinity” sets forth not persons but substance, and if the substance of the Trinity is one, then according to these people there will be the substance of one substance—something that is plainly most absurd. It follows, therefore, that the designation “Trinity” indicates three persons of one essence, one omnipotence, and one divinity.

But now let the blessed Proclus come forward, himself also about to bear witness to the truth. I ask that you listen to him with kindly minds. Command that the support of your prayers be rendered to me for this work.

THE LETTER OF PROCLUS OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO THE ARMENIANS CONCERNING THE FAITH, TRANSLATED BY DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS.

[Col. 0409]

[Col. 0409C] To the most God-loving and venerable bishops, priests, and archimandrites of the orthodox holy Church throughout Armenia: Proclus sends greetings in the Lord.

It was no slight matter, brothers, that disturbed our minds and wounded us with the deepest grief: the report of the newly sprouted weeds of error which the exceedingly crafty enemy of the common nature has recently sown in your region. For a report of intolerable sadness habitually wounds the soul that has not been trained by such meditations; and the more destructively it is hurled, fixing its darts on high, the more it strives not to attack the body but to overthrow the state of the mind, spreading the opinion that the venerable garment of faith has either been miserably torn apart or entirely stolen away.

Every virtue is rightly sought by those whose reason has not been obscured by material things [Col. 0409D], and every form of wickedness is rightly judged something to be fled by those who think rightly, since it directly opposes the essence and unquestionably exists contrary to nature. For just as what is most useful must necessarily be guarded, so what is unprofitable and proved harmful must either be driven away when present or carefully prevented if it is feared that it may occur.

There are therefore many forms of virtue. These have been variously defined either by the pagans, whom error chokes and whose ignorance of divinity obscures the light of discernment, or by Christians, who, possessing the eyes of their minds illumined by right faith, behold the Sun of Justice more clearly through confession. The former, wandering in their counsels as though in darkness and possessing understanding rushing headlong without a guide, [Col. 0410C] rely upon uncertain thoughts, investigating in their decisions nothing beyond the fleeting and unstable nature of visible things; while their gaze upon true contemplation is either entangled in temporal causes or blinded by errors.

[Col. 0410C] For they say that there are four forms of virtue: justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance. Although these are good, they nevertheless crawl upon the ground and are directed toward earthly things, while lower matters are approved in comparison with the heavenly height. They called fortitude a struggle against the flesh; temperance that which gains victory by subjugating the affections; prudence that which preserves desired principles in civic conduct; and justice the finest equal distribution. They sanctioned this order of life, as they supposed it, by law, restraining immoderate and illicit desire through such definitions.

[Col. 0410D] But what is lofty and higher than the present life they were unable either to conceive or to express. Relying on a foolish and darkened heart, they attempted to confine virtue, so far as they were concerned, within visible things alone, attributing to it nothing excellent or worthy of a heavenly dwelling.

Those, however, whose hearts possess eyes illumined by faith, whose leader and teacher is the most blessed Paul, define virtue as that which, always raising us toward God, governs us in an orderly manner on earth. This venerable Apostle therefore enumerates many forms of virtue, but especially commends faith, hope, and charity. Faith, transcending nature, bestows blessings upon human beings, joining them to invisible realities even while they still bear garments subject to manifold passions.

[Col. 0411A] For faith attributes to human beings who walk upon the earth and roll in the dust the discipline of the nature of angels and of the other incorporeal powers, a discipline unknown to those who do not understand the sublimity of their purpose. Faith presents us in every form before the royal throne and the Invisible One, who lacks every form [the Latin construction is uncertain], and conveys a sure revelation of the uncreated nature that remains forever without beginning. By its radiance it also dispels material perception and overcomes the dense and clouded vision of our mind, enabling us clearly to behold those things which can then be seen in part when they are judged invisible, and to grasp them when they are believed to be inaccessible.

Hope, as the saying goes, does not deign to cling to dreams, [Col. 0411B] but firmly holds what has been believed. It prepares future things for itself amid the present, and, to exclude doubt, embraces in thought what is not yet present as though it were present, bringing almost before our eyes the things that are awaited. In overcoming obstacles, hope attaches to almost visible realities the things that are desired, utterly surpassing the empty transience of time through love of the future.

Charity, however, is the summit and head of our holy religion. Through it God, although He was continually present on earth, deigned to come to us in the flesh. Faith and charity therefore rightly agree with one another: faith is the mirror of charity, and charity is shown to be the firm foundation of faith.

We believe that God the Word was incarnate without suffering any passion; and we believe this piously. For this [Col. 0411C] faith is recognized as the foundation of our salvation. Therefore we love Him who, for our sake, assumed the form of a servant, though He endured no alteration whatever of His nature, nor was any addition made to the Trinity.

Thus every Christian who is not rich in faith, hope, and charity is not what the name signifies. Even if he appears to chastise his little body and to be free from the passions of the soul, advancing only in moral virtue, he by no means obtains the crown of victory, since he has not extended himself toward that knowledge of divinity which bestows crowns upon those who struggle bravely through virtue.

Therefore faith, which is the head of all good things, as I have said, must be preserved unimpaired, admitting nothing discordant that is devised by human invention and disturbed by no profane novelty of speech. Remaining within the boundaries of the Gospel and the Apostles, it must not be violated by anyone’s obstinate fury.

[Col. 0411D] For through it we have been saved, and in baptism we have subscribed to it with our tongue. The height of faith casts down every rising boldness and presumption—not merely human presumption, but also that of those who are exalted by nature and incorporeal essence. Blessed Paul says (Galatians 1): “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.” For an angel has been commanded to minister, not to compose a doctrine. It is exceedingly dangerous for individuals not to remain within what has been assigned to them, but to desire to rise above the measure of what has in no way been granted to their nature.

Therefore, even if substance should present something that appears worthy of faith, an innovated proclamation will not be acceptable. Let us preserve with sleepless care what we have received, constantly raising the eyes of our mind toward the treasure of faith.

[Col. 0412A] What have we received from the Scriptures, except that God created the world by His Word and brought into being from nothing the creature that did not exist? And because by the natural law He honored the rational creature, He gave it a command, so that what was best would not remain hidden from its judgment, but that it might avoid harmful things by a better purpose.

And when that creature, by its spontaneous will, had fallen into worse things and had been cast from the earthly paradise through disobedience, He who formed nature instructed it through fathers, patriarchs, the Law, judges, and prophets, so that it might beware of sins and take care to do what is right. Yet sins gained dominion over us even with our consent, and because of them the devil raged toward the destruction of nature.

[Col. 0412B] For the natural law had become obsolete and soiled, and written transgression distorted it. The prophets too, like human beings, warned what ought to be done, but they could not free humanity from the impending danger. Then God, formless, without beginning, boundless, and almighty—the Word coming in the flesh, for He possesses the power to do whatever He wills—became flesh and assumed the form of a servant, born from a Virgin, willingly showing everywhere that He had truly deigned to become human.

Bodily nature, beginnings, conditions, and passions necessarily follow one another. For the Evangelist does not say (John 1) that God entered into a perfect man, but that “the Word became flesh,” touching the very beginnings of our nature. Just as a human being naturally brought forth does not immediately proceed as perfect in activity, but first the deposit of seed itself becomes flesh, and then, with the passage of time, receives the power that contains the completion of the senses and activities, so God the Word, touching the very beginnings and root of human formation, first became flesh—not, God forbid, being changed into flesh.

[Col. 0412C] His divinity remained superior to every change, because change is the suffering of a flowing nature; whereas it belongs to the everlasting and eternal essence, existing in this manner, to remain immutable. Thus, using both expressions of divine Scripture, we say that He became flesh and that He assumed the form of a servant.

From both statements, rightly understood, the seeds of salvation arise for us. For by saying that the Word became flesh, the Evangelist declares the indivisible unity of that supreme union. Just as singularity cannot be divided into two singularities—for once divided into these it would no longer be singularity but duality—so what is one according to the supreme union can in no way be divided into two.

[Col. 0412D] By saying that He assumed the form of a servant, the immutability of the divine nature is indicated. For whatever comes to be has either been made from what did not previously exist, as heaven, which previously did not exist, or has been changed from what exists into something else, as the waters of the Nile were changed into blood. But neither mode is compatible with the divine substance. God the Word neither proceeded from anything that existed, since He always remains without beginning, nor was He changed from any matter, since He persists in His immutability.

Therefore, through these expressions Holy Scripture bears witness both to the immutability of the Godhead and to the indivisible nature of the mystery, demonstrating what was made and indicating what He assumed: by the first, commending the singularity of the nature and person of both; by the second, proclaiming the immutability of the divine substance.

[Col. 0413A] God the Word therefore became a perfect human being, without the nature of the Godhead being changed, in accordance with a miracle that exceeds the understanding of our mind. We perceive this by faith; we do not arrive at it by investigation.

Having become human and related to us according to the flesh, He granted salvation to the race through the likeness of its passions, paying the debt of sin by enduring what belongs to humanity and dying for all. He destroyed the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil, as the most just God. He also made possible what was impossible under the Law, fulfilling all righteousness, and restored the former nobility and splendor of our substance by becoming human; He honored the one whom He Himself had formed from the earth.

[Col. 0413B] There is therefore one Son, one Lord. For we confess a Trinity of one essence, admitting no fourth person whatsoever into the Trinity. But, as we have said, there is one Son, born without beginning from the Father, through whom we believe the ages were made: a branch from the root, coeternal, sprung from the Father in an ineffable manner; the word proceeding inseparably from the mind and remaining intimately within it.

For although He was seen on earth, He was not separated from His Begetter. He willed to save the one whom He had created—indeed, He saved him—graciously dwelling in the womb, the common gateway of nature, which He both sanctified by His presence and marked by His birth with a birth beyond nature, incomprehensibly demonstrating Himself to have become human.

[Col. 0413C] Christ is not one and God the Word another, God forbid. Divine nature knows no two sons: one only-begotten Son was begotten. For where there is no union of begetters, there you cannot find a distinction in those who are born.

“In the name of Jesus Christ every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2). If Christ is another apart from God, Christ must necessarily be merely human. How, then, do the heavenly beings venerate Him beyond the merit of His nature, and bow the knee to one who is lesser? How do we understand the prophetic oracles that cry out that “our God was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3)?

[Col. 0413D] The prophet calls “vision” the manifestation that took place in the flesh, and “dwelling among them” the temporal sojourn by which He lived with human beings. His goodness, without envy, declared the advent of His loving-kindness: for, as almighty, He remained what He was for His own sake and became what He willed for our sake.

If at any time the beginnings of infancy, His lying in a manger, His growth according to the flesh in due time, His sleeping in a boat, His weariness from traveling, His hunger after fasting, or all those things that truly happened to a human being cause scandal, let those who criticize them know that they deny the human nature in Christ. By denying the nature, they do not believe in the dispensation; by refusing to believe in the dispensation, they will suffer the loss of salvation.

[Col. 0414A] Let contentious persons show whether anyone, from the creation of the world—which established that humanity was cast into this life—entered by any path other than this flesh; then let them weave their ravings. But if these are the beginnings of common nature, and God the Word truly became human, why, while confessing the nature, do they condemn the passion?

Let them choose one of two alternatives: either, ashamed of the humiliations, let them deny the nature and, afflicted with the diseases of Manichaeism, be counted among the impious; or, if they accept the gain that comes from the incarnation while confessing the substance, let them not be ashamed of the passions that follow upon the substance.

I marvel also at the madness of those who walk along new paths of deception. I know piously, as I have been taught, one Son, whom I confess to be the substance of God the Word incarnate. Since the one who endured the passions and performed the miracles is one, why do they silence the more divine matters and disparage the humbler ones?

[Col. 0414B] To establish faith that the Word remained what He was, He became flesh (John 1), that is, an infant and a perfect human being, without that great mystery being violated by any change. The same one performed miracles and endured insults: through the signs He indicated that He had remained what He was; through the passions He revealed that He had become what He had formed.

We therefore proclaim one and the same Son, both coeternal with the Father and incarnate in the last times, inserting nothing adulterous into the divine nature. For nothing superfluous can exist upon the throne.

But perhaps they will bring forward that often-repeated argument of theirs, weaving syllogisms weaker than a spider’s web:

“If the Trinity is of one essence, surely the Trinity remains impassible. But if the Trinity and God the Word are contemplated in the Trinity, the Trinity remains impassible, and God the Word is shown to be impassible. If God the Word is impassible, then the one who was crucified will be found to be someone other than the impassible God the Word.”

[Col. 0414C] Truly those who utter such things weave spiderwebs; those who devise these most foolish propositions write upon water. Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools, and their senseless heart was darkened (Romans 1). A diseased eye cannot receive the rays of the sun clearly, and a feeble mind cannot behold the height of faith.

What, then, do we say to this? According to the account of the Godhead, the holy Trinity is both of one essence and remains impassible. For when we say that the Son suffered, we do not understand Him to have suffered according to the account of the Godhead. The divine nature receives no passion whatsoever. But by confessing that God the Word, one of the Trinity, became incarnate, we provide those who inquire faithfully with the basis for understanding why He deigned to become incarnate.

Since God the Word had decreed to destroy the passions whose end was regarded as death, and the inviolable nature could not assume passion—for every passion is shown to introduce struggle into composite things, whereas in a spiritual and singular substance there is no composition, and passion could not reach what was not composite—He willed, as I have said, to destroy the passions that had oppressed the rational body and whose destruction was its supreme defense.

[Col. 0415A] God the Word, therefore, was incarnate from a Virgin and was found in appearance as a human being, since He willed thus to empty Himself, in a certain manner assuming the form of a servant (Philippians 2), yet admitting no circumscription of His divinity. Through this He also brought salvation to the whole human race, destroying the passions in His flesh while preserving His own divinity impassible.

Therefore Gabriel, indicating the authority and power of the One who was born, said to Mary: “He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1). The people cannot belong to a human being but to God. Nor did the one who entered this life together with corruption free the world from iniquities, since he had no blameless beginning of birth. Rather, God and human together, not divided into two but remaining one, saved His people: by being born from a woman He demonstrated Himself to be human; by being born without a husband while preserving His mother’s virginity intact, He clearly indicated Himself to be God.

[Col. 0415B] Who is He? Jesus Christ, who came upon the earth and lived among human beings (Baruch 3).

But if Christ is merely human and is not Himself God the Word, how did He create all things in the beginning, when then, as the impious assert, He did not exist? Since humanity is the last of created things, if Christ is merely human, it follows that He could not have created what existed before Him, as though He had come into being afterward.

And how could Paul say, “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things”? If all things were made through Christ, it is clear that Christ is God the Word, as the Evangelist bears witness: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him” (John 1).

[Col. 0415C] Paul too, interpreting this, says: “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8). Thus it is said that Christ is God the Word.

If they bring forward those statements found in the divine writings in which Christ is called human, as Peter says: “Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you” (Acts 2), and Paul likewise bears witness: “In the man in whom He determined to establish faith for all” (Acts 17), and the Lord Himself cries out concerning Himself: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man?” (John 8), let them know that through negligence they deprive themselves of understanding of Holy Scripture—or rather, through malice abandon it—because they wish to turn what has been well written toward their own perversity.

[Col. 0415D] Christ is also truly called human, but He became what He previously was not, while nevertheless being God. For just as He is uncreated as God, so that same one is a perfect human being, admitting no suspicion whatsoever of mere appearance.

And just as He is consubstantial with the Father according to divinity, so the same one is shown to be like the holy Virgin according to the flesh. Everywhere the truth of the mystery shines forth, with every falsehood entirely removed.

But if the Virgin did not give birth to God, neither was she regarded as remaining intact through a great miracle. Many other women also brought righteous persons into the world. The prophetic tongues, however, foretelling the ineffable nature of this mystery, said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a Son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.” Gabriel interpreted this by saying, “God with us” (Isaiah 7; Matthew 1; Luke 1).

[Col. 0416A] Why do they diminish the glory of the one who gave birth because of the lowliness of the one who was born?

But perhaps they object as follows: “Everything that is born is shown to be like its begetter. Therefore, if the one whom she bore is human, necessarily the one born from her is human.”

You present this as though it were a plausible argument. But a mother gives birth to one entirely like herself when birth occurs according to nature. The beginning of natural childbirth, however, is corruption, since it is preceded by intercourse. But where there is not even a suspicion of this dishonor, there is plainly a miracle beyond human understanding. Where birth is beyond nature, the one who is born is God.

[Col. 0416B] We therefore confess that He made the world from nothing, gave the Law, inspired the prophets, and in the last times became incarnate. We also confess that He sent the Apostles for the salvation of nations and peoples.

Let us therefore flee the counsels of seduction—I mean the destructive and God-opposed contagions of the heretics: the madness of Arius, who divides the inseparable Trinity into substances; the audacity of Eunomius, who confines the incomprehensible nature within the limits of human knowledge; the rage of Manichaeus, who separates the Holy Spirit from the essence of the Godhead, although He proceeds inseparably.

[Col. 0416C] Let us flee also this most recent and novel blasphemy, which is recognized as surpassing the impiety of the Jews in many respects. The Jews, by denying the Son, strive to tear the branch from the root. These people, introducing another above the one who exists, attempt to proclaim the undefiled substance as though it were multiplied into many offspring.

Let us therefore say with Paul (Ephesians 2): “Christ is our peace, who made both one.” Through baptism He reformed Jew and Gentile into one new human being, joining by His power those whom their manner of life had separated.

Therefore let the inventors of this new impiety tremble at the condemnation that hangs over them. For when the separated have returned to one concord, and the one who united the two is, so far as they are concerned, divided, they must fear the judgment awaiting them.

But, leaving aside the length of this discourse, I shall proceed to a concise statement of sound doctrine.

If anyone wishes to know truthfully how the very same one is one and remains not only the Son of Abraham, but also, in the last times, progresses according to the flesh in wisdom and age—for His divinity always possesses what is perfect—let him ask Paul. Paul himself will immediately proclaim the mystery of piety, showing that the one who arose from the Jews according to the flesh is the eternal God.

[Col. 0416D] Speaking of the Hebrews and praising that rebellious and ungrateful nation, because of its root, Abraham, and because of its seed, Christ, he declares as follows: “To them,” he says (Romans 9), “belongs the adoption as sons.”

For he cries out in the prophets: “Israel is my firstborn son and my glory.” Divine miracles bestowed infinite glory upon those who at that time were approved in character; so did the covenants through which the multiplication of Abraham’s seed was promised; the giving of the Law, written on the mountain by the finger of God; the service by which they ministered to divine worship; and the promises by which either the land of Palestine or, certainly, the blessing in Abraham’s seed was granted to all the nations.

[Col. 0417A] Their fathers, from whom, in this night of ignorance, the lights of faith are shown to have arisen, and from whom is Christ.

The most blessed Paul did not stop there. For the essence of the Word who exists without beginning is not the same as the birth from Mary. Rather, he immediately added “according to the flesh,” so that he might signify the manifestation that took place in the flesh, not that divine and eternal birth.

Who, then, is this Christ who was born from the Virgin, whom a cave received as though He were a thing of no worth, who lay in a manger, who grew in time according to the flesh, and who, descending to the lower regions of the earth, endured all that belongs to the flesh with wondrous condescension, to establish faith that He truly became human? He is no other than the one who descended; the same one who descended is the one who ascended. For He did not ascend first but descended, since He is not God by promotion but, because of the mercy that we needed, graciously became human.

[Col. 0417B] Let no one ask me or anyone else who He is, but ask the Apostle, who says by revelation that the Son is of the Father, when he says (Galatians 1): “When it pleased Him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace, to reveal His Son in me.”

Who this one is, Jesus Christ will truly teach by crying out (Romans 9): “From them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.”

[Col. 0417C] What opportunity for the slander of those who love perversity do these words of Paul allow? He said “Christ” to show that He truly became human; he said “from the Jews according to the flesh” to indicate that He did not begin to exist from the time when He was incarnate; he said “who is” to declare Him without beginning; he said “over all” to proclaim Him Lord of the whole creation; he called Him “Lord,” lest, misled by His passions and His human condition, we dare to deny His undefiled substance; he called Him “blessed,” so that we might worship Him humbly as almighty and not attack Him with slanders as though He were a fellow servant; he said “forever,” to demonstrate that the one who created us by His Word must, because of His divinity, be honored by us with perpetual worship.

[Col. 0418A] Since we have Christ as existing, as God, and as blessed forever, let us venerate Him as Lord, saying to the advocates of foreign doctrines: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is none of His” (Romans 8). But we possess the mind of Christ. Therefore we await the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who will give the crown of glory to those who live piously, but will repay those who provoke Him according to the deserts of their audacity.

We send this to your charity in response to the booklets that you took care to send us, affirming that certain pestilential men, bringing forth monstrous doctrines, have invaded your province, wishing through certain writings and objections of falsely named knowledge to corrupt the simple, unadulterated beauty and steadfastness of the true faith.

[Col. 0418B] But I again admonish you in the words of blessed Paul (Colossians 2:8): “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men who deliberate vain things and not according to Christ.”

No one can lay another foundation of holy faith besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. Stand therefore of one spirit, united in mind, laboring together for the faith of the Gospel, and in nothing terrified by your adversaries (Philippians 1), preserving the traditions that you received either from the holy and most blessed Fathers known to have proclaimed the faith at Nicaea, or from the holy and venerable Basil, Gregory, and the others who held the same opinion, whose names are written in the book of life.

[Col. 0418C] I, together with those who are with me, send abundant greetings to the entire brotherhood that is with you in Christ.

[This is absent from the Greek.] Given at Constantinople, in the consulship of the most pious emperors Theodosius Augustus V and Valentinian IV.

[Col. 0417]

## ON THE DISCOVERY OF THE HEAD OF JOHN THE BAPTIST

### Prologue of Dionysius Exiguus on the Discovery of the Head of Saint John the Baptist

[Col. 0417C] Dionysius to my venerable lord Gaudentius, abbot.

The care and diligence of the dearest brothers whom you govern through the grace of Christ compelled me to render into Latin the account of the discovery of the head of blessed John the Baptist, which was written in Greek. [Col. 0417D] They said that it was fitting that, on the birthday of the one greater than whom no one has arisen among those born of women, this account concerning him should be made known to the faithful.

With willing minds, therefore, I explained what was requested within the brief space available, especially because I learned that Your Holiness also wished this to be done. Nor do I fail to see that this was accomplished without divine guidance. That same holy John, the Lord’s forerunner, the herald of truth, the summit of all the prophets, and the founder of monks, just as he first manifested himself to monks—those who carried his most sacred head from the house of Herod, once an impious king—[Col. 0418C] then, after it had been removed to Emesa and remained unknown for many years, again revealed himself to monks; so now he has deigned, through the service of monks, though humble ones, to make known this account concerning himself to the Romans.

[Col. 0418D] I believe that he delights in the service of a venerable purpose, in order that through those who pursue a solitary life he might unfold his glory in Christ. We say this not because we presumptuously claim for ourselves the conscience of any distinguished mind, but because the pious profession itself displays holy zeal, even though our sluggish way of life does not equal it.

What manner of life that most blessed man then led—what believer could be unaware? Apart from that extraordinary generosity of divine grace by which he was conceived according to the promise, and while still enclosed within his mother’s womb recognized, from the womb of the barren woman whom he made fruitful, the Author of all things in the womb of the holy Virgin, [Col. 0419A] There was also his singular glory: he was the Baptist of Christ and the friend of the heavenly Bridegroom.

He often lived alone in deserted and hidden places, persevering day and night in fasting and prayer, clothed in camel’s hair and nourished by locusts and wild honey. These things are shown to be signs of the greatest self-restraint and frugality. Renouncing the whole world with its pomp and pleasures, he deigned to see nothing other than Christ. To Him, when He came to His baptism, he also bore witness, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold Him who takes away the sins of the world.”

[Col. 0419B] Although by such distinguished deeds and such magnificent examples he revealed models of virtue to all, the rulers nevertheless, together with the elders, scribes, and Pharisees, reproached his merits with senseless insolence. Our Lord attests this in the Gospel and says: “John the Baptist came neither eating nor drinking, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’”

Just so, even now many Christians, plainly like Pharisees, if they happen to see servants of God practicing abstinence, burst into the same reproaches and curses, and do not hesitate to pursue with their insults what they ought to attain through imitation. Thus a commendable life, exposed to malicious rumors, may nevertheless maintain a praiseworthy perseverance and kindle the fervor of an ancient rivalry.

We endure this hatred because of the likeness of our conduct, so that what our Lord says in the Gospel may also be confirmed in us: “If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of this world, therefore the world hates you.”

[Col. 0420A] Saint John encountered this hatred of the world. His feast is celebrated today by the Church throughout the whole world. He also endured in the remaining portion of his body, during the time of Julian—more a tyrant than a ruler—the treatment that the holy Gospels report was inflicted after his body had been handed over by his disciples for burial.

For the savage cruelty of the pagans, corresponding to the character of the most impious apostate Julian, broke open the tomb of the most blessed man, senselessly drew out his bones, burned them in fire and reduced them to ashes, and scattered them everywhere in mad fury.

But the grace of Christ, which directs the hearts of His servants, had brought monks from Jerusalem to that place in those days for the sake of prayer. When they saw this most wicked deed being perpetrated by the impious, they transferred the same venerable relics while the pagans themselves looked on in astonishment. Soon afterward they departed, carrying the venerable treasure with them.

[Col. 0420B] Behold, once again the service of monks is divinely arranged: just as the head of this holy man was discovered through monks, so the remaining relics of his body were preserved through monks. They were immediately sent to Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria. Later Theophilus, bishop of the same city, destroyed all the shrines of the idols and deposited the relics in the basilica that he had built with pious devotion under the name of that same most blessed John the Baptist, amid the immense veneration of the people.

But now it is time for us to relate to you the history mentioned above, and for this labor of ours to obtain effectively the support of your prayers.

## ON THE DISCOVERY OF THE HEAD OF JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Note: [Col. 0419] The Latin and Greek versions of this work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0419]

Concerning the first discovery of the precious head of the distinguished and glorious prophet and forerunner, John the Baptist. Translated by Dionysius Exiguus.

[Col. 0419C]

Two monks who had set out from the East, desiring to behold the place of Christ’s precious cross and his glorious tomb—Christ, who for our salvation became human and endured death, through which he bestowed life and immortality upon us—as well as the venerable places of his resurrection and ascension into heaven, arrived at Jerusalem.

To one of them the holy John appeared, the Forerunner of the Lord’s coming and Baptist of the eternal King, and said: “When you come to the former house of King Herod, take with you my head, which you will find buried in the ground.”

When morning had dawned, the monk reported the vision he had seen to his brother. The latter, suspecting it to be an illusion of the imagination, persuaded the man to whom the mystery had been revealed that it was nothing, so that he would think likewise. When they had neglected the matter, on the following day the herald of truth appeared to both of them separately and, appearing to them in the same way, spoke thus:

“Driving every doubt of unbelief from your hearts, let your thought not falter concerning the truth of the vision.”

When each had reported the agreement of the vision to the other, strengthened by the double vision and fearing the punishment of disobedience, they immediately fulfilled what had been commanded them. With divine grace going before them, they placed in a sackcloth bag the head of the Baptist, which had been cut off for justice and piety. I think that the prophet was pleased with such a covering, since formerly in the desert his body had been clothed with camel’s hair.

The monks therefore returned, carrying the head which Herodias had received on a platter as the reward for her dancing daughter, as though she had obtained the long-desired quarry of the hunt. Moreover, thinking that the rebukes of the prophetic tongue had now ceased, she by no means allowed that venerable head to be buried with the rest of the body. She feared its reunion and undoubtedly reasoned that, if the saint’s body remained whole, it would easily rise again, whereas this could not happen if she herself retained the head. Therefore she did not hand it over to an ordinary burial, but buried it within the enclosure of her own house.

For the love of the illicit union, betrayed by her own contrivances, imagined images of the rebukes, and that impious daughter of the devil feared the severed head of the righteous man. Thus, deceived by the perversity of her thoughts, she thereafter believed that she herself would remain hidden.

The monks, then, who had been deemed worthy of so great a revelation of Christ’s Forerunner, took up the venerable head and hastened to return home.

At that time a certain potter in the city of Emesa, oppressed by many hardships and lacking all necessities, was unable to struggle any longer against extreme poverty. Overwhelmed by great weariness because of the distress of his want, he believed that he could preserve his life only by departing. As he fled, it happened that he encountered these monks, who were carrying the most precious treasure of the desert.

When he had become their companion and fellow traveler, they entrusted the burden to him, as travelers commonly do when journeying together, explaining to him the vision that had been revealed to them. But while the potter remained ignorant of the mystery, the Forerunner appeared to him and instructed him to conceal himself from his companions and flee, taking with him what he was carrying.

He did so and returned to his own house, from which he had departed. From that time onward he flourished in every kind of prosperity. He understood who was the author of his prosperity and offered him, with devoted zeal and according to his means, the honor due to him.

When he saw that death was approaching, he carefully sealed the jar in which that gift had been enclosed and entrusted it to his own sister. He told her of his former poverty and disclosed the wealth now in his hands. After recounting the hardships of his earlier poverty and explaining how he had been rescued from them, he begged her to treat the deposit honorably and not to open the jar before the outcome of the matter revealed what was inside.

He was thinking, I believe, that the vessel would be like a womb for the Forerunner: just as he had made the Lord known while the Lord was in his mother’s womb, so surely, alive after death, he would reveal at the proper time the mystery of the jar. Therefore he did not conceal the author of his unexpected transformation [another reading: “with the author inspiring his transformation”], but said:

“O woman, experience itself will teach you, and you will learn the manner and conduct of our life from the time when we were deemed worthy to possess this treasure. If, then, you also show reverence toward it, you will enjoy an abundance of all good things, both present and future. But if perhaps the length of time takes away your strength, or violent illness of body wears you down so that you cannot render the service owed, do not delay to hand this gift over to some pious and faithful man.”

After her brother’s death, she is shown to have cherished the holy trust for as long as her strength remained equal to her devotion. But when she yielded to the necessity of old age, she explained what her brother had entrusted to her and handed it over to those who were prepared to receive the pious deposit.

After many people had received this gift in successive transmission, a certain monk named Eustathius, a presbyter of another sect, finally received what was kept in the jar, just as it had been sealed. Those who had handed it over had evidently been unable to discern his religion and had considered him a pious man. He, however, most craftily attributed to himself the healings bestowed through the power of the holy head upon those who approached it and attempted, like a thoroughly wicked wine-seller, to adulterate the truth.

At last he became known to those servants who rightly, holily, and inseparably glorified the blessed Trinity. He, who under the pretext of honoring the Father was proved to be insulting Christ, the Son of God, by diminishing him, began to be expelled from the city of Emesa, with the judges also cooperating.

He begged those who were seeking to separate and drive him away salutarily from the holy flock to grant him at least one day’s time to remain in the cave where the holy deposit was known to be kept, since he was already being pressed by the narrowness of the night. But God’s providence frustrated his hope. He could not obtain that what he was attempting should be accomplished.

Thus venerable men took possession of the same cave, pursuing the discipline of a solitary life. After many had succeeded one another in the monastery, at last, under the archimandrite Marcellus, divine grace deigned to reveal him whom Gabriel announced in the Gospel and whom a barren mother bore: the inhabitant of the desert, the greatest reprover of impiety and vindicator of the law, the Lord’s Forerunner, the friend of the Bridegroom, the Baptist of the Savior, the herald of truth, and the most ardent lover of righteousness.

The aforementioned venerable archimandrite Marcellus related the manner of his apparition in these words.

## On the First Discovery of the Precious Head of the Venerable and Glorious Prophet, the Forerunner and Baptist John

[Col. 0420C]

Two monks setting out from the East, and desiring to see for themselves the place of the precious cross and the tomb of Christ, who out of compassion for us became human and endured death, the bringer of immortality, as well as the places of his resurrection and ascension, arrived at Jerusalem.

To one of them the Forerunner of the Master’s coming and Baptist of the King of all, John, appeared and said:

“Run to the former dwelling of Herod and take up my head, which lies buried beneath the earth there.”

When dawn arrived, the monk related the vision to his companion. The other, thinking that the matter was an illusion, persuaded the one who had seen the vision to share his opinion.

When they had consequently grown negligent, on the following day the herald of truth again appeared to each of them separately in the same manner and said:

“Having banished every unbelief from your mind, do not let your reasoning falter concerning belief in the vision.”

When one had related the revelation to the other and they had been assured by the doubling of the vision, fearing the penalty arising from disobedience, they immediately carried out what had been commanded.

Led by grace, they took up the Baptist’s head, which had been cut off for piety, and placed it in bags made of camel’s hair. The prophet, I think, was pleased with this, just as formerly in the desert the garment made of camel’s hair had covered his body.

Carrying the head, they returned—the head which Herodias had received on a platter from her daughter, having obtained the long-sought quarry—and, thinking that the reproofs of the prophet’s tongue had ceased, she by no means allowed it to be buried with the rest of the body. She suspected the danger arising from their reunion and all but reasoned that, if the saint’s remains were complete, resurrection would be easy for them, but that it would not be easy while the head was guarded by her.

Therefore, as was to be expected, she did not consign it to an ordinary burial. Rather, she ordered it to be buried within the enclosure and secured by the application of locks. For the love of the unlawful union, betrayed by her thoughts, dreamed of the rebukes and feared, I think, the severed and unabashed head.

Thus the unlawful woman, the devil’s disciple, made sport of by the perversity of her thoughts, thought that it would henceforth remain hidden.

The monks who had been deemed worthy of the vision, when the Forerunner had appeared to them through the grace of the Spirit, took up the head more precious than all gold and hastened to return home.

At that time a certain potter of the Emesenes, living in misfortune and having poverty as his companion, overcome by helplessness, set out in flight. It happened that he encountered the monks who were carrying the treasure of the desert. He became their conversation-partner and fellow traveler, as commonly happens on journeys; and the aforesaid men entrusted him with carrying the gift, having kept safe what had been revealed.

While the potter was ignorant of the mystery, the Forerunner appeared to him and said:

“Conceal yourself from the monks traveling with you, take the bag you are carrying, and flee.”

Having done this, he returned home. He continued to flourish in every prosperity and forgot his former misfortune. Knowing the author of his prosperity, he honored him with gratitude according to his ability.

When he was about to depart from human life, he sealed the casket containing the gift and entrusted it to his own sister. He told her of the poverty he had first experienced and disclosed the abundance now in his hands. After describing the inescapable bonds of his former poverty, explaining how he had escaped them, and asking her to maintain the honor of this treasure but not to uncover the casket before what was inside indicated its release, he thought, I believe, that the container would again be a mother’s womb for the Forerunner. The one who had made the Master known in his mother’s womb and had indicated him by his leaping would surely also indicate, while living after death in the container, the time of its opening.

He did not, however, leave unmentioned the account of his sudden transformation, but said:

“You, woman, know from experience, having learned the change in our life and what we have become from what we were, after finding this treasure. Therefore, hold this in honor and reap the return of good things.

“But if time, with the whitening of your hair, should take away your strength, or bodily disorder should violently loosen your power [sic], and you should grow faint in your devotion, hand this over to some pious person.”

As long as she possessed strength corresponding to her zeal, she cherished the trust. But when she yielded to the necessity of old age, she explained to those who were to receive it what her brother had said to her and handed over the treasure, more precious than all gold.

After many had acquired this gift through successive transmissions, a certain monk named Eustathius, a presbyter of another doctrine, received what was kept in the jar. Those who had given it to him apparently did not know how to distinguish religions at all and considered him pious. But he, craftily appropriating to himself the healings that flowed from the apostolic head to those who approached it, adulterated the truth.

Eventually he became known to those who rightly, without confusion, and with consubstantial faith glorify the all-praised Trinity. He who under the appearance of honoring the Father insulted him by diminishing the Son was expelled from the Emesenes with the cooperation of the authorities.

Kneeling before those who were piously hastening to separate the impious man from the Savior’s flock, he asked them to grant a respite in his late expulsion and to allow him to inhabit the cave for one day. But by God’s providence he was deprived of his hope.

Devout men pursuing the solitary life took possession of the same cave. After many had succeeded one another in the monastery, in the time of Marcellus, the most pious archimandrite, God’s grace was pleased to reveal him whom Gabriel announced, the offspring of the barren woman, the fairest creature of the desert, the reprover of lawlessness, the advocate of the law, the Forerunner of the Master, the friend of the Bridegroom, the Baptist of the Savior, the herald of truth, and the most ardent lover of piety.

The most pious archimandrite Marcellus explained his manifestation in the following account.

## On the Second Discovery of the Precious Head of the Holy and Glorious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John

[Col. 0423C]

### In the Second Discovery of the Precious Head of the Holy and Illustrious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John

Translated by the same interpreter.

[Col. 0423C]

He appeared, he says, as the thrice-blessed and universal apostle, and faithful friend of our Savior Jesus Christ, in the middle week of the holy fasts, on the eighteenth day of the month Peritius, that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, in the seven-hundred-and-sixty-third year [another reading: the seven-hundred-and-third year], in the sixth indiction, while Valentinian and Marcian, most pious emperors and servants of God, were reigning, under the most holy bishop Uranius of the city of Emesa. To him also this same thing was revealed on the twenty-fourth day of the same month, that is, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

He revealed it to me, Marcellus, established in great fear and reverence, in the form of a fiery star, according to the most trustworthy visions set out below—he who created all things by his power and prepared them in his wisdom, who knows all things before they come to be and orders everything for the salvation of the human race, who is blessed above all forever. Amen.

Therefore God deemed me, his servant, worthy to be an observer of the proposed vision.

For I saw in a night vision, and behold, the doors of our monastery were open. Being placed in great fear, I ran to close them. Then again I looked and saw a river rushing toward our doors. When I had seen this, I was astonished and wondered where such an immense quantity of water came from.

While I was considering this within myself, I lifted my eyes and saw the presbyter Marcellus, who was second after the archimandrite Maxentius, coming from the southern side of the river. We heard the voices of many companies from the eastern side of the basilica of Saint Julian the martyr. A great sound from them was carried to us, and through the waters themselves the people hurried toward us with energetic eagerness.

As I wondered how they could come swiftly to us while walking in the midst of the waters, and as each company sang in its own language, suddenly the voice of those who were shouting from the east was heard:

“Behold, Saint John the Baptist is coming down.”

When I was standing at the southern door, the eastern doors were opened, and the companies of singers immediately entered. Leaving aside the spectacle of the river and standing at the beginning of the staircase, I observed their holy service, which they celebrated in the monastery.

Standing on that same staircase, I saw two courtyards, one facing west and the other south; between the two courtyards was a large church. Each company entered the courtyard that faced east, and they worshiped toward the church [al.: worshiping, toward the church]. When they entered the southern courtyard, they immediately became silent.

When the companies had fallen silent, others came forward and shouted:

“Behold, Saint John has arrived.”

When I was standing in the same place on the staircase, Saint John, the Lord’s Forerunner, came, and I saw him in the church that had been shown to me. Behold, one man was at his right and one at his left.

While he was standing in the church, the people of the companies began successively to approach him and receive his blessing. Then, while singing, they proceeded to the basilica of Saint Stephen the martyr [Note: [Col. 0425D] Another reading: “toward the western side, as though toward the basilica”], where they were to assemble.

When the companies had dispersed, I too thought of approaching him, so that I might receive his blessing. It seemed to me that I should enter through the doors by which the companies had entered. Since I had not seen them give anyone the kiss of peace, except that they had kissed only his feet [al.: his breast], I approached him from the front [al.: inner side] with fear and reverence, lowered my head to the ground, and took hold of his feet. He himself took hold of my chin and kissed me. When I had received this favor, I immediately awoke.

A few days later I saw again, and behold, the doors of the monastery on the southern side were open. I shouted, as it were, to the brothers, asking why they had left these doors [al.: thus]. I hurried with rapid steps to close them, and behold, I saw Saint John standing at the outer door, with those two whom I had seen before. I approached to receive his blessing, and again, raising me up, he gave me the kiss of peace.

His garments were white. Then, drawing a vessel full of honey from his bosom, he gave it to me, saying:

“Receive this blessing.”

He poured the vessel of honey over my hands. I asked him:

“Holy Lord John, where have you come to us from?”

He replied:

“I have come from Sebaste.”

I went before him, and both he and those who were with him entered our monastery. Again he poured the vessel of honey over my hands.

When I had carried his blessing to the upper dining room, he entered the oratory. When I descended to the oratory where he was, behold, I saw a column of fire before him. Seized by very great fear, I awoke.

After this, before the door of the monastery where the holy deposit was kept had been handed over to us, during the holy days of the fast, after we had taken our evening meal, I said to our brothers:

“Let each of you not neglect to repeat his psalms.”

They left me in the dining room and descended to the beginning of the staircase that faces both monasteries. When they had sat down to repeat the psalms, Brother Isaac raised his eyes to the right and saw fire burning in the boards of the door of the cave where the venerable head of Saint John the Baptist had been placed.

When the brother saw this, he cried out and said:

“My lord, my lord, fire has been kindled at the door of the cave.”

I answered:

“Do not be afraid, brother, but fortify yourself with the sign of Christ and remain there.”

The brothers, closing the door out of fear, hurried to me. Recognizing the mystery from the visions previously shown to me, I said to them:

“Do not be afraid, my brothers, for the Lord will make this prosperous for us.”

Five days later, the venerable presbyter-archimandrites Maxentius and Stephen came to the holy bishop on Sunday evening and reported everything concerning the cave, which adjoined our monastery, so that the two might be joined together. The bishop ordered this to be done.

The presbyter Stephen said to him:

“By our command I shall tomorrow early hand the cave over to Brother Marcellus.”

In the morning he came and handed the monastery over to us in the presence of the presbyters Palladius, Peter, Gennadius, and Stephen, archimandrite of the monastery of Bethgalorum [al.: Bethgaalorum]. Opening the door, which had been secured, we entered together and worshiped [al.: prayed]. Seeing that the place was extremely neglected, he urged us to take care of it diligently. Then the same presbyter Stephen departed to visit the monasteries established in the villages.

I, Marcellus, taking the brothers, began to devote care to the monastery that had been given to us [al.: to care diligently for it]. While we were cleaning the place, Peter, presbyter of Bethmamat, came and said to me:

“Stephen, archimandrite of Bethgaalorum, asks you, for the Lord’s sake, to come with us to the monastery of blessed Carterius.”

I replied that I could not come, because I had to care for the place entrusted to me. He compelled me to depart with him.

As we were traveling together, I said to him:

“Let us go up and greet Cyriacus, the deacon and archimandrite.”

When we had gone up and greeted him, we began intending to proceed to the aforementioned monastery of blessed Carterius. The deacon Cyriacus said to me:

“Have you come for this reason, to depart without delay?”

I replied:

“We must walk quickly, because another monastery has also been entrusted to us by the bishop, and we are earnestly caring for it.”

We therefore descended and reached the monastery so often mentioned. After we had greeted the brothers and arranged what was necessary, we were returning. The aforesaid presbyter-archimandrites Peter and Stephen said to me:

“We bid you farewell; pray for us.”

Then I said to them:

“Today we have received the monastery, and you wish to leave? Please stay and console us.”

And I compelled them to remain.

When evening came, after the prayers and after we had eaten, we rested: both of them in the upper dining room, while I was there in the inner chamber.

[Col. 0429B]

As I slept during the night in which the door of the monastery, or cave, was opened—that is, on the following third day of the week, after the night prayers—something like a man’s hand struck me three times on the right side, and I heard a loud voice saying to me:

“Behold, the door is open; therefore recognize him who opened the entrance for you, lest you neglect it.”

I turned in great fear, sat up, and saw a flaming star at the door where I was resting. Conceiving still greater fear, I signed myself with the cross of Christ, but it did not move at all from that place.

I therefore rose and placed my hands on the door where it was, and again it was found at the next door. When I had opened [read: “when I had opened”] the door, one of those who were resting there noticed it. When I reached the second door, the star was found at the third door.

Then I saw it within the steps of the staircase. The doors of both monasteries were likewise open, and the door of the cave stood open. Behold, the star itself went before me, and I followed it, entering until it stopped in the small apse of the cave. Seeing this miracle, I worshiped the Lord, lying prostrate on the ground for many hours.

Then I remembered that I had as guests the venerable men Peter and Stephen, presbyters and archimandrites. So that they would not suspect where I had been during the night, I rose from prayer. Going up again, when I wished to enter the chamber, they said to me:

“Where have you been for so long?”

I replied:

“I went down for necessary work.”

When I wished to enter where I had rested, they said to me:

“Are you entering again?”

But, realizing that I had been stunned by the revelation I had seen, I asked pardon like a madman and immediately withdrew.

When morning came, they said farewell to me and departed to their own cells. As soon as they had left at dawn, I ordered the brothers who were with me:

“Close the doors. Remain outside, and if anyone comes seeking me, say that I am occupied.”

For the presbyter Palladius often came in and read the Gospel. When he came as usual, the brothers denied him access, explaining the truth: that the Gospel too was under the archimandrite’s key. He excused himself.

He came a second time, and a third time as well, and thus entered.

I took a censer, placed incense in it, and earnestly entreated the merciful Lord to show me the place of the heavenly treasure. Taking a rake, I began to dig and reached a place built of lime and ordinary tiles. The farther down I dug, the louder became the sound that came back, as if from the reverberation of a jar.

[Col. 0431]

After I had dug and descended to the ground level, I found something like sand poured from bronze. Laboring greatly, I could scarcely remove the sand. After the sand had been removed, a single larger tile appeared. When I lifted it, I found beneath it a marble slab. Lifting the slab, I found the jar.

With fear and reverence I lit a lamp, placed incense in the censer, carefully touched the jar, worshiped the Lord, remained astonished for a long time, and then covered the holy jar again.

Immediately the deacon and archimandrite Gennadius came to us. Greeting me at the door of the cave, he said:

“Come, I beg you; let us enter the cave together.”

After we had worshiped there [al.: prayed there], he gave me and my brothers the kiss of peace and said:

“I have just come from my monastery of Caperetum. I saw the following dream. It was as though we were both standing in a certain cave in which there was a great quantity of loaves, exceedingly clean, like the sun, and a portion placed upon the loaves. An immense multitude of people came and took from them. They did not run out, nor did the people who had received them cease. When we were already failing because of the crowds, the loaves began to fly into our hands, and all who gathered for this grace of the gift received them.”

After he had related the dream to me, I replied:

“What you saw is good.”

Reflecting within myself what the vision meant, and considering again what had preceded it, I said that this vision was from God.

Knowing that these things had happened by divine agency, I explained how Saint John the Baptist had deigned to appear. As soon as he heard, he remained astonished and began to ask me to show him the place, which I did.

Afterward we both went out and considered what ought to be done. It seemed to me that I should first go and inform the presbyter Stephen, archimandrite of the monastery called Claramnium [al.: Daramium], so that through him the bishop might be informed.

When we came to his monastery, we did not find him. For he had gone, as we said, to the monasteries in the countryside, from the day on which he had given us the monastery and opened the door of the cave.

When we had gone out, it seemed best to summon to us Cyriacus, the deacon and archimandrite, and reveal to him the mystery through which Saint John had deigned to appear to us. We sent Brother Isaac, saying:

“Come to us quickly.”

When the brother came to him and told him, he immediately obeyed and came. After we had greeted him, he told us the dream he had seen, and it agreed with the vision that the deacon Gennadius had related to me.

After we had prayed, we made known to him the revelation of Saint John the Baptist, and he said:

“Let us consider what should be done.”

I said:

“I think it is fitting that we make this known to the bishop.”

Learning again that the aforesaid presbyter and archimandrite Stephen had not returned from the countryside, we remained there for five days after the revelation had been shown to us.

On Saturday afternoon, while we were sitting and conversing, Sallus [Salius], the tax collector, and Maris [al.: Marius], the linen worker [Lechtarius], came in to us, spoke with us, and immediately departed. I told Brother Isaac to close the door after them.

While we were again sitting and speaking, I was suddenly struck on the knees so violently that I bent completely over and could not rise at all or perform any task.

Then Gennadius and Cyriacus, the deacons and archimandrites, said to me:

“Did we not tell you, ‘Do not delay, but let us go and report this to the bishop,’ since the presbyter Stephen is said not yet to have arrived?”

I remained in great distress. They celebrated the evening service, came in to where I was lying, and announced:

“We have satisfied Saint John by an oath, undertaking on your behalf that the bishop will learn the whole matter from you before sunrise” [al.: “that the bishop will learn the whole matter from you tomorrow after sunrise,” and similar readings].

I replied:

“You have done very well by making this promise.”

Immediately I was relieved of my pains.

On the following Sunday, together with the deacon Cyriacus and the monk Julian, we came to the bishop as he was leaving the church after the morning prayers and reported:

“Saint John the Baptist has been revealed.”

He was astonished and said:

“No one knows this, and which of you would dare to touch it?”

The deacon Cyriacus said to him:

“When will you deign to come?”

He replied:

“Tomorrow I shall come.”

On the following day the bishop came with presbyters and deacons. When they entered the place, they fell on their faces and worshiped.

But the presbyter Malchus [al.: Malachus], one of those who had come with the bishop, moved by unbelief, said:

“From what is it certain that this is the head of the Forerunner?”

He reached out his hand to touch the jar, and immediately his hand withered and adhered to the jar; he could not pull it away.

After all had earnestly prayed, and all had glorified God and prayed on his behalf, he could scarcely at last withdraw his hand, but it remained powerless.

The bishop, together with all who were with him, took the jar containing the holy treasure deposited there and placed it temporarily in the diaconicon, that is, in the sacristy of the church, until a basilica should be built in its name.

When that had been completed and the day of its holy deposition was approaching, Saint John appeared to the man whose hand had withered and said:

“During the procession, when the deposition is made, place your hand upon the jar, and immediately it will be healed.”

When he had done this, it was restored to its former health.

The deposition of Saint John the Forerunner and Baptist took place in his church on the twenty-sixth of October, in the year 763, in the sixth indiction, while the religious, pious, and orthodox Augusti Valentinian the Younger and Marcian were reigning, rulers worthy of everlasting remembrance: to the praise and glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory with the undefiled Father and the most holy and life-giving Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Here ends the translation of Dionysius Exiguus, which is supplemented from R. P. Combefis. The following sermons have been transcribed here in the place of an appendix. — Editor.]

## In the Second Discovery of the Precious Head of the Holy and Illustrious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John

[Col. 0424C]

The thrice-blessed and universal apostle, and true friend of our Savior Jesus Christ, appeared in the middle week of the holy fasts, on the eighteenth day of the month of February, in the seven-hundred-and-sixty-third year, in the sixth indiction, while Valentinian and Marcian, the pious emperors and servants of Christ, were reigning, under the most holy bishop Uranius; and the revelation was reported on the twenty-fourth day of the same month.

It was revealed to me, the sinner Marcellus, in great fear and trembling, in the form of a fiery star, according to the visions set out below, which I hold to be trustworthy.

God, who created all things by his power and fashioned them in his wisdom, who knows all things before their creation and orders everything for the benefit of all human beings, who is blessed forever, deemed me also, his servant Marcellus, worthy to become a witness of the vision set forth.

For I saw in a night vision, and behold, all the doors of our dwelling were open. Being in great confusion, I went down to close them. Again I saw a river drawing itself toward the door of the monastery.

When I saw this, I was astonished, wondering where such a multitude of waters came from. While I was considering the matter, I heard the sound of many companies coming from the east and bringing a noise toward us. They were approaching us over the waters, and I was amazed at how they could walk toward us in the midst of the waters. Each company had its own language and sang, and I heard the voice of those who were shouting:

“Behold, Saint John the Baptist of our Savior Jesus Christ is being revealed.”

As I stood at the southern door, the eastern doors were immediately opened, and the companies entered. Leaving aside the sight of the river, I ran in and stood at the beginning of the staircase. I saw their holy service being performed in the monastery.

Standing on that same staircase, I saw two courtyards, one looking toward the west and the other toward the south, with a large church between them. Each company entered the courtyard facing west and worshiped toward the church. Then they entered the southern courtyard and immediately stopped.

After the companies had stopped, others shouted:

“Behold, Saint John.”

I saw him in the church that had been shown to me, with one man at his right and one at his left. Immediately the companies began entering one by one in succession to receive his blessing.

When the companies had been filled, I too thought to approach and receive his blessing. I planned to enter through the doors by which the companies had entered. Since I had not seen anyone give him the kiss of peace except upon his breast, I approached him from the front with fear and trembling, lowered my head to the ground, and took hold of his feet.

He touched my beard and gave me peace with his holy mouth. Immediately afterward he drew from his bosom a vessel full of honey and gave it to me, saying:

“Receive this blessing.”

I went before him, and he and those who were with him entered our monastery. Behold, I saw a pillar of fire preceding him, and, becoming terrified, I awoke.

After this, on the evening of the holy fasts, I said to the brothers:

“Let each of you repeat his psalm.”

While they were sitting and repeating the psalms, Brother Isaac raised his eyes and saw a fire burning in the small openings [sic] of the little door of the holy cave where the head of Saint John was kept.

When the brother saw it, he cried out:

“Lord, my father, behold, a fire is burning in the opening of the cave.”

I said to him:

“Do not be afraid, brother, but, having sealed yourself, remain at peace.”

Knowing the mystery, I was overcome by great astonishment.

On the following day, while I was sleeping in that same night after the hour of the night watch, behold, something like a human hand struck me three times on the right side. And behold, a voice spoke to me:

“Behold, I have been given to you. When you rise, you will find a star going before you. Wherever it stops, dig there, and you will find me.”

I went out in fear and saw a fiery star standing at the door where I had been. Becoming afraid, I signed myself.

Behold, the same star went before me, and I followed it inside until it stopped at the apse of the cave, where the holy head of the Forerunner and Baptist John was located.

Having seen all these things, I immediately worshiped the Lord, falling on my face upon the ground for many hours. Then I took incense, placed it in the censer, prayed and entreated, took a digging tool, and began to dig. I found a place built of sharply cut lime [or: slaked lime] and five-palms-long material [the Greek wording is uncertain]. As I dug, a great sound and pounding came back, as though from a jar.

After I had dug and descended level with the ground, I found something poured out like brass-colored sand. After laboring greatly, I could scarcely remove the sand. Then a single tile emerged with the sand. Beneath the tile was a marble slab. When I lifted the slab, I found the jar.

Immediately, with fear and trembling, I took a lamp and incense, worshiped again, and afterward covered the same jar.

At once the men around Gennadius, the archimandrite and deacon, came to us. Meeting me at the door of the cave, he said:

“Come; let us both enter inside.”

After we had prayed, he gave me the kiss of peace and said:

“I saw a vision there: you and I were standing in this cave, and a great quantity of loaves lay in it, clean as the sun, with a portion placed upon them. Behold, a multitude of people came down into the same cave and took from us some of the loaves mentioned above. Thus they did not run out, and the people taking them did not cease. When we were overcome by the great crowds, the loaves began to fly into our hands.”

After he had related this vision, I said:

“Your vision is good.”

Reflecting, I said:

“What does this vision signify?”

Then, considering it again, I said:

“This vision is from God.”

Knowing that it was from God, I revealed to him the manifestation of Saint John. As soon as he heard it, he remained astonished and began to ask:

“Where is the place?”

I immediately showed it to him.

After this we both went out and considered what we ought to do. I decided first to go and reveal it to the priest Stephen, archimandrite of Daromium, so that he might make it known to the bishop.

When we went to his monastery, we did not find him, because he had gone to the local monasteries. As we were returning from there, I decided to summon the deacon Cyriacus, archimandrite of those in the holy place, and reveal to him the mystery of Saint John’s manifestation.

I sent Brother Isaac, saying:

“Come to us quickly.”

When the brother had gone and spoken to him, he immediately obeyed and came. After we had greeted him, he too related to us the vision he had seen, which agreed with the vision of the deacon Gennadius.

After we had prayed, we made known to him the revelation of Saint John, and he said:

“What must be done?”

I said:

“It is fitting that we make this known to the bishop.”
