When we learned again that the aforesaid priest Stephen, the archimandrite, had not returned from the local monasteries, we remained for five days awaiting him.

On Saturday afternoon, while we were sitting and conversing, I was suddenly struck on the knees, so that I bent over completely and could neither move nor rise nor do anything else.

Those around the deacons Gennadius and Cyriacus said:

“Did we not tell you that we should go and make this known to the bishop, since the priest Stephen has not yet come?”

I remained in even greater distress. After they had completed the evening service and come to where I was lying, they announced:

“We have sworn to Saint John and undertaken that the bishop will learn the matter before sunrise.”

I said to them:

“You have arranged this well.”

Immediately I was relieved of my pains.

On the following Sunday, together with the deacon Cyriacus and the monk Julian, we entered and made the matter known to Bishop Uranius as he was leaving after the morning prayers. We said that Saint John the Baptist of Christ had been revealed.

When he heard this, he remained astonished and said that no one knew of it and that no one should touch it. The deacon Cyriacus said to him:

“When will you come?”

He replied:

“Tomorrow I shall come.”

On the following day he came with presbyters and deacons. When they reached the place, they fell down and worshiped.

But the presbyter Malchus, one of those who had accompanied the bishop, doubting, said:

“From what is it evident that this is the head of the Forerunner?”

He placed his hand upon the jar, and immediately his hand withered and adhered to the mouth of the jar; he could not pull it away.

After all had earnestly prayed, and all had glorified God and prayed that he might be released, he could scarcely at last withdraw his hand. It remained weak.

The bishop, together with all who had come with him, took the holy jar with the treasure deposited inside it and placed it in the diaconicon of the most holy church until its shrine should be built.

When they were about to make its holy deposition, the Forerunner appeared in a vision to the presbyter who had doubted and said to him:

“During the procession of my deposition, place your hand upon the jar, and immediately you will be healed.”

When he did this, he was restored to health.

The deposition of the holy Forerunner and Baptist John took place in his church on the twenty-sixth of October, in the seven-hundred-and-sixty-third year, in the sixth indiction, during the pious reign of our Christ-loving, pious, and orthodox emperors Valentinian the Younger and Marcian, worthy of everlasting remembrance.

To the glory and praise of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory together with the undefiled Father and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## Sermon on the First, Second, and Third Discoveries of the Precious Head of Saint John the Forerunner and Baptist

Translated by R. P. Combefis.

[Col. 0433A]

Again the divine Forerunner has come to us; again the time for prayer approaches, about to produce a festive gathering and celebrate here an assembly of thanksgiving in the form of a sermon.

There are many solemn festivals of the herald, all at once distinguished and illustrious. Anyone can draw from each of them an illustrious theme, so that each may contribute something worthy of mention and one person may remember one thing, another another. For even to remember and praise a single one of them according to its merit is difficult for speech—indeed, impossible.

For it is not only the Forerunner’s birth that surpasses the power and capacity of thought and speech; so too does that earlier conception and his leaping in his mother’s womb, which prophecy also followed. Moreover, there is his upbringing, unlike that of anyone else. And the coming of so great a man to the Jordan—what power of speech could fail to be surpassed and driven into difficulty by it? But what can one say about the Lord’s coming to him, with the Lord bowing his head, the touch of his hands, and the mysterious purification of baptism?

All these events separately constitute their own feast for me, together also with the glorious beheading which the greatest of men endured, when Herod cut off his head as the price of a wanton and shameless dance.

But since remembering these things does not belong to the present occasion, as they have their own appointed days and have been briefly related above, let us, if it pleases you, pass over them and turn our discourse to other matters, which we have now decided to pursue.

The purpose assigned to this discourse is plainly to explain the discovery of the precious head—that is, its appearance and bringing into public view. For we know that this was not a single discovery, but a second and a third as well.

Since, therefore, by the hidden counsel of God it was concealed three times and emerged from the bosom of the earth the same number of times, it will be worthwhile, after mentioning first the first discovery and then the second, to proceed in order from there to the third. The present discourse takes the third as its theme, although it is fitting that it should also adhere to the others and not depend individually upon any one of them, as though it made use of all of them.

Let the discourse therefore approach the matter in this way and display the subject for which it was instituted, since it plainly lacks no other names by which it might be designated. From this point the narrative must begin.

[Col. 0433D]

The remarkable John, the great herald and Forerunner of Truth, had already been beheaded by Herod. After her shameless dance, Herodias had safely placed his head in a hidden recess of the palace.

For the wicked woman feared that, if it were reunited with the remaining trunk, he might rise again to expose her crime. Yet she did not long escape the reward for what she had done. She herself met death by a most shameful fate, and afterward her daughter as well: in winter, the girl’s neck was cut off by the ice of a river, so that a punishment equal to the crime might overtake her.

Thus, as we have said, after John’s head had been cut off and deposited by the shameless woman in the hiding places of the earth, that precious jewel and most useful treasure remained for many years unseen by the common people, untouched, and inaccessible.

Perhaps the divine herald arranged this providentially so that, if it were easily possessed, it would also be easily lost and its desire easily despised. Moreover, while persecution arising from the worship of idols was growing stronger under the instigation of Diocletian and Maximian, it was hardly fitting that so noble a treasure should be exposed to a worthless human race and cast before swine, since it was more illustrious than every pearl.

For this reason, I think, the sacred head remained hidden, so that it would not be known by the common people or reveal itself. But if there is some other and more obscure reason why it was hidden and its discovery postponed, let those who contemplate greater things and devote their minds to higher matters know it.

When the time was now approaching at which it was to be revealed and brought forth from the earth’s hiding places, it was revealed and brought forth from its hiding place at the time and in the manner pleasing to him who brought it forth. The time was the period when Constantine the Great had assumed the imperial scepter. As for the manner, let us see how and through whose agency it was manifested, and how it first came to be discovered.

Two monks came from the East to Jerusalem, eager to see the Lord’s tomb and visit all the holy places there. The divine Forerunner appeared to one of them and said: “Go together to the house of King Herod and take up my head, which is buried there beneath the ground.” When that brother had reported the vision, while the other himself refused to believe it, and while both delayed going to the place where they had been commanded, John appeared to both of them a second time, repeated the same command, and sharpened their eagerness. They immediately set out, full of confidence—for the Forerunner himself, having appeared to them, was making their journey easy—dug up the place at once, and brought out the head, which shone as with a flash of light and breathed forth a fragrance of the sweetest and indescribable perfume. They placed the head in a sack of camel hair—for so, I think, it seemed fitting for the Baptist, who himself covered his body with camel hair—and departed.

As they were traveling, a certain potter encountered them, a man struggling with extreme poverty and reduced to the greatest distress. When he had met them and, as is customary, joined them as a companion on the road, he also became the companion of their burden, being ordered by them to carry the sack. Foolish and careless men, who entrusted their good and their treasure [Col. 0435D] to another. The poor man carried it, unaware of the treasure entrusted to him, for the monks had not told him. But the divine Forerunner appeared to him; and since it seemed altogether advantageous that the gift should pass to him, he both revealed what he was carrying secretly and commanded him to flee with it. He secretly fled more quickly than his companions, carrying away with him only that great treasure; and from that time it produced innumerable benefits for him. He prospered in wealth, enjoyed good fortune, and succeeded in all other things.

When he was about to leave this human life, he entrusted the gift to his sister, having safely placed it in a little chest, and warned her not to take it out before he announced that his life was ending; for it was truly a great thing and would provide great benefits. “For,” he said, “it has brought us great blessings, such as no one could easily attain even by speaking of them. You too will soon become a participant in these things, provided that you honor this pledge and venerate it. When you in turn are about to depart this life, entrust it to one of the faithful, and leave it by your will to someone dear to you and of honorable character.”

After giving these instructions to his sister, he departed from life. She, as was natural, became exceedingly joyful because of the gift, embraced it wholeheartedly, venerated it just as her brother had done, and herself received many blessings from it. When her own life was also drawing toward its end, she entrusted the treasure to those around her, giving many careful instructions and earnest requests concerning its preservation.

When many others, each succeeding another, had received the gift from it, and it had passed at different times from one person to another, it finally came to a certain monk named Eustathius. His understanding, however, was unsound in the faith, although his error had escaped the notice of the others. He too, trafficking in grace, concealed the entrusted relic and at the same time concealed the belief that he held with it—for he was an Arian.

When the people of Emesa, from which he also originated, finally recognized his character and his faith and were about to expel him from the city, he begged them to grant him a delay of even one day and then expel him. This was a stratagem full of malice and trickery. He had placed the sacred head in a certain cave, put it into a jar, laid a stone slab over its mouth, and heaped sand over it. For this reason he was seeking a delay, so that he might remove the pledge from there and, in his madness, make it his own possession.

But the people of Emesa did not allow him to remain even for a moment; they sent him away immediately, since the divine man had evidently stirred their impulse and urged them to accomplish the good deed without delay. Afterward monks took possession of the cave, men who pursued the best manner of life. They inhabited the place, yet did not know that the hidden pledge, that most abundant treasure, lay concealed within it. In this way the first discovery was completed, having taken place, as is conjectured, around the twenty-fourth of February.

Since, as they say, the pledge was again concealed, when the aforementioned Eustathius had devised his stratagem through the perversity of his mind, it is worthwhile to say how, at what time, and through whose agency the revered head was discovered for the second time, so that we may proceed from this to the third discovery, for which this discourse has been undertaken.

[Col. 0437D]

A certain Marcellus, distinguished in life and religious in character, who served as superior of the monastery situated beside the cave, saw one night during the middle of the week of fasts a dream of the following kind. He related the vision to the brothers under his authority, in approximately these words:

“I seemed to see all the doors of the monastery open, through which a certain river passed with a great roar and rush of waters.”

Struck with astonishment by this, he turned the vision over in his mind, not knowing what interpretation to form or what the apparition signified. “And indeed,” he said, “while I was in this state, a voice immediately came down from above, possessing a certain dreadful and great sound. At the same time a sweet chorus of psalm-singers was heard. Those who performed this service were divided into separate ranks. The meaning of the voice was this: ‘Behold, the great John, the Baptist of Christ, is being revealed.’ Each of the ranks that uttered this voice entered through the eastern gate.

“When I was struck with amazement at what had appeared and was leaning upon a ladder placed there, I saw two more courtyards. One extended toward the east, the other toward the south. Between them stood a most beautiful church, into which the ranks entered one by one and reverently rendered worship. Then two other men of remarkable appearance suddenly became visible to me, crying out these words: ‘Behold for yourself the great John in the church; see him and believe.’ I saw him shining with great brilliance. He looked upon the entering ranks with smiling eyes and bestowed upon each in order the gift of his blessing.

“When those blessings had been given and their procession had come to an end, I too approached to receive a blessing from him. I fell at his feet, trembling and entirely afraid. But he immediately raised me up, filled me with confidence, and kindly admitted me to the kiss of his awesome mouth. Then, drawing from his bosom a vessel full of honey, he placed it in my hands and ordered me to take it.

“As soon as I had received it, I went out from there, and seemed to lead the way. He immediately followed behind me, and together we entered the monastery. The ranks I had seen followed him, and among them I saw a kind of fiery column shining before them. At this I was seized by still greater fear and, troubled, awoke from sleep. Such was what happened to me in the dream: it was long and had a lengthy interpretation, no less dreadful than true, since both aspects were present in it.

“In the meantime, uncertain and hesitating, I ordered my subordinates each to perform twice the customary measure of prayers. One of them, named Isaac, while still chanting and lifting his eyes to God, saw before the cave a fire burning and entering within the doors of the church. He immediately showed me what he had seen. I ordered him to remain silent—for I had already perceived the meaning of the matter from the preceding vision—and freed him from fear, for he seemed to me to have been terrified. After five more days had passed, another vision came to me.

[Col. 0439D]

“For a hand appeared during the night and struck my right thigh. A voice resounded from it, crying out these words: ‘Rise; behold, I have been given to you as a gift. You will also find a star that will point out the place.’

“I immediately rose, and the star went before me on the way until, having come to the place, it stood above the spot where the cave was. Beside it there was also a shell-like structure, beneath which the sacred pledge had been buried. When I had seen so clear a sign, I fell on my knees, earnestly entreating him who had appeared to me, and began to dig the place with a mattock. When I reached a considerable depth, I encountered some sand that had been poured over the place; after it there was a tile, and then a stone slab. Beneath it I found the most precious pledge, covered by a certain jar and concealed within it.

“Rejoicing in spirit at this, I immediately covered the place again as I had found it, removing nothing and disclosing to no one what I had seen.”

[Col. 0441A]

Shortly afterward the abbot Gennadius also came to us, a man who had received from God the gift of immense grace. He too had seen a certain vision resembling the one I had seen a little earlier, and he explained it to me in every detail. Then, setting aside all hesitation, I revealed to him what had been shown to me, relating everything word for word and concealing nothing from him. Seized with joy and amazement, he begged me to show him the excavation, the place, and the spot where the sacred pledge had been deposited. I did indeed show it to him and did not deprive so great a man of the sight.

When we had separated from one another, I was again tossed about on a sea of thoughts, considering what I ought to do. Then this great opportunity appeared to me: to discuss the matter with the bishop—for at that time Uranius presided over the Church of the Emesenes—and to make him an assistant in what had been revealed, as well as to follow his counsel in the matter.

Since I did not carry this out immediately but delayed undertaking the action, being distracted by thoughts in various directions, and since I referred the matter to others, namely the deacon Cyriacus and certain others, I then came to recognize the consequences of my lack of deliberation and how much harm my delay had caused me. For late on Saturday, while I was sitting with those who were present and conversing with them, someone suddenly struck me on the knee and rendered my whole body immobile, so that I could scarcely bend toward the ground.

When those present saw this, and especially the Gennadius whom I have mentioned, they turned to prayers and vows and begged the great Forerunner to free me from the accident and restore my feet sound as before. For they knew [Col. 0441C] why I had been punished in this way: the cause was my neglect and delay in the matter.

When, immediately after the vow had been made, I recovered my feet prepared for walking, I went with those companions straight to the bishop, considering no task more urgent. I disclosed everything to him: the dream, the vision, the cave, the place, the buried jar, and finally the sacred head, the reason for all these things. The bishop immediately applied himself to the matter and gladly obeyed the command. At daybreak on Sunday he came to the place with lamps and, extending his hand reverently and in fear toward the jar, brought out the head—a sight dreadful to those who saw it and incredible to all others. For hairs appeared to be attached to it, a sweet fragrance issued from it, and an indescribable radiance shone forth.

[Col. 0441D]

The presbyter who accompanied the bishop, named Malchus, was somewhat doubtful and hesitant as to whether this was the Forerunner’s head. He thrust out his hand more boldly toward it—for the wicked customarily envy the good—and immediately reaped the fruit of his unbelief: his right hand withered and remained attached to the jar to which he had brought it. It would have remained so unless those who were present had for many hours entreated the saint to heal the man who was guilty and to reconcile himself with him who had doubted.

After the Forerunner’s head had been recovered—on February 24, the same day on which the first discovery had occurred—Bishop Uranius deposited the precious pledge in his own church. Shortly afterward he also built a church for the Baptist, and when many laborers had joined in the work, he transferred the gift there, bestowing upon the city of Emesa and upon every other city and region an abundant and inexhaustible treasure.

Thus far concerning the second discovery and manifestation, which took place when Valentinian and Marcian held the imperial scepters. It is worthwhile also to relate the recent event, the third discovery, for which this discourse has been composed and which is better known and more illustrious than the others.

When the sacred head had been deposited at Emesa, as we have said, and offered an abundant gift of grace to those who came from nearby, from afar, and from every direction, the treasure remained attached to that place for many years. Although it was confined to that location, its powers were not thereby restricted; it poured forth benefits abundantly, so that they reached everyone.

But what are the secret purposes of God, and how incomprehensible are his judgments! Although he allowed the region of Emesa and the city itself to be conquered by barbarian hands and to come under their dominion, he did not deem it right that the most precious head should remain with them or belong to them. And so it did not. Through the agency of a pious and honorable worshiper, it was taken from there and transferred elsewhere—to Comana, a small and obscure city which, enriched by that pledge, became illustrious and thereafter more renowned than the others.

The vessel that contained and enclosed the treasure within it was a certain silver urn fitted together with golden plates, so that the precious pledge might be preserved in a precious vessel. Most people, however, knew nothing of the place where it had been deposited, especially the citizens of the imperial city: partly because the transfer had been made secretly and without witnesses, and partly because the time when it had occurred was unknown. No one, as far as we have been able to learn, openly transmitted this information.

Thus the head remained at Comana, perhaps not even securely known to the inhabitants themselves. Both the passage of time and the course of events had covered the matter with deep ignorance, especially when the Iconoclasts arose. So far were they from honoring the relics of the saints that wherever they learned that such relics existed, they committed them to the flames. For that reason no one afterward saw or knew of the most sacred pledge.

When affairs returned to the Orthodox, when the scepters were again entrusted to faithful emperors, and when the impious Iconoclasts perished with a great crash, receiving the punishment they deserved, the Forerunner willed that his head should also reveal itself. He decided to give this astonishing gift not to this or that city—small towns enclosed within small boundaries—but to the greatest and most royal of all, namely Constantinople. Thus the inviolable treasure would be preserved, the city would be honored by its deposit, and the sacred gift itself would, as was fitting, borrow something of its splendor from the city, being accorded greater honors and more devoted veneration while in its possession.

At that time Michael and Theodora had assumed the scepters, and Ignatius, the successor of Methodius, a man distinguished by many virtues, governed the Church. Under these illustrious rulers the most precious pledge was brought into the imperial city and attained this third and final discovery.

[Col. 0445A]

The manner of its discovery was as follows.

One night, while a bishop who shared Theophorus’s name and character was offering praises to God, a divine vision from heaven came to him: the city of Comana possessed the most precious head, enclosed in a silver urn and deposited in a sacred place; and it was worthwhile that it should be transferred to Byzantium. This also seemed fitting to the Forerunner. The bishop declared what he had seen to the emperor. Since both were well disposed toward the undertaking, they immediately sent men to retrieve the treasure.

When these men had reached the place and learned, according to the indication given them by the bishop, where the head had been deposited, they reverently brought it out. Before the news of the matter had yet certainly reached the city, the emperor and the patriarch, together with all the nobles in the palace and all the clergy and monks, poured out beyond the city with incense and lamps to meet it. With great ceremonial they escorted the head in procession, touching to it their eyes, lips, foreheads, and above all their breasts.

Then the bishop, taking it up with trembling hands, brought the treasure into the palace church and deposited it there—on May 25. This is the day of the celebration, namely the feast of the Third Discovery or Deposition. Let it be called by both names, since one solemnity is celebrated under both names.

It was fitting that the worshiper of the Trinity, who had plainly revealed its mystery to others, should also make his own head be found three times; that he should neither fall short of nor exceed this number; and that by this means, as by others, it might be united to the First and Light-giving Trinity and honored by its number. For the number is precious and worthy, so to speak, of universal acceptance.

There are three whom we worship, distinct in persons though united in nature. Three parts are also discerned in the soul, by which the rational animal is stimulated and governed. There are three dimensions of the body, by which it is defined. Three laws were given to humanity for its ordering: the natural, the written, and the law of grace. Through three kinds of contemplation the mind raises its desire: the natural, the intelligible, and that which exceeds every power of understanding. For it has nowhere farther to extend itself, even if it should become supremely perceptive.

There are also three immersions in baptism, which represent and obscurely signify the Trinity. There are three breaths of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples by the Savior, through which they received an abundant gift of grace. There are also three changes of circumstances, called earthquakes, although one of them has not yet occurred.

Why should I say more about the number three and the Trinity? Just as the Trinity is the chief principle of our faith, so the third among numbers is preeminent, and this discovery is numbered with it and thereby receives greater honor. It is not the first, since the number one is imperfect and without quantity; nor is it the second, since the number two is mingled with matter, from which John was pure. Therefore it is the third, because the third is precious and especially beloved by him, being honored by the Trinity and numbered with it.

[Col. 0447]

Since we know you, most blessed Forerunner, to be a worshiper of the Trinity and its finest advocate—for its sake your neck was cut off—do not cease to make it gracious toward us, so that we may walk both in other ways and in the path that leads to it, avoiding through your guidance everything crooked and being directed toward straight roads. Your abundant love and affection for us are not hidden from us; nor is it hidden how each day you lavish rich grace upon us, presiding over your flock and generously rewarding those who continually attend your temple with great gifts.

May we also obtain these gifts; and when we depart from here, may we stand before the holy Trinity and be illumined by its light, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong all honor and worship, together with the unbegotten Father and the most holy Spirit, now and unto the ages of ages. Amen.

## Discourse on the first, second, and third discovery of the precious head of the Forerunner

[Col. 0434A]

Again the divine Forerunner has appeared among us; again discourse has come to celebrate and to keep festival with those assembled, giving thanks. Many are the festivals of the wondrous herald that I have, and all together are bright and renowned. Anyone who wishes may make each occasion bright by contributing whatever he can, and one person may recall one festival while another recalls another; for it is not merely difficult but impossible for a single person to remember and celebrate them all worthily. Indeed, even to mention one of them and speak of it adequately is difficult, not only for discourse but impossible.

For the Forerunner’s birth alone is not the whole matter, nor is it superior to discourse [the text has “and not superior and discourse,” *sic*], but there is also the conception preceding it, and surely the leaping in his mother’s womb, which prophecy accompanied. There are also his upbringing and rearing, unlike those of anyone else. And his arrival at the Jordan—what discourse does it not surpass and into what perplexity does it not throw us? What could you say of the Master’s appearance before him, of the bending of the divine head over him, of the touch of the hand, and of the ineffable baptism?

Each of all these events has its own festival among us, together also with the glorious beheading that the all-great one endured, when his head was cut off by Herod because of an obscene and unrestrained dance. But since the present occasion is not the time to recall these things, each of which has its own appointed celebration and which we have mentioned briefly above, let us set them aside and, if it seems good, turn our discourse to other matters and state its purpose.

[Col. 0434C]

The purpose of the discourse is certainly to address the discovery of his precious head—that is, its display and manifestation—for we know not one discovery only, but also a second and a third. Three times it had already been hidden according to an ineffable providence, and as many times brought forth from somewhere beneath the recesses of the earth. It is therefore fitting that we first mention the first, then the second, and in due order the third, which is the subject of this discourse. Yet it is also appropriate that the discourse should attach itself to both the other occasions and be separated from neither, as it makes use of both. Let it therefore proceed to its task in this manner and show the purpose for which the discourse has been composed, though it necessarily falls short of the others. Its narrative will begin from here.

At that time the wondrous John, the great herald of truth and Forerunner, had been beheaded by Herod; and Herodias, after her shameless dance, had placed his sacred head somewhere within the royal residence, in certain inaccessible recesses and hidden chambers. The lawless woman feared that it might again be joined to the remaining body and rise once more to condemn her.

Although she did not long remain without receiving the recompense for what she had done—for she herself died by a most shameful death, and afterward her daughter also, whose head was severed by the ice of a river during winter, so that she might receive a punishment proportionate to her crime—the head, as we have said, having been cut off and securely buried by the unchaste woman in the earth’s hiding places, remained for many years, that precious and most beneficial treasure unseen by the multitude, untouched and inaccessible.

Perhaps the divine herald arranged this so that, if possession of it were easy, our loss of it and our contempt for it might also be easy. Moreover, while the persecution raised by those around Diocletian and Maximian prevailed in support of idolatry, it was not fitting that the precious object should be revealed to dishonored men, lest the holy thing be given to dogs and what was brighter than every pearl be thrown before swine.

For these reasons, as I think, the sacred head remained hidden, unknown to the multitude and not revealing itself. If, however, it was concealed in some other and more secret manner and the discovery was postponed, let those who contemplate greater things and devote themselves to higher matters know the reason.

When the time had come for it to be revealed and brought out from the earth’s hiding places, then it was both revealed and brought out from its hiding place, at the time and in the manner in which the one who revealed it was pleased. The time was when Constantine the Great assumed the imperial scepters. Let us see by what means, how, and through whom it came to manifestation, and how it attained this first discovery.

Two monks, coming from the East and arriving at Jerusalem in order to see the Lord’s tomb and visit all the holy places there, received this message. The divine Forerunner appeared to one of them and said: “Go together to the dwelling of Herod the king and bring up my head, which lies there beneath the earth.”

When the man who had seen the vision reported it to his companion, while the latter remained doubtful and both delayed their arrival, John again appeared to both of them, making the same revelation and sharpening their eagerness. They immediately reached the place, filled with courage—for the one who had appeared to them was smoothing their path—dug up the spot at once, and brought up the head, shining with light and radiance and breathing forth an indescribable fragrance.

They placed it in sacks made of camel hair—an honor, I think, to the Baptist, since he too covered his body with camel hair—and returned from there. As they were traveling, a certain potter met them on the road. He lived in extreme poverty and was oppressed by destitution. Having encountered them and, as was natural, sharing their journey, he also became a bearer of the sack they were carrying, being asked by them to carry it.

Foolish and careless men, who handed over their own good to another. The poor man carried it without knowing about the treasure, for they had not told him. But the divine Forerunner appeared to him; and since he judged that it was beneficial for the gift to become his, he revealed what was hidden and commanded him to flee with it.

He secretly escaped from his fellow travelers and fled more quickly, carrying with him so great a treasure. From that time innumerable blessings flowed to him; he prospered in wealth and good fortune, and everything else went well with him.

When he was about to depart this life, he entrusted the gift to his own sister, having secured it in a small chest. He charged her not to take it out before he had announced his departure from life; for the object was truly great and would provide great benefits.

“For it has brought great blessings to us also,” he said, “blessings which it is not easy even to describe. You too will soon share in them, if you honor and care for this object. After you, entrust it to some faithful person who knows how to dispose of good things properly.”

After giving these instructions to his sister, he departed from life. She, as was natural, became exceedingly joyful because of the gift, cherished it with all her heart, honored it as her brother had, and likewise experienced many graces from it [the Greek has “many graces to her,” *sic*].

When she too approached the end of life, she entrusted the treasure to those who were with her, taking many precautions and giving many instructions concerning its safekeeping.

When many people in succession received the gift from it, and it passed at different times from one person to another, it finally came to a certain monk named Eustathius, who did not possess a sound mind, although his condition had escaped the notice of the others.

He, too, trafficking in grace, both concealed the entrusted treasure and concealed with it the doctrine he held—for he was an Arian. When the people of Emesa, from which he had originated, recognized him and were about to expel him from the city, he earnestly begged them to let him remain for one day and then drive him out, having maliciously calculated this stratagem.

For he had deposited the head near a certain cave, placed it in a jar, laid a stone slab over it, and heaped sand upon it. For this reason he sought an opportunity to remove the gift from there and, in his folly, make it his own.

But the people of Emesa did not allow him to remain even briefly; they drove him away immediately, since the divine man had clearly sharpened their impulse and urged them to perform the good deed without delay. After this, monks took possession of the cave, men pursuing an excellent life. They inhabited it but did not know what was concealed within it: a treasure rich and all-beneficial.

This, then, was the end of the first discovery, which, as may be seen, took place on the twenty-fourth of February.

[Col. 0438C]

Since, as the discourse says, the precious object was again hidden when the aforementioned Eustathius, through perversity of mind, had performed his wicked deed, it is fitting to say how, when, and through whom the all-honored head attained its second discovery, so that from this we may proceed to the third, for which this discourse has been undertaken.

A certain Marcellus, distinguished in life and beloved by God in character, who presided over the monastery beside the cave, saw one night during the middle of the week of fasts a dream of the following kind. He related what he had seen to those under his authority, setting it out word for word:

“All the doors of the monastery,” he said, “seemed to me to be open, and through them a river passed, drawn along with a great rushing sound.”

Struck by this with astonishment, he turned what he had seen over in his mind, not knowing how to interpret it or toward what the vision pointed. “And while I was in this state,” he said, “a voice immediately descended from above, possessing a loud and startling resonance. With it there was heard a sweet melody of people singing psalms. Each rank of singers was separate. The voice conveyed this message:

‘Behold, the great John, the Baptist of Christ, is being revealed.’

At the same time each of the ranks entered through the eastern doors.

“While I was beside myself with amazement at what I had seen, I leaned against one of the ladders there. I again saw two courtyards: one turned toward the east and the other toward the south. Between them stood a beautiful church. Each rank entered it in turn and reverently rendered worship.

“Then two other men, extraordinary in appearance, immediately appeared to me and cried out:

‘Behold for yourself the great John in the church; see him and believe.’

I saw him shining with great splendor. He looked upon the entering ranks with smiling eyes and blessed each in order. When those ranks had received the blessing and their part in the ceremony had ended, I too approached to receive a blessing from him.

“I fell at his feet, trembling and entirely terrified. He immediately raised me up, filled me with courage, and graciously granted me the loving kiss of that dreadful mouth. Then, bringing out from his bosom a vessel full of honey, he placed it in my hand, saying: ‘Take this.’

“As soon as I had taken it, I went out from there, going before him as though I were leading the way. He himself then immediately followed me, and we both entered the monastery. The ranks I had seen followed him; among them I also saw a fiery column shining before them.

“At this I was seized by even greater fear and, troubled, awoke from sleep.

[Note: [Col. 0440D] So in the manuscript. The reading ἐγρήγορα, ‘I awoke,’ may perhaps be preferable. —Editor.]

“Such was my dream: it was long and had a lengthy interpretation, and it was more dreadful than true, since both qualities were present in it. I, however, having fallen into anxiety because of this vision [the text reads τοῦδε; perhaps τοιοῦδε, ‘of such a one’], ordered the monks under my authority each to complete twice the customary prayer.

“One of them, named Isaac, while still chanting and lifting his eyes toward God, saw a fire burning before the cave and entering through the doors of the church. He immediately showed me what he had seen. I told him to remain quiet, since I had already anticipated the matter from the vision shortly before, and for the moment I freed him from fear; for he seemed to me to have been terrified.

“After five days had passed, another vision came to me.

[Col. 0440C]

“A hand appeared during the night and struck my right thigh. A voice echoed from it, crying out: ‘Rise; behold, I have been given to you as a gift. You will also find a star pointing out the place to you.’

“I immediately rose, and the star went before me along the road until, having reached the place, it stood above the spot where the cave was. Beside it there was a shell-like structure, and there the head had been buried.

“When I had seen this manifest sign, I bent my knees and earnestly entreated him who had appeared to me. I began to dig the place with a tool. When I reached the depth and found some sand poured over it, followed by a tile and then a stone slab, I found beneath the slab the precious treasure, covered by a certain jar and enclosed within it.

“Having become joyful because of this, I covered the place again as it had been [the text reads εἶχον, perhaps εἰκός, ‘as was likely’], removing nothing from it and not yet making the vision public.”

[Col. 0440D]

Shortly afterward the archimandrite Gennadius came to us, a man deemed worthy of great grace. He too had seen a vision resembling this one of mine, which he explained to me in every detail. Then I, without further doubt, revealed to him what I had seen, recounting each thing word for word and concealing nothing. Seized with pleasure and amazement, he earnestly asked me to show him both the excavation and the place where the sacred treasure had been deposited. I showed it to him and did not deprive so great a man of the sight.

When we had separated from each other, I was again assailed by thoughts, considering what I ought to do. Then this opportunity appeared to me: to communicate the matter to the bishop. This was Uranius, who presided over the Church of the Emesenes; I should make him an assistant in the revelation and a counselor.

Since I did not carry this out immediately but hesitated over the undertaking, turning this way and that and entrusting the matter to others, to that Cyriacus the deacon and to certain others, I then recognized the consequences of my lack of judgment and the harm that my delay had caused me.

For late on Saturday afternoon, while I was sitting with those who were present and conversing with them, someone suddenly struck me on the knees and rendered me entirely immobile, scarcely allowing me to bend toward the ground. When those present saw this, and especially that Gennadius whom I mentioned earlier, they turned to prayer and entreated the great Forerunner to release me from the misfortune and restore my feet sound as before. They knew the reason for which I had received this blow: my negligence and delay had caused it.

When, together with the prayer, I found my feet able to walk, I hurried to the bishop with those men, setting no other task before this one. I revealed to him everything I had seen: the dream, the vision, the cave, the place, the buried jar, and finally the sacred head, because of which those things had occurred.

He immediately took charge of the matter himself and gladly undertook the command. As Sunday was dawning, he arrived at the place with lamps. Extending his hand toward the jar with reverence and fear, he brought up the head. It was a dread-inspiring wonder to those who saw it and incredible to those who did not. For hairs could be seen attached to it, and an indescribable fragrance and radiance shone forth.

[Col. 0442C]

The presbyter who accompanied the bishop was named Malchus. He was somewhat doubtful and disputed whether this was truly the Forerunner’s head. He boldly laid his hands upon it—for the wicked customarily resent what is good—and immediately reaped the fruit of his unbelief: his hand withered and became attached to the jar to which he had brought it.

The hand would have remained so unless those who were present had entreated the saint for many hours to grant healing to the man who had erred and to be reconciled with him who had doubted.

When the Forerunner had taken up the head from there—it was then February 24, the day on which the first discovery had also occurred—he deposited the precious object for the time being in the church belonging to him. Shortly afterward, having built a church for the Baptist with the assistance of many people, he transferred the gift there, making it an abundant and inexhaustible wealth for the city of the Emesenes and for every other city and region.

This was the second discovery and manifestation, when Valentinian and Marcian held the imperial scepters. It is fitting that we also speak of the recent event, the third, for whose sake this discourse was composed, and which is more evident and better known than the others.

When the sacred head had been deposited in the city of the Emesenes, as we have said, and an abundant gift of grace had been set before those who came from nearby, from afar, and from every direction, the treasure remained there for many years without being moved. Although it was confined to that place, its operations were not confined; it poured forth grace without stint and extended it to all.

But the secret purposes of God and the incomprehensibility of his judgments permitted the places of Emesa and Emesa itself to be conquered by barbarian hands. The Good One did not judge it right that the all-honored head should become theirs or remain among them. Therefore it did not. It was taken from there by someone faithful and devoted to good things and transferred elsewhere. Comana received the gift: a small and obscure city, but from that time made illustrious and more conspicuous than the others.

The vessel that held and enclosed the treasure within it was a silver object fitted with golden plates, so that the precious object might be protected. Most people, especially those who inhabited the imperial city, did not know where the gift had been deposited, both because the transfer had taken place secretly and because the time when it had been moved from Emesa to Comana was unknown. No one, at least as far as we ourselves know, clearly made the matter known.

The head therefore remained at Comana, perhaps not even securely known to those who lived nearby. The times and circumstances had produced great ignorance, especially when the Iconoclasts arose. They not only failed to venerate the relics of the saints but burned them wherever they learned that they existed. Accordingly, no one saw or recognized this wholly sacred treasure.

When affairs returned to the Orthodox, when the scepters again passed under faithful emperors, and when the impious Iconoclasts perished amid the tumult, receiving the punishment they deserved, the Forerunner willed to reveal his own head. He judged that this wonderful gift should be given not to this or that city, enclosed within small limits, but to the largest and most royal of all—that is, the city of Constantine.

Thus the treasure would remain inviolate, the city would be ennobled by its deposit, and the gift itself would, as was fitting, become more honored through the city, both by being venerated more greatly and by being celebrated with greater praises.

At that time Michael and Theodora had assumed the scepters, and Ignatius, entrusted with governing the Church after Methodius, a man distinguished by many graces, was in charge. Under these renowned rulers the immensely valuable treasure was brought into the imperial city and attained this third and final discovery.

The manner of the discovery was as follows.

One night, while that archbishop, whose name and character were like those of Theophorus, was offering hymns to God, a divine vision from above came to him: the city of Comana possessed the precious head, hidden in a silver vessel and deposited in a sacred place; and it was fitting that it should be brought to Byzantium. This seemed also to the Forerunner to be the right course.

The bishop made what he had seen clear to the emperor. Since both were favorably disposed toward the matter, those who were to retrieve the treasure were immediately sent out. When they reached the place and arrived at the spot where the head lay, as the archbishop had indicated to them, they reverently took it up and brought back to the imperial city a gift worthy of God.

Before they had yet arrived, the emperor and the patriarch, together with all who were in the palace and all who were among the clergy and monks, went out before the city to meet it, carrying incense and lamps. With a great escort they prepared the head’s entrance, touching to it their eyes, lips, foreheads, and above all their hearts.

The archbishop took it up with trembling hands, brought it into the church in the palace, and deposited the treasure there. It was then the twenty-fifth day of May. This is the day of the festival, the feast of the third discovery, or deposition. Let both terms be used, since there is one celebration for both.

It was fitting that the man who honored the Trinity and explicitly revealed it to others should also reveal the discovery of his head three times, neither falling short of nor exceeding that number, so that in this respect too, as in others, it might be united to the primordial and illuminating Trinity and honored by its number.

The number is precious and worthy, so to speak, of everything. There are three whom we worship, understood as three hypostases, though united in nature. Three parts are distinguished in the soul, through which the rational animal is brought forth and directed. There are three dimensions around the body, within which it is bounded.

There are also three laws given for correction: the natural, the written, and the law of grace. Through three contemplations the mind raises its desire: the visible, the intelligible, and that which is beyond understanding. For it has nowhere else toward which to stretch, even if it should become exceedingly perceptive.

There are three immersions in baptism, which represent and symbolize the Trinity. There are three inspirations of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples by the Savior, through which they received abundant grace. There are also three changes of things, called earthquakes, although one of them has not yet occurred.

Why should I say more about the three and the Trinity? Just as the Trinity is the chief principle of our faith, so the third is preeminent among numbers; this discovery has been numbered with it and thereby becomes more venerable.

It is not the first, since the number one is incomplete and without quantity. Nor is it the second, since the second is mingled with matter, from which John himself had purified himself. Therefore it is the third, because the third is precious and especially beloved by him, being honored by the Trinity and counted together with it.

Since we know you, most blessed Forerunner, to be both a worshiper of the Trinity and its finest advocate—for its sake your head was cut off—do not cease to make it gracious toward us, so that we may walk in the path that leads to it as well as in all other good ways, turning away through you from everything crooked and being directed toward straight roads.

We know your love and affection for us, and how each day you lavish abundant grace upon us, presiding over your flock and rewarding with great gifts those who attend your temple. May we also enjoy these gifts; and when we depart from here, may we stand before the holy Trinity and be illumined by its light, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom all honor and worship are due, together with the unbegotten Father and the most holy Spirit, now and throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## Encomium of our holy father and confessor Theodore the Studite on the third discovery of the venerable head of the most holy Forerunner

*(From manuscript codex of the Royal Library, no. 273. It also exists in two other royal codices.)*

[Col. 0447A]

This present day, most devout hearers, brings us together by announcing a third remembrance of the Forerunner. For whenever a treasure is unexpectedly discovered, everyone gathers joyfully and seeks to see the desired object. What festival, then, ought more rightly to demand the delight of a day of celebration than the occasion when, by God’s benevolent will—he who orders all things for the salvation of the human race—the supremely venerable head of the Baptist has just been revealed, far more precious than all gold and precious stones?

Let us therefore exult and rejoice in it, since for people of religious mind the reception of spiritual gifts is itself a cause of exultation. Let us sing in gladness; let us praise in thanksgiving. This is one solemnity, that another; this is one encomium, that another.

The festival of the Nativity bears the appearance of a rising. It presents the spiritual luminary as emerging wondrously from the mother’s womb into the world. The festival of the Beheading signifies a setting: it represents the same divine luminary as descending beneath the earth at the completion of the course of the entire spiritual day and scattering there, among those in Hades, the first rays of Christ’s advent.

The day we celebrate now points to something more hidden, namely the resurrection unto eternal life. For the Forerunner has arisen and, as it were, been restored to life again through the revelation of his most sacred head.

What a wondrous thing! The earth did not endure to retain this treasure within itself for many more years and deprive us of it through its loss. Rather, at the proper time, like a new and ripened fruit, it brought forth its own fruit.

Heaven saw the sacred head and rejoiced; the human race looked upon it and poured itself forth in praise; the demons perceived its power and were shattered. It shone more brightly than the sun with the light of truth and more brilliantly than the moon with the radiance of piety. By the multitude of its miracles it surpasses the variety of the stars.

What streams of healings, clearer and more abundant than every spring, immediately flowed forth from it? The Spirit at once breathed grace more fragrantly and powerfully than all the lilies of the field. The whole world smelled its sweetest fragrance and rejoiced. All drank from it and seized for themselves as much as they sought and desired, in proportion to the measure by which their souls were stirred.

For grace is exceedingly abundant: as much as the will appointed by the faithful soul has capacity for, so much is received. “The head of those who surround them [namely, sinners] is the labor of their lips,” says David (Ps. 139:10); but for us this head has emerged as the release from labors, the driving away of diseases, the flight of demons, and the generous bestowal of every divine gift.

It is the head of him who leaped for joy in the barren womb at the presence of the Word of God incarnate in the Virgin’s womb. Of him the most sacred David says: “Man shall go forth, and the heart is high; and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63:8).

It is the head of him who was filled with the Holy Spirit while still in the womb, concerning whom the great Zechariah says: “And you, child, shall be called prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76).

It is the head of him who from his earliest years until his manifestation established a way of life for Israel in the desert, concerning whom the prophet Isaiah says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isa. 40:3).

It is the head of him who preached a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, concerning whom Scripture speaks: “Behold, I send my angel before you” (Mal. 3:1).

[Col. 0449B]

Why need I say more? It is the head of him who was worthy to touch the divine head, to whom the Lord said: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

But how could any mortal ever praise that most blessed head as it deserves? What earthly tongue could adequately celebrate that wholly wondrous head, radiant with the splendors of incorruption?

O divine and sacred head, vessel of the most sincere and pure thoughts! Spiritual censer of the fragrance of a sweet spirit! Most abundant storehouse of the riches of grace and wonders!

I praise your divinely woven locks, more precious than the gold of Ophir, surpassing in beauty the bridal ornaments of brides. No razor of vice—namely, the deceit of sin—rose over them, as once it rose over Samson when Delilah raged against him.

I magnificently proclaim your sacred and splendid beard, like Aaron’s (Ps. 132:2), from which the dew of healing flowed into the souls of the faithful, more precious than the dew of Hermon that descends upon the mountains of Zion.

I venerate your luminous eyes, most brilliant torches of the spirit, purer than the eyes of a dove and more precious than the most costly emeralds.

Your ears, breathed upon by God and fashioned as instruments attuned to heavenly voices, I exalt in praise. I shall apply to you, in a moral sense, the words of Scripture:

“How beautiful are your cheeks, like those of a turtledove” (Song 1:9; 4:3), as it is written in the Song: “Your cheek is like the rind of a pomegranate; your lips are like a scarlet thread; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon; and your speech is sweet and comely” (Song 7:4; 4:3).

I praise the enclosure of your teeth, shining with the whiteness of milk, from which the word of divine preaching proceeded to the ends of the earth.

Finally, I praise your neck, white as silver, which the most wicked sword pierced, and from which, in place of blood, fountains of miracles flowed forth.

What do you say, Herod? For now I must address my speech to you. Have you obtained what you sought? Have you gained possession of what you desired? Certainly not.

Behold, once again the witness of truth, that sword of the Spirit which condemns you, that most free tongue of piety: it lives and is not dead; it has been released, not bound. It cries out against you more clearly than Abel’s blood:

“It is not lawful for you to have your brother Philip’s wife” (Mark 6:18).

It exposes your crime; it would restrain you from the wicked bed and remove anger from the crime as it advanced upon you. Did you understand? Not at all. Were you chastised and did you repent? Not in the least. You did not lessen your lust; you made your whole soul into a Maenad. As the reward of a spectacle, you produced the most divine head, dripping with streams of blood, upon a platter.

Oh, what brutality! Oh, what a most shameless banquet! The same thing is happening even now: although the head of John is not being taken, the members of Christ are being made into the members of a harlot. For what else do drunkenness and feasting produce, according to the Apostle’s meaning?

Come forward, you wicked and criminal Herodias. Did you gain anything useful from your rash undertaking? Did you bury the Baptist beneath the earth? Is there, then, no one who still contradicts and opposes you?

Your hope was empty; the tale you played out was powerless; your zeal and effort were futile. The order of events has been reversed: to the extent that you thought you had hidden your crime, to that extent your crime has been proclaimed. Where you thought it could lie concealed, your deed is transmitted throughout all generations.

You and your husband perished together by a bitter death, your two bodies corrupted and stinking beneath the tomb and swarming with worms. But the head that you cut off leaps upon the earth. The hands of saints attend it; choirs of priests accompany it in procession; companies of monks entreat it; crowds of nobles glorify it and escort it with praises.

It gathers a far greater multitude of people, an assembly collected by God’s will. Indeed, in a word, it gathers the multitude of angels themselves and joins us to their fellowship of praise, since this glorious celebration is exceedingly dear to the angels and contends with them in equal name and glory.

It pours forth the perfumes of grace, surpassing nard, saffron, cinnamon, and every aromatic spice. It cries out and proclaims, without a voice, your ever-criminal undertaking, exposing it perpetually.

Such is the end of wickedness, and such infamy accompanies it. Understand this, kings of the earth, satraps and powerful men, governors and subjects, and the whole human race, so that in marriage, as in all other matters, you may pursue what is lawful and not fall into the same offense as that wicked pair, stained with equal disgrace.

But when we have crowned the golden head, as far as was permitted, with flowers of praise more precious than gold [Col. 0451D], come, I ask, let us likewise take up the other members, lest, praising the Forerunner only in part, we seem to offer a praise diminished and less than is just. What, then, is brighter and more radiant than those hands which were deemed worthy to lay hands upon Christ at his baptism? Since God is fire, understand that, through contact with the divine head, as though by union with fire, the Forerunner’s hands became fiery, without any change in their nature. His back is “in the pallor of gold,” according to what is sung (Ps. 67:14), as he bears Christ’s cross upon his shoulders. His belly is “an ivory box upon a sapphire stone” (Song 5:14), as Scripture says, since he cast out the pleasures of the belly that dwell at the navel. His loins embrace the sanctity of chastity, for he attained the gift of virginity. “The contours of his thighs are like necklaces” (Song 7:2), since he was girded with the sword of freedom from disturbance. “His legs are marble columns founded upon golden bases” (Song 5:15)—namely, upon the virtues. His feet have divine steps, for he prepares the paths of the Lord. Every member of that most sacred and undefiled body is a weapon of righteousness, an elect and sanctified vessel. Chastity raised him to manhood; continual prayer brought him to perfection.

Nor should I omit those things that are external—his garment and his belt. The patriarch Jacob made a variegated tunic for Joseph, his beloved son; but the great evangelist Matthew describes John’s garment as plain and without ornament. For he says: “His clothing was of camel’s hair, and a leather belt around his loins” (Matt. 3:4), thereby also obscurely indicating symbols that bring about the death of sin, although the variegated garment may there be interpreted in another sense as well.

What mind and tongue could be equal to mine, so as to be filled with praise of you in each of your members, O greatest adornment of humankind? But since I am cramped and destitute on both sides, may you, as most humane, forgive me, strengthen me—especially me, your least servant—together with my spiritual father and the flock entrusted to you, and preserve unharmed in Christ Jesus our Lord all who praise your divine magnificence. To him be glory and dominion, with the most holy Father and the life-giving Spirit, now and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily of our holy father and confessor Theodore the Studite on the third discovery of the honored head of the holy Forerunner

[Col. 0448A]

The present day, bringing the third announcement of the Forerunner’s memorial, calls us together, O lovers of Christ. For if, when some treasure has been found by chance, all people eagerly hasten together, seeking to see what they desire, how worthy of joyful celebration must be the most revered head of the Baptist, recently revealed through the good pleasure of God, who orders all things for the salvation of our race—more precious than all gold and costly stones.

Let us therefore rejoice and exult in him, if indeed the reception of spiritual gifts is an exultation for those who love God. Let us sing with gladness; let us hymn him with thanksgiving. This is another festival, another doxology. The feast of his birth resembles a rising, for it made known to the world the intelligible morning star rising from the mother’s womb and working wonders. The feast of his beheading resembles a setting, for it shows that the same divine luminary, after completing the course of the whole intelligible day, came to be beneath the earth and there sent the preliminary radiance of Christ’s presence to those in Hades. But the present feast hints at something more mystical: the revival of eternal life. For he has risen, and has in a way come to life again, through the manifestation of his most sacred head.

O wonder! The earth could not bear to keep this hidden treasure within itself for long and deprive us of it. At its appointed time it gives forth its fruit, like some fresh and ripened crop [Col. 0448C]. Heaven saw it and rejoiced; the human race looked upon it and acclaimed it. The demons perceived it and were shattered. It appeared brighter than the sun in the light of truth, purer than the moon in the radiance of piety, more varied than the stars in the multitude of miracles. For immediately it poured forth streams of healings, clearer and more abundant than those of every spring; at once it breathed forth the grace of the Spirit, more fragrant and more vigorous than all the lilies of the field. The whole inhabited world spiritually smelled the fragrance and rejoiced.

Everyone drew forth and plundered what he sought, what he desired, and toward which he was hastening. For grace is inexhaustible, and it is shared in proportion to the increase of the believer’s intention.

This is “the head of their circuit”—that is, of sinners—as David says: “The labor of their lips” [Col. 0448D]. But for us this head has been shown to be a deliverance from labors, a defense against sufferings, a means of driving away demons, and a source of every divine gift.

For it is the head of him who leaped in the womb of the barren woman in exultation, because of the Word of God who was made flesh in the virgin womb; concerning him the divine David says: “A man shall go forth, and a deep heart, and God shall be exalted.” It is the head of him who, while still in the womb, was filled with the Holy Spirit; concerning him the great Zechariah says: “And you, child, shall be called prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.” It is the head of him who was nourished in the wilderness from his very swaddling clothes until his manifestation to Israel; concerning him the prophet Isaiah says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” It is the head of him who proclaimed a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins; concerning him the sacred writing says: “Behold, I send my angel before your face.”

And why say more? It is the head of him who was deemed worthy to touch the divine crown, to whom the Lord says [Col. 0450B]: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” And how could any mortal praise it according to its worth—the head wholly blessed? What tongue of one born on earth could adequately hymn it, when it is altogether wondrous and flashes forth the gleams of incorruption?

But, O divine and holy head, dwelling-place of the most passionless and purest senses, spiritual censer of the fragrance of the Spirit, precious treasury of the wealth-producing wonders of grace: I praise your God-woven locks, more precious than gold from Ophir, more beautiful than the necklaces of brides. No razor of wickedness, no deceit of sin, rose upon them, as once upon Samson through the starry-haired Delilah.

I magnify your sacred beard, greater than Aaron’s, from which healing dew flowed—beyond the dew of Hermon descending upon the mountains of Zion—into the souls of believers [Col. 0450C]. I honor your luminous eyes, the transparent lamps of the Spirit, purer than the eyes of a dove and more precious than emeralds and other costly stones. I glorify your godlike ears, the listening-places of heavenly voices.

I shall fittingly apply to you the figurative words of Scripture: “How beautiful are your cheeks, like those of a turtledove,” according to the Song. “Your cheek is like the rind of a pomegranate. Your lips are like a scarlet thread; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon; and your speech is sweet and beautiful.” I hymn the barrier of your milk-white teeth, from which the word of the divine proclamation proceeded to the ends of the inhabited world. Finally, I praise your silver-like neck, through which the murderous sword was driven [Col. 0450D], and from which, in place of blood, the fountain of miracles poured forth.

What do you say, Herod? For my speech must now turn toward you. Do you have what you sought? Do you enjoy your desire? Not at all. Behold, once again you have the witness of truth: the reproving sword of the Spirit, the bold tongue of piety. He lives and has not died; he has been released and is not bound. He cries out to you more loudly than Abel’s blood: “It is not lawful for you to have the wife of Philip your brother.” He exposes your hatred, wishing to restrain you from your unlawful bed and rescue you from the anger that hangs over the impious. Have you perceived this? Not at all. Have you come to your senses? Not at all. You did not yield to pleasure. You sacrificed your whole soul to madness. In return for a game, you brought forth upon a platter the most divine head, dripping streams of blood [Col. 0452A]. Alas for such inhumanity! Shame upon the most licentious banquet! This is precisely what is being accomplished even now. And if the fornicator does not raise the head of the Baptist, at least he makes the members of Christ members of a prostitute. For what else do drunkenness and revelry accomplish—according to the apostolic meaning—if not this?

And you too, shameless Herodias, tell me: have you purchased the fruits of your bold undertakings? Have you placed the Baptist beneath the earth? Is there, then, no one who will still answer you and contradict you? Yet your hope is vain, your plot powerless, your undertaking stale. Matters have turned against you. As much as you thought to conceal, so much has your crime been proclaimed; to the extent that you thought you would remain hidden, to that extent your audacity is transmitted through generations of generations.

[Col. 0452B]

And you, too, have been caught in a bitter death together with your husband, rotting and stinking beneath the tomb, both of you swarming with a multitude of worms. But the head that you severed leaps above the earth. Holy hands escort it; choirs of priests accompany it in procession; companies of monks bear it in litanies; mixed crowds magnify it. It gathers a vast multitude of people, a festival assembled by God; indeed, so to speak, it gathers together the multitude of angels themselves and joins them to us in singing the hymn of praise, since the all-glorious celebration of their namesake, equal to them in name and glory, is especially dear to them. The perfumes of grace gush forth, surpassing nard, saffron, cinnamon, and every perfumer’s spice. It cries out and proclaims, triumphantly and without a voice, your criminal deed forever.

Such, then, are the ends of lawlessness, and such triumphs accompany it. Know this also, kings of the earth, satraps and powerful men, rulers and subjects, and everyone who lives, so that, observing the law in all things, including marriages, you may not suffer the same fate as those wicked people, being branded with equal disgrace.

But since we have crowned the golden head, as it is, with flowers of praise more precious than gold, come now, let us also take up the other parts, lest, praising the Forerunner only in part, we appear deficient in our praise. What, then, is brighter and more radiant than those hands which were deemed worthy to lay hands upon Christ at his baptism? For if the divine is fire, understand that, through contact with the divine head, as though by union with fire, the Forerunner’s palms became fiery without being changed in their own nature.

His back is “in the pallor of gold,” according to what is sung, as he bears Christ’s cross upon his shoulders [Col. 0452D]. His belly is “an ivory box upon a sapphire stone,” as the text says, casting out the pleasures of the belly that are located at the navel. His loins, embracing sanctifying chastity, have taken up the gift of virginity. The contours of his thighs are like necklaces, since he has girded himself with the sword of apatheia. His legs are marble columns founded upon golden bases, namely, the virtues. His feet are God-trodden, preparing the paths of the Lord. Every member of that most sacred and passionless body is a weapon of righteousness, an elect and sanctified vessel. Chastity brought him to manhood; unceasing prayer perfected him.

Nor should I omit the external things—his garment and his belt. The patriarch Jacob made a variegated tunic for Joseph, his beloved son; but the great evangelist Matthew describes this man’s garment as plain and unadorned. For he says: “His clothing was of camel’s hair, and he had a leather belt around his loins.” From this too he obscurely suggests the symbols that bring about the death of sin, although the variegated garment there should be understood in another way as well.

What mind and tongue could be equal to mine, so as to be filled with praise of you in each member, O greatest adornment of humankind? But since I am narrow and impoverished on both sides, may you forgive me, as one most humane, and strengthen me—especially me, your least servant—together with my spiritual father and the flock entrusted to you. Preserve unharmed all who hymn your divine majesty, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and dominion with the all-holy Father and the life-giving Spirit, now and always and unto ages of ages. [Col. 0454B] Amen.

# The Book on Easter, or the Paschal Cycle

[Col. 0453]

## History of the Cycle of Dionysius — May God Turn It to Good

## Dedication

To the illustrious president of the renowned commonwealth of Wrocław and to the other distinguished leaders of the most splendid senatorial order, most honorable, most noble, magnificent, exceptionally vigorous, most eminent lords, patrons and most kindly protectors, the most devoted client and citizen

**Benjamin Hoffman**

humbly offers this academic specimen as a public monument of piety and respect, praying with all his heart for prosperous success in all affairs and for every joyful and auspicious outcome, and commending himself and his studies to their further goodwill.

## § I

[Col. 0453C]

The lunar cycle of nineteen years, which Christians throughout so many past centuries have used to arrange their calendars, is commonly called the Dionysian cycle—not because it was first discovered by Dionysius Exiguus, but because he restored it and adapted it for the proper determination of the Paschal feasts for the year 532 after the birth of Christ and the ninety-four years immediately following. Translated from Greek into Latin, it was conveyed from the Eastern Church to the Western Church [Col. 0454C].

**Note [Col. 0453C].** Sigebert, *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 27: “Dionysius, a Roman abbot, surnamed Exiguus, renowned for his double knowledge of Greek and Latin … himself also wrote, after Cyril, a cycle of five cycles, beginning from the year 532 of the birth of Jesus Christ, which is the final year of the great cycle of 532 years, completed once from the birth of Christ.”

## § II

Its first origin is traced back to the astronomy of the ancient Greeks, who, no less than Christians later, celebrated their festival days according to cycles of this kind. For their laws and oracles alike prescribed that solemn rites should be performed **κατὰ τρία**—that is, on the same day, in the same month, and in the same season of the year [Col. 0455A].

**Note [Col. 0455B].** Geminus, that very ancient and excellent writer on the old Greek and Egyptian year, in his *Introduction to the Phenomena*, p. 32 of Petavius’s edition: “What was prescribed by laws and oracles,” he says, “was that sacrifices should be performed according to three things (**τὸ θύειν κατὰ τρία**), namely, according to the fatherland, the months, the days, and the years.” All the Greeks observed this distinction in such a way that they made their years correspond with the sun, but their days and months with the moon. They paid particular attention to this in the Olympic games, which were celebrated at the first full moon after the summer solstice—much as the Paschal term is the first full moon after the spring equinox. See Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, book IX, chapter 39, p. 92.

Now the seasons and changes of the year depend upon the sun’s motion. When the sun returns to the same point of the ecliptic, it is said to have completed a solar year. The months, however, were counted according to lunations—that is, according to the conjunctions of the moon with the sun—and twelve of these constitute one lunar year, which is approximately eleven days shorter than the solar year.

Because of this inequality between the solar and lunar years, fixed solemnities could not consistently be kept at once in the same season and in the same month without intercalation. Yet it was not possible for those who did not wish to disrupt the order of the lunar months or depart from the smallest lunar reckonings to intercalate eleven days each year. They therefore judged that only whole months, gathered from the remaining days of several years, should be intercalated, so that after a certain interval the beginnings of the solar and lunar years would again coincide [Col. 0455B].

**Note [Col. 0455C].** Geminus explains the purpose of the Greeks in devising these cycles in the following manner, in the work cited, p. 39: “The solar year has the sun’s circuit through the twelve signs, which produces 365¼ days; but the lunar year contains the period of twelve lunar months, amounting to 354 days, since neither a month nor a solar year consists of complete days. Astronomers therefore sought a period that would contain complete days, complete months, and complete years.” And on p. 34: “The period of this cycle contains complete months, complete days, and complete years.”

Although this had long been attempted without success through the dieteris, tetraeteris, octaeteris—that is, cycles of two, four, eight, and more years—Meton finally discovered the enneadecaeteris, that is, a cycle of nineteen years [Col. 0456A]. By intercalating seven lunar months, it was thought that the solar and lunar years could be reconciled with the greatest accuracy.

**Note [Col. 0455C].** The method of this Metonic enneadecaeteris, later corrected by Calippus and others, has been thoroughly explained among the ancients, after Geminus, by Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 6, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 13; among later writers, especially by Joseph Scaliger, book II of *On the Correction of Time*, under the heading “On Meton’s Great Year”; by Dionysius Petavius, book II of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapters 9 and 13; and in his *Dissertations on the Uranologion*, book I, chapters 1 and following; by Henry Dodwell, *On the Ancient Cycles of the Greeks and Romans*, dissertations 1 and 2; and by many others, who have set the matter forth at length. It is not necessary here to examine their disagreements and controversies among themselves.
