Meton, son of Pausanias, published this cycle when Apseudes was archon at Athens—that is, in Julian-period year 4281, the 321st year from the founding of the City, 433 years before the birth of Christ [Col. 0456A].

**Note [Col. 0455D].** Diodorus Siculus, book XII, p. 305: “At that time Apseudes was archon at Athens, and at Rome the consuls were Titus Menenius and Proculus Geganius Macerinus; when … at Athens Meton, son of Pausanias, renowned for his astronomical knowledge, published the enneadecaeteris so called, beginning on the thirteenth day of Scirophorion, the Attic month. For in so many years the stars return to the same configuration and complete, as it were, the revolution of a great year. For this reason some call this the year of Meton.” In this dating the reckoning by archons appears preferable to that by consuls, who held office several years earlier. Apseudes held office in the year mentioned above, Julian-period year 4281, the fourth year of the eighty-sixth Olympiad, and the 321st Varronian year from the founding of Rome. Hence the tables of the Metonic cycle begin with the following Varro­nian year, 322, in Dodwell, work cited, p. 716.

## § III

Meton’s discovery did not remain merely an idle speculation. It was transferred to civil uses and employed in determining the calendar [Col. 0456B].

**Note [Col. 0456B].** Petavius, following Scaliger, denies that the Metonic period, or cycle of nineteen years, was civil and popular, in book II of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 13. Yet Diodorus Siculus seems to assert this clearly when he writes, in the work cited, that most Greeks, down to his own time, used that enneadecaeteris without departing from the true reckoning of time. He writes: **Διὸ μέχρι τῶν καθ’ ἡμᾶς χρόνων οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν Ἑλλήνων χρώμενοι τῇ ἐννεακαιδεκαετηρίδι οὐ διαψεύδονται τῆς ἀληθείας**—“Therefore, down to our own times, most of the Greeks, using the nineteen-year cycle, do not depart from the truth.”

Geminus confirms the same point when he teaches that the nineteen-year cycle was devised so that festivals might be celebrated according to it more accurately and more suitably to laws and oracles than previously, when the octaeteris and heccaidecaeteris were used, pp. 32, 36, 37. Dodwell, in his work *On the Ancient Cycles of the Greeks and Romans*, dissertation 1, establishes the civil use of the Metonic cycle by many arguments and by the testimony of Aratus, Festus Avienus, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and others. Even Petavius himself, in the place cited, holds that at least the popular octaeterides had been corrected by suitable **προσθαφαιρέσεις**—additions and subtractions—on the basis of the aforementioned nineteen-year period, and thus does not deny all civil use of it.

As Greek power expanded, the cycle was propagated more widely. Although Athens and certain other Greek cities, after being brought under Roman power, gradually imitated Roman institutions and exchanged their lunar months for solar months of the kind contained in the Julian year [Col. 0456B], they did not all do so at once.

**Note [Col. 0456C].** How long the Metonic-Calippic form of the year and lunar months continued to be retained in the individual cities can scarcely be determined precisely, nor is it of much concern to us. At least before the Julian reform, and thus before the year 709 from the founding of the City, it is not likely that any Greek city preferred Roman months to its own. Concerning the months of the Athenians—who, having been subdued by Sulla in the year 668 from the founding of the City, were the first of all to adopt the Roman year—Dodwell observes, dissertation 2, §13, that their last contemporary mention occurs in the decree which the Athenians issued in honor of Hyrcanus, dated the eleventh of Munichion under the archon Agathocles, in Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book XIV, chapter 16. In §§14–15 he demonstrates that this magistracy falls in the very year of confusion, 708 from the founding of the City, which immediately preceded the first Julian year.

**Note [Col. 0456D].** Dodwell, dissertation 2, “On the Civil Use of the Calippic Cycle,” § 16: “Gradually thereafter, following the calendars corrected by Julius Caesar, the Roman solar year was adopted in the provinces—but so slowly that certain Greek cities retained the lunar year and even lunar months until the fourth century after Christ. From this we may infer that the free cities of the provinces were not compelled by any public Roman edict to use the Julian year.”

Moreover, those very cities that adopted new civil months continued to celebrate the solemn rites handed down from their ancestors and fixed to specific times according to the ancient custom. For this reason they established a correspondence between their old lunar months and the new solar months [Col. 0457A], which alone prevented the memory of the old Metonic-Calippic year from disappearing.

**Note [Col. 0457B].** The same Dodwell proves this at length in the place cited, § 23.

## § IV

Since Christians too, in celebrating their solemn sacred rites, especially Easter, took account alike of the solar and lunar courses, and sought to determine the days of those rites in agreement with both by means of some cycle, it was natural above all for the Eastern Christians to adapt to this use Meton’s celebrated nineteen-year cycle, introduced for a similar purpose and approved by the Greeks through so many centuries [Col. 0457B].

**Note [Col. 0457B].** The Paschal enneadecaeteris had long been ascribed to Meton as its author and was therefore called Meton’s cycle. Ambrose, letter 73 to the bishops of Aemilia, writes that the Council of Nicaea entrusted this task to the Church of Alexandria, so that it might determine the date of Easter each year; this was done by means of Meton’s nineteen-year cycle.

At first they had indeed employed other cycles, particularly the octaeteris and heccaidecaeteris.

**Note [Col. 0457B].** Joseph Scaliger, book II of *On the Correction of Time*, pp. 144 and following, lists and explains the earliest Christian cycles. Although Petavius, book II of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 62, disagrees with him on certain points, all agree concerning the octaeteris and heccaidecaeteris formerly used by Christians. Such was the well-known cycle of Hippolytus, preserved on the Verona stone and illuminated by the commentaries of so many scholars; such also was the Rheims cycle, edited by Dodwell at the end of his *Cyprianic Dissertation* from the Rheims manuscript and, if we believe him, cited by Cyprian. We shall present it below together with Joseph Valesius’s explanation and correction.

But the same consideration that formerly moved the Greeks to prefer and substitute the enneadecaeteris for the octaeteris prevailed among Christians. The Eastern Christians therefore gave it first place, and later the Western Christians did likewise.

## § V

Among the Eastern Christians, the first whose memory is preserved is Anatolius, an Alexandrian by birth and bishop of Laodicea by office [Col. 0457C]. In the third century, and therefore already before the Council of Nicaea, he applied that lunar cycle to the Paschal question and prescribed the enneadecaeteris in canons which he called Paschal, reckoned from the twenty-sixth day of Phamenoth, the Egyptian month corresponding to 22 March [Col. 0457D].

**Note [Col. 0457C].** You may read the account of this Anatolius in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 32. Valesius shows in his notes that he flourished during the reigns of Aurelian and Probus. He is commonly commended, especially by Petavius and Bucherius, as the first author of the Paschal enneadecaeteris. Bucherius writes in his commentary on Anatolius’s Canon, chapter 3, p. 463: “He was the first, so far as I believe, to attempt to adapt the lunar enneadecaeteris to the calculation of Christian Easter; no one before him having even worn it smooth.”

**Note [Col. 0457C].** These facts are taught by Anatolius’s own words, which Eusebius quotes from his Paschal canons in the place cited, p. 286: “In the first year you have the new moon of the first month, which is the beginning of the entire nineteen-year cycle (**ἀρχὴ τῆς ἐννεακαιδεκαετηρίδος**): according to the Egyptians, on the twenty-sixth day of Phamenoth; according to the Macedonians, on the twenty-second day of Dystrus; but, as the Romans would say, on the day before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.” See the discussions of this passage by Petavius in his notes on Epiphanius’s *Heresy* 51, pp. 194 and following, and in book VI of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 2, and by William Langius, *On the Years of Christ*, book I, chapter 7.

Bucherius brought to light and illustrated with a commentary the whole ancient Latin translation of Anatolius’s book, together with Victorius’s Paschal canon. The editor himself doubts whether that translation corresponds exactly to Anatolius’s work. Dupin, in *New Ecclesiastical Library*, volume I, p. 193, almost entirely rejects it as spurious; but William Cave nevertheless defends it against him in *Literary History*, part II, under the year 270, chiefly on the ground that everything cited from Anatolius by Eusebius and Bede is found in that translation.

The year of the Christian era derived from this first Easter described by Anatolius is 276.

**Note [Col. 0457D].** Aegidius Bucherius demonstrates in detail, in his commentary on Anatolius’s Canon, chapter 3, that the first Easter described by Anatolius falls not in any other year than 276 of the Christian era, the first year of the emperor Probus.

But since that cycle was burdened with many defects [Col. 0458B], it does not appear to have acquired great authority.

**Note [Col. 0458B].** Aegidius Bucherius lists and examines those defects in the preface to his commentary on Anatolius’s Paschal Canon, chapter 3. Among them are that it interrupts the sequence of leap years; moves the civil equinox from 21 March to 25 March; differs from the Alexandrian and Latin reckonings in the golden numbers and in the indication of the moon’s age; and, most seriously and least tolerably, determines that not only the fourteenth moons, or Paschal terms, but even the Easters themselves return to the same cycles after an interval of nineteen years, although it is manifest that such a revolution cannot occur before 532 years—that is, before the nineteen-year lunar cycle has been multiplied into the twenty-eight-year solar cycle.

**Note [Col. 0458C].** Bucherius, commentary on Anatolius’s Paschal Canon, chapter 3, p. 463: “I scarcely think that the cycle of Anatolius was ever brought into use, unless perhaps for a few years at Laodicea, where Anatolius was bishop, or even in neighboring places. For that it could not have endured long is sufficiently shown by the Sunday letters alone, which are placed with such great error. And the cycle of Eusebius of Caesarea, which began to be used not much later, could easily have displaced it.”

If it had any authority, it successively lost it when better cycles appeared afterward.

## § VI

Later, the Paschal nineteen-year cycle is believed to have been established by the authority of the Council of Nicaea [Col. 0458B].

**Note [Col. 0458C].** Dionysius Exiguus, at the beginning of the preface to his cycle: “We have taken care to explain the reckoning of the Paschal feast, following in all things the venerable decision—true and complete in this matter—of the three hundred and eighteen bishops who assembled at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, against the madness of Arius. They fixed the fourteenth moons of Paschal observance as stable and immovable by means of a cycle that continually returns upon itself every nineteen years … They established this rule of the aforesaid cycle not so much through worldly learning as through the illumination of the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 16: “The Council of Nicaea established the nineteen-year cycle because of the Paschal fourteenth moons, since, after nineteen years, each moon returns by an unerring course to the same day of the solar year, two hundred and thirty-five times.”

Ambrose appears to support this view when he begins his letter 83 to the bishops established throughout Aemilia—numbered 23 in the new Paris edition—with these words: “That it is no small mark of wisdom to determine the day of the Paschal celebration, both divine Scripture teaches us and the tradition of our ancestors. When they assembled at the Nicene synod, among those decrees of faith that were as true as they were admirable, they also, concerning the celebration mentioned, gathered the most skilled calculators and compiled the reckoning of nineteen years, establishing, as it were, a certain cycle from which a pattern might be generated for the remaining years. They called this cycle the enneadecaeteris, following the principle that we should not waver in vain conjecture concerning such a celebration, but, having discovered the true reckoning, should ensure that the devotion of all converge, so that everywhere on one night the sacrifice for the Lord’s resurrection may be offered.”

But if we examine the acts of the council itself, we find that a decree was indeed made that Easter should be celebrated not with the Jews but everywhere on one day, together with the Western, southern, and northern Churches, specifically with the Roman and Alexandrian Churches [Col. 0459A].

**Note [Col. 0459B].** The synodal letter of the Nicene Fathers, in Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, p. 29, and Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book X, p. 31: “We further announce to you concerning the agreement regarding the most holy Easter that this matter too, with your prayers assisting, has been successfully settled, and that all the brethren in the East who formerly celebrated Easter with the Jews will henceforth celebrate it in agreement with the Romans, with you, and with all who from the earliest antiquity have celebrated Easter with us.”

Compare the letter of Constantine the Great in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book III, chapter 19, p. 439; Socrates, work cited, pp. 33–34; and Theodoret, work cited, pp. 33–34.

History of the schism that arose at the end of the second century over the Paschal controversy teaches that this day was Sunday, sacred to the memory of Christ’s resurrection.

**Note [Col. 0459C].** Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 23, p. 190: “At that same time”—during the reign of the emperor Commodus—“a serious controversy arose … and synods and gatherings of bishops convened for that reason. Then all, with one accord, handed down by letters to all the faithful the ecclesiastical rule that the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection should never be celebrated on any day other than Sunday.”

More specifically, that Sunday was assigned to the sacred celebration which immediately follows the first full moon after the spring equinox [Col. 0459C].

**Note [Col. 0459C].** Thus three criteria of the lawful Easter were established, listed by Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 70.2, p. 823, in these words: “There are three things to which the celebration of Easter is bound: first, the course of the sun, because of Sunday (**διὰ τὴν κυριακὴν**) and the month; then likewise the course of the moon, because of the law that commands the Pascha to be sacrificed on the fourteenth moon (**ἐν τῇ τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτῃ τῆς σελήνης**). Therefore it cannot be celebrated before the equinox (**ἰσημερία**) has been completed.”

Yet we do not read in the acts that the Nicene Fathers established anything concerning the method of investigating or determining that day; still less do we possess a distinct Nicene canon concerning the time of celebrating Easter.

**Note [Col. 0459C].** Schelstraten, *Council of Antioch*, Antwerp edition, 1681, p. 158, and Joseph Saenz de Aguirre, volume I of the *Great Collection of the Councils of Spain*, part I, preliminary dissertation 8, p. 117, assert that a distinct Nicene canon concerning the celebration of Easter was enacted. They were deceived by failing to examine correctly the words of Balsamon and Zonaras. D. Thomas Ittignis refutes them systematically at the beginning of his preface to his *History of the Council of Nicaea*.

Indeed, if the Alexandrian enneadecaeteris had been prescribed by that council of 318 Fathers, they would not have needed to charge the bishop of Alexandria with investigating every year the date on which Easter was to be celebrated [Col. 0459B] and announcing it, with great labor, to the other bishops of the Christian world.

**Note [Col. 0459D].** Cyril, in the prologue, p. 481, Bucherius’s edition: “Since the Paschal rule was disturbed throughout the whole world by these and similar disagreements, it was decreed by the agreement of the holy synod of the entire world that, because a Church had been found at Alexandria so distinguished in this science that it knew on which day of the Kalends or Ides, and at what age of the moon, Easter ought to be celebrated, it should inform the Roman Church by letter every year. Thus, by apostolic authority, the universal Church throughout the whole world would know, without dispute, the determined day of Easter.” Compare the words of Ambrose cited in § 4.

Nor would so many Churches, which embraced the Nicene decrees with both hands, have employed different Paschal cycles [Col. 0460A].

**Note [Col. 0459D].** Not only did Western Christians retain Victorius’s cycle of eighty-four years long after the Council of Nicaea, but so did Eastern Christians and even the Alexandrians themselves. “Different cycles, spread throughout the whole world, held their ground unshaken, and from this there arose great confusion throughout the entire Church, in the praetorium and in the palace. Moved by this, the emperor Theodosius asked the holy Theophilus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, to explain the mystery of Easter by a clear method and to send it to him,” as Cyril of Alexandria testifies in his prologue, p. 482, Bucherius’s edition.

On this principal ground learned men have been led to believe that Dionysius Exiguus is mistaken here, and that Ambrose’s words imply only that the Council of Nicaea provided the occasion for constructing Paschal cycles, specifically the nineteen-year cycle.

**Note [Col. 0460B].** Aegidius Bucherius, commentary on Victorius’s Paschal Canon, chapter 3, p. 94, and Du Pin, *New Ecclesiastical Library*, volume II, p. 316.

## § VII

It is not unlikely that Eusebius of Caesarea’s book *On Easter*, presented to the emperor Constantine around the time of the Council of Nicaea [Col. 0460C], was attributed by some to the council itself and thus gave rise to the opinion concerning a Nicene enneadecaeteris.

**Note [Col. 0460C].** Eusebius himself speaks of this book in *The Life of Constantine the Great*, book IV, chapter 34, p. 542: “When we had dedicated to him”—the emperor—a certain book in which the hidden meaning of that feast had been explained, how he in turn repaid us with the honor of his reply may be understood from the following letter of his.” The emperor’s letter follows in chapter 35 and confirms the same point.

For everyone agrees that Eusebius’s Paschal cycle was none other than the nineteen-year cycle.

**Note [Col. 0460C].** Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 61, after mentioning Hippolytus’s **ἐκκαιδεκαετηρίς** (sixteen-year cycle), continues: “And it gave Eusebius the opportunity to compose a cycle of nineteen years concerning the same Easter, that is, an **ἐννεαδεκαετηρίς** (nineteen-year cycle).”

Likewise Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 42: “Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, was the first to compose the order of the nineteen-year cycle, in order to discover the fourteenth moons of the Paschal feast and the very day of Easter, since the moon of any age returns after that interval to the same day of the solar year.”

Gennadius, Ceolfrid in his letter to Naiton, king of the Picts, preserved in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book V, chapter 22, and Morinus, bishop of Alexandria, agree. Near the end of his disputation *On the Paschal Reckoning*, Morinus’s words in Digby manuscript 63 of the Bodleian Library are as follows: “Observe, therefore, the lunar course according to the rule of the Greeks, in the Egyptian manner, and not according to the epacts, that is, the lunar additions; for there one proceeds from moon 4 to moon 16, whereas here to 15, according to the composition of Eusebius, who first wrote the cycle of nineteen years, followed by Athanasius, Theophilus, Cyril, and Dionysius Exiguus, until Victorius wrote to Hilary, pope and bishop of the city of Rome. Then the Alexandrian and Antiochene disputants ceased to compose cycles one after another.”

## § VIII

After Eusebius, we see from Morinus [Col. 0460B] that Athanasius too is numbered among those who wrote a cycle of nineteen years. Dionysius Exiguus also appears to say the same.

**Note [Col. 0460D].** Dionysius Exiguus, letter 1 to Petronius, p. 482, Bucherius’s edition: “The blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, who also took part in the Council of Nicaea itself, at that time being deacon of the holy bishop Alexander and his assistant in all things; and afterward the venerable Theophilus and Cyril did not depart at all from the constitution of this revered synod. Rather, they are shown to have carefully retained the same nineteen-year cycle, which in Greek is called the enneadecaeteris, and not to have interrupted the Paschal course with any variations.”

But this Athanasian and Nicene enneadecaeteris itself may perhaps rest upon a similar conjecture—or, if it ever existed, it must have withdrawn suddenly from human knowledge together with the Eusebian cycle. Certainly it was unknown both to other ancient writers and to Cyril and Victorius, who in their prologues commend no author of the nineteen-year cycle earlier than Theophilus.

## § IX
Especially, however, Theophilus perfected the Alexandrian method of the nineteen-year cycle. He was Timothy’s successor in the Alexandrian episcopate from the year 385, otherwise known for the Origenist controversies. According to this method, at the emperor Theodosius’ command, he established a paschal cycle of 418 years [Note: These are Cyril’s words in the Prologue, p. 482], that is, 418 years, which contain exactly twenty-two nineteen-year cycles [Note: Hence I do not see sufficient reason why Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, book II, chapter 67, should agree with Paul of Forosemprone in thinking that Theophilus’ cycle was bounded by 487 years, contrary to Cyril’s very clear testimony, which he himself quotes from the Sirmondian manuscript, later made public through the work of Bucher, assigning 418 years to that cycle—not 428, as is perhaps read in Petavius, p. 225, through a typographical error]. He investigated the dates of the Paschal feasts.

For the rest, he did not present the emperor with the designation of all the Paschal feasts, but only of one hundred, and published it for general use [Col. 0462A], beginning from the first year of Theodosius, that is, from the common era 380 [Note: Cyril, in the passage cited: “Theophilus … calculating from his first consulship [that of the emperor Theodosius] up to one hundred, indicated in writing under what day of the calendar or Ides, and under what moon, Easter ought to be celebrated.” A fragment of Theophilus’ writing survives in Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 57, and another in Stoffler, *Roman Calendar*, proposition 34, letter A. In these we read the same thing that Cyril reported from them, expressed in these words: “We have written down this question, having examined it as far as our strength allowed, and have transmitted the day of the Paschal solemnity, calculated from the first year of your consulship through the following one hundred years.” The Prologue of Theophilus edited by Bucher agrees with this; at its end, p. 473, he says: “Having therefore arranged this matter moderately according to our ability, we also carefully set down the reckoning of each year relevant to the computation of Easter, attaching one hundred years from the first consulship of the most religious emperor Theodosius, while at the same time making known the date of the fourteenth moon and the day of the Lord’s Easter.” The same is attested by Dionysius Exiguus in the preface to his Cycle, where he says that Pope Theophilus dedicated a course of one hundred years to the elder emperor Theodosius, and by Proterius in his letter to Leo, p. 82 of Bucher’s edition, where the hundred-year course of Easter is said to have been drawn up by the most blessed Father and bishop Theophilus. I pass over Leo’s letters 64 to Marcian and 65 to the empress Eudoxia, as well as the agreement of Marianus Scotus, Sigebert, and others. Joseph Scaliger was therefore unquestionably mistaken when, in his additions to book II of *The Correction of the Times*, p. 743, he wrote that Theophilus had established an *enneēkonta-pentaetēris* (ἐννεηκονταπενταετηρίς), or great period, of five cycles. Calvisius followed him in his customary manner. For Theophilus did not establish a paschal period that would return in a recurring circuit; rather, he proposed a table intended only for the use of the next one hundred years, as Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, book II, chapter 67, and Norisius, *Dissertation 3 on the Ravenna Cycle*, chapter 1, correctly observe.]

The Paschal table of Theophilus no longer survives. Hence its character can be inferred only conjecturally from the cycles of later computists, which were modeled upon it [Note: Bucher, *Commentary on Victor’s Paschal Canon*, chapter 5, pp. 131–132: “Although that little table of Theophilus no longer survives, its character can be sufficiently inferred from the expanded cycles of Dionysius Exiguus, which were arranged almost according to its design as well as its teaching, unless perhaps it consisted of fewer lines. The first of these probably displayed the years of Diocletian; the second, the nineteen-year cycle; the third, the age and weekday of the moon at the beginning of the month Thoth; the fourth, the fourteenth moons, or Paschal limits; the fifth, the day of Easter; and the sixth, the age of the moon on that day, or something similar. For the cycle of Sunday letters, which is also called the solar cycle, does not yet seem to have been in use, as the period of our Victor appears to show; although it is much later, it displays nothing of this kind. Ambrose and Dionysius mention the first line, as I noted above; Theophilus himself mentions the fourth and fifth in his Paschal Prologue, which we print at the end of this work; and Cyril likewise mentions the fifth and sixth in his own. Thus Theophilus first fully perfected the nineteen-year cycle, which had not previously been sufficiently developed, whoever its originator may have been; then he distinguished it by a more detailed exposition of the Paschal feasts and adapted it to the understanding of ordinary people.”]

## X.

Cyril, Theophilus’ nephew and successor in the Alexandrian see, did not indeed alter Theophilus’ method of determining the days of Easter, but endeavored to bring it into the form of a more perfect cycle [Note: According to Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 35, Cyril was born of Theophilus’ brother; according to Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 7, and others, of his sister (see Dupin, *New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, p. 41). When Theophilus died in the year of Christ 412, Cyril succeeded him in the Alexandrian episcopate, as Theodoret and Socrates likewise testify in the passages cited. This escaped Joseph Scaliger, who thinks that Cyril’s period was corrected and revised by Theophilus in the reverse order, *The Correction of the Times*, book II, p. 152; Petavius notes this error under his name in the passage cited, p. 225].

For, in order to transfer to the nineteen-year cycle as well the excellence which the Latins proudly claimed for their own cycle in restoring the weekdays, he devised a cycle of ninety-five years. This contained five nineteen-year cycles and, in his judgment, restored perpetually both the restoration of the weekdays (*apokatastasis*, ἀποκατάστασις) and the lunar phases in the same order as before [Note: Read Norisius, in the passage cited. Cyril himself explains the reasoning behind his plan in the Prologue, p. 482, in these words: “Since various cycles scattered throughout the whole world have also taken firm possession of the minds of our people, this one that has recently been published”—that is, Theophilus’—“could scarcely reach more than a few. When I saw that its excessive profundity exceeded almost everyone’s understanding, I asked for the Lord’s revelation, and in this little book I have presumed to set forth what I was granted to draw from that very source; yet I learned that even those among whom I saw the cycle itself had not understood it. And lest the infinite mass of 418 years”—for Theophilus had calculated Easter for that many years—“should bring some people either weariness in learning or laziness in writing it out, I shortened the same cycle to ninety-five years, which I found to recur through those years without any difference.” Bucher thinks that *volvere* should be read *volvi* or *revolvi*.

Petavius, however, *On the Doctrine of Time*, book II, chapter 67, p. 226, judges this great cycle of Cyril, composed of five nineteen-year cycles, to be much worse than the greater cycle of Theophilus, which Cyril wished to correct, and less suitable for the restoration of the weekdays—the principal object sought in cycles, especially the larger ones [Note: The reference is to Norisius, in the passage cited].

That period of Cyril began in the year of Christ 437 and ended in the year 531 [Note: Dionysius Exiguus writes in the preface to his Cycle: “Since the holy Cyril began his first cycle with the one hundred fifty-third year of Diocletian and ended the last in the two hundred forty-seventh year, we, beginning instead with the two hundred forty-eighth year of that same tyrant rather than ruler, and so forth.” Norisius, in the passage cited, p. 145. Among the Alexandrians, Diocletian’s year 153 began on 29 August in the year of Christ 436. Therefore the first Easter marked in Cyril’s cycle fell on 16 Pharmuthi, 2 April, in lunar cycle 1 and solar cycle 26, C. Cyril himself, in the *Heortastica* 25, announced that this Easter would occur “on the approaching Sunday, the sixteenth of that same month Pharmuthi” (ἐπιφασκούσῃ κυριακῇ τῇ ἑκκαιδεκάτῃ τοῦ αὐτοῦ φαρμουθί μηνός), which the translator incorrectly rendered: “As Sunday dawns, the fifteenth of the same month of April.” It should be written: “The sixteenth of that same month Pharmuthi,” which among the Romans was 11 April. Now, when ninety-five years are subtracted from the year of Christ 437, the cycle likewise ended in the year of Christ 531, on 29 August. For the following year was bissextile, and therefore the first day of Thoth fell on 30 August, since the Egyptians placed the intercalary day after the fifth of the epagomenal days (ἐπαγόμενων). Thus Norisius. His opinion concerning the beginning of the Cyrillian cycle—reckoning it from the Dionysian year of Christ 437—and placing its end in 531 is most clearly confirmed by Cyril’s final nineteen-year cycle, prefixed to Dionysius’ Cycle in the Digby manuscript. Its final year, Diocletian’s 247, is immediately followed in the accompanying Dionysian cycle by the Christian era, which Dionysius substituted for the Diocletian era, in the year 532. Petavius is therefore mistaken about the beginning of the Cyrillian cycle when he thinks it began in the year of Christ 436, *On the Doctrine of Time*, book II, chapter 68, p. 229; and Scaliger is mistaken about its end when, in book II of *The Correction of the Times*, p. 155, subtracting the calculations less accurately, he writes: “The first year of the Cyrillian period is the year of Christ 437; therefore the ninety-fifth is 532 after Christ.”]

The order in which it was arranged is best shown by its final nineteen-year cycle, which Dionysius Exiguus prefixed to his own Cycle [Note: This has not yet, so far as I know, been published; it will be brought to light below from the Digby manuscript together with the Dionysian cycle].

## XI.

This cycle of Cyril was therefore still in force in the East and prescribed the time for celebrating Easter when Dionysius Exiguus, at the request of Petronius and others [Note: Dionysius Exiguus, near the beginning of his preface to Petronius: “The reckoning of the Paschal feast, which the persistent requests of many have long and repeatedly demanded, we have now undertaken to explain, assisted by your prayers”], in the year of the Christian era 525 [Note: That Dionysius wrote his Cycle in the year of Christ 525 is clearly proved by the Paschal Arguments published together with it, in which all examples are taken from that year as the present one. Dionysius’ letter to Petronius, prefixed to the recently completed Cycle and explaining its method at greater length, was written in the same year. For in the royal Paris manuscript cited by Petavius, as also in Colbert 1020 and Remigius 298, these words are appended to it: “For at present it is the third indiction; in the consulship of Probus the Younger, the thirteenth cycle, the nineteenth-year cycle, and the tenth lunar cycle.” See Petavius, *Appendix to the Works on the Doctrine of Time*, p. 889, and Pagi, *Criticism on Baronius’ Annals*, year 525, no. 7. Scaliger is therefore wrong, in book II of *The Correction of the Times*, p. 154, and Petavius in the chronological table at the year 526, p. 837, to say that Dionysius Exiguus composed his Cycle in the year 526, although Petavius himself seems later to have changed his opinion, in the *Appendix*, p. 890], undertook a plan to reconcile the Greek and Latin cycles, which had hitherto differed greatly and often not without immense [Col. 0464A] dissension and hostility [Note: These cycles differed from one another in various ways. To touch only upon the principal points: in every such cycle the position of the equinox, the Paschal limits—that is, the fourteenth moons—and the days of the Paschal Sundays had to be defined. In all these matters they diverged from one another. The Alexandrians assumed the equinox to be connected with 21 March and therefore recognized no fourteenth moon as Paschal if it preceded that day. The Latins, by contrast, judged a fourteenth moon falling on 18, 19, or 20 March to be Paschal and maintained that Easter could rightly be celebrated on the following Sunday. Thus, whenever these limits occurred, the Latins differed from the Alexandrians by an entire month in celebrating the Paschal feast. More specifically, years 8 and 19 of the Alexandrian Paschal cycle were embolismic, or had thirteen lunar months; in the Latin cycle these corresponded to the fifth and sixteenth years and were ordinary years, with twelve lunar months. The Latins therefore celebrated the Paschal season in March, while the Alexandrians celebrated it in April. Likewise, when the Alexandrians decided that the fifteenth moon could be regarded as the Paschal day, whereas the Latins, following both the ancients and Victor, admitted only the sixteenth moon—so that they would not be forced to commemorate the Passion before the fourteenth moon, on which the Savior suffered—whenever the fourteenth moon fell on a Saturday, the fifteenth moon was sacred to Easter for the Alexandrians; the Latins postponed it to the twenty-second moon, and thus differed from them by eight days. The extreme Paschal limits were therefore, for the ancient Latins, 20 or 21 March and 22 April; for the Alexandrians, 22 March and 25 April; and for Victor, 22 March and 24 April. Consequently the order of the holy observances was disturbed whenever such a case occurred, in which they were compelled to follow different principles and diverge from one another. Petavius supplies particular examples in book II of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 65. The distinguished former mathematician of Jena, Georg Albert Hamberger, places the difference between the Alexandrian and Latin cycles briefly before the reader in his *Dissertation on the Basis of Ecclesiastical Computation*, p. 19. After Petavius, Algidius Bucher pursued the subject more fully in his *Commentary on Victor’s Paschal Canon*, chapters 4, 5, and following. Add Norisius’ *Dissertation on the Latin Paschal Cycle*, pp. 97 and 129 of the Leipzig edition].

, or rather to introduce into the Western Church the lunar numbers and Paschal limits of the Easterners as more accurate.

Yet it was not open to him simply to transfer Cyril’s cycle to the Romans without any alteration, translating it only from Greek into Latin. For, apart from the fact that it had already nearly reached its end [Note: Cyril’s cycle ended in Diocletian’s year 247, the Christian era 531. Thus, in the year in which Dionysius undertook this task—Diocletian’s year 241, Christ’s year 525—only six years remained from the last, that is, the fifth, cycle of blessed Cyril, as Dionysius himself writes in the preface to his Cycle], it did not restore the days derived from the solar year in the same order as before when the cycle repeated itself [Note: Dionysius Exiguus himself observes in the preface to Petronius that this cycle of ninety-five years does not agree with its own recurrence, and locates the defect of the Cyrillian cycle in the fact that, when a leap day intervenes, the Sunday of Easter does not recur with its moon in the same way. This is explained as follows. Ninety-five Julian years contain 34,698 days and 18 hours. The number 34,699, however, is divisible by seven. Therefore, after ninety-five years the weekdays do not return unless the leap day is advanced and the remaining six hours are added to complete a day. Thus, in two cycles, or 190 years, there are 69,367 days and 12 hours. But this too is not divisible by seven; twelve hours are lacking. Cyril’s cycle is therefore inferior to Theophilus’ cycle, in which less remains in the reckoning of the hours. Neither cycle exhibits the restoration of the weekdays, which is found only in the cycle of 532 years. When that cycle has elapsed, the new moons return not only to the same weekdays but also continue in the same sequence. Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, book II, chapter 67. But an even greater variation occurred, which neither Scaliger nor Petavius observed, whenever, in a leap year, the Paschal fourteenth moon fell on a Sunday and transferred the feast to the following Sunday and the twenty-first moon. For then, when the cycle was renewed, Easter moved backward into the preceding week. Thus, in the leap year of Christ 448, with solar cycle 9, D, C, and lunar cycle 12, the Paschal new moon, fixed according to the Alexandrian canons to 22 March, produced the fourteenth moon on Sunday, 4 April; hence Easter was postponed to 2 April, the twenty-first moon. But ninety-five years later, that is, in the year of Christ 543, with the same lunar cycle 12, solar cycle 20, D, the Paschal fourteenth moon is marked in the Ravenna and Dionysian cycles as “the day before the Nones of April,” while Easter is marked “the Nones of April, moon 15”; consequently Easter occurred one week earlier, or six days before, than it had been celebrated in the year 448. Norisius, *Dissertation on the Ravenna Cycle*, chapter 2].

Moreover, because of the different beginnings of the Roman and Egyptian years [Col. 0465A], the lunar numbers—that is, those designating the new moons—could not be established identically in both systems [Note: The Alexandrians had adopted the Julian form of the year at Augustus’ command, but in such a way that they reckoned its beginning not from the Kalends of January but from 28 August. Consequently, from the Kalends of January to 28 August, exactly the same lunar numbers were placed in the Roman calendar as in the Alexandrian; but from 29 August through the end of December, the Roman numbers were one less than the Alexandrian. In the Roman calendar the numbers begun in January proceed in an unbroken series through the end of December; in the Alexandrian calendar, after 28 August, the sequence is interrupted because of the new beginning of the year. Petavius, book VI of *The Doctrine of Time*, chapter 5].

Dionysius therefore composed a new cycle instead, conforming as far as possible to Cyril’s, and appended to it, for its elucidation, the Egyptians’ so-called Paschal Arguments, translated into Latin [Note: Dionysius, near the end of his preface to Peter: “We have also appended the Arguments sought out by Egyptian ingenuity, by which, if they should perhaps be unknown, the Paschal headings may readily be found” [Col. 0465D]. These Arguments, interpolated by Bede and others and adapted to the reckoning of later times, will be presented in their proper place in their entirety and in the form in which Dionysius himself composed them].

## XII.

No cycle was ever more famous than that of Dionysius, nor did any obtain greater or more lasting authority throughout the Christian world. For it was the first to settle those long-standing controversies of the Romans with the Alexandrians and other Easterners concerning the time for celebrating Easter [Note: Henry Norisius is right, *On the Ravenna Cycle*, chapter 3: “After Dionysius Exiguus published his ninety-five-year Paschal Cycle, the Roman Church, at last wearied of the long disputes over the proper determination of Easter which it had waged for several centuries with the Alexandrian Church, indeed with the entire East, accepted the Dionysian Cycle, which was based upon the Egyptian canons”]. Following their example, it was received both in Italy [Note: In Italy the Milanese, together with the bishops of Emilia and Liguria, had already before Dionysius used the Alexandrian method for determining Easter, as Ambrose’s testimony shows. They therefore readily accepted Dionysius’ cycle. The Church of Ravenna, together with its associated bishops, likewise followed it from the beginning, as is revealed by its inscription on the Ravenna marble, from which H. Norisius had it engraved and illustrated with a learned commentary] and in the other western Christian kingdoms, where it governed the reckoning of the ecclesiastical year for many centuries [Note: That is, in the Roman Church until the time of Gregory XIII, by whom the Gregorian Calendar was introduced and named. See Thuanus, books LXXVI and LXXIX; Chytraeus of Saxony, books XXVI and XXVIII. Compare Petavius, book V of *The Doctrine of Time*, chapter 1 and following], and introduced the Dionysian era of Christ, which we still use to this day [Note: There is not complete agreement about who originated the Christian era that we use today. Some make it later than Dionysius and think that it was introduced only through Bede’s authority; there will be an opportunity to discuss them later. Others, by contrast, place it earlier than Dionysius. Among these is Johannes Harduinus, who maintains that the common Christian era was already in use throughout the Christian world at the beginning of the fifth century, nearly 120 years before Dionysius, as he is called, the Little, whom they imagine to have devised it. He seeks the sole foundation of this opinion in a coin of the emperor Gratian, on which is written: “GLORY OF THE NEW AGE.” See his dissertation *On the Coin of Gratian Augustus* in his works, p. 504. From this he creates a new emperor, hitherto unknown to all historians and different from the one whose reign is placed from the year 375 to 383, under whom that coin was supposedly struck in the year 501, at the beginning of a new Christian age according to the common era. But among the ancients the word “age” has so broad a range that it is sometimes used generally for “time”; even in its stricter meaning it is not always confined to an interval of one hundred years. For who does not know that the Romans did not always celebrate their secular games at the beginning of a new century of years after the founding of the City? Augustus celebrated them in the year 737 after the founding of the City, Domitian in year 841, and Severus in year 957. Thus “new age” and “glory of the new age” may be understood of the glorious auspice of a new reign, and there is no need to bind the expression to the first year of a new century. G. G. Leibniz and others demonstrate this at greater length against Harduinus in the dissertation *On the Coins of Gratian Augustus Bearing “Glory of the New Age”*. Woltereck included their dissertations on the same subject in *Select Works on Numismatics*, nos. 28 and 29. Petavius seems to have found a clearer trace of the common Christian era before Dionysius in Panodorus, an Egyptian monk, who, according to George Syncellus, connected the year of Christ’s birth with the Antiochene world-year 5493 in a chronology published at the beginning of the fifth century but lost through the injuries of time. After Petavius, Antonius Pagi demonstrated in detail, in his dissertation *On the Greek-Roman Period*, that this world epoch was artificial and had been adapted to the nineteen-year lunar cycle of that time, namely, Theophilus’ cycle. If 5493 is divided by 19, the nineteen-year cycle, the remainder is lunar cycle 2, which corresponds equally to the first year of Christ according to the common era. Indeed, since not a few people before Dionysius had been concerned to investigate the year of Christ’s birth, it is unlikely that he began an entirely new method of reckoning, wholly different from the opinions of everyone else; rather, he seems to have retained one of the opinions most widely accepted at that time. Now, if we follow Pagi in his *Criticism on Baronius’ Annals*, year 527, no. 8: “In the time of Dionysius two eras of the Incarnation were current among the Easterners: one in the Alexandrian patriarchate, the other in the Antiochene. The former derived the first year of the Incarnation from Julian year 43 and world-year 5501, and based itself on the view that Christ assumed flesh in March of Julian year 43; the Antiochenes, however, began Christ’s Incarnation on 25 March of Julian year 46 and world-year 5493, although in the course of time both the Alexandrians and the Antiochenes more commonly began their world-years and Incarnation-years from the Kalends of September. This second Eastern era of the Incarnation was more acceptable to Dionysius … Therefore Dionysius began the Christian era now used among the Latins with the Antiochenes, from Julian year 46 and 25 March, so that the second year of the Dionysian Cycle was the first year of the Christian era.” We readily admit this if it is understood as any kind of investigation or calculation of the time of the Savior’s birth. But if they are speaking of the custom of numbering and reckoning years from that time as a solemn epoch, I fear that it cannot be proved by any certain argument or indication. We are therefore not dissatisfied with the common opinion, according to which Dionysius is believed to have introduced this custom first, when in his Cycle he substituted the years of our Lord Jesus Christ for the Diocletian era familiar to the Alexandrians. Concerning this he himself writes in his preface to Petronius: “Since the holy Cyril began his first cycle with the one hundred fifty-third year of Diocletian and ended the last in the two hundred forty-seventh, we, beginning with the two hundred forty-eighth year of that same tyrant rather than ruler, did not wish to attach the memory of an impious persecutor to our cycles, but chose instead to mark the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be more familiar to us, and the cause of mankind’s restoration—that is, the Passion of our Redeemer—might shine forth more clearly.” But who would believe that, if this era of Christ had been current in the East from the beginning of the fifth century, Theophilus and Cyril would not have marked the years in their cycles and Christian calendars with it rather than with the era of Diocletian or any other?]

## XIII

Even after the time of Dionysius there were those who preferred other cycles, once they had been adopted in practice, especially the Victorian cycle, to the Dionysian, and who often celebrated Easter at a different time according to those cycles [Note: From the earliest period of Christianity, an eighty-four-year cycle had become established. In the West it was refined through the work of Victor, and in it Easter was announced thirty-two times on a week different from that of the Alexandrian cycle, as Bucher shows in his *Commentary on Victor’s Paschal Canon*, chapter 8, p. 164, and Henry Norisius in his *Dissertation 2 on the Latin Paschal Cycle*, p. 181. Compare § 11].

To this group belong the Gauls [Note: In Gaul the Victorian cycle flourished as though in its own native and domestic seat. The Fourth Council of Orléans, held in 541 under King Childebert and attended by fifty bishops from most of the provinces of Gaul, expressly decreed in canon 1: “Let holy Easter be celebrated by all priests at one time according to Victor’s table.” Each year the bishop was to announce this feast to the people in the church on the day of Epiphany. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 17, and the Rheims Chronicle in Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, vol. I, p. 358, mention an example of Easter celebrated according to this decree and Victor’s cycle in the year 577, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, whereas according to Dionysius’ cycle it fell on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, moon 21. Another example of Easter announced in the year 590, the fifteenth year of the younger King Childebert, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, moon 22—and therefore eight days later than Alexandrian or Dionysian Easter—occurs in the same Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 23. Scaliger reports in his additions to the Eusebian notes, p. 276, that in a very ancient manuscript of Eusebius he read the following annotation under the fifth year of King Childebert: “Easter was on the tenth day before the Kalends of April; the Lord’s Ascension was on the Kalends of May, according to the cycle, the number of years being reckoned back 140 from the beginning of the cycle.” Explaining these words, Norisius writes in his *Dissertation on the Ravenna Paschal Cycle*, chapter 3, p. 180: “This cycle is plainly the Victorian cycle, which, reckoned back from its beginning—as I stated above—to the year of Christ 560, produces the year 140, coinciding with the year of Christ 699, in which Easter fell on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.” Bucher also shows by examples from the years 735 and 740, and confirms by the testimony of Fredegar, at the end of chapter 10 of his commentary on Victor’s Canon, that even in the eighth century after Christ the Victorian rule for announcing Easter still prevailed among the Franks. These facts certainly seem to support Joseph Scaliger’s opinion, *The Correction of the Times*, book II, p. 150, that the Victorian cycle retained supremacy in the Gallican churches until the time of Charlemagne. Antonius Pagi does not depart far from this when he writes in his *Criticism on Baronius’ Annals*, year 760, no. 6: “The Gauls followed the Victorian cycle, and finally, under Charlemagne, if not earlier, yielded to the opinions of the Alexandrians”];

the Spaniards [Note: The Rheims Chronicle, in the passage cited: “In the year 577 the Spaniards and Franks disagreed about the celebration of Easter, the Spaniards celebrating Easter on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, but the Franks on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.” These words show that at that time the Spaniards followed neither the Dionysian nor the Victorian cycle. The same is confirmed by canon 1 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in 633: “In Spain there is usually diversity in the proclamation of the Paschal solemnity. For different observance of the tables of the Paschal feast sometimes produces error.” That diversity arose chiefly from the period when the Arian heresy prevailed in that kingdom. After King Reccared embraced the Catholic religion, the Dionysian cycle also gained strength among the Goths inhabiting Spain. The Council of Toledo seems to indicate this very cycle when it continues in the passage cited: “Therefore it was decided that three months before Epiphany the metropolitan priests should inquire of one another by letter, so that, instructed by common knowledge, they might make known to their provincial clergy the day of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ and announce that it was to be celebrated at one time.” For they interpret that common knowledge as Catholic knowledge. Isidore, certainly, metropolitan of Seville, who attended that synod, not only commended the cycles of Cyril and Dionysius in book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 17, but also continued the later one from the year 627 through 721];

the Britons [Note: The Britons here means the ancient and native inhabitants who believed that, just as the Christian religion had been transmitted to them from the time of Constantine the Great and his father Constantius—or, according to some, from the earliest times of Christianity (see Ussher, *British Antiquities*, chapter 1 and following)—so they had to hold firmly and observe with the utmost strictness the rites and institutions handed down to them by their ancestors together with that religion. Accordingly, after being driven from their homeland by the Anglo-Saxons in the fifth century and forced into a corner of Wales, they not only abhorred the pagan superstitions of the Anglo-Saxons but later also disagreed with them concerning the Christian, or rather Roman, ceremonies that Augustine, commonly called the apostle of the English, had brought into England at the end of the sixth century after being sent by Pope Gregory. One of the principal points of disagreement between the ancient Britons and the English, the new Christians, concerned the date of Easter: the latter determined it according to Roman practice and the cycle of Dionysius, while the former followed the ancient Latin custom and the eighty-four-year cycle. Bede speaks of this in his *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 2: “For they did not observe the Sunday of Easter at its proper time, but from the fourteenth to the twentieth moon; this reckoning is contained in an eighty-four-year cycle.” Bucher and Norisius explain the structure of this cycle in the passages cited. It is well known that the Council of Whitby—named after the monastery of Whitby, situated in the region of York and later destroyed by the Danes (see Pagi, *Criticism on Baronius’ Annals*, year 664, no. 3)—was held between the priests of both parties in the presence of Alchfrith, son of the king of the English. There Wilfrid, abbot and later bishop of York, defended the English position concerning the time for celebrating Easter with such success that the Britons and Scots left defeated by Alchfrith’s judgment and lost their case. For this achievement Walafridus obtained the following praise in his epitaph:

> He who also corrected the Paschal seasons of the cycle  
> of the Catholic Church according to the true rule of the canon,  
> which the Fathers established, once doubtful error had been removed,
It thus demonstrates to its own people the proper observance of the rite. Accordingly, in England the Scottish practice was suppressed—or, as Bede puts it, *detected and eliminated* (Hist. eccl. V.20)—but in Ireland, the homeland of the Scots, and in Wales, the land of the Britons, it by no means ceased. Although later Bishop Elbodus introduced the Dionysian cycle into Venedotia, or North Wales, as Jacob Usserius demonstrates from Humphrey Lhuyd’s *Fragmenta Britannica*, fol. 55, and the *Chronicon Cambriae*, p. 17, in his chronological index appended to the *British Antiquities*, p. 1172, the southern Welsh retained the ancient practice much more tenaciously. Bede is to be understood as referring to them when he writes (V.23) that even after the Iona Scots had been brought over to the judgment of the English Church in 728, the Britons still remained old-fashioned and lame in their ways, venerating Christ’s solemnities without communion with Christ’s Church. *[End of an inherited note.]*

The Scots [Note: Bede and other medieval writers place the Scots in Ireland, as in their proper homeland. In his *Ecclesiastical History* II.4, Bede says that Laurence, successor to Augustine, the first bishop of the English, cared not only for the new Church gathered from the English, but also extended pastoral concern to the ancient inhabitants of Britain and to the peoples of the Scots who inhabit Ireland, the island nearest Britain. Laurence likewise addressed a letter to the inhabitants of Ireland as follows: “To the brother bishops or abbots throughout all Scotland.” Isidore of Seville clearly shows what Scotland this was in *Origins* XIV.6, in these words: “Scotland, which is also Ireland, the island nearest Britain, is called Scotland because it is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots”; and Orosius says in I.2: “Ireland is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots.” Usserius, *British Antiquities*, ch. 16, p. 731, shows that this was the island’s proper name until the tenth century, when the new name Ireland became current. Compare William Temple’s discussion, following George Buchanan and others, of the ancient origin, territories, and distinction of the Scots in the *Introduction to the History of England*, p. 22ff. These Scots, therefore, no less than the ancient Britons, rejected the Roman rules introduced into England for celebrating Easter. In this sense Laurence says that they differed in nothing from the Britons, in the passage just cited, and throughout this controversy they are usually mentioned as allies of the Britons. Although in the course of time the Scottish peoples dwelling in the southern parts of Ireland learned, at the admonition of the bishop of the Apostolic See, to observe Easter according to the canonical rite—as Bede puts it in III.3—the northern province of the Scots and the entire nation of the Picts, during the reign of Oswald, king of Northumbria, who was killed in 642, continued to celebrate the Lord’s Easter according to the ancient custom. This practice lasted among them until the eighth century began. At that time Adamnan, abbot of Iona, sailed to Ireland, preached, and explained by a modest exhortation the legitimate time of Easter. He brought many of them, and almost all who were free from the jurisdiction of the Ionians, back to Catholic unity and thoroughly instructed them to observe the legitimate time of Easter (Bede V.16). Adamnan could not persuade his own Iona monks—that is, the Scots in the island of Iona—to accept the Roman Easter. Iona, separated from Britain by a narrow strait, had been handed over to the Scots by the Picts because, through the preaching of the Scots, the Picts had received the faith of Christ (Bede III.3). See Bede V.16. At length, however, after Adamnan’s death, they too yielded to the custom that was gaining ground. For in the year 716 from the Lord’s incarnation, when, after Osred had been killed, Coenred assumed the government of the Northumbrian kingdom, there came to them from Ireland the God-beloved and most honorably named father and priest Ecgbert. Moved by his pious and earnest exhortations, they abandoned that long-established tradition of their ancestors and instituted the celebration of the principal solemnity according to the Catholic and apostolic—Roman—custom, as Bede testifies in V.25. He adds, after some intervening material: “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 728, when the Lord’s Easter was celebrated on 24 April, Ecgbert, after celebrating the solemnities of the Mass, departed to the Lord on that same day . . . . It was a remarkable dispensation of divine providence that the venerable man not only passed from this world at Easter, but also celebrated Easter on that day, whereas it had never previously been customary to celebrate it in those regions.” This conversion occurred in the time of Dunchad, the tenth abbot of Iona; Usserius gives their succession from the *Ulster Annals*, *British Antiquities* XVI, p. 701ff.]

—and the Picts [Note: The Picts, inhabitants of the northern part of Britain, received from the Scots in the sixth century both the Christian religion and the time for celebrating Easter, and did not accept the Dionysian cycle before the eighth century. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* III.4, says: “At the time of the greatest solemnity they followed uncertain cycles, since, placed so far beyond the world, no one had brought them the synodal decrees concerning the observance of Easter . . . . This kind of Easter observance continued among them for a considerable time, that is, until the year 716 of the Lord’s incarnation, for 150 years. But then, when the most reverend and holy father and priest Ecgbert came to them, an Englishman who had long been an exile in Ireland for Christ’s sake and was most learned in the Scriptures . . . . they were corrected by him and transferred to the true and canonical day of Easter.” The Picts owed their knowledge of Easter and the laws for celebrating it properly according to the Dionysian cycle chiefly to Ceolfrid, abbot of Wearmouth, whose letter to them is worthy of reading in Bede V.22. When Naitan, king of the Picts, received it, he immediately ordered the nineteen-year Easter cycles to be copied, learned, and observed throughout all the provinces of the Picts, while the erroneous eighty-four-year cycles were everywhere erased.]—indeed, in Italy itself [Note: That the Dionysian cycle of the Roman Church was not immediately accepted throughout Italy, nor the Victorian cycle abolished, is shown by Victor, bishop of Capua, in a fragment of his book on Easter preserved in Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time* 49. He writes: “When we were carefully investigating on which day the venerable solemnity of Easter most properly occurred, in the thirteenth indiction of the present year—that is, in A.D. 550, as Scaliger correctly observes, *On the Correction of Time* II, p. 154—we said that, according to the venerable decrees of the Fathers, the Lord’s Resurrection was without doubt to be celebrated on 24 April. Some people, however, considered our answer wholly unreasonable, because a certain Victor, in the Easter cycle he published, had assigned the day of the Lord’s Resurrection differently, although he had also designated the day which we likewise profess should be celebrated.”]

—not everyone immediately followed the institution of the Roman Church. Nevertheless, these peoples gradually and little by little conformed themselves to that practice, so that after the time of Charlemagne, except perhaps for the Britons in Wales, scarcely any trace of disagreement remained [Note: Already in 664, at the Council of Pharres, Wilfrid opposed the universal—at least transmarine—agreement to celebrate Easter according to the Alexandrian or Dionysian cycles, using these words against the Scots, who clung to the ancient custom: “The Easter that we celebrate we saw celebrated by all at Rome, where the blessed apostles Peter and Paul lived, taught, suffered, and were buried. We saw it celebrated by all in Italy and in Gaul, through which we traveled for the sake of learning and prayer. We discovered that throughout Africa, Asia, Egypt, Greece, and the entire world, wherever Christ’s Church is spread, among diverse nations and languages, it is observed according to one and not a different reckoning of time—except only by these people and those who share their obstinacy, namely the Picts and Britons, who, with them, fight in their foolish labor against the whole world over two remote islands of the Ocean, and not even all of those.” In the eighth century Bede celebrated that agreement with still greater authority in *On the Reckoning of Time* 14. After reviewing the various rules of Anatolius and Victor, he continues: “Moreover, the Egyptians, whose opinion the Catholic Church now follows, etc.” Similar words occur in the Digby manuscript, written in the ninth century and, as we shall show elsewhere, copied from a much older source. Under the title “A writing of the chief notary to Pope John concerning the Easter reckoning,” the following is read after other material: “For they never celebrate holy Easter except according to the apostolic and Catholic faith, as it is celebrated throughout the world by the Christian people—that is, according to the apostolic rule of the 318 holy Fathers and the computation of St. Cyril and Dionysius. For throughout the whole world the one dove of Christ, that is, the immaculate Church, celebrates the holy day of the Resurrection at Easter. For the Apostolic See of Pope Victor did not approve the rule of Easter, and therefore does not follow its arrangement for Easter.”].

## § XIV

Where the Dionysian cycle had been accepted, not only were tables copied that indicated the time at which Easter was to be celebrated each year according to that cycle, but knowledge of the Easter reckoning was likewise disseminated through written instruction and oral teaching [Note: Thus, when under King Naitan the Picts decided in the eighth century to celebrate Easter at the same time as the English, nineteen-year Easter cycles were immediately sent throughout all the Pictish provinces to be copied, learned, and observed (Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* V.22).] And just as in the Middle Ages almost every liberal discipline was located among religious or ecclesiastical men, so this discipline too was entrusted to their care [Note: There survive many decrees not only of councils but also of Christian kings and emperors commending the study of Easter computation to members of the sacred order. For example, among Charlemagne’s capitula issued to priests at Salz in 804 occurs the injunction that they should know chant and computation. Chapter 5 of the capitulary issued in 805 commands that all learn computation correctly. Chapter 22 of the capitula of Walter of Orléans requires all priests to possess skill in calculation and diligently instruct their own people in it. Hincmar, cap. 8: “Let him also be fully instructed throughout the yearly cycle in the necessary computation and in chant.” I omit other such items found everywhere. To attain that end more effectively, when Charlemagne left Rome in 787, he took with him not only Roman singers and highly expert grammarians but also computists—that is, men skilled in the Dionysian cycle—as Ademar relates in the *Life of Charlemagne*, ch. 8. Indeed, according to Einhard, Charlemagne himself learned the art of computation. See Stephen Baluze’s notes on the capitularies, col. 1135.] and was especially at home in monasteries. An outstanding example of this is provided by the monastery of St. Remigius, formerly entrusted to the care and protection of the archbishop of Rheims, primate of all Gaul [Note: From Tilpinus through Hugh of Vermandois, the archbishops of Rheims used the title of abbots of St. Remigius and, under that title, presided over the monks of this monastery, although they entrusted most of its administration to the provosts or priors—known as the claustral priors—whom they appointed. Mabillon demonstrates this in *Benedictine Annals* II.26, p. 356.], which flourished in the other literary studies [Note: John Launoy describes the schools of Rheims, once more illustrious than those of Paris, in his *On the More Celebrated Schools*, ch. 21. With regard specifically to the monastery of St. Remigius, apart from the many learned men—Ebbos, Anshelms, and Roberts—whom it produced, this is demonstrated by the library of St. Remigius, perhaps the oldest of all the libraries in Gaul that still exist. I remember seeing its catalogue, written in the time of Hincmar of Rheims. As a rare treasure, it had somehow come into the Thuan Library and was restored to the monastery of St. Remigius through the care of Charles-Maurice Le Tellier, archbishop of Rheims. Among its books, besides others illustrating Charlemagne’s edict cited under letter c, occur: “C. I. Guido’s Music. XXXII. Tables of Computation. D. XI. Holy Canons. XXIV. Book of Canons and Decrees of the Popes. LXIV. Salic Law and the laws of the Ripuarian Franks, Frisians, and Alemanni. E. XII. Book of Computation. XXII. Book of Computation. XXVIII. Collected Canons.” Although some books listed there have been lost and scattered through the injury of time, quite a number remain, bearing Hincmar’s own signature and other evidence of venerable antiquity.] and above all taught the principles of ecclesiastical computation with the greatest diligence [Note: Nothing demonstrates this more clearly than an inscription excavated at Rheims a few years ago, which, so far as I know, had not yet been published. Henri Eget, a most learned and humane man, dean and treasurer of the abbey of St. Remigius, shared it with me, together with a French translation and part of an exposition.

**Ancient inscription found in the foundations of the new monastery of the Abbey of St. Remigius at Rheims, 1 April**

> A. 8 ICCCXIII.
>
> HUIC CLAUSTRO POLLENT STUDIO COMPOTIS APTA
>
> SICFARII FULTI SOLAMINE PRAEPOSITURAM
>
> INGENIO DECORANS PRIMAM QUAM CLAVIS EOE
>
> PARTE DOMUM CLARO STATUIT FUNDAMINA CONDENS
>
> IN MELIUS RELIQUAS ETIAM SI NOSCERE QUAERAS
>
> COMPTA SALUTIFERI QUIBUS INSUNT DINDIMA JUSSIS.

**Supplied French translation, rendered in English:** “The study of Computus, for which Sicfarius provided solid rules, flourishes in the schools of this monastery. He honored the dignity of prior by his intelligence; and, by having the magnificent apartment visible on the eastern side built, he also restored the library, in which, by his salutary commands, are found the authors who wrote best on our sacred mysteries, for the benefit of those who wish to acquire an understanding of them.”

This inscription was carved in large Roman letters on a stone six feet long, two and a half feet wide, and five fingers thick. It was found about three feet below ground in the foundations of the monastery of St. Remigius. It served as a kind of lid for a stone coffin, ornamented with certain figures and containing the bones of a deceased person with remnants of clothing. It was found upside down, with its inscribed surface facing downward; and, lest anyone suppose that it was an epitaph, the writing had been blunted with a hammer and was almost obliterated. The inscription therefore undoubtedly once stood over the door or façade of the buildings in which the monastery’s schools were maintained under Charlemagne’s institution in the Aachen capitulary of 789, ch. 70.

Sicfarius, named in it, was provost or claustral prior of St. Remigius a little before the middle of the ninth century, about the time when Ebbo was expelled from the archbishopric of Rheims. His immediate predecessor was Raduinus; his successor Rodefridus, who held this office under Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims. Most of the manuscripts listed in the catalogue of the library of St. Remigius mentioned above, col. 472, note e, seem to have been copied in Sicfarius’s time. Of these, a book of computation still survives in the library of St. Remigius, containing a most ancient copy of the Dionysian cycle and of related materials to be discussed below; it assisted us in publishing this very cycle.]

In this respect it surpassed the other churches of that kingdom [Note: Almost every church, even the smaller ones, had its own book of computation, modeled on the computation of the cathedral church. Thus the library of St. Remigius possesses a ninth-century book, written in Hincmar’s time, concerning the revenues of the church of Rheims. In its inventory of the books of a church dedicated to St. Medard in the village of Peina, it lists a book of computation in these words:

“In the aforesaid village there is a church consecrated in honor of St. Medard, and there are there altar coverings . . . one volume of Gregory’s Missal, one manual, one lectionary from various sources, one collectary from Easter to Advent; one Psalter, one book of Computation, one antiphonary; one volume of an exposition in the baptistery; one volume of Jerome on Matthew.”

Shortly afterward, concerning the village of St. Remigius (*vicus S. Remigii*) the following is read:

“In the aforesaid village there is a church dedicated in honor of St. Remigius, containing: altar coverings . . . the Letters of Paul, the seven Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse with an exposition; one volume of the canonical penitential; one Psalter; two quires on Computation; seven quires of canons; one old volume of the Missal of Gelasius; one old volume of lectionaries.”

Several other manuscripts on the computation of Easter and the Dionysian cycle are found in the Colbert Library. They were gathered here and there from French monasteries under the auspices of Jean-Baptiste Colbert, royal minister, through the care and scholarship of Étienne Baluze, a man of eminent distinction. Through this very indication and his kind recommendation, I was fortunate enough to be given the opportunity to examine them.]

and in it [the monastery of St. Remigius] shed particular light upon the subject.

## § XV

Just as Dionysius Exiguus did not insert the entire cycle of Cyril into his book on Easter, but rather constructed a new cycle on its model, so those who later took up this work did not so much copy Dionysius’s cycle as continue it and adapt it to later times [Note: Hence in manuscripts copied from Dionysius’s book one finds, in place of the Dionysian cycle, words such as these: “This cycle of Dionysius consists of five nineteen-year cycles, that is, of ninety-five years; it begins in the year 532 from the Lord’s incarnation and ends in the year 626. We have therefore omitted this cycle, since it has wholly elapsed.” These words occur in the Rheims manuscript 298, according to the old catalogue, D.IX, and in Colbert manuscript 1020, which we shall describe more fully below. Petavius likewise testifies that he found them in the royal manuscript in Paris, in his notes to the appendix *On the Doctrine of Time*, p. 890.]

Of their great number [Note: How many people undertook this task at various times is listed by Ceolfrid, abbot, in a letter written around 710 to Naitan, king of the Picts, which Bede reproduces in V.22. He writes: “His successor, Cyril, comprised a sequence of ninety-five years in nineteen-year cycles. After him Dionysius Exiguus added an equal number of other years in the same orderly pattern, extending to our own times. As their end now approaches, there is today such an abundance of computists that even in our churches throughout Britain there are many who, having committed to memory the ancient Egyptian methods, can very easily extend the Easter cycles over any desired span of time, even if they wish to extend them as far as 532 years. Once these have been completed, everything relating to the succession of the sun and moon, the month and the week, recurs in the same order as before. For this reason we have refrained from sending you the cycles for the times immediately ahead, because, since you sought instruction only in the reckoning of the Easter season, you have proved that the Catholic Easter cycles themselves are sufficient for you.”]

the best known are St. Isidore of Seville and the venerable Bede. Isidore extended the Dionysian cycle to A.D. 731 [Note: Isidore describes the nineteen-year cycle immediately following the completion of the Dionysian cycle, extending to the year 721, in *Origins* VI.17.], while Bede extended it to the year 1063, thereby completing the great period of 532 years, which, revolving back upon itself, restores the same Easter Sundays [Note: That the great Easter period of 532 years was known in England in Bede’s time is clearly shown by Ceolfrid’s letter written in 710, whose words we quoted shortly before. Bede himself testifies in *On the Reckoning of Time* 63 that he extended the Easter cycles—as I may put it in Ceolfrid’s words—to 532 years and thus continued Dionysius’s tables to the year 1063. After saying that, once 532 years had passed, everything relating to the course of the sun and moon would be restored in the same sequence as before, he adds:

“Now, so that this may become clearer, I have decided to place before the present work the same cycle in complete order, beginning with the year 532 of the Lord’s incarnation, where Dionysius first began the cycle, and carrying the work through to the year 1063 of that same holy incarnation. Thus all who read it may be able not only to look ahead to the present and the future, but also to review the entire past state of the Easter season with an unfailing gaze, and, for clarification of the ancient reading, may more clearly recognize all the years that at some time had come into question, when they occurred and what their character was.”

*Works of Bede* II, p. 169.

Scaliger either failed to notice or misunderstood these words when he supposed in *On the Correction of Time* II, p. 155, that the Easter period had been carried by Dionysius himself to the year 1063 and by Bede to the year 1595. Petavius likewise did not avoid this error when he wrote in *On the Doctrine of Time* XII.3, p. 404: “But Bede added several other cycles up to the year of Christ 1595.” Both men were perhaps misled, like many others, by the tables of John of Noyon inserted into Bede’s works. They are therefore commonly regarded as Bede’s, but wrongly, as will soon be demonstrated.]

Although the so-called Bedan cycles found in his works are not those written by Bede himself, but those restored by John of Noyon according to his understanding of Bede [Note: These cycles occur in vol. I of Bede’s works, p. 303 of the Basel edition, with the following preface by John of Noyon:

“Bede wrote eighty-four nineteen-year cycles—or, if you prefer, and it amounts to the same thing, twenty-eight sets of three—from the birth of Christ to 1595. Some of them have been corrupted through the ravages of time and the incompetence of copyists, while others have perished altogether. We have restored some elsewhere and corrected others, as far as we could, so that they might be complete through 1595. A later age, when the limit of these years has been reached, will add more.”

They are repeated in part in the same volume, p. 359.]

Thus the older cycles, displaced and obscured by the newer ones that were currently used for calculating Easter, gradually perished and withdrew themselves even from the knowledge of learned men. Consequently, people came to think that the true form of the complete Dionysian cycle had to be investigated and restored only through conjectures—and conjectures that were by no means especially fortunate [Note: Henri Noris, who devoted more study and effort than almost anyone else to illuminating this subject, counted the Dionysian cycle among things entirely lost in his dissertation *On the Ravenna Cycle* V, p. 216.
