Binius shows that he was ignorant of its form when, in his notes to the Life of Felix V (*Labbe’s Councils* IV, col. 1650), he wrote that a fragment of it was found in Marianus Scotus’s *Chronicle* under the year 527. In Marianus, however, under the year 526—the year is cited incorrectly as 527—there is not a fragment of the cycle but a letter by Dionysius to Boniface concerning the reckoning of Easter. Petavius published it in the appendix to his work *On the Doctrine of Time*, as did Aegidius Bucherius in his *Commentary on the Doctrine of Time*, p. 489; we shall provide it below in its proper place, restored and improved from several manuscript copies. Labbe therefore correctly wrote in the margin beside Binius’s words: “Binius is mistaken.”

Nevertheless, William Cave, apparently having only Binius’s edition of the Councils before him, repeated the error in his *Literary History* under the year 533. In nearly the same words he listed among Dionysius’s writings an Easter cycle of ninety-seven years beginning in 527, whose fragment was supposedly found in Marianus Scotus’s *Chronicle* under 527. Yet Dionysius’s cycle is not ninety-seven years but ninety-five, and it begins not in 527 but in 532.

Dionysius Petavius comes closer to the truth when he writes in the appendix to *On the Doctrine of Time*, p. 890: “The Dionysian table consisted of eight or nine lines, containing the years from the Lord’s incarnation, indictions, epacts, concurrents, the nineteen-year cycle, the fourteenth lunar day, Easter day, and perhaps the Sunday letter, in the same manner as they are prescribed in Bede’s cycles.” As for the years of the incarnation, Dionysius testifies that he prefixed the fifth nineteen-year cycle of Cyril to his own cycle. It therefore began in the year of Christ 513, when Cyril’s fifth nineteen-year cycle began, though Dionysius distinguished the final six years remaining from that same cycle from the earlier years already elapsed. It is plausible, however, that for the year now reckoned as 513 in the common era Dionysius assigned the year 514, since he placed the Lord’s incarnation in the year bearing Golden Number I, which is year 4713 of the Julian period, and the year conventionally called 513 is in fact the year 514 from that point.

In describing the Dionysian cycle, Petavius undoubtedly followed the tables included in Bede’s works under the title “Nineteen-Year Cycles of Bede,” together with the cycles written by the Roman Dionysius, called Exiguus, and Cyril, extending to the year 1595. As we showed shortly before, however, these tables were composed by John of Noyon from his own ingenuity rather than copied from the manuscripts of Bede or Dionysius Exiguus. Petavius therefore had good reason to doubt what in them should be attributed to Dionysius, what to Bede, and what finally to Noyon or to computists of later times. Accordingly: first, he is uncertain whether the Dionysian table consisted of eight or nine lines; second, he unnecessarily conjectures that Sunday letters may have been added; and third, he declares it plausible—although it is entirely false—that Dionysius assigned the year 514 to the year now numbered 513 in the common era.]

For these conjectures, together with other errors, gave rise especially to the widespread and still almost universal opinion that the common Christian era differs from the ancient Dionysian era and is one year lower [Note: Petavius defended the opinion that the ancient Dionysian Christian era differs from our present common era, and that the latter was introduced through an error of Bede, in his notes to Epiphanius’s *Heresies* 1, p. 112, and in *On the Doctrine of Time* XII.2, p. 402. By his authority rather than by any adequate argument he persuaded many learned men of this view, including Wilhelm Langius, *On the Years of Christ* I.1, p. 4; Aegidius Strauchius, *Brief Chronology* IV.40, p. 787; Papebrochius, preliminary dissertation to the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. I, April, §24, fol. XIII; Samuel Basnage, *Political Ecclesiastical Annals* I, p. 183; G. Albert Hamberger, dissertation *On the Origin and Author of the Christian Era*, and others. It rests on no other foundation than the false conjecture about the form of the Dionysian cycle—one that Petavius had never himself inspected—which we have just discussed. Even a single inspection of the true Dionysian cycle refutes it. See the sound observations against this error of Petavius by Antonius Pagi in his *Criticism of Baronius’s Annals* under 527, p. 533, and by Henri Noris in his dissertation *On the Ravenna Cycle* III, p. 215.].

## § XVI

To make it clearer how little authority should be assigned to the cycles of Dionysius reconstructed by such conjectures, we shall examine somewhat more carefully those of Noyon, which almost everyone has hitherto followed and accepted as Dionysian, and shall show how far they differ from the genuine cycles of Dionysius.

1. The cycles that John of Noyon calls “according to Dionysius” begin with the first year before the common Christian era and continue through the year 1595 of Christ. The Dionysian cycles, however, run only from A.D. 532 through 626.

2. The Noyon cycles display the Sunday letters in a separate column and place them incorrectly [Note: Thus for A.D. 532 they give B instead of D C; for 533, A instead of B; for 534, G F instead of A; for 535, E instead of G; for 536, D instead of F E; for 537, C instead of D. The error continues in the same way to the end.]

—and letters that Dionysius, if they were not entirely unknown to him [Note: It may still be questioned whether the use of Sunday letters was known to Dionysius Exiguus when he composed his Easter cycle not long after the beginning of the sixth century. Aegidius Bucherius certainly does not recognize their use in the fifth century, *Commentary on Victor’s Easter Canon*, p. 132. I am aware that they appear in a calendar said to have been written under Constantius and reproduced by Lambecius in vol. IV of his *Commentary on the Vienna Library*, and that this is commonly regarded as the first and oldest memory of Sunday characters. But for this very reason the antiquity of the Vienna calendar is suspect to scholars. In Noris’s judgment, if someone argued that such letters had been added by a later hand, he could not be convicted by any certain testimony, dissertation III *On the Easter Cycle*, p. 192. Whatever the truth may be, this much can at least be asserted with certainty: in all of Dionysius’s surviving writings there is no trace of Sunday letters, although almost all chronologists assign them to him as their principal author.], at least omitted, since their place in his cycle is occupied by the concurrents [Note: Below we shall show how the concurrents were formerly used in place of Sunday letters and how they corresponded to them. It is surprising that Petavius did not notice this, since in the appendix to *On the Doctrine of Time*, p. 890, he attributed Sunday letters to Dionysius, like Noyon, together with the concurrents.]

3. In the nineteen-year cycle immediately preceding the year 532, as in all the others, the Noyon cycles consistently employ the Christian era. Dionysius, however, explicitly states that he retained in his cycle the era of Diocletian, which Cyril had used, and substituted the Christian era for it only from the year 532 onward [Note: In the preface to the *Easter Cycle* addressed to Petronius.]

4. In the same cycle the indictions are counted differently from Cyril’s and incorrectly [Note: Thus in A.D. 513 they add indiction VIII instead of VI; in 514, IX instead of VII; in 515, X instead of VIII. This deviation continues through the final year of the cycle.]

I say nothing of the many errors, especially in the sixth column, where the fourteenth lunar days are given, and in the seventh, where the Easters themselves are incorrectly designated and transferred to the wrong days [Note: Thus the Easter of 566 is transferred from 28 March to 1 April; that of 567 from 10 April to 12 April; that of 568 from 1 April to 1 May; that of 569 from 21 April to 22 March; that of 571 from 29 March to 30 March; that of 583 from 18 April to 19 March; and that of 588 from 18 April to 28 April.].

## § XVII
Among all that has so far been published concerning the Dionysian cycle, if antiquity and authority are taken into account, the first place is easily held by the copy of the inscription on stone at Ravenna, visible in a chamber of the metropolitan church [Col. 0477B], edited and illustrated by Heinrich Noris [Note: Dissertation on the Ravenna Paschal Cycle of 95 Years, together with the eras of the Syro-Macedonians, first published at Padua and reprinted at Leipzig in 1694.]. For he seems not without justification to commend that stone, as a monument of the Dionysian cycle, as having been approved and received at the very beginning—that is, in the sixth century itself—by the metropolitan church of Ravenna and by the bishops attached to it, whom they call suffragans [Note: In the place cited, p. 173 of the Leipzig edition.]. Yet anyone would be mistaken if he thought that the whole diagram of the Dionysian cycle was contained in it. Since the diagram consists of eight columns, the first four in the Ravenna monument—which contain the numbers and characters of particular years, namely the Christian era, the indiction, the epacts, and the concurrents—have been omitted; consequently only the four later columns appear, which seemed sufficient for designating the recurring dates of Easter: namely, 1. the lunar cycle; 2. the paschal fourteenth moons [Col. 0477C]; 3. the day of the Sunday festival; 4. the moon of that Sunday. These are not divided into columns, but arranged in a circle, so that at a glance they represent a circle [Note: Such wheels, as they are called, are frequently encountered in ancient books written on the reckoning of time. I especially recall two of the oldest manuscripts of this kind, in which, appended to the letters and paschal arguments of Dionysius, they came to my notice while I was engaged on another task: one, written in the ninth century, in the library of Reims, at Saint Remigius, no. 298, D. IX according to the old catalogue; the other in the Cotton Library, under the image of Caligula, A. 15.]. Noris himself is so far from passing off his Ravenna wheel as the complete Dionysian cycle [Col. 0478A] that he regards the latter as entirely lost [Note: See § 15, col. 475, note. [ [Col. 0477C] In the preface of the Paschal Cycle addressed to Petronius.]].  

§ XVIII

Since matters stood thus, I fully accepted the judgment of learned men that the Dionysian Cycle no longer survived in complete form and could be restored only by conjectures of this kind, until I happened to obtain an opportunity to examine the Digby manuscript in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. The more carefully I investigated whether this book contained the very authentic tables of the Dionysian nineteen-year cycles [Greek: ἐννεαδεκαετηρίδων], such as had once been published by the author himself, the more certain evidence I found and was able to establish that it did. Since that book provided the principal occasion for this treatise, it does not seem out of place here to supply a somewhat fuller description of it than is contained in the catalogue of the manuscripts of England [Col. 0478B] [Note: In the catalogue of the manuscripts of England and Ireland, published at Oxford in 1697, the Bodleian Library, class 5, among the manuscripts of Kenelm Digby, p. 80, no. 1664, 63, our manuscript is described in these words: “A very ancient book or treatise on the Reckoning of Easter, with an old calendar and the oration of Theophilus of Caesarea on the same subject, etc.; the letter of Proterius; the treatise of Dionysius Exiguus, abbot; the Computation of Reginald the priest; another treatise on the Egyptian Paschal Tables, etc. All these are written in a very ancient script, from the earliest period of the Christian Saxons in England.”].

It is written on parchment, of a smaller format, slightly larger than what we call an octavo; its letters are very similar to those which Mabillon assigns to the eighth century [Note: Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book V, plate 9, p. 361.]. The first place in it is occupied by a paschal cycle beginning with Diocletian’s year 229—that is, A.D. 513—and extending through twenty nineteen-year cycles, consequently down to A.D. 892. Of these nineteen-year cycles we shall publish the first six and shall demonstrate that they constitute the very cycle of Dionysius. They are followed by a concise reckoning of time, carried from the creation of the world down to the death of Charlemagne, and by a Roman calendar with golden numbers, or the cycles of the Latins and Alexandrians [Note: This double calendar is that which appears in Bede’s works, vol. I, p. 242, under the title *Ephemeris*, and in Petavius, book VI of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 5, although it differs in many respects from both.]. Then follow the paschal canons, the prayers and letters of Theophilus, Proterius, Cyril [Col. 0478C], Paschasinus, and Dionysius, and other writings of the ancients concerning the explanation of the paschal cycle, collected by a certain priest named Regenbold [Note: He identifies himself by name shortly after Dionysius’s second letter to Boniface in these words: “The book on the Computation ends. Regenbold, priest of Pentonia, wrote this little book, and whoever reads it, let him always pray for him.” That these words belong not to the copyist but to the compiler is clear from the fact that they are not placed at the end of the book, but are followed by several further words written in the same hand.]. Finally there are added the Egyptian paschal arguments from Dionysius’s translation, enlarged and [Col. 0479A] interpolated with certain additions. These additions, however, can easily be distinguished both by their own indications and by comparison with other manuscripts. Apart from them, I do not remember ever having seen the paschal arguments anywhere in such complete form; hence, in editing them, we shall follow the Digby manuscript above all.

If you ask about the age of the book, it was undoubtedly written at the beginning of the ninth century. This is shown, besides the forms of its letters, by the chronology appended to the cycles, which, as we demonstrated shortly before, extends to the death of Charlemagne and the accession of the emperor Louis the Pious [Note: The words of the manuscript are these: “According to Bishop Julian, from the beginning of the world down to Christ there are reckoned 5,425 years. According to Jerome, however, from Adam down to Christ there are 5,029 years. From the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ down to the death of Charlemagne and the empire of Louis there are 814 years, and in that year the indiction was VI.”]. Nevertheless, it was copied from a much older exemplar. For the first continuator of the Dionysian cycle—whether he was Regenbold or whoever else he may have been—who added the next five nineteen-year cycles, extending from the year 627 to 721, and whose very words are preserved in the Digby manuscript, lived at the beginning of the seventh century, and thus in the earliest period of the Christian Saxons [Col. 0479B] in England. He undertook this task in A.D. 616, when the end of the last Dionysian nineteen-year cycle was approaching [Note: This is clearly shown by his words, which are read immediately after Dionysius’s second letter and before the passage marked (j), which we have cited: “The successor of Dionysius, Dionysius, formerly the most learned abbot of the city of Rome, endowed with elegant knowledge of both languages, namely Greek and Latin, meanwhile composed five nineteen-year paschal cycles by his keen intellect, taking his beginning from the year 532 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, indiction X, and carrying the continuous series of the aforesaid cycles down to the year 626 of the incarnation, indiction XIV. Since, therefore, his fifth cycle is now being completed, and ten years still remain to supplement it, our small ability foresees that we should compose, in a reasonable arrangement, five further nineteen-year cycles in the number of five, after the pattern of the preceding cycles. Beginning with the six-hundred-and-twenty-seventh year of the incarnation, indiction XV, and extending to the seven-hundred-and-twenty-first year of the incarnation of the Lord, indiction IV, we have established and set down a fixed limit. Therefore we have instructed the reader that, when the fifth cycle of the aforesaid venerable Dionysius has been completed, he should pass over to our five subsequent cycles, as we have said; and without any cloud of error he will find, by a trustworthy reckoning, the most solemn paschal days and the moons in their proper order.” The same words, almost verbatim, are found in the Remigian manuscript 298, under the title “Prologue of Felix, abbot of Gillitanus,” after the preface, or, as it is commonly called, the first Paschal Letter of Dionysius Exiguus.].

Since, therefore, ten years remained from that cycle, during which he himself wished his paschal book to remain in use, he prefixed to his own work the Dionysian cycles, which were otherwise destined to end only in the year 626, unlike the younger computists who published their cycles after A.D. 626 [Note: See § 15, col. 475, note. [ [Col. 0479B] The words of the manuscript are these: “According to Bishop Julian, from the beginning of the world down to Christ there are reckoned 5,425 years. According to Jerome, however, from Adam down to Christ there are 5,029 years. From the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ down to the death of Charlemagne and the empire of Louis there are 814 years, and in that year the indiction was VI.”]]. For a similar reason, though in an extremely rare example, the second continuator, who extended those paschal cycles beyond A.D. 721, retained all the cycles he had found in the earlier edition, including the Dionysian cycles, which all the other later computists omitted; thus he may perhaps have preserved them complete for us in the single Digby manuscript.

§ XIX

Afterwards, when opportunity arose, I diligently investigated and examined books of this kind on the paschal computation, especially in the Cotton, Colbertine, and Remigian libraries—the first among English libraries and the latter two among French libraries being easily the richest in manuscripts of this kind. I was able to find only one in which the Dionysian cycles had been retained. It is manuscript 1020 of the Colbertine Library, in which, after Dionysius’s preface, or letter to Petronius, those nineteen-year cycles are found, arranged in the same series of columns [Note: The form and arrangement of the Dionysian cycle in the Colbertine manuscript are as follows: ], and in some respects more accurately than in the Digby manuscript, extending from A.D. 532 to A.D. 1063; although the last cycle of Cyril, which in the Digby manuscript precedes the Dionysian cycles, is missing.

Since Dionysius published his nineteen-year cycles not naked or by themselves, but together with a prologue, paschal arguments, and other material relating to the subject, the order in which all these things were arranged can be learned more accurately from other ancient paschal books than from the Digby manuscript [Note: See the preface of Dionysius Exiguus, toward the end.]. Accordingly, in arranging, supplementing, and correcting these materials, besides the Colbertine manuscript we used:

1. A manuscript of the Cotton Library—which is joined to the Royal Library in London and consists entirely of excellent manuscripts collected with great care—in the case of Caligula A. 15. Besides the paschal letters of Theophilus, Cyril, Paschasinus, Proterius, and Dionysius, this manuscript also contains Dionysius’s paschal arguments, cited above before the paschal wheel [Note: § 17, note. [ [Col. 0480D] See § 15, col. 475, note. [ [Col. 0479B] The words of the manuscript are these: “According to Bishop Julian, from the beginning of the world down to Christ there are reckoned 5,425 years. According to Jerome, however, from Adam down to Christ there are 5,029 years. From the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ down to the death of Charlemagne and the empire of Louis there are 814 years, and in that year the indiction was VI.”]]. The material is adapted to A.D. 688, from which its antiquity may also be judged [Note: In this manuscript, beside certain examples dated A.D. 687 or 688, the year 525 has been written by another and ancient hand [Col. 0480D]. Hence it is clear that the manuscript was collated with the older paschal treatises of Dionysius, all whose examples are drawn from A.D. 525. Although I do not deny that treatises adapted to A.D. 688 by some computist of the seventh century could also have been copied without alteration by a more recent scribe, other indications show that the Cotton manuscript is not later than the eighth or ninth century.].  

2. Manuscript CCLXX–XXVIII of Saint Remigius at Reims, D. IX according to the old catalogue [Col. 0480C]. After Bede’s books *On the Nature of Things*, *On Times*, *On Measures and Times*, and *On the Reckoning of Time*, as well as chapters to which the computists, summoned for consultation, gave answers, and the paschal letters of Cyril, Paschasinus, Proterius, Theophilus, and Morinus, there is a book of Dionysius Exiguus. In it Dionysius’s letter to Proterius is prefixed in place of a preface, just as in the Colbertine manuscript. Although the nineteen-year cycles themselves are omitted for the sake of brevity, as we observed above [Note: § 17, note. [ [Col. 0481B] Especially from the Cotton manuscript in the case of Tiberius E. 4, from the Bodleian manuscript F. NE, 3, 5, and from the Royal Paris manuscript, whose variant readings du Fresne excerpted in the *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 479.]], the paschal arguments expressly attributed to Dionysius, illustrated by examples from the year 791, are found there. The manuscript itself was written at the beginning of the ninth century [Note: On the last pages of the book these words are found: “By the work of Bertigarius the monk, the book of Saint Remigius.” They indicate that it was copied through the care of Bertigarius, abbot of Saint Remigius, under Charles the Bald. In the chapters to which the summoned computists are said to have replied, the first question is: “How many years from the incarnation of God down to the present do they wish to retain?” Answer: 809.].

3. We supplemented and corrected the paschal letters of Dionysius and the others not only from these books but also from several other ancient manuscripts [Note: Especially from the Cotton manuscript in the case of Tiberius E. 4, from the Bodleian manuscript F. NE, 3, 5, and from the Royal Paris manuscript, whose variant readings du Fresne excerpted in the *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 479.].

§ XX

The authenticity [Greek: γνησιότητα] of this Dionysian cycle, as well as of the paschal arguments corresponding to each of its columns, is proved not only by the authority of the manuscripts mentioned above, which are extremely ancient in this field [Note: In the Digby manuscript, after Dionysius’s second letter to Boniface, fol. 69, the following is read:

**The successor of Dionysius**

“Dionysius … composed the preceding cycles, beginning with the year 532 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, indiction X, and carrying the continuous series of the aforesaid cycles down to the year 627 of the incarnation, indiction XIV.”

Add the rest, cited more fully above in § 18, note (b). In the Colbertine manuscript the following title is prefixed to Dionysius’s preface to Petronius and to the cycle tables appended to it: “Here begins the book of Dionysius Exiguus. To the most blessed and greatly desired father Petronius, etc.” Exactly the same words are found in the Remigian manuscript, after the discussion of Morinus, bishop of Alexandria, on the Reckoning of Easter.], but also by the clearest other indications that can be expected in such a matter.

First of all, it is noteworthy that everything Dionysius himself recorded concerning this work agrees exactly with the Digby manuscript, which we principally followed. For example, he writes that he prefixed to his own cycles the last cycle of Cyril, ending in Diocletian’s year 247 [Note: Dionysius says in his first letter, or rather in the preface to his cycle: “We have endeavored, with such diligence as we could command, to set forth this cycle of ninety-five years; we have prefixed in our work the last cycle of that same blessed Cyril, that is, the fifth cycle, since six years still remained from it; and then we confess that we arranged five others according to the rule of that same pontiff, or rather of the oft-mentioned Council of Nicaea.”]. In our manuscript that cycle is indeed prefixed and ends in Diocletian’s year 247.

He testifies that he substituted the Christian era for the era of Diocletian used by Cyril [Note: Dionysius, in the passage cited: “Since the holy Cyril began his first cycle from Diocletian’s 153rd year and ended the last in the 247th, we, beginning with the 248th year of that same tyrant rather than prince, did not wish to attach the memory of an impious persecutor to our cycles; instead, we preferred to mark the times by the years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be more familiar to us, and the cause of human restoration—that is, the passion of our Redeemer—might shine forth more clearly.”]. But nowhere can one see more clearly how this was done than in this edition of the cycles themselves.

He shows that he began the cycle with Diocletian’s year 248, or A.D. 532 [Note: It is a common error, already noted above, to say that the Dionysian cycle began with Diocletian’s year 247 and thus included in its first year Cyril’s last Easter—which fell on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May in A.D. 531. Thus, following Paul of Forosemprone and others, Petavius himself judges in book XII of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 2. But Dionysius himself expressly affirms, in the words just cited in the note [ [Col. 0481B] Especially from the Cotton manuscript in the case of Tiberius E. 4, from the Bodleian manuscript F. NE, 3, 5, and from the Royal Paris manuscript, whose variant readings du Fresne excerpted in the *Paschal Chronicle*, p. 479.]], that he began with Diocletian’s 248th year. The same is testified by Bede, who read the Dionysian cycle, in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 55, in these words: “By placing the five-hundred-and-thirty-second year of the Lord’s incarnation at the head of his first cycle, he clearly taught that, according to his cycle, this was the year in which the mystery of that most holy incarnation began.” On the authority of both writers, as well as on the evidence of the Ravenna cycle, Noris refutes Petavius, *Dissertation on the Ravenna Paschal Cycle*, pp. 205 ff. Our cycle agrees exactly with that Ravenna cycle in this respect as in others, and begins in this manner: “A.D. 532, indiction X, epact none, concurrent IV, lunar cycle XVII, paschal fourteenth moon on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, Easter on the third day before the Ides of April, moon XX.”].

He established the end in the year 626 [Note: Most chronologists have erred no less concerning the end than concerning the beginning of the Dionysian cycle, making it 532 years long and thus extending it down to A.D. 1063. We noted this error in Scaliger in § 15, note [ [Col. 0481C] Dionysius in his first letter, or rather the preface to his cycle: “We have endeavored, with such diligence as we could command, to set forth this cycle of ninety-five years; we have prefixed in our work the last cycle of that same blessed Cyril, that is, the fifth cycle, since six years still remained from it; and then we confess that we arranged five others according to the rule of that same pontiff, or rather of the oft-mentioned Council of Nicaea.”].]. Among others, Charles du Fresne followed him in the preface to the *Paschal Chronicle*, § 33, p. 28. Petavius, who had previously held the same opinion and had attributed two cycles to Dionysius—one larger cycle of 532 years and another smaller one of 95 years—corrected his error in book II of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 67, after encountering Dionysius’s letter. He declared there that it was plainly evident from the letter that the cycle established by Dionysius was not 532 years, as he himself, along with nearly everyone else, had thought, but 95 years, in the appendix to his work *On the Doctrine of Time*, p. 890.

Nevertheless, Antonius Pagi again undertook the defense of the common opinion, by relying only on the words of the Dionysian preface: “Let the reader turn to our FIRST cycle, which we began with Diocletian’s year 248” [Col. 0482D]. But Noris rightly observes, *On the Ravenna Cycle*, chapter 1, p. 161, that this passage must be understood of the first nineteen-year cycle, of the kind of which that entire period of 95 years contained five complete cycles. For Dionysius’s words are clearer than any possible objection: “This cycle of ninety-five years, which we have made,” and so forth.

If anyone should still refuse to be satisfied by this evidence, the very words of Dionysius’s successor, which we cited from the Digby and Remigian manuscripts in § 18, note [ [Col. 0481B] On the last pages of the book these words are found: “By the work of Bertigarius the monk, the book of Saint Remigius”; by which it is indicated that it was copied through the care of Bertigarius, abbot of Saint Remigius, under Charles the Bald. In the chapters to which the summoned computists are said to have replied, the first question is: “How many years from the incarnation of God down to the present do they wish to retain?” Answer: 809.], could overcome all the obstinacy of objections. There Dionysius is most explicitly said not to have carried the series of his cycles beyond the year 626 of Christ, indiction XIV.

A similar formula is found in ancient paschal books which omit Dionius’s cycles as already past. It is appended to his preface and was taken from three manuscripts and published in § 15, note [ [Col. 0481B] On the last pages of the book these words are found: “By the work of Bertigarius the monk, the book of Saint Remigius”; by which it is indicated that it was copied through the care of Bertigarius, abbot of Saint Remigius, under Charles the Bald. In the chapters to which the summoned computists are said to have replied, the first question is: “How many years from the incarnation of God down to the present do they wish to retain?” Answer: 809.].

He also designates its eight columns [Note: Dionysius jointly mentions all the columns of his cycle, and indeed the same columns displayed in our edition, in the preface in these words: “Although the years of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve their own order in an uninterrupted series” (column 1), “and the indictions” (column 2) “run through their customary revolution over fifteen years, and although you may find the epacts also” (column 3), “which the Greeks call additions, namely the annual lunar additions of eleven, which return upon themselves at the end of thirty days, marked according to fixed rules; and likewise the nineteen-year recurrence” (column 5) “and the paschal fourteenth moons” (column 6) “may be found by the recurring revolution of all ages; nevertheless, the concurrent days of the weeks” (column 4), “the days of the Lord’s Easter” (column 7), “and the moon of that Sunday” (column 8) “cannot preserve a similar constancy of order.” Bede describes each of these columns methodically in *On the Reckoning of Computation*, chapter 17, and *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapters 45 and following. Verses commemorating the same columns are found both in Bede’s works, vol. I, p. 358, [Col. 0484C] and in the Digby manuscript:

“First, the line, O Christ, contains your years;

the second holds the indiction of the cycle;

the third preserves fixed numbers for the epacts;

the fourth counts the seven days of the leap year;

the fifth computes for you the cycles of the lunar year;

the sixth now designates the fourteenth moons;

the seventh shows the season and day of Easter;

the final order displays the moon’s age.”].

Both points can be recognized here with the utmost clarity. He composed the paschal arguments in the consulship of Probus Junior, in lunar cycle 13, indiction III—that is, in A.D. 525 [Note: The often-mentioned preface of Dionysius should be read toward the end, and what we noted above in § 11, note (d), concerning his age should be compared.]. Yet in the frequently mentioned manuscript, faithfully copied by us, all the examples of the paschal arguments are drawn from that year, A.D. 525. Moreover, individual passages cited partly by Dionysius and partly by Bede and other ancient writers are found here in exactly the same words, as we shall demonstrate in the notes to the paschal arguments. To all this may be added, as a final confirmation, the exact agreement of the Ravenna marble [Note: On this marble, see § 17.].

§ XXI

If others have not regretted carefully pursuing the calendars and forms of reckoning of the most ancient peoples from the creation of the world, and searching for their traces throughout the whole record of antiquity; if many have thought that the calendars of the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Persians, Greeks, and Romans—already long obsolete and unknown—ought to be rescued from decay and oblivion with great labor; if, specifically, Bucherius was not blamed for bringing the cycle of Victorius, once approved only by certain churches in the West and obscured by more than a thousand years of darkness, back into the light and explaining it in a sufficiently substantial commentary; then much less, it would seem, can anyone rightly criticize whatever labor and study have been devoted to publishing and illustrating the Dionysian cycle, which the entire Christian world used for so many centuries to establish the reckoning of the year.

For although this cycle too was abolished in the Roman Church 136 years ago, and at the beginning of the eighteenth century in the whole Roman Empire [Col. 0483C], it nevertheless remains in force today in certain Christian kingdoms which have adopted neither the Gregorian nor our new calendar. Moreover, even the modern reckoning of the calendar, especially the Gregorian one, in which epacts have been adopted in place of golden numbers, is greatly assisted by the old method and the doctrine of the golden numbers, as Petavius acknowledges along with Clavius [Note: At the beginning of book VI of *On the Doctrine of Time*.].

And even if it were abolished everywhere, it should at least not be neglected because of the remarkable usefulness it provides in correctly judging ancient chronology. For the principle remains valid by which Bede writes that, in the eighth century, he was moved to review the cycles of Dionysius—although they were already past—and to place them before his own work: “So that all who read may be able to contemplate with an unerring view the whole past course of paschal time, and, for the clarification of ancient reading, may recognize more clearly all the years that have at some time been called into question, when and of what kind they were” [Note: Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 63.].

Certainly Scaliger, Petavius, and other very learned writers on the doctrine of time would have avoided many errors if they had examined the true cycle of Dionysius; among them, not the least is the error that is still almost universally held, by which the present era is attributed to Bede as its author and is considered one year less than the Dionysian era.

What is more, for this one reason alone the monument can be pleasant for anyone to know, since it places clearly before our eyes the occasion, purpose, year, and author by which that era, so familiar to all, was first introduced and began to be used in place of the Diocletian era. It also gives everyone the opportunity to judge how well or badly certain people have restored by their conjectures the Dionysian cycle, which they thought had perished.

[Col. 0483]

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS

[Note: This title is found in the Remigian manuscript 298 and in the Colbertine manuscript 1020 in exactly the same words.] (C)

## PREFACE

[Note: This preface—for it is called that by Petavius himself on p. 61—was published by Petavius in the appendix to his work *On the Doctrine of Time*, p. 874, and by Aegidius Bucherius in his *Commentary on the Doctrine of Time*, p. 485, under the title “The first letter of Dionysius Exiguus on the Reckoning of Easter.” We have collated it with several other manuscript codices, specifically the Bodleian manuscript F. N E, 3, 5, which is listed in the catalogue of the manuscripts of England, p. 122, no. 2372; the Cotton manuscript Tiberius E, T; and Digby 63, without neglecting the variant readings excerpted by Charles du Fresne from the Paris manuscript in his *Selections for the Illustration of the Paschal Chronicle*, no. 22, p. 479. For the sake of brevity, in the notes we shall designate the Royal Paris manuscript by A, the Bodleian by B, the Cotton by C, and the Digby by D. The Colbertine and Remigian manuscripts agree almost entirely with the Paris manuscript, so that if you know one of these, you know them all.]

[Col. 0483D] [Note: At the beginning of the volume, col. 19, we transcribed this letter, having already despaired of finding the most precious edition of Guillaume Jans. Later, when we planned to reprint it, together with other omitted material, as a supplement, we did not hesitate to place the same letter here, both for the sake of the completeness of the work and because of the abundance of notes with which it is enriched in this edition. EDITOR.]

To the most blessed and greatly desired father, Petronius, bishop: Dionysius Exiguus.

The reckoning of the paschal festival, which the persistent insistence of many people has long and frequently demanded from us, we have now taken care to explain, aided by your prayers [Note: D: “we are explaining.”]. In all things we follow the venerable 318 bishops who assembled at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, against the madness of Arius [Note: C adds: “examples.”], and their complete and true judgment on this matter. They fixed the fourteenth moons of paschal observance, through a circle of nineteen years that continually returns upon itself, as stable and immovable [Note: What the Fathers of Nicaea established concerning the time for celebrating Easter is shown in *The History of the Dionysian Cycle*, § 6, where this passage of Dionysius is examined as well.], so that through all the ages they proceed without variation, from the same beginning at which they recur [Note: All our manuscripts confirm this reading, so that those who substitute *reponuntur*—“are replaced”—are plainly wrong.].

They sanctioned this rule of the aforesaid circle not so much by worldly expertise [Note: We restore this word from A and C in place of *singulari*, which is found in the others.] as by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and they are seen to have placed it like a firm anchor in this reckoning of lunar measurement. Afterwards certain people, either despising it through arrogance or transgressing it through ignorance [Note: Thus C; the others read *inscientia*, “lack of knowledge.”], led on by Jewish fables [Note: He alludes to the ancient eighty-four-year cycle of the Latins, once used by many Western churches and originally received from the Jews, although it was later altered and corrected in some places. Epiphanius reports that the Jews had already employed an eighty-four-year cycle, composed from the Callippic period and the octaeteris, under the rule of the Syro-Macedonians, in order to investigate correctly the date of Easter, or rather the time of the new moon, in *Against the Alogoi*, heresy 51. See the commentary of Aegidius Bucherius on the paschal canon of Victorius, chapter 6, pp. 132 and 140, and Noris’s special dissertation on the Latin Paschal Cycle.], handed down a different and contrary form for the single festival [Note: A: “the ancient festival.”]. And because no structure can stand without the solidity of a foundation, they preferred to establish the Lord’s Easter and the reckoning of the moon quite differently in certain years, arranging disordered cycles [Note: Thus all our manuscripts; Bucherius, however, reports that other copies read *ordientes*, “beginning” or “setting in order.”]. These cycles not only display no stability of recurrence, but also exhibit a course notably marked by error.

But the blessed Athanasius, archbishop of the city of Alexandria [Note: See *History of the Dionysian Cycle*, § 8.], who himself was present at the Council of Nicaea as deacon of Saint Alexander [Note: C: “of the Alexandrian pontiff.”] and assistant in all things, and afterwards the venerable Theophilus [Note: See *History of the Dionysian Cycle*, § 9.] and Cyril [Note: There, § 10.] did not depart at all from this venerable ordinance of the synod [Note: C and D: “reverent”; A: “reverent.”]. Rather, carefully retaining the same nineteen-year cycle, called in Greek *enneacaidecaeteris*, they are shown not to have altered the paschal course with any variations [Note: The Gallic manuscripts read this way; the English manuscripts have “circle.”].

Finally, Pope Theophilus [Note: Read chapters 67 and 68 of book XI of *On the Doctrine of Time*. From them you will learn that Gennadius was mistaken in thinking that the ninety-five-year cycle had been established by the Council of Nicaea and presented by Theophilus to the emperor Theodosius. Cyril, the successor of Theophilus, was the first to construct it, as Dionysius indicates here. PETAVIUS.], dedicating a cycle of one hundred years to the elder emperor Theodosius, and Saint Cyril, composing a cycle of ninety-five years, observed in every respect this tradition of the holy council concerning the observance of the paschal fourteenth moons [Col. 0486B]. And because the rule of this same circle ought to be fixed more firmly in the minds of those who are eager to know what is true, we have thought it right to write it down after our preface.

Therefore, this cycle of ninety-five years [Note: [Col. 0486B] Thus D. It is absent in C; in others, however, *autem* is read. Much has been said by others, and we have set forth much in various places, concerning the Dionysian cycle; nowhere, however, shall we collect its substance more suitably than in connection with Dionysius’s own words. The Alexandrian year (for from it the discussion must take its beginning) precedes the beginning of the Roman civil year by four months, and that of the ecclesiastical year, which proceeds from Pascha, by more than seven months [Col. 0486C]. Again, Dionysius Exiguus began the years of his cycle from the fifteenth paschal moon, as is clear from the diagram in Letter 2. Hence the paschal new moon occupies the end of the year, Pascha itself the beginning of the year. Cyril is said to have begun his cycle in the 153rd year of Diocletian, which among the Alexandrians began on 29 August, in the year of Christ 436, when the Roman lunar cycle was beginning at 19 but the Alexandrian at 1. Thus the first Pascha of Cyril’s cycle was in the year of Christ 437. After four nineteen-year cycles and thirteen years of the fifth—that is, after eighty-nine years of Cyril’s ninety-five-year cycle had been completed—Dionysius Exiguus, observing the defect of that cycle, applied himself to correcting it. For in Letter 2 he writes that six years of Cyril’s fifth nineteen-year cycle still remained. Therefore Dionysius was devising these things between Pascha of the year of Christ 525, indiction III, and that of 526, indiction IV, as is understood from his words, which we corrected from Marianus Scotus in Book XII, near the end of chapter 3. The last Pascha of Cyril’s cycle [Col. 0486D] fell in the year of the common era 531, as the 247th year of Diocletian (rather, 248th) was ending, with golden number XIX. Therefore the first year of the Dionysian cycle began with the fourteenth paschal moon, which is XV Kalends of May, or 17 April; and the new moon, so to speak, of Dionysius’s first year is that very seventeenth day of April. Since Bede and the others had not hitherto noticed this, they threw the Dionysian era and cycle out by one year. The first year of the Dionysian cycle began in the year 4712 of the Julian period, golden number XIX, and ended in 4713 on 5 April. But one must by all means see what we wrote on this matter in Book XII, chapters 2 and 3. PETAVIUS.—Inspection of the genuine Dionysian cycle published by us teaches that Petavius erred here. It is true that Dionysius, in his letter to Boniface, numbers the LUNAR years N B from the fourteenth paschal moon, which in the year of Christ 531 was 17 April, namely when he teaches how to test whether the fourteenth moon, or paschal limit, of the year in question, 532 [Col. 0487B], has been correctly found and fixed. But it is wrongly inferred from this that, in Dionysius’s view, the first year of the Dionysian cycle, reckoned according to the era of Christ and being the SOLAR year N B, began with that fourteenth paschal moon of 531. It is remarkable that Petavius and so many others who followed him did not notice this.] we have endeavored, with all the diligence at our command, to set out, preferring in this work the final cycle of the blessed Cyril, that is, the fifth cycle [Col. 0487A] [Note: [Col. 0487B] Thus A and B. Others read “circle.”], since six years still remained from it; and we declare that thereafter we have arranged five more according to the rule of that same pontiff—or rather, according to that of the often-mentioned Council of Nicaea.

Since Saint Cyril began his first cycle in the 153rd year of Diocletian and ended the last in the 247th [Note: [Col. 0487C] C reads “might shine forth.”], we, beginning with the 248th year of that same tyrant rather than prince, did not wish to attach the memory of an impious persecutor to our circles, but preferred to mark the periods of years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be more familiar to us and the cause of humanity’s restoration—that is, the passion of our Redeemer—might shine forth more clearly [Note: [Col. 0487C] A reads “the cycle itself.”].

[Col. 0487B] Moreover, we thought the reader should be warned that this circle [Note: [Col. 0487C] A reads “the one set before.”] of ninety-five years, which we have constructed, when, after its period has ended, it begins to return to the same point, does not preserve in every respect the stability proposed [Note: [Col. 0487C] The Dionysian table consisted of eight or nine lines, etc. We have already cited Petavius’s note above in *History of the Dionysian Cycle*, § 15, note (a), and indicated what he correctly and incorrectly conjectured in it about the form of the Dionysian cycle.]. For although the years of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0487C] C reads “the same.”] preserve their order in an uninterrupted sequence, and the indictions run through their customary fifteen-year revolution [Col. 0488A], and you find the epacts—which the Greeks call *epactae*, that is, annual lunar additions, eleven of which return into themselves at the completion of thirty days—marked out by fixed rules, and likewise find the nineteen-year recurrence and the fourteenth paschal moons recurring throughout all ages [Note: [Col. 0487C] This is explained in Book II of *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapters 67, pp. 226–227. PETAVIUS.], nevertheless the concurrent days of the weeks [Note: [Col. 0487C] A reads “of the week.”] cannot preserve a similar consistency, nor can the day of the Lord’s Pascha [Note: [Col. 0487C] See Petavius’s discussion of this passage in Book II of *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 67.], nor the moon of that Sunday [Note: [Col. 0487C] See Petavius’s discussion of this passage in Book II of *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 67.].

The calculation of the concurrent weeks [Note: [Col. 0487C] A and C read “weeks”; others, “seven days.”]—which arises from the course of the sun—ends in a continuous seven-year [Note: [Col. 0487C] C reads “seventh.”] circuit. In it, you will count one for each year, but in the one year in which there is a leap day you will add two. This is also why this circle of ninety-five years does not seem to agree in every respect with its recurrence [Note: [Col. 0487C] B and C read “recurrence.”]. For although it does not differ in the other years [Note: [Col. 0487C] C reads “fall short.”], in those alone in which the leap year intervenes [Note: [Col. 0487C] C reads “twice.”], the Sunday of Pascha with its moon falls according to a different reckoning [Note: [Col. 0488C] D reads “runs through.”].

[Note: [Col. 0487D] Thus, at the beginning of the Dionysian cycle, in the year of Christ 532, solar cycle 19, D C, golden number I, the Sunday of Pascha is marked as 13 April, with the moon at age XX; but after the ninety-five-year cycle has elapsed, in the year of Christ 627, the Sunday of Pascha is marked in Isidore’s cycle as the day before the Ides, that is, 12 April, with the moon at age XXI. Consequently, because the leap year is inserted in the year of Christ 532, in the repeated period, as Dionysius says, the Sunday of Pascha with its moon falls according to a different reckoning: it moves to the following day, and the moon’s age increases. An even greater variation occurred whenever the fourteenth paschal moon, falling on a Sunday in a leap year, transferred the feast to the following Sunday and to moon XXI. Then, in the restored cycle, Pascha moved back to the preceding week. Thus, in the leap year of Christ 448, solar cycle 9, D C, lunar cycle XII, the paschal new moon fixed in Cyril’s cycle, according to the Alexandrian canons, appeared on 22 March [Col. 0488B]; the moon reached age XIV on 4 April, a Sunday, and Pascha was therefore postponed to 11 April, moon XXI. But ninety-five years later, namely in the year of Christ 543, with the same lunar cycle XII, solar cycle XX, and letter D, the fourteenth paschal moon is marked in the Dionysian cycle as 4 April [II Nones of April]. Pascha, however, falls on 5 April, moon XV, and therefore one week earlier—or six days earlier—than it was celebrated in 448. NORIS, *Dissertation 3 on the Paschal Cycle*, [Col. 0488C] p. 165.]

But those who proceed through all periods according to a fixed order [Note: [Col. 0488C] Because of the defect of the cycle, Cyril’s concurrents and likewise the dominical letters could not retain their sequence. Dionysius therefore added another sequence of concurrents and letters, beginning with the first year of his ninety-five-year cycle, which is the year of Christ 531. Hence, instead of the manuscript and Bede reading *mobilium casuum*, we judged that *mobilium casum* should be corrected. PETAVIUS.—Petavius erred twice here: first, in believing that a series of both concurrents and dominical letters had been inserted in Dionysius’s cycle; see *History of the Dionysian Cycle*, § 16. Second, in writing that its beginning was reckoned from the ordinary year 531; see the same work, § 20, and col. 481, note (g).] can regulate the movement [*casum*, “falling”] of the shifting paschal days by their stable cycle without any difficulty [Note: [Col. 0488C] Thus B and D, certainly more correctly than *casuum*, as in Bucherius. Dionysius speaks of the falling of the movable paschal days, as Noris observes in the cited passage, p. 169. Petavius therefore rightly conjectured and corrected here. C reads quite differently, *immobilium cursum*, “the course of immovable things.”].

And so, after the completion of ninety-five years [Note: [Col. 0488D] Dionysius placed the final cycle of Cyril before his five cycles; six years remained from it. He therefore advises that, when his ninety-five years have been completed, one should return to the same beginning—not to Cyril’s fifth cycle, but to the first of his own. This raises a very difficult question. Dionysius seems to have regarded a cycle of ninety-five years as one that would reproduce in a circuit the feasts, Sundays of Pascha, and lunar days. Yet only a few lines earlier he had denied that this could happen, and the facts themselves show that it is impossible, as you will learn from the table that we described in Book XI of *On the Reckoning of Time*, p. 227. Accordingly, the author of the preface placed before Dionysius’s circles in Bede interprets that first Dionysian cycle, to which one is to return after ninety-five years have been completed, as the great cycle of 532 years. But nothing of the sort can be extracted from Dionysius’s words. For he calls “his first cycle” the one he had just said he himself had established, namely one of ninety-five years. I would indeed believe that Dionysius attached to the same ninety-five-year cycle duplicated lines for the concurrent days, dominical letters, Sundays of Pascha, and lunar days, and indicated during which revolutions of the cycles the respective series of concurrents, letters, and so forth should be taken. Perhaps he also added those very series of changing characters on the model of the method of the Victorian period of 532 years. In Victor’s great cycle there are five complete nineteen-year cycles, together with fifty-seven years, or three cycles. Dionysius therefore established six such lines containing the sequence of concurrents, letters, and so forth. In the year of Christ 437, when Cyril’s first Pascha occurred, the solar cycle was 26, the dominical letter C, the concurrents 4, and Pascha fell on 2 April. After ninety-five years had elapsed, in the year of Christ 532, the concurrents were 4 and the dominical letters D C. But the leap-year calculation causes confusion. For in the fourth year of Cyril’s cycle, which was the year of Christ 440, the letters were G F, the solar cycle 1, the lunar cycle 4, the concurrents in March 1, and Pascha fell on 7 April. But in the fourth year of Dionysius’s first cycle, which was the year of Christ 535, the dominical letter was 6, the concurrents 7, and Pascha fell on 8 April. Thus the annual characters do not return in a circuit after ninety-five years. The discrepancy gradually becomes greater, as is clear from the table in Book II, p. 227. Dionysius therefore adapted different sequences of these characters to his nineteen-year cycle, which he undoubtedly took from the method of the greater cycle, as we have said. PETAVIUS.—Petavius’s conjectures are futile; by them he tries to resolve a difficult question that he himself has invented. We can dispense with all of them if we examine more carefully not merely Dionysius’s cycle, which was unknown to Petavius, but even this very preface. For when Dionysius says that his ninety-five-year cycle does not preserve the proposed stability in every respect, he clearly shows which columns of his cycle retain that stability and which do not. To the former he assigns (1) the years of Christ, (2) the indictions, (3) the epacts, (4) the nineteen-year cycle, and (5) the fourteenth moons; to the latter, (1) the concurrents, (2) the days of Pascha, and (3) the moon of the Sunday. After ninety-five years have been completed, therefore, he carefully orders a return to the first cycle N B [Col. 0490B], so that through those cycles that retain a fixed course the progress of those that seem to falter may be supported—that is, so that the calculation may be established according to the laws of the Alexandrian cycle, which he calls the paschal parameters.], when he wishes, with careful attention to these matters, to return to the beginning, let him proceed not to the fifth cycle of Saint Cyril, which we were necessarily obliged to set before the reader, but attentively to our first; and let him support, in the order we have described, through those elements that retain a fixed course, the progress of those that seem to falter [Note: [Col. 0490C] C reads *ex*, “from.”] [Note: [Col. 0490C] C reads *eorumque*, “and their.”] [Note: [Col. 0490C] C reads *sustinet*, “supports”; D, *sustinent*, “support.”].

We also judged that the following point must be noted with no less care [Note: [Col. 0490C] C reads *minima*, “least.”], lest we be deceived in recognizing the first month. For nearly the whole error of the paschal discrepancy arises from this, that the beginning of the period is not understood [Note: [Col. 0490C] These four immediately preceding words are absent in A.]. When Almighty God commanded that this most sacred solemnity be celebrated by the children of Israel, who were being liberated from Egyptian slavery, he said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, in the Book of Exodus [Note: [Col. 0490C] Exodus 12:2.]: “This month shall be the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year.”

And again in the same place [Note: [Col. 0490C] Ibid., verse 18.]: “In the first month,” he says, “on the fourteenth day of the month, in the evening [Note: [Col. 0490C] Thus C and D; perhaps more correctly than the others, which read *vesperum*, “evening” in a different form.] you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the same month, in the evening.”

In Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0490C] Deuteronomy 16:1.] the same lawgiver Moses also admonishes the people concerning this matter, saying: “Observe the month of new fruits and the first month of spring, so that you may keep the Passover to the Lord your God, for in this month the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt by night” [Note: [Col. 0490C] A reads “at night.”]. By such great divine authority it became clear that the paschal feast ought to be celebrated in the first month, from the fourteenth day, in the evening, until the twenty-first.

But since it is not clearly stated there from what point this month takes its beginning or where it ends, those venerable [Note: [Col. 0490C] A and C add this word.] 318 bishops mentioned above, diligently investigating the observance of ancient custom handed down from holy Moses, as is related in the seventh book of the *Ecclesiastical History*, said that the new moon occurring from 8 March through 5 April [Note: [Col. 0490C] C reads “on the Nones of April.”] constitutes the beginning of the first month; and that the fourteenth moon should be carefully sought from 21 March through 18 April [Note: [Col. 0490C] C reads “to be investigated.”]. Since the moon does not revolve at an equal rate with the course of the sun [Note: [Col. 0490C] C reads: “because it does not move equally with the course of the sun,” etc.], it catches up with the occurrence of the vernal equinox over such a span of days [Note: [Col. 0490C] A reads “does not follow.”], which, according to the opinion of all Easterners, and especially of the Egyptians, who are more skilled than anyone in calculation, is specifically marked from 21 March.

Even if [Note: [Col. 0490C] Let this decree of Dionysius—or rather of the Council of Nicaea—be noted, against the doctrine of Scaliger, Calvisius, and similar calendar-makers, who think it unlawful to celebrate Pascha on moon XV. For when moon XIV falls on a Saturday, on 21 March, Pascha is celebrated on the following day. This can occur only with lunar cycle or golden number XVI, and with solar cycle 3, 20, or 25. Thus it occurs four times in the entire Victorian period: in the years of Christ 72, 319, 414, and 509, which belong to the first period; in the second period, in the years of Christ 604, 851, 1041, and 1136. Accordingly, it occurs once in Cyril’s nineteen-year cycle and likewise once in the Dionysian cycle. In the latter, it occurs in its seventy-third year, which is the year of Christ 604. PETAV.] the fourteenth moon should fall on a Saturday—which is clearly seen to occur once in ninety-five years—the same holy synod unambiguously established that Pascha must be celebrated on the following Sunday, that is, on 22 March, with moon XV. In every possible way it thus admonished that no one should seek the fourteenth moon of the paschal feast before 21 March, since it was established that this belongs not to the first month but to the last.

Nor did we think this should be passed over [Note: [Col. 0490D] This is a noteworthy passage. From it we learn that in Dionysius’s time there were some who confined the lunar month to thirty days, which was especially the conviction of the ancient Greeks, as we demonstrated in Book I of *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 7. PETAVIUS.]: those are greatly mistaken who, thinking that the moon completes the course of its circle in periods of thirty days, count twelve lunar months as 360 days, to which they add five days, called intercalary by the ancients, so that the solar year may appear to be completed. Careful investigation of the truth has shown that in two lunar cycles not sixty days but fifty-nine should be counted. Consequently, the total of twelve lunar months is 354 days, to which the Egyptians add the annual epacts, that is, eleven days, so that the lunar measurement may finally be brought into agreement with the solar reckoning [Note: [Col. 0491C] C reads “dimension.”].

That this is entirely true and certain is confirmed by the judgment of the Fathers cited above, who, following this Egyptian calculation, handed down the observance of the fourteenth moons of the paschal feast. But some, ignorant of such precision—or rather of such an ordinance—while seeking other bases for calculation [Col. 0491B] [Note: [Col. 0491C] C reads “require.”], depart from the path of truth [Note: [Col. 0491C] C reads “departed.”].

Hence it often happens [Note: [Col. 0491C] There is no doubt that those whom Dionysius criticizes here followed astronomical tables and took account of the *proēgēsis* (προήγησις), the lunar advance. In the year of Christ 325, golden number III, the mean astronomical new moon fell on 30 March, Tuesday, at 23:34 from midnight on the Regiomontan horizon. Thus the paschal new moon [Col. 0491D] was on 31 March; on that day the mean full moon fixed by the Council of Nicaea occurred on 14 April, Wednesday, at 17:56. The limit was therefore fixed on 13 April, which was then moon XIV. In the year 534, however, with the same lunar cycle III, the mean new moon at Regiomontanus fell on 30 March, Thursday, at 13:31, and the full moon on 14 April, Friday, at 7:53. But because 534 is the second year after a leap year, and the preceding year was likewise close to it, six hours being subtracted from the later date, if it had retained the same position in the Julian four-year cycle as the earlier one, the new moon would have occurred at 7:31; thus the *proēgēsis* amounted to approximately sixteen hours in two hundred years. Accordingly, the astronomical lunar new moon fell on 31 March and the fourteenth moon on 12 April. This was why some in Dionysius’s time thought that moon XV was the moon which in the age of Nicaea had been XIV. They should not therefore be censured except insofar as, by private authority, they weakened the civil and ecclesiastical observance. Otherwise they were correct in their astronomical calculation of the moon itself, although their *akribeia* (ἀκρίβεια), their precision, was less relevant to the Church’s paschal rite. PETAVIUS.] that, as the often-mentioned Fathers place the fourteenth moon, these men suspect it to be the fifteenth, and proclaim that what is the twenty-first is the twenty-second.

But we, who cherish the love and care of the Christian religion, must in no way depart from the constitution of so many pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0492C] We supply these four words from C and D, since Petavius and Bucherius omitted them. The latter also adds: “IN no way,” etc.]; rather, we ought to preserve with the most sincere devotion the paschal rule established by them [Note: [Col. 0492C] Thus we write from B, C, and D instead of *observatione*, which appears in the printed editions.].

It is not difficult to show how greatly we rely upon the authority of these Fathers in the Churches spread throughout the whole world, since the holy council that met at Antioch [Note: [Col. 0492D] The printed editions incorrectly read “at Nicaea” here, which conflicts both with the sense and with manuscripts B, C, and D, from which we restore the correct reading.] not long afterward judged that the definition which they had first issued concerning the calculation of Pascha [Col. 0491C] [Note: [Col. 0492D] Thus B and D. Others read *protulerant*, “had issued.”] must in no way be violated.

Finally, in the holy canons, under title seventy-nine—which is the first canon of the Council of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0492D] This first canon of the Council of Antioch is canon LXXX in the *Code of the Canons of the Universal Church* edited by Christoph Justellus.]—the following is expressly found:

“We decree that all who dare to dissolve the definition of the holy and great council assembled at Nicaea in the presence of the most devout and venerable emperor Constantine concerning the saving solemnity of Pascha [Col. 0492A] are to be excommunicated and expelled from the Church” [Note: [Col. 0492D] B and C read “we decreed.”], “provided that they persist contentiously [Note: [Col. 0492D] Thus C. Others read “contentious.”] against what has rightly been decreed. Let this be said concerning the laity. But if any of those who preside over a Church—whether bishop, presbyter, or deacon—after this definition should attempt, for the subversion of peoples and the disturbance of Churches, to gather separately and celebrate Pascha with the Jews, the holy synod has judged him from this point onward alien to the Church [Note: [Col. 0492D] This word is absent in C.], since he would become a cause of corruption and disturbance not only to himself but to many. It not only removes such men from the ministry, but those also [Note: [Col. 0492D] C reads “those men.”] who afterward attempt to communicate [Note: [Col. 0492D] C reads “by communication.”] with one condemned in this way are condemned [Note: [Col. 0492D] C reads “are to be condemned.”] and deprived of every external honor which the holy rule and the priesthood of God [Col. 0492B] had granted them.”

The venerable Pope Leo, prelate of the apostolic see, pronounces similar things [Note: [Col. 0492D] Leo, Letter 55 to the Empress Pulcheria. There Saint Leo does not deal with paschal decrees, but with diocesan boundaries which Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, wished to alter. Read the letter. BUCHERIUS.], saying: “Against the statutes of the ancestral canons, which many ages ago were founded in the city of Nicaea by spiritual decrees, no one is permitted to undertake anything; so that if anyone should wish to decree something different, he should diminish himself rather than corrupt those statutes. If these are preserved inviolate, as they ought to be, by all pontiffs, there will be peace and firm concord throughout all the Churches.”

And again: “In all ecclesiastical matters,” he says, “we obey those laws which the Holy Spirit established, through 318 bishops, for the peaceful observance of all priests, so that even if many more should decide to establish something different from what they established, whatever differs from the constitution of those men must be held in no regard.”

[Col. 0492C] We believe that sufficient warning has been given to everyone that henceforth the most sacred Pascha must not be celebrated in any other way than that established by the holy Fathers. If anyone should perhaps, with an obstinate mind, despise the testimony of so many priests, he will also find equivalent testimony briefly reported in ecclesiastical history; and from the accounts of many pontiffs, especially of the blessed Athanasius, whom we mentioned above, he will learn that these same things were widely known.

The same matter is attested by the letter of Saint Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, addressed to the same Pope Leo concerning this very paschal question. When we translated it from Greek some years ago, we took care to append it to this work. We have also added the arguments discovered through Egyptian ingenuity, by which, if they should perhaps be unknown, the paschal headings [Note: [Col. 0493A] By the word “headings,” Dionysius means those eight columns of which his cycle consists. In his book *On the Reckoning of Time*, Bede calls them at one point “verses,” chapter 45; at another “orders,” chapter 46; “lines,” chapter 48; “limits,” chapter 60; and “headings,” as in chapter 59: “In the seventh heading,” he says, “of the nineteen-year cycle, the Sunday of Pascha is included.”] can easily be found—that is, what year it is from the incarnation of the Lord, what the indiction is, what the lunar or nineteen-year cycle is, and whatever else is sought by a similar abbreviated calculation [Note: [Col. 0494A] C reads “of a similar calculation”; C reads “are sought”; the Rheims manuscript, “will be sought.”]. May divine grace deign to preserve your blessedness, who pray for us.

The preface ends here [Note: [Col. 0494A] With these words the preface concludes in manuscripts Rheims 298 and Colbert 1020.].

# THE NINETEEN-YEAR CYCLE OF DIONYSIUS

[Col. 0493]

Here begins the nineteen-year cycle, which the Greeks call the *Enneacaidecaeteris*, established by the holy Fathers, in which you will find the fourteenth paschal moons at all times without any error—provided only that you remember for each year which lunar cycle and which nineteen-year cycle is in effect. For at present it is the third indiction, in the consulship of the younger Probus; it is the thirteenth nineteen-year cycle and the tenth lunar cycle [Note: [Col. 0493C] This heading, in the same order and words, is found after Dionysius’s preface in the manuscripts just mentioned and in the Paris manuscript, which Petavius shows that he used in volume II of *On the Reckoning of Time*, p. 889. Of these, only the Colbert manuscript exhibits Dionysius’s cycle itself beginning with the year of Christ 532; we have therefore compared it here with the Digby manuscript.].

[Note: [Col. 0493] The following ornament represents Dionysius’s *Nineteen-Year Cycle*. Notes are anchored within this ornament. These notes can be viewed as a block by double-clicking the note icon that follows the ornament icon.]

[Note: [Col. 0493D]]

**b** Dionysius cited this year not only in the heading of his cycle but also in Letter 2, using the same characters by which this book is marked. The words of the letter are these: “Who can doubt that, after the year had passed, in the third indiction, the fourteenth paschal moon was on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, that is, on 24 March?” Scaliger unjustly accuses Dionysius of error here: “Behold,” he says, “in those words cited above he says that in the year of Christ 525, indiction III, the paschal limit fell on 24 March, although it was actually 23 March.” Book II of *On the Correction of the Calendar*, p. 156.

Petavius defends Dionysius in Book II of *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 68, p. 230, where he says: “In criticizing Dionysius, Scaliger is greatly mistaken. Dionysius thoroughly observed the Nicene cycles and golden numbers, and did not recognize the lunar advance. In cycle 14, with golden number XIII, the fourteenth paschal moon falls on 24 March, since the new moon is on 11 March, to which day it is permanently attached, even though in Dionysius’s time the astronomical new moon had moved to 10 March.” I confess that I cannot understand how cycle 14 can be joined with golden number XIII in these words.

**c** In this year Dionysius wrote the letter commonly numbered 2, addressed to Boniface, concerning the reckoning of Pascha. Its words, repeated by Marianus Scotus under the year 526 and generally not sufficiently understood, receive illumination from this table and in turn illuminate it; they show that the table was before Dionysius’s eyes when he wrote the letter in question. “Let us show,” he says, “the example of the present year. The indiction is IV, the lunar cycle XI, and the nineteen-year cycle XIV; and because it is the sixth year of the *ennead*, it must be an embolismic year.” Compared with the table, this passage clearly shows at once what the lunar cycle and the nineteen-year or paschal cycle are and how they differ. Scaliger wrote almost ridiculously about this distinction in Book II of *On the Correction of the Calendar*, p. 145; Petavius, William Lang, Noris, and others have already noted this.

**a** Bede recalls this year with its characters from Dionysius’s cycle in his book *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45, in these words: “Since, therefore, in the second year of the cycle which Dionysius first wrote, the five-hundred-thirty-third year from the incarnation of the Lord was completed, it is plainly, according to the conjunction of the heavenly bodies, the year in which He deigned to become incarnate. For this second year of the nineteen-year cycle is the eighteenth year of the lunar cycle; it has XI epacts, V concurrent days of the week, and the fourteenth moon of Pascha on 25 March [‘the eighth day before the Kalends of April’].”

# PASCHAL ARGUMENTS

Here begin the arguments concerning the paschal headings, investigated with Egyptian ingenuity, so that they may indicate the present [Note: [Col. 0497A] This is the heading as it appears in the Digby manuscript. We thought its wording should be retained, especially because in publishing these arguments, as well as Dionysius’s cycle itself, we chiefly followed that manuscript. The Cottonian and Rheims manuscripts differ little from it, except that the latter expressly attributes these arguments to Dionysius. We therefore add his words: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: Here begin the arguments of the Greeks concerning the paschal headings, investigated with the ingenuity of the Egyptians, which Dionysius, most holy abbot of the city of Rome, endowed with elegant knowledge of both languages, namely Greek and Latin, composed and wrote.” Dionysius himself claims them at the end of the preface to his cycle in these words: “We have also added the arguments discovered through Egyptian ingenuity, by which, if they should perhaps be unknown, the paschal headings can easily be found—that is, what year it is from the incarnation of the Lord, what the indiction is, what the lunar or nineteen-year cycle is, and so forth.” Ceolfrith mentions the same arguments in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 22. After praising Dionysius’s nineteen-year cycles, he adds: “As these approach their end, there is today such an abundance of calculators that even in our Churches throughout Britain there are many who, having committed to memory those ancient EGYPTIAN ARGUMENTS, can easily extend paschal cycles through any periods of time.” Bede’s preface to the booklet *On the Arguments of the Moon* explains the sense in which the word “argument” is used here as follows: “An argument is a swift proof of general matters, which establishes confidence in a doubtful matter; and *argumentum* is so called as an indication of an acute mind, or as the invention of an acute mind. An argument and an argumentation differ in this respect: an argument briefly sets out the subject at the beginning of a book, whereas argumentation establishes confidence in assertions in a disputation.” Bede also partly added Dionysius’s paschal arguments to his own nineteen-year cycles under the title “Canons of the lunar nineteen-year cycles”; but they were enlarged, abridged, altered in many respects, and adapted to the reckoning of his own time, so that they deserve to be called Bedean rather than Dionysian. Charles du Fresne, in his *Selections for the Illustration of the Paschal Chronicle*, no. 24, p. 481, presents “the Egyptian arguments” mentioned by Dionysius in his letter to Petronius and by Victorius in his paschal canon. But either he himself was deceived by this title, or at least he sold smoke to the reader. For under it he published nothing other than a calculation based on those arguments, showing how one might determine on which weekday the fourteenth paschal moon falls in each year—and even that only for the first three years of the fourth nineteen-year cycle. We confidently believe that our Digby manuscript has a better right to this title, for this reason among others: we have not yet seen anything cited from Dionysius’s arguments by ancient writers that is not found in them exactly. See *History of the Dionysian Cycle*, § [lacuna] 0, and the notes appended to the individual arguments.].

[Col. 0497]

## FIRST ARGUMENT

[Note: [Col. 0497A] This argument, with the example of the year of Christ 771, occurs in Bede’s *Book on the Reckoning of Computation*, chapter 18, volume I of the works, folio 515; and with the example of the year 944 in *The Arguments of the Moon*, in the same work, folios 206 and 208. From this one may infer that it was written in this form not by Bede but by some younger author of the tenth century. The form found among the lunar canons, p. 373, adapted to the year 703, is more correctly attributed to Bede. Let us therefore hear Bede here as though he were Dionysius’s interpreter: “If you wish to know what year it is from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, find out how many orders of indictions there have been—for example, forty-six in the fifth year of the reign of the emperor Tiberius. Multiply these by fifteen; the result is 690. Add twelve regular years, because, according to Dionysius, the Lord was born in the fourth indiction—for example, in the present case 1; the result is 703. These are the years from the Lord’s birth.”]

## On the Years of Christ

[Col. 0497A]

If you wish to know what year it is from the Incarnation of [Col. 0498A] our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0497A] That is, once the number of indictions is known.], calculate fifteen times thirty-four [Note: [Col. 0497A] There had been that many cycles of indictions, to put it in Bede’s terms—that is, the complete cycle of indictions had been continued backward so many times and had returned to its starting point within the period from Christ’s birth to A.D. 525.], making 510; always add twelve regular units [Note: [Col. 0498A] For that many years remained from the cycle of indictions, which had begun three years before Christ’s birth, before the first complete cycle of indictions after Christ’s birth began. The following passage, found in manuscript Rheims 298 under the title “On the Years of Christ,” helps to explain this place:

“Dionysius adds twelve regular units here because, when the Incarnation took place, three years of that indiction had elapsed; and therefore, so as not to disturb the order of the indictions, he did not assign the twelve remaining years of the indiction to the number of the indiction, but called them regular units, because they are shown to correct the reckoning of the years of the Lord. And this number of the years of the Lord is investigated by means of the indictions, because both wise and foolish people know the indictions.”], making 522; [Col. 0499A] add also the indiction of whatever year you wish—for example, the third, in the consulship of Probus the Younger—and altogether there are 525 years.
