These are the years from the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0499D] The example is taken from the year of Christ 525, as though it were the present year, and is consistently retained in the subsequent paschal arguments. It clearly reveals the time at which these writings were composed—namely, precisely when Dionysius gave Petronius his preface, or letter, on the Reckoning of Easter. For in this letter he shows that six years still remained in the last, that is, the fifth, cycle of the blessed Cyril (A.D. 531). Indeed, in the same letter Dionysius describes, according to his established practice, the method of the cycle recently composed by him, together with that of the arguments appended to it, in the words quoted shortly before. From this you may recognize not only the γνησιότης [authenticity] of Dionysius’s paschal arguments but also the completeness of our Digby manuscript. Certainly, among such a large number of witnesses, no other could be found that corresponded so well with everything Dionysius reports about his paschal writings and the other ancient authors report about the same works. In the others, both different computational examples and other alterations occur.].

## ARGUMENT II

[Note: [Col. 0500B] This argument, omitting the example of the year 525, appears in Bede’s Arguments on the Moon, vol. I of his Works, col. 206, and, with the example of the year 771, in the book On the Reckoning of Time, chapter 18, col. 516; likewise, with the example of the year 775, in the Lunar Canons, p. 373.]

### On the Indiction

If you wish to know which indiction it is—for example, in the consulship of Probus the Younger—take 525 years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0500B] In the Cottonian manuscript 588 is read here; but the same hand has written 525 above that number. From this one may infer that the English calculator, toward the end of the seventh century, copied these Arguments from the book of Dionysius and adapted them to the reckoning of his own time. It is sufficient to have noted this once, since the same practice can be observed in nearly all the other examples of that manuscript [Col. 0500C], although at times, through negligence, only Dionysius’s numbers have been retained.]. Always add 3; the total is 528. Divide this by 15; 3 remain. It is the third indiction. If nothing remains, it is the fifteenth indiction.

## ARGUMENT III

[Note: [Col. 0500C] Bede mentions this third argument in On the Reckoning of Time, chapter 45, in these words:

“To discover how many lunar epacts there are, Dionysius orders one properly to take the years of the Lord, divide them, multiply them, and divide them again, but to subtract or add nothing; for, since the epacts begin in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, they did not require anything to be added to or subtracted from the years of the Lord, with which they had begun, in order to find their position.”

Compare the Arguments on the Moon, vol. I of his Works, col. 207, and On the Reckoning of Computation, chapter 18, col. 516.]

### On the Epacts

If you wish to know how many [Note: [Col. 0500C] This is how the Cottonian manuscript reads, and we give it preference here. In the Digby manuscript, perhaps through a copyist’s error, it reads: “what year it is.”] epacts there are—that is, lunar additions—take the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, however many there have been: 525. Divide these by 19; 12 remain. Multiply by 11; the result is 132. [Col. 0500A] Divide these again by 30; 12 remain. There are twelve lunar additions.

[Another computation [Note: [Col. 0500C] These words indicate that this new method of computation, which is also found in Bede’s book On the Reckoning of Computation, chapter 18, col. 516, was not transmitted by Dionysius but was added by a later calculator. The Cottonian manuscript confirms this, since it omits the words enclosed in brackets.].—Compute from the first year up to whatever year you wish—for example, the tenth year. Always leave out 1; 9 remain. Multiply by the annual epacts, nine times eleven, and you will have nine elevens, 99. Divide these by 30—that is, three thirties, 90; 9 remain. The ninth is the epact of the nineteen-year cycle. Thus in the eleventh year: leave out one, 10 remain; ten elevens make 110. Divide these by 30; 20 remain. The twentieth lunar epact will belong to the eleventh year of the nineteen-year cycle. In this abbreviated fashion you will calculate all nineteen years.]

## ARGUMENT IV

[Note: [Col. 0500D] This argument on the concurrent days, with only Dionysius’s example from the year 525 omitted, is repeated in Bede’s Arguments on the Moon, vol. I of his Works, col. 208; in the Lunar Canons, p. 373; and in On the Reckoning of Computation, chapter 18, col. 516. Dionysius is explicitly credited with it in On the Reckoning of Time, chapter 45, p. 154, in these words:

“If we wish to know the solar additions, that is, the concurrent days of the week, Dionysius orders the years of the Lord to be taken; and he teaches that, after adding their quarter, four regular units must always additionally be added, and that the result must finally be divided by 7.”

Bede also gives the reason for this rule: “For there were five concurrent days in the year in which the Lord was born; and, so that the fixed sequence of the computation might proceed, the calculator necessarily had to append the four that preceded them.”]

### On the Concurrent Days

If you wish to know the solar additions—that is, the concurrent days of the week—take however many years there have been from the Incarnation of the Lord, for example 525; always add the third indiction and one quarter of the years that have elapsed—that is, now 131—which together make 656. Add 4 to these; the result is 660. Divide these by 7; 2 remain. Two are the solar epacts, that is, the concurrent days of the week, according to the indiction stated above, in the consulship of Probus the Younger.

[Another recently discovered method, which I have better explained by setting it out briefly [Note: [Col. 0501C] This was added by a later calculator around A.D. 581. It is absent both from the Cottonian manuscript and from Bede’s Lunar Canons, p. 373; and in the Digby manuscript itself it seems not to have been copied in full.]. Compute in a similar way from the year following the consulship of our lord Tiberius the Younger Augustus, except that at the end, where the calculation above has four added, you should now add 1 instead of 4.]

## ARGUMENT V

[Note: [Col. 0501C] Bede mentions this fifth argument in On the Reckoning of Time, chapter 45, and gives its rationale in these words:

“Dionysius himself, in a certain way silently, shows us in the Paschal Arguments that he wrote what we are saying. For, to discover which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, he orders the years of the Lord to be taken and, before dividing them by nineteen, commands that one be added, indicating that, when the Incarnation took place, one year of the nineteen-year cycle had already been completed.”

See also the Lunar Canons, vol. I, col. 373, and On the Reckoning of Computation, chapter 18, col. 516. Petavius corrects Scaliger’s inept criticism of this rule in book II of On the Doctrine of Time, chapter 68, p. 231.]

### On the Nineteen-Year Cycle

If you wish to know which year it is of the cycle of 19 years, [Col. 0501B] take the years of the Lord—for example, 525—and always add 1; the result is 526. Divide these by 19; 13 remain. It is the thirteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle. If nothing remains, it is the nineteenth [Note: [Col. 0501C] Read “nineteenth,” not “ninth.”].

## ARGUMENT VI

[Note: [Col. 0501C] Concerning this sixth argument Bede continues in On the Reckoning of Time, [Col. 0501D] chapter 45:

“Likewise, to learn which year of the lunar cycle it is, Dionysius advises taking the years of the Lord, always subtracting two, and then dividing by nineteen, so that, once the two years that then remained have been removed, he might divide the rest of the calculated years by the nineteenth part and retain whatever remained.”

The argument itself, with only Dionysius’s example omitted, is read in Bede’s book On the Reckoning of Computation, chapter 18, col. 516; but not without errors that disturb the sense and can be corrected from these very words of Dionysius.]

### On the Lunar Cycle

If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is, contained within the nineteen-year cycle, take the years of the Lord—for example, 525—and always subtract 2; 523 remain. Divide these by 19; 10 remain. It is the tenth lunar cycle of the nineteen-year cycle. Whenever nothing remains, it is the nineteenth.

## ARGUMENT VII

### On the Fourteenth Moon in the Month of March

[Col. 0501C] If you wish to know in which years of the nineteen-year cycle the paschal fourteenth moon falls in the month of March, you will find the seven years written above in March: years 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 16, and 18. You will calculate the remaining twelve with certainty in April, according to the rule appended below.

## ARGUMENT VIII

[Note: [Col. 0501D] This argument of Dionysius is repeated in Bede’s Lunar Canons, vol. I of his Works, p. 374, and adapted to a later period. We shall quote its wording, so that each may illuminate and correct the other:

“If you wish to know when the bissextile day occurs, take the year of the Lord, as the present year is 688. Divide it by 4. If nothing remains, it is a bissextile year; but if 1, 3, or 2 remain, it is not a bissextile year. And lest some obscurity of error perhaps arise for you, throughout the entire computation that you conduct, if nothing is left over, know that it is the same computation by which you are proceeding.”]

### On the Bissextile

If you wish to know when the bissextile day occurs, take the years of the Lord—for example, 525. Divide these by 4. If nothing remains, it is a bissextile year. If 1, 2, or 3 remain, it is not a bissextile year. Lest some obscurity of error perhaps arise for you, throughout the entire computation by which you proceed, if nothing is left over, recognize that it is the same computation by which you are proceeding—for example, if you are dividing by 19 and nothing is left over, it is 19; if by 15, it is 15; and if by 7, it is 7.

## ARGUMENT IX

[Note: [Col. 0502C] This ninth argument is separated in the Cottonian manuscript from the preceding material by certain intervening matter that has no relevance here; but here, as elsewhere, we follow the Digby manuscript. That it belongs to Dionysius is proved by the example employed in it. For the third indiction, Easter celebrated on March 30, and the twentieth moon are features that correspond only to the year XIII in the Dionysian cycles prefixed to the final cycle of Cyril—that is, to A.D. 525, the year in which, as is clear from the preceding material, Dionysius wrote his Arguments.]

### On the Paschal Moon in March

[Col. 0502B]

If you wish to know what the moon is at the paschal feast, when Easter is celebrated in the month of March, count the months from September through March; there are 6. Always add 2 regular units to these; there are 8. Add the epacts—that is, the lunar additions—of whatever year you wish, for example, of the third indiction [Note: [Col. 0502C] This third indiction corresponds to the year of Christ from which the examples of nearly all the Arguments are taken, 525, as does the celebration of Easter on March 30. See the first cycle, which is Cyril’s final cycle. In the Cottonian manuscript the passage reads: “The first indiction, 14, and the day of the month on which Easter is celebrated, that is, March 29, together make 51; subtract 30, and 21 remain. The twenty-first moon is on the day of the Lord’s resurrection.” These features indicate the year of Christ 688.], 12; there are 20. And add the day of the month on which Easter is celebrated, that is, March 30; together there are 50. Subtract 30; 20 remain. The twentieth moon is on the day of the Lord’s resurrection.

### In April

But if we celebrate Easter in April, count the months from September through March; there are 7. Always add 2 to these; there are 9. Add the lunar epacts of whatever year you wish, for example, of the fourth indiction, [Note: [Col. 0502D] The Digby manuscript reads “third,” but this is plainly a copyist’s error. The whole example corresponds to the year 526, the fourth indiction. We have therefore not hesitated to substitute “fourth indiction.” In the Cottonian manuscript an example drawn from the year of Christ 689 is appended to this argument, in these words: “For example, the second indiction, 25; there are 34. And the day of the month on which we celebrate Easter, that is, April 11, which together make 45. Subtract 30; 15 remain. The fifteenth moon is on the day of the Lord’s resurrection.”], 23; these make 32. And add the day of the month on which we celebrate Easter, that is, April 19, which together [Col. 0503A] make 51. Subtract 30; 21 remain. The twenty-first moon is on the day of the Lord’s resurrection.

If you count from September through [Note: [Col. 0503D] Cottonian manuscript: “through December.”] December, always add three regular units in these four months; but in a bissextile year alone you will count only two regular units for the months stated above, and, instead of 31 days, you will take 32 in December at the end of each year [Note: [Col. 0503C] The Cottonian manuscript reads: “And by 31, one day, 31 in each year, etc.” The passage appears corrupt in both manuscripts; we leave its disentanglement to others.].

## ARGUMENT X

### On the Day of the Week of the Paschal Feast

If you wish to know which day of the week it is, count the days from January up to whatever month you wish—for example, to March 30 [Note: [Col. 0503C] This is the date on which Easter fell in the year of Christ 525, the 211th year of Diocletian, according to Cyril’s final cycle prefixed to the Dionysian cycle.]; the total is 89. Always add 1 to these; the result is 90. And always add the solar epacts—that is, the concurrent days of the week—of whatever year you wish, for example, 3, of the second indiction; together there are 92. [Col. 0503B] Divide these by 7; one remains: this is the Sunday of the paschal feast [Note: [Col. 0503C] The Digby manuscript reads “the Sunday Easter”; the Cottonian, “the Sunday of Easter.”]. In this way, by calculation, you will discover which weekday any day from the kalends of January through December 30 is, provided that you take together the one regular unit and the concurrent days, which always begin with the month of January.

## ARGUMENT XI

[Note: [Col. 0503C] The material appearing here after Argument X is read in the Digby and Cottonian manuscripts in the same way, except that in the latter the example from the year 675 is replaced by the year 688 or 689. The new example itself, from the year 675—a year otherwise not used by Dionysius—raises the suspicion that the Arguments in which it occurs were either added or at least altered by a later calculator [Col. 0503D]. Nor do they seem to be free of errors. Nevertheless, whatever the facts may be, we have thought it useful to transfer the material here in full, as it is found in the Digby manuscript, leaving to others the authority to judge and correct it.]

### On the Moon of the Earliest Easter

If you wish to know what moon it is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April (March 22) [Note: [Col. 0503D] It is well known that the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, or March 22, according to the practices of the Alexandrians preserved by Dionysius, Bede, and others, was the first, or earliest, day on which the paschal rites of any year could fall, just as the seventh day before the Kalends of May, or April 25, was the last and most remote. Bede says in the penultimate lunar canon:

“From the eleventh day before the Kalends of April through the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on whatever Sunday the moon occurs, you shall celebrate holy Easter in every way. Before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, even if the moon occurs, or after the seventh day before the Kalends of May, you shall in no way celebrate Easter.”

How the Alexandrians extended the final limit of Easter, which they had anciently fixed on April 21, to April 25 is shown by Bucherius in his Commentary [Col. 0504C] on Victor’s Paschal Canon, p. 104. Anyone wishing to learn more about the rationale and difference between the paschal limits according to the Latins and Alexandrians should consult Norisius’s dissertation On the Latin Paschal Cycle, p. 96. On that very day, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April (March 22), immediately following the spring equinox, the epacts were inserted. See Bede, On the Reckoning of Computation, chapter 14. Accordingly, what was learned from the investigated moon of that day was, according to Bede’s lunar canon, as follows:

“If you wish to know what the epact is, in whatever year you wish, calculate what the moon is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, and that moon itself will be the epact. For example, if the moon is 9 on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, it will itself be the epact; or whatever number you find the moon to have, that number will be its epact.”

The present argument therefore demonstrates the foundation of this computation of the epacts.], take the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ—for example, 675 [Note: [Col. 0504C] The Cottonian manuscript has 688.]. Divide these by 11; the result is 110. Divide by 30; 20 remain. The twentieth moon is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. If it is 7, it is the seventh; if one, the first.

## ARGUMENT XII

[Col. 0503C]

If you wish to know the weekday of the kalends of January in each year, take the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ—for example, 675 years. Subtract 1; 674 remain. Divide these by their fourth part, and add the fourth part that you have divided to 674; together they make 842. Divide these by 7; 2 remain. The second is the day of the kalends of January. If 5, it is the fifth weekday; if 1, Sunday; if nothing, Saturday [Note: [Col. 0504C] In the Cottonian manuscript this argument reads as follows:

“If you wish to know the weekday of the kalends of January in each year, take the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, 689. Subtract 1; 688 remain. Divide these by their fourth part, and add the part that you have divided to 688; together they make 860. Divide these by 7; 6 remain: the sixth day is the kalends of January. If 10, the fifth weekday; if 1, Sunday; if nothing, Saturday.”].

## ARGUMENT XIII

### On the Moon of the Kalends of January

[Col. 0503C]

If you wish to know what moon it is on the kalends of January, know which lunar cycle it is—for example, cycle 15. Keep 1 for yourself—that is, the very kalends of January—and multiply five times fifteen: they make 75. Add these to 1; the result is 76. Again multiply six times fifteen: they make 90. Add these to 76, and the sum of the numbers is 166. Divide these by 30; 16 remain. The sixteenth moon is on the kalends of January, and there are 16 points [Note: [Col. 0504D] The Digby manuscript has “points” in the plural. Here we follow the Cottonian manuscript. Likewise in Bede’s Lunar Canons, p. 373: “If you wish to know how many points each moon shines on a day,” etc. Compare col. 211. Indeed, in Argument XVI of the Digby manuscript itself it reads: “One point, however, is a quarter of an hour.”]. In this way you will always calculate through the nineteen lunar cycles and will discover without error what moon it is on the kalends of January.

But when you come to the seventeenth lunar cycle [Note: [Col. 0504D] Cottonian manuscript: “the sixteenth lunar cycle.”], and multiply seventeen times five above the kalends of January, making 85 [Note: [Col. 0504D] Cottonian manuscript: “80 days.”], if you divide by 60 and add that unit itself, the result is 86. Then multiply seventeen times six [Note: [Col. 0504D] Cottonian manuscript: “six times fifteen.”]; the result is 102. Add these to 86 [Note: [Col. 0504D] Cottonian manuscript: “87.”]; the result is 188. Divide that by 30; 9 remain. The ninth moon is on the kalends of January, and there are 26 points. You will do the same in the eighteenth and nineteenth cycles. But from the first lunar cycle through the sixteenth, do not divide by 60, [Col. 0504C] lest you fall into error.

## ARGUMENT XIV

### On Which Weekday the Fourteenth Moon Falls in the First Year of the Nineteen-Year Cycle

[Col. 0505A]

Here begins the calculation of how the weekday of the fourteenth paschal moon of each individual year [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Cottonian manuscript reads: “what weekday the fourteenth paschal moon was in each year.” We have followed the Digby manuscript, in which the word “is,” or something similar, must be understood or supplied.] may be discovered—that is, of the first nineteen-year cycle.

In the first year, since it has no lunar epacts, because, together with the eighteenth year of the preceding nineteenth cycle and its eleven epacts [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Digby manuscript reads “its eleven epacts.”], after one day has also been added by the Egyptians, they make 30—that is, a complete lunar month—and nothing remains from the epacts; and because in that year the fourteenth paschal moon falls in April, always keep 35 regular units in that year. Subtract 30, that is, the complete moon itself; 5 remain. On the fifth day from the kalends—that is, April 9—the fourteenth paschal moon occurs. Keep the 5 stated above; add the concurrent days of that same year, 4; the total is 9. Also add the regular units always assigned to April, 7; the total is 16. Divide these by 7—that is, twice seven, 14; 2 remain. The fourteenth paschal moon occurs on the second day of the week, and the Sunday of the paschal feast is on the twentieth moon.

In the second year.—The second year of the aforementioned cycle, from which the epacts of 11 begin. In that year the fourteenth paschal moon falls in March. Always keep 36 regular units for that year; always subtract the 11 epacts; 25 remain. On the twenty-fifth day from the kalends of March, which is April 8, the fourteenth paschal moon occurs. Keep the 25 stated above; add the concurrent days of that same year, 5; the total is 30. At the end of this month always add 4 regular units; divide these by 7—that is, seven fours, 28; 6 remain. The fourteenth paschal moon occurs on the sixth day of the week, and the Sunday of the paschal feast is on the sixteenth moon.

In the third year.—Again, in April, in the third year of the first cycle mentioned above. Always keep at the beginning of that month [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Cottonian manuscript omits the words “in that month.”] 35 regular units. Subtract the epacts of that year, 22; 13 remain. On the thirteenth day of the month, that is, April 13, the fourteenth paschal moon occurs. Keep these 13; add the concurrent days, 6; the total is 19. Always add the lower regular units for April, 7; the total is 26. Divide these by 7—three sevens, 21; 5 remain. The fourteenth paschal moon will be on the fifth day of the week, and the Sunday of the paschal feast on the seventeenth moon. In this way you will calculate each year from the first through the ninety-fifth.

Whenever the fourteenth paschal moon falls in March, keep 36 regular units at the beginning; subtract from these the epacts of whatever year you wish, add the concurrent days, and at the end always increase the total by 4 regular units. In April, however, always keep 35 at the beginning; from these, after subtracting the epacts mentioned above and adding the concurrent days of that year, increase the total at the end by 7 regular units. For you will calculate all the paschal arguments more easily [Note: [Col. 0505D] Cottonian manuscript: “more broadly.”] and more briefly.

The reader should also know this: whenever, in either of the two months mentioned above, the result in the first rule happens to be such that, after the epacts have been subtracted [Note: [Col. 0505D] Thus the Digby manuscript; but the Cottonian has “corresponds.”], more than 30 remain [Note: [Col. 0505D] Both manuscripts read this way; but perhaps one should read “after the epacts have been subtracted,” or “after subtracting the epacts.”], discard 30. If one, two, or more remain, that number of days of the month from the kalends of January is the date on which the fourteenth paschal moon falls. But when, after the epacts have been subtracted, less than 30 remain—for example, 20, or more or fewer—it is clear that, once in the nineteen years, the fourteenth paschal moon will be on April 30 [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Cottonian manuscript reads: “when it remains, that is, the fourteenth paschal moon occurs on that day of the month from the kalends. For if exactly 30 remain after the epacts have been subtracted, which clearly occurs once in fourteen years, it will be paschal on the thirtieth day from the kalends.”].

## ARGUMENT XV

### On the Day of the Equinox and Solstice

On the day when the Lord Jesus Christ was born according to the flesh from the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem, the day begins to grow. The first equinox is on March 25, on which day day and night are equal. On that same day Gabriel announces to the holy Mary, saying:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

On that day Christ also suffered according to the flesh. The second solstice is on June 24, when Saint John the Baptist was also born, after which the days begin to grow shorter. The second equinox is on September 24, on which day John the Baptist was conceived. From that point onward the day becomes shorter than the night, until the nativity of the Lord and Savior.

From March 25 to December 25, 271 days are counted. Therefore, according to the number of days, Christ our Lord was conceived on a Sunday, March 25, and was born on a Tuesday, December 20. Christ our Lord. From the day on which he suffered, there are 133 years [Note: [Col. 0506D] The Digby manuscript reads 30, plainly through a copyist’s error. But the numbers that follow also seem not to be free of error.], 3 months, which are 1,214 days. Thus, according to the number of days, it follows that he was born on a Tuesday and suffered on a Friday: born on December 25, he suffered on March 25. From the time Jesus Christ our Lord was baptized, there are 2 years and 90 days, making 820 days, with their bissextile days [Note: [Col. 0506D] That is, with the bissextile days included]. Thus he was baptized on January 6, a Thursday, and suffered, as I said above, on March 25, a Friday. Including the bissextile days, the total is 1,215 days, and from January 6 to March 25 there are 90 days.

## ARGUMENT XVI

### On the Reckoning of the Bissextile

It should not be believed, as some think, that the bissextile is made because of that day on which Joshua prayed that the sun should stand still, since that day both existed and passed away. Rather, it is called bissextile because one point is added to each month. One point, however, is a quarter of an hour. Four points make one hour; twelve points amount to three hours. Therefore, in four years, the three hours—which are twelve points—make one day; this is added to February when it has February 24, so that it has the same date on the following day. For example, if today is February 24, that day is added when the fourth year has been completed; nevertheless, the following day is also called February 24. And therefore it is called bissextile, because February has February 24 twice.

God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh. Therefore, so that this may be understood more fully, calculate how many hours one day contains [Note: [Col. 0507A] Digby: “calculate how many hours one day has”; Cottonian: “how many hours the days have,” with a division.], and divide them into seven parts; whatever remains from this is the bissextile. First calculate 300 days and how many hours they contain: ten times three hundred are 3,000. Again: twice three hundred are six hundred; [Col. 0508A] therefore in three hundred days there are 3,600 hours. Again: ten times sixty are 600, and twice sixty are 120. Therefore in sixty days there are 720 hours. Again: ten times five are 50, and twice five are 10. Behold, in five days you have 60 hours. Thus in a complete year of 365 days there are 4,380 hours, and as many again in the night; altogether, the days and nights of the entire year contain 8,760 hours.

Divide these into seven parts. First: seven thousand make 7,000; 1,760 remain. Again: seven times two hundred make 1,400; 360 remain. Again: seven times fifty make 350; 10 remain. Again: seven times one make 7; 3 remain. These three hours make one day in four years.

# LETTER OF PROTERIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO POPE LEO

[Note: [Col. 0507C] For the subject and date of Dionysius’s letter to Proterius, see book II of On the Doctrine of Time, chapter 64, p. 222. Uncertainty had arisen concerning Easter in the 171st year of the Diocletian era, A.D. 455; Proterius was consulted and replied to Saint Leo. Petavius.

[Col. 0507D] Sigebertus refers as follows in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 27, to this letter, written in Greek by Proterius and rendered into Latin by Dionysius:

“He translated from Greek into Latin the letter of Proterius of Alexandria, written to Pope Leo, concerning the celebration of Easter in the year of the Lord 455.”

That he appended the translation to his own paschal cycle is himself attested by these words near the end of his preface to Petronius:

“We have judged it appropriate to attach to this work the letter which we translated from Greek some years ago.”

Published by Petavius in the Appendix to his work On the Doctrine of Time, p. 871, and by Aegidius Bucherius in his Commentary on Victor’s Paschal Canon, p. 82, we have compared it with several manuscript copies and supplied and corrected it here and there, especially against the Bodleian manuscript F. N E. 3, 5; the Cottonian manuscript, in the Caligula A. 15 chest; and Digby 63. We shall designate the first of these by B, the second by C, and the third by D.]

[Col. 0507B]

To my most beloved lord, brother, and fellow priest Leo, Proterius sends greetings in the Lord.

Our most pious and faithful emperor Marcian recently addressed us in a venerable letter, in which he asserted that some people believed that the day of the paschal feast, which, with the Lord’s favor, is to be celebrated in the eighth indiction, had not been carefully written down. Yet he did not indicate this as though he had been moved by a personal concern, but because he had received a written communication from your holiness. He commanded that we investigate the matter carefully, applying an exceptionally fine examination that would contain great diligence and effort.

Therefore, I could not neglect the matter, but immediately undertook to examine it, since from the time when I received the memorandum of your reverence I had devoted the greatest care to this subject—now consulting legal books, now examining the principles laid down by the ancient teachers [Note: [Col. 0508D] C reads “containing the stated principles.”]—from which it is possible to investigate this kind of computation with greater precision.

I also took the hundred-year course of Easter, set out by our most blessed father and fellow bishop Theophilus, and ran through the whole of it. I found it so carefully and completely arranged that, whoever he may be, no one could in any way criticize or condemn the authority of this writing. For it would have been inconsistent with the character of a man so watchful and so dear to God, one also endowed with knowledge of the divine Scriptures, to have been able, in so great and necessary a matter, to err by neglecting the labor of careful investigation.

But perhaps, as your holiness writes [Note: [Col. 0508D] C and D read “wrote.”], it is the error of a faulty manuscript or [Note: [Col. 0508D] The word “writer,” inserted here in both printed editions, is absent from the manuscripts.] a copyist; and therefore we ought to transfer the day of that holy feast—God forbid [Note: [Col. 0508D] On the basis of all our manuscripts, we have substituted these two words for the reading in the printed editions, “which has passed away.”].

Let it rather be celebrated [Note: [Col. 0508D] Thus we read with C, instead of “is celebrated,” which appears in the printed editions.] as the hundred-year course of that same most blessed father and our fellow bishop Theophilus sets it out; for it agrees completely with the pages of the ancients, namely, on the day of the month Pharmuthi according to the Egyptians, which is April 24. We, the entire Egyptian region, and the whole East will likewise celebrate that day [Note: [Col. 0508D] D reads: “thus we shall celebrate the authority of that day.”], with God’s favor.

So that we should not be thought to write or wish to establish absolutely whatever seems to us, we have also inserted into this letter the reasons by which Your Holiness may perhaps judge that the truth of the Church of the Egyptians—which was the mother of this undertaking and carefully set it down in writing—ought not to be censured.

Long ago the Lord indicated the time of Passover through Moses, saying: “Keep the month of new growth,” declaring that this was the first; and again he says: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year; and you shall make Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month.” But the Lord who spoke these things through Moses, being the fullness of the Law, when he deigned to become human, on the fifth day of the week [Note: Thus all three of our manuscripts read, instead of “the fifth feria,” as in the printed editions], on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, eating the Passover with his disciples in the upper room, was shortly afterward betrayed by Judas; and on the following day, the fifteenth day of the moon—that is, Friday—he was crucified. Descending to the underworld and completing the dispensations of our salvation, he rose from the dead in the evening of the Sabbath, as Sunday was dawning; and it is clear that on that day the moon of the first month existed according to the Hebrews.

We Christians therefore seek at Passover not only the fourteenth day of the moon—for the Jews do this and have no festival—but also, with greater care, the day of the resurrection of our Redeemer, which is the seventeenth day of the moon of the aforesaid first month of new growth. If [Note: Petavius’s edition reads “which,” without sense and contrary to the testimony of all our manuscripts] the full moon always occurred in the same way [Note: The edition of Bucherius and manuscript D read thus, more correctly than Petavius’s edition, which here seriously disrupts the sense] on the fifth day of the week, when the Savior ate the Passover with his disciples, every ambiguity would be removed. But because the lunar cycle is unequal to the course of the sun, and the paschal fourteenth moon often falls on a Sunday, it is not possible to celebrate the feast then; nor can we break the fast on the preceding day, Saturday, when the moon is thirteen days old. The feast must be deferred to the following week, especially since within it we have the fifteenth moon, when, as the Apostle wrote, “Christ our Passover was sacrificed.”

For on the fourteenth moon of the first month, according to the Hebrews, as stated above, Jesus ate the typological Passover; but on the following Friday, the fifteenth moon, he was fastened to the cross for us as a slaughtered lamb; and on the evening of the Sabbath, as Sunday was dawning, on the seventeenth moon, he rose from the dead.

Therefore, since in the coming paschal solemnity, in the eighth indiction, the twenty-second day of the month Pharmuthi—which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, it is appropriate to defer the feast to the following week. For within it we have the three-day mystery, namely the fifteenth moon, when Christ was crucified, joined to the fourteenth; and also the sixteenth and the succeeding seventeenth. On the twenty-eighth day of the month Pharmuthi—which is the ninth day before the Kalends of May—we shall end the fast in the evening of the Sabbath. Then, on the following Sunday as it dawns, on the twenty-ninth day of that month Pharmuthi—which is the eighth day before the Kalends of May—we shall celebrate the feast with complete sincerity.

For in ancient times also, whenever the fourteenth moon fell on a Sunday, the feast was postponed to the following week, as is shown in the eighty-ninth and ninety-third years of the reign of Diocletian. Thus our most blessed Fathers are also declared to have acted at that time (in the year of Christ 373).

In the eighty-ninth year [Note: Saint Ambrose mentions both cases in his letter of the same subject to the bishops of Emilia. Diocletian’s eighty-ninth year began with Thoth fixed in the year of Christ 372. Therefore, in the following year, 373, while that same year of Diocletian was passing, controversy arose over Easter: the lunar cycle was XIII, the solar cycle XVIII, the dominical letter F, the paschal new moon fell on 2 March, Monday, and the fourteenth day on 24 March, Sunday. Therefore some celebrated at the term; the Catholics, however, on the last day of March. Damasus was then presiding over the Roman Church; the legitimate bishop of Alexandria was Peter, who had succeeded Athanasius, already dead since 371. Thus one must conjecture what Saint Proterius means when he says that Father and Bishop Anastasius was then still alive. Did he write “Athanasius” and, deceived by his own error, believe that the man who had died two years earlier was still living at that time? Petavius.]

of the reign of Diocletian, while our Father and bishop Athanasius, of blessed memory, was still alive [Note: We restore the name “Athanasius” from manuscripts B and D, instead of “Anastasius,” which appears in both printed editions. Aegidius Bucherius noticed that an error lay here; his note is: “Read ATHANASIUS, and learn that he could not have died before this year of Christ 373, 2 May—or, according to the unnamed chronographer cited by Scaliger in Eusebius, VII Pachon. See Petavius’s preceding note”], when the paschal fourteenth moon had fallen on the twenty-eighth day of the month Phamenoth—that is, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April—on a Sunday, the feast was transferred to the following week, so that the Lord’s Passover was celebrated on the fifth day of the month Pharmuthi, that is, on the day before the Kalends of April.

In the ninety-third year [Note: The year of Christ 377, lunar cycle XVII, solar cycle XXII, dominical letter A. The paschal term was Sunday, 9 April. It was therefore rightly celebrated on the sixteenth day of that month. Petavius] of the reign of the same Diocletian, when the paschal fourteenth moon had fallen on the fourteenth day of the month Pharmuthi—which is the fifth day before the Ides of April—and on a Sunday, the postponement was likewise made to the following week, so that the Lord’s Passover was solemnly celebrated on the twenty-first day of the month Pharmuthi—which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

In the one hundred and third year of the reign of the aforesaid Diocletian (in the year of Christ 387), when the paschal fourteenth moon was going to fall on the twenty-third day of Pharmuthi—which is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May—and on a Sunday, the following week was again chosen; and the Lord’s Passover is known to have been celebrated on the twenty-eighth day of that month Pharmuthi—which is the seventh day before the Kalends of May—because of the constricted time that was approaching.

Likewise, when in the one hundred and sixtieth year [Note: The year of Christ 444. See Book II of *On the Calculation of Time*, p. 221. Petavius] from the reign of Diocletian the paschal fourteenth moon fell on the twenty-third day of Pharmuthi—which is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May—and on a Tuesday, we remember that we celebrated the Lord’s Passover on the twenty-eighth day of that month Pharmuthi—which is the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

It is therefore necessary that in the two-hundred-and-fifty-fifth year [Note: This is how it is read in the editions of Petavius and Bucherius, which differ from the manuscripts no less than from one another. For B has “in the one-hundred-and-sixty-fifth year,” while D has “in the two-hundred-and-sixty-fifth year from Diocletian,” and so forth. But the characters mentioned by Proterius agree with none of these years. Hence Aegidius Bucherius adds in the margin: “Read 171, which is the common year of Christ 455, indiction VIII.” Petavius similarly says in his notes: “Write,” he says, “in the one-hundred-and-seventy-first”] from the reign of Diocletian, at the coming paschal feast of the eighth indiction, on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi—which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—when the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, the feast should appropriately be extended to the following week according to the preceding arrangement, so that we celebrate the Lord’s Passover on the twenty-ninth day of the month Pharmuthi—which is the eighth day before the Kalends of May—because of the constriction again approaching, just as our Fathers did when they postponed fourteenth moons falling on a Sunday.

For if, as I have said, the fourteenth moon repeatedly falls on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi—which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—and we celebrate Passover on that Sunday, we shall find that on the preceding day, Saturday, the twenty-first day of the same month—which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May—the moon is thirteen days old, and that it is not lawful then to end the fast. Passover is not eaten on the thirteenth moon. Therefore, since the fourteenth moon falls on Sunday, the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi—which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—and since it is not appropriate to fast on Sunday, because that is characteristic of the Manichaeans, it follows that we must proceed to the following week, within which, as we have said, we have both the fifteenth moon, when the Lord was crucified, and the sixteenth moon, together with the seventeenth moon, when he rose from the dead.

Thus, on the twenty-eighth day of Pharmuthi—which is the ninth day before the Kalends of May—we shall end the fast in the evening of the Sabbath according to custom, and on the following Sunday, the twenty-ninth day of that month—which is the eighth day before the Kalends of May—we shall celebrate the paschal feast.

We must also inform you of this: in the coming [Note: B should be corrected to read: “and in the coming one-hundred-and-ninety-eighth year.” This is the year of Christ 482. The lunar cycle was VIII, the solar cycle XV, and the dominical letter C. Therefore the paschal new moon was on 5 April at Nicaea, and the term was Sunday, 18 April, or the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. Passover therefore had to be extended to the seventh day before the Kalends, that is, to 25 April. Petavius.—Bucherius agrees. The Bodleian manuscript reads: “in the coming two-hundred-and-sixty-seventh year.”] two-hundred-and-sixty-fifth year of the reign of Diocletian, when the fourteenth moon again falls on the eighteenth day of Pharmuthi—which is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May—the Lord’s Passover will, God permitting, be celebrated on the twenty-eighth day of that month—which is the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

But some, perhaps ignorant of the subtleties of the paschal computation and led astray by Jewish fables, will think that we are moving into the second month if we extend the feast so far, asserting this—I do not know from where. For when the fourteenth moon of that month falls on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi—which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—how could we endure the accusation that we celebrate Passover in the second month? The Jews, because they do not know the Lord, do not know the time of Passover either. Hence they often depart from the first month and, to some extent, suppose that they celebrate Passover in the twelfth month [Note: Manuscripts B and D add the word “suppose”].

But our most blessed Fathers, establishing the nineteen-year cycle with greater precision—a cycle that cannot be violated—set down this nineteen-year computation as a kind of step, foundation, and rule. They did so not according to the Jews’ present ignorant and foolish practices [Note: Perhaps “calculations.” Bucherius], nor according to the supposed and fabricated wisdom of foreigners, but established by the grace of the Holy Spirit [Note: Manuscript B reads: “but by the grace of the Holy Spirit”]. In the revolution of the often-mentioned nineteen-year cycle they carefully recorded the paschal fourteenth moons.

These matters having been completed, we must also attend to the fact that those who absolutely determine the beginning of the first month’s lunar course from the twenty-fifth day of Phamenoth—which is the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—are greatly mistaken. They do so because the beginning of spring appears then to have been fixed with every care by those who were able to discover it; and, clearly according to the course of the sun, the equinox is known to occur on the twenty-fifth day of Phamenoth—which is the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

But the beginning of the first month according to the course of the moon must not be fixed absolutely from this equinox. Otherwise the moon’s entire cycle ought to agree with the sun’s cycle. Yet because it is certain to everyone who has understanding that the sun’s course by no means catches up with the moon’s extremely rapid motion, let us now, God permitting, briefly instruct the doubtful that we cannot in any way pass into the second month.

For if the beginning of the month were established at the equinox—that is, on the twenty-fifth day of Phamenoth, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—according to the course of the moon, it would be reasonable for some to think that we could pass into the second month. But now, because in the eighth indiction, which is to come, the fourteenth moon of the first month is found on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi—which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—it is certain that the beginning of that first month according to the moon’s course falls on the ninth day of Pharmuthi—which is the day before the Nones of April.

Therefore, since the fourteenth moon is found on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi—which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—when we celebrate the Lord’s Passover on the twenty-ninth day of that month Pharmuthi—which is the eighth day before the Kalends of May—we do not at all pass into the second month, since we unquestionably have the moon then twenty-one days old.

How, then, shall we run into the second month, when the beginning of the first month according to the course of the moon, as stated a little earlier, is on the ninth day of Pharmuthi—which is the day before the Nones of April—and the fourteenth moon occurs on the twenty-second day of that month, that is, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May? Once this has been made clear, it is certain that we do not in any way run into the second month when we celebrate the Lord’s Passover on the twenty-ninth day of Pharmuthi—which is the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

Let those who are in doubt in those regions learn through Your Holiness that we are celebrating Passover lawfully in the eighth indiction [Note: D reads “we shall celebrate”]. For this reason I have written [Note: D reads “written”], following here also the ecclesiastical formulas of the Fathers and taking from them the occasions for this discussion. For thus our predecessors [Note: So manuscripts B and D; the former has “my predecessors” instead. The editions of Petavius and Bucherius read “our forerunners”] also, whenever doubt arose, hastened to announce the matter so that the holy feast might be celebrated everywhere in harmony.

Even now, according to the ancient custom, we believe that this is proclaimed by the Lord in the churches: that there is one faith, one baptism, and one most sacred paschal solemnity, celebrated by all Christians everywhere in Christ Jesus our Lord, because in him “we live and move and have our being.”

We did not think it sufficiently certain to transfer this letter into the eloquence of the Latin tongue, lest perhaps those among us who speak Greek more readily [Note: This is how Petavius’s edition and the manuscripts read; we have therefore preferred to follow them rather than Bucherius, who reads “you” here], and who are no longer able to express these matters carefully [Note: The editions of Petavius and Bucherius incorrectly insert “for”; it disrupts the sense and is absent from the manuscripts], should injure the truth through an inarticulate and unsuitable mode of expression, one that perhaps could not be translated with the ardor and knowledge demanded by the subject.

Greet the fraternity that is with you. The fraternity that is with us greets you in the Lord.

And in another hand: “I pray that you may be well and remember us, my lord, most beloved and most longed-for brother” [Note: The final word, which is added in the manuscripts, was omitted by Petavius and Bucherius].

[Col. 0513]

[Note: If you wish to know why we have placed this letter, already copied in column 23, here again, see what we noted concerning the letter addressed to Petronius in column 483; the same judgment must be made concerning the present letter. Editor.]

## Letter of Dionysius on the Paschal Computation, Written in the Common Year of Christ 526 [Note: The fact that this letter was written in that year is proved by the chronological characters already noted above, and is confirmed by Bucherius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, p. 489; Noris, *On the Ravennate Cycle*, p. 200, and others. Although already published by Petavius and Bucherius, we collated it with two Cottonian manuscripts, Tiber. E. 4 and Calig. A. 15, with Digby 63, and with Bodleian F. N. E. 3, 5. We shall designate the first of these C1, the second C2, the third D, and the fourth B.] (C)

[Col. 0513A] Dionysius Exiguus sends greetings to the most highly revered lords Boniface, first notary, and Bono, second notary [Note: This word is absent from both Cottonian manuscripts].

Having long been urged by the holy and venerable Bishop Petronius, I was at last compelled to entrust to writing the rule of paschal observance. I had believed that every ambiguity and opposition arising from diversity would henceforth be removed—especially since I had taken the greatest pains to set forth the authority of the three hundred and eighteen holy bishops who assembled at Nicaea. In that venerable council they regularly established the nineteen-year cycle and recorded the fourteenth moons of paschal observance as immovable throughout all time according to the law of its revolution [Note: Both C manuscripts read thus. Petavius has “according to the law of his cycle”; Bucherius, “according to the law”].

But since, when a question concerning this matter arose, Your Holiness has now brought forth from the archive of the Roman Church writings of Paschasinus, the venerable bishop who is known to have presided over the holy Council of Chalcedon on behalf of the most blessed Pope Leo, writings sent to that same pope at the same time and agreeing with the holy Fathers by evident reasoning, we have inserted them into the present work so that we might also rely upon the testimony of this man, who by a manifest miracle confirms the paschal decrees of the venerable pontiffs [Note: B and D read “these”; Petavius and Bucherius, “to this work”].

Since his writings also mention common years and embolismic years, and since many people earnestly inquire into this computation, which is said to have descended from Hebrew tradition, wishing to know whether it appears to agree with this ancestral rule [Note: Others read “with the ancestral rule.” Bucherius; C1, C2, and B agree], we have thought it necessary to arrange this information also, in compressed form, so that it may not be shown to disagree in any respect.

Let us therefore understand that this same nineteen-year cycle always revolves within itself through an eight and an eleven. The number itself is expressed by eight and eleven. The eight-year period, then, which begins with the first nineteen-year cycle, namely the seventeenth lunar cycle, proceeds as follows: it has first and second years that are common, that is, shorter; a third embolismic, that is, longer; a fourth and fifth year likewise common; a sixth embolismic; a seventh common; and an eighth embolismic. Thus, in the eight-year period, five common years and three embolismic years are continually assigned.

A common year contains twelve lunar months, which produce 354 days. An embolismic year is shown to contain thirteen lunar months and 384 days.

The eleven-year period proceeds according to this rule [Note: Thus the Cottonian manuscript reads. The printed editions have “runs through”]. It begins with the ninth nineteen-year cycle, which is the sixth lunar cycle [Note: Thus Digby and Bodleian, from which we have corrected Petavius’s reading: “in the tenth year, lunar cycle…”]. Its first and second years are common, its third embolismic, its fourth and fifth common, its sixth embolismic, its seventh and eighth common, its ninth embolismic, its tenth common, and its eleventh embolismic. Thus the eleven-year period is completed by seven common years and four embolismic years.

The reason for the embolismic years is evidently this: they make good the deficiencies of the common years, so that the lunar course may be equalized with solar time. Although the moon traverses the solar cycle in each of its months, it cannot complete it in twelve of its own months [Note: Thus B and C. The printed editions read “it prevails”].

Indeed, in common years the moon is seen to fall eleven days short of the reckoning of the solar year. In embolismic years, however, the moon appears to exceed the same solar year by nineteen days [Note: This word is absent from D]. Therefore let us bring forward the years of the eight and the eleven according to the order of the aforesaid cycle, and we shall clearly prove that over eight years and eleven years the lunar course contends with the sun, when the moon gathers as many days as the sun has traversed.

In the eight-year period, we said that there are five common years and three embolismic years. Five times 354 makes 1,770 days [Note: C1 adds “days”], and three times 384 makes 1,152; together, therefore, they make 2,922 days.

Likewise, eight solar years, when reduced to a total—that is, eight times 365 and a quarter—also make 2,922 days.

In the same way, if you gather the years of the eleven-year period, which are seven common and four embolismic years, by the calculation we have given, you will find nearly the same total as that produced by eleven solar years, namely 4,014 [Note: These words are absent from B and both C manuscripts, but D retains them. C1 has inserted the following, though in a place belonging elsewhere, and referring to the present passage: “Let us therefore gather the eleven-year period by the solar and lunar course: seven common years and four embolismic years. Seven times 354 days make 2,478, and four [times 384 days, namely the embolismic years] make 1,536. Together they make 4,014. Likewise, let us calculate eleven solar years by the same method of reckoning. Eleven times 365 days and a quarter make 4,017 days and 18 hours. Therefore in the eight-year period [perhaps ‘in the eleven-year period’ should be read] the sun appears to surpass the moon by three days and 18 hours. That is why he said ‘you will find nearly the same,’ because he foresaw that there would be some difference, arising especially from the quarters.”].

This, then, is the reason for the embolismic years, as we said earlier: through their additions they compensate for the losses of the common years.

But now I shall show you the very beautiful and excellent arrangement of the nineteen-year cycle, by which you may henceforth remove any ambiguity, should one arise. Let no one be so overcome by excessive astonishment that, once the light of truth has been shown to him [Note: This is absent from C1], he does not rejoice and, abandoning the darkness of ignorance, immediately yield to so great a rational order.

From the fifteenth moon of the paschal feast of the preceding year, for example, to the fourteenth moon of the following Passover, a common year will have 354 days, and an embolismic year 384. But if one day more or less should occur, the error is evident.

The exception is the first year [Note: Dionysius’s sentence here is extremely perplexed and confused. Its meaning can be understood approximately as follows. Every common year consists of 354 days, while an embolismic year consists of 384. The first nineteen-year year alone must be excepted, for it contains only 353 days. Its first day is the fifteenth paschal moon of golden number XIX, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, or 17 April; its last day is the fourteenth paschal moon of golden number I, namely 5 April. Therefore 353 days belong to that year. For golden number XIX, in relation to the earlier epacts XVIII, adds not eleven days, as in the other years, but twelve; from these the epacts XXX, or 0—that is, none—are formed, corresponding to golden number I, as is demonstrated in Book IV of *On the Doctrine of Time*. Hence the lunar leap arises, when one day is suppressed and disregarded. Dionysius devised a wooden remedy for this difficulty: he ordered the same day to be counted twice. For the last day of that year, bearing golden number XVIII—that is, 17 April, or the fourteenth paschal moon of golden number XIX—is counted as the first day of the following year, which begins while golden number XIX is passing. Thus both days are counted fully: the former as 384, the latter as 354, as is clear from Dionysius’s diagram. Yet he is not consistent with himself, calling the same year at one point the last and at another the first. It has been demonstrated in Book VI of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 10, that the first year of the nineteen-year cycle is the one that begins with the fourteenth moon bearing golden number XIX, namely on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, and ends on the Nones of April; it has 354 days, as he explicitly asserts in the diagram. The second begins with the moon of golden number I, namely on 6 April, and ends on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, which is the fourteenth moon of golden number II. Thus the first year of the cycle, bearing golden number XIX, has epact XVIII; the second has 0, or XXX. But here Dionysius indicates the opposite and overturns his own position. For in the words “except the first year,” etc., he calls “first” the year that began at the Passover of golden number XIX and occupied approximately nine months, up to the end of December. When he then says that this same first year of the nineteen-year cycle proceeds from the last Passover’s fourteenth moon—that is, from the nineteenth year—he calls “last” the very year he had just called “first.” These statements are crude. Dionysius seems to have intended to use “first” and “second year of the cycle” for “first” and “second golden number. Petavius.—It is remarkable that so great an astronomer did not notice here the distinction so clearly emphasized by Dionysius himself between the lunar, or paschal and ecclesiastical, year and the solar, civil, specifically Roman, year. Dionysius teaches that the former, counted from one paschal term to the next, consists of 354 days, or 384 if it is embolismic; but he elsewhere acknowledges that the latter begins among the Alexandrians on 29 August and among the Romans on the following Kalends of January, and is completed in 365 days and approximately six hours. It was the former, not the latter, that he took pains to count from the fourteenth moon of the last Passover—that is, of the nineteenth year—to the fourteenth moon of the first. Conversely, he instituted the counting of the latter, the solar year, not the former, the lunar year, according to the Christian era. Because Petavius and certain other learned men who followed him failed to attend to this, they tried, from a misunderstanding of Dionysius’s words, incorrectly to extract the claim that Dionysius counted the years of Christ nearly a full year earlier than is customary today in our Christian era, namely from March or April preceding the beginning of our year. See the discussion, after others, by the distinguished former mathematician Georg Albert Hamberger, who, following Petavius’s view and relying on this very passage of Dionysius, argues at length and laboriously—but unsuccessfully—against Bede as though he were the author of the new era, in his dissertation *On the Origin and Author of the Christian Era*, Jena 1707, published edition, pp. 14 ff. But Dionysius’s complete disputed words should be understood and explained as follows: “Except the first [lunar] year of the aforesaid nineteen-year cycle”—adapted to nineteen solar and Julian years, and named from them—“which lunar or paschal year we count from the fourteenth moon of the Passover of the last, that is, nineteenth, solar year—which was Julian period 5244, Dionysian era 521—to the fourteenth moon of that same first solar year, which, placed at the head of Dionysius’s cycle, was the year 532 of the Incarnation, as Bede expressly testifies in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 47.” Thus the lunar or paschal year occupied the end of the preceding solar year and the beginning of the succeeding one; hence Dionysius’s words contain nothing crude or mutually contradictory].

of the aforesaid nineteen-year cycle, which we count from the fourteenth moon of the Passover of the last—that is, nineteenth—year to the fourteenth moon of that same first year [Note: Others read “we have caused.” Bucherius].

For this reason that last year, still retaining eighteen epacts—that is, lunar additions—assigns twelve days to the first year, rather than eleven, as is customary in the other years [Note: Petavius’s edition reads “it retains, first”; the reading retained here, from Bucherius, is supported by Digby and both Cottonian manuscripts]. And because the cycles revolve at the end of thirty days [Note: B reads “revolves”; D, “revolve”], no epact is placed at the beginning of the cycle itself; the second year, however, receives eleven epacts. Therefore, as we said, from the fifteenth moon of the first cycle to its end, there is no doubt that we find the prescribed number of days in common and embolismic years. If at some time the inexperience of calculators should explain the matter otherwise, this method of reckoning will expose the falsity of their reasoning.

And so that this may be understood more clearly, let us demonstrate it by the example of the present year. The indiction is the fourth [Note: We explained this passage in Book XII, chapter 3, at the end; there we also showed that a little later one should read “the year having passed, in the third indiction,” not “in the fifth,” as appeared in writings and print in Bede and had misled us. Thus this letter was written in the same Julian year as the earlier one. Petavius.—Petavius rightly judged that this should be read so, confirmed not only by Marianus Scotus under the year 526, where he cites Dionysius’s words, but also by all our manuscripts. Yet I do not understand how he can infer from this that this letter was written in the same Julian year as the earlier one, namely the preface to Petronius. For we have shown above by compelling arguments that this preface was written in the year of Christ 525, Julian year 570, whereas the other letter of Dionysius to Boniface was written in the common year of Christ 526, Julian year 571; this is made abundantly clear by the characters added here, indiction 4, nineteen-year cycle, or golden number XIV, and so forth].

and the lunar cycle is the eleventh; the fourteenth nineteen-year cycle [Note: D reads “the fourteenth of the nineteen-year cycle”]. Since it is the sixth year of the eleven-year period, it must be embolismic.

Let us therefore carefully inquire how many days there are from the fifteenth moon of the past feast to the fourteenth moon of the present one, and we shall undoubtedly discover when we ought to celebrate Passover.

After the year had passed [Note: Namely, the year of Christ 525, Alexandrian lunar cycle 13, dominical letter E. Bucherius], during the third indiction, the fourteenth moon was on the ninth day before the Kalends of April—that is, on 24 March [Note: The words “at Passover” are absent from Petavius’s edition. D reads “through the fourth indiction, the paschal fourteenth moon,” etc. Perhaps one should read “the paschal moon”]. Who could doubt this who has even a little knowledge of the care required for this matter?

Therefore let us take the eighth day before the Kalends of April as the beginning of our reckoning. We have seven days of March, thirty of April, thirty-one of May, thirty of June, thirty-one of July, thirty-one of August, thirty of September, thirty-one of October, thirty of November, thirty-one of December, thirty-one of January, twenty-eight of February, thirty-one of March, and twelve days of April, which is the day before the Ides of April. Together these make 384 days.

But if, according to the definition of those who calculate the moon otherwise than the truth requires, we suppose the fourteenth moon to occur not on the day before the Ides of April but on the third day before the Ides, they will count 383 days, with the total reduced by one [Note: Thus D and both C manuscripts. The printed editions read “we shall count”], which cannot be conceded in any way.

And so, whenever such a doubt arises, let us always diligently count the days from the fifteenth moon of the past feast to the fourteenth moon of the Passover we seek [Note: D reads “which”]. If it is a common year, we shall find 354 days; if it is embolismic, 384. No inequality will occur at all [Note: Alternatively, “unequally.” Bucherius and C2 read “nor otherwise”], because the rule of this cycle stands upon this principle, whose clarified formula we shall set forth in the following description.

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle [Note: Petavius and Bucherius here and in the years that follow alike read “in the nineteen-year year … lunar …,” but all our manuscripts everywhere have the genitive rather than the ablative, with more evident sense and greater agreement with Dionysius’s cycle table], the lunar cycle being the seventeenth, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May to the Nones of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days [Note: In the first and second years the printed editions have “there are”; in the remaining years, “there come to be.” The manuscripts use the latter wording everywhere].

In the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar cycle being the eighteenth, from the eighth day before the Ides of April to the eighth day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the third year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar cycle being the nineteenth, from the seventh day before the Kalends of April to the Ides of April, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar cycle being the first, from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May to the fourth day before the Nones of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the fifth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar cycle being the second, from the third day before the Nones of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the sixth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar cycle being the third, from the tenth day before the Kalends of April to the fourth day before the Ides of April, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the seventh year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the fourth, from the third day before the Ides of April until the third day before the Kalends of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the eighth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the fifth, from the day before the Kalends of April until the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May [Col. 0518C], since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the ninth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the sixth, from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May until the seventh day before the Ides of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the tenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the seventh, from the sixth day before the Ides of April until the sixth day before the Kalends of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the eleventh year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the eighth, from the fifth day before the Kalends of April until the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

[Col. 0519A] In the twelfth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the ninth, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May until the day before the Nones of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the thirteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the tenth, from the Nones of April until the ninth day before the Kalends of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the fourteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the eleventh, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April until the second day before the Ides of April, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the fifteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the twelfth, from the Ides of April until the Kalends of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days [Col. 0519B].

[Col. 0520A] In the sixteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the thirteenth, from the fourth day before the Nones of April until the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the seventeenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the fourteenth, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April until the fifth day before the Ides of April, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the eighteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the fifteenth, from the fourth day before the Ides of April until the fourth day before the Kalends of April, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the nineteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar date being the sixteenth, from the third day before the Kalends of April until the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, since it is an embolismic year [Col. 0520B], there are 384 days.

[Col. 0519]

TO THE MOST NOBLE AND MOST LEARNED MAN BENJAMIN HOFFMANN OF BRESLAU, JO. GUIL. JANUS.

[Col. 0519B] The life and writings of Dionysius Exiguus—an educated man, as those times were, and one who rendered distinguished service to sacred and literary studies—although they could not, owing to the defects of the age, be wholly erased or consigned to oblivion, have nevertheless been less illuminated than they deserved. Among his contemporaries, almost Cassiodorus alone preserved the memory of his virtues; and all who have hitherto transmitted anything about the life of Dionysius have followed him as their sole authority. Certainly, you will find nothing else worthy of belief about him among the older and more recent ecclesiastical and literary writers.

Most call him an abbot, whereas Cassiodorus called him a monk. Yet the monastery of which he was abbot is unknown, as the Benedictine Fathers, who prepared the final Rouen edition of Cassiodorus’s works, rightly observe. Antonius Pagi, however, led by Cassiodorus’s authority, entirely denies Dionysius the dignity of abbot and argues that it was first attributed to him by Bede. Yet the Prologue of Felix, abbot of Gillitanum, clearly shows that he was called abbot of the city of Rome at least a full century before Bede. Felix prefixed that prologue in A.D. 616 to the cycle of Dionysius, which he had continued, in the History of the Dionysian Cycle, published from the Digby and Rheims manuscripts.

Meanwhile, the common view can easily be reconciled with the position which Pagius defends as though it were new, if one distinguishes the common meaning of *abbot* from its proper and particular meaning. For, as Cangius rightly observes, among Latins and Greeks all monks were generally called abbots, especially those venerable for age [Col. 0519D] and holiness of life; in this sense we commonly call them Fathers. “It is,” says Augustine, “a mark of honor that every day we say to old men: Father.” The Greek lexicon in the royal manuscript, codex 2062, has: ἀββὰς, ὁ γέρων, ὁ πατὴρ — “abba: the old man, the father.” Thus Cassian calls Moses and Germanus, fellow monks, abbots; and the rule of Saint Columbanus mentions a thousand abbots under one archimandrite.

In this sense, then, our Dionysius too was called an abbot, more as a mark of honor than of office. But concerning the life of Dionysius, since some matters omitted by ecclesiastical writers may perhaps deserve annotation and a more suitable occasion will be provided, let us now concern ourselves chiefly with his works.

Two works above all brought their author fame and esteem: the collection of canons, first joined with the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, and the book on Easter. The former, edited and illuminated above all by Christophe Justel, is widely known and celebrated among learned men; the latter, considered almost entirely lost—or at least regarded by the most learned as lost—we now bring to light, restored as far as possible to its integrity.

It might perhaps have remained much longer hidden in my files had your industry and eagerness, most noble sir, not intervened. When you were seeking a subject for a public disputation and did not reject this one when it was offered to you, you repeatedly recalled me to it, although distracted by other occupations; you put into order with me the materials scattered here and there, and voluntarily offered the expense of publication [Col. 0520C].

Let this, then, be a public testimony both to your love of good literature and to the learning and diligence which you prove daily in my schools and those of other academic teachers, and which you adorn and commend by a character formed for every kind of honor and moderation. I can sincerely offer you this testimony of praise, since you live under the same roof with me and, for several years now, have been known to me more closely and familiarly.

May the immortal God continue to favor your highly praiseworthy efforts and grant the most desired success to you who strive toward all that is excellent, so that you may fulfill the joy of your parents and most honorable family, meet the expectations of the distinguished and flourishing leaders of your fatherland, whose exceptional kindnesses toward you you cherish with a most grateful heart, and one day adorn and bind sacred and literary affairs to yourself by your merits. Farewell.

Since, Hoffmann, you cultivate through diligent study the doctrines of the cycle,

a portion of the Pierian choir dear to me:

who, then, would wonder that you strive learnedly to expound

the difficult numbers of the cycle?

Well done in your virtue! Now gather new strength,

And carry the glory of your learning to the stars.

FRIDERICUS STRUNZIUS, P.P., congratulates the most learned man, the RESPONDENT, on this public specimen of more elegant learning.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 547. FACUNDUS [Note: [Col. 0521] In Facundus and Ferrandus, through a typographers’ error, harmless in itself, the chronological order has been altered somewhat. EDIT.] BISHOP OF HERMIANUM.

[Col. 0521]

NOTICE (from Gallandius).

[Col. 0521A] I. Facundus, bishop of Hermianum in the African province of Byzacena, flourished after the tenth year of the consulship of Basil, that is, in A.D. 551, during the reign of the emperor Justinian, as Victor of Tunnuna [Note: [Col. 0521C] Victor of Tunnuna, *Chronicle*, p. 10, in Scaliger, *Thesaurus temporum*, Amsterdam edition, 1658.] and Isidore of Seville [Note: [Col. 0521C] Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 19.] report. Yet the edition in Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library* incorrectly gives “after the fourth year of the consulship of Basil” [Note: [Col. 0521C] Fabricius, *Ecclesiastical Library*, p. 54.], whereas the others, including the Breulian edition, consistently give the tenth year [Note: [Col. 0521C] Isidore of Seville, *Works*, ed. du Breul, Paris, 1601, p. 528.]. Nor can it properly be read otherwise, especially if one observes that Isidore was accustomed to follow Victor of Tunnuna.

Cassiodorus also mentions this same Facundus, saying [Note: [Col. 0521C] Cassiodorus, *Commentary on Psalm 138*, near the end.]: “Facundus, the venerable bishop, a destroyer of heretics with penetrating certainty, recently writing to the emperor Justinian, treated the two natures of the Lord Christ in two books with remarkable acumen and clarity.”

Here, according to the judgment of learned men, “Senator” should be understood to refer to the first two chapters of Book I out of the twelve which he sent to Justinian, not to two books that had long since perished, as the illustrious Maffeius [Note: [Col. 0521D] Maffei, *Ecclesiastical Opuscula*, appended to the *Theological History of Gratian*, p. 201.] and Fabricius [Note: [Col. 0521D] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae Latinitatis*, vol. II, p. 433, Hamburg edition.] believed.

While living at Constantinople, this bishop of Hermianum composed a Commentary in twelve books concerning the affairs of the African Church, specifically in defense of the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon. Before it had been completed and fully treated, he says [Note: [Col. 0521D] Facundus, Preface below, col. 527.], Pope Vigilius was brought to Constantinople. From this it is clear when Facundus wrote his books.

For, as Sirmondus rightly observes [Note: [Col. 0522C] Sirmondus, note b on Facundus, cited work.], we learn from the Appendix to Marcellinus Comes, whose author is very ancient [Note: [Col. 0522C] Marcellinus, *Chronicle*, under the year 547.], that Pope Vigilius entered Constantinople on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, after the sixth consulship of Basil—that is, in A.D. 547.
