Pagius confirms this dating from Procopius [Note: [Col. 0522C] Procopius, *Gothic War*, Book III, ch. 16.] and Theophanes [Note: [Col. 0522C] Theophanes, *Chronography*, under the twenty-first year of Justinian.] [Note: [Col. 0522C] Pagius, under the year 547, § 4.].

Thus, at the beginning of the year 547, when Vigilius arrived in the imperial city, Facundus had not yet completed his work, as we have just learned from him; but since he appears to affirm that it was then almost finished, the emperor Justinian must have received it from the author in that very year, 547 [Col. 0522A]. I wished to record this so that, with the great Baronius [Note: [Col. 0522C] Baronius, under the year 547, § 32.], we might affirm that Facundus wrote these books while still within the Catholic communion—at the very time, namely, when Pope Vigilius himself is known first to have undertaken the defense of those same Chapters.

II. Many distinguished and orthodox statements worthy of a bishop certainly occur in that work; some of them Peter de Marca, a man of distinction, chose to transcribe [Note: [Col. 0522D] De Marca, *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and Empire*, Book III, ch. 15, § 10, p. 324, Paris edition, 1704.]:

“I can bring forward nothing more illustrious,” he says, “than an excellent passage of Facundus of Hermianum, which also commends the supreme authority of the Roman pontiffs. He is discussing Pope Vigilius, whom the opponents of the Three Chapters claimed to have consulted. ‘He,’ says Facundus [Note: [Col. 0522D] Facundus, Book II, ch. 6, below.], ‘received the first and greatest authority not for the destruction of the judgment of the Fathers—that is, of Pope Leo and the Council of Chalcedon—but rather for its defense and vindication; and he has no greater power than his fellow priests against the truth, but for the truth. For the Apostle Paul says: “We can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth” (2 Corinthians 13:8).’”

Elsewhere the same illustrious man writes about Facundus [Note: [Col. 0522D] De Marca, cited work, Book II, ch. 10, § 14, p. 147.]:

“He vigorously attacks, at length, the audacity of rulers who attempt to refer canonical questions to their own judgment, and he appeals to the example of the emperor Marcian, about whom these are his words [Note: [Col. 0522D] Facundus, Book XII, ch. 3, at the beginning.]:

“‘That most modest emperor, knowing that King Uzziah had not escaped unpunished because he presumed to sacrifice—something permitted to every priest, even one of the second rank—recognized that he himself could much less escape unpunished either by examining what had already been established concerning the Christian faith, which is wholly impermissible, or by establishing new canons, which is permitted only to priests of the first rank when many have assembled together. Therefore that temperate man, content with his own office, wished to be an executor of the ecclesiastical canons, not their author or enforcer. This is the firm boundary that must be set for royal authority in such matters [Col. 0523A], lest we be thoughtlessly drawn into the kind of flattery by which the Greeks transferred to their rulers the entire authority over ecclesiastical discipline.’”

Thus far the most learned man. The great Baronius had also long before reported other statements consistent with these from the same Facundus [Note: [Col. 0523D] Baronius, under the year 547, §§ 34, 35, 41 and following.].

III. Would that this Hermianian prelate had persevered in the same position to the end of his life! For, having been placed in exile because of his stubborn defense of the Three Chapters, he began to take the side of the schismatics. There he also wrote a book against Mocianus, or Mutianus, a scholasticus who had rightly rebuked the African bishops because, on account of the Three Chapters, they had separated themselves from Pope Vigilius and from the Church after his *Judicatum*.

Indeed, from a letter of Facundus himself, first published by Dacherius [Note: [Col. 0523D] Dacher, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, pp. 307 ff., new edition.], entitled *A Letter of Catholic Faith in Defense of the Three Chapters* [Col. 0523B], he appears to have died in schism. On this matter see Natalis Alexander [Note: [Col. 0523D] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, sixth century, ch. 4, article 7, § 2.]. These matters have been treated at greater length by the father of ecclesiastical annals [Note: [Col. 0523D] Baronius, under the year 547, §§ 36 and following.] and the distinguished Norisius [Note: [Col. 0523D] Norisius, *Historical Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, ch. 4, *Works*, vol. I, pp. 594 and following.].

After these observations, it is worthwhile to append what Peter de Marca writes while discussing the decree of Vigilius confirming the Fifth Synod [Note: [Col. 0524D] De Marca, *Dissertation on the Letter of Vigilius*, § 17, in *Councils*, vol. VI, p. 254, Venice edition, Labbé.]:

“Lest anyone should regard this decree of Vigilius as ambitious, he himself assigns the reasons that moved him to this judgment. Namely, the offenses and scandals which the enemy of the human race had introduced by the dispute over the Three Chapters had already been settled; peace had been restored to the Church after their condemnation; and truth had shone forth in these ambiguous controversies. Hence,” he adds, “it may be inferred that the bishops of the Illyrian and African provinces had repented of their former judgment and, after consulting with Vigilius, had embraced communion with the Easterners.”

So far he. Yet there were learned men, including Garnerius [Note: [Col. 0524D] Garnerius, Dissertation on Liberatus’s *Breviarium*, ch. 5, § 1, p. 229, Paris, 1675.], who doubted the integrity of the decretal letter of Vigilius, which the same distinguished archbishop first published and illuminated in his dissertation.

Whatever the truth may be, whether Facundus later laid aside his former position, returned at last to his senses, and, at least toward the end of his life, repented and joined himself to the Catholic communion after renouncing the unjust schism, we leave his case entirely to the judgment of God.

IV. But so that readers may have at hand a general account of the Three Chapters by which they can form a firm and settled judgment concerning them, we consider the following statement certain and well established, together with the great man [Note: [Col. 0524D] Baronius, under the year 546, § 38.]:

“Although the Catholic Church, after many controversies had arisen and immense divisions had been produced, eventually followed the judgment of the emperor Justinian against the Three Chapters, nevertheless, at the very beginning of the question proposed—and indeed of the judgment asserted by the emperor—many orthodox men, and even Vigilius himself, the Roman pontiff, rose up against those same Three Chapters as defenders of the Council of Chalcedon, to whose prejudice the emperor’s action seemed to have been enacted.

“But when it was clearly and fully understood that the condemnation of the Three Chapters had in no way diminished the sacred Council of Chalcedon, the Apostolic See itself approved and retained the emperor’s assertion, first promulgated by imperial edict and afterward confirmed by the Fifth Synod. All Catholics proceeded to the same judgment, together with the Fifth Synod, the Roman pontiffs themselves, and the others in communion with the Apostolic See.

“Those who later disagreed with them were treated and rejected as schismatics. Yet before the final assent of the Apostolic See, it was not a sacrilege to fight for the Three Chapters, especially since at one time they had someone to follow in that assertion: Vigilius himself, the Roman pontiff.”

Thus far the founder of the ecclesiastical annals, who elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0524D] Idem, under the year 547, §§ 28–30.] explains what those Three Chapters were and at the same time refutes a certain learned man’s new and false opinion concerning them.

V. Yet we must not fail to mention Sirmondus, a man of distinction, when he speaks about this matter and especially about our author. He writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0524D] Sirmondus, Preface to Facundus.]:

“In the case of the Three Chapters defended by Facundus, if one wishes to speak the truth, it would have been more honorable to fall with Vigilius than to conquer with Justinian. If he had preferred always to follow Vigilius as his leader, rather than, after Vigilius had judged that he must yield to Justinian, criticize him together with his Africans, no one would rightly judge Facundus blameworthy for undertaking the defense of the Chapters—a defense to which Vigilius himself later voluntarily returned.

“But Facundus and his colleagues, in resisting Vigilius, were deceived by the error in which they were held, an error made clear by Victor’s and Isidore’s testimonies concerning Facundus: namely, they were persuaded that the Chapters could not be condemned without injury to the faith and the overthrow of the Council of Chalcedon; therefore they would not permit them to be condemned.

“Vigilius, on the other hand, understanding that the controversy was open and that whichever way it turned had no bearing on the doctrine of the faith—a point which Gregory the Great, Pelagius, and others often attested after Vigilius’s time—sometimes used the freedom which the case allowed, though otherwise he was always more inclined, as was proper, to defend and approve the Chapters.

“For at the beginning, when the evil first arose at Constantinople, he opposed their condemnation with great force. Although he afterward issued the *Judicatum* condemning them, in order to prevent schism and purchase public concord at the cost of sacrificing his own judgment, nevertheless, when he observed that matters had turned out otherwise than he had hoped and that the defenders of the Chapters were being disturbed by this moderation of his, while his opponents were abusing it, he soon returned to his former defense and remained firm in it.

“And when he perceived that an attempt was being made to extort condemnation by force from those unwilling to give it, he regarded the Greek synod with suspicion and refused to take part in it. He set forth at length, in an edict, his own judgment that the Chapters should not be condemned; and finally, when the synod condemned the Chapters, he refused his assent, lest he should again offend the provinces, most of which were protesting.

“From these facts it is clear that Vigilius’s changing counsels did not display the inconsistency which some have perceived in them, but rather a steady and fixed constancy in preserving the peace and harmony of the Church which he governed.

“Out of this same concern for peace, his successors, when they saw that only a few still resisted in order that there might be one mind and voice throughout the Church, eventually gave their assent; and by their confirmation they granted both the force and the name of a general council to a synod whose authority had until then been uncertain.”

Thus far the most learned man.

VI. As for the value of this work of Facundus, the Sirmondus just mentioned judges [Note: [Col. 0525D] Sirmondus, Preface to Facundus, at the beginning.] that “every learned man, by attentive reading of it, will recognize that this author provides abundant material by which he may rightly sustain his mind and zeal through the usefulness, abundance, and variety of the matters he treats.”

Some rather difficult passages nevertheless occur from time to time in these books and require an attentive reader. Such is the celebrated passage on the sacred Eucharist, where he says [Note: [Col. 0525D] Facundus, Book IX, ch. 5, after the middle.]:

“We call the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, which is in the consecrated bread and cup, his body and blood—not because the bread is literally his body and the cup literally his blood, but because it contains within itself the mystery of his body and blood,” and so forth.

Although Sirmondus explained these words of Facundus with sufficient solidity, heterodox men eagerly seized upon them, including Cave [Note: [Col. 0525D] Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, p. 520.], to pass over others, so that they might persuade themselves and others that the Hermianian bishop of old had finally become a patron of their own cause—one who, if the gods please, did not believe that the substance of bread and wine was transformed into Christ’s body and blood when the sacred mystery of the altar was celebrated.

To dispel these utterly empty acclamations, it was enough for Dacherius, from Facundus’s own *Letter of Catholic Faith in Defense of the Three Chapters*, which he first published, to demonstrate [Note: [Col. 0525D] Dacher, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 307, note a, new edition.] that Facundus had no authority in the Church, since he had departed from Catholic communion and remained in schism until his death; consequently, heretics boast of him as their leader in vain.

But this is to cut the knot with a sword rather than untie it. Natalis Alexander untied it, and with a learned hand indeed. It is not appropriate here to report the whole sequence of his exposition [Col. 0526A], which is too lengthy; we therefore refer readers to it [Note: [Col. 0525D] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, sixth century, ch. 4, article 7, § 2.].

Another passage of Facundus also requires a kindly interpreter: the passage in which he comments on verse 8 of chapter 5 of the First Epistle of Saint John [Note: [Col. 0525D] Facundus, Book I, ch. 3, below, col. 535.]. The learned Mill [Note: [Col. 0525D] Mill, *Prolegomena to the Greek New Testament*, no. 1006.] touches on this passage briefly; the learned Bernard de Rubeis explains it more fully [Note: [Col. 0526D] B. de Rubeis, *Dissertation on the Three Heavenly Witnesses*, chs. 7 and 10, no. 2.].

Moreover, whoever carefully reads the twelve books of this author—I set aside his other two short works, which follow those books—may perhaps discover here and there some passages that delay him and demand serious consideration. Yet whenever this happens, let him remember that even the best ancient writers sometimes slipped and stumbled in certain matters. These things, as I judge, should rather be forgiven than counted as faults. For I am of the mind that:

> Where many things shine in a poem, I shall not be offended by a few blemishes,  
> Which either carelessness has scattered,  
> Or human nature has insufficiently guarded against.

[Note: [Col. 0526D] Horace, *Art of Poetry*, lines 351–353.]

VII. It remains for us now to say briefly, as is customary, something about the care taken in preparing this edition of Facundus.

First, we followed Sirmondus’s edition, which appeared among his various works from the Royal Printing House at Paris in 1696, revised through the efforts of the distinguished Baunius. We know that the Venetian edition which followed it in 1729 is full of no small number of errors.

From this later edition, however, we supplied the variants to Sirmondus’s notes. These were drawn by Joseph Blanchinus, a man of distinction, through careful collation with an excellent manuscript codex of the eminent chapter of Verona [Col. 0526C]. These readings illuminate, correct, and supplement Facundus’s text. The dignity of the codex is displayed by the illustrious Scipio Maffei [Note: [Col. 0526D] Maffei, *Ecclesiastical Opuscula*, appended to the *Theological History of Gratian*, p. 88.].

In addition, we appended to the notes of the celebrated Verona codex several observations which we gathered by comparing various editions of works published by learned men; here we wish to add one or two that had escaped us.

Baunius had long ago observed [Note: [Col. 0526D] Baunius, Preface to vol. II of Sirmondus’s *Works*, § 4.] that the passage in Facundus, Book II, chapter 6 (below, col. 578), beginning with the words “Recognize again, Augustus,” and extending to the concluding words “who would dare to resist the truth,” is not, as it might seem, Facundus’s own address to Augustus Justinian in his own words, but is taken from Saint Leo’s letter to Leo Augustus [Note: [Col. 0526D] Leo, Letter 133, vol. I of Quesnel’s second edition, p. [.....]44.].

Consequently, the reading in that passage of Facundus, *quia prius legitimus*, etc., must also be corrected. Without doubt it should be restored as *quia post legitimas*, etc. (“because after the legitimate [—]”), as it appears in Leo’s letter and as the sense of the passage absolutely requires. We have this correction recorded in that place by Blanchinus’s work from the aforementioned Verona codex.

Quesnel first recognized it [Col. 0527A] [Note: [Col. 0527A] Quesnel, note on Leo’s letter, vol. II of the cited edition, p. 507.], and afterward the brothers Ballerini [Note: [Col. 0527A] Ballerini, *Works of Leo*, vol. I, p. 1345.].

Next, concerning Facundus’s Book III, chapter 3, Montfaucon [Note: [Col. 0528A] Montfaucon, Preface to vol. VII of Chrysostom, § 3.] points out that the passage quoted by the author from John Chrysostom (below, col. 593) occurs in Homily 83, or alternatively 84, on Matthew [Note: [Col. 0528A] Chrysostom, *Works*, vol. VII, p. 791.].

Finally, concerning Book IV, chapter 2 (below, col. 620), where the Martyrdom of Marcianopolis is mentioned, Wesselingius observes [Note: [Col. 0528A] Wesselingius, *Ancient Roman Itinerary*, p. 229.] that one should read “Marcianopolis.”

But enough of effort. [Greek: ἅλις σπουδῆς.]

[Col. 0527]

TWELVE BOOKS OF FACUNDUS, BISHOP OF HERMIANUM [Note: [Col. 0527C] “In the African province of Byzacena”: before Facundus, the bishops of this city are recorded as Maximianus in the First Carthaginian Collation, number 187, and Donatus in the manuscript list of bishops who came to Carthage by order of King Huneric in the sixth year of his reign to give an account of their faith. After Facundus, Benadus appears in the Council of Byzacena, whose letter is preserved in the Roman synod of Martin I, session 2. In the letter, Benadus signs among the others as “Benadus, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Hermianum.”], TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN, IN DEFENSE OF THE THREE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON. (C)

PREFACE.

[Col. 0527B] Since the Acephali, opponents of the holy Council of Chalcedon, were seeking through certain persons to insinuate, to the council’s prejudice, that the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa—which the aforesaid synod, after it had been brought before it, judged to be Catholic—should be condemned under an anathema; and likewise Theodore of Mopsuestia [Note: [Col. 0527] From the old codex of the chapter of Verona. The same should be understood in the following notes.], together with his teaching, which was praised in that same letter of Ibas; as well as certain writings of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, who at the aforementioned Council of Chalcedon affirmed the dogmatic letter of Pope Leo—persuaded by the brothers, I wrote this work to the emperor at Constantinople.

While it had not yet been completed or fully treated, the Roman bishop [Note: [Col. 0527C] Vigilius. Baronius rightly rejects Anastasius the Librarian, who wrote that Vigilius arrived at Constantinople on the eve of Christmas at the end of 546. He proves clearly that this could not have happened, but does not say when Vigilius arrived. The Appendix to Marcellinus Comes published by us does show that Pope Vigilius entered Constantinople in the sixth year of Basil, that is, in A.D. 547. Facundus was therefore already engaged in writing this work nearly a hundred years after the Council of Chalcedon, as he relates in Book II, chapter 1.] was brought to Constantinople.

When we were debating the matter in the course of his examination, he ordered the proceedings to be interrupted in the midst of the dispute, and requested from all the bishops who were present that each should answer in writing what he thought concerning these Chapters. Since, therefore, through the master of offices, I was compelled to respond under severe pressure, I was scarcely granted seven days’ respite, two of which were feast days.

Accordingly, so that I might say everything that I judged most necessary, I excerpted certain passages from these books, since I could not undertake to say everything anew, especially since that response exceeds three thousand lines. Indeed, since, as I have said, I had not yet fully worked through those books, certain testimonies contained different readings because of the corrupt state of the manuscripts from which we had taken them or because of the carelessness of translators; and these were copied into that response in the same form.

For this reason I have taken care to state and announce beforehand that no one who, after reading the aforementioned response, happens upon these books should be offended by this difference, but should pardon the hurried work there and trust this version instead. For some things presented there in confusion have here been treated more moderately and in better order.

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0527]

CHAPTER ONE. That Justinian rightly professed, in his confession of faith, that one of the Trinity was crucified, that blessed Mary was truly and properly the Mother of God, and that Christ has two natures.

[Col. 0527D]

[Col. 0528D] **The Confession** [Note: [Col. 0527D] He refers to the confession which Justinian published at Constantinople and sent to the various provinces in the third year of his consulship, in the year of Christ 533. It exists in both Greek and Latin in *Codex* VI, *On the Holy Trinity*, and explains in the same words the three points that Facundus mentions here: concerning the two natures in Christ, the one of the Trinity crucified, and the blessed Virgin as κυρίως καὶ κατ’ ἀλήθειαν *Deipara*—“truly and in reality the Mother of God.”] of your faith, most merciful emperor, consonant with the definitions of the great Council of Chalcedon, I have always approved and have defended against the objections of many. For since two heresies refuted by that same council are now raging—heresies which, although opposed in their contentions, attack the mystery of the divine incarnation with equal hatred, namely those of the Nestorians and the Eutychians—what could have been said more salutarily or more clearly against both heresies than what you yourself confessed: that one of the Trinity was crucified for us? The Apostle taught you to believe him to be the great God when he said:

> “For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live chastely, justly, and devoutly in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Tit. II, 2).

For this reason you also said that the blessed Virgin Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God. For you do not recognize one God the Word and another Jesus Christ, whom you declared to be one and the same in two natures, consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and the same consubstantial with us according to his humanity. Concerning him you consequently also said this:

> “For just as he is perfect in divinity, so the same one is perfect in humanity.”

It is certain that you uttered all these statements in accordance with the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon. For that the Lord Jesus Christ is one of the Trinity is clearly shown by the address of that same council delivered to the emperor Marcian. There, while defending the letter of blessed Leo, bishop of the Roman Church, against the abuse of heretics, it says after some intervening material:

> “It is easy to recognize that, when a question has arisen because of ambiguity, we are known to have adapted our confession to the interpretations of the Fathers, making it clear that in no respect have we brought forward a disposition of mind discordant with their understanding, but that we use them as witnesses for the firmness of our faith.” [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Verona manuscript reads *utimur*, “we use,” rather than *utamur*, “let us use.”]

> “Thus Thus we embrace the letter of Athanasius to Epictetus; thus everywhere we present Gregory’s letter to Cledonius as though it were our own. And what need is there to say more? For if they judge it deserving of blame that the doctrines of the Church should be declared through letters on each question, anyone could first single out the most blessed Cyril, who expressed in his letters to the Easterners what he believed; and he would likewise subject the great Proclus to this reproach, because he sent to those same Easterners a volume to the Armenians in conformity with the faith. To these, as sharing the blame, would be added the most wise John, bishop of Antioch, who, rejecting the abuse of the heretics and declaring the doctrine of the Apostles, sent the confession of the whole East, as though from one most holy mouth, to Proclus and to him who at that same time governed the affairs of the world.”

In this volume to the Armenians, which, as the aforementioned council says, the great Proclus also sent to the Easterners in conformity with the faith, he confessed as follows (Roman edition, p. 128):

> “For neither, when we say that the Son suffered, do we think that he could suffer according to his divinity, since the divine nature receives no passion whatsoever. But, confessing God the Word incarnate, one of the Trinity, we provide a basis for understanding to those who faithfully ask why he deigned to become incarnate.”

Writing also to blessed John of Antioch, to whom he sent what he had written to the Armenians in order to preserve the fellowship of their common faith, so that, just as all believed one and the same thing in their hearts for justification, so also there might be one and the same confession from the mouth of all for salvation, he says as follows (Liberatus, chap. 10):

> “But when we again call God, that is, Christ, passible, we confess that he suffered not in what he was, but in what he became, that is, in his own flesh; and in proclaiming this we are in no way deceived. For we confess that one of the Trinity was crucified according to the flesh, and we by no means blaspheme by calling the divinity passible.”

And the most wise John of Antioch, together with the Eastern council, approved this sound doctrine of his in their letters. In these letters the Council of Chalcedon testifies that he rejected the abuse of the heretics and declared the apostolic doctrine. In his reply to the same blessed Proclus he said:

> “We both requested, and mentioned with every pleasure, the volume written to the Armenians by our most reverend son, the deacon Theodosius, who is worthy, because of the diligence in him beyond his years, to serve your arrangements.” [Note: [Col. 0529D] The same manuscript reads *reverendo*, “reverend,” rather than *reverentissimo*, “most reverend.”]

> “What gave us pleasure was not merely the beauty of the composition, nor the abundance of arguments worked out against the two opposing parties, as much as the very care and piety concerning the sacred doctrines. It was piety because, in what you said, you proceeded by rightly confessing the word of truth, the royal way of the divine Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0530D] The same manuscript reads *Scripturarum viam*, “the way of the Scriptures.”], and did not presume, without scriptural testimonies, to proclaim anything on your own authority. It was care because, together with the divine Scriptures, you set forth the sayings of the Fathers to prove what you were saying.”

The aforementioned John, writing also to blessed Cyril together with the same council of the East, stated that he had approved that very volume to the Armenians in these words:

> “When the most holy bishop Proclus sent us the volume which he had written to the Armenians, a volume that was truly right and devout, and sought our agreement, we did everything and fell short in nothing.” [Note: [Col. 0530D] The same manuscript has *sanctus Joannes*, “holy John,” rather than *supradictus Joannes*, “the aforementioned John.”]

It has therefore appeared, most religious emperor, that you confessed one of the Trinity to have been crucified for us according to the judgment of the great council, since this confession of yours is contained in those letters, to which that council accorded such authority that, following their example, it judged that the letter of blessed Leo should be defended (after the acts of the council).

We also find in the address of that same council confirmation of what you said: that blessed Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God. There it is said:

> “The enemy of the common nature did not escape the notice of the sleepless eye; but, like lamps, he immediately displayed our Fathers to those whom the error of darkness had overwhelmed, so that they might open to all the understanding of the faith and carefully proclaim the benefits of the incarnation: how the mystery of the dispensation had been arranged from the beginning out of the womb; how the Virgin was also called Mother of God because of him who deigned, even after childbirth, to sanctify her virginity and, as was fitting for God, to seal the womb with integrity; and how she was called, in truth, the Mother of God because of the flesh which she supplied from herself to the Lord of all.”

Here too it has been shown that the same holy council taught that the Virgin, the Mother of God, was called so in truth because of the flesh which she supplied from herself to the Lord of all. Nor does it matter whether she is called the Mother of God “according to truth,” that is, truly, or “truly and properly,” as you yourself confessed.

For what the Apostle John calls the true Son of God, Paul calls his proper Son. Thus he writes:

> “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know what is true and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ” (I John V, 20).

But, writing to the Romans, he says:

> “If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own proper Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 31).

Therefore, when John calls our Lord Jesus Christ the true Son of God, this is no different from Paul’s calling him the proper Son of God. And so we must likewise understand that when the holy Council of Chalcedon confessed blessed Mary to be truly the Mother of God, it meant no differently from your confession that she is truly and properly the Mother of God.

But if this seems insufficient to anyone, and he still hesitates to call her truly and properly the Mother of God, let him await the fuller explanation of this very matter which we shall provide below.

Since you also confessed, in accordance with the Council of Chalcedon, that the Lord Jesus Christ exists in two natures, this too is demonstrated by the definition of that council. It established that one and the same Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, is to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation; the distinction of the natures nowhere being removed by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved.

All these things therefore prove that your confession of faith accords with the definitions of the great council. [Note: [Col. 0532D] The same manuscript has “the Council of Chalcedon.”] For this reason we have always rejoiced in the correctness of your confession and have especially gloried in you on its account (after the acts of the council). For what should be praised first in a human being? What is more fitting in a ruler than the Catholic faith, which is the foundation of all our good and without which nothing good exists in us? For everything that does not proceed from faith is sin.

## CHAPTER II. How the Eutychians fraudulently attack the Council of Chalcedon under the name of the Three Chapters; and how, before answering them, he sets forth his confession of faith

But I ask you, most merciful emperor, to receive my arguments either with gratitude or with patience. For I have undertaken to demonstrate that, in defense of the same faith which you hold, and for the preservation of the decrees of Chalcedon, in which that faith is both clearly expressed and confirmed, I have not thought that we ought to agree with those who recently advanced a contrary opinion.

For the restless and shameless spirit of the heretics, which is readily and eagerly disposed to attack ancient decrees, always rises to its own confusion. Since it has often been frustrated when it tried to overturn the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon by open opposition, it has now crept in with a crooked and concealed malignity, believing that the plots of its faction could not be understood.

It found the desired opportunity in the fury of certain people who, under a Christian name, secretly follow the pagan doctrine of Origen in the Church. And because, through the urgency of your religious zeal, that profane doctrine has been condemned again and again, its followers have thereupon flared up against the Church, seeking to disturb it by whatever incursion they could make.

And this whole matter did not escape public knowledge, especially since Domitian, the bishop of the city of Ancyra in the first province of Galatia, who was an open supporter of the very Origenist heresy, confessed—God forcing the truth from him—in a petition which he wrote to the most blessed Pope Vigilius that his Origenist associates, when they saw that they could not defend their own doctrine and had no hope remaining in the conflict, had stirred up these scandals in the Church as revenge for what had been done against Origen. [Note: [Col. 0531D] He discusses Domitian again in Book IV, chapter 4, where he also quotes the words of this petition. What he asserts here from Domitian’s petition is also affirmed by the deacon Liberatus in his *Breviary*: namely, that the Origenists, inflamed by grief over the condemnation of Origen, drove Justinian toward the condemnation of the Three Chapters; and that the architect of the intrigue, belonging to the same sect, was Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, who suggested to the emperor that the Acephali could in this way be brought to accept the Council of Chalcedon and communion with the Church. After the council, five Greek-Latin letters were published on the two matters. The beginning of the first, against Origen, is “Ἡμῖν μὲν ἀεὶ σπουδὴ”—“It has always been our concern”; the beginning of the later one, concerning the Three Chapters, is “Εἰδότες ὡς οὐδὲν οὕτω”—“Knowing that nothing is so …”]

Thus the perfidy of the Eutychians, acting as these people’s accomplice, secretly attacked through them what it had often attempted in vain on its own against the Council of Chalcedon—through people whom we did not regard as suspect in this matter.

Yet they too did not dare openly to criticize the great council. Rather, under a certain pretext of defense, which their deceptive promise commended to your piety, they tried to weaken its authority. For, as you know very well, they claimed that all Eutychians who were offended by its decrees would enter into communion with the Church if the letter of the venerable Ibas, bishop of Edessa, written to Maris the Persian, were condemned as Nestorian, while it were denied that the council had approved it. The aforementioned council, when Ibas was accused on account of that letter as though it were injurious to blessed Cyril, had pronounced the letter orthodox.

They acted craftily, so that while they summoned the uninformed and ignorant with the false and shameless claim that the council could be defended by denying this, whatever lies the Eutychians dictated in condemnation of the letter could be written down without anyone resisting or taking care to ensure that they were affirmed by the subscriptions of our people—which is deeply lamentable. Thus, when it was later demonstrated, by the simple production of the acts—which was extremely easy—that the letter had been accepted by that council, nothing would remain for us to answer the Eutychians, who were always branding it as Nestorian. [Note: [Col. 0533D] The Verona manuscript has *est*, “is,” rather than *erat*, “was.”] [Note: [Col. 0533D] The same manuscript has *possimus*, “we may be able,” rather than *possemus*, “we might be able.”]

While they were thus acting fraudulently and promising some sort of unity—a unity which, even if it had followed, ought rather to have been called confusion—it was granted that the letter which those holy and venerable Fathers had approved as orthodox should be anathematized, not by itself alone, but together with those who had approved it. [Note: [Col. 0533D] The same manuscript has *anathema*, “anathema,” rather than *anathematizata*, “anathematized.”]

And so, to confront such unspeakable audacity, since we have sufficiently experienced the custom of those very Eutychians, who impose the crime of Nestorianism on all who resist them for the truth, I have resolved first to disclose, not merely in simple speech—as I have already done in approving your confession—but also to establish with the necessary proofs and defend against its attackers, the faith which I hold concerning the life-giving incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. In this way I may avoid, by as full a manifestation of the truth as I can provide, the calumnies of those whose frauds and lies I have undertaken to expose and whose errors I have undertaken to refute.

I do this so that they may not turn away from recognizing the truth which we are about to make known the minds of any simple people who do not know us, by bringing disgrace upon our name. For it is also well established that not only do the Eutychians, convicted of their own vanity, accuse us of being Nestorians, but the Nestorians themselves—whom the defense of our faith no less refutes—in turn accuse us of the Eutychian heresy.

And although we neither fear these accusations nor marvel at them as though they were new—for the Arians once falsely branded our fathers as Sabellians, while the Sabellians branded them as Arians—we must nevertheless, as the Apostle urges (Rom. 12:17), provide what is good not only before God but also before all people, and forestall the accusations of detractors, especially in a matter of faith.

Let this, then, have been said for the satisfaction of those who, because they are unaware of the necessity, also attend less carefully to what is being said. Those who are more discerning will certainly understand how the defense of the faith, which I share with your piety, also advances the defense of the present cause.

For if I prove that this faith rightly and prudently resists both Nestorians and Eutychians, and that we have already shown it to accord with the definitions of the great Council of Chalcedon, it will seem exceedingly absurd to believe that the letter approved by that council is Nestorian, since by its own definitions that council so skillfully countered the deceit of the Nestorians.

Moreover, since on account of these matters the Nestorians and Eutychians slander the council—whether in the judgment pronounced concerning the letter of Ibas or in the other matters on either side—their whole vain purpose will come to nothing. They will recognize that they labor in vain if, when we assert our faith, they see the decrees of that council confirmed, the authority of which they seek to remove elsewhere by a deceitful and circuitous route in order to weaken it.

Since, therefore, the order proposed is useful both to the defender and to the defense of the cause, in this volume we shall briefly defend the three matters mentioned above. For what could more clearly prove against the calumniating Eutychians that we are completely alien to the deceit of the Nestorians than for us to assert these two things: that one of the Trinity was crucified for us, and that blessed Mary is rightly and truly and properly called the Mother of God?

Or what could likewise demonstrate more clearly against the calumniating Nestorians that we are farther removed from the disagreement of the Eutychians than for us also to affirm this third point: that the same Lord Jesus Christ is perfect in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity?

## CHAPTER III. How it is more fitting to say, against the Nestorians, that one of the Trinity suffered than that one person of the Trinity suffered; how the term “persons” began to be used in the Trinity because of Sabellius; and concerning baptism in the name of the Lord Jesus
Certainly, we must not be silent about the fact that there are also Catholics who, as we believe, unaware that this had previously been confirmed by the aforementioned council, contend unnecessarily over the wording. For they think that one should not say that one of the Trinity was crucified for us, but rather that one person of the Trinity was crucified.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] Those who disliked the expression “one of the Trinity crucified” were chiefly concerned lest they should appear, with the Eutychians, to say that the divinity suffered. Others, on the contrary—for example, John Maxentius—called those who spoke of “one person of the Trinity” under suspicion, as though, with Nestorius, they were introducing a fourth person. For the rest, Ferrandus, a Carthaginian deacon of the same period and nation as Facundus, teaches in his letter to Anatolius, a Roman deacon, that both expressions are pious and correct and are said in one and the same sense; and before both of them, Pope John II teaches the same in his letter to Avienus, the Senator, Liberius, and others.]

[Note: [Col. 0534D] The same manuscript: “from the place previously mentioned.”]

We ought therefore first to join these people, as being close to us, so that they too may hold with us this confession, in which, as it seems to many, the deceit of the Nestorians cannot be concealed.

[Note: [Col. 0534D] In the same manuscript, the word *videtur* is absent.]

Otherwise, by contending idly over a word, they may settle the substance of the controversy without sufficient examination. For when they assert that our Lord Jesus Christ is one person of the Trinity, while they do not deny that he is one subsistence of God—existing through the union of the natures, that is, of divinity and humanity—and say that the God is the same as the man, not God in one way and man in another, but both alike, that is, naturally, they seem to me to be contending merely over the wording.

Indeed, they demonstrate this in their own argument. “If,” they say, “we say that one of the Trinity was crucified for us, and someone asks what we mean by ‘one,’ we cannot answer ‘God’ or ‘Son,’ because there are not three gods or three sons in the Trinity, from whom one could be said to have been crucified. Therefore we correctly say that one person of the Trinity was crucified, since there are three persons in the Trinity, from whom one can be said to have been crucified.”

But this is not a general rule of speech; it is a private law that they have made for themselves through their contentiousness. For it is so far from being necessary to understand three gods or three sons when one of the Trinity is said to have been crucified that Scripture could say in Genesis: “Behold, Adam has become one of us” (Gen. 3:22). This is certainly not understood as spoken from the person of the Father alone, nor of the Son alone, nor of the Holy Spirit alone; rather, the whole Trinity itself—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is introduced there as speaking. Hence the plural expression “of us” is used.

Why, then, does Scripture not say there, “Behold, Adam has become one person from our persons,” but rather, “Behold, Adam has become one of us”? Is it “one God from us,” as though from three gods? Or “one Father from us,” as though from three fathers?

[Note: [Col. 0535D] Perhaps: “from three gods.”]

Or “one Son” or “one Holy Spirit from us,” as though from three sons or three Holy Spirits? Who, even if insane, has ever said this?

[Note: [Col. 0535D] The Verona manuscript: “Who would have said this?”]

No one can speak about the Trinity better than the Trinity itself has spoken about itself. Therefore, when our Lord Jesus Christ is called “one of the Trinity,” it does not follow that “one God” or “one Son” must be understood as one from three gods or three sons.

There are nevertheless three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—from whom one is rightly called the Lord Jesus Christ. The Apostle John also speaks in this way in his Epistle of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: “There are three who bear witness on earth, the spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one” (1 John 5:7). By “the spirit” he signifies the Father, just as, according to John’s own Gospel, the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman, saying:

“Believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth; for the Father also seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:21–24).

By “the water,” however, he signifies the Holy Spirit, as he explains in the same Gospel when he records the Lord’s words:

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

Then he adds: “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:37–39).

By “the blood,” he signifies the Son, because he himself, from the holy Trinity, shared in flesh and blood.

Thus the Apostle John does not say, speaking of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, “There are three persons who bear witness on earth, the spirit, the water, and the blood, and these three are one.”

[Note: [Col. 0535D] The same manuscript reads, *et hae tres unum sunt* (“and these three [feminine] are one”); but the preferable reading is: *tres sunt (qui) testificantur in terra, spiritus, aqua et sanguis, et hi tres unum sunt* (“there are three [who] bear witness on earth, the spirit, the water, and the blood, and these three [masculine] are one”). “What then …?”]

What answer, then, do they give on behalf of the Apostle John? Who are these three said to bear witness on earth and to be one? Gods? Fathers? Sons? Or Holy Spirits?

Certainly not. These three are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, although no single name is found that is commonly predicated of all of them in the masculine gender, as “persons” is commonly predicated of them in the feminine gender.

Or, if perhaps those who contend over the word do not wish the Trinity, which is one God, to be understood in the statement, “There are three who bear witness on earth, the spirit, the water, and the blood, and these three are one,” let them answer on behalf of the Apostle John according to the very words he used. Can these three, who are said to bear witness on earth and to be one, be called spirits, waters, or bloods?

Yet the blessed Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage, understands this testimony of the Apostle John as spoken of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the letter—or book—which he wrote on the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0536D] The same manuscript reads, “on Unity.” Indeed, in the book *On the Unity of the Church* there are words which Facundus reports.]

For he says:

[Col. 0536C] “The Lord says, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30); and again, it is written of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: ‘And these three are one’ (1 John 5:7).” (Vol. II.)

Accordingly, those who needlessly occupy themselves with traps in wording ought to consider that we do not say, simultaneously and in conjunction, “one Son of the Trinity was incarnate,” lest we seem to introduce three or two sons. Rather, after first saying what the great council confirmed—“one of the Trinity was incarnate,” or “suffered,” or “was crucified”—when we are asked which one of the Trinity we mean, we rightly answer afterward, “the Son.”

It would not, however, be correct to say simultaneously, “one son of the Trinity was incarnate, suffered, or was crucified.” But it does not follow that what cannot correctly be said together cannot correctly be said separately.

Lest they pretend not to understand this—or perhaps truly cannot—let them either be convicted or instructed by the example of their own words. For they themselves correctly say that one person of the Trinity was crucified, as that blessed man of admirable learning, Augustine, also teaches in the work he wrote *On the Predestination and Perseverance of the Saints*:

[Note: [Col. 0536D] The same manuscript reads, “says.”]

[Col. 0536C] “The faithful person who believes and confesses that the true human nature in him is our nature, although it was singularly assumed by God the Word and exalted into the one Son of God, so that the one who assumed and that which he assumed might be one person in the Trinity.” (Vol. II.)

[Col. 0537A] Therefore, since they too, as we have taught,

[Note: [Col. 0537D] The Verona manuscript reads, “as we have said.”]

correctly say, in accordance with the teaching of the Fathers, that one person of the Trinity was crucified, and when asked whose person they say it is, rightly answer, “the Son,” they will not nevertheless be able to say correctly, simultaneously and in conjunction, what they say correctly in isolation—namely, “one person of the Son was crucified from the Trinity,” as though there were two persons of the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0537] See the distinguished Wesseling, *Probabilia*, ch. 36, p. 324, on this passage.]

Thus, although it is not correct to say together, “one person of the Son from the Trinity was crucified,” it is nevertheless correct to say separately, “one person of the Trinity was crucified,” and likewise to say separately of that person that it is the Son’s; so, although it is not correct to say together, “one son of the Trinity was crucified,” it is nevertheless correct to say separately, “one of the Trinity was crucified,” and likewise of that one, that he is the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] The same manuscript reads: “yet it is correctly said separately, ‘one person of the Trinity was crucified’; and likewise, etc.”]

Therefore it is correct to say both “one of the Trinity was crucified” and “one person of the Trinity was crucified.” But to speak of “one person” excludes the new evasions of the Nestorians less effectively. Convicted by countless testimonies of the Fathers that God the Word and the assumed man are one person, they either think—or pretend to think—that this was said by the Fathers according to the dignity of authority in the sense that the man Jesus Christ bore the person of the Word, just as the Apostle also bore a person when, writing to the Corinthians, he says: “For whatever I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—for your sake, in the person of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan” (2 Cor. 2:10); not in the sense that God and man were one and the same.

Since, however, it is rightly said both that one of the Trinity and that one person of the Trinity was crucified for us, those who did not wish to say that one of the Trinity was incarnate, suffered, or was crucified ought now to understand and approve the benefit by which the deceit of the Nestorians has been sufficiently excluded by the holy and great council.

[Note: [Col. 0538D] The same manuscript reads *quia* (“because”) instead of *qua* (“by which”).]

Even if no benefit invited us to do so, and even if this had not been confirmed by the authority of so great a council, they would act more modestly by acquiescing in the wise Gregory, who decided that there should be no disagreement over diversity of vocabulary (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 39). In that discourse entitled *On the Lights*, he spoke as follows:

[Col. 0537D] “When I name God, you are enlightened by one light, and at the same time by three: by three, according to the properties or persons of each. For there must be no disagreement on account of diversity of terms, when the diversity of all expressions directs the understanding toward the same meaning.”

Since, therefore, a great benefit invites us to this confession; since the expression under discussion is neither unheard-of nor novel, so that we are free to deliberate whether it should be admitted; since we have shown that it accords with the testimonies of divine Scripture and has also been confirmed by so many Fathers; and since there ought to be no disagreement over the word, it should please everyone that one of the Trinity, or one from the Trinity, be said to have been crucified for us.

Yet if anyone examines the matter carefully and traces the question back to its deeper basis, he will find that we do not say “one for one person,” but rather that “one person is said for one of the Trinity.” For in this way

[Note: [Col. 0538D] The same manuscript reads, “always.”]

the Church of Christ, even before it used the term “person” to distinguish the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,

[Note: [Col. 0538D] The same manuscript reads, “persons.”]

believed and proclaimed three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as we showed above from the testimony of John the Apostle, where it is said: “There are three who bear witness on earth, the spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one” (1 John 5:7).

The term “persons” was therefore adopted for ecclesiastical teaching only when Sabellius was attacking the Church, so that those who had always been believed and called three—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—might also be called, together and by a common designation, “persons.”

Afterward they were also called “subsistences,” because the Church decided to apply this term as well to personal distinction, in order to signify the Trinity. Thus the question at one time concerned the new terms “person” and “subsistence”: whether they ought to be admitted to signify the Trinity, which is God, just as the term “Trinity” itself had been admitted. It did not concern what the Church had always held and proclaimed: that there are three who bear witness on earth, and that these three are one.

Hence the aforementioned man Augustine, in the fifteenth book of *On the Trinity* (chapter 3), says:

[Note: [Col. 0538D] The same manuscript reads, “the most learned man.”]

[Col. 0538C] “It is clear in the substance of truth that not only is the Father not greater than the Son, but even the two together are not something greater than the Holy Spirit alone; nor are any two in that same Trinity something greater than one; nor are all three together something greater than each individually.”

The exceedingly cautious and wise man did not say, “Both persons together are something greater in the substance of truth than the Holy Spirit alone”—although he could correctly have said this if he wished—but rather “both.” Nor did he say, “Any two persons in that same Trinity are something greater than one,” but “any two in that same Trinity are something greater than one.” Nor did he say, “All three persons together are something greater than each individually,” but “all three together are something greater than each individually.”

If I wished to gather expressions of this kind from the writings of the most approved Fathers, time would run out before examples did.

There is therefore nothing for which we should be reproached on account of our wording when we say that one of the Trinity was incarnate, suffered, or was crucified. The holy Council of Chalcedon, instructed by the authority of divine Scripture and the testimonies of the most ancient Fathers, saw that this had been usefully written by Proclus to the Armenians and approved in the council by the most wise John of Antioch and the other Eastern bishops; accordingly, it too confirmed the expression in a fitting manner.

Therefore, those who, having accepted this religious and necessary expression, had previously contended needlessly over the word, ought now to press and constrain the Nestorians together with us, so that they may say not only “one person of the Trinity”—which, as we have already said, they wrongly interpret—but also “one of the Trinity suffered,” a statement which they cannot evade by any deception.

We press these Nestorians even more forcefully if we say to them:

It is certain that you agree with us that the Trinity, which is one God, was signified by the Apostle when he said:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever” (Rom. 11:33–36).

By “from him,” he means from the Father; by “through him,” through the Son, as he says elsewhere: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we are in him,”

[Note: [Col. 0539D] The Verona manuscript reads, “into him.”]

“and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we are through him” (1 Cor. 8:6).

By “in him,” he means in the Holy Spirit, of whom Solomon says: “For the spirit of God has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice” (Wisdom 1:7). To have all things “in him” means nothing other than that all things are contained by him.

Since this is so, how is the Lord Jesus Christ not one of this Trinity, when, as we have shown, the Apostle himself says: “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we are through him”?

Again, when the Lord Jesus Christ himself, revealing this Trinity to us, said to his disciples in the Gospel, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), how could the Apostle Peter, exhorting the Jews, say: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38)?

Or, as we likewise read in the same Acts of the Apostles (chapter 19), when Paul, the fellow apostle of Peter, found certain disciples at Ephesus who had received only John’s baptism, why were they, after being instructed by him, baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, unless the Lord Jesus Christ were one of the Trinity, in whose name alone baptism was commanded?

[Note: [Col. 0539D] The same manuscript reads *similiter* (“similarly”).]

The fact that those whom we have mentioned are reported to have been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus should not, I think, be understood to mean that they were not baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as though the form of baptism established by the Lord were preserved even in the wording of those accounts.

[Note: [Col. 0539D–0540D] Saint Ambrose held another view: in book 3 of *On the Holy Spirit*, he judged that the apostles baptized only in the name of the Lord Jesus, while the mystery was nevertheless complete, because whoever named the One signified the Trinity. Saint Athanasius had written the same in his work *On the Trinity*, extant only in Latin: “Did the apostles become transgressors of the Saviour’s command and baptize so great a multitude contrary to his tradition? For it is not written that they baptized them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, but only in the name of the Lord Jesus. Did they therefore transgress? Far be it. For although the name of the Son alone is mentioned, the Father and the Spirit are thereby also declared.” The same deacon Ferrandus holds this view in his letter to Anatolius.] Rather, because it had to be indicated that they had received the new baptism, it was judged sufficient, to distinguish that new baptism, to mention only the name of the Lord Jesus—a name that did not occur in John’s baptism or in the other baptisms of the Jewish rite.

In fact, they seem to me to have been baptized with those sacred words, namely, “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Nor do I think that the statement “Let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ,” or that some were baptized “in the name of the Lord Jesus,” was spoken falsely—far be that from us. For the apostles certainly baptized in the name of Jesus, although they did not baptize in the name of the Lord Jesus alone, that is, of the Son, but also in the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0540D] The same manuscript reads, “of the Lord Jesus.”]

Accordingly, I think that when baptism was celebrated, that form of baptism was also preserved in the sacred words themselves; but in the narrative it was sufficient, in order to distinguish it from other baptisms, to mention the Lord Jesus alone.

For this reason, I believe that, when the name of the Lord Jesus was used to indicate the new baptism, it was preferred to the mention of all three persons because we are buried with him through baptism into death.

Nevertheless, this would not be said unless, as we have already asserted, the Lord Jesus Christ were one of the Trinity.

Instructed by these and many other considerations, before I learned that this had been approved by the great Council of Chalcedon, I believed that the Lord Jesus Christ was one of the Trinity: God born from God before the ages, and the same one born as man from the Virgin in the fullness of time; the one who, existing as the Father’s only-begotten Son, became the only-begotten Son of his mother; so that, as Ambrose understood and sang, he might be believed to be a giant of twofold substance, by the distinctive character of both true births; and that he might be consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and consubstantial with his mother according to his humanity.

And just as he is believed to be consubstantial with the Father because he is his own and true Son, so he is also believed to be consubstantial with his mother because he is likewise her own and true son.

## CHAPTER IV

That the blessed Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God, against certain Catholics and against the Nestorians. The testimonies of Hilary, Augustine, and the presbyter Leporius are examined.

But who except the most absurd person would deny that the true and proper mother of a true and proper son is herself truly and properly a mother? We have also shown that this accords with the judgment of the great Synod of Chalcedon [Col. 0540D], and we promised that we would establish it in the second part of our division.

It must be made clear, however, that certain persons who are also in communion with the Church [Col. 0541A] [Note: [Col. 0541D] Although after the Synod of Ephesus there was no room among Catholics for doubt that the Virgin Mary ought truly and properly to be called *Deipara*, θεοτόκος (“God-bearer”), since that synod plainly decreed this against Nestorius, Pope John shows from Justinian’s letters, in the same epistle to the senators, that some besides Facundus nevertheless disputed this term without cause in these times.] think that this confession—that we call blessed Mary truly and properly the Mother of God—ought not to be accepted, even while they admit that Nestorius deserved condemnation because he denied that she was the Mother of God.

Before we answer the Nestorians, I think we must answer these people [Note: [Col. 0541D] Veronese manuscript: “we must demonstrate.”]—as has already been done in the preceding question—that it is altogether foolish and shameful both to approve Nestorius’s condemnation and to deny that blessed Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God. For if there could have been any question on this point, it was settled together with Nestorius himself, who denied that she was the Mother of God. It seemed difficult to believe, and worthy of dispute, whether that Virgin had given birth to God; but that she truly and properly gave birth to whomever she gave birth to appears to be a matter worthy of no dispute [Note: [Col. 0541D] The same manuscript reads *nullius* (“of no one”) for *nulli* (“to no one”).].

Therefore, those who concede that the Virgin gave birth to God—which is beyond comprehension and uniquely proper to one mother—why do they deny that she truly and properly gave birth to him, when this is common to all mothers and worthy of no question? Moreover, they dare to assign to the Eutychian doctrine what we say: that blessed Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God. They do not understand either what they are saying or the matters about which they make their assertions, as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 1:7).

The holy Synod of Chalcedon, by which Eutyches himself was condemned, says—as we have mentioned elsewhere (*In the Address to Marcian*):

> “How the Virgin was called Mother of God on account of him who deigned even after birth to consecrate her virginity and, as was fitting for God, to seal the womb with integrity; how she was called mother according to truth on account of the flesh which she supplied from herself to the Lord of all.”

[Col. 0541C] Since, then, according to the teaching of these Fathers, she was called mother according to truth precisely because she supplied flesh from herself to the Lord of all [Note: [Col. 0541D] The same manuscript reads “Mother of God.”], which Eutyches denies, how can this be thought assignable to the Eutychian doctrine, when it is found to be more opposed to it? For he cannot call the blessed Virgin truly and properly the Mother of God, but only nominally and superficially, since he does not believe that she supplied flesh from herself to the Lord of all.

This confession, therefore, by which blessed Mary is called truly and properly the Mother of God, destroys not only the Nestorian heresy but also the Eutychian. If they do not believe that our position belongs to the right faith, and suspect that we conceal something in these words, let them question us about the matter in whatever way they wish and draw out through their questions what we believe.

But if they do not doubt the correctness of our faith, and merely think that the correct faith is not being expressed in correct words, they say that we are perfect in understanding but not perfect in our statement, although the Apostle exhorts us to be perfect in both, saying: “But be perfect in the same understanding and in the same judgment” (1 Cor. 1:10) [Note: [Col. 0542D] The same manuscript reads: “be perfect.”]. Let them themselves explain whether that Virgin—whose being Mother of God they do not deny—is to be called so truly and properly, or nominally and superficially.

If they say that it does not follow that, if she is not truly and properly the Mother of God, she must therefore be nominally and superficially the Mother of God, let them state in what manner we ought, against them, to proclaim her Mother of God. For everyone who resists another’s assertion ought to say something either contrary to it or different from it.

Thus, when the Arians said that the Son was inferior to the Father, we say against them that he is equal to the Father. When the Manichaeans said that the flesh of that same Son of God was imaginary—that is, false—we say against them that he became human in true flesh. [Note: [Col. 0542D] The same manuscript reads *sic* (“thus”) for *sicut* (“just as”).] In this way, those who attack what is true and Catholic assert something of their own. No one resists another’s teaching in any other way than by saying something against it; and when someone has contradicted it, only then is it investigated whether that contradiction is acceptable.

But in the case of those who forbid us to call Mary truly and properly the Mother of God, while they do not say in what manner she should be called the Mother of God, there is no need to ask whether their contradiction is acceptable. For those who say nothing against it—how can they even appear to be saying anything? Therefore, our labor in resisting their absurdity is not so great as the danger to our reputation, lest we appear to answer unnecessarily those who offer no contradiction.

Although those who deny what we say—namely, that Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God—have so far affirmed nothing of their own, they must nevertheless be asked whether they dare to deny what necessarily follows from their position: what they forbid us to confess. Let them add the negation and say that she is not truly and properly the Mother of God [Col. 0542C]. I will not now say whether Catholic ears can endure this, but let them see whether their own faces can bear this profane and detestable statement.

If, however, they do not dare to say, “She is not truly and properly the Mother of God,” why do they forbid us to confess what they do not dare to deny? Let them therefore acknowledge, together with the holy Synod, whose decrees they profess to accept, that blessed Virgin was called the Mother of God according to truth because she supplied flesh from herself to the Lord of all. Let them not claim that they oppose the Eutychians by denying that Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God, when they are rather shown, unknowingly, to favor them: they resist the judgment of the Synod of Chalcedon, in which the Eutychians were condemned, and deny what is contrary to their vanity.

They should also beware, having experienced the perfidy of the Nestorians, to whom we must now respond concerning this confession as well. Otherwise, by saying—as though in defense of the distinction between the natures—that not the man Christ Jesus but God the Word is the proper and true Son of God, or that not God the Word but the man Christ Jesus is the proper and true son of man, they themselves may appear not to believe that the same person is God the Word whom they believe to be man, but to regard one person as God and another as man.

If, however, the God who is man is the same, and the man who is God is the same, then God the Word is just as properly and truly said to be the son of man as the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is properly and truly said to be the Son of God. No confusion of the natures is introduced by this; rather, the unity of the person is indicated.

The Apostle John was not introducing a confusion of the natures when he said: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given understanding [Note: [Col. 0543D] Veronese manuscript: “has given us understanding.”], so that we may know him who is true, and we are [Note: [Col. 0543D] Perhaps *we may be*] in his true Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 5:20). Nor was Paul doing so when he said: “If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:31–32).

If John calls Christ—that is, the Anointed One—the true Son of God, and testifies that he came, while coming and being anointed, insofar as concerns the distinction of the natures, belong more to humanity than to divinity; and if Paul calls him God’s own Son, yet teaches that the Father did not spare him, but handed him over for us all and gave him everything—things which likewise, when the natures are being distinguished, cannot be attributed to divinity—neither of them is believed to have confused the natures by proclaiming such things. Rather, they expressed the unity of the person.

Let the Nestorians answer, then, how the same principle of personal unity, without any confusion of the natures, does not demand from us that we say truly and properly that God the Word is the son of man and that blessed Virgin Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God.

The centurion, moreover, who guarded the body of the crucified Lord of glory, saw the elements of the world thrown into confusion when the Creator of the world expired [Note: [Col. 0543D] The same manuscript reads: “the same world,” etc.], and recognized him as the true [Note: [Col. 0543D] The same manuscript reads: “truly.”] Son of God. For he said: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:55).

Blessed Hilary confirms the truth of this statement, saying as follows (*On the Trinity*, Book III):

> “Those who had crucified him confess him truly to be the Son of God; the outcome agrees with the proclamation. The Lord had said: ‘Glorify your Son’ (John 17:1). He testified not only by the name ‘Son,’ but also by the propriety expressed in the words ‘your Son.’ Many are sons of God among us, but this Son is not such as they are. For he is both the proper and true Son: by origin, not adoption; in truth, not merely in name; by birth, not by creation. Therefore, after his glorification, confession of his truth followed. For the centurion confesses the true Son of God, so that none of the believers might doubt what one of his persecutors had not denied.”

If, then, according to Hilary—an exceedingly learned bishop and courageous confessor, testifying in accordance with apostolic teaching—the one who was crucified is the proper and true Son of God, there is no doubt that God is also truly and properly the Father of the crucified Son.

Since this is so, just as we need not fear that, when God is called truly and properly the Father of the crucified Son, it will follow that the humanity assumed and crucified by the Word of God was changed into divinity, or that human nature, which is composite, became consubstantial with the simple nature of the Father, so it does not follow, when we say that Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God, that the divinity of the Word was changed into flesh, or that the divine nature, which is simple, became consubstantial with the composite nature of the mother.

Otherwise, if it is blasphemous and absurd to say that blessed Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God, then, without further argument, it is blasphemous and absurd to say that God the Word is truly and properly the son of man [Note: [Col. 0544D] The same manuscript reads: “that God also, reciprocally, [is …].”]. If it seems blasphemous and absurd to say that God the Word is truly and properly the son of man, then it will consequently seem blasphemous and absurd to say that the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is truly and properly the Son of God.

But divine Scripture, which says nothing blasphemous or absurd, says, on account of the unity of the person, that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, is the true and proper Son of God. He gave himself as a ransom for all; in the true Son of God we are; and the Father did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all.

Therefore, on account of this same unity of person, blessed Mary is rightly called truly and properly the mother of that only-begotten Word of God.

For this reason, the most learned and distinguished teacher of the Churches of Christ, Augustine, in the work mentioned above, which he wrote *On the Predestination and Perseverance of the Saints* (chapter 15), says:

> “The Teacher of the Gentiles cries out at the head of his Epistles, Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, through the resurrection of the dead (Rom. 1:1–4). Jesus was therefore predestined so that he who was to be the son of David according to the flesh might nevertheless be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, because he was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. This is that singular and ineffable assumption of humanity by God the Word, so that the Son of God and the son of man might be called truly and properly one and the same: the son of man because of the humanity assumed, and the Son of God because of the only-begotten God who assumed it; lest we should believe not in a Trinity but in a quaternity.”

This learned man therefore taught that the assumed humanity is truly and properly called the Son of God and that the assuming God, on account of the assumed humanity, is truly and properly called the son of man [Note: [Col. 0544D] The same manuscript reads: “the man, on account of the assuming only-begotten God, truly,” etc.]. Otherwise, there would have been no need for him to add the words “truly and properly,” except to commend this great mystery, through which God became the son of man and man became the Son of God.

For who could doubt that a man is truly and properly called the son of man, or that God is truly and properly called the Son of God? The same person, therefore—God the Word, who is also the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus—is called the son of man as truly and properly as he is called the Son of God.

But if God is truly and properly called the son of man, it is necessary that, reciprocally, blessed Mary be called truly and properly the Mother of God. When Augustine added the words “lest we should believe not in a Trinity but in a quaternity,” he compelled us altogether to say that blessed Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God, lest we appear to believe not in a Trinity but in a quaternity.

Therefore, the denial of this devout and necessary expression should not be regarded as insignificant, since it is followed by such great blasphemy.

It is certainly not surprising that Augustine declares God to be truly and properly called the son of man, since in a sermon on the Epiphany (*On the Time*, Sermon 33), whose beginning is, “Recently we celebrated the day on which the Lord was born from the Jews; today we celebrate the day on which he was worshiped by the Gentiles,” he speaks as follows:

> “The star led the Magi precisely to the very place where God the Word was an infant.”

[Note: [Col. 0545D] The Veronese manuscript reads *Qui* (“Who”); perhaps *Qui ergo* (“Who, then”).]

If, then, he calls the Word, who is God, an infant, how could he not declare that God is truly and properly the son of man? For if that infant is truly and properly called the son of man, and that infant is God the Word, then God the Word is truly and properly called the son of man.

Again, in another sermon for the same day (*On the Time*, Sermon 30), whose beginning is, “The Magi came from the East to adore the Virgin’s childbirth,” he says:

> “Moreover, the same star that led the Magi to the place where God the infant was with his Virgin mother,” etc.

Who, then, can deny that God is truly and properly called the son of man, while resisting the teaching of this most learned man—unless he either denies that God was an infant or denies that the infant was truly and properly the son of man?

Since piety does not permit us to deny the former, and human nature does not permit us to deny the latter, we must believe without hesitation that God is truly and properly the son of man. Once this has been established, there is no doubt that that Virgin too must reciprocally be called truly and properly the Mother of God.
