Likewise, when a certain presbyter named Leporius in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0545D] The same manuscript reads *Galliam*.] had been corrupted from the true and ancient faith of the Church and presumed to teach the same things that Nestorius later taught, he was expelled on account of that error and came to Africa to be instructed. There, as the Apostle teaches (Gal. 6:1), he was instructed in a spirit of gentleness by the spiritual Fathers Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and the aforementioned Augustine, together with the other African bishops, and renounced the most perverse novelty of his doctrine.

The same Leporius wrote a *Book of Satisfaction* to the Gallic bishops. The venerable Fathers Aurelius and Augustine, together with the others mentioned, approved it in such a way that, to establish the truth, they also added their signatures to it [Note: [Col. 0545D] We later obtained the complete *Book of Satisfaction* of Leporius, part of which we published from Cassian in volume I of the Councils of Gaul, together with the subscriptions of Aurelius, Augustine, and others, mentioned here. We hope that it will shortly be made public in its entirety.]. In that book, after much discussion [Note: [Col. 0545D] The same manuscript reads “after many things.”], he says:

> “Therefore God the man Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is properly born of the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin [Note: [Col. 0546D] The same manuscript reads “ever-virgin.”]; and thus the Word and flesh become one in mutual union, so that, while each substance remains naturally in its own perfection, without prejudice to itself divine things may be communicated to humanity and human things may participate in divinity. There is not one God and another man; rather, the same Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who is God and also man, and reciprocally man and also God, is named and truly is so.”

Since that wicked error—which, while destroying the whole mystery of our salvation, thinks itself cautious and careful—first appeared among the Latin Churches, it was not, as among the Greeks, increased through disputes. Rather, through the great and anxious devotion of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0546D] The same manuscript reads *satagente* (“striving”) for *satagendo* (“by striving”).], as soon as it was detected it was condemned even by its own author. It seemed to those holy Fathers that the error could be abolished in no other way than if the very author of the error confessed in writing that God was properly born from the Virgin Mary.

For he says, as we have mentioned:

> “Therefore God is properly born of the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-Virgin.”

Thus he says that God was properly born from the Virgin, while also saying that the man Jesus Christ, reciprocally, is named and truly is the Son of God. Hence he added:

> “And thus the Word and flesh become one in mutual union.”

He did not thereby prejudice the distinction of either nature, since he confessed that, while each substance remains naturally in its own perfection, without prejudice to itself the divine participates in the human and the human in the divine. He did not call one person God and another man, but confessed that the same Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is called and truly is the God who is also man, and reciprocally the man who is also God.

If God is truly man, and is truly man only by being born from the Virgin, why should God not be said to be truly born from the Virgin? And if God properly became man, and became man properly only by being born from the Virgin, why should he not also be said to have been properly born from the Virgin?

It is exceedingly absurd that God, who by being born from the Virgin truly and properly became man, should not be said to have been truly and properly born from her: that the reality produced by that birth should be true, while the birth itself that produced that reality should not be a true birth.

Nor is this less absurd: someone who is not offended when the prophet says, “Mother Zion says: ‘A man,’ and a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5), and who calmly and faithfully accepts that the Most High himself, who founded Zion, became man in her; and who is not offended when the Evangelist says, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14)—if he hears that things belonging to man are attributed to the Most High who became man, and things belonging to flesh are attributed to the Word who became flesh, should nevertheless take offense, as though he had not previously believed the reason for these statements when he believed that the Most High became man and that the Word became flesh.

It is more to say that the Most High became man than to attribute things belonging to man to the Most High; and it is more to say that the Word became flesh than to attribute things belonging to flesh to God the Word.

Since, therefore, the Spirit of God judged it more fitting and useful to commend to us in this mystery the union of the divine and human natures by saying what is greater—namely, that the Most High became man and that the Word became flesh—why should anyone, grounded in this authority and without prejudice to either nature, fear attributing to the Most High what belongs to humanity and to the Word what belongs to flesh, on account of the sacrament and dispensation of his incarnation?

Speaking of God the Word, the same John does not hesitate in his Epistle to attribute to him what belongs to flesh [Note: [Col. 0547D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “to attribute to him what belongs to flesh.”], since in his Gospel he proclaimed that the Word became flesh [Note: [Col. 0547D] The same manuscript reads “flesh,” rather than “having been made flesh.”].

For in his Gospel he began his discourse in this way:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

And later:

> “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Likewise, in his Epistle he began in the same way:

> “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life; and the life was made manifest, and we have seen and testify and announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was made manifest to us” (1 John 1:1–2).

Thus, announcing to us concerning the Word of life, who was from the beginning, and not inserting in these statements the name of the flesh assumed by him, he says of the Word himself that he had looked upon him with his eyes and touched him with his hands. He does not hesitate to attribute what belongs to flesh to the incarnate Word.

Why, then, do the Nestorians, as though more cautious and more diligent than the Apostle John—or rather, than God the Word himself, who spoke about himself in the Apostle John—shrink from attributing what belongs to humanity to God and from calling blessed Mary truly and properly the Mother of God? They do not shrink from calling her truly and properly the mother of a man, unless it is because, not believing that the one who is man is the same as the one who is God, they wish to introduce for us two sons—not in words, perhaps, but in reality [Note: [Col. 0548D] The same manuscript reads: “in the realities themselves.”].

But we know that the Apostle said:

> “For I myself could wish to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites. To them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the exaltation, and the promises; to them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:3–5).

We do not think there is one Christ and another God who is over all. Rather, believing that the same Christ is God over all, we call his mother, blessed Mary the Virgin, truly and properly the Mother of God.

## CHAPTER V. That Christ has two natures, not one composite nature, against the Eutychians and Semi-Eutychians. Concerning Pope Julius and Cyril of Alexandria, whose writings the opponents bring forward

[Col. 0548A]

Suffice it to have said this against the perfidy of the Nestorians; these things, as I think, defend us more than adequately against the calumnies of the Eutychians, who, when they are refuted by Catholics, fasten upon them the charge of Nestorianism. And therefore let us now demonstrate that the third proposition, contrary to the aforesaid Eutychians, is correct: namely, that we confess our Lord Jesus Christ to be perfect in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity. By this we shall also overturn the calumnies of the Nestorians [Note: [Col. 0548D] The same manuscript reads, “avoid.”], who think that, in order to confuse Christ’s two natures, we say that the Lord Jesus Christ is one of the Trinity and that Mary is truly and properly the mother of God.

We therefore proclaim that Christ, the Son of God, as has been said, exists in two natures. Nor do we allow that one nature of his has been composed from divinity and humanity, lest he not be consubstantial with the Father, whose nature is simple, and lest, just as he is of another person than the Father, he should likewise be said to be of another—that is, a different—nature. Indeed, he will not be consubstantial with us either unless he has two natures: one, namely, in which he is consubstantial with the Father, and another in which he is consubstantial with us.

But the senseless contention of the Eutychians opposes this most evident reasoning, asserting that the unity of God the Word, which is immutably simple, could be composed with the humanity assumed into one nature. The Eutychians are divided into two groups. One follows throughout the opinion of Eutyches, its leader; the other, although dissenting from him in certain matters, nevertheless disdainfully refuses to return through repentance to the Church, so that what is said of them in the Psalms may seem applicable: “They were divided, and were not pierced with remorse” (Psalm 34:17).

For because, in their contentious vanity, they presumed to confuse things utterly different—namely, the creating nature and the created nature—having been handed over to the fabrications and errors of their own hearts, they have rightly and justly been divided, although they flow from the same filthy spring. But those who, although—as we have said—they depart in certain matters from the opinion of Eutyches himself, their author and head, nevertheless disdain to follow the teaching of the Catholic Church, whose head is Christ, perfect in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity, are called by the Greeks Acephali, “Headless,” since they remain, as it were, without a head [Note: [Col. 0547D] Others give different explanations for this name, such as Leontius, *On the Sects*, chapter 5; Ado of Vienne in his *Chronicle*; Nicephorus, book XVIII, chapter 45; and others. In any case, it is established that the Acephali eventually came universally to be called all the Monophysites who posited one nature in Christ and attacked the Council of Chalcedon, although among themselves they differed in various other errors. Anastasius of Antioch aptly alluded to the ten leaders of these men in his work *On the Economy of Christ* (Περὶ τῆς Χριστοῦ οἰκονομίας, *Peri tēs Christou oikonomias*) and called them a “ten-horned orchestra” (δεκακέρατον ὀρχήστραν, *dekakeraton orchēstran*). He says: “The holy Church casts out Eutyches, Dioscorus, Theodosius, Peter, Timothy, Julian, Gaianus, Barsanuphius, Jacob, and Severus, the chief of this ten-horned orchestra, and the remaining heresiarchs who teach in Christ, in Arian fashion, one nature” (Ἀποβάλλεται … ἀρειανικῶς ἐν Χριστῷ δογματίζοντας).]

that is, Semieutychians, as we may more expressively call them. These schismatics of the divided Eutychians say that, if the Son of God is also proclaimed to have one nature, that same one nature can be understood to be consubstantial with the Father’s nature in one respect and with ours in another. But this is to say that it is consubstantial neither with the Father’s nature nor with ours. For when this one nature of the Son of God is said to possess something which the Father’s nature does not possess, and again something which ours does not possess, this amounts to denying that it is consubstantial both with the Father’s nature and with ours.

For the reason we rightly say that the Son is consubstantial both with the Father and with us is precisely that, although we say that he is one person [Note: [Col. 0549D] The Verona manuscript reads, “that it is his.”], we nevertheless do not deny that he subsists in a certain duality of natures, so that according to one nature he is called consubstantial with the Father, and according to the other, with us.

But the one nature which they themselves say belongs to Christ they altogether deny to be contained in any duality. Thus, when they are asked what the duality consists of, since they can no longer say that it is a duality of natures, they are compelled to say that it is a duality of persons—which they deny with us in opposition to Nestorius. And since, when one nature is compared with another, consubstantiality cannot be declared unless the whole is equated with the whole, so that no difference in definition intervenes, there cannot be one definition of a nature composed from divinity and humanity, if this is believed of the Son, and of the Father’s simple nature, which is wholly divine, or of ours, which is wholly human. Therefore the Son will not be consubstantial both with the Father and with us.

[Note: [Col. 0549D] The same manuscript reads: “the whole is certainly compared with the whole; it cannot be,” and so forth. Another reading continues: “If this is believed of the Son, they must confess two natures of the one Son of God, which they themselves also do not deny, namely, that he is consubstantial both with the Father and with us.”]

Even if this is believed of the Son, they must confess two natures of the one Son of God. This has been demonstrated by innumerable testimonies of the ancient Fathers in defense of the great Council of Chalcedon and in the refutation of Eutychian madness, as you, among many others, have also acknowledged. From these testimonies we shall still produce some—not many in number, but weighty in authority, since they were confirmed by the authority of the Council of Ephesus. For they were brought forward there against Nestorius, and by them he was convicted and condemned.

Since, therefore, both groups of Eutychians claim to follow the authority of that council, I think it sufficient for their refutation if, leaving aside other matters, this one point becomes clear: that the council itself also affirmed Christ to have two natures when, in its proceedings against Nestorius, it cited from the second book of blessed Ambrose to the emperor Gratian (chapter 4), saying [Note: [Col. 0550D] The same manuscript reads, “saying” rather than “who says.”]:

> “Let empty disputes about words, then, be silent, because, as it is written, the kingdom of God is not in persuasive speech but in the demonstration of power. Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh: the Son of God speaks as one in both, because both natures are in him. And although the same one speaks, he does not always speak in the same manner.”

Observe in him now the glory of God, now the sufferings of a human being.

> “As God he speaks what is divine, because he is the Word; as a human being he says what is human, because he spoke in my substance, and so forth.”

They hear these words of Ambrose recited at the Council of Ephesus (session 1). They recognize from them that Nestorius was condemned on the basis of the words: “Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh,” and that although the Son of God is one, he speaks in both—that is, in both natures, divinity and flesh. Hence Ambrose adds: “because both natures are in him.” Yet they are not ashamed openly to lie that they preserve the decrees of that council, while denying that Christ exists in two natures and fabricating the claim that one nature was instead made from two.

Let them also consider what was brought forward from the words of blessed Gregory of Nazianzus against the teaching of Nestorius himself (Letter 1 to Cledonius):

> “If anyone introduces two sons, one from God the Father and the other from his mother, and not one and the same son, he will be deprived of the adoption promised to those who believe rightly. For there are two natures, God and human being, just as there are soul and body, but not two sons; nor are there two human beings here, although Paul (2 Corinthians 4:16) has called what is within and what is outside a human being by those names. And, to speak briefly, there is one thing and another from which the Savior consists; and although the invisible is not the same as the visible, nor the timeless the same as that which is under time, yet they are not one person and another—far from it. For both together are one combination: God incarnate and the human being deified, or by whatever name one may call it. I say that they are one thing and another. But it is otherwise in the Trinity. There one is another and another, so that we do not confuse the individual subsistences; there are not, however, one thing and another, for the three are one and the same in divinity.”

[Note: [Col. 0550D] The same manuscript reads: “but not two sons, nor gods, nor are there two here,” and so forth. The Greek text corresponds: υἱοὶ δὲ οὐ δύο, οὐδὲ θεοί—“but not two sons, nor two gods.”]

Since, then, here too they hear that there are two natures, God and human being, and that Christ is not, as these men wish, said to be one nature composed from both; and since they at the same time observe that, just as in the Trinity the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, and these three names do not signify one person, although they belong to one nature, so also in Christ there is not one nature, although there is one person—how do the Eutychians, if they believe Gregory, or rather the Council of Ephesus, fail to see that it is the same kind of profanation to say that Christ has one nature as to say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one person? The aforesaid council, with Gregory as its witness, demonstrated that the two cases are alike.

What, then, can help them against these most evident testimonies of the Fathers? They say, in support of their most empty error, that Julius, bishop of Rome, wrote somewhere—I do not know where—that Christ has one nature [Note: [Col. 0549D] The letter to Dionysius which the Acephali attributed to Pope Julius was believed by Gennadius, in *Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 2, to have genuinely belonged to Julius. Facundus suspects here that it was forged, as does Eulogius of Alexandria in his third oration preserved by Photius. Leontius of Byzantium, however, who also quotes the words of the letter which the Eutychians misused, teaches in chapter 8 of *On the Sects* that it belonged not to Julius but to the heretic Apollinaris. Anastasius likewise asserts this in his *Excerpt of Passages* (Ἐκλογὴ χρήσεων), as did, before both of them, Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, in his disputation with the Acephali at Constantinople: “We have clearly shown that that famous letter of blessed Julius, written to Dionysius, was manifestly by Apollinaris.” Leontius also denies that another letter, addressed to Prosdocimus, or Docium, whose testimony was used by the Council of Ephesus, belonged to Julius; he says that it was written by Timothy, a disciple of Apollinaris. Others, however, including Ephraem, patriarch of Antioch, in book III of *The Sacred Laws*, preserved by Photius, maintain without controversy that this letter belonged to Julius. There Ephraem quotes part of another statement from the same letter, which Anastasius the presbyter gives in full in chapter 38 of his *Excerpt of Passages on Divine Theology and Economy* (Ἐκλογὴ τῶν χρήσεων περὶ τῆς θείας θεολογίας καὶ οἰκονομίας), except that he calls the addressee Acacius rather than Docium. It reads as follows: “From the letter of Julius, bishop of Rome, to Acacius: Let anyone who does not confess that the Son from Mary is God the Word incarnate, consubstantial with the Father, existing from the beginning, unchangeable in the incarnation, and impassible in his sufferings, be anathema.”]

whereas at that same holy Council of Ephesus only this statement of blessed Julius against Nestorius was read from his letter to Prosdocius [Note: [Col. 0551] On this passage see Mazochius, *Spicilegium Biblicum*, vol. I, p. 34, note 10; compare Coutant, *Appendix to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 73, note.], in which he says (session 1):

> “For the completion of the faith it is proclaimed that the Son was incarnate from the Virgin Mary and dwelt among human beings, not that he worked in one human being; for this had occurred in the prophets and apostles. He is perfect God in the flesh and perfect human being in the spirit. There are not two sons, one the proper Son assuming a human being, the other a mortal received by God; rather, there is one only-begotten Son in heaven, the only-begotten God on earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0551D] The same manuscript reads, “the Son of God.”]

Apart from this letter to Prosdocius, nothing else from the sayings of blessed Julius was brought forward at that council—if indeed he wrote anything else—and nothing further from this letter. Why, then, was it not rather that statement concerning one nature which they circulate as having been written by blessed Julius, or similar statements which they assert other venerable Fathers wrote, that was read at the council against Nestorius? Such statements would appear more directly opposed to his teaching.

For what controversy would then have remained concerning the one subsistence, or person, of that God-human being, if it were proved that the Fathers had also proclaimed him to have one nature? Therefore, so that every question may be removed: if that letter was not composed later, or if—as is more credible—the council indicated that it did not belong to blessed Julius; or even if it believed that it did belong to him, a position I do not assert, then, when the council brought forward another statement by that same holy Julius against Nestorius rather than that letter itself, it did not judge the contrary error to be defeated on the basis of what had been said incautiously.

Let them understand that we give the same answer concerning the other statements which they circulate under the names of other ancient Fathers of the Council of Ephesus, whether false or wrongly understood. For if they had been genuine, or were to be understood as they wish, the Council of Ephesus would immediately have refuted Nestorius with them.

The Eutychians and Semieutychians therefore have no grounds for complaining about the great Council of Chalcedon, since, in accordance with the decrees of the earlier Council of Ephesus—which they accept with us—it affirmed that Christ exists in two natures.

Nor can they rightly object against this evidence from the sayings of blessed Cyril, which they similarly misunderstand, as must be believed, although they were uttered with another intention. For even if these sayings are thought to differ from the testimonies of the Fathers confirmed at the Council of Ephesus, they cannot be preferred or compared with the synodal decrees accepted by the universal Church.

Moreover, blessed Cyril himself was the first of the Council of Ephesus, and he should not rashly be believed to have contradicted himself. But even if he had done so, one ought not to follow what he said privately to individuals as he saw fit, but rather what he is demonstrably shown to have taught publicly with the deliberation and consideration of the council.

For when holy John of Antioch and the other Eastern bishops, together with the bishops of the other provinces, thought that blessed Cyril proclaimed Christ to have one nature—as the Eutychians now think—and consequently, though with a zeal for the faith that was in some respects commendable, nevertheless unjustly judged him a heretic, almighty God, whose wise and marvelous goodness can turn the evil of human ignorance to the advantage of instruction, brought the matter to such an outcome that the false suspicion of those Eastern and other provincial bishops concerning blessed Cyril left us nothing to suspect.

When the care of restoring peace among the Churches subsequently arose, since a serious schism had been stirred up by this suspicion, the Eastern bishops, through the venerable Paul, bishop of Emesa, asked blessed Cyril himself to confess most clearly, if he wished every scandal and offense to be removed, that Christ, one God and one human being, exists in two natures. Cyril gladly embraced and confessed this, since he was conscious that he had never believed otherwise.

Thus almighty God made evident to everyone the sound faith not only of the Eastern and other Fathers but also of blessed Cyril himself: neither had they asked for anything improper, nor had he refused what they requested. At the same time, God made the truth of Catholic teaching much more ready and much more evident against the future Eutychians.

So great was the concern and diligence of those Eastern Fathers against the error that Christ has one nature that, in the letter they sent to Cyril, they wrote down the words of the orthodox confession they expected from him and entrusted them to the aforesaid bishop Paul, so that blessed Cyril, transferring them into his own letter, might write back to them and leave no ambiguity from which the controversy might later arise again. Cyril accepted this, as we have already said, with the greatest satisfaction, testifying that he had always believed in the same way, and wrote back to the holy John of Antioch:

> “Since an unnecessary and unwarranted division of the Churches has occurred, we are now especially satisfied, since my most reverend lord Paul has produced a document containing an irreproachable confession of faith and affirmed that it was composed by your holiness and by the most religious bishops who are there. The document is written as follows, and these words have also been inserted into this letter.”

And after some intervening material:

> “We therefore confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect human being, consisting of a rational soul and a body: begotten from the Father before the ages according to divinity, but in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same person born from the Virgin Mary according to humanity; the same person consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with us according to humanity. For a union of two natures has occurred; therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, one God.

> “According to this understanding of an unconfused unity, we confess the holy Virgin Mary to be the Mother of God, because God the Word, having become incarnate and human, from the very conception united to himself the temple taken from her.

> “We know that the evangelical and apostolic sayings concerning the Lord were handed down by the preachers of the divine word in some places as referring to one person and in other places as distinguishing two natures; some fitting God according to Christ’s divinity, others humble according to his humanity.

> “Attending to these sacred words of yours, and finding ourselves to hold the same understanding—for there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism—we have glorified the Savior and Lord of all, rejoicing together with one another and with you, because the Churches among us and among you possess a faith agreeing with the divinely inspired Scriptures and the tradition of our holy Fathers.”

Therefore, when Cyril, in this confession by which he removed from himself the reproach of an unworthy suspicion and was reunited with the Churches of the East and of the other provinces, says that a union of two natures has occurred in Christ—for these same two natures belong to one person and one substance—and acknowledges that some evangelical and apostolic sayings concerning the Lord are to be joined as referring to one person and others divided as referring to two natures, how do the Eutychians or Acephali attempt, from the sayings of blessed Cyril himself, to establish not two natures of Christ but one nature composed from two?

For if the evangelical and apostolic sayings concerning the Lord speak not of one nature composed from two but as of two natures, they plainly testify that Christ exists in two natures.

Which sayings of blessed Cyril, then, are to be followed without any exposition or discrimination, if, as we have said, some of his other statements appear to differ from these? Are we to follow those by which, or by statements resembling which, he incurred an unfavorable suspicion, or those by which he was cleared of that suspicion? Clearly, without any interpretation, we must accept with certainty those statements which plainly removed every suspicion from those who were in doubt.

Therefore, whatever and however many false or wrongly interpreted statements they produce under the name of blessed Cyril against the definition of the Council of Chalcedon, they cannot be preferred or compared with the statements by which, at the Council of Ephesus, with Cyril himself presiding over the decision, Nestorius was rejected, nor with those by which Cyril himself was afterward cleared before his fellow bishops.

Let the reader also take into consideration that Cyril produced these statements when the Nestorian heresy was already scandalizing the whole Church, while the Eutychian heresy had not yet arisen; and he will not be surprised that Cyril was less vigilant against the error of the Eutychians than against that of the Nestorians.

Nor do I think that the following should be omitted, in which both the freedom of the aforesaid Eastern Fathers in preserving the integrity of the Catholic faith and the confession of blessed Cyril himself on this very point are more fully manifested.

When it seemed insufficient for the benefit of the Church that these priests of the Lord should communicate this confession of faith to one another only by letters, which could reach the knowledge of only a few, the venerable Paul, bishop of Emesa, delivered a discourse on the Lord’s incarnation in the Alexandrian church, in the presence of blessed Cyril himself. In that sermon (Council of Ephesus, part III, homily 2), among other things, he says:

> “What does ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14) mean—namely, in our nature? Observe John proclaiming two natures and one Son: one thing is the tabernacle, another the one in the tabernacle; one thing is the temple, another the one who inhabits it, God. Pay attention to what is said. He did not say ‘one and another,’ as though speaking of two persons, two Christs, or two sons, but ‘one thing and another,’ as though speaking of two natures. When, therefore, he said, ‘he dwelt among us,’ and proclaimed two natures, he then added, ‘and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten.’ He did not say ‘of two sons,’ but ‘as of the Only-begotten.’”

After the sermon of the aforesaid venerable bishop Paul, Saint Cyril addressed the people, saying:

> “The blessed prophet Isaiah, proclaiming in melodious words the teachers who were to come in Christ, says: ‘Draw water with joy from the springs of the Savior’ (Isaiah 12:3). Behold, then, we have drawn water from the holy spring; I mean from the teacher who, enlightened by the banquets of the Holy Spirit, has expounded to us the great and sacred mystery of the Savior, through which we have been saved by believing in him, and so forth.”

Since, then, not only does the Council of Ephesus declare that Christ must be proclaimed in two natures [Note: [Col. 0553D] The same manuscript reads, “confessed.”], but blessed Cyril also acknowledges in his letter, by which he communicated with the Eastern bishops, that all the Egyptian priests hold the same doctrine, saying that the Churches among us and among you possess a faith agreeing with the divinely inspired Scriptures and the tradition of our holy Fathers; and since, moreover, he commends Paul, bishop of Emesa, who in Cyril’s presence and in his church discussed the two natures of Christ, repeating the same point frequently and exalting it with great praise [Note: [Col. 0554D] The same manuscript reads, “who commends.”], while even the people present at the discourse applauded, as we read, saying:

> “You have spoken well [Note: [Col. 0554D] The manuscript reads, “You have come well.”], orthodox bishop, teacher of the world: whoever believes in this way is loved.”

—and since throughout all this we hear nothing of a single nature of Christ said to have been composed from two, how is it that the Eutychians, a large part of whom are in Alexandria, do not believe according to this orthodox and ancient teaching of the world, assigning it to the Nestorian heresy which their ancestors loved?

Let them therefore cease from this dreadful folly, by which, while saying that Christ has one composed nature, they do not understand that they are blaspheming God, whose nature they believe can be composed [Note: [Col. 0555D] The Verona manuscript reads, “could have been composed.”]. Nor should they say that blessed Cyril taught things contrary to one another, since by this they provide no defense for their own error but inflict upon him the gravest crime of betrayal.

## CHAPTER VI  
### How the Eutychians, by asserting that Christ has one composed nature, assist the Nestorians; and how they wrongly use the example of human nature composed of soul and body

We must now also demonstrate how these same Eutychians or Semieutychians, who deny that the Son of God has two natures, contrary to the Council of Chalcedon and indeed also to the Council of Ephesus, thereby assist the Nestorians, whose falsehood they think to resist by denying the truth.

For by asserting that the Son of God has one nature, they are shown rather to say that the human being Christ Jesus is of another substance and exists outside the Son of God. They falsely attribute this to us, although we say that the one Son has two natures.

If they are asked whether they confess the Son of God, whom they say has one nature, to be consubstantial with the Father, they will not be able to deny it. If they are then asked whether the Father is of a simple nature, they will likewise admit this.

Therefore they will be compelled to say that the Son of God, whom they declare to have one nature and to be consubstantial with the Father, is also of a simple nature—that is, of divine nature alone. Consequently, the human being Christ Jesus will be of another substance [Note: [Col. 0555D] The same manuscript reads, “subsistence.”], to whom the human nature is assigned separately.

Thus, while they deny that the one Son has two natures, they will be convicted of introducing one subsistence of the Son of God and another of the assumed human being.

The holy Council of Ephesus was not unaware of this plausible reasoning. When it condemned Nestorius for proclaiming not only that the Son of God existed in two natures, which is holy, but also in two subsistences, which is profane, it rebuked him—not because he confessed two natures of the Son of God, but because he falsely asserted two subsistences. Nor did it demonstrate, by the testimonies of the ancient Fathers with which it convicted him of the novelty of his perverse doctrine, that the Son of God has one nature; rather, it demonstrated that he has one person.

And certainly, for restraining and utterly extinguishing the error of Nestorius, who attempted to introduce two sons among us, nothing would be more useful or powerful, if truth permitted it, than for the Fathers to prove by their testimonies, or for the council to decree by its own definition, that the Son of God has one nature.

But since the Council of Ephesus rebuked Nestorius, who proclaimed in that mystery not only two natures but also two subsistences, not on account of both claims but solely because he divided one Son into two subsistences—and since it brought forward against him those testimonies of the Fathers by which Christ is shown to exist in two natures—it must rightly be judged to have affirmed that the one Son of God has two natures, since it did not likewise reject this in Nestorius, whom it rejected for another reason.

Therefore, restrained by this authority, let the Eutychians now cease arguing against the sound and necessary confession of the Church, which proclaims, according not only to the Council of Chalcedon but also to the decrees of the Council of Ephesus, that Christ exists in two natures.

For even if they could make their case appear coherent, they ought not to have trusted the reasoning of human arguments so as to contend that Christ has one nature; rather, they ought to submit to the authority of the Fathers, in whom the Spirit of God spoke.

But their wisdom will not permit this. The Apostle says of it: “The wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace; because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God: for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (Romans 8:6). Thus, in the unity of person—or subsistence—they follow with us the divine authority, since human reason cannot investigate the secret of so great a mystery.

But concerning the point on which, thinking that one nature has been made from two, they depart from the most firmly established authority of the Fathers, let us see whether their reasoning can stand even according to the wisdom of the world, as they confidently assert.

They say, then, that just as one human nature is composed from two natures, namely, soul and flesh, so one nature of Christ is composed from divinity and humanity; and therefore we confess Christ to be from two natures, but not in two natures.

Indeed, there is no reason why each human being should not also be said to exist in two natures, namely, flesh and soul. Yet because these two are composed into one, it is certainly and indisputably correct to call this one human nature: a human soul could indeed be composed into one nature with its flesh.

But concerning the divinity of the Word, which is immutably simple, it is said not without immense blasphemy that it could have been composed into one nature with the humanity assumed.

Let them further consider that both soul and flesh came into being for the sake of their union, and that neither has as the end of its nature to exist individually and separately. Rather, they tend toward their union and, in a certain way, owe their existence to one another. For just as flesh was made for the soul, so the soul was made for the flesh [Note: [Col. 0556D] The same manuscript reads, “and the soul was made for the flesh.”]; and the natural goal of their inclination is that they exist together.

We must not believe the ravings of Origen [Note: [Col. 0555D] Jerome, in Letter 60, calls Origen’s statements both nonsense and ravings, and the Fathers, Greek and Latin alike, frequently reject them—for example, Antipater, bishop of Bostra, in chapter 7 of his *Dissertation on Origen*. He writes: “He who made the human being from the beginning made them male and female; according to him, he did not first make minds and then human beings from sins” (Ὁ ποιήσας τὸν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ ἀρχῆς ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς· οὐ πρῶτον νόας κατ’ αὐτὸν, καὶ ἐξ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀνθρώπους). And later, treating the divine blessing by which the human race was propagated, he says: “It was not multiplied from sins and apostasy, as their writing teaches, but from the blessing of God, as the prophet declared. For if the human race is multiplied from transgression and from the cooling of what is good, it would rightly be called not a blessing but rather a curse,” and so forth; these matters are discussed at length throughout the chapter.], who supposes that the substances of human souls existed long before they were in bodies, and not only existed but sinned; that they were first minds and later became souls, when, in accordance with the merits of their sins, they were thrust into bodies.

The Apostle says: “Rebecca, having Isaac our father from one act of intercourse” (Romans 9:10), and so forth. For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil according to election, so that God’s purpose might remain, not from works but from the one who calls, it was said to her: “The elder shall serve the younger.”

We therefore believe Paul, who teaches this, somewhat better and more faithfully than Origen, who dreams that their birth was the punishment for some unknown evil: namely, that when Jacob and Esau had not yet been born, they had done nothing good or evil, and had been distinguished not by works but by the grace of the one who calls.

Moreover, when souls are separated by death from their bodies, they likewise tend toward their union, and therefore they produce one human nature.

It is impious to believe this of the nature of the Word of God: that it did not at some time subsist alone, but that union with human nature was the cause of its existence, so that, once united to it, its natural inclination might come to rest [Note: [Col. 0557C] The Verona manuscript reads, “for itself.”].

Nor can it be said of human nature that it cannot subsist without the composition of the Word of God into one nature with it. We see that human nature is content with its own form and does not tend toward something to which it is naturally attached in such a way as to become one nature with it.

The Eutychians therefore gain no support from the example of human nature for asserting that Christ has one nature, even if, setting aside the authority of the Fathers, they were permitted to argue from human reasoning about the mystery of the divine incarnation, which exceeds the measure of human reason.

This example is more suitably referred to the unity of person, on the authority already cited, and we know that it was referred to this by the holy Fathers.

For this reason blessed Augustine, renowned for the purity and prudence of his Catholic teaching, spoke about Christ in his book *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, which is called the *Enchiridion* by almost everyone familiar with it (chapter 36):

> “Certainly, from the moment he began to be a human being, he began to be no other than the Son of God, and this one and only Son, because of God the Word, who, by assuming that human being, became flesh; and he is God. Thus, just as any human being is one person, namely, rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, the Word and the human being.”

He does not say: “Thus Christ is one nature, the Word and the human being.”

Let us now briefly gather together what has been established.

It has first become clear that, in accordance with the judgment of the great Council of Chalcedon, you, emperor, have confessed that the Lord Christ, one of the Trinity, was crucified for us; that Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God; and that the same Lord Jesus Christ exists in two natures.

It has also become clear that, in declaring and defending this faith of ours, the aforesaid council, on the authority of the divine Scriptures and the testimonies of the Fathers, defined or confirmed these same points.

At the same time, those who, while communicating with the Church and venerating the authority of that holy council, nevertheless, in a superfluous contention over words, deny that it ought to be said that one of the Trinity was crucified and that Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God, have been shown to act against that same council and, conversely, to assist the Eutychians by their contentiousness.

It has also become clear that the Eutychians themselves, who, as though in opposition to the teaching of Nestorius, deny that the one Son of God has two natures, thereby grant the Nestorians an undeniable victory and criticize the Council of Ephesus, which they pretend to accept.

Thus contention, which is neither capable of reason nor willing to be satisfied with the authority of the Fathers, deserves to be blinded, since it first contradicts itself in opposition to the truth.

## BOOK TWO

### CHAPTER ONE  
### How the opponents of the Council of Chalcedon composed the condemnation of the Three Chapters and prefixed it with the emperor’s title

[Col. 0557D]

Since I consider the integrity of the faith which I share with your Piety, religious prince, to have been sufficiently both declared and defended, and since nothing has been left to the calumnies of heretics whereby they might either accuse us of holding an erroneous view of the mystery of the divine Incarnation, or attack the great Synod of Chalcedon, whose decrees we have shown to accord with this same faith of ours, we now proceed confidently to expose their hidden frauds and detestable lies. Through their agents and supporters [Col. 0558D], they have attempted, under the pretext of defending the aforesaid synod, to overthrow it. For I trust that it will become clearer than daylight not only to Your Serenity but to every reader who is not of the kind described by the prophetic saying, “He refused to understand, that he might do good” (Psalm 35:4), that what they boast was written in the synod’s defense was in fact done to nullify it.

We ask only this of Your Clemency, whose title adorns you: since, through the stealth of heretics, many things have been done and written to the prejudice of the Church, which the zeal of God impels us to rebuke, may our reply cause you no offense. For the adversaries of truth acted cunningly through their accomplices, as they are accustomed to do, so that the very things they had caused to be written might also be prefaced with the title of your name.

[Note: On this work, Liberatus, final chapter: “By a cunning fraud,” he says, “the Acephali asked that he dictate a book condemning the Three Chapters. When this book had been published and made known to the whole world, the case would become irrevocable when the prince was ashamed to amend it.” And he composed a book on behalf of our abandoned cause, known to us all. Vigilius also mentions it in his letter condemning Theodore of Caesarea. Facundus therefore did not doubt that Justinian was the author of this book, but artfully conceals the fact so that he may attack him more freely. For from this point onward he will devote himself entirely to criticizing him. Thus those are mistaken who think that Facundus is attacking Justinian’s edict or letter mentioned in the preceding book. To pass over the fact that the letter was published much later, it certainly does not contain those things which Facundus repeatedly adduces from the book he refutes.]

They thought that, by invoking the terror inspired by your person, they would escape condemnation or even exposure of their own temerity and falsehood. But we do not wish those writings to be called yours when we know that they contradict your recognized faith. For if, in accordance with your laws, you have rightly and beneficially decreed that any rescripts of yours which, having been obtained by stealth, are contrary to the very laws that you promulgated—laws by which you are served and which you are permitted to violate—should be voided, and that writings found to oppose your general constitutions should not be said to have been issued by you, how can we not rightly and deservedly say that those writings which oppose the constitutions of your fathers, to which you, as a religious ruler, must necessarily be obedient, and which neither you nor all human beings together with you are permitted to violate, are not yours? [Col. 0559B] Therefore, obeying the Apostle Peter, who says, “Fear God; honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17), we refute, for fear of God, what is contrary to the Church of Christ; and, for the honor due to the king, we do not call yours what ought to be refuted.

Let those writings belong, then, to the men who foolishly thought that things unable to stand by reason could be fortified by the false title of your name. Let them rather be charged to those whose fraudulent inventions and prolonged labors we know to have composed them against the holy Synod of Chalcedon.

For what need was there, I ask, to disturb the peace of the Church with the tumult of superfluous, not to say harmful, controversies? What need was there to reopen the decrees of that synod, not only against the reverence due to religion but also against the modesty of humanity [Col. 0559C], when by the consent of the whole Church they had remained inviolate for nearly a hundred years under your guardianship?

[Note: The Verona codex has: “even under your guardianship.”]

Or what need was there to examine the statements calumniously made about Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, who had long since died in the peace of the Church, and thus, wherever he is thought to have fallen—or even where he made a merely human slip of the tongue—to rage against him with such abuse as would not be fitting to inflict upon him, had he still been alive, unless he had first been reproved and convicted and, after a first and second correction, had stubbornly resisted the truth?

But because the same Theodore is praised in the letter of the venerable Ibas, which the aforesaid synod declared orthodox, the heretics believed that the synod’s authority could be dissolved if they now caused him, more than a hundred years after his death, to be condemned as the author and teacher [Col. 0559D] of Nestorius, and consequently caused the letter itself to be condemned as though it praised a heretic.

What will they do, however, since Theodore of Mopsuestia is not only praised in that letter, but is also shown to have been approved and highly commended during his lifetime by the holy Fathers who associated with him in preaching the word—for example, by John of Constantinople and Gregory of Nazianzus—and after his death by John and Domnus of Antioch, as well as by the entire synod of the East assembled at Antioch? Will they therefore also cause all these venerable teachers of the Church of Christ, or their statements, to be anathematized?

For the letter of Ibas cannot otherwise be regarded as justly condemned under anathema because of its praise of Theodore unless all these most blessed Fathers, or at least their writings, are likewise rejected; in those writings, as we shall demonstrate, Theodore is praised far more extensively than in the letter.

Nor have the statements said to have been written—I know not when—by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, against blessed Cyril been condemned at this time for any other reason than that, through this also, the Synod of Chalcedon might appear blameworthy, since that same Theodoret took part in its deliberation and definition, and there defended Pope Leo’s letter, which refuted the madness of Eutyches, showing to those of lesser understanding that it was correct.

For, as will be shown below, others also whose memory we share wrote against blessed Cyril; yet they were not named in this anathema, because they were not present at the Council of Chalcedon.

I have decided to treat the whole case concerning all these matters in the following order. First, by producing clear evidence, I shall demonstrate that the supporters of the heretics did these things to nullify the aforesaid great council and the decrees of Pope Leo. Next, since it is falsely asserted that the letter of the venerable Ibas was not received by that same Council of Chalcedon, I shall show that, because they cannot prove this, they attempted by such a lie to lead us toward its condemnation. Finally, I shall prove that the holy synod cannot rightly be blamed for declaring it orthodox.

At the same time, something unexpected, and something you will find difficult to believe, will be demonstrated, August Emperor. For while the Eutychians accuse the aforesaid synod of having supposedly confirmed, by approving that letter, that blessed Cyril was a heretic, of having accepted the defense of Nestorius, and of having censured the Council of Ephesus, I shall demonstrate the opposite: if it had rejected the aforesaid letter as heretical, it would rather seem, on that account, to have believed blessed Cyril a heretic, excused Nestorius, and censured the Council of Ephesus.

## CHAPTER II

### That the Letter of Ibas, even if the Council had not declared it orthodox, could not be condemned without censuring the Council

We must now address the first part of this division. We say, then, that even if—as some have falsely claimed—the Synod of Chalcedon did not approve the letter of the venerable Ibas and did not submit it to examination at all, it would nevertheless have been condemned, because of its praise of Theodore, to the nullification of the synod itself.

This is clearly shown by the address which, as we demonstrated in the preceding book, the synod wrote to the Emperor Augustus Marcian, whose authority Your Piety has also confirmed by your own law.

But before we produce or examine the testimony of that address concerning this matter as well, I think it necessary to recall your aforesaid law, which, as we have said, bears witness to its authority. Its title is as follows [Col. 0561B] (*Code*, “On the Supreme Trinity,” book VII):

“On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith, and that no one should dare to dispute it publicly.”

Its opening is:

“Emperor Justinian Augustus to Epiphanius, most holy and most blessed archbishop of this royal city and universal patriarch. Desiring that Your Holiness know all matters pertaining to the ecclesiastical order.”

And later:

“The same holy Synod of Chalcedon also received and confirmed, through its report, the letter of the great Proclus written to the Armenians concerning the necessity of saying that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our God, is one of the Holy Trinity. For if we depart from the aforesaid four holy synods, or from what they have established, we give heretics the opportunity—those who have been deposed by them and by their doctrines—to display their pestilence once again in the holy Churches of God.”

It is enough to have cited these words from your law in confirmation of the aforesaid address [Col. 0561C].

[Note: The Verona codex has: “address or report.”]

This is a law whose title forbids anyone to dispute the Catholic faith publicly. Whether this law is being observed, when the judgment of a universal synod is now being disputed in the Church after nearly a hundred years, is for Your Piety to judge. Or consider whether, if the four holy synods and what they established are being overturned without any transgression, the venerable Ibas’s letter—he was bishop of Edessa—which the great Synod of Chalcedon declared orthodox, is now condemned as impious and Nestorian.

What benefit is there in having foreseen that this would give heretics—those deposed by the synods and by their doctrines—the opportunity to display their pestilence once again in the holy Churches of God, while failing to foresee that this should happen?

But we must now establish what we intend from that address itself. Accordingly, when the aforesaid synod addressed the Emperor Augustus Marcian (*After the Acts of the Council*), confirming by the authority of the Fathers both the rationale of its decrees [Col. 0562A] and the letter of blessed Leo, it replied as follows against the Eutychians, who blamed it for defining that Christ has two natures:

[Note: The same codex has: “of its own decrees.”]

“When the question arose in an ambiguous form, we are known to have adapted our confession to the interpretations of the Fathers, satisfying ourselves that in no respect had we brought a mind discordant with their understanding; rather, we use them as witnesses for the firmness of our faith.”

And to show that the heretics were blaming not so much the synod itself as the ancient teachers of the Church whose judgment it had followed in this matter, the synod recalled in the same address the letters of certain Fathers, including the volume of the great Proclus to the Armenians, which your law mentions, and the letter of the most wise John of Antioch, in these words:

“Nor will they exempt the great Proclus from this reproach, although he sent to those same Orientals a volume addressed to the Armenians concerning what accords with the faith. To the charge they will add the most holy John, bishop of Antioch, who, rejecting the insults of the heretics and declaring the dogma of apostolic teaching, sent the confession of the entire East, as though from a single mouth, to the most holy Proclus and to him who at that time governed the helm of the world. Therefore, let them not censure the letter of the bishop of the Roman city, admirable as he was, as though it were an obstacle of innovation,” and so forth.

In this confession of the most wise John of Antioch and of the entire East, sent to the most holy Proclus and to the Emperor Theodosius—and on its model the Synod of Chalcedon defended the letter of the admirable bishop of the Roman city, that is, of blessed Leo—the synod testifies that John rejected the insults of the heretics and declared the apostolic teaching. We demonstrated in the first book that through this confession it was also confirmed that the Lord Jesus Christ is one of the Trinity. In it Theodore is praised with much greater commendation than in the letter of the venerable Ibas.

For in his reply to Proclus concerning the confirmation of the volume sent to the Armenians, John, together with the Synod of the East, writes as follows:

[Note: Liberatus, chapter 10, speaking of the Armenian monks who accused Theodore of Mopsuestia: “Then,” he says, “John of Antioch, having assembled a synod, dictated three letters on behalf of Theodore of Mopsuestia: one he addressed to the Emperor Theodosius, another to Cyril of Alexandria, and a third to Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, praising Theodore in them and explaining his wisdom. The words of the first and third are those quoted here; those of the second are quoted in book VII, chapter 4. But Justinian teaches in his edict that these praises of Theodore should be considered no more weighty than the writings which that same John and the Orientals had composed against Cyril and the orthodox faith and in favor of Nestorius.

“‘But if they produce testimonies of John of Antioch and of the Eastern synod under him in favor of Theodore and his impiety, they must also accept those things which, as far as depends on them, the followers of John dared to write for the condemnation of Cyril among the saints and the rejection of the true faith, and which they wrote while defending Nestorius and his evil doctrine for a very long time.’”]

“Not only do we, while living, continually suffer such calumnies from those who wish to disturb the Churches; but blessed Theodore also, who made a good departure from this life, shone brightly in teaching for forty-five years and defeated every heresy, without suffering any disparagement anywhere from the orthodox during his life. After his departure from this world following a long period of time, after many struggles, and after writing ten thousand books against heresies, and after he had been approved in the sight of priests, emperors, and peoples, he is now in danger of having to endure what belongs to heretics and of being proclaimed their associate.”

To the Emperor Theodosius, who at that same time governed the helm of the world, he writes as follows:

“For when we speak of Theodore, we speak of a man illustrious in the episcopate, who reached his end after nearly fifty years of vigorous opposition to all heresies. In the commentaries which he delivered throughout all the churches of the East, and by which he is clearly shown to have been highly esteemed in the imperial city, no one—neither his predecessors nor his contemporaries—ever judged him a heretic. On the contrary, all the priests, because of the grace of teaching which he possessed, always held him in admiration, and he enjoyed the glory of a higher honor.

“And not only by the priests, but also by your most sacred grandfather—whom we call thrice blessed, who received the scepters of imperial power from God and transmitted them to you, Theodosius—was he so regarded. That great emperor, having desired to see the man, became a great hearer of his teaching in the church; nor did he think that he had found another teacher of such stature. He greatly admired his teaching, and at that time delighted in and was astonished by his conversation—he whom some now despise, as though taking upon themselves the role of testing and rejecting deceased teachers according to their own will.

“Moreover, your imperial government has frequently testified to him, out of respect for him and for his spiritual wisdom, and he has been honored in your letters.”

[Note: The Verona codex has: “glory, and possessed.”]

And later, concerning him:

“This is that most devoted disciple of Flavian, the great pontiff of the holy Church of God of the Antiochenes, and fellow disciple of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople, whose memory you have restored, thereby bringing the greatest glory from this act to the rule of Your Piety.”

They say other things as well, which will more appropriately be recalled when we produce the testimonies of the other holy Fathers who likewise bore witness to Theodore.

Since John of Antioch and the other Eastern bishops, in those same letters—which the Synod of Chalcedon acknowledges that it followed as a model in its definitions—proclaim Theodore of Mopsuestia with praises as one declaring apostolic doctrine, so that it might accept the letter of blessed Leo, how could the letter of Ibas not have been condemned, because of its praise of Theodore, for the nullification of the synod—even if, as has been said, the synod had not declared it orthodox and had not submitted it to examination?

[Note: The same codex has: “extol with praises.”]

For if Theodore, as they claim, was indeed the teacher of Nestorius but blasphemed with even greater impiety than Nestorius, and if all Theodore’s statements against Christ surpass the madness of the devil, so that not only Theodore himself is justly condemned but also the letter that praised him, then the Synod of Chalcedon will likewise be justly condemned. It not only received as Fathers the greatest praisers of Theodore, the aforesaid bishop of Antioch and the other bishops of the East, but also confesses that it followed in its definitions the very letters in which they praised him.

You therefore perceive, most clement Emperor, that even if we too were to deny, against the testimony of our conscience, that the letter of the venerable Ibas had been judged orthodox at the synod, and were to add to this falsehood the claim that it had not been submitted for judgment, we could not defend the aforesaid synod if we condemned that same letter because of its praise of Theodore.

[Note: The same codex has: “we could not defend the aforesaid synod.”]

As for those who appear to be false brothers in the Church—would that they were outside it!—they now do not resist those who deny this; indeed, they themselves are even praised.

[Note: The same codex has: “indeed, they praise.”]

They introduced this deceitfully in order to lead us astray, so that afterward they might say to us, either themselves or those who are outside:

“You rightly condemned Theodore, since all his statements surpass the madness of the devil; and consequently you also rejected Ibas’s letter and denied that it had been received by the synod, counting it as a crime if it were said to have declared orthodox the letter that praised a blasphemous and impious man. How, then, do you accept the Synod of Chalcedon itself, which most clearly bears witness that those letters declared apostolic doctrine and rejected the insults of the heretics, in those letters in which Theodore’s teaching is praised with much greater commendation than in Ibas’s letter?

“Moreover, it is a graver offense that the synod subjected itself to the judgment and authority of those letters than if it had judged wrongly about Ibas’s letter itself—which, you say, it did not. They will also add: ‘This is that apostolic teaching of your Leo which you extol: the letter of which the Synod of Chalcedon attempted to defend by the testimony or example of those letters, which exalted the profane Theodore—whom you condemned for his impiety—with the highest praises.’”

When they bring these objections, what, I ask, shall we answer? What shall we say, when by our own judgment we close our own mouths, except perhaps this one conclusion to which everything compels us: that the synod did not judge rightly concerning the doctrines of the Christian faith?

This follows if it is a charge of heresy to have praised Theodore, who is commended in those letters, while the aforesaid synod confesses that it followed their model in its decrees by which it approved the letter of blessed Leo.

But if we wish its authority to remain unimpaired for us, we shall not call the letter of the venerable Ibas Nestorian because of its praise of Theodore, whom we find praised more extensively in those letters that it preferred.

Just as the testimony of those letters convicts those who, though bound by the authority of the Council of Chalcedon, by which those letters were praised, refuse to say that the Lord Jesus Christ is one of the Trinity, so too it will convict those who, approving the decrees of that council with similar faith, wish to reject as Nestorian the letter of the venerable Ibas because it praised Theodore.

These points have been established even if, as we have already said, the synod did not declare the letter orthodox and it could not be shown to have been read before it.

But since they admit that it was read there, let us grant them still more and, for the moment, set aside even this judgment of the synod, by which it declared that the most holy [Col. 0565A] John of Antioch, rejecting the insults of the heretics and declaring the dogma of apostolic teaching, sent the confession of the entire East, as though from a single mouth, to the most holy Proclus and to him who at that time governed the helm of the world.

[Note: The Verona codex has: “most wise.”]

Let us suppose, then, that just as they deny that the same synod declared the letter of the venerable Ibas orthodox, they also deny that it approved the letters of the most wise John and of the entire Eastern council, in which Theodore of Mopsuestia is praised much more extensively, and that it followed their model in its definition, as we have shown.

Even in that case, will the aforesaid letter not appear to constitute a reproach against the synod for whatever reason? For if it is to be believed that the condemnation of the letter as Nestorian after nearly a hundred years belongs to zeal for the Catholic faith, then that holy synod restrained the Nestorian heresy by not condemning the same letter when it had been read before it—if, that is, it was only that synod, and not the entire Church of Christ, spread throughout the world, that always received the synod’s decrees with the greatest authority.

It is therefore indisputable that the Synod of Chalcedon can be defended not by the false denial devised by heretics to deceive the easily persuaded, but only by the reasoning of truth. With God’s help, after examining the frauds and lies of those heretics, we shall give that reasoning.

## CHAPTER III

### That they condemned Ibas’s letter because it confesses two natures in Christ; for what purpose they demand the subscriptions of bishops; and why they themselves refuse communion with those who condemn

[Col. 0565C]

So that it may become clearer to Your Clemency that the synod did not deny that the letter had been accepted perhaps merely because no equally ready argument by which it might be defended had occurred to them, but rather that everything said to have been undertaken in its defense was done to the prejudice of that synod itself, consider, I beg you—or even ask those who wrote such things—why so much was written against the letter itself; why so many faults were attributed to it [Note: The same codex: falsely “were attributed”]; although they were not charged by Ibas’s own accusers; and finally why it was condemned as impious and Nestorian.

Did not the necessity of defending the synod demand this as well, since it ought rather to have been excused, so that—even if it was thought necessary to fear [Note: The same codex: “to lie”]—the synod might appear fortified on both sides of its defense, by their saying both that the letter had not been accepted and that, even if it had been accepted, the synod was not to be blamed? But now they heap many charges upon the letter itself, inventing what seem to be acceptable grounds for its condemnation—something the heretics desired—and they loudly assert that it was not accepted, though no one can demonstrate this.

For when they came to the passage of the letter itself where Ibas reports and says:

> “Many, however, having no fear of God before their eyes, under the pretext of ecclesiastical zeal hastened to bring to completion the enmities which they secretly harbored in their hearts. One of these is the tyrant of our city, whom you yourself do not fail to know. Under the pretext of the faith, he persecutes not only those now living, but also those who long ago departed to God. One of these is the blessed Theodore, herald of the truth and teacher of the Church. Not only during his life did he strike the heretics in the face through the truth of his faith, but even after his death he left spiritual weapons in his own books for the sons of the Church, as your Reverence also learned through your conversation with him and was instructed by what he wrote. This man, who dares everything, presumed to anathematize openly in the Church—the man who, out of zeal for God, not only converted his own city from error to truth, but also instructed Churches situated far away by his teaching.”

When, then, as I said, they came to this passage, in which the same venerable Ibas, writing to Maris the Persian, censures a certain man for having presumed to anathematize Theodore—although they did not set down the words of the letter itself in their book exactly as they are found, but excerpted whatever they wished at their own discretion—they nevertheless did not hesitate to add this also, saying:

> “One must look openly at the letter to Maris, which says everything without God and impiously, showing only this correctly: that Theodore was anathematized by him in the Church throughout the East.”

I wish, therefore, that they would answer me and demonstrate—not those who wrote such things, for they themselves know what they have done, but those who subscribed to such statements—how they can establish that the letter written to Maris says everything “without God and impiously.”

Did it also condemn the confession of Christ’s two natures? Or do these words not occur in that same letter?

> “For the Church says—as your Holiness knows, as it learned from the beginning, and as it has been confirmed by divine teaching from the books of the blessed Fathers—‘two natures, one power, one person,’ which is one Son, the Lord Jesus Christ.”

It is therefore already clear, as I think, even to those who may have thought otherwise, that the letter was condemned craftily, under the pretext of some new exactness, in order to deny Christ’s two natures. For why would they say that it says everything “without God and impiously,” unless they intended to include among those things also its confession that Christ has two natures?

And lest what they said—“everything”—be understood according to some customary manner of speech, they showed that they had inserted the word deliberately and carefully by adding an exception and saying:

> “Showing only this correctly: that Theodore was anathematized by him in the Church throughout the East.”

If, then, with that one thing excepted, it says everything “without God and impiously,” there is no doubt that they intended that “everything” to include the statement that Christ has two natures.

But the letter does not, as they boast, show this correctly—that Theodore was anathematized throughout the East in the Church—for it reports that this was done by one man. Rather, it shows correctly that the man whom only one person presumed to anathematize ought not to be anathematized. Whoever approves that presumption unquestionably condemns the other bishops of the East who judged it impious.

To show by yet another indication that they added the statement that the letter says everything “without God and impiously” in order to deny the two natures of Christ, which the same Ibas confessed in the letter mentioned above, recall, I beg you, emperor, what formula of condemnation of that letter was first issued, and what has now been composed.

At first it had been said:

> “If anyone says that the impious letter to Maris, said to have been written by Ibas, is correct, or is its defender, and does not rather subject it to anathema, because it treats Saint Cyril badly—he who says that God the Word became man—and disparages the twelve chapters of that same Saint Cyril, attacks the First Synod of Ephesus [Note: The Verona codex: “attacks with insults”], defends Nestorius, and praises Theodore of Mopsuestia, let him be anathema.”

Now, however, after all these grounds had been removed—I do not wish to say whether they were true or of what kind, lest it appear to have been condemned solely on their account and not also because of the confession of Christ’s two natures contained in it—a different formula for subscription was subsequently issued, and it was ordered to be made in these absolute terms:

> “If anyone says that the impious letter to Maris is correct, or defends it, and does not anathematize it, let him be anathema.”

Since, then, in the formal declaration concerning the book itself they pronounced that it says everything “without God and impiously,” and in the formula of subscription—which they later altered—they removed all the other grounds, whatever their character, for its condemnation, so that it might appear to have been condemned not for certain things but for everything, what else is to be understood except that, under the pretext of false exactness, they wished to destroy the confession of Christ’s two natures?

They have corrected other matters as well, and are still correcting them in that certain book of theirs—if that alteration is to be called a correction, by which the lie is not removed but increased. Therefore, if after this response of ours they alter other things too, they ought not to charge us as though we had falsely criticized statements that they made differently. If they would ever stand firm, and cease both to be changed and to change their position, our response too would be found appropriate to their words.

But if someone cannot investigate their deceptions from the matters we have mentioned, because not everyone applies himself to reading, what person of sound mind would not be troubled if the mere consideration of what they have done were insufficient for recognizing the previously untested designs of the heretical faction?

First, a matter judged by a universal council nearly a hundred years ago is suddenly reopened, without even any cause provoking it [Note: Perhaps: “without any cause at all having provoked it,” with *causa* placed earlier, etc.].

Next, after a formula for subscription was issued, which no one was permitted to exceed, bishops were compelled, wherever they were found, to subscribe to another’s decree, in order to increase the number—so that, once it had been circulated through various provinces, it might appear to be confirmed by the subscription of all the priests.

For the Eutychians knew that the private will of anyone could not prejudice the universal synod, which they had always sought to undermine. Through their agents, therefore, they did what heretical malice commonly practices: they arranged matters so that the letter might seem to be proved Nestorian by the judgment of the whole Church, even though they accuse the universal synod concerning its acceptance. No other reason either appears or is stated for sending the subscription to so many provinces.

And if we could not understand even this, what sane person would not ultimately be alarmed if an antidote were forced upon him when he had neither requested nor administered it? The very name of an antidote indicates that it is given against something. Therefore, if there is no disease against which it is given, it is imposed only under suspicion that health is to be taken away.

We urge this upon you, religious emperor, not by an argument foreign to you, for these are your own words. When you wrote to the most blessed Roman bishop in order to confirm or further publicize the condemnation of Theodore of Alexandria [Note: I think he was a monk, one of the sect of Severus the Theopaschite, who wrote books against Themistius, the leader of the Agnoetae; Photius discusses them in the *Bibliotheca*, no. 708: *Theodore the Alexandrian monk against Themistius*. Both were heretics and belonged to the Theopaschite party, attached to Severus. The rest is owed to Facundus, since other writers are silent about Theodore, and no letters concerning him from Justinian or the Roman pontiff survive], and of others like him, you added this very point that we are making, saying:

> “Moreover, we do not know what reason there is for your saying that a general council ought to be held. No unknown heretic has arisen; no new impiety has appeared in our times; nor is anything found in the faith that needs to be reconsidered.” 

And you added what we too say in the present case:

> “For whoever applies to healthy things what is ordinarily applied to wounds does not wish to restore health but to drive it away.”

This is your reasoning, most serene emperor. If we do not avert our gaze from it, we can judge nothing else concerning the present matter except that, in condemning this letter, the supporters of the heretics did not wish to restore health but to drive it away.

For this reason, therefore, we are not misled by the false title of your name into calling those things yours that we see to be contrary to this sound reasoning; nor do we believe that the holy and universal synod has been cleansed by such means, as though it had until now remained impure [Note: The same codex: “uncleansed”] and required a defense based on falsehood and compulsion, although its authority is true and has always been honored by the devotion of all Catholics.

If it seemed that the heretics should be answered in this way on behalf of the synod—by denying that it pronounced the letter of the venerable Ibas orthodox—this could not be confirmed by the subscription or testimony of those bishops whom, if the Eutychians believed them, they would not separate themselves from the communion of the Church.

For this reason no one has ever used his own witnesses against heretics; rather, people have relied on divine authority, necessary reasoning, and the testimonies of the ancient Fathers, whose teaching they pretend to accept with us.
