But it is said that the Eutychians are deeply distressed by the injuries to the blessed Cyril contained in the letter, and that for this reason they take offense at the synod, which they say accepted it. What, then, if we deny that it was accepted—will they believe us? Or did they believe us, that is, Catholics, and not rather themselves see that it was accepted, since they complain about it on that account?

If it is also said that they believed us because it was accepted, how will they again believe us if we say that it was not accepted? But if they did not believe our testimony, and themselves recognized what is evident, will they believe our subscriptions more than their own judgment?

The deceitful supporters of the heretics did not therefore wish to accomplish through the subscriptions of those bishops that the Eutychians should be convinced that the venerable Ibas’s letter had not been accepted by the synod. Rather, they wished the letter to appear, through their very denial, not to have been worthy of acceptance.

But let us suppose that they thought the Eutychians would believe our false testimony. Why, then, did they not at least formulate the matter in these terms: “If anyone says that the letter to Maris was accepted by the Synod of Chalcedon, let him be anathema”? Instead they chose to say:

> “If anyone says that the letter to Maris is correct, or defends the impious letter [Note: The Verona codex: “the impious letter to Maris, or defends it,” etc.], and does not anathematize it, let him be anathema.”

Was this not done so that they might condemn, at the will of the heretics, the holy Fathers who assembled in council, who did not anathematize the letter, and indeed judged it orthodox?

And although, in order to lead us to condemn it, they invented the claim that the same Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon did not pronounce it orthodox—a matter we shall investigate later—it nevertheless remains certain that, when it was read before them, they did not subject it to anathema [Note: The same codex: “to the anathema”].

Or, because they did not use the verb of past time and say, “If anyone did not anathematize the impious letter to Maris,” but instead said, “If anyone does not anathematize it,” are we therefore to think that they did not devise this for the condemnation of the Synod of Chalcedon?

Indeed, if this were required of those subscribing, the matter would be open [Note: Perhaps: “they would require it to be made open,” etc.], and it would no longer be suspicion [Note: The same codex: “subreption”], but manifest contradiction [Note: Perhaps: “they would require the matter to be made open,” etc.].

But they did not consider this necessary, since we always say, “The Prophet says,” “The Apostle says,” “The Evangelist says,” and this means the same as if we said, “That particular person said it.”

Moreover, we say that the Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon live both before God and among us in their constitutions, because, as the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:32).

The blessed Leo, bishop of the Roman Church, also indicates that this should be understood in this way when writing to the venerable Anatolius, bishop of this imperial city:

> “Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after condemning the sacrilegious Arius together with his impiety in the city of Nicaea, established laws of ecclesiastical canons that would remain until the end of the world, live among us and throughout the whole world in their constitutions.”

If, then, all the venerable Fathers live in their constitutions, surely those who assembled at Chalcedon, as living men, not only did not anathematize the letter of the venerable Ibas, but even now do not anathematize it, nor will they ever anathematize it.

Since this is so, it is certain that they intended this anathema to reach those same Fathers.

Moreover, once this argument too has been removed, it cannot plausibly be said that the measure was not established for the condemnation of the Synod of Chalcedon, but only so that those who were physically present might be condemned if they did not pronounce anathema upon Ibas’s letter.

For how can we be condemned, though we were not judges in the case, while those Fathers remain uncondemned—who, when the same letter had been read before them in their own judgment, did not condemn it, and by whose example we too were led not to pronounce anathema upon it?

The form of judgment must proceed from the condemnation of those from whose error the form of sin proceeded; and those who are found to be the authors of error deserve a greater punishment than those who merely follow it.

Since, then, they have judged and decreed, at the will of the heretics, in condemnation of the holy synod, that anyone who does not anathematize the aforementioned letter of the venerable Ibas is to be anathema, consider, I beg you, what levity, confusion, and disgrace it is that they compel us to communicate with them while remaining in the position that we not only do not pronounce anathema upon it, but even deny that anathema ought to be pronounced.

We omit saying that, if we communicate with those who have already pronounced anathema upon us, we shall communicate not only in the condemnation of the Synod of Chalcedon, but also confirm, by that very communion of theirs, their sentences against us. It is perhaps said that they themselves also desire this.

But we say rather that, if they had any regard for divine religion or human reason, it ought also to have seemed to them profane and exceedingly shameful to turn against themselves, by communicating with us, the anathema that they decreed against us.

Hence it is sufficiently clear how great is the seriousness and integrity of those who presume to reconsider the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon.

Accordingly, let them count it as a benefit rather than an injury that we do not communicate with them until they remove from our midst [Note: The same codex: “until it is removed”] this anathema, which, like a great chasm lying between us, separates the restless and exceedingly arrogant presumers from the poor in spirit, who rest in the understanding of the faith and judgment of the Fathers—presumers who think themselves so abundant in wisdom that, as though weaned above their mother, they despise the institutions of the Church, although it is written:

> “My son, keep your father’s law, and do not reject your mother’s teaching. Bind them continually around your soul, and tie them around your neck” (Prov. 6:20).

And again:

> “Hear, my son, your father’s discipline, and do not cast aside your mother’s teaching; for you shall receive a crown of grace upon your head and a golden necklace around your neck” (Prov. 1:8).

O what a great evil it is to wish to exchange the golden necklace for a millstone! We ought, by keeping the discipline and law of God the Father and by reverencing the institutions of our mother, to receive the crown of grace upon our head and the golden necklace around our neck. Instead, by rejecting what our holy mother established, we give scandal to her children and fall under the judgment of which the Lord says:

> “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be drowned in the depth of the sea. Woe to the world because of scandals! For it is necessary that scandals come; nevertheless, woe to that person through whom the scandal comes” (Matt. 17:6–7).

If, then, causing one little person to stumble is so grave that it would be better for the one who causes the stumbling to have a millstone hung around his neck and be drowned in the depth of the sea, how much more serious is it to disturb the whole Church through mere restlessness of mind and the desire not to remain silent!

## CHAPTER IV. That they falsely boast that they condemned the letter because it treated Cyril badly, although Gennadius and Isidore treated him more harshly, and they do not criticize them

What, indeed, is this claim of theirs—that they condemned this letter because its author appears in it to have held an evil opinion of the blessed Cyril, since he wrote against that same Saint Cyril and his twelve chapters? The blessed Gennadius too, bishop of this imperial city [Note: The successor of Anatolius, to whom Leo’s hundredth letter was written. Leontius quotes another passage from his second book addressed to Parthenius in his *Commonplaces*, concerning the origin of souls: “Gennadius of Constantinople, from the second discourse addressed to Parthenius”], of blessed memory, is not named by them in this condemnation, although in his reply he treated Cyril much more vehemently and abusively.

For he speaks against him as follows:

> “Woe is me because of evils! Alas, alas! From where else could anyone begin in the present circumstances? What and how many blasphemies of Cyril the Egyptian have I encountered, and what and how many blasphemies have I heard! Who will truly give water to my head and a spring of tears to my eyes, so that I may mourn this day and night? For he has stretched out his tongue for falsehood and not for faith; he has been strengthened upon the earth [Jer. 9:1, 3]. Indeed, peace for sinners is deception. ‘For this reason,’ he says, ‘their pride has taken possession of them to the end; they have conceived and spoken wickedness; they have spoken iniquity on high; they have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has traversed the earth’ (Ps. 72:6, 8–9). These are the words of the Psalmist; the earlier ones are those of the prophet Jeremiah. Well done, blessed Paul: ‘From among yourselves,’ he says, ‘men will arise speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them’ (Acts 20:30). Woe to the evil one of Alexandria, his associate and now this man’s second self, by whom we lament that she has been corrupted and who corrupts; the mystery of iniquity has now become complete, and I fear that perhaps he who restrains will never be removed from the midst (2 Thess. 2:7). Well done, prophet Jeremiah! A terrible ecstasy has come upon the earth in fulfillment of that same voice: ‘The prophets prophesied wicked things; the priests clapped their hands, and my people loved it so’ (Lam. 2:14–15). For what in them is small or moderate? He hurled against the holy Fathers every kind of surpassing blasphemy, against the apostles who preceded them [Note: The same codex: “superior”], and against the Savior himself; he plotted against the Resurrection. He insults the humanity assumed from us and for us [Note: The same codex: “the humanity of the Only-Begotten”], and insists that his divine nature, which is impassible, is subject to sufferings [Note: The same codex: “but his divine nature”].”

Behold how many and what kinds of accusations Saint Gennadius poured out against the blessed Cyril. Yet no odium attaches to his name on this account, because he was not present at the Council of Chalcedon.

Indeed, in replying to the first of the same blessed Cyril’s chapters, in which Cyril said:

> “If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is God in truth, and therefore does not confess that the holy Virgin is Mother of God—for she bore in the flesh the Word of God made flesh—let him be anathema,”

Gennadius attacked him in these terms:

> “God will anathematize you, whitewashed wall (Acts 23:3); for it is most just that you, like Ananias, the chief priest of the Jews, who moved his tongue against the disciples of Christ, should experience from them a similar indignation.”

And there are other statements, which anyone who wishes may find in the same work.

Why, then, in this avenging of the injuries—as they call it—done to the blessed Cyril, is the name of Saint Gennadius not brought forward instead, both because of the authority of his position as bishop of the imperial city and because of the magnitude of his curses and insults?

But if they took into consideration that Gennadius would not have written such things about Cyril unless he had understood the speaker’s intention imperfectly, I too accept this prudent and pious consideration. For he may have believed what was correct concerning the Christian faith, and in good faith blamed the blessed Cyril because he did not understand him; yet they considered it condemnable to condemn a good intention.

And if they also took into consideration that, if what the blessed Gennadius had written a hundred years earlier were condemned now, the whole Church would be subjected to criticism because it had not condemned it before, this too will be acknowledged by any wise and moderate person as a wise and moderate consideration [Note: The same codex: “what wise and moderate person would fail to recognize this? But,” etc.].

But why was this consideration not applied more fully to the letter of the venerable Ibas? For although I do not say that it was approved by the universal synod, it is certainly shown to have been read there, and it is not shown to have been rejected—unless it was condemned as profane for the destruction of that synod itself, and not because of any injury to Cyril.

Finally, they similarly criticized the statements of the venerable Bishop Theodore of Cyrrhus, in which he is said to have written things contrary to the blessed Cyril, under the pretext of this same retaliation. They wished him for this reason to appear blameworthy, because he was present at the Council of Chalcedon along with the other Fathers and, when the letter of the blessed Leo—which the Eutychians anathematize—was reread there, he defended it against the hesitation of the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops.

Otherwise, why would they proceed so openly against Ibas’s letter and Theodore’s writings, while remaining silent about the names of others whose dignity was greater, whose reputation was more illustrious, and whose statements against the blessed Cyril are seen to be more vehement and sharper? [Note: The Verona codex: “They wrote more vehement things against Cyril,” etc.]

For the exceedingly holy man Isidore, an Egyptian presbyter of Pelusium, a great glory in the Church of Christ, whom many know to have written two thousand letters [Note: Of these, the earlier letter to Cyril is book I, letter 370, and the later is letter 310. As for Isidore’s letters being counted altogether as two thousand, he may perhaps have seen the codices of the Acoemete monastery at Constantinople, which contained that number, as I remember having noted in an old manuscript from an ancient translator of them in these words: “I have reviewed and translated all these letters of the blessed Isidore, presbyter and abbot of Pelusium, from his two thousand letters, which are distributed in five hundred each among four very ancient codices of the Acoemete monastery.” Nor have more than two thousand and thirteen appeared in print through the three editions to date. Moreover, Suidas—or the author whom Suidas copied—is authority for the claim that Isidore wrote ten thousand letters, and among them interpreted sacred Scripture in three thousand. Suidas says: “Isidore, the presbyter of Pelusium, etc., wrote letters interpreting divine Scripture, three thousand, and another seven thousand, and various other works.” Thus the corrected codices read],

and who, on account of the merits of his life and wisdom, was both honored and called “father” by Cyril himself, wrote—or rather wrote back—to him as follows:

> “The examples of divine Scripture terrify me, and they compel me to write back what I ought. For whether I am a father, as you yourself said, because of the condemnation of Eli, who did not chastise his sinning sons (1 Sam. 4), or whether I am your son, as I more truly know, because you bear the appearance of that great Mark, I fear the condemnation of Jonathan, who did not restrain a ventriloquist addressing his father [Note: The same codex: “questioning”], and who died first in battle along with the one who sinned, although he could have restrained him (1 Sam. 15, 21; 1 Chron. 10:13). But so that neither I may be condemned nor you yourself be condemned by God, cease from contention. Do not exact from the living Church the vengeance for your personal injuries inflicted by mortal men, nor build for it eternal discord under the pretext of piety.”

Nor are Isidore’s writings, in which he says that Cyril was building eternal discord in the Church under the pretext of piety, marked with the same hostility with which the statements of Bishop Theodore and the letter of the venerable Ibas are denounced.

The same holy Isidore writes to him again:

> “Compassion dulls the sharpness of the eyes, but rivalry blinds completely. Therefore, if you wish to become the executor of neither kind of judgment [Note: The same codex: “If you wish to cleanse yourself of both kinds of blurred vision, do not become the executor of violent judgments,” etc. In the printed editions, in the translation of Jacobus Billus Prunaeus, this appears as book I, letter 310: “Therefore, if you wish to be pure and free from both kinds of stain, do not deliver violent judgments.”], entrust the matters to a just examination. For even God, who knows all things before they happen, wished humanly and kindly to descend and see the cry of the Sodomites (Gen. 18:21), teaching us the method of careful investigation.

> “For many of those who gathered at Ephesus mock you as though in a comedy, saying that, in judging a private injury [Note: The same codex: “avenging”; in the printed editions: “taking vengeance”], you did not investigate orthodoxly the things of Christ. They say that he is the cousin of Theophilus [Note: Isidore’s Greek word is ἀδελφιδοῦς, meaning ‘son of a brother or sister’ (a nephew). The evidence establishes that he was the son of a brother, not of a sister, as Isidore’s translator renders it. Theophanes calls him ἀνεψιός in his *Chronicle*; ἀδελφιδοῦς is also used by Socrates, book VII, chapter 7, and by Theodoret, book V, chapter 35. Theodoret in turn calls Theophilus Cyril’s θεῖος—not maternal uncle, but paternal uncle: θεῖος πρὸς πατρός, as in Nicephorus, book XIV, chapter 25. Thus there is also an error in the *Tripartite History*, book X, chapter 25, where Cyril is called Theophilus’s cousin, instead of the term used by Theodoret, ἀδελφιδοῦς, ‘son of his brother.’ Shortly afterward, where the translator reads Θεοδώρου, the Greek has θεοφόρου: ‘he scattered the manifest madness of the God-bearing and God-loving John,’ so that the subject is one John, not Theodore], and that he imitates that man’s will. For just as the other openly spread madness against Theodore and our John, so this man too desires to boast, although there is much difference between the persons under examination.”

Behold, in this letter too he accuses him of conducting the case more through violent emotion and rivalry than through just examination, as though blinded in mind by passion and competition. He says that many mocked him because, in the case of Nestorius at Ephesus, he had sought vengeance for a private injury rather than investigating orthodoxly the things of Christ, just as Theophilus, his cousin and predecessor, had sought human glory in the condemnation of John of Constantinople.

For this reason Saint Gennadius too said of the blessed Cyril, as we showed above:

> “Woe to the evil one of Alexandria, his associate and now this man’s second self”—

intending Theophilus by the first and Cyril by the second.

And although this learned man judges the cases of John and Nestorius to be different, saying, “Although there is much difference among those examined”—thereby condemning Nestorius himself—he nevertheless believed that in both cases the motivating purpose had been rivalry.

In other letters as well he writes to him in similar terms [Note: He refers to letter 324 of book I, which begins: “You must, O marvelous man, remain always steadfast, betraying the heavenly things neither through fear nor by appearing contrary to yourself,” and so forth], stating that through his fickleness he was betraying heavenly things and, overcome by a desire for empty glory, was making himself contrary to himself in his writings.

We must not, therefore, believe that Gennadius and Isidore, men of the highest reputation, were more innocent in this matter than the venerable co-bishops Ibas and Theodore; rather, they were more fortunate because they were not found to be participants in the Synod of Chalcedon.

## CHAPTER V. That the letter is rashly condemned after the examination of the Synod of Chalcedon, whose decrees Pope Leo and the bishops of the East affirm must not be supplemented by anything else
If you will deign to consider these matters with a calm mind and a better intention, with him opening your heart and closing it against the insinuations of the impious—for, as it is written, “the Holy and True One has the key of David; he who opens and no one shuts, and he who shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3:7)—you will recognize

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “us” for “you.”] from the manifest evidence of what occurred that all these things were devised by heretics and established by their supporters to nullify the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and the letter of Pope Leo, whose defender Bishop Theodoret was at that same council. Unless these matters are rescinded by a better judgment, it is vain to deny—or, if that could be believed—that the venerable council approved the letter of Ibas.

For since it is clear that the letter was brought forward there by its bishop’s accusers, unquestionably, as we have already said above, if it is now justly condemned, it ought then all the more to have been condemned. But since no such action is shown to have taken place, that council appears to have done something less than it should have done—not, indeed, to say that it restrained heresy—and these men ought to add and supply what it omitted.

Blessed Leo, however, the faithful and confident defender of the Church, and no feigned or timid opponent of heretics, says that everything was so defined there that he confirms that nothing can be added to its perfection. For when the Eutychians, then as now, were attempting by many and various schemes to weaken or diminish the authority of that council, and were seeking to reopen the judgments made there, so that under the pretext of a more careful consideration something might appear either to be corrected or supplied in them, he prudently and bravely resisted their plots, writing as follows to the emperor Leo (Letter 88):

> “We must detest and steadfastly avoid what heretical fraud strives to obtain, and matters that have been piously and fully defined must not be recalled for debate, lest we appear, at the will of the condemned, to doubt those things which clearly agree in every respect with the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic authorities. Therefore, if there are any who dissent from what has been established from heaven, let them be left to their own opinions and withdraw from the unity of the Church with the perversity they have chosen. For it is utterly impossible that those who dare to contradict the divine mysteries should be joined with us in any communion. Let them boast in the vanity of their eloquence and glory in the cleverness of their arguments, which is hostile to the faith. We choose to obey the apostolic commands, which say: ‘See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit of men’ (Col. 2:8). For according to the same Apostle (Gal. 2:18), ‘If I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor,’ and I subject myself to those conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the blessed Emperor Marcian, but I also, by my own confession, have confirmed. For, as you have said piously and truthfully, perfection admits no increase, and fullness no addition.”

Your Serenity therefore clearly sees that, just as nothing can be corrected in the decrees of that council, so nothing can be added to them. Consequently, those who rashly condemned the letter of the venerable Ibas are proved to have acted not only against the council itself but also against the judgment of this apostolic man.

For even if they say that they did not presume to correct anything in its decrees, they cannot deny that they judged something lacking from their fullness, so that what the council itself had done insufficiently in a case that had been examined there for so long, they might supply as though with a wiser and more careful consideration.

How, then, shall we be able to avoid the taunts of the heretics, who say:

> “Where are those magnificent words of your Leo, with which, arrogantly enough, he declared concerning the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon: ‘Perfection admits no increase, and fullness no addition’? Behold, your own testimony proves that he was loudly proclaiming windy words in vain. For what was judged at that council you either correct, or, if you do not correct it, you certainly supply and complete it; and you show that those things did not possess the perfection and fullness that was proclaimed. Nor can you any longer say that we have withdrawn from your communion without reason.”

Or ought we to have been in communion with that council when, after the impious and Nestorian letter had been brought against Ibas by his accusers—as you yourselves have also confessed—and read aloud before everyone, it was, to use the words you vainly denied, pronounced orthodox

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “let us not say.” Another reading is: “and, having been pronounced orthodox, it is certainly proved to have been condemned.”]

and you approved it to such an extent that you judged it worthy of condemnation only later, when, returning to our position after almost a hundred years, you saw that it necessarily had to be anathematized in order to purge yourselves from its guilt?

And they will not say these things without reason. For since these supporters of theirs have judged that we, who were not judges in the case, must be cleansed from the Nestorian charge by condemning this letter, they have consequently judged those Fathers, in whose judgment the letter was examined but not condemned, not to have been cleansed from the same charge.

Behold what kind of prejudice they sought to bring against us; behold how they wished to strengthen the calumnies of heretics against the Church—men who contradict not only blessed Leo but also the letters of so many bishops of those councils.

[Note: These were, evidently, the councils of all the provinces of the East which, by order of the Emperor Leo, were convened concerning Timothy of Alexandria and the Council of Chalcedon, which the followers of Timothy rejected, and which sent their opinions in written replies to Leo. The letters of the individual councils are extant, gathered into one volume after the acts of the Council of Chalcedon. Cassiodorus calls this volume the *Encyclical*; at his request it was translated into Latin by Epiphanius the Scholastic. The words cited by Facundus are partly from the Province of Europe, no. 27, and partly from Sebastian, bishop of Beroea in Thrace II, no. 30.]

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “the encyclical letters of so many bishops.” Baluzius shows in the *Nova Collectio conciliorum* that these letters had from ancient times been called *encyclica*.]

They contradict the letters of such great bishops, in which, when asked about the aforementioned council, they replied to the Emperor Leo:

> “We can neither move nor alter one iota or one stroke of the things defined by that council.”

And again:

> “For just as the sun lacks nothing that would demonstrate that it is the sun, so the great, holy, and universal Council of Chalcedon lacks absolutely nothing of what is good. It needs neither addition nor subtraction, having been seasoned by the Holy Spirit as though by a certain divine salt. For those who were condemned in it at that time”—  
> [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “according to the time.”]  
> “were judged unworthy of the priestly order and were condemned as impious by the decree and judgment of the great God. But those who were received by it, having previously suffered an unjust and tyrannical accusation, were immediately and justly received by the decree of the Holy Spirit. Among them is the second Abel of our times, blessed Flavian.”

They say many other things, whose repetition would take too long.

How, then, are we to receive the accomplices of heretics when they issue new and contrary decrees, as though insufficient religious care had been taken in the decisions of that council, when the ancient Fathers declare that they cannot move even one iota or one stroke in them? Or what, after all, do we suppose to be lacking from the sun that shines upon the whole world, which ought to be supplied by their additions? Just as they vainly attempt to obscure its unconquerable radiance, so they can add nothing to its fullness.

## CHAPTER VI  
### That they say in vain that they await the response of Pope Vigilius, since he will not in the least depart from the footsteps of his predecessor Leo

They also say that, concerning this great presumption of theirs, they have consulted the Roman Church and are now awaiting the judgment of its bishop, blessed Vigilius. What people of this age think about him, that they should presume to define so great a crime—something that, despite the intention of blessed Leo and under so many of his successors, had never until that time been attempted—he himself, without doubt, understands as a prudent man. Indeed, who would not understand it, unless he were foolish?

For if, as they say, they have even dared to consult him about this matter and are awaiting his judgment in the case, I do not see how they have not already passed judgment concerning him. But they will learn how greatly their suspicion has deceived them. For he received his first and greatest authority not for the destruction of his father’s judgment but rather for its defense and vindication.

[Note: Avitus of Vienne called this authority “the primacy of the universal Church” in his letter to the senators of the City concerning the judgment of Pope Symmachus. Concerning the claim of the condemnors of the Three Chapters that they were awaiting the judgment of Vigilius, see also Book IV, chapter 3.]

He possesses no power against the truth, but more power than his fellow bishops on behalf of the truth. For the Apostle Paul says: “We can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth” (2 Cor. 13:8).

What hope is left for them in the response of the Roman bishop, when the venerable Leo mentioned above, by forceful and repeated judgments restraining unlawful attempts, wisely forestalled their plots, so that we do not now await his successor as a judge in doubtful questions, but await him as the avenger of an utterly certain transgression?

[Note: The same manuscript reads “await” in place of “await.”]

The many and explicit prohibitions of his predecessor increased the guilt of the transgressors, but left nothing to anyone else’s judgment. For to whom else, more than to Leo, would it have been permitted, in return for the great labors that he sustained with unwavering courage on behalf of the aforementioned council, to reconsider anything that it had decreed?

But far be it from that holy man to have considered lawful what he recognized as inexpedient, or, after conquering, to lose the crown of his great struggle. For what would remain intact, or what could stand immovable, if the judgment of so great a council were regarded either as imperfect and needing supplementation or as doubtful and requiring renewed examination?

Authority is effective not only in matters of doubt or definition concerning the faith

[Note: In the same manuscript the words “of doubt, or” are absent.]

but also in all those things that have been modestly and properly arranged there for the preservation of peace and unity, which wise men care about above all.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, perhaps, “recognize again Leo’s words.” The following words are marked off as Leo’s in our manuscript; they occur, word for word, in Leo the Great’s letter to the Emperor Leo, no. 133 in Quesnel’s edition, down to “who dare to resist the truth.”]

Therefore recognize again from this, O august and venerable emperor, for what great protection of the whole world divine Providence has prepared you, and understand what assistance you owe your mother, the Church, which especially glories in you as her son.

Do not allow struggles that have been extinguished to rise again in renewed movements against the triumph of the almighty right hand—especially since those condemned heretical attempts have long been entirely forbidden this—and since the fruit of pious labors is that the whole fullness of the Church may remain secure in the solidity of its unity, and that nothing at all be reconsidered of what has been well arranged.

For to wish to contend against legitimate and divinely inspired constitutions

[Note: The same manuscript reads “after legitimate”; so also does the cited letter of Leo.] is not the disposition of a peaceful mind but of a rebellious one, as the Apostle says: “To quarrel about words is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear” (1 Tim. 1:14).

For if it is always permitted to debate through human persuasions, there will never be a shortage of people who dare to resist the truth. And indeed, what will be the end of disputes and conflicts if it is once permitted to pass judgment on matters established by the agreement of the whole Church? Why should the judgment itself not again be judged?

Therefore that most prudent man, giving no opportunity at all to those who sought one, issued this warning: “Let nothing at all be reconsidered of what has been well arranged.”

Thus, if nothing is to be reconsidered, he did not admit even that which might be thought insignificant.

Yet these men, who hope that they can prevail upon the Roman bishop to attack the judgment of his illustrious predecessor, boast that they have removed the offenses arising from that council. They say that the Eutychians have always refused to communicate with us on its account, because, as though even that great council

[Note: Perhaps, “as though.”]—than which no other was more numerous for the truth of the faith—could, after so lengthy a deliberation and under the pressure of the objections of heretics, who are usually especially fervent in novelty, have negligently overlooked anything, or if the aforementioned Leo, when repeatedly pressed to reconsider something established by it, could have both heard and settled no such harmful arguments that presented a plausible appearance, then he must be thought to have been immovable in his firmness, wisely guarding against the possibility that, once an entrance had been opened by any pretext to those who struck wickedly, the fury of those lying in wait for Christ’s Church might burst in.

But these people, who are excessively diligent, do not wish all this to be attributed to prudence and caution rather than to negligence.

What, then, will they do when the whole Church, by God’s favor, does not overstep the eternal boundaries established for it by its Fathers, whose negligence it prefers to imitate rather than their obscure diligence?

Whose judgment we ought to follow is sufficiently obvious. Should we follow the judgment of those who thought that, if they reconsidered—or rather, censured—the judgment of the Fathers, the Acephali would communicate with the Church, which did not happen at all and which, even if it had happened, ought not to have been approved? Or should we follow the judgment of the most wise Leo, who, as is shown in his other writings, declared that no limit would thereby be imposed upon the churches’ collisions, but that, once permission to rebel had been granted, their conflicts would be expanded rather than quieted?

That this was truly said is proved by the evident outcome of events—or rather, by the ruin that resulted from them. I believe that even without our saying anything it is clear what belonged to divine Providence and what to human recklessness.

If blessed Leo, although dealing with a more recent council

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “a still more recent.”]

and one defended by no prior assertion of his predecessor, did not allow anything to be recalled for debate, how can it be believed that holy Vigilius, his fourteenth successor, could judge something new—especially when Leo himself says:

> “For, according to the Apostle, if I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor, and I subject myself to those conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the blessed Emperor Marcian but I also, by my own defense, have confirmed.”

[Note: The same manuscript reads “by my consent.”]

He knew, of course, that the Apostle had said:

> “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything other than what we have preached to you, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:8).

[Note: The same manuscript reads “when Leo himself,” and “had written back.”]

For if blessed Leo, after accepting the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, wrote back to it as follows:

> “Let the brotherhood and the hearts of all the faithful know that I have communicated my own judgment to you not only through the brothers who carried out my office but also through my approval of the synodal acts” (Letter 65),

and is shown to have criticized and censured nothing in those acts except that it was reported

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “that was read there.”]

that the venerable Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, had sat in a place preceding Maximus of Antioch—

[Note: In the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, after the legates of the Apostolic See, Anatolius is always named and subscribes first—Dioscorus of Alexandria, whose case was being discussed, having been rejected and excluded—and Maximus of Antioch follows Anatolius. Anatolius claimed that this position was owed to him by the decree of the Second General Council, which had placed the see of Constantinople immediately after that of Rome. But the Apostolic See did not recognize this decree, as foreign to the Council of Nicaea, which assigns the second place to the bishop of Alexandria and the third to the bishop of Antioch. Therefore, while Pope Leo approved the Council of Chalcedon, he excepted this point and rebuked Anatolius’s arrogance and ambition in many letters to the Emperor Marcian Augustus, to Anatolius himself, and to Maximus of Antioch. The matter is discussed again in Book V, chapter 4.]

How, if he had allowed this letter of Ibas—which is said to be Nestorian and therefore plainly belongs to a matter of faith—or anything of that kind contained in the acts of the council, having been read there and not condemned, to be anathematized or at least examined, would he not have made himself a transgressor, subjecting to doubt what he had already declared that he approved?

And therefore, even if no prohibition of his had preceded, and even if he had not responded to the Emperor Leo on behalf of the council with the words, “Perfection admits no increase, and fullness no addition,” this alone would have been sufficient: in those acts he had censured only the presumption of the bishop of Constantinople. It would clearly appear that nothing in them that could be thought Nestorian had been left to the judgment of his successor.

For if they contained anything heretical that, when brought before the judgment of that council, had not been found to be condemned, Leo would have censured it first when it was brought before his examination.

Therefore, if that letter is to be condemned by everyone as Nestorian—the letter that was brought against Bishop Ibas by his accusers and is contained in the synodal acts—not only did the council itself restrain Nestorian heresy, but so also did Leo, bishop of the Apostolic See, by whom the council was approved. He would be convicted not only by consideration of the truth but also by the example of his previous action.

For when blessed Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, sent him the acts in which Eutyches, when questioned, replied:

> “I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature,”

the same most religious and prudent man, Leo, with those acts before him, wrote back to the aforementioned Flavian as follows (Letter 12):

> “I am astonished that so absurd and perverse a profession, rebuked by no censure from the judges, and uttered in such a way that it seemed to offend no one, was heard. For it is as impious to say that the only-begotten Son of God existed from two natures before the union as it is sacrilegious to assert that, after the Word became flesh, there was in him a single nature. And lest Eutyches think that what he said was therefore correct or tolerable because it was not refuted by any sentence of yours, we urge the diligence of your Charity, dearest brother, that, if by the inspiration of God’s mercy the case is brought to a satisfactory conclusion, the imprudence of the unlearned man may also be cleansed from this plague of his understanding.”

I should therefore like to be instructed what we can say in reply to the Eutychians when they say:

> “Why is your Leo found to have been diligent, as you think, against Eutyches in examining the acts conducted before Flavian, but negligent against Nestorius in approving the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, so that he confirmed the Nestorian letter contained there—unless it was because, being preoccupied by the contrary error of Nestorius, he resisted Eutyches?

> “For why does he call Eutyches’ profession absurd and perverse—the profession in which he said, ‘I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union’—although Eutyches had not been accused of it in Flavian’s judgment, and why does he blame it for having been condemned by no rebuke from the judges, since it seemed to him extremely foolish and impious? Yet he pretends not to notice that the Nestorian letter brought by Ibas’s accusers before the Council of Chalcedon and reread there was not condemned, although you now acknowledge that it ought to have been anathematized there.

> “For even if, as you imprudently denied, it was not pronounced orthodox by that council, it ought nevertheless to have been condemned, lest it appear to have been approved by those who did not know better.”

Since, then, according to these clear and unavoidable arguments, the condemnation of this letter necessarily entails so great a crime even on the part of blessed Leo,

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “condemnation.”]

 I do not know what they expect from the judgment of his successor—unless it is that which is also a monstrous error to utter,

[Note: The same manuscript reads “to utter.”] and which heretics could never have hoped for: that Leo, that most glorious author and defender of the great and universal Council of Chalcedon, should be condemned together with it.

But how great a punishment is deserved by the fact that they have dared not only to attempt this but even to await it from his successor, we leave to his own consideration. He cannot be unaware how gravely the Church would be offended if, God forbid, he were to leave such a great crime unpunished.

They indeed trust—holding incorrect views about the obedience you owe to Christ and the devotion you display toward his churches—that they can be defended against the force and justice of the canons.

But it is more fitting for them to fear lest, with the Lord guiding your heart, they should perhaps experience that you have received authority from above not as a protection but rather as a vengeance upon transgressions.

Let those who rashly attack their father’s judgment cease to trust in some unknown refuge, which was fabricated for them not by Romulus the Christian—for his God is the one truly called “the strong Lord and mighty, the mighty Lord in battle” (Ps. 23:8)—but by their empty suspicion.

Nor should they presume upon your agreement in such an action. You were deceived while occupied with the many affairs of the state into consenting that this should be done. They will therefore deserve punishment all the more because, wishing to use your person as a pretext to make the restraint they offered to heretics go unpunished, they did not allow it to be brought to your attention that what was being done was contrary to the decrees of the Fathers. In this way, through the authority of your consent, they also gathered many accomplices for themselves, as though impunity followed from numbers, according to the saying of someone: “Whatever is sinned by many goes unpunished.”

They paid too little attention to the fact that neither can the multitude of sinners resist the divine judgment, nor can the authors of recklessness deceive human judgment by means of a multitude.

Those who were led on by their faction or compelled by oppression are left to God’s future judgment; but those same factious and presumptuous men will receive the sentence they deserve, all the heavier because they harmed so many.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER ONE  
### That, when they denounce the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, they reproach the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon and of Pope Leo

The care demanded by the work we have undertaken requires us to demonstrate in this book, in many ways, what we began to show in the preceding book: namely, that the accomplices of heretics have also subjected Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia—who died in the peace of the Church and was praised by the holy Fathers, as we have already mentioned—to an anathema, thereby attacking the great Council of Chalcedon and the decrees of blessed Leo.

And because, in order to draw the simple-minded into agreement with themselves, they say that blessed Cyril condemned certain writings of that same Theodore, let us prove this also: even if it is true, they acted against Cyril’s judgment, although they vainly attempt to excuse their presumption by his example.

Just as they were plainly shown to have falsely boasted that they condemned the letter of the venerable Ibas because of the insult it allegedly contained against Theodore, so by their own testimony they may be convicted of having attacked the judgment of the council in condemning Theodore.

Where we demonstrated that, even if the Council of Chalcedon had not pronounced that same letter orthodox, it would nevertheless have been condemned in order to nullify the council, because it praised Theodore, there we also showed at the same time that Theodore himself had for that reason been condemned.

From this it necessarily follows, concerning the aforementioned letter of the venerable Ibas, what we have already said: if what these men established is said to concern the truth and judgment

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “indictment.”]

of the Catholic faith, when they say:

> “If anyone does not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia and his doctrines, and those who have held or hold opinions like his, let him be anathema,”

then it will be established that the council was not Catholic, since it did not condemn Theodore, even though it heard the praises of his doctrines recited from the aforementioned letter.

But neither will Leo, bishop of Rome, escape this charge. Although he said that he approved the acts of the aforementioned council, he did not censure the fact that he found no disapproval there of Theodore’s praises.

This point must be kept in mind wherever we complain of the council’s condemnation, since it is not censured without implicating blessed Leo as well.

Moreover, what we proposed for the consideration of prudent men concerning the manner in which that letter was condemned—must it not also be considered in the condemnation of Theodore? For even if he were still alive and were proved to be a heretic, once the Nestorian error in which he is said to have been previously involved had been condemned, it would not have been necessary to seek the judgment of so many bishops against him.

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “there was need.”]

Such a gathering of judgments had never been necessary for the condemnation of ancient heretics, but sometimes was required for the exclusion of new ones, if, after being admonished, they had refused to correct their errors.

The supporters of heretics have now sought to have Theodore declared the teacher of Nestorius by the universal Church so that, since they can easily show not only that the letter of the venerable Ibas, containing his praises, was approved by the council—something falsely denied—but also that the letters of the most wise John of Antioch and of the Eastern council, addressed to blessed Proclus and to the Emperor Theodosius, praised the same Theodore much more extensively, they might thereby establish that the aforementioned council was Nestorian.

For the very formula of subscription issued in Theodore’s condemnation seems to show nothing else, when it says:

> “If anyone does not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia and his doctrines, let him be anathema,”

something that, as far as I remember, never occurred in the condemnation of any heretic: namely, that those who did not pronounce anathema upon him should themselves also be anathema.

For many heretics and many of their doctrines remain unknown, and their names are unknown as well; those who do not anathematize people whom they do not know ought not therefore to be anathematized.

But, as has been said, in order to reach their attack upon the Council of Chalcedon, which, when the praises of Theodore himself were read aloud from the letter of the venerable Ibas, pronounced neither him nor his doctrines anathema, they issued this formula of subscription contrary to custom and humanity—as though no one could be proved Catholic in any other way than by pronouncing anathema upon Theodore of Mopsuestia and his doctrines.

If we accept this decree, we shall have nothing with which to answer the heretics on behalf of the Council of Chalcedon when they say:

> “This is how you thought to excuse that council in the book to which you gave your assent: you said that, not content with Ibas’s denial concerning the letter to Maris, nor with the testimony given on his behalf by the clergy of Edessa, the council, while confirming the judgment of Photius and Eustathius”—  
> [Note: The same manuscript reads “Eustachius,” or “Eustathius,” as it is read in the Council of Constantinople II, the Fifth General Council, session 6.]  
> “required Ibas, for the destruction and exclusion of the impious letter to Maris, to anathematize Nestorius and his doctrines.”

And indeed an orthodox council ought to have acted in this way, whatever the origin of the letter that had been brought against Ibas as his own: in order to remove suspicion completely, it should have compelled Ibas to anathematize Nestorius, whose name was mentioned in it.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “in that [letter],” namely, in the letter of Ibas praised a little above.]

How, then, if the aforementioned Council of Chalcedon was truly orthodox, when it required Ibas to anathematize Nestorius and his doctrines—which it had not praised—did it not also require him above all to anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia,

[Note: The same manuscript reads “Theodore of Mopsuestia.”]

whom it heard praised in the aforementioned letter as a blessed herald of the truth and a teacher of the Church, as having struck down heretics during his life by the truth of his faith, and as having left spiritual weapons in his own books to the churches after his death?

[Note: The same manuscript reads “to the sons of the Church.”]

Or was it that Theodore, concerning whose blasphemies you said that they surpassed the madness of the devil, who, through zeal for God, as is written there, not only converted his own city

[Note: The same manuscript reads “as there.”] from error to truth but also instructed churches situated far away by his teaching?

When the Council of Chalcedon heard all these things from the letter brought against Ibas, it did not compel Ibas to anathematize Theodore, who had been so praised. The reason was plainly that, while accepting the impious error of Nestorius, the council concealed his name but defended Theodore of Mopsuestia, who was Nestorius’s teacher, just as it was said concerning such matters in the aforementioned book, whose definitions you subscribed.

When these things are brought against us, what shall we be able to say in reply if one is not orthodox who does not pronounce anathema upon Theodore of Mopsuestia and his doctrines?

Therefore you recognize, O Augustus, that these decrees were established as a reproach to the Council of Chalcedon, even if we say that the aforementioned letter was merely read there and not accepted.

And so, as we have said, the accomplices of heretics are convicted by their own reasoning and testimony of having issued such decrees against the great council.

For if, as they falsely persuade us, the council is excused on the ground that, not content with the denial of the venerable Bishop Ibas concerning the letter to Maris, nor with the testimony given on his behalf by the clergy of Edessa, it required him to anathematize Nestorius, whom it had not praised in the letter itself, then it cannot be excused for not requiring him especially to anathematize Theodore, who was praised there together with his doctrines, since according to these men no one can otherwise be proved Catholic.

## CHAPTER II  
### That Theodore cannot be accused as the teacher of Nestorius, since he holds the orthodox faith concerning Christ against the error of Paul of Samosata and Nestorius; and concerning the creed said to be Theodore’s
What of the further fiction that the same Theodore was denounced by blessed Leo as though he were Nestorius’s teacher? Can we suppose that they uttered so manifest a lie, without any regard for human shame, for any other reason than so that the authority of a great witness might burden the cause of that synod—since neither he himself nor the letter that praised him was condemned there—as the authority not merely of a Nestorian, that is, a Catholic? Thus he said:

> “It is therefore necessary to understand clearly that blessed Leo, confirming what was done at Ephesus against Nestorius by blessed Cyril, and commanding that these things be preserved, calls the twelve chapters of blessed Cyril, by which Nestorius’s error was condemned, ‘defined’; but he anathematizes the teachers: Paul of Samosata and Theodore of Mopsuestia as teachers of Nestorius, and the impious Manichaeus and Apollinaris as teachers of Eutyches—although it cannot be proved that blessed Leo said Theodore of Mopsuestia was Nestorius’s teacher.”

But let them produce either a letter or any other writing in which they establish that he said this. Indeed, they ought to bring forward where blessed Leo said it, if they were confident that they were speaking the truth. But, so that this may not remain doubtful, let us demonstrate in Theodore’s own words how far he was removed from the error of Paul of Samosata. In the thirteenth book of the work that he called *Mystical*, he said:

> “Paul of Samosata is an angel of the devil, who dared to call the Lord Jesus Christ a mere man and denied the existence of the divinity of the Only-Begotten, which exists before the ages.”

Likewise, in the work that he published against Apollinaris [Note: Those who favor Theodore of Mopsuestia’s reputation praise his struggles against the Arians and Apollinarists, as Theodoret does in Book V, the final chapter of his *History*: “For thirty-six years he continued in the episcopate, drawing up his battle line against Arius and Eunomius and overthrowing the brigand-band of Apollinaris.” Theodore wrote another work against the Apollinarists. The Fifth General Synod and Leontius of Byzantium, in Book III *Against Nestorius and Eutyches*, mention this work. The Greeks consistently call him Ἀπολινάριος (*Apollinarios*), both the earlier Apollinaris of Hierapolis, who lived under Marcus Aurelius and is mentioned by Eusebius in Book IV, chapter 26, and the two Apollinarises of Laodicea in Syria, the younger of whom—that is, the son—was the founder of the heresy from which the Apollinarists received their name. Most Latins call them *Apollinares* rather than *Apolinarii*, without noticing the different origin of the word.] he spoke as follows in Book III:

> “For it is evident that Paul of Samosata was indeed bishop of the Church of the Lord God at Antioch; but, suffering from the error of Theodotus and Artemon, who said that the Lord Jesus Christ was a mere man [Note: The same manuscript reads *qui primi purum* (“who first [said] a mere [man]”).], not recognizing him as God the Word and as the Son of God, existing in his own substance before the ages from God the eternal Father.”

[Note: The manuscript of Verona reads *Theodoti* (“of Theodotus”). Sirmond corrects the reading *Theodori* in a preceding note.] [Note: *Theodoti* should be read. The reference is to Theodotus the Leather-worker, who was the first to teach that Christ was merely a man and was condemned for that reason by Pope Victor. An ancient author says in Eusebius, Book V of the *History*, chapter 27: “Victor also excommunicated Theodotus the Leather-worker, the founder and father of the god-denying apostasy, who first said that Christ was a mere man.” Artemon followed the heresy of Theodotus; Paul of Samosata followed Artemon, as the same author and the bishops of the Antiochene synod affirm in Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 24.]  

Would Roman Leo have called Theodore, who spoke such things about Paul of Samosata and taught such things about Christ, a teacher of Nestorius together with Paul? Yet these men confidently assert whatever they wish, as though proclaiming words were the same as proving the truth.

But far be it from us to believe this about that most holy man. Even if Theodore is shown to have erred in certain matters, he should not therefore be falsely accused in matters in which he is not culpable. Whoever rebukes and accuses an involuntary error ought not to entangle himself in a voluntary lie, since it is written: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm V, 7).

Nor are we so greatly astonished that the Eutychians lie in this way through their agents as that they are believed so rashly and so readily. How, then, can the same Theodore be said to have taught that Christ was a mere man—that is, a man only, and not also God—when he therefore calls Paul of Samosata a devil and declares that Theodotus and Artemon, who said these things, did not hold sound doctrine but rather suffered from their own error?

What, then, did he himself believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be? Certainly what he reproved them for not recognizing: God the Word, and the Son of God existing in his own substance, since he also says that he existed eternally before the ages from God the Father. Therefore, contrary to what is falsely alleged in the criticism of the holy synod, he did not believe or teach two sons, as though he said that the man Christ was of one substance and God the Word of another. For, as his words make clear, he recognized the Lord Jesus Christ himself to be not a mere man but also God the Word—not merely by the authority or dignity of the person, but God and the Son of God in his own substance, just as he was man and the son of man in his own substance.

What opening, what suspicion of Nestorian error remains in these words? Here is Theodore’s faith, open and free from every ambiguity—the faith for which he is praised in the letter of the venerable Ibas, as also by the most learned Fathers.

The Eutychians therefore have no grounds for accusing the synod of Nestorian doctrine because it declared orthodox the aforesaid letter, which contains praise of Theodore. Just as someone is not to be called a Manichaean because, in this testimony, he confessed the Lord Jesus to be God the Word and the Son of God in his own substance, existing eternally before the ages from God the Father, while saying nothing about his humanity, so Theodore should not be accused as Nestorius’s teacher when, discussing Christ’s humanity, he does not speak of his divinity—or when, compelled by the contradiction of the Apollinarist heretics, he distinguishes the natures more sharply than he otherwise would, in order to escape the slander of their heirs, the Eutychians.

Now receive another of their lies [Note: The same manuscript reads: “another evident lie of theirs.”], which they similarly fabricated in the same book, saying:

> “For it is necessary to observe carefully that when the Apostle, who signified the person of the Word as being in the form of God, which is in the essence of the Father (Philippians II, 6), said this, he did not say that the one who was in the form of a servant took it upon himself, lest he indicate the Word united to a pre-existing man, according to the madness of Theodore and Nestorius.”

Yet they do not show where Theodore said that the Word was united to a pre-existing man.

We shall therefore demonstrate simply, even in this matter, that they said this deceitfully in order to bring reproach and hatred upon the great synod, using Theodore’s own words. He did not say, as they falsely claim, that the Word was united to a man who already subsisted; rather, he said that from the very formation of the man in his mother’s womb, the nature of man subsisted as one person with the nature of God the Word. For in the thirteenth book *On the Incarnation* he says:

> “It is good at this point above all to conclude what power the things that have been said possess—whether ‘to live,’ or ‘to be baptized,’ or ‘to be crucified,’ or ‘to die,’ or ‘to be buried,’ and ‘to rise again.’ We do not say these things by applying them to some mere man. Indeed, in each of the things mentioned we do not hesitate to add this, so that we may provide no occasion for those who slander us to speak evil. Rather, he was inhabited by God the Word from the very formation in his mother’s womb; and he was inhabited not according to ordinary indwelling, nor according to the grace understood to exist in many, but according to a certain surpassing indwelling, according to which we also say that the two natures were united and that one person came to be through the union.”

[Note: The manuscript of Verona reads *voluimus* (“we wished”) rather than *volumus* (“we wish”).]

Behold: while we wish to expose another of their lies, we see here that all, or nearly all, of their accusations against Theodore concerning Christ’s incarnation are excluded. For they accuse him of saying that Christ was a mere man. But he himself says:

> “Whether ‘to live,’ or ‘to be baptized,’ or ‘to be crucified,’ or ‘to die,’ or ‘to be buried,’ and ‘to rise again,’ we do not say these things by applying them to some mere man.”

If, then, he does not apply these things to some mere man, he consequently confesses that God too lived among us, was baptized, crucified, died, was buried, and rose again in the flesh he assumed. And to show his concern he adds:

> “In each of the things mentioned we do not hesitate to add this, so that we may provide no occasion for those who slander us to speak evil.”

Yet even so he could not cut off the opportunity sought by those who were looking for an opportunity.

They also accuse him of denying that blessed Mary gave birth to God. But he himself says that from the very formation in his mother’s womb [Note: The same manuscript reads *utero matris* (“his mother’s womb”).] God the Word inhabited a man united to himself, according to what the Evangelist says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

They also accuse him of saying that God the Word dwelt in the assumed nature of man in the same way as he dwelt in many saints and prophets, rather than that, through the union of both natures, one person came to be. But he himself says that he did not dwell according to ordinary indwelling, but according to a certain surpassing indwelling, according to which “we also say that the two natures were united and that one person came to be through the union.”

Here let your piety also observe the fabrication concerning blessed Leo, namely, that he supposedly said Theodore was Nestorius’s teacher. For when the same blessed Leo, writing to Maximus, bishop of Antioch (Letter 66), teaches that the rock of the catholic faith, whose name blessed Peter the Apostle received from the Lord, anathematizes Nestorius because, separating the nature of the Word and of the flesh in the conception of the blessed Virgin and dividing the one Christ into two, he wished there to be one person of the divinity and another of the humanity, Leo could not condemn Theodore as his teacher when Theodore had already forestalled Nestorius’s error and taught instead that from the very formation in his mother’s womb the nature of God the Word subsisted as one person with the nature that was assumed.

We have brought forward these passages from Theodore’s writings in order to convict the falsity of those who were not ashamed openly to lie while trying to exclude the letter of the venerable Ibas on Theodore’s behalf, and, on behalf of the letter of the venerable Ibas, the Council of Chalcedon. At the appropriate place we shall produce so much evidence of such weight that, even if the calumniators and deceivers themselves do not repent, at least others who readily believed them may do so.

Who could recount either all their falsehoods or everything scattered throughout that book to increase the charge against Theodore and against the letter of Ibas in which he was praised, so that hatred might thereby be stirred against the great synod because it declared that letter orthodox? Whether they mention Nestorius, or some Cyrius of whom I know nothing, or John the Greek [Note: In the manuscript, instead of *Graeci* (“of the Greek”), there is another deleted word, of which the final letters appear as “. . . . . te.”], they do not wish to mention them without adding insults; and when they produce testimonies of the Fathers, they do not wish to praise them without censuring someone else.

Let us nevertheless expose another great and twofold lie of theirs. They wished to make the Council of Chalcedon appear condemned not only by the Council of Ephesus but also by the judgment of Chalcedon itself, saying:

> “The synod at Ephesus under blessed Cyril, and at Chalcedon, condemned Theodore’s creed and subjected it to anathema together with its author.”

Yet the Ephesian synod reports that a certain Charisius, a presbyter and steward of Philadelphia, accused certain priests named Antonius and Jacobus of association with Nestorius and testified that they had handed on not the Church’s creed but another creed to the converted heretics called the *Tessarescaedecatites*, who celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon not with the Church but separately. Nowhere does it say there, either through Charisius himself or anyone else, that this creed belonged to Theodore. [Note: These matters occur in session 6 of the Ephesian Synod, together with a copy of the *Exposition of the falsified creed*; it is read again in session 4 of the Fifth General Synod. The author discusses it again in chapter 5 of this book.]

Blessed Cyril, writing to the Easterners, says:

> “A definition was produced in the holy synod at Ephesus, said to have been deposited by Theodore, as those who presented it asserted.”

But he does not affirm that it belonged to Theodore. Nor does he report that it was condemned together with its author, as these men fabricate—for that would not have been just. Our law, as it is written in the Gospel, does not judge a person unless it first hears him and learns what he has done (John VII, 51).

It is therefore false also that they said Theodore’s creed was condemned at the Ephesian synod together with its author. At Chalcedon, Theodore is mentioned nowhere else except where his name was read from the letter of the venerable Ibas.

Let them therefore recognize that they have achieved nothing by their surreptitious maneuvers, by which they tried to make the Council of Chalcedon appear self-contradictory—approving a letter that praised Theodore, whom, together with his creed, it supposedly condemned.

From these facts the supporters of the heretics are fully and more than sufficiently exposed: just as they subjected the letter of the venerable Ibas to anathema in order to destroy the Council of Chalcedon, so also did they subject Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, to anathema in order to destroy the decrees of Pope Leo, by whose authority the acts of that synod were approved.

## CHAPTER III. How they unskilfully accuse Theodore of teaching, in his exposition of the centurion’s story, that Christ was a mere man because he said that Christ feared and was troubled in his passion, although Christ and the martyrs actually trembled before death

Now let us bring forward those matters in which they are also shown, by their own judgment, to have attacked the testimony of blessed Cyril. For, while claiming that he was the author of some work [Note: Cyril wrote, as Liberatus reports in chapter 10, three books against Diodore and Theodore, as authors of Nestorian doctrine. Fragments of this work are quoted in the fifth session of the same synod, including the passage that Facundus cites under this title: “From the second book of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, *On the One Christ, against Theodore*.” But the synod’s text differs greatly and is otherwise arranged, so that Cyril’s words strike at Theodore, whereas here they are transferred in his praise, with the final part omitted. The text reads as follows: “No one would wish to reproach these labors, but rather would honor them, if they contained sound doctrine. He says that Theodore’s books could have been praised if they taught nothing corrupt; but shortly thereafter he demonstrates that some things in them are impious.”], in which certain statements of holy Diodore, bishop of Tarsus, and Theodore are censured, they cannot deny that he said there:

> “Twenty books, or perhaps even more, were written by the great Theodore against the heresies of the Arians and Eunomians, and besides these he interpreted other evangelical and apostolic writings. No one dared to reproach these labors; rather, everyone sought to honor, by a favorable judgment, the zeal for sound doctrine that is in them.”

Yet these men, on the contrary, criticize the same Theodore in his exposition of the Gospel, although whoever authored that work testifies that no one dared to reproach his labors but rather honored them by a favorable judgment. On this basis they call him impious because he said that the Lord, in his passion, feared [Note: Theodore’s words to this effect are found in Book III *Against Apollinaris*, cited by the synod in session 4, section 11: “And, being placed in great trembling during the time of the passion,” he says, “he needs the appearance of an angel strengthening him for endurance and bearing the evils that were imminent.” He had also invented the prayer of Christ being strengthened by an angel, mentioned in the same work, section 4, and in Leontius, who attacks Theodore at length on this point in Book III, chapter 37.] and was troubled, even to the point of saying:

> “We shudder even at the mere memory of his blasphemies, and we beseech God to be gracious to us because we are compelled to endure such things on our lips, asserting that he who gave his servants who undertook martyrdom for his name such grace that they approached their sufferings with joy, readiness, and eagerness could himself tremble in his passion.”

This criticism and condemnation of Theodore’s writings attacks the sound doctrine of blessed Leo, the author of the Council of Chalcedon [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *impugnant* (“they attack”).], who, writing to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, says (Letter 78):

> “Use, therefore, dearest brother, the invincible proofs of the catholic faith, and defend the preaching of the Evangelists by the testimony of the holy places in which you dwell. Bethlehem is with you, where the life-giving birth of the Virgin descended from David shone forth, and where she received in a manger, amid the narrowness of an inn, the child wrapped in swaddling clothes. With you is the infancy of the Savior, declared by angels, adored by the Magi, and sought by Herod through the deaths of many infants. With you are the places where his childhood grew, where his youth matured, and where, through every bodily development, the nature of true man advanced to perfect manhood—not without the hunger of eating, not without the rest of sleep, not without the tears of compassion, nor without the fear of dread. For one and the same person worked great miracles of power in the form of God and endured the violence of suffering in the form of a servant.”

[Note: In the same manuscript, *omnia* (“all”) is lacking.]

If heretics ask us why we do not also condemn Leo, who preached—and compelled others to preach—that Christ endured the violence of suffering not without the fear of dread, what shall we answer concerning Theodore, now condemned for such a confession? Shall we deny that this letter belongs to Leo, fleeing for refuge to their usual lie [Note: The same manuscript reads *mendacii* (“of the lie”) rather than *mendacium* (“lie”).], or shall we concede that Leo himself, together with Theodore, must be condemned?

Behold what is said to have been written in defense of the Council of Chalcedon and of Roman Leo—arguments which, by their own prejudicial force, compel us to condemn both the synod itself and Leo. Those who, out of fear of God, refused to associate themselves with such things and taught that they had been composed to prejudice the Church are said to deserve exile and imprisonment [Note: The same manuscript reads *ducantur* (“let them be led”) rather than *digni* (“worthy”).]

This is not surprising. The world has always repaid the truth that reproves it in such ways.

Moreover, what are we to make of the fact that in the same book in which Theodore is said to have gone beyond the devil’s madness because he confessed that our Lord feared and was troubled in his passion, Athanasius is approved because, writing in Book III *Against the Arians* [Note: Below, near the end of this chapter, this is again cited. In the printed editions the work is *Oration IV against the Arians*; the other passage from Athanasius that follows is taken from the work *On the Incarnate Appearance of God the Word*. It concerns the human nature assumed by the Word.], he says this about the properties of Christ’s two natures:

> “For to be troubled is proper to the flesh; but to have power to lay down and take up the soul whenever he wills is not proper to man, but belongs to the power of the Word.”

Behold, in that same book—not elsewhere, but in the very book in which they forget themselves—they admit that blessed Athanasius truly said that the Lord was troubled in his passion. Why, then, while approving Athanasius in this matter in order to prejudice the great council, do they condemn Theodore?

Blessed Athanasius also spoke in this way in the book he composed on the Trinity:

> “The Word and Son of God was always the Lord God; he did not become the Lord Jesus Christ after the crucifixion. Rather, as I have said, his divinity made his humanity Lord and God. And when he says, ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak’ (Matthew XXVI, 39, 41), he shows two wills here: one human, belonging to the flesh, and another belonging to the divinity. The human will, because of the weakness of the flesh, refuses the passion; his divinity is willing.”

Since holy Athanasius therefore professes two wills in Christ—one human, refusing the passion because of the weakness of the flesh, and another, belonging to his divinity, willing—the Eutychians should now understand that, just as it necessarily follows that if Theodore is justly condemned for such a confession, Roman Leo cannot be acquitted, so necessarily Athanasius himself, whom they claim to venerate, cannot be acquitted [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “so it necessarily follows that, once Theodore and Leo have been condemned, neither can he whom they say they venerate be acquitted.”].

But why should I speak of Athanasius, when they did not hesitate to attack the Evangelists themselves, as they seek, through Theodore’s condemnation, to insult blessed Leo and the Council of Chalcedon because it declared orthodox the letter of Ibas containing praise of Theodore?

For again, when Theodore opposed the Apollinarists, who, like the Eutychians now, wished to abolish Christ’s human nature, and when, in proof of Christ’s humanity, he said that as the hour of the passion approached Christ prayed more earnestly and was strengthened by an angel, they say:

> “How did the worker of angels need the comfort of an angel, as the Apostle says: ‘For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible’ (Colossians I, 16)?”

They also add what we mentioned above, saying:

> “Or how did he tremble before the passion, who gave his servants who undertook martyrdom for his name such grace that they approached their sufferings with joy, readiness, and eagerness?”

All these things they said there not against Theodore, nor against the letter of the venerable Ibas that praised Theodore, nor against blessed Leo, who taught similar things, but rather against the Evangelists John and Luke. John reports the Lord saying:

> “Now my soul is troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour” (John XII, 27).

Luke says:

> “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him; and being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (Luke XXII, 43–44).

Therefore, let all who think soundly recognize that those most serious insults which they heaped upon Theodore on account of this statement, wishing through them to stain blessed Leo and the Council of Chalcedon, were directed rather against the Evangelists.

But if we accept their question—“How did the worker of angels need the comfort of an angel?”—and conclude that he needed no comfort at all in the nature he assumed, then we shall also reject the Apostle Paul, who says:

> “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that although he was rich, he became poor for your sake, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (II Corinthians VIII, 9).

Contradicting everything written about him, we might also say: How did the bread of angels need breasts and his mother’s milk? How did he need to be carried in human arms and a human bosom, when he upholds all things by the word of his power? How did he need sleep, when he does not slumber while guarding Jerusalem?

Thus we would say in words alone that he has two natures, while in reality abolishing what we profess with our lips, just as we claim to honor the Council of Chalcedon while opposing its judgment.
