They would not resist the Gospel by saying, “How did he tremble before the passion, who gave his servants who undertook martyrdom for his name such grace that they approached their sufferings with joy, readiness, and eagerness?” if they were speaking about human affairs either of human beings or at least as of human beings.

What, then? Did the martyrs not tremble before dying? Were they not moved by natural feeling and struck with fear at death, which is indeed a punishment not arising from nature but from sins? Do we believe that they approached their sufferings with joy and eagerness because of their hope of future things [Note: The same manuscript reads “future good things”], so that they were in no way moved by fear of present evils? Certainly not. If they could, they would wish not to reach what they were seeking through death.

For this reason the Lord himself also said to Peter:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you: When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.”

The Evangelist explains that he said this to signify by what death Peter would glorify God (John XXI, 18–19).

They hear the Truth saying, “Another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish,” yet they vainly assert that the martyrs felt no trembling before their passion.

They might as well say that if someone, despairing of life because of a fatal ulcer, is promised by a physician that his health can be restored by the knife, he rejoices so greatly in hope of future health that he does not fear the present pain of the incision.

Let them also consider what the Apostle Paul says, speaking of the death of the body:

> “For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, an eternal house not made with hands in the heavens. For in this also we groan, desiring to be clothed with our dwelling that is from heaven, if indeed we are found clothed and not naked. For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Corinthians V, 1–4).

The Apostle therefore calls the body a house or tent and says that he would not wish to be stripped of it; rather, it could happen that he would be clothed over with immortality, so that he might pass into it without the stripping away of the body.

But I do not know what they mean when they say that the martyrs, to whom it was said, “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew X, 23), did not tremble at dying but rather trembled at not dying. They would not wish to die, if it were possible [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “and they would not wish not to die, if it were possible,” followed by further wording.], but through devotion and obedience they placed God’s will above their own natural will.

The Lord’s words also signify this. When he said, “Father, if you will, take this cup from me,” he immediately added: “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Luke XXII, 42).

When he said, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew XVI, 28), he did not command something contrary to nature, as though the human mind should be touched by no trembling before death. Otherwise he would be said to have opposed his own command, since he himself gave counsel to flee. Rather, so that one fear might be conquered by another, he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body.” He then added: “Rather, fear him who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna.”

Let us now consider what the holy John of Constantinople, the fellow disciple of the aforementioned Theodore of Mopsuestia, said. In explaining the same passage from the Gospel according to Matthew, he spoke as follows:

> “He prays with greater intensity, so that the matter may not appear to be a pretense, and sweat pours forth again for the same reason. And lest heretics say that he was pretending to be in agony, for that reason there were also sweats like drops of blood, and an angel appeared strengthening him, and a thousand indications of fear. And lest anyone say that these words are fabricated, for that reason there is also the prayer. His saying, ‘If it is possible, let it pass,’ shows his humanity; but his saying, ‘Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will,’ shows how, through zeal for virtue and patience, we are taught to follow God even when nature draws us back.”

In the commentary he composed on the Gospel according to John, in chapter 26, which begins, “Whoever loves his soul will lose it,” he also spoke as follows:

> “Lest they say that, being foreign to human pains, he philosophizes easily about death and, free from danger, admonishes us, he shows that he does not refuse even agony for the sake of the dispensation. These things belong to the economy, not to the divinity. Therefore he says: ‘Now my soul is troubled’ (John XII, 27). Otherwise, if this is not the meaning, what connection is there between what was said and his saying, ‘Father, save me from this hour’? Why would he be troubled so as even to seek deliverance, if escape were possible? These are the things belonging to the weakness of human nature. But, he says, I do not know what to say while asking for deliverance. For this reason I came to this hour—as though he were saying: Even if we are troubled and disturbed, let us not flee from death. For I too am troubled now, but I do not say that I should flee; it is fitting to bear what has come upon me. I do not say, ‘Deliver me from this hour,’ but what do I say? ‘Father, glorify your name.’ And although my disturbance compels me to say this, I say the opposite: ‘Glorify your name’—that is, while I proceed to the cross. This greatly demonstrates what is human and shows a nature that does not wish to die but desires the present life, showing that he was not foreign to human sufferings. For just as it is not a crime to drink, nor to sleep, so it is not a crime to desire the present life. Christ had a body free from sins, but not freed from bodily necessities; otherwise it would not have been a body.”

[Note: The same manuscript reads *propter hoc enim* (“for this reason indeed”) rather than *propter hoc* (“for this reason”).] [Note: The same manuscript reads *clarifica* (“make clear/glorify”) rather than *glorifica* (“glorify”).]

Did Theodore of Mopsuestia, who is condemned to the prejudice of blessed Leo and the Council of Chalcedon, confess a thousand indications of fear in Christ’s passion in order to assert Christ’s humanity, as his fellow disciple blessed John did? Or is he shown anywhere by them to have said that Christ was so troubled and disturbed in his passion—as this distinguished doctor of the Church did—that he even sought deliverance, if escape were possible? John also bears witness to many other things that indicate Christ’s human nature: a nature unwilling to die but desiring the present life, since just as it is no crime to drink or sleep, so neither is it a crime to desire life in the present world.

What is more, and what decisively refutes a certain [perhaps merely] recent doctrine, John concludes his statement with this:

> “To remove these sufferings from Christ is nothing other than to deny the very substance of his body,”

when he says:

> “Christ had a body free from sins, but not freed from bodily necessities; otherwise it would not have been a body.”

Why should I produce further testimonies on this subject, either from the Fathers already mentioned or from others, when in their own book they have already answered themselves sufficiently by bringing forward against themselves the testimony of holy Athanasius, as we recalled above? He says:

> “For to be troubled is proper to the flesh; but to have power to lay down and take up the soul whenever he wills is not proper to man, but belongs to the power of the Word.”

What, then, do they say there, as though it were something great, that blessed Athanasius said in the same third book *Against the Arians* about Christ?

> “Whom would God, being God, fear, or why would he fear death, since he himself was life and delivered others from death? Or how, when he said, ‘Do not fear the one who kills the body,’ would he himself fear?”

They should understand that he said this according to Christ’s divinity, in opposition to the Arians, who transferred the things belonging to his humanity to the dishonor of his divinity. For how could he say both things—not merely in the same work but in the same book—unless perhaps we believe Athanasius to have been like these men, so that he too may be said to have contradicted himself in this way?

I would say the same about the testimonies of the other Fathers, which they boast that they have gathered there against the evangelical teaching. There are also many other passages in that book in which they attack themselves, speaking things contrary to one another. To pursue them now would be too long, and we leave the task of refuting them better to you, since it can be done very easily. That work, whoever composed it, ought rather to be adorned with the title of your name, by which the falsehood cleverly devised to prejudice the great synod is refuted.

## CHAPTER IV. How they unjustly slander Theodore, as though he had taught in his exposition of the story of the centurion that Christ was a mere man
Now let us disclose another matter in which, once again, by their own testimony they are convicted of having attacked the judgment of blessed Cyril, whom they boast of having followed, when, to the prejudice of the great synod, they likewise accuse that same Theodore of having said, while interpreting the Gospel according to Matthew, “that the centurion approached Christ for the healing of his servant, not as the Son of God [Note: This passage of Theodore was also read in the fourth session of the Fifth Synod, no. 3; but the interpretation is different, as also in Vigilius’s *Constitutum*, chapter 53, in these words: ‘For the centurion did not approach him as the Son of God, existing before the whole creation and creator of all things.’], and existing before every created being, and the maker of all that exists.”

In this chapter, however, their fraudulent falsehood is sufficiently apparent. For they accuse Theodore precisely where he ought rather to be defended against their accusation. In explaining this passage of the Gospel, he does not, as they pretend, show what he himself thought about Christ, but rather what the centurion had thought about him.

Indeed, he also shows what he himself thought. For the man who said that the centurion, through ignorance [Note: The Verona manuscript has *per ignorantiam*, “through ignorance.”], had approached Christ not as God, and as existing before every created being and the maker of all that exists, undoubtedly himself recognized Christ as not merely a man, as Nestorius did, but also as God, existing before every created being and the maker of all that exists.

But we shall show how they habitually placed Theodore’s corrupted statement in their book, arranging it as they wished; and afterward we shall explain, from the written records, how his words actually stand, so that in this one instance you may be able to recognize how many inappropriate things they inserted elsewhere into his statements which he did not say, and how many relevant things which he did say they removed. [Note: The same manuscript reads *facile cognoscere*, “to recognize easily.”]

For this is what they said:

“But let us also convict the remaining blasphemies of Theodore in a similar manner. For the impious Theodore himself, raging against Christ and not acknowledging the miracles performed by him as miracles performed by God, while perversely interpreting in the Gospel according to John [Note: The same manuscript has *Matthaeum*, that is, Matthew, specifically chapters 8 and 9.] the centurion’s words addressed to the Lord during the healing of his servant, says the following:

‘He rightly added that statement, “For I too am a man,” as if to say: “There is nothing marvelous about your being able to do this, since you are a man who receives power from God; for I, although I am a man, receive those who obey me, possessing authority to command once, as I wish, through the generosity of the giver. Therefore there is nothing unreasonable in your also receiving this power from God and, by merely commanding with a word, expelling diseases.”’

For the centurion had not approached him as the Son of God, existing before all creation [Col. 0596A], and the maker of all that exists.”

We have transferred these words from their book into ours. And although even in these words—which they composed according to their own inclination—the speaker’s intention could not be wholly obscured, since, as has been said, he expressed not his own faith but the opinion of the ignorant centurion, nevertheless, so that this may appear more clearly, let us set out Theodore’s complete words:

“He was entreating him,” he says, “to heal the servant. The Lord says to him: ‘I will come and heal him.’ For this reason he especially promised to go promptly, so that the centurion’s virtue might become evident when he refused. ‘For I am not worthy,’ he says, ‘that you should enter under my roof; therefore say only a word, and this will be sufficient for the healing.’ [Note: The same manuscript reads *curae*, “for the healing.”] First, then, he displayed great reverence, and secondly, the greatest faith.

“Then, also showing his own faith with prudence: ‘For I too am a man under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.’ It was an act of prudence, according to the reasoning that seemed right to him, to believe such things about Christ. ‘For I too am a man; yet I am master of those over whom I have received authority: whatever seems right to me is done by my subjects. Therefore there is nothing unreasonable in your also receiving this power from God and, by merely commanding with a word, expelling diseases.’

“For the centurion had not approached him as the Son of God, existing before all creation, and the maker of all that exists. For at that time even the disciples did not know these things before the crucifixion, as we shall show more carefully below, with the Lord’s help; rather, he approached him as a man who, through virtue acquired from God, had received power greater than human power. Hence he said to him: ‘For I too am a man.’”

This, then, is how Theodore’s words stand. Now compare the two passages [Note: The same manuscript has *utraque*, “both passages.”] with one another, as is worthy of you, emperor, and you will discover how much they inserted and how much they removed, so that the truth might not appear.

Above all, who does not see that they removed the statement, “It was an act of prudence, according to the reasoning that seemed right to him, to believe such things about Christ,” for no other reason than that Theodore might appear to have expressed in those words his own faith rather than the opinion of the ignorant centurion [Note: The same manuscript has “not so much the centurion’s”; in the same manuscript, *magis* (“rather”) is absent.]?

Or consider the final statement, which they did not wish to include, where he says: “For at that time even the disciples did not know these things before the crucifixion, as we shall show more carefully below, with the Lord’s help.” Gather the conclusion of the sentence together with these words, and you will find that Theodore believed Christ to be not a man who had acquired from God power greater than human power, but the true Son of God, existing before all creation and the maker of all that exists.

For how could he have said, “Nor was it then for the disciples to know these things before the crucifixion,” unless he himself knew them and believed that the disciples had also come to know them after the crucifixion?

Who, moreover, would not shudder at such enormous frauds and lies as these? If what is written is not considered—“You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5:7)—and if the fear of God is disregarded, then, at the very least out of human shame, they ought to have refrained from the manifest falsehoods that could so easily be detected. Yet, speaking about Theodore, they say:

“We shudder even at the mere memory of his blasphemies, and we beseech God to be propitious to us because we endure such things altogether upon our tongue.”

What holiness of conscience, and what sincerity! How do those who invent so many things that were never said prove that they shudder at the memory of blasphemies spoken by another? Or how could God fail to be propitious to them when invoked with such simplicity and truthfulness?

These are the men who teach a new truth, unknown both to Leo of Rome for as long as he lived and, until now, to the whole Church. I beg you: let such men be cast away and driven from your ears, and let them no longer be free to preface their lies with the title of your name.

For if they accused Theodore’s plainly expressed view of the centurion—through which, as we promised, we have shown that he is rather defended against their accusation—with such shamelessness, and if they tried to obscure it by inserting some things and removing others, so as to twist it into the opposite meaning by a savage interpretation, what should we suppose they did elsewhere, where the aforementioned Theodore, contradicting the Apollinarists, spoke in certain places more combatively than modestly and cautiously?

And if the authority of blessed Cyril held them, as they boast, they would not merely say that Theodore had wrongly interpreted the evangelical writings, in which, as they assert, he testifies that no one dared to criticize his labors, but that the zeal for correct doctrine contained in them was honored by a favorable judgment. Rather, they would also not condemn similar statements in other writings of the same Theodore; they would instead believe that they themselves had been unable fully to understand their meaning, lest, by rashly rejecting such passages, they should consequently appear, by the similarity, to condemn those very things in his labors which they do not deny were approved by blessed Cyril.

But if they condemned Theodore because the Nestorian error believes Christ to be not the Son of God, existing before all creation, and the maker of all that exists, and if they condemned him as holding similar views, then it necessarily follows that, since the same Theodore was approved as having believed Christ to be the Son of God, existing before all creation and the maker of all that exists, he was unjustly condemned as a teacher of Nestorius, whose error he appears to have opposed in the strongest manner.

You see, therefore, devout prince, how, even if we had no other evidence, this one matter would sufficiently and convincingly demonstrate that the letter of the venerable Ibas, which the synod approved, was unjustly condemned because of its praise of Theodore.

## CHAPTER V  
### How they falsely accuse Theodore of having denied the persons of the Trinity with Sabellius and taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one person

What of the fact that, likewise in order to heighten the injury done to the holy synod—where, while Theodore’s praises were being read, he was not anathematized—they say that he also denied the Trinity and, in accordance with Sabellius, believed the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one person?

Do they not say this also contrary [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *non contra*, “not contrary.”] to the judgment of blessed Cyril, if, in that work, he censures certain writings of Saint Diodore and of his disciple Theodore? For whoever he may be, he testifies in the meantime that Theodore wrote more than twenty books irreproachably against the heresies of the Arians and Eunomians. This he could not have done otherwise than by confessing the Trinity, since he also correctly interpreted the evangelical and apostolic writings, in which Matthew reports that the Lord commanded:

“Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

And Paul said to the Corinthians:

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:13),

as well as other similar passages [Note: The same manuscript has “many similar passages”], through which the Trinity has been revealed to us in the evangelical and apostolic writings.

Since, then, blessed Cyril is said to have declared that Theodore expounded these matters irreproachably, how can it be asserted, contrary to his testimony, that Theodore denied the Trinity and taught that the three are one person?

“For they said:

‘Nevertheless, so that all Christians, recognizing Theodore’s madness, may not be carried away by his impious doctrines, we have inserted into the present book a few passages from his blasphemies, written down from the creed composed by him in the controversy, which are contained in the very sermons:

“We confess the Father perfect in person, and the Son likewise, and the Holy Spirit also in the same way” [Note: In the Ephesian synod, where we said that this creed is found, the Greek reads: *Ὁμολογοῦμεν δὲ Πατέρα τέλειον προσώπῳ, καὶ Υἱὸν ὁμοίως, καὶ Πνεῦμα δὲ ἅγιον ὡσαύτως*—“And we confess the Father perfect in person, and likewise the Son, and likewise also the Holy Spirit.” In the same passage, in Facundus, one may suspect that *ὡσαύτως* (“likewise”) was likewise written. The interpreter of the Fifth Synod has it, “in the same way.”] [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *itidem*, “likewise.”]”’

And this, indeed, is what the impious Theodore said. But the hearer must observe that, by saying “likewise” and “in the same way” in the person of the holy Trinity [Note: The same manuscript has *itidem*, “likewise”], he is shown to be speaking of one person belonging to the three names of the holy Trinity, in accordance with the madness of Sabellius.”

Since, then, they said, “The hearer must observe,” they do not appear to me to be contemptible. Rather, as they advised, we must examine and disclose both those words which they say are Theodore’s and those by which they attempted to refute them, so that it may easily be discerned who appears to speak more in accordance with Sabellius:

Whether it was he—whoever he may be—who said, “We confess the Father perfect in person, and the Son likewise, and the Holy Spirit also in the same way” [Note: The Verona manuscript has *itidem*, “likewise”];

or these men, who say, “The hearer must observe that, by saying ‘likewise’ and ‘in the same way’ in the person of the holy Trinity” [Note: The same manuscript has *itidem*, “likewise”].

For these men appear rather to speak according to the error of Sabellius, which they claim to refute, since they say “in the person of the holy Trinity,” and not, as the truth requires, “in the persons of the holy Trinity.”

After first speaking carelessly in this way, they subsequently labor to establish—and attempt to prove to us, as though we doubted it—that there are three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

To them I give this brief answer: that the creed in which they claim the Trinity to have been denied is affirmed, by the testimony of earlier authorities, not to be Theodore’s. For he could not have denied the Trinity whom blessed Cyril, as they report, indicates to have interpreted more than twenty, or perhaps even more, books against the heresies of the Arians and Eunomians, in addition to these evangelical and apostolic writings; and that no one dared to criticize these labors of his, but rather honored, by a favorable judgment, the zeal for correct doctrine contained in them.

Finally, the same Theodore says the following in his second letter to Artemius, presbyter of Alexandria:

“They ought to know that we worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, declaring that in these the divine, eternal, and uncreated Trinity is complete. Since each of these is of the same essence—that is, of the eternal and truly divine cause of all created things—the Father is to be worshiped not for any other reason but on account of his own essence.

“So also the Son: he receives this not for another reason, but because he is of that essence, and of such an essence, in relation to which these things were fittingly accomplished. Likewise, recognizing that the Holy Spirit too is of the same essence, we worship him on account of his own essence.

“Thus we also speak of three persons, each one perfect and of the same essence, eternal and divine, and we consider them to be the cause of created things; and we worship three persons, believing them truly to be of one divine essence.

“How, then, could it be possible to add above these a fourth person, that assumed form of a servant? We do not consider it to be of the same substance; we do not acknowledge that worship is owed to it for its own sake, or that it should receive adoration on account of its own essence; nor do we worship it alone, separately, in its own person, as they suppose it to be divided.”

After recalling these statements, should they boast that the creed was fabricated by Theodore, in which they assert that the Trinity was denied? Or should we doubt that we ought to believe the holy Fathers, who testify that he was alien to the mind of Nestorius?

For in this testimony he not only confesses the three persons and the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but also denies that it is possible to add to these, as a fourth person, the assumed form of a servant. Against Apollinaris and Eutyches he had asserted that it was of another substance, not the same as that of the Godhead, while nevertheless denying against Nestorius that it was divided as though existing in a person of its own, since he knew that it belonged to one of the subsistences of the Trinity.

And if we lacked these testimonies from his writings, together with the many others that we shall produce later, his accusers ought to have been ashamed to fabricate such absurd and mutually contradictory claims about anyone at all.

For while they themselves say that he denied the Trinity, as though God were solitary and had neither a Son nor a Holy Spirit, they then say, in opposition to this, that he proclaimed two sons. But how, I do not know, can he be said both to have denied one and to have proclaimed two?

Ridiculous, devout emperor—ridiculous, but grievous. Behold the kind of nonsense to which bishops are compelled to subscribe, and, if they do not, are judged worthy of exile. Behold to what purpose even the Roman bishop is brought in, lest the ambitious fraud of the heretics should appear to have left anything unattempted.

## CHAPTER VI  
### How Theodore did not nullify the prophecies concerning Christ, even if he sometimes interprets some of them morally; and how he was consistently praised by Cyril
Yet consider another matter also, by which likewise they made the great synod still more conspicuous: they endured Theodore to be praised as though entangled in the crimes not merely of one heresy, but of two [Note: [Col. 0600D] Same manuscript, “had endured” (pertulerint)]; and by their own testimony they are proved contrary both to themselves and to the judgment of blessed Cyril, when they say that the same Theodorus [Col. 0600C] also cuts away all the prophecies made concerning Christ [Note: [Col. 0599D] The matters contained in the same session of the synod, no. 20 and following, belong to this chapter.]. Although they condemned him disgracefully, as though for Jewish impiety, saying that he did not believe Christ to be God [Note: [Col. 0599D] In Justinian’s edict, no. 11: Οὐδὲ γὰρ εἶναι τὸν Κύριον Θεόν: “For neither does Theodorus say that the Lord is God.”], they again, on the other hand, fasten upon him the charge of the Manichaeans, whom we know not to accept the Old Testament. For the Jews too do not deny that Christ was announced through the prophets; but they still await as future the one whom we believe has come.

Who could find it even slightly credible that a bishop in the Catholic Church should be said to have believed and taught that the prophets had foretold nothing about Christ, and should have remained in communion with that Church? For this is not, as with many heretics, a hidden error, or one disguised with some semblance of plausibility, so that it would not immediately offend religious ears when one hears that the prophets prophesied nothing about Christ. This is precisely to abolish all the prophecies made concerning Christ, which Theodorus is alleged to have done.

Although, therefore, what has been fabricated about him here appears incredible of its own accord, even this, according to their own account, is said against the judgment of blessed Cyril. For if Theodorus cut away all the prophecies made concerning Christ, he did not rightly interpret the Gospel writings, in which Luke records that the Lord said:

> “These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you: that it was necessary for everything written about me in the Law of Moses, and the Prophets, and the Psalms to be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44).

Nor did he rightly explain the Apostle, who at the beginning of his Epistle says:

> “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:1);

and six hundred other passages of this kind, with which the Gospel and apostolic writings are filled.

But let us consider what Theodorus said when explaining the foregoing passage in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans:

> “And because what was being said about Christ by them seemed in some way new, he adds, ‘which he had promised beforehand through his prophets,’ wishing by the prophecy to show the antiquity of the teaching. Hence, also magnifying the prophecy, he properly added, ‘in the holy Scriptures.’ For he did not mean a letter or a holy character, but the prophecy itself, which existed through the Holy Spirit granting them revelation. Thus he rightly called it prophecy [Note: [Col. 0601D] Verona manuscript: “as” (sicut)]. So also elsewhere he said: ‘Every Scripture inspired by God is useful’ (2 Tim. 3).
>
> “What, then, do these words say? ‘Concerning his Son.’ And since ‘son’ is a common designation, and when it is spoken of divinity it is also understood of humanity, wishing to make more explicit from what source he now intends to speak of him, or for what reason he has added the testimony of the prophets, he says: ‘Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.’ He clearly shows that he is introducing speech about the assumed man; yet he does not leave unindicated the sign of divinity. For by adding ‘according to the flesh,’ he sufficiently shows that he also knows how to understand the designation ‘son’ in another way, since according to this sense he knows him to have been made from the seed of David, as though according to another sense he did not know him in this manner—that is, according to divinity.
>
> “For there are two natures, but they understand one thing through conjunction [Note: [Col. 0601D] Same manuscript: “are understood” (intelliguntur)]. One is the nature of the assumed man, but the other is that of God the Word. Both come together into one because of the assumption and because of the union that resulted from the assumption, which the form of a servant has toward God” [Note: [Col. 0601D] Same manuscript, “God the Word.”].

Here Theodorus confesses both that the prophets spoke about the Lord Christ and that the Lord Christ himself is man and God. He says that the Apostle demonstrates the antiquity of his teaching through the prophecy made concerning Christ, and he also says that the designation “son,” when spoken of divinity, is understood of humanity as well; and that, when he introduces discourse concerning the assumed man, he nevertheless does not leave the sign of divinity unindicated.

More clearly still—and in a way that no malicious interpretation could twist into a deviant meaning—he says that the Apostle knows the Son of God, according to the flesh, to have been made from the seed of David, as though according to another sense he did not know him in this way: that is, according to divinity. Although, therefore, Theodorus teaches that he is one and the same Son in both respects, according to the one and the other, he does not teach that the one according to the flesh, made from the seed of David, is one person or subsistence, as Nestorius did, and that the Son of God according to divinity is another; rather, he says that the Apostle knew him to be the same Son both according to the flesh and according to divinity.

Accordingly, he added:

> “For there are two natures, but they are understood as one thing through conjunction.”

And although one is the nature of man and the other the nature of God the Word, both nevertheless come together into one because of the assumption and because of the union that resulted from the assumption.

He confesses, moreover, in accordance with the Apostle, that God formerly promised Christ through the prophets, and that the prophets spoke concerning his Son. Therefore this man does not abolish all the prophecies made concerning Christ.

Certainly, since it is true that the opponents of the holy synod make these accusations against him because he is said to have interpreted certain passages in the Psalms morally which ought rather to be understood as spoken about Christ—without examining how they themselves presented these passages, or how they were presented by him [Note: [Col. 0601D] Same manuscript, “are presented.”]—nor now proving that this matter does not make him a heretic, since it is often judged praiseworthy if even things spoken prophetically are expounded morally, these words of the same Theodorus in his book *On Allegory and History*, which he wrote against Origen—and on account of which he also incurred the hostility of the Origenists—put an end to these disputes [Note: [Col. 0602D] Same manuscript: “we put this end to the disputes, because the same Theodore,” etc.]. He says to Cerdon:

> “I attribute the fact that you praise our work in this way to no one else than to the friendship which you have for us, and which you have always shown in many important matters; and especially because you admire what has been written in the Psalms, which we also wrote first of all the others.
>
> “We did not, however, exercise as much diligence concerning this matter as we ought to have done. For we suffered whatever happens to beginners, being at that time inexperienced in writing. Indeed, the works that are ours underwent many alterations at that time, which it is not appropriate to recount now. For this reason many things were composed by us rather carelessly, especially those which came first” [Note: [Col. 0602D] Same manuscript, “when.”].

Here, even if the things they censured in his interpretation of the Psalter made him a heretic, he himself, reconsidering that interpretation, acknowledges that the same interpretation displeased him, and corrects with the maturity of later age the frivolous statements of a confident youth. He should therefore be approved all the more even in this very matter: he ought not merely to be censured for his error, but praised for his correction, since divine Scripture says: “He who slips, but not deliberately”; and, “Who is there who has not sinned with his tongue?”

Here too he showed by his voluntary self-reproach that he had fallen unintentionally—and, what is more, in a work in which he had been praised by a friend. Would that those who betrayed the Church knowingly and willingly might deign to imitate him, even when reproved by others!

These things are sufficient for Theodorus’s vindication. But those who count it heretical for certain things spoken prophetically about Christ also to be expounded morally ought to consider how they can defend blessed Cyril. For in the work which they say he wrote in criticism of certain statements of Diodorus and Theodorus, something of this kind is found; if they still claim that it was composed by him, they establish that he was a heretic.

The author of that work treats a passage in which the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> “For he did not subject the world to come, of which we are speaking, to angels. But someone testified somewhere, saying” (Heb. 2:5, 9):
>
> “What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8:5).
>
> “For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him. But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him. We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.”

The author of the aforementioned work, then, in treating this testimony—which the Apostle testifies that the prophet spoke beforehand about Christ—affirmed that it had been written about other persons, but that it had been transferred by the same Apostle, with skill, in order to reveal the mystery of Christ. He says:

> “Paul, however, a very wise craftsman, in introducing the divine mysteries, sometimes also brings forward those things which in the divine Scripture were spoken about certain other persons, in order to reveal the mystery of Christ. Nevertheless, he does not separate them from the persons concerning whom we know they were spoken, nor does he refer everything belonging to them to Christ; rather, he sometimes takes up a very small part, which he can skillfully refer to his purpose without any danger.”

Whether they wish these words to be those of blessed Cyril or of someone else, we leave it to their judgment to decide. For if they are blessed Cyril’s, and if anyone who has treated prophetically spoken passages also morally is to be called a heretic, then they assert much more strongly that he himself was a heretic, since, contrary to the Apostle’s testimony mentioned above, he confirms that the words were spoken not prophetically about the mystery of Christ but about certain other persons.

If, however, they would prefer to say that that work is not by blessed Cyril, they cannot excuse by his example their presumption in condemning Theodorus together with his doctrines. Whoever is said to be the author of that work, it can contribute nothing to their defense, since nowhere is he found either to have pronounced an anathema against Theodorus or to have condemned his doctrines.

They ought therefore to consider whether, by affirming that work to have been written by blessed Cyril, they have anything with which to answer if someone says to them:

Since you presume to be judges of the dead and to condemn as heretics those who died in the peace and honor of the Church, what judgment do you pass on Bishop Cyril, who unteaches what the Apostle Paul teaches and asserts that the things written prophetically about Christ were spoken about certain other persons, but that they were introduced by the Apostle—more skillfully than truthfully—in order to reveal his mystery?

As though there were such a lack of divine Scripture, or such negligence on the part of the Apostle Paul in revealing the mystery of Christ, that he could not have found a testimony truly written about Christ himself, one whose smallest portion he need not sometimes skillfully and “without danger,” as he says, refer to his purpose, but which he could simply and securely, whole and uncorrupted, refer to his purpose exactly as it stands.

But when the same Apostle says, “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3), if he spoke skillfully rather than truthfully, then Christ Almighty—who is also our truth—is being accused of having been unable to find a true testimony in his own Scripture with which to reveal his mystery.

Let them therefore see how they will answer these points—those who, in condemning Theodorus to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon, object, in order to excuse themselves, that they did so because blessed Cyril censured his statements in that work. For they cannot persuade even the Jews if it is said that the man in whom Christ spoke introduced, artificially, a false testimony spoken about other persons in order to reveal the mystery.

Finally, they cannot satisfy even Catholics who ask why the Apostle introduced sayings spoken about others in order to reveal the mystery of Christ, by saying that some usefulness at least prompted him to do this. For it is far removed from the truth of our faith to say that Christian usefulness can be untruthful—even without considering the judgment of blessed Cyril. If the Apostle said that the prophetic passage had been written usefully concerning Christ, then blessed Cyril wrongly said that it had not been written concerning Christ; and he ought not to have betrayed what Paul intended to keep concealed.

Especially since he was uselessly trying to persuade people of this, teaching that the Apostle should not be believed, and thereby teaching still more strongly that he himself ought not to be believed.

Let these men know, however, that it does not follow that someone abolishes all the prophecies made concerning Christ merely because he rightly treats certain things mystically spoken about him also in a moral sense. Let them hear the Apostle writing to the Ephesians and saying:

> “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31).

Yet what he says is a great mystery—“The two shall become one flesh”—he interprets differently when writing to the Corinthians, saying:

> “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not. Or do you not know that the one who cleaves to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, he says, ‘The two shall become one flesh’” (1 Cor. 6:15–16).

Behold, that great and celebrated mystery which he indicates to exist in Christ and in the Church, the Apostle Paul, without blasphemy, applies even to a fornicator and a prostitute. He neither lies nor is mistaken, nor does he, by writing such things, abolish the prophecies made concerning Christ, since divine speech, like a pearl penetrable from every side, must often be opened by the straightest, balanced, and moderate understanding.

Let them also hear Christ himself in the Gospel, not abolishing the prophecies made concerning him. When the Pharisees tested him and said, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause whatever?” he answered in this way:

> “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. 19:3, 7).

That great and singular mystery which the Apostle truthfully said to exist in Christ and in the Church, Christ himself, who is our truth, declares to have also been written for the general preservation of the marital covenant.

These things are sufficient to prove that it is often judged praiseworthy if even things spoken prophetically are expounded morally.

Meanwhile, Emperor, you perceive and increasingly recognize through the very clear evidence of these many proofs that the Nestorian character of the Letter of Ibas cannot be established from the praise of Theodorus. For this reason, as we have already said, the heretics sought to deny that it had been received by the synod—a claim that is plainly false—so that, first, while we offered no resistance, indeed while we affirmed it, they could heap upon it whatever accusations they wished; and then, by means of our own denial, they could show that it ought not to have been received.

But now hear how, not merely in the matters we have mentioned, but in absolutely everything for which they condemned Theodorus of Mopsuestia, they trampled upon the judgment of blessed Cyril, who, resisting those accusing the statements of the aforementioned Theodorus, wrote as follows to blessed John of Antioch and the entire Eastern synod:

> “As for the audacity and contest which you all jointly undertook on behalf of the admirable man who deserved the greatest glory among you—I mean Theodorus—you protested against certain people who, as it appears, were hostile toward him and were using as an occasion the contrary doctrine by which they were held, in order to demand the condemnation of certain chapters that, as some said, had not been understood in the better sense, and by which they had disturbed your Holiness.
>
> “Even now, as your letter shows, they are undertaking this journey to the imperial city, to see whether they can prevail, through the gathering of certain people, in persuading the authorities that the passages they produce should be subjected to an anathema by imperial decree, together with those who wish to defend them.
>
> “To this I say, as it seems to me—and to every person of sound mind—that it is impious to reproach or bear ill will toward those who do not know how to walk rightly, but rather to leave as far behind as possible those who think in this way. Unless perhaps one ought to entertain what they are trying to construct [Note: [Col. 0605D] Same manuscript: “continue” (continuare)], especially since the person whom they subject to blame is not clearly present, the refutation of the chapters is uncertain, and those who do these things will be found running into uncertainty and striking the air.”

Here we have proved that not merely certain matters, but everything which they accuse in the statements of Theodorus of Mopsuestia, was condemned contrary to the judgment of blessed Cyril, since “the person who is to be subjected to blame is not clearly present,” and “the refutation of the chapters is found to be uncertain.”

But let your Piety also deign to note that he does not say that those who struggled to prevent the condemnation of certain chapters of the admirable man who deserved the greatest glory, Theodorus, were possessed by the disease of Nestorius. Rather, he says that those who were hostile toward Theodorus were themselves using as an occasion the contrary doctrine by which they were held.

Rebuking them also for not knowing how to walk rightly, he advises us, as far as possible, to leave those who think in this way as far behind as possible, and not to entertain in our minds what they were trying to construct: namely, that when there was no definite person who could either interpret favorably what he had said, as blessed Cyril himself did with his own chapters, or, if he did not do so, be subjected to blame, the refutation of the chapters would be vain.

Thus, by his own example, he humanely warned that many things might be said with a proper intention which could nevertheless be understood otherwise [Note: [Col. 0606D] Same manuscript, “he was warned.”].

Let us know, therefore, most merciful Emperor, in accordance with Cyril’s judgment, that those who do these things will be found “running into uncertainty and striking the air.”

For this reason, again, at the end of that same letter he says of such people:

> “But those who provide causes of this kind shall rightly hear, even if they do not wish to: ‘Forget yourselves, when you stretch your bows against dust. For he who was registered among you no longer remains; and let no one accuse me of having proceeded to these words, but let him yield to the exceedingly famous predecessor.’
>
> “For it is grievous to insult the dead, even if they were laymen, much more those who ended this life in the episcopate. For it appears most just to prudent men to yield to him who knows beforehand the will of each person and knows what each of us will be.”

It is evident from these words, most merciful Emperor, that Bishop Cyril judged it grievous to insult the dead, even laymen. How much more grievous, then, is it to pronounce an anathema upon those who ended their life in the episcopate, and to seize the judgment of their case from God, who knows beforehand the will of each person and the intention with which he speaks, and who also knows what each of us will be, and what sort we are found to be in that judgment, when we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may render an account of what he did in the body, whether good or evil? [Note: [Col. 0606D] Same manuscript: “what sort he is found to be” (qualis inveniatur).]

What Catholic heart would not be offended that these judges of the dead say that the same blessed Cyril proved contrary to them, and that he later judged differently concerning certain writings of the aforementioned Theodorus, thereby falling into the very fault which he censured in the restless presumption of others? For the Apostle says:

> “For if I rebuild the things which I destroyed, I prove myself a transgressor” (Gal. 2:18).

Since Cyril himself had taught that those who were hostile toward the admirable man who deserved the greatest glory, Theodorus, and who sought to have certain of his chapters condemned as not understood in the better sense, were rather using as an occasion the contrary doctrine by which they were held, and since he declared that they did not walk rightly, how would he not make himself a transgressor and turn against himself everything he had said in his attack on others, if he too later wished to condemn certain chapters of Theodorus?

Or how would he not be caught contradicting himself, when he had instructed us, while seeking other things, to leave such people as far behind as possible, but later entertained in his mind what they were trying to construct, so that, when there was no definite person whom they could subject to blame, he made the refutation of Theodorus’s chapters uncertain, as he himself defined it, running into uncertainty according to his own judgment and striking the air?

It is exceedingly harsh to suppose this rashly of Cyril: that, forgetting himself and not considering that he was mortal, he would stretch his bow against dust—that is, against a dead man reduced to dust—when it was not impossible that he himself would suffer the same after death, when he could no longer defend or better interpret his own statements.

In accusing Theodorus’s partisans, he himself said:

> “For it is grievous to insult the dead, even if they were laymen, much more those who ended this life in the episcopate.”

Yet is he rashly to be believed capable of insulting Theodore, who died in the episcopate, rather than, as he was exhorted [Note: [Col. 0607B] Verona manuscript: “urged” (hortatus)], yielding to God, who knows beforehand the will of each person and knows what each of us will be?

Who would dare say this of Cyril, unless he wished to call down upon him not another’s judgment but his own?

For what someone else perhaps would not dare to say about him, he himself has already said:

> “For those who provide causes of this kind shall rightly hear, even if they do not wish to.”

He therefore cannot rashly be believed to have provided causes of this kind against his own judgment.

But now, Emperor, you recognize that it has been shown in many ways, as we promised, that the accomplices of the heretics, in order to abolish the great Council of Chalcedon and the decrees of blessed Leo, condemned Bishop Theodorus of Mopsuestia with excessive boldness under an anathema, and that they vainly strive to defend their presumption by some sort of patronage from blessed Cyril.

Here your Serenity could also observe that, in seeking to demonstrate these points, we have shown three other claims to be false, although they had another purpose and arose incidentally: namely, what they said about Theodorus himself—that he believed Christ to be merely a man and not also God; that he denied the Trinity according to Sabellius; and that he abolished all the prophecies made concerning Christ.

We judge these things sufficient for those who wish to know the truth with faithful and pious intent. But for the sake of argument we shall say more, since what is sufficient for belief is not sufficient for contention.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0607]

## CHAPTER ONE

That they ought not to follow Cyril if it is conceded that he at some time censured Theodorus, since they do not follow him in what he wrote against Chrysostom.

So that our opponents may know how powerful truth is—truth which no one can unwillingly evade when it pursues him—let us concede that Bishop Theodorus of Mopsuestia was censured by blessed Cyril in certain chapters of his writings. If he had been merely censured by them as well, and not condemned under an anathema, could they by Cyril’s example evade the conviction of truth?

For when Cyril himself defined that, since the person who is to be subjected to blame is not clearly present, the refutation of the chapters is uncertain, and that it is grievous to insult the dead—even if they were laymen, much more those who ended this life in the episcopate—because it appears most just to prudent men to yield to him who knows beforehand the will of each person and knows what each of us will be, how would they think that they were following Cyril’s judgment if he later said something contrary? No one can follow things running in opposite directions, and each person vainly trusts that he can be cleared by that judge or witness who, in one and the same matter—not for one reason and another, but for this very reason—is both defended and censured.

Therefore, even if blessed Cyril had later written something against Theodorus, these men could not rightly be believed to have followed his judgment; rather, they would appear to have sought to prejudice the Council of Chalcedon.

Unless perhaps they answer without any consideration of human feeling that Cyril is to be rejected when he forbids insult—not merely to admirable men deserving the greatest glory, as he himself said, but, what alone is sufficient, to those who died in the peace of the Church—but followed when he considers those same men worthy of accusation.

And if they say this also with shameless obstinacy, what will they say about the fact that they do not follow him in the condemnation of Saint John of Constantinople, the fellow student of that same Theodorus, concerning whom he said such and so much that only the necessity of our case can excuse us for mentioning it?

For, writing in reply to blessed Atticus, bishop of this imperial city, he says:

> “When I read the letter sent by your Reverence, I learned that the name of John had been written in the sacred diptychs” [Note: [Col. 0607D] John Chrysostom’s name was first entered into the sacred registers by Alexander of Antioch, who wrote to the emperor and all the bishops of the Churches so that the others might do the same. Atticus eventually entered it at Constantinople as well, and encouraged Cyril by letter, although Cyril strongly resisted ordering that it be entered in Egypt; but in vain, as this letter of his to Atticus shows. Cyril later yielded, partly through the persuasion of Isidore of Pelusium and partly, as they say, after being warned by a divine vision, and, after convening a synod, added John’s name to the diptychs, as Nicephorus relates from the philosopher Nicetas. In Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 14, chapters 26 and 27, the mutual letters of Atticus and Cyril are also found.] [Note: [Col. 0608D] Cyril’s Greek has ἐν ταῖς ἱεραῖς δέλτοις, “in the sacred tablets.” Atticus had also called them μυστικὰς δέλτους, “mystical tablets”; and Nicephorus, speaking of Alexander of Antioch (ch. 25), says ἐκκλησιαστικὰ δίθυρα, “ecclesiastical diptychs”: Πρῶτος τὴν Ἰωάννου προσηγορίαν τοῖς ἐκκλησιαστικοῖς διθύροις ἐνέταττε, “He was the first to enter the name of John in the ecclesiastical diptychs.” Cyril later used κατάλογον τῶν ἐπισκόπων, “the list of bishops,” because the names of bishops were inscribed in the diptychs.].

> “But, questioning those who came from there, I learned that he was listed not in the order of the laity but among the bishops. Foreseeing this and considering it within myself, I asked whether those who had done this were conforming to the rules of the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea. Extending the eye of my mind a little toward that great assembly of those same holy Fathers, I see the whole assembly, as though with certain eyes, rejecting this and prohibiting us with all its strength from joining in such an agreement.
>
> “How, then, can he be counted among the priests of God and be clothed with the lot of those from whom he was expelled? Or how can he be in the order of bishops who was excluded from the walls of the Church?”

Later in the same letter he says:

> “Command that John’s name be removed from the list of bishops. For if we think this means nothing, let the choir of the apostles not be troubled by having a betrayer counted among them. But once Judas has been introduced, where is Matthias placed?
>
> “If, therefore, no one, excluding Matthias, writes Judas into the choir of the apostles, I ask that the second rank of blessed Arsacius remain and be preserved after Nectarius of blessed memory, lest the name introduced by force exclude the memory of the blessed man.”

Further below he says:

> “Therefore let the expelled Jeconiah not be counted with David, Samuel, and the prophets; nor, because it happened to please foolishly, let us on that account introduce, as though it were both profane and holy, the corpse of Eudoxius into the holy places” [Note: [Col. 0609D] Eudoxius, the Arian bishop of Constantinople. Atticus had written that his remains were buried in the church of the Apostles: “For neither did the honorable burial of Saul harm David, nor did Eudoxius, the follower of Arius’s impiety, lying beneath the very altar, harm the apostles.” Cyril rightly disapproves this as having been done unjustly (ἀδίκως) and contrary to the canons.].

These are the most bitter words of blessed Cyril—words abhorrent to Christian minds—which Cyril, forgetful of himself, poured forth against the sweetest father of the Church, sweeter than Attic honey. We repeat them with sorrow because certain people have wished to resurrect causes already buried with their authors and to bring them back into disputes, to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon.

For who would not shudder to recall that Cyril does not hesitate to call John—and, what is more cruel, John already dead, God forbid—Judas, Jeconiah, and profane, and, comparing him with Eudoxius, the Arian bishop of this city, says that he was excluded from the walls of the Church?

John, for the sake of preserving the unity of the Church which he loved, preferred to bear the loss of his own case. For if he had wished to assert it, since his life was exemplary and his eloquence extraordinary, and since he enjoyed great favor among the Christian people, who esteemed him for his exceptional merits, and since he also had the defense of the Apostolic See, without whose judgment he had been condemned, he could easily have obtained victory—a victory which pursued him even after his death.

But fearing that, once acquitted by the judgment of others, he might not be received by some because of the obstinacy of his opponents, and that the Church might thereby be divided, with some communicating with him and others rejecting his communion, he most wisely and with extraordinary piety chose to relinquish the chair of his episcopate, which he knew he had received for the Church’s benefit, rather than allow Christ’s one inheritance to be divided through his defense.

But woe to the world because of scandals, through which John, for such merits, is called Judas, Jeconiah, and profane, and is compared with the Arian bishop Eudoxius.

What, moreover, is the meaning of the charge that blessed Atticus was censured for having listed the name of his predecessor John not among the laity but among the bishops, as though he had acted contrary to the rules of the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea? It is asserted on this basis that he ought to have entered John among the laity, because one who had been excluded from the walls of the Church could not be retained in the order of bishops; nor could the name of Judas the betrayer be introduced into the choir of the apostles, or Jeconiah be counted with David, Samuel, and the prophets.

As though, if John had been excluded from the walls of the Church, and Judas and Jeconiah were to be retained, it would accord with the rules of those Fathers for him to be listed in the order of the laity!

Since it is not denied that John ought for the time being to have been listed in the sacred diptychs in some order, even the testimony of his own accuser sufficiently proves that he ought neither to have been excluded from the walls of the Church nor called Judas, Jeconiah, or profane.

But since these excessive lovers of Cyril, and followers of Cyril beyond all measure, do not follow his example in the case of John of Constantinople, how can they be thought to have followed Cyril in the case of his fellow student Theodorus?

You understand, therefore, Emperor, that the disturbers of the Church are vainly attempting to obscure by the example of blessed Cyril their most evident connivance, which they extend to the Eutychians against the holy council.

For while Cyril calls John profane and excluded from the walls of the Church, they regard him as he ought to be regarded: an admirable man deserving the greatest glory. But although Cyril likewise calls Theodorus an admirable man deserving the greatest glory, they wish to regard him as profane and excluded from the walls of the Church.

## CHAPTER TWO

That they ought not to follow Cyril in the condemnation of Theodorus, since they rightly do not follow him in the condemnation of Diodorus, whom the Fathers and orthodox leaders commend, while only the heretical Apollinarists, together with Julian the Apostate, censure him.

What more is there, since, as we have already mentioned, they say that Theodore was so reproved by the same Cyril that they also claim that the holy Diodore, Theodore’s teacher, was likewise censured by him and in the same matter? If, then, they followed Cyril’s authority in condemning Theodore [Note: [Col. 0609D] Codex Veronensis: “they would condemn.”], although they do not dare to say that he anathematized Theodore—indeed, he forbade the anathematizing of Theodore’s writings—why nevertheless did they not also condemn Diodore? Was it because he was not praised at the Council of Chalcedon, and therefore they did not judge him worthy of condemnation, whereas they condemned Theodoret because he is found to have been praised both in the letter of Ibas, which the council declared orthodox, and in the decrees of the Eastern synod, which that same Council of Chalcedon approved, so that by this condemnation they might trample upon the council’s authority? Precisely so; no prudent person can deny it. For they ought first, and all the more, to have condemned his teacher Diodore, as the author of their common error.

Yet I shall not omit to set forth, whatever its worth, the argument that may appear to suit their defense. Perhaps they will say: “If someone does not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia and his doctrines”—by the addition they made, they will be understood to have intended the holy Diodore, and those who either held or hold views similar to his. But why, I ask, if they followed the authority [Note: [Col. 0611D] Codex Veronensis: “the authority; just as they followed the acts,” and so forth.] of blessed Cyril, was Diodore, his teacher, not named first and before him [Note: [Col. 0611D] In the same codex, the word *non* (“not”) is absent.] so that at least the decree might have read: “If anyone does not anathematize Diodore and his doctrines, let him be anathema, as one who is said to have wickedly imbued Theodore with them”; and then it could have continued, “and those who either held or hold views similar to his”? But now the accusation is openly and manifestly directed against Theodore, his disciple; Diodore is not counted among the condemned—or, if he too is implicitly understood to be rejected, this is not said.

Moreover, blessed Cyril is said to have written something in accusation of the holy Diodore in such a way that nothing is said to have been written in his defense; but in accusation of Theodore he is said to have written in such a way that he is shown also to have written in his defense. It is therefore clear, if we are willing to see it [Note: [Col. 0612D] The same codex: “if we are willing to see it, or rather, if we are willing to say openly that …”], that for this reason—because Diodore was not named—they condemned Theodore with his doctrines, and those who do not anathematize him: he had been praised both in the letter of the venerable Ibas, which the synod declared orthodox, and in the letters of the Eastern Fathers, to which it granted preeminent authority.

Otherwise, if the error alleged against both men is considered, it is said to have been Diodore’s no less than Theodore’s. If the persons of teacher and disciple are considered, either both, or at least the originator of the error, ought to have been named and condemned first. If the authority of blessed Cyril is considered, Diodore is plainly and unambiguously the one to be censured; for he is said to have attacked him in such a way that no other statement of Cyril’s in his defense can be found. Why, then, so much against Theodore and nothing against Diodore? Who, paying even a little thoughtful attention to this, would not immediately understand the deceptions of the heretical faction: in the common case only Theodore was named, although, if not both [Note: [Col. 0612D] The same codex: “or certainly one rather than the other.”], but one of them had to be named, Diodore ought rather to have been named?

Therefore it is useless to deny what is plain to everyone—indeed, clearer than light—or, if we do not wish to say so, what is manifest: in order that these things might be carried out against Theodore, it was not the Church that needed to pass judgment upon a dead man, but rather the heretics who wished to prejudice the Council of Chalcedon.

If they say that they did not dare to condemn blessed Diodore for this reason [Col. 0612A]—because, as we shall also show below, he possessed the finest and greatest testimony from Saint Athanasius; from Peter and Timothy, bishops of Alexandria; from Basil of Caesarea; from John of Constantinople; from Epiphanius of Cyprus; from the Egyptian bishops who had been sent into exile by the emperor Valens; and from the council of one hundred and fifty priests who had assembled with Diodore in this city against Macedonius, and that Cyril ought not to have been preferred to so many and such men—I shall for the moment leave unanswered the fact that, even in Theodore’s case, Cyril alone ought not to have been preferred to such Fathers, by whose testimony Theodoret too is commended.

For the present I hold only this: they themselves show, as justice dictates, that they abandoned the judgment of blessed Cyril. Let us therefore begin to review the testimonies of the venerable Fathers mentioned above, by whom Diodore is commended—Diodore whom they say was censured by Cyril together with Theodoret and in the same matter, as though he taught what Nestorius taught. Since Theodore could not justly have been condemned without his teacher, with whom he is said to have shared the same case, once we have proved that Diodore ought not to be condemned, it will become much more evident to everyone that Theodoret was unjustly condemned solely as a prejudice against the Council of Chalcedon.

Blessed Athanasius therefore writes to the aforementioned holy Diodore:

> “To my lord son and most beloved fellow priest, Diodore, bishop of Tarsus: Athanasius sends greetings in the Lord. I give thanks to my Lord, who establishes his teaching wherever he lays its foundations, and especially through his own sons, as the fact itself demonstrates in your case. Even before your Reverence wrote, we learned how great a grace had been wrought at Tyre through your perseverance; and we rejoice with you, because through you Tyre too came to know the right word of piety. For my part, dearest and most beloved, I took the opportunity to write to you. But I was surprised that, when I wrote, you did not write back. So do not be slow to write continually, knowing that, as a son, you make me, your father, rest, and, as a herald of truth, you make me exceedingly glad. Do not contend with the heretics, but overcome their verbosity by silence and their malice by gentleness. Thus your word, seasoned with salt, will possess grace; while they will be condemned in the conscience of everyone.”

What does your justice decree here, most serene emperor? Do you judge it equitable that this herald of truth, Diodore—whom the learned and good Athanasius, a man free from spite and envy, so greatly rejoices over because Tyre too came to know the right word of piety through his perseverance, and whom he even urges to write continually, saying that Diodore makes him rest in him as a father in a son—should be condemned as a heretic, when he too is said to have been censured by Cyril? It is exceedingly harsh for us to believe this of your fairness. Indeed, the presumptuous men themselves saw that it was unjust.

But if the teacher Diodore cannot justly be condemned as a heretic—against whom Cyril is said to have inveighed in such a way that no other statement of Cyril’s in his defense can be found—how could his disciple Theodore, who is said to have been accused in the same case, have been condemned as a heretic, except as a prejudice against the Council of Chalcedon, when another statement of Cyril’s in Theodoret’s defense is in fact found?

Peter too, the successor of that same holy Athanasius, writing to bishops, presbyters, and deacons who were in exile for the true faith, says:

> “The love with which I rejoice in Christ over you did not permit me to endure patiently; rather, even while writing, I am as though I were not writing, and again I am compelled to write.”

And below:

> “I therefore use you as counselors in the matters that arise; and what ought I to do, being so continually troubled? Timothy, who, while spreading the report that he himself is a bishop, may thus more confidently inflict injury and violate the laws of the Fathers? For he wished to anathematize me, Basil of Caesarea, Paulinus, Epiphanius, and Diodore, the bishops, and to communicate with Vitalis alone.”

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Timothy, a disciple of Apollinaris, whose mention will occur in Book VII, chapter 3. Pope Damasus, in his letter to the Easterners, writes of him: “Why is it that you again demand from me the deposition of Timothy, who was also deposed here by the judgment of the Apostolic See, with Peter, bishop of Alexandria, present, together with his teacher Apollinaris?” And in the letter of the Easterners to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, in the acts of the Council of Ephesus: “The thrice-blessed Damasus deposed Apollinaris, Vitalis, and Timothy, the heretics.” He is also cited in Anastasius’s *Eclogue*: “The impious Polemon, a disciple of Apollinaris, against Timothy, his fellow disciple.”]

Here too Peter, the successor of Athanasius, judges it equally wicked to anathematize Basil of Caesarea, Paulinus of Antioch, Epiphanius, and Diodore, as the most powerful defenders of the truth, and to communicate instead with Vitalis of Antioch, whom Apollinaris had ordained. We have therefore learned, from Peter’s judgment, that this Diodore shared the same doctrine as Basil, Paulinus, and Epiphanius. Who, then, even if Diodore is believed—according to the report—to have been censured by Cyril together with Theodore, would judge that he ought to be condemned on account of Cyril’s opinion? Or who would judge that Theodore was condemned without Diodore, with whom he is said, as a disciple, to have been censured by Cyril, on account of Cyril’s opinion and not as a prejudice against the synod?

Timothy too, Peter’s successor, who had been present with the same Diodore at the council assembled in this royal city against Macedonius, writes to him as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0613D] Codex Veronensis: “blessed Diodore.”]

> “To my lord, honorable in all things, most holy bishop and fellow priest, Diodore: Timothy sends greetings in Christ. I could never adequately proclaim your virtue, the perfection of your life, and your zeal for your right and apostolic faith, however hastily I might proceed; for words do not equal realities. You have certainly been granted not only to believe in Christ Jesus but also to suffer for him. Our divine father Athanasius long ago bore witness to your Reverence that this right and blessed disposition of yours toward God, and your unwavering conscience regarding the mystery of piety, were present in you; and he led us, his disciples, to love your perfection and to pray God that your life might be preserved through many cycles of years, for the benefit of the Churches of Christ.”

You see, as I think, most merciful emperor—for the matter is entirely clear—what virtue, perfection, and zeal for the right and apostolic faith Diodore always possessed, whom they report to have been censured by blessed Cyril together with Theodore, and how his glory increased along with his age. As a young man he is praised by Athanasius; as an older man he is praised by Peter; as an old man he is praised by Timothy. His entire life was spent in praise, and after his death he is said to have been accused together with Theodoret by the successor of Athanasius, Peter, and Timothy. Who could bear this calmly? Who could hear it patiently?

But let us turn away from such matters to attend rather to better ones. I am pleased to repeat the words of this holy man Timothy, who, having inherited both Athanasius’s virtue and his see, said to Diodore: “You have certainly been granted not only to believe in Christ Jesus but also to suffer for him.” He added:

> “Our divine father Athanasius long ago bore witness to our piety [Note: [Col. 0614D] The same codex: “to your piety.”] that this right and blessed disposition of yours toward God, and your unwavering conscience regarding the mystery of piety, were present in you; and he led us, his disciples, to love your perfection.”

In this he proved himself a worthy successor of Athanasius: without attacking Athanasius’s testimony, he was led by him to love Diodore’s perfection—Diodore whom Athanasius himself loved—and to pray God that his life might be preserved through many cycles of years for the benefit of the Churches of Christ.

But passing over the bishops of other cities, we must also consider what testimony holy Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia gave to Diodore. Writing to Patrophilus, bishop of the Church of Aegae [Note: [Col. 0614D] In Basil’s Letter 92, the text is corruptly read as “to Patrophilus, bishop of the Church in Agai” instead of “in Aegae.” Pliny too calls it Aegae in Book V, chapter 27. It was a city of Cilicia Secunda. The letter that follows is Basil’s Letter 167, written to Diodore while he was still a presbyter at Antioch.], he says:

> “We received Diodore from the beginning as the nourishment of blessed Silvanus; now we love and praise him because of the grace of the Word that is present in him, through which many of those who come to him are made better.”

Writing to Diodore himself, he says:

> “I read the books sent by your Honor, and I read them a second time with great care, not only because of their brevity—for I am in every respect a weak reader—but also because the argument varies, and contrary oppositions and responses to them are readily discerned. The style is simple and without any rhetorical flourish. This seemed to me fitting for the style of a Christian who writes not for display but for the benefit of human beings.”

And below:

> “For I am certain that you, who possess so great a zeal for writing, will write other works also. For you do not lack occasions for writing; while it is pleasant and dear to us to read your writings.”

And shortly afterward:

> “I have now sent through the chief reader a larger codex, having first read through it as far as I was able. I kept the smaller one, wishing to have it copied, but at present I have no swift copyist available; for the envious people of Cappadocia have been reduced to such poverty.”

Although this Diodore is said to have been censured together with Theodore—or rather, even before Theodore, as his teacher—nevertheless, since the holy and learned Basil so loved and praised him, and since he honored him on account of the grace of God through which many who came to him were made better, and since reading his writings was so pleasant and dear to him that he even had them copied for his own reading, the supporters of the heretics do not dare to condemn Diodore with his doctrines. Still less, for the reasons recalled above, would they dare to condemn Theodore with his doctrines, except as a prejudice against the Council of Chalcedon.

Let us now turn also to that golden mouth, John of Constantinople, whom Domnus, bishop of Antioch, as we shall show below, testifies to have been Diodore’s disciple. In John, above all, the teaching of so great a teacher gave evidence of its own integrity and virtue, and his fertile breast responded with the richer abundance of the sower’s hope. Let us observe with what praises he himself also extolled Diodore.

For in a certain sermon he spoke of him as follows:

> “This wise and most courageous teacher, having recently ascended this chair after exposing his bodily weakness, made me the beginning of his discourse, calling me John the Baptist, the voice of the Church, the rod of Moses, and saying many other such things about me. He praised me, and you applauded. But I, sitting far away, sighed most bitterly.”

And after a little:

> “Emperors too sometimes do this: removing a diadem suited to themselves, they place it on the heads of their sons. Then, when they see that the child’s head is smaller than the crown, they wish merely to place it upon him, even though it is unsuitable, satisfying their own inclination by that act alone; afterward they remove it and place it upon themselves. Since, then, this father has placed upon us a crown suited and fitting for himself, and since it has appeared greater than our head, let us remove it from our head and place it upon the head of this father, where it is fitting. Among us there is the name of John, but the meaning is found in him; we receive the title, but he possesses the philosophy.
