Therefore, in justice, he ought rather to be the heir of the title itself than we. For synonymy is ordinarily produced not by a community of names but by a kinship of realities, even when the names differ.”

And below:

> “Since, therefore, this is unquestionably the rule and complete definition of synonyms according to divine Scripture, come, let us show how this wise father of ours imitated John’s way of life, so that you may recognize that he also ought rightly to possess John’s title. John had neither table, nor bed, nor house upon the earth; and neither did this man ever have them. We ourselves are witnesses of this: how he lived out his whole time, demonstrating an apostolic life, possessing nothing of his own but always being nourished by his companions. He remained in prayer and the teaching of the Word and preached. John preached beyond the river in the wilderness; and this man too, at times teaching the whole city beyond the river, proclaimed saving doctrine. John lived in confinement and lost his head because of the boldness he displayed for the law; and this man too was often deprived of his homeland because of the boldness he showed for the faith. He was often deprived of his head for the same reason—not in reality, but in intention. For the enemies of truth could not endure the power of his tongue; they continually laid ten thousand snares, and the Lord delivered him from them all.

> “Come, then, let us now hear his tongue—the very tongue because of which he both suffered danger and was saved. Of that tongue, if someone were to say what Moses said of the land of promise, he would not at all be mistaken. What did he say of it? ‘A land flowing with milk and honey.’ The same must be said of this man’s tongue: a tongue flowing with milk and honey.

> “Therefore, so that we may be filled with milk and honey, let this discourse of ours now be silent, and let us listen to the lyre and the trumpet. When I perceive the sweetness of his words, I call his voice a lyre; but when I perceive the strength of his ideas, I call it a certain warlike trumpet, such as the Jews possessed when they destroyed the walls of Jericho. For just as then the sound of the trumpets, rushing upon the stones faster than fire, consumed everything, so his voice, rushing no less than that trumpet upon the schemes of the heretics, overturned their arguments—that is, every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God. But lest we say these things through our own tongue rather than through his, let our discourse here fall silent, giving glory to God, who has granted us such teachers.”

I consider it superfluous to commend, in my words—far inferior to those of the most eloquent John—the outstanding praise he bestowed upon Diodore, by which he commended to us both his teaching and his life, even though John’s beauty has been somewhat diminished by the necessity of translation, or by the ability of the translator. Let it be enough for us to consider this alone: comparing Diodore with John the Baptist in manner of life and martyrdom, John transferred both his own name and his crown to Diodore.

Again, in another sermon, he said of his teacher Diodore:

> “We do not, as it appears, spend our lengthy discourses without purpose. Rather, in celebrating the martyrs, we are reminded of a living martyr, close to martyrdom, a river of spiritual life. For this man is a living martyr; indeed, he is a martyr because he has often died in intention. Look at his mortified members; look at the form he bears, which is human, while his understanding is angelic.”

And after a little:

> “But let us return again to this martyr, on whose account we have said these things. How did he die, mortifying his members and trampling the desires of nature in a human body, and demonstrating to us an angelic life? If you wish to see that he also died in reality, remember the time when a harsh war rose up against the Church, armies were set in motion, and weapons were prepared, when everyone was gathering beyond the river. Then he came forth, standing before the others like a tower set in their path, or like some great and lofty cliff; receiving and breaking the waves of the opposition, he preserved the rest of the body of the Church in tranquility, beating back the storm and providing us with a calm harbor.”

Do you therefore judge it just, pious prince, that this living martyr—indeed, a martyr many times over, a continual martyr through the mortification of his members, bearing only the outward form of a human being while demonstrating an angelic life—whom John his disciple also describes as a tower standing in battle against the enemies of the faith, and as a massive cliff against which the waves of opposition were shattered, should receive such a recompense for his labors and struggles from the Church of Christ, namely, to be excluded from it as a heretic? I do not think so.

And yet, as a prejudice against the Council of Chalcedon, Theodore is alleged to have been excluded for this reason: that Cyril judged him to have been Diodore’s follower.

There are still many statements of great John concerning the same holy Diodore, which we omit because we are hastening to other matters.

We know also that Epiphanius of Cyprus, a very learned man, wrote books on heresies in which he carefully explained both their authors and their causes. He not only failed entirely to identify Diodore as the author of any heresy, but in his letters he honored him so greatly that he declared him to be a son, disciple, and successor of Elijah and the other prophets, and said that he had received from the Lord a grace akin to theirs.

It therefore seems appropriate to demonstrate this, as we have done in other cases, from the tenor of his own letter:

> “To my honorable brother and fellow priest, Diodore, beloved bishop: Epiphanius sends greetings in the Lord. The Lord, though bestowing greater grace than he received, asked the Samaritan woman for water to drink. He himself was the existing fountain, yet he sat beside the well and was found weary from the journey, so that in the present discourse he might not exceed the truth of the incarnation.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But his disciples and servants too, from whom others asked something, gave them more than they received from them. Elijah, who was properly a figure of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0617D] Codex Veronensis: “a figure of his own”], asked for the measure of necessities to the extent required; yet he filled abundantly with blessing the woman who provided for him, asking bread from the widow but, through the occasion of his request, bestowing an abundance of blessing. So too your Honor, by asking for what our poverty can provide, gives more than you take.

> “Your petition to God supplies inexhaustible abundance from little to our small container, and from the very least it bestows upon our jar an inexhaustible fullness. At the beginning of your letter, honorable sir, you ask about the stones arranged and set into the breastpiece of the priest’s rational, upon Aaron’s chest; about their names, colors, kinds, and locations; about the contemplations of those stones that lead toward piety; about which tribe each stone was assigned to; about where it was found and from what homeland.

> “As I said, the discovery of these matters was altogether difficult for us, as it was for that widow because of her poverty. But just as a miracle came to her through blessing, and the mystery of the Lord was revealed to the Samaritan woman in place of material water [Note: [Col. 0617D] The same codex: “the gift of mysteries”], so for us, though we are small, abundance has arisen on every side through a new understanding, a new knowledge, and a new reasoning, as though from a great outpouring of rains through the prayer of Elijah and the other prophets. You are their son, disciple, and successor, honorable sir, receiving from the Lord this grace akin to theirs and granting it to us through prayer.”

It would be no small indication, most merciful emperor—even if the testimonies of the other Fathers were lacking—that Diodore was the author of no heresy: Epiphanius, a most discerning man, deservedly renowned for his teaching of the Catholic faith, did not mention him among the founders of heresies, although he did not omit even those who, before the Lord’s coming, introduced new teachings.

Since Epiphanius possessed such diligence and knowledge that he did not remain silent even about the ancients who taught new doctrines in the time of the Jews, how could he have passed over Diodore, the teacher of Theodore, if Diodore had been the inventor of the new doctrine followed by Nestorius?

In addition to these things, we add the great testimony to holy Diodore given by the Egyptian bishops who were exiled at Diocaesarea [Note: [Col. 0617D] Peter of Alexandria states in his circular letter that eleven Egyptian bishops were driven into exile under Valens, at the instigation of the Arians and through the agency of Magnus, count of the sacred largesses, and were ordered to reside in the Palestinian town of Diocaesarea. Theodoret quotes part of this letter in Book IV, chapter 20 of his *History*.] under the emperor Valens.

For when the monks settled in Nitria wrote against Apollinaris, they said after a little:

[Note: [Col. 0618D] The same codex: “to the monks settled in Nitria.” For it was to these monks that the Egyptian bishops exiled at Diocaesarea under Valens were writing.]

> “The remarkable Apollinaris, receiving such letters in our name, and also receiving his own letter in the name of Adelphus and Isidore according to his wish, despised us to such an extent that afterward he dared in his own letters to accuse the irreproachable and most religious archbishop of Antioch, Paulinus, who had always been in communion with our thrice-blessed father Athanasius and with all the orthodox bishops in the West.

> “When we were disturbed by the receipt of such letters and suspected the accused of either heresy or schism, we often wished to write back to him. But while these things were taking place, by God’s providence his dispositions and definitions concerning the faith were made known and sent to us, agreeing with what many who had previously come to us had told us about Apollinaris himself: that he did not hold a right view concerning the incarnation of the Savior.

> “To these were added other letters in which he accused the venerable archbishop of Cyprus, Epiphanius, an orthodox man who had always been in communion with our most blessed father Athanasius. He also rejected the most holy man of Tarsus, who was likewise in communion with our blessed father Athanasius, and our own fellow bishop Diodore [Note: [Col. 0619D] Codex Veronensis: “our co-bishop.”], in his own letters, as unjustly as he could, unless he had withdrawn from communion with the aforementioned orthodox bishops, Paulinus and Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0619D] The same codex: “adjudged” rather than “rejected.”].”

After considering what these confessors say, we must acknowledge that Diodore ought not to be condemned: we see that he was adjudged by such men and for such a cause. For it is not fitting that we be found partners of the heresiarch Apollinaris, or opposed to the irreproachable and most religious Paulinus of Antioch and the venerable bishop Epiphanius of Cyprus, so that we should refuse communion with Diodore’s memory as though he were a heretic—one who was condemned by a heretic precisely because he had not withdrawn from communion with the aforementioned orthodox men.

To this we may add the authority of the council of one hundred and fifty bishops assembled in this royal city against Macedonius, among whom was this holy Diodore. Add also that he died full of days, with great glory, in the peace of the Church. It will surely appear exceedingly bold to anathematize as a heretic, against the authority of all these men, so great and eminent a teacher of the Church on account of Cyril’s complaints. It must be believed that those who judge the dead also took this into consideration.

But since, on account of the same complaints—or, if the claim is true, only after the teacher Diodore had first been excluded—the disciple can be excluded, how can anyone believe that Theodoret alone was excluded by these men for any reason other than the overthrow of the Council of Chalcedon?

Our Jerome too, a very learned man, whose reading was so extensive that he read all or nearly all the commentators on the divine Scriptures, whether in Greek or Latin eloquence, wrote a book entitled *On Illustrious Men*. In it he mentioned not only Catholics but also heretics who had written something from the holy Scriptures in either language. He did not omit to state who had been founders of heresies, who their defenders, or who had been accused of heresy by some while others defended them.

Yet he did not report that the holy Diodore had even come under suspicion of heresy. Concerning him he says:

> “Diodore, bishop of Tarsus, became especially distinguished while he was a presbyter at Antioch. His commentaries on the Apostle and many other works are extant, belonging more to the character of Eusebius; although he followed Eusebius’s sense, he could not imitate his eloquence because of his ignorance of secular literature.”

This statement of blessed Jerome, in which he reports that Diodore was inferior in eloquence, agrees with the words of blessed Basil that we have recalled. Writing to Diodore about the book he had sent him, Basil said:

> “The argument varies, and contrary oppositions and responses to them are readily discerned; the style is simple and without any rhetorical flourish. This seemed to me fitting for the style of a Christian who writes not for display but for the benefit of human beings.”

We already had abundant material in what has been said to demonstrate our proposition. But since we ought not to detract either from the glory of blessed Diodore himself or from the investigation of the case [Note: [Col. 0619D] The same codex: “conviction of the case.”], we do not think we should omit how your religious predecessors, the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and the elder Theodosius, bore witness to him.

When they wrote to Auxonius, proconsul of Asia, concerning the restoration of the churches, they said after a little:

> “Let those alone possess the churches who are in communion with Nectarius [Note: [Col. 0620D] The same codex: “the bishop of Constantinople.”], bishop of Constantinople; Timothy, bishop of Alexandria; Pelagius of Laodicea in the East; Diodore of Tarsus; the whole council established under the vicar of Asia; Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium; and Optimus of Antioch. In the Pontic council, let them be in communion with Helladius, bishop of Caesarea; Otreius, bishop of Melitene; Gregory of Nyssa; Terentius of Scythia [Note: [Col. 0619D] In the *Theodosian Code*, Book 3, *On the Catholic Faith*, where this rescript is found, the name is incorrectly printed as “Terennio.” In the commonly circulated copies of the Constantinopolitan synod, he is called “Gerontius”; but in the Anician codex it is correctly “Terentius,” as here. He was bishop of Tomi in Scythia. Shortly afterward, Martyrius of Marcianopolis in Moesia is again mentioned as bishop, not “Marmarius,” as in the *Theodosian Code*. All copies of the Constantinopolitan synod likewise call him “Martyrius,” and he subscribed to that synod.]; and Martyrius of Marcianopolis [Note: [Col. 0620D] The same codex: “Marcianopolitanus.” Martyrius of Marcianopolis in Moesia subscribed to the Constantinopolitan synod in the year 381, under Theodosius the Great.].

> “But those who do not honor the same faith shall be excluded from the churches as heretics and shall never thereafter return to them.”

For after this law, the religion of all Christians ought to have been purified in every respect.

Since these religious emperors therefore established it as a certain indication that anyone who did not communicate with blessed Diodore—holding the same views as Theodore—was to be regarded as a heretic, by what reasoning has it now been decreed that anyone who does not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia, his doctrines, and those who either held or hold views similar to his, is to be regarded as a heretic?

But because Diodore, the greatest preacher of truth, had learned, according to the Apostle’s teaching, to wage war in the strength of God with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, attend, I ask you, most merciful emperor, to how he always ran with a strong and courageous purpose through glory and disgrace, through ill repute and good repute. For just as he was always approved by the teachers of the Church and accused by the heretics, so too he is always found praised by religious emperors and censured by the impious.

Julian, the emperor faithless to Christ, writes thus to Photinus the heresiarch against Diodore:

> “You, Photinus, seem plausible and almost on the point of saving [Note: [Col. 0621D] The impious apostate evidently considered it absurd that God should become man. Cyril, however, refuting Julian in Book VI, teaches that it was the work of divine counsel and wisdom that, when Christ assumed human nature, he despised in that nature all human pomp and glory. Human beings judge things one way, God another. Cyril says: ‘You seem wise, noble sir, and whatever is considered important among us, you perhaps suppose that God also regards as greatly important. But you have entirely failed to understand what lies between them, what is elevated by divine glory, and what is petty in our human thought,’ and so forth. The Greek is: “You seem wise, noble sir, and whatever is considered important among us, you perhaps suppose that God also regards as greatly important. But you have entirely failed to understand what lies between them, what is elevated by divine glory, and what is petty in our human thought,” and so forth.], doing good by no means to bring into the womb the one whom you believed to be God. But Diodore, the magician of the Nazarenes, sharpening irrationality with his pigments and enchantments, has appeared as a sharp-witted sophist of a rustic religion.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But if the gods and goddesses, all the Muses, and Fortune come to our aid, we shall show him to be weak and a corrupter of the laws, arguments, and mysteries of the pagans and of the gods below, as well as of that new Galilean god of his, whom he foolishly proclaims eternal, exposed to an unworthy death and burial, stripped of fabricated [text incomplete].”

“of Diodorus’ deity.” As those convicted of error are accustomed to pretend that they are defeated by craft rather than by truth [Note: [Col. 0621D] The Verona manuscript has “truth.”], he continues:

“For this man, sailing to Athens for the detriment of the common good and philosophizing recklessly, having taken part in the discipline of music, armed his hateful tongue with the compositions of a rhetorician against the heavenly gods—so utterly ignorant of the mysteries of the pagans, and, as they say, miserably imbibing the whole error of his degenerate and unlearned [Col. 0621C] theologians, the fishermen. For this reason he has long been punished by those same gods. For having been afflicted for many years and fallen into corruption of the chest, he has reached the ultimate punishment. His whole body has been consumed: for his cheeks have collapsed, while the wrinkles have descended deeply into his body. This is not an indication of philosophical conduct, as he wishes it to appear to those deceived by him, but assuredly of justice and of the punishment of the gods, by which he is struck according to fitting reason, living a harsh and bitter life until the very end of his life, with his face exhausted by pallor.”

From the testimonies of the holy Fathers we have already recognized the bishops among bishops whose judgment we ought to follow in the common case of Diodorus and Theodore: whether that of Athanasius, Peter, Timothy, Basil, John, Epiphanius, and the Egyptian bishops exiled at Diocaesarea for the true faith, and of the Council of Constantinople, as well as of the most learned man Jerome; or that of Apollinaris and his disciples, who, even if they had been Catholics, ought not to have been preferred to such men. [Col. 0622A]

Now, from princes we have recognized the princes whose judgment they ought rather to follow in this same case of Diodorus and Theodore: whether that of Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius the Great, or that of Julian the sacrilegious apostate, who therefore calls Photinus plausible and near to salvation, because he did not, like Diodorus, introduce into the womb the one whom he believed to be God.

Who, moreover, could tolerate Diodorus’s being accused by Julian because he confessed that God had been born of a virgin, and also being accused by Christians as though he had denied this? Or who, on hearing Julian threaten Diodorus because he proclaimed Jesus the Galilean to be the eternal God—a claim he could not deny, since Jesus had died and been buried—and say that he was therefore punished by his own gods [Col. 0622B] with the supreme penalty, because, miserably imbibing the error of the fisherman-theologians, he proclaimed such things: who, I say, would judge that Diodorus too should be rejected by Christians, as one who believed Jesus the Galilean to be merely a man and not also God?

We therefore put this choice before the supporters of the heretics: let them either choose to imitate the venerable Fathers and religious princes, and, together with them, approve Diodorus and Theodore; or, if they prefer to follow Apollinaris and his disciples, and Julian, let them not condemn Diodorus for any other reason than that for which Apollinaris and his disciples, and Julian, believed him deserving of condemnation.

But if they cannot condemn Diodorus because he introduced into the womb Jesus the Nazarene, whom he believed to be God in two natures—calling him eternal, the one who was buried and died—how could they justly condemn Theodore, his disciple? The testimony of both men confirms that their case was the same and their accusation one and the same. Therefore, however late, let them cease calling “Theodorians” those who followed the testimony of so many Fathers, so that they did not dare to condemn Diodorus [Note: [Col. 0622D] The same manuscript has “Theodore.”].

Otherwise, it is the mark of an exceedingly hard and stubborn heart to believe of those who approve neither Diodorus nor, consequently, Theodore, and reject neither of them, that they neither praise them as they were praised by the holy Fathers nor condemn them for the reason for which they were condemned by the sacrilegious.

But behold, most serene emperor, even if we grant them what they wish—that Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, was censured by blessed Cyril—it will appear to no one of even slight understanding that, in condemning him under an anathema, they followed the judgment of that blessed Cyril, since they reject it in the case of Saint John of Constantinople, his fellow disciple and teacher of Diodorus [Note: [Col. 0622D] For in his earlier letter to Succensus, Cyril openly affirms that Diodorus, when he cast off the Macedonian error, fell into another, which was later condemned in Nestorius, his disciple, so that he posited two sons: one born from David’s seed of the holy Virgin, the other the proper Son of God the Father.]; rather, they sought a prejudice against the Church, so that by his condemnation the holy [Col. 0623A] Synod of Chalcedon—which condemned neither him nor his letter praising him—might appear to have been Nestorian.

## CHAPTER III  
That Pope Vigilius, writing while on his journey, disapproved and corrected the condemnation of Ibas and Theodore; and that various provinces protested to Vigilius that he should not tolerate this.

It is remarkable that, after they had carried out the condemnation of these men, they should say that they would consult the Roman Church and await the judgment of Vigilius, its bishop—although, so far as they were concerned, they did not permit him to judge according to his own conviction. For they had first decreed that, if anyone did not anathematize Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, together with his teachings, and the letter of the venerable Ibas, he should be anathema.

But behold: while still coming from his journey, he issued the decision that seemed right to him and ordered the author of this deed to correct his hasty transgression; and he declared that, unless what had been wrongly done were quickly removed, he would also exact punishment. He protested and said, with the Apostle Timothy:

> “Lest perhaps, when I come, I may find you not such as I wish, and I may be found by you such as you do not wish” (2 Cor. 12:20).

For this reason, with the greatest prayers and effort, he asked your Clemency through his legates—as various provinces protested to him while he was coming—that you should not allow what had been done to stand.

[Note: This refers to Menna, patriarch of Constantinople, who first assented to the condemnation of the Three Chapters and for that reason was rebuked by Vigilius in a letter written while Vigilius was on his journey. Vigilius then imposed upon him a four-month excommunication, as Anastasius reports in his Ecclesiastical History, following Theophanes.]

He judged the crime of this deed to be so great that he considered it necessary to rebuke its authors with the testimony of that teacher of the nations who, writing to his disciple Timothy, says:

> “Guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some, professing it, have fallen away from the faith” (1 Tim. 6:20).

What, then, is still in question as to whether the deed we lament was committed against the faith and the Council of Chalcedon, when the man whose judgment they claimed to await had judged that “profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some, professing it, have fallen away from the faith,” were to be rebuked in the authors of this very deed?

Finally, he stated that he had seen on his return in Sicily the blessed Dacius, bishop of Milan, and his other fellow priests, as well as Stephen, the deacon of venerable memory,

[Note: The same events are related in Vigilius’s letter to Menna, part of which Facundus quotes against Mutianus. Stephen had shortly before succeeded Pelagius, also a deacon, who had served for many years as representative of the Apostolic See in Constantinople. Stephen, however, did not hold this office long, for he died before Vigilius arrived.]

who was here his representative for the Roman Church, over which by God’s grace he presides; and through many sons of the Church he established that, on account of this affair, Stephen had suspended himself from communion with Menna, bishop of this imperial city, and had received under due satisfaction those who had communicated with him. He would not have done this unless he, like the others, had judged that what had been done was contrary to the Council of Chalcedon.

He also showed that it was not only the holy and venerable men whom we have mentioned who had judged the matter with him. For he did not conceal that the entire Roman community, as he was departing, and Africa, as he was coming, together with Sardinia—although he had not passed through those regions, they nevertheless addressed him through his representative by a public protest—had done the same, as had the provinces of Greece and Illyricum,

[Note: After this, a synod was also held in Illyricum concerning the same matter. Victor of Tunnuna writes in his Chronicle: “In the eighth year after the consulship of Basil, the Illyrian synod was held in defense of the Three Chapters under the emperor Justinian.” Justinian also issued a rescript against the Illyrian synod, as Isidore testifies in On Illustrious Men, chapter 18.]

through which he had come, so that he should in no way acquiesce in the novelty that had been introduced.

This matter, therefore, must not be regarded as a civil affair, nor as one that ought to be endured for the sake of the peace of the Churches. Rather, it should rightly be judged to have been stirred up against the very condition of the Catholic faith by the stealthy action of heretics. On its behalf, the greater part of the Christian world—as much as could do so—publicly confronted the foremost Christian priest.

Indeed, even before we received the letter of the Roman bishop himself, the Roman community and Africa had already made known to us by no small indication what they thought about the novelty of this deed. For the venerable Pelagius and Anatolius, Roman deacons, faithfully exercising the concern for the Church of God required by their office and position, wrote to Ferrandus, a Carthaginian deacon of praiseworthy memory,

[Note: Victor himself notes that Ferrandus was held in high esteem in the Church of Carthage at this time, in the sixth year after the consulship of Basil. His letter to Anatolius, deacon of the city of Rome, is extant, but concerns a different subject. This letter, however, appears to be mentioned in the catalogue of twelve authors commonly appended to Isidore’s little work On Illustrious Men. Ferrandus, it says, issued a rescript to Pelagius and Anatolius, Roman deacons, who had consulted him about whether anyone might be condemned after death. Among other things, he wrote as follows: “What benefit is there in disturbing the Church for those who sleep? If someone was accused while still in this body of death and condemned before he deserved to be absolved, and was snatched away from the Church, he can no longer be absolved by human judgment. If someone was accused but was overtaken by a sudden summons before the day of the sacred examination, while established within the bosom of Mother Church, he must be understood to have been reserved for divine judgment. No human being can pronounce a manifest sentence concerning this matter. If God has granted him pardon, our severity does no harm; but if God has prepared punishment, our kindness is of no benefit.”]

asking that, after careful consideration of the matter with the most reverend bishop of that same Church of Carthage, or with others whom he knew to possess both zeal for the faith and knowledge of divine Scripture, he should answer their consultation as to what seemed should be observed by everyone in common.

In the very letter of consultation it is not concealed that these things had been set in motion by the Acephali—whom, as we have said, we may more significantly call Semi-Eutychians—against the Council of Chalcedon and the decrees of Pope Leo, through those who, under the name of Catholic, offer their support to that party.

Moreover, the man who had been consulted, replying to those who questioned him, taught that the letter approved by the universal synod ought not to be reconsidered, since, if that were done, not merely its decrees but the statutes of all the councils would be thrown into doubt.

## CHAPTER IV  
That the primates and bishops of the East who themselves consented acknowledged that the condemnation of the Three Chapters had been carried out against the Council of Chalcedon; and that he rebukes them for not resisting the emperor.

It is not unusual for the Apostolic See to rebuke those who rashly violate the judgment of the Fathers as transgressors against the faith, or for men who are themselves undefiled and entirely remote from such presumption to protest publicly against such a deed and declare that, if it were once admitted, not only the definitions of Chalcedon but those of all councils could no longer stand.

What is unusual, what is remarkable, and what displays the great force of truth is that the very men who presumed to do this were compelled by the inward goadings of conscience to confess that these measures had been devised for the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon.

For when Menna, bishop of Constantinople and the first confirmer of their actions, was still hesitating to give them his written consent, as he had been commanded, he protested that the deed was being carried out against the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: This is relevant to what he says in his book against Mutianus: “Recall what we did elsewhere: how Menna of Constantinople, Zoilus of Alexandria, Ephraemius of Antioch, and Peter of Jerusalem, before they either consented or yielded, protested that this ought not to be done.” He discusses these four in order and soon afterward the other bishops as well. For the emperor compelled them all to condemn the Three Chapters, enriching those who assented with gifts and removing from office or punishing those who resisted with exile, as Liberatus records at the end of his Breviary.]

But after he had consented, the aforementioned Stephen, deacon and representative of the Roman Church, of venerable memory, confronted him and asked why he had acquiesced in what he had previously condemned, and concerning which he had promised to do nothing without the Apostolic See, contrary to his former judgment. Menna replied that he had yielded on the condition that he had been sworn to receive back his signed document if the Roman bishop did not approve these measures.

By this he sufficiently showed that he was more concerned about human than divine judgment. But even if he receives back his own signed document because the Roman bishop does not approve it, and nothing of what he fears comes upon him from human judgment, will he for that reason escape the sentence of God, the judge and avenger? No secret oath administered to him by another will ever secure this for him; only his own correction can do so.

We swore once to God, O emperor, when, in the baptismal rite involving the death of his Son, we promised that we would guard the deposit of the faith by which we have been saved. To give or receive an oath against this, therefore, is a great crime of perjury.

For if it is considered exceedingly terrible when human beings enter into an agreement with one another under oath, so that they even have people baptized in the midst of their agreements, what must be thought of the oath by which we have entered into a covenant with God—and we who swore it have been baptized?

But consider, I beg you, the action of this great mystery itself: how, as those who are to be cleansed in the bath of regeneration, we stand in the sight of God and the holy angels, condemning hidden shame, with the Church as witness. Nothing there was covered; nothing was concealed. Finally, having stripped off the body, we received that great sacrament of faith and promised to preserve it. Not only with our voice, but also through the posture of our entire body, we profess that we have put off the old man with his deeds.

Why, then, now resuming the act of the old man which we renounced, do we secretly make some extraordinary compact concerning the faith, with the Church unaware—the very Church that was our witness when we publicly and nakedly swore that we would preserve it in simplicity?

Who, moreover, could despise the authority of these men? Who would hesitate to follow their judgment, seeing that truth is proclaimed by them freely and fearlessly?

[Note: Codex Veronensis: “Truth is proclaimed by those who, under the trust committed to them concerning the faith, make decisions about the matter of faith.”]

Zoilus, too, bishop of the city of Alexandria, when he learned that the Roman bishop was coming, sent someone to meet him in Sicily, complaining that he had been compelled by necessity to affirm that decree. After the Roman bishop arrived, he openly reproached Zoilus to his face for this, while we and others were present.

Likewise Ephraemius of Antioch, when he was first ordered to confirm this by writing in response, refused to consent. But after he was informed that he would be excluded unless he did so, he was found to be a lover of his own honor rather than of the truth.

And what of Peter of Jerusalem? Does not public report relate that, when a multitude of monks had assembled before him, he declared under oath that whoever consented to that novel decree would act against the Council of Chalcedon? Yet he did not refrain from consenting to it.

We recognize that this was contracted, as though by inheritance, from the transgression of that first woman who, after saying that she had been forbidden to eat from the tree that was in the middle of paradise, afterward seized what she herself had declared unlawful and persuaded her husband to eat.

And what shall we say to these things except what the Lord himself said:

> “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

But what shall we say about the bishops of the other cities? When they were compelled to write, they openly protested that this was being done against the great synod. After signing, they gave documents to Stephen, the Roman deacon mentioned above, to be sent to the Apostolic See, confessing in them that they had signed under compulsion from the bishop of Constantinople. If they are sought out by your Piety, they will also be able, in your presence, to bear witness to our assertions.

Therefore, not only those who did these things, but also those who consent by communicating with those who did them, cannot excuse themselves on the ground of ignorance. They pretend in vain; they say in vain that they do not know what happened—whether because they love temporal profits or because, without even receiving payment, they neglect their own souls.

For whom would the mere confession of the transgressors be insufficient for understanding the merit of the case—a confession made publicly both in words and in documents? Their errors are manifest, while they defend their own mistakes with arguments that appear plausible, as though steadfastly. Can this fact be unknown to them, when it has been condemned by the confession of its authors?

To all this must be added the confession of Domitian of Galatia, formerly bishop of Ancyra, whom we have said confessed that his accomplices, the Origenists, contrived these things to disturb the Church.

For in the document that he wrote to Vigilius, complaining about those who opposed the teachings of Origen—who asserted that human souls had pre-existed their bodies in a kind of blessed life, and that all those destined for eternal punishment would be restored to their former blessedness together with the devil and his angels—he also says the following:

> “They rushed forward to anathematize the most holy and glorious teachers, under cover of the doctrines that had been raised concerning pre-existence and restoration, anathematizing, under the appearance of opposing Origen, all the saints who lived before and after him. But those who had proposed to defend this kind of doctrine were in no way willing to carry it through. Abandoning that conflict, they turned instead to attack Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, and began to contrive that he too should be anathematized, in order, as they thought, to abolish what they had established against Origen.”

[Note: Codex Veronensis and the manuscript read “had been established.”]

When these matters have been considered, most merciful emperor, who would not understand that, if the primates of the Churches whose confessions we have recalled had stood firm for the truth, they could easily have obtained from you that what they now complain they did unwillingly should not be done?

Were we really ordained bishops for this alone: to be enriched by the gifts of rulers and sit with them among the greatest powers, as though fortified by the privileges of the divine priesthood? And if, through the deceptions of wicked men—who have never been lacking in any age—something should be slipped past them amid the many concerns of their government that harms the Church of God or disturbs the peace of the Church, are we then not to suggest to them what is true for their own salvation, and, if necessary, resist by the authority of religion, patiently enduring even their displeasure if it should arise?

And where then will be the prophetic saying:

> “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame” (Ps. 118:46)?

Unless, perhaps, shepherds are indeed devoted to milk and wool, but, when it comes to turning aside the wolves’ attacks and guarding the sheepfolds, are deserters.

What, after all, have we suffered, or what did we fear suffering at the hands of a Christian emperor, while contending in defense of the same faith that he holds?

Perhaps someone else might say that, although the spirit was willing, the flesh was weak and could not endure prolonged torture. Everyone’s own weakness of conscience may incline him to grant indulgence to those who yield. For human hearts, on account of the devotion of their faithful beginning, commonly obtain pardon for faint-heartedness if they do not persevere to the end.

But in this matter, what excuse can finally be offered? Especially since your Clemency, mindful even in this affair of the name you bear, has acted harshly toward none—not even toward the heretics who contradicted you.

Therefore, if anyone has suffered anything on this account, the blame must rather be assigned to the envious suggestions of those who concealed their conduct from others and complained that only one person contradicted them.

For as soon as reflection upon this deed became known, did it not offend the hearing of the Christian people, when it was said that one man had wished to do this,

[Note: The same codex reads “had not wished to do this.”]

as though it were the mark of great and singular justice not to condemn so many venerable Fathers

[Note: The same codex reads: “venerable Fathers, although they themselves, as has been said, in order to be without excuse, [acted] against Chalcedon,” etc.]

who had recognized that this was being done against the Council of Chalcedon and had openly detested it?

[Note: The same codex reads “had publicly testified.”]

Yet these men signed the definitions of the book in which it is said:

> “If anyone says that we have said these things in order to abolish or exclude the holy Fathers who were present at the Council of Chalcedon, let him be anathema.”

Thus they made themselves anathema by assenting when they said that these things had been written against the holy Fathers who were present at the Council of Chalcedon, so that, if anyone said this, he would be anathema.

Even if this had not been the case, ought it to be included among the canons and statutes by which divine matters are decided that, if anyone believes something different about the author—whoever he may be or may be called—of that book than the author himself wishes, he should be anathema as a heretic? If such a decree and statement seemed necessary, it ought rather to have been phrased so that anyone who used the statements in that book to abolish or exclude the holy Fathers who were present at the Council of Chalcedon would be anathema.

As matters stand, however, no one is permitted to oppose such statements, while no one is forbidden to use them for the exclusion of the holy synod.

But since, as we had foretold, we have proved that the letter of the venerable Ibas and the writings of Theodoret, as well as Theodore and his doctrines, were condemned to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon, we must now, having completed this volume, demonstrate the second point of our division that we promised.

For it is vain to deny that the same letter was approved by the synod. The Eutychians spread this lie through their supporters in order to mock us.

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER I  
That the Council of Chalcedon truly declared the letter of Ibas orthodox, and that the opponents falsely say that it was not accepted by the council.

Now attend, Augustus, to how this too is demonstrated by clear and manifold evidence—the point that I promised I would demonstrate next: that the supporters of the heretics wished to deceive us by an open lie when they said that the letter of the venerable Ibas had not been accepted by the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: The case of Bishop Ibas and his letter was discussed in Sessions 9 and 10 of the Council of Chalcedon. After the proceedings previously held at Tyre and Berytus in the same case had been reread, Ibas was declared innocent, and the letter, as Facundus says, orthodox. Consistent with this is what Innocentius, bishop of Maronia, writes in the conference held at Constantinople between the orthodox and the Severians: “OBJECTOR: Then Ibas too was justly received by the Council of Chalcedon? BISHOP: By imperial authority the judgment of Ibas and of his accusers was delegated to Photius, bishop of Tyre, Eustachius, bishop of Berytus, and Uranius, bishop of the city of Imeria. These most reverend men, greatly abhorring Nestorius’s blasphemies, examined him with every care and declared him free and without fault, as both their proceedings and report show. How could the council condemn one whom the judges had acquitted?” Yet this shows that the letter was suspect to the council: “When the aforesaid letter was read in the holy Council of Chalcedon, it did not see fit to receive him, because of the suspicions inserted in it, unless he too anathematized Nestorius and all his decrees. After he anathematized them, he was then received into the holy council.” Hence the Fifth General Synod, which in Session 6 plainly condemns the same letter as heretical, maintains that the Council of Chalcedon had no different view of it, setting aside, as it says, what one or two persons had said in its favor by calling it orthodox.]

When the accusations brought against the aforementioned bishop Ibas by the deacon Theophilus, who was his opponent, were read out from the earlier proceedings conducted before the most reverend bishops Photius, Eustachius, and Uranius, the following judgment was given:

> “We have learned from the judgment of the most reverend bishops that Ibas has been shown to be innocent. For, having read his letter, we have learned that he is orthodox; and for this reason we decree both that the honor of the episcopate be restored to him and that the Church from which he was unjustly expelled while absent be restored.”

[Note: These are the words of the legates of the Apostolic See, who pronounced judgment first. The words that follow—“From what was recently read”—belong to Maximus of Antioch. Finally, the words “Previously, from the documents reread,” belong to Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia. Vigilius also cites and examines these same judgments of the bishops in his Constitutum.]

You see how the heretics, through their agents, wished to mock us by claiming that this letter had not been accepted by the council, when it is plainly evident that, from its reading, its author Ibas was judged innocent and orthodox, and for this reason they decreed that both the honor of the episcopate and the Church from which he had been unjustly expelled should be restored to him.

They knew that the piety of the Church could not endure it if the letter that the synod had approved were said to require condemnation—or rather, if the synod itself were condemned because it had judged the letter orthodox.

For they did not merely presume, as we have already said, to accuse and reject Ibas’s letter as Nestorian. They also attacked its approvers, those who call it correct and do not subject it to anathema. And who are more properly understood to be its approvers than the Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon and judged it orthodox?

Knowing these things, and supposing that they could thereby bring the agreement of Catholics to the condemnation of the letter itself, they claimed that it had not been accepted by the great council, although we know that the council once again pronounced as follows:

> “From what was recently read, it is clear that the most reverend Ibas is innocent of all the charges brought against him, and from the rescript of the letter reread, which was produced by his opponent, it appeared that his composition was orthodox.”

Could we, then, in opposition to these most evident judgments concerning the letter, after their condemnation had begun, answer the heretics when they reproached us by saying that the Council of Chalcedon had declared orthodox the letter that, in our judgment, was Nestorian? Could we say that this was false and demonstrate, on the contrary, that the council itself had rejected and condemned it?

You see, therefore, emperor, that the enemies of justice wished to mock the Church of Christ and divert us from the truthful defense by which the same letter can be defended more effectively and more strongly, leading us instead to the empty refuge of a false denial. They wanted us for the moment to affirm that it was Nestorian while denying that it had been accepted by the council; then, once convicted by them through the manifest and shameless lie that it had in fact been accepted, nothing would remain for us to say in defense of that council.

Therefore we do not accept the counsel of falsehood, nor will the heretics be able to make us like themselves. We both say that the letter was accepted and demonstrate that it was accepted in every respect, because the Church’s defense of the truth is always truthful and has never needed falsehood.

Before anything else, however, we must examine what sort of claims they spread through their supporters in order to deceive us into denying that it had been accepted.

Let us first consider whether we should say or believe what they attempted to persuade us of: that the synod declared orthodox not the letter of the venerable Ibas, but some writing—a petition and supplication—that the entire clergy of the city of Edessa had sent on behalf of Ibas, to the bishops Photius, Eustachius,

[Note: Codex Veronensis reads “Eustacius,” or “Eustathius.”]

and Uranius.

But what shall we answer when they themselves, or those whom the heretics favor, later tell us that that writing—the petition and supplication—was called by the synodal proceedings “the instruction and supplication of the entire clergy of the city of Edessa,” while the judgment of the synod testified that, from the rereading of his letter, he had appeared orthodox?

[Note: Its heading is thus written in Greek: “Διδασκαλία καὶ παράκλησις παρὰ παντὸς τοῦ κλήρου τῆς Ἐδεσσηνῶν μητροπόλεως”—“Instruction and supplication from the whole clergy of the metropolis of Edessa.” In the subscriptions of the clerics it is called only διδασκαλία, “instruction,” which the translator of the synod sometimes renders “instruction” and sometimes “petition.”]

And when Ibas the bishop requested that the petition and supplication sent by the entire clergy of the city of Edessa to the bishops Photius, Eustachius, and Uranius be read on his behalf, the judgment of the synod, as the very words we have cited make clear, pronounced concerning the rescript of Ibas’s own letter, produced by his opponent, that its composition appeared orthodox?

They will therefore easily prove—if proof is even needed here—that what Bishop Ibas requested to have read on his behalf was one thing, and what was produced against him by the man who was his opponent was another.

They will also add that it was irrelevant to pronounce concerning the petition and supplication of the clergy of the city of Edessa that its composition was orthodox, since the judgment of the synod was expected to concern Ibas’s letter: whether they judged it heretical or orthodox.

When they also raise the objection that the same synod likewise said, “Previously, from the documents reread, the most reverend Ibas was shown to be innocent; for in the passages where he appeared to speak wrongly in criticism of the blessed Cyril, he rightly rejected in the latter passages what he had criticized,” shall we then be unable to utter a word in reply? Shall we be unable even to breathe?

For what had Bishop Ibas said about the blessed Cyril in that petition and supplication that the entire clergy of the city of Edessa had sent on his behalf, such that he was said to have rejected it in the latter passages?

But whoever reads his letter sent to Maris the Persian, which we shall include in the following book, will recognize all these matters there.

But behold: if they will demonstrate by numerous documents that the synod judged the letter of Ibas orthodox—the letter on account of which Ibas himself had been accused—shall we not also demonstrate where the entire clergy of the city of Edessa was accused of having sent an unorthodox petition and supplication on behalf of Ibas the bishop, so that it seemed necessary for the synod to pronounce concerning it that its composition was orthodox?

Or even if this could be demonstrated, would the approval of that petition and supplication absolve Bishop Ibas rather than the petitioners themselves?

We ought also to recite the words of the judgment itself, in case, just as happened concerning Ibas’s letter, one of the Fathers should have said in that synod:

> “The writing of the petition and supplication of the entire clergy of the city of Edessa has appeared orthodox to us.”

But we shall be unable to show anything of the kind, and we know very well that there was no need to declare that petition and supplication orthodox, since no such question was being disputed concerning it. The supporters of the heretics invented these things in order to induce us to condemn that letter.

For why would the entire clergy of the city of Edessa be declared orthodox when Bishop Ibas was accused? Or why would Ibas the bishop be absolved when the entire clergy of the city of Edessa had been declared orthodox?

Finally, even they themselves, compelled by the truth—whether unwillingly or unknowingly—revealed that they had spread these claims fraudulently.

For after their many and varied inventions, after their great and fruitless efforts by which they attempted to obscure clear light with empty words in order to deceive the simple, they said in the same book of theirs:

> “John the heretic, while criticizing the holy synod, is shown to hold the same views as the letter to Maris; but by confessing that it was expelled and destroyed by the holy synod, he likewise confesses that Theodore the impious of Mopsuestia was expelled by it. And since calumniators do not consider what was defined at the end, but perhaps statements made by some before the judgment was complete, it is necessary to understand, if we have a correct intention, that in synods those things that perhaps were said by some before the final judgment do not prejudice what was defined by all together at the end, even if they appear discordant with the common decision. Finally, the holy Anatolius said that Dioscorus was not condemned on account of the faith; and this neither prejudiced the common decision of the synod nor freed Dioscorus from judgment, since he remained in the perversity of Eutyches.”

In all these matters, I now omit arguing that this unknown John the heretic has not been shown to have held the same views as the letter to Maris, or that, if he did hold them, he should therefore be detested.

I omit the fact that it has not been proved that this same John confessed that the aforesaid letter had been destroyed and expelled by the holy synod.

I omit the fact that nothing prejudices Theodore merely because he is said likewise to have declared him expelled by the synod, since, if this were demanded of him, he would be unable to prove it.

This is the one point I wish to make: although in hesitant and inconsistent words, they revealed that they knew the letter had been accepted by the synod, but that they invented all those claims in order to mock us.

For how, if they did not know that the synod had pronounced judgment concerning the letter, could they say that in synods those things do not prejudice the final definitions that were perhaps said by some before the judgment was complete?

Thus, although they claimed that certain statements were discordant, they nevertheless confessed that they knew the synod had judged the letter of the venerable Ibas.

They reveal the same thing later in their book, saying:

> “These statements have been made so that it might be shown to everyone that, in the synodal proceedings that took place—or if, as often happens, some discordance was produced by the judges—no one pays attention to what is said piecemeal, but only to what is finally defined by all in due order.”

For us it is enough to have learned their deceit from their own confession.

Nevertheless, we do not agree with these inventions either.

First, we refuse to be discovered, together with them, not only as liars but as unstable even in our lie, by saying that the synod pronounced not concerning Ibas’s letter but concerning the writing of the petition and supplication of the entire clergy of the city of Edessa that it was orthodox,

[Note: Codex Veronensis reads: “pronounced that it was orthodox, and again, concerning the letter itself, the synod pronounced; but in synods,” etc.]

and then saying that, in synods, those things do not prejudice what was perhaps said by some before the judgment was complete.

Second, the same judgments are found concerning Ibas’s letter,

[Note: Perhaps “the same judgments.”]

[Note: The same codex reads “the synod’s judgments.”]

not before the judgment was complete, but at the end, as they themselves say, and they are not the judgments of some but of all, with no one dissenting.

For they demand of us and say:

> “Prove the disagreement of the council that you allege. Show where, when some pronounced Ibas’s letter orthodox, others contradicted them and said that it was impious and profane. And after the disagreement that you say occurred before the judgment was complete, demonstrate the synod’s harmonious final judgment rejecting this Nestorian and blasphemous letter. Otherwise that synod too was Nestorian which judged such a letter orthodox.”

It is therefore evident that, after all these lies had been vainly invented, so great a synod could not be excused but rather appeared inexcusable, as though it had nothing by which it could truthfully be defended.

## CHAPTER II  
That they falsely say that Ibas denied before the judgment of the bishops Photius and Eustachius that the letter was his own.

Therefore, neither do we say what they likewise asserted in their frequently mentioned book, falsely bearing the title of his name: namely, that Bishop Ibas denied before the judges Photius and Eustathius that that letter was his own [Note: [Col. 0633D] Justinian likewise asserts in his edict that he did not dare call it his own: “At Chalcedon, after the impious letter had been read, Ibas, having been accused, did not dare to claim it as his own” (ἐν Χαλκηδόνι, κατηγορηθεὶς Ἴβας μετὰ τὴν ἀνάγνωσιν τῆς ἀσεβοῦς ἐπιστολῆς οὐκ ἐτόλμησε ταύτην οἰκειώσασθαι) [Col. 0634D]. In any event, nothing of the sort is fabricated in the Fifth Synod. The conjecture brought forward is frivolous and is skilfully refuted by Facundus.] For this too is plainly false; and if we wish to speak against our conscience, we are again convicted by those very men who sowed these lies, since they later said:

“Show us the actual words of his denial, if he said: ‘This letter brought forward against me is not mine; I did not write it; I did not dictate it.’ Show us also the replies of his accusers, by which they tried to convict him, as in the other matters as well, of denying this; show us also which witnesses they brought forward to prove this to him. Show us the judges’ sentence by which they declared that they acquitted him for the reason that it could not be proved to have been his, which he had denied to be his” [Note: [Col. 0633D] The same manuscript reads: “to have been that letter, or at least [Col. 0634D] because Ibas himself denied it to have been his.”] “And what of these things have we produced when they demand them?” [Note: [Col. 0634D] The same manuscript reads: “what have we produced when they demand them?”] Is any such thing contained in the proceedings held before Photius and Eustathius [Note: [Col. 0634D] The same manuscript reads “Eustacius,” or “Eustathius.” The same spelling should also be read shortly below and elsewhere.] and Uranius?

Or, since all these things fail us, shall we make that foolish reply which they inserted in their book, saying:

“Now, in the same proceedings held before Photius and Eustathius, Ibas’s own defence is also found, in which he says in response to these matters that, after the union of the Orientals and Saint Cyril, he had committed no injury against him.”

And they add:

“If, therefore, he indicates that the impious letter was written after the time of the union, while Ibas says that after the union he committed no injury against Saint Cyril, it is plainly shown that Ibas denied the letter to Maris.”

But this invention is altogether feeble and worthy of ridicule. For although, before the letter brought forward against him had been produced in the trial before the most reverend bishops Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius, the most reverend Ibas had disputed with his accusers concerning the name of blessed Cyril, while after his own letter had been produced against him he is shown to have made no word of denial in reply, nevertheless the proceedings do not contain the words in the form in which these men have composed or weakened them in order to obscure the truth.

There, when his accuser, the presbyter Maras, objected to him and said:

“Did you not say, when it was demanded in secret, ‘We regarded Cyril of blessed memory as a heretic, and we did not receive him until he anathematized his chapters’?” [Col. 0634B]

The same most reverend Bishop Ibas replied:

“I truly do not remember. But if I did also [Note: [Col. 0634D] Perhaps: “I said again that …”] say [Note: [Col. 0634D] The same manuscript reads: “and I said,” or “I said that,” etc.] that, in truth, the Oriental council received him after he retracted his chapters.”

And again, when the aforementioned Maras said that he had stated concerning the blessed Cyril just mentioned:

“We regarded him as a heretic until he anathematized his chapters,”

the same most reverend Bishop Ibas said:

“After he interpreted his chapters, I so far refrain from anathematizing the man; for I both received letters from him and sent letters to him, and he communicated with me and I communicated with him.”

Ibas therefore did not deny that he had at some time considered Cyril a heretic. Rather, he said that after the union had been effected he refrained from anathematizing the man, which the letter itself also makes clear.

But what Bishop Ibas said—“After he interpreted his chapters, I so far refrain from anathematizing the man”—is not the same as what these men put into his mouth, namely, that “after the union of the Orientals and Saint Cyril he committed no injury against him.” They present it as though it followed that, because Ibas had by then refrained from anathematizing blessed Cyril, he could neither previously have believed nor later have said that Cyril had once fallen into error, whom he had falsely thought rather to have been converted from error.

For this reason we likewise reject this fabrication of our own accord, rather than have it rejected by those who invented it, since it is later refuted by our own confession.

But if you wish, Augustus, to know that the actual denial is demonstrated not by these obscure and deceitful inventions, but by documents that are manifest and evident of their own accord, [Col. 0634D] attend, I ask, to the character of Ibas’s denial on another point in the same controversy, to the corresponding reply of his accusers, and to the judges’ interlocution.

I have therefore thought it necessary to transfer into this book, by way of example, certain passages from the same proceedings, where the aforementioned Maras, one of Bishop Ibas’s accusers, said [Note: [Col. 0635D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “He said: ‘We first raise a question concerning the faith.’ The most reverend bishops said: ‘What question concerning the faith do you have to raise?’ Maras, addressing them, said,” etc. This agrees with the proceedings of the Synod of Berytus recited at the Council of Chalcedon, act 10.]:

“Why do you raise a question concerning the faith?” Maras, addressing them, said [Note: [Col. 0635D] More correctly in the Synod of Chalcedon: Μάρας εἶπε· Προσομιλῶν εἶπεν, “Maras said: ‘Addressing them, he said,’” that is, he spoke publicly. The person meant is evidently Ibas, to whom the following words belong. There are also other passages, both in this text and in the preceding text of the Synod of Berytus, which show that Facundus used a corrupt manuscript, since the readings in the Chalcedonian text are more correct.]:

“‘I do not begrudge Christ that he was made God; for insofar as he himself was made, I too was made.’

“The most reverend bishops said: ‘Let the most reverend Ibas confess whether these words were spoken by him.’”

The most reverend bishop said:

“Anathema to him who said it and to him who makes the accusation; for I did not say it.”

Samuel said:

“We have witnesses to this matter, some of whom are standing here. We ask that they be summoned by you and received, so that they may testify in their own voices whether they heard him [Note: [Col. 0635D] The same manuscript reads: “whether they did not hear him.” See the passage cited above.] saying this.”

The most reverend Bishop Ibas said:

“I would suffer myself to be cut into ten thousand pieces rather than utter this word. Far be it from me even to think this word. But I know that each person is saved by confession.” [Col. 0635B]

The most reverend bishops said:

“Do you say that the most reverend Bishop Ibas said this in church?”

Samuel said:

“It is customary on the holy day of Easter, or on the day before it, to give something from the hand to the clergy for the festival. When he is about to give these things, he first addresses them, and then gives them. He addressed them in this way both before everyone and in the presence of the clergy, so that they might receive the things given for the festival; and he will be convicted by some of the clergy standing here, who heard him say this.”

The most reverend bishops said:

“How long ago do you maintain that the most reverend Bishop Ibas said this?”

Samuel said:

“It is about three years, more or less, since these things were said.”

Do you observe, Augustus, how Ibas the bishop was first questioned by the judges as to whether that blasphemy had been uttered by him; how his accusers also requested that witnesses be produced against him [Note: [Col. 0635D] The same manuscript reads: “how he himself also denied it and cursed it; and how the accusers also …”]; how the judges asked the accusers where, when, and in whose presence they claimed that he had uttered this particular blasphemy [Note: [Col. 0635D] The same manuscript reads “that he had uttered it”]; and how, although they were obstinate, they identified the place, recalled the time, named the witnesses, and showed sufficiently in the remainder of the proceedings how many times these words had been spoken and how many times repeated?

What comparable evidence can we prove concerning that letter, so that we may say that the aforementioned Ibas denied it to have been his, when the judges themselves already knew it to have been his to such an extent that they did not even think he should be asked whether it belonged to him?

Thus, as I said, the supporters of the heretics wished in vain to lead us into saying that Ibas had denied before the judgment of the bishops Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius that the letter was his. But if it is not demonstrated in their judgment that Ibas denied that the letter was his, how, accepting their persuasion, shall we say that he later denied in the synod that it was his, although he had not previously done so, when in that synod sentences are instead found to have been delivered concerning the letter itself, and Bishop Ibas himself is acquitted by its rereading?

For they also said this in their book:

“But even at the holy Council of Chalcedon, wishing to demonstrate that he himself was free from the accusation concerning the letter, Ibas, immediately after its rereading, said the following: ‘Order the letter of the Edessene clergy to be reread, so that you may recognize that I am unrelated to the charges brought against me and that I suffered violence.’ And the letter sent by the Edessene clergy was reread; in it they testified under oath that they were aware of no accusation made against him and did not know him to have done anything contrary to the orthodox faith.” [Col. 0636B]

In these words, one thing must first be noted: they do not depart from their customary deception, in that they call that document, which the entire clergy of the city of Edessa presented on behalf of the aforesaid Ibas, a letter [Note: [Col. 0636D] The same manuscript reads: “which the city had sent, they called a letter,” although it is there called a petition and supplication, and they wished …], intending through the term “letter” to turn the synod’s judgment concerning Ibas’s own letter to another meaning for us. Thus, if we believed that the synod had pronounced orthodox that petition and supplication of the Edessene clergy rather than the aforementioned letter, we would be led into its condemnation.

Next, how could the testimony of the entire Edessene clergy have been sought for the denial of the letter, when the accusers falsely claimed that the Edessene clergy had been witnesses not to the letter written to Maris but to that blasphemy, which was beyond suspicion? [Col. 0636C]

In that matter, therefore, it was necessary for their testimony to be reread to the synod, since they had been named by the accusers. Finally, they too testified not concerning this letter, but only concerning that blasphemy.

Let them show us in the very petition and supplication where they said that the letter was not written by him to Maris the Persian [Note: [Col. 0636D] The same manuscript reads: “that he himself had not written that letter to Maris the Persian, just as they clearly testified that they had not heard that blasphemy from him; and then perhaps they will persuade us also to say that the oft-mentioned letter was not denied in the judgment of the most reverend …”]; and then perhaps they will persuade us also to say that Bishop Ibas later denied in the synod that the oft-mentioned letter, which he had not denied before in the judgment of the most reverend Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius, was his own.

Otherwise it will be clear to everyone that they fabricated these things in order to mock us: if we followed this lie, they would later convict and confound us by the manifest judgments of the synod itself—judgments which, even if we could prove them, would show that they were delivered not by all but by some [Note: [Col. 0636D] The same manuscript reads: “which were certainly delivered there concerning the same letter; nevertheless, whoever might deliver them concerning that letter could not do so if …”] concerning that same letter, if Bishop Ibas denied it to be his.

For it was said there, as we recalled above:

“From the judgment of the most reverend bishops we have learned that the most reverend Bishop Ibas has been shown to be innocent. For, when his letter had been read, we learned that he was orthodox; and this we decree: that the honor of the episcopate be restored to him, and that the Church from which he was unjustly expelled while absent be restored to him”; together with other similar statements contained in those proceedings. [Col. 0637A]

How, then, would we not be convicted of accusing as insane the Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon, if we said that they had judged that he should be restored both to the episcopate and to the Church on account of that letter which Ibas had denied to be his? [Note: [Col. 0637D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “that the episcopate and the Church should be restored.”]

Let your serenity also observe how they reveal that they know the truth, namely, that Bishop Ibas did not deny that the letter was his. For they said this as well in their book, as we recalled in our second book:

“We ought to examine the letter to Maris, which says everything without God and impiously, but demonstrates this one thing correctly: that from that time onward Theodore was anathematized throughout the churches of the East.”

They would not have said this if they believed that Ibas had denied the letter itself.

But let them answer us: whose testimony did they use when they said that from that time onward Theodore was anathematized throughout the churches of the East? If Ibas denied that letter to be his, and they say that it was fabricated against him by the accusers, then without doubt they used false witnesses, since they claimed on their authority that from that time onward Theodore was anathematized throughout the churches of the East.

But if, as is more credible, they deny that they used false witnesses, they again reveal that they know that Bishop Ibas did not deny the letter to be his, and that the synod pronounced the letter itself orthodox. [Col. 0637C]

Finally, what need was there for a letter to be condemned by the judgment of the universal Church—a letter not only private and, as they assert, in no way pertaining to the synod, but also one whose author was uncertain? That is, if it is proper to call it a judgment at all, when the subscriber did not disclose what he thought but rather copied a formula presented to him.

Therefore, even if all the points stated above were lacking, the very manner of the act would sufficiently indicate that they knew it had been received by the universal council. Otherwise they would not have sought, except to the detriment of that council, for the universal Church to condemn it.

Let the supporters of the heretics therefore cease—now that they have been caught and exposed—from deliberately proclaiming to deceive us that the synod did not pronounce Ibas’s letter orthodox [Col. 0637D], lest they appear to wish to steal from us not something that we saw with our own eyes in broad daylight, but the very eyes with which we see.

CHAPTER III. That they falsely say that Theodoret did not sit in the Council of Chalcedon until after the condemnation of Eutyches and Dioscorus [Col. 0638A], and that the authority of the synod is not impaired if those who have come to their senses from heresy sit in it.

Certainly, let us examine also the following point, which they similarly wished us to assert in excuse of that synod: namely, that we should say that the judgment concerning Ibas’s letter did not at all pertain to its decrees because, supposedly, after the condemnation of Eutyches and Dioscorus and after the definition of the faith, Theodoret and Ibas sat in the council. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “concerning the letter of Ibas produced against him,” etc.]

Thus, in their book, they thought it appropriate to say the following about the most reverend bishops Theodoret and Ibas:

“Because they had been accused of accepting the doctrine of Nestorius, they were not summoned to sit with the holy synod. But after judgment had been passed concerning Eutyches and Dioscorus, and after the holy synod had established the orthodox constitutions of the Fathers—by which they adjudged and subjected to anathema Nestorius and Eutyches, together with those who followed their wicked decrees—then the aforesaid Theodoret and Ibas approached the holy synod.”

Who, ignorant of what took place at that synod, would believe that they could have fabricated such things about a public case conducted in the sight of everyone? What, then? Did Bishop Theodoret not sit with the holy synod until the eighth action, after judgment had been passed concerning Eutyches and Dioscorus and after the holy synod had established the orthodox constitutions of the Fathers?

How, then, is it recorded in the acts of that same synod that, in the very first action, Theodoret sat among the other bishops, in the consulship of Marcian Augustus, on the eighth day before the Ides of October?

[Note: When, in the first action, the bishops of many provinces protested, Theodoret obtained only with difficulty, by the authority of the judges, that he not be expelled from the synod. Later, in action 8, he was ordered to pronounce an anathema against Nestorius, and thus, with the consent of all, he recovered the see of his Church and his place in the synod.]

Are these words not contained there?

“The most glorious judges and the most distinguished senate said: ‘Let the most reverend Bishop Theodoret enter, so that he may participate in the synod, since the most holy Archbishop Leo restored his episcopate to him, and the most sacred and most pious emperor decreed that he should be present at the holy synod.’

“The most reverend Bishop Theodoret, coming into the midst, said: ‘I have presented petitions to the most sacred and most Christian lords of the world, and I have related the wounds inflicted upon me; I beg that these petitions be read.’”

[Note: The same manuscript has “to the most sacred, pious, and most Christian...”]

After this statement of the same most reverend Theodoret, when the most glorious judges and the senate again declared that Theodoret had received his proper place from the most holy bishop of the illustrious city of Rome, and that he had the testimony of Maximus, Bishop of Antioch, that he was of the Catholic faith, as is written there, he sat in the midst. While he was present and seated among the other bishops, the proceedings that had taken place at Ephesus under Dioscorus were read aloud. When Dioscorus, together with Juvenal of Jerusalem and certain others, appeared to be liable to condemnation, they decided first to refer the matter to the emperor.

It must plainly be acknowledged that Bishop Ibas did not sit in the synod until his case had been discussed and settled in the seventh and eighth sessions.

[Note: A synodical session is one thing, and an action another, since several cases or actions are sometimes dealt with in a single sitting. In the Council of Chalcedon, the first six sessions contain six actions altogether, one action in each. The seventh session, however, embraces three actions—the seventh, eighth, and ninth—while the eighth contains only one action, namely the tenth. In all, the sessions of the universal synod—or, as Liberatus calls them in chapter 13, the secretaries—numbered twelve, whereas the actions numbered sixteen. Ibas’s case, therefore, which we observed above to have been discussed in the ninth and tenth actions of the synod, is correctly assigned by Facundus partly to the seventh and partly to the eighth session, since, as stated, the ninth action belongs to the seventh session and the tenth to the eighth. Accordingly, what is cited shortly afterward from the eighth session is found in the tenth action.]

Before this, Nonnus, who had been ordained in his place, is recorded as having sat in all the actions. Indeed, in the sixth sitting, after the definition of the faith had been completed and duly subscribed by all the bishops, the emperor intervened and ordered all the bishops to wait several days, so that the private cases of any persons might be settled there.
