After Ibas, then, had been cleared in the eighth session, he subscribed the decisions that had already been established in the preceding actions. This is clearly shown by the judgment of Saint Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople, which he delivered among the others concerning Ibas’s case in the eighth session, when he says:

“The judgments of the most reverend judges demonstrate that the most reverend Ibas is innocent

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads: ‘The faith of the judgments of the most reverend bishops, and the reading of all the documents produced, show the most reverend Ibas to be innocent...’ The same words are found in action 10 of the Council of Chalcedon.] of the charges brought against him by his accusers. Therefore I remove every present suspicion concerning him, since he both agrees with and subscribes to the judgment now issued by the holy council concerning the faith and to the letter of the most holy Archbishop Leo of Rome; and I judge him worthy of the episcopate and of having charge of the Church in which he formerly served. As for the most reverend Bishop Nonnus, who was appointed in his place, the most reverend Maximus, Bishop of Antioch, shall provide a disposition.”

Here, then, it is proved, as stated, that after the eighth session, in which he was cleared, he subscribed the judgments previously reached by the council. For Saint Anatolius, in his judgment, as we have recalled, said that he “agrees with and subscribes to” them—not that he “agreed with and subscribed to” them.

We should therefore not be troubled by the fact that, although in the preceding actions Ibas is nowhere recorded as having sat, he is nevertheless found in them subscribing, together with Nonnus, who had been ordained in his place, to the judgments of the council.

For after the eighth session, in which Bishop Ibas, once cleared, recovered the episcopate of his Church, we do not find that the aforesaid Nonnus either sat or subscribed in the other actions in which Bishop Ibas himself participated.

In the second action—which is written after the third in the manuscripts but in fact took place in the same consulship, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, and in which discussion of the decrees of the faith begins—Theodoret sat in the one hundred and eleventh place.

After the creed of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers who were at Nicaea and of the one hundred and fifty who were at Constantinople had been read, together with the two letters of blessed Cyril—that is, to Nestorius and to John of Antioch—and after the letter of Pope Leo to Flavian had likewise been read, certain persons, as we already said in the second book, were doubtful about some words in that letter. They were reassured when Theodoret gave an explanation.

Thus the acts of that same action record:

“When the passage was being read from the same letter that runs as follows:

‘Although in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of God and man, nevertheless the source of the common dishonor in both is one thing, and the source of the common glory is another. For his humanity, which he received from us, is lower than the Father; from the Father he has divinity equal with the Father.’

“When the most reverend Illyrian and Palestinian bishops were doubtful,

[Note: The same manuscript reads: ‘the most reverend bishops.’]

“The most reverend Bishop Theodoret of Cyrus said: ‘There is also an example of blessed Cyril which reads: “both made man and not abandoning what is proper.” For he remained what he was; yet one thing in another, namely the divine nature in the humanity, is entirely understood to be present.’

“The most glorious judges and the most distinguished senate said: ‘After all this, who still doubts?’

“The most reverend bishops shouted: ‘No one doubts.’”

All this I have transferred into this book from the acts of the synod itself. How, then, can it be said of the most reverend Bishop Theodoret that he did not sit until the eighth action?

In the third action, in which Dioscorus was condemned—which took place in the same consulship, on the third day before the Ides of October, was held without the judges and senate, and is found joined to the first action in the manuscripts—I believe that this is because, in the first action, the same Dioscorus had already been judged deserving of deprivation of the honor of the episcopate, so that his condemnation might follow immediately. In any event, not only the dating of the days but also the substance of the actions themselves, namely the second and third, when they are read, shows that in the manuscripts the third was placed before the second.

In this third action, Nonnus, who had been ordained in the place of Ibas, subscribed in the fifty-fifth place, saying: “Nonnus, bishop of the city of Edessa, have subscribed.” Ibas himself, as we find, subscribed to his condemnation in the one hundred and seventy-seventh place, in these words: “Ibas, bishop of the city of Edessa, have subscribed.”

Then, in the fourth sitting, in the same consulship, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, we find that Theodoret, the one hundred and twelfth bishop, sat and intervened in the thirty-eighth place concerning the aforementioned letter of Saint Leo. It is written:

“The most reverend Bishop Theodoret of Cyrus said: ‘The letter of the most holy Bishop Lord Leo agrees with the faith expounded by the holy and blessed Fathers at Nicaea, with the creed composed at Constantinople by the one hundred and fifty, and with the letters of blessed Cyril.’”

[Note: The same manuscript reads “archbishop.”]

As for the fifth action, which took place in the same consulship, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in which the exposition of the faith was first read and then reported to the emperor so that it might afterward be confirmed by the subscriptions of all, we can prove nothing. For, as I said, the subscription was postponed; and in the report itself, which relates by whom the same exposition of the faith was reread, the Roman legates and fifty-two other bishops are named, and it says, “with those and the rest of the holy and universal synod seated,” but it is silent about the names of the others.

In the sixth action, in the same consulship, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in which the emperor was present and all subscribed the definition of the faith, anathematizing Nestorius, Eutyches, and all who held contrary views, Nonnus is found to have sat twenty-eighth and to have subscribed thirty-first, in this manner:

“Nonnus, bishop of the metropolis of Edessa, have subscribed by defining.”

Ibas also, although, as we said, he is not recorded as having sat, is nevertheless found to have subscribed ninetieth, in these words:

“Ibas, bishop of Edessa, have subscribed by defining.”

Theodoret likewise is found to have sat one hundred and seventh and to have subscribed one hundred and thirty-third, in the same words:

“Theodoret of Cyrus, have subscribed by defining.”

[Note: In the acts of the synod: Θεοδώρητος ἐπίσκοπος Κύρου ὁρίσας ὑπέγραψα, “Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, having defined, I subscribed.” Cyrus was a city of Euphratesian Syria over which Theodoret presided. Some call it Cyrrhus, Κύῤῥον, as do Pliny, Ptolemy, and Stephanus; others call it Cyrus, Κύρον, as it is commonly found in Theodoret himself, in Procopius’s *On Buildings*, and in Hierocles’ *Synecdemus*, where the cities of that province are listed: Ἱεράπολις, Κύρος, Σαμόσατα, “Hierapolis, Cyrus, Samosata,” and the rest. In the same way, the inhabitants are called by writers either Κυρησταί or Κυῤῥησταί; and on ancient coins of the Antonines and Philips one may read: Διὸς καταβάτου Κυῤῥηστῶν vel Κυρηστῶν seu Κυρεστῶν, “of Zeus Who Comes Down, of the Cyrrhestians or Kyrestians or Cyrestians,” with a temple or image of Jupiter Catabates, who was worshiped in that city.]

How, then, were the supporters of the heretics not ashamed to lie in the face of such overwhelming evidence, saying that Bishop Theodoret did not participate in the council until after the definition of the faith? And yet, after being caught in so many falsehoods, they still demand that the letter which the universal synod approved nearly a hundred years ago now be condemned on their testimony.

Who will pass a just judgment, rather than condemning those who fabricated such things? Or how will they be admitted either to bear witness or to accuse anyone against the canons of the Fathers, when we prove them to be liars in matters of such importance? And if anyone refuses to agree with such lies, he is called a heretic—as though it were characteristic of heretics to refuse to lie.

Moreover, since they subscribe to these falsehoods and establish their defense of the synod upon them, what will we be able to answer the Eutychians when they convict us by manifest truth? Or how great will appear the necessity that drove us to resort to such lies, in which there is no place to hide, as though nothing remained by which we could truthfully defend that holy synod?

Those who, while pretending to refute the accusations of the Eutychians, actually strengthen them will not persuade us to say that Theodoret did not enter the synod before judgment had been passed concerning Eutyches and Dioscorus and the exposition of the faith had been completed. For if we say this along with them, we are certainly convicted, and we do not evade the accusations of the heretics but strengthen them more and more.

Let those who strive to persuade us of such things know that we understand that they are practicing hostilities in too close concert with the Eutychians.

It is true that Theodoret, like Ibas, did not participate in the definition of the council of Chalcedon. But was this what had to be said in order to show that the letter of the venerable Ibas did not pertain to the decrees of that council, because judgment concerning it took place after the definition of the faith?

Then the canons of ecclesiastical discipline, which were usefully established there after the definition,

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “after the definition of the faith.”]

will likewise be said not to pertain to the same synod. And would that they would teach us to which synod we ought to assign them, if the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon do not belong to the Council of Chalcedon!

Furthermore, how can that synod be excused by an assertion that contradicts and destroys itself? Those who, in its defense, wanted us to say that no one should attend to what certain persons may have said before the judgment was completed, but only to what was defined in the final order, now themselves argue the opposite: that we should defend the synod on the ground that judgment concerning Ibas’s letter took place after the definition. Thus they later convict us not only by the evidence of the matter itself but also by the contradiction within our own assertion.

Yet reason does not so fail us in defending the synod concerning Ibas’s letter that we should wish to excuse it uselessly against the accusations of the Eutychians by means of an argument that cannot defend it against the Nestorians.

For if the definition of the faith made in that synod is defended against the accusations of the Eutychians on the ground that, because Theodoret and Ibas had been accused of accepting the doctrine of Nestorius, they were not summoned to sit beforehand with the holy synod, then it cannot be defended against the accusations of the Nestorians on the ground that Anatolius of Constantinople—who had previously usurped for himself the first place there before the Bishop of Antioch—and Maximus of Antioch himself, as well as Juvenal of Jerusalem, sat there, although they had previously been tainted either by the doctrine or by the communion of the Eutychians.

For venerable Anatolius had been ordained by the Eutychians after blessed Flavian had been expelled for the true faith; holy Maximus had likewise been ordained by them in place of Bishop Domnus; and Juvenal, having fallen into the very Eutychian doctrine, had been excluded from the Church. This is made clear by the letters of blessed Leo and by the records of other writers.

Let us not, then, defend the faith established in that synod in such a way that we say things which, while helping us not at all against the Eutychians, greatly assist the Nestorians against the Church.

Can Theodoret and Ibas really have as much power to incline the council to their view as the bishops of Constantinople, Antioch, and Jerusalem, who sat there first after the legates of the apostolic see—to say nothing of the many others who, through the violence of Dioscorus, had previously been compelled to affirm the Eutychian doctrine?

Or is it as difficult for us to defend the Council of Chalcedon against the Eutychians concerning Ibas’s letter as it is against the Nestorians—not only on account of the persons of the many bishops who were altogether present at that council, but also on account of the intervention of Saint Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople, who said in that council that Dioscorus, an affirmer of the Eutychian doctrine and oppressor of the Catholic faith, had not been condemned for the faith?

[Note: Perhaps “who called Dioscorus...”]

[Note: Nicholas I, in Letter 8 to the Emperor Michael, says that Dioscorus was condemned chiefly because he had dared to pronounce excommunication against Pope Leo. “Without any controversy,” he says, “they punished him for this: although inferior, he attempted to assail his superior with every kind of insult; this is attested by Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople, who says: ‘Dioscorus was not condemned for the faith, but because he excommunicated Lord Archbishop Leo.’” This does not mean that it was unclear that Dioscorus was involved in the heresy of Eutyches, which he had openly defended; but, as the legates of the apostolic see argued when delivering sentence against him in action 3, he could have been pardoned, as could the other bishops who had sinned under his leadership, had he not compounded his earlier crimes by subsequent offenses, especially that excommunication against Leo. But, according to Facundus, Anatolius’s judgment concerned something else: the faith of Dioscorus.]

From this the Nestorians say to us: “How did you accept that synod, in which not only many bishops, but bishops holding the more distinguished places, sat—bishops who had been ordained by the Eutychians and were proved to have followed the doctrine of Eutyches and Dioscorus? Or how do you maintain that it was convened to condemn the impiety of Eutyches and Dioscorus, when Anatolius of Constantinople there approved the impiety of Dioscorus, which he shared with Eutyches, by declaring that he had not been condemned for the faith?”

If these arguments do not move us when advanced by the Nestorians, the arguments of the Eutychians will move us even less.

For we can easily show the Nestorians themselves that what they say—that the definition made by the Fathers who had repented of Dioscorus’s presumption and assembled with the others at Chalcedon is without authority—is comparable to saying that the teaching of the Apostle Peter, which he preached about Christ with the other apostles, is without authority because he had once denied Christ or because he was rebuked by Paul when, by not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize.

It would likewise be comparable to the Sabellians’ saying that they therefore do not accept the Church’s teaching concerning the Trinity because far more bishops

[Note: In the false synod of Ephesus, the “Robber Synod”—λῃστρικῆς—as is clear from the acts read at Chalcedon, there were no more than 130 bishops. At Ariminum, according to Athanasius in his *Book on the Synods*, more than four hundred were counted: Ἦσαν δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ ἐπίσκοποι υʹ, καὶ πλέον, “There were four hundred bishops in it, and more.” At this point the translator, reading κʹ instead of υʹ, rendered the number as fifty rather than four hundred. Others also agree about the number, such as Sulpicius Severus in Book II of his *History*: “Four hundred, and sometimes more, Western bishops were summoned or compelled to attend.” If we believe Severus, who writes that no more than eighty of them were Arians, it follows that more than three hundred were orthodox—twice as many, plainly, as at the Second Council of Ephesus.]

who had assembled at Ariminum had been compelled to embrace the Arian doctrine by Constantius.

Therefore, just as we say to the Sabellians that the Church’s confession concerning the Trinity is not for that reason to be shunned—because at the Council of Ariminum many, yielding to the Arian doctrine, falsely claimed that the three persons of the same holy Trinity were different natures—so we say also to the Nestorians that the holy confession of the Council of Chalcedon concerning the one subsistence of Christ, that is, of God and man, is not for that reason to be shunned—because earlier, under the oppression of Dioscorus, many, yielding to the Eutychian doctrine, falsely claimed that there was one nature of that same subsistence.

Or, because they complain that the Greeks—though not all, indeed fewer in comparison with the whole number—fell into the view of Dioscorus, let them follow the view of so many Latins who cannot be accused by them of agreeing with Eutyches, Dioscorus, or anyone else, yet hold concerning the incarnation of Christ the very doctrine established by the Council of Chalcedon.

We have also answered concerning the intervention of Saint Anatolius regarding the person of Dioscorus: it must not be said that it pertains to the crime of heresy to have agreed in some respect with Dioscorus in a sound opinion.

For Saint Anatolius did not approve the very impiety of Dioscorus; rather, he wished him to be excused from that impiety. It is one thing to excuse a heretic because he is thought to be Catholic, and another to approve and defend the heresy itself. Likewise, it is one thing to accuse a Catholic because he is thought to be a heretic, and another to condemn and reject the Catholic faith itself.

For someone who approves and loves chastity may, without approving fornication, approve a fornicator if he is mistaken about the person; and without rejecting chastity, he may reject a chaste person if he is similarly mistaken about the person.

Finally, as they most readily concede, just as the Eutychians are not thereby defended from the crime of their doctrine because, thinking that the ancient Fathers believed what they themselves wickedly believe, they approve us, whose faith they attack, so the crime of the Eutychian doctrine must not for that reason be charged against Saint Anatolius because he either thought well of Dioscorus or excused him as though he were free from the guilt of the Eutychian doctrine, when he had himself refuted and condemned that doctrine.

## CHAPTER IV

That Pope Leo confirmed not only the definition of the faith of the Council of Chalcedon but all its acts and decrees, except for the arrogance of Anatolius, which he rebuked. He did not exclude approval of the letter of Ibas.

But since this too has become sufficiently clear—that even if, as has been fabricated, Bishops Theodoret and Ibas had not been present at the Council of Chalcedon before the definition of faith, he would not thereby have been excused—let us also investigate what sort of argument it is by which they say that only the definition of faith, and not the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, was conveyed to the Roman Church, and from this wish us to believe that blessed Leo confirmed the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon only in that definition of faith, and that we too should condemn the aforementioned letter of the venerable Ibas. Yet Leo says, as we already recalled in the second book:

> “Let the brotherhood and the hearts of all the faithful know that I have united my judgment with yours, not only through the brethren who carried out my commission, but also through my approval of the synodal acts.” [Col. 0645A]

He therefore declares that he approved not only the definition of faith, but the synodal acts themselves.

As for what they say they have extracted from certain letters of blessed Leo, deceiving the simple—as they extract other passages also—that he said the Council of Chalcedon had been convened solely to extinguish heresy and to confirm the catholic faith, and whatever similar statements we find in his letters, so that by this means also they may lead as many as they can to condemn this letter, as though it had not been approved by him: what they take from these statements was not said for that purpose. Therefore let us show why and how he said it.

For Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, because—as we have recalled—he had presumptuously taken his seat in the same synod before Maximus of Antioch, was addressed by blessed Leo in a letter to Anatolius as follows (Letter 53):

> “I grieve also that your Charity has fallen into this error, attempting to violate the most sacred constitutions of the Nicene canons, as though this time had opportunely presented itself to you, when the Alexandrian see had lost the privilege of the second rank and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of the third dignity, so that, with these places subjected to your jurisdiction, all metropolitan bishops might be deprived of their proper honor. By these unheard-of and never-before-attempted measures you are so carried away that you drag the holy synod, convened through the zeal of a most Christian prince to extinguish heresy alone and to confirm the catholic faith, into an opportunity for ambition, and compel it to grant you its connivance.” [Col. 0645B–C]

Let us not, then, infer from these and similar statements—which most blessed Leo wrote either to Anatolius himself or to others against Anatolius—that he rejected the judgment of the Council concerning the letter of Ibas. For he said that the holy synod had been convened “to extinguish heresy alone and to confirm the catholic faith” because it was to dissolve what had been usurped out of the ambition of the bishop of Constantinople, as will become much more evident from his other writings.

Otherwise, he would be said to have nullified the other things enacted at that synod. Yet when he wrote similarly concerning that same holy synod held at Chalcedon, he made his intention clear to everyone by adding these words (Letter 61):

> “I also admonish Your Holiness concerning the observance of the statutes of the holy Fathers, which have been fixed by inviolable decrees in the Nicene synod, so that the rights of the churches may remain as they were ordered by those three hundred and eighteen Fathers inspired by God. Let no one wickedly desire what belongs to another, nor seek his own advancement through another’s diminution. However much the exaltation of vanity may equip itself with forced flatteries, and however much it may think that its desires are to be strengthened by the name of councils, whatever differs from the canons of the aforementioned Fathers will be weak and void. The apostolic see makes the greatest reverent use of their regulations. From the reading of my writings, by which I resisted the efforts of the bishop of Constantinople, Your Holiness will be able to recognize that, with the help of our God, I am a guardian both of the catholic faith and of the constitutions of the Fathers.” [Col. 0645D–0646A]

[Note: The Verona manuscript has “three hundred and seventeen.”]

[Note: The same manuscript has “let him wickedly desire ambition”; in Quesnel’s edition, Letter 87, “let him wickedly desire ambition.”]

[Note: Isidore Mercator has “assents” rather than “flatteries.”]

Behold, then, that in this letter also, which blessed Leo wrote to the holy synod, he declares that nothing else displeased him in that synod except that Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, presumptuously took his seat before the bishop of Antioch.

Otherwise, he will be said to have condemned not only the judgment pronounced concerning the letter of Ibas, but also the restoration of the episcopate to that most reverend Bishop Ibas, and all the canons which the holy Fathers usefully established there concerning ecclesiastical discipline—discipline which Leo, his enemy, would then be shown to have attacked—as well as all the other matters specifically decreed there concerning various persons.

Or, if they do not dare say this openly about blessed Leo, let them understand with us that, when he wrote to the bishop of Constantinople about only two matters enacted at the Council of Chalcedon—namely, the question of faith, for which the council itself had been convened, and the bishop’s proud arrogance—he said:

> “You drag the holy synod, convened through the zeal of a most Christian prince to extinguish heresy alone and to confirm the catholic faith, into an opportunity for ambition.”

And when he found such expressions in his letters, he was judging by these words only the two matters we have mentioned, about which he had spoken, not the other things enacted there.

Thus the Apostle, writing to the Philippians about Timothy, says:

> “I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, so that I too may be encouraged when I learn how things are with you. For I have no one of like mind who will sincerely be concerned for you. For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:19–21). [Col. 0646C]

He was not directing his words against Titus and Luke, or against Epaphroditus and Mark, or against his other companions, concerning whom he says in the same letter:

> “I urge Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord. Yes, I also ask you, my true companion, help them, women who labored with me in the gospel, together with Clement and my other fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life” (Philippians 4:2–3).

Rather, he was speaking against those of whom he says there:

> “Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the mutilation” (Philippians 3:2). [Col. 0646D]

It was only in comparison with these people that he said of Timothy:

> “I have no one of like mind who will sincerely be concerned for you,”

and only with regard to them that he added:

> “For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.”

Finally, speaking of blessed Timothy himself, he says:

> “You know his tested character, how, as a son with his father, he served with me in the gospel. I hope, therefore, to send him as soon as I see how things stand with me. And I trust in the Lord that I myself will come shortly to you” (Philippians 2:22–24). [Col. 0646D–0647A]

[Note: The Latin editions read *you will know*; in accordance with the Greek text, read *know* (*γινώσκετε*).]

Then he immediately adds:

> “I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, and your apostle and minister to my need, since he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Indeed, he was ill, near to death; but God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow. I have sent him all the more eagerly, so that when you see him again you may rejoice, and I may be less sorrowful. Receive him, therefore, in the Lord with all joy, and hold such men in honor, because for the work of Christ he came near to death, risking his life to supply what was lacking in your service to me” (Philippians 2:25–30). [Col. 0647A–B]

Was it this Epaphroditus, the apostle of the Philippians, and Paul’s other holy fellow workers in the gospel, whom the Apostle Paul had in mind when he said:

> “I have no one of like mind who will sincerely be concerned for you; for they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ”?

Or rather, was he speaking of those whom we mentioned above?

Can Epaphroditus be said not to have been of like mind, when, after he had been restored from his illness, Paul says that God had mercy even on him, lest he should have sorrow upon sorrow because of him?

Or was the holy Epaphroditus not sincerely concerned for the Philippians, whom he longed to see, and for whose sorrow over his illness he himself was distressed because they had heard that he was ill—and who, for the work of Christ, had come near to death, risking his life to supply what was lacking in their service to Paul? [Col. 0647B–C]

For this reason he rightly commended him to them, telling them to hold such men in honor.

Thus, when the Apostle Paul wrote to the Philippians about Timothy, he did not have Titus and Luke in mind, nor Epaphroditus and Mark, nor his other fellow workers whose names are in the book of life, when he said:

> “I have no one of like mind who will sincerely be concerned for you; for they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.”

Rather, he had in mind those about whom he had said:

> “Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the mutilation.”

So too, when most blessed Leo wrote, he did not have in mind the judgment pronounced concerning the letter of Ibas, nor the restoration of the episcopate to the aforementioned Ibas, nor the other decrees made at the Council of Chalcedon concerning particular persons, nor the canons of ecclesiastical discipline beneficially established there by the holy Fathers, when he said:

> “You drag the holy synod, convened through the zeal of a most Christian prince to extinguish heresy alone and to confirm the catholic faith, into an opportunity for ambition,”

and similar words. Rather, he had in mind the proud arrogance of the bishop of Constantinople, as his very words show.

For nothing else is found in those same letters of his that he rebuked.

[Col. 0647D–0648A] The same manuscript has: “and compel it to grant you its connivance” [read: “and compel it to grant you its compliance”], “and similar words.”

We must therefore understand the words of Leo of Rome in this way, and support the writings of the apostolic see by the examples of the apostolic writings, if we do not wish to provoke a greater disturbance in the Church than we now endure by attacking all the canons usefully established by the holy Fathers at that synod, together with the other matters confirmed there in the particular cases of various persons.

Who, however, would dare say of blessed Leo that, if the letter approved by the synod were Nestorian, he would have set aside the blasphemy by which Christ is denied to be God, and complained only that one bishop at that synod had not taken his proper seat?

Therefore, either this is the only offense that blessed Leo did not conceal displeasing him at the Council of Chalcedon, or, if some other offense is alleged, it is certainly less serious than the offense committed by the bishop of Constantinople. Leo could never, while abandoning the question of heresy, have complained about the seating of one bishop.

Let it be shown to us wherever blessed Leo said (Letter 62) that he did not confirm everything enacted at that synod, that he detested the judgment of the synod concerning the letter of Ibas, and not rather that he chastised and restrained the ambition of the bishop of Constantinople. Once that bishop is cleared, the synod alone will be subject to accusation—if the letter it approved is truly Nestorian.

Writing also to Maximus of Antioch, from whom the aforementioned Constantinopolitan Anatolius had attempted to take away the dignity of the third see, the same blessed Leo makes what we assert clear to everyone. After many remarks, expressed both with acceptable reasoning and with vehement rebuke, concerning that same presumption, he concludes the letter as follows:

> “Whatever is brought before the episcopal judgment apart from the particular matters of synodal councils may have some basis for judgment, if nothing concerning it has been defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. For whatever disagrees with their regulations and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see. You will be instructed how carefully this is guarded by us from a copy of the letter that we sent to the bishop of Constantinople to restrain his ambition. You will make it known to all our brothers and fellow priests, so that they may know that ecclesiastical peace must be preserved through harmony pleasing to God. You should also take care to prevent anyone except the Lord’s priests from presuming to claim for himself the right to teach and preach, whether he be a monk or a layman who boasts in the name of some learning. For although it is desirable that all the sons of the Church should think what is right and sound, nevertheless no one outside the priestly order may be permitted to assume the office of preacher, since all things in the Church ought to be ordered, so that in the one body of Christ the more excellent members may fulfill their office and the lesser members may not resist the superior.” [Col. 0648B–D]

[Note: This sentence is inserted in the edition of Saint Leo.]

These points are manifest, as I think, and require no interpreter, so that it may be understood that blessed Leo said these things against the ambition of the bishop of Constantinople, not against the judgment pronounced concerning the letter of Ibas.

Similarly, when he wrote to the emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria (Letters 74 and 75)—letters which it would take too long to cite—he complains of no other matter.

What is worse, no one pays attention to the matters for which these statements were made; instead, other passages written with a different intention are turned by savage interpretation against the faith.

Pope Gelasius, a better and more acceptable interpreter of the words of his predecessor, contradicts them in our support. Writing to all the bishops established throughout Dardania, he confirms that the statements we have mentioned were written by blessed Leo not to destroy the judgment pronounced concerning the letter of Ibas, but to restrain the presumption of the bishop of Constantinople.

For he says:

> “Just as a small city does not diminish the prerogative of the present kingdom, so imperial presence does not alter the measure of religious administration. Thus that famous city, under the power of the present empire, remains secure, free, and exalted in its religion, if, in the presence of that power, it preserves its proper measure without any disturbance. Finally, if they flatter themselves because of the emperor’s presence and think that the person of the bishop of Constantinople can thereby be made superior, let them hear Marcian, the emperor of that same city. When an intercessor approached on behalf of the enlargement of the city and its priest, he could obtain nothing contrary to the rules; and Marcian praised Pope Leo of holy memory with the highest commendation because he had tolerated no violation of the canonical rules. [Col. 0649B–C] Let them hear Anatolius, the bishop of that same see, who confessed that the Constantinopolitan clergy, rather than he himself, had attempted such things, and who declared that everything rested upon the authority of the apostolic bishop. Let them also hear blessed Pope Leo himself, bishop of the apostolic see, by whose authority the Council of Chalcedon was confirmed: whatever had been delegated there beyond what had been established by him for the faith and catholic and apostolic communion, and whatever, under cover of that assembly, appeared to have been attempted by a new action contrary to the Nicene canons, he nullified by an appropriate refutation.” [Col. 0649B–C]

[Note: In the Roman council under Boniface, in the year 530.]

[Note: The reading may be *by the same* rather than *under the same*.]

Did wise Gelasius understand that his predecessor, blessed Leo, had said what we have quoted on account of the synod’s judgment concerning the letter of the venerable Ibas, rather than, as we have said, on account of the ambition of the bishop of Constantinople?

For why would he append, concerning the letter of Ibas:

> “Under cover of that assembly, a new action contrary to the Nicene canons appears to have been attempted”?

Let no one therefore attempt to twist his words into another meaning.

Neither the evident facts themselves nor Gelasius, a truthful interpreter, permits this. Let us therefore allow the apostolic see to interpret itself, and let us more wisely observe from what it later said through Gelasius why Leo had earlier made those statements.

There is another letter of the same blessed Gelasius by which these misguided interpreters of Leo’s writings may likewise be refuted; but we have judged that this one alone is sufficient to cancel their argument.

[Note: The same manuscript has “even this one alone.”]

Very well, then: setting all these matters aside, suppose that Leo did say those things to the Romans in order to destroy the synod’s judgment concerning the letter of Ibas. How will the synod then be excused, since it is convicted both of having received that letter—which they falsely deny—and of having been wrong to receive it, according to Leo’s rebuke?

Therefore, if these sorts of words attributed to blessed Leo are understood in that way, they will undoubtedly serve not to repel the accusation against the synod, but to confirm it. And if that letter is called Nestorian, blessed Leo may perhaps, as has already been said, be defended from the Nestorian charge; but the Council of Chalcedon will plainly be condemned by Leo’s own testimony. The Eutychian heretics will then seem not without reason to have withdrawn from our communion—if, indeed, those who, with Leo as their witness, will prove that the synod whose name is pronounced in the confession of the sacrifice is Nestorian are still to be called heretics.

Let us nevertheless see how even blessed Leo himself can be excused, since this too has been said to us concerning him:

Why did he not attack so great a crime in clear and evident words? Why did he not openly and unmistakably overturn the judgment of the synod approving a Nestorian letter? Why did the apostolic see not condemn with such authority and severity what had first been announced by its legates, to the detriment of the faith, that the Church could afterward have no doubt—unless it was not with a true conscience but deceitfully and only in name that he rejected Nestorius, having been forestalled by the precedent of his predecessor Celestine? [Col. 0650B–C]

[Note: The same manuscript has “of the apostolic see.”]

Otherwise, he would also have refuted Nestorius’s doctrine in the letter of Ibas.

He clearly rebukes and condemns it in vehement, lengthy, and numerous letters, writing not only to the aforementioned Anatolius but also to the entire synod, to Maximus of Antioch, and to the emperors themselves. He commands that it be made known to all priests that he was displeased that one bishop had presumed to sit somewhere other than his proper place. Yet he is silent about and ignores the synod’s judgment by which the Nestorian letter was approved—or, if he does not remain silent, as you say, he nevertheless says nothing openly and nothing clearly.

This is precisely what the Lord rebukes in the hypocritical scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23:23): that they tithe mint, dill, and cumin while neglecting the weightier matters of the law and faith.

This is precisely what he similarly reproves in the blind guides themselves: straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel.

What can we say in reply to this? What can we answer on behalf of blessed Leo, whose concern and diligence for the catholic faith, whose labor and zeal, whose freedom and steadfastness, Your Piety knows very well, and whom the whole Church never ceases to praise?

But that letter is not Nestorian. Surely no insignificant little fox would have gnawed it in some later age; rather, the most courageous Leo would have attacked it at once.

How, then, do they say that the judgment of the synod concerning the letter of Ibas was not confirmed by blessed Leo, while they admit that he confirmed what the synod had established there concerning the faith, when in another part of the acts, from which that same letter was read, it is found that Ibas, its author, had been accused of Nestorian heresy?

For his accusers said:

> “Because he is a Nestorian and calls blessed Bishop Cyril a heretic.”

And again, the same passage contains:

> “Maras said: ‘We first raise the question of faith,’”

followed by other chapters after “we raise.”

> “The most reverend bishops said: ‘Although we proposed to you that the examination of these three chapters should follow, we have not thereby denied an inquiry into the remaining matters.’”

Maras said:

> “We first raise the question of faith.”

By these statements and others like them it is proved that Bishop Ibas was accused above all concerning the faith. For this reason they brought forward the letter in question against him.

The letter itself also proclaims two natures and one person of the one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ; for this reason the synod declared it orthodox. It would not have used that word if its judgment did not concern the faith.

But there is no reason for us to linger here any longer. Let them themselves deny that it is Nestorian, and let them deny that it pertains to the question of faith. If it is called Nestorian, then it is certainly accused concerning the faith; and since it is said to have been received by the holy synod, it consequently is also said to have been confirmed by blessed Leo, whom they do not deny to have confirmed what was established there concerning the faith.

Even if they are granted the further point that, apart from the definition of faith, Leo neither confirmed nor condemned the other things enacted at that synod, they still could not escape the charge of rashness—those inventors of a new rigor who dared to establish and say:

> “If anyone says that the letter to Maris is correct, or defends it and does not anathematize it, let him be anathema.”

[Note: The same manuscript has “the impious letter.”]

For the Council of Chalcedon calls it correct; Leo, even if he does not confirm it, does not anathematize it. Therefore, according to these people, Leo has been made anathema together with the Council of Chalcedon.

## CHAPTER V

### That it is not permissible to dispute after the decrees of the councils, and that the Eutychians are not to be heard if they resist the council’s definition concerning the letter of Ibas

Since it has been demonstrated by the clear and manifold force of the evidence that it is falsely denied that the synod pronounced the letter of the venerable Ibas orthodox, and since it has likewise become clear that blessed Leo did not judge it Nestorian—for without doubt he would also have condemned it by an explicit and forceful judgment—this is sufficient for the defense of that letter: so great a synod approved it, as did the author of the synod itself, an apostolic man renowned throughout the whole world for his teaching of the truth.

[Note: The same manuscript has “the Council of Chalcedon pronounced.”]

This is our first, immovable, and secure argument, which protects and strengthens us against all the questions raised by those who contradict us: that, as the Apostle says (2 Thessalonians 2:2), we should not quickly be shaken from our judgment or terrified, even if we cannot adequately give or receive a reason here for why the synod judged it orthodox.

For there is no other usefulness in holding councils than that we should believe on the basis of authority what we cannot grasp by understanding, and that, whenever reason comes less readily to us, faith should quickly come to our aid lest we fall.

For if it were permissible to dispute after a decree and say, “Let that letter first be proved correct, so that it may be believed to have been received,” there would be no reason for councils ever again to be convened, nor could questions be called settled—or even capable of being settled—if proof were always demanded.

[Note: “Every synod has unshaken authority, and one who re-examines a matter already judged wrongs the synod,” as Athanasius says in *Apology* 2: “Each synod possesses unshaken strength, and the one who judges is dishonored if the judgment is undertaken by others.” Facundus again says more to this effect in Book XII, chapter 2.]

Why should one not similarly say:

> “Let it first be proved that the Father and the Son are of one essence, so that we may believe that this was settled by the Council of Nicaea; and, because the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, let it first be proved that the Council of Constantinople decreed this, since it cannot otherwise be believed”?

In that way, with all questions remaining in their former condition, it would appear not only that nothing had been settled by the constitutions of the councils, but also that their memory had been preserved only for the perpetual renewal of disputes.

Therefore the method and order of inquiry after a council’s definition, confirmed by the agreement of the whole Church, must not be the same as before the definition.

Before the definition, reason required that, if the letter were proved orthodox, the synod should judge that it ought to be received. Now, however, reason requires that, since it was received by the synod, it should be judged orthodox.

If we maintain this observance, the cleverness of the heretics will have no power over us, provided that we do not presume to judge what we are unable to understand.

Nevertheless, we have understood something: we have understood the frauds of the heretics and refuted their errors.

[Note: The same manuscript has “we shall have understood.”]

It is therefore no small thing that we truthfully disprove error, even if we cannot teach the whole truth completely.

The Lord says to Jeremiah:

> “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth, and I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant” (Jeremiah 1:10). [Col. 0652D]

The prophet is therefore commanded first to uproot, tear down, and destroy errors and falsehoods, and then to build and plant knowledge and truth.

This is the perfect work and the preacher’s goal. If we cannot attain it, it is nevertheless certain that we have made a beginning. We have uprooted, torn down, and destroyed what had to be uprooted, torn down, and destroyed. If we are less able also to build and replant, let us leave that to better men, and meanwhile be content with the authority of the Fathers.

But someone may say:

“Are you going to bring the authority of the Council of Chalcedon against the Eutychians, in order to prove that the venerable Ibas’s letter is not Nestorian because the council judged it orthodox, when they instead accuse that very synod as Nestorian because it received the letter?”

First I answer that I am not obliged to give the Eutychians an answer on this point. The order of reason does not permit me to explain to them why our Fathers made their decision concerning the letter of the venerable Ibas.

They must first acknowledge with us what we have shown to have been confirmed even by the Council of Ephesus: that our Lord Jesus Christ is to be believed to exist in two natures. This is the principal point of disagreement between us and them. Only then, having become friends, may they ask that the reasoning behind the judgment of the Fathers be supplied to them.

If they remain enemies and despise God’s commandments, resisting the definitions of the holy Fathers, they must be scorned and rejected. They inopportunely seek from us knowledge of a matter which the Lord says in the Gospel is owed only to friends:

> “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:14–15). [Col. 0653B]

The reasoning of the Father’s counsel is therefore not owed to servants of sin who despise God’s commandments, even if they improperly and prematurely demand that we give it to them.

Thus the Apostle Peter commands us to be ready to answer everyone who asks us for a reason concerning the faith and hope that is in us (1 Peter 3:15), so that readiness itself corresponds to what the Apostle Paul, his fellow apostle, teaches: that we should know how we ought to answer each person (Colossians 4:6).

Knowing, therefore, how we ought to answer each person, we say that they must first agree with us concerning the confession of the two natures of Christ. This is either the sole or at least the chief cause of our disagreement. Only then may the remaining questions be sought, with the proper order preserved.

While that question remains between us, who would not judge it either superfluous or out of order to dispute with them concerning the synod’s judgment about the letter of Ibas?

Hence blessed Leo, when he promised to send chosen legates to the emperor Leo Augustus, said (Letter 78):

> “Let Your Piety, venerable emperor, know in advance that those whom I promise to send will not go forth from the apostolic see to fight against the enemies of the faith, nor to contend against anyone. For concerning the matters defined at Nicaea and Chalcedon, as it has pleased God, we dare enter into no discussion, as though those things which such authority has fixed through the Holy Spirit were doubtful or weak. We do not refuse the support of our ministry for the instruction of our little ones, who, after the nourishment of milk, desire to be filled with more solid food. Just as we do not despise the simple, so we refrain from rebellious heretics, remembering the Lord’s command: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine’ (Matthew 7:6). For it is exceedingly unworthy and unjust to admit to the freedom of debate those whom the Holy Spirit, through the prophet, signifies by saying: ‘Foreign sons have lied to me’ (Psalm 17:46). Even if they did not resist the Gospel, they would nevertheless show themselves to be among those of whom it is written: ‘They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him’ (Titus 1:16).” [Col. 0653C–0654A]

Our reasoning is therefore confirmed by the authority of blessed Leo: no proper order permits us to dispute with the Eutychians concerning the judgment pronounced about the letter of Ibas.

Furthermore, how can they themselves contend with us and accuse the holy synod of receiving a letter that contains an improper suspicion of its author concerning blessed Cyril, unless they first confess that the same suspicion of Ibas was false—namely, the suspicion by which he thought that blessed Cyril denied Christ’s existence in two natures?

Only then will they be able to accuse that letter of unjustly criticizing blessed Cyril; only then will they have reason to complain about the insult against him, if they too do not say, together with the aforementioned Ibas, that he proclaimed Christ to have one nature.

Otherwise, they will not be able to accuse that most reverend Ibas of a false criticism—unless perhaps they persuade us both that blessed Cyril proclaimed one nature of Christ composed from divinity and humanity, and that orthodox Ibas ought not to have condemned this, although the whole Church confesses that it is blameworthy.

You see, therefore, devout emperor, that for the present defense of this letter it is sufficient for us that the synod judged it orthodox and that it was not, as had been fabricated, expelled by blessed Leo, but rather confirmed by him together with all that was established there concerning the faith.

Therefore, as has been said, the mere proof of these matters is sufficient for us. No Catholic can resist the authority of so great a synod, and reason does not permit us to contend with the Eutychians—much less among ourselves, once the principal question has been settled—concerning the judgment pronounced about the letter of Ibas.

This is especially so because they could not complain of an insult against blessed Cyril, which they pretend to deplore out of hostility to the great synod, unless they first confess that he proclaimed Christ to exist in two natures.

[Note: The Verona manuscript has “will be able,” rather than “were able.”]

But since, as I think, the matters that had to be said have been sufficiently explained, and since the heretics have been driven far from examining this letter because many faults have been falsely and deceitfully charged against it through their surreptitious insertions, compelled by this necessity, I will not deny some small assistance to the instruction of our little ones, so that they may not be scandalized by such matters—not as one great as Leo, but as one somewhat greater among them—as a minister.

[Note: The same manuscript has “of my ministry.”]

For blessed Leo himself also granted this.

This, however, is on the one condition: that I do not place the merit of the case in my own reasoning, which I shall have to render an account of, since you plainly see that the matter is settled. Rather, let it rest upon the authority of the great synod, which we hold amid the waves and storms of the heretics as a safe and firm anchor for the soul.

Binding ourselves to this authority with devotion and obedience, let us first oppose to the barking of those who attack us the weight of the judgment of the Fathers, which we have shown to have been pronounced concerning the aforementioned letter. Then, in a most tranquil harbor of faith, let us seek the reasoning of the case—or show that we have found it—so that what is believed by faith may also be known by understanding: namely, that the great synod cannot justly be criticized because it judged the letter orthodox.

This is what, in the division of this work, we promised to demonstrate last.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0655]

## CHAPTER ONE

### That the Council of Chalcedon judged rightly in pronouncing the letter of Ibas orthodox, and followed the practice of Sacred Scripture, which is accustomed to reach a judgment about many matters from the greater and better part.

[Col. 0655A] Let us now begin to prove and demonstrate what remains: how unjustly the Council of Chalcedon is accused concerning the judgment it delivered on the letter of the venerable Ibas. For when the aforementioned Bishop Ibas approached that great council, complaining and lamenting that he had suffered injustice from Eutyches and had been burdened with false accusations, and that at the Second Council of Ephesus he had been condemned in his absence and while innocent—just as the testimony of reliable documents demonstrated—under Dioscorus, the defender of Eutyches and of the doctrine of Eutychianism, and had been dragged through forty stations in various provinces and transferred among more than twenty prisons—

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Ibas, accused of the Nestorian heresy by the clergy of Edessa, was first brought before Proclus of Constantinople. Letters of his survive in which he informs John of Antioch of the entire matter. After John’s death, he was again accused by the clergy before Domnus, John’s successor; when they were not received by him, they went to Flavian, who had succeeded Proclus in the imperial city. With the consent of Flavian, the emperor Theodosius appointed as judges of Ibas the bishops Photius and Eustathius, together with Uranius. After a double investigation, at Tyre and at Berytus, they acquitted Ibas. Thereafter, at the wicked Second Council of Ephesus, he was condemned in his absence by the faction of Eutyches and removed from his episcopate. When he complained about this before the Council of Chalcedon, the council, approving—as stated above—the proceedings at Tyre and Berytus and rejecting those of Ephesus, restored him to his former rank in its tenth session.]

At these words the bishops applauded and said: “No one condemns a person in his absence. Those who condemned him contrary to the canons acted wrongly. Let what was done against a person in his absence be annulled. We all say this: no one condemns a person in his absence.”

Afterward the deacon Theophilus, who was among the adversaries of the venerable Ibas himself, produced contrary proceedings: the records of those who had disputed with him before the bishops Photius, Eustathius [Note: [Col. 0655D] The same manuscript reads “and Eustathius,” or “Eustathius.”], and Uranius, appointed by the emperor Theodosius. He promised to demonstrate from their reading that Ibas had not been condemned unjustly. In the judgment of Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius, the accusers had claimed that they would prove the aforementioned Bishop Ibas to be a Nestorian. They attempted to establish this from a letter that he had once written to a certain Persian named Maris, because in it he seemed, in accordance with their suspicion, to have spoken of blessed Cyril, the condemner of Nestorius, otherwise than the facts warranted—a suspicion that he shared, as we showed in the first book, with the bishops of the East and of other provinces.

Yet just as he could not be judged a Nestorian at the very trial of Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius on account of that letter, since the sound confession of faith contained in it prevented this, so he was not condemned before the great council. When the aforementioned letter was read there from the same proceedings produced by his adversary, he was rather acquitted on the basis of its contents. For [Col. 0655D] in it he confessed two natures in such a way as to offend the Eutychians; hence they sought to have it condemned, and likewise because, in opposing the Nestorians, it confesses that there is one person, namely one Son, the Lord Jesus Christ.

The Eutychians, however, wishing to undermine the authority of that holy council, pretend that they are grieving over the injury done to blessed Cyril. On this basis they declare the council culpable because it pronounced the aforementioned letter orthodox. They add other criticisms of the letter itself—criticisms that not even the accusers of Ibas, although slanderous and obstinate, are shown ever to have raised anywhere in the course of the many trials they experienced. Yet they are not ashamed to appear more shameless than accusers who have so often been refuted.

Those accusers objected only to this against the aforementioned Bishop Ibas from his letter: wishing to make him appear a Nestorian, they claimed that in it he had disparaged blessed Cyril, the condemner of Nestorius. But concerning the other matters [Col. 0656B] that these men now add, they did not even dare to make the slightest mention. We shall refute them in order, setting forth the entire text of the letter.

It seems to us, however, that we must first say a few words about the claim that the council approved a disparagement of blessed Cyril, and about the matter with which the adversaries chiefly and principally accuse it—either scandalizing the less instructed by it, or, if they cannot do that, agitating them. Some of these men, although they defend that same holy council because of their piety and devotion to the faith, nevertheless, because they cannot resolve the question, persuaded by the supporters of the heretics, assert that the letter was not accepted by the council.

We are ashamed that assistance is being supplied to the adversaries by an obvious lie. Even if it had not been obvious, it ought still to have been unworthy of a Christian conscience to defend the truth by lying. Truth has its own arguments, not borrowed from falsehood, arguments that do not conflict with the testimony of conscience and that, remaining unconquered, shatter the slanders of its adversaries. If someone cannot discover such arguments, let him choose silence rather than lying and be content with the authority of the decrees alone.

For if the heretics see us using their lie in matters that are clear, what will they think us to be in other matters that appear obscure? Therefore, religious emperor, attend now to how forcefully and effortlessly I shall dissolve the slanders of the heretics, producing examples from divine Scripture to show how Scripture customarily delivers judgment on many matters from the greater and better part. The holy Council of Chalcedon followed this pattern in every respect when, although the venerable Ibas suspected blessed Cyril otherwise than the facts warranted, it nevertheless judged his letter orthodox because of the true confession of faith that it maintains concerning Christ [Note: [Col. 0657D] The Verona manuscript reads “contains.”]

Thus Scripture itself praised Asa, king of Judah, although we know that he was censured in no small number of matters. We must first recall what his faults were, and then how he was praised despite them.

First, it is said that he shared with many kings the fault that he did not destroy the high places (1 Kings 15:14). Although the Lord was worshiped there, this was nevertheless done against his command, since he had ordered that sacrifice be offered to him in the temple. Next, after giving the silver and gold found in the treasuries of the royal palace, he improperly sought the aid of the king of Syria against Baasha, king of Israel (ibid., 18). For this the prophet Hanani rebuked him, saying that he had acted foolishly by trusting in the king of Syria and not in the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 16:7). Moreover, because of this rebuke, in his anger he delivered the prophet Hanani himself into prison.

Finally, Scripture says of him: “In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa became diseased in his feet, with a severe illness; yet even in his sickness he did not seek the Lord, but physicians” (ibid., 12). We do not believe that he was condemned for seeking the assistance of physicians, which was appointed by God, but because he trusted so much in their skill that he expected help from them rather than from God through them.

Although he is therefore found blameworthy in these matters, he did not abandon the worship of the Lord, nor did he serve the idols of the nations. Rather, as it is written, he removed all the inventions that his fathers had made, and he removed Maacah [Note: [Col. 0657D] The same manuscript reads: “and Ana his mother,” and so forth. Asa’s mother is called Ana in the Greek version of the Septuagint (τῶν LXX, “of the Seventy”), but Maacah in the Hebrew text and in the Vulgate edition.] his mother from the worship of the sacred grove; he cut down the grove itself and burned it in the torrent of the Kidron. Accordingly, divine Scripture praised him by saying: “Asa did what was right in the sight of the Lord, like David his father” (1 Kings 15:11).

And lest someone perhaps say that Scripture praised his earlier conduct but that he later became depraved, hear what the same Scripture again declares about him: “Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was perfect with the Lord all his days” (ibid., 14). It would not say “all his days” if he had at some time departed from the condition for which he had been praised.

Since, then, the Scripture of God praised King Asa, who was blameworthy in so many respects, on account of his worship of the one true God—indeed, it compared him with and likened him to the holy king David, declaring that his heart was perfect with the Lord all his days—how can any religious person dare to criticize the Council of Chalcedon for preserving the custom and pattern of divine Scripture? The council pronounced the letter of the venerable Ibas orthodox: the letter confessed two natures and one person in Christ, matters that pertain especially to the worship of God. It disregarded the fact that the author of the letter had suspected blessed Cyril otherwise than the facts warranted, judging it superfluous to take this into account or to assign it any weight in a question of Christian faith.

Blessed Cyril himself likewise regarded such matters as superfluous when he wrote to the Eastern bishops through Paul, bishop of Emesa, saying: “Since an unnecessary and unwarranted division of the Churches has taken place, we have now been fully satisfied, as my most reverend lord Paul has produced a document containing an irreproachable confession of faith.”

Since blessed Cyril himself, recognizing that the faith of the Eastern bishops was correct, did not judge them heretics because of the false suspicion they had held concerning him—for he ought not to have done so—how could the holy Council of Chalcedon have appeared to oppose that same blessed Cyril if, because of this false and unnecessary suspicion, it had not pronounced orthodox the true and necessary faith concerning Christ contained in that letter?

The most reverend Bishop Ibas had thought that blessed Cyril, when the Eastern bishops sent him their confession, had not recognized in it the common faith but had corrected his own error. Neither we nor the holy Council of Chalcedon approved this. There it was said:

“Previously, after the records had been reread, the most reverend Ibas was shown to be innocent. For in those matters in which he appeared, while speaking wrongly, to blame the most blessed Cyril, he later rightly confessed and rejected the things for which he had blamed him.”

That letter, however, was not to be rejected as Nestorian because of this suspicion concerning blessed Cyril. The name “Nestorian” designates a wholly different error and the gravest impiety toward Christ. The author of the letter did not blame the Catholic faith that Cyril truly held, which is not subject to blame; rather, he blamed Cyril himself, thinking that, by resisting the doctrine of Nestorius immoderately, Cyril had ignorantly fallen into the opposing doctrine of Apollinaris.

If we distinguish these two matters, we do not call Nestorian a letter that the council called Catholic. It is one thing falsely to believe something concerning a person of this kind; it is another to hold an erroneous opinion concerning the foundation itself of the Christian faith.

Unless perhaps someone should say that, because of the injury done to blessed Cyril, the council ought to have condemned the sound faith of Cyril confessed by that letter—or ought not to have approved it—although, as we have shown, divine Scripture praised Asa, king of Judah, with such distinction. This would be as though it were a greater crime to suppose that Bishop Cyril had fallen into error than to suppose that a prophet had fallen into error—to say nothing of the fact that Asa delivered into prison a man who rebuked him for his sin.

Now receive another example, by which we defend without lying the judgment of the council concerning the letter of Ibas. We also remember that Jehoshaphat, king of Judah and son of the aforementioned Asa, did not remove the high places, like his father, among the other kings (2 Chronicles 20:33) [Note: [Col. 0658D] The same manuscript reads “we find.”]

Next, he was joined by kinship to the irreligious king Ahab of Israel. He even went to Ahab’s aid and, disregarding the word of God that had previously been announced to him through the prophet Micaiah, fought unsuccessfully against the king of Syria (2 Chronicles 18:1). Because of this, after Ahab had been killed in that same battle, Jehoshaphat was rebuked when Jehu, son of the prophet Hanani, said to him: “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has come upon you from the presence of the Lord” (2 Chronicles 19:2).

Finally, after being rebuked for his association with King Ahab, Jehoshaphat also formed a friendship with Ahaziah, an equally irreligious king of Israel, who had succeeded his father Ahab both in the kingdom and in every abomination. Hence Eliezer, son of Dodavahu the prophet, rebuked him, saying: “Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the Lord has broken your works” (2 Chronicles 20:37).

Although he too was censured and blamed in so many respects, because he worshiped the one God and removed from the land the remnants of the idols that had remained in the days of his father, divine Scripture praises him in this way: “Jehoshaphat walked in the way of Asa his father and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the Lord” (ibid., 32).

If, then, holy Scripture declared that King Jehoshaphat, whom we know to have erred in so many matters—not only rebuked by prophets but also, after their warnings, having disregarded the prophets themselves—did not turn aside from what was right in the sight of the Lord because of his worship of the true God and because he did not turn away to worship foreign gods, how can the Council of Chalcedon be impiously blamed for preserving the custom of divine Scripture and pronouncing the letter of the venerable Ibas orthodox because of the true confession of faith that it contains, in which God is rightly worshiped?

Or is it perhaps a lighter fault to have been joined by friendship and kinship to irreligious men and to have disregarded prophets sent by the Lord than to have formed a false opinion about Cyril, a bishop?

But let us now produce a third example, which will also be the last, showing how, as we have said, divine Scripture customarily delivers judgment on many matters from the greater and better part. The holy council followed this pattern when it approved the letter of the venerable Ibas.

For Scripture likewise relates the following concerning King Hezekiah: “In those days Hezekiah became sick unto death” (2 Chronicles 32:24). He prayed to the Lord, and the Lord heard him and gave him a sign. But Hezekiah did not repay him according to the favor bestowed upon him; instead, his heart was exalted, and wrath came upon him, upon Judah, and upon Israel [Col. 0659D] [Note: [Col. 0659] The same manuscript reads “Jerusalem.” The text of sacred Scripture agrees with this in 2 Chronicles, chapter 32, verse 25.]

For this reason Isaiah prophesied against him, saying: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when everything in your house, and whatever your fathers have stored up until this day, shall be carried away to Babylon; nothing shall be left, says the Lord. And some of your sons who shall issue from you, whom you shall beget, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon” (2 Kings 20:17; Isaiah 39:6).

Although his heart was so exalted that on account of it he received this most severe punishment from the justice of God, the same Scripture says of him: “He did what was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done” (2 Kings 18:3; 2 Chronicles 29:2). And again: “He trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel, and after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him. He clung to the Lord and did not depart from him, and he kept his commandments, whatever he commanded Moses; and the Lord was with him in everything” (2 Kings 18:5).

How, then, did divine Scripture praise the man whom it described in such terms that even his sons would be carried into captivity and serve as eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon? Even if we set aside what it said of him—“He did what was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done”—and again, “He trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel, and after him there was none like him among the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him”—how was it said of him: “He clung to the Lord and did not depart from him, and he kept his commandments, whatever the Lord commanded Moses”?

Is it perhaps being said that the exaltation of his heart, which so displeased the Lord, clung to the Lord, did not depart from him, and kept the commandments that the Lord had given, when pride is the beginning of every sin?

What else can we say except that, by these words, Scripture wished it to be understood that Hezekiah did not worship the gods of the nations as other kings had done, nor did he depart from the worship of the one true God. Rather, he observed whatever the Lord had commanded Moses concerning this matter, and, as it is written, “he destroyed the high places, crushed all the idols, cut down the sacred groves, and crushed the bronze serpent that Moses had made, to which the children of Israel had offered sacrifice until that time” (ibid., 4).

Accordingly, he is said to have clung to the Lord, not to have departed from him, and to have kept all his commandments, whatever the Lord commanded Moses—not because of that exaltation of heart for which he deserved so great a measure of divine judgment.

## CHAPTER II

That the council pronounced the letter of Ibas orthodox because of its confession of the two natures in Christ, not because of its false suspicion concerning blessed Cyril.

[Col. 0660D] Therefore that holy council too, not exceeding the pattern of canonical Scripture in its judgment, pronounced his letter orthodox according to the Catholic and universal confession of two natures in one person of Christ, not according to the private suspicion that Ibas, together with others, had held concerning blessed Cyril [Note: [Col. 0659D] Liberatus also affirms this in chapter 13. Vigilius explains in his *Constitutum* in what sense it was called orthodox. Yet among all the judgments of the bishops concerning Ibas that are read in the Council of Chalcedon, only three—which Facundus recited in the preceding book—mention his letter to Maris, and only two of these pronounced it orthodox. Therefore the Fifth Council, as noted in its proper place, refutes those who argued that the council had accepted the letter, establishing that the judgment of the others concerning it had not been the same.].

By the very term with which it called the letter orthodox, it showed that it had approved the confession of faith contained in it. For it was not the praise of blessed Cyril but the true confession of Christian faith that deserved this name.

Otherwise, we would have to call the Eutychians orthodox because they magnify blessed Cyril, thinking that he held what they hold—which the most reverend Ibas, though he ought not to have attributed it to blessed Cyril, nevertheless rightly judged blameworthy.

But if the praise of blessed Cyril does nothing to help the Eutychians be judged orthodox, and if they are instead pronounced heretics because they deny the two natures of Christ, then the suspicion concerning blessed Cyril ought not to have weighed against the letter so as to make it heretical. Rather, because it confessed the two natures of Christ in the unity of his person, it ought to have been pronounced orthodox [Note: [Col. 0661D] The Verona manuscript reads: “The false suspicion concerning blessed Cyril ought not to have weighed against the letter of the venerable Ibas,” and so forth.].

Accordingly, just as it does not follow that, because we pronounce the aforementioned Eutychians heretics, we must therefore condemn in them their praise of blessed Cyril, so it does not follow that, because the holy council pronounced the letter of the venerable Ibas orthodox, it thereby appears to have approved the injury done in it to blessed Cyril.

“But,” someone says, “if the Council of Chalcedon did not accept the injury done to blessed Cyril, why did it approve without qualification the letter that spoke wrongly about him, and pronounce it orthodox without any exception? It ought to have said that its author had erred in certain respects.”

It is indeed shown by the matters recalled above that the council did not rebuke the author of the letter for this error, because, in those matters in which he had appeared to blame the most blessed Cyril while speaking wrongly, he himself had later rightly confessed and rejected the things for which he had blamed him.

Nevertheless, even if the council’s judgment contained no such statement, it would still not be credible that it approved the injury done to blessed Cyril in the letter of the venerable Ibas, since the testimony of the records of the council itself shows that it praised Cyril’s faith with many and harmonious voices.

And even if this evidence were lacking, no one could demonstrate in the council’s judgment that it approved everything contained in the letter. Therefore, if another person were permitted to accuse the council on the ground that its judgment did not say that it approved some things in the letter, I too would certainly be permitted to excuse that same council on the ground that its judgment did not say that it approved everything.

For just as the council did not say that the letter was correct in some respects, so it did not say that it was correct in all respects. If it had said “in all respects,” I would understand this as referring to the confession of faith that we hold concerning Christ, just as we understand the statement that Asa’s heart was perfect with the Lord all his days to refer to his worship of the one true God; and just as we understand the statement concerning Jehoshaphat—“He walked in the way of his father Asa and did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the Lord”—to refer to this; and just as we understand that Hezekiah was said to have clung to the Lord, not to have departed from him, and to have kept his commandments, whatever the Lord commanded Moses, for this reason.

Moreover, as we have already said, the very term “orthodox,” which was applied to the letter, is customarily assigned by a council to a confession of Christian faith.

It is nevertheless astonishing that those men say that a letter which correctly confesses the mystery of Christ’s incarnation could not, or ought not, to have been judged orthodox by the council because of the passing and very slight suspicion that it contains, while they themselves said: “One must look openly at the letter to Maris, which says everything without God and impiously.”

For if they thought it most just to define as godless and impious that letter which confessed the two natures of Christ in the unity of his person, how could it seem unjust to the holy council to pronounce it orthodox on account of the same correct confession of faith that it contains, when the council is not found to have approved it in every respect?

Therefore, if the letter of the venerable Ibas is to be approved for the confession of faith concerning Christ that it contains, but rejected for the suspicion that its author held concerning blessed Cyril, judge, I beg you, religious emperor, whether the council should be blamed, since its judgment does not show that it approved the letter in every respect, or whether those should be blamed who dared to declare that the entire letter speaks without God and impiously.

The holy Council of Chalcedon, although it marked in the most reverend Ibas that his suspicion concerning blessed Cyril was false, would nevertheless, even if it had not done so, have been shown—as we said—to have followed the pattern of divine Scripture by pronouncing his letter orthodox because of its correct confession of Christ’s incarnation, which pertains above all to the worship of God.

But what pattern or rule will those men be said to have followed who, because of one man’s suspicions concerning another man, rashly called even the correct confession concerning Christ impious?

## CHAPTER III
