That the council could not condemn the letter of Ibas without likewise condemning Cyril for heresy; and that, in replying to Nestorius, Cyril deliberately spoke more sparingly concerning the distinction between the two natures.

With these points established, which sufficiently defend the judgment of the great council against the calumnies of the heretics from the censure of blessed Cyril that has been accepted, as they claim—you surely already gather in your mind, pious prince, that we can refute much more easily those charges which were not even brought by the venerable accusers of Ibas themselves, but which they allege as crimes contained in his letter. We now transfer the complete text of that letter [Note: [Col. 0661D] It is found in Greek and Latin in act 10 of Chalcedon, from the proceedings of the synod of Berytus, where it had first been produced by the adversaries of Ibas. It is also found in the Fifth Synod, but in another translation. Thus this third version, used by Facundus, exists nowhere in full, but everywhere without a beginning and lacking its preface. Therefore, in the Greek copy it is entitled as follows: “From the letter written by Bishop Ibas, after the prefaces.” [Col. 0662D]] from the proceedings of the synod into this book, as we promised.

After the prefaces, then, it reads as follows (Council of Chalcedon, act 10):

> “In brief, we hastened to report to your luminous wisdom—which recognizes much in little—what was done here previously and what is now being done; for we know that what we write to your holiness, and what is taking place here, will become known to everyone there through your diligence [Col. 0663A], since they have accepted no alteration of the Scripture handed down by God.
>
> “I shall begin this account with statements which you yourself also know. A dispute arose between these two men, Nestorius and Cyril, while your holiness was here, and they wrote harmful books against one another, which became a scandal to their hearers. For Nestorius said in his books, as your holiness knows, that blessed Mary is not the Mother of God; so that many thought him to be the one who, following the heresy of Paul of Samosata, said that Christ was merely a man.
>
> “Cyril, wishing to destroy the books of Nestorius, stumbled and was found to have fallen into the doctrine of Apollinaris. For he too wrote in the same manner as that man, saying that God the Word himself became man, as though there were no distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it [Col. 0663B].
>
> “For he wrote twelve chapters, which I think your holiness also knows, stating that there is one nature of the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that, as he says, one ought not to divide the words spoken either by the Lord himself about himself or by the Evangelists about him.
>
> “These statements are full of every impiety even before we say so, as your holiness knows. For how can the words ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1:1) be understood of the temple born from Mary? Or how can the words ‘You made him a little lower than the angels’ (Psalm 8:6) be spoken of the divinity of the Only-Begotten?
>
> “For the Church speaks as your holiness knows and as you learned from the beginning, and divine teaching, confirmed by the books of the blessed Fathers, declares: two natures, one power, one person—which is one Son, the Lord Jesus [Col. 0663C] Christ.
>
> “Because of this dispute, the victorious and pious emperors ordered the leading bishops to assemble in the city of Ephesus and to judge the books of Nestorius and Cyril before everyone. But before all the bishops who had been ordered to assemble arrived at Ephesus, Cyril himself, anticipating them, took possession of everyone’s ears with a drug that blinds the eyes of the wise.
>
> “He found an opportunity in the hatred that existed against Nestorius and, before the most holy and reverend Archbishop John arrived [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: ‘was present at the synod.’], they deposed Nestorius from the episcopate without judgment or investigation.
>
> “Two days after his condemnation we arrived at Ephesus. When we learned that, in the condemnation of Nestorius which they had carried out, they had introduced the twelve chapters written by Cyril as contrary to the true faith, and had confirmed them and agreed with them as consonant with the true faith, all the Eastern bishops condemned Cyril himself and decreed excommunication against the other bishops who had agreed with his chapters [Col. 0663D] [Col. 0664A]. After this disturbance, each man returned to his own city.
>
> “Nestorius, however, because he was hated by his own city and by its leading men, could not return there. The Eastern council therefore remained out of communion with those bishops who had communicated with Cyril. Because of this, great sorrow arose among them, and bishops were in conflict with bishops and peoples with peoples; and what is written was fulfilled in deed: ‘They will be enemies of those of his own household’ (Matthew 10:32) [Note: The same manuscript reads: ‘of his own domestic servants.’]
>
> “From this, many slanders against us arose from the pagans [Note: The same manuscript reads: ‘from pagans and heretics.’]. No one dared travel from one city to another or from one province to another; rather, each person persecuted his neighbor as an enemy [Col. 0664B].
>
> “Many people, without the fear of God before their eyes, hastened, under the pretext of ecclesiastical zeal, to bring to effect the enmities which they secretly harbored in their hearts. Among them was the tyrant of our city [Note: He calls his predecessor Rabula by this name. Rabula had anathematized Theodore, as Liberatus also reports in chapter 10 of his *Breviary*. In the Fifth Synod there is a letter of Cyril of Alexandria to Rabula, bishop of Edessa, in which Cyril praises him for expelling the Nestorian heresy which arose from Theodore the Cilician; and another letter of Rabula to Cyril, in which he denounces Theodore as the author of Nestorian doctrine.], whom you yourself do not fail to know. Under the pretext of faith, he persecutes not only those now living but also those who long ago preceded us to God.
>
> “One of these is blessed Theodore, herald of the truth and teacher of the Church. During his life he not only struck heretics in the face through the truth of his faith, but after his death he left spiritual weapons in his own books for the sons of the Church, as your reverence learned when you conversed with him and were instructed by what he wrote.
>
> “This man dared to anathematize him publicly in the Church [Note: The same manuscript reads: ‘This man, who presumes everything, dared to anathematize [him] publicly in the Church,’ and so forth. The text agrees with Ibas’s letter to Maris the Persian in act 10 of the Council of Chalcedon and in collection 6 of the Fifth Ecumenical Council.], although, through his zeal for God, he had converted [Col. 0664C] not only his own city from error to truth but also instructed Churches situated far away by his teaching. Much examination of his books was therefore undertaken everywhere—not because they were alien to the true faith, for I often saw him reading Theodore’s books frequently while Theodore was still alive—but because of the hidden enmities he held against him, since Theodore had openly convicted him in the synod.
>
> “While these evils continued, and each person departed as he wished, as it is written, our God, who is to be worshiped and who always cares for the Church by his mercy, moved the heart of the most faithful and victorious prince to send the venerable [Note: The same manuscript reads: ‘that he might send a great man, known in his palace, who might compel the venerable …’] and most holy Archbishop John of the East, so that he might be reconciled with Cyril; for Cyril had been deposed from the episcopate by him.
>
> “After he received the emperor’s letters [Col. 0664D], he sent the most holy and reverend Paul, bishop of Emesa, writing through him the true faith and commanding him that, if Cyril agreed with this faith and anathematized those who say that the divinity suffered, or those who say [Col. 0665A] that there is one nature of divinity and humanity, he should communicate with him.
>
> “The Lord, who always cares for his Church, which he redeemed with his own blood, willed to soften the heart of the Egyptian, so that he might agree to the faith without difficulty, accept it, and anathematize all who believed without it. When they communicated with one another, the dispute was removed, and peace was made in the Church. There is no schism in it, but peace, as there was previously.
>
> “What words were written by the most holy and reverend Archbishop John, and what reply he received from Cyril, I have joined to the letter which I sent to your reverence and transmitted to your holiness, so that, on reading it, you may know and announce to all our peace-loving brothers that the dispute [Col. 0665B] has now ceased, the middle wall of enmities has been removed, and those who had attacked the living and the dead in a seditious manner are in confusion, making satisfaction for their excesses and now teaching the opposite of what they previously taught.
>
> “No one now dares to say that there is one nature of divinity and humanity; rather, they confess the temple and the one dwelling in it, who is one Son, Jesus Christ.
>
> “I have written these things to your holiness out of the great affection I have for you, knowing that your holiness exercises yourself night and day in the teaching of God, so that you may be useful to many.”

This is the complete text of that letter, which, as we have already shown, the great Synod of Chalcedon pronounced orthodox after it had been read aloud before them.

I shall therefore undertake, with the help of the Savior, to defend the judgment [Col. 0665C] of that synod not only against those statements which were censured in the aforesaid letter in writing by the supporters of the heretics and condemned as Nestorian in criticism of the judgment mentioned above, but also against whatever else we know to have been repeatedly attacked in the reckless words of irreligious men. Through the structure of this exposition, wherever appropriate, we shall also show that, if the synod had judged the same letter heretical, it would thereby rather have established that blessed Cyril was a heretic, excused Nestorius, and criticized the Council of Ephesus.

Accordingly, let us transfer into our work the statements which they said should be censured in writing, in the wording and context in which they were set down by them [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “they have brought [them forward] in the very wording,” etc.], so that no one may think that we have omitted anything relevant to the case. [Col. 0665D] Thus they said:

> “The accusers of Ibas entered and themselves requested that what had been charged against Ibas at Tyre before the God-loving bishops Photius and Eustathius be read again. When the proceedings were reread, a certain letter was found among them, presented as having been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian and filled with every impiety.
>
> “For it contains the following: ‘Cyril, wishing to destroy the books of Nestorius, stumbled and was found to have fallen into the doctrine of Apollinaris [Col. 0666A]. He too wrote in the same manner as that man, saying that God the Word became man.’
>
> “And later: ‘For how can the words “In the beginning was the Word” be understood of the temple born from Mary? Or how can the words “You made him a little lower than the angels” be spoken of the divinity of the Only-Begotten?’
>
> “Again: ‘Cyril, anticipating everyone with a drug that blinds the eyes of the wise, took possession of their ears, and they deposed Nestorius from the episcopate without judgment or investigation.’
>
> “He adds that, in the condemnation of Nestorius which they carried out, they introduced, confirmed, and agreed with the twelve chapters written by Cyril as contrary to the true faith, as though they were consonant with the true faith.
>
> “And shortly afterward, disparaging the bishop of Edessa, he says: ‘This tyrant of our city, who presumes everything in the Church, dared publicly to anathematize blessed Theodore, herald of the truth and teacher of the Church [Col. 0666B].’”

To anyone who reads them, it is clear that we too have set down all these things not as they are contained in that letter, but as they themselves, tearing them out and mangling them according to their own will, have asserted them and stitched them together into a single patchwork. But so that your serenity may recognize their customary frauds more clearly than daylight, and the leaps they made in their account—not, as they wished to appear, to avoid prolixity, but rather to obscure the truth, so that the intention of Ibas’s speaker might in no way become apparent—compare what they included with the text of the letter which we cited above. It will then be for your wisdom to discern whether the passages they skipped and refused to touch would have made the narrative lengthy, or whether they would rather have disclosed the very matter [Col. 0666C] which they feared more clearly.

Of all the points they censured in this letter, we first clear two, because they are joined together in a single chapter but have been improperly divided by these men. The first is what they placed at the beginning, saying: “Cyril, wishing to destroy the books of Nestorius,” and so forth. The second is what they placed in the second position, namely: “For how can the words ‘In the beginning was the Word’ be understood of the temple born from Mary?” and so forth.

First, it must certainly be admitted that this letter sufficiently shows that the most reverend Ibas, as has been said, together with the Eastern bishops and those of other provinces, understood the meaning of blessed Cyril’s statements less well and suspected that he denied a distinction of natures in Christ. Consequently, he judged that Cyril had fallen into the doctrine of Apollinaris, who did not believe that God the Word had become man by assuming human nature, but thought that a part of the substance of God the Word had been converted into flesh [Col. 0666D] [Note: Augustine, *On Heresies*: “The Apollinarists most obstinately assert that something belonging to the Word was converted and changed into flesh, and not that flesh was assumed from Mary’s flesh.” This monstrous heresy, when it first reached Athanasius’s ears, was refuted by him with the greatest care in his letter to Epictetus, bishop of the Corinthians; Epiphanius consequently copied that letter in full in his treatment of the heresy of the Dimoerites, or Apollinarists.].

For this reason he added there and said:

> “For he too wrote in the same manner as that man—that is, Apollinaris—saying that God the Word himself became man, as though there were no distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it.”

The venerable Ibas [Col. 0667A], then, did not fail to know that God the Word became man; rather, against the madness of Apollinaris, he denied that he became man by conversion. Blessed Cyril himself, in the book called *Scholia*, under the heading “How Christ is One,” says:

> “Therefore, even if others have been called Christs by a similar designation, there is nevertheless one, Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist—not that the creator of all things became man.”

We should not think that Cyril wrote this against the prophet who says, “The mother of Zion shall say: ‘A man, and a man was made in her’; and he himself, the Most High, founded her.” Rather, he wrote it with the intention that God the Word, the creator of all things, did not become man in the sense of Apollinaris—that is, by conversion.

Either, therefore, in both passages we understand that God the Word, the creator of all things, is denied to have become man because he did not become man by conversion, and neither passage will be censured as involving the Nestorian error; or, if this is not granted, the same fault will apply to both.

Even the Eutychians themselves do not want blessed Cyril to appear Nestorian when he says that the creator of all things did not become man, or that God the Word, through whom all things were made [Col. 0667B], participated in flesh and blood in the same way as we do and was called man [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “but that God …”]. Yet the very expression “was called” opens the way to slander, as though he had merely been called man and had not truly become man [Note: The same manuscript reads: “and had not truly become man.” It is therefore fair that they should not want the letter of the venerable Ibas to appear Nestorian, since, while censuring the same blessed Cyril, it says: “For he too wrote in the same manner as that man, saying that God the Word became man”; for he too, and so forth.].

For Ibas himself immediately adds there:

> “As though there were no distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it.”

But if the great synod rejected this letter as heretical, would it not, as we have said, thereby rather make blessed Cyril [Col. 0667C], who similarly said that the creator of all things did not become man, appear to have believed as a heretic? If the venerable Ibas had read other statements of the same blessed Cyril, or had attended to them as he ought, he would undoubtedly have found that Cyril too, against Apollinaris, denied—according to the intention we have explained—that God the Word became man, and taught a distinction of natures.

But in answering Nestorius, who divided the one Christ into two sons, Cyril had no need to argue against him more clearly and explicitly concerning two natures. Indeed, so as not to give any opportunity to Nestorius’s error, he spoke more sparingly about the distinction of the natures, lest, when he himself distinguished the natures, Nestorius should introduce two persons.

The Eastern Fathers therefore heard or reread the words of the speaker, yet did not perceive [Col. 0667D] his intention, according to which words must be judged. For one must attend not so much to what is said as to why each thing is said. We could indeed produce many testimonies from divine Scripture concerning the difference between intention and words—if that difference should properly be called a difference—showing how Scripture often seems to deny something which ought not to be denied, in order to indicate something else that is more necessary [Note: The same manuscript reads: “how something seems to be denied.”].

But since the matter with which we are now concerned has been peacefully settled by its own authors, these two examples will suffice for us.

For who [Col. 0668A], unless he were instructed by other testimonies of divine Scripture, would believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was either good or God, hearing Mark the Evangelist relate the following about him?

> “And when he had gone out onto the road, a certain man ran up, knelt before him, and asked him, saying: ‘Good Teacher, what shall I do to receive eternal life?’ But Jesus said to him: ‘Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God’” (Mark 10:17).

The Lord said this in order to admonish him that he should believe him to be God if he wished truly to confess him as good, because, as the examiner of the heart, he saw that the man believed him to be merely human and not also God. Although to some heretics who do not understand it he may seem to have denied that he was good, to Catholics who do understand it he plainly appears rather to have indicated that he was God.

For who, hearing only what the same Evangelist Mark similarly relates about the Lord, would not deny with the Manichaeans [Col. 0668B] that he was the son of David? Taking advantage of this very testimony, the Manichaeans reject the mystery of his incarnation.

> “Jesus,” he says, “was responding and teaching in the temple: ‘How do the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself says in the Holy Spirit: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.” David himself therefore calls him Lord; so how is he his son?’” (Mark 12:35–37).

By saying this, then, he did not deny that he was the son of David—that is, a man—as the ignorant suppose. Rather, he indicated what was necessary: that he was God, David’s Lord. For if he is neither God, because he says, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God,” nor man [Col. 0668C], because he says, “David himself calls him Lord; so how is he his son?” what are we to say that he is?

A prudent reader will find other expressions of this kind in the divine writings. According to them, an interpreter who explains a speaker’s words in such a way that he too seems to deny something which ought not to be denied, in order to indicate something else that is more necessary, should not be condemned as a heretic. Rather, he should be judged from his other statements. In the same way, no Catholic dares to censure the divine Scriptures themselves in such passages; instead, from their other, clearer statements, he recognizes how he ought to understand what is obscure.

Accordingly, if blessed Cyril, seeing Nestorius [Note: The same manuscript reads: “seeing Nestorius.”] attempt to introduce a certain wicked duality, narrowed his speech [Col. 0668D] more toward matters concerning unity, so as not to give any opportunity to his error, then, conversely, the earlier teachers of the Church, when answering Apollinaris, who most foolishly confused the diversity of the natures, pressed more strongly upon their distinction.

Thus Cyril, while resisting the Nestorian, ought not to be thought to have denied the distinction of the natures, just as those who resisted Apollinaris ought not to be thought to have denied the unity of the person. For the order and manner of the struggle are not always the same; rather, the cause of the attacker determines how the defender ought to oppose him.

## CHAPTER IV. [Col. 0669A] That Ibas, wrongly suspecting Cyril, censured in his letter not Cyril’s faith but what he falsely thought to be Cyril’s faith, and in reality approved Cyril’s faith concerning the incarnation of Christ.

These things, however, have been said not because the venerable Ibas held a wrong belief about Christ, but because he held a wrong belief about the blessed Cyril himself; nor because the confession of the preacher concerning the Christian faith is displeasing, but because the suspicion of one human being concerning another is displeasing in his letter. For what Catholic could take exception to the natural distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it, when the Church of God confesses the Word to have become flesh in such a way that it does not deny what is added there, namely, that he also dwelt in us?

The Word indeed became flesh because the eternal Son, who is the Father’s Word, himself became man in the fullness of time [Col. 0669B]. He dwelt in us because his immutable divinity underwent no change, but, remaining what it was, inhabited the nature that had been assumed. Therefore, “the Word became flesh” refutes the Nestorians, while “he dwelt in us” refutes the Eutychians, or their progenitors the Apollinarists: for “the Word became flesh” signifies that there is one person, whereas “he dwelt in us” signifies that two natures remained. There cannot be two persons, since the one who is the Word himself also became flesh; nor can there fail to be two natures, since what inhabits is one thing and what is inhabited another.

If anyone, without inclining to either side, investigates the matter without contentiousness, he will find that both the intention of the holy Eastern Fathers [Col. 0669C]—although they held a wrong opinion about the blessed Cyril—and that of the blessed Cyril himself was always the same: to teach that the one Lord Jesus Christ was perfect in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity, lest he be thought to have two persons because there are two natures, or to have one nature because there is one person.

It sometimes happens among men who hold the same opinion that, although they agree about the very matters under dispute, they nevertheless suspect one another of something else—either because the speaker expresses less clearly in words what he has conceived in his heart, or because the hearers pay insufficient attention to the speaker’s intention. The impiety by which someone holds a wrong belief about God must be distinguished from the ignorance by which, as one human being judging another, someone suspects his neighbor of something else. And even if [Col. 0669D] suspicion of one human being concerning another seems blameworthy, the intention by which the truth of the faith that we hold concerning Christ is asserted must nevertheless be approved.

Those discoverers of a new kind of diligence who wished to obscure this intention—how faithfully and simply do they act! After quoting from that letter the words, “For he too wrote similarly to him, because God the Word himself became man,” they passed over what follows: “as though there were no difference between the temple and the one dwelling in it.” Why, we wonder, did they do this? Was it because those very few syllables would make the passage too long? Or rather because they would plainly reveal the speaker’s intention?

O faith! O integrity! O conscience of those who rightly handle the word of truth! Surely these men can say with the Apostle: “We renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in cunning nor adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of truth commending ourselves to every human conscience before God” (II Cor. 4:2).

But now that their frauds have also been detected and exposed in this matter, observe, I beg you, most serene emperor, how from the other words that follow it becomes even more and more evident [Col. 0670A] [Note: [Col. 0669D] Veronese Codex, “even more and more.”] that the most reverend Ibas did not speak against the faith that we hold concerning Christ in his letter, but understood the intention of the blessed Cyril less fully in his Chapters.

For he continues, as the complete wording of the letter itself has it:

“For he wrote [Col. 0670B] twelve Chapters, which I think your Reverence also knows, because there is one nature of the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and because, as he says, one ought not to divide the statements spoken either by the Lord himself concerning himself or by the Evangelists concerning him.”

Who would not see that, as has been said, the most reverend Ibas understood less fully not the mystery of Christ’s incarnation but the intention of the blessed Cyril, since he, like the other Eastern Fathers—and even those Acephali who pretend to venerate him—thought that Cyril had proclaimed one nature of the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ and had said that one ought not to divide according to the natures the statements spoken either by the Lord himself concerning himself or by the Evangelists concerning him?

Finally, they also demanded from him through the venerable Paul of Emesa [Col. 0670C] [Note: [Col. 0669D] The same codex: “the bishop Paul of Emesa.”] that he should openly confess in writing:

“The venerable and most reverend John of Antioch, after receiving the emperor’s letters, sent the most holy and most reverend Paul, bishop of Emesa, writing through him the true faith and instructing him that, if Cyril agreed with this faith and anathematized those who say that the divinity suffered, or those who say that there is one nature of the divinity and humanity, he should enter into communion with him.”

Indeed, because the blessed Cyril, having received the embassy of the Easterners [Col. 0670D], hastened more to fulfill what was being requested by his fellow priests than to provide a sufficient defense of the statements by which they had been offended, he was thought to have been converted at the admonition of the Easterners, as though his former error had been condemned. He, however, eager to restore unity, did not wish to linger in defending his statements, lest, while he contended at length to prove that he had not said what was attributed to him, and that those who understood him less fully had therefore formed a different opinion, the controversy should find no end because of this disagreement.

The most reverend Ibas likewise indicates this in the words with which he subsequently reported that the same blessed Cyril agreed without hesitation with the faith of the Easterners, accepted it, and anathematized all who believed without it.

But is it a Nestorian crime to have thought that the blessed Cyril had been converted? Let those who called this letter Nestorian answer us [Col. 0671A], whether it is to be called Nestorian heresy to divide into two persons the one God and man, Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made and who himself was made among all things, or to have thought that Cyril, his servant, had been converted. We greatly excuse Nestorius if we say that his heresy consisted in having thought that Cyril had been converted.

Therefore, if the Council of Chalcedon had rejected this letter as Nestorian for that reason, it would rather have seemed, in the very matter that we promised to demonstrate, to have excused Nestorius. But that devout council ought not in this way to mitigate Nestorius’s grave crime, since it well knew that the blasphemy that gave its name to this heresy was very different [Note: [Col. 0671D] Nestorius imagined two persons in our Savior. For he did not believe that the one who was God was the same as the one who was man, but held that there was one Son of God and another son of Mary. He said that Mary was not θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), but χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*), that is, that she had given birth not to God but to a man, and that the Word, the Son of God, had not become man from Mary by assuming human nature, but had later descended upon the man born from Mary at his baptism [Col. 0672D]. Finally, he said that Mary had given birth to a temple for God, not to the one who dwells in the temple. This, then, was that wicked duality which Facundus said in chapter 3 that Nestorius had attempted to introduce.]

That blasphemy empties the mystery of the divine incarnation [Col. 0671B], upon which our salvation rests; it asserts one subsistence for man and another for God, thereby alienating the human nature from God, although that nature was healed in its first fruits by the Word who assumed it.

The council, however, saw Ibas’s letter as plainly confessing what those men were afraid to touch: that, although there are two natures, there is nevertheless one power, one person, namely, one Son, the Lord Jesus Christ. Consequently, whoever calls this letter Nestorian unquestionably asserts, together with the Eutychians and against the Church, that it is Nestorian to proclaim one person of Christ in two natures. For there is no other reason why the Eutychians now defame the Church and call the faithful of Christ Nestorians than that they profess two natures belonging to the one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore, while restraining the heretics, let them not pretend [Col. 0671C] that they condemned the letter of the venerable Ibas as Nestorian because it said that the blessed Cyril had been converted. If that is blameworthy, it is nevertheless not a Nestorian crime. Rather, the supporters of the heretics are shown to have declared it Nestorian for this reason: that its author confessed in it that Christ has two natures.

Nor should they now say that the letter blamed the faith of the blessed Cyril, since they cannot prove this at all. First, because after the union had been made between the Easterners and Cyril, it approves his faith. In addition, even before the union, it attacks not the faith that Cyril truly held, but the faith that it thought he held.

As we have already proved from the words of the letter itself, Ibas thought that the blessed Cyril had proclaimed God the Word to have become man [Col. 0671D] in such a way that there was no distinction of natures—that is, no distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it—but that there was one nature of the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore, whoever says that the most reverend Ibas in his letter argued against the faith that the blessed Cyril truly held [Col. 0672A], and not against the faith he thought Cyril held, himself plainly confirms that the blessed Cyril had proclaimed God the Word to have become man in such a way that there was no distinction of natures, but that one nature of divinity and humanity had come into being. This is what the most reverend Ibas blamed through his letter.

Who, then, are the ones who assert that the blessed Cyril was a heretic? Is it we, who say that Ibas did not attack his faith, or those who say that Bishop Ibas attacked Cyril’s faith? [Note: Veronese Codex: “his very faith, or those, etc.”]

We, who say that he did not attack the faith of the blessed Cyril, certainly deny that Cyril removed the distinction of the natures and said that one nature composed of divinity and humanity existed. But the supporters of the heretics, who say that Ibas argued against Cyril’s faith, themselves unquestionably assert the claims of the Eutychians, who say that the blessed Cyril did not believe in a distinction of natures, but taught that one nature had been formed from divinity and humanity.

Accordingly, if the Council of Chalcedon also had believed [Col. 0672B] that the most reverend Ibas had attacked the faith that the blessed Cyril held, rather than the error into which it thought he had fallen, it would unquestionably itself have affirmed that Cyril had proclaimed Christ to have one nature.

You recognize, therefore, devout emperor, that what we said is once again being demonstrated: if that great council had rejected this letter as attacking the faith of the blessed Cyril, it would rather have appeared thereby to believe the blessed Cyril himself to have been a heretic.

For this reason the supporters of the heretics also tried to persuade us to affirm this, so that nothing would remain with which we could answer the Eutychians whom they restrain when they say:

“If you have declared the letter of Ibas to be Nestorian—let it be said to belong to anyone else—which thought [Col. 0672C] that it was heretical to deny the distinction of natures and to believe that there is one nature of the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, how are you not Nestorians in your own judgment, since you likewise say that it is heretical to deny the distinction of natures and to believe that there is one nature of the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ?

“Or how can you now say that the blessed Cyril taught a distinction of natures, rather than saying that there is one nature of divinity and humanity, when you condemned that letter precisely because it had attacked his faith, and it is found to have attacked in him the fact that he had denied the distinction of natures and had taught that there is one nature of divinity and humanity?”

And for this reason we neither condemn that letter nor say that it attacked Cyril’s faith, because what it attacked was not Cyril’s faith.

For it is utterly and truly full of impiety [Col. 0672D] to understand, as referring to the confusion of natures, what the Evangelist said about the temple born from Mary: “In the beginning was the Word”; or, concerning the divinity of the Only-Begotten, which can neither increase nor diminish, to believe that it was diminished in its own nature, being made a little lower than the angels [Col. 0673A] [Note: [Col. 0673D] Veronese Codex: “as it is not said even in one and the same [man].”]—just as we say, in one and the same man, that the inner man was formed in the image of God, while the outer man was created from the clay of the earth according to the outline of his limbs and the distinction of sex.

But the blessed Cyril is never shown to have thought that the temple, which took its beginning from the Virgin Mary, and God the Word, who was in the beginning and is without beginning, are of the same nature.

This was the belief of the Apollinarists; from the Apollinarists the foolish Eutychians derived it [Note: [Col. 0673D] The error of Eutyches was contrary to that of Nestorius: he asserted one nature composed of the Word and humanity, whereas the Catholic faith, opposed to both, asserts one person in Christ against Nestorius, while at the same time acknowledging in him, against Eutyches, two natures that are neither confused but distinct and perfect, divine and human [Col. 0674D].]

If Cyril too held this view, it would most truly be said that he had fallen and had been found to have lapsed into the doctrine of Apollinaris. But we do not now believe that this is true, because it is not proved that he ever held such an opinion.

## CHAPTER V

That the false suspicion of Ibas concerning Cyril [Col. 0673B] ought not to have prevented the council from declaring Ibas’s letter orthodox, since the comparable suspicion of the Easterners did not prevent Cyril himself from subscribing to the confession of the Easterners.

But someone says again: “How, then, did the synod pronounce orthodox an epistle which censured the blessed Cyril, whom you say never proclaimed anything of the kind?” I answer: because that epistle proclaimed the faith of the blessed Cyril. For if, after the union effected between the Orientals and Cyril himself, it approves his faith, while we believe that Cyril’s faith had always been the same, it necessarily follows that Ibas also approved his faith before the union, although he did not know that it was Cyril’s.

Consider, moreover, the synod’s own judgment, and you will find that in that epistle—disregarding human suspicions—it approved those things [Col. 0673C] that pertain to the faith of Christ, for the sake of revealing and confirming which the synod had assembled. It would be called orthodox not as an honor to Cyril, nor as an injury to any heretic, but because it contains the true faith concerning Christ.

If anyone censures the Council of Chalcedon because, setting aside a man’s suspicion concerning another man, it pronounced the epistle of the most reverend Ibas orthodox, he must also censure the blessed Cyril himself. For Cyril likewise, disregarding the same suspicion held by his fellow Oriental bishops—who, assembled with bishops from other provinces, had condemned his chapters—transferred into his own epistle the confession of faith that they had sent him through the venerable Bishop Paul, entered into communion with them, and professed that he believed and proclaimed the same things concerning the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. He did not ask them to condemn the suspicion they had held concerning him, nor did he consider it necessary even to offer them satisfaction for it [Note: [Col. 0673D] In the same manuscript, τὸ nec (“nor”) is missing.]

Yet the Council of Chalcedon is not censured only together with the blessed Cyril for having pronounced this epistle orthodox, but together with the entire Council of Ephesus [Col. 0674A], since that council likewise embraced their communion [Note: [Col. 0673D] The same manuscript reads: “but together with the entire Council of Ephesus.” For it was not the blessed Cyril alone who, making nothing of the Orientals’ suspicion, judged them orthodox; the other Fathers who were with him at the Council of Ephesus did so as well, and they entered into communion with them, etc.].

Thus it now appears that the great council is accused not because it called the epistle of the venerable Ibas orthodox, but because it did not itself censure the blessed Cyril together with the Council of Ephesus. Since, then, everything we promised has been set forth, recognize that if the Council of Chalcedon had rejected the epistle of the venerable Ibas as heretical, it would rather have seemed to believe that the blessed Cyril was a heretic, that he had excused Nestorius, and that he had censured the Council of Ephesus.

Accordingly, in this too the council mentioned above followed the example of the blessed Cyril himself—or rather, of the Council of Ephesus. Just as that council, by prudent judgment, accepted the entirely correct faith concerning Christ held by all the Orientals, although they had formed an incorrect suspicion concerning Cyril himself, so this council likewise accepted the entirely appropriate faith concerning Christ contained in Ibas’s epistle, although the epistle contained certain inappropriate suspicions concerning the blessed Cyril.

Should this holy synod, then, be thought to have gladly accepted insults against the blessed Cyril, whom it is shown to have imitated by disregarding utterly alien suspicions—and whose example it would have accused had it not disregarded them? Or should it for that reason not have acquitted the most reverend Ibas and restored to him his episcopate and the Church from which he had been unjustly expelled in his absence by the faction of Eutyches, merely because he had been mistaken about the person of the blessed Cyril and had at some point thought that he had erred—although he approved Cyril’s faith not only knowingly after the union with the Orientals, but also unknowingly before the union?

“But,” they say, “after this union he ought not to have spoken such things about the blessed Cyril.” I, however, say that he ought not to have done so even before the union—indeed, not even before the Council of Ephesus. Cyril ought first to have been questioned, and then censured if he did not give satisfaction.

But what we are now asking is whether this fault of the venerable Ibas—which, as we have already proved, was also noted by the synod—ought to have been considered so serious that his epistle should be pronounced heretical, even though it approved the faith of the blessed Cyril in the confession that the Orientals had sent him through Bishop Paul for his signature, although at that time it did not yet understand his intention in the twelve chapters.

The great synod recognized that the same faith was present both in those chapters and in the confession signed by the blessed Cyril. It therefore judged that it made no difference in what words Ibas approved the faith proclaimed by Cyril, since it was clear that he had approved what it was necessary for him to approve [Col. 0674D].

Therefore it neither believed nor ought to have believed anything else except that the Oriental Fathers—including Ibas himself—and the bishops of the other provinces had failed to grasp the intention of the blessed Cyril’s chapters, and so censured them even though they had been accepted by the Council of Ephesus [Col. 0675A].

In the same way, at one time certain Catholics in the matter of the divine Trinity were unwilling to accept three hypostases [Note: [Col. 0675D] The Greeks, as Saint Augustine teaches in *On the Trinity*, book V, chapter 8, customarily said μία οὐσία, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις (*mía ousía, treîs hypostáseis*), which in Latin, as he himself explains, means “one essence, three substances.” But because usage had established among the Latins that *substantia* was understood in the same sense as *essentia*, they did not dare to say “three hypostases,” lest they seem to be saying “three essences.” Instead they said “one essence” or “one substance,” but “three persons.” Those who said “three hypostases”—the Greeks and Orientals—understood nothing other than three persons, as Epiphanius testifies in *Heresy* 73 and Gregory of Nazianzus in Oration 21. They distinguished ὑπόστασις (*hypóstasis*) from essence, whereas the Latins, in Gregory’s view, were unable to make the distinction because of the poverty of their language.

Yet the Latins alone, and not the first, were not the only ones who failed to distinguish οὐσία (*ousía*) from hypostasis. For the Nicene council, in its exposition of the faith, condemned those who said that the Son of God was ἐξ ἑτέρας ὑποστάσεως ἢ οὐσίας (*ex hetéras hypostáseōs ē ousías*, “from another hypostasis or essence”), apparently using the two expressions as equivalent, although Saint Basil takes a different view in Letter 78. Saint Athanasius likewise teaches that the Father and the Son are μία οὐσία, μία ὑπόστασις (*mía ousía, mía hypóstasis*, “one essence, one hypostasis”) in *Oration* 5 against the Arians and in his letter to Liberius; in his letter to the Africans, however, he explicitly affirms that ὑπόστασις οὐσία εἶναι (*hypóstasis ousía eînai*, “hypostasis is essence”).

Finally, at the Council of Alexandria, as reported by Athanasius himself in his letter to the Antiochenes, when the bishops disagreed—some preferring to say “three hypostases,” others “one”—those who said “one” professed that they considered hypostasis and essence to be the same: ταὐτὸν εἶναι εἰπεῖν ὑπόστασιν καὶ οὐσίαν (*tautòn eînai eipeîn hypóstasin kaì ousían*, “to say hypostasis and essence is to say the same thing”). Although that council discovered that both sides were correct in their understanding and differed in wording rather than in doctrine, it nevertheless judged that, henceforth, the appearance of novelty should be avoided and nothing beyond the Nicene formula should be sought. It communicated this decision in its synodical letter to the Antiochenes. But that decree achieved nothing. For, as has been said, it prevailed among the Greeks and Orientals that they should insist emphatically on three hypostases and compel others to adopt the same confession.

Hence Jerome’s complaint against the Antiochenes to Damasus, Letter 57: “Now, alas! after the Nicene faith, after the Alexandrian decree jointly issued by East and West, a new name—‘three hypostases’—is being demanded of me, a Roman, by an Arian bishop and by the Campenses.” As for our own people, who had resisted as long as they understood ὑπόστασις to mean “substance,” once they began, following the example of the Greeks, to distinguish that word from substance and to interpret it as “person” or “subsistence,” they no longer hesitated to profess, and to require others to profess, three hypostases together with the Greeks.]

Although they understood three persons, they were not therefore judged heretics by wise men [Note: [Col. 0676B–C] For since some used “hypostases” in the same sense in which others used “persons,” neither group could rightly condemn the other, since, as Nazianzen writes, the words were leading to the same understanding: ῥημάτων εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν φέροντων διάνοιαν (*rhēmátōn eis tēn autēn pheróntōn diánoian*). Thus at the Council of Alexandria neither those who asserted three hypostases were considered Arians—because they understood hypostasis not as substance but as person—nor those who asserted one hypostasis were considered Sabellians, because they understood hypostasis not as person but as substance.] For it was discovered that they were offended not by the reality signified by that name, but rather by the name itself by which it was signified.

Accordingly, Ibas’s epistle cannot be judged heretical unless it is said that the chapters of the blessed Cyril contain the correct faith, whereas the confession of the Orientals to which he subscribed was Nestorian; and unless it is also said that Ibas and the Council of Chalcedon accepted that confession in their own definition. In that case, Ibas and the aforesaid council would be accused, while Cyril, after Nestorius had been condemned, would be confirmed as having turned toward the Nestorian heresy.

For this reason it has been believed that the blessed Cyril had not previously held a correct position in his chapters, but was later corrected by the admonition of the Orientals. When the union of the Churches was effected, it was not the Oriental Fathers who were compelled to subscribe Cyril’s chapters; rather, Cyril himself was sought out to subscribe to the confession sent to him by them.

Some have therefore believed that Cyril’s retraction of his chapters [Note: [Col. 0676C–D] Cyril wrote twelve chapters, or anathemas, against the errors of Nestorius. They were appended to his own epistle and to the Alexandrian synod’s letter to Nestorius, and were read together with that epistle in the first session of the Council of Ephesus. The Oriental bishops, in their private gathering, branded and condemned these anathemas as heretical. Cyril, however, so as to remove every pretext, first retracted and explained his chapters at the urging of the synod, attaching to each anathema what he called an ἐπίλυσις (*epílysis*), or explanation. He then composed an apology for the same chapters against the Orientals, in whose name *antirrhēseis*—“refutations”—were circulated, each directed against one of the anathemas. Andrew, bishop of Samosata, is thought to have been their author; Cyril mentions him in Letter 30 to Eulogius. Finally, after receiving Theodoret’s book against the same chapters, composed at the command of John of Antioch, he undertook a second defense of them, in which he refuted each of Theodoret’s *anatrophai*—“overturnings”—with a corresponding apology. All these works may now be found published in Greek and Latin after the Council of Ephesus.] was made after the Council of Ephesus not so that matters previously closed to some might be opened, and things that had seemed obscure might be made clear, but rather so that he might correct in them the former error which, as was thought—and as the Eutychians still think—consisted in his saying that Christ has one nature.

Thus it came about that the union was thought to have occurred through the conversion of the blessed Cyril. And indeed, who would not be seized by this suspicion? We are speaking of human hearts, and we bear human hearts. The Oriental Fathers, who had judged these chapters in need of correction, were not compelled to correct anything; whereas the blessed Cyril not only subscribed, at their insistence, to the confession of faith which they had formulated and considered necessary, but also retracted his own chapters.

As for the objection that they spoke not so much against the blessed Cyril as against the Council of Ephesus, because through insufficient understanding they had formed an incorrect opinion concerning chapters that had already been accepted: in the following book, since that subject seems more appropriate there, we shall say much about it—much, as I believe, that should not be disregarded.

But if it is heretical to believe that Cyril had been converted, why, I ask, should the blessed Theophilus not much more be called a heretic? He wrote such and so many things about Saint John of Constantinople, whose authority and teaching the Church of Christ ought to venerate far more [Note: [Col. 0676D–0678D] He later calls it an “enormous book,” from which the following passages are drawn. Theophilus of Alexandria had been hostile to Chrysostom not only while Chrysostom was alive—to such an extent that he eventually drove him into exile—but also after his death, preventing his name from being entered in the diptychs. Yet by God’s singular providence he was not permitted to breathe his last until, by honoring Chrysostom’s image, he had been reconciled with him, as Damascene relates from the *Chronography* of Isidore the Deacon, *On Images*, book III, at the end.]

so that necessity alone can excuse us even for recalling them [Col. 0677A] [Note: [Col. 0677D] The Verona manuscript reads “the necessity of the case.”]

“Brothers,” he says, “John persecutes with the unclean spirit by which Saul was strangled; and again, he has killed the ministers of the saints.” He says that John was polluted and impious in the Church of the firstborn, pestilential, mad, and raging with the insanity of a tyrannical mind, and that in his madness he gloried and had handed his soul over to the devil to be violated.

We have set down all these statements exactly as they appear in Theophilus’s own book [Note: [Col. 0677D] The same manuscript reads “of the blessed Theophilus.”] He also calls John an enemy of humanity, one who by his crime surpassed the boldness of robbers, the leader of sacrilegious men, an impious priest, offering sacrilegious offerings, shameless and hard-faced beyond endurance.

He adds that John was not caught in snares from which he might ever be released, but in snares by which he would hear God threatening him according to the merit of his crime and saying: “Judge between me and John: I expected him to execute judgment, but he committed iniquity, and not justice, but a cry.”

He also says that, just as Satan transformed himself into an angel of light, so John was not what he appeared to be. He calls him not merely like Satan, but an unclean demon, dragging along the filth of his words like a torrent. He declares that John had been impious toward Christ and was the companion of Judas the betrayer.

He further adds that John was accused of stretching out impious hands against God, and that what the Apostle James said of certain people greedy for worldly things—“You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4:3)—the blessed Theophilus asserted that the blessed John had said about Christ: “He dared to say in church that Christ had prayed and had not been heard because he had prayed badly” [Col. 0677C].

Who among the heretics blasphemed more terribly than the blessed Theophilus reports that the blessed John blasphemed? Theophilus says that John had surrendered himself to participation in Jewish impiety and, with his customary rashness, offered what the Jews had offered: himself and the peoples, deceiving them, and emulating Dathan and Abiram. “Let him hear,” he says, “with the Jews: your iniquity has been greatly magnified” [Note: [Col. 0677D] The same manuscript reads “your iniquity.”]

He adds: “Arians and Eunomians delight in John’s blasphemies against Christ; Jews and idolaters, the Gentiles, have been justified in comparison with you.”

Again he says: “John is not merely not a Christian; he is worse than the king of Babylon, much more criminal than Belshazzar. John is more wicked than idolaters and pagans. To you,” he says, “present disgrace and eternal punishment in the ages to come will be repaid.”

The blessed Theophilus also seemed to say this: “The Savior cried out and said, ‘Take John and cast him into outer darkness.’” And again: “He supplied the most abundant fuel for his own fire before the tribunal of God.”

Nor were all these things sufficient for his anger and fury [Note: [Col. 0678D] The same manuscript reads “for the fury of Theophilus”], unless he also said of the holy man John just mentioned that another punishment had to be sought for him, because the magnitude of his crime surpassed the multitude of his torments.

If anyone wishes to test whether we have set down not merely the ideas but the very words, and to learn how often Theophilus repeated them, let him read the enormous book—translated by the presbyter Jerome—which is excessively horrible not only for its insults but also for its frequent repetition and recapitulation of curses. The blessed Theophilus expected that through Jerome’s eloquence the Latins would learn what kind of man John had been.

But in that book we learn not what kind of man John was—for he deserved none of these things—nor what kind of man Theophilus was, whose virtue had been proved in many respects and ought not to be judged from this incidental illness; rather, we learn what wretched human life is, concerning which it is written: “For there is temptation upon the earth” (Job 7:1).

For if such things happened to such men, what ought we not to fear—for ourselves and for those like us? Yet here I should like to question the judges of the dead, who, for the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon, want us also to judge the dead: by what reason, and by what justice, is the charge of heresy assigned to Cyril because he is said to have been converted, while Theophilus is not judged a heretic [Note: [Col. 0678D] The same manuscript reads “is not said to be a heretic”], although he accuses Saint John, the most illustrious teacher of the Church, of having said that Christ prayed and was not heard because he had prayed badly?

Theophilus is also said to have attributed such statements to John that Arians and Eunomians delighted in his blasphemies against Christ, as did Jews and idolaters, and that he had surrendered himself to Jewish impiety.

If they have no answer—because they judge that Theophilus should not be called a heretic on account of human insults—let them cease also to accuse the Council of Chalcedon of having judged the epistle of the venerable Ibas in the same way.

Following the judgment of this venerable Theophilus, his predecessor, the blessed Cyril himself later, as we showed in the fourth book, forbade John’s name to be recited after his death among God’s priests during the sacrifice, even contrary to the judgment of the apostolic see, which, through the most blessed Pope Innocent, had released the condemnation of the aforesaid Saint John, who was then in exile.

And just as his predecessor Theophilus had said that Arians delighted in John’s blasphemies, so Cyril himself compared John to Eudoxius, the Arian bishop. Yet no one judged either Theophilus or Cyril a heretic on account of this opinion, because the case that deserves that name is entirely different.

The holy synod also took this into consideration in the epistle of the venerable Ibas. Disregarding and setting aside human suspicions concerning another human being, it pronounced the epistle orthodox because of the true confession of the Christian faith that it contains.

It must also be believed to have foreseen this: if it had judged the epistle heretical on account of the slight and temporary suspicion that its author, together with the Orientals and bishops from various provinces, had held concerning the blessed Cyril, then by the same reasoning Theophilus would much more have been judged a heretic. For Theophilus said that John had been impious toward Christ and had dared to say in church that Christ had prayed and had not been heard because he had prayed badly, and that Arians and Eunomians delighted in his blasphemies against Christ, as did Jews and idolaters.

This suspicion of his was neither slight nor transient. He transmitted it even to his successor Cyril, so that Cyril too excluded John from the ecclesiastical walls [Note: [Col. 0679D] The Verona manuscript reads “excluded”], called him a Judas and a Jeconiah, declared him profane, and thought him comparable to Eudoxius, the bishop of the Arians.

Therefore it is not justly said that the holy synod ought to have condemned Ibas’s epistle as heretical on account of the suspicion that its author once held concerning the blessed Cyril together with many others. Rather, if it had presumed to do this, it would thereby have made the blessed Cyril himself appear condemnable, as has already often been shown.

For who—even among the calumniators themselves—would deny that Cyril wrote more serious things about Saint John than Ibas wrote about Cyril?

These scandals, and any others of the kind [Note: [Col. 0679D] The same manuscript reads “any such scandals”], rightly offend us in Fathers whom God established in his Church as luminaries, so that we might be enlightened from above by their excellent knowledge and teaching. Yet they seem to me to be regarded in the same way as the eclipses of the heavenly luminaries themselves: although they sometimes suffer a diminution of their brightness, they do not cease to be luminaries, remaining what they are.

Indeed, it often happens that these luminaries of the Church also, because we are separated from them by a great height, appear obscure to us through a kind of cloud of our ignorance, although they remain radiant in themselves.

Let the statements of Theophilus and Cyril concerning that great luminary, John of Constantinople, therefore be regarded as a kind of eclipse of luminaries. Let the statements of the Orientals and of the other Fathers who had gathered with them from different provinces likewise be regarded as another eclipse of luminaries, since, slightly darkened by a failure of understanding, they formed an opinion about the luminary Cyril different from what the matter actually was.

Those whom Christ has preserved in the enduring peace of his Church, as in the firmament of heaven, we ought to venerate and accept. We should not stir up endless conflicts over controversies that have now ended, nor rashly condemn the dead; rather, we should consider that we too shall die, and should believe what accords with Christian piety: that, for their labors in the Church of Christ and for the merit of the peace that they themselves preserved for the Church, if, before passing from this life, through human error rather than diabolical envy, they were unable to amend anything done against certain private persons, they are at rest with him through the Lord’s forgiving indulgence, awaiting securely the judgment of eternal recompense; for they never ceased to pray to him not to remember the sins of their youth and ignorance.

Therefore we must fear lest those whom we judge here and now—where everything is permitted to us, though not everything is beneficial—should, when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, and all the nations are gathered before him, become our judges.

The reasoning and comparison that we offered in the preceding book, when we were discussing the statement of the venerable Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, should also be applied here. He declared that Dioscorus had not been condemned for the faith. For just as it did not make Dioscorus a heretic that he wished Dioscorus himself to be excused from perfidy, since it is one thing to excuse a heretic because he is thought to be a Catholic, and another thing to approve and defend the heresy itself, so the epistle of the venerable Ibas could not justly be regarded as heretical—even if it is established that it did not narrate what actually happened as it appeared at the time, but accused the blessed Cyril [Note: [Col. 0680D] The same manuscript reads “had accused”]. For it is one thing to accuse a Catholic because he is thought to be a heretic, and another thing to disapprove and censure the Catholic faith itself.

And just as our statement benefited the defense of the venerable Anatolius—that someone can approve chastity and love it, yet approve a fornicator without approving fornication, when he is mistaken about the person—so let the following statement also benefit the defense of the most reverend Ibas, of the other Orientals, and of the bishops of the other provinces: someone can approve chastity and love it, yet, without disapproving chastity, disapprove a chaste person when he is similarly mistaken about the person.

For if the venerable Ibas, or the other Orientals and bishops of the other provinces whom we have mentioned, were mistaken about the person of the blessed Cyril rather than about the rule of faith—just as Cyril himself, together with Theophilus, was mistaken about Saint John—the holy synod understood this. It therefore pronounced Ibas’s epistle orthodox and accepted those men as Fathers.

But we, through contentiousness and the empty glory that we also seek everywhere to acquire through presumption, judging ourselves wiser than so great a synod, have transferred a very slight suspicion concerning a person to the rule of faith. We have enlarged a speck into a beam—not one of the same size, but of the same kind—and have turned a contemptible straw into an enormous battering ram that would uselessly batter the whole world of the Roman Empire.

Who could consider worthily, or explain in words sufficiently, how wisely God uses even human ignorance to instruct those who are predestined? His omnipotent goodness, whenever he wills, turns every harmful thing toward great benefit.

For that ignorance of Cyril’s fellow bishops concerning the blessed Cyril—which had at one time been contrary to the peace of the Churches—now benefits the Church’s instruction and defense, if anyone considers it carefully. It is a more evident proof of the true faith when the same judgment is found among those who disagree with one another than when it is found among those who are at peace.

For although the Oriental bishops, together with others, thought wrongly about the blessed Cyril and therefore attacked him vehemently [Note: [Col. 0681D] The Verona manuscript reads “attacked him vehemently”], we nevertheless learned through the venerable Bishop Paul of Emesa that both sides were contending for one and the same faith.

The Orientals expected from the blessed Cyril no other confession than that which the Church had always held and still holds. And the blessed Cyril joyfully fulfilled what was expected, receiving with eagerness their confession concerning the mystery of the divine incarnation and declaring it to be his own.

Therefore anyone who thinks rightly about Cyril, who believes him to have possessed a truly apostolic disposition, ought to consider how greatly he could have rejoiced when he saw the zeal of the Fathers—especially the Oriental Fathers—burning against him on behalf of the truth of the faith that he himself also held.

That his colleagues were mistaken about him would not have mattered so much to the most holy man as the fact that they were contending for the truth of the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0681D] The same manuscript reads “were contending in defense of the Christian faith”]. He preferred his fellow bishops to condemn the error into which they thought he had fallen, without regard to his person, rather than to defend him for his own sake in a way contrary to the truth [Note: [Col. 0681D] The same manuscript reads “which is.”]

Let us hear the Apostle speaking to the Galatians: “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:3).

Since the Apostle preferred that not only he himself, but even an angel from heaven preaching something contrary to what he had preached, should be accursed rather than that Christ’s faithful should be moved from the firmness of the Gospel preached to them, how much joy should we believe the blessed Cyril could have felt when he saw himself attacked by his fellow bishops on account of the faith that he held and wanted all to hold?

Because they were mistaken about him, he did not believe that the stability of the Christian faith rested there, nor did he think that their error would last long, since it was within his power afterward to reveal the reasoning behind his statements and calm the agitation of those who judged otherwise.

But because they asserted faithfully and steadfastly what belonged to the truth—even though it had not been necessary to assert it against Cyril—he judged that there lay the stability of the true faith, their salvation and his own, and the future stability of all the Churches: namely, that no one should thereafter doubt the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, concerning which the same judgment was found even among those who disagreed and held different opinions about one another.

Why, then, do we, fainthearted people, grieve over the joy of the magnanimous Cyril? Why do we disturb the Church over the very matter from which it ought to be defended against every disturbance? Why do we give heretics cause to laugh over something by which they ought to be confounded?

All this is the work of rash and ignorant presumption, which neither knows how to answer those who contradict it nor submits to the definitions of the Fathers. This is why it is easily deceived; this is why it is ensnared by the stratagems of heretics—more restless than strong.

We, however, first and foremost submit with calm and humble hearts to the decrees of the holy Fathers and are strengthened by their authority. Then we also understand that the holy synod, prudently discerning the intention of Eutyches and of Ibas, justly condemned Eutyches as sacrilegious and pronounced his doctrine heretical, even though he praised the blessed Cyril, because it rejected Cyril’s faith, which was the more important matter to consider.

In the same way it justly acquitted the most reverend Ibas and pronounced his epistle orthodox, even though the epistle censured the blessed Cyril, because it approved Cyril’s faith, which was the more important matter to consider.

Consider what that distinguished bishop, the most vehement despiser of empty glory [Note: [Col. 0681D] The same manuscript reads “that most vehement despiser of his empty glory”] and most sincere lover of truth, Augustine, says [Note: [Col. 0681D] The same manuscript reads: “Augustine says, at the beginning of the books he wrote on the Trinity, ‘We ought to consider this.’ ‘I believe,’ he says, ‘that some slower readers will think in certain passages of my books that I held an opinion that I did not hold,’ etc. The words before ‘I believe’ belong to Facundus, not Augustine; the following words are found in *On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 3, no. 6.]:

“I certainly think that some slower readers will suppose, in certain passages of my books, that I held an opinion which I did not hold. Who does not know that their error ought not to be attributed to me if, as though following me but failing to apprehend me, they stray into some falsehood while I am compelled to make my way through certain dense and obscure places? For no one would rightly attribute to the sacred authorities of the divine books themselves all the many and varied errors of the heretics, although all of them endeavor to defend their false and deceptive opinions from those same Scriptures.

“The law of Christ—that is, charity—plainly admonishes me and commands me with most gracious authority that, when people think I held something false in my books which I did not hold, and that falsehood displeases one person, I should prefer to be censured by the one who censures falsehood rather than praised by the one who praises it. For although I did not hold that opinion and therefore was not rightly censured by the former, the error itself is rightly censured; but I am not rightly praised by the latter, who thinks that I held what the truth censures, nor is the opinion itself rightly praised when the truth censures it” [Note: [Col. 0682D] The same manuscript reads: “one person dislikes it, another approves it; I should prefer it,” etc., at the cited passage.]

If, then, we think well of the blessed Cyril, and attribute to him wisdom and charity, let us believe, together with that just man Augustine, endowed with wisdom and piety, that when Cyril was falsely thought to have held in his chapters what he did not hold, he would have preferred to be censured by Ibas, who censured falsehood, rather than praised by Eutyches, who praised it.

And if he were alive now, he could himself answer us when questioned and say:

“By my venerable brother Ibas and my other fellow bishops, although I, who did not hold this view, was not rightly censured, the error itself was nevertheless rightly censured. But by the wicked man Eutyches [Note: [Col. 0682D] The same manuscript reads “the wicked man”], and by his accomplices, neither am I rightly praised, since they think that I held what the truth censures, nor is the opinion itself rightly praised when the truth censures it.”

## BOOK SEVEN

### CHAPTER ONE

That when Ibas said in his epistle that Christ had one power, he did not deny two natures in Christ, but asserted one person.

[Col. 0683]

I am not unaware that, to inexperienced assessors of matters, an argument for resolving questions may seem slow and less effective. For, because it proceeds by a cautious and investigated rather than a hurried step, surveying everything, it is criticized by them for slowness. Moreover, since, given the difficulty of its task, it must disclose through a more subtle treatment certain secrets and inner recesses of the truth—which cannot be brought to light quickly—in order to exclude either the slander of one lying in ambush or the ignorance of one who understands less—both of which operate at the surface of things and words—those who are both incapable of reasoning and impatient with it endure this most painfully. No one complains more about the delay of a reasoner than the person whose slowness is being assisted by it.

But we are more afraid of offending the judgment of the wise, by whom we shall certainly be blamed if we omit what the usefulness of the case most demands. [Note: [Col. 0683D] Codex of Verona: “then.”] And therefore we must inquire what sort of other considerations there are on account of which the venerable letter of Ibas is said not to have deserved to be judged orthodox.

For the same most reverend Ibas, confessing his faith, says:

> “For the Church speaks thus, as your Holiness also knows, and as it learned from the beginning, and as it has been confirmed by divine teaching from the books of the blessed Fathers: two natures, one power, one person, which is one Son, the Lord Jesus Christ.”

For this reason some again criticize him in the opposite direction, because he said that the Lord Jesus Christ has one power. They ask: How can one power belong to two natures that are very far apart from each other, namely, divinity and humanity? Consequently, when one power is asserted, the diversity of the natures is removed, so that, according to the madness of Eutyches, one nature also seems to exist.

[Note: [Col. 0683D] By contrast, Justinian in the edict and the Fifth Synod draw from these words a suspicion of Nestorian doctrine. They maintain that Ibas, in Nestorius’s manner, understood “two natures” as two persons [Col. 0684D], but said “one power” and “one person” not according to hypostasis (οὐ καθ᾽ ὑπόστασιν), but according to one dignity and the same honor (κατὰ μίαν ἀξίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν τιμήν).]

By saying this, they certainly confirm with us that the aforementioned letter is not Nestorian, since they think that the statement that the one Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, has one power accords with the error of Eutyches—that is, with the error opposed to the Nestorians. Hence it is also believed that he was not criticized by these supporters of Eutyches.

But why the most reverend Ibas, or the synod that declared his letter orthodox, should be censured on account of this word, I do not know. For he did not add this against the distinction of the natures, about which he had spoken correctly above, as though he had thought that the power of the created substance was one and equal to that of the Creator’s substance. [Col. 0683D] [Note: [Col. 0683D] The same codex: “that.”] Rather, he considered that the same power belongs to one person.

For if charity, poured out through the Spirit of our Lord himself into many persons, had such strength that it could rightly be said in the Acts of the Apostles, “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32) [Note: [Col. 0684D] The same codex: “rightly be said.”], how could it not rightly be said that there is one power belonging to that person whose gift brought it about that this multitude had one heart and one soul?

And if it is answered that the heart of that multitude of believers could therefore rightly be said to have been one, and its soul one, because all were of one nature, that is, human nature, whereas the Lord Jesus Christ has two distinct natures, let them understand first that the heart and soul of those believers were not one on account of their being of one nature, but rather because the one Spirit of Christ granted them this unity. For it is not nature that makes us of one mind, but fellowship of spirit.

Next, let them consider what the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

> “Do you not know that the one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body? For, he says, ‘The two will be one flesh.’ But the one who joins himself to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:16).

Now, if it has rightly been said not only of natures but also of distinct divine persons [Note: [Col. 0684D] The same codex: “different.”], “The one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit,” how can what the holy synod approved in the venerable letter of Ibas not rightly be understood—namely, that there is one power of the one person of the Lord Jesus Christ?

And if every faithful person, by cleaving to the Lord through good will alone, is one spirit with him, although he is not one person with him, how much more could it rightly be said of Christ that there is one power, where, through the union of the natures, the person of God and man has become one?

Moreover, if someone pays careful attention, what the Apostle says, “The one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit,” is greater and more elevated than if he had said, “He is one power.” For that spirit from which the power proceeds is understood to be the cause of the power; the power, however, is not the cause of the spirit from which it proceeds.

Therefore, they cannot justly criticize the venerable letter of Ibas, or the judgment of the synod that judged it orthodox, for what is lesser and was said of one person, when they do not dare to criticize in the apostolic writings what is greater and was said of two persons.

The intention of the speaker must therefore be considered in every matter. A great synod could examine that intention more carefully in the case of Ibas himself, even apart from the official proceedings, and thus judge his letter orthodox. And in all matters whose reasoning is less evident, not merely piety, but humanity itself, ought to consider this.

## CHAPTER II. That when Ibas said that Nestorius had been condemned without judgment and investigation, he did not disapprove his condemnation, but only the fact that the Eastern bishops had not been awaited

Let us therefore return to those passages in the same letter which the supporters of the heretics criticized in writing, so that they might reject it as profane and impious. These are what follow:

> “Cyril forestalled the ears of everyone with a pigment that blinds the eyes of the wise,” and so forth;

and again:

> “Because in the condemnation of Nestorius which was carried out by them, they introduced the twelve chapters written by Cyril, although they were contrary to the true faith,” and so forth.

These two passages are contained under one chapter, just as the two earlier passages were; but they have been habitually torn apart and abridged by these men, so that the integrity of the intention would not appear in them.

The beginning of the chapter itself, badly broken up by them, is as follows, as it is contained in that letter:

> “On account of this contention, the victorious and pious emperors ordered the leading bishops to assemble in the city of Ephesus and to have the books of Nestorius and Cyril judged before everyone. But before all the bishops who had been ordered to assemble had arrived at Ephesus, the same Cyril, anticipating them, forestalled the ears of everyone with a pigment that blinds the eyes of the wise.
