He found an occasion arising from the hatred that existed against Nestorius [Note: [Col. 0685D] Codex of Verona: “whereby.”], and before the most holy and most reverend Archbishop John had arrived at the synod, they deposed Nestorius from the episcopate, without judgment and investigation having taken place. Two days after his condemnation we came to Ephesus; and when we learned that, in the condemnation of Nestorius carried out by them, they had introduced and confirmed the twelve chapters written by Cyril, although they were contrary to the true faith, and had agreed with them as though they were consonant with the true faith, all the Eastern bishops condemned the same Cyril and decreed excommunication against the other bishops who had agreed with his chapters.”

In these bitter and swollen words, the most reverend Ibas seems still to exhale, as it were, the undigested bitterness of an old grievance: although the emperors had ordered that, in the case of Nestorius, holy John of Antioch also, together with the Eastern bishops, and the other leading bishops together with their colleagues, should sit as judges, Nestorius was condemned before those men had yet arrived at Ephesus.

From this arose the entire cause of the division; from this all the tumult took its origin; from this the Easterners and the other Fathers, offended, came already with hostile minds to believe that blessed Cyril, conscious of wrongdoing, had evaded the judgment and investigation of those Fathers [Note: [Col. 0685D] The same codex: “of his own,”] in order not to await their arrival.

For they thought that, if judgment and investigation had also been conducted concerning his chapters, which he later retracted, Nestorius alone could not have been found culpable.

For this reason, then, the venerable Ibas said that Nestorius had been condemned “without judgment and investigation”: as though there had been no examination of the sayings of blessed Cyril, whose intention they understood less well. Yet, as he reported, the emperors had ordered the leading bishops to assemble in the city of Ephesus precisely so that, before everyone, not only the books of Nestorius but also those of Cyril might be judged.

It is therefore not necessary to understand what he says—“without judgment and investigation having taken place”—as referring to Nestorius, as though Nestorius had been condemned without judgment and investigation. It can instead be understood as having been said because the chapters of blessed Cyril, about which we have now given sufficient explanation, were not investigated in that judgment.

And even if we grant that the phrase “without judgment and investigation” was said about Nestorius, [Note: [Col. 0686D] The same codex: “and investigation not having taken place.” The reading is confirmed by what is said above and below.] must we, even after granting this, necessarily understand that Nestorius was excused by these words?

Why should we not believe that the most reverend Ibas, not excusing Nestorius but expressing indignation that the Easterners had not been awaited, said in that council that what had been judged and investigated there had been concluded “without judgment and investigation”—as though the judgment were not legitimate, nor the investigation legitimate, where those men were absent who had likewise been appointed investigators and judges?

I believe—and we ought to believe—that unavoidable circumstances may have arisen for the Easterners and the Fathers of the other provinces, causing them to delay their arrival; and, on the other hand, that some comparable necessity prevented blessed Cyril and the others who had arrived earlier from waiting for them any longer.

What can we say here except what we have already said, when we were discussing the curses uttered by Cyril himself against holy John? “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7). For such scandals arise among mortals not only from voluntary movements of the mind, but also against their will and knowledge.

## CHAPTER III. That Ibas could have been mistaken in his judgment concerning Nestorius, just as Anatolius was concerning Dioscorus, Athanasius concerning Timothy, the Palestinian synod and Pope Zosimus concerning Pelagius and Coelestius

All these circumstances, by which it could become clear for what reason the most reverend Ibas, offended together with the others, and especially with the Eastern bishops, spoke as he did about blessed Cyril, these teachers of their novel truth avoided inserting into their book, lest that letter, which the synod declared orthodox, should seem to have excused Nestorius.

If he had in fact done this, the response we gave to the Nestorians on behalf of blessed Anatolius, by whom Dioscorus was condemned—Anatolius, who, wishing to excuse Dioscorus, said that he had not been condemned for the faith—we could with no injustice also give to the Eutychians on behalf of the most reverend Ibas.

For it is one thing if someone is simply deceived by a heretic concealing his tricks, so that he thinks him orthodox; and another thing if he recognizes and follows and defends the heresy itself.

Yet, if someone carefully considered the case of both men, the case of Bishop Anatolius would prove more serious. For he, as has been said, wished in that synod to excuse Dioscorus, the defender of the heresy of Eutyches and of Eutychian doctrine, from the charge of heresy, in the very synod in which Eutyches, together with his doctrine, and Dioscorus, as its defender, were condemned by Anatolius’s own decision among the others.

Ibas, however, was not present at the Council of Ephesus, in which Nestorius was condemned. Indeed, because the Eastern Fathers and the other bishops of the various provinces who had assembled with them at Ephesus had not been awaited, he was gravely offended at the condemnation of Nestorius.

For if those who write down what is worth reading should also deign to read other works, they will find that Timothy, the disciple of Apollinaris, was commended by blessed Athanasius to the Apostolic See as though he were orthodox, through ignorance, in the time of blessed Damasus. [Note: [Col. 0687D] Codex of Verona: “of Pope Damasus.”] They will also find that Pope Damasus himself received him simply, without restraining his heresy.

They will further find that Pelagius, the heresiarch—as the Pelagians are called—was acquitted in the judgment of the Palestinian bishops. He had concealed what he thought against the grace of Christ and interpreted his perverse opinions with cunning; yet through the same ignorance he was acquitted.

Finally, they will find that blessed Zosimus, likewise, the bishop of the Apostolic See, contrary to the judgment of his predecessor, holy Innocent, who first condemned the Pelagian heresy, approved as true and Catholic the faith of Pelagius and of his associate Coelestius. [Note: [Col. 0687D] From this passage and from what Saint Augustine writes in Book II of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 3, it is clear that those are mistaken who have thought that Zosimus’s letters on behalf of Coelestius were forged. Yet, even if we acknowledge them as genuine, the Pelagians had no great reason to triumph on their basis. As Augustine says, Zosimus approved in them the willingness to reform, not the falsity of the doctrine. For when Coelestius professed himself ready to be instructed by his memorandum and replied that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent, he appeared to be returning to a better frame of mind. But when the Africans replied—having recognized Coelestius’s cunning—that it was not enough for him to boast of the letters of Innocent unless he openly rejected what he had wrongly set down in his book, and when he had withdrawn from examination, Zosimus condemned him again, together with Pelagius.]

Coelestius had been convicted in the Church of Carthage and had appealed to the Apostolic See; Zosimus himself had examined the proceedings. Zosimus furthermore blamed the African bishops because Pelagius and Coelestius were considered heretics by them. Before the African bishops themselves had exposed their deceits much more clearly, he regarded Pelagius and Coelestius as orthodox. [Note: [Col. 0687D] The same codex: “to the African bishops.”]

And yet the Church does not regard Athanasius, Damasus, those Palestinian bishops, or Zosimus as heretics because they thought well of heretics. Rather, on account of the merit of their faith, it judges and honors them as Catholics. For the uncomprehended cunning of wicked people ought not to be counted as a crime against simple persons.

Accordingly, even if the letter of the venerable Ibas were proved to have excused Nestorius, it ought not on that account to have been judged heretical by the synod, but orthodox on account of the merit of its faith.

Moreover, it is not necessary to make this response to the Eutychians in defense of the holy synod, since it is sufficiently evident from the words of the letter itself—and it will become much more evident from what was done concerning the venerable Ibas himself—that Ibas did not say, as some wished to make it appear, “They deposed Nestorius from the episcopate without judgment and investigation,” in order to excuse Nestorius.

For even if they refuse to understand this as referring to the chapters of blessed Cyril, as we established earlier, nothing prevents us from believing that the same words were said because the venerable Ibas, on account of the injury done to the Eastern and other Fathers, who were not awaited so that they might be present for the judgment and investigation, disdained to say that Nestorius had been deposed by those men also, after judgment and investigation had taken place. [Note: [Col. 0688D] The same codex: “without judgment and investigation.”] He attributed so much authority to holy John of Antioch and to the rest of his provincial bishops—or to the bishops of the other provinces—that he did not consider what had been done without them either judged or investigated.

For the number of those leading bishops was not small, nor was their authority small. They had come with the bishops of their own dioceses, as they had been instructed, to Ephesus with the aforementioned holy John of Antioch and the other Easterners, and had expressed their position.

Nine provinces, in fact, had supplied bishops in addition to them: Bithynia, Pisidia, Second Cappadocia, Pelagonia, [Note: [Col. 0688D] Thus the old copies read. It might appear that “Pelagonia” means Macedonia II, in which there was a city called Pelagonia, as Hierocles teaches in the *Synecdemus*. Likewise, in the Fifth Synod, Benignus is subscribed as bishop of Heraclea of Pelagonia, to distinguish it from other cities of the same name. However, in the acts of the Council of Ephesus, from which Facundus took this number of provinces, “Pelagonia” is not written, but “Paphlagonia,” under the heading “Concerning the Schismatics”; and in the letter of the Easterners to Bishop Rufus: “those who inhabit the East; likewise the Bithynians, the Paphlagonians, Second Cappadocia, Pisidia, Thessaly, Mysia, Rhodope, and many others from various provinces.” Therefore it should be read that way here as well. On the other hand, in Vigilius’s *Constitutum*, “Heraclea of Paphlagonia” is incorrectly written instead of “of Pelagonia.”] Europe, Second Mysia, Rhodope, Thrace, [Note: [Col. 0688D] The same codex: “Dacia.”] and Thessaly.

But what bearing did this have on the Council of Chalcedon—that the same venerable Ibas, whether arrogantly, or from pain at the injuries he had suffered, or for whatever other reason, sent such a letter—when he had said nothing profane in it concerning the Christian faith, for the sake of which they had assembled?

## CHAPTER IV. That they produced Ibas’s letter in mutilated form, omitting the passages from which it would be clear that he had not excused Nestorius

Now pay attention with us, Augustus, so that you may detect the customary thefts of thieves: how, from the statement they quoted—“Cyril forestalled the ears of everyone with a pigment that blinds the eyes of the wise, and they deposed Nestorius from the episcopate without judgment and investigation”—they not only cut off its head, nor were they content merely to remove its ending together with its head; rather, so that it might be exposed more clearly that they had done this not for the sake of brevity but to obscure the truth, they also stole from the middle of it other passages which would easily demonstrate to readers that the most reverend Ibas had spoken in this way not to excuse Nestorius, but on account of the injury done to the bishops of the East and to the others.

Compare what they maliciously excerpted with what we have set down according to the wording of the letter itself, and you will see not only what they stole, but also the reasons for their thefts.

Why, above all, did they avoid the beginning of the narrative of the letter itself, from which they ought to have begun, unless it was because they wished to snatch something away from those who did not know what the letter itself contained, or who understood it less well?

> “I begin the narrative,” he says, “with words that you yourself also know. A contention arose while your Reverence was here, between these two men, Nestorius and Cyril; and they wrote harmful books against each other, which were a scandal to those who heard them. For Nestorius taught in his books, as your Reverence also knows, that blessed Mary is not the Mother of God, so that many thought that he was the one who held the heresy of Paul of Samosata, who said that Christ was a mere man.”

Then follows the passage from which these men began:

> “But Cyril, wishing to destroy the books of Nestorius, went astray and was found to have fallen into the doctrine of Apollinaris. He too wrote against him in a similar way, because he said that God the Word himself became man.”

And then follows the passage they again suppressed:

> “As though there were no distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it.”

Why, then, as I said, did they avoid touching the beginnings of the narrative itself, from which the method of teaching the truth more properly urged them to begin, unless it was because what accords with the truth is contrary to falsehood?

For, wishing to slander this letter by claiming that it had excused Nestorius, they wished to conceal what was said there about Nestorius himself and blessed Cyril:

> “They wrote harmful books against each other which were a scandal to those who heard them.”

How could the most reverend Ibas have seemed to excuse Nestorius, if it had been known that he said that he too had written harmful books that were a scandal to those who heard them?

He would therefore have seemed to have gone astray not by excusing Nestorius, but by accusing blessed Cyril at the same time. For just as he judged Nestorius blameworthy because he denied that blessed Mary was the Mother of God, so he also considered holy Cyril blameworthy because he thought that Cyril, like Apollinaris, had written that God the Word became man in such a way that there was no distinction between the temple and the one dwelling in it.

For this reason, the statement quoted by these men should not be thought to have been said in order to excuse Nestorius—although, I do not know whether they omitted it because their consciences resisted it or because, intent on other frauds, they passed over it in their own book of slanders and lies. Nevertheless, since we see it being brought forward by their associates or henchmen, we do not omit refuting it by a similar argument.

When the aforementioned venerable Ibas was narrating and saying:

> “All the Eastern bishops condemned the same Cyril and decreed excommunication against the other bishops who agreed with his chapters,”

he immediately added:

> “And after this disturbance, each man returned to his own city. But Nestorius, because he was hated by his own city and by the leading men who were in it, could not return there.”

They therefore object to us and say: Behold, here again Nestorius was excused by Ibas, because he did not say that Nestorius was unable to return to his city as a heretic, but because he was hated by it and by the leading men who were in it.

As though they could prove that the most reverend Ibas said that Nestorius was hated by his city and by its leading men, not on account of his heresy but on account of some other cause, so that he could not return there—although above he had already said that Nestorius had written harmful books that were a scandal to those who heard them because they denied blessed Mary as Mother of God.

We answer them in this way, leaving aside the other arguments by which this slander is refuted in many ways and with the greatest ease:

Did the most reverend Ibas ever say anywhere that Nestorius was indeed hated by his city and by its leading men, but not as a heretic, so that he could not return there?

“No,” they reply.

Did he at least say that he was hated by his city and by the leading men who were in it on account of some other private reasons, so that he could not return there?

“Not that either,” they reply.

If, then, the most reverend Ibas did not say this—although, if he had said it, it would not follow that someone described as hateful for other private reasons should thereby be considered not hateful on account of his heresy—how can you show that Nestorius was excused by these words of the venerable Ibas?

Or would it perhaps seem to you appropriate to the testimony of an orthodox priest to say that he was hated by his city and by its leading men?

“It would not,” they reply. “Nevertheless, the words of this letter imply that Nestorius could not return to his city not as a heretic, but because he was hateful there on account of other private reasons.”

But I infer that those words signify rather that Nestorius was hated by his city as a heretic, so that he could not return there.

Which implication will seem acceptable? I think it will be the one that accords with the preceding words, where it was said that Nestorius had written harmful books that were a scandal to those who heard them because he denied Mary as Mother of God, rather than the one that appears to conflict with all these statements: namely, that Nestorius was hated by his city on account of his harmful books, by which, in denying Mary as Mother of God, he had scandalized those who heard him, and therefore could not return there. [Note: [Col. 0689D] Codex of Verona: “to conflict. Although it is more suitably implied that Nestorius …”]

Nevertheless, for the sake of completeness, let us suppose that the venerable Ibas did not mean this by implication, but said openly that Nestorius was indeed hated by his city and by the leading men who were in it, but not as a heretic; rather, he was hated on account of other reasons, so that he could not return there. Let us also suppose that we lacked the other arguments already mentioned, and the many more that we shall mention, by which it would be sufficiently demonstrated that even this statement was not made to excuse Nestorius.

Would it then be necessary, considering the words we have imagined in themselves, to understand them in such a way that Nestorius appeared to be excused by them?

They could also be understood in another way: although Nestorius was a heretic, his own city did not believe this about him and did not prevent his return as a heretic; rather, he could not return because he was hated there for other reasons.

They could likewise be understood in this way: although Nestorius was a heretic, and although his own city also regarded him as such, this was not the reason he could not return there, since he had not been condemned by the Eastern bishops and the bishops of the other provinces whom the emperors had ordered to judge his case; rather, he could not return because he was hated for other reasons.

It would be as though the venerable Ibas, attributing great authority to his metropolitan and to the other Eastern bishops and bishops of the other provinces who had not been awaited, were saying that Nestorius, although a heretic, had not yet been condemned by them and could therefore return to the city and await their judgment, unless he was hated there for other reasons.

For when those Easterners and those who were with them had prevailed so greatly against the Council of Ephesus in support of the acceptance of the chapters of blessed Cyril that they condemned blessed Cyril himself and Memnon, bishop of Ephesus, and, at the emperor’s command, the count of the imperial treasury likewise handed them over to custody, [Note: [Col. 0691D] John. In the acts of the Easterners after the Council of Ephesus there is a letter of the Emperor Theodosius sent to the synod through John, the count of the imperial treasury: “a *sacra* having been sent through John, the count of the *sacrae*.” This is followed by a letter from the same John, count of the imperial treasury, to the emperor, in which he reports that he had handed Nestorius over to Candidianus, count of the domestics, for custody, and Cyril and Memnon to James, likewise count and prefect of the Fourth Schola.] what prejudice would there be if Ibas had also said this: that in the case of Nestorius, although he was a heretic, yet had not been excluded by the Easterners, the opinion of those who had been condemned as heretics and could be sent into custody had not been considered; rather, because he was hated by his city for other reasons, he could not return there?

But none of this is contained in his letter. It says only:

> “But Nestorius, because he was hated by his own city and by the leading men who were in it, could not return there.”

We have already answered the slanderers concerning this, perhaps at greater length than was necessary.

## CHAPTER V. That they falsely say that Ibas was compelled by the synod to anathematize Nestorius, and that his accusers never charged him with excusing Nestorius
To such an extent, however, were the most reverend Ibas himself and his letter removed from this suspicion—that he had excused Nestorius—that not even the judges themselves, Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius, after the same letter had been produced and read again, compelled the aforesaid Bishop Ibas to anathematize Nestorius. For it is not true [Note: [Col. 0691D] Justinian nevertheless asserts this very thing in his Edict. [Col. 0692D] “Therefore,” he says, “the aforementioned Photius and Eustathius, because of the assurance supplied by the accusers, formally declared in writing that the said Ibas had done everything contrary to the letter, as the judgment delivered by them on this matter demonstrates.” The Fifth Synod likewise, in Action 6: “Photius and Eustathius, not satisfied with his denial, established by their decree that Ibas should go to Edessa and openly anathematize in the church Nestorius and his impious doctrines, which the impious letter defended.”] what those men inserted in their book—men who love to lie as much as they are permitted to do so with impunity—when they say:

“Finally, Photius and Eustathius, lovers of God, [Col. 0691D] observing Ibas’s denial concerning the letter [Col. 0692A] made to Maris, issued a judgment for the destruction and exclusion of the impious letter.”

As we said above, Ibas approached this judgment and asked the holy synod that it be read aloud. The judgment, however, reads as follows: that Ibas should openly anathematize in his own church Nestorius, the author of malignant impiety, and those who use either his books or his writings.

It is therefore not true what they said. For, as we have already shown, it is not demonstrated that Ibas denied that the letter to Maris was his; nor did the venerable bishops Photius and Eustathius judge that Ibas should openly anathematize in his own church Nestorius, the author of malignant impiety, and those who use either his books or his writings. Rather, the aforesaid Bishop Ibas himself voluntarily and additionally promised this, with no one forcing or asking him to do so, [Col. 0692B] as is shown by the decree of the aforesaid bishops Photius and Eustathius.

For when the venerable Bishop Uranius, who had sat with them as judge in this case by imperial command, was already absent, and the judges made themselves mediators of peace between the parties, after some further proceedings, when many matters had been raised and inserted into the record, they said:

“Leaving aside for a little while the order of judicial inquiry and looking toward the common benefit of the holy Churches, we made ourselves mediators of peace between the parties in place of judges. Employing many counsels and proposing piety everywhere, we prepared Bishop [Note: Codex Veronensis: “the most reverend bishop,” and so forth.] Ibas, who himself wisely understood that, in satisfaction for the matters that had been stated, he should give in writing what he believed or understood concerning our pious faith. This he also did.

“In addition, the aforesaid most reverend man promised that in the church of his own city he would openly anathematize [Note: The same codex: “and in the church of his own city openly anathematize.”] the author of malignant impiety [Note: The same codex: “the author, Nestorius.”] and those who think as he does, as well as those who use either his books or his writings.

“He confessed that he believed as the letters contain, which passed between John, of venerable and holy memory, bishop of the great city of Antioch, and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria [Note: The same codex: “bishop of the great city of the Alexandrians.”], through the ministry of Paul, bishop of the city of Emesa, of blessed memory; and from these there also arose universal agreement.”

Behold: the venerable Photius and Eustathius, having become mediators of peace in place of judges, say that they themselves did not judge, as is falsely alleged, for the destruction and exclusion of the impious letter to Maris, so that, on his return, [Note: The same codex: “the most reverend Ibas.”] Ibas would openly anathematize [Col. 0692D] Nestorius in the church of his own city. They judged that Ibas had said, not in defense of Nestorius, [Col. 0693A] but because of the injury done to the Orientals and to the others who had not been summoned with them, the things which certain people misinterpret in that letter.

Otherwise, they would not say that the returning [Note: Codex Veronensis: “the most reverend Ibas.”] Ibas had promised this “in addition,” namely, that he would anathematize Nestorius in the church of his city. Rather, they would say that they themselves had necessarily demanded this of him.

It is also plainly evident that, by their customary fraud, [Note: The same codex: “therefore, by their customary fraud.”] they suppressed what we included from the same proceedings: that Bishop Ibas confessed that he believed as the letters contained which passed, through the mediation of Paul, bishop of the city of Emesa, between John, bishop of Antioch, of blessed memory, and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria. They did this so that, from the testimony of the bishops Photius and Eustathius—which they falsely claimed had been made for the destruction and exclusion of the letter of the venerable Ibas—its truth might not instead be demonstrated. For this testimony itself did not keep silent about the matter. [Note: The same codex: “this.”]

If what we are saying still seems obscure to anyone, and if he desires to know the case more fully, he should be advised merely to read the same proceedings—not as though he needed assistance in understanding them. For what appears obscure here is found there clearer than daylight.

But it is entirely false also that, in the same book of their lies, they said:

“The holy synod, [Note: This is also alleged both by Justinian in his Edict and by the Fifth Synod. The latter teaches that Ibas’s letter was condemned by the Council of Chalcedon precisely because it approved the judgment of Photius and Eustathius, who had condemned it as impious.] not satisfied either with the denial made by Ibas concerning the letter to Maris or with the testimony given on his behalf by the clerics of Edessa, but confirming the judgment of Photius and Eustathius, asked Ibas, for the destruction and exclusion of the impious letter to Maris, to anathematize Nestorius and his doctrines, which that same letter praised.” [Col. 0693C]

Where, then, did the most reverend Ibas deny that the letter was his? Or where did that letter praise Nestorius and his doctrines, as they put it? In that letter he said that Nestorius had written harmful books which had been a scandal to those who heard them, because he denied that blessed Mary was the Mother of God. Let them quote from it the praises of Nestorius and his doctrines that they allege.

If they have nothing to quote, they ought to be ashamed of lying so openly and so repeatedly. I confess that I am weary and wholly ashamed of having to accuse so many lies; yet, while passing over much, I am compelled by necessity to refute certain people.

Although it is their responsibility to prove what they have said, we shall nevertheless prove to them—not only from the evidence of the letter itself, which contains nothing of the sort, but also from the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon, [Col. 0693D] for which they themselves fabricated a testimony—that the most reverend Ibas not only did not praise Nestorius and his doctrines in his letter, but also, as we proposed to demonstrate long ago, made no defense of Nestorius.

For when the same letter was reread before the Council of Chalcedon from the proceedings of the bishops Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius, it noted only that Ibas had blamed blessed Cyril because he had insufficiently understood the intention of his chapters, not that he had excused Nestorius.

He gave the following judgment, as we explained in the fifth book:

“From the matters reread earlier, the most reverend Ibas was shown to be innocent. For in the passages in which he appeared to speak wrongly in blaming the most blessed Cyril, he later rightly confessed and rejected the things for which he had blamed him. But because he excused Nestorius, he is not found to have been rebuked by the synod. The synod would undoubtedly have rebuked him if he had excused Nestorius, whom it itself had condemned”—all the more so if he had also praised him, as they say.

The judgment of that same synod, then, if it is to be believed in anything, proves that Nestorius was neither praised nor excused in Ibas’s letter. [Note: The same codex: “Nestorius; and therefore it should neither be supposed nor fabricated that the synod made Ibas anathematize Nestorius for the destruction and exclusion of the letter to Maris; for it not only…” [Col. 0694D]]

That synod not only made him anathematize Nestorius, but also Eutyches—something these men did not wish to mention. Yet Bishop Ibas had not been accused concerning the Eutychian doctrine; rather, he complained that he had suffered injustice and false accusations from Eutyches himself.

But because that holy synod had assembled not only to condemn Eutyches but also to confirm the condemnation of Nestorius, and because it recognized that Ibas’s letter was orthodox and especially opposed to Nestorius and Eutyches, it judged him worthy to join with it in condemning the heretics whom he refuted.

If the Eutychians think that the synod ought to have rejected Ibas’s letter, which confessed two natures in the unity of the person, as though it were Nestorian, then it would plainly have excused Nestorius as far as it was concerned and would have freed him from the charge of heresy. We demonstrated this also in the preceding book, as we had promised.

Therefore let those who have called this letter Nestorian take care lest they themselves rather appear to excuse Nestorius by asserting that, in accordance with his teaching, it confesses that the one person of the two natures is one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

For this letter cannot rightly be said to have defended Nestorius, whose confession appears contrary to the Nestorian doctrine. Seeing this, the holy synod reasonably judged the letter to be orthodox.

Yet it seems to me insufficiently evident how shameless those people are who accuse the letter of the venerable Ibas of having excused Nestorius, if they are refuted in their lie merely by the testimony of the bishops Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius, or even by that of the Council of Chalcedon. They must also be confounded by the example of Ibas’s own accusers, whom we have shown to be more calumnious and more shameless than themselves.

For those accusers too produced the letter for this one purpose, as the records in which the matter is contained demonstrate: to prove from it that Ibas had disparaged blessed Cyril, not that he had wished to excuse Nestorius. And when they wanted the same Ibas to appear Nestorian, they tried to prove this more from his disparagement of blessed Cyril than from an alleged defense or praise of Nestorius, as is now being fabricated.

They said of him: “He is a Nestorian, and he calls Bishop Cyril a heretic.”

What need was there for this roundabout method—to show as a Nestorian, on account of this, a man who had disparaged blessed Cyril, the condemner of Nestorius—when this could have been demonstrated concisely from his defense of Nestorius himself or from praise of his doctrines, if the letter had excused Nestorius as they say? [Col. 0695A]

They would have said simply that he had defended Nestorius or praised his doctrines. [Note: Codex Veronensis: “that that letter had praised the doctrines of Nestorius. For let them produce the passage where even Ibas’s lying accusers dared to lie so far as to say that he had excused Nestorius in that letter or praised his doctrines. But if…” At this point, up to page 449, the collations are missing because two folios have been removed from the codex.]

If not even Ibas’s own calumniators brought forward anything of the sort from that letter, how much more do these men appear to have surpassed their malice and shamelessness, since they accuse him after the judgment of that council of something which the others did not even attempt to allege—not in the complaints deposited before the emperors, nor in the episcopal trials repeatedly conducted before the Council of Chalcedon, nor at the great and universal council itself!

Those men, although utterly obstinate and blinded by their very obstinacy, saw that it would be disgraceful for them and incredible to others if they said that Nestorius had been defended in that letter. Our wise men, however, thought not only that this could be said by them, but also that we could believe it. Let them consider whether such lying is fitting for them; but let them recognize that, to us, what they say is incredible.

You perceive, therefore, most merciful emperor, that the letter of the venerable Ibas is cleared even by the testimony of his own accusers from the false charge that it excused Nestorius. It requires no further assertion on this point, since even its own accusers sufficiently excuse it.

But what shall we say about the calumnies of our own times? What once embarrassed the most shameless accusers now does not embarrass judges—and what judges? Judges not of human authority, but, as they imagine, of divine authority. For they are judges of judges and judges of the dead.

From what has been done concerning the venerable Ibas, we have proved sufficiently and more than sufficiently that the claim that Nestorius was excused in his letter is being spread by a malicious interpretation.

If anyone also considers that the same venerable Ibas could not have acted against the judgment of Saint John of Antioch, to whom such great authority was accorded, nor against that of the other Orientals and of the others who had come with them to Ephesus from various provinces—men who, although they condemned Nestorius without the judgment of the council assigned to judge him, nevertheless did not judge that he should be absolved—he will recognize much more clearly that Ibas in no way excused him.

I believe that Ibas’s accusers also considered this, when, after long deliberation, they constructed so many unheard-of calumnies against the aforesaid most reverend Ibas. Yet they judged it utterly shameless to say, against everyone’s conscience, [Col. 0696A] that Ibas had at some time excused Nestorius before many people.

For after Nestorius’s condemnation, when the Oriental bishops and the most reverend Ibas himself arrived at Ephesus with Saint John of Antioch, they complained only about the fact that the chapters of blessed Cyril had been approved there, as their writings make clear. They brought no complaint at all concerning the condemnation of Nestorius.

The venerable Ibas himself narrated this in his letter as follows:

“Two days after his deposition, we came to Ephesus. When we learned that, in the condemnation of Nestorius which had been carried out by them, they had inserted, confirmed, and accepted the twelve chapters written by Cyril, although they were contrary to the true faith, as though they agreed with the true faith, all the Oriental bishops condemned that same Cyril and decreed excommunication against the other bishops who had accepted his chapters.”

The venerable Ibas therefore said that the Orientals had taken offense only on account of the chapters of blessed Cyril, whose intention they did not understand—not on account of Nestorius’s condemnation.

How, then, could he excuse Nestorius, who had written harmful books, contrary to the judgment of blessed John of Antioch, who held primacy over him, contrary to that of the entire Oriental council, and contrary to his own judgment? Or how could his accusers have hoped that anyone would believe them if they accused Ibas on this point against the public record?

Therefore, whether that letter is said to belong to Ibas or is asserted by his accusers to have been fabricated, it must not be supposed that they would have omitted to accuse him here if they had thought the charge credible.

It is even more absurd to suppose that, when Ibas’s accusers fabricated the letter in the name of the venerable Ibas so that he would appear Nestorian, they would not attempt to charge him with defending Nestorius either in the many episcopal trials before the Council of Chalcedon or at the council itself.

For if those words—“They deposed Nestorius from the episcopate without judgment or inquiry”—and again, “Nestorius, because he was hated by his own city and by the leading men who were in it, could not return there”—signify that Nestorius was excused, why should they be believed to have fabricated them against a bishop when they did not accuse him of excusing Nestorius?

From this it is sufficiently indicated both that the letter belongs to Ibas and that he is falsely said to have excused Nestorius.

Nor is Nestorius found to have been blamed by the Oriental bishops through the aforementioned Saint John of Antioch only after his condemnation; he was blamed even before he was condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] The complete letter of John of Antioch to Nestorius, from which these excerpts are taken, is found in Part I of the Synod of Ephesus, no. 25.] For when John wrote to him that he was foolishly refusing to call blessed Mary the Mother of God, he said:

“I do not exhort your holiness to correct the term as though I were accusing you, nor, so to speak, out of childish opposition. But because, as we have learned, you have repeatedly said to many people that, without being ashamed of this pious confession, you alone refuse the name: if some among you in the church should also request this of you, you will never refuse to call the holy Virgin ‘Mother of God.’

“Accordingly, I exhort you regarding what I know you do not err in: that name and term have already been established, written, and spoken by many Fathers for that reality. Therefore one must not deny the Word, whose reality you are shown to hold in mind according to its meaning.

“No ecclesiastical teacher refuses this name. For those who have used it are both numerous and distinguished; those who have not used it have not blamed those who did. And we, as it appears, foolishly fall into the perverse opinions of the heretics—as though this were a matter requiring a double examination—and disregard the consciences of our brothers, struck without any benefit, by refusing a name whose meaning we fully and rightly accept. We greatly err; rather, we place ourselves in danger concerning the ineffable dispensation of the only-begotten Son of God.

“For when this name, or its signification, is removed, it follows that neither is he God who, for our sake, assumed the inerrant dispensation of the body, nor is the Word of God the one who, emptying himself and taking the form of a servant, displayed toward us the immeasurable greatness of his mercy—as was accomplished through this divine dispensation.”

Since, then, Nestorius is shown to have been rebuked by the Orientals both before his condemnation and afterward—although afterward they were indignant and deeply grieved by the injury done to themselves, they did not absolve him, but, after condemning the venerable bishops Cyril and Memnon of Ephesus on the basis of mere suspicion, left Nestorius in the condemnation he had deserved—how could even the most obstinate accusers of the venerable Ibas fail to be ashamed, in the face of the many people whose recent memory of events would contradict them, to say that Ibas had excused Nestorius in his letter?

They therefore saw that, in view of all the matters we have recalled, no one would believe that the words “They deposed Nestorius from the episcopate without judgment or inquiry” had been spoken in defense of Nestorius. Rather, they could be understood as referring to the chapters of blessed Cyril, which he later interpreted—as though Nestorius had been condemned concerning them without judgment or inquiry—or to the fact that, as we have already said above, Ibas disdained to call it judgment and inquiry when the Oriental bishops and the bishops of the other provinces, who had been jointly appointed as investigators and judges, had not been present.

They also saw that the other statement, which we have likewise refuted in many ways, would not be understood as having been made in his defense: “Nestorius, because he was hated by his own city and by the leading men who were in it, could not return there.”

They considered it disgraceful for them, however shameless they were, to bring a calumny from this statement. They thought it easier to persuade the judges of what it is horrifying even to mention: that Bishop Ibas had said, “I do not envy Christ for having been made God; for insofar as he was made, I too was made”—than to claim, against the conscience of so many people, that he had defended Nestorius in that letter.

## CHAPTER VI

That it did not seem to the synod that Ibas’s mistaken suspicion concerning Cyril’s chapters was sufficient cause for judging his letter condemnable.

[Col. 0697D]

[Col. 0698A] Therefore, the only charge that heretics or their supporters, together with the malicious and obstinate accusers of the venerable Ibas, can bring against him from his letter is that, concerning blessed Cyril, he judged otherwise than the matter actually stood. Yet in this too they prove more malicious and obstinate, dragging a man’s ignorance concerning another man into the charge of heresy. For they do after the council’s judgment what those others did before it; they do not permit calumnies refuted long ago to be laid to rest, but revive, through renewed controversy, accusations buried long ago with their authors.

But concerning this ignorance, through which the most reverend Ibas, together with the bishops of so many provinces, was mistaken regarding the person of blessed [Col. 0698B] Cyril, much has already been said, and it has been shown more than sufficiently that this circumstance does not make a person a heretic. But since we see some people more lenient toward their own sins and more severe toward the sins of others, displaying their holiness by magnifying the offenses of their neighbors, let us also remove that resentment by which they complain bitterly, saying that in these chapters blessed Cyril was not so much blamed as the Council of Ephesus, which had already accepted them; and that this letter cannot be approved unless that same council is disapproved. By this they wish to make the great Council of Chalcedon, which judged the letter orthodox, appear to oppose the decrees of that Council of Ephesus.

But I say that for this very reason it more emphatically pronounced the often-mentioned letter orthodox: it saw that the letter, [Col. 0698C] in accordance with the decrees of that Council of Ephesus, confessed that the one Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, exists in two natures. Accordingly, it wisely recognized that the author of the letter, together with the Eastern bishops and those of the other provinces, had understood nothing amiss in all the matters enacted there, save how the chapters of blessed Cyril had rightly been accepted. They thought that Cyril had said that God the Word became man in such a way as to remove the distinction between the natures and to assert one nature of the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ—something which every Catholic abhors.

But the great Council of Chalcedon, recognizing the intention of those chapters, which the Council of Ephesus had carefully learned from blessed Cyril while he was present, judged that Ibas and the others, as absent persons—as the outcome of the case demonstrated—had failed to understand it. It judged that it made no difference that, in those same chapters, they had understood the intention less fully, both of blessed Cyril who spoke and of the holy Council of Ephesus which approved him, since the faith of both parties had been the same: all alike believed that God the Word became man in such a way that, in the one person of Christ, the distinction of the two natures remained.

In this matter, then, there was no ignorance on either side and no disagreement. And if either party had understood the other, or each other, differently—and this does not pertain to heresy—the judgment of both parties concerning the Christian faith was nevertheless the same. But if someone says that Ibas and the Eastern bishops and those of the other provinces—for the case of all these people is one and the same—ought to have followed the authority of the Council of Ephesus even in matters they did not understand, he too must first [Col. 0699A] consider what the Council of Chalcedon must be believed to have considered: since so many dissenting persons had been summoned to assemble together at that council, its authority at that time could not have been as great as it is now, since it had not yet been confirmed by the judgment of the great Council of Chalcedon. Antiquity itself, moreover, adds much strength to authority.

Next, by what rashness or profanation can it be said that blessed Cyril dared to retract, at the wish of those Easterners, what was no longer his own but belonged to the entire Council of Ephesus and had been confirmed by its authority? And if it is attributed to the Nestorian heresy that the Easterners, together with the bishops of the other provinces, not understanding the intention of his chapters, believed that the Council of Ephesus ought not to have accepted them, then blessed Cyril will be said to have shared in the same Nestorian heresy, since he communicated with those very Easterners, who held that view concerning his chapters, whose reconsideration they had demanded, and subscribed to their confession.

For if this opinion is valued so highly that it is to be judged heretical, Cyril ought not merely to have yielded in anything to those same Easterners. Rather, he ought to have compelled them, even in matters they understood less fully, to submit to the authority of the council; he should have required them publicly, and in a written confession preserved for posterity, likewise to condemn their presumption by which they had condemned the aforesaid chapters in a published decree. He ought not even then to have subscribed to the Easterners’ definition, but rather to have demanded that they subscribe to those same chapters—not interpreted according to their wishes, but as they had previously been accepted by the Council of Ephesus—and to have them anathematize as heresy the very suspicion by which they had condemned the chapters, and only then to receive them into communion.

Therefore neither could the other Fathers who had assembled with him at Ephesus, and who had communicated with the aforesaid Easterners while they held this belief about the Council of Ephesus, be excused. [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *poterunt* (“will be able”), rather than *potuerunt* (“could”).]

But because both blessed Cyril and the others who had approved those matters at Ephesus understood that their ignorance concerned not the Christian faith itself but the intention of their own statements, it seemed shameful and unworthy to them to contend over this matter and thereby prolong the churches’ dispute. We, however, are reviving after a hundred years, through restless ignorance, a dispute that the moderation of the holy Fathers had brought to rest. [Note: The same manuscript reads “moderation and reason.”]

And if only we were disturbing some of the churches that had been stirred up in the first dissension, rather than also forcing churches situated far away to investigate causes long ago consigned to oblivion—causes which, even when we know them, we are reluctant to remember—and, once found, to debate them under the necessity of giving an answer, not without offending those who hear us. [Note: The same manuscript reads “those,” rather than “some.”]

But concerning the further point they make—that the council ought for this reason to have judged the letter heretical, because after unity had been achieved its author, Ibas, ought not to have said or thought such things—we have already replied in the preceding book.

But how can the holy council, by approving this same letter as containing a correct confession of faith, be said to have attacked the decrees of the Council of Ephesus? If it had judged the letter heretical on account of this suspicion, it would rather appear to have criticized both blessed Cyril and the Council of Ephesus itself, since they communicated with the Easterners who held that suspicion, plainly judging them orthodox.

You see, therefore, Emperor, that what we demonstrated in the preceding book, as we had promised, is here once again and repeatedly displayed. Consequently, if the Council of Chalcedon is called Nestorian because it judged this letter [Col. 0700B] orthodox, then blessed Cyril and the Council of Ephesus will likewise subsequently be said to have turned aside into the Nestorian heresy, because they judged orthodox the Easterners who held this very belief—and not only the Easterners, but also the bishops of the other nine provinces mentioned above, who together condemned blessed Cyril himself, Memnon of Ephesus, and the aforesaid chapters, and pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the other bishops as well, because they had accepted them. [Note: The same manuscript reads “they judged orthodox,” rather than “they judged the Easterners orthodox.”]

Now this suspicion of the Easterners and the other Fathers concerning the Council of Ephesus—that, believing it to have transgressed the traditions of the Fathers, they contended against it on behalf of the very faith they commonly held—seems to me like the suspicion that arose among the people of Israel in the days of Joshua son of Nun (Joshua 22). At that time, commendably zealous for the worship of God, one part of that people was aroused against another part that was equally zealous, because it did not understand the latter’s intention.

For when that same people of Israel was proceeding to take possession of the whole land that God had promised to Abraham, the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, before they had crossed the Jordan (Numbers 32), had chosen to dwell in the region of Jazer and the region of Gilead, because the area was suitable for livestock, of which they had a great abundance. They did not wish to receive an inheritance beyond the Jordan with the tribes of Israel. Nevertheless, they proceeded with their brothers into the land of Canaan to fight the nations whom the Lord drove out before them.

After the Lord had given Israel the whole land that he had sworn to give their fathers, and they had received it as an inheritance, those same sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh returned to the land of Gilead—that is, to the land of their possession, which they had received as an inheritance. As it is written (Joshua 22:10), they came to Galioth of the Jordan, [Note: Some Greek copies likewise retain the Hebrew word, reading Γαλιλὼθ (*Galilōth*) and Γαλιὼθ (*Galiōth*). Symmachus, the translator, renders it as ὅρια (*horia*), “boundaries” or “borders”; Saint Jerome rendered it as *tumuli*, “mounds,” and in *Hebrew Names* explained *Galioth* as “hills.”] which is in Canaan, and there they built an altar above the Jordan. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “and there they built an altar above the Jordan, an altar immense to behold, with this intention, namely, lest, because they were beyond the Jordan in the land of Canaan, etc.”]

In Canaan the other tribes had received their possession, where the tabernacle and the altar of God were located. But these men, on the near side of the Jordan, had erected that altar with a religious intention and in burning zeal for God, so that their descendants would not become strangers to the worship of God—as though separated from his people by the Jordan as a boundary. They intended it to serve as a testimony and memorial for their descendants that they too belonged to the worship of God and to his people.

But when the other tribes beyond the Jordan, who had obtained their inheritance in the land of Canaan, were unaware of this intention and thought that the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh had built the altar for the purpose of separating themselves from the assembly of all Israel and, contrary to the observance of divine worship, offering sacrifices to the Lord upon it—something that was not permitted except upon the one altar located before his tabernacle—then, burning with the same zeal for God and contending for the same worship of God, they all assembled at Shiloh in order to go up and attack them.

When the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh explained to them the reason and intention for which they had erected the altar, the others said: “Today we know that the Lord is with us, because you have not committed a trespass in the sight of the Lord, and because you have delivered the children of Israel from the hand of the Lord” (Joshua 22:31).

You see, therefore, Augustus, that for the sake of the same religion by which God is rightly worshiped, devout and entirely upright people can not only disagree with one another but even commendably fight against one another, when it is not the principle of divine worship but one party’s intention that remains hidden from the other.

Accordingly, those who say to us, “If you accept the Council of Ephesus, condemn the bishops of the Eastern province and of the other nine provinces,” will rightly hear this answer: if they too accept the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, let them condemn the tribe of Levi and the other nine tribes, which, while the intention of their brothers was hidden from them, assembled to attack them.

And certainly there were prophets among that people as well. Yet no one blames them for failing to perceive the prudent purpose of their brothers’ hearts, since it could easily have been revealed to them through prayer by the grace of the prophecy they had received. But all the Eastern bishops and the bishops of the other provinces, who failed to understand the intention of blessed Cyril’s chapters and therefore blamed the Council of Ephesus for accepting them, were bishops, not prophets.

If, then, we do not blame the prophets for failing to know the religious intention of their brothers, but rather praise them because, moved by that same religious intention, they were aroused against them, how can we blame the Eastern Fathers and the others—who were not prophets—for having been aroused by a religious intention against those who approved the chapters? [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “because they did not know the religious intention of Cyril’s chapters; or, if it is said that it is not praiseworthy that they were aroused by the same religious intention against those who approved them. Seek …”]

Examine the intention of the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, [Col. 0702A] and, on the other side, that of the tribe of Levi and the other nine tribes of Israel, and you will find that both parties were concerned for divine worship. Examine their ignorance, and you will find that neither party was ignorant of matters pertaining to divine worship; rather, one party was ignorant of the other’s intention.

Examine the intention of the Council of Ephesus and, on the other side, that of the bishops of the Eastern province and of the other nine provinces, and you will find that both parties were concerned for divine worship. [Note: This has appeared just above and therefore seems unnecessarily repeated here.]

Examine their ignorance, and you will find that neither party was ignorant of matters pertaining to divine worship; rather, one party was ignorant of the other’s intention.

This is sufficiently clear from the fact that, through the venerable Paul, bishop of Emesa, the Eastern Fathers did not ask blessed Cyril to confess anything improper, nor did blessed Cyril refuse anything that they had requested. [Note: The same manuscript reads “anything requested by him.”]

But if we cannot condemn the Eastern Fathers and the others who were with them for ignorance of another party’s intention—just as we cannot condemn those many tribes of Israel—how could the Council of Chalcedon condemn the letter of the venerable Ibas, which complained, in accordance with their suspicion, about the acceptance of blessed Cyril’s chapters?

For is either Bishop Ibas or the other bishops of the many provinces ever shown to have blamed the Council of Ephesus because it had established that Jesus Christ, the one Son of God and man, must be confessed as being in two natures? Could it therefore be believed that they resisted the faith which they held concerning Christ’s incarnation and proclaimed something else? There is consequently nothing in this letter concerning the intention of the chapters of blessed Cyril and of the Council of Ephesus about which the Eutychians can complain. [Note: The same manuscript reads “concerning the criticism” rather than “concerning the intention.”]

## CHAPTER VII. That “the temple and the one dwelling in it” was rightly said, and that Ibas’s letter ought not to have been condemned by the council because of its praises of Theodore, since Theodore was likewise praised by Chrysostom and by the Nazianzen.

I see, however, that of everything they criticized in that letter, one chapter remains—the passage containing praise of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia. Since they said much about this passage and boast that they especially exercised their calumnies against it, thereby compelling us also to offer an extensive reply, I choose for the moment to defend something else, although it appears later in the order of the argument: namely, the statement which they rashly criticize—not in writing, but merely in words—at the end of the letter:

> “For no one dares to say that the divinity and humanity have one nature; rather, they acknowledge [a distinction] between the temple and the one who dwells in it, who is the one Son, the Lord Jesus Christ.”

This is indeed of the same character as the passage we defended above, where he speaks as though there were no difference between the temple and the one who dwells in it. Yet, lest we seem to have omitted anything, let us refute the same calumny here also.

For they say that the words, “But they acknowledge [a distinction] between the temple and the one who dwells in it,” imply a division of the one Son, Jesus Christ—as though he intended one subsistence or person of the temple and another of the one who dwells in it. But on this basis they could also make the same accusation against the words of the Lord himself, where he said to the Jews concerning the temple of his body, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), as though he intended one person for the temple of his body that was to be raised and another for the one who would raise it.

What uncertainty, moreover, has the venerable Ibas left us in his letter, when he first disclosed the intention of his mind and, showing that he had written these things not for a division of persons but for a distinction of natures, prefaced his statement with the words:

> “For no one dares to say that the divinity and humanity have one nature,”

and then added:

> “But they acknowledge [a distinction] between the temple and the one who dwells in it,”

and so concluded his thought by saying:

> “Who is one Son, Jesus Christ”?

What could have been said more explicitly or more fully? Yet, as I see it, whoever says that there is one Son in such a way as not to empty the mystery of his incarnation, together with the Eutychians, by denying his two natures, is judged to believe in two sons.

They also say that he ought not to have mentioned the temple first and then the one who dwells in it—as though the order of speech itself would allow him to mention first the one who dwells in it and afterward the temple. Indeed, the order is also suitable to the doctrine: since we reach knowledge of Christ’s divinity through his humanity, his humanity should first be mentioned as the temple, and afterward the divinity dwelling in the temple.

For this reason also the venerable Paul, bishop of Emesa, spoke as follows in the sermon which he delivered in the Alexandrian church in the presence of the blessed man himself, and which the blessed Cyril praised with such great commendation, as we showed in the first book:

> “See John proclaiming two natures and one Son: one thing is the tabernacle, and another the one in the tabernacle; one thing is the temple, and another the one who inhabits it—God.”

Consequently, if the venerable Ibas is blamed because in his letter he placed the temple first and then the one who dwells in it, the blessed Cyril must also necessarily be blamed because he praised the sermon of the aforementioned bishop Paul, in which he mentioned first the tabernacle and the temple and afterward the one in the tabernacle and God who inhabits the temple.

You recognize, therefore, emperor, that the great Council of Chalcedon approved, according to the judgment of the blessed Cyril, the letter of the venerable Ibas, which says:

> “But they acknowledge [a distinction] between the temple and the one who dwells in it, who is the one Son, Jesus Christ.”

For if it rejected the letter as heretical on this account, it would rather appear that it had confirmed the blessed Cyril as a heretic, since he approved the same statement in the sermon of his fellow bishop Paul.

Let us now return to the chapter that had been passed over, which they recall in these words:

> “And shortly afterward, disparaging the bishop of Edessa, he says: ‘This tyrant of our city presumed to anathematize publicly in the church the most blessed Theodore, herald of the truth and teacher of the Church, who presumes everything.’”

They included this passage from the letter because, as has often been said, they accuse the aforementioned Theodore of proclaiming the teachings of Nestorius, so that by this means they might demonstrate that the letter was Nestorian because it praised Theodore, and thus also prove the Council of Chalcedon Nestorian because it declared orthodox the letter that praised the man called the originator of the Nestorian error.

But since Theodore himself was not praised only in Ibas’s letter, and since we have already shown in the second book from the letters of the blessed John of Antioch and of the entire Eastern Council assembled at Antioch that he was praised by many holy Fathers, and shall show below from the letters of other Fathers, as we promised, I nevertheless consider it necessary to demonstrate from this letter itself that this opinion concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia was not Ibas’s alone.

For Ibas also declares that Maris the Persian himself, to whom he is writing, was aware of what he had said about Theodore, and confidently states that public knowledge itself bears witness on his behalf. But these men, with their customary fraud, avoided mentioning the passages by which this is shown.

For who cannot see in these words the venerable Ibas’s confidence in the truth? Unless the facts were certain and manifest, he would never have said to the man to whom he was writing, concerning the person who had anathematized Theodore:

> “You yourself are not unaware of him, who, under the pretext of faith, persecutes not only those now living but also all who formerly departed to the Lord. Among these is the blessed Theodore, herald of the truth and teacher of the Church, who during his life not only struck heretics with the blows of the truth of his faith, but after his death also left spiritual weapons in his books for the children of the Church.”

Then he also shows that the knowledge of the very man to whom he is writing bears witness on his behalf, when he says:

> “As your Reverence also learned by conversing with him and was instructed by what he wrote.”

And later, concerning the same Theodore:

> “Who, because of his zeal for God, not only converted his own city from error to truth, but also instructed Churches situated far away by his teaching.”

Finally, Theodore himself openly rebuked in his own synod the man whom Ibas called the tyrant of his city. If these things were not true, how could the most reverend Ibas have said them, in opposition to the testimony of all the Eastern bishops? Indeed, he would also have endangered his own position, if Theodore were regarded as a heretic, since Ibas said that in the council Theodore had rebuked some tyrant of his city.

He accused all the Eastern bishops, then, if he claimed that in their synod a heretic had possessed the confidence to rebuke someone in order to excommunicate the supporters of heretics.

They deliberately avoided touching upon this chapter, lest they be exposed. Recognizing that these things were true, the venerable Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius, when the aforementioned letter was reread in their judgment, did not demand that Ibas anathematize Theodore.

And in order to convict them by their own testimony—whatever its worth—they themselves certainly said in that book of lies, as we mentioned earlier:

> “Finally, Photius and Eustathius, observing Ibas’s denial concerning the letter, issued a judgment for the destruction and exclusion of the impiety of the letter to Maris. They affirm that this judgment required Ibas publicly to anathematize in his own church Nestorius, the prince of malignant impiety, and those who use his books or writings.”

Here I do not mean merely that, forgetful of themselves, they first called Theodore the originator and teacher of the Nestorian error and of Nestorius, and then themselves again called Nestorius the prince of malignant impiety, thereby denying that Theodore had been the common author of the error—as though they could speak the truth only through forgetfulness.

Rather, let your Piety consider this point with us: those who wished to demonstrate from this that the letter of the venerable Ibas was Nestorian claimed that the bishops Photius and Eustathius, observing his denial concerning his own letter, had issued a judgment for the destruction and exclusion of that letter requiring Ibas to anathematize Nestorius and his doctrines. We have proved that they falsely asserted this.

Without question, they thereby confirmed through their own judgment that Theodore was not a heretic. For although they heard the most distinguished praises of his teaching, they did not demand that the aforementioned most reverend Ibas renounce Theodore together with Nestorius, whom Ibas had not praised.

Since, as we have already shown, they compelled him neither to pronounce an anathema against Theodore nor even to do so against Nestorius, if the Eutychians or their followers believe anything on the basis of the testimony of these men, let them neither falsely claim that Nestorius is excused in this letter nor call Theodore the originator of Nestorian impiety. In their judgment they find that he was praised even before the Council of Chalcedon, but they do not find him condemned.

But, mindful of our promise, let us now approach those illustrious lights of the Church, whose testimony the Council of Chalcedon trusted more, so that it did not judge the letter of the venerable Ibas heretical because of its praise of Theodore.

Let us first summon as witness the most renowned teacher of the Church and most steadfast confessor of the truth, John of Constantinople. Writing to the aforementioned bishop Theodore of Mopsuestia while in exile, he says (Letter 112):

> “If it were possible for me to come and embrace your Reverence and affection, and to rejoice in your presence, I would do so with great speed and eagerness. But since this is not available to us, we now accomplish the same through letters. For even if we are led to the very ends of the world, we cannot forget the integrity and favor of your affection, nor its guileless sincerity—an affection ancient and from the beginning, which you have now also displayed. For it was not hidden from us how eagerly you hastened to speak and act on our behalf, my most honored and holy lord. Even if nothing more had been accomplished, you nevertheless have God as your debtor for your zeal and eagerness, and your reward is complete. We, too, do not cease, knowing the grace of your holiness, to praise your Reverence to everyone and to ask that the same affection may remain flourishing in every respect. For while sitting in the desert, we do not reap the fruit of an ordinary intercession when we possess in Cilicia such a treasure and such hidden riches. For this is the affection of your strong and vigilant soul.”

**Editorial note:** The Verona manuscript has *fervor* instead of *favor*.

**Editorial note:** Montfaucon has shown at length that Facundus’s reading is sound and should not be disturbed, in his edition of Chrysostom’s works, volume III, column 669, note a (in the later edition), on Letter 112 of the holy teacher, and especially volume VI, pages 515–516, in the preface.

**Editorial note:** In John Chrysostom today, instead of *in Cilicia*, one reads *in the heart* (*ἐν καρδίᾳ*) in Letter 112, which is entitled *To Theodore the Bishop* and does not specify the place. It reads:

> “For while sitting in the desert, we do not reap an ordinary consolation when we possess in the heart such a treasure and wealth stored up—the love of your watchful and noble soul.”

It is not easy to determine how this variation arose. Mopsuestia, moreover, the see of Bishop Theodore, was a town of Cilicia Secunda. Hierocles has: “The province of Cilicia Secunda, under a governor; nine cities: Anazarbus, the metropolis; Mopsuestia,” and so forth.

Your Serenity will observe with me from the tenor of this letter that, just as John of Antioch and the Council of the East testified, Theodore—who was condemned as the supposed originator of the Nestorian error—had been a fellow student of this blessed John.

This is sufficiently indicated by John’s words, when he says that Theodore’s affection toward him had been ancient and from the beginning. The same point will also be proved by the letters of the Lord Bishop of Antioch.

Why, then, should the great Council of Chalcedon be accused? Knowing that the holy John, writing to Theodore, had said:

> “For it was not hidden from us how eagerly you hastened to speak and act on our behalf, my most honored and holy lord,”

the council believed that the man who had hastened to speak and act so zealously on behalf of John, transported into exile, and who had thereby made God his debtor for a full reward, was not a heretic.

It considered it incredible that a teacher of Nestorian treachery would seek to have the true teacher of religion, who was certainly opposed to him, brought back from exile and, by the authority of his position, allowed to dispute freely in the Church against his corrupt doctrines.

Unless perhaps that synod is condemned as impious for this reason: because, thinking piously about John of Constantinople, it judged him to be such a man that a heretic would love him enough to wish him recalled as his assistant into his own Church—or that John himself would likewise love and praise a heretic with such great commendation.

But when John also said:

> “We possess in Cilicia such a treasure and such hidden riches,”

why should the synod be blamed if it revered the treasure of John and his hidden riches and refused to anathematize them? Or ought it itself to have decreed and said, “If anyone does not anathematize Theodore, let him be anathema”?

Is it not better—not to mention the other Fathers—to hear an anathema together with John than to pronounce an anathema against John? For if the man who does not declare Theodore of Mopsuestia anathema is himself anathema, then John of Constantinople, the most illustrious bishop of the Church and the most steadfast confessor of the truth, is anathema, since he did not anathematize such a treasure and such hidden riches as Theodore possessed in Mopsuestia of Cilicia.

Yet that man of great weight and always-anticipated authority will not be lacking to us in defense of the great synod, which did not demand that Bishop Ibas condemn Theodore of Mopsuestia when it heard his praises read from Ibas’s letter.

Let the blessed Gregory of Nazianzus also appear, himself adding to the charge against the rash, since he writes as follows to Theodore while he was still young and newly grown, congratulating him on his perfection:

> “We rejoice in the tokens of your affection, especially at such a time, and from such a young man who is at once newly grown and perfect—and, to embrace you in terms drawn from Holy Scripture, established over youth. For Scripture calls those who surpass their age in understanding by this name. The ancient fathers ask that the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, together with all other things, be granted to their sons—unless someone finds it pleasing to understand these things more deeply. But we repay all things to you spiritually. May the Lord fulfill all your requests, and may you become the father of such sons—for it is fitting that I pray for you briefly and familiarly—as you have shown yourself to your fathers, so that in other respects also we may boast because of you.”

**Editorial note:** The Greek reads *Ἀγάπης συμβόλοις ἡδόμεθα* (“We rejoice in the tokens of affection”). This appears to be the correct reading, not *συμβούλοις*. In Gregory’s Letter 219, and in the letter cited here as Letter 220 together with the following two, the simple title is *To Theodore* (*Θεοδώρῳ*). Letter 225, however, has the fuller title *To Theodore, Bishop of Tyana* (*Θεοδώρῳ ἐπισκόπῳ Τυάνων*), and everyone conjectures that this letter belongs to that Theodore, as will be discussed shortly.

**Editorial note:** The Verona manuscript has *you show* instead of *you have shown*.

How, then, is the holy synod blamed because it did not condemn Theodore, when it knew how great a man had praised him for his perfection—namely, Gregory of Nazianzus, who called him young but said that he surpassed his age in understanding and was established above his youth through the height of his wisdom?

What is more pleasing and delightful is that, although he was distinguished in knowledge, he displayed such humility and reverence toward his fathers that Gregory bestowed upon him this blessing in recognition of those merits: namely, that he might have sons such as he had shown himself to be toward his fathers.

If that synod religiously and piously believed that this blessing had not been uttered in vain, then it is the synod that is being frustrated as impious and profane.

Let us pass to another letter.

**Editorial note:** This is Gregory’s Letter 88, which in the Greek manuscripts is addressed to “An Anonymous Person” (*Ἀνωνύμῳ*), but which is correctly entitled in the Latin manuscripts, *To Theodore, Bishop of Tyana*. Facundus is therefore mistaken in thinking that it was written to Theodore of Mopsuestia. It was written to the metropolitan of the province in which Nazianzus was located, as the words of the letter make clear. It says:

> “If the province had another head, it would be necessary to cry out and protest to him; but since your Reverence stands above it, it is necessary to look to you.”

Nazianzus, moreover, was a town of Cappadocia Secunda, whose metropolis was Tyana. Hierocles writes in the *Synecdemus*: “The province of Cappadocia Secunda, under a governor; eight cities: Tyana, Faustinopolis, Cybistra, Nazianzus, Sasima,” and so forth. The letter therefore belongs to Theodore of Tyana, as Justinian also observes in the Edict and the Fifth Council, against those who referred it to Theodore of Mopsuestia.

For when the same blessed Gregory was worn out by age and also suffering from a long illness, and complained that for this reason he could not bear the burden of his Church or resist the Apollinarians, who were ravaging the flock of God, because of this twofold weakness, he decided to lay down the care of the episcopate and, leaving his city, to live with monks in the countryside, where he also died. He chose Theodore, from throughout the East, to defend and visit that same Church of his, declaring that the province had no other head from whom it could seek help.

Thus he writes to him again:

> “It is time for me to say the words of Scripture: ‘To whom shall I cry out when I suffer violence? Who will stretch out a hand to me in my oppression? To whom shall the burden of this Church, lying so wretchedly and falling apart, pass?’ I testify before God and the elect angels that the flock of God is suffering unjustly, living without a shepherd and without a visitor because of our sluggishness. For illness holds me and has quickly carried me away from the Church, and now I am altogether expecting the end, being even more afflicted in reality. If the province had another head, it would be necessary to cry out and protest to him. But since your Reverence has been placed above it, it is necessary to look to you. Take care of your Church in whatever way you can, and do not contemptuously disregard it in its distress.
