To pass over other matters, you will learn from my lords and fellow presbyters Eulalius, my fellow bishop, and Eleusius, whom we have sent with great urgency to your Reverence, what the Apollinarians who are now rising have done in some respects and threaten in others. To suppress these things belongs not to my age but to your prudence and virtue, since God has granted you, together with others, the ability to defend the Church in common. But if, despite my saying and writing these things, I am not heard, the only thing left will be to proclaim publicly to everyone and make it known that the Church needs a bishop, lest because of my weakness it be struck.”

> “For the rest, you will see to it.”

Oh, how strong and unconquerable are the merits of the righteous, most merciful emperor! They are shown to be incapable of being overcome all the more certainly and clearly the more zealously and violently they are attacked.

For who could know or seek out so many impregnable testimonies in support of the judgment of the Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon, unless adversity provoked it? Therefore it seems to me that adversity ought to be received not only patiently but even gratefully. For while it strives to obscure the justice of the saints, it always makes that justice clearer.

Is the justice of those Fathers not more fully demonstrated when they are shown to have trusted the testimony of John of Constantinople and Gregory of Nazianzus more than that of those who wanted certain chapters of Theodore condemned, making them, as the blessed Cyril says, an occasion for the contrary doctrine to which they were attached?

Let it not, then, be judged condemnable that the synod did not condemn Theodore, whom Gregory judged to be the singular head of the entire province and to whom he entrusted the flock of God committed to his government.

Gregory begged Theodore to stretch out a hand to him against the Apollinarian heretics, testifying before God and the elect angels that, while Gregory was held back by the sluggishness of illness, Christ’s flock needed Theodore’s visitation and assistance. What fault is there in this?

The synod does not condemn Theodore, and for that reason it is thought heretical. Gregory entrusted Theodore with prudence and virtue, and no slight complaint is raised on that account. Yet, good heavens, such envy is stirred against the Council of Chalcedon because it did not attribute imprudence to him!

But will Gregory of Nazianzus, John of Constantinople, and the others whom we have mentioned and shall mention be called men possessed by the Nestorian disease because they not only did not reject Theodore but even prevented him from being rejected? Or will anyone dare to call them by a new and hitherto unheard-of name, “Theodorians”?

If no one dares to do this, why do they call others “Theodorians” who hold to their Catholic faith and preserve their judgment, and who do not dare, to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon, to condemn Theodore? By this insult they simultaneously dishonor the council mentioned above, where Theodore was not condemned even when his praises were read.

If there is doubt about their religion and faith, let them be examined. If the question concerns the reason for condemning Theodore, the opinion of the Fathers whom they follow is clear.

For surely a person who refuses to agree with novel presumptions should not thereby be forced to accept a new name. Nor is it shameful that we endure this together with such great Fathers. For just as it is criminal to praise him against their judgment, so it is praiseworthy to be accused together with them.

Since we recognize that the great synod is being accused in the case of Theodore of Mopsuestia together with these lights of the Church, we ought not to be disturbed by any calumnies of the Eutychians; rather, we should confound them by the authority of those very men.

And so, having recalled the testimonies of these venerable Fathers, who bore witness to the same Theodore while he was alive, let us now proceed to the testimonies of two men who likewise honored his memory, after he had departed from this life, with great and abundant praise.

Thus we bring the present book to an end, so that the reader’s attention may be renewed by a new beginning elsewhere.

# BOOK EIGHT

## CHAPTER ONE

### That many ancient Fathers wrote things consonant with what is criticized in Theodore of Mopsuestia, according to the testimony of John of Antioch and the Eastern bishops

Receive, most serene emperor, the many further testimonies of holy and venerable Fathers by which the Council of Chalcedon is still accused of having failed to contradict them—Fathers by whom Theodore of Mopsuestia, even after his death, was praised much more extensively than in the letter of the venerable Ibas.

Let us therefore first return to the letters of the holy John of Antioch and of the Eastern Council, as we promised in the second book.

The blessed Proclus had sent synodical letters to the East, together with a doctrinal volume addressed to the Armenians, which, as we have already shown, the Eastern Council approved. Taking advantage of this mission, certain men tried to insinuate themselves into the matter, so that excerpts from the statements of ancient teachers of the Church, with their names placed above them, might also be subjected to anathema.

**Editorial note:** The bishops of Armenia and Persia had sent through their envoys to Proclus certain chapters excerpted from Theodore’s writings, so that they might be condemned on his authority, together with those in Syria and Cilicia who were said to hold the same opinions. Proclus included these in his volume addressed to the Armenians and sent it to the Eastern bishops. They could not tolerate the condemnation of Theodore and opposed it in a letter to Proclus and in other letters to Cyril and others. Concerning this matter, and the entire controversy over Theodore’s anathema, much is said at length in the fifth action of the Fifth Council and in Liberatus, chapter 10 of the *Breviarium*.

The Eastern Council, stirred by such an attempt because it had thought that this had been ordered by the blessed Proclus himself, replied that it approved the doctrinal volume sent to it. It then wrote to him on Theodore’s behalf the things we recalled in the second book, as well as many others which we intend now to mention, having omitted them earlier:

> “Our souls have been wounded exceedingly, because we continually endure not only such calumnies against the living from those who wish to disturb the Churches, but also the charge that the blessed Theodore, who lived his life well, who shone brilliantly in teaching for forty-five years, who defeated every heresy, and who during his life suffered no reproach anywhere from the orthodox, is now, after his departure from this life following a long period of time, after many struggles, after writing ten thousand books against errors, and after being approved in the presence of priests, emperors, and peoples, in danger of enduring the fate of heretics and of being proclaimed their foremost—”

And they add what had been omitted, saying:

> “They have filled us with this confusion and turmoil—not us alone but also the Christian peoples. When these people learn of such things, they do not allow ecclesiastical celebrations to be completed without disturbance; rather, they stir up seditions against us and refuse even to hear what sort of anathema was being devised against the Fathers who have fallen asleep. They threaten ten thousand evils against us if anyone should presume such a thing.

> “Let your Holiness also know this: when we searched the writings of the ancient teachers of the Church, we found ten thousand such passages and others similar to the excerpts which certain men, by an evil practice, collected from the books of the blessed Theodore, cutting away the remainder of the body of the text, and presented to your Holiness.

> “For in the writings of the great martyr Ignatius, who, second after Peter, the first of the apostles, organized the Church of the Antiochene see; in the writings of the most blessed Eustathius, who was the first among the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea to confirm the orthodox faith; and in those of the most holy and blessed Athanasius, who endured countless struggles for the evangelical doctrines; and, in addition, in those of Basil and both Gregories, who shared the same opinion; and in those of the most blessed Flavian, Diodore, and John, who were the distinguished lights of the entire East; and again in those of the most blessed Ambrose, who illuminated all the regions of the West; and in those of the most blessed Amphilochius, the most approved teacher; and also in those of your father, the blessed Atticus; and in those of ten thousand others, to avoid going through them one by one, we found statements consonant with the chapters excerpted in this way.

> “If these Fathers are anathematized, it is necessary to include under the anathema also the statements made by the Fathers mentioned above. Who, then, will henceforth support our teachings when such admirable and famous men have been condemned after death?

> “It is not for us to insult the beliefs of those glorious men who have gone before, nor to judge those who died honorably, but this belongs to the one Judge of the living and the dead.”

Here I should like the Eutychians to explain what the holy Council of Chalcedon ought to have observed, when the praises of Theodore were read in the letter of the venerable Ibas, Theodore having been praised by the Eastern Fathers with much greater commendation—not to mention John of Constantinople and Gregory of Nazianzus.

Would it have justly condemned the letter because of its praise of Theodore, while failing to condemn the letter of the Eastern bishops in which it was confirmed that one of the Trinity was crucified for us?

Or could it justly condemn Theodore alone, without Ignatius, Eustathius, Athanasius, Basil, both Gregories, Flavian, Diodore, John, Ambrose, Amphilochius, Atticus, and the other ten thousand—if, as John of Antioch and all the Eastern bishops say, statements consonant with certain chapters of Theodore are found in their writings?

But if such statements are not found, and these men, while shielding Theodore, wished to deceive us, could the Council of Chalcedon even then justly condemn Theodore alone, without John of Antioch and all the Eastern bishops who, while concealing the errors of that same Theodore, accused Ignatius the martyr—who, second after the apostle Peter, organized the Church of the Antiochene see—and the other glorious Fathers whom they mentioned, of having held opinions consonant with Theodore?

For if Ibas’s letter is judged impious because it contains his slight suspicions concerning the blessed Cyril, then John of Antioch and all the Eastern bishops ought to have been accused of incomparably greater impiety. They had deliberately assembled in council, explicitly accusing so many and such great Fathers—and, as they said, ten thousand others—of having written things consonant with Theodore, whom these men call a heretic.

Thus Theodore of Mopsuestia could not justly have been condemned by the Council of Chalcedon except either together with the martyr Ignatius and the other most glorious Fathers mentioned with him, if they had written statements consonant with certain excerpts from his chapters, or together with John of Antioch and all the Eastern bishops, if they had falsely claimed that those Fathers had written things consonant with Theodore.

But we must not omit the fact that it could not justly have condemned the Eastern Fathers themselves without Proclus of Constantinople.

For if those who wrote to him falsely claimed that the martyr Ignatius and the other Fathers mentioned with him had written things similar to Theodore—who is now accused as a heretic—Proclus ought not to have remained silent through a deceitful and destructive pretense. Rather, he ought immediately to have opposed them with the greatest indignation, since what they were saying would not have been true.

This was especially necessary because, not in a slight or passing word but in a synodical judgment confirmed by the subscription of all the Eastern bishops, he saw a horrible crime being attached, to the prejudice of the Church, to such blessed Fathers.

Since this is so, let them cease accusing the great synod because it did not condemn Theodore. It could not justly condemn him either without the martyr Ignatius, Eustathius, Athanasius, Basil, both Gregories, and the others listed in the same way, or without John of Antioch, the Eastern Council, and Proclus of Constantinople.

But first let them say together with which of these men Theodore ought to have been condemned; only then should they accuse the Council of Chalcedon of negligence or restraint.

## CHAPTER TWO

### That it is falsely said that Proclus disparaged Theodore’s name, since his writings plainly refute this
Let us now see what blessed Proclus replied when John of Antioch and the Eastern synod wrote to him, so that the shameless falsity of the heretics may become apparent—heretics whose supporters Catholics ought not to have believed when they fabricated the claim that the same holy Proclus, in writing to the aforementioned John of Antioch [Note: We have seen a fragment of Proclus’s letter to John, sent with the tome, in Book II. This belongs to another letter that he wrote in reply to John after receiving his earlier letter and complaint concerning Theodore’s chapters. It is therefore clear that Proclus’s policy was the same as Cyril’s: in consideration of the Easterners’ offense, Theodore’s name should be spared, while his perverse doctrines should nevertheless be condemned. For this reason he had suppressed Theodore’s name in the chapters, although the Easterners could not even be persuaded of this.], had spoken ill of Theodore and said that in the tome which he sent to the Armenians he had inserted chapters of that same Theodore, full of Jewish impiety, in order that they might be condemned under an anathema.

When the aforementioned John of Antioch and his synod complained and objected, Proclus replied as follows:

> “When did I ever write to Your Holiness that either Theodore or certain others who died long ago should be subjected to an anathema, or that anyone’s name should be mentioned specifically? [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “I made mention.”] But I think—as the very letter addressed to Your Holiness loudly proclaims—that the letter contains nothing difficult or perverse. Yet, since it is necessary to remove every suspicion and sew shut the mouths of detractors, I subscribed to the tome that was sent and rejected the chapters appended to it, since they lacked the subtlety of piety. I did not write to you, most beloved of God, either about Theodore or about anyone else who has already died, that he should be anathematized or repudiated. Nor did the most beloved Theodore, the deacon sent by us, receive any such instructions.”

Even this most evident denial by blessed Proclus does not yet confound the heretics or their supporters. They still dare to say that after his death he spoke ill of Theodore of Mopsuestia and accused him, as though he were a heretic, of impiety, although Proclus explicitly protests that he had sought not only for Theodore, but for no one at all among those who had already died, to be anathematized or repudiated, nor had he mentioned anyone by name.

Far be it from Proclus’s conscience that he should seek childish glory through the malicious defamation of venerable names and the public disparagement of deceased priests who had died in the peace of the Church, and should thereby aspire to appear learned or religious. He therefore denies that he had mentioned anyone by name; and he says that his letters not only bear witness, but cry out against the deafness of contentious men, that they contain nothing perverse—defining as perverse, plainly, the action that he was falsely thought to have sought: that bishops who had never been censured during their lives should be condemned after death, contrary to the custom of the Church.

He also writes to Maximus [Note: The same manuscript reads: “to Maximus the deacon.” Facundus likewise calls this same Maximus a deacon below, at col. 0728.], one of the two through whom, as has been said, he had sent the synodical letter to the Eastern bishops, saying:

> “Your Reverence remembers that, when I entrusted you with a letter to the most holy bishop of Antioch [Note: The same manuscript reads: “archbishop.”], I instructed you that everything ought to be done according to his will; that nothing should be undertaken to confuse or agitate Churches possessing peace; that the tome should indeed be signed, but that the appended chapters, without a name, should be rejected and repudiated as lacking the subtlety of piety. How, then, have I now learned through letters that the names of Theodore of Mopsuestia and certain others have been placed before the chapters for condemnation by an anathema, when they have already departed to God, and when it is superfluous to insult after death those who have already left this life and whom we never censured while they were alive? I therefore ask you: hasten, like a son, to investigate [the matter], but leave everything to the authority of that most reverent fellow-priest, John. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “as a son obedient to his father, to inquire into nothing further.”] After the tome has been signed and the chapters—whose authors we do not know—have been rejected, immediately prepare for the deacon Theodore to come to the imperial city, so that the churches of the most holy city may not be filled with storm and tumult, and so that you may grant something to the desire of the impious Nestorius, who thinks that he has many people who share his opinions.”

Here, as you can see, Emperor, the matter is not inferred from the course of our reasoning but is demonstrated most clearly by the very words of blessed Proclus. For if the synod of Chalcedon, as certain persons did, had rejected the letter of the venerable Ibas on the grounds that it praised Theodore as one who shared Nestorius’s opinions, it would thereby have seemed rather to excuse Nestorius, as we have said and demonstrated, and to grant something to the desire of the Nestorians, who think that they have many people who share their opinions.

Thus the most wise man Proclus [Note: The same manuscript reads: “the most prudent Proclus.”] understood what the learned men refused to understand: if Theodore of Mopsuestia, together with certain others whose names had been placed before certain chapters for condemnation by an anathema, were condemned, Nestorius could object and say:

> “How have I been expelled from the Church as though I were the inventor of a new doctrine, when Theodore, a most learned man, proclaimed by the most learned Fathers, and others who, like him, died without accusation in the peace of the Church, are said to have held the same opinions? You, therefore, rather than I, must be called the inventors of a new doctrine, since you depart from the teaching of those whom the Church has always honored. For I too am proved Catholic by your own testimony: if I teach what Theodore of Mopsuestia and the others taught in the Church, and if their teaching was either praised by the holy Fathers or—what is certain for the present—was never found blameworthy by anyone throughout the whole time they lived, then my teaching too is blameless.”

But if this reasoning—not mine, but that of the most prudent and holy Proclus—is now disregarded, although the Church had until then preserved it and lived in peace, why, I ask, is silence kept concerning the names of the others who at that time had likewise been placed before the chapters for condemnation? Why, we may ask, are those men, though equally accused, now spared, while Theodore of Mopsuestia alone is named in this condemnation? Is there anything else that we can understand or suspect here except that he alone was praised in the letter of the venerable Ibas, which the synod of Chalcedon judged orthodox?

Moreover, the wise man Proclus did not dare to insult this Theodore after his death, since Christian piety did not permit such a thing; nor would he have had anything to answer if someone had said to him:

> “Why do you accuse him of Jewish impiety and seek to condemn a dead man whom, while he was alive and teaching openly in the Church, you never dared to rebuke? For if he appeared to be condemned as a heretic, you ought first to have admonished him while he was alive, when he could either explain himself concerning the matters that offended you and offer or accept a better account, or else be justly condemned for his obstinacy.”

But now you are doing nothing other than leaving an interminable scandal to posterity, so that the Church may always be shaken by great disputes: some following the judgment of the ancient Fathers who praised him, and others following your judgment, since you presume to accuse him after his death.

This clear reasoning, evident to all, guided the good and wise Proclus, so that he wrote nothing evil either about Theodore, as the heretics fabricate, or about anyone else who had died in the peace of the Church. For this reason, rebuking his deacon, he says that he had not instructed him to undertake anything that would cause confusion or tumult among Churches possessing peace. Accordingly, he not only censures the fact that the names of Theodore of Mopsuestia and certain others had been placed before certain chapters, but also admits that he did not know to whom those chapters belonged.

How, then, could the holy synod, having observed Theodore’s praise in Ibas’s letter, compel Ibas himself to anathematize Theodore, when it knew that the judgment of holy Proclus—whose teaching it upheld—had determined not only in Theodore’s case but in the case of all who had departed this life without accusation that it was superfluous to insult them after death?

## CHAPTER III. That the Synod of the East wrote to the Emperor Theodosius, and Theodosius to the Synod, concerning the non-condemnation of Theodore

But let us now return to another part of that letter, written by the aforementioned synod of the East to the emperor Theodosius, which we judged it inappropriate to mention in the second book and had postponed for explanation here [Note: This letter of John and the Eastern synod to Theodosius was discussed in Book II. It is the letter that the synod of Chalcedon praises in its address to Marcian. “The wise John,” it says, “of the Antiochenes, sent the confession of the East, in one voice, to him who governs the scepter of the inhabited world.” The Greek reads: **Ὁ σοφὸς τῆς Ἀντιοχέων Ἰωάννης, τῆς ἑώας ἐκ μιᾶς γλώττης τῷ τῆς οἰκουμένης σκῆπτρα διέποντι τὴν ὁμολογίαν ἐξέπεμψε**—“The wise John of Antioch sent the confession of the East, with one voice, to him who governs the scepter of the inhabited world.”].

When this same Eastern synod, writing to the emperor Theodosius against those who wished to condemn certain chapters of Theodore, had said many things about Theodore himself—that he was held in singular honor not only by priests but also by his most sacred grandfather, Theodosius, thrice-blessed and receiving the scepters of imperial power from God, as a most devoted disciple of Flavian the Great, bishop of the holy Church of God at Antioch, and a fellow student of blessed John of Constantinople—it added the following:

> “But if someone should say that something obscure is found in his writings or in those of others, there is no need to subject it to renewed examination. For those whose life in the priesthood and ministry had an excellent end, we dedicate a splendid glory to them, and we do not judge them on the basis of the matters with which some savagely accuse them. For since those who teach in the Church are human beings, it is impossible for them to escape the criticisms of their slanderers. And what shall we say about the teachers of the Church? Even the holy Gospels themselves are received by many heretics according to their own will; they twist the divine sayings and tear the body of the Church into many parts. These things, in brief, we all—the bishops who by God’s grace have assembled at Antioch—have taught Your Piety.”

After this, when they had mentioned by name many ancient teachers of the Church, just as they had done in writing to Bishop Proclus, asserting that those teachers had taught the same things as Theodore, they finally say:

> “We consider it also useless to the pious empire itself that men should be driven here and there and not be allowed to rest from this unwelcome disturbance caused by men. We therefore ask that the causes of the storm be brought to an end, and command that tranquility be established for the Churches of God.”

Nothing, as I judge, most religious prince, had this holy synod of Eastern priests left for us to do before Your Clemency. For they carefully stated that it was useless not only to the peace of the Churches but also to your own empire that men should be driven here and there and not be allowed to rest. [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “They said beforehand.”] Yet it came about that these things became known to you too late, since those who could have done this did not wish to, while those who wished to were prevented from doing so by them.

For what Christian would not yield to the great authority of these men? What prudent person would not submit to their considered judgment? Finally, instructed by their writings, the emperor Theodosius also followed the judgment of his holy grandfather Theodosius concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia, and did not disregard or postpone putting their wholesome decrees and admonitions into effect, as we shall show below.

Nor was the case of Theodore of Mopsuestia then the same as it is now. He was not being sought for condemnation together with his doctrines to the prejudice of the great synod, as is now the case; nor was anyone being compelled to anathematize those who did not pronounce an anathema against him.

What, then, as something new or heretical, could the synod of Chalcedon condemn in the letter of the venerable Ibas: that Theodore, praised by so many Fathers and held in singular honor by the elder emperor Theodosius, who received the scepters of imperial power from God, was also praised by Ibas himself?

Nor ought the holy synod to have treated lightly the judgment of that blessed emperor, to whom the Church had to grant as much authority as he himself had never claimed any authority against the Church.

Therefore, most merciful emperor, I ask and beseech you, out of the reverence that you owe to Christ God and to his priests, to receive obediently the exhortation of your holy Fathers. For all these ancient Eastern bishops now speak to you; they now urge you with the words that they once addressed to the younger Theodosius:

> “But if someone should say that something obscure is found in the writings of Bishop Theodore or of others, there is no need to subject it to renewed examination. For those whose life in the priesthood and ministry had an excellent end, we dedicate a distinguished glory to them, and we do not judge them on the basis of the matters with which some savagely accuse them. For since those who teach in the Church are human beings, it is impossible for them to escape the criticisms of their slanderers. And what shall we say about the teachers of the Church, when many heretics also receive the holy Gospels themselves according to their own will, twisting the divine sayings and tearing the body of the Church into many parts?”

Therefore listen, most religious prince—listen, we beseech you—as we give you this salutary exhortation: listen to your fathers, if you wish Christ to hear them praying on your behalf. It is a serious matter that those whom the younger Theodosius once received while they were present in the body and sojourners from the Lord should now, when they are absent from the body and present with God, be rejected by Justinian, who is acclaimed for zeal for the faith.

Theodosius had no example of an emperor obedient in this matter to invite him to follow; you, however, have an example before you. Theodosius had not yet experienced the benefit of that obedience; you, however, have learned from the outcome of events how that storm was calmed by his prohibition.

You therefore respond far more usefully, most merciful emperor, to the expectation of the whole Church than he did, since the present case for not condemning Theodore is incomparably greater than it was in those times.

For if John of Antioch and all the Eastern bishops whom we have mentioned—or Domnus, likewise of Antioch, whose letter we shall also quote in part [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “nevertheless, a certain part”]—may appear to some to have contended only for Theodore, we, who fear anathematizing Theodore and all those who do not pronounce an anathema against him, are contending not only for Theodore, nor only for the Council of Chalcedon, where he was not condemned even though his praises were later recited, but also against the condemnation of John and Domnus of Antioch, of all the Eastern priests, and of blessed Proclus. They not only failed to pronounce an anathema against him, but forbade us to do so.

What, then, the younger Theodosius replied when the aforementioned blessed Proclus approached him, so that you may reply more advantageously, must be explained. The letter reads:

> “The emperors Caesar Theodosius and Valentinian, victorious, triumphant, most pious, ever Augusti, to John, beloved of God, archbishop, and to the synod assembled with him at Antioch.
>
> “Our empire learned of the crowd and disturbance that arose in the East through our most religious and most holy father and bishop Proclus. Since, therefore, we provide for the quiet and peace of all, and especially for the Catholic faith, which also preserves our empire, we write to Your Holiness so that you may maintain peace and give no heed to those who wish, to their own destruction, to disturb the most holy religion.
>
> “For the intention of our divinity is that all people should live in quiet, and especially the holy Churches of God, through which we too are saved and our empire flourishes. Therefore, while providing by this decree for the tranquility of the Church, we expect nothing more useful from you than that you, together with the whole Church, establish that no one henceforth presume to do anything of this kind against those who have died in its peace.” [Note: The same manuscript reads: “we expect nothing more useful.” The reading is: “There is nothing more useful than this,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER IV. That the same synod of the East also wrote to Cyril concerning the non-condemnation of Theodore
I shall add also another letter of the oft-mentioned holy John of Antioch and his synod to the blessed [Col. 0718B] Cyril [Note: [Col. 0718D] Cyril himself mentions this in the same letter to Proclus, which survives only in Latin in the Fifth Synod: “But now,” he says, “as my lord, the most holy bishop of Antioch, John, wrote to me, the beginning of another storm has arisen among them; and there is very great fear that perhaps some unstable persons may return to their former position.” This is the third of those letters which, as was noted in Book II, John wrote on behalf of Theodore because of the chapters appended to Proclus’s Tome, according to Liberatus’s *Breviary*.] written against condemning the statements of Theodore.

“To the God-beloved [Note: [Col. 0717D] This letter of John of Antioch is found only in Latin among the letters of Cyril of Alexandria, *Works*, vol. V, part II, p. 192.] and most holy bishop Cyril, John of Antioch, and the God-beloved bishops who assembled with him from each province in the East by the grace of God, in the city beloved by Christ, Antioch, because of the letter of the most holy bishop, our lord Proclus.”

And further, speaking of those very men who, as has been said, were insisting that certain chapters excerpted from Theodore’s books should be condemned, they say:

“But now these same men, as though rising from sleep, went to the imperial city and, disturbing it, disturbed ecclesiastical peace as far as lay within their power. For when the most holy bishop Proclus sent us his Tome—which is truly correct and devout, and which he wrote to the Armenians—and sought our agreement, everything was done by us, and we fell short in nothing. Indeed, at the present time this was also superfluous, because now, by the grace of God, everyone everywhere preserves one and the same devout understanding. Matters which seem almost necessary often acquire an increase of disturbance unless they are done at the appropriate time.

“There is another evil in the haste of these men, with hands extended [Note: [Col. 0718D] The same lacuna occurs in the same place (*Cyril’s Works*), p. 193.] [Note: [Col. 0718D] Something appears to be missing here.], and another Tome containing certain excerpts from the blessed Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, and from what he appears to have said in various books, which they wish to subject to anathema. For this reason we ask you to apply your mind to us more diligently than to other matters, and deign to consider that this is an evil undertaking unless you strive to extinguish it by common agreement. For God has given you not only the will but also the ability, so that you may help everyone together [Col. 0719A] [Note: [Col. 0719D] In Cyril’s edition just cited, p. 193: ‘that you may live in the communion of all.’ This seems less correct.].

“We confess that there are some things in that Tome which are uncertain and capable of being understood otherwise than they were said. But we see most of them to be clear and correct, without any ambiguity. Yet among those matters that are thought obscure, we find many similar statements made by many glorious Fathers earlier than him; and a considerable danger is involved here, lest in these matters we also undo their [Note: [Col. 0719D] In the same place: ‘them,’ namely, the Fathers. But the reading ‘their’ seems preferable, with ‘statements’ understood.] statements by rejecting the statements of a man who, although he died in the episcopate, was adorned throughout his whole life and everywhere with ten thousand struggles against the Arians [Note: [Col. 0719D] The Verona manuscript reads: ‘against the Arians and Eunomians, and other heretics.’] and other heretics. If this happens, we shall also be forced to retract and reject many things plainly stated by other holy Fathers.

“For among these excerpts we have found certain similar statements in the thrice-blessed and noble Athanasius, others in the blessed Basil, others in both Gregories; many, moreover, in Amphilochius, repeatedly stated, and not a few in our common Father, the blessed Theophilus. Indeed, there are matters which your holiness also confesses in this way, and you hold the same understanding of them. Some things were also said by the God-beloved [Note: [Col. 0720D] The same place: ‘by the beloved.’] Proclus himself in that same Tome which he sent to the Armenians, and they agree with many of these statements in meaning.

“Time would fail us if we were to go through the blessed Eustathius, bishop of the city of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0720D] The same place: ‘Eustathius of Antioch.’], who stood for the true faith at the Council of Nicaea, and your great and renowned Alexander of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0719D] The same manuscript reads: ‘your Alexander.’]; and, after those most holy bishops, Meletius and Flavian, by whom many statements agreeing with these were made. What shall I say about those in the West who were distinguished according to the doctrine [Note: [Col. 0719D] The same manuscript reads: ‘the same doctrine.’] and the same confession, whom your holiness knows even better?

“Therefore, I beg you, consider into what precipice those men are driving us who contend in words to no useful end. What injury, corruption, and confusion would not arise from this, if we opened the door to those who seek to overturn the statements [Note: [Col. 0719D] The same manuscript reads: ‘who wish to overturn the statements.’] of the Fathers who have passed away [Note: [Col. 0719D] Perhaps: ‘who wish to overturn them.’]? What harm would not be manifest in not only refuting their statements but also anathematizing them? For although one thing may please one person and another thing may not, in the statements of some people—whether ancient or later, whether or not they are of our own time [Note: [Col. 0719D] The same manuscript reads: ‘now ours.’]—there is one consideration. But to impose an anathema upon them as well appears presumptuous and harsh, even if the persons are not anathematized together with their statements.

“For who among us can hope that he can persuade another, or that none of these things would always provide an occasion for the people to be disturbed? [Col. 0719D] This indeed tends to happen both with the living and with those who have passed away [Col. 0720A]. We say this not only to one who is unaware of these matters, but also to one who is able to consider more fully than anyone else [Note: [Col. 0719D] The same manuscript reads: ‘than all of us.’ The same is found in Cyril at the place cited.] the magnitude of this absurdity.

“What welcome thing would we not thereby provide to the defenders of Nestorius? For who would not honor him if he were anathematized together with this man and with others who laid down their life in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0720D] The same manuscript reads: ‘were anathematized.’ The same is found in Cyril at the place cited.]? Or where would his opinion not thereby receive increase? And who among deceived men, seizing this as an opportunity, would not call him a confessor, as though he had suffered what he suffered because of that man [Note: [Col. 0720D] The same manuscript reads: ‘who suffered what he suffered.’ (The same is found in Cyril at the place cited, although there it reads ‘for her.’)], which even those who shone in the Church have suffered?”

Who among people of sound judgment does not know that Theodore, the blessed, said those things which were harsh because he was compelled by necessity? For the whole East, in common, placed him among those who had lived before us [Col. 0720B] as possessing great power of doctrine against the heresies. In fighting and contending against them, he employed a certain division—not arising from a perverse understanding, but because he judged that this method would be more effective against the heretics. He neither ignored nor denied the supreme unity—far be it from him, for all his books are full of this kind of teaching—but divided the properties of the natures more fully, as the struggle he had against the heretics dictated that he should do. Your religiousness also plainly adopted this approach in your earlier letters, for the satisfaction of certain of our venerable fellow bishops. This too is characteristic of your virtue and wisdom.”

But I, religious prince, am moved by these statements to the extent that the venerable Fathers, through the wisdom granted them by God [Col. 0720C], anticipated everything that we might have been able to say on Theodore’s case on behalf of the great synod. To the same extent, however, I grieve and blame those who were not accustomed to show these things to you beforehand [Note: [Col. 0720D] The same manuscript reads: ‘did not allow us to show these things to you beforehand.’]. For who could believe that your religiousness would resist so great an authority, or that such prudence would resist such reasoning? These words of the Eastern synod would move not merely the mind of a God-fearing and wise prince, but that of any person whose humanity had not utterly deserted him.

For if they were then able to extinguish the blazing flame, how much more could they now obtain from you that no one should revive what had been extinguished? But if those men are called as though rising from sleep who, having contradicted nothing while Theodore was alive, went at that time to the imperial city after his death and disturbed ecclesiastical peace as far as lay within their power [Col. 0720D], what should be said about these supporters of heretics, who after a hundred years have begun to awaken even more disastrously from the sleep of those who had then risen to their own ruin [Note: [Col. 0721D] The Verona manuscript reads: ‘from the sleep of those who at that time, to their own harm, etc.’]?

How, then, can the Council of Chalcedon rightly be blamed, since it trusted the Eastern Fathers assembled in council—men whom it knew neither to have denied that certain statements in Theodore’s writings could be understood otherwise than they were said, nor to have failed to affirm that those statements which they understood to have been expressed in a correct sense had been so expressed? They declared that they saw many other statements of his to be clear and correct, without any ambiguity. The Council also knew that these same Easterners had testified that many similar statements had been made by many of Theodore’s earlier and glorious Fathers concerning those statements of Theodore which were thought obscure.

But it did not wish to reject the statements of that man who, although he died in the episcopate [Col. 0721B], was adorned throughout his whole life and everywhere with ten thousand struggles against the Arians and Eunomians and other heretics. Should it be blamed for this moderation and reasonableness? Especially since a serious danger threatened: once his statements had been condemned, the entire teaching of those Fathers might also be destroyed.

That synod, therefore, ought to be called extremely deliberate and provident rather than Nestorian. It prudently removed the occasions by which the people could be disturbed and provided neither an excuse nor even authority for Nestorian error. It would certainly have done so if it had judged Theodore—praised by so many Fathers—to be the author of Nestorian doctrine.

“For this reason they themselves also said: ‘Or what among these things would not provide occasions for the people always to be disturbed? What welcome thing would we not thereby provide to the defenders of Nestorius? For who would not honor him if he were anathematized together with this man and with others who laid down their life in the episcopate?’” And the other things which they recalled seem to us also to contribute more to Nestorius’s defense.

Moreover, that holy synod would appear tacitly to have reproached the blessed Cyril and the other Fathers who assembled with him at Ephesus, because they considered it unjust to judge as heretics the Easterners mentioned above, who defended Theodore and praised him much more highly. For was it only the blessed Cyril who knew the Easterners’ judgment concerning Theodore? Should we not believe that his aforementioned fellow priests who were with him at Ephesus—especially the Egyptians—also knew it, although all of them remained in communion with those men [Col. 0721D]?

Thus, emperor, you recognize that the three points which we appended to the division of this work are here once again demonstrated repeatedly together. For if the Council of Chalcedon had condemned the letter of the venerable Ibas because it praised Theodore, it would be proved to have excused Nestorius and blamed the blessed Cyril and the Council of Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0721D] The same manuscript reads: ‘had rejected the letter of the venerable Ibas as heretical; hence it would rather be proved to have excused, etc.’].

For these reasons it acted altogether piously and prudently when it distinguished Theodore’s case from Nestorius’s case [Col. 0722A]. Nestorius concealed his perfidy under the pretext of a harmful zeal, denying that the holy Virgin was the Mother of God; and, when admonished and rebuked, he had incurred the offense of the whole Church [Note: [Col. 0722D] The same manuscript reads: ‘had despised.’]. Theodore, however, did not contradict the Church but responded to the heretics [Note: [Col. 0722D] The same manuscript reads: ‘rather responding to the heretics on behalf of the Church, etc.’]. He spoke in certain ways such that, unless the reader attends to the speaker’s intention, he may be offended by the words. Nor did he deny that Christ is one in two natures, as we have shown; rather, compelled by the necessity created by the heretics’ attacks, he was forced to distinguish the properties of the natures very sharply.

Hence it was said:

“For the whole East, in common, placed him among those who had lived before us as possessing great power of doctrine against the heresies. In fighting and contending against them, he employed much division—not arising from a perverse understanding, but because he judged that this method would be more effective against the heretics. He neither ignored nor denied the supreme unity—far be it from him, for all his books are full of such teaching—but divided the properties of the natures more fully, as the struggle he had against the heretics dictated that he should do.”

If it is permitted to later generations to scrutinize the simple statements of the ancient preachers as though they were the fraudulent statements of heretics, without considering that they were directed against heresies of their own time, not against future heresies of which they had no knowledge, we shall condemn many without hesitation together with Theodore. For, as these Eastern Fathers testify, many things are found in them which require not a severe judge but a devout interpreter.

Because the testimony of those Easterners is not believed, we therefore produce a few of many examples from the statements of the ancient teachers of the Church, so that the Eutychians or their supporters may not be able to conceal the fact that, in the condemnation of Theodore’s doctrines—which they sought in the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon—the teaching of those Fathers whom they claim to venerate would also be condemned.

But even apart from these matters, or after setting them aside briefly, the holy synod cannot be blamed for not judging the venerable Ibas’s letter heretical on account of its praise of Theodore. First, because it followed the judgment of so many Fathers, which alone is sufficient for its defense. Second, because it is not necessarily blameworthy if it believed either that those who complained about certain writings of Theodore were providing an occasion for the contrary doctrine to which they were committed, or that they blamed those writings because they understood them insufficiently, or that Theodore himself had not expressed in sufficiently suitable words what he meant. This can happen even to many Catholic teachers.

For often, when one intends to resist opponents, one exceeds the proper measure in speaking; and it is not easy for a human being to avoid future controversies when he rises with the full effort of his mind against those of the present. Theodore frequently acted, both in books and in sermons to the people, against the Synousiasts [Note: [Col. 0721D] The Synousiasts, Συνουσιασταί, were called Apollinarians because they taught that Christ had one nature, a “mixed” and composite nature—σύγκρατον—of God and man, human and divine. Since the Eutychians later taught the same thing, he calls the latter their ancestors. Those who formerly wrote against the Apollinarians often gave their books the title κατὰ Συνουσιαστῶν, “Against the Synousiasts.” Thus, in the Fifth Synod, there is cited Theodore of Mopsuestia’s book *Against the Synousiasts* or Apollinarians. Likewise, Diodore of Tarsus’s *Against the Synousiasts* is cited by Leontius of Byzantium in Book III; likewise a book of Cyril of Alexandria with the same title in Anastasius’s *Ecloge χρήσεων* (“Collection of Extracts”), chapter 5; and, in the same author, an extract from Theodotus of Antioch: Θεοδότου Ἀντιοχείας ἐκ τοῦ πρὸς Ἡρακλείδην, κατὰ Συνουσιαστῶν (“From Theodotus of Antioch, from [his work] to Heracleides, Against the Synousiasts”). He says: Εἰ δὲ ἐφ’ ὧν ἡ οὐσία καὶ μία αὐτή, αἱ ἰδιότητες τῶν ὑποστάσεων ἀκέραιοι μένουσι· πολλῷ δικαιότερον ὅτ’ ἂν δύο διάφοροι φύσεις ἐφ’ ἑνὶ προσώπῳ γνωρίζονται, ἀκέραια τε τῆς ὑπάρξεως τά τε τῶν φύσεων ἰδιώματα σώζεσθαι: “If, where the essence is one and the same, the properties of the hypostases remain intact, then it is much more just that, when two different natures are recognized in one person, both the integrity of the existence and the properties of the natures should be preserved.”]—or, as they are called from the name of their author, the Apollinarians, the progenitors of Eutychian madness [Col. 0723A]. They arose in his time and said that Christ had one nature. If, in resisting them, he is perhaps found to have stumbled in a word through human frailty, what impiety did the synod commit by believing, on the testimony of so many, that he remained Catholic in his understanding? Especially since Nestorian perfidy had not yet arisen, which would always have made a disputant cautious on the other side; he was attending only to the matter he had set out to defeat.

But if Theodore is shown to have been overtaken by some inexcusable error, the holy synod did not act impiously by believing—since it held a devout view of the Church of Christ—that, after being admonished in due time, he could have corrected himself and remained a bishop within it, and that for this reason, in view of the many other matters on which he thought correctly, his teaching was not undeservedly praised.

You recognize, Your Serenity, that these words of the Eastern Fathers concerning Theodore—“For the whole East, in common, placed him among those who had lived before us as possessing great power of doctrine against the heresies”—agree with the letter of the blessed Gregory of Nazianzus. Writing to Theodore himself, Gregory says:

“If the province had another head, it would be necessary to cry out and appeal to him; but since your Reverence has been placed above it, it is necessary to look to you.”

And again:

“To suppress these matters is not within the power and weakness of our age, but within your prudence and strength, since the Almighty has granted you, together with others, the ability to defend the Church as a whole.”

What the blessed Cyril also wrote in reply to the Eastern synod, forbidding the condemnation not only of Theodore’s person but also of his statements, we have recalled in the third book.

## CHAPTER V

That Domnus of Antioch praises Theodore in his synodical letter to the emperor Theodosius, and that all those same Fathers teach that one must not insult the dead who have departed in the peace of the Church.

Now, therefore, let us recall the synodical letter of Domnus of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0723D] It is remarkable that there should be such silence about this synodical letter of Domnus, who, as will be stated at the end of Book XII, was the first of all to resist Eutyches. He had succeeded his uncle John, inheriting not only his office but also his zeal, though he was more inclined toward the Nestorian party. Hence he rejected and condemned the Edessene clergy who accused Bishop Ibas, as Liberatus relates in chapter 10. At the Second Council of Ephesus, however, he was deprived of his episcopate after letters were produced [Col. 0724D] that he had written to Dioscorus against Cyril’s Twelve Chapters, as the same Liberatus reports in chapter 12.], who, like his predecessor John, also wrote to the emperor Theodosius:

> “Your Piety is compelled to learn that the presbyter Eutyches is attempting to renew the impiety of Apollinaris the heresiarch, to undermine the apostolic teachings, corrupting the doctrine of the mystery of the incarnation, calling both the divinity of the Only-Begotten and the humanity one nature, asserting that commingling and confusion have occurred, attaching the saving Passion to that undefiled divinity, and presuming to anathematize Diodorus and Theodorus, men who were pillars of truth and defenders of piety, who clearly displayed their strength against every heresy. In this he resembles the vanity of Apollinaris.

> “For Apollinaris raised his tongue against the great Diodorus because Diodorus rebuked him for acting impiously. This too is a clear sign of the affinity between their doctrines: whoever attacks the great champion of piety, Diodorus, with blasphemous words, thereby shows, conversely, that he himself embraces a likeness to that man’s vanity.

> “But this great Diodorus has as a witness to his piety and illustrious struggles that great man Basil. [Col. 0724B] He became renowned at the time when the patrons of Arius’s impiety were ensnaring the minds of the emperors and stirring their power against the truth. In Antioch, moreover, he pursued a course of struggle, contending against the harshness of the heretics.

> “The holy man of God, Meletius—after whom the guardians of the apostolic doctrines among us are named, for the followers of Arius call us Meletians—appointed the most sacred Diodorus governor of all Cilicia [Note: [Col. 0724D] Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, Book V, chapter 4: ‘The divine Meletius made Diodorus shepherd of the Tarsians and entrusted the Cilician people to him.’ Since Cilicia had not yet been divided into two parts, Tarsus was the capital of the entire province. After the division, Tarsus remained, as is clear from Hierocles, the metropolis of First Cilicia, while Anazarbus was that of Second Cilicia.], and entrusted the administration of Tarsus to him.

> “In the imperial city, together with Gregory and the others who shared his zeal, he ordained the thrice-blessed Nectarius archbishop. He was the teacher of the great John, who adorned the see of the imperial city and filled the whole world with his teaching.

> “He nourished that universally renowned Theodorus in pious doctrines [Col. 0724C] and, teaching him clearly and courageously to labor, sent him into battle against the ranks of the heretics.

> “The most sacred Diodorus flourished together with the great Athanasius, Peter, and Timothy; Theodorus, however, together with Theophilus—men who, like luminaries, illumined the world and adorned the see of Alexandria. Those men were their admirers throughout their lives, and no one anywhere dared openly to accuse them.”

From what we have now brought forward it is also evident that the universally renowned Theodorus was a fellow student of the great John, with whom, as Domnus attests, he was nourished in pious doctrines by the holy Diodorus, just as he had been by Flavian of Antioch. It has likewise been disclosed that the Eutychians inherited their hatred of Theodorus [Note: [Col. 0723D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “against Theodorus, just as also against his teacher Diodorus, the Eutychians inherited [their hatred] from Eutyches himself,” and so forth.] from Eutyches himself, their father, [Col. 0725A] who called the divinity of the Only-Begotten and the humanity one nature, asserting that commingling and confusion had occurred and attaching the saving Passion to that undefiled divinity.

It is therefore not surprising if the unhappy branches correspond to their exceedingly bitter root. But here I await the judgment of your Piety: to whose opinion do you think we ought to attach ourselves in the case of Theodorus of Mopsuestia? Is it to the madness of Eutyches and his heirs, who, because of the particular folly by which they are possessed, have always been vainly armed for his condemnation? Or is it to John of Constantinople, his fellow student, and Gregory of Nazianzus; then to John of Antioch and the entire council of the East; to Cyril and Proclus, who wrote in reply to him; and to this Domnus of Antioch?

I think, most merciful emperor, that you judge it a great crime and a great profanation to trample upon the judgment of these luminaries of the world concerning Theodorus of Mopsuestia, and to pass over into the darkness of Eutychian blindness, so that in the Catholic Church we may practice the enmity of heretics and fight against our own people with another’s hatred.

But if it is profane for us to trample upon the judgment of the Fathers in the sole condemnation of Theodorus, in order to satisfy the desire of the Eutychians, how much more profane would it be to condemn the venerable Fathers themselves, by decreeing—or assenting to those decreeing—that whoever does not anathematize Theodorus of Mopsuestia should be anathema.

Therefore, whatever your religious devotion compels you to judge profane, the venerable Council of Chalcedon also judged profane, as it ought to have judged it: namely, that in the case of Theodorus it should follow the judgment of Eutyches, against whom it had been assembled, rather than that of these Fathers, whose testimonies refuted Eutyches. For this reason, while bearing witness with Domnus of Antioch and many Fathers that the universally renowned Theodorus had been nourished in pious doctrines by Diodorus, together with the great John who adorned the see of the imperial city, it ought not to have condemned the letter of the venerable Ibas, or Theodorus, when it observed that praises of him were recited from it.

For the council also knew that Theodorus, together with his teacher Diodorus, was subjected to the common accusation of the Apollinarists and Eutyches. It likewise knew that Diodorus had as a witness to his piety and illustrious struggles the great Basil and the holy Meletius, after whose name the Arians call us Meletians; and Gregory and the other Gregory, with whom he ordained the blessed Nectarius bishop in the imperial city; and that he flourished together with the Alexandrian bishops, namely the great Athanasius, Peter, and Timothy, as we have also shown from their letters in the fourth book; just as Theodorus himself flourished with Theophilus, men who, like luminaries, illumined the world.

In any event, the great Council of Chalcedon could not escape the charge of intolerable presumption if it followed the Apollinarists and Eutyches, who attacked Diodorus and Theodorus with false accusations, although they had lived blamelessly in the preaching of the word together with Basil, Meletius, both Gregories, John, Nectarius, Athanasius, Peter, Timothy, and Theophilus. Was it not to display Apollinarists and Eutyches as wiser and more diligent than these men, and to condemn so many venerable Fathers who are shown to have found nothing to reproach in Diodorus and Theodorus? The foolish presumption of the Eutychians ought therefore to have been trampled down and crushed by the authority of these Fathers, rather than the council being deceitfully excused—though what we have said can be defended more soundly and forcefully by an acceptable argument and evident truth [Note: [Col. 0725D] The same manuscript reads: “than what we have said.”].

Since so many and such great teachers of Christ’s Church praised the life and doctrine of the universally renowned Theodorus, testifying that he labored clearly and courageously to overthrow the ranks of heretics, and since no one accused him, while certain men condemned him and his doctrines, what arrogance have I displayed, religious emperor, since someone has thought or said of me that, standing between the two parties, I neither wished to praise nor to condemn him? This is especially so because, as we said above, they subjected to anathema not only Theodorus alone, but all who do not anathematize him.

How could it more easily be proved that Theodorus ought not to be anathematized than by showing that they joined all who do not anathematize him to his condemnation? How cruel and exceedingly unjust this would be is very easy to see, even if no judgment of the Fathers prohibited it. For ought those who did not anathematize Theodorus of Mopsuestia to have been anathema—whether because they did not know who he was and were uncertain whether any of his errors existed, or because they feared to anathematize one who had died in the peace of the Church?

For if someone, wishing to quibble, were to object to them and say, “What had the innocence of infants or the necessity of the mute done to deserve being anathematized by you, since they can pronounce anathema neither against Theodorus of Mopsuestia nor against anyone else?” they would, I think, be greatly troubled, according to their own expertise.

How much the minds of those very heretics have been darkened by the zeal of their madness—not only in everything else but especially in this matter—is sufficiently clear. While they strive through the long-winded evasions of their faction to bring about the annulment of the Council of Chalcedon, they have failed to realize that the very Fathers whom they claim to venerate would also be condemned together with Theodorus.

Let them, then, or their supporters, show us—if they are truly capable of anything—how Theodorus can simultaneously be pronounced such a heretic that those who until now were called Nestorians are already called Theodorians after his name, while the eulogists of his faith and doctrine are not considered heretics—not to mention the whole Church, which honored him as long as he lived.

Here let them demonstrate the subtlety of their doctrine. Here let them exercise that insolent intellect and shameless learning of theirs—men who think they philosophize expertly, who can slander the dead when they cannot defend their own statements. Therefore, now that they have been admonished, they ought to disapprove to us of what was done [Note: [Col. 0726D] The same manuscript reads: “with us.”].

But if they refuse, let Catholics at least cease to judge the dead either unjustly or with excessive severity, and to destroy the authority of the Council of Chalcedon with such arguments of heretics [Note: [Col. 0727D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “with such an argument.”].

For what need is there of this excessive justice, which, while favoring heretics who argue badly, has rebounded harshly and cruelly to the insult of the holy Fathers? Does it not seem that such conduct is expressly forbidden in Ecclesiastes, where it is written:

> “Do not become excessively righteous, and do not argue excessively, lest you become bewildered; do not act exceedingly impiously, and do not be hard, lest you die before your time” (Ecclesiastes 7:17).

And since it continues by saying, “It is good for you to hold fast to this, and from that do not withdraw your hand, because the one who fears God escapes all things,”

For the fear of God, we preferred to spare the venerable Fathers and escape this guilt rather than associate ourselves with those who stained their hands by condemning them through an ill-considered subscription.

It therefore belongs to the justice of your Piety that, since you do not judge contemptuous of their fatherly judgment those who boast that they have understood more wisely than such Fathers and served the faith more usefully, you should judge me much less severely hereafter, since I appear to follow in the case of Theodorus not my own judgment but that of so many Fathers.

The holy Council of Chalcedon followed that judgment as well, knowing that Theodorus had been proclaimed, while still alive, by John of Constantinople and Gregory of Nazianzus, and that after his death he had been defended against the calumnies of heretics by John and Domnus of Antioch, by the entire synod of the East, and by Cyril of Alexandria and Proclus of Constantinople through arguments of many kinds.

This more strongly proves how foolish it is to regard the council as heretical for this reason: that in the case of Theodorus it trusted the testimony of those Fathers whose faith it upheld in its definitions and by whose authority it rejected the heretics.

It should certainly be observed and impressed upon the hearts of the faithful—not so much for the sake of the case of Theodorus of Mopsuestia as for the sake of all who have ended, or shall end, their lives in the peace of the Church—that all these Fathers whose judgments we have recalled, though using different words, pronounce with one and the same meaning that anyone who, during his life, does not stubbornly resist the corruption of the Church ought not, after death, to be repudiated together with his writings.

Saint John of Antioch and the entire synod of the East, writing to the blessed Proclus, complain among other things as follows:

> “What value can henceforth remain in the doctrines of men so admirable and so renowned if they are condemned after death? It is not for me, therefore, to insult the glorious opinions of those who have gone before, nor to judge those who died honorably, but this belongs to the Judge alone of the living and the dead.” [Note: [Col. 0727D] Perhaps: “It is not for us.”]

Writing also to the emperor Theodosius, they say:

> “But if someone says that something obscure is found in his writings or in those of others, there is no need to reopen the matter [Note: [Col. 0727D] The same manuscript reads: “there is no need to reopen this.”]. For those whose life in the priesthood and ministry had the best possible end—we assign the glory that was owed to them; and we do not judge them by those matters concerning which certain men accuse us with savage hostility.” [Note: [Col. 0728D] The same manuscript reads: “accuse them.”]

Proclus likewise replied to the aforesaid John and to the eastern synod, who were lamenting and complaining:

> “When did I write to your Holiness that either Theodorus or certain others who had previously died ought to be subjected to anathema?”

And further:

> “Nor did I write to you, most God-loving man, concerning Theodorus or anyone else who has already died, that he should either be anathematized or repudiated.”

Again, writing to the deacon Maximus, he says:

> “How, then, have I now learned from letters that the names of Theodorus of Mopsuestia and certain others have been placed before the Chapters for anathematization, since they have already departed to God? It is superfluous to insult those who have already left this life after death, whom we never blamed even while they were alive.”

The aforementioned John of Antioch, writing to Cyril together with the eastern council, says:

> “What injury, corruption, and confusion will be generated here if we open the door to those who wish to overturn the statements of Fathers who have departed? What damage will not become evident if we not only refute their statements but also anathematize them?”

Cyril, replying to the same John and his synod, says:

> “Unless, perhaps, we must take into consideration what they persist in doing, especially since the person whom they subject to blame is no longer present, the indictment of the Chapters is uncertain, and those who undertake these things are found to be running into uncertainty and beating the air.”

And further:

> “Yet, even unwillingly, they shall hear the just rebuke, those who provide such causes: ‘Forget yourselves, for you are bending your bows against dust; for the one whose name is written among you no longer remains.’ Let no one blame me for proceeding to speak in this way. It is a grave matter to insult the dead, even if they were laymen, and all the more those who laid down this life in the episcopate. For it appears most just to prudent men to yield to the one who foreknows each person’s will and knows what each of us will become.”

These principles must be kept in mind and opposed not only to those living now but also to future presumptuous men, should any arise again, so that no one may dare to condemn anyone except one who stubbornly resists correction.

But if it should be proved that any one of these Fathers who responded for Theodorus with harmonious and unanimous voice [Note: [Col. 0728D] The same manuscript reads: “and as though with one voice.”], God forbid that such a thing should be found in the conscience and truth of the saints, had later deviated from the common judgment of all and adopted a judgment contrary to himself and to so many Fathers, then it would be the judgment of that individual who had departed from everyone—not the common judgment of all in favor of Theodorus—that ought to be set aside.

Therefore, if there are some who, while attacking the blessed Cyril, say that he later spoke differently about Theodorus of Mopsuestia than he did in this judgment, which he shared with John of Antioch, the eastern synod, and Proclus of Constantinople, and in which he is shown to agree with his fellow student John of Constantinople, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Domnus of Antioch, they must not be accepted against that same Theodorus—or rather, against the blessed Cyril himself. By speaking in this way, they make him appear, as far as they can, inconsistent and changeable.

For in defense of the Council of Chalcedon, which did not judge Theodorus deserving of condemnation, the testimonies of so many other Fathers would unquestionably suffice, even if we possessed no judgment of Bishop Cyril in his favor. Finally, even if these testimonies were absent, the communion of the Catholic Church would suffice, in whose peace he died—not only without any accusation, but also with great glory.

## CHAPTER VI. That it ought not to count against Theodorus if Cyril later wrote against him, and that Theodorus cannot be condemned without Diodorus

Those who, wishing to condemn Theodorus to the prejudice of the holy council, say that the blessed Cyril later became opposed to so many venerable Fathers, to the Church, and to himself, must therefore be rejected and rightly restrained.

But so that we may leave no reader suspicious or doubtful—whether Cyril wrote anything against Theodorus or did not write anything against him—the defense of the council must stand firm for us in every respect. Therefore, something certain must be established concerning this uncertain matter: namely, that the council rightly proceeded as it did and did not condemn Theodorus or his doctrines when it observed that his praises were recited before it.

Certain writings against Theodorus and certain writings in favor of Theodorus are found under the name of the blessed Cyril. It is therefore necessary that either both sets belong to the blessed Cyril, or neither, or that one of the two does.

If both are said to belong to the blessed Cyril, then, since he appears contradictory to himself in both, the holy council could not follow him simply as such. It ought to follow him in those matters in which he does not oppose the judgments of the other Fathers and of the Church.

If neither set is said to belong to the blessed Cyril, there is no reason why the holy council should be thought obliged to oppose the judgments of so many Fathers and the judgment of the Church.

But if one set is said to belong to the blessed Cyril, the holy council is to be praised for believing that the writings belonging to him were those that did not oppose the judgments of the other Fathers or the judgment of the Church.

Even if some certain and manifest indication proved that the writings against Theodorus, rather than those in his favor, were truly Cyril’s, and if it were shown that this could not have escaped the notice of the same council, who would even then blame it for not also blaming Theodorus?

For do you believe that those writings against Theodorus are Cyril’s in which it is nevertheless said:

> “Twenty books, or perhaps even more, were written by the great Theodorus against the heresies of Arius and Eunomius; besides these, he also interpreted the evangelical and apostolic writings. No one dared to criticize these labors, but they sought to honor by a favorable decree the zeal for sound doctrines that is found in them.”

How could Cyril blame Theodorus as the originator of Nestorianism or of any other heresy, when Theodorus could neither have written twenty or more books irreproachably against the heretics nor correctly interpreted the evangelical and apostolic writings if he held any erroneous belief about the Christian faith?

Indeed, we refute all heretics chiefly from the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures. It is wholly contradictory to say simultaneously that someone correctly interpreted the evangelical and apostolic writings and that he did not think correctly about the Christian faith.

And even if these writings against Theodorus, which alone would be thought to belong to the blessed Cyril, did not refute themselves, no one except the most unreasonable person would judge that the council ought not to have followed the judgment of those Fathers concerning Theodorus who, living with him in the same province and conferring frequently and familiarly about the rule of the faith [Note: [Col. 0729D] The same manuscript reads: “and conferring familiarly in conversation about the rule of the faith”], knew perfectly well with what intention he said things that seemed to offend certain people who were ignorant of that intention.

For it would have been exceedingly grave to follow merely the sounds of words—or rather, the signs of sounds traced in ink on little sheets—and to disregard the testimonies of holy consciences, writings composed not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on little sheets but on tablets of flesh [Note: [Col. 0730D] The same manuscript reads: “on the fleshly tablets of the heart”], which bore witness to Theodorus’s doctrine.

Who except a thoughtless person would believe, who except an immodest person would say, who except an obstinate person would affirm, that Cyril should have been preferred—or, not to say preferred, even compared—by the holy council with John of Constantinople in the case of Theodorus, not only because of John’s greater authority arising from his merits, but also because the council ought to have believed John more concerning Theodorus, as an old friend and his fellow student from the beginning, than Cyril?

The council knew that Cyril had also written against that same John, already dead, contrary to the judgment of the apostolic see, ordering Bishop Atticus to remove his name from the catalogue of bishops, as though he were profane and excluded from the ecclesiastical walls, on the grounds that the traitor Judas ought not to be enrolled among the apostles, nor the expelled Jeconiah counted with David, Samuel, and the prophets.

The council also knew that Cyril had maintained communion with the aforementioned Theodorus as long as he lived and had never reproved him while alive, when Theodorus could both interpret himself and make clear anything in him that might seem doubtful.

The council would therefore act religiously if, approving Cyril’s faith insofar as he did not disagree with the Fathers, it did not approve the suspicion he held against Theodorus contrary to the judgment of so many Fathers. Likewise, while approving the faith of John of Antioch and the other Eastern bishops, as well as of the other priests who had assembled with them at Ephesus from various provinces—insofar as they did not disagree with the Fathers—it rejected the suspicion they had held against the blessed Cyril.

This is especially true because, if that council is said to have believed that Theodorus of Mopsuestia had been blamed by the blessed Cyril, it cannot be denied that it also believed that the holy Diodorus had been blamed by him at the same time. For, as we recalled in the fourth book, whoever is believed to have blamed both of them blamed both equally in the same work and in the same matter of faith.

Therefore, if there had been no judgments of the Fathers in favor of Theodorus—which the council would unquestionably have opposed if it had presumed to condemn him—it is clear that Theodorus the disciple could not justly have been condemned on Cyril’s authority without his teacher Diodorus.

Nor could it have condemned Diodorus, whom, as we have shown, the great lights of the Church had praised: Athanasius, Peter, and Timothy, bishops of Alexandria; Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia; John of Constantinople; Epiphanius of Cyprus; the Egyptian bishops who confessed the faith and were sent into exile under the emperor Valens; and the great testimony of the council assembled at Constantinople against Macedonius, which Diodorus is clearly known to have attended.

He also had the testimony of the devout rulers Gratian, Valentinian, and the elder Theodosius; and finally of the apostate emperor Julian, who censured him for confessing that God was born of a virgin and for proclaiming Jesus the Galilean both eternal God and dead.

Since, therefore, the holy council could in no way condemn Diodorus contrary to the testimonies of these men, how could it condemn Theodorus, his disciple—even if, as has been said, he were supported by no testimonies of the Fathers—when it could not justly condemn him without his teacher, who held this same faith?

There is therefore no reason to criticize the council on account of what the blessed Cyril is said to have written against Theodorus, because it declared the letter of Ibas, which contained praises of him, orthodox. For even if Cyril had written against Theodorus and had written nothing in his favor, the sound judgment and freedom of the Council of Chalcedon would still deserve praise for not approving Cyril in every respect.

The sound judgment and freedom of Paul, the least of the apostles, is likewise praised: when Peter, the first of the apostles, was led into hypocrisy and was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, Paul boldly rejected his conduct, opposed him to his face, and rebuked him publicly before everyone.

It would therefore not be novel or contrary to Christian religion for that holy and great council not to accept Cyril’s judgment against the judgment of so many Fathers in the case of Theodorus, just as no one says that Cyril ought to be accepted in the case of John of Constantinople.

## CHAPTER VII. That if Theodorus had been suspected of heresy, the Fathers of his time would by no means have concealed it, and that the judgment of those Fathers concerning Theodorus ought to be believed rather than that of Cyril alone
[Col. 0731D] But if we lacked, in defense of that great synod, the written testimonies even of those Fathers by whom the faith and teaching of Diodorus are commended—and without Diodorus we have shown that Theodore cannot justly be condemned—should he be judged blameworthy because he did not despise the testimony of the Church, in whose perpetual peace Diodorus and Theodore remained in outstanding honor? Or will the Eutychians dare to accuse the Church of that period of the Nestorian doctrine, when neither Eutyches nor Nestorius had yet arisen? I do not think they would openly and publicly venture this.
