Just as, therefore, the natural law, one and wholly implanted in the human mind, which the Lord recalls in the Gospel when he says, “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them; for this is the law and the prophets” (Matt. 7:12), is found to be much stronger than that which is contained externally in written letters—for from that inner rule all the individual things given to us externally in writing as law descended, and are parts of it; nor can all of them collected together, or even multiplied, exceed the measure of that inner law—so that one general testimony of the Church is stronger than the many testimonies which we have produced separately and privately on behalf of Diodorus and Theodore [Col. 0732B]. For these too are parts of the one general testimony of the Church, and however greatly they may be multiplied, they will not exceed its authority or limit.

But just as, when a person abandoned that natural and inner law [Note: [Col. 0731D] Codex Veronensis: “natural law.”], which exists as a whole at once, and fell into external things, it was necessary to admonish the contemptuous person of inward matters separately and externally [Note: [Col. 0731D] The same codex: “to admonish the contemptuous person of inward matters separately and externally”; thus we too judged it necessary to refute, by private testimony, those who despise the general and public authority of the Church, etc.], not because we prefer parts to the whole or members to their entire body, but because we judged the slanderers of the great synod more suitably refuted in this way—so likewise nothing is stronger than the general symbol of the Christian faith by which we are initiated, although it is not handed down in writing. Nevertheless, against those who corrupt its meaning and power [Note: [Col. 0732D] Or “truth”?] [Col. 0732C], we also use the private testimonies of the Fathers contained in writing, since all those testimonies serve that one general symbol and do not exceed its established limits.

And therefore, as has been said, even if we lacked these testimonies of the Fathers committed to writing, which we have brought forward in defense of the Council of Chalcedon on behalf of Diodorus and Theodore [Note: [Col. 0732D] The same codex: “cleansing.”], no wise person would say that he ought to consider himself either more religious or wiser than those same holy Fathers and many others who shone as lights of the Church in the times of Diodorus and Theodore. Those whom they did not exclude while they were alive—when, if they had been heretics, they could have corrupted others even more—how could the pious synod, after their death, judge them worthy of exclusion? If something in their words seemed to offend certain people, it ought rather to have believed that they had spoken with another intention, or corrected them at the time after a friendly admonition, than to presume to place itself above so many venerable Fathers in religion or wisdom [Note: [Col. 0732D] The same codex: “above herself.”]

For, as we have learned, the Church never had at one time teachers so numerous and so distinguished as in the days of Diodorus and Theodore. To pass over, because of the difference of language, the most learned men of the Western Church—although many of them were also educated in Greek eloquence and could have recognized their intention by reading the writings of Diodorus and Theodore—and to pass over also the most learned men of Greece who were not bishops, Athanasius meanwhile lived among them, as did Peter, Timothy, and Theophilus of Alexandria, preaching the word; then there were Meletius and Flavian of Antioch; Nectarius, John, and Atticus of Constantinople; Amphilochius of Iconium; Epiphanius of Cyprus; Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia and his brother Gregory of Nyssa; Gregory of Nazianzus; Gelasius of Caesarea in Palestine; and Theotimus of Tomi in Scythia [Note: [Col. 0733D] Incorrect. Read “of Tomi.” For Tomi is the metropolis of the Scythians, “a great and prosperous coastal city,” as Sozomen says, Ecclesiastical History VI.21; see Wesseling on the Ancient Roman Itinerary, p. 227, col. 2.].

None of these is shown ever to have judged Diodorus a heretic [Note: [Col. 0733D] “Theodore” should apparently be added.], or, according to the Codex Veronensis, “Diodorus or Theodore.” Rather, together with them he endured the hostility of the Apollinarian heretics, as though they were proclaiming two sons by asserting two perfect natures in Christ. Therefore, even if they might have read the writings of Diodorus and Theodore with insufficient attention, they would certainly have been made more attentive by the accusations of the heretics.

What need, then, was there, to the insult and sacrilege of so many Fathers, to pronounce Theodore impious, wicked, and worse than demons? Even if he were proved to have erred in certain matters, he ought not to have been judged worse than demons after dying in the peace and honor of the Church. Nor, in connection with his praise, did the most reverend judges Photius, Eustathius, and Uranius rebuke Bishop Ibas, before whom his letter was first brought forward and examined.

Nor did his accusers themselves—whether when they approached the emperor against him, or when, after bringing forward the accusation [Note: [Col. 0733D] The same codex: “defense.”], they produced the aforesaid judges and, in their examination, attacked him with many great and unheard-of charges, engaging him in repeated and prolonged conflict—ever attempt to oppose anything concerning Theodore’s praise. They would certainly have done so if Theodore had ever been judged a heretic by the Church of Christ.

Accordingly, we say to the Eutychians: since they dissent from the synod which pronounced orthodox the aforementioned letter, confessing two natures in Christ and one person, let them at least agree with the venerable Ibas’s accusers as refuted by that synod, and let them find fault in that letter with nothing beyond what those most slanderous, shameless, and obstinate men charged.

But how could the aforesaid synod, in condemning Theodore—even if, as has been said, it were in no way opposed by the written testimonies of so many Fathers—fail either to call the Fathers mentioned above heretics, if it thought that, understanding them, they assented to the allegedly wicked doctrines common to Diodorus and Theodore [Note: [Col. 0733D] The same codex: “say this if it believed that they consented.”], or to call them excessively ignorant if it thought that they were unable to understand those doctrines?

For we are not arguing about obscure persons whose teaching might be said to have remained hidden. It is written of Theodore that he shone clearly in doctrine for forty years [Note: [Col. 0733D] The same codex: “forty-five years.” That is the number given by the letter of the Antiochene synod held under John in 435 and addressed to Proclus of Constantinople, as is clear from the fragment cited above in chapter 1.], that he defeated every heresy, and that he wrote ten thousand books against errors against which the entire East collectively set him forward as possessing great doctrinal power. It is also written that in the expositions which he delivered in all the churches of the East and in this imperial city, he was approved in the presence of priests, emperors, and peoples.

If the holy synod rejected such a man, how could it fail, as we have said, either to call all the venerable Fathers of that period heretics or ignorant? Which of these alternatives it would prefer to state, I do not know; but I do know that it would necessarily have to state one of them.

Much more, then, now that testimonies of those Fathers on behalf of Diodorus and Theodore are not lacking and have also been committed to writing: if it presumed to condemn Theodore for holding what Diodorus held, it would be forced to say either that all these Fathers were heretics or that they were ignorant and uninstructed.

But is Christ so angry with the world that Christian ears could bear to hear that the synod ought to have judged Athanasius, Basil, both Gregorys, and John heretics, so that the rash condemnations of Theodore might be judged orthodox? Or, as the preferable alternative, would it be said that they ought to have been judged ignorant, so that the astonishing expertise of these men might be exalted, as they chiefly desire?

But to say something further, or rather to repeat it more fully: is Christ so angry with the world that the ears not merely of Christians but of any human beings could bear to hear our teachers called more learned than such teachers? Or perhaps it will be thought that those Fathers ought not to be called heretics by the synod, because they did not agree with the doctrines of Diodorus and Theodore, nor ignorant, because they knew those doctrines were not right, but merely negligent, because they had taken insufficient care to correct them or expel them from the Church?

Yet the very fact that they remained silent at the time, although they possessed both great learning for understanding and adequate speech for responding, may rightly be held as consent. Thus nothing else would be accomplished except that those holy Fathers would be declared heretics by the synod [Note: [Col. 0734D] The same codex adds: “by the synod, which, although it could, neither wished to exclude them nor their doctrines, which it knew to be impious. But let us concede even this, as we concede many things, to those who presume against the truth: they are not declared heretics by the synod. Although…”].

Although, therefore, in such a case a negligent person might perhaps be judged more tolerable than a heretic, he would nevertheless undoubtedly be worse than an ignorant person. But the venerable Fathers, whom that synod would not dare to call ignorant, it would much less presume to judge negligent, which is worse.

It therefore judged them diligent, since it knew that in their time they had expelled the heretics who arose. To pass over those whose names were erased together with their heresies—namely, the Basians, whom we also call Anthropomorphites [Note: [Col. 0735C] The author of the exceedingly foolish heresy of the Anthropomorphites, as Jerome calls it in Letter 61, was Audius, or, as Theodoret has it, Audaeus (Greek: Αὐδαῖος), who attributed a human form to God, saying that God was “anthropomorphic” (Greek: ἀνθρωπόμορφον). They were therefore called Anthropomorphites from their doctrine and Audiani from their teacher. In Saint Augustine, Heresy 1, “Vadiani” is written; for “Vadiani,” as appears here, “Basiani” has been printed.], Semi-Arians, Aetians, Antidicomarites [Note: [Col. 0735C] In Epiphanius, Ἀντιδικομαριανῖται. They asserted that Mary had joined with her husband after Christ’s birth. Against them Epiphanius wrote a lengthy letter to the Arabs, where the heresy arose. Theodore, bishop of Cyprus, is also said to have written against them.], Messalians, whom we also call Euchites [Note: [Col. 0736C] The meaning of the two names is the same. For the Messalians, in the language of the Syrians, are the “Praying Ones” (Greek: Εὐχόμενοι), because they prayed almost continually. Epiphanius also mentions another kind of Messalian, originating among the Gentiles, who called themselves Euphemites, Martyrianes, and Satanianes; he explains the reasons for these names in Heresy 80. “Sacianes” therefore seems to have been written here through error for “Satanianes”; and shortly afterward “Marrianes” and “Photianes” should likewise be restored to “Marcellians” and “Photinians,” whom Epiphanius joins together in Heresies 71 and 72, and whom the law also associates in Codex Theodosianus 16.5.65, On Heretics.], Euphemites, Martyrianes, and Sacianes [Note: [Col. 0735D] The editor of the Sirmondian edition, in the preface to volume II, §4, quotes the following passage at this point from Cotelerius, Ecclesiastical Greek Monuments, volume I, p. 777: “I would not reject the conjecture of the entirely authoritative Jacques Sirmond; but why should we not read Saccianes, which means the same as Saccites and Saccophori? Indeed, perhaps Facundus had written Satianes, misled by a similar copy in our Greek editions of Epiphanius’s Anacephalaeosis and Ancoratus, where, with the spelling shortened, Satianes is found. Let these matters therefore remain conjectural.” And shortly afterward, p. 785: “To what I noted above … I now add that the more probable reading in Facundus is Satanianes or Satanies.”]—there also arose and were expelled in their time the Marrians [Note: [Col. 0736D] Cotelerius, at the cited place, p. 780, thinks that “Arians” should be read here, through a scribal error in which a duplicated m was reduced to a single letter.], Photinians [Note: [Col. 0735D] Codex Veronensis: “Photinians” (from Photinus).], Macedonians, who are also called Pneumatomachi; Aetians, who are also called Eunomians; and the Apollinarians.

How, then, could those who were proven champions of the faith in the case of so many heresies be believed negligent by the holy synod only in the case of Diodorus and Theodore? Therefore, either they understood the statements of Diodorus and Theodore better, just as they wished their own statements to be understood by others—which we neither wish nor are able to do [Col. 0735B]—or they demanded from them an explanation of why they had spoken in that way, or they discovered that they had already changed their opinion, or, as a last resort, they caused them to change it after admonishing them.

For what wise Catholic could believe that they could otherwise have remained in the Catholic Church? Yet although I, an unlearned man and a speaker of Latin, have been able, a hundred years later, to understand or explain, according to my capacity and ability, so many things that were said in a case conducted among the Greeks, how much more must we believe that that assembly of holy Fathers, dealing with a matter that was their own and still fresh in memory, was able to understand it—especially with the aid of him who said, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20)?

For when he is faithfully invoked not only by the priests but also by all his people, whose faith and expectation depend upon their authority, he first gives all who are assembled one heart and one soul, so that none of them wishes his own opinion to prevail unless it is the opinion of truth. How often do the more learned there yield to the less learned, and the majority to the minority, when he is in their midst? How often does he himself knowingly work through those who do not know, he who is able to do everything beyond what we ask or understand, or who promised that he would be with us all days, until the consummation of the age [Note: [Col. 0735D] The same codex: “and he who.”]?

Would that secular power never usurped for itself in these matters what was not entrusted to it—matters in which it has never usurped anything successfully. But Christ cannot be absent from his priests assembled in his name, since, being omnipotent truth, he cannot in any way lie. Nor was he absent from that synod, which, in the matter of faith, followed the common teaching of all the Fathers; but in Theodore’s case it followed not Cyril alone—or, if we believe what is said, not even Cyril, since his judgment appeared contradictory or uncertain [Note: [Col. 0735D] The same codex: “grant,” i.e. “concede.”]—but the other Fathers, whom it ought to have preferred in authority, number, and reason.

For who would not prefer John of Constantinople to Cyril, many approved men to one, and a most certain and consistent defense to an uncertain and inconsistent accusation? [Note: [Col. 0735D] The same codex: “would not prefer by just reasoning.”]

Let heretics therefore make no further slander on this account, nor let Catholics be offended. The faith of John and Proclus of Constantinople, of Gregory of Nazianzus, of John and Domnus of Antioch, and of the Eastern Council, as well as of the Church from which Theodore was not expelled, was also Cyril’s faith. Concerning Theodore alone, as also concerning Diodorus—concerning whom Athanasius and the others, as well as the Council of Constantinople, likewise bear witness [Note: [Col. 0735D] The same codex: “likewise Athanasius and the others, and …”]—a different opinion is said to be found in Cyril alone. And what is a sign of the most certain truth, the agreement of one and the same faith is demonstrated in the very disagreement.

For the thing which Cyril is said to have blamed Theodore for was manifestly wicked, and Theodore’s defenders did not deny this [Note: [Col. 0735D] The same codex: “it is manifestly wicked and contrary to religion, and Theodore’s defenders did not deny that it was wicked; but …”]; rather, it was said that Theodore had not held this view. Thus Cyril thought that Theodore should be prosecuted because he had supposedly held the same views that Nestorius had held wrongly [Note: [Col. 0736D] The same codex: “should be accused”; and: “he had held the same views that Nestorius had held wrongly. For this reason the Eastern saints defended him, asserting that he had not held the same views that Nestorius had held wrongly; and consequently …”]. Hence, although the two sides held different opinions concerning Theodore, both firmly maintained the condemnation of Nestorius without any difference.

What help, then, does this give the Nestorians, who are said to make wrongful use of Theodore’s statements, as also of those of others who shone in the Church, if there was some differing opinion among the Fathers concerning him? He was accused precisely because he was thought to have held views similar to Nestorius; and he could not otherwise be excused unless he were shown to be alien to Nestorius’s error.

The same Nestorians must also remember that in the letter of the Eastern Fathers replying to blessed Proclus, Theodore is excused in the very passage in which, as we have shown, they affirm that one of the Trinity was crucified for us. In that letter it is said: “But that the entire Eastern Council rejected the novelties of Nestorius, your Holiness also knows, since you have already received our letters on this matter a second and a third time.”

Nor should the Eutychians or Semi-Eutychians conceal the fact that, meanwhile, they have been unable to produce anything in the name of blessed Cyril, whom they claim to follow, in which Theodore is blamed for proclaiming Christ in two natures. For whether Theodore is truly or falsely reported to have been blamed by Cyril for believing in two sons, it has not yet been fabricated that Cyril rebuked him in Theodore’s writings for proclaiming that Christ has two natures. The Eutychians do not deny that he proclaimed this; indeed, they falsely claim that he thought there were also two persons.

Why, then, did blessed Cyril not at the same time blame him for proclaiming two natures, if it is to be counted as Nestorian heresy to believe and teach that Christ has two natures? Rather, the most wise John and the Eastern Council, writing to blessed Cyril himself, clear Theodore of the charge that, by dividing the properties of the natures more sharply in opposition to the heretics, he might also be thought to have asserted two persons in Christ.

How, then, could the Eastern Fathers judge that Theodore should be excused from the Nestorian charge precisely because he divided the properties of the natures more sharply, if it is a Nestorian crime to assert two natures in Christ? Or how could blessed Cyril himself fail to judge those same Eastern Fathers heretics and exceedingly foolish, since they tried to defend Theodore, who was burdened with an uncertain crime, by means of a certain crime? [Note: [Col. 0737C] Codex Veronensis: “judge the Eastern Fathers.”]

Especially since they themselves affirmed that blessed Cyril had taught no differently, saying to him, as we recalled above: “For there are also matters which Your Holiness likewise confesses in this way and concerning which you hold the same understanding.”

Accordingly, if proclaiming two natures in Christ must be ascribed to Nestorian heresy, blessed Cyril, who made no response against this, confirmed a great crime against himself by his silence, from which he cannot be cleared unless it is judged Catholic to assert two natures in Christ.

You understand, therefore, Emperor, that if there is said to have been any dispute among the Fathers concerning Theodore, it confounds the Nestorians and the Eutychians alike. But the holy synod, holding the one common faith of the accuser—if indeed he is truly said to have accused him—and of those defending Diodorus [Note: [Col. 0738C] The same codex: “the faith of those defending Diodorus and Theodore.”], judged that, in Theodore’s case, those men should be followed whose authority was greater and who, having lived with him and known him well through long familiarity, understood the intention with which he had written the things for which the ignorant thought he should be accused.

This was consistent with justice; it was also consistent with piety, which, insofar as reason permits, ought to favor the person’s defense more than his accusation. It was also consistent with the assertion of the true faith which that synod had undertaken against Nestorius and Eutyches: lest Nestorius be said to have held views similar to those of Theodore, who was commended by so many Fathers; lest authority thereby be given to Nestorius’s error; or lest the judgment of the forefathers of the Apollinarians, of Eutychian madness, or of Eutyches himself seem to have been followed in Theodore’s case. Thus, according to the judgment of blessed Cyril, it might rightly be said even of that synod that it had set itself fiercely against Theodore, a remarkable man deserving the greatest glory, in order to create an opportunity for the contrary doctrine by which it was held, seeking to have certain of his chapters condemned because they were not understood according to their better meaning.

Since these matters have thus been established and confirmed, the fact that Theodore was recently condemned by certain people must be attributed to the restraint which they offer to the Eutychians and to detestable presumption. Therefore, just as no wise person can approve these rash men against the testimony of the holy Fathers and of the Church, so he cannot disapprove the great Council of Chalcedon together with those same Fathers and the Church in which Theodore remained.

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 0737]

## CHAPTER ONE

That Theodore himself is proved to have been Catholic by his writings, and that all the objections brought against his teaching are refuted by an exposition of a single Psalm, Psalm 44.

[Col. 0737D]

Remembering our promise, let us now present, at the appropriate place, not a few passages from Theodorus’s writings [Note: [Col. 0737D] The Verona Codex has *proferamus*, “let us bring forward.”], as we did in Book Three when the falsehood of his opponents had to be refuted, but many more—passages by which it may abundantly [Col. 0738D] be shown how far he was removed from those things fabricated about him to prejudice the great Council of Chalcedon. Thus it may be demonstrated no longer by the testimony of the Fathers but by the facts themselves that the disturbers of the Church, who criticize the venerable Ibas’s letter in praise of Theodorus, did not fail to find the truth as though it were hidden, but deliberately refused to see it even though it was manifest.

As we have already said, there are therefore three matters for which they slander his statements. The first is that they accuse him [Col. 0739A] of believing, in accordance with Sabellius’s madness, that the divine Trinity is a single person. The second is that, contradicting themselves, they assert conversely that he introduced a quaternity by proclaiming two sons [Note: [Col. 0739D] This was the principal charge against Theodorus, which Justinian designates and condemns in these words in his edict: “If anyone supports Theodorus of Mopsuestia, who said that the Word of God is one and Christ another, let him be anathema.” Theodorus, a presbyter of Raithu, plainly teaches that the man of Mopsuestia held this heresy: he said that Christ was one man among many, who, because the Word of God dwelt in him “according to divine good pleasure” (*κατ’ εὐδοκίαν*), had become a participant in “divine worth” (*θεϊκῆς ἀξίας*). Accordingly, he held that there were two natures in him, distinct and joined to one another only by relationship. “He says,” he writes, “that he knows two self-bounded natures (*δύο φύσεις … ἰδιοπεριωρίστους*) in Christ, joined to one another only by some relationship” (*σχέσει τινὶ καὶ μόνον ἀλλήλαις ᾠκειωμένας*). This amounted to professing two persons in Christ, verbally and in reality. Since this later became Nestorius’s doctrine, he calls Theodorus “the ancestor of Nestorius” (*πρόγονον Νεστορίου*). The Fifth Council, in its fourth session, confirms that these and other similar opinions were held by Theodorus, both from various passages in his own books and from the testimony of Cyril and others. Facundus, however, defends Theodorus in such a way that he endeavors to show that in many of his books he held the correct faith, and argues that if anything contrary occasionally slipped from him, it should be interpreted more charitably.], that is, by asserting that the person of the Word of God is one and that of Christ another, Christ having been merely human and not also God, as the Jews supposed.

The third is that they say he nullified all the prophecies made concerning Christ. This is the error of the Manichaeans, whom we know to have been perversely opposed to Jewish unbelief. For the former, detesting the New Testament, claim to accept the Old; the latter, detesting the Old, claim to accept the New Testament. These charges, as has been shown, are so absurd and mutually contradictory that no one would have considered them worthy of refutation or attention. They ought rather to have been despised [Col. 0739B] and rejected in silence, unless the forced subscription of so many bishops compelled us to answer such nonsense.

For what would we fear from this? Or is it perhaps to be believed that anyone even moderately sensible would assent to these ridiculous claims, which destroy one another even if no one refuted them [Note: [Col. 0739D] The Verona Codex has: “even if no one”]? How could it become more plainly apparent to everyone what sort of people the critics of the Council of Chalcedon are—people who set themselves above John of Constantinople, Gregory of Nazianzus, John and Domnus of Antioch and the Eastern Council, as well as Proclus of Constantinople and Cyril of Alexandria, in religious authority and learning—unless they were proved both to love falsehood with extreme irreverence and not even to know how to lie?

Now, most serene emperor, hear what that same [Col. 0739C] Theodorus says while discussing the forty-fourth Psalm:

“What, then, will be found greater than the things accomplished by Christ amid such a transformation of the world, when everyone acknowledges him as the God of all, and those who hasten to devote themselves to piety and virtue glorify God’s only-begotten Son while offering worship worthy of the Holy Spirit? Concerning these things blessed David says: ‘My heart has uttered a good word’ (Psalm 44:1).”

Here your Piety sees that all the heretics’ slanders have at once been destroyed. For who, believing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one person, would say that those who hasten to cultivate piety and virtue glorify God’s only-begotten Son while at the same time offering worship worthy of the Holy Spirit? If he believed that the one whom he called the Holy Spirit was the only-begotten Son of God, it would have been enough to say, “glorifying God’s only-begotten Son”; there would have been no need to add, “while offering worship worthy of the Holy Spirit.”

Accordingly, Theodorus believed and taught that there are three persons: he called the Father one, whose son is the one he called the Only-Begotten, and the Holy Spirit another [Note: [Col. 0739] The same codex reads: “and another the Son himself, the Only-Begotten, and another the Holy Spirit.”], to whom those who hasten to cultivate piety and virtue offer worship worthy—that is, worship of the same kind as that offered to the Son.

Nor did he proclaim Christ to be merely human, since he declares that nothing is greater than Christ’s works and confesses him to be the God of all, by whom such a transformation of the world was accomplished. That he did not nullify all the prophecies made concerning Christ is clear because, again, in his exposition of the same Psalm he said:

“Since he first mentioned kingdoms, and afterward recalled the destruction of enemies and the subjection of the rest, so that no one might suppose that kingship had only recently come to him, or that he could again be deprived of the same authority, he then adds: ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever’ (ibid., 7). That is, in due order the enemies will be destroyed, while all the rest will be subjected. For you do not possess a kingship introduced later, but have reigned over all from eternity; you reign forever, and your kingdom remains forever.

“The Jews understand these things as empty fables, supposing that they were spoken of a human king. For to which merely human being could this distinction of virtues or such greatness of expressions apply? To whom would the words ‘and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully’ apply (ibid., 5)? Divine Scripture always speaks in this way of all the righteous, because they possess virtue through divine assistance.

“But it is also clear here that he is not speaking of some impious person who relies on his own virtue. To which human being, then, does he say, ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever’? If he speaks of a divine king, it is clear that the queen too is not a woman but the Church, whom Christ betrothed to himself through faith, intending to unite her to himself through the devotion of the soul. For it is customary in divine Scripture to call those who are joined to God through knowledge his spouse, in order to display their complete union and oneness with God.”

A little later he says:

“As John the Baptist also says: ‘He who has the bride is the bridegroom’ (John 3:29). Since, then, the congregation of human beings who are joined to God through knowledge is always called God’s spouse, he appropriately called Christ the king. Necessarily, therefore, there is a queen, who is the royal wife, receiving no other advancement in these matters than that which she shares from her husband’s dignity. Accordingly, he calls the Church queen, showing how great a dignity she has obtained from union with Christ, a dignity conferred on her through faith. Since these things cannot be said of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0741D] The Verona Codex has *possint*, “cannot.”], what follows clearly establishes this.”

What, then, do the heretics appear to accomplish in the present chapter by criticizing the Council of Chalcedon on account of Theodorus’s person? We see all their slanders equally excluded in him. He did not believe the Father to be the same as the Son, since he says: “What has been said concerning the Son cannot be said concerning God the Father.” Nor did he believe the Word of God to be one person and Christ another, since he confesses that the prophet said to Christ: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Psalm 44:7), and denies that he possesses a kingship introduced later, teaching instead that he reigns from eternity.

Theodorus, therefore, must not be accused of Jewish impiety, as though he had considered Christ merely human, since he rather mocks the Jews, saying: “The Jews understand these things as empty fables, supposing that they were spoken of a human king.” And, indicating what he himself believes, he says that no human being can possess such a distinction of virtues or such greatness of expressions as those addressed to Christ: “Your right hand has led you wonderfully” (ibid., 5). For divine Scripture says that all righteous human beings possess virtue through divine assistance; but he asserts that Christ, as God, has no need of divine assistance.

Likewise, farther below he says: “But if he speaks of a divine king, it is clear that the queen too is not a woman but the Church, whom Christ betrothed to himself through faith, intending to unite her to himself through the devotion of the soul.” And to show again that he believed Christ to be God, he says:

“For it is customary in divine Scripture to call those who are joined to God through knowledge his spouse, in order to display their complete union with God.”

Thus he declares to be God the one whom above he called Christ. Therefore farther below he also says that the congregation of human beings who are joined to God through knowledge is always called God’s spouse.

That he did not nullify all the prophecies made concerning Christ is evident from the fact that he confesses this very prophecy to have been spoken of Christ and of his spouse [Note: [Col. 0741D] The same codex has: “and of his spouse, the Church.”]. Again, interpreting the following verses of the same Psalm, he says: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (ibid., 8). It is clear that these words cannot again be spoken of God:

“But since these things do not apply to God the Father, ‘Therefore God, your God, has anointed you’ makes it clear that what follows is spoken of Christ. In this he wonderfully distinguished the natures and demonstrated the unity of the person. He distinguished the natures in that he uttered words expressing different meanings; for there is a great difference between ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever’ and ‘Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.’ But he showed the unity of the person by gathering things that are different into the unity of one person.”

It is not now necessary to linger here and show that in the same way he removed from himself the reproach of all the slanders. One point might perhaps seem to require interpretation for the sake of his accusers: he said that he “distinguished the natures and demonstrated the unity of the person.” But, interpreting himself, he teaches in what sense he said that they were distinguished, when he immediately added:

“He distinguished the natures in that he uttered words expressing different meanings. For there is a great difference between ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever’ and ‘Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.’”

He therefore asserted that they were distinguished only insofar as the meanings concerning the living God are distinct. It is clear that they differ from one another—not in such a way as to produce two persons, as we also showed shortly afterward when he said that even in one human being the soul is naturally distinct from its body.

Accordingly, he added this as well and said:

“But he showed the unity of the person by gathering things that are different into the unity of one person.”

You recognize, then, emperor, that the truly wise John, writing with the Eastern Council to blessed Cyril concerning blessed Theodorus, said truthfully:

“For the whole East in common held him forth as possessing great excellence of teaching against the heresies. In fighting and battling against them he made use of much division, not deriving this from a perverse understanding, but judging that this was the more effective way to employ it against the heretics. Nor was he ignorant of or denying the supreme unity—far from it, for all his books are full of this kind of teaching—but he divided the properties of the natures more explicitly, as the struggle he waged against the heretics dictated that he should.”

For who, from the passages we have cited, would not recognize that all Theodorus’s books are filled with opinions of this kind, when from a single passage of his writings—that is, from the first part of his exposition of Psalm 44—we proved for the third time that all three charges maliciously circulated against him were false? Thus [Note: [Col. 0742D] The same codex reads: “From this, therefore.”] the discerning reader may understand how many similar passages, arranged both together and separately, may be found throughout all his books.

## CHAPTER II  
### That Theodorus confessed Christ to be not merely human but also God by nature

It seems to us, however, that we ought to produce more passages from his writings in which he confesses Christ to be not merely human but also God according to nature, existing essentially as the true Son of God and the maker of all things—precisely what they most seriously accuse him of denying.

While discussing what is written in the Gospel according to Matthew—“When Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, he questioned his disciples, saying: ‘Who do people say that the Son of Man is?’” (Matthew 16:13)—he spoke as follows:

“For the Lord Christ was both God and human, each alike according to nature. He appeared from one aspect, while from the other—that is, insofar as he existed according to the divine nature—he was invisible. One aspect alone was manifest to everyone, namely, what could be seen: for at that time everyone thought that he was human and nothing more. What was hidden in him had previously been incredible to everyone. But, from the greatness of the things that took place around him, from the novelty of the miracles that he performed for the instruction of those who witnessed them, and from the grace of the Holy Spirit who came upon the apostles, it was later understood and believed that he was the true God, essentially existing as the true Son of the eternal God.

“Since, at the earlier time, it was not known that he existed according to essence, and since, from what appeared to those who saw him, he was thought to be a mere human being, he spoke many things according to humanity and according to the nature that appeared. Anyone can find this in the things written in the Gospel, if he examines them attentively.”

Do you suppose now, most merciful emperor, that those who believed the deceitful assailants of the Council of Chalcedon have recognized that they were deceived [Note: [Col. 0743D] The Verona Codex has: “have recognized that they themselves had been deceived.”], so that, for the council’s destruction, they thought Theodorus should be condemned as the author of Nestorian error?

For what more carefully considered or more subtle argument against the Nestorians could Catholics find than the statement that Christ was God and human, and that each was alike according to nature? He does not mean that Christ was human according to nature alone, while God was merely like God—that is, according to a relation of dignity, an authority belonging to a person, or a title conferred by grace, which is all that those same Nestorians commonly say. Rather, the one Christ is according to nature and alike in both: appearing from one aspect, while from the other—that is, insofar as he existed according to the divine nature—he was invisible.

Theodorus therefore confesses the same person, who is both, to be both visible and invisible. He adds:

“One aspect alone was manifest to everyone, namely, what could be seen: for at that time everyone thought that he was human and nothing more. What was hidden in him had previously been incredible to everyone.”

How, then, can it be said that this man considered Christ merely human and nothing more, when he himself attributes this judgment to the ignorance of the people of that time, who thought this and found what was hidden in him incredible? He even confesses that, from the greatness of the miracles and from the grace of the Holy Spirit descending upon the apostles, Christ was later understood and believed to be the true God, essentially existing as the true Son of the eternal God.

What, then, shall we say? Does it seem credible to those who understand that the one whom he taught was later understood and believed to be God was himself neither understood nor believed by Theodorus? Repeating and emphasizing this very point as though against the slanders directed at him, he says again:

“Since, at the earlier time, it was not known that he existed according to essence, and since, from what appeared to those who saw him, he was thought to be a mere human being, he spoke many things according to humanity and according to the nature that appeared.”

He again says that it was due to ignorance that Christ was not understood to be God according to essence but merely a human being, not also God. Yet he himself is portrayed as having been ignorant of this! A little later he says again:

“Near the time of his passion the Lord said to the disciples: ‘If you knew me, you would also know my Father’ (John 8:19); and to Philip: ‘I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father’ (John 14:9). He showed that they knew neither the divine nature of the Only-Begotten nor the true God, the Father. Therefore they did not in any way attend to him when he spoke of his own Father as speaking of God; rather, with their understanding divided, they thought those things were the same as these. For this reason Philip was also led to say: ‘Show us the Father, and that is enough for us’ (ibid., 8).

“For if he had understood completely that he was calling ‘his Father’ the one who truly was his Father, from whom he truly existed as God from God, he would never have said: ‘Show us your Father,’ knowing well that the divine nature is invisible to human beings. Accordingly, the Lord also said to him: ‘I have been with you for so long, Philip’ [Note: [Col. 0744D] In the same codex *Philippe* is absent; it is also absent from the text of John 14:9.], ‘and you have not known me, Philip?’

“His desire to see the Father was evidence that he did not know either who he was according to nature or whom he was calling Father—the Son existing from him. And, explaining this, he added: ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father also.’ ‘If you know who I am,’ he says, ‘you will know him also, contemplating through me, insofar as this is possible, the nature of the Father, whose Son I am, existing from him according to essence and existing of the same essence as he.

“‘Since you do not know me, you do not know my Father, whom I name. But by knowing me, you will know the Father whom I named: seeing me through the contemplation of understanding, through me you will see him also in every respect.’

“He also added: ‘Until now you have asked nothing in my name’ (John 16:24). By this he made clear that, because they did not yet understand his divine nature, they neither offered prayers to him as God nor made any requests in his name, as they ought to do in the name of the one who exists as God and Son of God, the maker of all.

“And because of their weakness he spoke about the Father in likenesses, since they were not able fully to understand what was being said—either of which Father he was speaking or in what manner he existed—this is indicated even more plainly. For he said: ‘I have spoken these things to you in figures; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father to you openly’ (ibid., 25).

“What, then, was it that he had not spoken openly concerning the Father, except that they truly did not know the divine nature of the Only-Begotten, from which they could learn of God the Father, who was truly his Father, so that he was God from God, born from him according to essence? For this reason he spoke to them about the Father through likenesses: at that time using only the name before them, while reserving for the future the true understanding of it, when the grace of the Holy Spirit that came upon them would instruct them and make them capable of receiving such great teaching.

“For this reason the Lord himself, near his passion, in that same discourse, in order to show their weakness and indicate from what condition they could receive more perfect instruction, said: ‘I have many things to say to you’ (John 16:12). Why, then, do you not say them now? Because you cannot bear them now—not because I begrudge them, but because you are not yet capable of a greater apprehension of realities, being still affected by weakness, so that you cannot be instructed in the fullness of these doctrines.

“When, then, will they be able, and from where? ‘When the Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth’ (ibid., 13). For the grace of the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and through it you will know the whole subtlety of the doctrines [Note: [Col. 0745D] Perhaps *cognoscetis*, “you will know.”]. Therefore, if they were taught the divinity of the Only-Begotten, they would certainly also be taught that the Father is God, as the Father of the Son of God. What more perfect knowledge of the doctrines would remain for them?”

Having recalled these passages, you should attend not only to how far we are from the accusers of Theodorus—and, rather, from the accusers of the Council of Chalcedon—in accordance with the merits of the case entrusted to us, but also to how simply and faithfully we conduct the matter.

For the heretics, like thieves and dogs, do not bring forward Theodorus’s opinions intact, as they actually stand, sincerely and straightforwardly. Instead, as they also habitually do with the canonical Scriptures themselves, they steal a few obscure words from his statements and then mutilate those same words with a slanderous tooth [Note: [Col. 0745D] Dionysius of Alexandria, as Athanasius reports, complained in the same way that his opponents presented his statements not in their entirety but in mutilated form: “Then he accuses those who denounced him of not stating his words in full, but cutting them up” (*Ἔπειτα αἰτιᾶται τοὺς κατειπόντας αὐτοῦ, ὡς μὴ ὁλοκλήρους λέγοντας, ἀλλὰ περικόπτοντας αὐτοῦ τὰς λέξεις*). Gregory of Nazianzus likewise speaks of Apollinaris’s mutilation of the Apostle’s words in his address to Nectarius: “For again he cites an apostolic utterance, having cut away something from the whole body of its context” (*Λέγει γὰρ πάλιν ἀποστολικήν τινα ῥῆσιν τοῦ ὅλου σώματος τῆς συμφράσεως ἀποκνίσας*).]

We, however, as you see, prefer to risk the weariness caused by length rather than the suspicion of fraud caused by brevity and obscurity. In the passages we present, the reader need not ask what Theodorus said above, what follows below [Note: [Col. 0745D] The Verona Codex has: “or what follows below.”], or why he spoke in this way. We have set the whole case before the eyes of the judges [Note: [Col. 0745D] The same codex reads: “we have set the whole case just as it is.”]. We do not, as they do, select a few obscure words from many clear ones, nor bite off fragments from complete and finished statements [Note: [Col. 0745D] The same codex reads: “we have selected words, not fragments from complete statements.”].

As everyone can recognize from the passages cited, he asserts that it was not a mere human being—that is, one who is not also God—but the only-begotten Son of God, consubstantial with the Father, who suffered for us. He says that this same one, near the time of his passion, told the disciples: “If you knew me, you would also know my Father” (John 8:19); and to Philip: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9). He says that Christ showed that they did not know the divine nature of the Only-Begotten. Theodorus would not have said this unless he believed that the Only-Begotten, who possesses the divine nature, suffered for us.

Nor would he have included there the following words:

“For this reason Philip was also led to say: ‘Show us the Father, and that is enough for us’” [Note: [Col. 0746D] The same codex has: “that is enough for us,” adding: “For if.”].

“For if he had understood completely that he was calling ‘his Father’ the one who truly was his Father, from whom he truly existed as God from God” [Note: [Col. 0746D] The same codex has: “his God.”], “he would never have said: ‘Show us your Father,’ knowing well that the divine nature is invisible to human beings.”

## CHAPTER III  
### That Theodorus acknowledged one person in Christ’s two natures and was alien from both the error of the Jews and that of the Manichaeans
Therefore, did this man, who truly asserts that God from God, and the invisible Son of the divine nature, suffered for us, intend that two sons were to be understood—as though the one who suffered for us belonged to one hypostasis, and the Only-Begotten, who truly exists as God from God, invisible and of the divine nature, to another? Or could he say of the one whom he believed to be a mere man:

> “For if you know who I am,” he says, “you will also know him, contemplating through me, insofar as this is possible, the nature of the Father, whose Son I am, existing from him according to essence and existing of the same essence as he”?

And to show that it was not another, but the very one who is consubstantial with the Father, who undertook suffering for us, he repeats the same point and says again:

> “For this reason also the Lord himself, being near to his passion in that very discourse, in order to show their weakness and the point from which they could receive more perfect instruction, said: ‘I have many things to say to you.’”

Thus Theodorus says that it was the Lord himself, who is consubstantial with the Father, and not another, who suffered for us. Yet neither does he declare that the Father himself is the one who is the Son. Otherwise, when speaking about Philip, he would not say:

> “For the desire to see the Father was an indication that he did not know even him—that is, Christ”; or, in what follows there in the person of the Lord: “For if you know who I am,” he says, “you will also know him, contemplating through me, insofar as this is possible, the nature of the Father”—

and the other similar statements contained there, which concern the Father and the Son, whose nature is one, and which can be understood only as spoken with the distinction of persons.

At the end of that very statement he also indicates all three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—together, when he says in the person of the Lord:

> “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth. For the grace of the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and through it you will learn the whole subtlety of doctrine.”

Accordingly, if they were taught the divinity of the Only-Begotten, they would certainly also be taught that the Father is God. Why, then, have the accomplices of the heretics tried, to the prejudice of the holy synod, to obscure such overwhelming evidence—as though they could blind everyone’s eyes in the same way that they have blinded their own?

For, interpreting the Gospel according to John, he says:

> “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10),

and, saying that the Lord Christ came into this world, he rightly explained the words “he was in the world” as referring to his coming for manifestation.

> “For he was substance and nature in the world,” he says, “and before that as well.”

And as though this were not enough, he continued:

> “The world was made through him”—that is, what wonder is it if he was in the world, when the world would not exist unless he had willed it? Yet he was indeed in the world beforehand, and he himself also made the world, and the world did not know him. Here he rightly said ‘did not know,’ as though he were saying, ‘They did not recognize their own Lord.’”

[Col. 0747A] The statement of the most wise John is altogether confirmed by what he says about Theodorus together with the Eastern council.

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “He says about Theodorus, neither ignorant of nor denying the supreme unity.” Far be that from him.]

[Col. 0747C] In fact, as is evident, he neither ignored nor denied the supreme unity.

[Note: But only according to εὐδοκίαν, “good pleasure” or benevolent disposition, and by a certain relation (σχέσει τινί), as has been said. For Theodore rightly refuted union according to οὐσία, substance, against the Synusiasts, but did not acknowledge hypostatic union. This is shown especially by passages which Anastasius the priest quotes from his Letter to Domnus in the *Eclogue of Doctrinal Extracts*: “Theodore of Mopsuestia, from the Letter to Domnus: The union of the natures according to εὐδοκία produces, by virtue of their common name, one designation for both: one will, activity, authority, power, dominion, dignity, and sovereignty, in no way divided, since according to it one person of both comes to be and is spoken of.” The Latin rendering: “The union of natures which takes place according to εὐδοκία gives one common appellation to both, and a will, operation, authority, power, dominion, dignity, and rule in no way divided, since according to it the person of both is and is called one.”

After other matters:

> “And why say much? The account of union according to substance is true only of things consubstantial; of things of different substance it is false, since it cannot be free of confusion. But the mode of union according to εὐδοκία, preserving the natures unconfused and undivided, shows one person of both, one will, and one activity, together with the one authority and dominion consequent upon these.”

The Latin rendering:

> “The principle of union according to substance is true only in consubstantial things; in things of another substance it is false, since it cannot exist without confusion. But the mode of union according to εὐδοκία, preserving the natures unconfused and undivided, shows one person of both, one will, and one operation, together with the one authority and dominion which follow upon them.”

Again, after other matters:

> “For, joined to God the Word according to the mode of εὐδοκία, as we have said, the temple born of the Virgin remained undivided from the very womb, possessing in all things the same will and the same activity as he; and nothing can be more closely joined.”

The Latin rendering:

> “For the temple born of the Virgin, joined to God the Word according to the mode of εὐδοκία, as we have said, remained undivided from the very womb, having in all things the same will and the same activity as he; and nothing can be more closely joined.”]

For he said all those many things mentioned above, including his statement concerning Christ coming in the manifestation of the flesh: that he was substance and nature in the world and before it—that is, that the one who was later manifested in the flesh had previously existed in the world. He declared that there was nothing remarkable in saying that Christ had previously been in the world, since the world would not exist unless he had willed it. He again affirmed that the same one had made the world in the beginning, while asserting that the world, when he came in the last times, did not recognize its own Lord.

Accordingly, this man knew that Christ, coming in the manifestation of the flesh, was the maker of the world and its own Lord. By saying that Christ has two natures, he did not say that there are two sons, or two Lords, or two Christs, as the heretics falsely claim.

For in his book *To the Baptized* he spoke plainly:

[Note: The same manuscript reads *ad baptizatos scripto*, “written to the baptized.”]

[Note: See Touttée on this passage, *Ad Cyrillum Hierosolymitanum*, dissertation 3, chapter 4, no. 24, p. CXVI, Paris edition.]

[Note: The same work appears to be that which, throughout the fourth session of the Fifth Synod, is entitled *To Those Being Baptized*.]

> “For even if we say that there are two natures, no necessity compels us to say either two sons, or two men, or two Christs; for to think this is the height of madness.”

[Note: The same manuscript reads “two Lords, or two Christs” in place of “two men, or two Christs.”]

But consider more attentively what he says in the fifth book of *On the Incarnation*, chapter 52, against the Apollinarians and Arians, who ask whether the one is one and the other another, or whether they are the very same. In that passage his orthodox faith concerning Christ’s incarnation is not merely evident; it also becomes clear according to what principle, or according to what manner of speech, he expressed the other statements for which the heretics malign him.

[Col. 0747C] For he says:

> “When someone distinguishes the natures, he necessarily finds one and another; and I do not think that even they themselves oppose this, since it may be granted that one is God the Word by nature, while the other is whatever that which was assumed may be. Nevertheless, with respect to person, the very same one is found, the natures in no way being confused, but because of the union that has taken place between the assumed and the one who assumes.
>
> “For if it is fully granted that this is other than that by nature—and it is clear that what is assumed is not equal to the one who assumes, nor like him, nor the same as the one who assumes—it is nevertheless clear that the very same one is found through the union of person.
>
> “Thus it was necessary to distinguish the things concerning Christ. These distinctions are in no way contrary, for they also agree in many respects with the divine Scriptures. In this way there will be neither confusion of natures nor some perverse division of person. For the account of the natures must remain unconfused, and the person must be recognized as indivisible.
>
> “That distinction is by the property of nature, what is assumed being distinguished from the one who assumes; but their identity is by the union of person, the nature of the whole being considered under one designation, whether it is that of the one who assumes or of what is assumed; and, so to speak, in the appellation ‘Son’ we name together both God the Word and the assumed nature, whatever it may be, signifying it together with him because of the union it has with him.”

[Col. 0748C] Is there anyone, most merciful emperor, whose heart is so darkened and who is so completely alienated from human understanding that, hearing and rereading these words, he would think that Theodorus preached two sons? I judge that his accusers, in what they have done to annul the Council of Chalcedon, are acting deceitfully against their conscience rather than erring through ignorance in matters so manifest.

But this is what I ask you to observe more attentively:

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “Observe this proposition,” or “observe this point.”]

how he speaks, and in what manner of expression, when he seems to offend the inexperienced and those ignorant of his intention. For when, distinguishing the natures in Christ, he says “one and another,” he does not introduce two sons. Rather, he says that one is God the Word by nature—

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “the other is God.”]

—as he teaches most clearly here, while the other is what was assumed, although, with respect to person, the very same one is found.

These are not my words but his: he explains himself and teaches how he should be understood elsewhere, where he says that, repeating this very point as was appropriate, whenever anything of this kind is said, we must understand it in no other way.

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “he says.”]

> “For if it is fully granted,” he says, “that this is other than that by nature, and it is clear that what is assumed is not equal to the one who assumes, nor like him, nor the same as the one who assumes, it is clear that the very same one is found through the union of person.”

You see, Augustus, that he says the one who assumes is other than what is assumed not with respect to person but rather with respect to nature. He wishes this to be understood of the natures, between which there is great difference, and concerning which it is appropriate to say that what is assumed is not the same as the one who assumes. But of the person he says that the one who assumes and what is assumed are the same. Could anyone have said more than “the very same one”? In this statement he says it not merely once but again.

[Col. 0749B] He therefore continues:

> “Thus there will be neither confusion of natures nor some perverse division of person.”

What could we seek more clearly, or what more could we expect from him? Yet he still adds:

> “For the account of the natures must remain unconfused, and the person must be recognized as indivisible.”

And again, piling one statement upon another, if I may put it so, he says:

> “That distinction is by the property of nature, what is assumed being distinguished from the one who assumes; but their identity is by the union of person, the nature of the whole being considered under one designation, whether it is that of the one who assumes or of what is assumed; and, so to speak, in the appellation ‘Son’ we name together both God the Word and the assumed nature, whatever it may be, signifying it together with him.”

[Col. 0749D] He says “whatever it may be” because the heretics against whom he is arguing disagree among themselves concerning the incarnation, each in a different error. The Apollinarians believe that the Lord assumed the nature of flesh and soul without a mind; the Arians, only flesh.

[Note: Theodoret also observes this distinction between the Arians and the Apollinarians in *Dialogue* 2. But Saint Augustine, in *Heresy* 55, indicates that at first the Apollinarians agreed with the Arians that Christ had assumed flesh without a soul; later, overcome by evangelical testimonies, they said that there had been no mind in Christ’s soul, but that the Word himself had been present in it in place of the mind. For this reason some called them *Dimoiritae* (Διμοιρῖται), because they said that the Word had not assumed the whole human being.]

For this reason he also said above: “One is God the Word by nature, while the other is whatever that which was assumed may be.”

Now that he has established this clear rule for us—not merely once or twice, but repeatedly—and has emphasized it so often, whenever he is found speaking about Christ and distinguishing one from another, separating the one who assumes from what is assumed in such a way as to affirm that this and that are not the same, ought we to understand him as speaking of the division of one person, rather than of the difference between two natures? For he says that, with respect to person, the one who assumes and what is assumed are the very same; he repeats this very point and commends it in various forms of expression.

This principle of his ought therefore to help us with the passages that appear obscure, so that we may judge what may be doubtful from what is absolutely certain. Let us not look at the stolen fragments of his statements that the heretics cut away precisely so that the intention of the speaker may not appear in them.

What they tell us, then—that in discussing Christ’s incarnation Theodorus wrote that what was assumed is not the same as the one who assumes, but is one and another—we have shown by the present testimony that he did indeed say this, but with reference to the difference between two natures, not to the division of one person. It is like saying that the inner man, made in the image and likeness of God, is one thing, and the outer man, made more like the beasts, another—not because there are two persons, but because there are two natures.

His own explicit words also make this clear and commend it to us as something to hold firmly, through repeated emphasis. Let them therefore prove, if they can, where he said with respect to person that the one is not the same or is another, so that we too may admit that he was in error. We seek proof of this, not assertions thrown out on the basis of someone’s unknown suspicion or preference, so that he may be judged from his own words, not from the conjecture or slander of others.

But if nothing of this kind can be proved against him, how can they say that he ought to have been condemned by the Council of Chalcedon as the inventor of Nestorian doctrine?

Again, in the sixth book of the same work, chapter 54, against the same Apollinarians, who want us to appear to be *hominicolae*—

[Note: Ἀνθρωπολάτρας, “worshipers of a man.” Athanasius, near the end of *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, says: “And while slandering us, you say that we speak of two sons and call us worshipers of a man.”]

[Col. 0750C]—he replied as follows:

> “If, then, merely because we call Christ a man, it seems right to them that we should be called worshipers of a man, Scripture taught this before we did, through the passages in which it does not refuse to call him a man, just as above we showed in many places that Christ is called by this name.
>
> “But, they say, if we say that Christ is a mere man, we ought to be called worshipers of a man. This is now an obvious lie, if that is what they intended to say. No one has ever heard us say this, and I think that they themselves cannot accept so blatant a lie—not because they are unacquainted with lying
>
> [Note: The same manuscript reads *cognate*, “akin” or “related.”]
>
> “but because they see that they can easily be refuted, although, if they care little about this
>
> [Note: The same manuscript reads *eis*, “them.”]
>
> “perhaps even that may happen.
>
> “For we consider it the height of madness to say such things—that is, to deny the divinity of the Only-Begotten. Otherwise, what remains by which we are separated from the heretics? Why do we endure such and so many persecutions?
>
> [Note: The same manuscript reads: “have endured.”]
>
> “Or who does not know that the heretics have always waged war against us? Every mine and every deserted place is filled with our people because of the doctrine of piety.”

And after a little further he says:

> “But when the blessed Meletius first endured all these things, and afterward many with him throughout the provinces, cities, and places endured them from the heretics, for what reason did this happen? Was it not because they confessed the Lord Christ as true? Was it not because they preached the true Son of God, begotten from the Father’s essence, always existing together with the Father who begot him, while also adding a pious confession concerning the Holy Spirit? How, then, can we, who have suffered so much for this confession, endure being slandered by them as though we said that he was a mere man, when the facts themselves plainly refute this slander?”

I do not know how this man can be accused not merely imprudently but also shamelessly of calling Christ a mere man. For long ago he answered the Apollinarians—the authors of the Eutychian error, who denied Christ’s two natures and therefore slandered the orthodox as worshipers of a man because they confessed Christ as both man and God—that it was false to suppose that they called Christ a mere man. He affirmed that no one had heard them say this and declared that saying it would be the height of madness.

He says that the holy Meletius, bishop of Antioch, and the other Catholic confessors with him filled the mines and every deserted place because they confessed Christ as the true God, begotten from the Father’s essence and always existing together with the Father who begot him, while also adding a pious confession concerning the Holy Spirit.

Since the Lord says in the Gospel, “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37), how could the holy synod condemn this man—justified by his own words—on the basis of the words of the Apollinarians and Eutychians?

[Col. 0751C] Behold, he cries out and repeatedly insists that he does not say that Christ is a mere man, but that he is the true God and the true Son of God, begotten from the Father’s substance and always existing together with the Father who begot him. Yet certain people say that the synod ought to have anathematized him after his death as though he had called Christ a mere man, and not as though he himself were saying that Christ is the Son of God according to essence.

Here they should recognize—and not pretend that they fail to see—that when he says that Christ the Son of God was begotten from the Father’s essence and always existed together with the Father who begot him, and then adds, “while also adding a pious confession concerning the Holy Spirit,” he is likewise preaching the Trinity, which he is similarly alleged to have denied.

Let them therefore acknowledge their own credulity and finally understand that they have been deceived: they believed concerning Theodorus more readily in heretics or the supporters of heretics than in the holy Fathers of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0751D] In the tenth book of the same work, chapter 70, he also says:

> “Just as through such expressions from divine Scripture we are taught the differences of the natures—
>
> [Note: The Verona manuscript reads “the difference.”]
>
> “so also we learn their union, whenever he brings together the properties of both natures into one and speaks of them as one. For this is to show at once both the differing natures and the union of person: from the difference of the things that are said, the difference of the natures is understood; but when they are brought together, we perceive the union clearly.
>
> “The blessed evangelist John says: ‘The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him and said: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world. This is he of whom I said, “After me comes a man who has been made before me, because he was before me,” and I did not know him’” (John 1:29).
>
> “Here, by saying, ‘He saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Behold the Lamb of God,”’ John seems clearly to me to signify the humanity. This is what John the Baptist saw; this was what had received death—namely, the body that was offered for the whole world. But what follows, ‘who takes away the sin of the world,’ no longer applies to the flesh. It was not the flesh’s role to take away the sin of the whole world; that was certainly the work of divinity.”

Who would not have thought that such things were spoken after the emergence of the heresies of the Nestorians and Eutychians, unless the title identified the author of the statements? Thus this man proceeds uprightly between the two, refuting both by the testimony of divine Scripture—he who, they claim, ought to have been refuted by the Council of Chalcedon as the originator of the Nestorian error—so that the reader finds nothing else defined either by the Council of Ephesus or by that of Chalcedon itself.

Would that the Nestorians and Eutychians followed these teachings with us, for then they would not be heretics. Would that at last the Nestorians and Eutychians follow these teachings with us, so that they may not be heretics: in them the difference between the two natures in Christ is preached in such a way that the one person of both natures is preached at the same time.

Let the Eutychians therefore not pretend that they hate Theodorus because he supposedly preached two persons, one of the Son of God and another of the son of man, when the passages cited above show that they hate him rather because he preached that there are two natures belonging to one person. We do not require here an ingenious interpreter, but simply a reader who is not fastidious. The matter is open and clear and requires no interpretation; all that is needed is that those who resist the truth with closed eyes should now wish to see.

For in the twelfth book of the work mentioned above he also says:

> “If someone wishes to ask what, finally, I say Jesus Christ is, I answer: God and the Son of God.”

Behold the character of the confession of the man whom they falsely represent as having called Christ a mere man. We must fear that, when we refuse to let these slanderers accuse him of Jewish impiety, they may instead lay upon him the charge of the Manichaeans in the mystery of the incarnation, because here, confessing Jesus Christ as God and the Son of God, he said nothing about his humanity.

For what wonder is it if those who earlier falsely claimed that he preached God as solitary—

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “said that he preached [God], and [as] solitary.”]

without Son and Holy Spirit, and conversely taught two sons, should invent this also through a similar contradiction? Having said that he believed, like the Jews, in Jesus Christ as a mere man—as though he were not also God—they may again say, like a Manichaean, that because he believed the Lord Christ to be God and the Son of God alone, he denied that he was a man. For, as we have shown above, they have decided to stain him with both the Jewish and Manichaean error, as though he were nullifying all the prophecies fulfilled in Christ.

Everything is permitted to their wisdom, and there is nothing they may desire that they do not believe serves their purpose.

Just as he does not deny that Jesus Christ is a man because here, saying nothing about his humanity, he confesses him only as God and the Son of God, so also he does not deny that Jesus Christ is God when, saying nothing about his divinity or distinguishing the natures, he omits the fact that he is also the same God and Son of God.

The apostle Peter did not deny that Christ is God when, speaking to the Jews about his divinity, he tactfully remained silent about what they could not bear even to hear lightly, and said:

> “Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus the Nazarene, a man attested to you by God through mighty works, wonders, and signs, which God performed through him in your midst, as you yourselves know—this man, delivered up by the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men; but God raised him, releasing the pains of the underworld” (Acts 2:22).

Nor did Paul, his apostle—

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “his fellow apostle.”]

—deny that Christ is God when he said:

> “There is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony at its proper times” (1 Timothy 2:5),

as though Christ were not God, but merely mediator between God and human beings, or as though he were not the creator and ruler of all times, so that certain times could be called his, in the way that we customarily speak of any ordinary human being and say, “In his time he says or does this or that.”

But the intention of the speaker is always different according to the different circumstances.

[Col. 0753C] The Lord himself also says to the Jews in the Gospel:

> “But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God” (John 8:40).

Did he deny by saying this that he is God and Christ?

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “Did Christ deny this?”]

Accordingly, let us believe that his apostles and the teachers of the Church spoke certain things in this manner, as stewards of the divine mystery, not handing the same things to everyone, nor in the same way. If we wish to interpret more fully and reverently those who died in the peace of the Church, let us excuse the men in this way while condemning the errors.

In the fifteenth book, with which he concluded the entire work *On the Incarnation*, he also testifies that both natures came together in the person of one Son, saying:

> “For this reason both are rightly called Son, since one person exists, which the union of the natures produced.”

I have lingered longer over this work of his *On the Incarnation* than faith and reason required—or, if not longer than they required, longer than seemed necessary in view of the slanders and obstinacy. For what person of sound understanding—

[Note: The same manuscript reads *sentienti*, “of sound judgment.”]

—would not find the title of the work itself sufficient for recognizing Theodorus’s faith? Who, hearing that he had composed books *On the Incarnation*—or, to express this more precisely, by a less Latin but necessary word, *On the Inhumanation*, as the Greeks call it—would think that he preached two sons?

[Note: *Περὶ ἐνανθρωπήσεως*, “On the Inhumanation.” Justinian’s edict says: “against Theodorus, who speaks in his various discourses, impiously set forth, concerning the inhumanation…” The Greeks customarily gave this title to books concerning this mystery, which the Latins called *On the Incarnation*. Thus Athanasius’s second discourse is entitled *Περὶ τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγου*, “On the Inhumanation of God the Word,” and likewise the works of Cyril and other orthodox writers. The Arians and Apollinarians, however, because they denied that the Word had assumed the whole human being, avoided the title *ἐνανθρωπήσεως* and used instead *περὶ σαρκώσεως*, “On the Embodiment,” as Eudoxius of Constantinople does in Anastasius’s *Eclogue*, and Apollinaris himself, whose *Brief Treatise on the Embodiment* is mentioned by Theodoret in *Dialogue* 3. Catholics too sometimes used this expression, as Athanasius does in other books; indeed, in writing against Apollinaris he joined both expressions together: “A Manichaean, having disbelieved in the embodiment and inhumanation of the Lord, became impious in every respect.”]

For how could he fail to call the Son of God, that is, God the Word, also a man, when he said that he had become inhumanated? I do not shrink from the term required of me by the demands and usefulness of the faith, especially against those who say that the Son of God assumed not the whole human being—that is, flesh and a rational soul—but only flesh, or flesh together with a soul without reason.

How, then, could he teach that God the Word, whom he taught to have become inhumanated, was not himself also man? Or how, while teaching two sons—as though the Word of God belonged to one person and the assumed man to another—could he call God the Word himself inhumanated, if the same person were not God the Word and man? The two claims are mutually contradictory. They ought to have been ashamed to accuse so learned a man on this basis—or, if they refuse to call him learned, at least one who was commended by the testimony of the most learned men.

The Council of Chalcedon was clearly not a participant in such shamelessness. It should have understood that whenever Theodorus, necessarily distinguishing the properties of the natures more sharply against the heretics, asserted that the one who assumes is other than what is assumed, he was speaking of nature, not person, as we have shown above.

Let us now pass from this work *On the Incarnation* to another work that he published against Eunomius. There, in the tenth book, he says:

> “For all the Jews were awaiting the coming Christ on the basis of the prophetic utterances, expecting him to be a great person and the author of many benefits for them. Therefore, when Herod asked the scribes and Pharisees, after the arrival of the magi, where Christ was to be born, they answered him and named the place, saying that he would be born in Bethlehem of Judea. Yet they did not for that reason know Christ the Son of God as God; rather, they thought that Christ would be a mere man, according to the most reputable of the prophets, though somewhat better than these people. Anyone can see that the Jews still hold this opinion today.”
