Is it still just that the holy and great synod should be accused because it did not also accuse Theodorus of both Jewish unbelief and the Manichaean plague—condemning him with the Jews as though he had believed Christ to be merely a man, and with the Manichaeans as though he had not accepted the prophets who spoke about Christ?

For he reproves the Jews because, although they regarded him as somewhat greater than the most reputable of the prophets, they nevertheless did not know that he was God. Against the others, however, he says that the Jews awaited Christ’s coming on the basis of the prophetic utterances, according to which they also answered Herod when he asked, saying that he would be born in Bethlehem of Judea.

## CHAPTER IV

### That Theodorus used the likeness of a human being composed of soul and body to demonstrate only the unity of Christ’s person, not to confuse his natures
Therefore, since the Eutychians cannot be reconciled either to the great synod or to Theodore, no matter how many similar passages from his books are brought forward, let us rather show that he said something which they may think accords with their own error. For they could not be pacified by the passages already mentioned [Col. 0755B] or by others of the same kind, because they hate neither Theodore himself nor the Council of Chalcedon, as they pretend, on the ground that it proclaimed two sons—for this is plainly false—but rather because it most clearly said that there are two natures of one Son.

And since, as we recorded in the first book, these same Eutychians, or Semi-Eutychians, are accustomed to say that Christ has one nature composed of divinity and humanity, just as human nature itself is one, composed of soul and body, let us show them where Theodore also says that, just as the soul, united to the body, produces a man from both, so from the united form of God and form of a servant—that is, from divinity and humanity—there is one Christ. Thus perhaps those who have not spared him as a Catholic will spare him as one of their own, that is, as an Eutychian or Semi-Eutychian, and will cease accusing the great council for not condemning him.

He indeed set this forth not for the unity of nature but for the unity of person, as did other Fathers whose examples they misuse. For the nature of the Word of God, which is simple and immaculately simple, could not be composite. Thus he says in the fourth book Against Apollinaris:

> “Since, then, among us also a man is said to consist of soul and body, and we say that these are two natures, soul and body, but that one man is composed from both, in order to preserve both as one, must we confuse the natures and, reversing their terms, say that the soul is flesh and the flesh is soul? And since the one is immortal and rational, while the flesh is mortal [Col. 0755D] and rational [Note: Codex Veronensis: ‘irrational.’], should we, reversing the terms, say that the immortal is mortal and the mortal immortal, and that the rational is irrational and the irrational rational?

> “But neither have we learned this from divine Scripture, O wisest of all men, nor does anyone else say this to the present day who possesses a sound human mind, except you, who are altogether demented. By removing the dispensation made for our sake from the discourse concerning the assumption of the mind [Note: The same codex: ‘removing the assumption from the discourse’], you have incurred upon the mind itself a judgment full of all folly, speaking in all irreverence and laying down laws with great impiety.

> “For whatever things are distinct in one respect but have received unity in another preserve unimpaired the principle according to which they are distinct, and possess their unity intact. One thing is of one nature, as the Son and the Father; yet the distinction of persons remains. The essence exists inseparably as one, but the persons possess their proper distinction, so that the Father is not called the Son, nor the Son the Father.

> “Likewise, even if certain things are different in nature but have happened to be united in another respect, they neither lose their natural division nor fail to possess their proper unity, as the soul is united to the body and one man is produced from both. The division of the natures remains: the soul is one thing, and the flesh another; the one is immortal, the other mortal; the one rational, the other irrational. Yet one man is both. Neither of the two is ever called, absolutely and properly, ‘man’ in itself, except perhaps with some qualification, such as ‘inner man’ and ‘outer man’: not simply ‘man,’ but ‘inner’ and ‘outer,’ so that it may be evident that one thing is within the man and another outside him.

> “So also, in the Lord Christ, O remarkable man, we say that, while existing in the form of God, he is the form of a servant, neither the one who assumes becoming what is assumed, nor what is assumed becoming the one who assumes. The unity of what is assumed around the one who assumes is inseparable, incapable of being divided in any manner.” [Col. 0756C]

Thus, as we have said, let them spare Theodore as though he were a Semi-Eutychian, and let them not accuse the synod, which could not have condemned him either earlier or among themselves when he was accused—especially since he says that, just as the inner man and the outer man, that is, soul and body, although they are not of one nature, nevertheless make one person, so also in the Lord Christ the form of God and the form of a servant, although they are not of one nature, nevertheless made one person [Note: The same codex: ‘although they are not of one nature, nevertheless make one man; so also in the Lord Christ the form of God and the form of a servant, although they are not of one nature, nevertheless made one person. And so forth.’]

What confession of unity could be subtler or more explicit than that which is thought to demonstrate not merely that Christ is one, but even that his nature is one? Yet he did not shrink from this expression in order to articulate the unity of person. But just as, by saying this, he is not to be considered the head of the Acephali—for he says it not to deny two natures, but rather to assert one person—so neither is he to be considered the originator of the Nestorian error when, rejecting the confusion of the natures [Note: The same codex: ‘refuting’], he divides their properties more fully in the necessity of answering heretics, since this does not oppose the unity of person. [Col. 0756D]

From this the Semi-Eutychians may recognize the intention with which other Fathers speak—Fathers whom they suppose to have denied Christ in two natures—when they say that, just as soul and body make one man [Note: [Col. 0755D–0756D] Theodore of Hagiopolis set out the discrepancy of this comparison in eleven chapters, under the title: Ἕνδεκα κεφάλαια, ἐν οἷς δείκνυται τὸ ἀπεοικὸς τοῦ παραδείγματος τοῦ τινὸς ἀνθρώπου τῇ κατὰ Χριστὸν ἑνώσει: “Eleven chapters in which it is shown how the example of any man differs from the union according to Christ,” that is, from Christ incarnate.], so from divinity and humanity there is one Christ. This is said by them not for the unity of nature but rather for the unity of person, since Theodore himself, whom they accuse of being a Nestorian, and whom they cannot deny proclaimed Christ in two natures, uses this analogy, which they think suits their own madness.

The wise can therefore see how truth confronts its fugitives from every direction, so that wherever they turn aside, they find it standing face-to-face against them. For how could it fail to confront those whom it refutes even through their own accusations? They reject the doctrine taught through the Council of Chalcedon, namely, that the one God Christ has two natures; or else they accuse Theodore himself, whose praises were recited there, of the Nestorian heresy, thinking that Christ’s nature must be confessed as one. They strive to establish this on the grounds that the holy Fathers said: just as one man is made from soul and flesh, so one Christ exists in divinity and humanity.

Suspecting, therefore, that the Fathers said this for the assertion of one nature, rather than—as the truth requires—for the assertion of one person, they do not deny that it is wholly contrary to the Nestorian error, and thus, as we have said, they are refuted by their own authorities. For the holy Fathers referred that analogy of the union of soul and flesh not to prove that Christ has one nature to such an extent that Theodore also used it—a man whom they say believed not only what is true and manifest, namely, that Christ has two natures, but also what is false, namely, that Christ has two persons. Thus he used the analogy by which they think the holy Fathers taught not only one person but also one nature of Christ.

But just as it is said of the soul and flesh of one man [Note: Codex Veronensis: ‘says’]—which we had promised to demonstrate—that the division of the natures remains, and that the soul is one thing while the flesh is another, specifically by nature, not by person, since the one is rational and the other irrational, yet one man is both; so also, wherever—especially before the error of Nestorius was disseminated—we find certain doctors of the Catholic Church calling one the “assumer” and another the “assumed,” we must understand this as referring to nature, not to another person or subsistence [Note: The same codex: ‘another’]. This is like the case in which, in one man, one is called the inner man and another the outer man. We must do this if we neither wish to err ourselves, nor to slander them, nor to disparage the Church of Christ, in whose peace and honor they died, nor to lend authority to the Nestorian error by allowing Nestorius to be said to have proclaimed things similar to those who earned the highest praise by the Church’s judgment.

The truth, which permits the faithful no such belief, utterly refutes the slanders of his accusers by means of their other statements, in which they plainly spoke about the unity of Christ’s person. For Theodore alone did not speak in this way, as the ignorant suppose or his adversaries pretend; many other Fathers did so as well. As we promised, we shall now produce their examples, in which we wish to test the freedom of the Eutychians and their followers, and the zeal for the faith that they display against Theodore and the Council of Chalcedon: if they dare to pronounce even those who speak in the same way heretics, to say no more.

They spoke in this way in the Church of Christ as people secure and unconcerned, as though no question concerning Nestorius were troubling them—not in order to divide the unity of Christ’s person, which Theodore too professes to be inseparable and incapable of being divided in any manner.

It is especially welcome that he himself, by repelling one, reciprocally repels the other also of the empty and mutually destructive slanders of those who say that he believed Christ to be one person of the Trinity and proclaimed a quaternity by asserting two sons. For from the statements we have cited he teaches that, just as the Father and the Son are indeed of one nature but are not one person, so in man soul and body, or in Christ God and man, are indeed one person but are not of one essence. For neither is the form of God the form of a servant, nor is the form of a servant the form of God, although the unity of person remains inseparable and incapable of being divided in any manner.

## CHAPTER V. That the obscure and ambiguous statements of the Fathers ought to be interpreted from their clear statements, as he demonstrates by several examples.

From these therefore certain and evident statements of Theodore, we must understand the others which in his writings seem to some doubtful or obscure, if we do not wish to be counted among those of whom blessed Cyril said that they were hostile toward that same remarkable man, Theodore, deserving of the highest praise, making an opportunity for the contrary doctrine to which they were committed, so that they might seek to have certain of his chapters condemned as not understood in their better sense. This is a voice worthy of Cyril; it was fitting that an upright teacher of the Church should speak thus. For just as it belongs to heretical slanderers to interpret what is certain and manifest from what is doubtful and obscure in a distorted way, so it is customary to Catholic prudence and piety, from what is indubitable and evident, both to establish what is ambiguous and to clarify what is hidden.

Therefore we act better if we interpret more favorably the writings of very learned men who died in the peace of the Church, even if they were unable to avoid completely the slanders of future heresies. But if some orthodox people should think that something else ought to be done, they are not to be imitated in this by prudent men. If they weigh the considerations on both sides, they will easily recognize whose purpose they ought rather to approve: that of those who accuse, or that of those who excuse men who died in the peace of the Church and in the praise of the Fathers.

First, then, they ought to consider what is common to us both—since in relation to orthodox accusers we are similarly situated—and what belongs properly to each side, in which we differ from one another. Faith in God is therefore common to us. What is proper to each side, and in which we differ, is this: they cruelly and boldly condemn those who died in the unity and glory of the Church, whom God alone is [Col. 0759A] to judge; but we, considering that we are human beings, and that such conduct accords neither with piety nor with modesty, presume to usurp nothing that belongs to God.

They reject what is profound and disdain the opinions of the holy Fathers, by whom those men were approved and praised. We, agreeing with what is humble, receive those opinions obediently and with due reverence. They imprudently grant authority to the errors of heretics, asserting that the heretics taught things resembling the preaching of honored men. We, however, granting heretics no opportunity, answer cautiously that the Church of Christ never accepted such blasphemies, but rejected every innovation as soon as it arose.

Finally, they accuse and disgrace the very Church that gave us birth, as though she had at some time been corrupted by adulterous doctrines. We, however, deny that the virginity of our mother ever departed from the charity that is in Christ, asserting that those whom she honored were not heretics.

For these reasons, if we wish both to be subject to God and obedient to the holy Fathers; if, in the present matter, we wish also to silence the mouths of the Nestorians and to defend the Church that gave us birth from the accusations of the impious, then we should not only refrain from condemning those who died in the communion and praise of the Church, but should not say that they taught such things before Nestorius. Rather, we should interpret what seems obscure in their writings from their other statements, which are evidently contrary to the Nestorian error. Otherwise we may rightly and deservedly be reproached for being inferior to the Nestorians both in caution and in zeal, and for appearing less active than they in striving against the truth—or than we are in striving for the truth.

For if they wish to attach the most illustrious teachers of the Church to their own party, and attempt to obscure their statements, which are manifestly contrary to Nestorian doctrine, by means of other, less clear statements, twisting them to their own position, then we should much more rightly interpret what seems doubtful in their writings from what is certain, since by this means Nestorius is shown to have been justly condemned as the inventor of a new doctrine.

It is therefore established that certain ancient teachers of the Church said that God the Word handed over the assumed human being to death.

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “Let us therefore establish that certain …”]

[Note: It is sufficiently established, from the Fifth Synod and from Leontius of Byzantium, that what follows were statements of Theodore. Facundus, however, judged it more prudent to defend them as the words of several others who had spoken in the same way, rather than under Theodore’s single name.]

Now, if the Nestorians, misunderstanding this, should say that they intended to signify two persons—as though one were the person of God the Word who handed him over, and another the person of the man whom he is said to have handed over—ought we too to reinforce their accusations against the Church and testify that she once had teachers who did not preach one person of God and man, when we have many similar examples?

Hence there is the Apostle’s statement: “I bruise my body and bring it into bondage” (1 Cor. 9:27). He did not intend one person to be understood as the one who bruises his body and brings it into bondage, and another as the body itself. There is also the further statement of Tobit: “I and my soul give joy to the King of heaven” (Tob. 13:9). Anyone who pays attention will find many similar examples, not only in the divine Scriptures but also elsewhere and in our own daily speech.

If this can be said of a human being, of whom one nature—namely, the human nature—can properly be spoken, without any question compelling the contrary, by the Apostle and by Tobit, how much more could it properly be said of Christ, whom we believe to exist in two natures, in opposition to the Apollinarians, that God the Word handed over the assumed man to death for us? We say that the Father handed him over, and we believe that the works of the Trinity are inseparable.

Thus, when the prophet says, “My heart has forsaken me” (Ps. 39:13), without dividing himself into two persons or subsistences, why, if one of the Fathers is found to have said that God the Word was in Christ or was present with Christ, should he be thought to have introduced two persons of Christ? For if a man’s heart is said to forsake him, and no division of one person is understood to have taken place—although “to forsake” signifies a certain separation—why must two persons necessarily be thought to be signified when someone is said to be “in” or “present with” something, since the soul also is said to be in or present with its own flesh when it nourishes and sustains it and protects it from diseases and sufferings?

But let us also grant that the ancient teachers of the Church said that God the Word is principally and according to essence the only-begotten Son of God, while the assumed man, from the unity of his person, received the status that he should always be and be called the only-begotten Son, and should be understood together with him under the designation “one Son.”

[Note: *Πρωτοτύπως* (“principally,” “in the primary sense”). Theodore uses this word in Book XII *On the Incarnation*, when, in accordance with his own positions, he teaches that God the Word is truly the Son of God, while the assumed man “participates in” (*συνεπιδέχεσθαι*) the dignity of the Son through the union effected with the Word.]

Can we not understand this as spoken rather to distinguish the natures than to divide the person, just as we say that the inner man is principally called man, whose essence was made in the image of God; whereas the outer man, formed from clay, received from the unity of his person that he too should be called man and be understood together with him under the designation “one man,” although he himself was not made in the image and likeness of God, but seems more like the animals?

We also say, without dividing the one person, that the inner man, justified by the merit of his faith, passes into adoption as a son of God; while the outer man, through adherence to the inner, receives a dignity shared with him, as the Apostle also says: “Though our outer man is being corrupted, yet our inner man is being renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

If we say that not the inner man but the outer man is corrupted, or that not the outer man but the inner man is renewed day by day, do we thereby separate the human being from himself into two subsistences? Therefore, if similar expressions of the Fathers are found concerning Christ, we should refer them rather to the distinction of the two natures than to a division of the one person.

Furthermore, when the heretics called Synusiasts thought that Christ had been born of one essence,

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “that he was of one nature, and not …”]

and that he had not received flesh from the Virgin’s womb, but rather that God the Word had converted a part of his own substance—that is, of his divinity—into flesh within her womb, believing that he was incarnate in her but not from her, they said that he was consubstantial with the Father not only in divinity but also in the flesh. But all the Catholic teachers, on the contrary, asserted that Christ had been born from the substance of the Virgin.

The Apollinarians, again, defaming this teaching of truth, proclaimed that the Church taught that Christ was born from the Virgin as though he had also received his beginning from her according to his divinity—asserting that God the Word had been born from her womb, without beginning from the Father before the ages, as though he were saying that one who had not previously existed had come into being.

If, then, in order to remove this accusation, some ancient teachers of the Church, before the question of Nestorius had troubled the other side, said against them, “God the Word was not born from a woman”—as though they were saying: “The Church does not teach, as you slanderously claim, that the divine nature of God the Word came forth from the Virgin’s womb, but rather the human nature, which took its beginning from the seed of David”—ought we therefore not to investigate and demonstrate the reasons why they spoke in this way, but, by condemning them as authors of the Nestorian error, accuse the Church of Christ, in whose honor they died?

Or if, in opposition to the intention of those same Apollinarians, who were wrongly interpreting the words of the evangelist John, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and saying that the Word had become flesh by conversion, some answered by saying, “God the Word did not become flesh,” that is, did not become flesh by conversion, but assumed flesh while remaining what he was, are they to be judged contrary to the Gospel?

[Note: Leontius, Book III, quotes Theodore’s words from Book IV *Against Apollinaris*: “Who endowed with understanding could say, as you say, that the Word became man? For we emphatically affirm that he assumed a man, but we can never say that he became man.” From this it is clear that he denied not merely that the Word became flesh *by conversion* (*κατὰ τροπήν*), as Facundus wishes to suggest, but denied it absolutely, since he recognized no union of the Word other than one of disposition and good will (*τῆς διαθέσεως καὶ εὐδοκίας*).]

If that is so, the Apollinarians will appear to agree with the evangelical preaching. But if the Apollinarians, because of the intention of their mind, are judged enemies of the evangelical preaching, although they said, “The Word became flesh,” then those who, while remaining in the Church, contradicted such men should likewise be judged, according to the intention of their mind, to agree with the evangelical preaching.

For this reason Theodore also says against the same Apollinarians in Book IX *On the Incarnation*:

> “If indeed the statement ‘The Word became flesh’ was spoken according to some conversion, how should it be understood that he dwelt among us? For it is clear to everyone that what dwells is other than that in which it dwells.”

But the same interpreter of his own word, anticipating every slander, closes the matter for you:

> “For he dwelt in us, taking our nature and dwelling in it, and accomplishing in it all that pertains to our salvation. How, then, did the indwelling God the Word become flesh? Clearly, he was not converted or transformed; for otherwise he would not be said to dwell.”

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “How, then, did the one who dwelt among us become God the Word?”]

It is therefore clear from these words of Theodore that the ancient teachers of the Church did not deny, contrary to the Gospel, that God the Word became flesh. For how could they openly resist the Gospel and remain honored in the Church? But, as he teaches here, they denied that the Word became flesh by conversion, against the madness of the Apollinarians.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “They denied the flesh by conversion and transformation.”]

Likewise, when the Lord says in the Gospel, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), because the Arians abuse this testimony, we too, without resisting the Gospel in the intention with which they use it, deny that the Father is greater than the Son. If anyone here too attends to the sound of the words and not to the intention of the mind, he will think that the Arians, rather than we, agree with the meaning of the Gospel.

How the Apollinarians could say, “The Word became flesh,” and how the Catholics would answer, if they are indeed shown to have answered in this way, “The Word did not become flesh,” the Church will make clear—the Church that expelled the former and honored the latter.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “these,” namely, the Catholics.]

It follows, then, that if anyone refuses to expel these men from the Church, he admits the Eutychians, their most foolish offspring, together with their error.

[Note: Among other charges, Justinian alleges against Theodore in his edict that he said Christ attained adoption as sons (*υἱοθεσίας ἀξιωθῆναι*) through baptism. Leontius, from his Book III *On the Incarnation*: “And the glory which you gave me, I have given them.” What glory? Namely, participation in adoption. For he himself received this according to his humanity when baptized in the Jordan. This heresy, renewed several centuries later by Elipandus, a bishop, was condemned and copiously refuted by the Synod of Frankfurt, which decreed that Christ must be called the true and proper Son of God, not an adoptive son.]

Likewise, if the ancient teachers of the Church are shown to have said that Christ received the adoption of sons, neither they nor the whole Church that had such teachers ought to be judged heretical. For Christ deigned to receive the sacrament of adoption both when he was circumcised and when he was baptized; and the sacrament of adoption may be called “adoption,” just as we call the sacrament of his body and blood, which is present in consecrated bread and the cup, his body and blood—not because the bread is literally his body or the cup literally his blood,

[Note: Consecrated bread, having undergone a change in nature, is no longer bread; nevertheless it is called bread because it was bread and retains the appearance of bread. The same judgment applies to wine. Again, we call bread and wine the body and blood of Christ, as Augustine also affirms in Book III, chapter 4, of *On the Trinity*, not literally but figuratively, because the body and blood of Christ are contained sacramentally under the appearance of bread and wine. In my opinion, Facundus has no other meaning in these words. For he could not have doubted the reality of Christ’s flesh and blood in the Eucharist, since, after the Lord’s own profession, as Hilary teaches in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, no room for doubt has been left. Irenaeus, Book V, *Against Heresies*: “He acknowledged the cup that comes from creation as his own blood, and he firmly declared the bread that comes from creation to be his own body.” If he perhaps seems here to have expressed something rather harsh or obscure, he deserves pardon, and should receive from a kindly interpreter the same service that he himself repeatedly and diligently rendered to others whose statements were being criticized.]

but because they contain within them the mystery of his body and blood. Hence the Lord himself called the blessed bread and cup that he handed to his disciples his body and blood.

Accordingly, just as Christ’s faithful, when they receive the sacrament of his body and blood, are rightly said to receive the body and blood of Christ, so Christ himself, when he had received the sacrament of adoption as sons, could rightly be said to have received the adoption of sons.

Otherwise it should not be said of us either that we have received the adoption of sons, or that we have been redeemed and saved, since the Apostle says:

> “We ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we await the adoption of sons, the redemption of our body. For in hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:23–24).

Therefore, although according to the Apostle we still await adoption, redemption, and salvation, nevertheless, because we already receive the sacrament of adoption, redemption, and salvation, we are rightly called sons of God, redeemed, and saved. In the same way Christ, receiving the sacrament of adoption—not for his own benefit but for the confirmation of the sacrament itself—in circumcision and baptism, could rightly be said by the ancient teachers of the Church to have received the adoption of sons, just as the Apostle says:

> “For I say that Christ became a minister of circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers” (Rom. 15:8).

If they are also found to have said that after his passion—whether when he rose again or even when he ascended into heaven—the Lord was glorified or received power, this should be understood in the same way as it was said by the Apostle Peter:

> “The prophets searched and carefully investigated, who prophesied of the grace of God destined for you, searching into what person or what time the Spirit of Christ within them was indicating, when he testified beforehand to the sufferings destined for Christ and the glories that would follow” (1 Pet. 1:10).

And it should be understood as the Lord himself said after the resurrection:

> “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26)

And again:

> “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

Likewise, concerning the glorification that was to take place after his ascension, he says:

> “When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come.”

[Note: The Verona manuscript adds: “He will announce them to you. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.”]

It was also said of him:

> “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

We therefore act better if we believe that the interpreters of the divine Scripture spoke against heretics in the same manner as the divine Scripture itself.

Either something was added to the nature of Christ’s flesh when he rose, since that flesh, sown in dishonor, had already risen in glory; or the same glory and power became more widely known to the faithful after the resurrection. Thus he is said to have been glorified and to have received power when these things came to be known among believers, just as we say in prayer, “Hallowed be your name” (Luke 11:2), meaning that it may be made holy in the knowledge of the faithful.

Or, if any power and glory was bestowed upon the Church after his resurrection, he is said to have received it as the head in the members, that is, in faithful human beings. Hence the prophet says:

> “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; you received gifts among human beings” (Ps. 47:19).

By these and many other means, a pious and experienced reader can both understand the statements of the earlier Fathers and defend them against the slanders of heretics. But the unskilled and arrogant person, who hastens not to learn whatever he does not understand but to condemn it, must be thrown into confusion by such matters; and, if he can, he will throw others into confusion as well, refusing through arrogance to accept the explanation which, because of his ignorance, he was unable to discover for himself.

But who could endure the claim of some who say that they believe with us that Christ has two natures and do not deny that he is both God and man, yet, when they hear that he is the Son of God by grace, detest this expression as though it were said of one who is God alone and not also man?

Just as he is by nature the son of man because of his true humanity, and by condescension the Son of man because of his true divinity, so he is by nature the Son of God because of his true divinity, and by grace the Son of God because of his true humanity.

But if he is also called the Son of God by nature according to his humanity, one falls into the error of Apollinaris, who believed that God the Word had made flesh for himself from a part of his substance,

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “from a part of his divine substance.”]

which is wholly present everywhere and cannot be divided.

If they truthfully say that he has two natures, and both cannot be divine, since one nature is human, then plainly he is not the Son of God by nature according to his humanity in the same way that he is the Son of God by nature according to his divinity.

But if according to his humanity he is not the Son of God by nature, it necessarily follows that he is the Son of God either by merits or by grace—he who, from the moment he began to exist, was nothing other than the Son of God.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “either by merits or by grace he is the Son of God. But no merits preceded for which he should become the Son of God according to his humanity, since from the moment he began to exist …”]

It remains, therefore, that according to his humanity he is the Son of God by grace.

For this reason blessed Augustine, an eminent preacher of the Catholic faith, writing to Prosper and Hilary on the predestination of the saints, and teaching that God’s grace is not given according to our merits, says among other things in Book I, chapter 15:

> “The Savior himself, the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is also the most splendid light of predestination and grace. What preceding merits of his own—whether of works or of faith—did the human nature in him acquire in order to become this? Let an answer be given, I ask. By what merit did that man, assumed by the Word coeternal with the Father into the unity of person, become the only-begotten Son of God? What good, however small, preceded this? What did he do? What did he believe? What did he ask, in order to attain this ineffable excellence? Did not that man, through the Word acting and assuming him, begin to be the one Son of God from the moment he began to exist? Did not that woman, full of grace, conceive the one Son of God? Was not the one Son of God born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, not by the desire of the flesh but solely by the gift of God? Was there any fear that, as he advanced in age, that man might sin by free choice? Or was his will not free, and indeed all the freer because he could not serve sin? Certainly, all these things, singularly admirable—and whatever else may most truly be said as proper to him—were received by the human nature, that is, our nature, in him in a singular manner, without any preceding merits of its own.

> “Let this man answer God, if he dares, and say, ‘Why not I also?’ And if he hears, ‘O man, who are you to answer God?’ (Rom. 9:20), let him not even then restrain himself, but increase his recklessness and say, ‘How do I hear, “Who are you, O man?” when I am what I hear—that is, a human being—and so is he of whom I speak? Why should I not be what he is?’

> “But he is such and so great by grace. Why is grace different where nature is common? Certainly there is no partiality with God. Who—not a Christian, but even a madman—would say such things?

> “Let the very source of grace therefore appear to us in our head, from which, according to the measure of each, it is diffused through all his members. By that grace any human being is made a Christian from the beginning of his faith, by which grace that man, from the beginning of his existence, was made Christ, God. This man is reborn of the same Spirit of whom that man was born; by the same Spirit forgiveness of sins is effected in us by which it was effected that that man had no sin. God certainly foreknew that he would accomplish these things. This, therefore, is the predestination of the saints, which shone forth most fully in the Holy One of holies. Who can deny it, if he rightly understands the statements of truth?”

Let these men, then, if they can, dare to call this apostolic man a heretic and, with their customary presumption, condemn him—a man who teaches that Christ, according to his humanity, without any preceding merits, began to be the only-begotten Son of God by grace from the moment he began to exist; through which grace also all these singularly admirable things were singularly received by the human nature, that is, our nature, in him; and who asserts that, through the difference of this grace, he became so great and such a one, and not like us, although our nature is common to us.

He also asserts that by that grace any human being is made a Christian from the beginning of his faith, by which grace that man, from the beginning of his existence, was made Christ, God.

Let them dare, if they can, to call him a heretic; let them dare, in their customary presumption, to condemn him. Then they will truly learn what are the piety and steadfastness of the Church of the Latins, which God established and strengthened through his teaching, when they have immediately been anathematized by all and cut off like rotten and diseased members.

If, then, they wish to reopen the tombs of those who rest in peace and gnaw the bones of the dead, let them test their teeth on this adamantine man, and they will discover that their teeth will be broken in their mouths, so that under this appearance of piety they will bite no one thereafter.

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 0765]

## CHAPTER ONE

That the synod ought not to be criticized because it did not condemn Theodore, even though there are certain things in his writings that deserve blame, since it may have been possible that they were hidden from the synod, or that they should be interpreted more favorably, or that they were believed to have been inserted by his enemies.

If I may be believed, Emperor, I greatly regret the lot of my present undertaking, from which I expect not so much fruit as I have taken upon myself labor. For what more am I trying to persuade mortals by so many documents and arguments than that they should not presume to be judges of the dead? This requires no persuasion at all; nor would I wish to spend time on a matter whose loss no one can recover. But when I saw certain men secretly attacking the Church under the false name of defenders and, supposedly in her vindication, condemning as heretics those whom she had always honored, I did not think I ought to remain silent, lest I fall into what Isaiah says [Note: Perhaps, “lest I fall into that.”]:

> “See, all have been blinded; all have failed to understand; dumb dogs, unable to bark, dreaming in bed, loving sleep. And the dogs are utterly shameless [Note: The Verona manuscript has *improbi animo*, “shameless in spirit.” The Vulgate reads *impudentissimi*, “most shameless”; the Hebrew text and Greek version have ἀναιδεῖς τῇ ψυχῇ, “shameless in soul.”], knowing no satiety; and they are wicked, knowing no understanding. They have all pursued their own ways, each according to himself” (Isaiah 56:10–11).

“See how the just man perishes, and no one takes notice; and righteous men are taken away, and no one considers” (Isaiah 57:1). One might think this was spoken specifically about the present case.

Since, however, the circumstances of a question and of its answer are not identical, and what is briefly accused cannot immediately be briefly excused—just as defiling and wounding are not so difficult as the washing and healing that follow—it is necessary for us to act somewhat more energetically, especially since we know how difficult it is for the obstinate to reject what they have once rashly undertaken.

But I desire, most merciful Emperor, to seem excessive both to your modesty and to all men of the greatest seriousness into whose hands this may perhaps come, rather than to allow the obstinacy of those who resist to excuse the length of my discourse. For if we accomplish nothing with them even after so much effort, I shall be found provident rather than prolix.

Although, therefore, it was demonstrated above that some of Theodore’s statements, for which he is thought to have deserved condemnation by the Council of Chalcedon, were corrupted by the supporters of the Eutychians, while others resembled the teaching of the holy Fathers whom they themselves claim to venerate; and although it was also shown that the same Theodore was praised with great acclaim by those holy Fathers both while he was alive and after his death; and although, finally, it became plainly evident from clear proofs in his own writings that he was being attacked by the accusations of his adversaries through slander—nevertheless, since the attention of the religious reader expects not so much Theodore’s vindication, on which the standing of the Church does not depend, as the complete defense of the Council of Chalcedon, we must show how, even if certain things in Theodore’s books are judged blameworthy, the council is not to be criticized for not condemning him, when it heard his praises read from Ibas’s letter:

[Col. 0767B] so that the Eutychians may recognize how fruitlessly they spend days and nights in wicked counsels and accomplish nothing despite the great sums they expend on their associates and supporters.

Let us therefore suppose, as was said, that certain things in the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia appear reprehensible. First, how can it be proved that the Council of Chalcedon knew this? It could have remained unaware of it, just as it remained unknown even to Ibas’s accusers—although they were slanderous, obstinate, and practiced in malice. For when they repeatedly accused Ibas himself before the Council of Chalcedon in episcopal tribunals, they did not even attempt to bring against him anything concerning Theodore’s praise.

But it is one thing to say that the matter escaped the notice of the accusers and another to say that it escaped the notice of the council. Let it be different; let us concede that. But does it therefore follow that it must be established that the council was not unaware of it? Whatever they may say, however many words they may multiply, this too will undoubtedly be conceded: it is one thing to suspect, and another to demonstrate by certain reasoning that the matter did not escape the council’s notice.

For I think that, on the basis of their suspicion, they would not even say that the accusers of Ibas could have remained unaware of it, unless the outcome of events had defeated them. Therefore, even if that council were to be judged, it could not be judged on the basis of suspicion—especially the suspicion of enemies—but on the basis of certain proofs. For if suspicions are to pronounce the sentence of judgment, there is absolutely nothing that could not be judged one way or another. It was very wisely arranged, however, that we should call judges not conjecturers but investigators.

Yet these men want such a council, established for so many years by the peace of the universal Church [Note: The Verona manuscript has *auctoritate*, “authority.”], to be judged, while they bring forward nothing that we can know, but only this: they want us to suspect according to their own will. Therefore, if they want me also to criticize this council along with them, let them seek out and produce something capable of destroying it—something as certain to me as my own existence is certain to me.

Let us nevertheless see what follows from their suspicion; and if it is agreeable even to the Eutychians themselves, let them accuse us because we do not suspect along with them. For if it is believed that certain writings bearing Theodore’s name, which are called Nestorian, could not have escaped the notice of the Council of Chalcedon, how can it be believed that they escaped the notice of the Church, in whose peace and honor Theodore himself died?

And if the Council of Chalcedon is judged to have shared the opinions of Nestorius because it did not condemn the dead Theodore, whom it had been unable to question or correct beforehand, how will it be established that the Church of the earlier period did not share the same opinions as Nestorius—the Church that honored him, while he lived, among the most distinguished bishops?

But when it is said that the Church of Christ previously held the same opinions as Nestorius, the Nestorian heresy is undoubtedly excused—if indeed it is now to be called a heresy—since anyone who thinks otherwise is himself found to be asserting a new doctrine against the teaching of antiquity. This is the entire result that the Eutychians have been able to obtain at great expense through their agents.

But O pitiable good fortune of the Nestorians, for whom the Eutychians’ pay provides military service!

Moreover, since the Eutychians cannot accuse the Catholic Church, before the Councils of Chalcedon and Ephesus, of Nestorius’s doctrine—for Theodore the bishop died in her communion—they will not be able to accuse the holy Council of Chalcedon except imprudently. The council ought not to have acted against the judgment of that very Church, even if Ibas’s accusers had raised certain questions about Theodore’s praise.

Therefore, if they say that the Church of the earlier period is not to be blamed because it condemned neither Theodore nor the writings in his books that ought to be censured, since it did not know them, let them believe that the Council of Chalcedon too could have been unaware of them. But if they say that the Church in whose communion Theodore died understood those same writings—which they have now caused the Nestorians to misuse—according to a different and better sense, let them also believe that the Council of Chalcedon understood them in the same better sense.

Let these things suffice for the vindication of the great council. In Theodore’s case it can be defended no less than the earlier Church, which the Eutychians cannot accuse of Nestorian doctrine before Nestorius.

But since we are not content merely to overthrow the utterly foolish pride of the Eutychians—a pride that, though often cast down, still rises against the judgment of so many priests of Christ—but also wish to trample and crush it, what more can we bring forward after this complete defense, abundantly and beyond measure?

For it is more credible to assert that Theodore’s doctrine, while contained in writing, could have escaped the Council of Chalcedon than that it escaped the Church of the earlier period, in which, as is shown, he always also disputed publicly in his own voice.

For blessed John of Antioch and the Eastern Council say that, in the expositions he gave in all the churches of the East—expositions in which he is shown to have been highly esteemed in the imperial city—he was found to be orthodox in the presence of priests, emperors, and peoples.

It also seems easier and more natural that the Council of Chalcedon, following the prior judgment of the Church by which he had always been regarded as most learned, should have thought well of him than that the Church of the earlier period, without any preceding judgment, should spontaneously have accepted his statements by interpreting them in a better sense.

Finally, the council would have condemned him rashly, excessively, and impiously, without any example leading it to do so, even though he had died in the communion of the Church without complaint. The Church, however, acted prudently and religiously, with many precedents before it, in bringing a living man to examination when it could still correct him, if this seemed necessary.

It is certain, therefore, that the mad Eutychians or Acephali, since they do not know what they are saying, by the slanders with which they attack the Council of Chalcedon are rather bringing an accusation against the faith of the Church that existed before Nestorius—the Church in whose communion they falsely claim to have remained. Hence we too defend the Council of Chalcedon against their slanders, not without the Church of antiquity.

And therefore, even if it is conceded that the Church of that earlier period, or later the Council of Chalcedon, knew the things judged reprehensible in Theodore’s books and could not interpret them in a better way [Note: The Verona manuscript has *amplius*, “more fully” or “further.”], why are they still accused because they did not condemn Theodore, when they could have believed that these things had been inserted into his books by heretics, just as Theodore himself complained?

For at the beginning of one of his works, to which he gave the title *Against Apollinarius and His Heresy*, he says:

> “About thirty years ago we composed a book on the incarnation of the Lord, extending to fifteen thousand lines. Throughout that work we examined Arius’s and Eunomius’s errors concerning this matter, as well as Apollinarius’s vain presumption, so that, in my opinion, I might omit nothing that belonged either to the firm establishment of ecclesiastical orthodoxy or to the refutation of their impiety.
>
> “But those who presume upon everything with the greatest ease, and who had moreover been trained by Apollinarius, the founder of this heresy, made our work known to all who shared their views, if they could in any way find something capable of refuting what was written in it. Since no one dared to undertake the contest against us in writing, they imitated weak and cunning athletes who, when they cannot fight against stronger opponents, try to overthrow them by whatever ambushes and contrivances they can.
>
> “For they undoubtedly wrote among themselves certain foolish things which we had never said. Finally, they inserted these very things into one part of our writings and showed them to their associates, and sometimes even to our own people, who in their simplicity listened to everything with open minds; and they presented this, as they thought, as evidence of our impiety.
>
> “One of these writings said that there were two sons. [Note: This point of objection was discussed at the beginning of Book IX. Theodore shrank from seeming to say that there were two sons, although in fact he imprudently posited two: one natural, the Word of God; the other adoptive, born of Mary, who, as he taught, having been joined to the Word κατ᾽ εὐδοκίαν (“according to good pleasure”) and sharing in divinity, became a participant in the appellation and honor of Son. Thus, in the Exposition of the Creed, recited in the sixth session of the Council of Ephesus, he says: Καὶ οὔτε δύο φαμὲν υἱοὺς, οὔτε δύο κυρίους· ἐπειδὴ εἷς υἱὸς κατ᾽ οὐσίαν ὁ Θεὸς λόγος, ὁ μονογενὴς υἱὸς τοῦ πατρός, ᾧ περ οὗτος συνημμένος τε καὶ μετέχων θεότητος, κοινωνεῖ τοῦ υἱοῦ προσηγορίας καὶ τιμῆς: “And we say neither two sons nor two lords; for the Word of God, the only-begotten Son of the Father, is one Son by essence, and this one, joined to him and partaking of divinity, shares the name and honor of Son.” A little later, Ἀναιρεῖ πᾶσαν ἔννοιαν δυάδος υἱῶν τε καὶ κυρίων: “he removes every conception of a duality of sons and lords.”] Thus they represented us in this work as saying and maintaining very strongly that one ought to believe and say that there are two sons, although in that writing we plainly said everywhere that one ought not to speak of two sons.
>
> “It was therefore necessary that those writings should appear to their hearers not only foolish but also weak, since this could be shown neither by sound reasoning nor by anything suitable to the case. They had been written in a deliberately weak form for this very reason, so that the author could more easily be convicted by them [Note: The same manuscript reads *infirmius*, “more weakly.”].
>
> “One of our people, because of his excessive simplicity, believed that these writings were ours. For this reason he was considered trustworthy by those men to read the writings, and he reported to us what had been written.
>
> “When we had heard this, we indeed rebuked him for believing statements against us concerning matters which he had often heard us speak of both in church and privately, when he ought to have judged our spoken word more trustworthy than the writings, as evidence of the position which we are determined to preserve in our doctrines.”

You have learned, most merciful Emperor, with what envy and deceit the founders of the Eutychians, the Synusiasts, had always plotted against Theodore’s statements, and how they tried to turn the minds of the simplest Catholics away from his teaching—not only by wrongly interpreting what he taught in a correct sense against their folly, but also by corrupting his books through inserted falsehood.

Yet Theodore confidently charged them either with malice or with the simplicity of Catholics, since he openly proclaimed in the Church of Christ what conformed to sound doctrine, and since his spoken word was more trustworthy than his writings as evidence of his position. The writings of an absent man, which could be corrupted by enemies of the Church, ought not to have been preferred to the testimony of his voice.

What, then, if either the Church of that period or later the Council of Chalcedon, recognizing the things for which Theodore is blamed as though he were a teacher of Nestorius, and unable to interpret them in a better sense, believed that they had been inserted into his books by heretics in order not to condemn him? Should this pious belief be counted as a crime of heresy, when Theodore himself complains of this and many other clear writings of his demonstrate how far he was from Nestorius’s error?

But if some say that Theodore should not be believed because he falsely claimed that the Apollinarians had inserted certain heretical statements into his books—for, they say, he wrongly seized upon what he wished to attribute to them—I will not obstinately contend against them; I will still grant them permission to suspect what they wish.

Meanwhile, this is plainly true and cannot be denied: Theodore testified that those things were not his own. Let him therefore be accused, if it is shown that he lied, of having humbly been ashamed to confess certain errors of his past after he had come to his senses, although he wisely submitted to the truth. Yet even if he lied, he would not justly be called a heretic if in whatever manner he renounced his errors.

The same Theodore, writing to Cerdon concerning his exposition of the Psalms, as we recalled in the third book, says:

> “We did not exercise as much care concerning this matter as we ought to have done. For we suffered whatever happens to beginners, who, as it turned out, were inexperienced in writing. Indeed, many alterations were made at that time in what was received as ours, though it is not for the present occasion to recount them. For this reason many things were composed by us with greater negligence, especially those that come first.”

If, therefore, either the earlier Church or the later Council of Chalcedon believed that among the many things which Theodore confessed he had composed negligently through inexperience were passages in his books that could not be interpreted in a better sense, it must be said that the council restrained error by not judging him a heretic for matters in which he had voluntarily accused himself of ignorance and negligence, while believing him worthy of praise for the rest, which was free from blame.

## CHAPTER II  
### That although Theodore may at some time have erred, he could not be condemned as a heretic because he was not obstinate, since he voluntarily corrected certain things that had been censured

There is another point, certainly much stronger, that greatly assists us in defending the cause we have undertaken.

For when the holy John of Antioch censured Nestorius in his letter [Note: John’s complete letter to Nestorius survives in the first part of the Council of Ephesus; but where it mentions Theodore, the name Paul had intruded in place of Theodore. Facundus’s words therefore restore the passage as follows: Μέμνησαί που πάντως τοῦ μακαρίου Θεοδώρου ἐπισκόπου, ἐν ἐξηγήσει εἰπόντος τι τῶν οὐ δοξάντων καλῶς εἰρῆσθαι πρώτῳ τέ σοι, τῷ καὶ παῤῥησιασαμένῳ κατ᾽ ἐκεῖνον τὸν καιρόν, ἔπειτα καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἀκούσασι: “You surely remember the blessed bishop Theodore, saying in an exposition something not thought to have been rightly said, first to you, who also spoke freely at that time, and then to all who heard.” Before becoming bishops, Theodore and Nestorius had both been presbyters of the Church of Antioch. At this time Nestorius, still a presbyter and himself distinguished in teaching—as Gennadius testifies in chapter 53—and an extemporaneous declaimer, heard Theodore of Mopsuestia, already a bishop, preaching at Antioch.] because he denied that blessed Mary was the Mother of the Lord, and urged him to confess this, he says after a few words:

> “If it seems appropriate, I shall also remind you at a suitable time of an example of good conduct, which I wish you, most holy brother, to remember. For it is not long since something happened among us that might perhaps be consigned to oblivion.
>
> “You certainly remember blessed Theodore the bishop saying, in an exposition, something that was not thought rightly spoken—first to you yourself, who at that time had confidence in him, and then also before all who were listening.
>
> “And how, perceiving the injury and disturbance caused by the very considerable circulation of that statement, and understanding that disturbance produces discord, and even contradiction and contention among people who love to seek occasions for division from every possible matter and to enlarge the spark of scandal that had seemed small—as has now happened among you—how that very strong man rose up, and after not many days corrected for the benefit of the Church, without embarrassment, what he had said; and, by correcting it, immediately crushed the murmuring or accusation that had been made against him, never judging it shameful to correct himself.
>
> “All knew that it had been said by him negligently and less cautiously; nevertheless, those who had taken it up immediately accepted the correction.”

This entire passage confounds the arrogance of those who boast that they are more diligent and wiser than the most ancient Fathers. They say that the Church of that period negligently and foolishly listened to Theodore’s disputations, and therefore did not censure him for the matters for which they themselves censure him.

Far be it from the piety of the Council of Chalcedon to say or believe this! Far be it, I repeat, from it to believe that the Church of Christ could have failed either to understand or to disregard blasphemies spoken by Theodore against Christ, if he was, as they say, the author of Nestorian error. For what was not blasphemous or heretical, but merely was not thought rightly spoken, caused no small disturbance, as John of Antioch testifies; nor was that disturbance quieted until that very strong man rose up after not many days and corrected, for the benefit of the Church and without embarrassment, what he had said.

And truly, great courage was required for him to interpret himself, trample upon the glory acquired through long years of teaching, and descend without embarrassment to correct his statement—especially since, relying on his conscience, he could easily have disregarded the offense of his hearers, because he had not said it in the way they thought. Yet he did not allow that injury to persist for long. Quickly overcoming his shame, he hastened, after not many days, to remove the offense caused by a single statement.

John does not say that Theodore had understood something perversely, or even that he had spoken negligently and less cautiously [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “not less cautiously observed, but rather negligently and less cautiously spoken by him.”]. He speaks as of a man who was not perverse in his understanding of the matter, but whose language in this instance was insufficiently appropriate.

How, then, could a religious council fail to believe this testimony of the holy John when he rebuked Nestorius? Not only because John himself was so eminent, but also because, when writing to Nestorius and inviting him to correction by the example of Theodore, that very strong man who despised human glory, he could not have appealed so confidently to his own knowledge of a recent event—an event which not only Nestorius himself but the whole Church of Antioch could readily remember—unless he had relied upon the manifest truth of the matter.

For the bishop of Antioch could not publicly rebuke the bishop of Constantinople for asserting a new doctrine without the deliberation of the other priests belonging to his council. Since the holy council believed such testimony, how could it judge Theodore’s memory to be rejected from the Church as that of a heretic, when he had died in the peace of the Church and had loved that peace so greatly that he was not ashamed to subordinate the glory of his authority to the Church’s offense?

The same holy John explained why Theodore had incurred this offense, saying that he had said something that was not thought rightly spoken, thus placing the cause of the offense chiefly in the hearers’ estimation—a conclusion demonstrated by his immediate correction [Note: The Verona manuscript has “his easy and immediate correction.”].

From that correction, by which he better interpreted himself, either the Church that heard him disputing or the holy Council of Chalcedon afterward ought to have judged not only those statements that had offended the hearers at that time, but also other similar statements of Theodore.

But even if, contrary to the testimony of the holy John, it is said that Theodore offended his hearers not through an incautious and negligent expression but through a perverse understanding, even so he could not, once corrected, be judged a heretic either by the Church of that age or by the holy council.

The apostle James says:

> “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that they will incur a greater judgment” [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *sumitis*, “you will incur.”].
>
> “For we all offend in many things” (James 3:1).

Since, then, we all offend in many things, why are we not all heretics, unless it is not offense but the obstinate defense of an offense that makes a heretic?

I also confess that I take greater pleasure in Theodore, and much greater pleasure in this testimony of the holy John of Antioch, than in the other testimonies, whether John’s or those of the other Fathers. In those earlier testimonies, by which the greatness of his teaching is shown, I rejoice, certainly, but I recognize that this is something he shares with many. In this testimony, however, which reveals the manifest humility of his heart and his contempt for glory already acquired, for the sake of a brother’s offense, I find very few companions for him.

We have learned that many have excelled in knowledge and have won the greatest glory on account of it. But when they have fallen as human beings, they have refused to acknowledge themselves as human; and when simply admonished, they have scorned to believe the truth. Thus the very glory of their knowledge greatly harmed their salvation, for “knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1).

Theodore would therefore be less known to me, even though he has been praised by the testimonies of so many Fathers, if I did not learn from John’s testimony what he was like when he was being censured. Yet not everyone can imitate this, and therefore an example of his knowledge would be of little use. But to receive correction gladly and quickly and calmly to amend what has caused offense is found both imitable by everyone and far more useful.

Therefore, let the obstinate deign to learn from Theodore to preserve apostolic moderation and piety even when admonished about an easy slip of speech. For at one time Peter, the first of the apostles, as we have already said, when he was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, was rebuked by Paul, the least of the apostles (Galatians 2:14). He did not take this indignantly, nor did he despise the man who resisted him because of the glory of his primacy. For the love that confidently raised Paul to rebuke the former’s fault also taught Peter to incline himself obediently to receive correction from the least.

How, then, could the Church of that period, or the Council of Chalcedon, reject this man, who was proved not only in knowledge but also in humility of heart and moderation, when it heard his praises read from Ibas’s letter—especially since even his correction is an example of virtue, and since, having stumbled in speech, he displayed the form of Christian humility and an example of great piety?

Let the Eutychians now go and, if they can, add anything further to their slanders; let them invent whatever they please about Theodore; let them also accuse the Council of Chalcedon of restraining and consenting to evil. The light-minded and unstable in heart will undoubtedly recoil at these things. But the prudent and serious will understand that they add nothing against Theodore, whose vindication is sufficiently established by the fact that he was always ready to correct himself.

Whatever they may say against Theodore, therefore, let them know that, if their charges are accepted, they will be attributed not merely to Theodore and the Council of Chalcedon but to the whole Church, which neglected to censure a gentle and teachable man.

But I wish, most merciful Emperor, that those who blame Theodore might imitate to some extent his humility and reasonableness. Just as he gladly accepted correction and hastened to amend what he had said negligently and less cautiously, so may they also bear with us patiently and at last deign to correct what they have done cruelly and discordantly.

Moreover, Theodore was so far from being condemned by the holy council—as they think—as a teacher of Nestorius, that Nestorius was rebuked by Theodore’s example and condemned precisely because he did not imitate him.

What, then, do the Eutychians, who slander the Council of Chalcedon concerning Theodore, and the Nestorians, who are said to misuse the statements of that same Theodore, want us to conclude from this?

Nestorius, rebuked by Theodore’s example, did not immediately attempt to defend his wicked teachings from Theodore’s statements, as though Theodore held the same opinions, nor did he answer the holy John by saying:

> “Theodore, by whose example you rebuke me, whom you call blessed and very strong—he always taught the same things without offending anyone.”

If Nestorius had answered in this way, he could not thereby have prejudiced Theodore, any more than he could prejudice the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, since either he himself misused them or his followers now misuse them, as do all other heretics.

Nevertheless, since that man was ill-prepared to answer and sufficiently equipped for his own destruction, and since he attempted to draw nothing from Theodore’s statements in defense of his error, although he had been admonished by Theodore’s example, he showed clearly enough that he was not a follower of Theodore’s sound doctrine but its opponent.

## CHAPTER III  
### That although Theodore may have erred in certain matters, Ibas could have praised him for the other things he wrote correctly

[Col. 0774D]

These considerations, then, would amply suffice for the defense of the great Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: [Col. 0773D] The same manuscript reads *abundarent profecto*, “would certainly suffice,” even if it itself praised Theodore [Col. 0774D]. But now …]

But the council did not itself praise him; rather, it declared the letter of the one who praised him orthodox on account of the right faith that it contains. What prudent person, if he carefully considers the matter, could fail to recognize that these are different things? For it could have happened that, even if certain statements of Theodore appeared culpable, and the council neither ignored them nor was able to interpret them more favorably, it nevertheless believed that the most revered Ibas could have been unaware of them—

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The same manuscript reads: “nevertheless believed that the most revered Ibas …”]

—just as the Eutychians believe that the holy Fathers John of Constantinople and Gregory of Nazianzus, and the whole Church that observed Theodore teaching, could have been unaware of them, so that Theodore himself was not condemned while still alive.

Therefore, just as the holy council ought to have judged the ancient Church, of which the Fathers mentioned above had been members, not from its communion with or praise of Theodore—or even if it knew that he had erred in certain matters—but from the faith proper to that Church, as the Eutychians admit together with us, so it was right for it to judge that letter not from its praise of Theodore, but from the faith proper to its author, which is read there.

How, moreover, could the council have believed that the most revered Ibas could have been unaware of Theodore’s statements, said to have been written before Nestorius,

[Note: [Col. 0775D] The Verona manuscript calls them “Nestorian writings.”]

when it saw that Ibas’s own faith was opposed to Nestorian doctrine?

But let us grant even this to the Eutychians: let us grant that the Council of Chalcedon believed that the most revered Ibas was not ignorant of those statements of Theodore that appear blameworthy. Was it therefore not entitled to declare his letter orthodox on account of the right faith that it contains? Especially since the venerable Ibas could have praised Theodore and his teaching for this reason: he believed that whatever was judged reprehensible in Theodore’s books had either been inserted by heretics or had been censured by Theodore himself, as we have shown, or had been corrected. His teaching was not to be judged from the fact that, when he first began writing, he had at some point written something reprehensible or incurred an error of expression; it was rather to be judged by the fact that, if anything in it appeared culpable, he himself had censured and corrected it.

For if no wise person believes the Church to be heretical because it praises the teaching of blessed Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage, although he had determined—not merely in private, as he thought right, but also in a council assembled for that purpose—that every heretic returning to the Church should be baptized, and had consequently been criticized by Stephen, the Roman bishop, yet resisted him and defended his own opinion in a letter to Pompeius (Cyprian, Letter 14), employing as much human argument as he could and treating that same blessed Stephen abusively, although Stephen had rightly censured him—how could the letter of the venerable Ibas rightly be called heretical because it praised Theodore’s teaching? Theodore, although he had defined nothing contrary to the truth in a council, nevertheless voluntarily censured what he had composed badly in private; and when others reproved him for an error of expression, he hastened not to return an insult but to correct the offense.

Therefore, just as the Church, without approving the definition of blessed Cyprian and of his predecessor Agrippinus,

[Note: [Col. 0775D] Agrippinus was the first of all mortals, as Vincent of Lérins writes in *Commonitorium* 1, to judge that heretics ought to be rebaptized. He is called Cyprian’s predecessor, as by Augustine, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book II, chapter 7. How many predecessors before Agrippinus Cyprian succeeded is unclear. Cyprian himself states in Letter 73 to Jubaianus that he succeeded him after a long interval: “Many years and a long age have passed since, under Agrippinus of blessed memory, very many bishops assembled together and established this.”]

—who had previously made this determination concerning the baptism of all heretics—nevertheless counts not only them but also all the bishops who made that determination with them among the Fathers, and judges their faith and teaching, especially Cyprian’s, shining throughout the world, to be worthy of praise, so the venerable Ibas could praise Theodore’s teaching without approving anything culpable in it, even though he was not unaware that it contained certain culpable elements.

Whether, then, it was blessed Cyprian and Agrippinus, and the other bishops who made the same determination with them; or Theodore, even if he too is believed not to have corrected his errors; or the other teachers of the Church from whose opinions heretics attempt to construct their own errors—as we judge, they are all defended from the charge of heresy by the intention and purpose of their minds. For, while remaining in the Church’s communion before the Church had issued a definition on the matter, they either decreed or said such things out of excessive or immoderate zeal against heretics,

[Note: [Col. 0776D] The same manuscript reads: “and.”]

not after the Church had given its judgment on the question, when the heretics, having been separated from it, attacked the Church itself by asserting such things.

[Col. 0776B]

Perhaps someone will say: “Then the council ought at least to have condemned those statements of Theodore that caused offense, if it did not condemn Theodore himself because he had died in the peace of the Church, nor his entire teaching because he had spoken correctly in many matters.”

First, what council’s example could it have followed in doing this? Let some council be produced that condemned selected statements of a highly learned man who had persevered in the Church; then let them complain in this way, at least, about the Council of Chalcedon.

Next, when could all Theodore’s books have been examined, so that whatever might offend readers could be sought out with the greatest diligence and scrupulousness? For if this had to be done, that council ought to have reviewed all his writings, lest, if it censured him in part, it appear to have approved the rest. And what amount of time would have sufficed for this? Or when could such a number of bishops have reached agreement on each individual point, when the minds of hearers are affected in different ways, and what offends one person is received by another without offense because of a better understanding?

But if one does not submit to the judgment of the Eutychians, why should anyone say that at that council only Theodore’s statements, and not those of all the ancients who had completed their lives in the Church, ought to have been reviewed and debated? For if it censured certain writings of Theodore alone, it would appear to have approved everything written by everyone else, although the truth does not teach that everything is to be approved. And who knows even the names of all who have written about the Christian religion?

Since, then, the council could not examine everything written by everyone, it was not necessary for it to condemn Theodore’s statements, because the Apostle’s judgment is sufficient for us here: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thess. 5:21).

If this had not been the reason, what moderate and prudent judge would judge anything except the cases and questions brought before him? But when the accusers brought no charge against Bishop Ibas concerning his praise of Theodore, who had died in the communion of the Church, was it right for the holy council, convened for the faith and peace of the universal Church, to introduce a new question into a private dispute between litigants and spend time on it? It would have been as though it were not enough that they had contended through so many judgments in so serious and prolonged a conflict, but that the council itself had to add something worse either to the accusers’ obstinacy or to the misfortune of the bishop under accusation—especially since he lamented his situation while seeking the help of the holy council, reporting that he had already changed prisons more than twenty times and had come to it from forty stations.

Who, apart from the Eutychians—men from whom both reason and piety have departed, in whom only the human name remains—could say this?

Let the reader remember that we have said these things in defense of the great council without being compelled by any necessity, in order to trample down and utterly crush the arrogance of the witless Eutychians. We wished to mock them and to construct the case as though Theodore had written certain culpable things and had not corrected them; as though not only the aforesaid Council of Chalcedon had known of them and been unable to interpret them more favorably, but also the venerable Ibas, despite knowing those same things, had praised Theodore’s teaching. None of this has been established; we granted these points voluntarily so that it might become even clearer how foolishly the Eutychians complain about the council’s judgment concerning Ibas’s letter, since even with all these concessions it would not be shown blameworthy.

[Note: [Col. 0777D] The Verona manuscript reads: “so that it might not be shown blameworthy even with these concessions.”]

## CHAPTER IV. That the council ought not, after his death, to have condemned Theodore, who had died in the peace of the Church, even if he had been accused before it

[Col. 0777C]

We shall add something even to these arguments, so that we may suppose that what never actually happened did happen: that either Theodore himself or the venerable Ibas was accused before the council on account of the praise of Theodore.

If that council must therefore be called heretical because it declared orthodox a letter praising Theodore, then blessed Cyril and Proclus—whom they pretend to honor—will be defended from the charge of heresy, since they defended the Easterners who had Theodore accused before them and praised him even more highly. They did not condemn those Easterners as heretics; rather, by communicating with them, they confirmed them as orthodox.

I shall omit the fact that the judgments of Cyril and Proclus themselves are also held against that same accusation of Theodore: namely, that neither he nor his statements ought to be condemned.

Accordingly, even if Theodore or Bishop Ibas had been accused before the council on account of Theodore’s praise, the Eutychians could not accuse that council because it declared the letter orthodox unless they also accused Cyril and Proclus, since they judged orthodox the Easterners who, while defending Theodore after he had been accused before them, had also exalted him with the highest praises.
