If anyone were to weigh the merits of both sides a little more attentively, he would find the case of that holy council less serious than that of blessed Cyril and Proclus. For even if, as we have granted, Theodore had been accused before the council, it would have been a lesser matter for it to absolve Bishop Ibas, who had praised Theodore before an accusation had been lodged against him, than for blessed Cyril and Proclus to do what they did: they judged orthodox the Easterners by whom Theodore had been praised after his accusation.

Where can it be shown that anyone, even if he truly had been a heretic, was condemned by a universal council without an accusation having first been brought?

[Note: [Col. 0777D] The same manuscript omits *non*, “not.”]

Our Fathers first admonished all the heretics whom they expelled to think better; then they threatened condemnation if they did not repent, granting them time to confer with them, as seemed necessary.

We do not assert this without evidence. The examples of our predecessors testify to it. Following their pattern,

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The same manuscript reads: “whose pattern blessed Cyril preserved, and so forth.”]

blessed Cyril first corrected Nestorius—not because he had fallen, but because he refused to repent—and condemned him; yet he forbade the condemnation of Theodore, who had previously been accused.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The same manuscript reads: “who had not previously been accused.”]

Certain people have badly transgressed this rule of soundness and moderation, unwilling even belatedly to acknowledge their error. They claim that they can prove that certain heretics were condemned after death, as though this proved that they had not also been condemned while alive, or even if that has escaped our memory and knowledge. No one can know or remember everything, since not everything committed to writing has survived to the present.

But, to pass over this, they certainly cannot deny that those persons were first reproved, brought to judgment, and convicted; and that, even if they were not immediately stripped of the honors they held in the Church so that they might repent, they were nevertheless removed from fraternal communion.

Which of these things had already occurred in Theodore’s case, so that the council might adjudge him—even if he had been accused before it?

If someone maintains that certain people were condemned by the Church before correction, he attempts to set not so much those people as their condemners—our Fathers—against the Apostle, who commands that a heretic be avoided only after a first and second admonition (Tit. 3:10).

But far be it from us to believe

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The same manuscript reads: “Far be it from us to believe that …”]

that the catholic and apostolic Church was ever opposed to the Apostle! Therefore, if the authority of that order and moderation has any force among them—the order that the Apostle salutarily established for avoiding, that is, excluding, heretics, and that the Church has always maintained—let them cease attacking it with their contentions.

For they are not attacking the holy council, which would have done nothing contrary to the custom of the Church even if it had not condemned Theodore after he had been accused before it; they are rather attacking the entire Church, whose pattern the council followed.

But they argue as follows: Theodore was expelled from the Church for this reason: the holy Fathers, in their books written privately, condemned those who held opinions such as Theodore is said to have held.

Indeed, it has already been shown above—not only by the testimony of great men but also by citing Theodore’s own statements—what his opinion was. Nevertheless, because they maliciously tear out of his countless books certain passages that seem contrary to those we have cited and believe that he ought to be condemned on their account, claiming that our Fathers had earlier marked out all who held such opinions, we therefore produce in the following volume statements by those same Fathers similar to the ones they condemn, so that they may see their calumnies, devised against the great council, repelled on every side.

But even if these points were removed or temporarily set aside, if Theodore had already been expelled, as they say, then blessed Cyril, as well as John and Domnus of Antioch and the other Eastern bishops, were expelled along with him, since they would not permit the condemnation of one who had already been expelled. They would also be lying when they say that Nestorius was expelled by either blessed Cyril or holy Celestine, bishop of Rome.

For if Theodore had already been expelled because the holy Fathers, in their books, had condemned those who held such opinions, then Nestorius had been expelled all the more: he is shown to have held manifestly corrupt opinions, and he refused to remove the offense he had caused his hearers through profane novelties of expression.

But here I shall inquire into whatever conscience the Eutychians possess. Let us suppose that someone was accused before us who was said to deserve expulsion because he taught things contrary to certain statements of the Fathers. I ask their advice: what ought we to do?

Would it occur to us to expel him from the Church without admonishing or correcting him, merely because the Fathers, in books they had written privately, were found to have refuted those who held such opinions? Or would it not rather occur to us that he ought first to be questioned and admonished, with the statements of the holy Fathers shown to him, statements to which he was said to be opposed?

[Note: [Col. 0779D] The Verona manuscript reads: “the very statements of the Fathers.”]

And if he did not correct himself, should he not be summoned to a council? If he did not submit to its authority, should he then be expelled?

[Note: [Col. 0779D] The same manuscript reads: “if he did not submit to the authority of the council.”]

This surely appears to have been what ought to be done; this is the order we ought to follow; this is the consideration for humaneness that ought to be observed—even if the Apostle had not commanded it.

But if we ought not condemn a living man in his absence unless he had first been admonished and corrected, how could the holy council, even if Theodore had been accused before it, justly condemn him after his death?

[Note: [Col. 0779D] Those who defended Theodore relied especially on this exception, which Facundus presses in many places and which Vigilius himself states in the *Constitutum*: those who had ended their lives in the peace of the Church ought not to be condemned after death. The opponents of the Chapters, on the other hand, maintained that heretics could rightly be condemned and that those condemned had been heretics in the Church even after death; they argued that Theodore was falsely said to have died in the peace of the Church, since he had followed doctrines contrary to the Church until his death. Justinian argues in this way in the *Edict*, and the Fifth Council in Act 5.]

For, first, which accuser could be so certain that all those chapters being censured were Theodore’s, that, if he were told according to custom, “Swear by the name of the Lord that Theodore, whom you seek to have condemned after death, wrote these things,” he would dare to swear?

The great council could not lightly believe something that, if true, would have required serious condemnation.

For one situation arises when we read something merely for instruction and simply believe it to belong to the author whose name appears in the title, without prejudicing him by this belief of ours; another arises when the condemnation of the person believed to be the author is demanded in a judicial proceeding.

Therefore, even if this accuser swore that all those chapters belonged to Theodore, the council ought not for that reason to have been driven by his oath to condemn a man who had died in the peace of the Church.

What more, then, could that accuser have done than summon witnesses of suitable standing and sufficient number who were willing to testify under oath to the same thing?

Yet not even this—whatever more could have been done—would have sufficed for his condemnation.

For if, while Theodore was alive, witnesses had been brought against him, he ought not to have been condemned on their testimony alone without being summoned to judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0780D] The same manuscript reads: “on their testimony alone.”]

But if, after being summoned, he had refused to await the announced inquiry, whether from a guilty conscience or through obstinacy, then the matter would no longer have rested on witnesses testifying about an absent man; rather, one would have believed the man himself, who was judging himself.

If he were condemned without any preceding correction or summons, he would rightly complain of the judges’ injustice and reasonably say that they had maliciously or rashly believed false witnesses against an absent man.

For this reason, in that same holy council, the bishops repeatedly cried out on behalf of the most revered Ibas, saying: “Those who condemned him contrary to the canons acted wrongly; let what was done against an absent man be annulled. We all say this: no one condemns an absent man.”

But if witnesses ought not to have been accepted against a living man so that he could be condemned without being questioned or summoned, how could the holy council justly admit them even if they testified against Theodore in his own trial?

Would it be easier to lie about a living man and more difficult to lie about a dead one?

If those same witnesses were questioned about how they knew with absolute certainty that the statements being censured had been written by Theodore, what could they answer more credibly than that they had either found them in books said to belong to Theodore or had learned from Theodore himself, while he was alive, that they were his?

But we have already shown that the title of books is insufficient to secure the condemnation of a man who had died in the peace of the Church and with the highest praise of the Fathers—especially since Theodore had complained that certain of his books had been corrupted by heretics. Blessed Cyril said of him that, when no person was readily available to whom the fault could be attributed, an uncertain accusation of the chapters was being made, and that those who undertook such actions would be found running into uncertainty and beating the air.

How, then, could the council believe witnesses—even if they had been brought forward—who claimed that something was certain when Cyril had testified, with the events still fresh in memory, that it was uncertain?

If, instead, they said that they had learned from Theodore himself that the statements were his,

[Note: [Col. 0780D] The same manuscript reads: “that, while he was alive, they were his.”]

what could they answer if they were told: “Why, then, did you not bring these matters that you now accuse him of before the ecclesiastical authorities when he was still alive, when he could have been brought to judgment and could either have denied that they were his, interpreted them more favorably, or, as a last resort, rejected them if he could not defend them?”

There is therefore no basis for censuring the holy council concerning Theodore, whom it did not condemn, even if he had been accused before it and witnesses of suitable standing and sufficient number had been brought to his trial.

But let us grant this also to the Eutychians, and suppose that it was proved to the council that those chapters belonged to Theodore. How could it know the intention with which they had been produced?

We often do not express ourselves exactly as we think, and what we say is often not received by others in the precise sense in which we utter it.

But let us grant even this: let us suppose that the council knew Theodore had written those chapters while in error. How could it know whether they were among the statements—or similar to those statements—that Theodore himself, as has been said, had either censured or corrected in his writings?

For it is also rightly said that his censure or correction of those statements ought to have served as an excuse for other similar statements as well.

But even if it were not shown that Theodore had censured or corrected certain things in his writings, and it were believed that the Church had been unaware of the matters for which he is condemned, how could the council be certain

[Note: [Col. 0781D] The Verona manuscript reads: “how could it have been certain …”]

that, after writing those things, he had not come to know the truth through the inspiration of God, who secretly and wondrously works in the hearts of his own, so that the council ought to judge him as having died in error?

Even if it were proved that he had remained ignorant of something concerning the incarnation of Christ until the day of his death, nevertheless, since he had not been separated from the Church, how could the council be certain—as I have said—that in the very hour when he was about to breathe his last, the great and inscrutable mercy of God, which did not overlook the robber’s crimes but forgave them on the cross, had not also granted Theodore, for his many labors and struggles in the Church against heretics, repentance from his ignorance, so that, with his error condemned, he might follow the robber and immediately be with Christ in paradise—he who is now said to have been subject to condemnation for Nestorian doctrine even before Nestorius?

For how many heretics, how many Jews and Gentiles, have we learned by reliable testimony to have been converted at the very threshold of death? But because their error had been public, their conversion could not remain private: they begged to be reconciled and baptized by the Church, and finally they were reconciled or baptized.

But Theodore could secretly reject his own hidden ignorance, which no one had censured and which he is said to have possessed; concerning him the Eastern council also testifies that he suffered no denunciation from the orthodox during his lifetime, and Bishop Proclus says of him and others, “whom we never censured while they were alive.”

And even if he had abandoned this ignorance not secretly but with certain people aware of it, it could nevertheless have remained hidden from the holy council, and the council could not judge what was hidden, since that belongs properly to God, as Moses says: “The things that are hidden are for you and your children.”

Hence blessed Cyril also says: “It appears most just to prudent men to yield to the one who knows in advance the will of each person.”

Why, then, should this council be censured for yielding everything to God, who knows all things in advance, and for not daring, like certain others, to be the judge of hidden things—something that belongs to God alone?

Yet, as I think, no modest person would dare to determine even this: that all those should be considered heretics who, not obstinately but as imperfect people ready to learn, have known less than they should about the Christian faith, as did the apostles Thomas and Philip themselves.

For it is said to Thomas: “If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also” (John 14:7). And to Philip: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?” And: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (ibid., 9–10).

Who, then, would call such people heretics if, although still ignorant, they ended their present life in the Church, which they do not believe can err? Who would dare to suspect that the apostles just mentioned were heretics even at the time when they were ignorant of these things?

But we shall say much more about this later.

Since, then, the council was uncertain that all those chapters, on account of which Theodore was said to deserve exclusion from the Church, belonged to him—and since, even if it had been certain of this, it would still have been uncertain of the intention with which they had been produced—and since, even if it had known without doubt that he had erred, it would not thereby immediately be evident that he had not afterward corrected his error—and since, even if this too were established by some certain proof, no pious and serious person would dare to determine that all those who err in the Christian faith without obstinacy are heretics, if they ended their lives in the peace of the Church while still uninstructed—who, unless he were reckless, would say that amid so many uncertainties that council ought to condemn Theodore under an anathema?

Without doubt, Emperor, you consider how many things we have voluntarily granted or conceded to the Eutychians and their supporters, without any necessity compelling us to do so. Yet the truth does not permit them to declare blameworthy the judgment of the great council, which pronounced orthodox the letter containing praise of Theodore.

And if we had lacked all the arguments of conviction that, in view of our opponents’ proven obstinacy, we have brought forward, what religious person could criticize this council, which did not dare to usurp what had not been granted to it?

For the Lord granted his Church no power to bind and loose the dead, when he said to his disciples: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XIII, 18).

[Col. 0782D]

It received the power, therefore, to bind and loose only those who are on earth. For this reason it ought not to be censured because it did not dare to bind Theodore—even if it knew him to be culpable—since he was no longer on earth.

That presumption belonged to others who approved such a course, not to the council. For just as it was not right for the council to dare to loose after death those who had been bound on earth—which might indeed appear to bear some resemblance to piety—so it was not right for it to dare, after death, to bind someone who had not been bound on earth. That would be plainly impious and had not been entrusted to its authority.

Accordingly, the blessed Fathers also determined that it is not ours to judge those who have died honorably, but belongs to the one Judge of the living and the dead.

## CHAPTER V. That no one condemns Athanasius on account of the defense he undertook of Dionysius of Alexandria; and that it is much easier to defend Theodore
How, then, do they say that the synod is Nestorian because it did not defend or in any way excuse the writings of Theodore, whom they accuse as Nestorius’s teacher, when they do not dare to call Athanasius an Arian for defending the writings of his predecessor Dionysius? For when the Arians wished to enlist certain statements of the venerable Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, as testimony and support for their error—so as to show from this that Arius was not the inventor of a new doctrine, since Dionysius had once taught that the Son was a product, not naturally proper to the Father but alien to the Father’s essence, and that the same Son did not exist before he was made, along with other similar statements contained in that same work—Athanasius, a genuine and credible exemplar of catholic doctrine and virtue, steadfastly accepted those statements. Although they were harsh to our ears and difficult to excuse, he did not refuse to defend them. First, he wished Dionysius, their author, to be cleared by this means and shown free from the charge of Arianism: Dionysius himself had not, like Arius during his lifetime, been accused of impiety or expelled from the episcopate; nor had he, as though defending a heresy, departed from the Church as Arius did, but had remained within its unity. Then he attempted to interpret those very statements more favorably.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] The whole accusation against Dionysius, as Athanasius shows in his *Apology on behalf of Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria* (ἐν τῇ ἀπολογίᾳ ὑπὲρ Διονυσίου ἐπισκόπου Ἀλεξανδρείας), arose from a letter that he had written against Sabellius to Euphranor and Ammonius, on account of which he was compelled to clear himself at Rome before Pope Dionysius. That letter contained all the statements which Facundus incorrectly reports as having been made by him. Athanasius, moreover, maintains that Dionysius wrote these things against the Sabellians not through error or ignorance, but “by dispensation” (κατ’ οἰκονομίαν). Basil, however, in Letter 41, while arguing in the opposite direction, thinks that he “exchanged one evil for another” (κακοῦ κακὸν διαμεῖψαι) and fell through lack of caution. “For,” he says, “while violently opposing the impiety of the Libyan, he failed to notice that he had been drawn by excessive zeal into the opposite evil” (Ἀντιβαίνων γὰρ σφοδρῶς … τῇ ἀσεβείᾳ τοῦ Λίβυος, ἔλαθεν ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸ ἐναντίον κακὸν ὑπὸ τῆς ἄγαν φιλοτιμίας ὑπενεχθείς). They also disagree about the outcome. Basil asserts that Dionysius sowed the seeds of the Anomoean heresy. Athanasius, by contrast, says that the Arians unjustly boast of Dionysius as “of the same doctrine and of the same mind” (ὁμόδοξον καὶ ὁμόφρονα), a supporter of their position, whereas they ought to judge his faith and teaching from his other writings, not from this one letter alone.]

For this reason I think it more appropriate, if not to present everything—for that would be lengthy—at least to present some things in his own words.

“For,” he says, “the Lord also rebuked the Jews when they acted against the Law, saying: ‘Abraham did not do this’ (John 8:40); and that same Truth rebukes these impious and deceitful men, because Bishop Dionysius neither held anything of Arius nor was ignorant of the truth. But just as the Jews at that time, so these new men now have inherited from their father the devil this madness, rebellious against Christ. This is a great indication that they merely wish to slander that man and pay no attention to the fact that he was neither accused of impiety by other bishops nor expelled from the episcopate, as these men were from the clergy; nor did he, as though defending a heresy, depart from the Church, but died peacefully within it. His memory is still celebrated with the Fathers, and his name is written among them. For if he had held any of these opinions, or if he had not offered an explanation of what he wrote, he too would unquestionably have suffered the same things.

“These points would indeed have sufficed to rebuke the new Jews, who denied Christ, accused the Fathers, and are known to deceive all Christians.”

[Note: [Col. 0783D] The same manuscript reads “intend to deceive.” The Greek word in Athanasius’s letter *On the Opinion of Dionysius* is ἐπιχειρούντων, “those who attempt.”]

“Since, however, they think they have charges with which to accuse the bishop, let us take up some portions of his letter and examine them, so that their vanity may be exposed even by this means. Let them, however late, cease blaspheming the Lord among themselves, and let them confess—even with the soldiers, when they see creation bearing witness—that ‘truly this is the Son of God,’ and that he is not from among the creatures.

“They say, then, that in that letter blessed Dionysius said that the Son of God was a product and had been made; that he was not naturally proper to the Father but alien to the Father’s essence, just as a farmer is related to a vine and a shipwright to a ship; and that, as a product, he did not exist before he was made.

“Yes, he wrote this; we too acknowledge that this letter of his exists. But just as he wrote that letter, so he wrote many others; and they ought to read those as well, so that the faith of that man may be recognized from all his writings, not from this one alone.”

Then follows his explanation of the statements we have mentioned. The reader should seek it in his work, not here, since that would be lengthy.

You see, Emperor, what blessed Athanasius undertook to excuse in Dionysius, for no other reason than that what is said must be judged not from the superficial sound of the words but from the speaker’s intention. When the person who spoke is already dead, his intention is judged with greater reverence from his communion with the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] The same manuscript reads “more religiously from communion with the Church.”]

This is what he means when he says: “If he had held any of these opinions, or if he had not offered an explanation of what he wrote, he too would unquestionably have suffered the same things.” It is as though he were saying: We ought not to attend merely to what the words sound like; rather, we should believe concerning the Church of Christ—which is governed by the one who redeemed it with his blood—that, unless Dionysius had expressed these things with a good intention, or unless the offense had been removed by his other statements, he would certainly not have remained a bishop within it.

Thus Athanasius, who was an advocate of the unity of the Trinity not so much through verbal teaching as through suffering, and whose entire life was a martyrdom, submits himself to the authority of the Church. Because Dionysius remained in communion with it to the end, Athanasius judges that this alone is sufficient for his vindication, so much so that he does not merely refrain from condemning him for such statements, but does not even dare to censure him lightly.

[Note: [Col. 0785D] The Verona manuscript reads “at least censure him.”]

He knew that if he did this, he would censure the whole Church that had remained in communion with Dionysius.

And now certain men—would that we truly did not know who they are—dare, to the dishonor of the Church, to condemn Theodore, praised by so many Fathers; and, moreover, to accuse the holy synod because it did not presume to do so. But what indefensible matter had they already found in Theodore, if in Dionysius it could be excused that he said that the Son of God was a product, alien to the Father’s essence, and did not exist before he was made—when the Fathers at Nicaea anathematized those who say, “There was when he was not,” and “Before he was born, he was not,” and those who say that the Son of God was made or is of another essence?

But Athanasius, a man grounded in great reason and gravity, and one whom they rightly trusted as an exceedingly experienced leader in the greatest battles against the enemies of the Church, knew how to meet the deceits of heretics prudently, having been trained by those very dangers. For they too, with no lesser—indeed, more cunning—craft, frequently deceive the unwary, so that we will neither trust the counsel nor be strengthened by the example of those whom they have seen to be wise and courageous in the Catholic Church, as though in the camp of a great commonwealth. Since they cannot make such men their own, they try to make them suspect to us.

For this reason Athanasius was not moved like some frivolous man, susceptible to all their factions:

[Note: [Col. 0785D] The same manuscript reads “susceptible to all their actions.”]

he did not, as malicious and timid generals—or as generals both malicious and timid—are accustomed to do, cruelly and rashly condemn Dionysius merely because the Arians wished him to appear their accomplice and friend, thereby excluding from the heavenly camp the man whom he had as a defender alongside him against the enemies.

Therefore, most merciful Emperor, we ought to imitate this most learned and holy man and follow his policy and his observance concerning the peace of the Church. We laugh at the cruelty of those who are sluggish in defending their own people but hasty in condemning others, and who seek the disgraceful glory—shared with heretics—of criticizing their predecessors.

I believe that you instruct the commanders of your army to maintain in the camps entrusted to them the same caution toward the enemy’s deceit and the defense of their own men that Athanasius, the commander of Christ’s army, maintained. Therefore, do not consider the overseers of God’s Churches worthy of their office if you would judge men of that kind unworthy were they commanders of your camps.

Now, if the Nestorians say to me: “Theodore of Mopsuestia, who died while still a bishop, was praised with great commendation not only in the letter that our synod declared orthodox, but also in those letters on whose authority the dogmatic letter of Leo of Rome is defended. Yet he thought about Christ as Nestorius did, and, in defense of his doctrine, he brought forward—just as the Arians did concerning Dionysius—certain passages from Theodore’s books, directed to another subject and written against other people, which require to be excused,” I shall immediately follow the model that blessed Athanasius gave us concerning Dionysius. I shall answer these men on behalf of Theodore of Mopsuestia in the very words with which Athanasius answered the Arians:

“You slander that man to no purpose. He was neither accused of impiety by other bishops nor expelled from the episcopate, as Nestorius was; nor did he, as though defending a heresy, depart from the Church, but died peacefully within it. If he had held any of these opinions, or if he had not offered an explanation of what he wrote, he too would unquestionably have suffered the same things.”

Following the order of Athanasius’s further response, I shall say again: Just as Theodore wrote these things, so he wrote many others, and you ought to read those too, so that the faith of that man may be recognized from all his writings, not from these passages alone. I shall also produce many statements contrary to the Nestorian error, of which I have cited a few in the earlier books.

[Note: [Col. 0786D] The same manuscript reads “I cited in the earlier books.”]

I shall also demonstrate to them the reason why he wrote such things, and show that he spoke thus against the Synousiasts (Συνουσιασταί), who were especially active in his time, whenever an opportunity arose, with greater security because the opposing wickedness of Nestorius had not yet begun to cause alarm.

For me, and for any Catholics, these considerations alone are sufficient against the Nestorians—just as the considerations that then sufficed for the great Athanasius against the Arians were sufficient for him. But I shall not delay in showing, or rather recalling what has already been shown, what further arguments we have on behalf of Theodore than Athanasius had on behalf of Dionysius.

For the mercy of the Lord has provided—whether because of our ignorance, since we are less capable of defending our position, or because of the obstinacy of our opponents, who refuse to accept manifest truth—that Theodore can be excused in many more ways than Dionysius.

What we assert is that Nestorius differed so greatly from Theodore’s position that, when admonished by the most reverend John of Antioch,

[Note: [Col. 0786D] The same manuscript reads “admonished by his example.”]

he did not dare to defend his own evil statements with testimonies from Theodore’s statements. He certainly would not have omitted this unless he had seen that the teaching of the catholic man was contrary to his own. Blessed Athanasius had no such argument to use in defense of the venerable Dionysius, because Arius had not been admonished and convicted by the example of Dionysius in the way that Nestorius was by the example of Theodore.

Furthermore, Theodore voluntarily criticized himself in his exposition of the Psalms, confessing that many things had been composed by him carelessly, especially those written first; and he claimed that certain passages had been inserted into his books by the Apollinarists. We can therefore say to the Nestorians that those very passages which they think accord with their doctrine should be regarded either as among the many things carelessly composed by him or as among those which he complained had been inserted into his books by the Apollinarists.

We can also produce the statement that Theodore himself makes in Book Five *On the Incarnation*, which I included in my earlier work: wherever, in discussing Christ, he says “one” and “another,” he means “one” and “another” not in person but in nature.

All these resources, which we possess in abundance, were lacking to blessed Athanasius when he excused Dionysius’s letter. Since the Eutychians or Semi-Eutychian Acephali do not dare to blame Athanasius, how can they blame the Council of Chalcedon, which did not wish to excuse Theodore’s statements, but did not wish to condemn him without excusing him.

[Note: [Col. 0787D] The Verona manuscript reads “accused” (*accusatum*) rather than “unexcused” (*non excusatum*).]

## Chapter VI. That Basil excused certain harsher statements of Gregory the Wonderworker and of the Antiochene and Sirmian councils; and that the synod could likewise have excused Theodore if it had undertaken to do so

Saint Basil defended the great Gregory,

[Note: [Col. 0787C] This is Basil’s Letter 64 to the people of Neocaesarea, p. 849: “As though Gregory had said in the exposition of faith: ‘The Father and the Son are two in conception, but one in subsistence’” (Ὡς ἄρα Γρηγορίου εἰπόντος ἐν ἐκθέσει πίστεως· Πατέρα καὶ Υἱὸν ἐπινοίᾳ μὲν εἶναι δύο, ὑποστάσει δὲ ἕν). These words are not found in Gregory’s revealed *Exposition*, nor in the other work entitled *The Faith in Detail* (ἡ κατὰ μέρος πίστις). They must therefore have been in another work that he had written to Gelianus or Aelianus, as Basil reads it. Anastasius quotes a notable passage from the later *Faith in Detail* in his *Eclogue*. It is worth transcribing, because the corrupt Latin version not without reason misled Schobast: “From the Faith in Detail of the great Gregory the Wonderworker: ‘The true God is the incorporeal one manifested in flesh; perfect in true and divine perfection; not two persons, but two natures; nor do we say that four are to be worshiped: God, the Son of God, man, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore we anathematize those who are impious in this way, who place a man within the divine doxology. We say that a man is assumed by God for our salvation, so that we may receive the likeness of the heavenly one and be deified according to the likeness of the true God by nature, but by flesh the man, our Lord Jesus Christ.’” The translator, having found a corrupt exemplar, read the contrary meaning: οὐδὲ δύο φύσεις, “not even two natures,” instead of ἀλλὰ δύο φύσεις, “but two natures.”]

who received the epithet “Wonderworker,” so that he was and is called *Thaumaturgus* by the Greeks, not only against the Arians, who say that the Son is a creature and a product, but also against the contrary error of the Sabellians, who say that the Father and the Son have one subsistence, although the aforementioned Gregory himself appears to have said this as well.

Accordingly, when speaking about certain people who were attempting to excuse their perfidy by Gregory’s authority, Saint Basil says:

“They brought forward as a test a letter addressed to our like-minded brother Anthimus, bishop of Tyana, claiming that the great Gregory had said in the *Exposition of Faith* that the persons of the Father and the Son are two in conception but one in subsistence. But because this was not said dogmatically, but in the course of a disputation in a speech to Gelianus, those who glorify themselves in the subtlety of their interpretations were unable to perceive it. There are many false statements in what is written, as we shall show in those very speeches, if God wills.

“Again, in accommodating a pagan, he did not think that subtle reasoning about words was necessary. There are also places where one must comply with the custom of the person who is being contradicted, so as not to resist where resistance is unnecessary. Therefore you will find there many expressions that now provide heretics with their greatest strength, such as ‘creature,’ ‘product,’ and anything of that kind. Many statements, too, about the union that took place with the man they relate to the divine nature, because they listen to Scripture without understanding; among them is the statement they circulate.”

How, then, could the synod justly anathematize Theodore, who died in the peace of the Church, when Athanasius and Basil defend Dionysius and Gregory from such serious charges precisely because they died in the peace of the Church? Or how could it declare the letter of the venerable Ibas heretical because of its praise of Theodore, when it did not dare to call these writings of Athanasius and Basil heretical? Or how do the Eutychians blame the same synod because it did not presume to anathematize Theodore, who had not been accused before them, when they cannot blame these Fathers, by whom Dionysius and Gregory are also excused?

But let us produce something more important. Blessed Hilary,

[Note: [Col. 0788D] In his letter *On the Synods*: “The man of Samosata confessed the term *homoousion* wrongly, but did the Arians deny it more correctly? Eighty bishops, our Fathers, once rejected it, but three hundred and eighteen recently accepted it.” As he adds shortly afterward, both groups established the same thing by their approval and rejection. Athanasius likewise treats the same argument concerning the councils of Ariminum and Seleucia, praising both those who rejected the term at Antioch against the man of Samosata and those who approved it at Nicaea against the Arians: “But it is not right to accuse either these or those; for all professed the things of Christ, and all were zealous against the heretics. Some condemned the man of Samosata, others the Arian heresy; both these and those acted rightly and wrote well with regard to the subject at hand” (Ἀλλ’ οὔτε τούτους, οὔτε ἐκείνους ὅσιον αἰτιάσασθαι· πάντες γὰρ ἐπρέσβευον τὰ Χριστοῦ καὶ πάντες σπουδὴν ἐσχήκασι κατὰ τῶν αἱρετικῶν· καὶ οἱ μὲν τὸν σαμοσατέα, οἱ δὲ τὴν ἀρειανὴν αἵρεσιν κατέκριναν· ὀρθῶς δὲ καὶ οὗτοι κᾀκεῖνοι, καὶ καλῶς πρὸς τὴν ὑποκειμένην ὑπόθεσιν γεγράφασι).]

the most powerful and fiercest conqueror of the Arians and the most steadfast confessor of the Christian faith, in the letter that he wrote from exile to the bishops of the provinces of First and Second Germania, First and Second Belgica, First and Second Lugdunensis, the province of Aquitaine, the province of Novempopulania, the communities and clergy of Toulouse from the province of Narbonensis, and the bishops of the British provinces, approves not the private words of one man but the public decrees of councils.

In those decrees our eighty Fathers, against Paul of Samosata, rejected calling the Son *homoousios*, that is, of one essence with the Father. Hilary gives the following reason for their rejection of the term: the aforementioned heretic Paul confessed that the Father alone was God, while he said that the Son began with his birth from Mary his mother and was merely human. For this reason, Hilary explains, those Fathers preferred, after removing *homoousios*, to establish *homoiousios*, that is, “of similar essence,” because similarity does not allow union to be understood.

But when Arius later understood and taught *homoiousios* wrongly, denying that the Son was of one substance with the Father and saying that he was similar to the Father—as the apostle John says of himself and the other adopted sons, “Now we are children of God, and it has not yet been manifested what we shall be”—

[Note: [Col. 0787D] The same manuscript reads “what we shall be in the future.” The Vulgate has “what we shall be.”]

—and, “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2)—the other Fathers took up *homoousios* again.

Therefore Hilary, so as not to accuse the Church in either group of Fathers, since the Church honored both, resolved the question by saying that the eighty Fathers rejected *homoousios* against a heretic, while the three hundred and eighteen approved that same term against a heretic.

He adds this as well toward the end:

“Let us consider all those holy priests who are now at rest. What will become of us, who bring the matter to the point that, because they were not bishops, we too should cease to be bishops? We were ordained by them and are their succession. Let us renounce the episcopate, since we have received its office from those whom we have anathematized.”

All these statements—whether spoken privately by the holy Dionysius and Gregory or decreed publicly in the council by the eighty Fathers—

[Note: [Col. 0789D] The Verona manuscript reads: “not only seem difficult to excuse.”]

—seem not merely difficult to excuse, since they are found to have been produced before the definition of the Council of Nicaea.

There is something much more significant: in that same letter, Saint Hilary equally defends the Council of Sirmium,

[Note: [Col. 0789D] Photinus was expelled from the episcopate there in the year of Christ 351. Hilary writes in the same letter: “Let us now reconsider that faith which was composed not long ago, at the time when Photinus was expelled from the episcopate.” He gives the text of the faith composed at Sirmium by the Eastern bishops against Photinus: “We believe in one God,” and so forth. He transcribes it in full, together with the following twenty-seven chapters or anathemas. By “the Easterners” he means those whom Athanasius, discussing the same faith, calls Eusebians—namely, the Semi-Arians. Although the authors were of suspect faith, and the decrees themselves bore the mark of their authors, Hilary nevertheless did not hesitate to explain and defend them as having been necessarily composed against Photinus.]

which was convened after Nicaea. Its decrees said:

“If anyone, while saying that there is one God, does not confess that Christ, God and the Son of God before the ages, obeyed the Father in the creation of all things, let him be anathema.”

And again:

“If anyone calls God the Lord and Father, and the Son Lord from the Lord, two Gods, let him be anathema. For we do not equate or compare the Son with the Father, but understand him to be subject. For he did not descend upon Sodom without the Father’s will, nor did he rain from himself, but by the authority of the Lord, namely, the Father; nor does he sit at the right hand by himself, but hears the Father saying, ‘Sit at my right hand’ (Psalm 109:1).”

[Note: [Col. 0789D] The same manuscript reads: “the Lord and the Lord, the Father and the Son,” and so forth. Several other manuscripts support this reading, as can be seen in the new edition of Saint Hilary’s *On the Synods*, or *On the Faith of the Easterners*.]

Again:

“If anyone says that the Son is unborn and without beginning, as though there were two without beginning, two unborn beings, and two unbegotten beings, and thereby says that there are two Gods, let him be anathema. For Christ is the head that is the beginning of all things; and God is the head that is the beginning of Christ. Thus we refer all things through the Son to the One who is without beginning, the beginning of all things.”

And again, in Chapter 27:

“Confirming the understanding of Christianity, we say that if anyone does not say that Christ, God and the Son of God, existed before the ages and ministered to the Father for the perfection of all things, but says that from the time he was born of Mary he was called both Christ and Son, and from that time received a beginning so as to be God, let him be anathema.”

Saint Hilary asserts that all these things were necessarily decreed by the aforementioned Council of Sirmium against Photinus and by the Easterners.

[Note: [Col. 0790D] In the same manuscript the conjunction “and” is absent. The sense is therefore that the Easterners decreed all the foregoing in the Council of Sirmium.]

In providing a sufficient explanation of them, he demonstrates how they should be understood.

This, then, was the concern of Athanasius, Basil, Hilary, and all holy men: that if those who had died in the peace and honor of the Church were condemned as heretics, the Church itself—which had honored them so greatly—would be condemned.

Therefore, even if some people should be found who have been approved in many respects yet condemn Theodore as a heretic, they certainly do not do this with sound judgment; nor should they be followed in this matter, in which they do not follow the custom of the Church.

Accordingly, if the Council of Chalcedon, following the custom of the Church in defense of the Church itself, had likewise excused Theodore’s statements, who but a profane person would accuse it of such piety and caution? Yet it could not have done this without Athanasius and Hilary.

[Note: [Col. 0790D] The same manuscript reads “without Athanasius, Basil, and Hilary.”]

Moreover, it did not do anything of this kind. Instead, it incurs hatred because it declared orthodox another letter brought before it—not one accused of praising Theodore—on account of the confession of the true faith that it contains.

## Chapter VII. That the adversaries fell into four grave faults in the brief sentence of Theodore’s condemnation
Let us examine the very supporters of Eutyches, who, because something obscure is found in the statements of those resting in the peace of the Church, want them condemned rather than excused, and see whether they are so vigilantly cautious that they cannot in any way be criticized in what they have said and written. For if they are so circumspect that they are found at fault in nothing, it might perhaps be considered tolerable that, relying on their wisdom, they do not deign to stoop to us and to those like us who offend in many ways. But what shall we do, since we have heard of no books composed by them in another matter, by examining which we might prove their irreproachable expertise and ever-watchful caution? Do they therefore wish us to seek their perfect, nowhere-blameworthy knowledge in this book, which they wrote—or caused to be written—through a common and prolonged discussion, to the prejudice of the holy synod? Yet, even if we do not disclose all the errors it contains, since we have undertaken in this work to demonstrate something else, we have nevertheless exposed many errors by taking the opportunity [Note: The same manuscript has “his errors”], as well as many falsehoods and contradictions within it. Here we have also shown that, although they devote themselves to lying, they do not even know how to lie, nor how, through the same knowledge, they sometimes speak the truth against themselves.

But if, in this book to which they subscribed, they were intent on censuring the errors of others—whether false or true—and have been found at fault in so many matters, with what face do they presume to condemn the statements not merely of Theodore, but of any human being? These judges of the dead will blush if we consider their ignorance throughout the whole book; and for that reason I have proposed to inspect and demonstrate it in the very sentence by which they condemned Theodore together with his doctrines. For they said, as we reported:

> “If anyone does not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia [Note: As above, at the beginning of Book III. Justinian uses the same words in the Edict: “If anyone, therefore, defends Theodore but does not anathematize him, his writings, and those who have thought or think like him, let him be anathema” (Εἴ τις τοίνυν ἀντιποιεῖται Θεοδώρου, ἀλλὰ μὴ ἀναθεματίζει αὐτὸν, καὶ τὰ αὐτοῦ συγγράμματα καὶ τοὺς τὰ ὅμοια αὐτῷ φρονοῦντας ἢ φρονήσαντας, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω)], and his doctrines, and those who either have thought or think like him, let him be anathema.”

Consider, I ask you, how many and how serious are the faults I criticize in this sentence. The first is that they subjected him to anathema contrary to the judgment of the Fathers and of the whole Church, in whose peace he died.

The second is that, by condemning everyone who does not pronounce anathema against him, they decreed that the venerable Fathers whom we have mentioned, the very Church that was in communion with Theodore, and all the faithful presently living in the body of Christ—whether they do not anathematize him because they ended their lives in the peace of the Church, or because they have heard neither his errors nor even his name—should likewise become anathema. As we have already said, this was plainly done contrary to justice and to the custom of the Church; nor have we found any example in which those who do not anathematize a heretic whom they may be ignorant of were made anathema. These men too would not have decreed this except as an insult to the Council of Chalcedon, which, when his praises were read before it, did not pronounce anathema against him.

The third is that, condemning without any exception, in general terms, his doctrines and all those who do not pronounce anathema against them—even though they themselves do not deny that many of those doctrines are correct—they are shown to anathematize not only the Fathers mentioned above and other innocent persons of past or present times, but also the Catholic faith itself. For, as John, Domnus of Antioch, and the Eastern Council testify, Theodore overthrew every heresy by affirming that faith; and, as they meanwhile claim, he magnificently defended it against the Arians and Eunomians according to Cyril. They are therefore plainly convicted of anathematizing it.

The fourth is that they were not content to anathematize only those who think like him, but, again contrary to justice and the rule of the Church, added those who have thought like him [Note: The same manuscript has “who have thought like him”]. Although they have not proved that Theodore ever held any erroneous opinion, so far as they are concerned they have condemned everyone who, they suppose, was converted from the error into which they believe him to have fallen. Their conversion has done them no good, since they are condemned precisely because at some time they held such opinions.

What, then, will they do with Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus, who with familiar devotion adhered to the Lord himself while he lived here in the flesh? Yet each of them—first Martha and then Mary—is read to have said to him:

> “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:21, 23).

Although they believed that he was the Son of God who had come into the world [Note: The same manuscript has “Christ, the Son of God”], they would not have said, “If you had been here,” if they had known him to be present everywhere as God. They therefore held the same opinion that Theodore is said to have held, and they have been anathematized together with Theodore.

And how many such people do we recognize in the Gospels and apostolic writings, both at that time and even now—people in the flock of the faithful who please God merely by participating in the holy mysteries and by simply obeying the commandments? Even the first shepherds, his apostles, at times held such views; and we have seen all of them condemned in this anathema together with Theodore.

For even if Thomas and Philip, who say, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8), are said not to have believed Christ merely a man, but God—though lesser than the Father or separated from the Father—which is why it was also said, “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (ibid., 10)—they nevertheless undoubtedly held opinions like those Theodore is thought to have held. For it was no different or lesser ignorance either to believe God lesser, or to separate the Son from the Father. Unless perhaps we dislike the Nestorian error so much that we approve the Arian one. However they are said to have thought, they certainly held either the same or similar opinions.

Let those who know only how to slander others, but do not know how to defend their own statements, answer for this precipitous and inconsiderate judgment of theirs; and, if they can, let them release themselves from these bonds of manifest truth [Note: The same manuscript has “from the bonds”]. Perhaps we shall believe that they have received the power to bind those who are not upon earth—something the apostles themselves did not receive.

Behold four great faults, neither obscure nor drawn from hidden matters, but clear and manifest, which we have shown that they committed. How, then, was their subtle intellect, vigilant through laborious reflections during the night of obscure questions against the statements of others, found dull in their own case and lethargic in broad daylight?

In how many volumes of books are these censorious judges of the dead found to have committed errors so great in number and magnitude? Is it not one short sentence, which can be written with a single dipping of the pen?

> “If anyone does not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia, and his doctrines, and those who either have thought or think like him, let him be anathema.”

In these very few syllables, pondered over for a long time, so many wise men—and, what is more, the most scrupulous and slanderous examiners of the statements of others—fell into such error in the very sentence of their own slander that, even if what they assert about Theodore in condemnation of the holy synod were true, it could not be compared with their errors.

And these men dare to examine and criticize the learned men whose innumerable books could not have been produced with a single dip of the pen without containing great and numerous errors?

This too must be considered: Theodore, before the Nestorians had appeared, while directing his attention against others and confronting the Synusiasts who opposed him, incurred some incidental offense in the course of a discourse proceeding toward another subject [Note: Codex Veronensis has “a slanting offense.”] [Note: In the manuscript, “a slanting offense.”]. These men, however—whose conduct not undeservedly admits of no pardon—after a long hatred of peace, diligent and quiet, if indeed quiet, not only erred in many ways and gravely, but placed an anathema between themselves and so many Fathers, the whole Church that was in communion with Theodore, and even the apostles themselves.

Theodore did not do this in the matters for which they criticize him, yet he is now condemned under anathema merely because of the synod’s prejudice. Therefore, if a hundred years ago it seemed bold and harsh to the holy Fathers to impose anathema upon statements of those who had died in the peace of the Church [Note: The same manuscript has “that an anathema be imposed”], how much bolder and harsher is it now to condemn not only their statements—which it is established was formerly forbidden—but also their persons?

And those Fathers who forbade the condemnation of Theodore’s statements and those of others wisely said:

> “For who among us expects not to die? Or from whom has nothing been said that could offend another?”

They were surely taking care lest, by such an example, anathema should also be imposed after their death upon their own statements. How much, then, ought we to fear giving posterity an example by which not only the statements of those who spoke them, after their death, but their persons also may be condemned?

For if Theodore is believed detestable after so many years since his death, although he is not proved to have resisted correction while alive; if Theodore is condemned, although he condemned no one who died in the peace of the Church; if Theodore is excluded, although he is not found to have written anything to the prejudice of the Church that could disturb it—what will become of us, if, while many oppose our tumultuous presumption, we give posterity not merely an example but also a cause for presuming such things against us? If indeed that action ought to be called presumption, rather than, more properly, a reprehensible presumption.

Or will anyone think it improper that, lest so great a crime remain uncondemned, that very crime should instead be condemned together with its authors—those who, in condemning Theodore, anathematized so many holy Fathers, so many innocent people, so many persons pleasing and dear to Christ, and the apostles themselves [Note: The passage appears to be corrupt]?

Let them therefore correct their excessively profane rashness; or, if they think they have nothing to correct in what they did, let them give an account of their deed. Let them display the subtlety of intellect in which they greatly glory, not in criticizing the statements of others, but rather in defending their own.

This we ask of your justice: if they attempt to reply, let them no longer be permitted, under the title of your name, to write their own foolish and profane words [Note: The same manuscript has “foolish and profane”]. For although we have learned from the apostles who taught us that we ought to obey God rather than human beings, yet, insofar as it lies with us, we desire both to obey God and to obey human beings, provided that human beings will and command things that are not contrary to the obedience we owe God [Note: The same manuscript has “we desire more to obey”].

# BOOK ELEVEN

## CHAPTER ONE  
### That many ancient Fathers said things similar to those criticized in Theodore, and especially Eustathius of Antioch

[Col. 0793]

There are indeed many statements by which we have refuted from every side the slanders of the Eutychians, who accuse the great Council of Chalcedon even in Theodore’s case. What ground for complaint remains to them now, when we have shown that the same council is defended by invincible and evident reasoning, not only by demolishing the things they were shown to have fabricated [Note: Codex Veronensis has “conceding”], but also by freely granting them many things that were not fabricated, in order to turn them to ridicule?

Yet because we wished to prove to them more fully than we did above how they slander the teaching of many Fathers whom they themselves claim, together with us, to honor, and because we are contending not so much for the already sufficiently and abundantly vindicated synod as for those very Fathers, we have decided in this volume to present statements of great men similar to the more difficult statements for which they thought Theodore should be struck with anathema as if he were the teacher of Nestorius.

Thus, through numerous examples, they may see what the most wise John of Antioch, writing with the Eastern Council to blessed Cyril concerning certain chapters of the aforementioned Theodore, said [Note: In the fifth volume of Cyril’s works, part II, p. 193]:

> “But we have found many statements similar to those considered obscure, spoken by many of his predecessors and by glorious Fathers; and there is no slight danger that, if we reject the statements of that man who died in the episcopate [Note: The same manuscript has “who indeed died”], but who throughout his life was everywhere adorned with ten thousand struggles against the Arians, Eunomians, and other heretics, we may thereby also have to retract many things aptly said by other holy Fathers [Note: The same manuscript has “retract and reject”; and afterward].”

And later:

> “For who among us,” he says, “expects not to die? Or from whom has nothing been said that could offend another?”

This declaration by so great a council would indeed have been sufficient to restrain the rashness of the presumptuous: they would find that many statements similar to the chapters which they criticize in Theodore, because they provided an opportunity for the contrary doctrine to which they adhered, had also been spoken by many earlier and glorious Fathers.

But since the man who until now was rightly believed is no longer believed, and his sound reasoning is disregarded when he again says, “Or from whom has nothing been said that could offend another?”, necessity compels us to present some of the many similar statements of the Fathers and to show how they could cause offense, so that the Eutychians and their allies cannot conceal the fact that, in condemning Theodore’s doctrines, they must also condemn the teaching of those Fathers in whom similar statements are found.

For blessed Eustathius, bishop of Antioch [Note: It should be written Eustathius, Εὐστάθιος; this is what everyone calls him. Eustachius is also given elsewhere through a similar error; he was the judge of Ibas together with Photius, while others call him Eustathius. Various writings of this “holy Eustathius, bishop of Antioch and confessor” are cited by Theodoret in the Dialogues: an Interpretation of the Psalms; a Discourse on “The Lord created me”; a Discourse on the Soul; and also works On the Inscriptions of the Stela and of the Steps. His homily on the Hexaemeron is also seen in ancient libraries, as is his work On the Vision of the Ventriloquist Woman, whose book Saint Jerome mentions in On Illustrious Men. From this work Against the Arians, Anastasius also cites another passage in the Eclogue, in these words: “From Eustathius of Antioch, from the discourse Against the Arians: ‘For if he is created, then he is not begotten; but if he is begotten, then he is not created. For it is not possible for the genus of both to be predicated of the same nature; and it is a sign that it is impossible to say that, with respect to the same nature, the created and the uncreated coexist—for that is universally absurd to the teacher’” (Εὐσταθίου Ἀντιοχείας ἐκ τοῦ κατὰ Ἀῤῥιανῶν λόγου· Εἰ γὰρ κτιστὸς, οὐκ ἄρα γεννητός· εἰ δὲ γεννητὸς, οὐκ ἄρα κτιστός. Ἐπεὶ μηδὲ οἷόν τε περὶ τὴν αὐτὴν φύσιν ἑκατέρων στρέφεσθαι τὸ γένος· σημεῖόν τε, ὅτι ἀδύνατον εἰπεῖν περὶ τὴν αὐτὴν φύσιν τὸ κτιστὸν ὑπάρχειν, καὶ τὸ ἄκτιστον, καθολικὸν γὰρ παράλογον τῷ διδασκάλῳ)], who was first at the Council of Nicaea, says in the sixth book Against the Arians, concerning the Lord’s statement, “No one knows that day” (Matthew 24:36):

> “Let us say, then, for what reason the Son of Man is ignorant of the day of his own coming. For there is no doubt that the Creator and Maker of the human race devised this also, foreseeing the usefulness of human beings. For just as, for the salvation of human beings, he joined humanity to the Word and to God, so also, for the sake of the divine beneficence, he fittingly concealed the notable day of judgment from the man, lest perhaps, by a man announcing ineffable mysteries to human beings of the same kind, he should also reveal the day of the second coming.”

What such thing, I ask, have the Eutychians so far found—or pretended to find—in Theodore against the Council of Chalcedon? To pass over the fact that here he says that the Son of Man is ignorant of the day of his own coming, and did not even say “was ignorant,” so as to seem to have spoken of him as ignorant only before the resurrection, not also after the resurrection, when no ignorance will remain in any of his faithful: to pass over this, as I said, since it can easily be explained as spoken by blessed Eustathius with reference to the period Christ spent here before the resurrection—

and to leave aside also his statement that “for the salvation of human beings he joined humanity to the Word and to God,” which the Eutychians would undoubtedly have accused in Theodore, had he himself said it, as though a man had first existed who was then joined to the Word and to God—

this statement certainly, that the day of judgment was fittingly concealed from Christ so that a man would not reveal the day of the second coming to human beings of the same kind, is something we have not so far known the Eutychians to criticize in Theodore, nor anything comparable to this statement. For when the Apostle, caught up into paradise, heard secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak, and did not disclose them to anyone, but proved a faithful guardian of a divine secret, how can it be said that God concealed the day of judgment from Christ—not, I say, as God, which he is, but merely as a human being, who nevertheless would not have been inferior to Paul—so that he would not reveal it to human beings of the same kind, as though he could not preserve the secret entrusted to him, just as the Apostle preserved it?

Although the Eutychians would not lightly pass over Eustathius’s statement that human beings are like Christ in kind; rather, they would certainly slander him for believing Christ merely a human being and not also God, since he declared all human beings to be like him in kind.

Again, in the same book:

> “When the Son of Man sits,” he says, “on the throne of his majesty (Matthew 19:28), one person appears to speak about another, and he plainly speaks of one about another. Thus the divine Spirit appears clearly to speak of the man, saying, ‘When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty,’ plainly declaring that the man received the glories that came upon him, adorned with justice and virtue, and duly attaining the lofty throne of the kingdom.”

What shall we say here as well? Did Theodore ever treat Christ’s words about himself in such a way as to say that one person was speaking about another, as blessed Eustathius does when he treats his words, “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty”? Do they not attempt to infer, suspiciously or slanderously, from everything for which they criticize Theodore that he wished one person in Christ to be understood as God and another as man? Theodore, indeed, vehemently abhors this; but Eustathius openly says that, in the words of the one Christ speaking about himself, one person plainly speaks about another, and that the statement, “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty,” clearly speaks not of God but of a man.

Nor could the Eutychians tolerate in Theodore the statement that “the man received the glories that came upon him, adorned with justice and virtue.” They would certainly accuse him as though he were saying that Christ was merely a man and not also God, to whom glory had been added that he had not previously possessed, and that he had attained it through progress in justice and virtue, so that, in proportion to this merit, he duly received the throne of the kingdom [Note: Codex Veronensis has “so great a merit”].

Again, in the same book, discussing Christ’s words, he says:

> “‘All things have been delivered to me by my Father’ (Matthew 11:27) is plainly recognized as prophesying from the person of the man, just as we proved earlier. For this man receives the greatest and accruing virtues, advancing in dignity toward better things.”

Here too, when he declares that Christ, while speaking, prophesies from the person of the man, it is implied that he says the person of God to be another. For when, speaking of the man, he says, “This man receives the greatest and accruing virtues,” it has the same force as if he had said, “But that one does not receive them, as God.” By saying also that Christ advanced toward better things through receiving accruing virtues, he testifies that he received what he had not previously possessed and that he made progress.

In the eighth book he likewise says:

> “It must be considered how, while speaking to God and saying, ‘You have destroyed cities’ (Psalm 9:7), the Lord again introduces another, adding, ‘And the Lord remains forever; he has prepared his throne for judgment’ (ibid., 8–9). For he most clearly appears to speak of one about another: he indicated that the one who prepared the throne for him is judge, as though he had not previously possessed this honor. He seemed to speak in this way, for through prophetic figures he was indicating that the man, fittingly made a temple from the members of justice and dwelling in the most sacred Word, attained an everlasting throne through virtue. ‘Speaking to God,’ he says, ‘he again introduces another Lord.’”

If the Eutychians found this in Theodore, they would certainly constrain us with a twofold argument against the Council of Chalcedon, which judged orthodox the letter containing his praises, saying:

> “If he said this about the Father and the Son, how is the Son another Lord, when it is written, ‘For the Lord our God is one Lord’ (Deuteronomy 6:1)? For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not called Lord in such a way that there are three Lords rather than one Lord—just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not called God in such a way that there are three Gods rather than one God. But if, speaking of God the Word and the assumed man, he called the assumed man another Lord, he is accused of dividing the one Christ into two Lords.”

They would also affirm this by the subsequent words:

> “He appears to speak of one about another”;  
> “God the Judge prepared a throne for the assumed man, as though he had not previously possessed this honor.”

Since they prosecute with such hostility the letter of the venerable Ibas for saying “the temple and the one dwelling in it,” what words would suffice for them to exaggerate the charge if he had said what Eustathius says: “The man was fittingly made a temple from the members of justice, so that, dwelling together with the most sacred Word, he might attain an everlasting throne”? For if they say that “dwelling in” signifies two persons in what Ibas says, although the soul dwelling in its own body is one person together with it, how much more would “dwelling together,” and the man’s attaining an everlasting throne through that very indwelling, support the same charge?

Again, in the same book:

> “He does not say that the one who possesses the throne of the kingdom prepares another lot for himself, but rather that one for whom the power of the throne is not present does so. Therefore these things plainly refer to the man of Christ. They should not be attributed to the Almighty, who possesses his own scepter; nor to the Word, who possesses the very kingdom that the Father also possesses. Rather, in Christ it must be said: ‘The Lord in heaven has prepared his throne.’ For he is ruler of all creatures together because of the mingling of the divine Word.”

Let them therefore attend to the nature of this statement as well: he says that another lot was prepared not for God the Word, who possesses the kingdom, but rather for him in whom the power of the throne is absent—that is, for the man of Christ. He did not even say “the man of God the Word”; and he asserts that Christ himself, for whose man he says the throne was prepared, rules all creatures together with God the Father and his Word.

Yet even for these statements, which simple assurance spoke before Nestorius had arisen, his doctrine is not to be anathematized. This will be clear to us if the statements of none of the ancient preachers of the Church are condemned for such reasons. Otherwise, if the writings of any one of them are anathematized, it is necessary, as the most wise John and the Eastern Council said, to include also the statements made by other Fathers.

Let it be enough for posterity that, while resisting the heretics of their own times, they preserved the Church unharmed. Let it be enough that, preparing for us by their labor and diligence many weapons against them, they departed from this world with great praise.

Successors owe no injury to the labor of those who have died; insults must not be returned. If anyone is found ungrateful enough to deny the glory of triumph to those who died victorious after the struggle, I do not know whether anyone except us has brought such an insult.

One preacher of the Church so fought the heretics present in his own time that he gave future generations no, or at least very little, opportunity for attack: he should be judged worthy of the highest praise. Another, intent upon the enemies immediately before him, did not prudently and vigilantly meet others as though they lay hidden in ambush—for they did not yet exist, but would arise at some time [Note: The same manuscript has “less prudently”]. He may be considered worthy of little or even no praise, if that seems appropriate; yet he must not on that account be regarded as an incautious defender of his homeland amid its enemies.

Thus blessed Eustathius, although he could offend many by such statements, is not condemned as the author of the Nestorian error. Rather, he is honored together with many Fathers and above many of them, as the first figure at the Council of Nicaea; and, since the Eutychians raise no hostility against him on this account, he is solemnly named among his predecessors and successors in the liturgical sacrifices.

Perhaps they accuse nothing in this respect because, in the last testimony we cited, he said, “because of the mingling of the divine Word.” For whenever the Eutychians find one of the preachers of the Church saying that God the Word was mingled with a man, they consider the statement to have been made according to their own doctrine.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### That certain statements are found in blessed Athanasius no less difficult than those criticized in Theodore

[Col. 0798D]

We could produce many passages similar to those above from the sayings of that same blessed Eustathius, which could be treated in a single volume [Note: The same manuscript reads: “not in a single [volume]”]; but let these suffice for the reader, since we wish to pass on to the writings of others. From these, likewise, we shall cite not everything similar to what they said, but only certain passages.

What, then, does also Saint Athanasius say in his letter to the Antiochenes? [Note: Athanasius’s synodical letter to the Antiochenes was mentioned in Book VI, when we were discussing hypostasis. It is clear, however, that this was another letter, the one discussed here. Whatever Athanasius wrote in it for refuting the Apollinarians shows that he never distinguished two persons in Christ, but rather two perfect natures in one and the same person: “so that the two things might be one, perfect in every respect, God and man, the same person”—words belonging to Athanasius himself in Book I Against Apollinarius, *On the Incarnation of Christ*.]

[Col. 0799A] “For, instructed by the ancients and being a teacher of the Law, while reading the Proverbs of Solomon and finding two persons concerning the Lord, one concerning the man whom he was to assume from Mary for our sake, the other concerning the Word who was eternally begotten from the Father before all ages, he writes to Timothy concerning Jesus from Mary: ‘Remember that Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, is of the seed of David according to my Gospel’ (2 Tim. 2:8). But concerning God the Word, who is always with the Father, he said that he is all things.” [Note: The same manuscript reads “before all things.”]

I accepted this letter of Saint Athanasius to the Antiochenes—which states that there are two persons, the assumed man and the assuming God the Word, and that certain words of Scripture are appropriate to the Lord Jesus who is from Mary, while others are appropriate to God the Word—with such authority against the Apollinarians in the Church that those who had been converted from that heresy confessed in their own subscriptions that this was their belief.

Therefore Peter, successor to that same Athanasius, writing to the bishops, presbyters, and deacons who had been exiled and sent to Diocaesarea under the emperor Valens, says:

“He is without God, indeed wholly reprobate, who does not confess that the Savior saved the complete man by his coming. And if he saves the whole, he assumed the whole—not as an aid to salvation, but for the salvation of the whole. Therefore let no one who thinks that he holds a pious opinion prove himself more faithless. But if he wishes to inquire, let him learn from the letter that the bishop Athanasius of blessed memory wrote to the Antiochenes, in which he explains everything carefully. Orthodox believers, when they begin to read it, confirm that they hold this belief and have subscribed to it.”

[Col. 0799C] In that same letter to the Antiochenes, then, in which his successor Peter declared that the bishop Athanasius of blessed memory had explained everything carefully, this too is contained:

“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever” (Heb. 13:8).

“‘Yesterday’ signifies eternity before the ages; ‘today,’ the earthly age; and ‘for ever,’ the time after the passing of this life. But Jesus Christ, who is understood according to the man of the Savior, is not the same. For he who received growth in age, being at one time an infant and at another time beginning to be a man, approximately thirty years old, as Luke says, cannot be the same.”

How, then, when Theodorus has been condemned, is Athanasius not also accused as though he had taught two Jesuses and two Christs? For, first speaking of Jesus Christ, who is “yesterday and today and for ever,” he later says that Jesus Christ, who is understood according to the man of the Savior, is not the same, and he gives a reason why he cannot be the same.

Although, if Theodorus had said this, the Eutychians, according to their own accusations, would want these words to be understood as indicating not merely two, but even three Jesus Christs. For the statement does not say, “Jesus Christ, who is understood according to the Savior,” but “according to the man of the Savior.” Thus they could claim that one Jesus Christ was signified, another the man according to whom that Jesus Christ existed, and yet another the Savior whose man that same person was said to be.

Again, in the same letter:

“There is,” he says, “the Holy Spirit of life with the Father and the Son, passing through each of the prophets from generation to generation. He indicates what will be and what has been, having eyes before and behind—that is, as we have said, knowledge of future and past things—which he recounts through Solomon from the person of the Son of Man from Mary, and of the Son of God the Word, who was in the beginning with the Father. He signifies two persons: one, the man created and fashioned from Mary; the other, him who exists before the ages, without beginning, and whose birth is eternal.

“Since, therefore, deceivers in words, unlearned in observing the Spirit and thereby lead the unlearned into error, say, ‘The operation of the Lord’s body has existed for four hundred years,’ and ask how some apply to him what was said, ‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works’ (Prov. 8:22), when Scripture says that he was generated and created before the mountains and hills, before the fountains and before the age—when they say these things, they appear to be praised by certain people, because they do not distinguish which person, speaking by the prophetic Spirit, cries out concerning the Lord’s body and which person Scripture teaches concerning his eternal generation from the Father.”

There are many similar passages in this letter which the Nestorians, although directed against the Apollinarians, could also appropriate in defense of their own error. But Athanasius, or his doctrine, is not for that reason to be condemned. Therefore neither should Theodorus, or his doctrine, be said to have deserved condemnation by the synod for that reason.

We have decided, then, to pass on to other of his short works. Thus the same blessed Athanasius says in his exposition of the Creed. [Note: Athanasius’s work is entitled *Exposition of the Faith*.
