Here, as often elsewhere, Facundus used a defective translator, who had read ὧν (*of which*) instead of ὤν (*being*) in the words: “having been made for us the beginning of the ways, being on earth, he showed us light from darkness.” The meaning is: “Having become for us the beginning of the ways, while he was present on earth, he displayed light to us from darkness.”]

“He who, at the end of the ages, descended from the bosom of the Father, assumed from the immaculate Virgin Mary our man, Jesus Christ, whom for our sake he handed over to suffering.” [Note: These words occur in Athanasius, volume I, p. 99, in the edition of the Benedictines.]

A little later:

“Having been made for us the beginning of the ways, while he was on earth, he showed us light from darkness, salvation from error, life from the dead, and entry into paradise, from which Adam was excluded. [Note: In Athanasius, same work, p. 100, Montfaucon conjectures that the reading should be ‘on the earth, IN WHICH.’ The Greek is: ἀρχὴ ὁδῶν κτισθεὶς ἡμῶν, ἐν τῇ γῇ ὢν, ἡμῖν ἔδειξεν, κ. τ. λ. (“Having been made for us the beginning of ways, being on earth, he showed us,” etc.).] He entered it again through the thief, as the Lord said: ‘Today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke 23:43). Paul also entered it. He showed an ascent into heaven, where the Lord’s man, who had gone before us, entered for our sake, and in which he will judge the living and the dead.” [Note: “The Lord’s man” (*κυριακὸς ἄνθρωπος*). Augustine does not deny that Christ can in some sense be called the Lord’s man, although he later retracts this expression as used by himself, in Book I, chapter 19, since Christ is certainly the Lord. For this same reason Gregory of Nazianzus rebukes the Apollinarians, who habitually spoke in this way, in Letter 1 to Cledonius: “Let these men not deceive others, nor be deceived themselves, by accepting the Lord’s man, as they call him, as devoid of mind—or rather our Lord and God.”]

And a little further on:

[Note: Athanasius, same work, p. 101: “The salvation created for us as a planting is new and not old, for us and not before us. It is Jesus, who became man according to the Savior; this name is interpreted sometimes as ‘salvation’ and sometimes as ‘Savior.’” That is: “The salvation created for us as a planting, new and not old, for us and not before us, is Jesus, who became man insofar as he is the Savior.” Facundus’s translation must therefore be corrected.]

“That salvation which was created for us for our planting is new and not old, for us and not for those who came before us: Jesus, who became man according to the Savior, whose name is interpreted as shepherd, salvation, and sometimes also Savior.” [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: ‘Jesus is, who’; the Greek has Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν.] [Note: In Greek, *πὴ μὲν σωτηρία, πὴ δὲ σωτήρ* means “sometimes salvation, sometimes Savior”; hence “shepherd” is incorrect here.]

Let them therefore accuse him also, as though he were saying, according to Nestorius, that the Son of God is one person and our man Jesus Christ another. For he does not say that the Son of God himself handed himself over for us, as the Apostle said, but rather that the Son, descending from the bosom of the Father, assumed our man Jesus Christ. Which man? The one whom he calls “the Lord’s man,” in whom he will judge the living and the dead—as though, with a misguided understanding, he had considered the Lord the Son who will judge the living and the dead to be one person, and the Lord’s man in whom he will judge to be another.

Let them also accuse him because he similarly says, “It is Jesus, the man who became according to the Savior,” claiming that by saying “according to the Savior” rather than “the Savior,” he separated Jesus from the Savior.

He also wrote a book Against the Manichaeans. [Note: No work of Athanasius bearing this title, or having this beginning, survives today. Both the title and the opening correspond to a book by Serapion, bishop of Thmuis, Against the Manichaeans, which contains the words quoted by Facundus and attributed by him to Athanasius. The fraud concerning the author’s name, however, is less serious than the error concerning the name Jesus, which has been improperly inserted here into those words and is not found in Serapion. Serapion speaks only of people who are converted from depraved conduct to better pursuits; to apply this to Christ the Lord is impious. Someone who supplied this passage misled Facundus.]

Its beginning is: “Truth has dissolved error.” In it he says:

“When I see the man Jesus, I understand what he is; but when I contemplate the manner, I marvel and do not recognize it, for change produces astonishment. The essences, however, have not been changed: the body remains, not having become something else. For the body was not changed into something incorporeal, nor did another soul come into existence in its essence. But although the essences remained, the dispositions did not remain. For dispositions are by no means essential; otherwise they would remain with the essences and would not be taken away.”

If everything that our presumptuous defenders, in their stupidity, have been unable either to defend or to understand properly is to be condemned according to their own preference, how can these passages not also be condemned? [Note: The same manuscript reads “let them be condemned.”] Or, if they can understand and defend these passages properly, why do they not also understand and defend those of Theodorus which are censured [Note: The same manuscript reads “censure.”] to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon?

Behold, Athanasius also says that when he contemplates the manner in the man Jesus, he marvels and does not recognize it, because the change produces astonishment. Let them therefore tell us how Athanasius’s doctrine can be defended while Theodorus and his doctrines are condemned under anathema, if the sayings of the Fathers are to be judged according to the sound of their words and not according to the intention of their mind. Let them explain what change took place in the man Jesus without the essences being changed, or what dispositions in him did not remain while the essences themselves remained.

For if Theodorus were found to have said these things, they would detest him as though he had preached that Christ had been converted from a corrupt way of life and evil dispositions to better dispositions. Athanasius certainly did not mean this; and far be it from us to believe that he thought this—not only that the man Jesus had at some time been divided from God the Word by a personal division, as Nestorius held, but also that he had at some time been divided from him by evil dispositions.

Moreover, this final passage, as well as the earlier passages of his that we have recalled, requires an interpreter. With God’s help, they can be defended much more easily than the blessed Athanasius himself defended the words of his predecessor Dionysius. We could indeed show, insofar as the Lord grants us ability, how these passages are rightly to be understood, and repay this kind and devout Father the service which he himself previously rendered in explaining the words of his predecessor Dionysius. But this would be lengthy, and in this work we have undertaken not to interpret the writings of venerable Fathers, but to refute the accusations of the Eutychians on behalf of the great synod.

For their refutation it is enough if those Fathers whom the Eutychians do not dare to criticize are shown to have said things as similar to, or more difficult than, the statements for which they claim that Theodorus and the letter praising him ought to have been condemned.

## CHAPTER III. That Amphilochius of Iconium also wrote things similar to those criticized in Theodorus

Let us now produce certain statements from the writings of the blessed Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium. [Note: What was said above of Athanasius must be understood likewise of Amphilochius in these statements of his: he distinguishes two natures in Christ, not persons. For he expressly professed this in his letter to Seleucus: ‘the form of God and the form of a slave combine into one person, and [there is] one Son of two natures’ (τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ μορφὴν, καὶ τὴν τοῦ δούλου μορφὴν, συντελεῖν εἰς ἓν πρόσωπον· καὶ ἕνα Υἱὸν δύο φύσεων). This is also the point of what he says in another letter to Pancharius, deacon of Sida: ‘Truly impious and alien from truth is he who does not say that Christ, the Savior and Maker of all, according to both those things of which he naturally consists, is self-governing and active, and free from every necessity’ (Ἀσεβὴς ὄντως ἐστὶ, καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀλλότριος, ὁ μὴ λέγων τὸν Χριστὸν τὸν σωτῆρα τῶν ὅλων καὶ ποιητὴν, κατ᾽ ἄμφω τὰ ἐξ ὧν ἐστι κατὰ φύσιν, αὐτεξούσιον καὶ ἐνεργῆ, καὶ πάσης ἀνάγκης ἐλεύθερον). Finally, Theodoret, who adduces almost all these very statements of Amphilochius in the Dialogues, adduces them in order to show the properties of two natures in the one person of Christ.] The most wise John of Antioch, together with the Eastern council, pronounced him to be a most approved teacher. The emperors Gratian and the elder Theodosius also judged him to be such that they ordered—as we recalled in the fourth book—that only those should possess churches who were shown to be Catholics through communion with the aforementioned holy Amphilochius, Diodorus, and other similar men. [Note: The same manuscript reads “Valentinian and the elder Theodosius.”]

Speaking, then, about the statement “The Father who sent me is greater than I,” in a discourse beginning, “The contest of the heretics has made us weary,” he says: [Note: Theodoret, in Dialogue III, cites this passage as from the discourse *Against the Arians*; and Leontius in turn cites the words, ‘Distinguish, then, the natures,’ which Theodoret had cited in Dialogues I and II as from the discourse on ‘My Father is greater than I,’ while he himself cites them as from the discourse *Against the Arians*. From this it is clear that this book of Amphilochius had a double title.]

“You see that the Father is greater when he says, ‘Let us go’ (Matt. 26:46), not when he says, ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them’ (2 Cor. 6:16). You see that the Father is greater when he says, ‘I am the vine’ (John 15:1), not when he says, ‘I planted the true vine’ (Jer. 2:21). And, not to prolong my speech, I ask you briefly, heretic: Who suffered—the one who was born from God before the ages, or Jesus, who was generated from David in the last times? If the divinity suffered, you have spoken blasphemy; but if the man suffered, as the truth holds, why do you not apply suffering to the man, or join the humble words to him?”

Thus this most approved teacher too can be accused, as though he were indicating one person who said, “Let us go” and “I am the vine,” and another who said, “I will dwell in them” and “I planted the true vine.” He plainly teaches that it was not the one born from God before the ages who suffered, but rather the one generated from David in the last times. [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “Jesus, who …”]

In discussing the statement, “Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life” (John 5:24), he says:

“If you attribute sufferings to the flesh, attribute humble words to it as well; and to the one to whom you ascribe miracles, apply heavenly words. For God, who performs miracles, rightly speaks exalted words worthy of his works; but the man who suffers rightly speaks humble words worthy of his sufferings.”

Here too he may be blamed for saying that the God who performs miracles is not himself also the man who suffered.

Again, in a discourse beginning, “Come, today let us reach contentious arguments,” [Note: The Greek is *Φέρε, σήμερον* and so forth. It should have been translated “Come,” not “Bring.” I have already explained the kind of Greek versions Facundus was accustomed to use. I do not recall this Amphilochian discourse being mentioned elsewhere; the others, as I said, are cited by Theodoretus.]

Speaking about the statement, “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God” (John 20:17), he says:

“The Father is common: he is his Father by nature, but our Father by grace. He is also commonly called God [Note: The same manuscript reads: ‘God God’; but ...]; but he is our God because he made us exist from things that did not exist, while he is that man’s God according to the flesh. For he himself formed the flesh in the Virgin, he himself anointed it in the Jordan, he himself proclaimed it, he himself glorified it in the Passion, he himself raised it from the dead, he himself carried it up in the empty cloud, making it worthy to sit at his right hand. For the one who ascended to the Father possesses all these things by taking them with him; not the one who is in the Father.”

In this passage too he may be accused because he does not say that the one who is in the Father is the one who ascended to the Father.

Again, concerning the statement, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” in a discourse beginning, “Then, like a duly enlisted soldier,” he says:

“If the Son of Man must be handed over, how can you say, ‘If it is possible, let this cup pass from me’? And if you did not wish to suffer, why did you say, ‘Let this cup pass from me’? It is not I, who made heaven and founded the earth, but, according to you, a man, who speaks while shrinking from death.”

Again:

“Since I am God and man, say who suffered. If God suffered, you have spoken blasphemy; but if the flesh suffered, why do you not apply the suffering to him in whom you place the fear? For when one suffers, another does not fear; and when a man is crucified, God is not troubled.”

I think that in this chapter too the reader cannot fail to notice that he says that the man who suffered is one person and the God who felt no fear when the man was crucified is another.

Therefore, if anyone condemns Theodorus or his sayings, he is consequently compelled to condemn Eustathius, Athanasius, and Amphilochius—most approved teachers—or their sayings as well.

What, then? If some error appears to us in Theodorus, or in anyone who died in the peace of the Church, must it for that reason be approved and followed? Far from it. But we must first investigate the matter and consult those who are better instructed, lest what appears culpable to us have been uttered by its author with another intention. The one who spoke must not be judged merely on the basis of what seems to us to be the case, without being questioned—especially if he is found to have said other things contrary to the error into which he is believed to have fallen.

For often a scrupulous and subtle inquiry, just as it recoils from the exposed deceits of heretics, rejoices when it discovers the simplicity of Catholics. But if the error of certain people who died in the peace of the Church is so certain that it cannot be excused by the considerations we have mentioned, then the errors themselves should be confronted without bringing disgrace upon them, without offense or disturbance to the Church, and without naming the persons concerned. In this way due reverence may be shown to preachers who died in the peace of the Church, while the defense of the truth may cause offense to no Catholic.

We know that holy and serious men acted in this way, men who did not boast of criticizing others; and we imitate them all the more appropriately and profitably. Just as the teaching of those who stood outside the Church, although they wrote many true and necessary things, cannot on account of those correct and necessary matters be judged Catholic, so the teaching of members of the Church, even if they are shown to have erred in certain matters, must not on account of those matters be condemned as heretical.

## CHAPTER IV. That similar passages occur in Gregory’s books Against Eunomius to those criticized in the books of Theodorus
Now let us also produce what Saint Gregory says in the third book of his work Against Eunomius.[Note: Gregory of Nyssa’s books Against Eunomius number thirteen, though they are not all ordinarily cited in the same way. What is presented here first as coming from the third book of his work is likewise assigned to the third book by Anastasius’s Ecloge; but Leontius assigns it to the second book. In reality, these passages occur in the fourth book of the Greek-Latin edition; and in the fifth book occur all the remaining passages that Facundus cites from the fourth. It would be superfluous to investigate the reasons for this variation.]

“Neither does human nature,” he says, “give life to Lazarus, nor does an impassible power weep over the one lying there; but it is proper to the human being to weep, whereas giving life belongs to that which is truly life. Human want does not feed thousands of people; omnipotent power does not run to the fig tree. Who is weary from the journey? And who, without labor, established the whole world by a word? Who is this brightness of glory? And what is it that has been fastened with nails? Which form is struck with blows in the passion, and which is glorified from eternity? For these things are evident, even if they are interpreted by no discourse. For the wounds belong to the servant, in whom the Lord exists; but the honors belong to the Lord, around whom the servant is recognized.”

Do you observe how Saint Gregory, not supposing two Christs or two sons,[Note: Eunomius had, among other accusations, charged Basil with proclaiming two Christs and two Lords. Gregory, whose purpose in these books was to defend Basil, refutes the slander in Book IV: “He accused us of saying two Christs and two Lords, not having grounds to prove the charge from our writings, but using falsehood at will, according to what seemed expedient.” Greek: Δύο Χριστοὺς καὶ δύο Κυρίους λέγειν ἡμᾶς ᾐτιάσατο· οὐκ ἐκ τῶν ἡμετέρων ἐλέγχειν τὴν αἰτίαν ἔχων, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ δοκοῦν κατ’ ἐξουσίαν τῷ ψεύδει χρώμενος. Much less, then, should he appear to have held this view himself.] teaches that it was proper to the human being to weep, but that giving life belongs to that which is truly life; and, questioning the heretic as an orthodox Christian, says: “Who is weary from the journey? And who, without labor, established the whole world by a word?”—and so forth. Then he closes his argument by affirming that the wounds belong to the servant, in whom the Lord exists, while the honors belong to the Lord, around whom the servant is recognized.

Do we therefore believe that he said these things according to the error of Nestorius—as though the Lord who existed in the servant belonged to one hypostasis, and the servant in whom he existed to another? Or that the Lord to whom the honor must be attributed belonged to one person, while the servant who is recognized around the Lord, and to whom the wounds must be assigned, belonged to another?

Again, in the same work, Book IV, he says:

“For just as he who did not know sin becomes sin, in order to take away the sin of the world, so likewise the flesh that receives the Lord becomes Christ and Lord. For, through union, it is changed into what it was not by nature.”

And shortly afterward:

“Let it be known to the whole house of Israel that God made this Jesus Lord and Christ, whom you crucified. By this demonstration they think they can show that the essence of God’s Only-Begotten is a creature. What then, tell me: did the cross exist before the world? Did Pilate exist before all creation? Did Jesus come first, and the Word afterward? Is flesh older than divinity? Did Gabriel announce the Gospel to Mary before the establishment of the world? Did that man who is beside Christ receive the beginning of his generation under Caesar Augustus? But the Word was God in the beginning, and our King before the ages, as the prophecy also bears witness. Do you not see what sort of confusion, upward and downward, according to the proverb, you are stirring up concerning the Word of God? It was the fiftieth day after the passion when Peter preached these things to the Jews, saying: ‘God made this Jesus, whom you crucified, Christ and Lord’ (Acts 2:36). Do you not attend to the order of the words—to what is placed first and what second in what is said? For he did not say, ‘You crucified him whom God made Lord’; rather, he says: ‘You crucified him; this one God made Christ and Lord.’”

Here too, speaking of the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, he says that the flesh which receives the Lord becomes Christ and Lord. Yet it must not be supposed that Gregory believed that a mere human being, who was not also God, had first existed and then received the Lord. What, then, could the Semi-Eutychians or their supporters reply if they were told: “You think that Theodorus ought to have been condemned by the Council of Chalcedon; why do you not condemn Gregory?”

For while we believe that Christ—that is, the Anointed One—is none other than God incarnate, and while anointing is more appropriately associated with human nature, Gregory himself says: “The flesh that receives the Lord becomes Christ.” Yet he also says:

“Was it not that man who is beside Christ who received the beginning of his generation under Caesar Augustus? But the Word was God in the beginning.”

If, then, the flesh—that is, the man—received the Lord and became Christ, who likewise is that man beside Christ who received the beginning of his generation under Caesar Augustus? Or why does he assert that confusion, upward and downward, according to the proverb, is stirred up concerning the Word of God by what was said—namely, that God made this one whom you crucified Christ and Lord? And he urges Eunomius, against whom he is arguing, to pay attention to the order of the words and to understand what is first and what second in what is said. He then adds:

“For he did not say, ‘You crucified him whom God made Lord’; rather, he says: ‘You crucified him; this one God made Christ and [human] Lord.’”[Note: From what was said above, “human” seems to be required here.]

What then? Was he not Christ and Lord before the passion—the one who was afterward crucified—but became Christ and Lord only after the crucifixion, as a reward for his passion? And how was it said above that the flesh which receives the Lord becomes Christ and Lord? Did the flesh receive the Lord only after the crucifixion?

Accordingly, if these statements are brought as an accusation against the Eutychians, will they also condemn Gregory? Or will they try to understand and explain them more accurately?

Saint Athanasius too, in the book he composed on the Trinity, as we mentioned in our third book, spoke similarly in order to distinguish the natures:

“For the Word and Son of God was always Lord God, and he did not become Lord Christ after the crucifixion; rather, as I have already said, his divinity made his humanity Lord and God.”

But let us return to our subject. The same Saint Gregory says again in the same book:

“Having the divine Scripture in our hands for interpretation, the great Apostle forbids us to accept old-womanish novelties. When I perceive the cross, I understand the cross; and, instructed by the human name, I contemplate in the name itself the nature that is signified. I am therefore taught by Peter that this one was made Lord and Christ; and I do not hesitate to say that this one, who was made so before our eyes, was made so by him, because the saints agree with one another both in this and in all other matters. For just as this man says that the one who was crucified was made Lord, so Paul too says that he was supremely exalted after the passion and after the resurrection.”

Let the reader also observe in this statement that when Gregory says, “I am therefore taught by Peter that this one was made Lord and Christ,” and repeats the point by saying, “I do not hesitate to say that this one, who was made so before our eyes, was made so by him,” it has the same force as if he had said: “This one—not the one who was Lord before the ages.” Yet he does not thereby teach that there are two sons, one in this person and another in that.

Confirming his earlier statement, he again asserts that he was made Lord after the crucifixion when he says: “For just as Peter says that the one who was crucified was made Lord, so Paul says that he was supremely exalted after the passion and after the resurrection.”

Therefore, just as he asserts through the testimony of Paul that he was exalted after the passion and resurrection—Paul saying, “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:8–9)—so he also affirms that he was made Lord after the passion and resurrection, as the Apostle Peter says of him:

“Let it be known to the whole house of Israel that God made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36).

Again, in the same book, he says:

“So that what belongs to piety may be preserved concerning both, he demonstrates that the human things were glorified through assumption, while the divine things were in no way defiled through descent. He assigns humanity to the passions, but the operation of the resurrection to the divine power of the one who suffered. Thus the experience of death is referred to the one who shared in passible nature, because of the union of the human being with him; and likewise the higher and divine names descend to the human being.”

If Theodorus had said, “He assigns humanity to the passions, but the operation of the resurrection to the divine power of the one who suffered,” would learned men not have proclaimed this to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon, saying that he speaks of “the one who suffered” as though God the Word, who did not suffer, were a different person?[Note: The same manuscript reads “would not boast,” rather than “would not proclaim.”]

Or when he adds immediately afterward, “Thus the experience of death is referred to the one who shared in passible nature,” would they not accuse Theodorus, as they usually do, saying that he did not believe God and the man to be of the same person, since he said that what belongs to the one who suffered—that is, to the man—is referred to the one who shared in passible nature—that is, to God the Word? In this way the man’s passion would be attributed, by reference, to God the Word himself, just as the higher things, which belong to God the Word, and the divine names likewise descend to the human being.

Again, speaking of this same matter in the same book, he says:

“For if it were proper to say that something had happened by way of progress in that exalted nature—for example, that from a private person he became king, from the lowly the exalted, from a servant the Lord—it would perhaps be proper also to adapt Peter’s utterance to the divine person of the Only-Begotten.”[Note: The same manuscript reads “nature.”]

“But since the divinity, whatever it is that we believe it to be, always remains the same and stands above every addition, suffering no diminution, it is necessary in every respect to refer the statement to humanity. For God the Word, who was in the beginning, is also now what he was, and remains forever: always King, always Lord, always Most High, always God. He acquired none of these things by progress; rather, everything that is said of him subsists by the power of his nature. But he who was exalted from man to God through assumption, existing as one thing and made another, is properly and truly said to have been made Christ and Lord. For from a servant and subject he made him king, from the obedient one he made him Christ; he supremely exalted what was lowly, and he gave to the one who possessed a human name the name that is above every name.”

Having considered these things, let those who judged Theodorus, together with his doctrines, worthy of condemnation—as though he had said that something was added to Christ by progress according to his humanity—take heed. For whether Theodorus said this[Note: The same manuscript reads “whether Theodorus may have said this.”] or did not say it, Gregory meanwhile says that, by way of progress, Christ was made king from a private person, exalted from the lowly, and Lord from a servant in the humanity he assumed.

For God the Word, who was in the beginning, is also now and always what he was, and acquired none of these things by progress. But he who was exalted from man to God through assumption, while existing by nature as one thing and being made another, was properly and truly made Christ and Lord—the assumption of God the Word making him king from a servant and subject, and Christ from one who obeyed.

Let them therefore accuse Gregory also of introducing two sons, because he said: “God the Word acquired nothing by progress; but he was exalted from man to God through assumption.” Let them accuse him as though he were saying that the Lord Jesus was once so much a servant and subject that he was not also king and Lord; or that he was first merely obedient and afterward became Christ by the merit of that obedience; or that he was ever so lowly that he was not also exalted; or that he at some time possessed a human name without also possessing the name that is above every name. For Gregory said this as well:

“He supremely exalted what was lowly, and gave to the one who possessed a human name the name that is above every name.”

Let them also accuse him because he said: “He who was exalted from man to God is properly and truly said to have been made Christ and Lord,” as though the man, once made Christ and Lord, had ceased to be man, so that it could be said that Christ and Lord had been made from man.

From this the reader may infer how many such statements may be found in the books of this holy Gregory, since we have produced so many not only from the same work but even from the same book as we judged necessary for the case. Yet his doctrine does not deserve to be condemned under an anathema on account of such statements.

First, because those who ended their present life in glory are not worthy of infamy. Moreover,[Note: The Codex Veronensis reads “Therefore.”] the Eastern Fathers also said:

“But if anyone should say, holy emperor, that something obscure is found in the writings of Theodorus or others, it is not necessary to retract it. Since their life in the priesthood and ministry had an excellent end, we dedicate glory to them as their due, and we do not judge them on the basis of those matters with which some violently accuse them. For it is impossible, when those who teach in the Church are human beings, that they should escape the censures of their accusers.”

Further, because great harm and confusion also arise in the Church from this. Hence the Fathers mentioned above said again:

“What harm, corruption, and confusion would not arise from this if we opened the door to those who wish to overturn the statements of the Fathers who have passed away? What damage would not become manifest if we not only rejected their statements but also anathematized them?”

It is one matter if one statement pleases someone and another does not, whether the statements belong to ancient writers, later writers, or our own contemporaries. But to impose an anathema upon them as well appears bold and harsh, even if the persons are not anathematized together with their statements.

## CHAPTER V  
### That certain statements of John Chrysostom are also similar to those criticized in the writings of Theodorus

Let us now proceed to the statements of Saint John of Constantinople, so that either he too may bear, together with Theodorus—his ancient friend and fellow student from the beginning—the same odium from the Eutychians, or may repel it from that man and from the Council of Chalcedon.

In a certain sermon beginning, “Once again the race of horses,” he says:

“When, therefore, he says, ‘If it is possible, let this cup pass from me,’ and, ‘Not as I will, but as you will,’ he shows nothing other than that he truly clothed himself with flesh that feared death. To fear death, to wish to escape it, and to be in agony belong to the flesh. At this time he left it deserted and stripped of its proper operation, so that, by displaying its weakness, he might make its nature manifest.”

We have already demonstrated in Book III how the same blessed John taught that Christ, according to his humanity, feared death. But for the present we wish to attend to the fact that he says: “At this time he left it deserted and stripped of its proper operation,” although we believe that God the Word united the flesh to himself in one hypostasis in such a way that it can never be separated from him. Yet John declares that it was deserted by him, in a sound sense that the stupidity of the Eutychians could not investigate and their impiety could neither calmly nor reverently accept.

Again, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, Book III, he says:

“Consider how great is the distance between human nature and God’s nature, and how from this lowliness he led it up to that honor. He did not transcend by one degree only, nor by a second, nor by a third—behold!”[Note: In Greek: Βαβαῖ, “Good heavens!” or “Ah!” The Greek indicates an exclamation, not merely a simple continuation.]

“He did not simply say ‘up,’ but ‘above the heights,’ for he is superior to the powers above. Therefore he led up there the one who is from among us; from the lowest limit he led him up to the highest principality, beyond which there is no other honor: ‘above every principality,’ he says—not above this one but not that one, but above every power, virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named in heaven and on earth, he was made superior. This is worthy of wonder concerning the one who was raised from the dead, but not at all concerning the Word of God.”[Note: The same manuscript reads “to the highest,” corresponding to the preceding phrase: “From the lowest limit he led him up to the highest principality.”]

By saying here that the divine nature led up the one who is from among us, he did not intend two sons to be understood. Nor should we therefore take in that sense what he said at the end of this statement: “This is worthy of wonder concerning the one who was raised from the dead, but not at all concerning the Word of God.”

Again, in the same book:

“For he did two great things: he himself came to the deepest humiliation, and he raised man to great excellence; he saved him in his blood. He said the former when he said that he humbled himself so greatly; he says the latter afterward, calling it great and supreme. And even if we had not been made worthy of anything, that would have been sufficient; and even if, apart from this, we had been made worthy without being killed, that would have been sufficient. But when there are two things, what greatness of speech could fail to overcome and surpass?”

When I consider these things, the resurrection does not seem so great. Concerning this one he says, “The God of our Lord Jesus Christ,” not “the God of the Word.”

Who, then, could call John here an inventor of the Nestorian doctrine because he said: “He himself came to the deepest humiliation”; and again: “God the Word raised man to great excellence”; and: “The one in whose blood he saved us”? Or because he says below, “Concerning this one he says, ‘The God of our Lord Jesus Christ,’ not ‘the God of the Word,’” as though our Lord Jesus Christ were not, by the unity of hypostasis, himself also God the Word?

In his interpretation of the Epistle to the Hebrews, Sermon 14,[Note: Montfaucon, in the preface to volume XII of Chrysostom’s works, §8, writes: “It seems certain that copies of the Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews were issued after Chrysostom’s death, differing in many respects from the copy of the presbyter Constantine. As a witness to this we may cite Facundus of Hermiane, who in Book XI, chapter 5, quotes a passage from Homily 13, which he himself calls Sermon 14. This is because, in his copy, the long introduction or argument placed before the homilies was counted and entitled as Sermon 1—a practice we have observed more than once in other commentaries. In this matter Facundus does not entirely agree with the translator Mutianus.” The passage cited by Facundus is found in the same volume XII, p. 134.] concerning what is written, “As the priesthood according to Leviticus was brought to completion,” he says:

“Another prophet says, ‘No deceit was found in his mouth’; that is, no cunning. Perhaps someone would say this about God, and would not be ashamed to say that God is not cunning or deceitful. But concerning the one who is according to the flesh, he may perhaps have an explanation.”

Here too, although he says that the prophet’s statement, “No deceit was found in his mouth,” was written not about God the Word but about the one who is according to the flesh, he nevertheless did not intend two Christs or two sons to be understood.

In a sermon on the Lord’s Ascension,[Note: Chrysostom’s sermons on the Ascension are represented by different passages in Theodoret, Dialogue II, and Leontius of Byzantium, Book I, both drawn from the sermon beginning, “And when we celebrate the remembrance of the cross.” John Cyparissiota also cites passages from another sermon beginning, “Every festival is joyful.” Both sermons were printed in volume V of the English edition. The sermon used here by Facundus has not yet been published.] beginning, “Today we celebrate a marvelous festival,” he says:

“Certainly, one ought to express the distinction in this way. To his angels he says, ‘Who makes his angels spirits’ (Hebrews 1:7); but to the Son, ‘The Lord created me’; or, ‘God made him Lord and Christ.’ Yet neither statement was spoken about the Son, nor was the latter spoken about God the Word, but about the one who is according to the flesh.”

Do you see how John in this statement too says that “He created me” was spoken not about the Son but about the one who is according to the flesh? Yet he must not therefore be thought by true and devout believers to have denied that the one who is according to the flesh is the Son.

## CHAPTER VI  
### That when the holy Fathers err in anything, their intention should be excused, lest they be judged heretics

Why, then, are these statements—whether of Saint John himself or of the other Fathers whom we have mentioned, together with many others that we omit in order to avoid excessive length—not considered heretical? It is because the intention of those who speak excuses the offensiveness of their words; and words are judged more accurately according to that intention.

It is the intention of the mind that presides over our words and also over our deeds, as a kind of eye presides over the body. Concerning this the Lord says:

“The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?” (Matthew 6:22–23).

Thus the sound eye of these Fathers—that is, their intention, by which they answered heretics on behalf of Christ’s Church before the controversy concerning Nestorius had arisen—made the whole body of their doctrine luminous.

But if someone now uses these words of the Fathers, or even of divine Scripture, with an evil eye—that is, with an intention directed against the Church—in support of the Nestorian doctrine, his whole body will be dark.

It is not granted to us in this life that the work we undertake should equal the intention of our mind, or that our action should be as perfect and great as our intention. What shines perfectly in a good intention becomes somewhat dim in speech or action. If the intention itself grows dark, then the words and deeds proceeding from it will be much darker.

For this reason the Lord also added: “If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?”

Accordingly, the writings of these Fathers, and of any others like them, should be read in such a way that, wherever something offends us in them, we either interpret it more favorably or leave its interpretation to better judges. If the error is so certain that it cannot be excused, let us believe that they were later able to correct it—or, even if the place where they corrected it is not read—that we may not blame the Church of Christ more than we blame them for a lapse that escaped their notice.

If some, because of the ambiguity of a new question concerning which no single general judgment had yet been established—as happened at one time when the blessed Cyprian believed that all heretics should be baptized[Note: The same manuscript reads “the martyr Cyprian”]—or because of the security of that period, since they were not yet assailed, as we are, by opposing controversies; or because the matter perhaps remained hidden from the Church, so that they were not admonished; if, I say, they are judged to have remained in the error itself, let the religious intention of those who fell excuse their weakness.

And since they remained in the charity of the Church, let us believe that charity itself covered their faults, as it is written: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8).

For who in the Church of Christ is so inhuman and harsh that, even if he knew that Augustine, a man endowed with such piety, had erred in matters whose faith we are considering and had remained in error without being admonished, he would call or think him a heretic?

At the beginning of his books on the Trinity he says:

“I shall not be ashamed to inquire wherever I am uncertain, nor shall I be ashamed to learn wherever I err. Therefore, whoever reads these things, where he is equally certain, should proceed with me; where he is equally uncertain, he should inquire with me; where he recognizes his own error, he should return to me; where he recognizes mine, he should call me back.[Note: The words “where he is equally uncertain, he should inquire with me” are absent here.] Thus let us enter together upon the way of charity, making our way toward him of whom it is said: ‘Seek his face always’ (Psalm 104:4). And this pious and safe agreement I have entered before the Lord our God with all who read what I write, especially in all my writings, and most of all in those where the unity of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is sought. For nowhere is error more dangerous, nowhere is anything sought with greater labor, and nowhere is anything found more fruitfully.”

Who, then, would call Augustine a heretic when he entered the way of charity and advanced toward God, professing that he was not ashamed to learn wherever he might err, and urging others to call him back from his error? Who would do so if he should be proved to have erred in these matters, and to have remained in error without anyone admonishing him, when his very readiness to correct himself and his exhortation that he be recalled from his error ought to be esteemed more highly than correction itself?

For often people are corrected because they are weighed down by shame or constrained by necessity.[Note: The manuscript reads “we are corrected.”] But Augustine, without any shame, binds all who read his writings by a solemn divine testimony to recall him:

“And this agreement,” he says, “I have entered, pious and safe before the Lord our God, with all who read what I write.”

Would this agreement, which he believed he had entered with all who read his writings, not have been safe for him and pious before the Lord our God even if he had remained in some error without being admonished? Who but a cruel person would say or believe this?

Let us therefore regard other teachers of the Church as Augustine showed himself to us. We shall call no one a heretic who died in the peace and honor of the Church. What harm is there for me if I think this way about everyone—even if not everyone was such?

Someone may perhaps say: “You rightly believe this about Augustine, whose profession reveals his mind; but why should you believe this about others?” As though the person who objects knew for certain that the others had not said the same thing; as though he had read everything written by everyone and remembered it all; or as though Augustine’s mind was such because he spoke in this way, rather than his speaking in this way because his mind was such.

Accordingly, even if he had said nothing of this kind, his mind would nevertheless have had the same disposition: prepared to correct whatever had rightly caused offense. If we were to think well even of this disposition in him, our judgment would certainly be both pious and true, although it might seem uncertain.

Let us therefore think the same about the minds of others, because for the present this is pious, even if it appears uncertain. If we think badly of them, that too will not be certain—but it will certainly be impious. It is therefore better to choose between two uncertainties the one in which certain piety is approved than the one in which certain impiety is condemned.

I believe that even those who do not wish to think about the other teachers of the Church as they do about Augustine—because they do not find that those teachers similarly urged readers to correct them for their statements—should judge it impious to believe that none of the others was prepared to be corrected if something in his writings rightly offended the reader.

If it is impious to believe that no other person had the same disposition, how does he know that the man whom he considers worthy of condemnation was not such a person?

It follows in every way, therefore, that no one who died in the peace of the Church should be condemned merely for such ignorance, except through great impiety and rashness.

Accordingly, if someone had accused Theodorus before the holy Council of Chalcedon, and could have demonstrated—and did demonstrate—some of his errors, that council would undoubtedly have acted modestly and piously if it had also formed a favorable judgment concerning his uncertain intention.

But he was accused before that council,[Note: The same manuscript reads: “Theodorus was neither accused before that council, nor was…”] and his intention was not uncertain. In the preceding book we showed that he had voluntarily and deliberately confessed his negligence even in the work for which he was praised by his friend Cerdon, so that no one, led astray by the authority of his name, might follow one who was in error. He had not disregarded the offense of his hearers when he said something that he did not think had been correctly stated; rather, he overcame the shame that is harmful by removing the same offense that he had incurred through an inadvertent expression.

That correction cleansed him not only from the matters in which his error was plainly evident, but also from any similar matters.

Why, then, should he not be praised for the rest of his sound doctrine, when he ought to be praised even in the error itself through which he taught us by his example rather than by his words both to confess our errors voluntarily and to correct without shame an offense for which we have been reproved?

There is therefore no reason to blame the holy council concerning the case of Theodorus. It did not impose upon anyone, by the authority of his statements, that they should be read without examination, or that everything he wrote should be held by everyone as unshaken and beyond scrutiny.

His writings should therefore be included among those concerning which the Apostle says: “Test everything; hold fast what is good.”

We read the divine Scriptures, which are called canonical, in one way; we read the writings of those who advanced through their zeal for reading and writing and who, by the ability acquired through daily labor, spoke about these matters as they were able, in another way. Among the latter was that most wise and modest man Augustine, who says in the third book on the Trinity:

“Certainly, in all my writings I desire not only a devout reader but also a free corrector, and especially in those writings where I wish the greatness of the question itself could have as many discoverers as it has contradictors.[Note: The citation in Augustine reads “faith” rather than “Catholic truth,” and continues: “let the corrector not love himself more than Catholic truth.”] Yet just as I do not want my reader to be devoted to me, so I do not want my corrector to be devoted to himself. Let him not love me more than Catholic truth.

“As I say to the reader, ‘Do not serve my writings as though they were canonical Scriptures; when you find in them something you did not believe, believe it without hesitation in the canonical Scriptures; but in my writings, unless you understand as certain what you did not hold as certain, do not retain it firmly,’ so I say to the corrector: ‘Do not correct what is in my writings according to your own opinion or contentiousness, but according to divine reading or unshakable reason.’ If, by existing, you grasp some truth in them, it is not mine; but by understanding and loving it, let it be both yours and mine. If you convict some falsehood in them, it was mine through error, but now, by avoiding it, let it be neither yours nor mine.”[Note: The Benedictine edition reads “my writings” rather than “my letters.”]

Thus, as this most prudent man teaches, we read the canonical Scriptures in one way. In them, even what we do not believe must be believed without hesitation when we find it. We read the writings of Augustine himself, or of others like him, in another way. In those writings we must not firmly retain what we regard as uncertain unless we have understood it to be certain.

Writing also to Jerome, he says (Letter 19):

“For I confess to your charity that I have learned to show such fear and honor to the books of Scripture alone that are now called canonical that I firmly believe none of their authors erred in writing anything. If I encounter in them anything that appears contrary to the truth, I have no doubt that either the manuscript is faulty, or the interpreter has not grasped what was said, or I myself have failed to understand.

“But I read other writers in such a way that, however great their holiness and learning may be, I do not consider something true merely because they themselves thought so. Rather, I do so because either through those canonical authors or through probable reasoning they have been able to persuade me that it does not depart from the truth.

“Nor do I think that you, my brother, wish your books to be read as though they were those of the prophets or apostles, concerning whose writings it would be impious to doubt that they are free from every error. Far be this from pious humility and a truthful judgment about yourself. Unless you possessed these qualities, you would surely not say: ‘Would that we might be worthy of your embrace, so that by mutual exchange we might either teach or learn something.’”

Holding, then, to the judgment of this most wise man, let us neither attribute divine authority to noncanonical books nor deny human compassion to their writers whenever, as human beings, they have fallen.

What can a person do when corruptible flesh weighs down the soul and an earthly dwelling depresses the mind as it considers many things, while the necessity of an office he has undertaken compels him to teach? He must submit what he writes or says to the examination and judgment of the very Church on whose behalf and from which he received the perilous responsibility of teaching.

But if he has taken up an office that does not belong to him, if he has usurped what was not entrusted to him, he rightly lacks pardon and cannot in any way be excused, since he has thrust himself voluntarily and rashly into dangers belonging to others.

A teacher of the Church, however, is excused by the necessity of his position if he is prepared to correct whatever in his teaching has caused offense.

## CHAPTER VII  
### That many statements of Cyril too are similar to those criticized in the writings of Theodorus, of which he produces ten examples
But let us now also produce some passages from the writings of blessed Cyril, so that from this the reader may understand whether what they assert—that certain writings of Theodore were condemned as Nestorian by Cyril after Theodore’s death—is to be accepted to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon. And so that it may become clear that above we produced only a few testimonies from the many writings of the Fathers previously mentioned, let us produce twice as many from this man, who both condemned Nestorius and whom they have made the accuser of the writings of Diodore and Theodore—that is, ten examples—[Col. 0816B] and these themselves only a few out of many.

For in the book which he called *Scholia* [Note: [Col. 0815D] This plural title is more correct than the singular *Scholium* found in the common editions: Theodoret, Dialogue 2, Κυρίλλου ἀπὸ τῶν σχολίων, “Cyril, from the *Scholia*.” Anastasius the presbyter, in the *Eclogue of Usages*, ch. 3, recites the opening of the *Scholia*, which has been published only in Latin: Κυρίλλου ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῦ αʹ σχολίου· Τὸ Χριστὸς ὄνομα οὔτε ὅρου δύναμιν ἔχει, οὔτε μὴν τήν τινος οὐσίαν ὅ τι ποτέ ἐστι σημαίνει· καθάπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὸ Ἄνθρωπος, ἢ Ἵππος, ἢ Βοῦς· πράγματα [In the royal manuscript, πράγματος ἐνεργουμένου, “an act being effected.”] δὲ μᾶλλον ἐνεργούμενα περί τινα ποιεῖται δήλωσιν: “The name ‘Christ’ has neither the force of a definition nor signifies the essence of any thing whatever, just as ‘man,’ ‘horse,’ or ‘ox’; rather, it indicates things effected in relation to someone.” Each chapter therefore contained its own [Col. 0816D] scholium; hence the book’s title, *Scholia*.], in the seventh section, “What we call the union”:

> “The soul,” he says, “regards as its own everything that belongs to the body, although by its own nature it is free from the body’s passions, both natural and those which occur from without. For the body is moved toward natural desires, and the soul consents [Note: In Greek, συναισθάνεται, ‘feels together’ or ‘perceives together.’], not indeed becoming in any way a participant in the desire, yet it derives its own pleasure from the outcome [Note: Τὸ τῆς ὀρέξεως ἀποτέλεσμα, ‘the result of the desire.’]. And if perhaps its body is beaten down [Note: The Greek says something quite different: Κἂν εἰ καταξαίνοιτο τυχὸν τὸ σῶμα, καὶ σιδήρῳ καταξαίνοιτο, συναλγεῖ μὲν, ὡς ἰδίου πάσχοντος σώματος, ‘And if perhaps the body is struck, and struck with iron, it suffers pain together with it, since it is its own body that suffers.’ The faulty translation, which Facundus immediately follows closely, leads him astray.], or tormented, it certainly suffers pain because its own body is suffering; but in its own nature it suffers no torment whatsoever. Nevertheless, beyond these things also, we say that there is the union which took place in Emmanuel. For it was necessary that the soul united with its body should suffer pain, so that, by fearing sufferings, it might submit its neck to God.” [Col. 0816C]”

If the Eutychians found Theodore saying these things, how, we think, would they examine each point individually! First, they would ask how the soul is free from the body’s passions if it consents when the body is moved toward natural desires; or how, while consenting to natural desires, it nevertheless in no way becomes a participant in desire [Note: Codex Veronensis: “or, in no way having become a participant in desire, nevertheless from the outcome …”], yet derives its own pleasure from the outcome. Or how desire is attributed rather to the body, when the soul can desire even without the body, whereas the body cannot do so. For when it is said, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17), nothing else is meant than that the fleshly, earthly affection of the soul [Note: Codex Veronensis: “that is, earthly.”] desires against the good affection which it possesses from the divine Spirit; just as that affection which is given through the Spirit also desires against the fleshly affection. [Col. 0817A]

Next, in what way is it said [Note: Codex Veronensis: “the soul is said …”] that, when it is beaten down or tormented by its body, it suffers pain because its own body is suffering, while in its own nature it suffers no torment whatsoever? For if it suffers no torment whatsoever, how is it tormented by its body? Or how does it suffer pain without its own torment, since no one suffers pain together with another unless he himself suffers pain? Is it then tormented and does it suffer, but not according to its own nature? And what is there among existing things that is tormented outside its own nature so as to suffer pain?

Indeed, the nature of the soul is so far from being alien to passions [Note: Perhaps, “from passions”] that it often suffers many torments—even if on behalf of its body, nevertheless not from its body—that is, anxiety, fear, sorrow, weariness, jealousy, and the rest. Moreover, that rich man who did not show mercy to Eleazar is tormented in hell without his body. [Col. 0817B]

But setting these matters aside, I wish rather to consider how much envy the Acephali would arouse against the Council of Chalcedon if Theodore had said: “Beyond these things also we say that there is the union which took place in Emmanuel; for it was necessary that the soul united with its body should suffer pain, so that, by fearing the passions, it might submit its neck to God” [Note: Codex Veronensis: “that there is a union.”]

If Theodore had said this, with what great envy and detestation would they cry out, saying:

“Behold the man whose praises were contained in a letter which the Council of Chalcedon pronounced orthodox: a man who was so far from believing Christ to be God and the Son of God that he thought it necessary for him to suffer—not for the removal of our pains, by whose wound we were healed, but rather for himself—so that, through fear of sufferings, he would not become proud but would submit his neck to God.” [Col. 0817C]

They would also say that he did not even believe Christ to be a man of perfect virtue, since he thought that he was restrained from exalting himself by fear of temporal sufferings, by which virtue is ordinarily exercised. For if those who are restrained by fear of eternal punishment are imperfect—as the Apostle John also says of such people, “Fear is not in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and the one who fears is not perfected in love” (1 John 4:18) [Note: Codex Veronensis: “perfect love”; so also in the Vulgate]—how much more imperfect are those whom fear of present troubles holds back from sins?

But if someone, in answer to such complaints of the Eutychians, were to bring forward other writings of the same Theodore, of which we mentioned very few above, in which he confessed that Christ was by nature God before the ages and always equal to the Father who begot him, they would immediately reply:

“It would have been more tolerable for him not to believe that Christ, by nature God and always equal to the Father, was God—a belief which at some time even the apostles did not possess—than to believe that the one whom he believed to be the eternal God was restrained from exaltation by fear of sufferings.” [Col. 0818A]

Let us turn again to what he said in the same book, in the tenth section, or rather to what the title alone plainly presents at first sight. For in it he promised that he would demonstrate the following:

“That, although God the Word was united with true humanity, the subsistences nevertheless remained unconfused.”

To prove this he added:

> “The holy tabernacle was raised in accordance with God’s will through the desert, and in it Emmanuel was formed in many ways.”

And after other remarks:

> “But that the natures, or subsistences [Note: The Greek is found in Leontius, Book I: Ὅτι δὲ ἀσύγχυτοι μεμενήκασιν αἱ φύσεις, ἤγουν ὑποστάσεις, ἐντεῦθεν εἰσόμεθα· τὸ γάρ τοι χρυσίον ἐπαληλιμμένον τῷ ξύλῳ μεμένηκεν ὅπερ ἦν· καὶ κατεπλούτει μὲν τὸ ξύλον ἕως τοῦ χρυσίου τὴν δόξαν· πλὴν οὐκ ἀπέστη τὸ εἶναι ξύλον, ‘That the natures, or subsistences, remained unconfused we shall learn from this: gold applied to wood remains what it was; the wood was enriched with the glory of the gold, but it did not cease to be wood.’ If Cyril intended to speak of two hypostases in Christ, that is, two subsistences, he is rightly censured. But what could be more foreign to Cyril’s doctrine? Here, therefore, he used *hypostases* for substances, following Athanasius and the practice of the Alexandrians, concerning which we spoke in Book VI. The translator should therefore have rendered the term as ‘substances,’ not ‘subsistences.’ The comparison of wood and gold which he uses is also unequal and dissimilar in this respect.] remained unconfused, we learn from this: gold placed upon wood remained what it was; the wood was indeed adorned with the beauty of the gold, yet it did not cease to be wood. That the ark is understood as a figure of Christ can be demonstrated by many proofs.”

Let the reader therefore consider how it is asserted that, while the natures in Christ remained unconfused, the subsistences also remained—although they never existed, since that humanity always belonged to the subsistence of God the Word and never subsisted for itself as in a proper person. Rather, having obtained the subsistence of the one who assumed it [Note: Codex Veronensis: “having been born from the subsistence of the one who assumes it”], it passed into that subsistence by being born, or was born by passing into it; and its assumption itself was the cause of its birth and of everything that it became when born. [Col. 0818B]

Likewise, in his letter to Acacius of Melitene [Note: Cyril’s letter to Acacius, in Greek and Latin, was published after the Synod of Ephesus, no. 35. There, as we said, the phrase τῶν φύσεων, ἤγουν ὑποστάσεων διαφορά is more correctly explained as “the difference of the natures, or substances,” rather than, as here, “of the subsistences.”]:

> “If someone investigates how he was incarnate and became man, he will contemplate God the Word from God having assumed the form of a servant and having been made in the likeness of human beings, according to what is written; and in this respect alone the difference of the natures, or subsistences, will be considered.”

Here too he teaches that the difference of the subsistences is to be considered, just as that of the two natures.

Again, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, Book II [Note: Codex Veronensis: “Book III”], he says:

> “When we say that the Word became flesh, he communicated with the flesh according to subsistence, ineffably and in a manner that cannot be understood. Then, at that time, the person of each subsistence, received in understanding, likewise came together with the natures for unity.”

Who, knowing that Cyril proclaimed that God the Word communicated with the flesh in such a way that in this mystery not only two natures came together for unity, but also two subsistences and persons, would not be astonished to hear that he condemned the writings of Diodore and Theodore as Nestorian, and would not rather imitate his predecessor Athanasius, striving to excuse the writings of all who rest in the peace of the Church? [Col. 0818D]

Later, in the same work, Book IV:

> “Therefore,” he says, “the man of Christ our Savior blossomed again and was, as it were, reborn, like a second growth from a root, overcoming throughout the ages corruption and the power of the ancient causes.”

If one wishes to slander him, let this also be brought against him: that he believed in one Christ the Savior and another man belonging to that Savior Christ, since he did not say, “and was, as it were, reborn, like a second growth from a root, the Savior of us all” [Note: Codex Veronensis: “Christ the Savior,” but], but “the man of Christ, the Savior of us all.” Let them add further:

“If Christ, that is, the Anointed One, is man, since only human nature was anointed in him, who then is this other man who is called Christ’s? For the man of God the Word was not mentioned, but the man of Christ—though he is believed to be God in such a way that he is also believed to be man.”

In his exposition of the prophet Isaiah, Book IV, he says:

> “Therefore, with regard to the bitterness of the unbelievers and their foolishly contrived opposition, the Savior labored in vain for them, and expended his strength uselessly and to no purpose. For foolish Israel did not endure, as I said recently, his sacred proclamations, nor did it honor his labor. For it was labor for the Word to become as we are and to bear human lowliness. But, he says, ‘My judgment is with the Lord, and my labor is before my God.’ For the Father, he says, recognized the labors I completed for their salvation; therefore judgment was also pronounced by him.”

Behold: Gregory, as we mentioned above, says of God the Word that he established the whole world without labor; Cyril says that he labored to become as we are and to bear human lowliness [Col. 0819C]—as though his impassible divinity suffered constriction in a human body, although our soul does not suffer such constriction from the smallness of the body, but rather from the law of sin which is in our members and opposes the law of the mind. For the future life will suffer no constriction in an incorruptible body.

Likewise, in his commentary on the Gospel according to Matthew, Book II:

> “When Christ was baptized,” he says, “then he is said to be led by the Spirit—that is, to dwell spiritually, or to live a spiritual life.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Accustoming his own temple to spiritual life—the temple in which God the Word already dwelt—and transforming what is ours into an unfamiliar and undisciplined manner of life, restoring it in the newness of life which had not previously been known, he undertakes so lengthy a fast.”

Did Christ, then, not live a spiritual life before he was baptized? Or did he need John’s baptism in order to be consecrated by it and thereby be instructed to live spiritually, when even those who were baptized by the apostles in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ did not need to be consecrated by John’s baptism?

How, then, is it said that, once Christ had been baptized, he lived spiritually, and that what is written—“Then Jesus was led by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil” (Matt. 4:1)—is understood to signify that he dwelt spiritually and lived a spiritual life? Likewise, it is said that he was “accustoming his own temple to spiritual life,” as though previously a habit of carnal life had belonged to that same temple. Yet, since it was conceived from the Holy Spirit, it could not have been anything other than spiritual life. How, then, is it said to be accustomed to spiritual life, when it was ordered toward it not by effort but by nature? Nothing was ever lacking in it for the perfection and abundance of virtue, since it is written of him: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34). And again: “From his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace” (John 1:16).

Also, in his exposition of the Gospel according to John, Book I, he says:

> “We are shown to be gods and sons of God through faith. For the one who is by nature Son and God dwelt in us. Therefore, in his Spirit we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ The Word dwells, however, as in all people, and in the one temple which was assumed for us and from us, so that, possessing all in himself, he might reconcile all to the Father in one body.”

If the teachers of the Church are judged by the sound of their words and not by their intention, what shall we think of this man, who said: “The Word of God dwells as in all people, and in the one temple which was assumed for us and from us”?

Do we believe, then, that Cyril, the condemner of Nestorius, meant that God the Word dwells in that one temple which was assumed for us and from us in the same way as he commonly dwells in all people, rather than that the person of the indwelling God the Word and of the temple was one? This is so even though Theodore, who is condemned as the originator of the Nestorian error, says—as we mentioned in Book III:

> “The one inhabited by God the Word from the very formation in the mother’s womb was inhabited, not according to a common indwelling, nor according to the grace understood to be present in many, but according to a certain excellence, according to which we also say that both natures were united and that one person was effected according to the union.”

Let the Eutychians and their supporters therefore learn either to interpret the writings of the ancient preachers of the Church more accurately or to leave them to be interpreted by better interpreters, lest they be forced to call blessed Cyril worse than Theodore, whom they say was much worse than Nestorius.

Cyril should not therefore be thought to have said, “The Word dwells as in all people, and in the one temple which was assumed for us and from us,” as though there had not been one person of God the Word and the temple; rather, he said it because his divinity remained unaltered in its own temple [Note: Codex Veronensis: “his divinity also”]. For in this mystery of the incarnation two things must be understood and confessed: namely, that there is one person of God and man, and that two natures remained unconfused.

With respect to the unity of person, God the Word does not dwell “as in all people” in the one temple which was assumed for us and from us [Note: Codex Veronensis: “God the Word dwells in the one temple”]. But with respect to the fact that the two natures remained without confusion, God the Word dwells “as in all people” and in the one temple which was assumed for us and from us; for just as, while dwelling in all people, his divinity remains unaltered, so his unaltered divinity remained in the one temple which was assumed for us and from us.

Let us therefore believe that he spoke with this intention, so that we neither condemn the one who spoke nor approve an error. We could also offer a not inconsiderable account of other passages from his writings that have been mentioned, and certainly more learned men could offer an account of more passages. For this reason, the dead must not be judged rashly.

In the same work, Book IV, he also speaks in the person of the Lord:

> “‘Father, if it is possible’:
>
> ‘I cannot obtain life through death for those who had fallen into it, unless death dies when I die. It is certain, however, that he speaks according to the flesh: “Let this cup pass.” Yet because, he says, it cannot happen otherwise, “not as I will, but as you will.” Observe how human nature, failing once again insofar as it is concerned, is nevertheless raised up through the Word united to it toward divine boldness and youthful wisdom, and is instructed not to do what appeared to be done according to its own wills, but rather to follow the divine intention.’”

For this reason they said that Theodore blasphemed worse than demons, because he said that the Lord feared suffering. But if we accept this, we shall also be compelled to say that Cyril blasphemed worse than demons, since he urges us to observe how human nature, insofar as it is concerned, failing, is raised up through the Word united to it toward divine boldness.

As for what he added, “and is instructed toward youthful wisdom, so that it might not do what appeared to be done according to its own wills,” more learned men may interpret this, together with certain matters mentioned above—if the Eutychians and their associates are willing to accept it. [Col. 0821C]

For when something of this kind is found in Athanasius, who purified the writings of his predecessor Dionysius, which could offend the reader; or when something similar is found in Basil, who defended the sayings of the great Gregory; or in Hilary, who defended the decisions of the council convened against Paul of Samosata and those of the Council of Sirmium—it is wholly improper to think ill of men of such great piety. They judged others by themselves and strove to excuse the sayings of their predecessors; they believed that those predecessors had spoken and that the Church had received their words in a manner in which they could be understood, so that the bishops might remain within the Church.

And if any other venerable Fathers, whose excusing of the sayings of their predecessors we do not read, said something of this kind, they certainly must not be censured, when they too are believed to have possessed the same piety.

But when the Eutychians and their satellites say, to the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon, that blessed Cyril—not because of some circumstance that happened to arise, but deliberately and in a work composed for that purpose—marked out the sayings of Theodore, who had been praised by so many Fathers, what else are they doing [Note: Codex Veronensis: “what else do they do, except …”] than making him himself inexcusably culpable in the matters we have mentioned and in others like them?

For the Truth says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged, and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you” (Matt. 7:1–2).

If, then, they spare blessed Cyril himself, if they wish him to be excused in such matters, let them no longer speak against the Council of Chalcedon, alleging that it did not spare the dead when it accused men of distinguished testimony, men full of days, who died in the highest dignity of the Church.

They ought carefully to attend to this statement. When Cyril says that human nature is raised up through the Word united to it, so that it might not do what appeared to be done according to its own wills, but rather follow the divine intention, he teaches two wills—if indeed only two—since he says that the human nature alone has, not one proper will, but proper wills, which, as he himself put it, Christ was taught not to enact; and that there is another will of divine intention, which he was taught to follow.

But let the reader also observe what he says again in the same work and the same book about Christ’s two wills, concerning which we also showed in our third book that blessed Athanasius wrote:

> “What was voluntary and what was involuntary for Christ? Dishonor by the Jews, slanders, insults, blows [Note: Codex Veronensis: “blows, scourges, and spittings”], and, beyond these, accusations—and what is last in everything, the death of the body. But if it had been possible for him to obtain for us what he sought without suffering, he would not have wished to suffer. But because the Jews were altogether and inexcusably going to presume to do what was done against him, he accepted suffering and made voluntary what was not voluntary, for the benefit resulting from the suffering.”

Let them therefore attend to how blessed Cyril teaches that there were two wills in Christ, although not in the same words as Saint Athanasius, when he says that what Christ suffered was both voluntary and involuntary; that what he willingly suffered for our sake he would not have wished to suffer; and that he made voluntary what was not voluntary [Note: Codex Veronensis: “that it was voluntary for him”]. Yet let no one therefore believe that he proclaimed two Christs or two sons.

But if it is said that “voluntary” means that Christ willingly suffered these things for our sake, while “involuntary for Christ” means that he willingly suffered what he would not have wished to suffer, and that this does not manifest two wills, one of the divine nature and one of the human nature, but only a human will, one will and another because of different circumstances—and if this is said not to accord with the divine nature, since it is not fitting that it should simultaneously will and not will the same thing [Note: Codex Veronensis: “which does not accord with the divine nature”]—then it remains that, in addition to these wills, there was another will in Christ, the same will as in the Father and the Holy Spirit: the will of the divine nature, to which different and contrary things cannot belong.

Accordingly, we await this from the supporters of the Eutychians or Semi-Eutychians: let them not condemn, together with Theodore’s doctrine, the doctrine of blessed Cyril on these matters and on the rest of the same kind.

If they consider it impious to condemn blessed Cyril, let them not accuse Theodore to the prejudice of the holy council as though he were the originator of the Nestorian error.

But if blessed Cyril spoke such words, or words of such character, even after the question of Nestorius had arisen and spread abroad, what wonder is it if Theodore, before Nestorius had yet opposed them, incurred the slander or suspicion of an unexpected error?

From the matters we have mentioned you recognize, most merciful Emperor, that the most truly wise John of Antioch, writing to blessed Cyril together with the Eastern council so that certain excerpts from Theodore’s writings would not be condemned under an anathema, added and said:

> “For we have found certain passages like these excerpts in blessed [Note: Codex Veronensis: “thrice-blessed”] and noble Athanasius; some also in blessed Basil; some in both Gregories; many, moreover, in Amphilochius, who said them repeatedly; and not a few in our common Father, blessed Theophilus. For there are passages which your holiness also confesses in such a way that you hold the same understanding of them.
>
> “Having therefore been admonished by these examples, let us not judge the sayings of all who rest in the peace of the Church according to the opinion of heretics or of those who understand little, but rather according to the intention of those who spoke. For these things which, in whatever manner, appear to offend the reader were written not by separating themselves from the Church against the Church, but on behalf of the Church against heretics.
>
> “For can anyone prove that they said such things against those who believed that one person of God the Word and man had been effected in the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, and not rather against those who denied that two natures remained in one person of Christ?”

If someone should say that, at that time, when the Church was not being assailed by the same questions concerning heretics as those which assail us, these things were necessary against other heretics and harmless to Catholics, but that now, since Nestorians are seeking a simple opportunity to deceive, the faithful—and especially children—ought to be kept from reading such writings, who would find this sound and prudent counsel displeasing?

Since the enemies whom we now suffer are armed differently against the Church, its faithful and defenders should likewise exercise themselves in other weapons; and thus, without bringing infamy upon the ancient preachers of the Church, the Church may be defended against the snares of heretics [Note: Codex Veronensis: “the Church will be fortified. Nor, etc.”].

Nor will this appear to insult the dead, or to display ourselves as more religious or wiser by criticizing others, or to seek glory from the disgrace of the dead. Blessed Gregory notes this in his *Apologeticus*:
