> “Everyone,” he says, “wants to appear learned and Catholic if we criticize others and judge them impious.”

Since, then, the Eutychians and their associates were boasting that they were learned and Catholic, not because of the condemnation of one Theodore but because of their criticism of the great Council of Chalcedon, I thought it more appropriate to restrain them by the similar sayings of those Fathers whom they do not dare to condemn as heretics.

I did this not because I wish those same Fathers to appear blameworthy, as they wish Theodore to appear blameworthy in order to empty the authority of the great council, but to show them that without those Fathers whom they do not dare to condemn, they cannot condemn Theodore for similar statements, nor condemn the council itself because it did not condemn him.

Thus, when the Lord was passing through the grainfields on the Sabbath and his hungry disciples began to pluck the ears of grain and eat them, and the Pharisees censured them, saying, “Behold, your disciples are doing what is not lawful for them to do on the Sabbaths,” he replied:

> “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt?” (Matt. 12:2, 5)

Just as the Lord, in giving this answer to the Pharisees who censured the apostles, did not wish the prophet David and those who were with him, or the priests, to appear blameworthy, but rather wished the Pharisees themselves, restrained by the example of holy persons of unquestioned authority, not to censure innocent disciples, so we took no pleasure in offending the venerable Fathers. Rather, we wished to restrain the presumption of the Eutychians and their associates by presenting such examples.

This is what we say to them: if they can interpret more correctly the sayings we have mentioned of Eustathius, Athanasius, Amphilochius, Gregory, John, and Cyril, let them also deign to interpret Theodore more correctly. If they leave those sayings to more learned interpreters [Note: Codex Veronensis: “but if they leave them to more learned interpreters”], let them likewise leave Theodore’s sayings to them.

But if, while thinking that the sayings of the Fathers mentioned cannot be interpreted more correctly, they nevertheless do not judge their praiseworthy doctrine on the basis of those statements produced with less careful examination before the question of Nestorius became pressing, let them not allege that the holy council judged Theodore’s doctrine in this way.

For since it is not ignorance but obstinacy that makes a heretic, we have already said much about this in the preceding books, and we shall say something more in the following book.

# BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0823]

## CHAPTER ONE  
That it is not ignorance but an obstinate defense of falsehood that makes a heretic, and that those who have erred in certain matters must not immediately be judged heretics

[Col. 0823D]

# Defense of the Great Synod of Chalcedon

The Acephali accuse the holy Synod of Chalcedon because it judged orthodox the letter of the venerable Ibas, which praises the teaching of Theodore. Since the Council of the Orientals especially urged us to do so, we have been compelled to bring forward certain statements of the ancient Fathers which, to those who read them, may seem no less offensive than those things for which they blame Theodore himself. And since such offense must not be disregarded, and since we cannot excuse everything that we have brought forward from their statements—or, even if we could, time would not suffice to excuse all the other things in the writings of these and other Fathers that may give offense—we defend all who have died in the peace of the Church by this brief and safe argument: we show that we cannot rightly judge any of them heretics, even if some are found to have been ignorant of something concerning such questions.

No one should think that in the present book I have undertaken to define what makes a person a heretic. I have proposed only to demonstrate something which, as I believe, I have already demonstrated above by an acceptable argument: that no one living or dead in the Church who offers—or offered—himself as teachable in Christian doctrine ought to be judged a heretic on account of ignorance concerning such questions. For if the Church is now a school of Christ, and all her faithful are said to be Christ’s disciples, no one can truthfully be called a disciple who is not learning something; and one learns only what one does not know. Beyond doubt, then, either teachable ignorance does not make a person a heretic, or every disciple of Christ will be a heretic.

And who will now be called a Catholic, if everyone who learns something about the Christian religion is to be called a heretic? Even if some are believed to have learned everything so completely that they can no longer have anything to learn, nevertheless, because they were ignorant of something before they learned it, they will appear to have become Catholics from heretics. Thus it follows that no one will be found in the Church of Christ who is not said either to be or to have been a heretic. But to say or think this is both utterly impious and exceedingly absurd.

We must therefore know that it is not ignorance which is not obstinate against the teaching of truth that makes a heretic, but rather an obstinate defense of falsehood. We say that the following also belong to this obstinacy—or rather, we affirm that they hold the first place in it: those teachings which certain people devised not because they understood the divine Scriptures less well, but by openly resisting them and relying solely on their own presumption, such as Manichaeus and Origen.

[Note: The errors and delusions of both men were akin in many respects, and accordingly their audacity against the sacred Scriptures was comparable. Thus Athanasius, writing to the solitaries about the Manichaeans, had said that they adulterate the divine Scriptures with their fabricated arguments and tell fables. “For the Manichaeans,” he says, “peddling the divine Scriptures, tell fables through their own fabricated arguments” (Μανιχαῖοι γὰρ καπηλεύοντες τὰς θείας γραφὰς τοῖς ἑαυτῶν ἐπιπλάστοις λόγοις μυθολογοῦσιν). Justinian, writing to Mena about Origen, suggests that Origen undertook to interpret the sacred Scriptures in appearance only, “so that he might introduce the fables of the Greeks and his own Manichaean error” (ἵνα τῶν Ἑλλήνων μυθολογίας, καὶ τὴν Μανιχαϊκὴν αὐτοῦ πλάνην εἰσαγάγῃ).]

And the same applies to the others who, unlike those who followed the intention of the Scriptures and went astray in obscure questions, raised themselves above them and believed that they understood or spoke better than they did.

[Note: Codex Veronensis: “teach.”]

For if the person who does not yield to the Church’s decrees, established by the authority of those same Scriptures, must be called obstinate, how much worse an obstinacy must characterize the person who disdains to submit to the divine Scriptures themselves, and either removes the truth from their inviolable fullness or thinks that something is lacking which must be supplied by his own invention?

In what matters this obstinacy is to be regarded as heresy is a greater question and foreign to the purpose of this work.

[Note: The same codex: “foreign to the intention.”]

For now, let us carry out what we have proposed.

We say, then, that every heretic is alien from Christ. The Apostle says to the Corinthians: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1).

[Note: The same codex: “as though.”]

If, then, the Corinthians, who did not yet know the perfect knowledge hidden in the ministry,

[Note: The same codex: “mystery.”]

were not heretics because, as the Apostle says, they were infants in Christ, how can anyone—whether still living or dead in the Church of Christ—be judged a heretic merely because of partial ignorance, when no one rebuked him so that he could be said to have refused correction?

Writing also to the Philippians, he says: “I do not consider that I have apprehended it; but one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus. Let all of us who are perfect think this way; and if you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this to you. Nevertheless, let us walk according to that which we have attained” (Phil. 3:13–16).

[Note: ἀποκαλύψει: “he will reveal.”]

Since this is so, what are we to believe about these same Philippians, to whom the Apostle said that they thought differently and whom he admonished meanwhile to walk according to that which they had attained—that is, to make progress? Shall we pronounce such people heretics, or unlearned Catholics? We shall not dare to call them heretics, since the Apostle communicated with them together with the whole Church. It remains, therefore, that although unlearned and thinking differently from what the truth teaches, we should nevertheless say that they were Catholics.

He writes similarly to the Colossians: “Although I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and that which is lacking in the usefulness of your faith” (Col. 2:5). Should we therefore have called them heretics because the Apostle saw that something was lacking in them for the benefit of their faith? Far from it. For how could the Apostle be with such people in spirit and rejoice with their order?

What, moreover, are we to think about the woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, had spent all her possessions on physicians, and could not be cured by anyone? For she had not believed Christ to be God when she touched the fringe of his garment. When the Lord said, “Who touched me?” and Peter and those who were with him replied, “Master, the crowds press upon you and throng you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” (Luke 8:45), and when the Lord said again, “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me” (ibid., 46), he did not reveal what had happened, so that the woman who had been healed might instead become a witness to divine power. As the evangelist goes on to say: “When the woman saw that she had not escaped notice, she came trembling” (ibid., 47), fell down before his feet, and declared before all the people why she had touched him and how she had immediately been healed.

Thus, from Luke’s words, “When the woman saw that she had not escaped notice,” we understand that she had touched him in such a way as to remain hidden; yet she would not have believed that God could remain hidden. She therefore had not believed Christ to be God, since she had believed that he could fail to know what had happened, so much so that she thought it necessary to report to him what she knew had happened to her.

Another evangelist likewise reports: “But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him, and told him the whole truth” (Mark 5:33)—so that what the modesty of the sick woman had previously concealed, the devotion of the healed woman might confess.

Perhaps she therefore touched Christ from behind so that by this very act she might signify that she had touched not his preeminence, which precedes all things, according to the saying, “In the beginning was the Word,” but his humanity, through which the Word later became flesh (John 1:1, 14).

For just as words have been given to us for signifying things, so almighty God, to whose power all things are subject and whose wisdom uniquely knows how to adapt even the voluntary movements of those who do not know to the service of instruction, signifies whatever things he wishes through the action of his creature.

I therefore think it was not inappropriate that she approached only the fringe of his garment, since, in proportion to the measure of her faith, she could not approach the excellence of his majesty, but approached that which belonged to his gracious incarnation, through which he bowed down to the earth and became nearer to our lowliness.

Nor is it surprising if this woman’s faith was imperfect, or if in that very imperfection she received healing from Christ’s mercy, since even among the apostles themselves there appear to have been some of this kind, as we have already shown concerning Thomas and Philip, although through them he nevertheless performed works of power among the people.

Nor is it incredible that, although she did not believe Christ to be God, she nevertheless said, “If I touch even his garment, I shall be saved,” since it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that believers in Christ trusted so greatly in the power of even his disciples that not only were handkerchiefs or aprons carried from Paul’s body to the sick, and diseases left them and evil spirits went out (Acts 19:18), but also that the multitude of believers in the Lord, men and women, brought the sick out into the streets and placed them on beds and pallets, so that when Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow some of them (Acts 5:13–16). A multitude from the neighboring cities of Jerusalem also gathered, bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, and all were healed.

Should we therefore condemn this woman also among the heretics because of the faith by which she deserved to be healed, and about which the Lord said to her, “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 8:48)? If the faith of infants is to be condemned by those who seem to themselves to possess great and perfect faith, why should this woman not also be condemned?

Why should we not also condemn Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, since both said to the Lord, “If you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:21, 32)? As we have already said, they certainly would not have said this if they had believed Christ to be God. For who would think that God was absent from any place?

Martha, moreover, even when the Lord came to the tomb and commanded that the stone placed over it be removed, thought it necessary to inform him, as though he did not know, just as the woman healed of the flow of blood had done, saying, “Lord, he already stinks, for it has been four days” (ibid., 39).

Why, then, should we not also say that these familiar friends of Christ were heretics, if simple ignorance makes a heretic? Indeed, why should we not condemn all worshipers of God from the beginning of the world who, whether like the Corinthians, Philippians, and Colossians, or like these women, believed less than they should about those things by whose faith we are cleansed, yet completed a holy and simple life in obedience to God’s commandments?

What is remarkable here is that the imperfect and childish faith of the woman with the flow of blood obtained a perfect and great healing from Christ’s justice, while the faith of these sisters obtained the astonishing resurrection of a brother who had been dead four days. Yet our faith, which seems to us so great and perfect that we do not spare the dead—or, if what is said were true, those who are imperfect—can accomplish nothing of significance.

We argue incessantly and without order about the doctrines of the Christian faith, wishing to appear learned and religious in criticizing others; and we carelessly discuss heavenly mysteries which should be treated reverently and sparingly. Only an empty name now remains for things that were called mysteries. Necessary questions of faith, which should be entrusted to few, are treated as idle stories and common talk.

In all this we seem to ourselves to be acting on behalf of piety while disturbing the Church, in whose peace we reject as heretics those who have died with what we consider childish faith, although the apostles themselves were at times imperfect in faith and never heretics. Although they still believed little about Christ, they received great power over unclean spirits, so that they could cast them out and heal every sickness and every infirmity, when the Lord sent them and commanded:

“Go, preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’ Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. 10:7–8).

[Note: Codex Veronensis: “and thus he commanded.”]

If, then, the apostles were not heretics even during the period of their ignorance, how can anyone affirm that those who passed from this life in such a condition were heretics? And if those who had the truth itself present with them in the body could, without guilt, think something different or less about him, why should it be counted as the crime of heresy if someone in the Church, endowed with piety, devoted to obedience, submissive and teachable, should think differently about him, provided that he is ready to correct what has been reproved?

Therefore, all who are disciples of the truth and present themselves as teachable to reason and subject to the authority of the Church—if they think differently about those things by whose faith they are cleansed, whether because their understanding is inadequate or because they have not attended to the matter as carefully as necessary—are certainly impiously cursed as heretics.

[Note: The same codex: “we curse.”]

For whoever firmly establishes in his heart his belief in what the doctrine and faith of the Church teaches concerning such matters, even though he does not perfectly understand or express everything about them, is nevertheless not called an enemy of the truth, which is what a heretic is. He does not trust in his own knowledge, and in many things in which he errs or is uncertain he does not doubt that the Church rightly holds the truth. Situated in the Church as though in a school of truth, he has the pious intention of learning; he ought therefore to be perfected as a disciple.

This imperfect person does not presume, by his own authority, to teach anything fabricated by his own heart, as certain heretics do, nor does he follow those who teach such things. Rather, he relies upon the authority of the divine Scriptures.

[Note: Codex Veronensis: “Scriptures.”]

And when he has not attained their understanding—for in many matters, because of their great depth, human vision is obscured—

[Note: The same codex: “their true understanding.”]

he learns what the universal Church has determined concerning them and, with pious humility of heart, renounces his error, since he has never forbidden himself to think otherwise.

Just as there are some more perfect people who, through the great gift of wisdom, are able mentally to contemplate what others merely believe in the life of faith,

[Note: The same codex: “in faith.”]

so there are many imperfect people in the Church of Christ who are nevertheless perfect in preserving her unity. Although they err in many matters through their ignorance, they believe that the Church, through whose unity they trust they are saved, errs in nothing.

Therefore, even if we seem wiser than they—although Scripture says that piety is wisdom—we ought not to expel these worshipers of God from his Church or cast them out from the walls of spiritual Zion and count them among her adversaries.

“Surround Zion,” says the prophet, “and embrace her; tell it in her towers; place your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her houses” (Ps. 47:17);

or, as other manuscripts read, “Distribute her steps.”

[Note: The word “houses” is superfluous, since the Greek has καταδίελεθε τὰς βάσεις αὐτῆς, “divide her steps.”]

[Note: In the same codex, “houses” is absent.]

We must therefore surround all who belong to Zion with our defenses and embrace them in charity, not excluding anyone who occupies any rank within her. We should render great honor to those above them, as is owed to them, but not deny affection even to the lowest among them.

This is what the verse means by “Distribute her steps,” which is expressed elsewhere as, “Set love in order within me” (Song 2:4).

Just as the lower rank of certain people who are perfect in faith should not be despised because they cannot grasp the truth intellectually, since others of a higher rank can do so, neither should these people be despised or expelled from the Church—or, what is more cruel, condemned under anathema after death—because they may appear to have had imperfect faith. They were unable to direct their minds as they ought to all the many and great things contained in the Christian religion, yet they did not doubt that all things held in the faith of the Church were true and right, so that they might remain within it to be perfected.

By believing in this way, they too appear to be perfect in faith according to a certain rank, since they believed that they were to be perfected through the unity of the Church.

Those endowed with the more excellent rank of understanding were able to attain, insofar as this life permits, the very reality whose full revelation is reserved for the future. Those who were perfect only in faith approached it more closely. But those whom we have placed in the third and lower rank, although they look toward the same reality from a somewhat greater distance, nevertheless intend to come there.

If such people are judged heretics, what portion will remain for us—not merely of the whole people, but even of the very leaders of the churches—that ought to be judged Catholic? For even those of more excellent understanding, advancing through difficult paths because of the necessity of the office they have undertaken, are sometimes received into the bosom of mercy when they submit themselves to the authority of the Church whose teachers they are, so that no flesh may glory in his presence.

Heresy, therefore, must not be called anything except the stubborn contradiction of the proud person who forbids himself to think otherwise and, when admonished, scorns to submit to the truth. Such a person prefers to separate himself contumaciously from the Church, or to hide deceitfully within her, rather than change his perverse opinion.

We distinguish the ignorant from the deceitful by this: the ignorant are not necessarily shown to have been adequately corrected concerning what they understand less well, nor do they corrupt the minds of the simple by hidden arguments; rather, they ordinarily state freely and simply what they think.

If anyone wishes to learn, even in the case of Christ’s disciples whom he had while he lived among them in mortal flesh, how great is the difference between the spirit of one who patiently submits to reason and the spirit of one who is contumacious toward authority—the spirit by which heretics are driven, who are more ready to take offense and separate themselves than to learn—and the less capable understanding of pious people who patiently await the opportunity for instruction and preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, he will find an example in a single chapter of John the Evangelist.

There the Lord said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:52). And: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid., 57). “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me” (ibid., 58).

When the Jews argued and said among themselves, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (ibid., 53), many of his disciples, hearing this, said: “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?” (ibid., 61). Therefore, as the narrative continues: “Many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him” (ibid., 67).

Here is that spirit impatient of reason and contumacious toward authority by which heretics are driven: they are more ready to take offense and separate themselves than to learn.

The ignorance of pious people who patiently await the opportunity for instruction and preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace is disclosed in what follows. The evangelist adds, reporting the event in this way: “Then Jesus said to the Twelve, ‘Do you also want to go away?’” (ibid., 68).

He would not have said this if they had been equally incapable of understanding the mystery but not equally harsh or contumacious toward authority. Why would they be asked whether they too wished to go away if they had understood what had been spoken mystically? For those who understood the mystery could not take offense and depart.

They were asked so that they might answer whether, although they did not understand what had been said, the authority of the good teacher nevertheless held them. In them a salutary example of piety and gentleness was provided for us, so that whenever we do not understand, we may yield to authority.

Finally, when the Lord asked this question there, Peter answered in such a way as to say that he did not wish to depart—not because he understood the mystery, but because whatever that mystery might be, whatever was said by such a teacher undoubtedly pertained to eternal life.

[Note: Codex Veronensis: “whatever it might be.”]

For he says: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life; and we have believed and have come to know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John 6:69).

If he had understood the mystery, he would rather have said: “There is no reason for us to depart, since we believe that we shall be saved by faith in your body and blood.”

There is therefore a great difference between the harsh arrogance of heretics, which tears apart the body of the Church or hides within it with a deceitful heart, and the less capable understanding of Catholics, which is subject to Christ’s teaching and preserves the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace.

Those who separate themselves from the Church certainly do not have this Spirit, as the Apostle Jude says: “These are the ones who separate themselves, worldly people, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19).

Nor does the person who hides in the Church with a deceitful heart have this Spirit: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. 1:5).

We must not therefore confuse things that are so greatly distinct or regard as identical what is profoundly different.

For this reason the holy Fathers, whose apostolic rule certain people appear to have wrongly transgressed, did not condemn those teachers of the Church who, preserving her peace to the end, may have erred in certain matters of the Christian faith. Rather, they condemned those who, after a first and second correction, and after the rule of truth had been made clear through a synod preserving the paternal constitutions, presumed to believe and teach something else.

For they could not condemn those individuals alone without condemning the whole Church, which, although it noticed them, did not rebuke them for preaching such things.

[Note: The same codex: “condemn the teachers.”]

For these matters belonged to everyone, since no one had rejected them and they were not unknown to anyone.

You therefore see, most gracious emperor, how many people’s condemnation would follow if anyone were condemned on the presumption of later generations. Yet such importance is attached to remaining in the unity of the body of Christ and not presenting oneself as contentious, but submitting one’s teachable mind to the truth, that, for the sake of the fruit of peace and charity itself, whatever may perhaps be thought differently from what the true faith requires may be cleansed by the Lord, so that it may bear more fruit in peace.

“For the fruit of righteousness,” according to the Apostle Paul—

[Note: The same codex: “James.”]

—is “sown in peace by those who make peace” (James 3:18).

Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he removes; and every one that bears fruit, he prunes, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1–2).

Nor should it seem surprising that those who remain joined to the body of Christ and preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace are cleansed of their errors through charity itself, since it is written that “charity covers all offenses” (Prov. 10:12).

Just as, on the basis of the testimony of God’s Scripture, by which many people are praised, we do not dare to call their lives impious, although we are seriously offended by some of their actions, so we must not call the teaching of many heretical when it is attested and honored by the Church of God, although we may be seriously offended by some of their statements.

And just as we do not think that those people, although praised by divine Scripture, should be imitated in everything, so we should not think that these people, although honored by the Church, should be approved in everything.

We show this reverence to divine Scripture itself: we do not believe that it praised anything unworthily.

[Note: The same codex: “anyone.”]

[Note: The same codex: “which it praised.”]

Therefore, when we hear the Apostle praising Samson among other righteous people and saying, “For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, and obtained promises” (Heb. 11:32–33), and so forth, we understand that when Samson caused himself to be crushed under the ruin of the great structure together with the Philistines, he did this not because he could not endure his own misfortune, but because he had been inspired by the divine will.

Otherwise, he would not have been given sufficient strength to strike and overthrow with his own hands a structure of such size, in which the Philistine people celebrated their banquets. Nor, if he had inflicted death upon himself by his own will, would the Apostle have praised him among the righteous.

Therefore we judge his deed on the testimony of divine Scripture, not according to our own custom.

Likewise, when we see David praised by the same Scripture, although after committing adultery he also added murder to his crime, we believe that he was praised because we read in it at the same time that he repented of those crimes.

But when it also praises Aaron the high priest, who made a calf at Horeb so that the people might worship it (Exod. 32), and does not report where he repented of so great a sacrilege, the reverence we owe to the same holy Scripture requires of us that, although it is silent about this, we should nevertheless not believe that it could praise him unless he had repented of so great a sacrilege.

We must therefore maintain this same practice concerning those whose teaching has been received in the Church of God: if something in their words offends us, we should first inquire whether perhaps it was not they who failed to find the truth, but we who failed to perceive their intention adequately.

And just as we judge Samson’s deed on the testimony of divine Scripture and not according to our own custom, so we should judge the statements of these men on the testimony of the Church and not according to our own understanding.

If their error is certain, as in the case of David and Aaron, we should believe that they were praised only because of their correction of it—whether this can be shown, as we have shown that Theodore amended the things he had expressed less cautiously, or whether it perhaps cannot be demonstrated clearly. For the Church of God could not approve them in any other way.

Just as it is exceedingly unbecoming and offensive to search out the sins of those to whom God’s Scripture has borne witness as righteous, and then mark and enumerate them in detail because we wish to appear holy and undefiled, so it is exceedingly unbecoming and offensive to investigate with excessive scrupulousness the ignorance of those to whom the Church of God has borne witness as sound in doctrine, and, if we detect or suppose errors in some of them, heap them together and discuss them because we wish to appear learned and Catholic.

But just as with the sins of the former, so with any ignorance found among the latter, it is enough that, when we read, we disapprove of it, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thess. 5:21).

And just as we judge the lives of the former—not impious on account of certain blameworthy deeds, but righteous on account of their many more correct deeds—according to the testimony of God’s Scripture, so we should judge the teaching of the latter—not heretical on account of certain blameworthy statements, but Catholic on account of their many more correct statements—according to the testimony of God’s Church.

For this reason the holy Synod of the East, writing to Theodosius, said:

“If anyone, holy emperor, says that something obscure is found in the writings of Theodore or of others, it is not necessary to reopen the matter. For those whose life had an excellent end in the priesthood and ministry, we dedicate the glory that was bestowed upon them, and we do not judge them on the basis of those things for which some accuse them harshly.”

## Chapter II. That Matters Once Established in a Synod Should Not Be Reopened
But behold, what remained for us as the final means of demonstrating the whole case: we have also shown, sufficiently and more than sufficiently, that, in view of Theodorus of Mopsuestia’s praise, this letter cannot rightly be condemned as heretical. Nevertheless, as stated above, we establish its firmness not on our own reasoning—although that reasoning may appear unanswerable—but on the authority of the holy council by which it was received. [Col. 0833D] [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “by which it was received.”] [Note: The same manuscript reads “we establish the firmness of it.”]

Let this suffice for the instruction of our little ones, so that they may not be scandalized by what has been fabricated about that letter: namely, that we have excluded all such accusations by defenses of every diverse and manifold kind, converging from all sides in the service of truth. Nor should they ask themselves, saying, “Why did that council itself, which rightly judged the letter orthodox because it contains the right faith, not insert into its acts an explanation of all the charges by which heretics accuse it?” They must understand that, since the accusers of Ibas’s letter had brought no objection against it, the council had no need to linger over such matters. [Col. 0834A] [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Since the accusers of Bishop Ibas had raised no objection on this point, it had no need to do so.”]

But if the great council is thought deserving of blame because it did not anticipate the future accusations of heretics, then the prophets and apostles themselves must also be blamed, since many things occur in their writings whose meaning, although they could have disclosed it without any difficulty, is now explained with the greatest effort and labor by the most gifted and learned men. Let them therefore recognize that Christ exercises the faith and devotion of his Church through these difficulties. For surely the prophets, and still more the apostles, would have avoided or resolved the future questions raised by slanderers or by those who did not understand—questions which they foresaw. Let them heed what the apostle Peter says:

> “Our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, as he does in all his letters, speaking in them of these matters, among which there are some difficult to understand. The ignorant and unstable distort them, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction. You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, beware lest, seduced by the error of the wicked, you fall from your steadfastness.” (II Peter 3:15–17)

Behold: not only did they fail to avoid the future difficulties, although they foresaw them, but even when they saw them present, they did not resolve for us the questions raised from their writings against the Church by the ignorant and unstable. No Christian dares charge them with having spoken things which those same ignorant and unstable persons would distort because of the difficulty of understanding them. Rather, one trembles at God’s judgment in this matter, because through temptations of this sort the saying is fulfilled: “Let the one who is filthy be filthier still; let the righteous do yet more righteous things, and let the holy be holier still.” (Revelation 22:11)

Therefore, if we show any reverence toward synodal decrees received by the universal Church, then in everything obscure and difficult to understand that we find in them, we must recognize and approve the divine will. You recognize, most serene emperor, that the blessed Leo rightly restrained rash men from revising the aforesaid council, when he wrote to the emperor Leo, saying: “Let nothing at all be revised that has been properly arranged.”

Again, when the emperor Augustus mentioned above urged him by letter to come to the imperial city and either correct or supplement something in the statutes of that same council—something that could not be done without detestable betrayal—he replied as follows (Letter 125):

> “I have reverently received your Clemency’s letter, full of the power of faith and the light of truth. I would have wished to obey your piety in what it considers my presence necessary [Note: Leo edition: etiam in eo, “also in that”], so that I might attain the sight of your splendor with greater fruit [Note: Leo edition: majorem fructum conspectu, “a greater benefit through the sight”]; but I think [Note: Leo edition: id vobis, “this [will please] you”] that what reason has shown must be chosen will please you more. For while, with holy spiritual zeal [Note: Leo edition: et spiritali, “and spiritual”], you fortify the peace of the universal Church [Note: Leo edition: in universum, “in its entirety”], and while nothing is more suitable for defending the faith than to hold fast to what, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, has been irreproachably defined in every respect, we would seem to be overturning what has been well established and, at the demand of heretical petitioners, weakening the authorities embraced by the universal Church. Thus we would impose no limit upon the collision of churches, but, by granting license for rebellion, would spread rather than calm the conflicts.
>
> “Accordingly, after those impieties of the Ephesian council, by which the Catholic faith was rejected through the crime of Dioscorus and the Eutychian perversity was accepted, nothing could have been ordained more useful for preserving the Christian faith than that the holy Council of Chalcedon should abolish the aforesaid crime, and that such heavenly care should there be taken of doctrine that nothing should remain in anyone’s opinion discordant with the prophetic or apostolic preaching—while this moderation was preserved, that only the rebellious and obstinate were rejected from the unity of the Church, and forgiveness was denied to no one who had been corrected. What more reasonable, what more religious, could your piety decree than that no one thereafter be permitted to attack what has been established not so much by human as by divine decrees? Otherwise those who dared to doubt its truth would truly deserve to lose so great a gift of God.”

You see how he urges the emperor Leo to adhere to and uphold what, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, was irreproachably defined in every respect at the council mentioned above, so that no one thereafter might be permitted to attack what had been established not so much by human as by divine decrees. How, then, can the divine decrees be revised profanely—not to say condemned?

But who would not praise the dignity of this Roman bishop? Who would not honor such steadfastness? Could secular power in any way move him from his judgment that what had been divinely established must not be revised—him whom bodily force could not move from his place? Without doubt, he would shine wherever the sun might be; but in heaven the sun shines with far greater honor and propriety, where its position is highest and most fitting for illuminating all alike, lest it abandon many when it inclines toward a few.

Finally, moved by the authority of such freedom and reason, even the most religious emperor lays aside a useless—indeed, a many-sided harmful—desire and, as a son of peace, himself follows what reason has shown must be chosen. Yet Leo, as though fixed by an eternal law in a kind of firmament of his dignity and faith, shines with the radiance of truth and, like a most brilliant trumpet, thunders forth his authority to restrain the assaults of the restless. He says (Letter 78):

> “To seek what has been revealed, to revise what has been completed, and to overturn what has been defined—what else is this than to fail to give thanks for the grace received and to extend the wicked desires of deadly greed toward the food of the forbidden tree?”

In this and many other statements of the same kind, which that man of God wrote so often to the emperor Leo, I have demonstrated less than I wish, and less than I owe to my affection, how great was his concern and vigilance in preserving reverence for synodal decrees. For in all those matters mentioned above, he declared that he could neither revise further nor investigate what had once been defined by the Council of Chalcedon, since he knew that those decisions had been established not so much by human as by divine spirit.

In the matters I have now decided to mention, he also prohibited others from entering into any sort of dispute [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads disceptationem, “disputation.”] about the council mentioned above with heretics. For when he wrote not only to bishops but also to Catholic clergy and confessors from Egypt established at Constantinople, he admonished them as follows: [Col. 0836B] [Note: Two letters of Leo have been lost, fragments of which are appended. The first was written to the Egyptian bishops and clergy who, having been driven out by Timothy the Cat, had fled to Constantinople; for that reason they are called confessors. The second was addressed to the Constantinopolitan clergy. Both had the same subject: they were directed against Timothy the parricide, who had compounded his seizure of the Alexandrian see with the murder of Proterius, and in favor of the Council of Chalcedon, which he attacked, as Liberatus relates in chapter 15. It is therefore clear that these letters were written when Leo Augustus had sent an encyclical on the same matter to all the provinces; this encyclical is read after the council together with the replies of the provinces, as was mentioned in Book II and will be mentioned again in this chapter.]

> “Therefore, with every effort and labor of affection, you must strive to ensure that no disputation of those who lay snares be admitted, and that heretics not be able to obtain what plainly serves to attack the gospel faith. Nothing ought to be debated concerning matters defined by the authority of so great a council and of the most Christian emperor, and confirmed by the assent of the apostolic see, lest anything contrary to law appear to be violated. Much is detracted from faith and priestly steadfastness if one engages in a conflict of superfluous and highly harmful controversy with those who are filled with murder and madness, who wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ, and who are shown by their crime to be hateful to God.”

Leo, so strong and powerful, neither trusts his own strength nor allows others even to dispute or contend over matters defined at Chalcedon as God willed. Yet some presume even to issue decisions after assembling together, and to call heretical a letter which that holy and great council judged Catholic.

Writing also to the priests, deacons, and clergy of the Church of Constantinople, he says:

> “By God’s favor we have the great and divinely prepared assistance of the most Christian emperor. In my letters I earnestly implored him, as the case required, not to grant assent in any respect to the wicked petitions of parricides, nor in any way to permit the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon—which truly proceeded from heavenly decrees—to be violated as though they required revision. For it is evident that plotters [Col. 0836D] [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “the plots of the impious.” Another reading, “plotters against the pious,” which Quesnell noted in the margin of Letter 131 of Saint Leo from Facundus, seems capable of being relegated among the false readings; for Facundus did not reproduce it in accordance with the authority of our manuscript.] wish to creep in for this purpose: to make things consonant with the evangelical preaching and the traditions of the Fathers weak through a new judgment, so that [Note: The same manuscript reads et, “and”], when disputation is admitted, authority may be removed.” [Note: The same manuscript reads “so that, when disputation is admitted, authority may be taken away.”]

What, then, will the discoverers of this novel diligence [Note: The same manuscript reads novitio rather than novitii, a grammatical-form variant of “novel.”] say, who by their novel decree claim to have confirmed the Council of Chalcedon, whose statutes—consonant with evangelical preaching and the traditions of the Fathers—this great priest of Christ instead judged to be threatened with weakening by a new judgment? These statutes, just as they do not need strengthening, cannot be weakened. Nevertheless, insofar as these presumptuous men are concerned, they have made them weak by a new judgment, even if they had judged nothing contrary.

Accordingly, the emperor Marcian also considered it impious and sacrilegious to deliberate about anything after the judgment of the priests, and he permitted no one to reopen matters once rightly judged and properly arranged or to debate them publicly. In his edict, by which he denied everyone the discussion of what had been judged at Chalcedon, he declared:

> “He is truly impious and sacrilegious who, after the judgment of so many priests, leaves anything for his own opinion to deliberate. For it is the height of madness to seek a counterfeit light in the midst of clear daylight: whoever investigates anything further after the truth has been found is seeking a lie. Therefore, let no one—whether cleric, soldier, or person of any other condition—thereafter presume to discuss the Christian faith publicly before assembled and listening crowds, seeking in this way an occasion for tumult and unbelief. For anyone who attempts to reopen and publicly debate matters once judged and rightly arranged does injury to the judgment of the most religious council.”

And later, after establishing various penalties according to the condition of transgressors, he says:

> “Therefore all that was established by the holy Council of Chalcedon must be observed, and nothing afterward must be doubted. Having thus been admonished by this edict of our tranquility, abstain from profane speech and cease thereafter to dispute about divine matters, which is unlawful. For not only will this sin, as we believe, be punished by divine judgment; it will also be restrained by the authority of the laws and the judges.”

Behold Marcian, the emperor, the true father of the state and the true son of the Church—not the leader but the follower of priestly decrees—declares in his edict that whoever investigates anything further after the truth has been found is seeking a lie. Yet after this judgment of his, received by the Church of God, I do not know who boast that they have discovered another truth through their insolent investigation.

He says: “Anyone who attempts to reopen and publicly debate matters once judged and rightly arranged does injury to the judgment of the most religious council.” But these men say that they have honored the council, whose judgment they have judged. Indeed, by dissolving its judgment, they have called impious the letter which that council pronounced Catholic; and they strive to undermine the judgment of the holy Fathers, concerning which the emperor Marcian permitted no one even to dispute.

May his memory be among the blessings, and may all always return this saying to him for such merits: through him not only was the salvation of a desperate state given, but also rest was granted to the Church, long shaken by turmoil.

## CHAPTER III  
### That rulers ought to show obedience in matters of faith, not usurp for themselves what belongs to priests, as is taught by the example of the emperors Marcian and Leo

[Col. 0838B]

He recognized in which matters he should exercise imperial power, and in which he should show the obedience of a Christian. Therefore, so that he might not appear impious and sacrilegious, after the judgment of so many priests he left nothing to his own opinion [Note: The same manuscript reads, “he left nothing to be discussed.”]. He remembered the fate of Uzziah [Note: The same manuscript reads, “of King Uzziah”]. After he had prevailed over many nations and become glorious, his heart was lifted up, so that he placed incense upon the altar—something permitted only to the priests, the sons of Aaron. For this reason, leprosy confounded his most obstinate brow, which reverence had abandoned.

That most modest prince therefore knew that King Uzziah had not escaped punishment because he had presumed to sacrifice, although this is permitted to every priest, even one of the second order [Col. 0838C] [Note: He plainly calls the priest of the second order a presbyter, and shortly afterward priests of the first order, bishops. It has been observed that they were once distinguished in this way in the note on Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 25. Hence a presbyter was also called “a man of the second order” in the second synod of Pope Symmachus, chapter 6: “It is impious to say that a man of the second order in the Church is not bound by the obligation by which the supreme pontiff binds himself.” Likewise in Hincmar, Letter 7, chapter 20: “And if such things have been admitted concerning bishops, they are certainly not to be overlooked concerning presbyters, men of the second order.”]—all the more did he recognize that he himself could not escape punishment, whether for reopening for discussion matters of Christian faith that had already been properly settled, which is wholly impermissible, or for establishing new canons, which is permitted only to many priests of the first order gathered together in one place.

Accordingly, this temperate man, content with his own office, wished to be an executor of the ecclesiastical canons, not their author or enforcer. He neither established a new rule of faith against the error of Dioscorus, although the prejudice that Dioscorus had attempted to inflict upon religion at Ephesus had been removed, nor compelled the Fathers’ decree at Chalcedon to be reconsidered.

Yet Emperor Marcian may have been moved at that time not only by the fate of King Uzziah, though it was greatly to be feared [Note: The same manuscript reads, “warned in this way”], but also by the fate of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Although Korah was one of the sons of Levi, who had been chosen from the whole people of Israel and appointed to the sacred service of the Temple, nevertheless, because they all usurped the office of priests and dared to offer sacrifice to God—a matter far less serious than deciding questions of Christian faith—they were swallowed up by the gaping earth. By their new and singular destruction they left an example astonishing to all presumptuous men.

How, then, could a religious and wise emperor, a layman, believe that he would escape punishment for retracting what the holy Fathers had already decreed concerning the faith, or for himself issuing new decrees, when punishment did not pass harmlessly over the sons of Levi—that is, Korah and those of his tribe who followed him—even though they had been set apart from the people for the service of the Temple [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “having been set apart”]—nor over Dathan and Abiram, for doing what we have shown to be incomparably less?

Indeed, that people had already committed many grave sins, and had even been stained by the profanation of idolatry, which was considered the greatest of all sins, together with its priest. After they had seen Egypt devastated by miraculous plagues for the sake of their liberation and had crossed the middle of the sea on dry ground, they forced Aaron to make a calf for them at Horeb, worshiped the graven image, and exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass (Psalm 105:19–20), saying: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of Egypt” (Exodus 32:4). Aaron built an altar before it, brought burnt offerings, offered a sacrifice of salvation, and the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.

Yet when this evil was punished among them, nothing like what we read happened in punishment for their presumption, so that a singular and extraordinary penalty might reveal the singular crime of the presumptuous. For this reason Moses also says there: “By this you shall know that the Lord sent me to perform all these works, and that I do not act on my own: if these men die the death of all men, and if their visitation is the visitation of all men, then the Lord did not send me” (Numbers 16:28–29).

There Aaron, the high priest, both fashioned the calf, built the altar, brought burnt offerings, and offered the sacrifice. Hence it is written: “Moses saw the people, that they had been stripped bare. For Aaron had stripped them bare, so that they might be a joy to their enemies” (Exodus 32:25); and he obtained pardon for his deed. But there Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, although they were sacrificing to the true God, were punished with a new and incredible penalty because the office did not belong to them. So great is the weight assigned in divine justice to preserving the order that God has established in his service [Note: It appears that the text should read, “if it is not preserved”], that God judges this worse than rendering to false gods the service that is owed to him alone.

They certainly appeared to be despisers of the divine order when they rose up against Moses and Aaron, claimed to speak on behalf of the assembly, and uttered words in praise of God, saying: “Be assured that all in the whole assembly are holy, and the Lord is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the Lord?” (Numbers 16:3). But for that reason their pride could not be justified, since such words are commonly produced as a covering for contempt.

No one praises God better than the one who, approving God’s judgment upon himself, does not usurp what has been entrusted to others. Moreover, if Marcian should be thought to have remembered that commandment which is given concerning the Levites, the sons of Kohath—“They shall not touch the holy things, lest they die” (Numbers 18:3)—how could he believe that he would escape condemnation to eternal death if he either issued a new decree concerning the Christian faith or reopened what had already been decreed?

But it is not enough merely not to touch the holy things; they are also forbidden to look upon them, as it is written: “And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Do not destroy the tribe of the family of Kohath from among the Levites. Do this for them, and they shall live and not die when they approach the holy of holies. Aaron and his sons shall enter and assign each one his burden, and they shall not enter suddenly to look upon the sanctuary” [Note: The same manuscript reads, “the sanctuary, and they shall not die.” It adds: “Could Uzzah, son of Abinadab, have done too little? It should read Uzzah: in Hebrew and Greek, Οζά. He is called the son of Abinadab in the Hebrew text and the Vulgate edition, but in the Greek, Aminadab, in the Second Book of Kings, chapter 6.”] (Numbers 4:17–19).

Nor could the fate of Uzzah fail to terrify a Christian prince. When the ark was being brought from his father’s house, placed upon a new cart, and the oxen suddenly kicked, he stretched out his hand and held it lest it fall. The Lord was angered against him, as Scripture says: “And he struck him because of his rashness; and he died there beside the ark of the Lord” (2 Samuel 6:7). And so that an everlasting memory of fear might also be left for posterity, that place was called Uzzah [Note: The Vulgate has, “The striking of Uzzah.”] [Note: The same manuscript reads, “the striking of Uzziah.” It should read “Uzzah.”]

For this reason David too, who was joyfully leading it forward with all Israel, feared the Lord on that day and said: “How shall the ark of the Lord come to me?” (2 Samuel 6:9); and he was unwilling to divert the ark of the Lord to himself. If we follow the judgment of a wrongly presumptuous heart, would it not seem that he deserved greater punishment for failing to hold the ark of the Lord, which he believed was about to fall, when he could have held it? But we must judge according to reverence for the divine commandment, not according to the suspicion of presumptuous men.

For since Uzzah had learned that the Levites had been warned, “They shall not touch the holy things, lest they die,” how could he lawfully touch what was forbidden? Even in the critical moment, he ought not to have been moved by sudden fear at the wavering ark, but restrained by observance [Note: The same manuscript reads, “careful observance”] of the divine commandment.

Therefore, since Uzzah did not transgress with deliberate purpose and counsel, but was overtaken by an unexpected and accidental circumstance, and suffered the ultimate punishment for his rashness solely because he touched the ark without due thought, by what reasonable argument could Augustus Marcian presume to reopen for discussion what had been established at Chalcedon [Col. 0841A] [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “what was established in the council of rulers and in the great assembly, diligently sought out in the work of the Lord according to all his purposes, for discussion.”]?

Yet to preachers of the truth, who sometimes kick against the goad like the oxen of whom it is said, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (1 Corinthians 9:9), the Church appears to waver; they are its bearers and teachers [Note: The same manuscript reads, “its teachers are, as it were”], and it seems to waver like that ark. But it is not Uzzah’s office to hold it up. Its own David goes before it, leading it in exultation; he himself, strong of hand, invisibly governs it through those whom he has appointed to govern it. Therefore it may indeed waver, but it can never fall.

You therefore have nothing, Uzzah, with which to excuse yourself under the pretense of pious concern, since by divine judgment you are struck for your rashness. It is credible that Marcian, of august memory, was instructed and fortified by these and similar arguments and examples [Col. 0841B], lest he disgrace the dignity of the empire entrusted to him by usurping another’s office.

Even if what we have recalled occurred less readily to his mind [Note: The same manuscript reads, “occurred to him”], his own reasoning undoubtedly restrained this modest man. He could very easily have reflected and understood that it belongs to Christ alone to possess kingship together with priesthood. For although certain kings exercised priestly functions as figures of the one who was to come, when the manifest light came into the world, removing the shadows of things to come, Christ gave no one else what he reserved as his singular possession. Rather, distributing his gifts among different persons, he forbade kings what properly belongs to the priesthood [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Just as he forbade priests what properly belongs to kings, so he forbade kings what properly belongs to the priesthood.”].

Accordingly, how could a wise man fail to judge it profane to wish to appear to be what Christ alone is?

But when the Church, having found rest from the assaults of heretics through the decree of the holy and great council and through the authority of the emperor Marcian himself, was again harassed by their factions after Leo succeeded to the empire, Leo wished to confound them not merely by his own response but by the common response of the Church. He therefore did what was fitting for a Christian emperor: through the metropolitan bishops he sent general letters, asking about Timothy, the murderous bishop of Alexandria, and about the Council of Chalcedon, so that each bishop, meeting with his fellow bishops and clergy, might sign his response stating his judgment.

In these letters he also judged that the following should be added: “Respond without any fear, without favor toward anyone or hatred, yet placing before your eyes the fear of almighty God, knowing that you will give an account to the divine majesty concerning this matter.”

After receiving these letters, the same metropolitans, with their colleagues, responded from their respective provinces, as they had been instructed, with a judgment as harmonious and steadfast as the Spirit of truth commonly makes many spirits one. Although their responses were given from widely separated places, none of them differed from the others. They decreed that the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon must be observed irrevocably, protesting and saying—as we have already recalled in Book II—“We cannot either remove or alter one iota [Note: The same manuscript reads, “one iota”] or one letter of what was defined at that council” [Col. 0842A].

And again: “Just as nothing is lacking to the sun for demonstrating that it is the sun, so nothing at all of what is good is lacking to the great, holy, and universal Council of Chalcedon. It needs neither addition nor subtraction; it was established by the Holy Spirit like a kind of divine sun [Note: The same manuscript reads, “salt”]. For those who were condemned there in due course, judged unworthy of the priestly order, were condemned by the decree and judgment of the great God as impious. Those who were received there, having previously endured an unjust and tyrannical indictment, were immediately and justly received by the decree of the Holy Spirit. Among them is the second Abel of our times, the blessed Flavian.”

Those who dared to pass judgment upon the decision of so great a council despised all these considerations. They believed either that something might be lacking in it which they ought to supply, or that something might be present which they ought to correct.

It must be considered what responses Christian freedom—into which we have been called—gave at that time, when Leo, a most religious emperor, did not terrify the priests of God by the temporal power he had received, but rather inspired them, against human fear, with fear of almighty God. He said: “Respond without any human fear, without favor toward anyone or hatred, placing before your eyes only the fear of almighty God.”

He did not warn them that they would have to give an account of their response to him, so that someone might perhaps say that they had given the answer they believed would please the emperor who had addressed them. Rather, he said: “Knowing that you will give an account to the divine majesty concerning this matter.”

That prince should be understood to have said this not only for the sake of the discipline and observance of Christian religion, but also because no authority can belong to decrees imposed by coercion. It is the height of futility either to pronounce a judgment against someone or to accept a judgment assigned by force. The very name “judgment” disappears when one does not say what one thinks.

Consequently, nothing is contributed to the case judged in this way, while those who oppose it gain considerable strength from the fact. For it is proved that a person has not judged rightly when he judged under compulsion from another.

The Church was once disturbed in this way when, through the emperor Constantius, secular power usurped within it what had not been granted to it. For this reason the blessed Hilary, in a letter from which we quoted part in Book X, said: “After the prolonged and grievous sorrow of us all over the things that were irreligiously done by the impious, the communion of the Lord has been preserved among us only since the Church began to be harassed by these disturbances: bishops are driven into exile, priests are deposed, peoples are terrified, the faith is endangered, and the decrees of the Lord’s teaching are established according to human judgment and power.”

Therefore Leo, of pious memory, did not disturb the Church’s peace, because he did not presume to establish the decrees of the Lord’s teaching according to his own judgment and power, nor did he usurp anything entrusted solely to priests.

For this reason, too, the decisions made in his time are confidently opposed to heretics without any charge of violence, because he knew that, after the Lord’s coming, only pagan princes had held imperial power and priesthood together. He judged that it was unbecoming for a Christian prince to do what had once belonged to pagans.

If he had desired to exercise dominion over the Christian faith—which even the Apostle did not desire, when he said, “We do not lord it over your faith, but are fellow workers for your joy” (2 Corinthians 1:23)—he would first have decreed according to his own pleasure what seemed right to him, and afterward would have brought Christ’s priests forward unnecessarily and compelled them to give their assent by signing what he himself had devised.

If they accepted as council decrees what had been composed by the will of a single layman, then one who had no competence to judge such matters would be deciding everything, while those competent to judge would decide nothing.

That Augustus also remembered that a council compelled by force has never subscribed to anything except falsehood, as happened at Ariminum when Constantius applied compulsion and at Ephesus when Dioscorus used oppression [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “has never subscribed”]. For this reason he left confirmation of the faith to the judgment of the priests, to whose authority it had been entrusted. Such confirmation is truly made only when no judgment of secular power is subscribed.

For it is one thing when someone, occupying the place of a judge among the other bishops in a council, indicates by his signature what he thinks; it is another when he is brought forward as a witness and, worse still, unwillingly subscribes to another’s decision.

Therefore, although writings of this kind bear the false title of synodal decrees, they serve at least to show what sort of causes they were in which no one subscribed unless compelled; what sort of men those were who compelled others to subscribe; and what sort of men those were who yielded to human presumption.

The same most religious emperor also knew that very few people are led by reason, while many are led by authority. He therefore attempted not only to extract no judgment from the priests, but not even to anticipate it. Although the matter had already been decreed and was manifest, he chose to await their judgment, so that by this very act of waiting he might show the whole people how much reverence ought to be paid to priestly authority.

If he had wished to establish first what was just and afterward to seek the bishops’ judgment in order to strengthen what he had established, then, even if the decree had been just and religious, he would nevertheless have made it suspect to many by such presumption. Those less capable of reasoning would more readily have believed that the bishops had obeyed something other than the truth.

For if some bishops had subscribed to the decree but had instead feared to resist temporal power, then authority useful to many in matters of truth would have been abolished. And who can explain the evils that will follow upon those who do not observe the order established by divine providence?

Moreover, since the Semi-Eutychians have nothing to complain of in what was established in the times of both the emperor Marcian and Leo, why did their supporters wish to nullify those decisions by a new reconsideration? Did Marcian and Leo convene councils to confirm a hasty judgment of their own, and then, changing their minds, compel the priests of God to alter their earlier decrees according to the shifting of their own minds—so that the gravity of synodal authority would become a mockery and the reverent expectation of it a weariness?

They never removed from the preachers of the Church the administration of the divine sacraments. They knew that, just as the Lord said through Solomon in an admonition to kings, “Have they appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself. Be among them as one of them; take care of them, and so sit among them” [Note: Greek: Κάθισον, “sit” or “remain confident.”] [Note: The same manuscript reads, “remain confident.”] (Ecclesiasticus 32:1–2), so the same Lord spoke specifically concerning the preacher of the divine word in the Gospel: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds so doing” (Luke 12:42–43).

How could these words of the Gospel fail to move religious and wise princes, so that they would not insolently thrust themselves into the dangers of so great a responsibility?

First, this servant is said by the Lord to have been appointed not as a distributor but as a steward. He needs the most vigilant discernment if he is to fulfill the one office entrusted to him properly. Therefore the Lord seeks in him not only faithfulness but also prudence. He is not to distribute equally to the household entrusted to him, nor in the same manner, but according to each person’s capacity and disposition of mind, he is to dispense the Lord’s provisions moderately and suitably.

Next, he is commanded to give the measure of wheat at the proper time. Matters that would often be beneficial if brought forward opportunely have proved harmful when introduced at an unsuitable time. Thus the proper occasion must also be observed, so that the household may receive its measure of wheat at the proper time.

If anyone, ignorant of these dangers and eager to appear learned, disturbs the Church with questions raised spontaneously and at an unsuitable time, without any usefulness recommending them, he is not a steward of the Lord’s household but its dissipator and a scatterer of God’s mysteries.

Those princes feared becoming such men. Therefore, not only because the magnitude of so great a responsibility exceeded their strength, but also because they had not received it, they did not assume the office of this stewardship.

There is consequently no reason to call weak or inadequate the measures established against heretics in their times, since they were undertaken outside the judgment and authority of the priests. The princes themselves followed the priests’ judgment, remembering that just as the apostle Peter, when he says, “Fear God; honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17), commends the honoring of princes not only to laymen but also to the priests themselves, so Paul, his fellow apostle, is read as saying to all Christians: “Obey your leaders and be subject to them; for they keep watch as those who will give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for that would not be profitable for you” (Hebrews 13:17).

This command is given not only to the common people, nor only to nobles, but also to kings: they are to obey and submit to the leaders of Christ’s Church and understand that their souls have been entrusted to the priests’ account, if they do not bear the Christian name in vain.

Therefore they did not oppress any of the priests, so that the priests might do everything with joy and not with groaning, because, in accordance with the Apostle’s admonition, they believed that this would not be profitable for themselves.

Hence heretics are now oppressed by decrees of those same priests, because the men by whom those decrees were established are not themselves offended by being oppressed [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “are not themselves shown to be oppressed.”].

## CHAPTER IV. That the emperor Zeno, by presuming to decide matters of faith, disturbed the Church with a prolonged and grave schism.

But who will accept what the emperor Zeno later decreed, trampling underfoot the reverence due to God’s order and deciding according to his own will and authority? Who will pay attention to the fact that an inconsiderate power considered not what was expedient, but what was permissible to itself, and did not understand that unity is not produced by confusion? For if unity is to be achieved not through the conversion of heretics but through contagion and mixture, why were only the Acephali, and not all heretics, admitted into the Church while their errors had not first been condemned and the definitions established against those errors had not been received?

[Note: The Henoticon, or “Instrument of Union,” of Zeno—as Liberatus interprets it—was issued to the Alexandrians; some of its chapters are examined here. Evagrius gives the complete Greek text in Book III, chapter 24, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, and Liberatus gives another Latin version in chapter 18. The latter likewise reports that Acacius was its author on Zeno’s behalf, while Theophanes in his *Chronicle* relates that some said it had been dictated by Acacius himself: “Then Zeno also composed the Henoticon and sent it everywhere, dictated, as some say, by Acacius of Constantinople.” After the Henoticon was accepted, the orthodox at first became confused with the heretics in Alexandria; thereafter the same stain spread from Constantinople and Antioch, and finally throughout the entire East. Victor of Tunnuna writes: “In the consulship of Theodoric, the Eastern bishops, except a few, having been polluted by the communion and agreement of Zeno through the Henoticon, with Peter of Alexandria, Peter of Antioch, and Acacius of Constantinople, renounce the Council of Chalcedon.” Facundus likewise writes against Mutianus: “The emperor Zeno rejected the Council itself by a published edict.”]

For when he exhorted the aforementioned Acephali to return to the Church, he said at the outset:

> “Flavius Zeno, pious, victorious, triumphant, ever-great Augustus, to the orthodox bishops, archimandrites, and peoples established throughout Alexandria, Egypt, Pentapolis, and Libya.”

And after calling them orthodox, he urged them to join themselves to the Church, saying:

> “Join yourselves, therefore, to the spiritual mother, the Church, so that you may enjoy one divine communion.”

What a prudent and universally circumspect man—one who presumed to intrude upon the office of priests! He calls the Acephali orthodox, although they were nothing else than separated from the Church. Why, then, does he urge them to join the spiritual mother if, while remaining separated from her, they have continued to be orthodox? “So that,” he says, “you may enjoy one divine communion.” Were these men orthodox without divine communion, that is, alienated from God?

Or did they indeed possess divine communion, but not one communion with the Church? Can there therefore be two divine communions, disagreeing with and opposed to each other? But if there is one God of Zeno, there is also one divine communion. If two divine communions, disagreeing with one another, are spoken of, it follows that people must believe not only that there are two gods, but also that they disagree with one another.

And what evil do you not do, O Augustus, first power of the world, when, failing to consider that divine power is superior to you, you exceed the limits appointed for you? Calling those who disagree with the Church of God “orthodox,” you say that they partake of another divine communion. If you understood that this very fact—that everything is permitted to you—is the furnace of your testing, you would also recognize from the appearance, that is, the color, of the purple with which you are clothed a constant reminder, as though you were placed in the midst of flames.

Again he says:

> “For our holy mother the Church receives you as her own children; embrace her. For after a long time she desires to hear your sweet voice. Join yourselves, therefore, to her.”

For what benefit, I ask, should they embrace the Church? For what benefit should they join themselves to her, when he both calls them orthodox though separated from her and believes them to be participants in divine communion?

But hear what worldly power, trusting in itself rather than in reason, did thereafter. Wishing to satisfy those same Semi-Eutychians, he set out his faith in this edict, professing that he accepted the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus, but remaining silent about Chalcedon and refusing to confess the two natures of Christ—as though the sick were not to be healed with an antidote, but gathered together for contagion with others.

And although it is written, “I will speak of your testimonies before kings, and I shall not be put to shame” (Psalm 118:46), the king was ashamed to speak the truth before his subjects. This was what the despiser of God deserved from divine justice: since he refused to be subject to God’s order, he feared those subject to him.

Adding something still worse, he said “that the holy Catholic Churches existing everywhere, and the priests beloved by God who presided over them, should believe no differently.” It was as though the faith of all the Churches depended upon his will, and no one were permitted to believe otherwise than the emperor commanded.

I think he saw certain fearful men, or men greedy for temporal things, favoring him, and judged the others by them. Even though he had taken away their voice of contradiction, he could not change their mind. For worldly power has no further force over those whom it has drawn back from the free confession of faith, except to make them fall into what the Lord says:

> “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his majesty, and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke 9:26).

Worldly power can therefore take some people away from the Church, but it cannot acquire anyone for itself. It is better, then, that it keep itself within its own limits; when it oversteps them, it can destroy many and win no one.

Everything that we see teaching deliberately has its own workshops or craftsmen. We have never heard anvils sounding in a weaver’s shop, nor fire roaring there in furnaces. We have never found a shoemaker being asked what proportion of width corresponds to the length of a particular construction, or how much height suits the two together. Those things can be known completely by men instructed by the teachers of that very craft.
