The divine Scriptures alone are held in contempt, as though they had neither their own school nor teachers; and one who has never learned believes that he can dispute about them with the greatest skill.

Furthermore, when the affairs of the palace are transferred to the Church, how was he transferring the affairs of the Church to the palace? Finally, had he already subdued or pacified all the barbarian nations hostile to the state? Had he already removed rebellions and the causes of rebellions throughout the various provinces of his empire? Had he already brought a fitting conclusion to all the complaints arising from criminal or civil cases?

Since no one can be sufficient for these matters, how could he, if he considered the great dangers of his position and believed that he would render an account to God for everything, plunge himself into dangers belonging to others as well? Or how could divine justice fail to condemn such presumption?

Not content with these things, he also added this insult to the holy Council of Chalcedon, saying:

> “Gather yourselves together, therefore, doubting nothing. For we have written these things to you not to innovate the faith, but to satisfy you. Whoever thinks otherwise, whether now or at any time, whether at Chalcedon or in any council whatsoever, we anathematize.”

We believe that he was roused to this detestable crime by the praises of flatterers, who told him, as they usually do, that he surpassed all his predecessors in wisdom and religion; that none among all the priests of God, whether present or past, could be compared with him; and that the Catholic faith stood in him alone and continued only up to him.

Trusting them, he imagined that, through a singular wisdom which no one except his flatterers had attributed to him, he could discover a way of producing unity which no one before him, throughout so many ages, had been able to discover.

Finally, in the aforementioned edict he said:

> “Let members be fitted to members, which the enemy of good has long hastened to separate; for he knows that, if he attacks the whole body of the Church, he is easily overcome. From this division it happened, through so many generations and so many years, that some, deprived of the bath of regeneration, departed this life,”

and so forth.

If we agree with the proclamation of secular power, which after so many generations, by deceiving or concealing the truth, believed that it could produce unity, we too shall say that unless we are joined to the Eutychians, the body of the Church is not whole. But woe to us if we believe that, without the Acephali, we have remained mere trunks.

When the most blessed Leo said, “For it is in no way possible that those who dare to contradict the divine sacraments should be joined with us in any communion,” this man sent contradictors into the Church, giving holy things to dogs and throwing pearls to be trampled by swine.

Finally, turning against the very men who had committed this outrage, they tore them apart and separated them from the Church. For this reason also a great and prolonged schism came about, until the merciful God, through the ministry of your piety, restored them to unity.

[Note: According to the account he writes against Mutianus, the schism lasted nearly forty years, from the pontificate of Felix III until Hormisdas; in Hormisdas’s time the Easterners were received into communion and peace was restored to the Church in the year of Christ 519, chiefly through the efforts of Justinian, then still a count, with the emperor Justin. Vigilius writes in his encyclical: “And therefore, if the cause of the Church is being arranged so that he may now restore to it the peace which his most devout uncle, the prince, established in his time, I have no need of oaths, but immediately depart.” Justinian’s congratulatory letters to Hormisdas on the establishment of peace are extant. There is also extant an unpublished letter of Avitus of Vienne to John of Constantinople on the same subject, expressing public joy over that peace. “The illustrious man,” he says—Laurentius—“added that every cloud which had darkened and obscured the quiet of the Eastern peoples with uncertainty had been wiped away by the serenity of restored peace, and that you possessed with the Roman bishop the harmony which it would be fitting to present to the world as that of the twin princes of the apostles. For who, even if he can be called Catholic, would not rejoice in the peace of Churches so great and so distinguished, which the world beholds as a sign of religion set in heaven, like a double constellation? Who would not rightly delight in the return of the sick to health and in their sound condition, when, with the other sheep saved within the folds, that one which had wandered through the fault of an erring will is recalled while the heavenly enclosures resound with joy?”]

Thus you attained the greatest glory, which we hope you will preserve to the end, doing nothing contrary to this praiseworthy achievement of yours. But remember what joy there was then among the Christian people, when the whole Catholic world proclaimed you guardians of your fathers’ decrees, restorers of ecclesiastical peace, and avengers of the order that had been violated.

O how sweetly your name was carried on the lips of those who praised you! How pleasing was the sound of remembrance of that memorable work of yours!

Therefore, we beg you, consider and observe both what you yourselves accomplished at that time, and what the princes Marcian and Leo accomplished in their own times through the properly ordered office of the priesthood, and what Zeno did contrary to them, trampling upon the order of divine providence and abusing another’s office—when he believes flatterers, when he estimates himself by their praises, when he is lifted up by those applauses by which human frailty is altogether burdened.

He did not heed what the Apostle said in admonition:

> “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Galatians 6:4),

that is, let him trust the testimony of his own conscience, rather than abandoning it and glorying in the mouth of one who praises him.

Flattery indeed appears pleasant, but it is received to one’s ruin; truth is sometimes bitter, yet it is always salutary to those who receive it well. The former caresses and deceives; the latter disciplines and corrects.

## CHAPTER V  
### Conclusion of the Entire Work, with an Exhortation to Justinian to Recognize His Error after the Example of Theodosius

If the distinguished priests held to this, and did not wish to please princes in the manner in which deceitful parasites usually mock their unwary patrons, they would never have said, to the insult of the holy Council of Chalcedon:

> “If anyone says that the impious letter to Maris is correct, or defends it, and does not anathematize it, let him be anathema,”

nor would they have decreed that anyone who did not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia and his doctrines, together with those who either held or now hold opinions similar to his, should be anathema.

In this way, as we have shown, they condemned under anathema not only the aforementioned Council of Chalcedon and the Council of Antioch, but also the Church of earlier times which had been in communion with Theodore, and all the faithful present in the body of Christ who know neither his doctrines nor his name; indeed, they condemned holy persons beloved by Christ, the apostles themselves, and the Catholic faith.

And for this they think themselves excusable: that they did not do it of their own accord, but followed another’s judgment. They pay insufficient attention to the fact that shepherds ought to lead the flock, not the flock the shepherds. Therefore the error is attributed not to the flock, but to the shepherds of the flock, unless they have rebuked it.

The Lord says to Ezekiel:

> “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel, and you shall hear a word from my mouth. When I say to the sinner, ‘You shall die,’ and you do not speak so that the wicked may beware of his way, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand. But if you warn the wicked of his wicked way and he does not turn from it [the Verona manuscript: ‘and he has not turned from it’], he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but you shall save your own soul” (Ezekiel 3:17, 19).

It is certain that the princes of the people also belong to this house of Israel, and that watchmen have been appointed over them as well. If priests conceal their faults out of respect for persons, those faults will undoubtedly be charged against the priests as though they had enabled them.

Even if it is granted that they lacked the power to forbid these things, who will grant that they lacked the power to avoid them? Therefore, even if they could not prevent these things from being done, they could at least have avoided doing them.

Why, then, should a priest, whose duty it is to bear the sins of the people, fail to care for his burden by preventing from sin the one for whose sins he offers sacrifice? For it is written:

> “And Aaron shall bear the judgments of the sons of Israel” (Exodus 28:29).

By this we understand that priests will be judged for the sins of the people.

Hence the Apostle also said what we mentioned above:

> “Obey your superiors and submit to them, for they keep watch as those who will render an account for your souls” (Hebrews 13:17).

Here again it is said:

> “And Aaron shall bear their sins” (Exodus 28:38).

Therefore, if princes are not foreign to the people of God, and sacrifice is offered for them as well, priests must also bear their sins. Consequently, it should not be counted as recklessness or arrogance if a priest forbids even a prince to sin.

The statement of the man who says, “Do not increase the burden which I have undertaken to bear for your salvation,” is humane and worthy of every acceptance. For when a priest says to someone, “Do not sin,” he is saying nothing other than, “Do not increase the burden which I bear for you.”

Accordingly, if a prince also wishes to have a priest as an intercessor for his sins, he should not disdain to endure him as a corrector of his sins as well, so that the priest, interceding for him, may be heard. Otherwise what was said to Jeremiah may also be said to him:

> “Do not pray for this people, and do not ask or entreat me on their behalf, and do not come to me for them, for I shall not hear you” (Jeremiah 8:16).

Fearing this, the Emperor Theodosius, of blessed memory—whose memory in the Church of Christ will always be worthy of remembrance—although he often triumphed in battles against mighty barbarians and over the greatest tyrants, did not thereby earn true glory from the frequency of those victories, in which he cannot be compared with Trajan, a son of Gehenna.

Rather, he earned it through the humble and public repentance for his sin which he accepted calmly and humbly when the bishop Ambrose disciplined him after he had subdued his royal pride, and through the period of due satisfaction imposed upon him, which he completed while removed from communion with the Church.

He piously believed and wisely understood that he could reach life not through the temporal power by which he had even been placed over the priests of God, but through the fact that he himself was subject to them.

Therefore we must believe that, if God were now to raise up an Ambrose, there would also be no lack of a Theodosius. But when confidence in demanding is diminished, devotion in rendering is diminished as well.

He is not a great lover of truth for whom the authority of the person commends it. But since we have now at last reached the point toward which we were striving through the long circuit of our speech, I beseech you, most merciful emperor, by the gentleness and modesty of Christ, not to regard me as unworthy or to despise me.

For if the things being said are true, they ought not therefore to be rejected because an outcast brings them to your attention. What difference does it make through whose mouth truth speaks to you, since it once deigned even to speak through the mouth of a she-ass?

But if the prophet Nathan must be sought whenever a prince has sinned, where shall we now find Nathan, so that the prince who is certainly known to have sinned, like David, may be rebuked? Therefore let the one who has sinned not seek another Nathan, since I think he himself would not presume to compare his merits with those of holy David.

For David the king was far superior not only in his kingdom but also in the very prophecy over which Nathan alone possessed authority. Nathan vehemently exposed David’s hidden sin by rebuking it; we, however, humbly ask that what we cannot conceal, if we wish to, be corrected, and we do not exaggerate a sin that has not been committed against many.

Nor do we ask that something be corrected like the act which Ambrose punished by excommunication. That act, although wrongly done, was nevertheless believed to fall within Theodosius’s authority. But what has now been done—even if it had been correct—would not have been correctly done, because no king has been granted authority to do anything of this kind; it belongs to priests alone.

Nevertheless, taking care lest I appear to have exceeded the measure not of my office, but of my merit, I presume to make no accusation concerning this. I ask only, in all simplicity, that you consider with a faithful mind those very men whom we have shown to have been condemned in this novel decree.

First, consider Philip and Thomas, disciples of Christ, who were made anathema because they once held opinions similar to those which Theodore is said to have held. Then consider the holy Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon and declared, by their own judgment, that the letter of the most reverend Bishop Ibas was correct; they did not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia, even though they heard his praises recited from it. Moreover, they defended the letter of the blessed Leo by the example or testimony of those letters in which that same Theodore was both defended and praised.

Among these venerable Fathers, first contemplate in your mind the aforesaid Leo, who, because he did not anathematize the letter in question when he approved the acts of that council, was himself made anathema together with the Council of Chalcedon by which the letter had been judged orthodox.

Look also upon the Eastern Council, which we have shown to have been assembled by the most wise John of Antioch and approved by the Council of Chalcedon. It not only did not anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia and his doctrines, but even prohibited his being anathematized, because it found many similarly expressed statements among other earlier and glorious Fathers.

Behold, as though presiding over this holy Eastern Council, John of Constantinople, Theodore’s fellow student, and Gregory of Nazianzus. In agreement with their judgment, John defended Theodore’s writings against those who slanderously disturbed the Church.

Let the blessed Cyril also join this council. Agreeing with its decree and likewise forbidding certain sayings of Theodore to be condemned, he said that they would provide an occasion for the contrary doctrine held by those who wished Theodore to be condemned.

Let the blessed Proclus of Constantinople join it as well. He not only likewise forbade Theodore to be rejected, but also testified that he had never condemned him while he was alive.

Let the venerable Domnus of Antioch join it too. Holding to the judgment of his predecessor John and of his other earlier colleagues, Domnus was the first to resist Eutyches, who was attempting to renew the impiety of the heresiarch Apollinaris and was therefore presuming to anathematize Diodore and Theodore; he wrote to the Emperor Theodosius against him.

To all these men, so that a prejudgment might be made against Theodore’s person at the Council of Chalcedon, an equal anathema was pronounced, because by their example, testimony, or decree they prohibited anyone from saying that either they themselves or Theodore’s doctrines should be anathematized.

But behold, religious emperor: with every effort we have brought so many holy and venerable persons before the eyes of your mind. Who will grant that you too, considering that those condemned men belong to that company who, at the resurrection of the righteous, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, will themselves sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel, may look upon them with those eyes by which you do not doubt that you will be judged by them, rather than with the eyes by which you now see Christ’s priests temporarily subject to you?

Look, therefore, with the eyes of faith by which you believe in Christ, as though they were seated in a heavenly court: first and in the highest place, the reverend apostles Philip and Thomas; then, in the order that follows, all the most blessed Fathers whose judgments we have mentioned and whom we have shown to have been condemned together with them.

Although, on account of the greatness of the case, we can scarcely commend them in words—for their dignity does not permit it—who among those conscious of their condemnation could endure even the silent sight of them? Indeed, they terrify the faithful observer more by their silence itself.

For by this they seem to have reserved their condemnation for the future judgment, unless it is removed as quickly as possible; its sentence will be irreversible, and that which incurs it will be everlasting without end.

## CHRONOLOGICAL SUMMARY OF EIGHT YEARS

Arranging and elucidating the principal events that occurred in the affair of the Three Chapters.

**In the year of Christ 546.** The Emperor Justinian, at the urging of Theodore, Bishop of Caesarea, publishes a book against the Three Chapters and compels Menas of Constantinople and the other patriarchs, together with their bishops, to subscribe to their condemnation. For the same reason he also summons Vigilius from Rome.

**In the year of Christ 547.** Vigilius enters the imperial city on the eighth day before the Kalends of February and suspends Menas and the other condemners of the Chapters from communion. Later, at the request of the Empress Theodora, he restores Menas to communion on 29 June. Justinian unsuccessfully uses force in an attempt to extort a condemnation from Vigilius.

**In the year of Christ 548.** In the interest of peace, Vigilius is inclined to condemn the Chapters. He holds a meeting of bishops, which Facundus attended, and orders each of them to submit his judgment in writing. He sends the bishops’ replies to the palace; and on Holy Saturday he himself delivers the *Judicatum* to Menas. In it he condemned Theodore of Mopsuestia together with his doctrines, the letter of Ibas, and the writings of Theodoret, while preserving the reverence due to the Council of Chalcedon. The Africans, Illyrians, Dalmatians, and others nevertheless continued to defend the Three Chapters.

**In the year of Christ 549.** At the beginning of the year the deacons Rusticus and Sebastian desert Vigilius. Attacking the *Judicatum*, they denounce Vigilius throughout the provinces as a betrayer of the Council of Chalcedon. For this reason Anastasius, sent by Aurelian of Arles, brought a letter to Vigilius on the day before the Ides of July.

**In the year of Christ 550.** Vigilius writes back to Bishop Valentinian of Scythia on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, and to Aurelian of Arles on the third day before the Kalends of May, explaining that nothing contrary to the Council of Chalcedon had been admitted in his *Judicatum*. He deprives Rusticus and Sebastian, the authors of the false report, of the honor and ministry of their rank.

When Justinian pressed him to condemn the Chapters absolutely and without mentioning the Council, Vigilius persuaded him to refer the matter to a general council. In the meantime, after accepting with the signatures of the other bishops the *Judicatum* he had previously issued, he prohibited, with the emperor’s consent, any further discussion of the Chapters until the council.

**In the year of Christ 551.** At Theodore’s instigation, Justinian publishes edicts condemning the Chapters, contrary to the prohibition. Vigilius protests and imposes excommunication upon those who give their assent.

Enraged at this, Justinian causes Vigilius to take refuge in the Basilica of Saint Peter at Hormisdas in the month of August. There the praetor, attempting to carry Vigilius away by force, is repelled by a tumult of the people. At last, after receiving an oath from the emperor’s legates, Vigilius returns to the Placidian house.

But after suffering many further injuries and being subjected to plots, he again departs by night, on the Nativity of Christ, for Chalcedon and the Church of Saint Euphemia.

**In the year of Christ 552.** Six senators sent by Justinian to recall Vigilius return on the fifth day before the Kalends of February without accomplishing their mission. Peter the *referendarius* is also sent separately, once and again: first, on the day before the Kalends, with a document full of insults against Vigilius; then, on the day before the Nones, to urge his return.

On the Nones of February Vigilius writes an encyclical concerning his sufferings and publishes the sentence of deposition against Theodore which he had composed six months earlier. After Justinian withdraws his edicts and Menas, Theodore, and others offer statements of faith and repentance, Vigilius leaves Chalcedon and returns to Constantinople.

**In the year of Christ 553.** On the day of the Theophany, other professions are issued to Vigilius by the patriarchs Eutychius, who had succeeded Menas after his death, Apollinarius, and Domnus.

The Fifth General Council begins on the fourth day before the Nones of May. Vigilius declines to attend it, but in order to express his judgment in writing he sends Justinian a document dated the day before the Ides of May. In it he resumes the defense of the Three Chapters and forbids any alteration of matters judged by the Council of Chalcedon.

The Fifth Council nevertheless condemns the Three Chapters. Vigilius, because he refused to approve their condemnation, is driven into exile. After some years he is recalled through the efforts of Count Narses; while returning to Rome, he dies of illness in Sicily after the consulship of Basil, as Victor records in his *Chronicle*, in the seventeenth year—that is, in the year of Christ 558.

## FACUNDUS’ BOOK AGAINST THE SCHOLASTICUS MUTIANUS

[Note: Baronius, not without reason in my opinion, believes that this Mutianus is the same man who rendered Chrysostom’s Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews and on the Epistle to Philemon into Latin. Apart from the name, his age and profession agree. When this man rightly rebuked the African bishops because, on account of the Three Chapters, they had separated themselves from Vigilius and from the Church after his *Judicatum*, Facundus, then in exile, replied to him in this little book. It is therefore unsurprising if he appears more vehement against Mutianus, since he does not spare Vigilius himself, even though he was pope.] (C)

[Col. 0853C] It would have been proper, venerable sons, for me to dedicate this work—whatever its worth—to you under your customary names. But, fearing that, as men aware of our hiding places, you might fall under the accusations of the persecutors from whom we have fled, I did not wish to name you. Nor was it necessary to state this beforehand on your behalf, since you are not untouched by our distress; rather, I say it for the sake of others who do not know and into whose hands this may perhaps come.

I wish you to know, however, that the messenger whom you sent found me suffering from a serious illness, so that in such circumstances—as he himself will be able to report to your Eminence—I am scarcely able to postpone my fast until the third hour. [Col. 0854C] He also informed me, on your instructions, that, as a result of the merits of our age, Mocianus now dares to criticize the decrees of the councils and openly boast that the African bishops and those of other provinces acted improperly in avoiding communion with those who, after the decree had been openly promulgated and published, did not hesitate to attack the Council of Chalcedon. When do you allow us to cease, when to rest, if you compel us to answer Mocianus as well?

But I also learned this from the aforesaid messenger’s report: that Mocianus, wishing to turn ignorant people toward the forbidden communion of transgressors, circulates certain statements of blessed Augustine; and that what Augustine appropriately said against the Donatists, Mocianus inappropriately attempts to attach to the present case as a snare for the simple. Thus, at one time, Faustus the Gaul also [Note: The bishop of Riez. Avitus of Vienne, writing to the king of the Burgundians in Letter 4 and refuting a letter of Faustus himself to Paulinus, says that Faustus was British by origin but a resident of Riez. Sidonius likewise strongly implies that he was British in Book IX, Letter 9; this should be understood of the British in Gaul above the Loire, as Sidonius says elsewhere. Facundus therefore calls him a Gaul.] deceived the unwary and led them into assent to his error concerning free will, by wrongly understanding and incongruously applying statements of blessed Augustine himself. Yet he was exposed and convicted by Fulgentius of Ruspe, of holy memory.

What should surprise us in this? Augustine could not have spoken better than the prophets, the apostles, and the evangelists; yet by similarly misunderstanding and inappropriately applying their words, so many heretics attempt to defend their errors.

Nevertheless, I rejoice that you have reported his now openly admitting that the Church’s enemies condemned Bishop Theodore of Mopsuestia, who died in the peace of the Church, and whose teaching—its praises having been recited at the Council of Chalcedon without anyone objecting—as well as the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, which was judged orthodox there, and the writings of Bishop Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who there proved himself a defender of Pope Leo’s dogmatic letter, all these opponents condemned to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon.

For the holy brother Abba Felix [Note: An African, abbot of the monastery of Gillitani, or Guillensis. Vigilius condemned him, together with the deacon Rusticus, as an instigator of depravity. Later, because he and Rusticus disparaged the Fifth Council in their writings, he was expelled into exile by Justinian and died there. Victor of Tunnuna, *Chronicon*: “In the seventeenth year after the consulship of Basil, Felix, abbot of the monastery of Gillitani, departed this life to the Lord in exile at Sinope.”] [Note: On this passage, see Mazochi’s *Commentary on the Ancient Marble Calendar of the Church of Naples*, vol. I, p. 127, note 70, and p. 30, under 31 January.] reported to us, among the many other evils that he wrote about him, that he had become a friend of Theodore of Cappadocia and had repeatedly presented him to the emperor, because Theodore supplied him with certain articles for condemning, after their death, men who had died in the peace of the Church. He also maintained similarly at Carthage, as we have observed, that the aforesaid Theodore of Mopsuestia [Col. 0855C] had been justly and canonically condemned after his death.

Now, therefore, since you have informed us that Mocianus blames what he previously defended as right and blameless, while nevertheless asserting that communion with those very enemies of the Church must be endured, and misusing, in support of that assertion, the words of blessed Augustine spoken against the Donatists, he has compelled me—as you requested, without regard for the strength of my health—to answer his foolish assertions in whatever way I can. For, like a man driven into hiding and living in concealment, I now lack the books needed for consulting the necessary testimonies: because [Note: A mutilated passage, seen by Sirmond, which cannot be supplied from our manuscript, in which two complete lines have been worn away by the violence of time.] he alone is the one whom no one pleases. [Note: The book appears to be mutilated here; the words themselves show this, since they do not cohere with what precedes, and later, after several pages, he recalls matters concerning Hilary and others as though they had been mentioned earlier.]

But if it seems that we are like the Donatists, why is he himself not ashamed to be found like Tychonius, whom blessed Augustine accused of folly because, while criticizing the Donatists for their schism, he communicated with them? Or is Mocianus now doing anything else, when he affirms that Africa committed schism and was separated from the Church, yet communicates with it? And since he alone seems wise to himself, he has become one of those of whom the Apostle says: “They became futile in their reasoning, and their foolish heart was darkened” [Note: The Verona manuscript reads “their senseless heart” (*insipiens cor*).]; for “claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:21). [Col. 0856A]

But why is it reproached only to the Donatists—who leapt from schism into heresy and later came to think wrongly about baptism and the divine Trinity—and not to all heretics, whether by blessed Augustine himself or by other teachers of the Church, that they were unwilling to tolerate the wicked within the Church? It is because the Donatists separated themselves from the Church without any intervening decrees that they could claim were attacking ancient decrees concerning the faith. Others, however, who have been separated by the intervention of decrees, are blamed not for impatience in their separation but solely for their own doctrine, since they would have had a just and necessary reason for departing if they themselves had not been mistaken in their doctrine.

Blessed Gelasius, bishop of Rome, wrote a substantial work against the Acephali. Neither he nor anyone else blamed them for impatience, saying that, even if the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon were wrong, they ought to have endured communion with the wicked and not separated themselves from the Church. They are blamed only for this: that they refused to accept sound doctrine. Why, I ask, except that these men were separated from the Church because of intervening decrees, whereas the Donatists were separated for other reasons? [Col. 0856B]

Let this new teacher, therefore, no longer abuse, to his own destruction and that of others, the assertions and examples by which the Donatists were refuted. Let him rather attend to the fact that, according to the prophet’s saying, “He refused to understand, so as to act well” (Ps. 35:4), the case of the Donatists is one thing, while the case now before us is another, in which we follow the examples of so many of our fathers.

When Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, dared to do something against the authority of the Council of Chalcedon, the apostolic see did not act as has now been done, by establishing a decree accompanied by an anathema; instead, it permitted communion only with the council’s enemies. The apostolic see foresaw that this concession would lead—as the outcome demonstrated—to the destruction of the council in question. For afterward the emperor Zeno, who had ordered communion to be granted to them, advancing from lesser to greater things, rejected the council itself by a published edict. Nevertheless, despite the resistance of the aforesaid Zeno, the apostolic see condemned Acacius. Even after his death he continued to be condemned through the letters of bishops being ordained.

But after it happened that, in their letters of ordination, bishops condemned Theodore of Mopsuestia together with his doctrines, as well as the letter of Ibas and the writings of Theodoret, Acacius and the other adversaries of the Council of Chalcedon were exempted from condemnation. [Col. 0857A]

Because, therefore, the aforesaid Zeno, despising the decrees of the apostolic see, communicated with Acacius and compelled all the Churches established within the boundaries of his kingdom to do the same—and because Anastasius then succeeded him in the empire and in a similar presumption—the entire East, except for a very few who remained hidden within that multitude, continued for nearly forty years, until the time of Justin, removed from communion with the apostolic see. When, during that period, certain bishops of the same party sought to secure communion with the apostolic see for themselves and their Churches, they did not obtain it until, in the time of the emperor Justin, they subscribed to the condemnation of Acacius.

Yet none of them said: “We are not weeds, but we tolerate weeds, lest we uproot the wheat along with them.” Why would they not also have said this to the apostolic see, if the comparison were applicable to such cases? “Rather, we are acting rightly; we are abiding by the Gospel’s commandments, since we tolerate the weeds—more rightly than you, who, because of the weeds, uprooted the wheat along with them or withdrew from the wheat.”

What, then, shall we say here, religious sons? [Col. 0857C] Throughout so many years, was no one found among the Roman priests—from Felix, the condemner of Acacius, [Note: After the letter of Pope Felix III to Acacius concerning his condemnation, issued during the consulship of Venantius, there follows in the manuscript of Saint Mary of Verdun a very brief edict by the same pope, hitherto unpublished, in these words: “Edict of the sentence of Pope Felix, issued on account of the condemnation of Acacius, bishop of Constantinople. ‘Acacius, who, after being admonished by us a second time, did not cease to despise salutary statutes, and who believed that I was to be imprisoned among my own people, God has, by a sentence issued from heaven, made an exile from the priesthood. Therefore, if any bishop, cleric, monk, or layman, after this denunciation, communicates with him, let him be anathema, with the Holy Spirit carrying out the sentence.’”] to Hormisdas, who reconciled the Churches of the East—among whom was blessed Gelasius [Note: The reading may perhaps be *etiam* (“also”).], celebrated throughout the world with the glory of a reputation distinguished both for holiness of life and for knowledge—not one was found, either among the Roman clergy, [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “and among all the Christian people.”] or among the Christian people residing there, or in all the Churches of the West, who was as concerned for the unity of the Churches as this new teacher sent in the last days, so that no one recognized and taught that, in this very case too, communion with the wicked ought to be tolerated, lest the wheat be uprooted along with the weeds?

This would be credible only if one believed that knowledge and discipline concerning the preservation of unity began with blessed Augustine, whose appropriate writings against the Donatists this man now applies inappropriately to the present case. [Col. 0858A]

And therefore the distinguished doctor of the Churches, Hilary, and the other earlier Fathers mentioned above did not observe what pertains to preserving unity, since, before anything was decreed against the Council of Nicaea, they withdrew from communion with those who were contriving these things. Although, as we have said, they had previously condemned the Donatists, had the apostolic see, when later it condemned Acacius for violating the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon while Zeno resisted, not read these and similar writings of blessed Augustine? Or should we suppose that it was less capable by itself of understanding what pertains to the observance of unity, so that it condemned Acacius, whom the emperor would not allow to be expelled without expelling a great deal of wheat with him?

Nor should the Roman Church have reconciled the Churches of the East and received them into communion after due satisfaction; rather, the Churches of the East, which had tolerated the weeds, ought to have reconciled the Roman Church, separated from the wheat. Was this not done because that man could not yet teach throughout the Catholic Church what he now teaches? Or rather, because the one who wishes to impose this perverse and confused doctrine upon the Catholic Church had not yet come to the Catholic Church—and would that he had not colored it with Augustine’s name?

For he wishes the apostolic see, which at that time remitted the fault of the others, itself, together with the others who upheld its sentence against Acacius, to appear guilty of the schism that had occurred. And, sparing no one in his customary manner, he also wishes those Easterners to appear to have turned toward the schismatic Westerners, even though those Easterners themselves ought to have converted the Westerners to their own side. [Col. 0858C]

These points would indeed suffice for our refutation of him, if the adversaries—whom he himself also blames for not imposing an anathema on the Council of Chalcedon, though they acted against its authority in some respect rather than against all of us—were themselves condemned by us under an anathema.

But now, since those men have acted impiously, anathematizing us and our fathers and thereby separating themselves by this anathema from the entire Church of Christ, we who, with God governing us, remain steadfast in our fathers’ sentence and communion—yes, we—have determined, in accordance with the observance of the Christian religion, not to communicate with those who have separated themselves from the Church to which they have given an anathema.

I would not, therefore, grant this point to him either: that we have done what Hilary and his colleagues did. For, when no decree had yet been issued to the prejudice of the Council of Nicaea, and when the first efforts of their opponents had presumed to advance, they hastened to withdraw from communion with them. [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *praesensissent* (“had perceived”) for *praesumpsissent* (“had presumed”).] [Col. 0859A]

I would not grant him that the African Church separated itself from the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon; rather, it avoided communicating with those who had already separated themselves. Hence a more conscientious person, more fervent in zeal for God, could more acceptably blame us for delay, on the example of Hilary, than Mocianus could accuse us of schism or haste.

Who, unless senseless and wise in his own eyes, and, as the Apostle says, “puffed up without reason by his fleshly mind” (Col. 2:18), would dare, against the judgment of the entire Church and without considering the outcome that followed, criticize Hilary, that prudent and moderate governor of the Church? He would not even tolerate communicating by letter with the bishops of Gaul, because he believed that, in so great a matter, they had kept silent and had not resisted their adversaries.

Or who, not daring to criticize him, would criticize the African Church for fickleness or impatience? Once it saw that the Council of Chalcedon and all who held its sentence had been anathematized by an open and published decree, it avoided communicating with the condemners of its fathers and of itself—not as though this contradicted Augustine’s teaching against the Donatists, but as following the practice of Hilary [Note: The same manuscript reads: “as following Hilary.”] against the enemies of the universal council.

To make clear, however, how, with the assistance of God who governs and directs us, we follow Augustine and Hilary harmoniously, and do not set them against each other as though, by approving one, we must reject the other, but follow both according to the diversity of the cases, hear what I pursued in the judgment of Vigilius, [Note: This is the synod of Vigilius at Constantinople, mentioned in the preface to Book XII. “The Roman bishop,” he says, “was brought in; and while we were disputing in his examination, with the proceedings recorded, concerning this matter, he ordered the proceedings to be interrupted in the midst of the contest and asked all the bishops who were present to respond in writing, each stating what he thought about these Chapters.” The acts of that synod, apart from what Facundus quotes here, have perished, except that Vigilius’s judgment addressed to the archbishop Menas is known to have arisen from it. In that judgment he condemned the Three Chapters under a certain dispensation, while preserving reverence for the Council of Chalcedon, as is shown by the letter of the Roman clergy to the Frankish envoys in vol. I of the Councils of Gaul.] as the proceedings published for us from the office of the third session make clear.

“I ask of your justice,” I said, “that you inquire whether the letter of Ibas, which was condemned as though it were Nestorian, was received by the Council of Chalcedon; and, once it has been established that what the opposing party alleges concerning Theodore’s person does not harm the council, permit the matters they wish to present to be reread, lest what is being done appear to concern a reconsideration of the aforesaid council.

“For I openly confess to your Beatitude that I did not withdraw from communion with those who contradicted me because of the condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Even if that condemnation ought not to be approved, I nevertheless consider it something to be endured, and I do not judge it a matter so serious that we ought to separate ourselves from communion with the multitude. But because they attempted, on the basis of Theodore’s person, to prove Ibas’s letter Nestorian, and on the basis of Ibas’s letter to discredit the council by which it had been received—”

In these words of mine you recognize, first, that I was concerned for the standing of the general council, lest what the Acephali had always sought—the council’s being drawn into reconsideration—should break its authority. [Col. 0860A]

Next, observe that we are not now learning from this man that the wicked must be endured for the unity of the Church, as Augustine taught. When I said, “I openly confess to your Beatitude that I did not withdraw from communion with those who contradicted me because of the condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia; even if that condemnation ought not to be approved, I nevertheless consider it something to be endured, and I do not judge it a matter so serious that we ought to separate ourselves from communion with the multitude,” I showed that I remembered Augustine’s teaching.

But since I ought not to be opposed to Hilary and his colleagues, who, although they undoubtedly also tolerated many wicked men in the Churches [Note: The same manuscript reads: “in the Churches of God.”] and condemned schismatics, nevertheless judged that those rulers of the Churches [Note: The same manuscript reads: “even those.”] who attempted by their decrees to weaken the authority of the general councils, through which the Church is fortified, were not to be endured, I therefore followed this by saying that I had avoided communion with these men because they had attempted, on the basis of Theodore’s person, to prove the letter of Ibas—in which his teaching is praised—Nestorian, and, on the basis of Ibas’s letter, to discredit the council by which it had been received.

For what other reason can be given for condemning, after one hundred and twenty years from his death, a bishop who had died in the peace of the Church, together with his doctrines, or a letter whose author is said to be uncertain? They do not even admit that it belongs to Ibas; they merely say that it is said to be his. Or why would the subscriptions of so many bishops have been sought in this matter, unless the agreement not of a few but of a multitude could prejudice the universal council?

And because the judge pretended not to know this, I asked and said at the same time: “First, command me to demonstrate this, so that I may show that it is falsely denied that the letter was received by the holy Council of Chalcedon, and refute all the fabrications of those who, to the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon, condemned it as impious.”

But since an unspoken promise of his had been made before the trial—by which he had pledged himself to condemn these same Chapters, so that he might later clear himself as though through ignorance—he did not permit me to make the proof I was offering and which he himself ought earnestly to have demanded. Instead, having removed the proceedings through which the case had begun to be disclosed, and having interrupted his own judgment, he demanded from the bishops sitting with him that each of them sign in writing whatever opinion he had of the case once it had been presented.

And because those bishops had chiefly come to Constantinople in anticipation of his arrival, none of whose subscriptions in this matter had previously been recorded, and because they were confident of their own integrity, on the pretext of this questioning they too were compelled by the enemies of the Church to respond as they dictated, to the prejudice of the great council. [Col. 0861A]

And, lest they later withdraw and fail to submit to the judgment what they had answered in writing, they were brought openly under the supervision and guard of their accusers to deliver their profane and detestable responses to him. We saw these things with our own eyes. We saw the Acephali before the judge, joyful and exultant, when they brought bishops to him carrying those same responses.

When these things remain so fixed in the hearts of those who hear them, how could you detest and mourn them as we do, in whose minds the image of those evils still lingers?

He received the aforesaid responses and, after several days, carried them to the palace and handed them over to the other party, to be preserved, together with the signatures of the others who had subscribed earlier, to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon. [Col. 0861B]

But, lest he appear to have betrayed his own supporters, he deceived them with words of this sort, saying: “Why should we keep these responses contrary to the Council of Chalcedon in our possession, so that, if they are eventually found in the archive of the Roman Church, they may be believed to have been approved by us? Let us bring them to the palace, and let them themselves determine what should be done with them.” [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “and let them themselves now know what should be done with them.”]

As though he himself could not tear them up or burn them, or invalidate them by his own sentence, or return them to those by whom they had been given! He ought neither to have received nor extorted them from those men if he truly wished to guard against prejudice to the general council.

And by this customary fiction, pretending to guard against prejudice to the council, he did, at the will of his opponents, what—if we remain silent—prejudices him. For how could it not prejudice the council if approximately seventy bishops assembled at Constantinople with the Roman bishop, leaving aside those who had subscribed earlier, are shown to have condemned, together with their approvers, a letter approved by the Council of Chalcedon? And if they are shown to have anathematized after his death, with his doctrines, that bishop whose teaching was praised in the aforesaid Council of Chalcedon without anyone resisting, while the others knew of it and remained in communion with him?

For this reason, therefore, it was necessary not merely for us to withdraw from communion with those men, but also—since they seemed to occupy the more influential position in the Church, being the first to yield to this prejudice at the emperor’s command—to recall, as we have done elsewhere, how Menas of Constantinople, Zoilus of Alexandria, Ephrem of Antioch, [Col. 0861D] and Peter of Jerusalem, before either consenting or yielding, testified that this ought not to be done.

For this reason also we thought it necessary not to remain silent concerning the Roman bishop’s own written statements, whether those he made earlier under the impulse of ambition, when he was eager to become bishop, or those he later made for payment to the other party, lest true faith suffer prejudice through the authority of his name.

If this had not happened, and if he himself had not first anathematized the entire Church, we ought to have preserved his own sentence in that matter and followed the example of ancient integrity that he provided for us. For before he himself committed this act, writing about the journey to Constantinople to the bishop who had first assented to the prejudice of the great council, he anticipated him in his letter, saying:

“Therefore, we have believed it necessary to point out that our most clement lord and son, the emperor, through the illustrious man Leo, encourages us in his most serene address to preserve with you and with all our brothers and fellow bishops the peace which Christ the Lord, our God and Savior, loves above all holocausts, maintaining it with firm stability. We gladly embrace the exhortation of the most devout prince.

“But if you wisely consider the good of peace, as is fitting for the place of your priesthood, you must recognize and proclaim what peace ought to be maintained in the Church of God, since the Apostle, who affirmed that the Lord speaks through him, says: ‘May the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds’ (Phil. 4:7).

“Christ our God himself, wishing to display the marks of perfect peace [Note: One manuscript reads *praefatae* (“the aforesaid peace”).], says: ‘I leave you my peace; I give you my peace. I do not give to you as the world gives’ (John 14:27). What kind of peace the world can give, he himself teaches us through the prophet, who says: ‘Saying, Peace, peace, when there was no peace’ (Jer. 6:14).

“Let us also weigh, by the same reasoning, the fact that in the Acts of the Apostles the perfect peace of those who believed in the Lord is described in this way: ‘They were of one heart and one soul’ (Acts 4:32). Thus we find many things written that must be distinguished concerning earthly and heavenly peace. Since we do not believe that you are ignorant of these matters, let it suffice to have excerpted a few from the many, so that your Fraternity’s judgment may more readily determine which peace ought rather to be maintained by priests.”

Is it not clear and evident from the matters we have recalled that even the opponents who disagree with us in many respects nevertheless agree with us in this: that in such cases communion with transgressors must be avoided? And that the peace to be maintained by the priests of God in the Church is that which does not overturn the Church’s order? It is overturned if its general decrees concerning the faith are broken on any pretext by the decrees of other priests.

For this reason, when he came to the imperial city, he suspended from communion those who had communicated with such men. [Note: First of all, he punished Menas, who had first assented to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, with four months’ excommunication, as stated in Book IV. Theophanes, *Chronicle*: “so as to impose on Menas, bishop of Constantinople, a deprivation of communion for four months as a penalty” (Ὡς καὶ ἀκοινωνησίαν τεσσάρων μηνῶν δοῦναι Μηνᾷ τῷ Κωνσταντινουπόλεως ἐπισκόπῳ εἰς ἐπιτίμιον). Yet later, at Theodora’s request, as Theophanes also reports, he received him into communion on 29 June.] [Col. 0862D]

In the same letter he says:

“When it is not unknown to us that the deacon Stephen, formerly the representative of our Church—which by God’s grace we preside over—abstained from your communion for as long as he lived, together with many Christians; and when we were established on the island of Sicily, we learned from the report of our brother and fellow bishop Datius that he himself, other fellow priests of ours, and many Christian sons of the Church had likewise withdrawn from your communion; and when we sought the causes of the scandal that had arisen, the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop replied that this had been done by your Fraternity’s person, something that had never been committed by any of your predecessors during the times of our predecessors.”

Do you see that not only this judge and his deacon [Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “the deacon Stephen.”], but also Datius, bishop of Milan, together with other priests, did not think that communion with such transgressors ought to be endured?

Why, then, is any further question raised against us concerning this matter, when there is no contradiction among those who oppose one another, nor any disagreement among those who differ in many things? For the judge asserts that he issued that judgment unwillingly. [Note: This was discussed immediately above. The Roman clergy’s letter to the Frankish envoys calls it a *constitutum*. This is what they report Vigilius later received from the emperor: “God granted that in this manner the holy Pope Vigilius publicly received the *constitutum* that he had issued in this very matter at an assembly, declaring that if any Greek bishop, before the discussion of the universal council, did anything concerning these Chapters, or consented to those doing it, he would be alien from communion with the apostolic see.” Vigilius himself also refers to it in his letter to Rusticus and Sebastianus, sometimes calling it a *judicatum*, sometimes a *constitutum*. He shows that it was issued on Holy Saturday and sent to Menas of Constantinople. But another *constitutum*, quite different from this *judicatum*, was issued by Vigilius to Justinian several years later, when the Fifth Council was beginning, on the day before the Ides of May, in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil.] [Col. 0863B]

We reply that he sinned voluntarily, after making a promise out of ambition, and that he endured no torture to which he could be believed to have yielded. Although he asserts that he did this unwillingly, he says again in the same place that he did it in ignorance. We, however, prove that he could not have done in ignorance what he asserts he admitted unwillingly.

After this, he also wishes it to appear that he did nothing to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon. We counter his excuses with this argument: if he had done nothing prejudicial, he would never have attempted to clear and absolve himself either from the violence of the emperors or from his own ignorance.

Although, therefore, much disagreement is found between us concerning these and other matters, the parties nevertheless agree on this point, and it is established without controversy among all, that in such cases communion with transgressors must be avoided.

Finally, neither Sorcius, the chief glory of their party and one who ought not to be associated except with such men, contradicts this judgment; indeed, he says something even stronger. For, writing to the blessed old man Boethus [Note: This means “the primate.” Elsewhere we have shown that in Africa the primates of the provinces were accustomed to be called this because of the prerogative of age. Boethus was primate of the province of Byzacena. Victor, *Chronicon*: “In the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, Primasius too was exiled to the monastery of Acoemetae.” But when Boethus, primate of the council of Byzacena, had died before him, Sorcius immediately consented to the aforesaid condemnation in order to succeed him.], before sailing, in order to resume what he had condemned, he pronounced an anathema against those whom the African councils had not anathematized, saying:

“I anathematize Eutyches, together with all his followers and supporters, whoever attempt in any respect to weaken the Tome of the holy Council of Chalcedon; and whoever anathematizes the letter of Ibas, which that holy Council of Chalcedon received, is anathema to me.”

Therefore, if Mocianus dislikes the practice of Hilary and his other colleagues in the similar case of the Council of Nicaea, through whom the orthodox faith was preserved in that period [Col. 0864A] and handed down to us undefiled; if he also dislikes the concern and caution of the holy and learned orthodox man Jerome; if he dislikes the example formerly provided for us in the case of Acacius by so many bishops of the apostolic see concerning the Council of Chalcedon, an example confirmed by the consent of the universal Church; if he dislikes what the African councils have now decreed in opposition to the same council; if he dislikes what the bishops of other provinces, such as Illyricum and Dalmatia, also judged should be done; let him at least approve what Vigilius himself or Sorcius himself judged: that in such cases communion with such transgressors must be avoided.

For this reason, blessed Stephen, also a bishop of the apostolic see, when he learned that holy Cyprian and the other African bishops had decreed that all heretics should be baptized, although they had issued that sentence—as has been said—without any intervening anathema, and had not, while conniving with heretics, issued such a judgment against any earlier decrees of a general council, nevertheless immediately warned him that, if anyone dared to do this, he would be expelled from the Church. And the Church upholds Stephen’s sentence rather than Cyprian’s, not only concerning the refusal to rebaptize heretics but also concerning the refusal to tolerate those who rebaptize.

But the most prudent man Augustine, in order to rebuke the Donatists for their schism—for they attempted to defend the sacrilege of repeating baptism by the authority of blessed Cyprian—believed that Cyprian’s example was sufficient. Although Cyprian thought differently about baptism from the many bishops of other provinces, he did not nevertheless separate himself from the Church as the Donatists did. He would have separated himself if he had established an anathema between himself and those who disagreed. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “if he had fixed an anathema.”]

This example of blessed Cyprian, therefore, does nothing to support Mocianus’s assertion, as you see; rather, you should see how it supports us. We say, then, that just as, although we condemn the Donatists who rebaptize as separated from the Church, we do not condemn Cyprian and his associates, who did not divide themselves from the Church by imposing any anathema when they formulated their position on baptism—a position that now appears to have given the Donatists an occasion for error—so, although we condemn the Nestorians as separated from the Church, we do not condemn Theodore of Mopsuestia, who did not divide himself from the Church by imposing any anathema [Note: The Verona manuscript reads *se ab Ecclesia* (“himself from the Church”).], or who, if he wrote something that perhaps now appears to have given the Nestorians an occasion for error, [Col. 0865A] is not for that reason to be condemned as a heretic.

And just as it is enough for us to reject the opinions of Cyprian and his associates concerning baptism, without condemning them under an anathema, so, if Theodore perhaps wrote something wrongly through insufficient understanding, it is enough for us to reject it, without condemning him under an anathema. For the Church has always shown this reverence within the embrace of its peace and honor toward the dead: not only did it refrain from condemning under an anathema those who may have erred in such questions through the ignorance of human weakness, but it did not condemn their statements either, as it does those of heretics.

It is not ignorance arising from human weakness that makes a heretic, but obstinacy. Hence blessed Augustine says in his book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*:

“Although those who have departed from this life as Catholics and have left to posterity some Christian writings were, in certain passages of their little works, either not understood or, as is human weakness, not sufficiently capable of penetrating deeper matters with the acumen of their minds—”

“to penetrate hidden matters, and, straying from the truth through what seemed probable, they became an occasion for presumptuous and audacious men to devise and bring forth some heresy.”

Thus the Catholic Augustine says that those who departed this life were Catholics—men who, while established in the Church, were unable, through human weakness, to penetrate the more hidden matters with the sharpness of their mind, and who strayed from the truth through what seemed probable. He does not wish them to be called heretics, although they became an occasion for presumptuous and audacious men to devise and bring forth some heresy.

And therefore we do not call blessed Cyprian and his colleagues heretics, though through human weakness they erred in the question of baptism; [Col. 0865C] nor do we call Theodore of Mopsuestia a heretic, if it should perhaps be shown that he strayed in some respect from the truth and, remaining in that error, departed this life—men whom we do not deny remained in the Catholic Church to the end. [Note: Col. 0865D. The same manuscript has *quousque*, “until.”]

In vain, therefore, did he habitually gather together—who knows what—examples irrelevant to the case, by which he endeavored to prove that the aforementioned Theodore of Mopsuestia had been justly and canonically condemned. For a bishop who, when dying, made a heretic heir to his possessions is not to be condemned because he was unable, through mental weakness, to penetrate hidden matters, or because he strayed from the truth through what seemed probable; rather, he committed a manifest crime through the perversity of his will, not through the ignorance of weakness. [Note: Col. 0865D. The same manuscript reads, “is to be condemned.”]

Hence, when Philip said, “Lord, show us the Father, [Col. 0866A] and it is enough for us” (John 14:8), he went unpunished for having failed to know Christ for so long a time. But upon Ananias and Sapphira, who withheld part of the price of their property, the punishment of death immediately followed for the offense they had just committed. Simple ignorance arising from piety is therefore judged one way by the Lord, and the twofold awareness of perversity another way.

The Apostolic See, moreover, through blessed Gelasius, judges it impious to condemn anyone who has died in the peace of the Church, when he says:

“Let us leave to divine judgment what exceeds the measure of our authority. Nor will they be able to charge us with the offense of transgression if, while they are alive, we remit what God, by his gracious gift, has made possible for the Church, since they demand that we give either pardon or condemnation to the dead also, which it is manifest is not possible for us. [Col. 0866B] For when it has been said, ‘Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven’ (Matthew 16:19), he has reserved for his own judgment, not for human judgment, those who are now plainly no longer on earth. Nor does the Church dare to claim for herself what she sees was not granted even to the blessed Apostles. For if it is permitted to bind the dead, it is also permitted to release them; and if it is permitted to inflict condemnation upon the dead, it is also permitted to grant them pardon.”

[Note: Col. 0865D. These are the words of Gelasius from the Roman synod at which Bishop Misenus was acquitted. Other similar statements by him, to the same effect, are also found in several of his letters. Vigilius likewise treats the same argument more fully in his *Constitutum*, using the testimony of Gelasius. In that work, on account of the statements and errors attributed to Theodore of Mopsuestia and others, he condemns them in such a way that he nevertheless decrees that the authors themselves, having died in peace, are not at all to be condemned. But since the *Constitutum* of Vigilius is commonly confused with the *Judicatum*, and other matters throughout this entire case are often reported in disorder, it seemed worthwhile to set out here, in a brief summary arranged under their respective years, the principal points—especially those concerning Vigilius—as far as they could be ascertained from the letter of the Roman clergy to the legates, from Vigilius’s own encyclical, from the *Constitutum*, and from other sources. [Note in the edition, Col. 0865: We placed that summary at the end of Book 12 as a torch to illuminate all Facundus’s writings.])

But if it should perhaps seem to someone that he ought to hold the view by which certain people who have died in the peace of the Church are believed to be subject to condemnation, and not rather this position of the Apostolic See—which alone understands that such matters have been reserved to divine judgment—and if he should grant [Note: Col. 0866D. The same manuscript reads, “and which (the Apostolic See) maintains that, etc.”] that, if it is permitted to bind the dead, it is also permitted to release them, and that, if it is permitted to inflict condemnation upon the dead, it is also permitted to grant them pardon, it does not therefore follow that [Col. 0866C] Theodore of Mopsuestia must also appear to him worthy of condemnation.

For that view does not attack those who, like blessed Cyprian and his companions, were unable through human weakness to penetrate hidden matters with the sharpness of their mind and strayed from the truth through what seemed probable. Rather, it attacks those who are proved to have sinned knowingly and willingly.

Furthermore, it is known that judgment was once rendered in the case of Theodore when the Apollinarists, the progenitors of the Acephali, sought to have him rejected together with certain chapters of his writings, but were rejected by John of Antioch and the eastern council, as well as by Cyril of Alexandria and Proclus of Constantinople. Now, however, his case—settled and already consigned to oblivion one hundred and twenty years ago—is being revived to the prejudice of the great Council of Chalcedon.

Because they feared to share in that prejudice, [Col. 0867A] Marianus of Doracena [Note: Col. 0867B. The Veronese manuscript has *Marinianus*, “Marinianus.”] and Basiliscus, bishop of Serdica, together with Lampridius, presbyter and abbot of the Jerusalem monastery, Mocianus, at Constantinople, said that they had gone to hell, in order to recommend himself.

But this is not the road by which one proceeds to hell—the road held by Hilary and his colleagues, by Jerome in the case of the Council of Nicaea, and by so many later bishops of the Apostolic See when, in the time of Zeno, they saw the Council of Chalcedon similarly attacked.

Rather, the road to hell is the one which, in obedience to the will of Constantius, the multitude of Sirmium entered at Ariminum and Seleucia of Isauria. This man too followed that road: while the Vandals were reigning, he was an Arian; then, when Roman rule succeeded, he changed [Col. 0867B] so as to appear a Catholic; and now, with prejudgments against the Catholic religion arising even from the palace, [Col. 0868A] he follows the same course. For, as you see, his counselors furnished him with this undertaking. Not content with it, he still does not cease striving, through the destruction of others as well, to attain something more exalted.

This is how advancement is made in the present age. And whenever he can, through such assistants [Note: Col. 0868B. The same manuscript has “he finds such hearers.”], by his customary wickedness and by testimonies gathered from every direction that do not fit the case, he even argues that the Council of Chalcedon may be reconsidered.

When he cannot persuade people of that, he either excuses that wicked *Judicatum*, or defends the condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia; or, if he can accomplish none of these things, under the name of peace and of the king he endeavors to draw toward polluted communion those who are either desirous of temporal advantage or ignorant and heedless—inviting the former with promises and deceiving the latter with plausible arguments, since they merely read or [Col. 0868B] hear what has been written and do not inquire into the case for which it was written.”

[Col. 0867]

# Facundus’s Letter of the Catholic Faith in Defense of the Three Chapters

*(From volume III of Dom Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*.)* (C)

[Col. 0867C] Some people are troubled and ask what the case of the Three Chapters is, on account of which almost all the members of Christ throughout the world are scandalized. They say: What harm can be done to the Catholic Church by the condemnation that was issued against the Chapters, whether it concerns persons or writings? Especially, they say, since the very men who condemn them profess that they hold the same faith as those who do not condemn them, baptize with the same creed, and celebrate according to the same rite both the solemn order of the readings and the order of the sacrifice.

Since they demand that an answer be given them briefly, we must, with the Lord’s help, respond in this way. These very condemners of the Three Chapters cannot deny that their case was determined in the holy Council of Chalcedon nearly one hundred and twenty years ago. They must therefore first be compelled to say whether the Three Chapters harmed the Catholic Church in which they were baptized before their condemnation impiously arose, or did not harm it.

If they say that they did harm it, they are convicted of bringing upon the Catholic Church the stigma of error and crime. Either it was heretical—which it is impious to say—when those whom these men condemned as heretics were not only not condemned by that Church but were even praised by it, and their writings were declared orthodox by the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon; or else, enclosed in the cloud of ignorance, it must be branded with every heresy, since throughout so many years it neither knew nor was able to understand what these men learned fifteen or sixteen years ago from various and foreign doctrines, contrary to the apostolic command, and by obeying commands from the palace.

Consequently, these men themselves are heretics, and were baptized by heretics, nor have they yet been reconciled by anyone. For, as they themselves say, those who recently condemned or condemn the Three Chapters, and communicate with those condemners, are Catholics; whereas those who neither condemned nor condemn them, and do not communicate with those who condemn them, are heretics.

Since this is so, either that Church—which truly was, is, and will be the Catholic Church—neither condemned nor condemns the Three Chapters, and does not communicate with these most wicked condemners and those who communicate with them except after an appropriate satisfaction; and these men are unquestionably heretics, because they have recently admitted what they did not receive in the Church that regenerated them; or, if that Church was not the Catholic Church—which it is sacrilegious to hear—these men are likewise, without further circumlocution, heretics, because, as has been said, the very Church baptized them that never condemned these Chapters.

Therefore, whichever alternative they adopt, they must necessarily be proved heretics.

But if they say—and this is true—that the same Chapters harmed the Catholic Church not at all throughout more than a hundred years, as stated above, then they should recognize all the more clearly that they are inexcusably guilty. Let them consider how much evil they have committed against its decrees by condemning what it did not condemn. Let them understand what they have done and realize that they have been cut off from it. For, insofar as they could, they have torn apart its decrees, and by favoring the bands of heretics they have obstinately joined themselves to their wishes.

Indeed, the condemnation of the Chapters was sought and extracted by the Acephali heretics—that is, the Semi-Eutychians—and the writings issued against the Church by Vigilius and Pelagius, Roman prevaricators, and by Primasius of Byzacena, the principal teacher of the Acephali, bear witness to this.

[Col. 0869A] Since this is so, how can they now make good their claim that they hold one faith with those who do not condemn the Chapters? We confess in our one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and man, the distinct property of two natures in the unity of one person; this the Catholic Church has always preserved and taught.

But these men, obeying the Acephali, are shown to have anathematized the whole Church when they wrote:

> “We anathematize the impious letter of Ibas, which he wrote to Maris the Persian, together with those who defend it and say that it is correct, or that part of it is correct.”

They have unquestionably anathematized the Church that defended and defends it, and declared and declares it correct, since that Church confesses concerning the Incarnation of Christ—the mystery on which our salvation rests—what the same letter contains in every respect.

For the words of that letter, where the soundness of the Catholic confession is set forth, read as follows after other material:

> “But the Church says this: Two natures, one power, one person, who is one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Therefore, if this confession of the two natures of our Lord Jesus Christ in the unity of one person is, as they have said, impious and godless, let them themselves now say what is pious and consonant with the correct faith of Christians.

Truth therefore compels them, by refuting them through their works and writings, to confess either one nature in Christ, as the Eutychians or Acephali say, whose wishes they have obeyed and to whom they have yielded, withdrawing from the Church—or no nature at all. How impious and blasphemous this is, and how far removed from Catholic truth, anyone endowed with a sound mind will recognize without hesitation.

Now let us examine what they say in words: that they baptize with one creed. Let us see whether this is established as true for them in reality and in its effects.

To make this perfectly clear, we must first consider and weigh the force and greatness of the truth contained in the creed. For unless that by which one believes comes first, the power and gift of faith that follows cannot in any way be granted, as it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

Our Catholic teachers, the Fathers, therefore taught that a creed is an agreement or covenant made between a human being and God. Since we have made a covenant with God, and have thus been baptized in the one name of the holy Trinity, if anyone dissolves even one jot or one letter of the covenant that he made with God, he is unquestionably shown to have lost both the faith by which he believed in God and the God in whom he believed.

Who, then, violated this covenant, we shall soon see, when we set down the words of the creed—not in their full order, for the sake of avoiding prolixity, but in a brief selection.

The beginning of the creed is this:

> “We believe in one God, the Father almighty; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate; on the third day he rose from the dead; he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead,”

and so forth.

Here, surely, lies the whole present question concerning the judgment of the living and the dead. No heresy ever caused this clause to be added to the creed—just as the clause concerning the equality of the Father and the Son was added at Nicaea against Arius, or that concerning the omnipotence of the Holy Spirit at Constantinople against Macedonius. Yet it has been violated by no heresy except this one, which in recent times has arisen as though from a compacted refuse of all heretics, namely, through the condemnation of the living and the dead that they issued in writing, saying among other things:

> “If anyone defends the impious Theodore and his impious writings, but does not anathematize him and his impious writings, and all who accept or defend him and say that he expounded orthodox doctrine, and those who wrote on his behalf and held or hold the same opinions as he did, or write on behalf of him or his impious writings, and those who think or have at any time thought like him, let him be anathema.
>
> “If anyone defends the impious writings of Theodoret but does not anathematize them and those who have thought or think like him, let him be anathema.
>
> “If anyone defends the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian heretic, but does not anathematize it and its defenders, and those who say that it is correct, or that part of it is correct, and those who have written or write on its behalf, or on behalf of the impiety contained in it, and presume to defend it, let him be anathema.”

By this blasphemous sentence they have involved not only those dead men whom, while they were in the body, no one condemned and whose doctrine no one judged heretical—but which, as can be proved by the clearest documents, the authority of the Fathers in synod declared orthodox, and subsequent generations have devoutly preserved and still preserve—but also the very Fathers who praised those men and their writings, and us who are alive, in the same anathema, insofar as it lay within their power.

[Col. 0870D] Where, then, is the Christianity that they wish to display or claim? Where is their boastful declaration that they preserve the faith of the creed? They have arrogated to themselves, with excessively proud and lamentable audacity, the judgment that the Father gave to the Son alone. Through such presumption they are proved to have surpassed even the madness of the devil.

For he, in the utmost pride of his heart, said: “I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14). But these men, anticipating God’s judgment and carrying out the deadly condemnation of the dead and living who do not agree with them, have determined, as far as their intention is concerned, not merely to be equal or like their Lord—as the devil still said concerning the future, “I will be”—but to be superior to him.

And the wretches are not ashamed to say, with sacrilegious lips and shameless insolence, that they hold one faith with those who condemn!

As though demons did not also believe and tremble, yet are known to possess no operation except that of error—which these novel pests likewise exercise, themselves wandering in error and leading others into error. They lead people into error not merely by lying words, but also by violent persecutions, dragging and compelling as many as they can to agree with them or communicate with them.

The unhappy men neither consider nor perceive that it does not help them, but rather weighs heavily upon them, to profess in words that they know God while denying him by their deeds.
