For if they truly confessed—or if others confessed on their behalf when they were baptized—that they believed in God the almighty Father, in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit, as the authority of the creed holds, then they ought truly also to have believed and patiently awaited the same Son of God and man, Jesus Christ our Lord, who at the appointed time will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead. They ought not now, with impious and savage violence, to judge not only us who are alive but also the Catholic bishops who died long ago, and to condemn them as though by a perpetual sentence of anathema.

But perhaps, because of their holiness and the efficacy of their wondrous works, they claim that, as judges of the living and the dead—appointed by themselves, or rather by their father the devil—they have raised these very dead whom they condemned; and that, after hearing their case, they pronounced a sentence of judgment against them, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “I judge as I hear” (John 5:30).

We therefore ask them when they gathered up the ashes of those whom they condemned and raised them, or where they sat to judge them. Certainly the Lord will judge all nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat, although that expression also has another meaning. Yet was the valley of Jehoshaphat Constantinople, where this sacrilege was begun? Were the other cities and towns that signed and accepted the abominable decree of condemnation against the living and the dead the valley of Jehoshaphat?

Let them also say and show where they placed those whom they condemned, so that it may be known whether access to the place of the underworld has been opened to them alone, since no one except the condemners condemns them.

Let them next tell us, who are alive and whom they condemned together with the dead long ago, when they caused these men to die and immediately raised them again, as the Catholic Church confesses will happen with regard to those whom the Lord’s coming finds alive in the flesh, either at or before that judgment.

If they could not do these things, or the other things that we believe will come to pass at a time known to God alone, what madness seized their hearts? What smoky vanity, like a dark night of dense and tangible darkness, blinded their eyes so that they did not see or steadfastly hold what they received in the creed when they were baptized?

Instead, according to their own pleasure, sometimes corrupted by gifts, sometimes enticed by honors and ambitions, sometimes led astray by a foreign—or rather, serpentine—doctrine of cunning, and puffed up and inflated by the wind of pride, they raised the crests of their pride against God, seizing his judgment before him, creating a new error through the condemnation of the living and the dead, and restoring an old one.

For they have become supporters and associates of the Acephali, and have given their right hands to other heretics, so that they may, whenever and however they please, rescind or condemn the decrees of orthodox bishops.

[Col. 0872A] For the case concerns not, as certain ignorant people say, the Three Chapters, but the condemnation of all the bishops who, from the apostles and their successors down to the Council of Chalcedon—in which these same Chapters were judged orthodox—and from that time down to our own, persevering in one and the same defense and communion, departed from this life as Catholics.

We could demonstrate this here more fully by the clearest documents and truthful arguments drawn from the traditions of the Fathers, if brevity, which has been imposed, allowed it.

After carefully considering and weighing these matters, let anyone who fears God’s judgment, anyone who believes and confesses that the Son of God will come at the proper time as the manifest judge in the form of a servant that he assumed for us—the one whom, by believing, he learned to have come secretly in the fullness of time—judge whether such men, who in their audacity are more proud and exalted than the devil and even worse than the Antichrist, ought to be counted at least by the name of Christian, or rather called ministers of the Antichrist and avoided in every way.

Since this is so, how can their claim stand that they believe in God the Father and in his Son, which comes first in the creed, when they cannot accept what follows there concerning the one and same Christ, specifically said to be coming to judge the living and the dead?

For these men, as has been said and shown above, have hurled the arrows of their condemnation both against those long dead and against us who are alive.

But after these points, let us examine something else.

If they say that the dead whom they condemned taught perversely and wrote books with heretical meaning, we ask whether, while they were alive, they were admonished according to the custom of Catholic observance and discipline to hold sound and correct opinions; whether they stubbornly resisted; and whether, after being convicted of their error, they were summoned before a council and condemned, as Arius was at Nicaea, Macedonius at Constantinople, Nestorius at the First Council of Ephesus, and Eutyches and Dioscorus at Chalcedon.

If they say that this occurred, we shall immediately demand that they produce the synodal acts, as the acts concerning those men are produced, showing where their error was condemned and where a sentence was issued against them.

If they display such acts, we ask again how they remained hidden from the entire Catholic Church for more than a hundred years, when human laws bar human claims after thirty years, and when our Lord Jesus Christ, by divine law, gave his apostles power to bind and loose only things that are on earth.

Or where do we suppose that these acts lay hidden, so that recently they could come to the knowledge only of those who condemned them, and not of those who did not condemn them?

But if—as is more true and certain—they cannot produce any such ancient proceedings, because in truth they have nothing to produce, we on the contrary produce the synodal letters of the Council of Antioch in defense of Theodore and his teachings. Theodore, whom these men have now branded with the novel name and charge of heresy—that is, as Necrodioctists or Porcianists—has been condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0873] Perhaps “Sorcianists,” from Sursius or Sorcius, who is mentioned in the book against Mocianus, cols. 0861C and 0862B; unless perhaps “Porcius” should be read.]

We then display the acts of the holy Council of Chalcedon, whose authority no one contradicts except a heretic. There it is shown not only that the praises of blessed Theodore were received, read aloud, and proclaimed with admirable glory, but also that the venerable letter of Ibas—which these men condemned as impious—was there declared orthodox and praised.

It was likewise acclaimed at that council that Theodoret’s teaching had from long ago and from the beginning agreed with the orthodox faith; and both men—that is, Theodoret and Ibas—were judged worthy of the episcopate and appointed to govern the Churches entrusted to them previously.

After setting these matters forth, we propose to these condemners of the Chapters and to our own condemners, and to those who communicate with them, this question concerning the same great Council of Chalcedon: What do they think of it? Do they call it Catholic or not?

If they say, “It is Catholic,” we reply: “Then you are unquestionably heretics. For whatever or whomever the Fathers presiding there praised and declared consonant with the Catholic faith, you have condemned as heretical and impious.”

It follows, whether you wish it or not, as reason requires, that those whom they condemned as heretics—Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus—you declare orthodox, if not in words, perhaps through fear of men, then certainly in your deeds, in your unrestrained persecutions, in the expulsion of Catholic bishops, in the replacement of them by heretics, and in the written condemnations issued against Catholics.

Finally, among other matters, this case was also defined in that one and the same Council of Chalcedon: namely, the approval and condemnation of the Three Chapters.

For behold, on one side of that council stand, as it were, Theodore, although already dead yet living in the synodal letters containing his praises, which were left there and approved; and Theodoret and Ibas, praised and declared orthodox. On the other side stands Nestorius, condemned first at Ephesus and then bound by a renewed condemnation at Chalcedon; and Eutyches and Dioscorus, likewise condemned there as heretics.

What do you say? Is it not so? However thick the callus of hardness may be with which your brows are covered by your customary lies, will you be able to deny that this is so?

And if, in your confusion, you should wish to deny it, here are the acts of the Council of Chalcedon; here stand the six hundred and thirty bishops gathered there. Through those acts they cry out and say:

> “We received and approved the praises of Theodore, who died in peace and in communion with the Catholic Church, when they were read aloud to our assembly.
>
> “We declared the venerable Theodoret and Ibas orthodox, and we know with certainty that they subscribed with us to the definition of the Catholic faith.
>
> “We judged the letter that the venerable Ibas wrote to Maris the Persian, after it had been read aloud by us, to be orthodox, and we confirmed our judgment by subscribing to it unanimously.
>
> “We overthrew Nestorius, who had already been condemned, by a renewed condemnation together with Eutyches and Dioscorus, while the Holy Spirit presided over us. Whoever attempts to violate our judgment is a heretic; whoever tries in any respect to tear down our decrees is alien to the Catholic faith and alien to the Christian name.
>
> “For whoever condemns those whom we praised while declaring them Catholics, and conversely praises those whom we condemned as heretics, is a heretic. Therefore anyone who does not accept what we have rightly defined, or who proudly rebels against what has been determined by legitimate and Catholic order, is a heretic.”

Hearing these things, what, I ask, will you say to so many illustrious bishops, or to the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, which has always devoutly guarded their statutes and, to this day, guards them in their surviving works disseminated everywhere?

Unless, perhaps, you wish to tell the truth: how else was the heresy of the Necrodioctists or Porcianists to arise?

But if they say, “The Council of Chalcedon is heretical,” there is no longer any need to fight against them afresh, except that they should be regarded by all true Catholics as the man whom the Lord questioned in the Gospel about his name and who answered: “Legion, because we are many” (Mark 5:9).

For whoever presumes or attempts to contradict in any respect the authority of the holy and great Council of Chalcedon is at once an Arian, a Macedonian, a Nestorian, an Eutychian, and an Acephalian—or whatever else can be derived from and fitted to the various shoots of heretical impiety.

The intention of that council kept watch against both kinds of pestilence: it struck earlier heretics with a renewed condemnation, anathematized those then present, and, through the foresight of the Spirit of God, bound future heretics, together with their followers and participants of whatever kind, with the bonds of condemnation.

As for their claim that they celebrate the solemn order of the readings or the order of the sacrifice according to the same rite, we could answer briefly that, once they have been cut off—as we have shown—from Catholic unity, the invocation of the divine name in fictitious words is of no benefit, nor is a celebration appropriated and drawn from the Church.

The devil himself, when tempting the Lord, brought forward testimonies from Scripture—but ones by which he would be destroyed, not strengthened. And the holy Scriptures themselves consist not in reading but in understanding. Various heretics have retained, after being cut off, what they had received well and beneficially in the Catholic Church, but they have retained it perniciously and lethally.

We could also speak concerning the sacrifice of what the Lord said to Cain at the beginning of the world: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.”

We could likewise mention what the same Lord says through the prophet to transgressors and to priests who violate God’s covenant:

> “When you multiply your prayers, I will turn my face away from you. And when you offer sacrifice to me, I will not accept it from your hands, nor will I be appeased by you, for your assemblies are wicked” (Isaiah 1:13, 15).

There are many similar passages that it would take too long to enumerate.

But we judged it appropriate to produce against them one or two testimonies from the writings of the most glorious martyr and bishop Cyprian, concerning a similar case. Anyone who is intelligent in heart, considering and examining them carefully with the eyes of the heart, will recognize whether he ought any longer to desire the sacrifices of the new heretics.

In a letter concerning the holy martyr and bishop Cornelius of the city of Rome—whom the heretic Novatian had expelled and had installed himself in his place, just as has now been done by the recent heretics—Cyprian wrote to Magnus, saying among other things:

[Note: [Col. 0875D] In this testimony from Cyprian, Facundus omits some material and also changes the wording.]

> “But if there is one flock, how can one be counted among the flock who is not within the number of the flock? Or how can he be regarded as a shepherd who, while the true shepherd remains and, succeeding in due order in the Church of the Lord, presides there, succeeds no one and begins from himself, becoming alien and profane, an enemy of the Lord’s peace and divine unity, not dwelling in the house of God—that is, in the Church of God—in which only those who are harmonious and united dwell?

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Cyprian reads: “with a substitute appointment (*ordinatione succidanea*) presiding.”]

[Note: [Col. 0875D] The word “himself” is redundant.]

> “Finally, how inseparable is the sacrament of unity, and how hopeless they are, and how great a destruction they acquire for themselves through God’s indignation, those who create schism and, having abandoned the bishop, appoint another pseudo-bishop for themselves . . .

[Note: [Col. 0876D] For what is missing here, see Cyprian, Letter 76.]

> “But if someone objects and says that Novatian holds the same law that the Catholic Church holds, and baptizes with the same creed as we do, and knows the same God the Father, the same Christ the Son, and the same Holy Spirit, let him who thinks this objection should be raised know that this cannot help such men.

[Col. 0875C] “For Korah, Dathan, and Abiram also knew the same God as Aaron the priest and Moses. Living according to the same law and religion, they invoked the one true God who was to be worshiped and invoked. Yet because they transgressed the ministry of their office and, against Aaron the priest—who had received the legitimate priesthood by God’s favor and appointment—claimed for themselves the right to offer sacrifice, they were struck by divine judgment and immediately paid the penalty for their unlawful attempts. Their sacrifices, offered irreligiously and unlawfully against the right of God’s arrangement, could not be valid or beneficial.

“Therefore those who support Novatian or others of this kind contend in vain.

[Col. 0875D] “And so that it might be more clearly understood what divine judgment is directed against such audacity, we find that in such a crime not only the leaders and authors but also the participants are destined for punishment unless they separate themselves from communion with the wicked. The Lord commands through Moses, saying:

> ‘Separate yourselves from the tents of these exceedingly hardened men, and do not touch anything that belongs to them, lest you perish together in their sin’ (Numbers 16:26).

“And what the Lord had threatened through Moses he fulfilled: whoever did not separate himself from Korah, Dathan, and Abiram immediately paid the penalty for impious communion.

[Col. 0876A] “By this example it is shown and proved that all who irreligiously and rashly join themselves to schismatics against the rulers and priests of God are liable both to guilt and to punishment.”

[Note: [Col. 0876D] The manuscript reads: “will be liable.”]

> “As the Holy Spirit also testifies through the prophet Hosea, saying:
>
> ‘Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them will be polluted’ (Hosea 9:4),
>
> teaching and showing that all those who are polluted by their sin are joined to punishment together with the authors.”

What is clearer than this testimony? What is more illuminating? What could be said more truthfully?

Behold, it teaches that absolutely all who have been polluted by communion with the wicked are bound by equal guilt and equal punishment.

Why, then, do certain people, as though excusing themselves, say: “My bishop himself knows whether he has condemned anyone”? To such persons Scripture threatens, saying:

> “But you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you. When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 49:17–18).

Further on, the apostle Paul makes clear and proves that those who do evil are worthy of death and come under punishment, but not only those who do such things: also those who consent to people doing them (Romans 1:32).

Those who unlawfully mingle with the wicked, sinners, and people who do not repent are polluted by contact with the guilty; and while they are joined in guilt, they are likewise not separated in punishment.

But these men say: “We do not consent to the condemnation of the dead.”

O intolerable evil! O unheard-of disgrace! They say that they do not consent to the condemnation—as though merely in words—yet in their deeds they consent to the detestable communion, which is worse.

For the punishment remains all the more abundant for those who both know the truth and nevertheless communicate with the enemies of the truth.

If those with whom you communicate have created a heresy, as we have shown, by condemning the living and the dead; if they have gone over to the heretics by doing what the Acephali desired, then, having committed both offenses, they have certainly remained heretics.

How, then, can those who communicate with heretics deny that they are held by the crime of heresy? Or with what face do they imagine that they communicate with the Catholic Church?

Is it because, supported by the palace’s favor, they seized churches made with human hands after expelling the Catholics? Do you therefore imagine that the Catholic faith and Christian peace exist in walls?

If this is your opinion, listen to what the holy bishop Hilary, confessor and distinguished teacher, wrote to certain bishops in the time of the emperor Constantius, when the Arians had invaded almost all the local churches throughout the world under the name of peace and the king, just as the Eutychians or Acephali have now done. After other material, he writes concerning this matter:

> “I ask you, bishops who believe that you are such: With what support did the apostles use to preach the Gospel? By what powers did they receive assistance when they preached Christ and transferred almost all nations from idols to the Lord? Did they take for themselves some dignity from the palace?”

And further:

> “I give you one warning: beware of the Antichrist. For the love of walls has seized you disastrously; disastrously you venerate the Church of God in roofs and buildings; disastrously you introduce the name of peace under these structures. Is it doubtful that the Antichrist will sit in these places? Mountains, forests, lakes, prisons, and ravines are safer for me. For in these places the prophets lived and prophesied by the Spirit of God.”

These testimonies are sufficient for the present, given our brevity. If we wished to heap up or reason through more, we might perhaps burden the memory of our readers.

Now we must also briefly mention what they bring forward from the short works that blessed Augustine wrote against the Donatists. They say: “Saint Augustine said: ‘Peace is good; have peace. Unity is good; love unity. Let unity not be divided.’”

But they do not at all perceive how these and similar testimonies from that outstanding teacher strike them down, while they establish us.

If these men, who bring such statements forward against themselves, did not wish to divide unity; if they did not wish to wage war against the Catholic Church, by which peace would be violated, then they ought to have preserved and bravely guarded what they found in it, as has been shown above.

But what they did not receive from it, or from that Church, they ought to have fled and avoided as truly harmful and deadly.

According to apostolic teaching, peace is to be had with all people, if possible, but it is not to be kept with all. For it is one thing to have something and another to keep it.

Peace must therefore be maintained not only with schismatics and heretics but also with carnal Jews and pagans. Yet it must be that peace by which we desire and strive to acquire them for God and unite them to Catholic truth and unity. For this reason we also pray for them, according to God’s command, that they may be converted.

But peace must not be held in such a way that we go over to them and become what they are.

Finally, what blessed Augustine said and urged upon the Donatists—namely, to have peace and love unity—he said most excellently and beneficially. He desired them, just as we desire these men, to return to the Catholic Church after their error had been condemned, as he teaches most clearly in many works written against their schism.

He did not desire that he himself, or any orthodox person, should abandon the Catholic Church—God forbid—and be joined to their error through sacrilegious communion.

We say the same to these men, in the midst of great peace:

“Condemn the error that you introduced. Remove the evil of condemnation that you brought in, through which you have both become heretics and proved yourselves supporters of heretics. By having peace with us and holding, as before, to what you held, you will confound all heretics and restore yourselves to Catholic unity.”

Whoever reads these things, therefore, should not seek elegant expression but carefully contemplate the substance and weight of the truth.

If you have not been polluted by communion with prevaricators, pray to God that you may persevere. But if you have fallen either through ignorance or through violence, hasten to restore yourself by returning to Catholic truth and resuming communion with it. For forgiveness has been promised to all who repent.

Let no one be broken by despair. Let no one be entangled any longer in serpentine deceptions. For just as eternal punishment with the devil has been prepared for transgressors and for those who remain impenitent in heart, so an eternal and unending glorious reward has been reserved by the Lord God for those who preserve his covenant, guard the foundations of the Catholic faith, and avoid profane innovations.

## In the Year of Our Lord 547. Fulgentius Ferrandus, Deacon of the Church of Carthage

[Col. 0877]

## Notice

*(From Gallandius.)*
[Col. 0877D] **I.** Fulgentius Ferrandus—if you accept Chiffletius’s account [Note: [Col. 0877D] Chiffletius, preface to Ferrandus’s Works]—was either a relative or a kinsman of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe; and the distinguished family suggested both by his name and by the modest way in which he mentions the holy bishop almost persuades one of this. Among Saint Fulgentius’s disciples he was outstanding, and for that reason he calls him his teacher [Note: [Col. 0877D] Ferrandus, Letter 2, below, p. 889]: plainly a disciple worthy of so great an instructor.

The eminent writer, as usual, speaks at length and admirably about him [Note: [Col. 0878D] Noris, *History of the Controversy concerning One of the Trinity who Suffered*, ch. 9, Works, vol. III, p. 855]:

> Ferrandus, following the African bishops who had been deported to Sardinia by order of King Thrasamund, put on the monastic habit in the monastery constructed there by the exiled Saint Fulgentius. When the most merciful King Hilderic recalled the bishops from exile in the year 523, Ferrandus returned to Africa together with Fulgentius. Because of his exceptional excellence of character and learning, he was ordained deacon by Boniface, archbishop of the Church of Carthage, and was everywhere celebrated in the speech of all. He turned the books of Saint Augustine more than any others day and night with his own hands; this was counted to his praise by his teacher Fulgentius in the book *On Five Questions*, dedicated to Ferrandus himself. For, after quoting certain sayings of Augustine, Fulgentius says that they would be sufficient, especially in view of Ferrandus’s ability and zeal, by which he read Augustine’s words so acutely and so frequently that he could discover in them many parallels [Note: [Col. 0879D] Fulgentius, *On Five Questions*, ch. 14].  
> 
> He had everywhere acquired so great a reputation for learning that distinguished men sought his judgment on more difficult matters, just as he himself consulted Saint Fulgentius in the more serious controversies; at that time Africa had no one more learned than Fulgentius.

Thus far the distinguished scholar. Ferrandus flourished in the time of Justin and Justinian. Among the ancients, he is mentioned with praise by Victor of Tunnuna [Note: [Col. 0879D] Victor of Tunnuna, *Chronicle*, under the year 547], Facundus of Hermiane [Note: [Col. 0879D] Facundus of Hermiane, book IV, ch. 3], Cresconius, an African bishop [Note: [Col. 0879D] Cresconius, preface to the *Brief Summary of the Canons*], the anonymous author appended to Ildefonsus of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0879D] Anonymous, *On Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 11], Sigebert of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0879D] Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 11], and Gratian [Note: [Col. 0879D] Gratian, distinction 63, ch. 34]. Pagius [Note: [Col. 0879D] Pagius, under the year 529, §14] and Natalis Alexander [Note: [Col. 0879D] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, sixth century, ch. 4, article 5] assert, without witnesses, that Ferrandus lived until the year 548.

For the present, we know this much with certainty: he had already died in the year 547, when Facundus of Hermiane wrote his books in defense of the Three Chapters, as we shall show below. In them that African bishop calls Ferrandus “a man of praiseworthy memory in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0879D] Facundus of Hermiane, cited work]. Chiffletius observes [Note: [Col. 0879D] Chiffletius, preface to Ferrandus’s Works] that after his death the African Churches were disturbed for a long period by the controversy over the Three Chapters, and that, according to this evidence, Ferrandus died not long before that time.

**II.** To speak, with Baronius, of Ferrandus’s great reputation in his own age [Note: [Col. 0880D] Baronius, under the year 529, §9], and of the fact that he was accustomed to be consulted on extremely difficult questions: his surviving letters sufficiently demonstrate this and likewise indicate how highly he was esteemed. Among these letters, two first appear addressed to Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe; we have appended Fulgentius’s replies from the new edition of the holy Father’s works.

In the first letter Ferrandus proposes a twofold question concerning the salvation of an Ethiopian catechumen: he had been baptized when, already overcome by the force of illness, he was no longer in possession of his mental faculties, and he had died without receiving the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 0880D] Mangey, preface to the Works of Saint Fulgentius]. Hence Ferrandus was troubled by two doubts: first, whether another person’s confession of faith could suffice for an adult’s salvation; and second, whether one who had received the sacrament of baptism but, prevented by the speed of death, could not eat the Lord’s flesh, could nevertheless attain salvation.

Fulgentius considers these two questions separately. To the first he replies that a sincere desire for baptism, previously possessed, is sufficient, provided that baptism is conferred while the person is still alive, even though he perceives nothing. To the second he replies that it is no fault of anyone who has been baptized that, overtaken by death, he was unable to partake of the Eucharist, since through baptism itself he has received—not perhaps the sacrament, but at least the reality of the sacrament. For the power of baptism is such that it inserts us into the body whose head is Christ and makes us a true member of him; this incorporation is signified by the sacrament of the Eucharist itself.

In the later letter to Fulgentius, Ferrandus proposes five questions to him, and there survives a lengthy reply worthy of Fulgentius’s learning and genius [Col. 0879D]. Noris makes the following observation concerning the first two questions proposed by our Carthaginian deacon to the bishop of Ruspe [Note: [Col. 0880D] Noris, *History of the Controversy concerning One of the Trinity who Suffered*, ch. 9, Works, vol. III, pp. 855 ff.]:

> When disputes concerning “one of the Trinity” were being conducted with the utmost passion, Ferrandus asked Fulgentius—whom he always honored as his teacher—to resolve the two questions that had arisen from them. For many rejected the proposition concerning Christ, one of the Trinity, for two reasons: first, lest they seem to introduce a division and separation of the persons from the divine nature into the mystery of the most holy Trinity; and also lest, by admitting that one of the Trinity had suffered, they should be compelled to say that the divinity itself had suffered. Fulgentius examines both difficulties proposed to him in twenty-two chapters and especially in the final two completely penetrates the whole matter, citing the clear and splendid testimonies of Saint Augustine.

Thus far Noris.

**III.** The third letter is addressed to Anatolius, a deacon of the city of Rome. In it Ferrandus discusses the two natures of Christ, establishes the chapters of the Scythian monks by solid arguments, and refutes the opposing objections with great learning.

The same Noris, already cited, writes as follows concerning this letter [Note: [Col. 0880D] Noris, *History of the Controversy concerning One of the Trinity who Suffered*, ch. 9, Works, vol. III, p. 858]:

> When the same question concerning “one of the Trinity” subsequently stirred up contentious debates among learned men at Rome after the death of Hormisdas, Anatolius, a deacon of the Roman Church, uncertain which side he should take, consulted Ferrandus about the controversy. Ferrandus sent him a lengthy letter in which, with the highest learning, he thoroughly disposed of the entire question. He especially examined what was urged with the greatest force against the proposition concerning one of the Trinity suffering in the flesh, as though it were absurd—an objection that caused Anatolius even greater doubt and therefore was the only matter on which he consulted him.  
> 
> He also proposed another question for resolution, namely, whether the blessed Virgin could truly and properly be called the Mother of God. This had been another of the chapters of the Scythian monks, as I have shown elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0880D] The same author, cited work, ch. 3, p. 797], and it had also been debated at length in the East, as we learn from Facundus of Hermiane.

This and much else is said by the most learned scholar. Later, concerning the time when this letter was written, he says [Note: [Col. 0880D] The same author, cited work, p. 861]:

> No chronological indication appears in the letter mentioned above from which the year in which it was written can be known. Nevertheless, I think that it was composed before John II, in the year 535, brought those prolonged controversies to an end by an apostolic decree. For neither would Anatolius, a deacon of the Roman Church, have consulted Ferrandus concerning propositions that had been inscribed by the supreme pontiff among the dogmas of the faith as though they were doubtful matters; nor would Ferrandus, in his reply, have passed over in silence the pontifical sanction that thereafter left no room for doubt.

Baronius, however, assigns this letter of Ferrandus to the year of Christ 533. He reports that it had recently been published in his own time, together with Ferrandus’s other minor works, by the Portuguese Achilleus Statius [Note: [Col. 0880D] Baronius, under the year 533, §28]. Chiffletius subsequently corrected and supplemented it by comparison with two manuscript codices; following Baronius, he appears to assign it to that same year, 533, in which Justinian’s Edict on the Catholic faith is also recorded, during his third consulship.

**IV.** There follows the fourth letter, to Eugippius the presbyter, concerning the essence of the Trinity and the two natures of Christ.

Eugippius was Italian, a disciple of Saint Severinus, the apostle of the Noricans, and of Pope Gelasius, and abbot of the Lucullan monastery near Naples in Campania. There also survives a fifth letter of Saint Fulgentius to him, in which Fulgentius calls him his “fellow presbyter.”

Cassiodorus writes the following about him [Note: [Col. 0880D] Cassiodorus, *On Divine Literature*, ch. 23]:

> You should also necessarily read the works of the presbyter Eugippius. We too saw him: a man not exceedingly learned in secular literature, but completely filled with the reading of the divine Scriptures. Drawing from the works of Saint Augustine extremely profound questions and statements, and extracting various matters, he arranged them in a single volume, with a very necessary economy, in 338 chapters, for our kinswoman Proba, a consecrated virgin.

Here the Senator plainly alludes to the Augustinian *Collectaneum* compiled by Eugippius, “at the urging of Abbot Marinus,” and dedicated “to the lady Proba, venerable by merit and ever illustrious in the grace of Christ through the fruit of sacred virginity,” as Eugippius himself declares in his preface.

Fulgentius celebrates the praises of this virgin Proba [Note: [Col. 0881D] Fulgentius, Letter 2, no. 31]. He describes her as “born from grandfathers and great-grandfathers who had been consuls, and raised amid royal luxuries,” and addresses two letters to her, the fourth and fifth. From these facts, therefore, we know the period in which Eugippius flourished, the man to whom our Carthaginian deacon writes. On this matter, I would have you consult Sirmond’s letter to Chiffletius [Note: [Col. 0881D] Sirmond, Works, vol. IV, pp. 736 ff., Paris edition].

This also disproves the fiction of two Eugippi, one Italian and the other African, a view supported by Miraeus [Note: [Col. 0881D] Miraeus, note on Isidore, ch. 13, and Sigebert, ch. 39, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*], Bollandus [Note: [Col. 0881D] Bollandus, *Lives of the Saints*, January, vol. I, p. 483, no. 2], Cave [Note: [Col. 0881D] Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, under the years 511 and 553, pp. 498 and 527], and others.

Learned men fell into this error because they were led by Sigebert’s authority. Speaking of Eugippius, Sigebert says [Note: [Col. 0881D] Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 39]:

> Eugippius the abbot, at the urging of Reducus, bishop of Naples, extracting passages from the books of Augustine, bishop of Hippo, presented a book of great usefulness to the virgin Proba and, through the hands of that same bishop Reducus, offered it to the Church of Naples. He lived in the time of Pelagius II and the emperor Tiberius Constantine.

Sigebert is mistaken here in two ways. First, he writes that the Augustinian excerpts were compiled by Eugippius at the urging of Reducus, bishop of Naples, whereas Eugippius himself makes a different statement in his preface, as we learned shortly before from his own words. Second, he says that Eugippius lived in the time of Pelagius II and Tiberius, although it is plainly evident both from what has just been said and from what will shortly be said that the abbot of Lucullan was alive long before the pontificate of Pelagius II and the reign of Tiberius—that is, long before the year 578.

The illustrious Petrus de Marca, archbishop of Toulouse, first detected the origin of Sigebert’s error in a letter sent to Labbeus, which Labbeus published among the additions to his dissertation on ecclesiastical writers [Note: [Col. 0881D] Labbeus, *Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, pp. 775 ff.]. The learned Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0881D] Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 60 ff., new edition] later pursued the matter at greater length, as did, not long ago, Mazochius, outstanding in learning and scholarship [Note: [Col. 0882D] Mazochius, *Commentary on the Ancient Marble Calendar of Naples*, vol. I, pp. 123–135].

Let the reader consult these three authorities in order to understand more deeply both Eugippius’s period and the time when Ferrandus wrote to him; and let him not be carried away by the authority of the distinguished Noris, who, reproducing Sigebert’s words, did not realize that Sigebert had erred [Note: [Col. 0882D] Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, ch. 21, vol. I, p. 515].

Concerning this letter of Ferrandus, Chiffletius writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0882D] Chiffletius, preface to Ferrandus, §4]:

> We publish this letter from the printed editions, apparently truncated at the end, since we found no assistance in the manuscript codices for completing it. Since it is directed chiefly against Arianism and mentions a question proposed by an Arian count, I am led by conjecture to think that it was written while the Vandals still held power in Africa; indeed, during the reign of Hilderic, whose favorable disposition toward the Catholics opened the way for catechesis, and therefore before the year of Christ 531, when Hilderic was driven out and deprived of his kingdom by Gelimer.

Thus far Chiffletius. This letter also appears in the appendix to the Works of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe.

**V.** On the same subject as the preceding letter to Anatolius, Ferrandus wrote another, the fifth in number, to Severus, a scholasticus of Constantinople. Moved by the reputation of our Carthaginian deacon’s learning, Severus had requested his opinion by letter in the great controversy concerning “one of the Trinity who suffered.”

“Ferrandus sent Severus a most learned letter,” says Noris [Note: [Col. 0882D] Noris, *History of the Controversy concerning One of the Trinity who Suffered*, ch. 9, vol. III, pp. 856 ff.]. “But because he was a modest man and thought humbly of himself, he says: ‘Let those speak and proclaim to whom the honor of the priesthood has granted the authority to teach; we are prepared to learn, we do not presume to teach’ [Note: [Col. 0882D] Ferrandus, Letter 5, to Severus, ch. 1, below, p. 909]. He then adds: ‘Therefore, most prudent man, if you desire to hear anything concerning the truth, ask first of all the bishop of the apostolic see, whose sound doctrine is established by the judgment of truth and strengthened by the protection of authority.’”

A judgment truly worthy of so great a teacher: he leaves the controversy concerning “one of the Trinity” principally to the bishop of the apostolic see for judgment and definition. Ferrandus had evidently been instructed by his teacher Fulgentius and formed by Fulgentius’s teaching. Fulgentius’s celebrated golden saying is preserved in these words [Note: [Col. 0882D] Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and Grace*, ch. 11]:

> Illuminated by the words of the two great luminaries, Peter and Paul, as though by shining rays, and adorned by their bodies, the Roman Church, which is the summit of the world, holds and teaches—and the entire Christian world with it believes without hesitation for righteousness and does not hesitate to confess for salvation.

As for the time when this letter of Ferrandus was written, the learned scholar just cited says [Note: [Col. 0882D] Noris, cited work, p. 858]:

> The year in which the letter mentioned above was written is unknown. But since the African bishops returned from exile to Carthage in the year 523, the letter appears to have been written after the death of Hormisdas, when Ferrandus was already a deacon of the Church of Carthage.

Chiffletius, however, writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0882D] Chiffletius, preface to Ferrandus’s Works, no. 5]:

> I assign Ferrandus’s reply to Severus, the Constantinopolitan scholasticus, to the year of Christ 532, while Fulgentius the bishop was still alive. At the beginning of the letter Ferrandus seems quietly to complain that Fulgentius, rather than Ferrandus himself, was not consulted concerning so important a controversy. Moreover, I now present this letter of Ferrandus to Severus, previously encumbered with errors and mutilated at the end by several periods, complete and corrected, from the codex of Saint Augendus and also from the codex of the convent of the Discalced Carmelites at Clermont in Auvergne.

**VI.** Ferrandus’s sixth letter is said to have been sent to Pelagius, who later became Roman pontiff, and to Anatolius, deacons of the city of Rome. It concerns the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, and consequently supports the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon against the Acephali.

Facundus of Hermiane first mentions this letter in the following words [Note: [Col. 0882D] Facundus of Hermiane, book IV, ch. 3, near the end]:

> The venerable Pelagius and Anatolius, Roman deacons, fulfilling the concern owed by their office and position to the Church of God, wrote to Ferrandus, the Carthaginian deacon of praiseworthy memory in Christ, asking that, after careful consideration of this case—the case of the Three Chapters—with the most reverend bishop of that same Church of Carthage, or with others whom he knew to possess both zeal for the faith and knowledge of divine Scripture, he should reply what seemed to all in common ought to be observed.

The same letter is also mentioned by the anonymous author of the little work *On Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, usually appended to Isidore of Seville and Ildefonsus of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0883D] Anonymous author, *On Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 11]:

> Ferrandus published a reply to Pelagius and Anatolius, Roman deacons, who had consulted him about whether it is permissible to condemn anyone after death. In it, among other things, he spoke as follows: “What does it profit to disturb the Church on behalf of those who sleep? If someone, accused and condemned while still in the body of this death, was taken from the Church before he deserved to be absolved, he cannot thereafter be absolved by human judgment. If someone, accused and acquitted, was overtaken before the day of the sacred examination by a sudden summons, he is to be understood as preserved within the bosom of Mother Church for judgment by God. No human being can pronounce an open judgment on this matter: if God has granted him pardon, our severity does him no harm; but if God has prepared punishment, our leniency does him no good.”

These words occur in this letter of Ferrandus [Note: [Col. 0883D] Ferrandus, Letter 6, to Pelagius and Anatolius, ch. 7, below, p. 925]. From them it is clear that the passage reported by this anonymous author is mutilated and corrupt, and should therefore be restored as follows:

> What does it profit to contend with those who sleep, or to disturb the Church on behalf of those who sleep? If someone . . . was taken from the world . . . If someone, accused and acquitted, departed to the Lord in the peace of the Church, he cannot be condemned by human judgment. If someone, accused before the day of the priestly examination . . . is to be understood as reserved for divine judgment, and so forth.

Baronius saw this passage of the anonymous author [Note: [Col. 0883D] Baronius, under the year 529, §9], attributing it to Isidore of Seville; he considered Ferrandus’s letter lost, although he knew that this passage had been taken from it.

But Chiffletius eventually brought this very highly desired letter to light from the two manuscript codices of Saint Augendus and the Auvergne codex mentioned shortly before. Among other things, he writes the following in his preface to it [Note: [Col. 0883D] Chiffletius, preface to Ferrandus’s Works, no. 9]:

> Although in this letter you find nothing concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia or Theodoret, but only concerning the letter of Ibas, I would nevertheless ask you not to doubt that it contains a defense of all three Chapters. For since in that letter Ibas greatly praises Theodore of Mopsuestia and attacks Cyril, the holy bishop of Alexandria, with Theodoret’s own barbs, it is evident that this one letter embraced the arguments of the three Chapters in question.  
> 
> As for the entire history of the Three Chapters, apart from Liberatus in his *Breviary*, Facundus of Hermiane, and Victor of Tunnuna in his *Chronicle*, Baronius treated it fully and accurately in his *Annals*. Anyone who carefully watches that tragedy will understand that perhaps never did the evil demon employ a more wicked stratagem to disturb the tranquility of the Catholic Church and overthrow its peace. And I do not know whether, during that storm which raged most violently in Africa, Ferrandus himself may have died either in exile, as did many others, or worn down by grief within his own household walls. Certainly Facundus, writing to the emperor Justinian at that time, plainly indicates, when he mentions Ferrandus in book IV, chapter 3, as “a man of praiseworthy memory in Christ,” that Ferrandus had already departed this life.

Thus far Chiffletius.

The statements Ferrandus makes in this letter concerning the authority of councils and of the Roman pontiff are entirely worthy of being inscribed on cedar and therefore must not be omitted. He writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0883D] Ferrandus, Letter 6, ch. 7, below, p. 925]:

> Universal councils, especially those to which the agreement of the Roman Church has been added, hold the place of second authority after the canonical books.

A little later, speaking of statutes enacted by universal synods, he says [Note: [Col. 0883D] The same author, cited work, ch. 9]:

> For full confirmation, it is judged sufficient if, once brought to the knowledge of the whole Church, they cause no impediment or scandal to the brethren, but are established as agreeing with the apostolic faith and strengthened by the consent of the apostolic see.

He also teaches in the same place [Note: [Col. 0883D] The same author, cited work, ch. 6] that if anyone should appeal from the judgments delivered at the Synod of Chalcedon,

> there might perhaps, according to custom, be room for an appeal to higher judgments; but where would he go, or where in the Church would he find higher judges, when the apostolic see was already present before him in its legates, and, since that see consented, whatever that synod defined received invincible strength?

The most learned cardinal Noris, considering these words [Note: [Col. 0883D] Noris, *History of the Controversy concerning One of the Trinity who Suffered*, ch. 9, vol. III, p. 857], says that Ferrandus teaches, first, that “universal councils obtain the second place of authority after the canonical books through the consent of the apostolic Roman see, so that supreme authority in defining derives from the apostolic see and resides in it alone.” He further says that the same deacon of Carthage teaches that no one could appeal from the Synod of Chalcedon, because the apostolic see—to which alone one may appeal from synods—had consented through its legates to the synodal decrees; and through that consent the synod had received invincible strength.

These observations of Noris, subsequently copied by learned men such as Natalis Alexander [Note: [Col. 0884D] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, sixth century, ch. 4, article 5, vol. V, p. 407] and Joseph Augustine Orsi [Note: [Col. 0884D] Orsi, *On the Irreformability of the Roman Pontiff’s Judgment*, book III, ch. 17, vol. II, pp. 124 ff.], I have been pleased to record here once again.

**VII.** The six letters of Ferrandus reviewed thus far are followed by the *Paraeneticus* to Count Reginus, concerning the Seven Rules of Innocence.

Reginus himself provided the occasion for composing this work. Earlier he had asked Saint Fulgentius to explain two matters for him. First, what should be thought about the famous question recently debated at Alexandria—namely, whether Christ’s flesh was corruptible or incorruptible [Col. 0884C]. Second, what a religious commander ought to be in military actions.

But since Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, was overtaken by death when he had scarcely completed part of his reply to Count Reginus’s first question, Ferrandus, his disciple, completed the unfinished work of his teacher—namely, its latter part—at Reginus’s own request. To Ferrandus’s work we have appended the first part of Saint Fulgentius’s letter, so that the response to the count’s requests might at last be complete.

“This work of Ferrandus,” says Chiffletius [Note: [Col. 0884D] Chiffletius, preface to Ferrandus’s Works, no. 6], “which had hitherto been strangely disordered and deformed by errors, we have restored to its native beauty from the same codex of Saint Augendus mentioned above. It was written,” he adds, “not long after the death of Saint Fulgentius, which occurred, as I have shown elsewhere, on Saturday, the Kalends of January, in the year 533 of the Dionysian era.”

Thus far Chiffletius.

But learned men disagree about determining the year of Saint Fulgentius’s death. Baronius says [Col. 0884D] that this supreme glory of the African Church died on the Kalends of January in the year 529 [Note: [Col. 0884D] Baronius, under the year 529, §1]. Pagius [Note: [Col. 0884D] Pagius, under the year 529, §13] and Bollandus [Note: [Col. 0884D] Bollandus, *Lives of the Saints*, January, vol. I, p. 32, marginal note] nearly follow Baronius.

Noris, however, adhering to Chiffletius [Note: [Col. 0884D] Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, ch. 24, vol. I, pp. 532, 534], assigns the death of the holy bishop of Ruspe to the year 533, not to the year 534, as the brothers C. and I. Ballerini report less correctly [Col. 0885A] [Note: [Col. 0885D] Ballerini, notes on Noris’s Works, book II, ch. 14, vol. IV, p. 933]. On this matter as well they bring forward several further arguments in the cited place against Fontanini’s opinion; these should be read in their work.

**VIII.** The collection of Ferrandus’s works is brought to a close by his *Brief Summary of the Canons*. Whether this work can certainly be attributed to him, Christianus Lupus appears to doubt, though perhaps without sufficient reason [Note: [Col. 0885D] Lupus, *On Appeals*, dissertation 2, ch. 33, p. 741, Mainz edition, 1681].

Gulielmus Voellus and Henricus Justellus discuss this work at length [Note: [Col. 0885D] Voellus and Justellus, preface to the *Library of Ancient Canon Law*, pp. 6 ff.], and Pagius copied much of their material [Note: [Col. 0885D] Pagius, under the year 527, §§14–15]. They observe above all that among the Latins there is no collection older than Ferrandus’s, and they judge his work to be pre-eminent and entirely distinctive. In it, the author has gathered the whole of canonical discipline into 232 chapters, arranging each matter methodically and systematically, with the relevant canons and decrees noted under each.

They further warn that the illustrious author of the *Annals* erred twice: first, in attributing exactly 300 chapters to Ferrandus [Note: [Col. 0885D] Baronius, under the year 419, §90]; and second, in confusing Cresconius’s *Canonical Breviary* with Ferrandus’s *Brief Summary of the Canons* [Note: [Col. 0885D] The same author, under the year 527, §76]. Baronius says that Cresconius appended to his own collection the work that Ferrandus composed at almost the same time, but in an entirely different order—not citing the canons, but reciting them—and that Cresconius rightly called it a *Breviary*.

“For,” they say,

> apart from the fact that Baronius makes Cresconius Ferrandus’s contemporary, although Cresconius was in reality almost two hundred years later, it is absolutely certain from all the printed and manuscript books that Ferrandus’s work consists of only 232 chapters and is entirely different from the Cresconian collection. For although they agree in method and manner of presentation, Ferrandus’s order is much more impressive and precise than Cresconius’s.

These same learned men discuss many other matters concerning the ways in which Ferrandus and Cresconius differ and agree; these are to be taken from the preface cited above.

Yet the observations made about this work of Ferrandus both solidly and learnedly by the distinguished scholar Franciscus Florens in his dissertation *On the Origin, Art, and Authority of Canon Law* deserve particular attention [Note: [Col. 0885D] Franciscus Florens, *Juridical Works*, part I, p. 27, Paris edition, 1679].

We add only this point from Chiffletius [Note: [Col. 0885D] Chiffletius, preface to Ferrandus’s Works, no. 1]: in his *Brief Summary*, Ferrandus did not aim to collect every canon published before his time, but only those sufficient, in the circumstances of the time, for the discipline of the African clergy.

Lupus agrees with Chiffletius [Note: [Col. 0885D] Lupus, cited work] and further adds that our Carthaginian deacon may perhaps have arranged his *Brief Summary of the Canons* in order to abolish and proscribe the earlier codex of the African Church, in which contentious and deviant acts had been the alpha and omega.

Nor do we think that the observations made by other learned men concerning this *Brief Summary* should be omitted. First, the Franciscus Florens whom we have just cited believed that he had discovered certain blemishes in this work of Ferrandus, which he had undertaken to expose and remove in a new edition of Ferrandus that he was preparing [Note: [Col. 0885D] Florens, cited work, p. 28].

Prompted by this judgment, Paschasius Quesnellus attempted to test the matter in one or two chapters of Ferrandus, in order to support Florens’s assertion [Col. 0886A] [Note: [Col. 0885D] Quesnellus, dissertation 15 on the Works of Saint Leo, ch. 2, vol. II, pp. 389 ff., Lyons edition, 1700].

Learned brothers, the Ballerini, demonstrated that the efforts of both men rested on weak conjectures [Note: [Col. 0886D] Ballerini, notes on the Works of Saint Leo, vol. III, pp. 998 ff.]. Through their work, moreover, several obscure citations in the same *Brief Summary of the Canons* have been explained, while others have been supplied or corrected. These the same learned men hope will prove useful to a new edition [Note: [Col. 0886D] Isidore, *Treatise on the Ancient Collections of Canons*, part IV, ch. 1; Isidore, cited work, pp. 246 ff.].

As for the year in which Ferrandus compiled his *Brief Summary*, we have no certain knowledge, since he attached no indication of time to his work. Nevertheless, I willingly agree with the distinguished Florens [Note: [Col. 0886D] Florens, cited work]—an opinion that we saw shortly before was also approved by Voellus and Justellus—that our author is the oldest of the Latin Collectors whose works survive.

For Dionysius Exiguus, as they think, mentions him in the preface to his new translation of the Canons, which he was ordered to compile by Laurentius, “offended,” as he says, “by the confusion of the ancient translation” [Note: [Col. 0886D] In Voellus and Justellus, *Library of Ancient Canon Law*, vol. I, p. 101].

Whatever the truth may be, Ferrandus certainly lived at the same time as Dionysius and died before Dionysius. In publishing Ferrandus’s *Brief Summary of the Canons*, we followed Chiffletius’s exemplar, restored to completeness from the manuscript codices. We nevertheless compared it again with the edition later published by Voellus and Justellus [Note: [Col. 0886D] The same authors, cited work, pp. 448 ff.], which they copied from Pithoeus’s first edition, taken from an ancient codex at Troyes, and which those same distinguished men compared most carefully with two later editions: that of Altaserra, printed at Poitiers in 1630, and Chiffletius’s, printed at Dijon in 1649.

## IX.

It remains for us to speak of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe*, which we have judged should be appended to Ferrandus’s undisputed letters and works. But first of all Chiffletius must be heard; concerning this matter he writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0886D] Chiffletius, preface to the works of Ferrandus, no. 8]:

> “That this *Life*, which has hitherto been published anonymously, was written by Ferrandus was once my conjecture; and later I discovered that it had also pleased the most learned Peter Pithoeus in the preface to Ferrandus’s and Cresconius’s *Breviaries* [Note: [Col. 0886D] Pithoeus, preface to Ferrandus’s *Breviary of the Canons*, p. 303, Paris edition, 1687, fol.]. Aubertus Miraeus likewise says in his *Ecclesiastical Library* [Note: [Col. 0886D] Miraeus, note on the anonymous author of the *Little Book on Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 11]: ‘There are those who think that the *Life of Saint Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe*, which is in everyone’s hands, was written by that same Ferrandus the deacon.’

> “Furthermore, in the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portes, the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* is listed immediately before other works of Ferrandus—to Reginus, Severus, Anatolius, and Pelagius—a clear indication that this *Life* too came from the same workshop. I am additionally inclined to this opinion for the following reasons. First, in the letter on the Five Questions Ferrandus professes that he is addressing Fulgentius, ‘his absent teacher’ [Note: [Col. 0886D] Ferrandus, Letter 2, no. 1, below, p. 889], which he explains, as it were, in the prologue to Fulgentius’s *Life*, when he reports that he lived under Fulgentius’s instruction in the Caralitan monastery of Sardinia [Note: [Col. 0886D] *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, prologue, no. 3. See below, p. 961]. Next, although he lists in several places the books composed by Saint Fulgentius [Note: [Col. 0886D] Ibid., chaps. 22, 24, 28, 29], he nowhere mentions the letters sent to him concerning the two or five questions; nor does he mention the letter to Count Reginus, written shortly before Fulgentius’s death, whose thread he himself was judged worthy to carry through. These matters he passed over in silence out of modesty—something no one other than Ferrandus would have omitted. Moreover, since he does not say that he was present at Fulgentius’s funeral (which otherwise he certainly would not have omitted), this fits well with the case of a Carthaginian deacon who was living far from Ruspe. Finally, if one examines more closely the individual words, the joints and connections of the discourse, the frequent parallel cadences, and the entire character of the style throughout that history, one will say, I think, that no egg is more like another.

> “Accordingly, this *Life of Fulgentius*, which in my judgment is a genuine work of Ferrandus, I received from the preliminary section of the Paris edition of Fulgentius’s works and compared with the version which our John Bollandus, improved from very many copies, incorporated into his January volume [Note: [Col. 0887C] Lupus, *Dissertation on Appellations*, dissertation 2, chap. 3, p. 398; and chap. 33, p. 741], as well as with a good-quality manuscript from Dijon. I think it was written in the year following Fulgentius’s death, namely in the year of Christ 534, when Felicianus had already been consecrated bishop of Ruspe, on the Kalends of January, with Sunday coinciding with the anniversary of his predecessor’s death.”

Thus far Chiffletius. In addition to Pithoeus and Miraeus, whom he cited, Christianus Lupus subsequently adopted his view. Speaking of Ferrandus [Note: [Col. 0887C] Bollandus, *Acts of the Saints*, January, vol. I, pp. 32 ff.], he says:

> “For he is unquestionably the very man who wrote the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*.”

Natalis Alexander later joined Lupus [Note: [Col. 0887C] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, sixth century, chap. 4, art. 5, vol. V, p. 407]. Norisius, however, a man of distinction, judged otherwise [Note: [Col. 0887C] Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chap. 24, vol. I, p. 534]; and Pagius [Note: [Col. 0887C] Pagius, under the year 529, §14], Mangeantius, the editor of Saint Fulgentius’s works [Note: [Col. 0888C] Mangeantius, note at the beginning of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*], and, not long ago, Fontaninus [Note: [Col. 0888C] Fontaninus, *Inquiry concerning the Body of Saint Augustine*, etc., §3, p. 3] followed him eagerly.

But I am pleased to transcribe Norisius’s words:

> “Chiffletius thinks that the man who committed the deeds of his teacher to writing was Ferrandus the deacon, a man highly renowned for his distinguished learning, adding that he published that work in the year 534. But he is led to this opinion by slight conjectures, though he persuaded several learned men by them. As for his claim that the same man described Fulgentius’s deeds in the year 534, it is plainly false. For in chapter 29 he calls Boniface ‘of holy memory’ the primate of Carthage [Col. 0887C]; yet Boniface had certainly already died when those things were being written. He died in the year 535, during the consulship of Belisarius, as the bishop of Tours testifies—he who at that time was living in Africa.”

Thus far Norisius. As I reread these words and compare them with what that most learned man later wrote elsewhere about Ferrandus, it seems to me that he himself changed his opinion concerning the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* and finally attributed it to Ferrandus.

For, in another work, speaking of our Carthaginian deacon [Note: [Col. 0888C] Norisius, *History of the Controversy concerning Whether One of the Trinity Suffered*, chap. 9, vol. III, p. 855], he says:

> “Ferrandus, following the African bishops deported to Sardinia by order of King Thrasamund, had assumed the monastic habit in the monastery built there by Saint Fulgentius, the exiled bishop of Ruspe.”

But the distinguished author could not have learned this from anywhere except the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, since one reads it nowhere else. Speaking of himself, that author says [Note: [Col. 0888C] *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, prologue, §3. See below, p. 961]:

> “Converted by his saving admonitions [Fulgentius’s] to embrace the profession of monks, in that very small monastery which, banished to Sardinia for Christ’s sake, he had established for himself . . . I lived day and night in his presence, when the streams of his heavenly eloquence, sweeter to me than honey and the honeycomb, frequently drenched me.”

Here one sees that this writer says nothing about Ferrandus, but speaks throughout about himself. Since, then, the most eminent man stated that Ferrandus had assumed the monastic habit in the monastery established in Sardinia by Saint Fulgentius during his exile, and since he could not have drawn this information from any other writer than the one who, in composing the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, committed these words to writing only about himself, he therefore recognized that Ferrandus had narrated these things about himself and, consequently, that Ferrandus himself was the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*.

## X.

Having set aside the other editions of this *Life of Saint Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe*, we have committed it to the press in the form most diligently prepared by Mangeantius, the editor of the works of the same Saint Fulgentius, whom we mentioned shortly before.

There is no reason to mention here the supposedly revived Saint Ferrandus—that is, the *Life of Saint Hector Fulgentius Ferrandus*, first a Carthaginian deacon in Africa, then bishop of Carthage Spartaria in Spain, and finally archbishop of Toledo—which Joannes Ferrandus of Le Puy, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, published at Lyon in 1650. It is certainly a fictitious work. Its editor, exploiting the name and authority of writers of dubious reliability, assigned the African Ferrandus to Spain and made him a bishop there once and again. The work’s frivolity is plainly exposed by Chiffletius in his *Observations on Saint Ferrandus Revived*, which he appended to and published with five little works of the ancient writers on the Catholic faith at Dijon in 1656.

[Col. 0887]

# FULGENTIUS FERRANDUS: LETTERS AND LITTLE WORKS (C, S)

## FIRST LETTER

Ferrandus the deacon proposes two questions to Fulgentius: concerning the salvation of an Ethiopian catechumen who was baptized when illness had already deprived him of his mind and who died without having received the Eucharist.

To the most blessed lord and father, Bishop Fulgentius, who is to be received with every mark of veneration, Ferrandus the deacon sends greetings in the Lord.

**1.** Those who lack earthly resources and cannot obtain them through the sustained labor of a long undertaking or through the skill of an honorable craft, etc.—For the remainder, see among the works of Fulgentius, vol. LXV, col. 378.

## SECOND LETTER

Ferrandus proposes five questions to Fulgentius.

To the most blessed lord and father, Saint Bishop Fulgentius, who is to be regarded with every mark of veneration, Ferrandus the deacon sends greetings in the Lord.

**1.** I have often wished, with an eager desire to learn, to ask many things; but the infrequency of messengers, owing to the length of the journey, prevented me from addressing my absent teacher through frequent letters, etc.—For the remainder, see among the works of Fulgentius, vol. LXV, col. 392.

## THIRD LETTER: TO ANATOLIUS, DEACON OF THE CITY OF ROME

Concerning the two natures in Christ, and that one person of the Trinity can be said to have been born and to have suffered.

**1.** After the letter of the blessed Pope Leo and the salutary decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, holy brother Anatolius, the once-condemned impiety of Eutyches does not need to be refuted by a fuller discussion. Let the profane inventor of that wicked heresy lie buried in his own ashes. The authority of the priests who condemned him struck him once with the thunderbolt of anathema; why is there any need to infect an inanimate corpse again with the sword of truth? Let the prison of perpetual silence conceal a doctrine equally devoid of the light of reason. Sometimes the worst doctrines, when they are brought forward as though they were to be defeated, disturb the hearts of the simple with deadly poison. It is better not to know such things and, after crushing profane novelties, to preserve the Catholic faith inviolable, with those matters remaining firm which have also been strengthened by synodal definitions.

Or, if you think it more necessary that the lies of heretics always be refuted, unlock my tongue with the keys of your command: I shall hasten, insofar as grace grants me the ability, to obey cheerfully one who commands graciously. Extend the right hand of goodwill, and, protecting my exposed breast with the shield of prayer, come forth with me—if it pleases you—into the field of free combat. Against the impious ranks of those who, though wickedly slain, attempt to claim their ruinous inheritance, we shall fight without difficulty. Their weapons and their camp are not new. They still wish to overthrow the walls of apostolic preaching with those same darts which the standard-bearer of the heretics hurled vainly, becoming prey to the birds of the air.

As far as we have read, Eutyches carried two weapons of his error, with which, like a treacherous soldier, he wished to wound the Church emerging from the Lord’s side. For, denying that Mary remained ever-virgin through the working of the Holy Spirit, he refused to acknowledge that she had supplied the only-begotten God, who was to be born from a human womb, with the material of his flesh; and thus he refused to confess the Son consubstantial with his mother. By this means, wounding the integrity of Catholic unity with the harmful force of a turned-back blade, he hesitated to believe that the incarnate Word possessed two substances and completely cut off one of them.

But he who fights for his own people with the weapons of righteousness, in the right hand and in the left, immediately weakened and rendered powerless one of these positions, which would have inflicted deadly harm, so that now you can scarcely find anyone who dares deny that the Lord Jesus Christ possessed the reality of his mother’s body. Many, however, are frightened away from the opinion of two substances by the singularity of the one person. Nevertheless, lest we seem to have disregarded your command, we shall answer both propositions; and, following the rule of the Fathers, we shall speak to you also without fear of what you know so well.

**2.** I am confident that you know our position well: if, according to what the heretic thought—or rather, thought foolishly—the flesh of the Word of God, born according to the flesh from the flesh of the Virgin, is declared foreign to her, then the Son of God is asserted to have become the son of man without reason. For how is he naturally the son of man who has no origin from man? Yet he has no origin from man if, conceived in a virginal womb, he did not draw flesh from flesh.

It is certain that, without the seed of a father, he made his mother’s womb fruitful; but what kind of fruitfulness will Mary’s be if the flesh born through her is not from her? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” says the evangelist John (John 1:14). You ask from what he became flesh? Blessed Paul should answer your question: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. 4:4). God therefore sent his Son—that is, God made his Word flesh—but from where? From a woman. If, then, the Word became flesh from a woman, the flesh of the Word was unquestionably taken from a woman.

Here “woman” is always the Virgin Mary; she is called “woman” by reference to her sex. For this reason she conceived and bore God without violating her chastity: because God, having become man, received from her the reality of his flesh. Otherwise, if the Creator, who was to be created, fashioned for himself flesh of a new kind, either from nothing or from whatever source he wished, he ought to have appeared suddenly before mortal eyes, rather than endure for ten months the lodging of a tiny womb, whose capacity is insufficient for his greatness. [Note: [Col. 0889D] Here “rather” should be understood, as is often the case among ancient writers.]

What necessity would there have been for Joseph, the faithful bridegroom, when he saw his most chaste wife become a mother before they had come together, to suspect adultery, since he did not yet know the heavenly mystery? The only-begotten God would have become man without a human father and likewise without a mother, if he had been required to receive nothing from his mother. He would have come to the children of men as the son of no human being, if he were to share nothing with the children of men.

This opinion is exceedingly contradictory; the shame of truth overwhelms anyone who considers it at length. A virgin gives birth to a son while everyone marvels, and yet the womb of the mother is thought to have remained barren because it contributes nothing of itself to the limbs of the one being born? The earth produces senseless plants, and no one denies them the quality of earthly substance. Mary conceives the Son of God and gives birth to the Son of God, yet in him she does not recognize the property of her own substance?

It would surely be judged the more tolerable error of one who, suspecting that the Lord Jesus Christ received nothing from Mary, is silent even about his birth. For whoever introduces any difference between the substance of the begetter and that of the begotten does great injury to the birth. The Teacher of the Gentiles rebukes this most wicked blasphemy when, recognizing that the opening of his Epistle should be adorned with the clearer title of the true faith, he began to build up the Romans with these words:

> “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh; who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 1:1–4).

**3.** Let the heretic now say how the Son of God was made from the seed of David according to the flesh. Certainly Joseph contributed no seed to Mary, to whom the angel said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Why, then, is Christ again said to be from the seed of David? Why is he who was born among human beings without human seed said to have been made from the seed of David?

The force of this proclamation must not be considered lightly or superficially. Remembering his own teaching, the Apostle likewise admonishes Timothy, his dearest disciple, elsewhere:

> “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David according to my Gospel” (2 Tim. 2:8).

Who, then, inserted the seed of David into his birth, in the substance of his humanity? Where could this have taken place from the seed of David? If he was born without a human father, how could he be from the seed of David unless he received flesh from his mother, who belonged to the seed of David?

For Mary was from the seed of David, and Christ from Mary’s flesh—without marital seed, indeed, but with the property of nature. Therefore the Psalmist sings in prophetic spirit:

> “The Lord will give goodness, and our land will give its fruit” (Ps. 84:13),

because Mary bore her Lord in the manifest substance of the flesh which she had given him. For if Christ’s flesh had been born from elsewhere, the land—that is, Mary—would in no way have given its own fruit, but a foreign one.

Nor would the holy Apostle again have indicated that Christ was the seed of Abraham, speaking as follows:

> “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say, “and to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “and to your seed,” which is Christ (Gal. 3:16).

What could be clearer? What more evident? Is Christ not the seed of Abraham in the same way as he is from the seed of David—because of Mary, through Mary, and from Mary?

Let the impious disputant take away from Christ the material of the flesh which Mary supplied, and let him explain how Christ is the seed of Abraham or how he was made from the seed of David.

Did faithful Abraham seem to bind his servant with a superfluous ritual when, full of faith and also foreknowing future things, he said: “Put your hand under my thigh and swear by the God of heaven” (Gen. 24:2)? He might surely have said: “Touch my breast, splendid with holy thoughts; touch my hands, enriched by the gift of innocence; touch my head, liable to no crime.” Why are the more honorable members passed over, and why is he compelled to place his hand beneath the thigh alone when he is about to swear?

Something great was hidden in that thigh: the flesh of Christ was hidden there, which was destined to be born from his lineage. Therefore, when the thigh had been touched, a terrible oath is uttered by the God of heaven, because the God of heaven was to be born according to the flesh in the same way as those whom a generation signified by the name “thigh” identifies as sharing the same form as those from whom they are formed.

**4.** The flesh of Christ, therefore, was taken from his mother, and for this reason it is all the more real; but it is wholly holy, because it was cleansed by union with the divinity. In Christ’s flesh there is the nature of our flesh, but the guilt of nature is not found there.

Thus Christ’s flesh is both like and unlike Mary’s flesh: like, because it derived its origin from her; unlike, because it did not contract from her the contagion of an impaired origin. Like, because although they were voluntary, it nevertheless experienced real weaknesses; unlike, because it committed no iniquities at all, either voluntarily or through ignorance. Like, because it was passible and mortal; unlike, because it was undefiled and also life-giving to the dead. Like in origin, unlike in merit; like in appearance, unlike in power; like because it is “the likeness of sinful flesh,” as the Apostle says: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8:3).

See how Christ’s flesh is taught to have naturally received from Mary the cause of a new existence according to the regularity of human birth, while the necessity of marital intercourse was excluded. Thus it is not sinful flesh, because it is God’s flesh, yet it is the likeness of sinful flesh, because it was truly born from mortal flesh. It is also rightly mortal, because it drew its material from mortal flesh.

For in flesh that was entirely without sin, through what door would voluntary death enter unless it were born from the flesh of one in whom sin could exist, and through sin, death? Let us explain this more fully in clear words.

Christ’s flesh was not conceived in iniquities; why, then, does it appear to have experienced the condition of death? We plainly know that the Son of God died for us not by necessity but by will. Yet the holy Apostle is a witness to the truth when he says truthfully:

> “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death” (Rom. 5:12).

Sin did not enter Christ’s flesh. How, then, did death—although voluntary—enter, unless divine power caused him to be born without sin, while divine mercy caused him to die without sin?

Nevertheless, since his maternal substance was in him, nothing proves more effectively that Christ had flesh from a mortal mother than the punishment of death. Thanks be to him who, by assuming human nature without guilt but not without punishment, removed guilt, ended punishment, and healed nature, so that, because he shares nature with us—

For it was necessary that, like a priest, he receive from us what he was to offer for us. But if he did not receive from Mary the material of flesh, he did not receive from us anything that he could offer for us; and how could he perform the office of an eternal priest?

We ought to give our priest a victim to be sacrificed to God. The only-begotten Son of God the Father, having become our priest in mortal flesh, offered not gold, not silver, not the blood of goats, but his own body. Our victim, therefore, is his body; and if he received a body, he received a body from us. He received it when holy Mary conceived him.
