He must therefore be believed consubstantial with his mother, just as he is consubstantial with his Father. Being consubstantial with his mother, and therefore with us, he conquered the devil; for this reason, in his mercy, he lifted the entire human race from the depths of captivity.

Adam was conquered when he was persuaded by woman’s allurements to eat from the forbidden tree; Christ conquered when he was hung upon the tree of the cross amid Jewish fury and outcries. What benefit does Adam’s victory derive from Christ if Christ has no substance in common with him? And how could this have happened unless the Virgin Mary had borne him in such a way as to provide him, without iniquity, with the material of flesh in which he could be born in time and suffer?

**5.** Thus, entirely thus, true faith admonishes us to believe: Christ had a true body—not an airy one, not a phantasmal one, not fashioned from elsewhere, but fleshly; taken from the Virgin’s flesh, although not generated carnally; brought to life by the inspiration of a rational soul; such as ours, except without sin; such that the devil would be deceived by it, swallowing the hook while thinking it bait.

For if the devil had not seen in Christ the Savior a true body, consubstantial with his mother, he would neither have dared to tempt him nor to kill him. Moreover, in him he saw nothing of his own, as the Lord himself tells his disciples:

> “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30),

namely, nothing of sin. For in him there was the complete nature of his mother—that is, ours. The ancient creditor of sin, as though something were owed to him, attacked, crucified, and killed that nature; and through an unlawful exaction he lost whatever was owed to him: justly conquered and justly punished, because it was the flesh in Christ that conquered—the flesh that had been conquered in Adam.

For this was God’s justice: that through the flesh by which the author of death had been conquered in Adam, he should himself be conquered in Christ; and that the flesh without sin should die, so that all sin might be erased—the flesh which had died through sin. The grace of the Savior worked wondrously, so that the death which was the punishment of sin afterward became the medicine of sins.

Adam sinned and died, binding all his descendants with the chains of eternal death. Christ died, and because he had not sinned, he freed all sinners from death’s dominion. If, then, the nature of the flesh in which Christ had not sinned and in which he died were different, the devil would have been conquered not by justice but by power.

But he had to be conquered by justice. Justice itself consisted in this: that the Redeemer should come in the flesh which the tempter had caused to remain subject to punishment. Therefore God wished to become man, so that man might easily be reconciled to God through the God-man.

A great separation had arisen between the just God and sinful man. God was not near to man in substance, nor was the sinner joined to the just one by grace. God therefore humbled himself and became the just man, and God was reconciled to sinful man.

God became what he had not been—man; and man likewise became what he had not been—just. But if the just God had perhaps become a just man in such a way that he did not share the substance of the man who had been sinful, and possessed nothing proper to the substance of the sinner, sinful man would have remained so forever.

Now, however, through the likeness of substance, having become participants in grace, we have been justified in that only-begotten God who wished to become for us a man like us. Hence the most holy Paul, treating the mystery of the Incarnation, speaks of Christ to the Hebrews as follows:

> “For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make atonement for the sins of the people” (Heb. 2:16–17).

Who could explain the meaning of this passage in words worthy of it? “He had to be made like his brothers in every respect,” he says. O foolish heresy’s unskilled defender! How can Christ be made like his brothers in every respect if he was unlike them in substance? How can he be altogether like them in substance unless he received flesh from Mary?

Let the profane heart cease to meditate on such things. Whoever denies that Christ, the true Son of the true God, wondrously assumed the true reality of flesh from a true mother wishes to empty the entire work of the Mediator.

A mediator is mediator only between two parties, whom he himself properly and firmly joins together by existing between them, if he is like both in substance—those whom he brings near to himself by grace. But Christ, existing as Mediator between God and human beings, as the Chosen Vessel declares:

> “There is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5),

if he is not man from man, how is he God from God? If he is not consubstantial with the human being who is his mother, how is he consubstantial with God the Father?

If his divine substance is shared with God, while his human substance is not considered shared with human beings, he bears the person or performs the office of mediator in vain. Yet because he is a mediator in such a way that he is truly mediator both for the Father and for the mother, both for God and for human beings, he is consubstantial with God and with human beings. Consequently, he is plainly not of one substance but of two, since a mediator can never be mediator of one substance.

**6.** See, most holy brother, how secretly we have entered the threshold of another question, with truth itself opening the doors. For while we wished, through the office of the mediator, to discover—or rather to prove—the property, likeness, and reality of the human substance, lest we cut away the fruitfulness of the Virgin mother, the manifest distinction of two substances shone forth when the mediator was named and considered.

For the mediator is indeed one if you consider the person to whom the name “mediator” belongs; yet, existing as mediator between two things of dissimilar substance, he can fulfill the office of mediator only through two substances. For whoever possesses one person and one nature cannot in any way be mediator, or be called mediator, between two substances. With respect to that substance to which his one nature is least suited, he is wholly without the office of mediator.

He is a true mediator when, in order to join the division of two dissimilar substances, he possesses substantial communion with both. Through that communion he removes the division, so that the two may become one by coming together in one through that mediator with whom, before they came together, they had been one.

Let us consider this more fully in our mediator, the Lord Christ. His person is truly one—for it is unfitting that one mediator should have two persons—but he is nevertheless not of one nature, although he is one mediator.

For this one nature, since he is the mediator of God and human beings, must necessarily be shared either with God or with human beings. Yet, however much the heretic protests, one nature cannot be shared by God and human beings alike. God is the Creator; we are creatures. God is eternal; we are temporal. God is incomprehensible; we are comprehensible. God is without place; we are in place. God is infinite and immeasurable; we are bounded and determined.

Therefore I say again confidently: if Christ’s nature is one, it can be shared either with God the Father or with human beings; it can never be shared with both God and human beings.

Now Christ is of one substance with the Father—what the Greeks call *homoousion*—according to the unambiguous profession of the Council of Nicaea. Therefore Christ Jesus has one nature in common with the Father.

How, then, can he be our mediator unless he has that by which he is one with the Father and that by which he is one with us? He demonstrates this most clearly in the Gospel, now near his Passion, when he prays to the Father in these words:

> “That they may be one, just as we are one. I in them and you in me” (John 17:22–23).

Tell me, you who proclaim that Christ has one essence: how is he himself in us, and how is the Father in him? Because the substance of the Father and the Son is one. He is also in us because he wished to become a participant in our substance.

Therefore there is no longer one substance but two: one in which he is one with the Father, another in which he is one with us; one through which the Father is in him, another through which he himself is truly in us. He is the true mediator, possessing that by which he is near to God and that by which he is near to us, so that he may also make us near to God—through himself, who wished to become near to us.

But if perhaps you, whom consideration of the mediator reluctantly compels to proclaim two substances, wish to evade the force of the truth and do not entirely deny that one mediator has two essences, but affirm that one could have been made from these two, examine more carefully whether, if the Word and flesh began to be one nature, flesh and God the Father could be proclaimed to be of one essence.

For consequently, since the Word of the Father is the Son and the substance of the Father and the Son is unquestionably one, just as God the Father is of one substance with his Word, so he will also be found to be of one substance with the flesh of his Word, if flesh and the Word could become one substance.

**7.** This opinion will be joined by yet another absurdity: since all human flesh is of the same substance, and Christ’s flesh was human, and according to you began to be of one substance with the Word, and through the Word also with the Father, our flesh too would be said to be of one nature with the Father’s divinity. No Christian at all ought even to hear this, much less admit it as a suspicion in the slightest thought.

Whoever therefore asserts that Christ has one substance should consider something else that could easily become apparent to anyone, unless the smoke of contention obscures the eyes of his heart: by proclaiming one substance in Christ, he would also make it appear that the Father was born from the Virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, and buried.

For if the only-begotten God did not receive another nature from the flesh of the Virgin mother, so that he might be born in time, but the nature of the assumed flesh and the assuming divinity was somehow made one nature, then this one nature will either not belong also to the Father—and how then will it be proclaimed *homoousion* with the Father, which the Greeks call “of one substance” or “of one essence”? Or, if it will also belong to the Father, and the Son was born and crucified in it, let them see how the Father can be proclaimed either unbegotten or impassible.

Indeed, not only the Father but also the Holy Spirit—since he too is believed to be of one substance or essence with the Father and the Son—will be joined to the sufferings of the Son. Thus the entire economy of the Lord’s Incarnation will be thought to belong to the whole Trinity; and blessed Mary will be not only the mother of the Son of God but the mother of the entire Trinity.

Let us strive to make this plain through apostolic examples. The blessed Apostle says:

> “Our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed” (Rom. 6:6).

How was our old man crucified together with him, if only Christ was hanging on the cross, unless he hung according to that substance which he took from us?

Again, in another passage the same Apostle says:

> “He raised us together with him and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 2:6).

Let it be answered: how were we raised together with him, or how did we sit together in the heavenly places, unless through communion with that substance which he took from us?

If, then, the Son of God assumed human nature into the unity of his divine substance, so that there could be one nature of divinity and flesh, whatever was joined to his divinity was joined to the whole Trinity—especially since the works of the Trinity are inseparable, because the substance or essence of the Trinity is one.

The Trinity is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three in persons, one in substance or essence. But if the Son was born or suffered in this essence or substance, then the Father and the Holy Spirit were likewise both born and suffered.

If, however, only the Son suffered, as the ancient tradition of the Catholic faith has taught, he suffered in another nature. And what is that other nature except the human one? If, therefore, the human nature is one and the divine nature another, then one nature was not made in Christ from two.

### 8

The Arians are accustomed to raise against us the following proposition. “Has the divinity of the Son suffered, or has it not suffered?” If we answer, “It has not suffered,” they say: “Then a mere man was crucified.” If we answer what we ought to answer—“It suffered, but according to the flesh, while nevertheless remaining in that which it is, impassible”—they reply: “Then either the divinity of the Father suffered, if the divinity of the Son suffered, or the divinity of the Father and the Son is not one.”

To the Arians who put forward this argument, the Catholic tongue should respond as follows: The Father and the Son are one in substance, not in person; the nature of the Father and the Son is one, but the person of the Father is one and that of the Son another. The Son, however, assuming flesh—that is, the complete and perfect nature of man—was pleased to assume it in such a way that one person was formed of flesh and the Word, though not one nature. God, having become man, united human nature to himself in the unity of person, which he does not share with the Father, not in the unity of substance, which he does share with the Father. Therefore it was not the Trinity, but only the Son, who was both born and suffered.

The Son suffered according to another nature; but because he made one person of his divinity and his flesh, on account of the unity of person the divinity of the Son is said to have suffered whatever the flesh produced [or: endured?]. The person of the Son, however, is not the person of the Father, since the Father’s is another person; therefore only the Son suffered.

But those who, just as they want to preach one person of the Lord Jesus Christ, likewise want to preach one nature, what will they answer the Arians? All their arguments will undoubtedly fail them; either they will agree with the Arians and cease to preach one divinity of the Father and the Son, or they will join the Patripassians, to be miserably bound by a sacrilegious error.

Let heretical fury return to a devout understanding; and let the one who confesses that one nature was made from two in the Lord Jesus Christ tell me which of the two perished so that one might be made from two. The divine nature could not perish; the human nature ought not to perish. Or, if he dares to assert the destruction of neither, let him say whether one was changed into the other. And if he supposes that one could have been changed into the other, let him say in turn whether the divinity was changed into flesh or the flesh into divinity.

For if the divinity was reduced to the lower condition of flesh, it is recognized as having been degraded; and the good Creator would then appear to have procured misery for himself rather than granted mercy to us. But if the divinity, remaining inviolate, absorbed the substance of the flesh, so that the flesh began to be what the Word is, who could hear this with toleration: that a creature, previously subject to all accidents, arrived at the nature and power of the Creator, so that suddenly it existed without quality, without quantity, without time, without place, without position, without passions, without habit—its created condition having been lost and supported only by the power of making?

### 9

I fear that the enlargement of the creature may instead be the diminution of the Creator, as though God needed the addition of flesh in order to be enlarged; for that nature into which the other could be changed will also be said to have been much more readily changeable. Let us consign this exceedingly absurd opinion to silence. And if it is clearly evident that neither of these two natures could have been transferred into the other, let the opponent answer whether perhaps a mixture of the two natures, with the property of neither preserved, produced a new nature of a new kind.

And if he wishes to preach this one nature of the one mediator, I will not for the moment ask by what natural name he judges that it should be called—just as, from two natures, soul and flesh, one nature is made whose name is “man”; from two animals likewise one animal is born and is called a “mule”; and from two substances, fire and wood, one thing is made and is called “charcoal.” Neither soul alone nor body can naturally be called “man”; neither horse alone nor ass “mule”; neither fire alone nor wood “charcoal.” So let him be able to show, if one nature has been made from two natures—namely, divinity and humanity—what it ought naturally to be called.

For “Christ” is the name of an office; “Emmanuel” is a name that indicates and declares both substances as united. But the name of the nature of this substance, which is said to have been made one from two, I have neither read in Scripture nor heard from the tongue of any disputant. This name, as I have said, I earnestly demand.

Rather, I propose this and, whether he wishes it or not, set it before the preacher of one substance in Christ as something to be considered: If Christ’s nature is one, composed from two, the Father’s nature is not such, nor is that of the Holy Spirit. How, then, will the Son be *homoousios*—of one substance—with the Father or the Holy Spirit? The one nature of the Father and the Holy Spirit is simple and lacks composition; but Christ’s nature, which is established as one made from two, is composite and lacks simplicity.

What, then, shall we say? The force of truth compels us, even against our will, either not to preach one nature of Christ, or to deny that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity—have one substance or essence. But if we deny that the Trinity has one substance or essence, we appear to lend our agreement to the doctrine of the Arians.

Therefore, lest we appear like the Arians, let us not preach one nature of Christ, even though it is said to be from two; rather, let us confess one Christ from two and in two natures. Thus we shall neither be polluted by the poison of the Arians nor intoxicated by the superfluous argument of the delirious Eutyches.

The only-begotten God, the true and proper Son of God, was one when it was said:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.  
> *(John 1:1–3)*

He is one and the same when it is said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Therefore, before the Virgin Mary conceived, the triune God created us; and after she had given birth, through the fecundating power of the Holy Spirit, to Emmanuel—that is, “God with us”—the triune God redeemed us: before the dispensation of the flesh, our God was the Trinity; after the work of the cross and after the spoils of hell, our God is the Trinity.

Why is this so? Because just as the Father was, is, and will be one—the Father who was not born of the Virgin; just as the Holy Spirit was, is, and will be one—the Spirit who likewise was not born of the Virgin; so also the Son who was born of the Virgin is one. His assumption of another [substance] was into one person. [Note: The word “substance” seems to be missing here, at Col. 0897D.]

### 10

Therefore, through the birth of the flesh, the number of substances in Christ increased, while the singularity of person remained. Accordingly, although the nature of divinity is one and the nature of humanity another, that Trinity does not become a quaternity, because it is a Trinity of persons, and the person in Christ remained one.

Christ is therefore one, and always one, on account of the singularity of the one person, which in him can neither be divided, subdivided, nor doubled, although he is believed to exist from two and in two natures.

Let us therefore freely and without any fear confess the two natures of the one Christ—namely, the divine and the human, the Word and the flesh—appearing with clear distinctions. And, hearing simply throughout all the divine books what may rightly be understood according to the property of each nature, let us have no doubt that certain statements are applied to his divinity and others to his humanity, without any separation whatsoever.

If someone asks me whether the statement “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) was spoken according to divinity or according to humanity, I answer confidently: according to divinity, not according to humanity.

And if someone again asks whether the statement “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28) was spoken according to divinity or according to humanity, I answer confidently: according to humanity, not according to divinity.

Yet neither statement will for that reason cease to be Christ’s statement. Both belong to the one Christ, whose are both divinity and humanity. No separation has been introduced here, because we have said that one statement can be understood according to one substance, while denying that it is according to the other. For a statement belongs to whichever nature it suits; for that reason it does not suit the other without separation, because it belongs to the person whose are both natures.

Let no one impose upon us the necessity of preaching one nature. The Catholic faith knows no two sons and utterly detests those who assert a quaternity. Therefore, as I think, certain guardians of the rule of right faith have now been pleased to confess that one of the Trinity suffered.

This statement is understood to imply nothing other than that the one who suffered in the flesh was the very one who was born from God the Father—that is, Christ—lest it be thought that a mere man endured the injuries of suffering. This, then, is what the person who says that one of the Trinity suffered means. The one who suffered is not a fourth person, but belongs to the number of the Trinity.

For, while the Son of God remained impassible according to divinity, through the assumption of a passible nature he became subject to suffering. And although there is one nature in him by which he always remains impassible, and another by which he is said to have suffered temporally, nevertheless the impassible one himself suffered. The impassible one is not one person and the sufferer another.

This impassible one is the Son of God himself, the only-begotten God, naturally born before the ages from God the Father; and, when the fullness of time came, mercifully born from his mother because he willed it. Without him the Trinity never existed, since, as we have already explained above, the Trinity is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If you remove either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, the Trinity cannot exist.

Neither the Father, nor the Son according to divinity, nor the Holy Spirit is numbered among creatures; nor are the Father, the Son according to divinity, or the Holy Spirit said to be of this world or of creatures. Rather, only the Trinity is counted together among itself, and each of them, when said to be of the Trinity, is separated from all other creatures.

### 11

For every reality is either God or a creature. If it is God, it is not a creature; if it is a creature, it is not God.

God, however, is the Trinity of one substance or essence; creation is distributed among many kinds of different substances. Therefore, whoever is God and is properly—that is, truly—God is either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit.

And because neither the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone is the Trinity, but the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together are the Trinity, the Father is one of the Trinity, the Son is one of the Trinity, and the Holy Spirit is one of the Trinity.

What, then, does anyone mean who says, “The Son is one of the Trinity,” except: “Do not seek him among creatures”? The Son, therefore, according to divinity, because he is not a creature but the Creator, is one of the Trinity; and because he deigned to suffer according to humanity, for this reason he is said to have suffered as one of the Trinity.

The meaning is, so far as I infer—or rather, so far as I believe—the same as when one says, “God suffered.” Just as whoever proclaims that God suffered does not make the substance of divinity passible, but shows that the impassible divinity and the humanity that was subject to suffering constitute one person, so whoever proclaims that one of the Trinity suffered commends the unity of person in both natures, excluding the wicked and impious doctrine of the Nestorian heresy, which introduces two sons.

Let the one who wishes to deny that God suffered deny, then, that one of the Trinity suffered. But how God suffered, all the faithful understand well: namely, according to the flesh, according to which God was able to suffer. Otherwise no credible reason would remain for assuming flesh, if divinity could have been subject to suffering by itself.

These things are so familiar to almost all Christians that whenever they hear God proclaimed as having suffered, they understand none other than the Son of God, and suppose that he suffered in no other way than in the manner in which God both ought and could suffer—according to the substance of the flesh that he assumed from his mother.

Thus, whenever one of the Trinity is said to have suffered, no one is even compelled to ask, “Which one? The Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit?” As soon as you say that he suffered, they immediately understand the Son, whom they know alone to have suffered, as the Gospels testify. The knowledge of right preaching is vigilant in them even in this respect: although, when asserting that one of the Trinity suffered, I do not add “according to the flesh,” they nevertheless understand it as correctly said, as though I had added those words—provided only that the inclination to contention is driven far away, in those accustomed to attack everything they hear rather than believe it.

I have plainly been unable, after prolonged reflection, to discover anything from which this statement could receive support for the Eutychians, as some loudly claim. The first falsehood of the delirious Eutyches was that the only-begotten God, when he deigned to become man, did not assume flesh for himself from the Virgin’s womb. The second was that there are not now in Christ two substances, divine and human, but that one substance was made from these two.

Let us therefore examine both statements carefully, and if this assertion that one of the Trinity suffered can be fitted to either of them, let us investigate the matter with greater concern.

### 12

What, I ask, does it contribute to denying the reality of the maternal body in the Son of God when it is asserted that one of the Trinity suffered? Is he not truly the Son of God if he is one of the Trinity? And if he suffered, does he not truly possess the reality of a maternal body? Otherwise, remove the body assumed from his mother, and how could pure divinity have suffered?

Consider what Mary’s flesh is: undoubtedly passible and mortal. Therefore, for the flesh of the Word to be passible and mortal, it derives its origin from that flesh which was passible and mortal.

Recognize, then, in the offspring the likeness of kind through the testimony of suffering; and observe, whether you wish it or not, that the Eutychians are more thoroughly refuted than supported when it is asserted that one of the Trinity suffered.

Without doubt, the preacher of one substance in Christ is also refuted by these words. For that Christ is one of the Trinity pertains to divinity; that he is believed to have suffered pertains to humanity. The one who suffered would not be one of the Trinity unless he had the same divinity as the Father and the Holy Spirit. The one who is one of the Trinity would not have suffered unless he had a humanity consubstantial with his mother.

Let the preacher of one nature in Christ, then, be silent. For the person who confesses that one of the Trinity suffered recalls two natures.

Anyone who gnaws uselessly at well-spoken words by trying to understand them badly, and seeks to slander rather than to be taught, vainly torments his own suspicions. The statement that one of the Trinity suffered displeases the Nestorians, not without reason. They wish to introduce a fourth person, to whom they think the sufferings occurred.

But one of the Trinity suffered does not rightly please the Eutychians, if indeed it pleases them at all. They evidently and deliberately deny that the two natures of Christ remain, and this chapter openly contradicts them: one substance is indicated by the words “one of the Trinity,” and another by the fact that he is said to have suffered.

For the suffering mentioned bears witness to a passible nature. Once a passible nature is understood—especially in the one who is one of the Trinity—the distinction between the two substances is made exceedingly clear.

But perhaps an excessively suspicious or altogether slow listener desires instruction in plain language: whenever we take pleasure in confessing either that God suffered or that one of the Trinity suffered, since the Father is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and the whole Trinity together is God; and since the Father is one of the Trinity and the Holy Spirit is one of the Trinity, when we say that God suffered we should immediately add “according to the flesh,” lest either the whole Trinity be thought to have undergone suffering, or the Son himself be thought to have suffered in the substance of his divinity, which he shares with the Father.

In this matter, we should accommodate ourselves to such people. If they wish to hear it in this way, we should also speak in this way: One of the Trinity—that is, the Son, one person among three persons—suffered according to the flesh, which he assumed from us, so that he might deign to endure suffering for us.

### 13

Let us add explicit words, lest we give an opportunity for malicious interpretation and be thought to believe something other than what we hold.

Yet the person who is disturbed by these plainly spoken words and suspects them should be reminded that Christ’s divinity or humanity is not denied as often as the two are not pronounced together in the same utterance.

The Apostle says: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6). There he called Christ “Lord” and remained silent about “man”; yet he should not for that reason be thought to have denied it.

Again, writing to Timothy in another place, he says: “There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). There he said “man” and remained silent about “God”; yet he did not for that reason deny him. Such is the power of the ineffable mystery.

Thus God, mercifully made man, uniquely and wonderfully united two natures in one person, so that whether you call Christ Jesus God, you also understand him as man; and whether you confess him as man, you also understand him as God. In him there is a human divinity and a divine humanity.

Therefore, it is the person who does not understand the two natures in any other way than by hearing both named who sows the greater suspicion of separation or division.

Behold, in the Gospel we have heard Christ say: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), which he appears to have said according to his human nature. Shall we therefore suppose that he does not possess divinity, according to which he said elsewhere: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)?

When he said, “The Father is greater than I,” did he not remain silent about “I and the Father are one”? And when he said, “I and the Father are one,” did he not remain silent about “The Father is greater than I”? Yet he denied neither statement.

Let us therefore say to him, if it seems appropriate, when he says, “The Father is greater than I”: “Add, Lord, ‘I and the Father are one,’” lest the Arians fail to consider him equal.

Many similar examples present themselves to those who seek them with devout care.

Again, the Savior himself says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Sirach 24:5), which he spoke according to divinity. Let us say to him: “Add, Lord, ‘from the Virgin’s womb,’” which pertains to humanity, lest the Manichaeans or Eutychians suppose that you were not born from flesh.

Among those who understand how we believe, let us be permitted to speak simply.

The apostles baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Did they therefore deny the Father and the Holy Spirit because they remained silent about them? Or was that baptism not given in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit because the apostles are said to have baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus?

Because of the communion of one substance and because of the one name of the undivided Trinity, even when only the Lord Jesus is named, the Father and the Holy Spirit are understood to have been named as well, in the power of that name which is one among the three.

Likewise, if I name only the divinity of Christ, I have already named his humanity, which he united to himself from the Virgin; and if I name only his humanity, I have simultaneously named the divinity to which it was united.

These two substances in Christ may be mentioned separately, but they cannot be recognized in belief separately.

### 14

For behold, while blessed Paul was giving salutary instructions at Miletus to the elders of the Church, he said:

> Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.  
> *(Acts 20:28)*

Tell us now, Teacher of the Gentiles, and answer something that we, who are exceedingly suspicious, ought also to be answered.

You said that God acquired the Church with his own blood. Why did you not add “the Son”? What if someone should think you meant the Father? What if another should think you meant the Holy Spirit? For the Father is undoubtedly God, and the Holy Spirit is God.

Or, if you simply named “God,” when you said that he acquired the Church with his own blood, you should have explained how God has blood and added “according to the flesh,” lest anyone suppose that divinity too can have or shed blood.

I know what the Chosen Vessel would answer immediately to this question. “You know my preaching, my son; why did you consider my statement doubtful? I have already said: ‘He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all’ (Rom. 8:32), so that it might be believed that only the Son suffered at the hands of the nations.

“I have already said: ‘Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross’ (Phil. 2:6, 8), so that he might rightly be believed to have died in human substance.

“Yet, so that you might know him as God, elsewhere I spoke confidently: ‘From them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever’ (Rom. 9:5).”

I recognize, holy Paul, the teaching of truth in its fullness, and your statement in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles has never been doubtful to me. I understood that the God who acquired his Church with his own blood (Acts 20:28) is none other than Christ Jesus, the Son of God, and that he had blood only according to the substance of the flesh.

But I said these things on account of those who, now hearing that one of the Trinity suffered, say: “Add ‘according to the flesh,’” as though it ought to be understood otherwise if I do not add it, or as though adding it were very necessary, even though the meaning is evident without it.

Nevertheless, I gladly endure being required to say what I am ready to offer voluntarily. My tongue freely utters what my conscience retains.

The Son of God, one of the Trinity, Christ Jesus, who is one person among three persons, suffered according to the flesh.

But if you now believe, without malice, that one of the Trinity is said to have suffered, say it in the same good sense as I do. If you still doubt, say: “One person among the three suffered,” that is, “The Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, suffered according to the flesh.”

Otherwise, if you refuse to confess that one person among the three suffered, you will be found to confess a fourth person and, without any ambiguity, judged to be possessed by the error of Nestorius.

### 15

Therefore every Catholic should either hear simply and speak simply of one of the Trinity having suffered, or, speaking cautiously though not unbelievingly, confess that one person among the three suffered. Nor should anyone for that reason judge as a heretic the person who says that one of the Trinity suffered in the sense in which he himself also truly says that one person among the three suffered. At the same time, let us hasten to walk along the Lord’s way, holding fast to peace.

For “one of the Trinity” means the same as “one person among three persons.” If you say, “Christ has one person,” you say nothing other than, “Christ is one.” And if you say, “The Father is one” or “the Holy Spirit is one,” you say nothing other than, “The Father has one person” or “the Holy Spirit has one person.”

“One” can indeed also signify substance, but only if you add the proper and clear designation of substance, as when you say, “The Trinity is one,” and immediately add, “God.”

Otherwise, remove the noun you have added where substance is being signified, and say, if you dare: “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one.” Who would not immediately understand “are one” as said according to person, and refute the vanity of Sabellius?

You see, then, that “one” properly pertains to signifying person, although, when joined to the designation of a substance, it can also signify substance.

Let us therefore hear simply that one of the Trinity suffered—that is, one person from among three persons.

Let no one wish to object to me: “If we say one of the Trinity, let us say one of humanity, just as we say ‘God’ and again say ‘man.’” For when we say “God,” we rightly also say “man,” because “God” and “man” are names of substances.

But since “one” properly signifies person, let us not imagine saying “one and one,” lest we appear to assert two persons.

For this reason we confess one of the Trinity, and not one of humanity: God came into the Virgin’s womb and, by his coming, granting her the gift of fertility without the stain of lust, powerfully and ineffably united human nature to himself, with so great a bond of unity that the person of the Word became the person of the flesh, and thereafter the one person of the Word was also the person of the flesh.

Therefore we cannot in any way say “one of the Trinity and one of humanity,” or “one of the Trinity” and “one of humanity,” because in Christ Jesus humanity does not possess a proper person separately; rather, the person of the Word of God, by whom humanity was assumed, became its own person.

We therefore distinguish Christ’s two natures in names and functions, not in persons.

For this reason the Apostle confidently says:

> We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.  
> *(1 Cor. 2:23–24)*

Behold: Christ crucified is himself the power of God and the wisdom of God. Why, then, should one of the Trinity not be said to have suffered?

Or is Christ not the power of God and the wisdom of God, one of the Trinity? But let the person who denies this openly also say that, according to divinity, the Son is not one of the Trinity.

If, however, according to divinity Christ is one of the Trinity, and according to divinity he is the power and wisdom of God; and if Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God, then it is rightly said that one of the Trinity suffered.

### 16

No one should be disturbed if, as some say, the representative of Eutyches proclaimed this statement at the Council of Chalcedon. Truth often speaks even through the ignorant.

Our fathers, however, when assembled in the council, considered the speaker’s meaning rather than his words. They did not wish either to declare him Catholic on account of this statement or to insert the statement itself into the Catholic definitions at that time, lest they appear to have approved the speaker’s understanding [Note: Here, as above in section 2, something should probably be understood.]

Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit later wondrously instructed the faithful that the Eutychianists are also refuted by this statement, in which the preaching of two natures is complete. Thus they could not say: “If Christ is one of the Trinity, and the Trinity is of one substance, while Christ is God and man, then he is of one substance.”

For Christ is both one of the Trinity and God and man, yet he is not of one substance [with the Trinity]. Otherwise the humanity he assumed would also be consubstantial with the Trinity, which sound doctrine condemns.

I remember that I once understood three reasons that might compel some people to doubt this statement.

The first was fear that, with some separation intervening, the Trinity might be one thing and the one who is said to be one of the Trinity another, just as the Father is one and the Son another when the Son is said to be from the Father; and just as a city is one thing and a man who is said to be from the city another.

Yet although the Father is Father by having a Son, by the name “Father” itself he shows that he is not the Son. Therefore, when the Son is said to be from the Father, the Father is indicated as one and the Son as another.

A city is a multitude of human beings, not a human being; therefore, when someone is said to be from a city, he is found to be one thing and the city another.

But the Trinity is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore you can confidently say: “The Son is one of the Trinity.” There cannot be one Son and another Trinity, because without the Son there is no Trinity.

The second reason for doubt seems to arise among those unwilling to say that one of the Trinity suffered, lest the substance of divinity appear to become passible. But this is so impossible to Catholic ears and minds that to suspect it appears more a matter of malice than of caution—especially since, when one of the Trinity is said to have suffered, and the Trinity signifies three persons, anyone can easily see that one of the Trinity is proclaimed to have suffered on account of the one person of the impassible Word and the passible flesh.

The third reason for doubt is that, when we say “one of the Trinity suffered,” an extremely exacting questioner may say: “Which one?” And when we answer, “The Son,” he may again say: “Then if the Son is one of the Trinity, or is one of the Trinity, is the Trinity a Trinity of sons, or is the Son a son of the Trinity?”

When we answer, “God,” he may say: “How can anyone be one God of the Trinity, when there is no one God except the Trinity?”

This doubt is easily met if we consider what the Trinity is. For the Trinity—as must often be said—is a Trinity of persons. What, then, is the Trinity except three persons? And what are the three persons except the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

In this Trinity, therefore, you find neither three Fathers, nor three Sons, nor three Holy Spirits [Note: The wording appears to call for the reading “three Fathers,” as well as the “three Sons” and “three Holy Spirits” that immediately follow at Col. 0906D.]

Therefore you can confidently say, “One Son of the Trinity,” because there is only one Son in the Trinity.

By signifying his person, we say that one of the Trinity suffered, because he alone is rightly believed to have suffered: the one who, being truly and properly God, truly and properly became man, so that blessed Mary may rightly be believed truly and properly to be the Mother of God.

For from Mary, ever-virgin, neither divinity could be born without humanity, nor humanity without divinity.

### 17

Anyone who thinks that a mother would become consubstantial with the divinity is needlessly alarmed if Mary was truly and properly the mother of God. For certainly, because the one who is born is always truly and properly consubstantial with the one who gives birth, God received from her that by which he would become consubstantial with her, and thus deigned to be born from her. Therefore, just as truly as properly, Mary bore the Son’s divinity—but incarnate. For mortal human nature could not give birth to the eternal divinity without flesh. What, then, does “she properly bore” mean? She manifestly bore him, as signs and miracles testify that the one born from a human being is God. What does “she properly bore” mean? She herself supplied him with the material of flesh according to which he was generated—indeed through the activity of the Holy Spirit, yet from her own womb—and therefore she also properly bore the one who had to be born in this manner, because she bore him in human nature, which she unquestionably bore properly.

But whoever thinks or says that two substances could in no way be generated from one substance speaks truly, if he understands them to have been generated separately. But in that great and wondrous mystery which was manifested in the flesh, the divine substance was properly born according to the human substance, because it was not born separately, nor did the divinity unite to itself a humanity that had been properly born; rather, by uniting it to itself, it was itself properly born.

I shall state this still more plainly, according to the capacity of my weakness, if God removes from the light of this discussion the darkness of falsehood. The pure divinity was properly born from the Father; the same divinity, incarnate, was properly born from the mother. The difference between the two generations of the one Son of God is this: in the divine generation there was no humanity; in the human generation, the divinity was united to the humanity that was properly being born.

For if I say, or wish to say, “Mary ever-virgin properly bore the humanity, but did not properly bear the divinity,” she will seem in some sense to have borne a mere human being—whom she in no way bore in that manner, since she properly bore the Word made flesh. Therefore, rightly, as I think, we say and confess: “Mary is truly the mother of Christ God,” so that there may be no suspicion of a phantom. We also rightly confess: “Mary is properly the mother of Christ God,” so that it may in no way be thought that she conceived and bore a mere human being who would later, on account of the merits of good works, be advanced into God, or who would begin to be called or become God when the Son of God came upon him; rather, she is believed to have conceived and borne God—without beginning—made human from a definite beginning.

Another suitable way can plainly be found in which this statement may be made without scandal, if each person says it in this way: “Mary is properly the mother of Christ God,” so that this singular benefit of heavenly operation may not seem common to her with the others. For when the Savior himself was told by those announcing to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you,” he said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward the disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (Matthew 12:47–50).

Therefore, everyone who does the will of his Father is his mother. But Mary is properly his mother for this reason: by being born from her according to the flesh, he became her son. Many God-fearing women give birth to Christ God in their minds, not in the flesh; but Mary alone also gave birth to Christ God in the flesh. Therefore she alone is properly the mother of God, because no other woman is the mother of God in this manner.

When the blessed Apostle was writing to the Romans, he said: “If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32). Let someone tell me, then, whether the proper Son of God the Father is himself the proper son of the Virgin mother, or whether perhaps Mary did not have a proper son whom God has as his proper Son. But Mary too has a proper son, because she gave birth to him and did not adopt him; and she has as her proper son the one whom God has as his proper Son, because the catholic faith never proclaims two sons.

It therefore remains that, if he is God’s proper Son, he is also the Virgin mother’s proper son, and she properly bore him. Otherwise, if she did not properly bear him, he is not a proper son either. But he is a proper son; therefore she properly bore him—yet according to his humanity, according to which God could be born.

### 18

Now, at the conclusion of this work, it remains to provide, concerning the same two propositions over which a lengthy dispute has arisen among the contending brothers, a certain rule of faith, so that no ambiguity may seem to remain even to those inclined to suspicion, and so that the simplicity of those speaking may be made clear beforehand and scandal removed from those hearing them.

Therefore, anyone intending to say that one of the Trinity suffered should first assert that the almighty God is one substance and three persons. Of these, one person—that is, the Son—while remaining God, became human, was born, and suffered; neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was likewise incarnate, although the whole Trinity carried out the work of our redemption.

Let him confess that the Son suffered in such a way that the believer understands that he could not suffer in the very substance by which he is God and, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, but in that substance which he assumed from his mother without the Father and the Holy Spirit. Yet the faithful may rightly say that the Son’s divinity suffered, because the flesh that suffered belongs to him and pertains to his person, which is not believed to be shared by him with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

When he has understood both that the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, suffered and that he was not made passible in the divinity itself, but suffered in the humanity, which was passible, let him nevertheless confess that this one Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, has two natures, or substances. After he has explained these matters more fully, according to the measure of his intelligence or eloquence, let him profess that in all things he follows the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and the letter of Pope Leo.

Let him add that through the incarnation of the Son of God the Trinity did not increase, nor did a fourth person join the Trinity, because in Christ the very same person remained uniquely both of the divinity and of the humanity. Nestorius denies this by introducing two sons; therefore, rightly, the faithful Catholic tongue, answering his followers and removing the notion of a quaternity, says that one of the Trinity suffered—while indicating that, according to his divinity, he is one of the Trinity, but according to his humanity he suffered.

Therefore, anyone intending to say that Christ is one of the Trinity should first state what we have explained, especially when speaking to those who contradict or hold suspicious opinions; and no one builds up another person who thinks that such statements are instructing him in a bad sense. I do not want a preacher of the Word of God to be satisfied merely with the testimony of his own conscience. Let him try to bring to the hearts of others what he rightly and faithfully believes; let neither laziness nor pride hold him back, as though he were repeating something doubtful, until it is entirely free from ambiguity. Let him be as verbose as necessity requires, provided that he scandalize no one by obscure brevity.

Likewise, anyone intending to say that blessed Mary truly and properly bore God should first confess all the foregoing: the divinity of the Son of God, already born from the Father, could neither be born nor properly be born unless it had assumed the flesh of our race and the substance of a rational soul—that is, a complete human being. Nor was a beginning given to the divinity through temporal birth; rather, it was given to the flesh, whose beginning, or conception, was nothing other than the assumption of divinity.

Let him first also confess that the things belonging to the divinity cannot be separated from the humanity, nor the things belonging to the humanity from the divinity of Christ; but whether something has been said, done, or endured according to his divinity or according to his humanity, it is common to both his substances.

Because of the one person—a point which it is often no burden to repeat—which the preacher of right faith proclaims, although he knows that according to his humanity the divinity was properly born from the mother’s womb, he confidently says: “Mary properly bore God”—the one who is believed to be human in such a way that he is not denied to be God.

But the person who hesitates to state these propositions, if he hears all the things that commonly lie hidden under heretical meaning refuted in clear and unequivocal words, should lay aside suspicion and cease contention. From now on, accepting that one of the Trinity suffered, or that Mary is properly the mother of God, in the sense in which Catholics say it—even if heretics strive to affirm it in another sense—let him lend a receptive ear to orthodox teachers.

## LETTER IV. TO EUGIPPIUS THE PRESBYTER  
### On the Essence of the Trinity and the Two Natures of Christ

#### 1

Ferrandus the insignificant sends greetings in the Lord to his most blessed brother, Eugippius the presbyter.

Dearest brother, consider how much force the question recently proposed by the Arian count possesses. But first let us deliberate over the propositions or doctrines by which Arians and Catholics differ among themselves.

The Arians wish to proclaim the Trinity as undivided, just as the Scriptures proclaim one God. Catholics, however, hearing with saving understanding the precepts of the Law—“Hear, Israel: your God, the Lord, is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4)—lest they seem, under the religion of one God, to exclude faith in the Trinity, proclaim three persons of one substance and simply confess the Trinity itself to be one God. They understand the saying, “Hear, Israel: your God, the Lord, is one God,” as wisely spoken concerning the whole holy Trinity.

The Arians proclaim three substances of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore they divide their power, avoid unity, diminish their immensity, and, through their errors, subject the lesser Son to the greater Father; they also say that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son.

Catholics, on the contrary, lest they seem to introduce three gods among the nations, confess that God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit possess one honor, glory, greatness, eternity, divinity, equality, and essence. Desiring to place no one before another, they nevertheless understand that the Son was born from the Father and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

#### 2

If you wish to ask the Arians from where the Son comes, they are afraid to say, “from the essence of the Father,” lest the one who begets and the one begotten be proved to have one divinity and equality be confirmed. Again, they are afraid to profess that the Son was born from nothing, lest the Creator, by receiving an origin like that of creatures, be deprived of the privilege of the Only-Begotten and lose the glory of the creator.

On the other hand, they are much more afraid to assert that the Son was born from elsewhere—that is, from some underlying matter—lest anything seem to have existed before him, through whom all things were made.

To such errors Catholics respond: “Believe that he was born from the essence of the Father. If you deny this, say from where he is.” The Arians also say that the Son is lesser, because they deny that he is equal. Catholics, however, say that he is equal according to his divinity, but lesser according to his humanity.

His equality according to his divinity has no beginning; nevertheless, neither the equality appropriate to divinity nor the abasement corresponding to the flesh has an end. Therefore, whether he is called lesser according to the flesh and equal according to the divinity, he is the same and one Christ, truly the Son of God and truly the son of man.

For, remaining equal, he became lesser; having become lesser, he remained equal. Therefore he is wholly lesser and wholly equal, because both natures are preserved in him: the nature he had and the nature he assumed from his mother. Otherwise, if there existed in Christ only one person and one nature, one Christ could not be called both lesser and equal to the one Father.

#### 3

We also say of Christ that Christ is truly one. Yet whenever wise minds hear, “Christ is one,” they ought to consider in what way he is one: whether by possessing one person or one nature.

If he cannot be said to possess one nature, since we say that he assumed another, he can nevertheless be said to possess one person. For that person, always remaining the person of a nature that always remains, afterward voluntarily assumed such a wondrous nature without a person that, by receiving into its unity the human substance that did not have a subsisting and abiding person, it made that substance belong to itself. Thus that humanity became divine: from the moment it began to exist, it began to have the person of God; that divinity became human because it truly wished to unite human nature to itself in the unity of its person.

#### 4

We therefore say: “Christ is one, God is one, and he is the son of man”—that is, there is one person of Christ, God and man. Yet we do not say that there is one nature of Christ, God and man.

We agree with the Apostle, who wishes to establish the unity of the person: “For in what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, it was for your sake in the person of Christ,” he says to the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 2:10). Would he not have said “persons” more appropriately if he wished to signify two substances in Christ?

Similarly, clearly distinguishing the substances, he says elsewhere: “Although he was crucified through weakness, he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4). Was it not the same one who was crucified who lives? Yet the one who was crucified through weakness lives through the power of God.

Therefore, to commend and exalt the one person, Christ is proclaimed as one in such a way that sometimes one of his natures, either human or divine, is mentioned, while both are nevertheless understood. For unity is present, so that whoever names one signifies both.

For this reason the Apostle touches only upon the humanity when he says to Timothy: “There is one God, one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Of the divinity he says to the Corinthians: “For although there are those who are called gods—for indeed there are many—yet for us there is one God, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:5).

[The remainder is missing.]

## LETTER V. TO SEVERUS THE SCHOLASTIC OF CONSTANTINOPLE  
### That Our Lord Jesus Christ Is One of the Holy and Undivided Trinity

#### 1

You are trying to impose upon me the task of great men, because you are pleased to hear what I think concerning those who deny that our God Jesus is one of the holy and undivided Trinity. But this, I confess, my smallness of intellect either scarcely can undertake or does not dare undertake at all.

For who am I, or what sort of person am I, that I should be permitted to issue a settled judgment on doubtful matters and, by the authority of a choice, determine in more recent times whether new statements ought to be accepted? Would that God grant me to be content with the simple faith which the catholic Church teaches throughout the world, so that, if possible, during the whole of this miserable life, devoting myself to prayer and fasting, I might lament with my insignificant brothers the many and serious sins which I either already grieve to have committed or am still compelled to commit because of the frailty of the flesh!

Then I shall consider myself blessed, when, placed in the silence of the monastery, I sing at intervals that verse of the psalm: “I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue” (Psalm 38:1).

Let those to whom the honor of the priesthood grants the authority to teach speak and preach; we are ready to learn, but we do not presume to teach others. Therefore, most prudent man, if you desire to hear anything true, ask above all the bishop of the apostolic see, whose sound doctrine is established by the judgment of truth and supported by the protection of authority.

Ask also the many bishops throughout the various regions of the earth whose knowledge of heavenly commandments, divinely inspired, has gathered for them a great reputation together with reverence. Without doubt, these men are both capable of disputation and prepared by frequent practice to persuade. You will not be blamed if, while still uncertain, you consult them; and you will be praised if, once truly instructed, you follow them.

From me, however, seek what charity requires in such a way that you do not persuade me to incur the guilt of rashness.

**Note:** [Column 0911D] “Or should it read *laudaberis* (‘you will be praised’)? Immediately afterward, perhaps *doctos* (‘the learned’).]

#### 2

For me, the manifest statement of blessed Peter is sufficient; it speaks generally to all the faithful: “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the faith and hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15). When someone asks how we believe, we should immediately answer: We believe in one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the Father begotten by no one, the Son the Only-Begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit eternally proceeding from the unbegotten Father and the Only-Begotten Son.

Thus, although we have called this blessed Trinity one God, the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit; the Son is never the Father or the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit is at no time the Father or the Son. Rather, the Father is the Father of the Son alone; the Son is the Son of the Father alone; and the Holy Spirit is jointly the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

These three together are naturally one God, because they have one substance insofar as there is one God; they are three persons, because there are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and, because there is one God, they work all things together inseparably. Yet, because there are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we confess that certain properties belong peculiarly to each: begetting to the Father alone, being born to the Son alone, and proceeding from both to the Holy Spirit alone.

Thus we confess that the Father alone spoke from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17); that the Son alone was born from the Virgin and baptized by John in the river Jordan; and that the Holy Spirit alone descended in the form of a dove.

Long ago the truth refuted those heretics who wished to call the Trinity one God in such a way that the one whom they confessed as Father they imagined to be the Son himself and the Holy Spirit himself. According to them, the one who, while remaining in heaven, was the Father of the whole creation became the Son when he was extended into the Virgin and was born among human beings; and then, when the mystery of the human dispensation had been completed, he came upon the apostles in tongues of fire and was called the Holy Spirit. Compelled by this error, they believed not the Son of God the Father but the Father himself to have been crucified. Hence antiquity shows that they were also called Patripassians.

Thus Sabellius, because of the one substance, refused to acknowledge three persons, while Arius, conversely, because of the three persons, wished to proclaim three substances. The Apostolic Church, counting three persons against Sabellius but vindicating one substance or essence against Arius, remembers that it was told: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4). This one God is not solitary but is the Trinity—namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Having made this confession, we go on to unfold with reverent devotion the great and wondrous mystery of piety—“which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). For the redemption of the human race, we believe that he assumed human nature, so that the one who remained and remains God, the Only-Begotten, in the perfect Trinity, himself became from Mary the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). The same one whom God the Father had begotten before all ages was begotten by a human mother after the fullness of time had come.

#### 3

Our faith principally proclaims Christ the Son of God as the son of man in such a way that it calls him one Son of God and man. It does not revere one Christ in the divinity and another in the humanity, but the one who is Christ in the divinity is himself Christ in the humanity.

For this reason God became human: there is not one God and another human being, but the one who is God is wholly the same as the human being; and for this reason the one who is human is also God—Jesus Christ our Lord.

Remaining God the Son, one person within the Trinity, he came to the Virgin. He did not assume another person from her, but assumed another nature into the unity of his person in such a way that the person who had always existed assumed the nature of flesh, and that one person of Christ had two natures.

Nor ought we to doubt how human nature is believed to have had the person of the Word of God from its very beginning. We know that God did not assume a human being already formed, conceived, or beginning to live by some life of its own in its mother’s womb. Rather, before Mary conceived anything at all, before any cause of a human being formed or to be formed existed, God, wishing to become human, entered the palace of the virgin womb. By the power of his divinity he bestowed the gift of fertility and assumed from her, whom he wished to have as his mother, true flesh of our race.

By that assumption he was conceived and born. He did not assume another person, since he did not find a prepared human being; rather, he received human nature, in which God himself would be born as a human being. Thus human nature had a person from the moment it was created—but one person with God, who was created by assuming it.

Therefore, whoever you are who contradict this faith, show me at some point in Christ a humanity without divinity, and then I shall concede that the human nature alone also had its own proper person. But because the divinity of the Word of God existed without humanity, whereas humanity never existed without divinity, the divine nature had a person, which it granted to human nature when it assumed it.

Thus both the assuming nature and the assumed nature, united ineffably without any confusion, are believed to belong to one person: the humanity belongs to the one whose divinity it is, and the divinity belongs to the one whose humanity it is. Although the divine nature is one thing and the human nature another, there is not one Christ whose nature is divine and another Christ whose nature is human. Rather, the same one Christ possesses both human and divine nature.

For the Word of God did not dwell in Christ as it dwelt in the prophets; rather, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). This is the Lord Jesus Christ.

Finally, although Holy Scripture often speaks many things from the person of God through the prophets, it never said of any prophet that he was God over all. Of Christ, however, the Apostle boldly proclaims: “From them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5).

For if anyone denies that Christ, God and man, has one person, he proclaims two Christs. And if there are two Christs to be adored or worshiped, he worships not a Trinity but a quaternity.

If, again, anyone says that Christ has one nature, and although he does not dare deny that he is from two, nevertheless fears or hesitates to confess him in two substances, that person asserts either the abolition of one nature or the confusion of both. For unless he has simultaneously removed one from the two or confused both, he will have no basis for proclaiming one nature.

#### 4

Briefly refuting these positions by the testimonies of Scripture, so that the measure of the letter may be maintained, let us first consider the words of our Savior. In handing down the fixed rule of divine baptism, he was saying to his apostles [editorial note: read “he said”]: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

I ask those who think that Christ does not have one person: when the Son is named in baptism, if there is not one person of God and man, which person is being named? If they say, “the person of the Son of God,” and do not confess that the one who is the Son of God is also the son of man, then all the grace of the mediator is removed from the sacrament of regeneration.

For, as the Apostle says, “There is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). And if—which God forbid—when the Son is named in baptism only the person of the Son of God is named, and the person of the Son of God who is man is not mentioned, then the mediator is not named.

And how is the Father reconciled without a mediator? Or, if perhaps he is not reconciled, why is baptism given? But if he is reconciled, he is reconciled through a mediator. If he is reconciled through a mediator, this mediator is neither God alone nor man alone, but God and man: he unites humanity, possessing in one and the same person divinity with God and humanity with human beings, and for this reason he is the mediator.

For if one is God and another is human— that is, if Christ God has one person and Christ man another—then the person of Christ who possesses divinity with God is not our mediator, because he does not possess humanity with us; nor is the person of the son of man who possesses humanity with us our mediator, because he does not possess divinity with God.

Therefore, if when we are baptized we name only the person who possesses divinity with God, how are we reconciled without a mediator? It follows that, if we wish to name the mediator when the Son is named in baptism, we must not divide the Son. Rather, confessing that he is the God whom we confess to be human, we must truly confound those who deny the one person.

Otherwise, how will it be true that “whoever of us has been baptized in Christ has been baptized into his death” (Romans 6:3), if, when we name the Son in baptism, we name not one person of God and man but only the person of the Son of God, without the person of the son of man? If there had truly been two persons, the person of the son of man ought to have been mentioned in order to commemorate Christ’s death, into which the Apostle teaches us that we are baptized. For Christ could die according to his humanity.

But if the person who strives to deny one person in Christ asserts that, so as not to exclude the mystery of the incarnation from baptism, when the Son is named the person of the son of man is named, then we are not baptizing in the united name of the Trinity. For the Trinity cannot be named where God the Son of God is not named, if only the person of the son of man is emphasized.

#### 5

Therefore, so that the whole Trinity may be named in baptism, the grace of the mediator may not be silenced, and the remembrance of Christ’s death may be renewed, let it be truly acknowledged that Christ has one person. Thus, when the Son is named in baptism, it is understood that this one person is named—the person of whom Paul, the chosen vessel, also says: “For I too, whatever I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, did so for your sake in the person of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:10).

This person, possessing everything that belongs to God and everything that belongs to man, truly says what the evangelist John records: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

For how has no one ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, if Christ is not one person—the one who descended and ascended? If he is thought to have two persons, will there not unquestionably be one assuming person and another assumed person; one who was born from God the Father and another who was united to the Son of God when he wished to become incarnate?

If this is so, the assuming person descended so that the assumed person might ascend, and the statement “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” will already be false. The person of the Son of God descended, and the person of the human being ascended; thus the one who descended did not ascend.

The necessity of disputing compelled us to say this according to the wickedness of the false understanding of those who divide Christ. In reality, no one has truly ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven because the person who ascends and descends is one: according to the nature of his divinity, he descended by merciful condescension; according to the nature of his humanity, he ascended with the trophy of immortality.

The Teacher of the nations bears witness to this, saying plainly: “The one who descended is himself also the one who ascended” (Ephesians 4:10)—himself, plainly, not another. And if he is not another, then there is altogether one, the same, and inseparable person, of whom it is rightly said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John 3:13). For the sake of impressing this upon sluggish minds, it would most rightly be followed by the words: “the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

Here I ask: if there is not one person of God and man, how does he say, “the Son of Man who is in heaven,” when he was still speaking in the world, before he had suffered? How, I ask, how is the son of man in heaven before the death of the cross, before the glory of the resurrection, before the triumph of the ascension, unless he was joined in the unity of person to the Son of God, who never departed from heaven?

Therefore the son of man is in heaven because the Son of God is always there—the one who became the son of man.

It is astonishing—indeed, astonishing—unless it is understood. The Lord says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven.” And as though someone were asking, “Who is this?” he immediately and without hesitation replies: “The Son of Man who is in heaven.”

O Lord Jesus, in the beginning the Word, and the Word with God, and God the Word: before you descended, before you became flesh and dwelt among us, were you not God alone, consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and one person within the Trinity?

How, then, do you now say: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven,” and immediately, indicating the person who descended, continue: “the Son of Man who is in heaven”?

How did the son of man descend before you became the son of man? It is because you, who were from the beginning the Son of God, you, the Only-Begotten God, you, one person within the Trinity, became the son of man. And you became the son of man in such a way that your person was not one person and the person of the son of man another.

#### 6

This one person is finally commended when Christ asks the Pharisees: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” (Matthew 22:42). When they answer, “David’s,” Jesus says: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies beneath your feet’?” (Psalm 109:1).

David calls him Lord; how, then, is he his son? There the Pharisees were indeed convicted and humbled, but we too, if we inquire devoutly, have been instructed.

For why is he the son of David and the Lord of David, unless the Lord of David himself became the son of David? Indeed, if Christ were not one person, he could not be both the son of David and the Lord of David. But he is the son of David and the Lord of David because the person whom he possesses as Lord of David is the same person whom he possesses as son of David.

This one person said to Philip, who asked: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us”: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?” (John 14:8–9).

Since Philip saw with his bodily eyes only a human being who was speaking, he heard these words spoken to him by a human mouth: “Whoever sees me sees the Father.” Why this, unless the very human being is God, so that whoever sees him sees the Father?

Otherwise, if there were not one person of God and man, he would not say, “Whoever sees me”—already seen in the flesh, yet wishing to be seen still in his divinity—but would instead say: “Whoever sees my God sees the person of my God.”

What does it mean to say to one who sees him, “Whoever sees me,” except: “I am the one who is seen; I am the one who is not seen”? And whoever now sees me outwardly in the flesh, if he sees inwardly in the spirit, sees not another but me. Whoever sees me in this way also sees the Father.

And immediately afterward he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (ibid., 10). When would mortal flesh say, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” unless, because of the unity of person, he himself were the immortal God who was destined to be crucified as mortal man?

Hear him still further invoking the truth of the one person in many ways.
