When he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” (Matthew 16:13), and after the many and varied opinions of the people—some thinking Christ God, the Lord of the prophets, to be Elijah, others Jeremiah, others John the Baptist, and others one of the prophets—the Lord wished to distinguish himself from his servants and to impress upon those who saw him that he was one Christ. He said: “But who do you say that I am?” (ibid., 15).

Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16).

If there had not been one person of the Son of God and the son of man, how could blessed Peter, when Christ called himself the son of man, have added, as though contradicting him: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God”? Christ says, “me, the son of man”; Peter says, “You are the Son of the living God.”

If Christ’s person is not one, Peter is asked about one and confesses another. He is asked, “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” and he answers, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.”

But blessed Peter would never have deserved to be praised in his Master’s words unless he confessed the very one about whom he was questioned. The one who said to him, “You,” and from whom he had heard, “me,” is himself the son of man who is the Son of the living God.

Writing to the Hebrews, Paul likewise shows that he is always one person when he says: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). By repeating “he himself” once, he wished it to be understood three times, as though he were saying: “Jesus Christ himself yesterday, himself today, himself also forever.”

“Yesterday”: before he received flesh. “Today”: when, according to the prophecy of the prophet Jeremiah, it was said:

“This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him. He discovered the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36, 38).

Whether now, when he sits at the right hand of the Father forever, or when he is to come to judge the living and the dead—as the whole Church confesses in the Creed—he is always himself, never another.

### 7

For by assuming flesh he united the natures; he did not duplicate the person. He plainly united the natures, which remained without confusion and will remain so forever. He united them in such a way that neither was the divinity changed into humanity, nor was the humanity absorbed by the divinity; rather, each nature was preserved unharmed, exercised its own functions, was recognized by its own works, and was called by its own names, yet they were not distinguished as separate persons.

For the two substances—namely, the divine and the human—were not united in such a way that one substance came into being, but so that there might be one person, and that from them there might always exist one Christ. Far be it from us, while truth compels us to confess one person, to dare to deny two natures.

For if the Creator became a creature, if the Word became flesh, if God was found in appearance as a man, then neither could the Creator be created, nor the Word become flesh, nor God be man without the assumption of another nature. And if another nature was assumed, there are certainly two natures, not one.

But if it is asserted that one was made from two, it must first be stated what that one is that was made. Although it is scarcely possible for one thing to be made from two substances without either their confusion or the abolition of one of them, nevertheless, whenever one thing is made from two, a new thing comes into being; and if a new thing comes into being, it necessarily takes a new name of nature by existing newly.

For example, in us the nature of the soul is one, and that of the body another: the former spiritual, the latter earthly; the former invisible, the latter visible. And because one nature has been made from these two, it has acquired a new name, so that it is called “man.” The soul is named separately, and the body separately; neither can the soul be called the body, nor the body the soul. But body and soul together are rightly called “man.”

The nature of the soul is not the nature of the body, nor is the nature of the body the nature of the soul; but that which consists together of the nature of body and soul is one human nature.

Therefore, if it is maintained that the divine nature and the human nature have made one nature, let it also be discovered what nature that is—one that can be called neither divine nor human, but which, being new, is likewise called by a new name. Let no evasive disputant and contentious defender of one nature, at this point in the argument, give the nature which he fabricates as one from two any new name and answer that it is called “Christ,” because “Christ” is the name of an office, not of a nature.

For “Christ” comes from anointing; and anointing appears to be an indication of a temporal dispensation, not a designation of substance. Let the man who believes that one nature was made from two—this I say repeatedly—state what that one nature is. For this one can be called neither divine nor human, but by some other name. If someone should discover that name, the defender of one nature will at least have a tolerable case.

I, however, greatly fear confidently adopting the profession of one nature. For if Christ has one nature, it will either be wholly equal to the Father or wholly less than the Father. If wholly equal, in respect of what does he say, “The Father is greater than I” (John XVI, 28)? If wholly less, in respect of what does he say, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30)?

Either it will be impassible or passible. If impassible, in respect of what is Christ said to have suffered, died, and been crucified? If passible, then either Christ will no longer have one nature with the Father, so that God the Father is separated from his sufferings; or, if this one nature which he has in common with the Father is passible, the Father too will be passible, and the Patripassians will then boast that they are not catholic Christians but heretics.

I add still further: if Christ has one nature, it is asserted to be either invisible or visible. If invisible, what did those who crucified him see? What did the apostles see, even to the point of touching him? What did the angels promise would be seen when they said, “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I, 11)?

But if it is visible, what did he intend to manifest to his beloved in the future when he said, “And I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John XIV, 21), since he had already been manifested according to the flesh? Or why does the Gospel cry out in this way: “No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matthew XI, 27)? For undoubtedly we know what we see; and no one can say that one is not subject to knowledge whom he has confessed to be subject to sight.

### 8

It further troubles me that, if Christ has one nature, it is either spread everywhere or is local. If it is spread everywhere, why do we recite the words of the Creed in this way: “On the third day he rose from the dead, he ascended into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father”? If the nature of Christ is spread everywhere, how did he ascend into heaven? If it is spread everywhere, how is it specifically said of it, “He sits at the right hand of the Father”?

But if it is local, then certainly the wisdom of God, which is Christ (I Corinthians I, 24), “reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom VIII, 1). And what of the fact that, when departing from his disciples according to the presence of the flesh, he said, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XVIII, 1)?

Let us therefore be ashamed to deny two natures, so that in the one Christ it may be apparent which nature is equal to the Father, which less than the Father; which passible, which impassible; which visible, which invisible; which spread everywhere, which local. Yet let Christ be one—both equal and less, both impassible and passible, both invisible and visible, both spread everywhere and local: wholly equal, but not wholly [equal]; wholly less, but not wholly [less]; wholly invisible, impassible, and spread everywhere, but not wholly so.

Now, if you ask what “the whole Christ” is, I answer: the Word of God, the rational soul, and the flesh. For whether you say “the Word,” he is the whole Christ, but not the whole [of Christ], unless you add the rational soul and the body. Whether you say “the rational soul,” he is the whole Christ, but not the whole [of Christ], unless you add the Word and the flesh. Whether you say “the flesh,” he is the whole Christ, but not the whole [of Christ], unless you add the Word and the rational soul.

The whole Christ, therefore, is everywhere according to the Word, but the whole [Christ] is not everywhere, because the rational soul and the flesh, with which he is the whole [Christ], are not everywhere.

The whole Christ was among the dead according to the rational soul, but not the whole [Christ], because the flesh, with which he is the whole [Christ], was not there. The whole Christ was in the tomb according to the flesh, but not the whole [Christ], because the rational soul, with which he is the whole [Christ], was not there. Yet the Word of God was both with his soul among the dead and with his flesh in the tomb, because, being naturally spread everywhere, he was never absent from either his soul or his flesh.

Thus, whether the Word, the rational soul, or the flesh is signified, the whole Christ is signified, but not the whole [of Christ]. For he will not be the whole [Christ] unless the Word, the rational soul, and the flesh are together.

Why, however, is the Word the whole Christ, and the rational soul the whole Christ, and the flesh the whole Christ, except because there is one person of the Word, the rational soul, and the flesh? And again, why is the Word without the rational soul and the flesh not the whole Christ, or the rational soul and the flesh without the Word not the whole Christ, except because the nature of the Word is one, and the nature of the rational soul and flesh another—the former divine, the latter human?

The one person of Christ, however, which appears to unite two substances, divine and human—that is, simple and composite—is not composite, but simple in each and simple in both. It is as simple as it was before, in its unity, it assumed human nature, so that thereafter it might possess two substances: one, as we have said, simple, and the other composite.

### 9

But why should we linger any longer? This is my faith concerning the incarnation of Christ: I confess that Christ has one person in and from two substances. Nor does it trouble me how one person of Christ could have two natures, when we see that the one substance of divinity has three persons.

For if someone should say to me, “Show me in Christ, according to the number of natures, the number of persons,” I shall answer fearlessly: “You, too, show me in the Godhead, according to the number of persons, the number of natures.” For if there can be no nature without a person, neither can there be a person without a nature.

But if it is said that in the Trinity all three persons have one nature, because that one nature belongs to all three persons, then I shall likewise say that in Christ both natures have one person, because that which signifies the existence of each is also what distinguishes one from another.

Accordingly, someone might rightly appear as a preacher of two persons in Christ if that God had not been man, or that man had not been God, with his person distinguishing one from the other. For, according to the meaning of the definition given above, an incommunicable property would so signify one Christ as existing as the person of divinity that it would separate him from the other who was to be believed to exist in humanity.

Yet far be this from the minds of the faithful; let it be far from Christian discussions.

Therefore, if those whom he asserts deny that our Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy and undivided Trinity confess that he is one from the holy and undivided Trinity, If they confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is God, the Son of God, made the son of man; and therefore, when the Lord Jesus Christ is named, not a mere man but a divine and human substance is named; if they confess that the Trinity is God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and that this Son, without whom the Trinity never was and through whose assumption of flesh the Trinity remained the Trinity; if, as the Trinity always is, they understand that from the beginning of his incarnation he himself is the Lord Jesus Christ—what concern is that of ours, whatever words they may use to preach the right faith?

Rather, I think we must see and consider more carefully why some people deny, with excessive caution, that the Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy and undivided Trinity.

For, in my opinion, the proposition is made suspect in three ways.

The first way is lest the Lord Jesus Christ be thought to be proclaimed one of the holy and undivided Trinity in such a manner that he is one, while the Trinity of which he is said to be one is another. This would be like our believing that the Son is from the Father: plainly, the Son is one, and the Father from whom the Son is is another. Or, for example, when we indicate that someone belongs to this or that city, he is so distinct from the city that the city remains as it was with him even without him, although he alone cannot be called a city.

This interpretation serves especially those who wish to introduce a fourth person into the Trinity.

### 10

There is a second way. Perhaps the Lord Jesus Christ is deceitfully declared to be one of the holy and undivided Trinity for this reason: so that not his humanity—which, by being assumed into the unity of his person, began to be called the Lord Jesus Christ—but his divinity, on account of which he is asserted to be one of the holy and undivided Trinity, may be proclaimed passible whenever it is said that the Lord Jesus suffered for the salvation of human beings.

This interpretation either helps the Arians to diminish the divinity of the Son, or introduces the opinion that he has only one nature, while fearing to incur suspicion of two persons.

There is still a third way: lest, when we affirm that the Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy and undivided Trinity, we immediately be asked, “One what?”

**Note:** [Col. 0919D] Perhaps *affirming* (*affirmantibus*) should be read; I change nothing, since at the beginning of §11 the author shortly uses the word *firmare* (“to affirm”).

For example, if I wish to say, “Gabriel is one of the angels of God,” and, being asked, “One what?” I answer, “An angel,” because I have already mentioned all those angels. Or again, if I say similarly that the Ephesian Church is one of the seven churches to which the apostle John writes, and, being asked, “One what?” I immediately answer, “A church,” because I have already mentioned those seven churches.

Likewise, if I declare that three men have come to some place or departed from another, when I have said, “One of these came to me,” and am asked, “One what?” I immediately answer, “A man,” because I have mentioned those three men.

But when we say that the Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy and undivided Trinity, and are asked, “One what?” we cannot say, “One God,” because that Trinity is not a trinity of gods. Nor does reason permit us to say, “The Lord Jesus Christ is one God of the holy and undivided Trinity”; rather, we say, “The whole Trinity is one God.”

Similarly, when we say that the Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy and undivided Trinity, and are asked, “One what?” we cannot answer, “The Son,” because that Trinity is not a trinity of sons; there is one Son in the Trinity.

And if it is said that the phrase “The Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy and undivided Trinity” is equivalent to saying “one person,” this is said quite correctly—provided that, if this is the intended meaning, the phrase “one person” is added, lest it cause scandal to those who understand little or suspect wrongly.

**Note:** [Col. 0920D] *Potius* (“rather”) seems to be missing here.

In what ways, therefore, this proposition may be judged by some to be refuted or avoided, I have stated simply. For the rest, I have contradicted neither those who wish to say this nor those who do not, since I have already declared at the beginning of this letter that nothing certain can be defined by me.

### 11

But if a definite report has reached us—for I hesitate to affirm this because, since nothing has been indicated about it in your letters, I reasonably suppose that it has not—then I wonder how those who are said to deny that our Lord Jesus Christ is one of the holy and undivided Trinity are said to confess that he is one from the holy and undivided Trinity.

I should like to hear what difference these propositions are intended to convey. If it were permitted, I would ask them in person. I would like to speak, if the opportunity were given to enter into the discussion without a spirit of contention.

For if the Lord Jesus Christ is to be called “one from the Trinity,” he must certainly be called so on account of the unity of person, so that it may be shown that that only-begotten God himself became man. Why, then, should he not also be called “of the Trinity,” so that it may likewise be shown that he belongs to the essence of the Trinity, since, having assumed the form of a servant, he endured the insult of death?

But if he is not said to be one “of the holy and undivided Trinity,” but rather “from the holy Trinity,” in order to show that he has nothing in common in substance with the Trinity—just as we say that we are “from God,” and not “of God,” because our substance is one and God’s another—for everything that is “of” something must also necessarily be “from” that thing, but not everything that is “from” something can immediately also be “of” that same thing, as all things are from God but are not of God, whereas we rightly confess the only-begotten Son to be both of God and from God—then your prudence also sees that the Lord Jesus Christ is being proclaimed a mere man by them. And unless this interpretation is explained in some better or more suitable way, it must be judged exceedingly dangerous.

Therefore, I think we should desist from contentions. Rather, I urge that we wait and patiently bear this uncertainty until, by the authority of the universal Church, it is either declared worthy of acceptance or exposed as worthy of rejection.

For the true faith will not be preached any less if this proposition is left unmentioned, nor will it be considered any less firm if it is not strengthened by this proposition. Even if that were the case, it would nevertheless be more fitting for us to follow the apostolic words, where we are told: “Nevertheless, let us walk according to that which we have attained; and if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Philippians III, 16, 15).

This is what we have attained: to know that the Lord Jesus Christ has one person from two substances and in two substances or natures. Let us hold this, understand this, and proclaim this. And if we sometimes utter certain words less cautiously, or perhaps, through excessive concern, remain silent, as though we thought differently about something, God will reveal this also to us.

## LETTER VI. TO PELAGIUS AND ANATOLIUS, DEACONS OF THE CITY OF ROME

*In defense of the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, and consequently of the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon; against the Acephali.*

### 1

To the most blessed lords, Pelagius and Anatolius, holy brothers and fellow deacons, worthy of being reverently honored with devoted service: Ferrandus, the insignificant.

I suffered exceedingly great distress when we received your letter; the sign of my perturbation was a prolonged silence. For if you deign to consider how prompt I have always been to obey your commands, you will attribute the delay of this reply not to lesser devotion.

Why else would I have remained silent for so long unless I feared to speak before the proper time concerning the recently arisen question, while the African Churches were still silent? Nevertheless, compelled by your command, I speak simply what we believe, so that you may know that we are with you in heart, with you in faith, with you according to good hope, and with you in sincere charity. Whatever you communicate wisely, briefly, and truthfully, we believe, feel, and say the same.

### 2

I encourage the glorious ministers of the apostolic see with the apostolic words: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions which you have learned” (II Thessalonians II, 14).

It is not fitting that the deliberation of the ancient Fathers known to have taken part in the Council of Chalcedon should be blamed, their judgment retracted, or their decision changed. Otherwise, that venerable synod, which for so many years has been confirmed without any doubt among all the Churches of East and West, would suddenly lose its reverence; nor could it preserve inflexible strength in its definitions of faith if it began to be proved fragile or worthy of censure in any respect.

Whatever is established once and for all in a council and assembly of holy Fathers ought continually to retain perpetual firmness. For with what face shall we sing, “What we have heard and known, what our fathers have told us” (Psalm LXXVII, 3), if, whenever we please, we are permitted to rescind their decrees?

Through those most wise judges the Catholic Church said what the catholic Church would preserve—or rather, what it has preserved until now. Why, then, in today’s renewed debates, do we reject once again a letter which was not then rejected?

The Catholic Church is a sealed fountain; the apostle James cries out: “Does a fountain pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?” (James III, 11). If sweet water flowed from the mouths of the former priests when they issued definitions of the faith, how could it have happened that from their mouths, and not those of others, as if from their opening, there flowed in the matter of the venerable bishop Ibas not sweet water but water more bitter than gall?

I say this with fear and trembling, but I say it nonetheless: if the praiseworthy disputation of the Council of Chalcedon offered the faithful a bitter taste in any matter, then let us give the heretics the opportunity to denounce the potion of saving medicine as deadly, while we provide them the occasion, “while there is strife over words, while there is dispute over novelties, while ambiguity provides an occasion, while there is complaint about ears, while there is rivalry over parties, while agreement is difficult.”

Your Blessedness knows well that these words are not mine but belong to blessed Hilary, in the second book that he wrote to the emperor Constantius.

Consider, then, brothers, among what reefs the ship of evangelical preaching is tossed. Isaiah cries out: “Woe to those who call darkness light” (Isaiah V, 20). And we dare to assert that our fathers said darkness was light when they refused to condemn a letter favoring Nestorius, indeed when they wished even to receive it?

Will the prophetic curse, “Woe to those who call darkness light,” then be applied to our fathers? Were they not themselves like lights in the world, holding the word of life, whose faith silenced the faithless, and to whom the whole world rightly believing gave credence?

### 3

Is it said: “They believed rightly, but they received the letter of the venerable Ibas wrongly”? Were they truthful in their own confession but incautiously consented to a deceptive confession?

Who could endure the tortuous contentions of useless questions? If any part of the Council of Chalcedon is displeasing, the whole is thereby liable to displease. The most holy Paul, the chosen vessel, plainly declares: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (I Corinthians V, 6).

If, in that lump of holy definitions, even a small amount of sour admixture can be found, the whole lump will be judged harmful—or, if we moderate the force of the comparison, useless for making the bread that strengthens the human heart.

What benefit, then, was it that Nestorius and Eutyches were anathematized there? Behold, those who condemned Nestorius and Eutyches are accused of having received a letter favoring Nestorius’s blasphemies, whether ambiguous or manifest.

What then? If they admitted it unknowingly, they will appear—God forbid—to have incurred the stigma of ignorance, so that their authority is completely emptied. But if, knowing the facts, they thought one thing and declared another, they will not be free from the charge of deceit.

Those who resist their doctrines will then cry out all the more loudly in reproach:

“Behold, the synod assembled at Chalcedon, to which you unquestionably assign great weight of authority, at one and the same time condemned Nestorius and recalled Nestorius’s error, receiving a letter wholly contrary to the catholic faith—just as you have now begun to think, understanding, although late, what all those bishops refused to understand.”

Let us mourn and pray that such an error may quickly pass away when abolished, vanish when rejected, and be buried in perpetual silence.

The entire Council of Chalcedon, when it is the entire Council of Chalcedon, is true: no part of it has any fault. Whatever we know was said, done, judged, and confirmed there was accomplished by the ineffable and hidden power of the Holy Spirit.

Why do we disgrace the memory of so many righteous men by sudden contradictions, when Solomon, full of the Holy Spirit, plainly declares: “The memory of the righteous is with praises” (Proverbs X, 7)?

**Note:** [Col. 0923D] “To whom to give” (*cui dare*) seems to be the reading.

**Note:** [Col. 0923D] The Arvernensis codex reads *roboravit* (“strengthened” or “confirmed”).

### 4

What if, rising from their tombs before the God in whose presence they live and with whom they faithfully rest, those religious men should say at the final resurrection:

“Why did you reject the letter whose catholic wording we perceived, declared, and judged to be catholic, and whose judgment we confirmed by subscribing?”

Was it because the venerable Ibas criticized the holy Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian Church? Yet afterward he indicated that he had entered into communion with the holy Cyril. If he deserved blame for criticizing blessed Cyril, he deserved no small favor for restored communion.

That he blamed the chapters of Saint Cyril because, through inadequate understanding, he found them ambiguous and obscure in their wording, together with the Eastern bishops, was a matter of human weakness. That he more readily believed and most willingly consented to one who interpreted his statements correctly was wholly a matter of priestly charity, without any loss of truth.

Why should we condemn the letter in which both matters were narrated as past events through the faithful interpretations of that holy Cyril? Saint Cyril himself—Saint Cyril himself—hurried to remove the scandal of misunderstanding, not from the venerable Ibas but from many Eastern bishops, by interpreting his chapters correctly. And should we reject the letter for the sake of his injuries, when it merely explains historically what had happened?

If it is firmly maintained that the venerable bishop Ibas spoke contrary to the rule of the true faith in that letter, because of certain passages, whether ambiguous or obscure, which make this appear so, our judgment ought to be the better one, because we were able to investigate the meaning of the words from the mouth of the man who dictated the letter.

Finally, why should we think that the letter favored Nestorius when its author, in our presence, at our command, and in our hearing, did not hesitate to anathematize Nestorius with his living voice, accepting the Tome of Pope Leo and confirming with us, by subscription, his confession of the true faith?

When we hear these things, what answer shall we give to so many renowned governors and teachers of the Churches—especially when the just King has taken his seat upon the throne?

### 5

Let us beware, brothers, of the devil’s snares. If the wicked error of Nestorius is thought to lie hidden in this letter of the venerable bishop Ibas, which the Fathers received, it harms neither great nor small: for the error of Nestorius was publicly condemned at the Council of Chalcedon.

If the criticism of the most holy memory of Cyril causes scandal, so that the letter received by the Fathers should be rejected, Cyril was praised there, and greatly praised. For it is affirmed that the interpretation of his own statements removed the offense of an evil suspicion when the Eastern bishops were reconciled to his peace. In that peace all who communicated with one another likewise fell asleep, and they did not say that this letter, which reports such matters, was to be lightly condemned.

**Note:** [Col. 0924D] Perhaps the reading is “not even to be lightly condemned” (*ne leviter quidem culp[andam]*).

Rightly, then, in the presence of the religious emperor Marcian, all the priests who had begun the council of peace with peaceful minds and concluded it with definitions corresponding to ecclesiastical peace returned in fraternal peace to the places of their own flocks—without hatred, envy, or contention, concordant and unanimous, bearing common witness.

The apostolic see was there in its legates, holding primacy over the universal Church. There were the bishops of the other venerable sees, “wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” There was an immense crowd of pastors from lesser cities, governing the folds of the Lord’s flock with pastoral care.

No one there condemned anyone against the will of the others; no one absolved anyone against the will of the others. All, consenting with one another and gladly fulfilling the words of the Doctor of the Gentiles, obeyed him when he said: “I beseech you, brothers, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you” (I Corinthians I, 10).

Their judgment therefore remained, and in its stability remained wholly unchangeable, because the dignity of the priests who judged was not inferior, their number was not small, their authority was not lesser, their choice was not ignoble, their presumption was not excessive, their deliberation was not foolish, their agreement was not ordinary, their labor was not fruitless, and their conclusion was not contrary to the tranquility of the Churches.

They came to calm past contentions, cut off present ones, and even mitigate future ones. To add anything after their definitions, to change or diminish them, is nothing other than to sow new disagreements.

Let no one hasten to condemn what has been rightly deposited [or arranged]. Let no one correct what is right.

What will be firm if what the Council of Chalcedon established is called into doubt?

**Note:** [Col. 0925D] Here I restore *nihil aliud* (“nothing else”) from the Greek οὐδὲν ἕτερον.

### 6

I could here lament many more things mournfully, in the manner of a kind of tragedy; but it seems sufficient for me to cite what the Church of Justiniana Carthage, through the pen of its glorious bishop, blessed Capreolus of revered memory, reasonably determined when he wrote to the most merciful prince Theodosius:

“Nothing in divine or human actions, nothing in sacred or public affairs, can possess any firmness if posterity, after intervals of years and whatever succession of ages, presumes to amend—as though acting as an instructor—the things that have been closed by the due conclusion of a judicial sentence, as if correcting the Fathers.”

And in another letter addressed to the Council of Ephesus through the deacon Versulus:

“Whatever arises recently may require examination, so that, once proved, it may be received, or, once condemned, excluded. But if anyone admits that matters already judged should be called back for reconsideration, he will appear to doubt the faith which he himself has held until now.”

Behold, the memorable teacher of the Church of Carthage declares that not only synodal enactments but nearly all established judgments must not be called back for examination. How, then, are matters once judged now to be judged anew?

If, at that time, some accuser of the letter whose catholic wording had become clear had appealed to higher judgments, there might perhaps, according to custom, have been a place for appeal. But where would he go? Or where would he find greater judges in the Church, with the apostolic see present before him in its legates, and with that see consenting to whatever the synod defined and giving it unconquerable strength?

How, then, will a voice once taken away from those wishing to defend what they have wrongly undertaken be restored? Who, after so many and such great bishops, will be a new and suitable examiner of a matter already concluded?

From what regions or cities of the world will bishops better than the ancient bishops be assembled, and given authority to correct the judgments of their predecessors? Or with what hope will they confidently undertake to define anything, seeing the judgments of such men suddenly annulled?

How will what we are doing be pleasing to our successors, if through us they are taught to make void what they know their predecessors accomplished?

Whence comes this new precaution? Was there no one after Pope Leo, Anatolius, Maximus, Juvenal, or the other priests of that time among their successors who read more attentively and understood that the letter of the venerable bishop Ibas had been wrongly inserted into the synod?

Only now has the complaint of the heretics begun to move the Catholics, so that they consider rejecting this letter.

### 7

I have this to say: if the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon are reconsidered, let us also think about the Council of Nicaea, lest it suffer a similar danger.

Universal councils—especially those to which the consent of the Roman Church was added—hold the place of second authority after the canonical books.

Just as those who read divinely inspired Scripture are not permitted to criticize anything in it, although they are entirely unable to comprehend the heights of the heavenly oracle, but the devout reader believes what he does not understand so that he may deserve to understand what he believes, so, and in no other way, the councils which antiquity confirmed and devoted posterity preserved demand obedience from us, leaving no necessity for doubt.

They are far removed from the matters about which the Apostle says: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil” (I Thessalonians V, 21–22).

But those matters which are concluded by the judgment of holy bishops and, having been brought to the memory of blessed Peter, are examined and confirmed with the greatest care must be followed and embraced. They must not be held up for reconsideration under any pretext of piety—especially by later generations, when those who pronounced the judgment are already dead according to the flesh and already established in the place where, according to the Gospel, “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22).

**Note:** [Col. 0926D] “Peter” appears to be missing here.

What benefit is there in contending with those who sleep, or in disturbing the Church on behalf of those who sleep?

If someone was accused and condemned while still in the body of this death, but was taken from the world before he deserved to be absolved, he cannot thereafter be absolved by human judgment.

If someone was accused and acquitted and passed to the Lord in the peace of the Church, he cannot be condemned by human judgment.

If someone was accused but was overtaken by a sudden summons before the day of priestly examination, he is to be understood as having been reserved for divine judgment, while remaining within the bosom of Mother Church. No human being can pronounce a manifest sentence concerning him. If God granted him pardon, our severity does him no harm; if God prepared punishment, our kindness does him no good.

### 8

The Apostle forbids us to be wiser than we ought to be (Romans XII, 3). Whoever, therefore, thinks differently and considers his opinion right should speak, write, and dispute in this spirit of devout piety—especially in a matter of religion—so that he does not compel anyone by his words to obey against his will. Nor should he think that the opinion of one man has such force that it prejudices those who think otherwise.

Anyone who preaches the right faith may write what he thinks, but he should not call upon others to subscribe to what he himself has written.

How greatly, after the apostles, those most holy and illustrious teachers labored in preaching the word—men to whom the Lord had granted through the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge the ability to teach Catholics and overthrow heretics! Yet they left their books to posterity without anyone’s subscription.

Let us consider what the blessed Apostle advises: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others examine” (I Corinthians XIV, 29). Did he say, “Let them subscribe,” or “Let them be compelled to subscribe”?

He commands that what has been said be examined more carefully, lest easy agreement fall into error. Let everyone be free, after reading what one man has dictated, not to accept his words as though they were canonical Scriptures, but to consider what he should choose, what he should reject, what he should immediately follow, and what he should discuss with more prudent brothers.

Let no necessity be created for anyone to prejudice himself by subscribing, lest he later think one thing when the truth, once revealed, demonstrates that something else should be thought.

But let the devout writer patiently endure the devout concern of those who seek the truth, and let him not hasten to hold the hand of his hearers; rather, through a gracious understanding, let him be ready to consent to those who think better.

## 9.

The blessed bishop Augustine, offering an example of such humility in the charity of Christ to nearly all the teachers of the Catholic Church, says:

> “I shall not be embarrassed to ask whenever I am uncertain, nor ashamed to say so if I am mistaken. Therefore, whoever reads these things, let him proceed with me wherever he is equally certain; wherever he is equally uncertain, let him seek with me; wherever he recognizes his own error, let him return to me; wherever he recognizes mine, let him recall me. Thus let us enter together upon the way of charity, making our way toward him of whom it is said: ‘Seek his face continually.’ And this is pleasing, devout, and just before the Lord our God. Meanwhile, with all who read the things I write, etc.”  
> (Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book I, chapters 2–3.)

For, as we have already said many times above, divine commands are found only in the canonical books, and paternal decrees in general councils—commands and decrees that must not be rejected or spurned, but guarded and embraced. Holy Scripture says:

> “Hear, my son, your father’s law, and do not reject your mother’s counsel”  
> (Prov. 1:8; 6:20).

The father’s law, as I understand it, shines forth in the canonical books; the mother’s counsel is contained in universal councils. For this reason, the priests who assemble there subscribe their decrees, so that there may be no doubt about who conducted the discussion. Apart from those who establish what must be established, however, no one compels anyone else to subscribe. It is judged sufficient for full confirmation if, once brought to the knowledge of the whole Church, such decisions cause no offense or scandal among the brethren, but are affirmed to agree with the apostolic faith and are strengthened by the consent of the apostolic see.

### 10.

May your Blessedness therefore carefully attend to and preserve these three rules, which we have set forth in the order and language we were able to use—if, indeed, our humble counsel is acceptable.

First, let no reconsideration of the Council of Chalcedon or of similar councils be desired; rather, let what has once been established remain inviolate.

Second, let no scandals be generated among the living on account of departed brethren.

Third, let no one wish to confer upon his own book, through the subscriptions of many people, the authority that the Catholic Church has bestowed upon the canonical books alone.

This, too, may contribute to the tranquility of the churches: let no one wish to prescribe what the Church should follow, but let him hold to what the Church teaches. The Lord himself says through Moses in the song of Deuteronomy:

> “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will declare everything to you”  
> (Deut. 32:7).

Then the gracious teaching of the Teacher of the nations will also be fulfilled—his admonition to the Corinthians:

> “When you come together, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has an interpretation: let everything be done for edification”  
> (1 Cor. 14:16).

Behold: when questioned, I could not remain silent out of obedience. I have answered as a disciple to teachers, an unlearned man to the learned, an inferior to superiors. Examine this little answer, I ask, out of charity, to see whether it has been able to grasp the truth; and, if it seems good, let your discernment weigh whether it ought to be disclosed to the brethren.

# LETTER VII. TO COUNT REGINUS: AN EXHORTATION

## What a devout commander should be in military affairs, or, concerning the seven rules of innocence

### 1.

As soon as a person has grown free from the ignorance of childhood and become rational, he must be exercised in the labors of social life: either he begins to serve God, illustrious commander Reginus, or the world.

For this reason the Apostle Paul says:

> “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs”  
> (2 Tim. 2:4),

showing that there are soldiers of God, just as there are also soldiers of the world.

Thus the two forms of service signify two kinds of soldiers. One kind is bound by bodily service to labor with the world, according to the will of an earthly king; the other is led by spiritual service into the heavenly camp through the free grace of the heavenly Emperor.

The soldiers of the world are held subject to various passions and desires; the soldiers of God crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. The former are nourished by banquets; the latter by virtues. The former strive to seize what belongs to others; the latter strive either patiently to lose even what is their own or mercifully to distribute it. The former look after their private interests; the latter after the common good. The former undertake actions by which they may be raised up through false praises; the latter seek actions by which they may be honored with eternal rewards. Vanity gives the former an image of joy; truth bestows true joys upon the latter.

The former hasten to preserve and continually hold a perishable homeland, though they themselves are likewise destined to perish; the latter desire to possess one that will never perish, lest they perish eternally. For the former, living is a hardship and dying a punishment; for the latter, “to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” The former fight against visible enemies; the latter against invisible ones. Avarice makes the former cruel; mercy makes the latter kind. Envy makes the former quarrelsome; gentleness makes the latter peaceful. Through pride the former quarrel on behalf of their own men; through humility the latter each regard the other as superior to himself.

Through the former Babylon is ruled; through the latter, and in the latter, the heavenly Jerusalem is administered by the Lord.

It often happens that, although joined together in body and separated in mind, soldiers of God and soldiers of the world experience temporal prosperity and adversity together. But prosperity exalts the soldiers of the world and adversity casts them down. The soldiers of God, however, remain unmoved whether in prosperity or adversity, because their glory is the testimony of their conscience. They rest when the world suffers tribulation; they do not fear being confronted by the enemy of chastity when an abundance of pleasures is at hand, springing from the root of temporal happiness and producing the thorns of desire.

The soldiers of God gladly hear blessed John, crying out to his fellow soldiers with a stronger trumpet:

> “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world is passing away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever”  
> (1 John 2:15–17).

When they hear and obey this most salutary admonition, whenever the hidden dispensation of the most merciful Creator grants them the authority to judge and administer an earthly commonwealth, then, at least in part, worldly service is not burdened with grave sins. Then the restless are easily corrected, the fainthearted are consoled, and the weak are received; license for crimes is taken away from the wicked, and innocence gains the freedom to act well.

### 2.

Let us therefore pray continually to him who orders the world in equity, accomplishing everything according to the counsel of his will. Of him the Psalmist truly sings:

> “Whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths”  
> (Ps. 134:6).

May he deign to promote his soldiers, hidden beneath the appearance of worldly military service, to the highest dignities—ruling them inwardly and granting them the knowledge of how to rule others, just as he is known already to have granted this to you also, illustrious commander Reginus.

Accordingly, with commendable concern, you asked the bishop Fulgentius of the Church of Ruspe, of venerable memory, what rule of spiritual purpose you should retain while occupied with military affairs. Wisely indeed you had sought an answer of wisdom from a wise man; and holy prudence was lacking neither to the questioner nor to the one questioned.

You were already practicing what he could teach, and he could teach what you were practicing, so that you might recognize your conduct in his words, and he might approve his words from your conduct.

But now, because the incomplete dictation of a half-finished little book is known to have answered nothing concerning your question—for the opening sections of that glorious work spend a long time discussing the first question in your letter, whether Christ’s flesh was corruptible or incorruptible—while still engaged in that discussion, before beginning to speak faithfully and reasonably about the pious conduct of military affairs, that outstanding teacher passed on to the immortal joys of eternal blessedness, where he would contemplate face to face the Word of God, whom he always possessed in heart and mouth.

You therefore place an unbearable burden upon weak shoulders, ordering me to discharge, as though it were an inherited debt, the obligation of so great a man.

Am I filled with wisdom as he was? Have I the same eloquence? Has an authority of dignity like his been given to me? Or is even the innocence of my conduct such as his, when infirmity of mind and body weighs me down, entangled in past and present transgressions?

What, then, shall I do? I wish to satisfy your desire, but I cannot—especially when, reflecting and reconsidering the merits of my sins, I judge it nearly arrogant to lead others along the paths of righteousness along which I myself do not walk.

### 3.

Woe to me, miserable man, until the Most High takes pity. Behold, bound by the chains of ecclesiastical service, I am scattered among secular cares; and how dare I display the law of spiritual service in a world engaged in military service?

Should I weep, or speak? Should the life of another be instructed, or should my own life rather be corrected? The first virtue is to live well; the second is to teach rightly. But the one who does not live well teaches rightly in vain. Since I am not yet living well, how shall I teach rightly?

Nevertheless, because it is not a human being who teaches another human being, but God who is the teacher of all, and because you seek to hear not human commands but divine ones, pass over what I am and learn what you ought to be—or rather, what sort of person you may rejoice to be while we rejoice with you.

1. Believe that God’s grace is necessary for you in every action, saying with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10).

2. Let your life be a mirror in which your soldiers may see what they ought to do.

3. Do not desire to command, but to be of service.

4. Love the commonwealth as yourself.

5. Put divine things before human things.

6. Do not be excessively righteous.

7. Remember that you are a Christian.

It seems to me that through these seven rules people can be spiritual in military affairs and pleasing to God. They will suffer no loss of good character; rather, they will advance toward greater growth in righteousness.

If, then, you wish to be a perfect soldier of God among the soldiers of the world, hold firmly to what we have said briefly. If you confess grace, the Spirit of the fear of the Lord will rest upon you. If your life is a mirror in which your soldiers see what they ought to do, the Spirit of piety will rest upon you. If you do not desire to command but to be of service, the Spirit of knowledge will rest upon you. For the one who wishes to be of service knows how to command.

If you love the commonwealth as yourself, the Spirit of fortitude will rest upon you. If you put divine things before human things, the Spirit of counsel will rest upon you. If you willingly hear, “Do not be excessively righteous,” the Spirit of understanding will rest upon you. If you remember that you are a Christian, the Spirit of wisdom will rest upon you.

And through the abundance of the sevenfold Spirit, the merciful God will fulfill what the friends of his faithful servant Job said most truly:

> “In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil will not touch you. In famine he will rescue you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and you will not fear calamity when it comes. In devastation and famine you will laugh, and you will not fear the beasts of the earth; rather, you will have a covenant with the stones of the region, and the beasts of the earth will be at peace with you. You will know that your tent is at peace; and when you visit your dwelling, you will not sin”  
> (Job 5:19–24).

It is plainly necessary that, while preserving the order of the divisions, you listen carefully and attentively as I discuss each of these seven kinds individually. Know above all that no one can understand rightly without God’s grace, and no one can live justly without it.

For the Lord grants understanding; the Lord makes whomever he wishes devout. We possess nothing good from ourselves. As the Apostle James testifies:

> “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration”  
> (James 1:17).

# FIRST RULE. ATTRIBUTE ALL GLORY TO GOD

### 4.

The first rule, therefore, which you ought to hold amid military affairs, is that you attribute nothing proudly to your own strength, but refer everything that you accomplish wisely, bravely, or successfully to the praise of the most powerful Creator. Always remember what Moses said to the people of Israel as they entered the promised land, wishing all to possess the virtue of holy humility:

> “Do not say in your heart, ‘My strength and the power of my hand have made this great achievement for me’; but remember the Lord your God, because he gives you the power to accomplish this achievement”  
> (Deut. 8:17–18).

The prophet Jeremiah also gives fuller admonition:

> “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let the one who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows that I am the Lord, who practice mercy, judgment, and righteousness upon the earth”  
> (Jer. 9:23–24).

Therefore, frequently—and, if possible, continually—you will cry out with the voice of heart and body:

> “Lord, my strength and my help in the day of calamity”  
> (Jer. 16:19).

And again:

> “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my glory”  
> (Jer. 17:14).

By saying these things, you will appear to follow the teaching of holy Paul, who says:

> “Let the one who glories glory in the Lord”  
> (2 Cor. 10:17).

Then the prophetic sentence will be fulfilled in you:

> “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope. He will be like a fruitful tree beside water, sending its roots toward moisture. He will not fear when the heat comes, and its branches will be abundant. In the year of drought he will not fear, and he will not cease producing fruit”  
> (Jer. 17:7–8).

But he will fail if he forgets the one of whom the faithful Isaiah tells the faithful:

> “The everlasting God, the Lord who created the ends of the earth, does not fail or grow weary, and his wisdom is unsearchable. He gives strength to the weary and increases power and vigor for those who have no strength. Boys will fail and grow weary, and young men will fall in weakness. But those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength; they will take up wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will fly and not fail”  
> (Isa. 40:28–31).

Run swiftly, soldier of God, so that, joined to the company of such men, you may conduct military affairs securely.

If it should be necessary to use counsel, Wisdom immediately answers you:

> “Counsel is mine, and protection is mine”  
> (Prov. 8:14).

If you must fight in battle, you will hear the voice of the strongest David:

> “The Lord does not save by sword or spear; the battle is the Lord’s”  
> (1 Sam. 17:47).

If you plan to set guards against hostile attacks, the psalm answers the one who is considering this:

> “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain”  
> (Ps. 126:1).

If a small army must be led against innumerable enemy forces, you will immediately be strengthened by Judith praying. With a harmonious prayer, you will cry out in lament:

> “Your strength is not in numbers, nor is your power in the mighty; but you are the God of the humble, the helper of the needy, and the defender of the weak”  
> (Judith 9:16).

If harmony among the soldiers is sought, you will remember what is written:

> “The Lord is peace”  
> (Judg. 6:24).

If obedience is required, you will sing to the Lord your God in the words of the psalm:

> “You will rescue me from the disputes of the people”  
> (Ps. 17:44).

Under the name “people,” the multitude of soldiers may also reasonably be understood—especially because such a people is often full of dispute, natural severity supplying material for seditions.

The dispute of soldiers is dangerous, for it is close to slaughter and plunder. Obedience, however, is sweet when it willingly obeys the salutary admonitions of a most wise commander.

There can be no doubt at all that in military affairs the strongest commanders need the help of heavenly strength. David cries out and, as though speaking in the assembly of the human race, responds to those who trust in their own strength:

> “Blessed be the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war. He is my mercy and my refuge, my protector and my deliverer, who subjects peoples beneath me”  
> (Ps. 143:1–2).

Understanding that the Lord subjects peoples to you, you will undoubtedly hasten to do the Lord’s will. You will not terrify your subjects by power alone, but will offer them peaceful counsels in obedience, taking care to be the kind of person you wish to find in others.

# SECOND RULE. LET YOUR LIFE BE A MIRROR FOR YOUR SOLDIERS

### 5.

The second rule for one occupied with military affairs is that his soldiers should see in him, as in a mirror, what they ought to do; imitation should summon them to goodness more than power does.

A wise commander ought to go where he wishes to lead his subjects. He is called a commander because he leads; and he certainly misleads himself if he thinks he can walk along the royal road while, by providing a bad example, he leads those under him to the pit of an evil life.

Be, then, the standard-bearer of the holiest discipline. Raise the trophy of virtue, for the others constantly to behold. Appear as one to be imitated, so that anyone who hears you command will not rebuke you for acting otherwise.

Always place in your heart the words of the Apostle:

> “You are without excuse, every person who judges; for in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the very same things that you judge”  
> (Rom. 2:1).

What you declare blameworthy, therefore, you will first strive to avoid and only afterward condemn; whatever you declare praiseworthy, you will first practice and only afterward command.

The life of the best commander, compared with a mirror, is properly examined to see whether faith, justice, mercy, patience, self-restraint, and a prudent assessment of the future shine in it—not with a simulated color, but with an entirely genuine display.

You will be a faithful commander if, by the judgment of wise people and not by the words of flatterers, you are tested and known to believe rightly, deceive no one, and fulfill your promises.

You will be a just commander if, by the judgment of wise people and not by the words of flatterers, you are tested and known to punish those who persist in wickedness, favor the good, distinguish the merits of individuals, and render to everyone what is owed.

You will be a merciful commander if, by the judgment of wise people and not by the words of flatterers, you are tested and known to love the poor, govern your subjects, serve those in need, mercifully pardon those who ask forgiveness, teach wisdom to the foolish, call those who walk in crimes back from their evil way, pray to God for your enemies, and reconcile those who are at odds.

You will be a patient commander if, by the judgment of wise people and not by the praises of flatterers, you are tested and known to labor for the interests of others without the profit of desire; to endure injuries and not inflict them; to have no lust for revenge; not to be broken in any way by fear of adversity; not to be carried away by desire for prosperity; to persevere in what you have rightly undertaken; to hope in God’s mercy even when he delays coming to your aid; to do nothing hastily without counsel; to receive obediently whatever a superior commands; and to arrange without disturbance whatever you command an inferior.

You will be a self-restrained commander if, by the judgment of wise people and not by the praises of flatterers, you are tested and known neither to desire nor seize the property of others when you have the opportunity; to do nothing violently, nothing fraudulently, nothing without measure, nothing for pleasure, nothing out of avarice, and nothing forbidden by the laws or contrary to the custom of the city or people—provided that the custom itself neither harms religion nor opposes good morals.

Otherwise, a bad custom, like an old disease, kills unless it is driven out. Thus it is a virtue of self-restraint to do nothing contrary to good custom.

If you are indeed a self-restrained commander, you will also be found to assess future events prudently—whether by keeping watch against the plots of adversaries, or by knowing what outcomes are usually assigned to particular circumstances, where seditions arise, where new wars are born, where the relaxation of severity comes from, and where the ruinous license of plunder originates. If these things are cut off at their roots, they will open a path of peaceful administration for the wisest commander.

### 6.

The most faithful admonitions of John the Baptist must also be heard. Soldiers heard them when, in response to their question, “What shall we do, then?”, he did not say, “Go, lay down your weapons, flee from the conflicts of war, devote yourselves only to prayers, and disregard the emperor’s commands.” Rather, he proposed certain other things to be observed, saying:

> “Shake no one down, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your pay”  
> (Luke 3:14).

To shake someone down is to use violence openly; to accuse falsely is to seek an opportunity to cause harm.

For whoever refuses to be content with his pay either breaks apart the restraints of discipline all at once or seizes what belongs to others through reckless excesses. Saint John prohibited this when he said, “Shake no one down.” Or he seeks grounds for offense so that, under some appearance of justice, he may terrify the innocent and compel the unwilling to satisfy his avarice—or rather, his rapacity. Saint John prohibited this when he said, “Accuse no one falsely.”

After removing the perversity of this twofold evil, he added what should be followed:

> “Be content with your pay.”

The soldiers will be blessed if they keep these commands; the commonwealth will be blessed if it deserves to have such soldiers; and the commander will be blessed in whose army many such soldiers happen to serve.

Yet he will appear even more blessed if he himself is such a man—shaking no one down, accusing no one falsely, and content with his pay. For the greater he is in dignity, the more he can shake people down, make false accusations, and refuse to be content with his pay.

From this, affliction most often arises for cities; from this come the gravest cruelties, profits obtained through a thousand schemes, venality in judgments, leniency in battles, and the diminution of the entire commonwealth—if a commander begins not to be content with his pay and, desiring to enlarge his private advantages beyond public emoluments, cares only for his own usefulness while neglecting the welfare and security of his subjects.

Such a commander is not modest and agreeable toward his equals, but quarrelsome and avaricious; he is not gentle, approachable, and accommodating toward his inferiors, but cruel, partial, and difficult.

Under such a man military discipline quickly deteriorates. Why would soldiers wish to spare provincials when they have seen them suffer fraud at the hands of the commander himself? How will they be content with their pay when they perceive their commander acquiring distinction from the property of others?

When a commander shakes someone down, does he not use his soldiers as instruments of violence? When he makes a false accusation against someone, does he not carry out the business of fraud through them? By frequently ordering them to commit iniquity, he makes them despise equity.

Does a wise commander wish his soldier to be peaceful, pacific, and obedient? Then let him himself be just, merciful, temperate, and, in his administration, love not to command but to be of service.

Let him imitate Samuel in good actions. Let him acquire for himself the free confidence of modest and honorable liberty, so that with an open face he may say to those subject to him, as Samuel said:

> “Here I am. Testify against me before the Lord and before his anointed: whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I wronged by force? Whom have I oppressed? Or from whose hand have I accepted a bribe or even a sandal? Testify against me, and I will restore it to you”  
> (1 Sam. 12:2–3).

And let the response also be given to him that they gave Samuel:

> “You have not wronged any of us, nor oppressed anyone by force, nor crushed us, nor taken anything from our hands”  
> (ibid., 4).

Oh, how glorious a commander he will be before the face of the prince who has deserved to hear these things! The nobles will magnify him, the humble will bless him, and a reputation better than all riches will follow him.

He will be given, as it is written, “the chosen gift of faith,” and “a more peaceful lot in the temple of God,” the good fruit of good labors and a good reputation (Wis. 3:14).

And if he should perhaps be removed, or ordered not to administer the commonwealth, he will remain and endure in everyone’s affection as though present. Whoever succeeds him will find not something to criticize, but something to admire.

That is, if he prefers to be of service rather than to command. For many command, but altogether few are of service to the peoples over whom they command.

Whoever thirsts for private honors, despising the usefulness of his subjects, desires to command rather than to be of service. Such a commander is useless and unjust: he can neither govern a commonwealth that is standing nor restore one that has fallen.

# THIRD RULE. DO NOT DESIRE TO COMMAND, BUT TO BE OF SERVICE

### 7.

The third rule, therefore, for one occupied with military affairs is that he should command for the purpose of being of service.

You will appear to be of service if you understand the time and place of your administration. You will consider the time by carefully judging whether it is peaceful or disturbed by the turmoil of war. Often what discipline, acting as an avenger, pursues in the leisure of peace, cautious patience tolerates amid disturbances and swords.

You will properly consider the place by asking whether it is barren or fertile; whether it is sufficient to nourish the army or less suitable; whether it is deserted and uncultivated, or secure and carefully worked.

Whenever the place where you are seen to govern the army needs restoration, all private profits must be disregarded, even those that custom already freely claims for itself; and the judgment of severity must be tempered with somewhat greater strictness.

Apart from these considerations, you will also appear to be of service in two ways: if you harm no one, and if you prevent, as far as you can—or rather, as far as Christ grants you the ability—those who habitually or willingly cause harm.

An excellent commander will harm no one if, throughout his entire headquarters, no friend, client, physician, arms-bearer, or other person who is always attached to the commander’s side because of devotion to public office dares to sell the benefits that have been granted.

What does it help the wretched if the commander displays the self-restraint of a good commander while someone else uses his authority as an opportunity to satisfy avarice?

Let him have associates and ministers of the kind he recognizes that he himself ought to be. For whoever clings familiarly to a commander, to whom he entrusts many tasks, is the commander’s hand; and whatever such people receive is rightly believed without doubt to pass through to him. Nor can the reputation of an excellent commander be good when his ministries are bad.

Moreover, how will he correct outsiders unless he first corrects his own people? Who would doubt that those stationed in the army will more readily rush into committing crimes if they see the commander’s attendants perpetrating worse acts with greater license?

He will easily keep in check the whole populace, even an unruly army, if the men very close to the commander observe it.

Let him therefore beware—and beware diligently—that none of his men harm the wretched. Otherwise, while he considers himself good, he will be judged evil on account of the wicked, whom he must be said either to favor or to consent to, since they commit such acts in his presence. Even if he does not commit these acts himself, he will not be believed to possess goodness but only to feign it.

A wise commander cannot excuse himself through ignorance whenever he perhaps says, “I do not know; I have not heard; no complaint has reached me.” For it is necessary that he inquire into what is being done by his own men, since no one dares publicly accuse those whose violence some fear and others suffer.

Let the commander therefore not hesitate to become a most searching investigator. From this diligence he will gain the authority of public severity, so that he may be entirely of service, since he allows no one to be harmed either by himself or by another.

Through this diligence he can acquire such a good reputation that, even if a superior person wishes to harm his subjects, he may come to their aid through free intercession and easily persuade that mercy be shown to those whom he himself first spared.

### 8.

The path of our discussion has brought us beautifully to this point, where we must say that it is necessary for good commanders—even while making suggestions to rulers—to be of service to their subjects.

For we know that many, in order to please their superiors, take less care of their inferiors. I believe that those who conceal the poverty or troubles of the province they administer belong to this number. They report that everything they see fallen remains safe, considering it a glory if they lie that what they know to have perished is still standing.

They are compelled, in order to win credence for their shameful words, to multiply the losses of the wretched provincials. Through these losses they seem to provide something like profits—though profits wholly hostile to the commonwealth—to the most merciful rulers, while actually hindering the restoration of the region.

Where they strive to appear useful, there they are wholly useless. By imposing heavier burdens, they make exhausted peoples collapse, and they leave their successors nothing but mourning and tears.

I do not want you to be found like them. If you love being of service rather than commanding, accomplish something worthy of remembrance, something posterity will recall, so that no oblivion of your time may arise.

Take care to leave wealthy those whom you found poor; provide abundance where you yourself also endured scarcity. If your strength is sufficient, restore the province without delay. But if the will for this most merciful work is present while the ability is lacking, bring the matter to the attention of the superior authority.

Be a faithful witness to the sufferings of others. Beg and entreat until you obtain assistance. Labor long in asking, so that others may not endure prolonged hardships in laboring. For you will be judged to have provided whatever is provided to the whole community at your request.

Do not appear like those who wish to please for the moment. When they see, perceive, or sometimes even endure evils in the provinces where they serve, they report good things through false dispatches, thinking that by an exceedingly joyful report they are securing for themselves the appearance of being either useful to the administration they hold or necessary to it.

O crime worthy of lamentation! While they seek to command, they do not consider being of service; rather, they try to preserve the unjust power of private honor through the sufferings of others.

Yet the cunning of malignant ambition sometimes deceives them, until public opinion begins to speak of what they conceal and they are found to be liars in their own declarations.

May God always turn this madness and these practices away from the best commanders, who love to be of service rather than to command!

# FOURTH RULE. LOVE THE COMMONWEALTH AS YOURSELF
9. For then the commonwealth is well governed and can be delivered from great dangers, if its commander loves it as much as he loves himself. For there is an unmistakable declaration of the ancient law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19:18), which Paul, a fitting preacher of the New Testament, confirms and renews by repeating it thus: “The whole law is fulfilled in one saying: in this, that you love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal. 5:14). But whom should the wisest commander regard as a better neighbor than the commonwealth, whose affairs, condition, and welfare are entrusted to him? Let him therefore love it as himself, because by loving it as himself he will desire to see it peaceful, tranquil, prosperous, and calm without any disturbance, just as he himself strives, insofar as he can, to be peaceful, tranquil, prosperous, and calm without any disturbance.

Enter, then, excellent among men, whenever you consider what sort of person you ought to be in military affairs, enter the broadest recesses of your conscience. See there how you desire to possess happiness, and take careful heed that the commonwealth, which you love as yourself, may suffer no sadness. Consider that you do not wish any loss, pain, or disgrace to befall you; hasten to rescue the commonwealth from these evils.

If you are displeased when, as a private individual, you suffer violence, you ought to hate those by whose violence the commonwealth is afflicted. If you fear enduring the plundering of your own goods, remove from plunderers the practice of plundering. If you detest and truly regard as an enemy anyone who attacks you with false accusations, judge the accusers of the entire province accursed. Or is it perhaps difficult to suppose that an entire province suffers accusers? Believe me, it suffers them very often.

Its accusers are the ambitious men who, in order to be granted the power to oppress the poor, make impossible promises. To regions laid waste and already ruined by the incursions of war, they attribute their former condition of stability; they falsely claim that everything is still flourishing and that they are still able to bear not only their customary levies but even the burdens of new taxes, if these are imposed. Yet in hidden whispers they blame the officials of the fiscal exaction, falsely alleging that these men are idle or excessively lax and deliberately provide no revenues for the commonwealth; but, they say, once the administration has been entrusted to them, everything will be made prosperous through their excessive and faithful diligence.

But—O stubborn greed!—their diligence is better called cruelty, and their calculation, plunder. They desire to purchase the most burdensome offices because they plan to sell them; they promise falsehoods in order to steal what is true; they flatter in order to harm; they pretend to exercise a pious concern for the public interests, but are plotting to afflict and worsen everything at once. They desire to overthrow, not govern; to dissipate, not preserve; to devour, not nourish. They supply material for seditions, increase misery, and cause tears—doing this so that, when the province is nearly dead, it may not die too slowly.

“Fence your ears with thorns” (Ecclus. 28:28), lest you hear the voice of those who speak maliciously. When you see them praising the fertility of the fields, announcing abundant rains, and frequently depicting pleasant places, beware of a flattering tale. Such speech is birdlime: the will of a good commander must not become stuck there. Nor should you inquire whether they report anything truthfully. For, trained by the practiced craft of vice, they are no less cautious in doing harm even when they know that everything has perished. Nevertheless, they seek out a few quite rare places which, under the protection of the Lord’s mercy, have deserved either to remain unharmed or perhaps to suffer little damage.

By repeatedly reciting the names of these places, commending them to memory, they diminish by comparison with them the magnitude of the general calamity, and they say—as you have certainly been able to verify—“The province is sufficient for these levies; that place, after all, has so much revenue.”

“O wretched men, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Ps. 143:8)! If they have their eyes open to their own advantage, why does the people groan? Let them see whether a just balance is on their lips. First let them count how much has perished; afterward, how much has remained. Or do they see nothing where compassion is needed, while with watchful eyes they mark whatever may give rise to envy?

[Col. 0938B] 10. Keep your path far from them; let them always find your house closed. Let those who suggest harmful things displease you, and let them know that they have displeased you. For closely attached to them is also a thoroughly wicked crowd of informers, who, in secret murmuring, point out the resources of others to the best commanders, so that, captured by the snares of greed, they may lose the reputation of a pious administration if they heed wicked counsels and begin to consider taking away what is reported to them.

What else is being stirred up against innocent people except slander? Informers are truly a detestable and exceedingly abominable human race. [Note: Col. 0937D: Perhaps read *genus hominum* (“a race of men”).] In whose headquarters they have not emerged, that man loves the commonwealth as himself, unwilling to do to others what he would not wish to suffer himself.

For this is the fourth rule of innocence for one occupied with military affairs, which you hold and must hold firmly: that you love the commonwealth as yourself, with a free love. Filled with the abundant sweetness of this love, Moses, when he saw that the people of Israel—namely, his commonwealth—had sinned against almighty God and feared the future severity of the most just Judge, undertook to appease Him as He was angry:

“I beg you, Lord,” he said, “if you forgive their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me from your book which your hands have written” (Exod. 32:31).

Let us consider what it profited Moses to save others if he himself perished. But because he always loved the commonwealth as himself, by this sacrifice of love he appeased God; and neither did he himself perish, nor did he permit the people whom he governed to perish.

Holy David imitated him with equal strength of love when the angel was striking the city: “Let your hand be turned against me and against my father’s house. What have these sheep done?” (II Reg. XLII, 17).

Give me a man who loves the commonwealth in this way, and you will see how pleasing he is to God, even while occupied with military affairs. Surely you are worthy to live as one like these men: ready to labor for the rest of your subjects; ready even to undergo death, if God permits it, so that you may free your subjects from the danger of death. Fear, excellent commander, that the province should become worse more than that you yourself should become poorer through diminished resources. Regard a good reputation as riches beyond measure.

Nevertheless, because every person who loves himself ought to love God more than himself—for otherwise, loving God less, he does not love but hates himself—whoever loves the commonwealth as himself should love God more than the commonwealth and should place divine affairs before human affairs.

## FIFTH RULE. Put divine things before human things.
