11. This, then, will be the fifth rule of innocence for one occupied with military affairs: to consider temporal things in such a way that he gives greater attention to eternal things; to provide for present actions in such a way that he thinks more about future rewards.

For it frequently happens—as you cannot fail to know, since the Spirit of wisdom reveals all things to your understanding—that necessity compels something to be done which the eternal law forbids. To avoid introducing unfamiliar examples: if many heretics are found in a very powerful army, obstinately defending the false doctrine of their unbelief, and for this reason a Catholic commander is advised either to spare or to favor the heretics, or to grant the preachers of their unspeakable error permission to exercise their blasphemies, patiently enduring, for fear of the scandal he dreads, that those already once reborn should be defiled by a second baptismal washing—if he consents to so wicked a counsel, although he may appear to have provided his subjects with some temporal advantage, he has meanwhile harmed himself. Judged to have placed less hope in God’s help, he sometimes endures dangers worse than those he fears. Neither, remaining steadfast in his own faith, does he properly exercise religious zeal, nor does he escape the ruin of the gravest affliction, because he has preferred earthly things to heavenly and has not hesitated to offend the will of the Creator, wishing to please men whose minds are corrupt.

Therefore you will be blessed if, occupied with military affairs, you flatter no one on behalf of the true faith which you hold, and forbid the dogs advancing against it from the workshop of falsehood to bark. Place your hope in Him whose power no one can resist with impunity. If you offend Him, you rely on the multitude of your army without cause; if you have Him favorably disposed toward you, you will fear neither a proud soldier nor a violent enemy.

Above all, therefore, let this be your concern, while occupied with military affairs: that the Catholic faith may always conquer its adversaries. Defend it amid arms and swords; commend it to the minds of armed men.

12. The Catholic faith, then, is to proclaim one substance—or essence—of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit against Arius, and three persons against Sabellius, so that, when unity in essence and distinction in persons have been rightly understood, true equality in majesty may also be worshiped.

For they are three, because the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Yet these three are one, and supremely one, because separately the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. Nevertheless, they are not three gods, but one God, of whom Holy Scripture says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4).

The Trinity removes the suspicion of a solitary God and shows one God to those who believe in one substance. Not one in such a way that each individual is only half-full and the whole becomes complete in all of them, and therefore is one; but one in number, kind, power, and fullness. Whatever it possesses in all, it does not lack in each.

As much is in the Father alone as in the Son and the Holy Spirit; as much in the Son alone as in the Father and the Holy Spirit; as much in the Holy Spirit as in the Father and the Son. Finally, as much is in each of them individually as in two; as much in two as in three; as much in three as in each individually.

For there is nothing arranged there in degrees, nothing different in quality, nothing lesser in quantity, nothing separated by place, nothing later in time, nothing ineffective, nothing subject to suffering. The only distinction it admits is that they exist in relation to one another: the Father in relation to the Son, the Son in relation to the Father, and the Holy Spirit in relation to those from whom and with whom He is both Spirit and holy, so that He alone in the Trinity is called “holy.” It is proper to the Father to beget, proper to the Son to be born, and proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from both.

The Father is the Father of one Son; the Son is the Son of one Father; the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both Father and Son. Generation belongs to the Father alone, birth to the Son alone, and procession from both to the Holy Spirit alone.

When the necessity of our salvation awaited the birth of God as man from a human being for the liberation of human beings, the Father was not born according to the flesh, because He was never the Son; nor was the Holy Spirit, who was never at any time Father or Son. Rather, the Son was born, so that He who is the Son of God the Father might Himself become the Son of the Virgin Mother. Through this temporal birth, the number of the children of almighty God did not in any way increase, nor did the second birth of the only Son make two sons.

This is especially so because that same one Son, coeternal, consubstantial, and equal with the eternal Father, was alone to become also the son of man. When the fullness of time had come, so that He might become man from a woman and redeem men and women, He was born temporally in one sex in order to save both: choosing one sex in which He would be born and the other from which He would be born. Thus He assumed the truth of our substance without doubling the singularity of His person—a giant of two substances, yet of one and the same person.

The Word before the flesh: one nature and one person. The Word made flesh: two natures and one person. The Word before the flesh: *homousion* with the Father. The Word made flesh: *homousion* with both Father and mother. The Word before the flesh: ineffably begotten without a beginning in time. The Word made flesh: after the fullness of time had come, wonderfully and uniquely brought forth without the disorder of lust. The Word before the flesh: fashioning a new world. The Word made flesh: redeeming the world that was perishing.

The Word before the flesh: doing divine things. The Word made flesh: doing divine and human things together, and suffering as He willed. The Word before the flesh: God the only-begotten. The Word made flesh: Emmanuel, which is interpreted “God with us.”

Yet it is the same one: the Word made flesh, who earlier in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. For it was not that a man became God, but that God became man so that man might be God—that is, Christ Jesus.

Although He was in the form of God, He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. He humbled Himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted Him and gave Him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:6–11).

13. This is the Lord Jesus, who in the perfect Trinity is called the Son when we are commanded to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. He is great and small, exalted and humble, incapable of suffering and capable of suffering, immortal and mortal, living among human beings without sin and forgiving sins to human beings: in all things like us except for sin, and in all things like the Father, who sent Him to us in the likeness of sinful flesh and, because of sin, condemned sin in the flesh.

Truly and properly the Son of God the Father; truly and properly the Son of the Virgin Mother. Above the heavens, the life of the living; upon earth, the medicine of the sick; among the dead, the resurrection of the dead. Mediator of God and human beings because of His two substances, or natures, one of which He shares with God and the other with us.

In one and the same person, in which He truly became mediator, He did not receive the beginning of His divinity from Mary; but from her He received the material of the flesh which He assumed in order to be born. He possesses the flesh of our race—not airy, not imaginary, not brought down from heaven, not made elsewhere—human indeed, yet in no part polluted by the stains of original iniquity. It was formed not from the pleasure of flesh and blood but by the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon it, and was enlivened by the inspiration of a rational soul.

Properly and truly human—that is, from a mother—yet without a human father. Corruptible, because He voluntarily, yet truly, experienced hunger, thirst, pain, and death. Incorruptible, because, feeling in Himself the impulse of no sin, whether original or personal, He did not consent to iniquity through any desire.

Nor could He, after being buried, come to the corruption of decay, because of the gift of the resurrection. Carrying the spoils of the underworld, that same one Christ, always one, rose again, remaining with His disciples for forty days, and then wonderfully ascending into heaven.

There He now sits at the right hand of the Father, to come in glory, He who had first come in humility; to judge the living and the dead, and to condemn unbelievers, but to grant believers the forgiveness of sins and eternal life—provided, however, that they persevere in the Catholic Church, cleansed from the contagion of every vice.

For the Catholic Church is the station where the good physician heals our wounds. Whoever defends her even to the shedding of blood is a son of promise.

14. Therefore, excellent and faithful commander, hold all its doctrines, preach them, defend them; lead those who are willing to it, compel those who are unwilling—not through the pain of punishments or fear of a raging sword, but through moderate correction and severity filled with love.

Far be from you the fear that serves the devil. Let the heretics know that you are Catholic; let Catholics know that you detest heretics. During the period of your administration, let the synagogue of sinners diminish and the number of the elect increase.

If the man whose labor enlarges the boundaries of the empire becomes glorious, how much more glorious will be the man whose labor multiplies the Catholic Church? Rejoice in Christ’s gains; grieve over his losses.

Let the judgment of the apostle Peter always remain in your heart, condemning rulers with this question: “Whom ought one to obey?” he says, “God or human beings?” (Acts 5:29). Therefore, faithful commander, whenever the fervor of your faith scandalizes profane soldiers, say with mouth and heart: “Whom ought one to obey? God or human beings?”

When your conscience answers, “God,” speak, act, and command what God loves, so that whoever is now opposed to the truth may either follow willingly or remain grumbling, powerless to do anything against orthodox religion.

For there cannot fail to be others whom you please by your good work, whose hearts will cling to you more firmly. True faith has lovers everywhere. However much iniquity may be exalted, truth conquers.

But suppose that there are perhaps more heretics than Catholics in the army: you ought to strive with your strongest powers so that, if God’s grace looks favorably upon you, you may make all the strongest soldiers Catholic—or at least leave only a few heretics.

I am still saying too little. Perhaps you have been sent to regions where you find no orthodox believer, or at least only very few, hidden away. There too, courageously sow the word of life for the glory of Christ. Rebuke the multitude of the faithless without shame, fear, or hesitation. Do not first consider how you may govern them by imperial laws, but how you may correct them through spiritual words. At first, by the authority of your office, prevent those terrified by your name from resisting holy doctrine; then gradually persuade them to consent.

It is useful for you to think rightly if you do not abandon others in their error as well. The persistence of a good commander has often provided many with an opportunity for salvation. But if you perhaps despair that they can be saved, it is good to preach what accords with salvation, because God crowns the will, not the ability. It belongs to the duty of a diligent farmer to sow; it belongs to the heavenly gift for the earth to bear fruit and answer the wishes of its cultivator.

Having exercised this diligence toward your subjects, you will readily learn, even in dealing with exalted powers and the kings themselves through whose authority you have become a commander, both not to yield and to resist if they should happen to hold opinions contrary to the true faith—ready for martyrdom.

Otherwise, if one fears offending those below and therefore carries out the cause of his own religion less fully, how will he deserve to sing with the prophet David: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed” (Ps. 118:46)?

15. If only good commanders would begin to put divine things before human things, they would provide remedies for the greatest errors. This virtue extends widely and pours itself out through more and more paths of justice.

Put divine things before human things: let a widow not endure oppression for the sake of passing profit; let the property of an orphan have no need of a guardian’s favor; let an unjust litigant lose his most wicked victory; let the ears of priests open willingly to petitions. Let prayer be frequent. Let devotion to reading, although occupations press in from every side, burn with the fire of spiritual desire, with sluggishness removed.

Why does the best commander oppress a widow? Why does he allow an orphan to be harmed? Why does he judge on behalf of an unjust litigant? Why does he go to church with difficulty or rarely? Why does he not read? Is it not because he puts human things before divine things?

Therefore always put divine things before human things. All your works and words of religious devotion, even amid military affairs, will be preserved for you.

Who could offer the sacrifice of almsgiving as the best commander could, whose great power provides abundant opportunities for showing mercy—if only he puts divine things before human things? Or did the prophet Daniel speak to Nebuchadnezzar in vain when he said: “May my counsel please you, O king: redeem your sins with almsgiving and your iniquities with compassion for the poor, and God will be merciful to your sins” (Dan. 4:24)? Is it not because the opportunity for almsgiving is greater for those who are more powerful?

For such men it is also possible to perform the greater form of almsgiving: namely, to forgive those who offend. Those whose anger is a messenger of death grant pardon more laudably. Those who are permitted to exact the punishment of blood love their enemies more gloriously.

You have both works of mercy in your power if you put divine things before human things. You are especially shown to put divine things before human things when you swear falsely to no one and deceive no one by a deceptive oath.

Even if he is an ancient enemy, even if he has inflicted monstrous wounds on the vitals of the commonwealth [Note: Col. 0943D: The reading here appears to be *vulnera*, “wounds”], he must not be deceived by a false oath; even if his life hinders and his death advances peace, nevertheless, excellent commander, not even if you are compelled ought you to swear falsely.

Whether dealing with one man, with a people, or with many nations against whom you have undertaken to wage war, either undertake the struggle while remaining without an oath, or do not dare in any way to free or assist the commonwealth by committing the crime of violating an oath.

For what does it profit him to conquer whom the devil has conquered, so that he swore falsely in hope of victory?

It is good always to put divine things before human things and to speak freely and willingly in the words of holy Job: “As waves of the sea hung over me, so I feared God” (Job 31:23).

For this reason, when the Psalmist sang, “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest upon your holy mountain?” (Ps. 14:1), he answered himself in God’s person with these words: “He who speaks truth in his heart, who has not dealt deceitfully with his tongue, who has not done evil to his neighbor, and has not accepted reproach against his neighbor; he who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive” (ibid., 3–4).

Therefore he will dwell in the Lord’s tabernacle and rest upon His holy mountain who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive. But the man who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive is the one who fulfills in his actions whatever he swears in words.

Let no one think that an enemy to whom he swears ought not to be counted as a neighbor. For this very reason an oath is sworn: so that he may be regarded as a neighbor. From the moment, therefore, that he wishes to become a friend and embraces the law of peace, he is already a neighbor. And whoever swears faithfully to him swears to his neighbor and does not deceive.

[Col. 0944A] 16. A false oath is the worst sacrilege and, if you consider the matter somewhat more deeply, it is always useless, especially for those governing an army. The changeable hearts of young men are frequently bound by the bond of the oath, so that they may undertake wars with steadfast loyalty. Security for commanders is then firm if fear of religion does not allow soldiers to swear falsely.

How grave and harmful, then, that they should see or perceive that the oath can easily be dissolved and, by the example of their commander, be invited to regard perjury as a light matter!

Whatever you confirm with an oath, therefore, always keep valid—whether you promise favor to an enemy, pardon to an accused person, or rewards to those laboring with you. Make it credible by carrying it out, invoking the name of God. You must not make it void because of any consideration of advantage or fear of any danger.

Let the word whose faithfulness has God as its witness be firm and unchangeable.

There is plainly one reason for dissolving an oath: if, in anger, you have sworn something by which you could offend the God by whom you swear. For example, if you swear threateningly that the offenders can never make satisfaction to you; if you threaten, under oath, the destruction of a city or people; if you swear that prayer must never be offered in a church; or if, overcome for the moment by the weakness of human temptation, you swear to carry out anything else that fear of God forbids.

Then, plainly, the oath must not be fulfilled, because in this case you are not putting human things before divine things, but rather keeping divine things in view, so that you may regret having sworn in this way and be ashamed to fulfill what you swore.

Thus too divine things are put before human things, and the rule of those words begins to be observed—a rule that forbids people to swear quickly, indeed that wishes them never to swear: “Do not swear,” He says in the Gospel, “neither by heaven nor by earth; but let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no’” (Matt. 5:34).

Whoever puts this into practice is an imitator of the Son of God Himself, of whom blessed Paul speaks in this way: “There is not in him ‘Yes’ and ‘No’; but ‘Yes’ has been in him” (2 Cor. 1:18, 20) always.

For He is unchangeable, as the true God, and naturally one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Seeking His name, the most faithful Moses, trembling at the heavenly voice addressed to him, heard: “I am who I am. And you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14).

Surely great is the glory of remaining in Him who is and following Him who is. And because our weak nature makes us changeable, and we cannot be compared with the unchangeable God by equal power, so that, just as He is always in us, we might also be able to be in Him, let our speech at least be “Yes, yes; no, no.” Whether an oath is involved or not, let us strive to remain absolutely firm in the truth.

For truth is divine, and from it the Son of God said with complete truthfulness: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). And just as we remember John saying of love, “Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him” (1 John 4:16), so likewise, if we wish to say, we do not lie: “Whoever remains in truth remains in God, and God remains in him.”

Therefore let us put truth before all temporal advantages, and then we shall rightly be found to put divine things before human things. Let reason plainly demonstrate the truth to us, or let divinely inspired Scripture commend it, or let the faithful teaching of priests show it.

For under the appearance of truth, falsehood is very often defended. Unless pious humility of heart is present in good commanders, so that whenever they seek the truth they remove the authority of secular rank, human things will pitiably be placed before divine things. Then a man, although a commander, yet a disciple of the Church, will rashly dare to teach the Church and will refuse to follow the judgments of priests, preferring to judge priestly judgments.

17. On a certain occasion we have come to this subject, which, as I think, is necessary for one who always wishes to put divine things before human things.

As a good commander, consult the Church in all matters, if you think piously; hasten to obey priests; do nothing without their counsel, since you are aided by their prayers.

Above all, however, among the duties of religion, learn to offer obedience alone. And if some scruple troubles your mind, do not readily follow your own opinion, nor try to persuade others of it unless you have first learned that it has pleased the priests.

Remember what God says to you in Deuteronomy: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you everything” (Deut. 32:7). Consult, therefore, those whom God, the Lord of knowledge, has warned you ought to be consulted.

Even if fullness of knowledge and the ability to speak with greater eloquence are available to you, consult the priests with your head bowed in submission to holy humility. Consult them piously by asking what they answer, not violently by ordering them what to reply.

Never let it please you to rescind the decrees of the canons in the provinces where you exercise command. If you fear transgressing public laws established by a human being, how will you attempt to oppose the decrees of the Holy Spirit?

Do you not know that the Fathers spoke under the impulse of the Holy Spirit? If we rescind their commands, we heap insult upon Him who spoke through them. Perhaps the apostolic rebuke can fittingly be applied to us: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2).

Therefore, wishing to have zeal for God according to knowledge, keep the right order and beware of the wrong one. The right order is that priests teach and laypeople are taught; and that everyone who boasts of belonging to the Church should live by the laws of the Church, especially those confirmed by antiquity.

Hence even a custom without a law—which the tradition of the holy Church has nevertheless handed down to posterity for perpetual observance—seems to deserve observance with the same reverence and must not be removed if it is not contrary to the true faith.

Do not let the differing customs of Churches offend your minds while the faith is one. For this vice enters childish and almost foolish minds: they seek the custom of their own Church, where they were born or raised, in other Churches; and if they see any difference in custom, they suddenly suffer a scandal to their faith.

But you, wise man, if you approve the faith of the Church to which you have come, immediately follow its custom, and do not presume to introduce any novelty into the sacred rite.

For if a changed custom scandalizes you, it can likewise scandalize the people, whose goodwill the best commander always hastens to secure in good matters, frequently recalling the apostolic words: “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and to the Church of God” (1 Cor. 10:32).

It therefore seems better that, lest any stumbling block be given to the Gospel of Christ by scandalizing the multitude of Christian people, you, as a wise commander, patiently endure your own offense until you either somehow grasp the reason for the other custom—which has offended you—or embrace it with affection, provided, as must often be said, that no danger to the faith is feared.

Only what does not oppose the faith ought to be endured with equanimity, for the sake of avoiding scandal to the people. For this too certainly belongs to the preservation of the faith: avoiding scandal to the people. A scandalized people easily rushes into schisms, and you know how every faith is endangered in schism.

It is therefore good that, with your favor, consent, and complete lack of prohibition, each Church should follow its own custom according to the most pious decrees of the Fathers; and that you should become a participant in the custom maintained by the Church where, for a time or because of the needs of your administration, you have lived.

Otherwise, to love what one is accustomed to and vehemently recoil from what is unfamiliar is excessive justice, deserving not praise but the strongest reproach, if the judgment of the wisest Solomon is pleasing: “Do not be exceedingly just, and do not be wiser than necessary, lest you become stupefied” (Eccles. 7:17).

What does “lest you become stupefied” mean? Do not remain cold. Who remains cold? The one from whom the warmth of love is withdrawn.

Do not, therefore, be exceedingly just.

## SIXTH RULE. Do not be exceedingly just.

18. And let this be your sixth rule of innocence, as you are occupied with military affairs. Whatever you say, do, or arrange in order to please God and human beings, and wonderfully to exclude the coldness of iniquity through the fervor of charity, do not be excessively just, nor wiser than necessary. Does someone incur the guilt of a very grave offense and deserve to feel judicial censure? Moderate, excellent commander, the impulse of severity; and while punishments are being inflicted on the guilty, let piety say in your inner ears: “Do not be excessively just” (ibid.). Has someone, forgetful of friendship, neglected to render the duties owed? Is he worthy of rejection and deserving of harsh injury? Restrain, I beg you, your righteous anger; do not repay like with like. Do not regard him as though he were an enemy, but correct him still as a friend, with the most wise Solomon answering you: “Do not be excessively just.”

Be just, therefore, but do not be excessively just. Be just, so that you may correct the restless; do not be excessively just, so that you may console the fainthearted, receive the weak, and be patient toward all. Consider whom you command and what hard hearts you desire to bend; so that, now threatening, now striking, now granting pardon, you neither allow the sins of soldiers to remain altogether unpunished nor always inflict punishments proportionate to their offenses, saying to yourself: “Do not be excessively just.” How many things, most wise commander, must be overlooked, how many endured, how many touched lightly, how many even granted through the intercessions of priests, by one who wisely hears: “Do not be excessively just!” You can silently consider various kinds of faults for which the one who said, “Do not be excessively just,” wished to foresee a remedy.

Among other things, we shall wound no one with the hidden arrow of detraction, nor investigate too anxiously the conduct of those who live well in order to discover how they may be blamed, if faithful Scripture speaks to each one of us through the Holy Spirit: “Do not be excessively just.” For one who examines the whole life of his neighbor in every respect of justice, setting aside consideration of human frailty, strives culpably to be excessively just—as though anyone who begins to avoid sins could live without sin, especially since the Apostle James confirms: “For we all offend in many things” (James 3:2). Therefore the proud detractor is rightly called back from the exaltation of judging when he is told: “Do not be excessively just,” so that he may willingly fulfill what Paul, the Vessel of Election and teacher of the Gentiles, says: “If anyone is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

This, then, is what “Do not be excessively just” means: “Consider yourself, lest you also be tempted.” But whoever grows angry at those who offend as though he himself were entirely free from offenses immediately falls miserably into the abyss of cruelty. And while the aforesaid Apostle cries out, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ,” the person who bears no one’s burden through patience becomes unbearable to everyone; as hatred toward many gradually grows, he first opens the door to seditions and then to public battles. Desiring to be excessively just, he truly becomes unjust and unworthy of the name or office of commander.

Therefore, excellent commander, I repeat this necessary exhortation more often, and impress this sixth rule of innocence upon you with great insistence, as you are occupied with military affairs: “Do not be excessively just.” “Piety is useful for all things” (1 Timothy 4:8); it is not I but that same most holy Paul who says this. Although justice makes a commander terrible, piety makes him beloved. The administration of the commonwealth, the security of salvation, and the good of concord are better served when the excellent commander chooses to be loved rather than feared. A beloved commander is a wall for his homeland. But one who at all times appears to be feared through sustained severity makes all his subjects disloyal; he easily fears treachery and more easily suffers from it; he lives as a stranger among his own people; finally, he fears as much as he is feared. He cannot in any way escape this scourge of unhappiness unless, having become gentle and gracious toward all, he learns to say to himself when he judges another: “Do not be excessively just.”

### SEVENTH RULE. Remember that you are a Christian.

19. Remember that you are a Christian, so that you may more easily keep Christ’s commandments. For Christ, teaching gentleness, also tempered the justice of the Law, distinguishing the Law from the Gospel by this contrast. Since the Law did not permit killing, in the Gospel it is not even permissible to become angry. In the Law adultery was forbidden; in the Gospel, even looking at a woman in order to desire her is judged to be part of the adultery already committed. In the Law a bill of divorce was sufficient for separating spouses; in the Gospel, no cause for dissolving a marriage is permitted without the guilt of fornication. The Law prohibited swearing falsely; the Gospel commanded that one not swear at all. Establishing the measure of vengeance, the Law said to the ancients: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Leviticus 24:20); but Christ did not wish the disciples of the Gospel to await any vengeance. Rather, he instructed the person struck once to offer the other cheek to the one striking him. He commanded one who had been compelled to go one thousand paces to go two thousand, entirely prohibiting retaliation.

The Law permitted hatred to be repaid to enemies, but allowed love to friends; whereas the sacred commandment of the Gospel says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 5:44). And when the Gospel had shown that it excelled the Law in these greater virtues, it recalled the Christian from vainglory and summoned him to mercy, of which God alone is witness. At the same time giving believers the rule and words of prayer, it bound those who pray by this condition: whoever asks that his own debts be forgiven must profess that he forgives the debts of others; he will receive nothing from the Lord if he is unwilling to grant anything to his fellow servant.

For the simplicity of the fasting Christian also pleases the just Judge; and he is commanded to gather riches where he is commanded to have his heart: in heaven, that is, where he hastens to dwell, not on earth, from which he departs day by day. Otherwise he will remain wholly in darkness, unless the intention of his mind, like the eye of the body, shines simply upon the limbs of good works in order to illuminate them.

Moreover, when he is admonished not to serve two masters; not to be anxious about tomorrow; not to judge, lest he be judged; when he is blamed for seeing the speck in his brother’s eye but not seeing the beam in his own; and when he is commanded not to give what is holy to dogs or dare to cast pearls before swine; when he is told to ask in order to receive, seek in order to find, and knock in order that it may be opened to him—by many methods and arguments it is shown how greatly a Christian must take care of a praiseworthy purpose, lest the dignity of so great a name appear to go astray in him.

20. Therefore, so that your attention may return to each of the things that we inserted above from the Gospel, whenever the authority of your command compels you to draw the sword from its sheath, remember that you are a Christian, for whom it is not permissible to be angry with his brother without cause; and think for a long time, lest the vengeance you appear to inflict exceed the proper measure. For if it is sacrilegious for a Christian to become angry, how much more so to kill.

Thus punish the guilty person, Christian commander, so that, striking mercifully, you may wish to destroy not the human being but the vice; and hasten to preserve public discipline, lest it perish when the guilty person perishes. Everywhere mindful of your faith, both in avoiding crimes and in correcting shameful conduct. For the greatest power is accustomed to give itself free rein in the penalties of sin whenever false happiness itself becomes a greater unhappiness: because no one dares to restrain the person committing crimes, either what is permitted becomes pleasing, or everything that is pleasing is thought to be permitted.

When such temptations knock at the mind, even though the dignity of office and a numerous household of dependents are available; even though the sinner may perhaps be praised in the desires of his soul and the one who acts unjustly be blessed—ascending the watchtower of self-restraint, remember that you are a Christian. See that, for a Christian, looking in order to desire is part of adultery. Let blessed Paul the Apostle say to you: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Hebrews 13:4). Let Job, tested and not rejected, say: “For it is a great anger, and a fire burning on every side” (Job 31:12), to desire another man’s wife. Let the most holy Paul say again: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?” (1 Corinthians 6:15). Warned by these words, you will easily be able to return from the precipice of pleasure.

And whenever you swear by almighty God, perhaps compelled to do so by some great necessity of the commonwealth, at least remember to avoid perjury if you cannot altogether escape the oath. Remember, then—remember that you are a Christian. Conducting the military office laudably, make many friends for yourself through frequent benefits, although you are commanded to love your enemies. Be more good than severe, because this alone is the perfect praise of an excellent commander: always to forget injuries. Thus, through the discipline of this seventh virtue, while you continually say to yourself, “Remember that you are a Christian,” may you deserve to live happily both in this age and in the age to come, where Christian commanders will be granted perpetual rule.

[Col. 0949]

## FULGENTIUS FERRANDUS’ ABRIDGMENT OF THE CANONS (C, S)

[Col. 0949B] 1. That neophytes are not to be ordained (Council of Nicaea, title 2; Council of Sardica, title 14; Council of Laodicea, title 3).

2. That anyone chosen from the laity for the episcopate must first pass one year in ecclesiastical ministry through all the grades (Council of Suffetula).

3. That anyone who, after baptism, has enlisted in secular military service is to be excluded from ordination (Council of Zella).

4. That a bishop is to be ordained by three bishops, with the consent of the others given in writing, together with the confirmation of the metropolitan or primate (Council of Nicaea, titles 4 and 6; Council of Antioch, title 19; Council of Laodicea, title 12; Council of Carthage under Bishop Genethlius, title 10; Universal Council of Carthage, title 49; Council of Zella, from a letter of Pope Siricius).

5. That, in ordaining a bishop, additional bishops beyond the three are to be added if anyone raises an objection (Council of Carthage, title 50).

6. That one bishop is not to ordain another bishop, except in the Roman Church (Council of Zella, from a letter of Pope Siricius).

7. That a bishop who, after accepting the laying on of hands, refuses the ministry is to remain excommunicated until he consents (Council of Antioch, title 17). But if, though willing, he is not accepted by the people, he must await a plenary synod without loss of his honor (Council of Antioch, title 18).

8. That a bishop who has been ordained but is not accepted is not to occupy another Church; rather, he is to sit as a presbyter in the Church where he had been a presbyter (Council of Ancyra, title 18).

9. That the statutes of the councils are first to be impressed upon an ordained bishop (Council of Carthage, title 10).

10. That an ordained bishop is to receive from his ordainer a signed letter containing both the day of his ordination and the name of the consul (Council of Milevis, title 4).

11. That the decision of the mother Church is sufficient for choosing a bishop (Council of Septimunicum; Council of Macrian).

[Col. 0950B] 12. That a bishop is not to be ordained in a village or hamlet (Council of Laodicea, title 55).

13. That a bishop is not to be ordained for a diocese that has never had a bishop, except with the consent of the bishop to whom that diocese belongs, and then only by a plenary council and with the authority of the primate (Council of Carthage, titles 52 and 54; Council of Carthage in the basilica, title 5).

14. That a bishop ordained for a diocese is to possess that diocese alone (Council of Carthage, title 54).

15. That bishops, presbyters, and deacons are not to be ordained unless they have made all their people Christians (Council of Carthage, title 3).

16. That bishops, presbyters, and deacons are to abstain from their wives (Council of Carthage, title 1; Council of Zella).

17. That no bishop is to establish himself in a diocese after abandoning the mother Church (Council of Carthage, title 6).

18. That bishops or clerics are not to pass from city to city, nor from province to province (Council of Nicaea, title 11; Council of Sardica, titles 2 and 3; Council of Antioch, titles 3 and 21; Council of Constantinople, titles 2 and 3).

19. That bishops are to remain in another city for only three weeks (Council of Sardica, title 15).

20. That those who wish to remain in another city out of fear of persecution are not to be prohibited (Council of Sardica, title 22).

21. That no bishop, even if chosen by the people, is to take possession of a vacant Church except by the authority of a plenary council (Council of Antioch, title 45).

22. That no bishop appointed as administrator of a see is to hold it for more than one year; rather, he himself is to seek a bishop for them (Council of Carthage, title 9).

23. That episcopal administrators are to urge the congregations that do not have a bishop to accept one. If they neglect to accept him, then, after the administrator has been removed, they are to remain as they are until they seek a bishop for themselves (Council of Macrian).

24. That no bishop is to usurp another’s congregation (Council of Carthage under Saint Gratus, title 9; Council of Carthage under Bishop Genethlius, title 9; likewise Council of Carthage, title 5).

25. That a bishop who, without the judgment of the bishops, retains a congregation that he believes belongs to his own see is to lose the case (Council of Carthage, title 12).

26. That no bishop is to dare to claim a congregation belonging to another (Council of Juncus).

27. That a bishop is not to receive or ordain another bishop’s cleric (Council of Nicaea, title 12; Council of Sardica, titles 19 and 20; Council of Antioch, title 22; Council of Carthage under Saint Gratus, title 2; likewise Council of Carthage, title 28).

28. That no bishop is to ordain another’s monk in a church or make him superior in his monastery (Council of Carthage, title 14).

29. That a bishop is not to perform an ordination in the presence of catechumens (Council of Laodicea, title 4).

30. That if necessity compels a bishop to veil a virgin before the age of twenty-five, the council that established this number of years is not to hinder him (Council of Carthage, title 18).

31. That the bishop’s property is not to be subject to ecclesiastical property, but that he himself may dispose of it as he wishes (Council of Antioch, title 24).

[Col. 0951C] 32. That no bishop is to make outsiders, or even heretical relatives, his heirs (Council of Carthage, title 15).

33. That bishops and clerics are to confer nothing by gifts upon those who are not Catholics (Council of Carthage, title 23).

34. That bishops or presbyters are not to transfer to other places anything belonging to the places where they are ordained until they have first rendered an account (Council of Hippo Regius, title 5).

35. That bishops are to be compelled to return to the Church whatever they have acquired in their own name; but whatever is given to them they may bestow upon whomever they wish (Council of Hippo Regius, title 8).

36. That the bishop is to have authority over the administration of ecclesiastical property (Council of Antioch, title 25).

[Col. 0951D] 37. That without the bishop’s knowledge no one is to dare either to give or receive the offerings of produce owed to the Church (Council of Gangra, titles 7 and 8).

38. That the bishop of the mother Church is not to usurp anything that has been donated to churches established in the diocese (Council of Hippo Regius, title 9).

39. That the sons of bishops are not to be joined in marriage to pagans, heretics, or schismatics (Council of Carthage, title 21).

40. That the sons of bishops or clerics are neither to put on spectacles nor attend them (Council of Carthage, title 20).

[Col. 0952A] 41. That bishops are not to emancipate their sons unless the sons have already been tested (Council of Carthage, title 22).

42. That bishops are not to go indiscriminately to the imperial court (Council of Sardica, titles 9, 10, and 11; Council of Antioch, title 24).

43. That any bishop who has requested a public trial from the emperor is to be deprived of his office (Council of Carthage, title 9).

44. That each bishop may draw up petitions when something is to be requested in public courts against heretics (Council of Marazan).

45. That a bishop is to do nothing without the counsel of the metropolitan except what pertains to the governance of his own Church (Council of Antioch, title 9).

46. That bishops are not to sail without a letter of authorization from the primate (Council of Carthage, title 36).

47. That bishops are not to sell Church property without the advice of the primate (Council of Carthage, title 5; Council of Hippo Regius, title 9).

48. That, through the bishop’s foresight, a place of residence is to be chosen for virgins who are orphans (Council of Carthage, title 40 [Note: [Col. 0951D] The Treves manuscript incorrectly has title 11.]).

49. That the periods of penance are to be assigned to penitents by episcopal judgment (Council of Carthage, title 39).

50. That, by episcopal judgment, the period of penance or reconciliation is to be determined for a Donatist who, after having performed penance among his own people, converts (Council of Carthage, title 2).

51. That a bishop is to hear accused presbyters after summoning five bishops; deacons with three; but he alone is to investigate the cases of the others (Council of Carthage, title 17).

52. But that one bishop should not claim jurisdiction for himself was enacted in another Council of Carthage.

53. That no excommunicated bishop, presbyter, or deacon is to receive communion (Council of Nicaea, title 5; Council of Sardica, title 17; Council of Carthage, title 8 [Note: [Col. 0952D] The Corbie manuscript has title 9.]; Council of Antioch, title 2).

54. That if a bishop has been excommunicated by a synod, he is not to dare to communicate; and if he does so, he is not to have hope of restoration (Council of Antioch, title 4; Council of Hippo Regius, title 3).

55. That, if a bishop has a case, he is to be heard by twelve bishops (Council of Carthage under Saint Genethlius, title 8).

[Col. 0952D] 56. That bishops appointed as judges in a case are to hear it on the day fixed for the proceedings (Council of Septimunicum).

57. That if two bishops have a dispute in one province, they are not to summon bishops from another province for judgment (Council of Sardica, title 4).

58. That if there are many episcopal judgments concerning an accused bishop, the metropolitan of another province is to be summoned (Council of Antioch, title 14). What is to be observed in accusations against bishops (Council of Carthage, title 15).

59. That a bishop against whom judgment has been rendered may appeal to the apostolic see, if he wishes (Council of Sardica, title 5).

[Col. 0953A] 60. That if he appeals [Note: [Col. 0953D] Another item appears to be missing here.], no one is to be ordained in his see (Council of Sardica, title 6).

61. That if he appeals from the judges appointed by the primate, other judges of greater number are to be assigned. That if he appeals from these also [Possibly: “But if he appeals from these also”], the matter is to be deferred to the judgment of the council (Council of Thenit).

62. That if a bishop condemned by judging bishops is acquitted before more eminent bishops, it is not to harm those who judged him if they judged with good intent (Council of Carthage, title 11).

63. That a bishop who has been condemned by all the bishops of the province is not to have the opportunity to reopen the trial (Council of Antioch, title 15).

64. That a bishop condemned by the bishops whom he himself chose as judges is not to dare to appeal elsewhere (Council of Carthage, titles 3 and 15).

65. That bishops appointed as judges in any case are themselves to choose the place of hearing (Council of Zella).

66. That a deposed bishop is not to refer his case to the emperor (Council of Antioch, title 12).

67. That an accused bishop or anyone from the clergy who has been accused before the Church is not to proceed to public courts (Council of Carthage, title 18).

68. That a bishop who, after being summoned a second or third time, has scorned to come is to be suspended from the fellowship of the bishops (Council of Zella).

69. That no bishop, presbyter, or deacon is to celebrate Passover with the Jews (Council of Antioch, title 1).

70. That bishops, presbyters, or deacons are not to be contractors or agents (Council of Carthage, title 24).

71. That bishops or clerics are not to dine in a church unless they are passing through (Council of Carthage, title 38).

72. That bishops and presbyters are not to make offerings in their own homes (Council of Laodicea, title 56).

73. That a bishop is not to suspend from communion someone whom he claims confessed a certain sin to him alone (Council of Carthage, title 2).

74. That a bishop is not to choose his own successor (Council of Antioch, title 23 [Note: [Col. 0953D] Read: title 6.]).

75. That bishops are to attend the council; or, if they do not attend, they are to present their excuses in the tractoria or before the primate (Council of Laodicea, title 38; Council of Carthage, title 11).

[Col. 0953D] 76. That, except for the elderly who cannot be moved from their place and sick bishops, any bishop who, after being admonished, does not attend the council is to be deprived of communion (Council of Marazan; Council of Thusdrit; likewise Council of Thenit; Council of Septimunicum).

77. That a bishop who, without having accepted a legation, presumes to attend a universal council is not to be admitted to that council by the bishops who have accepted the legation (Council of Thusdrit).

78. That no bishop is to dare to place himself before his predecessors (Council of Milevis, title 2).

[Col. 0954A] 79. That chorepiscopi—that is, vicars of bishops—are to ordain neither presbyters nor deacons, but only subdeacons (Council of Ancyra, title 13; Council of Antioch, title 10).

80. That vicars of bishops may issue letters of authorization (Council of Antioch, title 8).

81. That the bishop of the first see is not to be called “prince of priests” or “high priest” (Council of Carthage, title 34).

82. That Mauretania Sitifensis is to have its own primate (Council of Carthage, title 6).

83. That bishops of the first see are to be constituted from the Council of Carthage whenever a dispute has arisen (Council of Carthage, title 7).

[Col. 0954B] 84. That the primates of the various provinces are to send the names of the bishops to the Church of Carthage (Council of Carthage, title 3).

85. That a presbyter is not to be ordained before the age of thirty, however worthy he may be (Council of Neocaesarea, title 10).

86. That one baptized in illness is not to be ordained a presbyter, except perhaps on account of a good life or a scarcity of men (Council of Neocaesarea, title 11).

87. That if an ordained presbyter has confessed [Possibly: “been convicted”] of a crime, or belongs among those who have lapsed, he is not to be accepted (Council of Nicaea, title 8; Council of Neocaesarea, title 11).

88. That a presbyter is not to attend a banquet for a second marriage (Council of Neocaesarea, title 7).

[Col. 0954C] 89. That no one is to dare to refuse communion on account of the offering of a married presbyter (Council of Gangra, title 4).

90. That a presbyter, without consulting the bishop, is not to dare to celebrate the rites to be performed in any place (Council of Carthage, title 7).

91. That a presbyter, without consulting the bishop, is not to consecrate virgins; and that he is never to prepare chrism (Council of Carthage, title 43).

92. That the presbyters of a city are to command nothing without the bishop’s order, nor do anything in any parish (Council of Ancyra, title 14).

93. That presbyters who abstain from meat may touch it, and may even eat vegetables that have been cooked with meat (Council of Ancyra, title 14).

94. That presbyters are not permitted to issue letters of authorization (Council of Antioch, title 8).

95. That presbyters are not to sell Church property without the bishop’s knowledge (Council of Ancyra, title 15; Council of Hippo Regius, title 11).

96. That a presbyter who has incurred guilt is to be heard by six or seven bishops (Council of Carthage under Bishop Genethlius, title 8 [Note: [Col. 0953D] The Treves manuscript has title 9.]).

97. That a presbyter who sacrificed to idols and afterward fought for the faith is not to be deprived of his rank; nevertheless, he is neither to sacrifice nor to preach [Note: [Col. 0954D] This canon is taken from the Council of Ancyra, title 1.].

98. That if a presbyter takes a wife, he is to be deposed; but if he has committed fornication, he is also to be compelled to perform penance (Council of Neocaesarea, title 1).

99. That a presbyter or deacon who, abandoning his own Church, has gone over to another is to be deposed if he does not return after being recalled by his bishop (Council of Antioch, title 3).

100. That a presbyter or deacon who, after being deprived of office by his own bishop, presumes to perform any part of the sacred ministry is not to have hope of restoration (Council of Antioch, title 4).

101. That a presbyter or deacon who has separated himself from the Church and erected an altar in his own house is to be deposed (Council of Antioch, title 5; Council of Carthage, title 7).

102. That presbyters or deacons, if they have been unjustly excommunicated, may appeal to neighboring bishops (Council of Sardica, title 18).

103. That presbyters of another region are not to celebrate the sacrifice in the presence of presbyters (Council of Neocaesarea, title 12).

104. That there are to be seven deacons (Council of Neocaesarea, title 13).

105. That deacons are not to be chosen by popular vote (Council of Laodicea, title 13).

106. That deacons are not to receive communion before the presbyter (Council of Nicaea, title 14).

107. That a deacon is not to sit in the presence of a presbyter unless ordered to do so (Council of Laodicea, title 19).

108. That a subdeacon is neither to distribute bread nor bless the chalice (Council of Laodicea, title 25).

[Col. 0955C] 109. That a deacon or any cleric invited to an agape is not to take away a portion (Council of Laodicea, title 24).

110. That a deacon or cleric is not to be a magician or enchanter, nor make amulets (Council of Laodicea, title 34).

111. That a deacon or even a layperson is not to depart anywhere without a letter of authorization (Council of Laodicea, title 39).

112. That deacons or any clerics are not to depart for foreign places without the bishop’s command (Council of Laodicea, title 40 [Note: [Col. 0955D] Treves 11; Corbie 20; both require correction.]).

113. That deacons or clerics are not to attend the spectacles displayed at weddings (Council of Laodicea, title 52).

114. That deacons, or any clerics, or even Christian laypeople are not to hold a banquet from contributions (Council of Laodicea, title 53).
