# LIFE OF SAINT FULGENTIUS, BISHOP OF RUSPE

(See *Patrologia*, volume LXV, column 117.)

## In the Year of Our Lord 540. Saint Justus, Bishop of Urgell.

[Col. 0961B]

## NOTICE (from Fabricius)

Saint Justus of Urgell, or Urgel, a bishop in Spain, subscribed to the Second Council of Toledo in the year 527 [alternatively 531], and to the Council of Lérida in 542 [alternatively 546]. His mystical exposition of the *Song of Songs*, addressed to Pope Sergius—not the Roman pope, but the bishop of Tarragona, his metropolitan—and mentioned by Isidore of Seville, chapter 21, Honorius III, 25, and Trithemius, chapter 210, was published by Menradus Maltherus at Haguenau in 1529; reprinted in the *Micropresbytericum* of Basel in 1550, in both editions of the *Orthodoxographi* in 1555 and 1569, and in the complete *Bibliothecae Patrum*, Paris, Cologne, and the latest Lyon edition, volume IX, p. 731; and separately under the care of Georg Rostius, Halle in Saxony, 1617.

The prefatory letter to Sergius was also published in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, [Col. 0961C] volume III, p. 312 (new edition, volume III, p. 119), and in the Councils of Spain with the notes of Cardinal de Aguirre, volume II, p. 273; as was another letter to the deacon Justus, at whose urging he declares that he undertook this work. See Nicholas Antonius IV, 1; *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*, volume I, pp. 208ff.; *Acta Sanctorum*, volume VI, May 28, p. 773.

[Col. 0961]

# LETTER OF SAINT JUSTUS OF URGELL TO POPE SERGIUS (C, S)

To my truly most devout lord, and especially rich by the grace of God, ever blessed in Christ, Lord Sergius, pope: Justus, bishop.

Knowing that you have labored with such diligent zeal for the refreshment of the poor that you have gained for them temporal consolation and for yourself an eternal reward, and now judging that you have devoted yourself wholly to the word of God, from which you have never been absent, for the cultivation of the soul, I have endeavored to send you a spiritual gift in bodily form. If Christ should make it most welcome to you, not because of our merit but by his own gift, it may perhaps happen that during the days of fasting you will come to the table somewhat refreshed and, before receiving food, feel that you have already tasted something beforehand.

In saying this I do not arrogantly seek to suggest the merit of this transmission before you have approved it; but with charity intervening, in which I possess you wholly, I confidently trust, presuming upon your mind as upon my own, that it will be acceptable to you without any doubt. Therefore, knowing that you are my true brother in Christ, I have judged that I should first offer you the little book on the exposition of the canonical book entitled the *Song of Songs*, which, with Christ’s illumination, we recently published.

In it you will recognize that I have received not our own things so much as those that are yours, since you love them in this way. I beg you to read it often with the same concern with which you are vigilant in Christ, so that, if you perceive anything there requiring correction, you may point it out with complete freedom. And so you may offer it to the other brothers in Christ for rereading or, if it should perhaps please you, for transcription.

It happened, however, that when the parchment began to fail, the same writing was accommodated in smaller letters and in gatherings of equal size, without being surrounded by carefully constructed lateral margins. Therefore, if you judge the work mentioned to possess any merit—for, as I said above, this very thing is yours, since the Lord has granted it—hasten to have the transcript more usefully arranged with greater care.

If the work proceeds worthy of praise, I shall report you to Christ as its author; but if it proves open to criticism, since it belongs to both of us, I shall immediately take you as my associate, because it is fitting that you should so arrange the beautiful things God has bestowed that you receive not reproach for negligence but the fruit of charitable diligence. Thus our brothers, who feast upon the expositions of the earlier Fathers, may also delight in some measure to feed upon these newer things that we offer them out of charity—not for our merit, but through God’s gift and their goodwill.

Now farewell in Christ, most devout lord, and cherish our littleness in the Lord by your holy prayers.

[Col. 0963]

# THE MYSTICAL EXPOSITION OF SAINT JUSTUS OF URGELL ON SOLOMON’S SONG OF SONGS (C, S)

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0963A]

### No. 1. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

This is the voice of the Church coming to Christ in a kiss, desiring that the offense which human beings had contracted with God by sinning might be undone, and desiring to find that peace through which, while we were enemies of God the Father, we are reconciled through his Son. Therefore the prophet says to God: “Give us your peace, Lord, and you have restored everything to us” (Isa. XXVI).

In the Gospel also (Luke XV), the father kissed the son returning from a distant region. At that time, in a certain sense, he gave a kiss to those coming to him, when he willed his only Son to be born as a human being, through whom he also granted that we might cling to him in the bond of peace. Finally, when Christ was born, the angels cried out with a united voice: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke VIII), because by saying such things they clearly taught us that he himself is our peace.

### No. 2. “For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest perfumes.”

We rightly understand Christ’s breasts as the apostles and evangelists; through them we are nourished in faith and refreshed by spiritual food. They are judged better than wine because the teaching of the Gospel is recognized as superior to the Law once given. There, there was a figure; here, the truth. There, as though with the harshness of wine, it showed that one should love only one’s neighbor and hate one’s enemy; here, the sweetness of grace urges us to pray for our enemies and teaches us to love those who hate us.

Christ’s breasts themselves—that is, the apostles—are also shown to be fragrant with the finest perfumes, because they shone with such great virtues [Col. 0963C] and such great miracles that the fragrance of their righteousness, diffused far and wide, delighted those who then looked upon them and continues to refresh all who hear them even now, just as one of them declares: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place” (2 Cor. II).

### No. 3. “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women have loved you.”

God anointed Christ with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. XLIV). His name also is like oil poured out: for all who are called Christians from Christ and are anointed with chrism, baptized in his name, and filled with the Holy Spirit are like the perfume that descends from the head into Aaron’s beard (Ps. CXXXII). This declares what is true, perfect, and most powerful: the Holy Spirit, poured out by God upon Christ, also descends to the hem of his garment and fills the whole Church, even to the end; by clinging to him, she is undoubtedly his garment.

For in the Transfiguration his face shone like the sun, as we read in the Gospel, and his garments became white like snow (Matt. XVII; Luke IX), such as no fuller on earth could make them. No teacher, after all, ever led his disciples to such brilliance as he did; or he makes believers in him washed clean from stains in this way, white like snow.

The young women, therefore—that is, the new Churches or the incorrupt souls—have loved him. Filled also with fragrant perfume, they say with the Apostle: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

### No. 4. “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance.”

The Lord says in the Gospel: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI). One is drawn to Christ who believes in Christ; but those run after him who imitate him or who, by his gift, make progress in following him.

### No. 5. “The king brought me into his chambers.”

Christ brought the Church into his chambers when he revealed to her the hidden mysteries of the Scriptures, as the Apostle says: “So that he might show in the ages to come the abundant riches of his grace in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus” (Eph. II).

Or, the saints are then brought wholly into Christ’s chambers when they are told at the end: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

### No. 6. “We shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts above one [reading uncertain].”

The saints exult and rejoice in the Lord when they remember how, through Christ’s breasts—that is, through the teaching of the apostles—they were nourished with spiritual milk. When they see this teaching of Christ as clearer than the commands of the ancient Law, they recognize Christ in it and through it. To them he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear. Amen, I say to you, many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matt. XIII; Luke X).

### No. 7. “The upright love you.”

For the perverse cannot love righteousness. Those are upright and love God who are not held captive by love of the creature, but, as befits the upright, placing the precious gift first, have clung to God, the author of all things, with the strongest love.

Those too are approved as rightly loving God who, established not only amid his benefits but also amid his scourges, give thanks in the same way as the one who said: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII)—that is, both when I receive joy as a gift and when I accept suffering, corrected by him.

As another man, tested by the most intense suffering, his flesh putrefying but his heart sincere, also said: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil? The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Let the name of the Lord be [blessed],” and so forth.

[Col. 0965A]

### No. 8. “I am black but beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar.”

Black through the confession of sins, beautiful through the grace of the sacrament: daughter of Jerusalem. For from that first Church which believed in Jerusalem the Church was born through the Gospel; or certainly, as the Apostle says: “The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. IV).

And rightly so, because she resembles the tents of Kedar, which is interpreted as “of darkness.” To his sons the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

She may also be called black when she is handed over to sufferings, reproaches, insults, and contempt. Consider her black and beautiful in Paul: “In everything we suffer affliction, but are not crushed; we are perplexed, but not abandoned; we are struck down, but do not perish” (2 Cor. IV).

“How like the tents of Kedar”: “We have become as the refuse of this world, the scum of all,” and, like Solomon’s skin, we always carry in our body the mortification of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh.

### No. 9. “Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.”

That is: do not despise me established in persecution. I have endured the heat of tribulations and have lost, as it were, the beauty of temporal joy: “For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV).

For among those am I of whom it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted”; and: “You will indeed have sorrow, but the world will rejoice; your sorrow will be turned into joy” (Matt. V; John XVI).

### No. 10. “The sons of my mother fought against me.”

That is, the sons of the Synagogue, who stoned the martyr Stephen while he was teaching and reproving them: “And a great persecution arose against the Church which was at Jerusalem, and all the brothers were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria” (Acts VII).

Or those also fought against the Church who persecuted Paul as he preached among the Gentiles, in every city. Likewise those who thought that burdens of the Law should be imposed upon those who had believed from among the Gentiles; blessed James, with the other apostles, wisely decreed that these burdens should be removed (Acts V).

For those also who had persuaded the Galatians believing in Christ to be circumcised are shown to have fought against the Church by disturbing the Gospel tradition. Of them the Apostle Paul says: “Even those who are circumcised do not keep the Law, but they wish you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh” (Gal. V). Of them he also said: “Would that those who are troubling you would mutilate themselves!” (Ibid.).

### No. 11. “They appointed me guardian of the vineyards.”

These vineyards too are the synagogues. For Saul had received authority and letters from the chief priests to hand over for punishment whichever believing men and women in Christ he might find (Acts XI and XXII), so that, while doing this, he might seem to guard the vineyard of the synagogues.

And it follows: “I did not guard my own vineyard.” For when Saul became Paul, and a persecutor became a preacher, while he preached the word of God and was wholly rejected by the Jews who contradicted him, he said to those same unbelievers: “It was necessary that the word of God be preached to you, but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of such salvation, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For thus the Lord commanded us through Scripture: ‘I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles, so that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth’” (Acts XIII; Isa. XLIX).

Or as he himself wrote to the Galatians: “You have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it, and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (Gal. I).

And again: “But whatever gains I had, these I counted as losses” (Phil. III), saying, as though under a riddle: “They appointed me guardian of the vineyards, but I did not guard my own vineyard.”

### No. 12. “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”

We read in the Gospel: “If they say, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ do not go out” (Matt. XXIV; Mark XIII). “Here” and “there” are recognized as parties; but Christ, lying down in the Catholic Church as at noon, has suffused the whole world with his radiance. He rests in those who burn in spirit and, through the love with which he illuminates the whole world, daily feeds the peoples who believe in him.

### No. 13. “Lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions.”

That is: if I do not recognize you dwelling in that brightness in which the whole company of your faithful stands, I shall begin to wander among the flocks of your companions—that is, among the gatherings of heretics.

The companions of Christ may be called companions in a certain respect because they profess his birth, passion, and resurrection. But since the Apostle says of them, “Having the appearance of godliness but denying its power” (2 Tim. V), they are proved to be no longer companions but adversaries.

### No. 14. “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks.”

This is Christ’s voice to the Church: “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women”—if you do not understand that you are the one to whom it is said in the psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear and forget your people and your father’s house, because the king desires your beauty” (Ps. XLIV)—because you alone have received the beauty of the incorruptible sacrament.

And he rightly says “among women,” that is, glorious among heresies. For they are appropriately called women because they have lost the virginity that exists in Christ.

Therefore do not wander by seeking me elsewhere in any way. For in you, where until now you did not seek me, I rest as at noon. Now understand where you should seek me feeding and guiding you, lest some pretense, as though in the night, lead you astray. For only in you, while I reign within you, does certain sincerity endure. Know that you are among those to whom, after my resurrection, I truly promised: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

But if, wavering in some way through doubt about my promises, you do not recognize either my presence or your own beauty, “go out and follow the tracks of your flocks.” For rightly will she proceed after the tracks of the flocks because she has abandoned the presence of the shepherd.

“And pasture your kids beside the shepherds’ tents”: delighting unjust people with the traditions or conventicles of heretics. Those deserve to be rebuked by such reproaches who do not recognize Christ in the Catholic Church, or themselves as the Catholic Church.

### No. 15. “To my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.”

The prophet Habakkuk says: “Are you angry, Lord, with the rivers, or is your fury against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea, when you ride upon your horses and your chariots are salvation?” (Hab. I).

Whom do we understand as the horses? The apostles and evangelists. Therefore Christ speaks to the Church.

“I have likened you to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots” when I converted the wise men of the world, calling them to my faith, so that, laying aside worldly pride, they might advance by running under me, who am true salvation; and, carrying me about through their devout preaching, might make me visible to the eyes of believers through faith.

And just as the prince of this world, who has now been cast out, used false philosophers like splendid chariots for destruction, so I, having filled the apostles with my wisdom, shall instruct believers for salvation.

### No. 16. “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.”

He proclaimed chastity as the companion of modesty. For it is said that the species of turtledoves, once deprived of bodily companionship, proceeds in solitude and no longer seeks carnal union.

Christ’s bride therefore possesses extraordinary beauty when, with modesty, she preserves chastity.

### No. 17. “Your neck is like necklaces.”

Those are indicated by the neck who do not cease meditating on the Law of God day and night, and who, like clean animals, continually return salutary teaching by ruminating upon it. Since these are splendid ornaments of the Church, they are described as the bride’s necklaces.

### No. 18. “We shall make golden necklaces for you.”

This is the voice of the teachers, who then arrange the ornaments of the Church mixed with gold and silver when they expound spiritual meanings with the brilliance of eloquence.

Necklaces flowing down from the head are customarily fitted to adorn the neck. Therefore those teachings are splendid which, proceeding from the head—that is, from Christ—minister in a spiritual office in such a way as to teach that our neck must be subjected to the yoke of Christ. Thus the Apostle says to such people: “Do not be wise in lofty things” (Rom. XI), and so forth.

### No. 19. “While the king was on his couch.”

The Gospels relate (Mark XIV; John XII) that two days before Passover, while the Lord was reclining, a woman who had an alabaster vessel poured genuine nard perfume over his head. This prophecy too says: “While the king was on his couch, my nard gave its fragrance.”

Both this and that event are therefore recognized as having been spoken or done figuratively. When our King was established on his couch—either on the cross, where he bowed his head and gave up his spirit, or in the tomb, where he rested buried in bodily form—the Church anointed him with the fragrant perfume of a devout confession, so that she might not cease proclaiming, for the salvation of believers, that he suffered voluntarily and rose from the dead on the third day by his own power.

### No. 20. “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh.”

The species of myrrh is known to be suitable for preparing the bodies of the dead. Therefore Christ is a bundle of myrrh: he suffered, died, and was buried.

“He shall dwell between my breasts.” The breasts of the Church are rightly understood as the learned, overflowing with spiritual milk, who nourish peoples being born in faith. They are those who, as commanded, do not cease by every means to proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

### No. 21. “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus.”

A cluster in Cyprus: Christ suspended on the wood of the cross. This kind of wood is always fragrant and incorruptible; for we mark the sign of the cross on the forehead together with the fragrance of chrism.

He says well, “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus for me,” because the sweetness of this cluster was granted not to those who crucified him, but to those who believed in the one who was crucified.

“In the vineyards of Engaddi”: among the peoples of the Synagogue, where the Lord’s passion was accomplished. Engaddi is interpreted as “the eye of my temptation.”

Read the Gospel, and you will find that the Pharisees and Sadducees intended nothing else in their questions than to test the Lord at every point and find grounds for accusing him. To them he says: “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” (Matt. XXII).

But although so great a good—the passion of Christ—was accomplished among them, it is plainly granted to us who have believed.

[Col. 0968C] ### No. 22. “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend.”

Christ declares the Church, whom he made his friend by the kiss of his peace, beautiful twice over, just as the Apostle taught that she is holy in body and spirit (1 Cor. VII), adding: “Your eyes are like those of doves.”

Nothing adorns the face of the body more than the arrangement of the eyes. Through them we appropriately understand the holy apostles, who were also able to foresee future things. Indicating their privileges, the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “You are the body of Christ” (1 Cor. XII). And elsewhere: “God appointed some in the Church, first apostles” (Eph. IV), and so forth.

When he says, “Your eyes are like those of doves,” he clearly reveals that these same apostles were commanded to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matt. X). Through the likeness of this bird he also demonstrates that they were filled with the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0968D] ### No. 23. “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved.”

The Psalmist proclaims Christ, whom the Church here recalls as beautiful and comely, saying: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips” (Ps. XLIV).

But this beauty of yours exists because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

When he adds, “Our couch is flourishing,” he shows that the Lord’s body, in which the Godhead rested, was pure and fragrant, born from the Virgin.

### No. 24. “The roofs of our houses.”

These houses in which Christ dwells are the saints, as the prophet says: “For I shall dwell in them” (Lev. XXVI; 2 Cor. VI).

The roofs and ceilings of these houses, however, made of cedar and cypress—woods recognized as incorruptible and fragrant—demonstrate the ordering of God and neighbor, granted from above through the Holy Spirit; that is, they show that the saints are to be such within themselves.

# CHAPTER II

### No. 25. “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

I am the adornment of the world, born from the virginity of the humble.

### No. 26. “Like a lily among thorns.”

To the man expelled from Paradise it was said: “Cursed is the earth in your works; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). This earth is understood as human flesh, which is accustomed to produce the goads of lust and the thorns of desire.

Therefore when he says, “Like a lily in the midst of thorns, so is my friend among the daughters,” he calls the heresies “daughters.” Since they are, as it were, reborn through baptism, they are called by the name of daughters; but, compared with thorns, they are shown to be corrupting and corruptible.

The Church knows nothing of this corruption. Compared with the purity of lilies, she gives off fragrance and shines in every direction.

### No. 27. “Like an apple among the trees of the forests.”

The Psalmist says: “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

There he is a son by adoption; here, by nature. Therefore among the saints or among the whole human race, although anyone may be counted by the title of son, no one is found like Christ. By the sweetness and refreshment of his fruit he surpasses the elect with incomparable beauty.

### No. 28. “Under the shadow of the one whom I desired.”

With the one whom I always sought to be present protecting me, I remained humble and secure.

### No. 29. “And his fruit is sweet to my throat.”

The Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

Although fruit therefore arises on the branch, it must nevertheless be attributed to the vine, from whose root the branch proceeded together with its fruit. Thus whatever the righteous bring to fruition in good works must all be referred to Christ.

In his fruits an incomparable sweetness is perceived. Those saints also who, under the image of the throat, were accustomed to ruminate what they had tasted—that is, to meditate upon the things of Christ—receive an exceedingly great sweetness from his fruit.

[Col. 0969D] ### No. 30. “He brought me into the wine chamber.”

As the Lord was about to ascend into heaven, he commanded the apostles not to depart from Jerusalem, saying to them: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world, and I am going to the Father; but you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

And as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. And when they had entered the upper room, they went up where Peter and John were staying. And shortly afterward: ‘All these were gathered with one accord with the women, and Mary, the mother of Jesus, and his brothers’; and there was a crowd of about one hundred and twenty people” (Acts I–II) assembled in this place.

When the Holy Spirit came upon them, they were filled; and when they began to speak in various languages, the people thought that they were full of new wine.

The Church is therefore brought into the wine chamber when this apostolic congregation, remaining in unity, is filled with the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle also says: “In one Spirit we were all baptized, whether slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (1 Cor. XII).

Because love is poured into the hearts of the godly through the Holy Spirit, he immediately added: “He ordered love in me.”

For this is ordered love: that a person love his neighbor as himself, but love God in such a way that he even renounce himself for God’s sake. In evil people too, what is loved is not the wickedness that they do, but the creature in whom they have been formed good by God.

This too is ordered love: that servants should not regard their lord as evildoers do, nor should they love one another with the detestable love of the wanton; but, even when necessary, they should correct one another freely, after superstition has been driven away, according to the saying: “Better are the wounds of a friend than the deceitful kisses of one who flatters” (Prov. XXVII); and again: “Those who rebuke shall be praised, and upon them blessing shall come” (Prov. XXIV).

[End of supplied source.]

## Number 31

“Support me with flowers; surround me with apples.” She desires to be joined to or surrounded by assemblies of the saints, she who languishes with devout and chaste love; for this languishing is not illness, but an ineffable longing, according to the saying: “My soul has fainted for your salvation, and I have hoped exceedingly in your word; my eyes have failed at your word, saying, ‘When will you comfort me?’” (Psalm 118). Happy are those who advance with such progress: for in a certain sense the one who greatly desires languishes and fails until he finds what he longs for or seeks.

[Col. 0970C]

## Number 32

“His left hand is under my head.” Solomon himself says in Proverbs: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom and abounds in prudence; length of days is in her right hand, and in her left hand are riches and glory.” Thus the chosen Church of Christ, having the left hand under her head, describes temporal things as subject to her; and she teaches that his right hand embraces her while she desires eternal things.

## Number 33

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does.” By the daughters of Jerusalem he means the holy and peaceful souls of teachers. By the clean and swift animals that do not cease ruminating and that feed in the fields of the holy Scriptures, he adjures them not to awaken her until she herself wishes it.

[Col. 0970D]

We know that the apostle Paul did this when he gave virgins advice, not a command, concerning the preservation of their holiness (I Corinthians 7); and in the Gospel the rich man is told: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and give to the poor” (Matthew 19). Elsewhere, eunuchs are praised—those who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven—and immediately it is added: “Let him who is able to receive it receive it.” Again, when the Apostle urges continence, he says: “I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but to encourage what is honorable and what may enable you to entreat God without impediment” (I Corinthians 7). And again to Philemon: “But without your counsel I wished to do nothing, so that your good might not be as though compelled, but voluntary.” For the beloved is in no way awakened until she wishes it when the vows of the saints are offered to the Lord by spontaneous choice.

[Col. 0971A]

## Number 34

“The voice of my beloved.” This voice of Christ, which is mentioned only in this prophecy, may appropriately be understood as that by which the race of dead human beings is raised in the Gospel, as he himself declares: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life” (John 5). And in the Apocalypse it is said: “Blessed is he who has a share in the first resurrection” (Revelation 20). He has a share in the first resurrection who, rescued from an evil habit, rises from death as Christ gives him life.

## Number 35

“Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains.” Christ comes leaping upon the mountains when he appears to the perfect as one more perfect; he leaps over the hills when, by the excellence of his majesty, he surpasses all the height of the saints.

[Col. 0971B]

## Number 36

“My beloved is like a doe.” He is like a doe because he appeared to us “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8); he is also like a fawn of the deer because, according to the flesh, he derived his origin from the saints who overcame the serpent.

## Number 37

“Behold, he himself stands behind our wall.” He stands behind our wall when he clothes himself with the veil of our body.

## Number 38

“Looking through the windows.” When he concealed something of himself but revealed something else, he looked out as though through windows and lattices. For he did not show himself completely, especially according to his divinity, when he said to Philip, who desired to see the Father: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me”; and elsewhere: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14). Or he looked out through the windows and lattices when he taught the people in parables. It may also be understood that he looked out through the windows when, during the Passion, his side was pierced by a lance and blood and water flowed forth, producing the sacraments of redemption and washing.

[Col. 0971C]

## Number 39

“My beloved speaks to me.” The beloved is often described in this book. For who is as beloved to the Church as the one for whom the martyrs laid down their lives? “Arise, hasten, and come”: arise, believe; hasten, and, having completed the course of devoted labor, receive the reward. “My friend,” reconciled to me through death; “my beautiful one,” made clean through washing.

[Col. 0971D]

## Number 40

“For winter has already passed.” Because temporal tribulation has come to an end.

## Number 41

“The rain has gone and departed.” Frequent and manifold temptation, or the persecution of the pagans, has ceased.

## Number 42

“Flowers have appeared on the earth.” The saints have multiplied throughout the world, arising in the month of renewals, when Easter is celebrated. To them the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3).

## Number 43

“The time of pruning has come.” Those who are planted in the house of the Lord, having been subjected to the pruning knife of discipline and cleansed from every superstition, are prepared for the fruits to come.

[Col. 0972A]

## Number 44

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in the land.” In the Gospel, the soul of an exceedingly chaste widow of eighty-four years, who did not depart from the temple but served with fasts and prayers, recognizes Christ and speaks about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel (Luke 2). He also commanded that pairs of these birds be offered in sacrifice; nothing is truly splendid in God’s offering unless the faithful, sanctified in body and spirit, are offered to the Lord.

## Number 45

“The fig tree has brought forth its unripe figs.” At last the Synagogue also produced Israelites who believed in Christ, just as the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery: a partial blindness has occurred in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

[Col. 0972B]

## Number 46

“The vines are flowering and have given their fragrance.” Congregations of clergy, monks, and virgins likewise flourish in the Church and have become known through good reputation and conduct.

## Number 47

“Arise, my beloved and my beautiful one.” By these loving appellations the Church continually exhorts the faithful, so that, leaving temporal things behind, they may long for eternal things.

## Number 48

“My dove in the clefts of the rock.” The Church is called a dove for no other reason than that she is without deceit and is filled with the Holy Spirit. She dwells in the clefts of the rock because she always finds refuge in the wounds of Christ, through which she was healed. She is also received into the cavern of the stone wall when she is cherished by the holy consolation of Scripture, or when she is wholly protected by the merits and prayers of the saints who preceded her. In these clefts of the rock, the apostle Thomas found protection like a dove when, after the resurrection, he touched the places of Christ’s wounds and, every doubt removed, faithfully cried out: “My God and my Lord” (John 20).

[Col. 0972C]

## Number 49

“Show me your face, Sion.” Sion is interpreted as “contemplation,” and it is rightly understood of those who say with the Apostle: “We, beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.” And again: “We do not contemplate the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen” (II Corinthians 3). For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal. She is therefore invited always to stand before God, like Elijah, who said: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand today” (IV Kings 3); and not to be among those whom the prophet condemns, saying: “They turned their back to me and not their face” (Jeremiah 2). And again: “Your voice,” he says, “is in my ears” (III Kings 17); and: “The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them and delivered them from all their tribulations” (Psalm 33).

[Col. 0972D]

## Number 50

“For your voice is sweet.” The prayers of the saints are always acceptable to the Lord and present with his favor, because they have received from Christ’s light what enables them to remain in the beauty of righteousness.

## Number 51

“Catch for us the little foxes.” The Lord says in a parable in the Gospel (Matthew 13) that when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared. [Col. 0973A]

That is: as the Church advanced in numbers, many heresies also arose, or they were discovered while remaining in that faith which they understood wrongly. So also Samson, whose name is interpreted as “sun,” captured three hundred foxes, attached fire to their tails, and set fire to the crops of the enemies (Judges 15). Heretics always appear conspicuous at their beginnings, as though by a fabricated religion, but in their end they draw fire upon themselves, being destined for the burning of Gehenna. Therefore: “Catch for us the foxes”—refute the heretics and confine their deceits by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. He calls them little foxes because they contain nothing great according to right faith in their understanding. They display everything they think; being small, they destroy the vineyards, overthrow the peoples, and corrupt them with wicked traditions. “Our vineyard has flowered.” The Catholic Church advances with unceasing growth.

[Col. 0973B]

## Number 52

“My beloved is mine, and I am his.” The Apostle says: “The two will be one flesh. This mystery is great, but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5). For concerning him the same Church says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15). And again the Father says to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2). Christ therefore has the Church in his body, and the Church has Christ as her head. Since this union cannot be separated, she rightly says: “My beloved is mine.”

## Number 53

“He who feeds among the lilies.” Christ feeds among the lilies when his body, which is the Church, is adorned with assemblies of saints and virgins.

[Col. 0973C]

## Number 54

“Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” Until the evangelical tradition advances into clearer light and the figures of the Old Testament—which, like shadows, preceded it in sacrificial rites and typical observances—are driven away.

## Number 55

“Return; be like a doe, my beloved.” When he tells the beloved to return and calls him like a doe and a fawn, he shows that Christ’s ascension into heaven is to be compared with clean and swift animals. For these, with a swift leap, cross over the highest mountains. Christ, however, surpassed everything that appears exalted, because the Apostle says of him: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2). Bethel is interpreted as “house of God.” Therefore, above the mountains of Bethel, he proclaims Christ more powerful than all the saints who are in heaven and on earth.

## CHAPTER III

## Number 56

“Upon my bed, by night, I sought him.” Among those who sleep in faith and have been destroyed by the darkness of ignorance, she sought Christ, whom the Church loves. But see what follows: “I sought him and did not find him.” The Lord says to Adam: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis 3). For those who are relaxed by some fault or by the stupor of inactivity do not quickly reach the eating of that bread which came down from heaven; rather, those who keep watch through holy labors find him.

[Col. 0974A]

## Number 57

“I will rise and go around the city.” I considered all the glory of the present age; I examined the assemblies of unbelievers and the various schools of philosophers. But I did not find there the one whom my soul loves.

## Number 58

“The watchmen found me.” The wise men of the world and the worshipers of idols disputed against me, examining many things to no purpose and composing many books through fruitless labors. To them I said: “Why do you weary yourselves with a vain and excessive effort? Why do you uselessly exhaust your intellects? Have you seen the one whom my soul loves?” Since you boast of glory under the false name of wisdom, “God made your wisdom foolish” (I Corinthians 2), because you were entirely unable to find Christ there.

[Col. 0974B]

## Number 59

“After I had passed on a little.” When I had passed beyond such people, who are thought to be distinguished in the world by their empty knowledge, and when I had resisted their superstitious inventions and judged their wisdom foolish, I found the one whom my soul loves. Hence the Apostle says of such matters: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, but not the wisdom of this age; we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom that God predestined before the ages for our glory” (I Corinthians 1). And because that wisdom, which is Christ, is not found among such people, he continues: “None of the rulers of this age knew it; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. Rather, as it is written: What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (ibid.). But because the bride finds him whom she loves among spiritual people, hear what follows: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (ibid.).

[Col. 0974C]

## Number 60

“I held him and will not let him go.” Thus I will cling to Christ and persevere in his faith until, preaching him among the peoples of the Synagogue as though in the house of his mother, I bring him into the chamber of my mother who gave birth to me, so that the Jews, who have until now denied him with their lips, may receive him in their hearts. With the eyes of their minds enlightened, may they at last find him standing in the chamber, in the secret place of the holy Scriptures, he who was formerly revealed to us. Or Christ is brought into the house of his mother when the Christian people, which is his body, is joined to the heavenly Jerusalem. There is what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart,” and so forth.

[Col. 0974D]

## Number 61

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” He has already established this statement above, and I remember that we discussed it at length with supporting testimonies insofar as God granted us understanding. But I think it was repeated in this book for the following reason: so that none of the teachers might either trouble those who are about to believe with gifts or frighten them with threats, but might preach only what is holy and lead those who are willing to believe or convert to the faith and religion.

## Number 62

“Who is this who comes up through the desert?” The Church comes up through the desert when the people of the Gentiles, taking possession of the multitude of believers through faith, advance. Concerning her it is sung in the Psalms: “He made the desert into pools of water, and the dry land into springs of water” (Psalms 106 and 113). “Pillars of smoke from spices” refers to the prayers that rise to the Lord from the contrition of the heart of the saints. Smoke ordinarily brings forth tears. Myrrh and frankincense, and all the powders of perfumes, signify the marks of mortification or the various gifts of grace that abound in the elect.

[Col. 0975A]

## Number 63

“Behold Solomon’s bed.” Solomon’s bed is Christ’s rest. This rest is appropriately understood as the Church, whom we read to have been chosen in the Psalms: “For the Lord has chosen Sion; he has chosen her as his dwelling. This is my rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen her” (Psalm 75).

[Col. 0975B]

The number sixty is significant because sixty consists entirely of its parts and ascends by tens. Accordingly, those appointed to guard the Church in the Lord’s presence are rightly described as the strongest of Israel. Through the prophet it is also said to her: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall never be silent. All hold swords and are most learned in war; each one’s sword is upon his thigh” (Isaiah 62).

To them the Apostle says: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth; put on the breastplate of righteousness; and having shod your feet for the preparation of the Gospel of peace, take up in all things the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6). Those, then, are most learned in war who know how to fight against the desires of their flesh. And he usefully carries a sword upon his thigh who mortifies carnal emissions and lusts with spiritual nourishment. Whoever of this kind is found in the Church is known to be among the strong, among the strongest of Israel, by contemplating God.

[Col. 0975C]

## Number 64

“King Solomon made himself a litter.” Wherever the presentation of food is mentioned, there the faith of believers is signified, through which Christ is perceived. When the Lord spoke to the Samaritan woman at the well, and she returned and announced his majesty to the other inhabitants of the city, his disciples arrived and asked him: “Rabbi, eat.” But he said to them: “I have food to eat of which you do not know.” And shortly afterward: “Many Samaritans from that city believed in him” (John 4). He showed that their faith would be food for him when he had shortly before told his disciples that he would eat what they did not know.

But in this passage, as what follows teaches, the term “litter” indicates more an instrument in which something is carried—or, as another edition has it, a carrying frame—than the food itself. “From the woods of Lebanon”: from the distinguished saints in the Church.

[Col. 0975D]

## Number 65

“He made its columns of silver.” He prepared the supports of the Church from his learned men, or from his apostles, just as Paul, the chosen vessel, wrote to the Galatians: “When James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, recognized the grace of God, they gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas” (Galatians 2).

## Number 66

Look upon him in the diadem with which his mother crowned him: in that crown of thorns which the Synagogue placed upon his head on the day of his betrothal. For he betrothed the whole Church to himself when, ascending the cross of the gallows, he taught all who believed in him to bear the sign of that cross upon their foreheads, as he himself says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw everyone to myself” (John 12). The day of his Passion was also the day of the joy of his heart; [the following clause is textually uncertain:] for just as Christ granted good things through his possession to the faithful, for generations and many ages.

“I have removed my tunic.” When I came to faith, I laid aside the old person according to my former way of life and put on the new person, who was created according to God (Ephesians 4). Yet then I see with sorrow the ministers of the sacraments through whom I ought to be adorned, infected with carnal vices. And therefore, because I perceive myself darkened by the evils I had renounced through the transgression of some, I say: “I have removed my tunic; how shall I put it on again? Or should I allow myself to be stained once more by evil living with the filth from which I was cleansed? Or is it right that I should regress through evil conduct from progress to decline, or from the brightness of righteousness to the blackness of sins?”

## Number 113

“The watchmen found me.” The powers of the world, who are known as though to govern the state, seized me.

[Col. 0981B] **No. 114. “They struck me; they wounded me with blows.”** They raged against me with punishments inflicted upon my body; and, loading me with chains, they shut me up in prisons. They prolonged my life through carefully devised tortures, not inflicting death quickly, so that I could not easily be freed from the punishments imposed.

**No. 115. “They took away my cloak.”** For when they demolished the churches down to the ground and burned upon pyres the altars together with the Gospels and the other canonical books; when they shut up the priests and condemned them to the mines; when no place for sacrifice, no freedom to baptize, and no permission to communicate was granted—when the persecutors were doing all these things, they in a certain manner took away a kind of cloak from Christ’s bride, that is, from the Church.

**No. 116. “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.”** He adjures all the saints, if through these tribulations they reach him after despising the life of the world, to make known that the Church, established amid these persecutions, burns with ineffable love toward God and is in no way chilled by such great and terrible distresses.

[Col. 0981C] **No. 117. “What is your beloved like?”** This is the voice of those asking, and of those seeking to learn the Church’s faith from her reply. “What is your beloved like, [as one] from the beloved?” That is, what is God from God, or the Son from the Father? By likeness in all things, he declares the equality of the persons. For they are believed to be undivided in the being of one nature and to remain in the same glory of majesty.

**No. 118. “My beloved is white and ruddy.”** White, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God” [Col. 0981D] (John 1). Ruddy, because, born of the Virgin, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” White in virginity, ruddy in the Passion. Thus the prophet also speaks of him: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63). Edom is interpreted as “blood”; therefore he is ruddy from the shedding of blood. “This one is beautiful in his robe, advancing in the multitude of his strength.” “Chosen from thousands.” He is the one of whom it is said in the Psalms: “Who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 44), and again: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips.”

**No. 119. “His head is finest gold.”** We read in the Apostle: “The head of a man is Christ, the head of a woman is man, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 1). Therefore, just as among metals nothing is like gold, so among creatures nothing can be compared with the Creator. The head of Christ is God, according to what we recalled shortly before from the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth.

[Col. 0982A] **No. 120. “His locks are like clusters of palms.”** These are recognized as clinging to their holy head, that is, to Christ: in the likeness of the raven, they acknowledge themselves to be sinners. One of them says: “If I wished to justify myself before you, my mouth would condemn me” (Job 9). Another likewise says: “For I acknowledge my iniquity” (Ps. 50). John, in harmony with the elect, declares: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us; but if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1). [Col. 0982B] Paul likewise says: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1). And because, according to the Gospel, “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. 23; Luke 4, 18), those who cast themselves down through confession of sin are not undeservedly compared with the height of palm trees, according to what is written in this book.

**No. 121. “His eyes are like doves.”** Filled with the Holy Spirit, his elect remain without any gall of bitterness and steep the people in the streams of Scripture.

**No. 122. “Which have been washed with milk.”** Having thereby become purer, because they believe without hesitation that Christ was born in the flesh, they acknowledge themselves to have been reborn, washed, and nourished through the visible sacrament. They dwell beside very full streams—that is, amid the most abundant gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0982C] **No. 123. “His cheeks are like beds of spices.”** Just as in the eyes of doves we rightly understand the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, so in the cheeks, which are near the eyes, we understand those Churches that believed through the apostles. Like beds of spices, they produce the sweetest fragrance from holy conduct, planted by perfumers—that is, by devout preachers—to whom the Apostle says: “Although you were a wild olive, you were grafted into them and became a sharer in the root and richness of the olive” (Rom. 11).

**No. 124. “His lips drip with myrrh.”** His teachers—through the Spirit or even through the flesh of the Virgin—and in this they proclaim his Passion, so that, for the sake of him who died for us, they do not refuse death.

**No. 125. “His hands are golden, turned work.”** Those who do not cease to perform what is good are assigned to the hands of Christ. Therefore they are golden, turned work, because they are always ready for every good work, “full of hyacinths,” according to the Apostle: “Rich in good works, generous in giving, and storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6).

[Col. 0982D] **No. 126. “His belly is ivory.”** Those who give birth to believers in faith are assigned to his belly. That belly of ivory is also not unfittingly understood as the font of baptism, from which we are reborn. And because the bones of ivory, from a dead animal, are known to be beautiful and incorruptible, therefore the Apostle says to us: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried [Col. 0983A] with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Gal. 3). “Marked with sapphires”: adorned with saints begotten from him and most illustrious in confession.

**No. 127. “His legs are marble columns.”** The legs, which support the whole body, are the saints, who support the house of the Church and are described as marble columns founded upon golden bases. These righteous people support the others through love and sustain them with the consolations of Scripture, as the Apostle says: “We who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not to please ourselves.” Shortly afterward he indicates the holy Scriptures as golden bases, saying: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15).

[Col. 0983B] **No. 128. “His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like the cedars.”** All the saints who have given forth the sweetest fragrance from good conduct and have endured in the integrity of incorruption have received, by God’s gift, the grace of such great blessings.

**No. 129. “His throat is most sweet.”** Those who expound his mysteries and meditate daily on his law provide the sweetest savor in sacred doctrine. “And he is altogether desirable.” There will be fulfilled what blessed John says in his Epistle: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

[Col. 0983C] **No. 130. “Such is my beloved.”** He persuades the righteous to direct their attention toward these varieties of graces and these adornments of the mysteries, suggesting that the bridegroom’s beauty is to be contemplated in his members.

**No. 131. “Where has your beloved gone?”** As though they were searching and saying: Since you have described his beauty so greatly that our hearts have been set aflame to seek him, now show where he has gone or where he has turned aside. The Church is rightly called a virgin, “most beautiful among women,” because Paul speaks thus to the faithful concerning her: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Cor. 11). Appropriately they say of him: “Where has your beloved gone? Where has he turned aside?” For he turned aside, in a certain manner, when, although he was in the form of God and did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, “he emptied himself, [Col. 0983D] taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). Therefore whoever seeks him exalted in the form of God will not find him unless he believes in the form of a servant, in which he humbled himself for this reason: to raise us who were lying low.

## Chapter VI

**No. 132. “My beloved went down to his garden.”** He went down to his garden when, at his coming, he visited Israel, his people, as he himself says: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 10). We understand the bed of spices as Saint Mary the Virgin herself, for from her the order of righteousness arose for us, the Lord Jesus Christ.

**No. 133. “To pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.”** So that he might reign among the nations or delight in the Churches, and take from them virgins and other saints.

[Col. 0984A] **No. 134. “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine.”** I am Christ’s kingdom and he is my king; I am his body and he is my head. He pastures among lilies when he rests in the hearts of virgins, or when he is daily increased and advances there through the grace he himself bestows.

**No. 135. “You are beautiful, my friend, beautiful,” and so forth.** Beautiful through righteousness; sweet and friendly because she is always peaceful; lovely like Jerusalem. The Lord says in the Gospel: “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they will be like angels in heaven” (Matt. 12; Luke 10). The Church is therefore rightly described as lovely like Jerusalem, since the likeness of angels is granted to her by the Lord forever.

[Col. 0984B] **No. 136. “Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.”** How many tyrants and persecutors, together with their author, the devil, tried to break and overcome the Church’s strength, yet were utterly unable to prevail. For the holy Church has an ordered battle line, when, with Christ approaching, neither persecution conquers the martyrs, nor carnal pleasure the virgins, nor greed the merciful, nor ambition for temporal glory the humble.

**No. 137. “Turn your eyes away from me, for …”** Do not always seek to behold me in the body; you see me better in spirit through faith. For this reason I ascended into heaven, so that I might not always appear to you as localized, since by the presence of my divinity I fill all things in such a way that I am everywhere, contain everything, and am contained by no place.

[Col. 0984C] **No. 138. “Your hair is like flocks of goats; your teeth are like a flock of sheep, all bearing twins, and the barren one,” and so forth. “Like the rind of a pomegranate.”** These four verses are plainly written twice in this place. By God’s gift we have already treated them above; nevertheless, there he foretold the conversion of the peoples of the Jews and the Gentiles with the fruit of a twofold love, and declared the glory of the martyrs together with their merits.

[Col. 0984D] **No. 139. “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines.”** In the number sixty, which is completed when six ascends by tens, we recognize the perfection of all good things consummated through the precepts of the Law. Observe briefly how six consists of all its parts: its sixth part is one, its third part two, and its half three. Who does not know that one, two, and three make six? In another number it is difficult to find this completion when its parts are distributed and then reduced to one. Thus the queens are called the perfect souls of the saints, who are not servants of sins; for it is written: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (1 Cor. 3). The concubines, who, like Hagar, “give birth into slavery” (Gal. 4), are rightly assigned to those who, having received the seed of God’s word, savor not spiritual things but carnal ones. The innumerable young women represent the multitude of those who are always ready to hear what is holy, yet do not strive to fulfill in their works what they hear. Of them the Apostle says: “Always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 3). [Col. 0985A] Although these are classes of people who are joined to Christ, as it were, through his teaching, nevertheless, because unity rather than diversity is commended among the elect, hear what follows.

**No. 140. “One is my dove, my perfect one.”** A dove, because she is simple and has spiritual understanding; perfect, because, abandoning the world, she loves me more than temporal things or herself, according to the saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19).

**No. 141. “One is the chosen one of her mother.”** Her heavenly mother, Jerusalem, of whom the Apostle says: “The Jerusalem above is our mother” (Gal. 4). She is therefore one for him, because in future blessedness she alone will be joined to him.

[Col. 0985B] **No. 142. “The daughters saw her and called her most blessed.”** What holy souls are there who do not exalt the Church with wondrous praises, since even the concubines—that is, the carnal—are not silent in proclaiming her, when they admire her as unconquered in the martyrs and victorious in the virgins?

**No. 143. “Who is this who comes forth like …”** She rises like dawn when, having rejected the works of darkness, she lives chastely and soberly among married people; beautiful as the moon when she shines with a bright radiance among the continent; chosen as the sun when she gleams in virgins with the beauty of perfection, like the good soil in the Gospel which, having received the seed of God’s word, produced thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold fruit; “terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.” Is she not terrible who overturned the rites of the nations and the worship of idols, and who, persevering in the faith of Christ, could not be overcome by the nations? She is also exceedingly terrible in that power given to her in Peter, where it is said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16 and 18).

[Col. 0985C] **No. 144. “I went down to the garden of nuts to see.”** The garden of nuts signifies the canon of the Old and New Testament. The appearance of a nut displays one thing in its shell and retains another in its kernel. If someone does not distinguish this in the holy Scriptures, and does not, as it were, seek the inner things within the shells of the nuts, he cannot reach the fruit of spiritual understanding. What he says—“to see [Col. 0985D] the fruits of the valley”—means: to see the fruit of the humblest people in the Church, as it is sung in the Psalms: “For you will save the humble people and will humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. 17).

**No. 145. “To see whether the vines had blossomed.”** To test whether the Church had advanced so far that there might spring up in her those who would attain the perfection of martyrdom and, because of the shedding of Christ’s blood, would be beautiful in their redness.

**No. 146. “I did not know; my soul troubled me.”** What did Christ not know except sin? He also did not know those who say in the Gospel: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and perform many mighty works in your name?” And then, he says, I shall say to them: “Truly I tell you, [Col. 0986A] I do not know you” (Matt. 7)—not that he did not know what they were like, but because he recognized that there was no good in them. “My soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.” We also find this Aminadab genealogically in Christ. Hence we understand these chariots to be taken in a favorable sense, in which we rightly understand the Evangelists. But when he says, “My soul troubled me,” this troubling is not contrary to tranquility but is found to accord with concern, according to what is said to Martha in the Gospel: “Why are you anxious and troubled” (Luke 10) about many things? And in the Psalms: “You moved the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, for it has been shaken” (Ps. 59). From where, moreover, do all the Gospel narratives proceed except through the Holy Spirit, according to the saying of the prophet Ezekiel: “Wherever the Spirit went, the wheels also were carried there with it” (Ezek. 3 and 10)?

[Col. 0986B] **No. 147. “Return, return, O Shulammite.”** Twice in the Book of Kings we find this Shulammite established in a praiseworthy position: both the woman who ministered to King David in his old age and, though an exceedingly beautiful virgin, remained in his embrace (4 Kings 4), and the woman whose son Elisha raised from the dead after he had been born according to the promise (3 Kings 1). Who, therefore, would doubt that holy Church is to be understood by this name? She is frequently told, “Return,” because once, in the younger son, she had turned away by going into a distant region (Luke 15); she returned when she turned back to God from her heart. [Col. 0986C] Or she is told “return” so often for this reason: that even if, after turning back, she should sin, she may not fall into despair, but may recover from the habit of sinning through the indulgence offered by hope. This voice is certainly shown to apply to the saints, who desire to behold the beauty of the one who has turned back.

## Chapter VII

**No. 148. “What will you see in the Shulammite, except …”** What is there to behold in the Church except the disposition of those who, always stationed in readiness as though in a military camp, do not cease fighting against the devil—so that the faithful may not lose their faith; the devout may not, once lifted up, become apostates; the merciful may not be hardened by greed; penitents may not return to their vomit; virgins may not lose the beauty of their integrity; and the continent may not lose the splendor of chastity? These are the Church’s choirs, continually engaged in battle and, with God protecting them, always unconquered.

[Col. 0986D] **No. 149. “How beautiful are your steps!”** How wondrous is the progress of those who announce God’s word in the Church of Christ, as the Apostle recalls what is written in the prophet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize good things!” And again he himself says: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace” (Rom. 10).

**No. 150. “The joining of your thighs.”** By the joining of your thighs we understand the union of the peoples coming from circumcision and uncircumcision: both those who were propagated bodily from Abraham’s thigh and those who merited to be in his seed—that is, in Christ. When they are joined in the unity of faith, they are described as necklaces fashioned by the hand of a craftsman. For what craftsman joined these peoples in faith like necklaces except the one of whom the Apostle says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 6)?

[Col. 0987A] **No. 151. “Your navel is a turned-work bowl.”** Those who are changed not at the extremity but in the middle of the Church’s body are called the navel. Turned-work bowls are useful vessels, turned for this purpose: they are ready to obey and for every good work (Eph. 2). They never lack drink, because they are always filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

**No. 152. “Your belly is like a heap of wheat.”** Those who always receive the holy nourishment of the Scriptures and heap up within themselves what is salutary are assigned to the belly’s likeness. They are rightly called a heap of gathered wheat, because from the sound teaching with which they are daily filled they abundantly refresh many; and this teaching advances so far that through devout persuasion it brings many even to the observance of virginity.

[Col. 0987B] **No. 153. “Your two breasts are like two fawns.”** The two Testaments are fitted to the two fawns of a doe, that is, to peoples who come from the transmission of sin. Those who are subject to original sin are nourished by the works proceeding from these, being reborn in Christ like fawns.

**No. 154. “Your neck is like an ivory tower.”** Knowledge of the Scriptures, acquired through frequent meditation, is represented in the beauty of the neck as an ivory tower. It is an ivory tower because those who attend to God’s word advance through daily progress to higher things by the brightness of righteousness.

[Col. 0987C] **No. 155. “Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon.”** Your spiritual teachers, established at the gate, are in Christ like flowing waters for instructing the peoples. They are called pools because they are filled with knowledge of the Holy Spirit. In another book Solomon himself says: “I made pools of water, to irrigate the forest of growing trees” (Eccl. 2).

**No. 156. “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.”** The nose of the Church consists of those who, perceiving the fragrance of righteousness that is in Christ, carry it into the inner chambers of the heart. Those who stand in great strength are arranged like the tower of Lebanon. We have already said above that Lebanon signifies whiteness; the whiteness of their stature faces Damascus, because their wisdom, which is from God, illuminates the world.

[Col. 0987D] **No. 157. “Your head is like Carmel, and your locks …”** On Mount Carmel the saints Elijah and Elisha often found a place of refuge (3 Kings 18). Therefore, in the head of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is exalted like Mount Carmel, both the righteous find a dwelling and the multitude of peoples, like a diversity of animals, receive the nourishment of wisdom. “The locks of this head are like royal purple joined to channels”: the more eminent saints—namely, the blessed martyrs of Christ—are understood as likened through purple to royal ornaments and as always joined to salutary teachings.

**No. 158. “Your stature is like a palm tree.”** Your perfection has reached its reward, and your teachers have been made sweet through the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0988A] **No. 159. “I said, ‘I will climb the palm tree.’”** Those climb the palm tree who advance in the cross of Christ. Of them the Apostle says: “Those who are in Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” They receive the rewards of this palm tree—that is, of the holy cross—who say with the same Apostle: “If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified” (Rom. 8).

**No. 160. “And your breasts will be like clusters of the vine.”** For no others are found who nourish those being born in faith except the teachers of the Church.

**No. 161. “And your fragrances will be like apples.”** The sweetness of your instruction will be spread through those who, living soberly and righteously, do not cease to offer the fragrance of good conduct.

[Col. 0988B] **No. 162. “Your throat is like the finest wine.”** The saints may also be understood in the throat, through whom the Law, the prophets, and evangelical teaching were proclaimed. This holy Scripture, endowed with an exceptional savor, smells and shines like the finest wine, and through the Holy Spirit it intoxicates those who drink.

**No. 163. “Worthy of being drunk by my beloved.”** They drink from sacred Scripture when Christians, who are his members, are satisfied by it with wondrous and incomparable sweetness.

**No. 164. “And for his lips and teeth to chew.”** The lips and teeth of Christ are the teachers of the Church. They do not cease to chew what is holy when they meditate daily on the things written for our instruction.

[Col. 0988C] **No. 165. “I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me.”** To this beloved the Church says in her own voice: “My soul has clung to you; your right hand has received me” (Ps. 62). Let us see elsewhere how she herself speaks to her beloved: “But we are your people and the sheep of your flock” (Ps. 78). And the prophet says concerning his turning toward me: “Before they call, I will answer; while they are still speaking, I will hear,” says the Lord (Isa. 65). But Christ’s turning toward the Church is nowhere so evident as when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

**No. 166. “Come, my beloved; let us go forth.”** Christ goes forth with the Church into the field when, together with the saints mentioned above, he visits the world, as it is written in the Gospel: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man” (Matt. 13; Mark 14); “the field is the world.” “Let us remain in the villages”: among the believing peoples spread throughout the surrounding regions, in whom Christ dwells through faith—not without the Church, since, reckoning these same people among his members, he makes them his Church.

[Col. 0988D] **No. 167. “Let us rise early and go to the vineyards.”** So that the souls who have already merited to be cultivated through faith may recognize in the morning that Christ has risen and may no longer doubt the resurrection of his body.

**No. 168. “Let us see whether the vine has blossomed.”** Let it appear whether the faithful confess with their mouth what they have believed in their heart, as the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10); or whether the blossoms produce fruit, that is, whether works of piety have emerged in them through holy desires.

[Col. 0989A] **No. 169. “Whether the pomegranates have blossomed.”** Whether those who have believed in Christ advance in such great love that they delight in every way even to be killed for him. If you wish to see the pomegranate, hear the Apostle Paul in the Acts of the Apostles: “I am ready,” he says, “not only to be judged in Jerusalem, but also to die for Christ” (Acts 21).

**No. 170. “There I will give you my breasts.”** In this holy confession my teachers will be joined to you, prepared to suffer for you; they too will reign with you without end.

**No. 171. “The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance.”** Those who are founded in faith with deep roots and are known to flourish through a certain austerity of discipline or frugality instructed the peoples through public preaching, offering the fragrance of sweetness from their most holy conduct.

[Col. 0989B] **No. 172. “All new and old gifts.”** For in the patriarchs and prophets as well as in the apostles and martyrs I myself have preserved for you things both new and old. The former foretold and believed that you would come; the latter do not cease to preach that you were born of the Virgin, suffered for the salvation of all, and after the resurrection were taken up into heaven.

## Chapter VIII

**No. 173. “Who would grant that you were my brother?”** Christ sucks the breasts of his mother when the Christian people are refreshed by the mysteries of the ancient Law, or when teachers refresh them with spiritual sacraments and most devout interpretation, as with true milk.

[Col. 0989C] **No. 174. “That I might find you outside and kiss you.”** “That I might find you,” she says, “whom the figures of the Old Testament concealed, in truth through the Gospel.” She rightly says, “I will find you outside,” because the father went out to meet the younger son returning from a distant region (Luke 15). “That I might kiss you,” she says, “so that I may be worthy to be reconciled to you, and no one may now despise me.” In other words, so that it might not be said to Peter concerning Cornelius, whom the grace of the Holy Spirit had preceded: “Why did you enter men who had the foreskin and eat with them?” Rather, let Peter himself declare: “In truth I perceive that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every place and among every nation, whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 11).

[Col. 0989D] **No. 175. “I will take hold of you and lead you.”** When I have taken hold of you and have clung to you through faith, it remains for me to bring you into the house of my mother—that is, into the assembly of Jerusalem. I shall bring you there when, together with all the good things I have obtained through your grace, I too shall have merited to be led there, that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem.

**No. 176. “There you will teach me, and I will give you a cup.”** There you will teach me, so that I may see no longer in a riddle through a mirror but face to face, and may then know not partially but as I have been known (1 Cor. 13), as he says: “And I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the juice of pomegranates,” when I have brought forth the finest and sweetest fruits of the holy martyrs, and the sons of men who hope in the shadow of your wings “will be intoxicated by the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delights” (Ps. 35).

[Col. 0990A] **No. 177. “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.”** These things written in this passage were already stated above and, with Christ’s illumination, have been expounded. I think they have been written again in this book so that they may be impressed more deeply upon the heart and, expressed twice, be renewed in more living memory. They command us to despise temporal things and teach that things placed beneath us are like the left hand established under the head; they urge us to await the heavenly glory that embraces us from above like the right hand. Or they teach this: that those who are to serve the Lord should willingly, not unwillingly, accomplish holy things, according to the Apostle Peter’s instruction: “Feed the flock of God that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly” (1 Pet. 5).

[Col. 0990B] **No. 178. “Who is this who comes up from the desert?”** She is rightly described as coming up from the desert, to whom the prophet says: “Because you were forsaken and hated, and there was no one passing through you” (Isa. 60), and so forth. Concerning her children also it is sung in the Psalms: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless region; they did not find a way to a city of habitation.
