Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them; and they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities; he led them by the straight way, so that they might go to a city of habitation” (Ps. 10). Therefore what follows is:

**No. 179. “Abounding in delights.”** Thus the people of Israel, coming out of the desert, enter the land of promise flowing with milk and honey; and the son who, desiring to be fed on the pods of pigs, could not be satisfied is brought in to be refreshed at the banquet that his father prepared from a fattened calf. Coming from the desert, the Church finds these manifold delights in Christ, and she is written as leaning upon her beloved, because that same beloved says through the prophet: “I made, I will carry, I will bear, and I will save” (Isa. 46).

[Col. 0990C] **No. 180. “Under the apple tree I raised you up.”** Beneath the fragrant gallows of the cross, where I died, there I raised you from the destruction of sins, when I commanded you, as a believer, to mark yourself beforehand with the sign of the cross.

**No. 181. “There your mother was corrupted.”** Where you merited to be raised up through my death, there the Synagogue was seized through its impiety, when, while shouting “Crucify him!” it answered Pilate as judge: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Luke 23).

[Col. 0990D] **No. 182. “Set me as a seal.”** So that you may be able to say with the Psalmist: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4). Since whatever is sealed cannot easily be violated, receive my faith in such a way that you preserve it whole and undefiled, and do not fear that the treasure of righteousness which I have placed in you, received through the sign of the cross, can in any way be touched by anyone.

**No. 183. “Set me as a seal.”** Understand that the seal is first to be placed upon the heart, then upon the arm: that is, run to my sign both in thought and in deed; and thereby demonstrate that you belong not to another but to me. With me protecting you, persevere intact.

[Col. 0991A] **No. 184. “For your love is strong as death.”** I loved you so greatly that I wished to die for you; and this was the strength of love, the bitterness of death. “Jealousy is hard as hell,” so that the saints also, conversely, may not fear to be killed for Christ, since they undoubtedly know that he accepted death for their salvation.

**No. 185. “Its lamps are lamps of fire.”** The vessels in which chastity dwells are always radiant and burning with the fire of the Holy Spirit.

**No. 186. “Many waters could not extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it, nor tribulations.”** No persecutions, however powerful, can disturb or overcome the love that is from God or directed toward God, according to what the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8).

[Col. 0991B] **No. 187. “If a man gives all his substance.”** It is as though he were saying: “Even if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and even if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). For nothing is more precious than this, as the Apostle John says: [Col. 0991C] “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God.”

**No. 188. “Our little sister, and she has no breasts.”** The Church coming from the Gentiles is still inexperienced in believing and not yet equipped with learned men for teaching, according to the Apostle’s words: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, nor indeed are you yet able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3). And elsewhere: “If you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are despised in the Church. I say this to your shame: is there no wise person among you who can judge between his brother?” (1 Cor. 6). In rebuking them for such great weakness, he shows that the people are still little in faith and not yet capable of spiritual nourishment.

[Col. 0991D] **No. 189. “What shall we do for our sister?”** How shall we arrange the Church at the time when she is to be called to faith?

**No. 190. “If it is a wall, let us build upon it.”** Those who began to grow in faith and became so established that by their strength they could encourage the weak are appointed, after receiving the privilege of honor, to teach the others, according to Paul’s instruction to Timothy: “Entrust these things to faithful people who will be able to teach others” (2 Tim. 2). And again to Titus: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what remains to be done and appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you.” When these arrangements are made in [Col. 0992A] the Church, silver battlements are added to the walls.

Num. 191. If it is a door, let us join it together. The Prophet says in the Psalms: “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140). Therefore, if someone is competent to speak and, like a door that opens and closes, understands the proper time for speaking or silence, let us join this kind of door together with cedar boards, so that, having received fragrant wood within himself, he may be able to say with Paul: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6).

Num. 192. “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.” This is the voice of the Church, advancing both in faith and for the sake of faith: “I am a wall,” because he himself built me who fights most powerfully on my behalf. “And my breasts are like a tower.” Through God’s construction they have grown in the height of righteousness, and they nourish within me the little ones who are in Christ; and until they reach the food of perfection, they do not cease to raise them, until the voice of Wisdom says to them: “Leave childhood behind, and come to walk along the paths of prudence.”

Num. 193. “From the time when I was made before him.” From the time when I found peace in Christ, I also received, with dignity, the defenses of walls and the bulwarks of towers; with them, I deserved from him who made me to be a city, possessing fortifications in the saints and retaining beauty in the elect.

Num. 194. “The vineyard belonged to the peaceful one.” Constant cultivation was applied by Christ to the Church, which possesses those peoples of whom it is sung in the Psalms: “Those who are planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of our God” (Ps. 91). “He handed it over to guardians.” He entrusted it to the apostles, or to their successors, the bishops, to govern. To it, under the name of Jerusalem, the Lord says through the Prophet: “Over you and over your walls I have appointed your guardians; all day and all night, until the end, they will not be silent” (Isa. 62).

Num. 195. “A man brings its fruits, a thousand silver pieces.” Christ is the one of whom the Prophet says: “Behold the man; ‘Rising’ is his name” (Zech. 6). He repays the kingdom of heaven for holy labors or almsgiving, according to what is said in the Gospel: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, because I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick and in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. 25). In the thousand silver pieces, the fullness of the entire recompense and the completed reward of the righteous is indicated.

Num. 196. “My vineyard is before me.” According to what is sung in the Psalms: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers.” For the Apostle says: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven at the command, at the voice of an archangel, and at the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who live, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4). Therefore, because after the resurrection the saints are always with the Lord, the Lord says: “My vineyard is before me.”

Num. 197. “A thousand of yours, O peaceful one, and two hundred for these.” For when twelve are multiplied by the number one hundred, they produce twelve hundred; and this number is fitting for apostolic men, who have been spiritually begotten from them through the Gospel in Christ and, established in complete perfection, answer their author with a hundredfold fruit, like that very good earth. They too are rightly described as “peaceful,” that is, as disciples of Christ, both because they guard the fruits of the Church and because, by the voice of their teaching, they deter the wicked outside, or by their prayers they do not cease to defend from wicked dogs and the bites of beasts the Church that Christ planted.

[Col. 0993B] Num. 198. “You who dwell in the gardens.” You who overflow among peoples established under the cultivation of righteousness, or who are continually watered by the water of spiritual teaching.

Num. 199. “Friend, listen; let me hear.” In the Gospel the Lord says to his disciples: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15); and again: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3). “Let me hear your voice”—the voice, namely, with which you say to the faithful when rewarding them: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

Num. 200. “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” You who lived among us on earth, hasten back to the heights above. And as you ascend into the heights, you who now appear to bodily eyes, be always present to the eyes of the heart, so that we may retain in faith the one whom we do not see with our sight. “Be like a gazelle and a young stag,” because you are the one who assumed the flesh of mortals and, with swift leaping, transcended all the heights of heaven. “Upon the mountains of spices,” existing higher than all the glory of the angels.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 540. VIVENTIOLUS, BISHOP OF LYONS.

[Col. 0993]

NOTICE CONCERNING FABRICIUS.

[Col. 0993C] Viventiolus, educated in the monastery of Condat, was bishop of Lyons in the year 516. He wrote certain works, of which nothing survives except one letter of no great length to Alcimus Avitus, among his letters, no. 59; a fragment of a speech at the Council of Agaunum in 517, in Labbe’s Councils, vol. 4, p. 1559; and a Tractoria-letter to the bishops of his province, summoning them to the Synod of Epaon in 517, in Hardouin, Councils, vol. 2, p. 1046. Add the Literary History of France, vol. 3, p. 94.

[Col. 0993]

LETTERS OF VIVENTIOLUS. (C)

FIRST LETTER TO AVITUS.

[Col. 0993D]

(Read it among the works of Avitus, Patrol. vol. 59, col. 272.)

LETTER II TO THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF LYONS. Tractoria. [Note: [Col. 0993D] Now published for the first time from a manuscript of the Library of the Augustinian Fathers in the city of Toulouse, from a copy sent to us by the Reverend Father Petrus Rocques, of the Society of Jesus.] A letter of Viventiolus, bishop of Lyons, to the bishops of the province of Lyons, summoning them to come to the Synod of Epaon.

To our most devoted lords, brothers and bishops, and to all the clergy, honored men, and landowners of our territory, Viventiolus, bishop, sends greetings.

[Col. 0994D] All priests ought equally to desire the discipline of our brothers and sons; but if something is committed by more honored clergy that is judged worthy of public reproach, it is more appropriate that it be exposed to correction [Note: [Col. 0994D] Perhaps *aculeo* is missing, or some similar word.] than nourished by silence. But just as this is simple and right, so we are offended by the slanders of malicious speeches and by the purpose of fearful murmuring. Therefore, lest anyone think that we in any way give assent to our own leniency or negligence, I announce by this present protest that a gathering of all the bishops of our rank will soon take place, around the beginning of September, in the parish of Epaon; there we compel the clergy to attend, as is fitting, while we permit the laity to be present, so that the people too may recognize what ought to be ordered by the bishops alone. And because it is just that all Catholics should desire to have clergy of good life, we open to everyone an opportunity to report what each person knows ought to be reproved. Let permission to bring charges against whomever one wishes be open to all; with the power of quarreling relaxed, let hidden murmuring born of wicked desires cease. Nevertheless, the accuser must undertake to prove what he has reported; [Col. 0996A] and no one should think that those who perhaps live rightly may safely be defamed by empty lies. Let no one bring an accusation unless he can establish it; the slanderer [Perhaps: the reviler] will receive the shame that virtue ought to fear. Patience in hearing and fairness in judging shall first be extended to both sides. May the Lord deem you worthy of his protection, brothers and sons whom we shall receive in Christ. Issued on the fourth day before the Ides of the fourth month, in the consulship of Agapetus (A.D. 517).

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 540. TROJANUS [Note: [Col. 0995B] This is found in quite a few manuscripts, but without the names of the cities. We have therefore supplied the designation on the basis of our conjecture; if it is correct, it must be said that Trojanus was the bishop of Saintes, of whom Gregory of Tours writes in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 59, and that he flourished at this time. For Eumerius of Nantes is established by the subscriptions of the Fourth Council of Orléans. JAC. SIRMONDUS.], BISHOP OF SAINTES.

[Col. 0995]

[Col. 0995B]

LETTER OF TROJANUS TO EUMERIUS, BISHOP OF NANTES. Concerning a boy who did not know whether he had been baptized. (C)

To his ever-lord Eumerius [Note: [Col. 0996B] He is called Evemerus by Fortunatus, book 4, chapter 1, in his epitaph.], bishop, Trojanus, bishop.

I received, from the deacons whom you sent to my humility, a letter from Your Holiness in which you ask about a certain boy who says that he does not know whether he was baptized, except that he remembers only this: that his head had been wrapped in linen. This is often done to the sick after an illness, so that the head may not become chilled and the illness return. To these men, therefore, I return in the Lord the service of the greeting they deserve, and I presume to give an unhesitating judgment according to what was established by our predecessors. Know that it was established that anyone who does not remember having been baptized, and for whom it is not proved that this was done by another person, should receive baptism without any delay, lest his soul be required of us if it has been separated from the baptized (Pope Leo I, Letter to Rusticus, chapter 16). Pray for us, my lord, deservedly most blessed in Christ.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 540. PONTIANUS, AFRICAN BISHOP.

[Col. 0995]

[Col. 0995C]

LETTER OF PONTIANUS, BISHOP, TO THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN. Concerning the Three Chapters. (C)

To the most merciful and most devout son, the Emperor Justinian, Pontianus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

From the very beginnings of justice you received your name in a primary way; and the just Lord so arranged matters that he gave you the name of justice before he later entrusted you with the governance of the empire. Thus the Creator’s grace was united not only in name but also in merit: his life was exalted through ruling, and his rule through living justly. You deigned to admonish us, who reside in the African regions, by letter concerning what faith you hold and defend. We have learned that the Lord established this with blessed Peter, saying: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16). Our spirit rejoiced, recognizing that you, most devout emperor, firmly hold what the apostolic faith proclaims, since we believe that you do not depart from the path of right belief. For an emperor ought to be such as we know you to be: devout, just, and faithful. At the end of your letter, however, we learned [Col. 0997A]—and this troubles us greatly—that we ought to condemn Theodore, the writings of Theodoret, and the letter of Ibas. Their statements have not yet reached us at all. But if they should reach us, and if we should read anything there that is apocryphal or spoken against the rule of faith, we can reject the statements without condemning in a precipitous judgment the authors of those statements, who are already dead. If they were still alive and, after being corrected, did not condemn their error, they would justly be condemned. But now, to whom will the sentence of our condemnation be read? There is no one in them who can be corrected. Yet I fear, most devout emperor, that under the pretext of condemning these men [Col. 0998A] the Eutychian heresy may be raised up; and that, while we do not disregard the smallest indications, we may come into collision with a greater heresy. And what business have we to wage war against the dead, where no victory can be found in the contest? They are already held by the true Judge, from whom no one appeals. Through him in whom you honor and love us, we beg your clemency that peace may remain during your reign, lest, while you seek to condemn men already dead, you kill many living people who disobey, and consequently be compelled to render an account to him who is to come to judge the living and the dead.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 542. SAINT CAESARIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES.

[Col. 0997]

NOTICE (from Gallandius).

[Col. 0997B]

I. Caesarius, a Gaul by nationality and a native of Chalon, distinguished by birth, while still a young man professed the monastic life in the monastery of Lérins under the abbot Porcarius, successor of Faustus of Riez, when he was eighteen years old [Note: [Col. 0997C] Cyprian, *Life of Caesarius*, chapter 1, no. 5, in the Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, August, vol. 6, p. 65.]. Because the austerity of his life had broken his bodily strength, he was sent to Arles to restore his health, and in that city he was entrusted to the most distinguished African rhetorician Pomerius for training in the liberal disciplines [Note: [Col. 0997D] The same, ibid., no. 8.]. Soon, however, dismissing the fictions of human learning, he was first ordained deacon and then priest by Aeonius, bishop of Arles and his kinsman, and was chosen to preside over a monastery on an island outside the city [Note: [Col. 0997D] The same, ibid., nos. 10–11.]. When Aeonius died—he had desired Caesarius as his successor—Caesarius, although unwilling, assumed the governance of the Church of Arles in the year 502 [Note: [Col. 0997D] The same, ibid., book 2, no. 1.]. [Col. 0997C] The holy bishop displayed many outstanding virtues and likewise left to posterity many examples of patience. These are to be gathered from Cyprian, Firminus, and Viventius, bishops; from Messianus, a priest; and from Stephanus, a deacon, the authors of his life. He presided with metropolitan authority over various councils: Agde in 506; Arles IV in 524; Carpentras in 527; Orange II in 529; and Vaison II, held in the same year. Finally, after completing forty years in the episcopate, he died on 27 August 542 [Note: [Col. 0997D] Messianus, *Life of Caesarius*, book 2, chapter 4, no. 34, in the Bollandists, loc. cit., p. 83.], when he was seventy-three years old. The learned Norisius discusses Caesarius’s age at length [Note: [Col. 0997D] Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book 2, chapter 22, pp. 518ff., latest edition, Verona.], and argues that our bishop was born in 470, entered the episcopate in 503, and died in 543. Most scholars, however—Cointius [Note: [Col. 0997D] Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. 1, p. 611.], Mabillonius [Note: [Col. 0998C] Mabillonius, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. 1, p. 89, and *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, first age, vol. 1, p. 654, note b.], Pagius [Note: [Col. 0998D] Pagius, under the year 544, § 8.], the Bollandists [Note: [Col. 0998D] Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, August, vol. 6, p. 55, commentary on Saint Caesarius, § 2, no. 18.], Sammarthanus [Note: [Col. 0998D] Sammarthanus, *Gallia Christiana*, vol. 1, p. 536.] and others—declare that the chronology we have just proposed should be retained. The tomb of Saint Caesarius, after it had been destroyed by the Saracens, was restored by Paulus, an illustrious man, in the year of our Lord 873; he added an epitaph, which Mabillonius published from an old manuscript much more accurately than Saxius and others [Note: [Col. 0998D] Mabillonius, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. 1, p. 90.].

II. Saint Caesarius, deeply devoted to Augustinian doctrine, wrote against Faustus an outstanding work on grace and free will, which the Synod of Valence and Pope Boniface approved. Some have thought that this work had long since perished; but unjustly, as the most learned writers of the *Literary History of France* judge [Note: [Col. 0998D] *Literary History of France*, vol. 3, p. 225.]. For it is clear from the author who inserted chapter 86 on Saint Caesarius into Gennadius’s catalogue—on this matter, consult Norisius [Note: [Col. 0998D] Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book 2, chapter 22, pp. 517, 520.]—that this work is nothing other than the Acts of the Second Council of Orange. And rightly so, it seems, if those Acts are compared with what that Gennadian writer has, when he says that Caesarius published, “on grace and free will, testimonies fortified by the judgments of the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers, in which he teaches that a human being can do nothing good from his own resources unless divine grace has first gone before him.” The holy Father also wrote very many homilies, almost all of which, as Mabillonius says [Note: [Col. 0999D] Mabillonius, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. 1, p. 89.], [Col. 0999A] were published together in the Augustinian appendix of the new edition. Oudinus was preparing to publish them, collected together with other little works of Caesarius [Note: [Col. 0999D] Oudin, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. 1, pp. 1344ff.]; but those learned men whom we have just mentioned present them in a more accurate arrangement [Note: [Col. 0999D] *Literary History of France*, vol. 3, pp. 198ff.]. Accordingly, of these we have committed to the press only those which Baluzius published, furnished with notes, from a very ancient manuscript in Paris in the year 1669. We have discovered, however, that some of them had already been published earlier [Note: [Col. 0999D] Ibid., pp. 209, 219ff.]. The editor’s annotations placed beneath the homilies refer to the pages of the Paris edition, which we have had placed in the margin of our copy.

III. Following Baluzius’s homilies, we have added Saint Caesarius’s Rules for monks and nuns, copied from the Holstenius manuscript of the Rules. First comes the Rule for monks, which Tetradius, a priest and abbot and Caesarius’s nephew, took down from the saint’s dictation and, at his command, sent to various monasteries. It had often been published previously in the *Libraries of the Fathers*, as well as by Prosper Stellartius among the *Rules of Monastic and Military Orders*. Cointius later incorporated it into his *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks* from Holstenius’s edition, which, being the latest, is also the best [Note: [Col. 0999D] Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. 1, pp. 489ff.]. He carefully compared it with the Rule for nuns, whose author was Caesarius himself, and explained several passages that seemed to present some difficulty. The Rule for monks is followed by another, for Virgins, which Mabillonius conjectures to have been the first monastic rule written for the benefit of nuns [Note: [Col. 0999D] Mabillonius, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. 1, p. 19, § 52.]. Nor should we omit what Martenius recorded [Col. 0999C] [Note: [Col. 0999D] Martenius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. 1, p. 3, note b.]: namely, that he had discovered this rule in an ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint Martin of Autun, at the end of which the following particularly noteworthy words are added, though they are absent from the printed editions:

“Caesarius the sinner ruled and wrote this rule of the holy virgins on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the time of the consul Paulinus.

“Simplicius the sinner consented and signed.

“Severus, bishop, consented and signed.

“Lupercianus, bishop, consented and signed.

“John consented and signed.

“Cyprianus, bishop, consented and signed.

“Montanus consented and signed.

“Firminus the sinner consented and signed.”

From these words the learned man argues for the date [Col. 0999D] when Saint Caesarius wrote this Rule, namely the year 534, under the consulship of Paulinus, the last of the Western consuls. Moreover, in Bollandus, at the end of the aforesaid Rule, the following subscription of the blessed bishop is found [Note: [Col. 0999D] Bollandus, *Acta Sanctorum*, January, vol. 1, p. 736.]: “Caesarius the sinner reread and subscribed this Rule of the holy virgins; [Col. 1000A] I noted it on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.” Elsewhere Martenius teaches [Note: [Col. 1000D] Martenius, *Literary Journey*, pp. 285ff.] that in the library of the monastery of Saint Maximinus at Trier there is a manuscript of the Rules of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, already published by Holstenius and written with considerable elegance, where near the end of the Rule for nuns there is a privilege of Pope Hormisdas, by which no authority whatsoever is granted to the bishops of Arles, Caesarius’s successors, over that monastery of virgins founded by Saint Caesarius. This privilege, absent from Holstenius’s edition, appears appended to the aforesaid Rule in Bollandus [Note: [Col. 1000D] Bollandus, loc. cit.]. Finally, we note that Cointius, whom we have praised, enlarged this same Rule, just as the preceding one, with notes [Note: [Col. 1000D] Cointius, loc. cit., pp. 472ff.], which we have appended in abridged form to our edition [Col. 1000B]. From the same learned man we also learn that the same Rule for nuns, received from Sirmondus, was first published at Poitiers in 1621 by Stephanus Moquotus, with observations by Franciscus Meinardus, a professor of Poitiers; and that shortly afterward, namely in 1626, Prosper Stellartius published it again at Douai in a work entitled *Foundations of the Orders*, leaving aside the other subsequent editions already mentioned.

IV. To these are added four letters of Saint Caesarius, preceded by a sermon of his to nuns. Of these letters, the first is addressed to the abbess Oratoria, though it is not preserved complete; the second is an exhortation to a virgin consecrated to God; the remaining two are said to have been sent to Caesaria, his sister, who had undertaken the governance of the monastery built through the efforts of her brother Caesarius. We have taken all these works from the frequently mentioned manuscript of Holstenius’s Rules. Finally, the collection is closed by the Testament of Saint Caesarius, taken from the same manuscript. This monument of ecclesiastical antiquity, excerpted from the archive of the Church of Arles by Claudius Saxius, notary, and received from Franciscus Claretus, archdeacon of that Church, while he was living in Rome, was first published by our Baronius [Note: [Col. 1000D] Baronius, under the year 508, § 23ff.]. Saxius also published it in his *Pontifical of Arles* [Note: [Col. 1000D] Saxius, *Pontifical of Arles*, § 30, pp. 101–105.], and finally Cointius in his *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks* [Note: [Col. 1000D] Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, under the year 542, § 23, pp. 616–618.]. Baronius long ago observed that the letters of Hormisdas, Roman pontiff, lend this Testament of Caesarius considerable authority and credibility [Note: [Col. 1000D] Baronius, loc. cit., § 28.], and Cointius did so after him [Note: [Col. 1000D] Cointius, loc. cit., § 24.]. Caesarius himself points to those letters when he says: “The authority of the holy Pope Urbicanus himself urged this.” By these words he evidently indicates that pontiff’s privilege, which is found in Bollandus appended to the Rule for nuns, as we noted above.

[Col. 1001]

THE LIFE OF SAINT CAESARIUS, BISHOP.

BOOK ONE. BY CYPRIANUS, FIRMINUS, AND VIVENTIUS, BISHOPS.

From manuscripts of Saint Martin of the Fields, of the Cluniac order, at Paris, compared with Mabillonius’s edition. (C)

PREFACE.

[Col. 1001A]

1. Since you, revered virgin Caesaria [Note: [Col. 1001C] This Caesaria is not the sister of Saint Caesarius, who died before him, as is clear from no. 44, but the abbess of the same monastery who succeeded her, as is said in that passage.], together with the community of nuns entrusted to your care, ask us to set down in writing, beginning at the outset, the life and conduct of blessed memory, Saint Caesarius, our founder [Mabillonius: your founder], through which his life enjoys its reward [Note: [Col. 1001C] Mabillonius’s edition differs considerably here in its wording; the reader may consult it.], although his blessedness cannot be expressed in mortal speech—though formerly, while he was still living here, it was reverently proclaimed throughout the whole world—we nevertheless believe that it would be wrong not to comply with so holy a desire. This is especially so because for your monastery, and even more for him, our account can take the place of his presence; and while we speak about him, we may rejoice that in some manner we are also seeing him. Therefore, with God’s help, [Col. 1001B] we shall undertake to fulfill what you request. We have learned many things about that most blessed lord [Mabillonius adds: Caesarius] through inquiry, many we ourselves witnessed, and some were reported by venerable priests and deacons, his disciples. Above all, however, we have relied on the accounts of the venerable priest Messianus and the most faithful man Stephanus, a deacon, who served him from adolescence; we shall include only those matters that are less burdensome and have been freed from prolixity.

2. We ask one thing of our readers in the devotion with which this little work is undertaken: if it should happen that we, simple reporters, come to the ears and judgment of men trained in literary studies, let them not reproach us because our style seems deprived of verbal ornament and the refinements of grammatical art. For when we narrate truthfully the deeds, words, and merits of so great a man, the light of his works and the adornments of his virtues are sufficient for us. Indeed, the aforesaid lord Caesarius, whom we have as our subject, was accustomed to say: “Some avoid rusticity of speech but do not turn away from the vices of life.” It is surely fitting for the pure sincerity of Christ’s virgins that nothing artificial, nothing fashioned by worldly art, should be presented to their eyes or offered to delight their ears; rather, they should receive words of the purest account flowing from the fountain of simple truth. And therefore this discourse of ours, content with the devotion of integrity, rejects worldly pomp and spurns, together with its works, the boastfulness of worldly glory; it takes greater delight in agreeing with the speech of fishermen [Note: [Col. 1001C] That is, of the apostles.] than with that of rhetoricians. Now, then, let each person seek by living to follow what he hastens to learn by reading.

CHAPTER ONE. The saint’s homeland, parents, clerical and religious life up to the episcopate.

3. Saint and most blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, is said to have been a native of the territory of Chalon [Note: [Col. 1001C] Chalon is a city of Gaul, situated in the duchy of Burgundy on the Saône, and an episcopal see under the archbishop of Lyons. It is sufficiently well known, commonly called Challon or Châlon-sur-Saône [Col. 1001D] to distinguish it from another city.]. His parents, of equally distinguished lineage, excelled all their fellow citizens in faith and conduct—this being a great and pre-eminent example of honor and nobility [Note: [Col. 1001D] The sense here is not entirely complete, but the same wording occurs in the manuscripts and printed editions.]. When this venerable and holy boy was seven years old or somewhat older, he would give to the poor, without any hesitation, the clothes he had around him. Often the blessed boy would return home half-naked; when his parents saw him and strictly questioned him about what he had done with his clothes, he would answer only that they had been taken from him by passers-by.

4. Just as certain little trees of noble stock are accustomed to bear fruit before they grow, and in them the smaller the age, the more pleasing the abundance, so in that holy man, amid the very rudiments of infancy, a joyful shoot of budding hope sprang forth so strongly that, before he blossomed through the span of his years [the fruit of his intelligence flourished. When he was eighteen years old] [Note: [Col. 1001D] This phrase is corrupt in Mabillonius, where it reads: “Before the space of one year had passed,” which is plainly erroneous. In our manuscript the words enclosed in brackets had been omitted, because the copyist had skipped from the first occurrence of the word *aetatis* (“of age”) to what follows after the same word, repeated later. Everything I have supplied in the text is found in our manuscript of Besançon and in the manuscript of Arles in Mabillonius’s notes.], desiring to attain the dwelling-place of the heavenly kingdom, without the knowledge of his household or parents, he prostrated himself before the holy bishop Silvester of that time [Note: [Col. 1002C] Saint Silvester is commemorated on 20 November, as our predecessors noted in volume 3 of the March issue, p. 516, where the discovery of his body is related in connection with other saints [Col. 1002D] who were found at the same time. We shall therefore provide more about him on that day. In the meantime, one may consult the reprinted *Gallia Christiana*, vol. 4, col. 863, where he is said to have administered that Church for forty-two years.], after first making supplication, asking that the bishop cut his hair, change his clothing, and bind him to divine service, and that he not allow the supplicant to be recalled by his parents to his former estate and pursuits [Mabillonius: “himself”]. When the bishop gave thanks to Christ, there was no delay in fulfilling his excellent vows. After serving there for two years or more in this beginning, inflamed by the prompting of divine grace, he resolved to free himself more strictly and more readily for divine service according to the Gospel, so that for love of the heavenly kingdom he might become a stranger not only to his parents but also to his homeland.

5. Thus, having wisely seized the freedom to flee the fetters of the world, the holy novice sought the monastery of Lérins [Note: [Col. 1003C] Baudrand describes the island of Lérins in his *Geography* as follows: “Lerina, an island of Narbonnese Gaul, called Lerinum and Lerinus by ecclesiastical writers, is now called Île Saint-Honorat by its inhabitants and Sant-Honorato by the Italians. It is a small island of Gaul off the coast of Provence in the Gallic Sea, where there is a celebrated monastery of Lérins, scarcely two leagues south of Antibes and five east of Fréjus. Together with Lero, it is commonly called the Islands of Saint-Honorat and Lérins, but Lero is larger and lies farther north than Lerina, from which it is separated by a narrow strait.” Vincentius Barralis, mentioned earlier, collected much information about the holy men who emerged in great number from the monastery of Lérins.]. As he traveled with only one servant, he was not seen by the searchers sent by his mother while crossing a river. The devil, however, entered a wretched man and, pursuing his journey, continually shouted from behind him: “Caesarius, do not go!” He immediately cured him by offering him a blessed cup of drink. This was learned from the report of his aforesaid companion, and it became clear that this was the first miracle he performed. Thus received by the holy abbot Porcarius [Note: [Col. 1003D] “This abbot Porcarius is different from another of the same name who suffered martyrdom in the eighth century,” Mabillonius says in his notes. Saint Porcarius II and his fellow martyrs are treated in the August volume 2, where, on p. 784, the distinction between the two Porcarii is established at greater length.], or by all the elders, he began to be prompt in vigils, watchful in observance, swift in obedience, devoted to labor, outstanding in humility, and singular in gentleness. Thus those who had undertaken to train him in the beginnings of regular discipline rejoiced to find him perfected in the growth of the entire formation.

[Col. 1003C] 6. After a short time he was appointed cellarer of the community. He therefore began attentively and diligently to distribute things to those who needed them, even if they asked for nothing out of love of abstinence; but to those whom he had determined did not need anything, he gave nothing, although they wished to receive it. As a result, those to whom holy discretion was displeasing begged the abbot that he ought to remove him from the storeroom; and this was done. Soon, setting aside care [Mabillonius adds: “in this way”], he finally devoted himself to the desired regularity of reading, singing psalms, praying, and keeping vigil, so that he made the body of his youth—which ought rather to have been treated gently than weakened—bent and broken alike by excessive hardship. Thus he would draw out, until the following Sunday, the food consisting of the small quantity of greens or porridge that he prepared for himself on the Lord’s Day [Mabillonius: “until the next Sunday”].

7. Such, then, were the good qualities that shone forth at the beginning of his merits; in the life that followed they were multiplied by manifold virtues. He wore down the strength of his flesh in order to strengthen the power of the spirit with the solidity of hope and faith. And, as the Apostle says, triumphing over himself and conquering himself so as to deserve to be crowned, he transcribed the outward man according to the commands of the inner man, and cast away the impulses of his rebellious body at the orders of his splendid mind. After this, however, when his stomach was failing, he suffered an attack of quartan fever [Note: [Col. 1003D] *Typus* or *typhus*, meaning an attack of fever or the fever itself, is not uncommon, as may be seen in Du Cange’s *Glossary*.]. When the holy abbot was deeply troubled by his illness, and the disease was divided, as it were, between master and disciple, so that the one suffered in spirit and the other in body, and when the holy Father saw that no remedy could be provided for him in the monastery—for even if a physician were present, the boy’s fervent devotion to spiritual matters would not permit any relaxation of the restraints of abstinence or the severity of vigils—the most blessed abbot ordered, indeed compelled, him to be brought to the city of Arles for the recovery of his health.

8. At that time there was a certain Firminus, illustrious and God-fearing, and his close associate, the noblewoman Gregoria, most illustrious among the women in the aforesaid city of Arles [Col. 1004C].

[Note: In Sirmond, volume I, column 827, there is a letter of Saint Ennodius to Firminus, whom Sirmond, in his notes, considers identical with this Firminus of ours.] Through their zeal, vigilance, and care for the clergy and monks, and for the citizens and the poor of the city, the city was thereby made more illustrious. Neither of them consumed their own resources in worldly luxury; rather, by transporting them through the poor, they sent them ahead for themselves to paradise.

They received the aforesaid Saint Caesarius into their household out of mercy. There was also a certain man named Pomerius, very familiar with these persons, skilled in rhetoric, and African by birth, whom his knowledge of the grammatical art made singularly distinguished and renowned there [Col. 1005A].

[Note: This passage is read in different ways. Sirmond, in his notes to Ennodius’s letter to Pomerius, quotes the words as follows: “Whom they held especially dear,” etc. Our manuscript has: “Whom he made singular for himself in the churches,” which appears corrupt. For this reason I have followed Mabillon’s edition here.]

They therefore conceived in their minds that Saint Caesarius, filled with so much divine grace and apparently supported by so great a gift of memory from Christ, might possess such strength that monastic simplicity might be powerful in him amid the disciplines of secular learning.

[Note: Mabillon, volume I of the *Annals*, p. 20, wrote the following about Pomerius:

“Pomerius, that African rhetorician to whom Caesarius was entrusted for education at Arles, appears to be a different man from Julianus Pomerius, who wrote books on the contemplative life, although both were Africans and both monks. For that Pomerius of Arles is addressed by the name of abbot in two letters of Ruricius, bishop of Limoges—namely, book I, letter 17, and book II, letter 9, as edited by Henry Canisius in volume I of the *Thesaurus Monumentorum*. Julianus Pomerius, however, when he was a bishop, wished—as he himself testifies—that, laying down the burden of his episcopate, he might flee far away and remain in solitude. These two things, episcopal dignity and solitude, do not suit Pomerius of Arles.”

Yet this opinion is not without difficulty. It scarcely seems credible that there were two Pomeriuses, both Africans, both having left their homeland, and both having become monks and rhetoricians by profession. Hence the Benedictines who produced the *Literary History of France*, volume II, p. 669, rightly refute Mabillon and take the word “episcopate” improperly, as meaning administration of the monastery, of which Pomerius was abbot. Their view is preferable, as being more consistent with the whole of antiquity.

Some writers think that Pomerius was abbot on the island outside Arles, where Caesarius later became abbot in place of Pomerius. This opinion appears probable, especially because Saint Ennodius, in a letter addressed to Pomerius, calls him an alumnus of the Rhône. That letter may be seen in the Sirmond edition cited above, column 826. More about Pomerius and his writings may be found in the *Literary History of France* mentioned above.]

9. But he did not accept the fabrications of human learning, whom divine grace had prepared to be instructed by itself. The teacher had therefore given him a book to read. Once, exhausted by keeping vigil, he happened to place it beneath his shoulder while lying on his bed. Although he then fell asleep, he was immediately struck by a terrifying vision from God. As he drifted into a light sleep, he saw, as it were, that the shoulder on which he was lying and the arm on which he had been leaning upon the book were being gnawed as a dragon bound them together.

Roused from sleep and terrified by the vision itself, he began to reproach himself even more terribly for having wished to join the light of the saving rule to the foolish wisdom of the world [Col. 1005B]. From that moment he despised these things, knowing that those in whom spiritual understanding had excelled would not lack the adornment of eloquent speech [Mabillon reads *esset*, “would be present,” for *deesset*, “would be lacking”].

10. After some days, the persons mentioned above made a proposal to Saint Eonius [Col. 1005D], bishop of the city, saying that they had among them a venerable monk distinguished by every praise, whose character he ought to learn through a familiar and private examination.

[Note: We shall discuss Saint Eonius on 30 August, the day on which he is commemorated.]

He therefore ordered him to be brought before him. When Saint Caesarius had been presented to him, the venerable Bishop Eonius carefully questioned him about what city he belonged to and from what parents he had been born. When he had disclosed his civic residence and his parents’ origin, the bishop rejoiced with holy eagerness and said:

“You are mine, my son—both a fellow citizen and a relative. For I remember your parents very well, and through kinship I embrace them in the memory belonging to your family.”

He then began to contemplate the young man, not as a stranger or outsider, but with a more attentive regard, through the innermost eyes of his heart. Soon afterward he requested him from his holy abbot Porcarius. At the request of the blessed Bishop Eonius, he was granted, although from one unwilling to grant him. Immediately he was ordained deacon, and afterward priest.

11. Nevertheless, he never abandoned the monks’ canonical chanting, nor even slightly left behind the institutions of Lérins. In rank and office he was a cleric; in humility, charity, service, and the cross he remained a monk.

At the church he was the first of those entering for Matins and the other assemblies, and the last of those leaving [Col. 1005D]. Neither sight nor sound could separate the blessed man’s mind from the nectar of heavenly goods, so that the appearance of his face always seemed somehow to shine with something heavenly [Col. 1006A].

Afterward, when the abbot of the island outside the city had died, blessed Father Caesarius was sent by Saint Eonius to govern as abbot the monastery [Col. 1006D] that had recently been deprived of its rector by death. He succeeded him in the same authority of reverence and was to form the monastery according to discipline.

[Note: “No trace now remains of this monastery, which Saxius considers to have been founded by Honoratus in his *Pontifical of Arles*. From it came Saint Ailbeus, or Alveus, the second Patrick of Ireland, concerning whom Colgan writes in the *Acts of the Saints of Ireland*, 12 September.” Thus Mabillon at this passage. Whether Saint Alveus flourished there under Caesarius, as some assert, will be examined in its proper place.]

He willingly undertook life in the suburban monastery, a life that he had always cultivated within the city by daily actions and had always desired by his vows. Through daily persistence and divine observances he so instructed the aforesaid monastery that, by God’s favor, it is still preserved there today.

## CHAPTER II

He is unwillingly promoted to the episcopate; arranges the divine offices and devotes himself fervently to preaching; provides for the sick, captives, and poor; is falsely accused and exiled; afterward, when his innocence is recognized, is honorably recalled; restrains fire, obtains rain, and other deeds.

[Col. 1006B]

12. When he had served in the office of abbot on the aforementioned island for a little more than three years, Saint Eonius addressed the clergy and citizens, and through intermediaries also addressed the leading men of the community, asking them that, when he himself, God willing, had departed to Christ, they should choose no one other than Saint Caesarius as his successor.

His purpose was that the ecclesiastical vigor which, as he lamented, had been weakened in many rules by his illness might, through Christ’s servant Caesarius, be restored to its proper condition and vigor, to the joy of the brotherhood. The successor’s labor would thus in some measure be the predecessor’s reward [Col. 1006D], since, by leaving behind such a successor, he would receive an increase of eternal inheritance even through the election of the holiest man [Col. 1006C]. After his departure there would not be lacking a companion in the vote of election, one who, while surviving him, would also stand as the authority behind the decree.

[Note: In our manuscript, which I have judged should be abandoned here, “successor” is corruptly read.]

After all these matters had therefore been faithfully arranged by divine Providence, blessed Eonius, secure concerning his successor, departed to the Lord.

When the matter had come to the knowledge of the Father of whom we speak, and the true report spread that he was to be ordained bishop, he sought a hiding place among certain tombs. But he could not remain concealed, since it was not guilt but grace that revealed him. Thus he was dragged alive from a tomb, and the brightness of life showed that he was not dead but hidden.

13. Compelled, therefore, to assume the burden of the episcopate, he carried the load placed upon Christ’s gentle beast with the moderation of humility. As a solicitous and prudent shepherd concerned for the progress of all, he immediately established [Col. 1006D] that every day the clergy should sing the Office of the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours in the basilica of Saint Stephen, with hymns [Col. 1007A], so that if any of the laity or penitents happened to desire to perform the holy work, he could attend the daily office without any excuse.

[Note: As Mabillon observes, he omits the office of Prime. He intended it to be said only on Sundays, Saturdays, and solemn feasts, as is clear from the appendix that he attached to the rule for nuns. At that time the canonical hours had not yet been arranged as they are today.]

He himself, rejecting every earthly anxiety and care, entrusted to the administrators and deacons, under adjuration before God, the apostolic diligence of management, and devoted his entire self to the word of God, to reading, and also to unremitting preaching.

Indeed, as a spiritual physician who cured the vices embedded in illnesses [and prevented those that would arise from evil thoughts], God granted him such a grace of speaking from his own resources [Col. 1007D] that whatever he could see with his eyes he might present, as a consoling analogy, for the edification of his hearers.

[Note: The words enclosed in brackets were absent from the manuscript that we otherwise follow. They are nevertheless found in Mabillon’s edition, to which, apart from a few words, the manuscript of Besançon agrees.]

He commended such a succession of sacred volumes and continually gathered new ones in such a way that he lost nothing of the old. He was like the temple of God, which daily receives new guests and cherishes the old, and which continually grows through the entrance of newcomers without ever being diminished by the departure of the old.

Whenever circumstances required, he recited examples and passages from the divine books with such precision that he seemed to be reviewing things known from a book, not bringing forth from the treasury of memory things once read. Thus he fulfilled the Gospel saying about a person who brings forth new and old things from his treasure.

When visiting bishops or priests, and all ministers of the divine order, whether citizens of the place or outsiders, had been greeted and prayed for, he would also ask briefly about the welfare and affection of their fellow citizens or their own people.

14. Soon, having taken up the weapons of holy preaching, he spoke about the shadow of present things and persuaded them of the eternity of blessedness. He invited some by gentle address, deterred others more sharply, corrected some by threats and others by kindness, recalled some from vices through charity and others through severity. Some he admonished generally, as though in proverbs; others he rebuked more harshly and under divine adjuration, threatening with tears the eternal punishments that would follow if they did not heed his warnings—all according to what he knew of each person’s virtues, character, or vices.

He delivered his preaching in such a way that he both stirred the good toward glory and recalled the wicked from punishment. Like a good physician, he provided different medicines for different wounds, offering not what pleased each person but what cured him. He did not consider the patient’s desire, but sought the health appropriate to the sick.

He sharply rebuked the bishops [Col. 1007D] and the other rulers of the Church, urging them to provide unceasingly spiritual food for the people entrusted to them. He said:

“You hold, in the name of Christ, the place of the first rank in the spiritual army, brother. Attend with pastoral diligence to the talents entrusted to you, so that you may return them doubled to the moneylender [Col. 1008A]. Hear the prophet: ‘Woe is me, because I have kept silent!’ Hear the Apostle speaking with fear: ‘Woe to me if I do not evangelize.’ Beware lest, while you occupy the place of the chair, another who might have responded better to the Lord’s interests be shut out, and that saying be spoken of you: ‘They took away the key of knowledge; they did not enter themselves, and they prevented others from entering.’”

Yet, by God’s inspiration, he possessed this particular gift: while addressing different words to different people, he set before each one the course of his own life, so that whoever heard him believed not only that he was a searcher of hearts, but also confessed him to be a witness of his conscience. And just as he was extremely strict toward himself, so he appeared severe toward others for the sake of their correction.

15. He also added and compelled the common people of the laity to prepare psalms and hymns and, in a loud and measured voice like that of the clergy, to sing—some in Greek and others in Latin—proses and antiphons, so that they would have no opportunity to occupy themselves with gossip in the church.

[Note: Hear what Mabillon notes at this passage:

“Saint Jerome, in the preface to book II of his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, reports from Varro that the Massilians, fellow provincials of the people of Arles, were trilingual and spoke Greek, Latin, and Gaulish. One may suspect that this use of languages was spread throughout Gaul from the celebrated academy of Massilia, on the basis of book VI of Julius Caesar’s *Gallic War*, where we learn that the Gauls used Greek letters in almost all matters, both public and private. From this passage in the *Life of Saint Caesarius*, however, we gather that the use of the Greek language remained among the people of Arles even into the sixth century, including among the laity and the common people, and was employed in sacred services.”]

He also established and introduced deeply moving sermons suited to the season or to the feasts.

He provided especially [Mabillon: “very well”] for the sick and helped them, assigning a very spacious house where they could hear the holy service without any disturbance from the basilica. He provided beds, bedding, provisions [the text has *sumptos* for *sumptus*], and a person who could serve and care for them. He did not deny captives and poor people the opportunity and freedom to make their requests.

He always instructed his attendant, saying:

“See whether any of the poor are standing outside the doors, lest perhaps, because of our quiet, some timid and shamefaced person of standing, waiting because of our sin, suffer injury” [Col. 1008C].

Drawing long sighs from the depths of his heart, he said:

“Christ has truly become one who waits, and one who chatters, and one who is deaf, and yet he asks, persuades, admonishes, and adjures everyone.”

[Note: Mabillon reads *protelator* (“one who prolongs”) rather than *praestolator* (“one who waits”). Here “Christ” designates the poor, or the members of Christ; the text does not deny their faults, but teaches that they must nevertheless be helped.]

He also added that, without doubt, the poor were given to us for our progress in the present age, so that now, with Christ as guarantor, we might entrust to them on earth what we would later receive in heaven.

16. But after a few days an adversity provoked by the devil’s envy disturbed the tranquillity of this holy man. Since it had no bodily vices to set against him, it brought an accusation of treachery against him.

Some time later, a certain depraved notary of the blessed man, named Licinianus, undertook against the apostolic man what the disciple Judas did not fear to perpetrate against our Savior, the Son of God [Col. 1008D].

Armed with the poison of a savage accusation, he suggested through informers to King Alaric that the most blessed Caesarius, who originated in Gaul, was striving with all his strength to subject the territory and city of Arles to the authority of the Burgundians [Col. 1009A]. Yet that outstanding shepherd, kneeling, was asking the Lord day and night for the peace of the peoples and the tranquillity of the cities in general.

For this reason especially we must believe that barbarian ferocity was stirred up by the devil’s prompting against the holy man, to send him into exile. For the enemy does not welcome or favor the person who prays that his works may be opposed.

17. At the instigation of those then in power, neither the credibility of innocence was considered nor the truth of the accusation sought. Condemned on false and unlawful charges, he was taken away from Arles and relegated as if into exile to the city of Bordeaux [Col. 1009D].

[Note: Burdegala, Bordeaux to the French, is a very famous city of Gaul on the river Garonne; at that time it obeyed Alaric, king of the Visigoths. Sigonius reports the whole event in *On the Western Empire*, book XVI, no. 504 of the new edition, and agrees correctly with the *Life*, except that he calls the notary, the saint’s accuser, Licumannus rather than Licinianus. Sigonius says that the event occurred around the consulship of Cethegus, that is, about the year 504, when he held the consulship without a colleague. We have said in commentary no. 16 that the year 505 should probably be assigned.]

But so that God’s grace might not remain hidden in him, it happened by chance that one night the city was burning in a terrible fire. The people quickly ran together and cried out to the man of God:

“Saint Caesarius, extinguish the raging fire by your prayers” [Col. 1009B].

When the man of God heard this, moved by sorrow and compassion, he threw himself down in prayer before the advancing flame, and immediately he halted and drove back the balls of fire. At this sight, all who had gathered celebrated through their voices the praise of God’s power manifested through him.

After this miracle he was held in such great admiration by everyone that in the same city he was regarded not only as a priest but as an apostle. The author of the persecution, that is, the devil, was confounded: the man whom he had attempted to declare guilty he saw excelling through miracles of divine action.

We have learned that this happened through a trustworthy account.

There, as everywhere, he instructed the Church to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s; to obey, according to the Apostle, kings [Col. 1009C] and authorities when they command what is just; and to hold in contempt, in a ruler, the depravity of the Arian doctrine.

Thus, with truth bearing witness, the lamp placed upon a mountain could not be hidden. Wherever he went, he illumined everyone, shining upon his lampstand [Mabillon: “the Lord’s lampstand”].

18. When the innocence of the blessed man had afterward been discovered, the wicked ruler requested that the holy bishop return to his former church and present himself once more to the city and clergy. The king ordered his accuser to be stoned.

The people had already begun to run together with stones when suddenly the king’s order reached the saint’s ears. At once the holy man rose in haste and intervened. He did not wish his accuser to be handed over so much to his own vengeance as he preferred, by his personal supplication, to preserve him for repentance, so that the Lord might heal through repentance the man’s soul, which the enemy had made captive through false treachery.

By mercifully forgiving the domestic enemy, he overcame the ancient adversary twice in one matter, with a clear conscience.

The servant of God also took particular care that no one, whether a servant or a free person serving him, should ever receive more than the lawful discipline, namely thirty-nine blows [Col. 1010A].

[Note: The measure of blows prescribed to the Jews in Deuteronomy 25:2–3 was that they should not exceed the number forty. For caution’s sake they deducted one from the number. Hence Paul, 2 Corinthians 11:24: “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one.”]

If someone had been found guilty of a serious offense, he permitted him to be beaten again after several days, but only a few times. He warned the leaders of the Church that if anyone ordered a negligent person to be beaten more severely, and the man died as a result of that discipline, the person whose command had caused it would be guilty of homicide.

When it was announced that the man of Christ was returning and was already approaching the city, the entire brotherhood and people of every sex went out to meet him, singing with candles and crosses and awaiting the holy man’s entrance.

Because Christ makes his own people rejoice through miracles and confounds the faithless by the manifest light of wonders, at the arrival of his servant the Lord drenched the dry earth, parched by a very long drought, with a most abundant rain, so that fertility followed with its fruit when the pleasing steward returned.

19. Afterward, one day, looking out from the altar, he saw certain people leaving the church after the Gospel readings. They disdained first to hear the blessed man’s word, that is, his preaching.

He immediately went after them and cried out to the people:

“What are you doing, children? Where are you being led, overturned by evil persuasion? Stand firm for your souls before the word of admonition, and listen attentively. You will not be permitted to do this on the day of judgment. I warn you, I cry out, I adjure you: do not therefore be fugitives or deaf.

“Behold the trumpet of my mouth, as though the soul of each one of you had been struck down by the devil’s sword. I shall not be held guilty of silence.”

For this reason he very often ordered the doors to be closed after the Gospel readings [Col. 1010C], until, by God’s will, those who had been fugitives might rejoice in their restraint and progress.

## CHAPTER III

A monastery is built for holy virgins and a rule is written for them; the saint, attacked by calumnies, is thrust into prison and afterward taken to Ravenna; captives are redeemed; miracles.

20. The man of God therefore conceived in his mind that, while the Lord always reigned, the church of Arles should be adorned not only with countless ranks of clergy but also with choirs of virgins, and that the city should be fortified. Thus, as a fruitful farmer, he might store a full harvest in the heavenly granaries and, surviving, teach that it should be carried in through the following of his example [Col. 1010D].

But adversity, arising from the devil’s envy, opposed these arrangements for a time. For while the Franks and Burgundians were besieging the city, after King Alaric had been killed in battle by the most victorious Clovis, Theodoric, king of Italy [Col. 1011A], had entered this province after sending commanders.

[Note: Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths in Italy, is very well known in history. Pagi places his entry into Italy in the year 489 and his death in 526. Like most of the Goths at that time, he was an Arian; otherwise he was commendable in character and government, and sufficiently kind toward Catholics and men distinguished for holiness, unless he had acquired certain blemishes.

We explained this event in commentary § 2, where we said that Alaric was killed by Clovis in 507, that the city began to be besieged in 508, and that the siege was lifted in 510.]

During this siege, the monastery that he had begun to build for his sister and the other virgins was largely destroyed, its timber and dining halls alike plundered and overturned by the barbarians’ ferocity.

When he saw the work, which he had hurried to advance and had constructed with his own hands and sweat, being overturned and destroyed, he began to be consumed by doubled sorrow.

21. Then a certain cleric, his fellow citizen and relative, terrified by fear of captivity and moved by youthful recklessness, armed by the devil’s prompting against the servant of God [Mabillon adds: “armed”], let himself down by night with a rope from the wall and voluntarily offered himself the next day to the most wicked besieging enemies.

[Note: That is, the devil brought this about so that an opportunity for calumny might arise against the saint.]

When the Goths within learned of this, they rushed upon the holy man, while a popular uprising and a crowd of Jews made an excessive uproar and shouted that the bishop had sent a fellow countryman by night to betray the city to the enemy [Col. 1011B].

[Note: That is, a fellow citizen, born in Burgundy, I think, since Caesarius was born there.]

No room was therefore left for faith, proof, or a clear conscience. The Jews especially and the heretics shouted the same thing without reverence or restraint:

“Let the bishop be dragged from the church residence and committed to the strictest confinement in the palace, so that during the night he may either be thrown into the depths of the Rhône or certainly be cast into the fortress of Ugernum [Col. 1011C] and held there, until adversity may rage more violently against him through exile and tribulation.”

[Note: “The fortress of Ugernum,” says Mabillon here, “must, according to Strabo, book IV, be situated between Nemausus and Tarascon, precisely where the city now called Beaucaire is seen, according to the view of Samson, royal geographer. John of Bularia, in his chronicle under the third year of Maurice, mentions the fortress of Ugernum and places it on the bank of the Rhône.”

Longueval, volume II, p. 299, observes that geographers do not agree about the site of this fortress. “Many,” he says, “think it is the city now called Beaucaire; it is more probably an island of the Rhône called Gernica, La Vergne.” The latter opinion is taken from Valesius, who discusses the fortress of Ugernum more extensively in *Notitia Galliarum*, p. 601, since that name is closer to it.]

The church residence and the bishop’s bedroom were therefore packed with Arian occupants. Yet one of the Goths, who, despite the objections of the others, had lain down in the saint’s bed, was struck by the Divinity and died the next day [Col. 1011C], so that no one thereafter dared, with a polluted conscience, to violate the servant of God’s place.

Although the Goths were unable, by God’s will, to raise from either bank the fast vessel—the *dromo* [Col. 1012A]—by which he had been lured, because of the enemy’s siege, they brought the holy man back by night into the palace and concealed his identity in silence, so that none of the Catholics could learn whether he was alive.

[Note: *Drumo*, more correctly *dromo*, designates a swift ship, from Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ δρόμου, “from running” or “course.”]

22. While these things were taking place, with the devil exulting and the Jews rejoicing—those Jews who everywhere spewed insults against our people without any regard for their treachery—one night a man from the Jewish group, from the place where they had happened to undertake the duty of keeping watch on the wall, threw a letter tied to a stone toward the enemy, as though he were striking the adversaries.

In it, identifying his name and sect, he invited them to bring ladders at night to the place of their guard, provided that in return for the benefit received no Jew inside would suffer captivity or the loss of his property.

In the morning, when the enemies had withdrawn somewhat from the wall, certain men went outside the outer wall and, as usually happens, found the letter among the ruins. They carried it inside and published it for everyone in the marketplace.

The man was immediately brought forward, convicted, and punished. Then the savage cruelty of the Jews, hateful to God and humanity, was finally exposed and confounded in the clear light of day.

Soon our Daniel—Saint Caesarius—was also brought out of the lions’ den, and the accusation of the satraps was made public. The saying was fulfilled concerning the author of their plot:

“He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit that he made.”

23. When the Goths returned to Arles with an immense number of captives [Col. 1012D], the sacred basilicas were filled, and the church residence too was packed with unbelievers.

[Note: At that time not a few among the Franks were still pagans, even though their king Clovis had converted to the Christian faith together with many others.]

Since these people were in great need, the man of God abundantly supplied them with food and clothing until he freed each one through the gift of redemption. He spent the silver that his predecessor, the venerable Eonius, had left for the use of the church table.

Following the example that the Lord dipped bread in an *arantine* dish—not in a silver vessel—and commanded his disciples to possess neither gold nor silver [Note: In our manuscript the word is *Araantino*. The word is equally unknown. Mabillon attempts to explain it as follows: “It appears to be derived from ἀραιός, which signifies something fragile, such as an earthenware or glass vessel; perhaps the author understood it in this sense, as may be gathered from what follows.”].

The holy work was carried out even to the provision of the divine ministry. Indeed [Mabillon reads “and with”], even censers, chalices, and patens, when given for the redemption of these people, were sold though consecrated for the temple’s service [Col. 1012C]. It even appears that blows of axes were struck against the pedestals and screens [Col. 1012D], as the silver ornaments were removed from the columns.

[Note: This phrase is confused in Mabillon and gives a different meaning, as anyone who compares the two texts together will discover.]

The man of God did this, saying that a rational human being, redeemed by the blood of Christ, must not, after losing the condition of freedom, become either an Arian or a Jew because of bondage, nor a slave from being free, nor free from being a slave.

24. Through this he adorned and protected the church; he did not disfigure it. He caused the womb of the mother to be opened for her children, not condemned. He said this very often:

“I would like certain priests of the Lord, or the rest of the clergy, who through some love of excess refuse to give the insensible silver and gold from Christ’s offerings for Christ’s slaves, to give me an account.

“I would like them, I say, to tell me, if these misfortunes happened to them by chance, whether they would wish to be freed by these insensible offerings—or whether perhaps they would count it sacrilege if someone came to their aid from the divine gifts.

“I do not believe that it is contrary to God for redemption to be given from his ministry, since he himself gave himself for the redemption of humanity” [Col. 1013A].

[Note: These words of the saint plainly show that there were people who criticized this charity of his. Caesarius could also have defended himself by the example of Saints Augustine and Ambrose, whom he imitated in this action. Hear Saint Ambrose himself, *On Duties*, book II, chapter 28:

“Let this be the greatest incentive to mercy: that we sympathize with the calamities of others and help their necessities as much as we can, and sometimes more than we can. It is better to provide grounds for mercy, or to endure envy, than to display lack of compassion. Thus we once incurred envy because we broke the sacred vessels in order to redeem captives—something that could have displeased the Arians. It was not so much the deed itself that displeased them as the fact that it gave them something with which to reproach us. Who, however, is so hard, unfeeling, and iron-hearted that he would be displeased when a man is redeemed from death, a woman from the impurity of barbarians—impurities worse than death—and young women, boys, or infants from the contagion of idols, with which they were being defiled through fear of death?”

Caesarius could have said precisely the same.]

We see that some people praise the holy man’s action on this account, yet in no way imitate it.

Was not Christ’s blood in glass, and his most precious body hung and shone upon wood for us? [Col. 1013B] Yet we believe and trust in the Lord God, through the mercy and faith—or prayer—of blessed Caesarius, that in his days the city of Arles was so besieged by enemies that it did not deserve to fall into captivity or succumb to plunder.

Afterward it passed from the Visigoths to the kingdom of the Ostrogoths [Col. 1014C].

[Note: Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, claimed the city for himself at the same time after it had been freed from the siege, as is clear from the tribute that he remitted to the people of Arles. See the commentary, no. 17.]

Today it is subject in the name of Christ to the authority of the most glorious King Childebert [Col. 1014D], so that, as we read, “they passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people,” and God did not permit anyone under that ruler to harm his people of Arles.

[Note: The city of Arles came to Childebert in the year 536, when Vitiges, king of the Ostrogoths, ceded to the Franks whatever he possessed in Gaul, and the Frankish kings, the sons and heirs of Clovis, divided that territory among themselves. More about this may be found in Cointius under the year 536, nos. 1 and following.]

25. Meanwhile he rebuilt, in the likeness of the earlier rule and with the singularity of a cloister, the distinguished monastery that he had begun to prepare for his sister.

He himself—if indeed nothing contrary to the mystery fitting for a Christian is involved—like a more recent Noah of our time, because of the storms and tempests, built an ark at the side of the church of the monastery for his companions or sisters. He summoned from the monastery of Massilia his venerable sister Caesaria [Col. 1014A], whom he had sent there for this reason: so that she might learn what she would teach, and might first be a disciple before becoming a teacher. He brought her into the prepared dwellings with two or three companions for the time being.

Crowds of virgins gathered there in great companies. Renouncing their possessions and parents, they rejected the deceptive and equally fleeting flowers of mortal life. They sought the embrace of Father Caesarius and Mother Caesaria, so that, with lamps lit together with him, they might await the door of the heavenly kingdom and, having entered appropriately, might deserve to cling to Christ’s perpetual embraces.

They were so enclosed that, until the day of their departure, no one was permitted to leave the monastery through the outer door.

26. For this reason, and because of this zeal, the devil undoubtedly raged against the servant of Christ like an inflamed and rabid lion. After preparing another accusation, he had the bishop taken from Arles and brought under guard into Italy, and to Ravenna, so that what is written might be fulfilled in him: “As gold and silver are tested in the furnace, so are the hearts of the elect before God.”

He therefore went to the palace and, with Christ as his guide, approached King Theoderic to greet him. When the king saw the fearless and venerable man of God, he rose respectfully to greet him; then, removing the headdress from his head, he graciously returned the greeting. First he asked about his hardships and journey; afterward he affectionately inquired about his Goths and the people of Arles. When the holy man [Mabillon adds: “bishop”] had left the king’s presence, the king addressed his attendants, saying:

“May God not spare those who have needlessly subjected this man of innocence and holiness to so long a journey. What sort of man he is is proved by this: when he entered to greet me, I trembled from head to foot. I see,” he said, “an angelic face; I see an apostolic man. I consider it sacrilegious to think anything evil about so venerable a man.”

Afterward, once he had been received at his lodging, the king sent him, as a gift, a silver dish for his meal, whose weight amounted to approximately sixty pounds, together with three hundred solidi. [Note: I think *pensa* is used here for “weight,” although among medieval writers it has other meanings as well.] He asked and said at the same time:

“Receive this, holy bishop. Your son the king asks that your blessedness graciously accept this little vessel as a gift and keep it for use in memory of him.” [Col. 1014B–C]

27. But he, who had never used silver at his table except for spoons [the manuscript reads *cochlearia*; Mabillon reads *cochlearibus*, “spoons”], had his servants publicly put the dish up for sale on the third day, and with its price began to free very many captives.

“Immediately,” they say, “his servants reported to the king: ‘Look! We have seen the lord’s gift for sale among the things being sold, and with its price Saint Caesarius is freeing crowds of captives.’”

For such an enormous multitude of poor people was about him, packed into the courtyard of his house, that, because of the density of the wretched petitioners, one could scarcely approach him even to greet him. [Note: The word *meditatu* is obscure, but its sense is inferred from what follows.] [Col. 1014D–1015A] Indeed, we saw innumerable crowds of unfortunate people running through the streets, going to and returning from the man.

When Theoderic learned what had happened, he praised and admired it so greatly that the senators and nobles attending upon his palace all vied with one another to have the reward of their offerings distributed by the blessed man’s hand. They proclaimed themselves divinely regarded because they had been deemed worthy to behold such a bishop, who in those times appeared, in word and deed, a true successor of the apostles and an apostolic man.

And because nothing travels faster than fame, as this most holy work increased, the holy man’s holy reputation immediately spread throughout Rome. There it began to be desired by the senate and nobles, by the pope and clergy, and likewise by the common people, with such ardor of charity that he had already taken his place in the embrace of each person’s heart before he was seen with bodily eyes. [Col. 1015A–B]

Meanwhile, he redeemed, as soon as he found them in Italy, all the captives from beyond the Durance, especially those of the town of Orange, which had been surrendered entirely to captivity. He had also freed some of them at Arles by paying their ransom.
