[Note: The Durance, called *la Durance* by the French, rises from Mount Genevra, one of the Cottian Alps in the region of Briançon in Dauphiné; it then flows through Provence and is received by the Rhône one league below Avignon.]

[Note: Orange—*Arausio*—is a town in Provence beyond the Durance. From this passage it may sufficiently be inferred that it was captured by the Goths after they had defeated the Franks and Burgundians near Arles and crossed the Durance.]

[Note: The text has *Arelatum*; Mabillon reads *Arelato*.]

And, so that their freedom might be restored more fully, he provided animals and wagons at his own expense for the journey and, with the assistance and arrangements of his own people, had them brought back to their homes.

28. During these events, in the aforesaid city of Ravenna, a certain widow had a young son who served in the prefectural offices and supported his mother’s poverty from his earnings and wages. This boy, struck by a sudden illness, lay lifeless. When every hope and comfort of human treatment had failed, his mother immediately abandoned and left behind her son and hurried to the man of God.

She prostrated herself, her eyes streaming with tears and adding loud wails. With faith alone still alive, she clasped the blessed man’s knees and cried:

“I believe that divine mercy has brought you here for this reason, holy [Mabillon adds: “man of”] God: so that you might restore my son to his mother.”

For a little while he refused the woman as she tearfully pleaded. Yet he considered it harsh not to hear such tears and, moved by his customary compassion, wishing to discharge the duty of charity in such a way and to exercise power in God’s name while avoiding vanity in everything, he secretly and quietly went to her dwelling.

After pouring out a prayer in the customary manner and prostrating himself, when he sensed through the Holy Spirit that the divine power corresponding to his calling was present, he departed. He left instructions with his notary at that time, now the venerable presbyter Messianus, that he should immediately inform him when the young man returned to himself.

While Messianus kept watch before the bed of the sick man, before an hour had passed the boy was recalled from the darkness of death. At once, opening his eyes, he addressed his mother:

“Go, mother, and hurry to the servant of God, by whose prayers I have been restored to you and to life; give thanks that God has brought this about through his merits and virtues.” [Col. 1015D–1016A]

She flew and hastened to him, offering thanks not so much in words as in tears, cries, and expressions of joy. She asked that, when he returned to Gaul, he would not allow the man whom God had restored to this light through him to depart from his service.

But that blessed man, of profound understanding, replied that she ought rather to give thanks to the One whose power and mercy are accustomed to be present to all who mourn and cry out. The greatness of this miracle therefore traveled not only through that city but throughout the entire province, carried by the devotion and reports of the faithful.

29. The deacon and physician Elpidius, a man close to the royal authority through his constant service, was not only harassed by the devil’s attacks and various other assaults, but was also frequently assailed in his house by a shower of stones. He begged the holy man of God to merit release from this harassment through his prayers.

Entering his house to sanctify it, Caesarius sprinkled it with an infusion of blessed water and freed him from the dangers of the customary harassment, so that nothing of the kind ever happened there again.

## CHAPTER IV. He travels to Rome and receives various favors from the bishop; then, having returned home, he shines through various virtues and miracles.

30. Afterward, when he came to Rome, he was presented first to Pope Symmachus [Note: Symmachus held the pontificate from 498 until 514, when he died on 19 July, as Pagius records there, no. 1. Caesarius’s dealings with Symmachus occurred in 513; we have set them out more fully in the commentary, §3.] and then to the senators and senatrices.

They all gave thanks to God and to the king that they had been deemed worthy to see with bodily eyes the one whom they had long since beheld with the eyes of the heart. Thus, recognizing the apostolic man not merely through the report of fame but through his bodily presence, they began eagerly to love and venerate him.

For this reason Pope Symmachus, moved by the great dignity of his merits, not only honored him most truly with the dignity of a metropolitan but also decorated him with the privilege of the pallium, granted to him in a special manner. He caused Caesarius’s deacons to take precedence in dress, wearing dalmatics in the manner of the Roman Church.

31. Then he returned home and entered the city of Arles, received with psalm-singing. He brought back from Italy, whither he had gone into exile, eight thousand solidi obtained through a ready ransom.

[Note: I suppose these were surplus funds received as alms, intended for spending at Arles on the redemption of captives or on other pious works.]

On the day he entered the city, he went into the church in the evening to give his blessing. And behold, one of the women, seized by trembling, crying out with foam at the mouth, and shouting so that everyone was terrified [Mabillon adds: “in the church”], broke forth. Seized by the hands on either side, she was immediately brought before the blessed man at the altar. Everyone pleaded that he drive away the affliction and restore the woman to health.

Then, following his customary practice, he prostrated himself in prayer for her. Placing his hand on her head, he anointed all her senses and her face with the touch of sacred oil. After this, the calamity that had been driven away in Christ’s name never again attacked the woman.

32. Meanwhile he had a special concern for captives above all others. He was so outstanding and so devoted in this ministry that no account could adequately describe it.

One day, when his holy hands lacked any gold or silver to give to the needy, a poor man appealed to him. He said:

“What shall I do for you, my poor fellow? I give you what I have.”

He then entered his cell and brought out a processional cloak [Note: That is, as I suppose, one used in processions or in a procession of supplicants] and a white paschal garment [Note: Mabillon explains this as a white *planeta*, or chasuble. I would rather understand it as a long linen garment, commonly called “white,” with which priests are clothed beneath the chasuble or *planeta* when celebrating Mass. He calls it “paschal” because it was of the finest quality and reserved for the Paschal festival]. He gave it to the poor man, saying:

“Go, sell it to any cleric you can find, and with its price redeem your captive.”

Not only were those who had sought him released from the bonds of captivity, but he himself also traveled to the city of Carcassonne to redeem captives.

[Note: Carcassonne—*Carcasso*, frequently called *Carcassona*—is a city in lower Occitania on the river Aude. It is well known and lies at a considerable distance from the city of Arles. From this it becomes especially clear how devoted the saint was to redeeming captives.]

He also sent abbots, deacons, and clerics on many occasions to different places for the redemption of the unfortunate.

33. He was granted as many virtues of divine grace as scarcely ever flourished among the many who serve God. Yet he always cultivated each virtue in himself as though he possessed that virtue alone. His most beautiful and delightful precedence always appeared so long as it was surpassed by those who followed.

Who could describe his patience, his purity, his charity, his spiritual fervor, his discernment, his kindness, his holy zeal, or his continual meditation day and night on the law of the Lord?

He was a defender of the faith, a model for priests, an ornament of churches, a preacher of grace, an extinguisher of quarrels, a seedbed of charity, a rule of discipline, a weighmaster of conduct, a balance of counsel, a defense of orphans, and a redemption for captives.

Never did slander, never a lie, never a curse against any person whatsoever proceed from his mouth. And not only did he slander no one; he would not even patiently listen to someone who slandered.

34. If one of his own people suddenly swore or perhaps cursed, he chastised him salutarily according to the person’s character. Yet this was his blessing in place of a curse whenever he became angry with anyone:

“May God erase your sin. May God take away your sins. May the Lord chastise your offense, so that it may not be held against you there. May the Lord correct your error here.”

The outward revealed what was within. His face was always serene and angelic, so that, according to Scripture, his face blossomed from a joyful heart. Thus he was never more relaxed than was proper in laughter, nor ever overwhelmed by excessive sorrow—unless perhaps he was mourning over the sins of others.

He never hated anyone, and he prayed with all the affection of his heart not only for his friends but also for his enemies. Nor did he teach in words what he failed to fulfill by example.

No hour of the day passed him without meditation on divine speech; nor did it pass him even while he slept, for he was often seen both sleeping and meditating. And when he seemed to cease from meditating on the psalms or from preaching, a reader or notary continued reading before him without interruption. Thus he could rightly and truly say: “The meditation of my heart is always in your sight.”

35. At a certain time, while he was traveling through the Alpine regions, the venerable holy bishop Eucherius was with him.

[Note: “Eucherius the younger, that is,” says Mabillon; “for it has been demonstrated above in the Acts of Saint Consortia that two men of this name occupied the see of Lyon.” But concerning Eucherius II, who would have been Caesarius’s contemporary, there is considerable disagreement among scholars, as may be seen in the new *Gallia Christiana*, volume IV, columns 20 and following, where the principal arguments of both sides are recorded. It is not the place here to settle the controversy completely, since that should be done when the Acts of Saint Eucherius come under examination. Nevertheless, I can readily show that a weak argument is being drawn from this passage in favor of the second Eucherius.

First, neither in our manuscript nor in Mabillon’s edition is Eucherius called bishop of Lyon; he is called only “bishop,” so that the word “Lyonese” appears to have been added by Surius, who wished in that way to make the matter clearer. The same word entered Vincent Barralis’s edition from Surius, whom he followed in many places.

Now it can be shown without difficulty of which city Eucherius was bishop. In the cited *Gallia Christiana*, volume I, column 798, the names of certain bishops who subscribed to the Fourth Council of Arles are produced from a very ancient manuscript codex of the Councils, together with the names of their cities, which were lacking in the printed councils. Among these bishops one reads: “Eucherius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Avignon”—that is, *Avennica*.

From this I infer that Eucherius of Avignon is the one who is recorded, without a city-name, as having subscribed to the four councils held by Saint Caesarius within a few years: the Fourth Council of Arles, the Council of Carpentras, the Second Council of Orange, and the Council of Valence. I infer further that no other Eucherius was the companion of Saint Caesarius in this passage than the aforesaid bishop of Avignon, since the proximity of the places strongly supports this, while the arguments advanced for Eucherius II of Lyon are of no weight, as can be shown in its proper place.]

It happened that, in the middle of the road [Note: *Strata* is often used for “road”], an unfortunate and sick woman came toward them with her hands and feet contracted, crawling along the ground. When Caesarius saw her, he asked Saint Eucherius what this was, that she was dragging herself along the ground in such a way.

Eucherius questioned the woman. She replied that she had been paralyzed for many years and that all her limbs were contracted.

Then blessed Caesarius said to Saint Eucherius:

“Get down and make the sign of the cross over her.”

Eucherius began, as though hesitating and making excuses. Caesarius did not stop insisting that he do so. He therefore got down, made the sign of the cross over her, and said:

“There, I have done what you ordered.”

He replied again:

“Extend your hand, take hold of her hand, and raise her.”

Eucherius answered:

“I will do anything else that you order, Eucherius, but I do not dare undertake this matter. You do it, since God has given you power to heal both the souls and the bodies of the sick.”

Saint Caesarius replied:

“For now, do what I say.”

When Eucherius resisted firmly, excused himself humbly and tearfully, and continued to argue for some time, Caesarius said to him:

“You would have entered fire for the sake of obedience, yet for the sake of mercy you are not ready to do what charity commands? Extend your hand in the Lord’s name and raise her.”

Then, obeying the command, he raised the woman with his outstretched hand. Her feet and all her limbs restored, she walked unharmed to her little lodging.

36. For who could recount with how many virtues he shone? It happened that wild boars frequently appeared in the suburban estate of his monastery. The counts of the city and the other men in military service would go out and would not allow people to live or work in their houses, but killed them with excessive slaughter—[the syntax is obscure; the sense appears to be that the men were slaughtered because they attempted to prevent the hunters].

After enduring these injuries and disturbances for a long time, the people came and appealed to their lord, crying out and saying:

“Do with us what you command, for we can neither serve you nor remain there.”

He carefully asked what their complaints were. They replied:

“Because of the wild boars, the counts, Goths, and various hunters come and kill us.”

Then, in a loud voice, raising his eyes and hands and looking toward heaven, he said:

“Lord Jesus Christ, let the wild boars have no further access to this place.”

From that hour until the present day, they have never bred there as they used to, nor did anything appear that could be hunted.

[Note: Mabillon reads *nec truerunt* and notes: “It seems that this should be read, not *nutrierunt*, since elsewhere *truo* was formerly used for *destruo*, ‘destroy,’ which suits wild boars very well.” Nevertheless, I prefer the reading of our manuscript, which has *nutrierunt*.]

He rightly commanded the beasts, since he had driven every vice away from himself. He was able to obtain this from God because he had never transgressed God’s command.

37. It also happened that the boy of the most illustrious man, the patrician Parthenius, who was regarded by his master as preeminent among the other servants, repeatedly fell to the ground with his senses overthrown under a most wicked temptation. Since his torment by the enemy seemed truly to be an illness of the soul rather than of the body, he was anointed with oil consecrated by the blessing of the most blessed man.

After this, the evil temptation departed from him so completely that Christ, through his servant, had restored him to health when the earthly physician’s care had failed; and the master himself placed him in charge of his household as an example and warning.

And because, for the purpose of displaying the merit of the most holy man, what follows may inspire even greater fear under the guise of wonder, it would be wrong to pass over this memorable deed in silence.

38. While the holy man was traveling around his dioceses, he was received by the owners of a villa called Launico. After he had departed, in the cell where he had slept, a certain pestilential physician named Anatolius—an object of great pity for such a crime—sought a prostitute for the bed where the holy man had lain.

Thereupon, immediately seized by public torment from the devil who had incited him, he was struck down before the eyes of the people. In a loud voice, while confessing the power of the servant of God through which he had been punished for his presumption, he publicly disclosed the crime he had committed.

39. We also know that the Lord performed many miracles through the intercession of the living [Mabillon reads: “servant of”] God, which would take too long to relate one by one.

One of our number, the writer of this account, had asked him for oil consecrated by his blessing as a support for himself. Having received a small flask full of it from him and carefully carried it home, he sought to preserve it as though it were a most precious relic.

After some time, when he was suffering from the burning of a tertian fever, he asked that the flask containing the oil be suspended above his head with the greatest reverence and as a powerful protection. After it had been wrapped in a perfectly clean cloth, it was broken—apparently through the negligence of the servants.

Yet the oil remained within it in such a way that no liquid flowed onto the ground or into the cloth. When, on seeing this, they hastily transferred it into another vessel, the broken flask immediately fell apart once it had been completely emptied. And, with the Lord’s help, the fever departed without any delay from the man who truthfully relates these events.

## CHAPTER V. His fervor in preaching, both personally and through others; certain regulations of his; his teaching called into suspicion and approved at Rome; hospitality.

40. Who could describe how greatly grace shone in him when he discussed the Scriptures and clarified obscurities? It was his greatest delight whenever someone challenged him to explain obscure matters.

He very often encouraged us, saying:

“I know that you do not understand everything. Why do you not ask questions, so that you may come to know? For cows do not always run to their calves; sometimes the calves run to the cows, so that they may satisfy their hunger from their mothers’ udders. You too must certainly do this: by questioning us, exercise us, so that we may be obliged to search out from where we can bring forth spiritual honey for you.”

Every virtue shone forth in him: virginity with purity, modesty with reverence, wisdom with simplicity, sincerity with gentleness, teaching with humility—in short, an unstained life, an irreproachable life, a life always consistent with itself.

Woe to me, wretched Cyprian, who was so lukewarm in learning that only now do I understand and repent! Why did I not drink from the stream of so great a fountain as much as my dryness required?

Who could ever imitate the ardor of his charity, by which he loved all people? He carried this above all in his heart and on his lips, and he laudably instructed us by gentle exhortation, speech, and example that we ought to love our enemies.

Hardly anyone prayed for his loved ones with the affection with which he prayed for his enemies. Although there were no grounds on which anyone could be his enemy—unless perhaps certain rivals seemed hostile because of envy or discipline—he nevertheless loved them not only with paternal but also with maternal affection. [Note: He very frequently inculcates love of enemies in his homilies, as will be clear to anyone who reads them.] He often impressed this upon us: when love extends even to enemies, it is impossible for one’s neighbor not to be loved.

41. He also taught from memory for as long as he was able, and always preached in the church in a loud voice. His provision in this work was so pious and beneficial that, when illness no longer allowed him to undertake the duty himself, he instructed presbyters and deacons and appointed them to preach in the church. Thus no bishop could excuse himself from this exhortation, necessary for everyone, by claiming any sort of inability.

He said:

“If the words of the Lord, the prophets, and the apostles are recited by presbyters and deacons, why should the works of Ambrose, Augustine, or of my littleness, or of any of the saints, not be recited by presbyters and deacons? ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ To those who have been given authority to read the Gospel, I believe it is also permitted to recite in church the homilies of the servants of God or expositions of the canonical Scriptures.

“By establishing this practice, I free myself from this obligation. Let the holy priests who disdain to fulfill it know that they will have to give an account of themselves on the day of judgment.

“I certainly do not believe that anyone could have so hardened a mind that, when God says to him, ‘Cry out, do not cease,’ he would neither cry out himself nor permit others to cry out. Let him fear this saying: ‘Woe to those who are silent about you, for many are talkative’ [Mabillon reads: ‘for many are mute’]. And also the saying of the Apostle [more properly, Isaiah 56:10]: ‘Mute dogs, unable to bark.’

“For how many sheep have gone astray while the priest remained silent! He will have to give an account for the souls of so many.” [Col. 1021B–C]

42. He also composed sermons appropriate to festivals and places, as well as against the evils of drunkenness and lust; against discord and hatred; against anger and pride; against sacrilegious persons and diviners; against the utterly pagan rites of the Kalends; and against augurs, tree-worshipers, spring-worshipers, and the vices of various kinds.

He prepared them in such a way that, if any visitor asked for one, he not only did not refuse to give it but, even if the visitor did not suggest that he ought to receive it, offered it to him so that he might take it away and read it himself.

To those living far away in Francia, in Gaul [Mabillon reads “in the Gauls.” At that time Francia was distinguished from Gaul. “Francia” may designate present-day Franconia or perhaps whatever the Franks then possessed even in Gaul. Later, “Francia” began to designate what is now the Île-de-France], in Italy, in Spain, and in various provinces, he sent priests with instructions about what they should have preached in their churches, so that, casting aside frivolous and fleeting things, they might become, in accordance with the Apostle, followers of good works.

43. Thus the good fragrance of Christ was spread far and wide through him. Carried abroad, it became fragrant everywhere among those to whose sight he was not presented; it touched the hearts of those whose bodies it did not touch.

[Note: This is the reading of our manuscript. Mabillon has: “It became fragrant everywhere through its benefits, so that no one…”]

He also added this rule: he never ordained a deacon in his church before the man had completed his thirtieth year of age.

[Note: He did not prescribe this law for others. For at the Fourth Council of Arles, which the saint presided over, canon 1 states that no bishop should presume to ordain a deacon before he has completed twenty-five years. Thirty years are required there for the ordination of a presbyter or bishop. See Labbe, volume IV, column 1622.]

He added this as well: no one was to be ordained, even at a more advanced age, unless he had first read the books of the Old Testament four times through in their proper order, and the books of the New Testament four times.

I, a sinner, testify on behalf of his holy conscience that whatever he commanded others, he himself did, and that he always fulfilled it for God’s sake. Whatever he prohibited from being done, he either avoided doing himself or prevented; everything was done in zeal for God.

44. He neither acted nor thought in a carnal manner, and he never wished to be idle in the work of God. He arranged and built a threefold basilica within a single enclosure. He constructed its central section in honor of the holy Virgin Mary, with more distinguished adornment; on one side he added the chapel of the lord John, and on the other that of Saint Martin.

And to remove from the sacred virgins whom he had gathered the concern for necessary burial, he newly caused *monobiles* [perhaps *immobiles*, “immovable”] coffins, excellently suited for burying bodies, to be hewn from enormous stones. He had them laid in ordered rows, packed across the entire pavement of the basilica, so that whichever woman of that community departed this life might find a burial place fully prepared and most holy.

Not long afterward, he buried the holy Caesaria, his sister and mother of the monastery, as she departed to Christ’s rewards. [Note: Saint Caesaria is treated on 12 January, where something is also said concerning the second Caesaria and the abbesses who followed her.] He placed her among those whom he had previously buried there, in the middle of the sanctuary, beside the place he had prepared for himself.

She was succeeded by the Caesaria who remains to the present day. Under her direction, the work undertaken with the sisters flourishes so remarkably that, amid psalms, fasts, vigils, and readings, the virgins of Christ beautifully copy the divine books, having Caesaria herself as their teacher.

45. As he was accustomed to do, the blessed man devoted himself to prayer, reading, and almsgiving, and preached continually every Sunday and on all feast days. Frequently, even at Matins and at the lighting of the lamps [Note: Mabillon notes in the margin: “that is, Vespers”], homilies were recited for the sake of visitors, so that no one could excuse himself on the grounds of ignorance.

He invited the obedient, instructed the diligent, and sternly admonished those who resisted, because, just as a worthy reward would be granted to the faithful on the day of judgment, so a punishment of worthy indignation would overtake these people.

He also established by rule that, out of reverence for the blessing, those who were marrying should receive a blessing in the basilica three days before their union.

Finally, by the gift of divine grace, he possessed such an abundance of good things—through the progress of his hearers, the imitation of his disciples, and the consecration of virgins—that he was crowned not with a single merit only. Surrounded by so many and varied crowns of his radiant merits, he was wholly transformed into a crown of the Church.

46. Many rivals arose to oppose his teaching about grace. But what a blessedness worthy of imitation! For through the whispers and malicious interpretation of certain people, an unfounded sinister suspicion arose in parts of Gaul against the preaching of the man of God.

For this reason, the bishops of Christ who lived beyond the Isère [Note: The Isère, or *Isara*, called *l’Isère* by the French, rises in the Cottian or Tarentaise Alps among the Sapaudi. It then descends from Savoy into Dauphiné, crosses it, and joins the Rhône slightly above Valence, near the confluence. See Valesius, *Notitia Galliarum*, p. 253] gathered in the love of charity and assembled in the city of Valence [Note: Valence is an episcopal city in Dauphiné, under the archbishop of Vienne, situated on the Rhône one league below the confluence with the Isère. It is commonly called Valence].

The blessed Caesarius could not hasten there, as he had arranged, because of his customary illness. Nevertheless, he sent eminent men from among the bishops, together with presbyters and deacons. Among them Saint Cyprian of Toulon [Note: *Telo Martius*, called Toulon by the French, is an episcopal city under the archbishop of Arles in Provence, famous for its harbor on the Mediterranean. This Cyprian is one of the authors of the Life; I discussed him at the beginning of the commentary] stood out as a great and distinguished man.

He affirmed everything he said from the divine Scriptures and proved it from the teachings of the most ancient Fathers: no one can seize for himself any progress in divine things unless he has first been called by the prevenient grace of God.

But while they sought to establish their own righteousness [Note: This was the aim of the Semi-Pelagians, who attributed the beginning of faith to the powers of free will; the passages of sacred Scripture set out below oppose them. One may consult the canons of Orange and the theologians who disputed concerning Semi-Pelagian errors. Yet in later centuries considerable controversies arose among them, because some represented as Semi-Pelagian errors quite a few positions that were in fact Catholic and accepted by both sides.], they were not subject to the righteousness of God, since they did not remember God’s saying:

“Without me you can do nothing.”

And:

“I chose you, not you me.” [Note: This text is absent from our manuscript, apparently omitted through the carelessness of the copyists.]

And:

“No one has anything unless it has been given to him from above.”

And through the Apostle Paul:

“By the grace of God I am what I am.”

And through another apostle:

“Every good gift is from above.”

And the prophet:

“The Lord will give grace and glory.”

Moreover, a human being truly takes up free will when he has been redeemed by Christ’s liberation, under which absolution he is able to attain the perfection of his fulfillment.

To their arguments the man of Christ gave a true and evident answer drawn from apostolic tradition. The blessed Boniface, pope of the Roman Church, had also learned of the same struggle [Note: More correct Latin would be *eadem colluctatione comperta*, “having learned of the same struggle”]. Trampling underfoot the position of the disputants, he confirmed Saint Caesarius’s exposition by apostolic authority.

By Christ’s gift, the bishops of the churches gradually accepted what the devil had desired to suppress by a sudden assault.

47. He frequently preached the following to everyone:

“If you love the word of God, you certainly retain what I have impressed upon you [the manuscript’s *impectoratum* is obscure; the sense is probably ‘impressed’ or ‘instilled’]. The complete perfection of the Decalogue was suited to divine love: whatever the charity of Christ has bound together in you, you too must return as a common possession through generosity shared with another human being.

“But do not think that only the souls of parents, friends, or dependents are to be nourished by this exhortation of ours. I testify before God and his holy angels that you will be answerable for the salvation of any of your weak slaves if, when you return, you do not impress upon them equally with friends or parents what we have preached.

“You should know that, in the present life, a slave has been subjected to you in bodily condition, but has not been enslaved by a bond of eternity.”

Again he said to those whom he had addressed:

“What have we said, brothers? What have we discussed, dear children? I ask you: what have our conversations been up to now? If you love them, you retain them; if you retain them, undoubtedly you have enclosed these words in your hearts.”

By such questioning, he extracted from them, even unwillingly, the effort to retain what they had heard.

48. At both lunch and dinner, it was read aloud daily without interruption at his table, so that both the inner and the outer man might rejoice, refreshed by this twofold nourishment. In this, then, strict and constricted enclosure, many who listened before him were, I confess, soon recognized—with sweat and great embarrassment—as forgetful; and a few, worse still, were able to repeat the little story entrusted to them only in disjointed abridgments. In the house of his church, whether he was present or absent, a meal was always prepared for the clergy and for any arrivals whatsoever. As long as he lived, no one came to Arles as to a foreign city, but as to his own home. And since we have presumed to touch on these few matters from among his countless deeds, let what is manifest suffice, even if hidden things remain concealed. Nevertheless, we ask you, holy brothers Messianus the presbyter and Stephanus the deacon, who know many things about him because you served him from your youth, to join your account to this little work.

# BOOK TWO

By Messianus the Presbyter and Stephanus the Deacon; from the edition of Mabillon (C)

## Chapter One

Various miracles, with certain admonitions and virtues interspersed

[Col. 1025A]

### 1

Messianus the presbyter and Stephanus said:

Concerning the conduct and virtues of our holy and most blessed Father, priest, and teacher, the lord Caesarius, we shall relate those things that we learned about him, either together or individually, or that we witnessed jointly with the most holy fellow bishops—that is, the lords Cyprianus and Firminus and the holy Viventio.[^c0110-1] They, having both taken up what was written above about him, referring to it from the beginning and bringing it to the conclusion of the section, were pleased to permit and instruct us each faithfully to recount what was well known to him concerning his deeds.

[^c0110-1]: The term “fellow bishops” does not refer to Messianus, who was only a presbyter, or to Stephanus, who was only a deacon, but to Cyprianus and the others, as Mabillon observes.

In Mabillon’s text the reading is “Vincentio,” doubtless, in my view, through a typographical error; for in his preliminary observations, when citing these words, he has “Viventio,” as do Surius and Barralis.

We have no need of secular eloquence—even if such eloquence were available to us—for the truth of holy actions surpasses every ornament of worldly speech. To demonstrate it fully, that purity and simplicity will suffice for us with which the most blessed Father himself also performed the miracles that we are about to relate. This is especially so because the lord himself often made this point in ordinary conversation: what was expressed learnedly provided understanding only to the educated, whereas what was expressed simply instructed both the educated and the uneducated in a fitting manner.

Therefore, with God’s favor, we shall undertake to make known to faithful hearers, in unvarnished and complete words, insofar as we can, those things that we know he truly did and said, so that from them the weak may receive compunction, the perfect joy, and those striving toward perfection an example. We shall therefore begin, as we remember them, briefly to unfold his holy works, with God’s help.

### 2

The daughter of Peter, the deacon of this church, in whom the entire welfare of his household seemed to reside, had been lying mute for three days because of a severe illness. On her behalf, one day he threw himself at the feet of the most blessed man and said:

“Have mercy, servant of Christ, on my old age. Pray for my daughter, for I trust that nothing is refused you by the Lord. Lay your hand upon her, and she will be saved. For three days now she has lain mute, her eyes closed, and hour by hour, moment by moment, I await her death.”

When he heard this, the saint, moved and compelled by the old man’s tears, went to his house. When he had entered and saw everyone in the house weeping bitterly with the father, he prostrated himself in prayer. There, like another Elijah,[^c0110-2] he drew himself toward her head amid the confined space between the chest and the bed. After offering a tearful prayer, he immediately began returning to the house of the church.

[^c0110-2]: Surius and Barralis read “Elisha,” and it is not sufficiently clear which reading should be preferred. For both Elijah (1 Kings 17) and Elisha (2 Kings 4) restored a dead child to life in nearly the same manner.

### 3

For it was his custom, whenever the Spirit suggested to him that his prayers for the sick had been heard, to depart immediately and quickly from the place, lest, if what he had obtained from the Lord by his prayers occurred in his presence, an occasion for arrogance should arise. Indeed, he often and sweetly said, as though figuratively, so that no one could understand:

“He to whom the care of souls has been entrusted ought strenuously to fear the practice of bodily pleasure.”

Finally, divine grace granted this more to the simple than to the learned. May the merciful Lord grant us, in the things he has given us, the discernment that pleases him![^c0110-3] Yet we, unworthy as we are, must by no means presume upon this.

[^c0110-3]: Barralis reads *utinam* (“would that”) here; Mabillon has *vitam* (“life”), perhaps through a typographical error, and certainly less correctly.

As he was leaving,[^c0110-4] the father began calling out again and again after him:

“I know that if you had prayed to your God, he would have restored my daughter to me.”

[^c0110-4]: *Eo* (“as he was leaving”) is missing from Mabillon’s edition.

Then Caesarius left one of his chamberlains behind and said:

“Go, keep watch there, then come after a little while and tell me what is happening.”

Before the hour had been completed, the chamberlain came and reported:

“Lord, the girl over whom you prayed has returned to herself. She says: ‘The lord bishop was here; through his prayers I have been restored and made well.’”

At this, the father came giving thanks and declared that through the saint’s prayers his daughter had already been recalled from death. For, with the Lord finally granting it today, she herself remains alive as a witness to this event.

### 4

Although, as is customary with God’s servants, they always excuse themselves from performing miracles, this servant of Christ was especially cautious. Even when, through the Lord’s prompting, he trusted that a miracle would presently be granted through him, he did not then seize the opportunity rashly, but sought carefully to evade it. Yet whether he stayed or fled, God was never lacking to him when he asked.

He always had God with him in his heart—not only in prayer and supplication, but also at table, on the road, in conversation, in company, in prosperity, in adversity, and even in sleep. Indeed, we ourselves, or our fellow servants who remained in his chamber, know what we say: amid the pauses of sleep, which age not only demanded but which illness sometimes forced upon him, he would say with his spirit always watchful—as though admonishing someone who was reciting a psalm—the sense is incomplete: “Come, say it.”

No one doubts that he was either singing psalms spiritually with the saints, or that he was certainly fulfilling the prophetic saying:

“I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

Frequently, too, while sunk in sleep,[^c0110-5] he preached about the future judgment or the eternal reward. Meanwhile, it is not a matter of my merits that I, unworthy as I am, should relate glorious things about the servant of God.[^c0110-6]

[^c0110-5]: [Col. 1027A]

[^c0110-6]: Up to this point the speaker is Messianus the presbyter; what follows therefore appears to be the account of Stephanus the deacon.

### 5

When, then, I was a deacon assigned, in my judgment, to serve him in his chamber, he ordered me, among my other duties, also to take charge of the nocturnal hours. Accordingly, when I had gone outside from the lower chamber where I stayed—for the holy man had always wished to observe moderation in everything, but was especially vigilant regarding the night office[^c0110-7]—he took the greatest care that, apart from what he privately said to himself, with God alone as his witness, none of his servants who stayed with him should be awakened before the appointed hour.

[^c0110-7]: This designates the nocturnal prayers, which are now commonly called matins.

Then, in a slow voice during sleep, he said:

“There are two things; there is no middle course. There are two: one either ascends into heaven or descends into hell.”

When I returned from outside, he awoke and said to me:

“What is it? Is it already time for the night office?”

I replied:

“It is not yet the hour; it is still too early.”

But he said:

“It truly is the hour.”

And in fact it was. Then we completed the night office. He said to me:

“In my sleep I was calling out with great intensity to someone: ‘There are two; there is no middle course. One goes either to hell or to heaven.’”

I replied:

“You are following your usual practice of crying out incessantly.”

Then I, a sinner, judged that he was always speaking about God and with God. For, as was said above, he was such a lover of every virtue that there was no good thing which he did not either practice eagerly himself or fervently wish others to possess and teach.

### 6

Among all the good things which he generally taught should be done, and the evils which he declared should never be done at all, he especially—and your kind and sincere conscience knows this—abhorred with the utmost impatience the vices of unbelief, lying, pride, lust, and drunkenness.

Good Jesus! With what groans, sighs, and tears he pleaded for sinners! You could already see the man of God as though he were presently beholding a wretched sinner being condemned to the punishments of Gehenna. Finally, in accordance with the Apostle, he never lived for himself alone and never prayed for himself alone.

### 7

At a certain time, as captives were being brought from every direction to be redeemed at Arles—not in vain, as though to crown his merits—a great multitude of redeemed freeborn persons and many nobles were fed daily by the holy man at Arles.

Then his steward came and began to protest to him:

“Let these captives go, lord, through the streets and beg for what they will eat. For if they are fed by the church today as usual, tomorrow you will have nothing from which bread can be made for your table.”

Then Caesarius entered his chamber confidently and, taking refuge in his customary resource of prayer—for he never wished to have a human witness there—asked the Lord to provide sustenance for the wretched. If anyone happened to arrive by chance while he was lying prostrate and praying alone, he strongly disliked it.

Accordingly, he wept so profusely that he immediately obtained what he asked for. Then, leaving the chamber with cheerfulness and confidence, and in a manner rebuking the steward’s unbelief, he said to the venerable Messianus the presbyter, who at that time was a notary:

“Go to the granary and sweep it so thoroughly that, if possible, not a single grain remains there. Let bread be made as usual, and let us all eat together. If tomorrow there is nothing to eat, let us all fast—provided that today the well-born men and the other captives do not go through the streets begging while we sit, eat, and drink.”

Then, calling one of us, he said privately in his ear:

“Tomorrow God will provide, for whoever gives to the poor will never lack.”

At that time, however, the captives still were not permitted to return to their own homes.

### 8

Why say more? What he ordered was done. All those dining at the church murmured, wondering where they would obtain food from that day onward. But the One who had provided for Elijah a widow with whom he might be sustained by coming to her also, without any doubt, indicated to this man through prayer that he should distribute everything to captives and strangers, reserving absolutely nothing for himself; and he was always enriched more abundantly.

Finally, on another day, when those who were supported by the church feared to see the dawn break, and were awaiting anxiously what would happen, Gundobad and Sigismund,[^c0110-8] kings of the Burgundians, knowing how eagerly the servant of the Lord hastened to works of mercy, sent three large ships—called *latenas*[^c0110-9]—filled with wheat before the light of day itself had appeared.

[^c0110-8]: Longuevallius, in *Historia Ecclesiae Gallicanae*, vol. II, p. 336, assigns the death of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, to the year 517. On p. 259 he shows that Gundobad recognized the truth of the Catholic faith through the influence of Saint Avitus of Vienne, but for political reasons remained attached to the errors of the Arians. His benevolence toward the holy man should therefore not seem surprising. Moreover, those kings may have done this on account of the Burgundian captives redeemed by Caesarius. We discussed Saint Sigismund, Gundobad’s son and successor, who was successfully converted from Arian errors to the Catholic faith, on 1 May, the day on which he is commemorated.

[^c0110-9]: The word is otherwise unknown to me and appears barbarous.

Everyone who the previous day had feared the danger of hunger in disbelief, seeing that the Lord was never absent from his servant, gave the greatest thanks with joy to God, who had come to their aid in their need.

### 9

At a certain time the patrician Liberius,[^c0110-10] having been pierced through to his vital organs by the wound of a spear while the Goths—whom they call Visigoths—lay in ambush, was attacked beyond the Durance. When everyone rushed after the assailant in confusion, he alone remained behind.

[^c0110-10]: The patrician Liberius was distinguished for his achievements and virtues. At that time he was praetorian prefect in Gaul on behalf of the Ostrogoths, whose territory he ably defended against the Franks. He later obtained the same praetorian prefecture at Rome, as Baronius reports in his *Annals* under the year 539, no. 47, where he quotes these words of Cassiodorus: “Consider, indeed, the patrician Liberius, also prefect of the Gauls, a soldierly man, most agreeable in fellowship, renowned for his merits, distinguished in appearance, but more beautiful through his wounds, having obtained the rewards of his labors, so that he did not lose the prefecture which he had administered well, and honor, doubled, adorned an outstanding man.” Cassiodorus said this and more, Baronius states, in the twelfth indiction, when Liberius obtained the praetorian prefecture at Rome, in the year 534. He subscribed to the Second Council of Orange, in Labbe, vol. IV, col. 1673, as follows: “Peter Marcellinus Felix Liberius, of illustrious rank, praetorian prefect of the Gauls and patrician, have subscribed in agreement.” From this and other evidence we understand that he was Catholic, even though he served an Arian king. Saint Ennodius of Pavia celebrates the man’s outstanding praises in three letters written to him; see Sirmond, book VII, letter 1, and book IX, letters 23 and 29, where Sirmond adds further information about him.

Terrified by the danger of his wound and despairing of his life, he fled as far as a man could, until he became bloodless, traveling nearly five hundred paces or more on his own feet to the opposite bank. But when he reached the place called Arnaginus,[^c0110-11] where the people of the village could come to meet him, he fell and lay there completely without hope or breath of life.

[^c0110-11]: Concerning this place Mabillon notes the following: “In the *Itinerary of Antoninus* it is called Ernaginum, lying about two miles from Arles toward Avignon.” The location is now uncertain. Valesius provides further information about Ernaginum from geographical writers in his *Notitia Galliarum*, p. 189, where it is also called Mansio Arnagine. He adds: “It is commonly called Eragnae, and is a place between Cavaillon of the Cavares and Tarascon of the Salyi.”

Nearly the whole city knows this story. Nevertheless, we learned of the holy man’s virtues with tears and great amazement from the magnificent man himself, who related what we are saying. At that time, they say, he told us:

“At my final breath, nothing else came to my mind except to cry out with tears: ‘All remedies have failed; ask my lord Caesarius to come to my aid.’”

We learned from the man who had been sent that this was true. For when Caesarius had wished to rest for a while in the field of his holy monastery and arrange certain matters, he had begun to linger there a little. Suddenly the messenger arrived, panting, and earnestly begged:

“Hurry, lord. Your son is asking to see him before he dies.”

Since the man of God did not wish anyone to leave this world without the medicine of repentance, he especially did not want this man to depart without that remedy. We therefore immediately reached the village of Arnaginus. As I said above, I shall relate what the man himself told me from among the many events.

### 10

While he lay there so lifeless that he recognized neither any of his other companions nor even his wife or only daughter, he himself said under oath that he seemed to hear a human voice speaking to him in the air—or perhaps in his ear—and saying:

“Behold, the holy bishop is coming.”

At that very voice I opened my eyes and recognized the servant of God coming. When he approached me, I began fervently to kiss his hands, as much as was necessary for me, who had lost all hope of life.

Then, as I believe, with God inspiring me, a sinner, I seized the *byrrus*[^c0110-12] of my lord and placed it upon my wound. After I had held part of his garment there for a little while, the blood—which had been flowing without stopping at all—ceased at that very hour, so completely that not only was health restored to me, but also the greatest strength. If I had been allowed, I would have tried to hurry to the city seated on horseback.

[^c0110-12]: We discuss the *birrus* in the commentary, no. 65.

This was also established as completely true among us, who were present.

### 11

The most illustrious woman Agretia,[^c0110-13] the wife of that same man, suffered from an illness like that of the woman who touched the extreme fringe of the Lord’s garment, and was freed through a similar faith and devotion.

[^c0110-13]: Barralis has “Agressia.”

When I came to meet her, she graciously received me in a familiar manner. Revealing her illness to my insignificance as though with matronly modesty, she began, under solemn appeal to the Lord, to ask me earnestly to bring her a piece of cloth from his *tesselli*, which had been against his naked body.[^c0110-14]

[^c0110-14]: “We interpret *tesselli*,” says Mabillon, “as square pieces of cloth applied to the stomach for warmth.” I have found the word nowhere else.

While I was in the blessed man’s chamber, I could easily have done what she hoped, but I began to fear that, by obtaining for her the remedy she sought, I might incur sin through theft. I therefore informed the chamberlain to whom the holy garments belonged that someone was asking for a *tessellum* to be carried away on the strength of her faith. He did not delay in giving me one old piece.

Lord Jesus Christ, you are glorious in your saints, and who is like you? Yet you promised that if anyone believed in you, he would also do the works that you do.

While the cloth was already being kept by me for delivery, evening came. It was customary for the *tesselli* to be warmed at the fire before he rested,[^c0110-15] and then, after the others had been removed, to be applied to him.

[^c0110-15]: That is, before he went to bed.

They were brought in according to what the servant thought was required. But Caesarius said:

“Not these. I want the others—and that one and that one.”

Other old pieces were brought. He said:

“This is not the one I am seeking,”

searching for what he did not ordinarily seek, so that it might become known what he foresaw in spirit. Then the man who had given me the cloth and I began, by gestures, to recognize that our theft could not have been hidden from the servant of God. It became clear and evident that your servant, Lord, could say to us, unworthy as we are, concerning those gifts which you had bestowed upon him:

“Someone touched me.”

### 12

Then, as though on behalf of the woman whom you, Lord Jesus, had healed through the prayers of your servant, I—fearing and trembling—began to confess to your servant what had happened, saying:

“Forgive me, lord. I myself have the cloth you are seeking. Your daughter—”

Up to this point he permitted me to speak. But he said with a whisper of silence:

“Be quiet.”

Then, taking hold of me with great compassion, he gave me yet another *tessellum*, saying:

“Go and carry both of them to the basilica of the lord Stephen. Place them beneath the altar and let them remain there. In the morning, take whichever one you wish to the woman who asked you, and bring the other back to me.”

I did as he ordered, unworthy servant that I was. Yet he never asked me whom I had taken it to, nor did he demand the *tessellum* back.

The woman continued persistently to insist that I bring her what she had requested. When she saw me approaching from a distance, she came rushing toward me with both hands extended. Before I had given it to her, and already eager to seize what I was presenting, she hurried to meet me.

Before I could lift the *casula*—the clerical or ankle-length garment, as I infer,[^c0110-16] beneath which I was carrying the little cloth—she hastened to take what she had requested with such eagerness of faith.

[^c0110-16]: Here *casula* designates a clerical or ankle-length garment, so far as I can judge. Certainly, in Labbe, vol. VI, col. 1535, at the First German Council, canon 7, it is decreed: “that presbyters and deacons should use *casulae*, in the manner of God’s servants, and not cloaks as laymen do.” See what is said in the commentary, no. 64.

When I brought out the *tessellum*, I gave it to her. She placed it around herself over her garments, first bringing it to her eyes and honoring it with devout kisses, as was fitting. Immediately, through the Lord’s gift, the effect of her faithful petition appeared. And already through the garment of the servant of the Lord they obtained what they are known to obtain also after his passing.

As she herself used to confess, when she placed the cloth against her breast, all her limbs and even her veins were immediately suspended in a shivering, just as those who are sprinkled with cold water react, and her body was shaken for a while by both horror and trembling. But the Lord’s mercy was present at once; the discharge ceased and never returned to her again. Thus the saying was fulfilled in her:

“Go, daughter; let it be done for you according to your faith.”

## Chapter Two

Various miracles performed by the Saint

### 13

It happened that, at a certain time, four bishops[^c0110-17] came to meet him, and he went down with them to the basilica of Saint Stephen for the lighting of the lamps—that is, vespers. When vespers had been completed and he had given the blessing to the people, as they were leaving, a woman encountered him in the *salutatorium*.[^c0110-18]

[^c0110-17]: Barralis adds “or five.”

[^c0110-18]: That is, in the sacrarium, so called because the bishop sat there before the solemn celebration of Mass and received the greetings of the faithful who commended themselves to his prayers or communicated some business to him, as our Menard says in *Conciliorum regul.*, chapter 5, §25. Mabillon agrees.

She had contracted such a dreadful illness that day and night her hands continually struck against each other as though they were rolling something. She cried out tearfully:

“Lord Caesarius, have mercy on the unhappy woman; pray for me, that my hands may be restored to me.”

As was his custom, he prostrated himself in prayer with the other bishops. When both of them had risen, he inclined his head toward one of the holy bishops and said:

“Please order, lord, that this woman’s hands be signed.”

The bishop obeyed most readily, but nevertheless the woman’s hands continued to roll about in their customary manner.

She cried out more loudly:

“Lord Caesarius, I cry out to you; I beg you, you sign them.”

He fell again into prayer, then rose and made the sign of the cross over her afflicted hands. They immediately became still. The woman, giving thanks to God and the holy man, returned healed.

### 14

For he came each year on the appointed days to the baptistery to bless the oil.[^c0110-19] When he entered the *cucumula*,[^c0110-20] and sat down to sign the infants, the little boys and girls sent there by their parents ran eagerly to him, bringing small vessels—some with water, others with oil—for him to bless.

[^c0110-19]: Although *baptisterium* can have various meanings, here it designates the place within the church set aside for baptizing.

[^c0110-20]: Mabillon says that *cucuma*, whose diminutive is *cucumula*, designates a vessel or even a hut shaped like a cucumber; here it refers to the vaulted baptistery. Barralis reads *cocinnulam*, which is equally obscure.

Since those carrying them brought jugs and flasks into collision with one another because of the crowd, the sound of their striking was heard and the striking was seen; yet the glass in which the blessing of the servant of Christ had been poured was never broken.

### 15

At another time, while he was visiting the dioceses, we came to a castle called Luco.[^c0110-21] There was a certain matron named Eucheria—also read *Euthyria*—who brought forward her maidservant and threw her prostrate at his feet. She tearfully begged him to intercede with the Lord for her.

[^c0110-21]: Luco, Le Lue, is a fortress in the diocese of Fréjus, on the little river Caraunnia, as Mabillon notes.

He, being a man filled with God and exceptionally inquisitive in all things, investigated the cause and asked what illness she had. They said:

“It is a demon whom the country people call Diana.[^c0110-22] She is tormented in such a way that she is beaten continually on almost every night. She is often brought into the church between two men so that she may remain there. Yet she is secretly exhausted by demonic blows, so that her voice is continually heard while she is utterly unable to answer those who attend her.”

[^c0110-22]: See the *Fragments of Capitularies* edited by Baluze, vol. II, *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, col. 3, chapter 5: “Nor should this be omitted: certain wicked women, having turned back after Satan and having been deceived by the illusions and phantasms of demons, believe and profess that during the night they ride upon certain beasts with Diana, the pagan goddess, and an innumerable multitude of women, crossing great stretches of land in the silence of the dead of night, obeying her commands as their mistress and being summoned on appointed nights to her service.” I believe this is the origin of the name, since the demon, than whom no tyrant is more cruel, exercised his power with extreme savagery over the wretched women once enslaved to his service.

Then everyone who was present with the servant of Christ asked that the truth of the matter be made visible. With the lord’s permission, the holy presbyter Lucius and the deacon Didymus, who at that time were traveling through the parishes, hurried to see her more privately; I too went along in their service.

If faithful people believe me, I declare before God that with my own eyes I saw the wounds she had received some days earlier on her back and shoulders coming to health, while those inflicted the previous day and during the very night remained fresh, interwoven among the wounds she had previously suffered.

Then she was brought before the saint again. Her eyes were so disturbed, and she appeared so confused and turned her face away from him so completely, that it was evident to everyone that she could not look upon the face of the servant of God. He placed his hand on her head and gave her a blessing. Then he blessed oil and ordered that she be anointed with it during the night. Immediately she became so well that thereafter the demon’s assault never returned to her.

### 16

At another time, when we had come to the dioceses, a child of about eight years, living in clerical dress, came to the altar. After the preaching—which he did not fail to deliver from memory not only in the city but also in all the parishes whenever he could—Caesarius returned from the screen to the altar and had already begun to celebrate Mass.

The child himself began to be gravely tormented by a most evil spirit, for he was horribly shaken by trembling and foam. Then no small terror seized everyone. But Caesarius lifted his eyes to heaven, directed prayers to the Lord for the child’s recovery, and again turned away from him to celebrate the Mass.

Then a certain presbyter of the Church of Citarista, named Ursus, threw the little boy at his feet. Caesarius looked at him with displeasure and said:

“May God forgive you, blessed one. This is the work of others, not mine.”

Although he denied it out of human humility, divine power was nevertheless not absent from his servant. As soon as the boy had been thrown at his feet, he rose healthy; and the evil spirit never returned to him. I also saw him later as a subdeacon in that same church.[^c0110-23]

[^c0110-23]: This miracle is also related in a letter of Messianus the presbyter, quoted in the commentary, §5.

### 17

When he had come to the parish of Citarista[^c0110-24] for the purpose of visitation, the daughter of a certain man, Novatus [alternative reading: *nominis*, “of a name”], seemed to have contracted such a dreadful and unprecedented kind of demon that whenever she set one foot outside the door of her house, a multitude of ravens immediately rushed upon her face, tearing at it.

[^c0110-24]: Cytharista, Cyreste, lies on the coast of Provence between Toulon and Marseille, as Mabillon notes.

They shook her with trembling, rolled her about amid foam, and disfigured every naked part of her body that they could reach—that is, her face, neck, or anything else they found.

When she was brought to the holy man, we saw the ravens flying over her and following her all the way to the basilica where the man of God was. Yet they did not dare to attack her violently either then or at that point.

When she came before him, he saw that her face had been horribly lacerated and said to us privately:

“I have never read, seen, or heard of the devil lying in wait for anyone in this manner.”

Then he placed his hand upon her head before the holy altar, blessed oil, and anointed her eyes and ears with it. In full view of everyone, she returned healthy through the streets to her home. During the two days we remained there, she attended the church, and thereafter that attack never returned to her.

### 18

After some time had passed, he came to the estate of our church, where there are also dioceses, a place called Succentriones.[^c0110-25]

[^c0110-25]: I find no information about this place, but it is clear that it was in the territory of Arles.

Large bath buildings with lofty roofs had been constructed there. Whenever anyone happened to pass by them, he was immediately called by name; at once he saw enormous stones falling either before his feet or behind him in terror. Everyone took care never to pass that way. Those who did not know were also warned not to fall into that danger, past which none dared proceed.

Then, behold, as the man of God was going to another church, having apparently been summoned [the text has *requisita*, perhaps *requisitus*], the cleric whose duty it was to carry his staff—an office belonging to the notaries—forgot it; I, useless as I was, served in that ministry.

The inhabitants of that place, when they found the staff, rejoiced and said that the Lord had granted them the opportunity to find something belonging to him. They marveled and gave thanks to God, and hung the staff itself on the wall. Immediately the devil’s ambushes were driven away, and from that time to this the adversary has not dared to inflict that most wicked harm upon anyone in that place.

### 19

At that time it also happened that a certain man from Gaul named Benenatus—though not so in his conduct—came and complained that he was being held captive with his nephews.

He had a little girl whom he dressed in male clothing and presented to Caesarius, saying:

“This is my nephew; he and I are being held captive together with his sister, who is hurrying here after us.”

The man of God, grieving over their captivity because of the affection that the Lord had inspired in him from childhood, gently kissed the man who had presented the girl, believing her to be a boy.

Having each received ransom, they went away; after reaching their destination, they returned. Two days later he brought back the same girl, as if in her proper clothing, in order to receive additional solidi. This was done at the suggestion of the holy presbyter James, who, in his holy simplicity, indicated that the whole matter should be sought out truthfully.

He then accepted ransom for this girl a second time. Those who were responsible for the matter then learned that he had presented the same girl whom he had previously displayed in male clothing.

I not only suggested this indignantly to the holy man, but the aforementioned presbyter did so as well, and with embarrassment.[^c0110-26]

[^c0110-26]: Barralis reads *suggerebat* (“was suggesting”) rather than *suggerebant* (“were suggesting”).

Then, as he was always exceedingly gentle and kind toward strangers, Caesarius said to the presbyter:

“Do not be angry, holy one. You did well to commend a stranger. For your good will God will repay you with a reward.”

And he said of the poor man:

“May God forgive him this sin, since he made me kiss a girl.”

Then he said:

“And may the girl herself receive this reward: because, although she presumed to kiss an unworthy priest, may he make her such a holy nun that she never kisses another man.”

But because God, the arbiter of future events, knew that she would certainly be unable to remain in virginity, lest the servant of God’s prayer prove fruitless, she departed from this world the very next day.

These events are known to have taken place publicly at Arles, at the basilica of the Apostles, where the holy man himself had his lodging.

20. At another time a certain matron in the city of Massilia [Col. 1035A] [Note: [Col. 1035D] Massilia is a very well-known city in Provence, on the Mediterranean Sea.] accidentally dislocated her foot, so that for a long time she could not put that foot on the ground; supported by the hands of her household servants, she could scarcely be brought to church, enduring the most severe pain. But because the Lord’s mercies are many, when he himself willed it, he brought about circumstances whereby the man of God might travel to that city. When the woman heard of his arrival, she had herself brought to him to offer her greetings. Having received his prayer and blessing, she did not presume to mention anything to him about her condition. But after returning from him, she asked to be allowed to approach his saddle-horse [Note: [Col. 1035D] *Sellaris* or *sellarius* is a horse carrying, or accustomed to carry, a saddle, as various examples show in Du Cange’s *Glossary*. *Supersellium* is the saddle-cloth placed over a horse’s saddle. The woman applied the afflicted part of her body to this. In Surius and Barralis, *Cella* is wrongly read here.] Having faithfully touched the disabled place against the saddle-cloth that covered the saddle, she immediately recovered her former health and, as though she had suffered no injury, returned sound on her own feet, without anyone supporting her, giving thanks to the Lord [Col. 1035B] to this very day.

21. One day, then—as many people know—a fire seized the house of a certain John in this city, next to the monastery of the virgins. It began to draw near, so that no one doubted that everything there would be burned. The handmaids of God, unable to go outside, threw their books and possessions, their cells [perhaps *saddles*], and themselves into cisterns where, by God’s providence, there happened to be no water, lest despair overwhelm them. The monastery’s superiors ran and informed their father, because the fire was already close to his cell. He hurried out in the middle of the night, came through the wall to the place where the flames were, and prostrated himself in prayer [for *prosternebat*, “was prostrating himself”], calling out to them from the wall: “Do not be afraid, blessed women.” At once the raging [Col. 1035C] flame, subdued by his power, extinguished the fire.

22. Nor will I keep this silent. What happened at a certain time in the Alpine districts is proclaimed as exceedingly famous. When continual storms were ravaging the estates of a most noble man with destructive downpours, and the force of hail was devouring all the crops of that place, so that year after year no hope of relief remained there, it happened again that his staff was accidentally left there. The owner himself ordered that a cross be made from that staff and, armed with faith, fixed it in a prominent place, so that when the hail came, the disciple’s staff might oppose it—the master’s cross. God deigned to work such great power there for the honor of his servant that afterward he granted that place the greatest abundance, from which he had driven away the storm.

[Col. 1035D] Likewise, one day a fire seized the house of a certain Vincent, whose wooden upper story was yielding to the flames. Seeing that he could do nothing, Vincent hurried with all possible speed to that lord, fell at his knees, and begged him to pray. Going outside, he made the sign of the cross against the flames; the fire immediately turned back and was so completely subdued that it left no mark on the boards of the upper story.

## CHAPTER III. Other Miracles; His Care in Instructing His Disciples and Exhorting All to Repentance; His Virtues and Visions

[Col. 1036A]

23. A certain presbyter also recently told us that, some years earlier, while he was still a layman, his daughter was being tormented by a demon. In grief and mourning he said to one of his friends: “What shall I do, unhappy man that I am, since my daughter is tormented by a demon? It would have been better for me if she had never been born, or at least if she had died.” The other replied: “Do not weep, but go and take her to Lord Caesarius; secretly present her to him, so that he may heal her.”

Without hesitation the man came to Arles, and while walking he encountered Caesarius. He threw himself at his feet with tears and said: “Lord, have mercy on me, miserable man that I am; heal my daughter.” Caesarius carefully asked him what was wrong, and he replied: “A demon.” He said to him: “Be silent, and return to your home. When the morning office is being said, return and bring the girl herself and her mother with you. Wait [Col. 1036B] [that is, remain] in the atrium of Saint Stephen’s until the morning office has been said; and when you see that the secret part has begun, come to the cell and knock.”

The man did as he had commanded. Caesarius secretly came out, knelt on the ground, and prayed with the girl’s father and mother. Then he rose, made the sign of the cross over her, and sent her away healed.

Again, as he was walking through a street of the city, he saw across the way in the marketplace a man who was being driven about by a demon. When Caesarius noticed him, he kept his hand under his cloak so that his companions would not see, and made the sign of the cross against him. The man was immediately freed from the enemy’s assault.

24. How holy and delightful it was when, day after day, without interruption, he pressed the word of God upon those who desired it at a suitable time and upon those who did not desire it at an unsuitable time! When it had already grown late and the time for rest had come, he would not allow even a moment of that hour [Col. 1036C] to be free from the divine Scriptures and holy instruction, and he would say to us: “Tell me,” he said, “what did we have for supper today? What dishes did we have?”

We remained silent and sighed, because our thoughts were being led where he was accustomed to direct them: he wanted us to speak about spiritual food, and therefore he questioned us. He would say again: “I know that, if I am concerned about what we ate for supper, you also remember what you had for lunch. But if we ask what was read at table, we do not remember.”

From this it becomes clear that what we retain tasted sweetly to us, while what we do not retain not only offered no flavor to the palate of our hearts, but perhaps even caused disgust. Groaning, he would say: “O unhappy forgetfulness of good things—what is more unhappy than this?” And beginning from the start, he would repeat what had been read or expounded. To us poor men he would say in a prophetic voice, with a groan: “Gather, gather the Lord’s wheat; for I tell you, it will not be long before you gather it. See what I am saying. Gather it, because you will seek this time; truly, truly, you will seek these days and greatly desire them.”

25. Although at that time our sloth received this saying carelessly, we now know that what he said has come to pass [Col. 1037A]. That prophetic word has been fulfilled in us: “I will send a famine upon the land”—a famine, he says, “not of bread or water, but of hearing the word of God.”

Although the sermons that have been established are recited, that unceasing voice has ceased which fulfilled the prophetic command: “Cry out; do not cease.” He often said this: “When anyone’s palate grows weary of the word of God, his soul is fevered. When it has recovered health, then it hungers and thirsts for what, while sick, it rejected and neglected.”

For who could ever express in words that sweetest and holiest *recinium* [Note: [Col. 1037D] Mabillon notes the following concerning this word: “The ancients called a square garment or toga a *recinium*, as if *rejicinium*, because they threw one half of it back over the shoulders. Here, by *recinium*, understand a mid-meal, which the French today call *le reciner*: it is only half a meal, the other part being deferred until supper.” In Surius it is written *reticinium*; in Barralis, *recticinium*.]

Thus the servant of Christ would say to us: “We have now finished supper as best we could.” Those standing by, or the chamberlains, would suggest—because of his weariness, since in his exhaustion he could scarcely breathe—that he should rest. [Col. 1037B] He would answer: “You are right. But wait a little.”

Then the chamberlains would say: “Lord, what are you saying? The table has been waiting a long time; you have wearied yourself by speaking so much and have not been silent until now. Refresh yourself for a little while.”

With the greatest sweetness he would reply again: “You are right; but since we have finished supper, we shall not have any *recinium*.”

26. He who is aware of hidden things knows what I am saying. When the Holy Spirit began to pour forth speech through him, he would expose everyone’s vices in turn, strike them with the scourges of his instruction, and, applying divine medicines, recall them to health without any delay. Like a spiritual and holy organ-player [Note: [Col. 1037D] This designates one who plays musical organs. See certain admonitions of the saint near the end of the commentary.] touching the hearts of each person, he caused us, when we left him, to echo somewhat among ourselves what had been said. We would say: [Col. 1037C] “Let each one of us give thanks to you, God, for I no longer retain the wrongdoing, nor does my spirit rage against that brother of mine. For certainly what your servant proclaims is true, and I would rather suffer injury than have this holy man appear against me as a witness on the day of judgment.”

Another said the same concerning pride, another concerning envy, and another, who had been suffering from some other vice, spoke similarly. Thus, all of us, healed in spirit and relieved, returned to our beds, giving thanks to God.

27. For what countenance, good God, holy Creator, what face or appearance could anyone ever describe? In you, holy Father, we long for the teaching, form, countenance, appearance, knowledge, and sweetness that you had from the Lord in a special measure beyond other men. How holy was your life, how pure and sweet your disposition! Lord Jesus, who could even imagine, much less express in words, how much you gave him?

When he went out to bless the fountains—as those who saw it and hear what I am saying can testify, for they are credible witnesses to themselves—who ever believed that he was an earthly man in that procession? Lord God of heaven, I confidently speak the truth: during those forty years in which he exercised his ministry, whoever saw him proceeding on that day always saw him as though they had never seen him before; he continually appeared new in everyone’s eyes. His face shone together with his soul, because his life truly grew through continual progress, so that he was always becoming better than he himself had been. Not without reason did what he bore within appear outwardly [Col. 1038B].

28. To him, many visitations not only of various saints were repeatedly shown, but also—something greater than all else—the Lord Jesus revealed himself to him in a vision together with all his disciples. Caesarius did not broadcast this indiscriminately or become elated in spirit [Note: [Col. 1035D] How modestly the saint thought of himself is shown by his ninth sermon in Barralis, p. 295, where, after praising the monastery of Lérins, he adds the following about himself: “For all whom this fortunate and blessed dwelling has received, it is accustomed to raise through Christ, on the wings of charity and humility, to the lofty heights of virtue. Although this has been happily accomplished in nearly all the inhabitants of this place, in me, however, because my merits resist, it is not shown to have been fulfilled. For when this holy island, like a distinguished mother and the one unique and singular nurse of all good things, once received my littleness in the arms of its piety, and brought me up—or attempted to nourish me—for no short time, although it raised the others to the summit of virtue, it could not remove all negligences from me, because the hardness of my heart resisted. Therefore, with all humility I beg, and with complete contrition of heart I beseech you, that what is denied by my merits may be supplied by your prayers; and that I, your special foster-child, may deserve to be helped by the support of your prayers, so that the fact that I was nourished in this holy place may bring me not judgment but progress.” He continues at greater length in the same vein there, and often elsewhere; these passages may be read in the saint’s writings.] Rather, under oath, he confessed it to one person alone, sufficiently faithful to keep silent; that person asserts before God that it happened.

Moreover, two years before his passing, the whole preparation for his departure, and what he was to receive in heaven for all his works, was shown to him in spirit, and he was told: “Rejoice in the Lord, for behold what you will receive for your service.”

There are still many other important matters that, because of their length, we pass over. Many who know these things with us will undoubtedly regret that we have omitted so much—things that they certainly know along with us. We ask them to forgive us, because it is sufficiently unbecoming, burdensome, or uncouth to presume to speak longer to educated ears, or, like a mute person unable to speak, to wish to keep murmuring on.

May God grant that we reach the end before we cease in our hearts to remember the love, nourishment, charity, preaching, and wholly holy memory of our lord and holy father Caesarius.
