Nevertheless, I shall report a few things that occurred concerning his relics after his passing, even before these matters were written down.

## CHAPTER IV. Certain Miracles Performed after His Death; The Saint’s Age and the Duration of His Episcopate; His Devout Preparation for His Foreseen Death and His Blessed Death; The Grief of All at His Death and Burial

[Col. 1039A]

29. A public *chartarius*, named Desiderius [Note: [Col. 1039D] Here *chartarius* designates a *commentariensis*, or notary, as we commonly say.], had long been so severely afflicted by quartan fevers that even in vigorous youth he had lost his strength. He drank a little of the water in which that holy body had been washed, and was so completely healed that not only did the fever itself not return to the young man, but, with the Lord’s favor, his former strength and vigor also returned.

The son of the illustrious man Salvius was being severely afflicted by tertian fevers. As is characteristic of such a man, Salvius diligently tried to cure him with frequent remedies appropriate to the illness, but he could not be helped at all. Then, as a Christian, he said: “Run, my son, and seek water in which the lord bishop was washed, or at least wash some relics from his clothing in water, drink it, and the Lord will grant health.”

As soon as this was done, all the fever and whatever other discomfort there was departed from him.

The son also of the late illustrious Martianus was so severely distressed by debilitating fevers that even the physicians despaired of him. But, as God mercifully inspires those whom he wishes to heal, he began with faith and eagerness to ask that something from the clothing of the Lord’s servant be washed and given to him to drink. Then someone ran to me—or to others who were absent but had preserved some relic of this kind. It was sought from someone, found, and given; he drank the water in which the garment had been washed and was made well. He himself remains a witness to this miracle.

[Col. 1039C]

30. On another occasion, as I was walking through a street, a certain Frank, already bent over and trembling from the chill of a quartan fever, was walking ahead of me. When I was preparing to continue quickly in the direction I had begun, he began to call after me: “Benedictus, if you have any, give me some of the cloth [Note: [Col. 1039D] That is, a piece of fabric; in French, *drap*.] of Saint Caesarius against the chills [*frigoras*, for *frigora*], because it helps many people; I want to drink the water.”

I, who wanted to hurry quickly on in the direction I had begun, said: “If you wait for me, tomorrow I will give you what you seek.”

But he said: “Today is my fever day, and I am already trembling all over. When am I supposed to wait for you?”

Then, considering that I had encountered him so many times before in the street for no good reason, I said to him: “Come, young man; I will give you what you seek.”

We immediately returned together. When we had entered my cell and had both washed our hands, I brought out a linen cloth [Col. 1039D] with which the holy body of the gentle lord [another reading adds “good lord”] had been wiped. I took a small piece to give him. But the Frank, with great fury [another reading: “fear”], said to me: “Take it away, man! Why are you lying? I heard that Benedictus had not linen, but cloths for use; I want to wash them and drink the water.”

Then I said to him with tears: “You are right; you heard correctly. But the body of that holy man was wiped with this linen cloth when he died.”

And he said: “Then give it to me, if I am to be well.”

As soon as he received the linen cloth [for “having received the cloth”], he felt health from the Lord at that very hour.

31. Since no language is altogether capable of adequately recounting the benefits of the prayers of the Lord’s servant, which Christ bestowed through him upon bodies and souls, let my rustic eloquence sound almost foolish; for although I am not skilled in speech, when speaking with the wise even a few testimonies are great gains for the account of events. Those who receive true statements with faithful minds possess their own understanding as testimony.

Nevertheless, I will not omit what happened recently in his cell, where his little body rested and from which he migrated to the heights. While the holy brothers there were saying their little chapters, with them officiating [another reading: “present”] [Note: [Col. 1039D] Barralis reads *capitulum*. The word *capitellum* has various meanings; here it seems to signify the shorter canonical hours. Tours uses the word in this sense in his *History of the Franks*, book IX, chapter 6: “And entering the oratory, he set me aside and himself recited one, then a second, then a third little office.”], one of the chamberlains whom he had kept in his service was arranging a lamp [Note: [Col. 1039D] *Cicindelis* or *cicindilis* designates a lamp, as I have already noted elsewhere.]. The lamp slipped from his hands onto a stone; it neither overturned [that is, “turned over”], broke, nor went out.

32. Thus, while this evangelist, as we read, appropriately and inappropriately carries out the outstanding and supreme work of the Word, and while he fulfills his sacred office, he is present by God’s will—not through his own handing it over, as the Arians alleged, but with him nevertheless continually praying for all—with peace and tranquility in the city of the Arlesians, under the reign, in the name of Christ, of the most glorious and thoroughly Catholic Childebertus [Col. 1040C] [Note: [Col. 1040D] I have already explained in the notes to Book I, chapter 3, when and on what occasion the city of Arles came to Childebertus. Childebertus was a Catholic, although the people of Arles had long been subject to the Arian Goths; he was also benevolent toward ecclesiastical persons, as his various foundations testify. It is therefore not surprising that the author of the *Life* praises his reign, although not all his deeds are otherwise equally worthy of praise.], gentle in power, impartial in severity, conspicuous in humility, not shaking the Lord’s priests with terror but binding them through reverence; preeminent among all in Gaul, equal in privilege and dignity among all the churches, and humanely recognizing the city in its high position.

The man of God, therefore, refreshed and joyful, looked down upon the threats, repeated accusations, falsehoods, and fabricated pretenses of the Ariomanites. He saw and rejoiced, and, gathered to his fathers in a good old age, full of days, he departed in the name of Christ.

33. As illness frequently left him half-dead before our eyes, and as meanwhile he was completing the seventy-third year of his whole life, while the cycle of years was completing its fortieth circuit in his episcopate [Col. 1040D], he perceived in spirit that the day of his passing was approaching. Amid the considerable pains he was suffering, he asked how near was the day of the deposition of the most blessed Augustine.

When he learned that Augustine’s commemoration was approaching, he said: “I trust in the Lord [Col. 1041A] that he will not separate my passing far from his. For, as you yourselves know, as much as I loved his thoroughly Catholic understanding, so much, although I am unequal to him in merits, I do not think that the day of my deposition will be set at a much greater distance from the time of his death. Meanwhile, the exodus of Israel from the land of Egypt is increasing and being completed—that is, the migration of the holy soul from this world of bodily life.”

34. He therefore ordered himself to be carried by the hands of the attendants to the monastery of virgins that he himself had founded, as though he wished to console the anxious women whose sleep suspicion of his approaching death had taken away, and whose food forgetfulness had removed. With the sound of the Psalms interrupted by tears, they uttered a moaning instead of a song and a groan instead of an Alleluia.

After consoling and addressing his daughters, he gave them not cheerfulness but increased sorrow. For it was already easy to recognize that the loving Father was soon to migrate to his heavenly homeland. He therefore addressed Caesaria, the foremost and venerable mother of more than two hundred girls [Note: [Col. 1041C] This is the second Caesaria, who succeeded Caesarius’s sister.], with his customary sweetness; he consoled her and encouraged her to strive toward the palm of the heavenly calling. He admonished them to keep the rule that he himself had established some years earlier.

In the same way, through his testament [Note: [Col. 1041C] We have given the testament in the *Commentary*, § 6.], he commended them by letters to his successors in the episcopate, to the rest of the clergy of the prefecture, and to the counts and citizens, so that in the time to come they would by no means suffer hardship. At that time the monastery had stood for a full thirty years [Note: [Col. 1041C] We discussed the monastery’s construction in the same work, § 2.].

He then gave them his prayer and blessing, said his final farewell, and, while they were crying out, returned to the church [Col. 1041C]. On the third day after the feast of Saint Genesius [Note: [Col. 1041C] The acts of Saint Genesius, martyr of Arles, have been illustrated under 25 August.] [Col. 1042A]—that is, six days before the Kalends of September, before the day of the deposition of Saint Augustine the bishop—and after the dedication of his monastery, having already said farewell to everyone the preceding day [Note: [Col. 1042C] In the *Commentary*, no. 18, we stated that the dedication took place on 26 September 512. [Col. 1041: The person who copied the Life of Saint Caesarius in the Royal Library omitted this commentary. Later, observing that it was frequently discussed in the notes, we placed it at the end of the volume, since no other place was then available to us. EDITOR.] From this, together with Pagi, we proved that he died in 542.], when the first hour was approaching, he joyfully surrendered his blessed soul to Christ among the hands of the bishops, presbyters, and deacons who were present.

35. The clothing of the holy body was torn away by various mourners and faithful people with such devout force that, while we presbyters and ministers were assisting, it could scarcely be restrained from taking the relics. From these, by God’s favor, as I said above, healings of the sick are continually and very frequently performed.

It produced marvelous joy in heaven, but on earth it left unbearable grief—a grief shared not only by the good but also by any wicked persons who witnessed it. For who, holy man or outsider, sang a Psalm at that funeral amid the tears? Everyone, good or evil, just or unjust, Christian or Jew, whether going before or following, uttered the same cries: “Woe, woe, and daily more woe, because the world was not worthy to have such a herald or intercessor any longer.”

He was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin, which he himself founded, where the holy bodies of the virgins from his monastery are buried. Let us also, with faithful devotion and due diligence, venerate on earth the one whose soul we trust, rejoice, and glory to see shining in heaven, to the praise and honor of Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through infinite ages of ages [Col. 1042C]. Amen.

[Col. 1041]

# FIRST PART OF THE WORKS. SERMONS. (C, G, S)*

## I.

The following sermons are attributed to Saint Caesarius of Arles in the Appendix to volume five of the works of Saint Augustine, namely:

Sermons 2, 4, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 19, 22, 28, 29, 34, 35, 37, 38, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 63, 66, 69, 76, 78, 89, 91, 93, 104, 107, 110, 112, 115, 116, 129, 131, 139, 145, 173, 174, 224, 225, 228, 230, 244, 249, 253, 256, 267, 269, 279, 281, 286, 288, 289, 292, 293, 301, 303, 305, 307, 308, 309, 313, 314.

## II.

*(From the *Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum* of Margarino de la Bigne.)*

# FIRST HOMILY. On Easter.

[Col. 1041D]

Rejoice, heaven, and be glad, earth. This God shone more brightly from the tomb than he had gleamed from the sun. Let hell grieve, because it has been undone; let it rejoice, because it has been visited.

Let it resound, because after long ages it has seen an unknown light and breathed again amid the darkness of profound night. O beautiful light, which sprang forth from the bright summit of heaven and, amid the sulfurous streams, clothed those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death with sudden radiance. At once, then, as Christ descended, the eternal night of the underworld shone forth. The groaning of the mourners fell silent; the burdens of the chains were loosed; the bonds of the condemned were shattered and fell. The torturers, their minds stunned, were struck dumb. The entire impious workshop trembled together when it suddenly saw Christ in its own dwelling.

Then the iron gatekeepers, as Christ descended, muttered such words amid the shadowy silences, blinded while fear pressed upon them: “Who,” they say, “is this terrible one, and this chorus in snowy splendor? Has our Tartarus received such a one? Has the world spewed such a one into our cavern? He is an invader, not a debtor; a breaker-in, not a sinner; we see a judge, not a suppliant; he has come to command, not to submit; to burst forth, not to remain.

“Where, do you suppose, were our gatekeepers sleeping when this warrior was troubling our barriers? If he were guilty, he would not be proud or bold. If any offenses darkened him, he would never scatter our darkness with his radiance. But if he is God, what is he doing in a tomb? If he is human, what has he dared? If he is God, why has he come? If he is human, why has he released captives? Has this one perhaps made terms with our ruler, or has he attacked and defeated him, and thus passed through our kingdoms?

“Certainly he was dead; certainly he was defeated. Our warrior was deceived in the world; he did not know what devastation that cross would bring upon hell—deceiving our joys, giving birth to our losses. Through wood we were enriched; through wood we are overthrown. That power, always feared by the nations, is perishing. No living person ever entered here; no one terrified the executioners. Never in this place, blinded by soot and perpetual black darkness, has an unpleasant light appeared. Or perhaps the sun has departed from the world? Yet neither the heavens nor the stars obey us, and still hell is shining.

“What shall we do? How shall we turn ourselves? We cannot defend our bloody dwellings against this one, nor can we maintain the guardianship of our underworld! We are disastrously disturbed. We could not darken the light, and now we fear for our own destruction.”

# SECOND HOMILY. On Easter.

The great and wondrous sacrament of Easter and baptism has long been known to us as consecrated even in the Old Testament, or Law [Col. 1043D]. It has been celebrated through the ages: blessed Moses led the Lord’s people out of Egypt and from the yoke of unworthy servitude (Exodus 15); it has been celebrated that he enabled the people to cross the deep Red Sea, while nature itself stood astonished.

Here, first of all, let us examine more carefully what such servitude, and what such a crossing, can contribute to edification. For the blessed Apostle, saying that “all these things happened to them in figure,” confirms by heavenly authority that the signs and miracles of that time belonged to the mysteries of the redemption to come. For he says: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.”

Already then, therefore, under the leadership of that people, divine power was serving our interests, rich in benefits but always in promises. Blessed Moses was indeed their leader, but the Son and the Holy Spirit went before them in the pillar of light and cloud. Here let us recognize above all that the people who strive to heed their leaders follow God, and reach salvation through the God-man.

Thus the children of Israel, while they did not resist the command of Moses their leader and of their priest, deserved God’s companionship on the difficult roads to the dwelling of freedom, rest, and kingship. Nor was it without reason that the enemy did not touch them: the light went before; the waves were afraid. So the Prophet testifies: “He rebuked,” he says, “the Red Sea, and it dried up” (Psalm 105). And again: “The sea saw and fled” (Psalm 114). What did it see? It saw, then, what must be believed in baptism.

Without doubt that terrible and hidden abyss shuddered before the majesty of the one who stood there, and yielded at the presence of its creator. Therefore the children of Israel passed safely either among the waves or beneath the waves, while steep masses of vast waters hung above them and the waves threatened on the right and left; while the insensible creature, sensing the maker of the element, provided a way surrounded by waters for those crossing and prepared a returned vengeance against those pursuing them.

In accordance with this, if we too have left vices and crimes behind as though they were Egypt, and if each of us runs with attentive heart after Christ, the Christian, who is likewise a Hebrew, will not fear Egypt—that is, the devil, the author of sin. For this is the nature and weakness of the enemy: when you withdraw, he yields; and, if you follow the law of the Lord as Moses, he enters behind you. Behold the enemy whom to flee is to conquer.

First, then, what else did that harsh and tyrannical servitude of Egypt signify except the devil’s exercise of dominion over the human race through sins? What else, I ask, were those base and dreadful commands of Pharaoh in mud and straw except the filthy and earthly services of diabolical pleasure and the detestable contagions of vices? For the fruitless and empty works of this life are straw—straw, I say, a material exceedingly friendly to flames.

But even the fact that Pharaoh orders the male children of the Hebrews to be killed and the females to be preserved, presenting the figure of the devil, shows the hostile spirit opposed to virtue and allied with the flesh, hostile to strength and consenting to pleasure: it was choking strength and nourishing desires.

This servitude, what is worse, belonged not only to that time, but even now wraps the souls of the negligent and unbelieving in the bonds of a seductive captivity, much more dangerously. For, as the Apostle also testifies, everyone is the slave of whatever conquers him: one obeys injustice, another anger; one pride, another savagery; one malice, another wrath; one greed, another lust.

I do not know how anyone can dare to call himself free amid these things when so many masters drag him apart into their own factions. What good is it to be free by nature if one is a slave in conscience? We see people outwardly exalted by the nobility of their birth, but inwardly degenerate through the weakness of their minds—masters of the innocent, and slaves of crimes.

The condition of household servants is already better, since their original station seems to have inclined them toward this. Good servants, you have your consolation: embrace honorable servitude in place of freedom. What an intolerable yoke, a foul domination, and a shameful subjection! Or what hope remains for one who serves, when eternal death is joined to servitude?

It is useless for someone to be conspicuous outwardly by birth or rank if he is not inwardly free. Crimes are repeated under a grave condemnation after they have been redeemed by Christ’s blood. It is an inexcusable evil for the servant of our Redeemer, the Lord, to be stained by sins after his death.

If, perhaps, the servant of some beloved human being is driven by the harsh commands of his master, he can escape and avoid the unjust master by fleeing or hiding wherever he can. Where will the servant of sin flee? Where will he drag himself? Wherever he flees, he does not flee himself. There is nowhere for an evil conscience to go. It follows itself—or rather, it does not depart from itself. There is scarcely any remedy from outside when the wound is enclosed within.

What good is it for a man to flee a sounding bow when he carries the arrow fixed within him? Although that serpent withdrew its bite, it left behind its venom. Each person committed sin in order to seize some pleasure. What condemns remains; what delights passes away. Completed wickedness remains; fleeting pleasure passes by.

From this servitude, and from these enemies pursuing God’s people as far as the shores of baptism, Christ frees countless thousands of captives through the irrigation of the sacred font, and crushes the head of the great dragon upon the waters.

Thus that most savage dragon felt his own poison poured back for his destruction. While he thought he was causing harm, while blindly making an assault against his Lord, while striking his torment against what was solid, he was driven back by his own blow and regretted that he had been strong; he recognized that he had lost all power to injure, though he had left the poisonous bites of his venomous teeth in the sacred body.

And therefore now he draws to his jaws, by the songs of his temptations, whatever unhappy people he foresees will readily grant him assent, so that, unarmed, he may await voluntary prey. Accordingly, cast down by the Lord, he does not attack the human race as though he were stronger, but, as one weakened, hisses wicked counsels.

So that you may escape his songs, gladly hear the voice of the sacred Incarnation from the utterances of God. Christ overcame him not in his divinity but in our flesh, to show that he could also be overcome by us. Christ, I say, killed him through his saints.

Perhaps this is the serpent which the blessed Moses’s rod, changed into a serpent, consumed (Exodus 4). By this event he then clearly showed that the author of death was likewise to be crushed by the rod—that is, by the royal power of Christ the Lord.

While Moses was fighting against the magicians, the rod was at one moment changed into a serpent, and at another the serpent returned to a rod. What does this mean? In the serpent, recognize the person of the accursed man who was to be crucified and cursed. In the rod, understand the scepter of royal dignity. What is the rod becoming a serpent? The same God changed into a human being.

[Col. 1046A] What is the serpent in the rod? It is man received into God. Thus, in man divinity was emptied, so that in God humanity might be glorified.

We still have, in the Heptateuch, under a simple and fitting sign, the insignia of sacred redemption. When, in the desert, the children of Israel were being struck down without any mercy by the bites of venomous serpents, it is written (Num. II) that blessed Moses, instructed by divine inspiration, set up a bronze serpent fastened to a piece of wood amid the crowds of the dying, and commanded those who were perishing, after receiving the poisonous blows, to hasten to the presence of the serpent in order to recover their health. When they fled to it, the healing remedy was as prompt as the joy of looking upon it was swift. A certain cure followed upon a momentary gaze, because a mystery lay hidden in the serpent [Col. 1046B].

If we say here that the visible form has placed before the name a type that ought to be shunned, who would not tremble even at hearing it? But who would dare even to think this, unless he himself had revealed the figure of the mystery who suffered the dishonor of the figure itself? He testifies to this by an oracle in the Gospel: “Just as Moses exalted the serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be exalted” (John III).

Let us see, then, what the sight of a serpent signifies against the venom of serpents. The serpent was accursed from the beginning. And the one who was to be hung upon a piece of wood, like the Savior, was filled with curses. For again he says: “Accursed is everyone who hangs upon a piece of wood” (Deut. XXI). We see, then, a serpent against a serpent: likewise, the condemned against the condemned, the accursed against the accursed, wisdom against cunning, [Col. 1046C] goodness against wickedness, vinegar and gall against venom, death against death, consuming the devourer and killing the slayer. Thus the Lord himself also speaks through the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; O underworld, I shall be your bite” (Hos. XIII).

But even now, if we wish it, a remedy against the serpent’s bite is given to us when we look upon the serpent. This is clearly fulfilled when sin is healed by knowledge of sin itself, and guilt is erased by confession of guilt. Thus, when a person says with the prophet, “For I acknowledge my iniquities, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. L), when he looks carefully upon his sin, he heals the serpent’s bite by looking upon the serpent. The serpent, therefore, against the serpent—that is, Christ pursuing sin under the appearance of a sinner [Col. 1046D]. And therefore the Apostle said: “And, because of sin, he condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. VIII). He wiped out original sin through flesh like sinful flesh, and, through sin, crushed sin—that is, death through death. Rightly did he call death by the name of sin, since it is clear that it was generated from sin.

Accordingly, the health that proceeds from the serpent is nothing other than divinity hidden, as it were, beneath sinful flesh. Since this is so, dearly beloved, let us look within ourselves; if we perceive any wound, let us flee from sin at once and take refuge in Christ. Let us raise the gaze of our hope toward him; let us direct the eyes of our mind toward him. But we must recognize what kind of bite this is. Whoever looks upon another’s evil, whoever sighs with anxious desire for another’s possession, whoever gazes upon another’s wife with importunate eyes that draw death upon himself, whoever sacrifices to the devil in another’s body—he has been struck in the heart by a poisoned arrow and pierced in his soul: though the bite may seem slight, he has been wounded with a fatal injury. Whoever retains malice or envy like a wound enclosed in his entrails has been torn by the bitterest and deadliest tooth. Whoever is empty of faith and full of hatred has been wholly devoured by the bites of that dragon.

Yet even if this is so, no one ought to despair. We read in the prophet Jonah (Jonah II) how even a creature is compelled to vomit out what it has swallowed. Therefore, amid our various bites, let us look toward Christ, so that he may look toward us. Here let us look toward our healer, since there he will no longer be seen by sinners except, perhaps, in judgment. [Col. 1047A] Or how will anyone be able to see the author of glory when he is about to utter the final farewell to the order of nature? Therefore, whoever, though redeemed, has refused to acknowledge him here will not be able to see him there, when condemned. Now, then, let us set him before our eyes through faith and works, and, with hope guiding us, let us hurl our eyes toward heaven.

Moses demonstrated the remedy in the Old Testament after the serpent had bitten. Christ also showed this: how, if you resist, it cannot bite. See how much the name of your God can accomplish through grace, since it accomplished so much in the figure. We are told that those who were to be redeemed looked toward the serpent and received a remedy. How much more healthful will it be if those who have already been redeemed look toward Christ!

## HOMILY III. On Easter.

[Col. 1047C]

The most holy solemnity of this day is called *phase* in Hebrew, *pascha* in Greek, and “passing over” in Latin. The Jews celebrated it after withdrawing from Egypt, following the long yoke of captivity. Behold, even now the people of God have been set free; behold, once again *phase* is enacted, once again the passing over is celebrated.

How is the passing over celebrated again? The same passage is made from slavery to freedom, from iniquity to righteousness, from guilt to grace, from death to life, through saving streams. You can once again enact the ancient miracles of the Red Sea by the power of that uplifted arm. The soul enters the life-giving waters, as though they had been consecrated red by the blood of Christ. It enters full of deadly debts, soon to be enriched by the blessed shipwrecks of sins [Col. 1047D]. In one and the same element of the saving waters, the sinner perishes like an Egyptian, while the just person remains wholly like a Hebrew. The guilty person is washed away; guilt is abolished.

Wonderful is the Lord’s clemency, which recalls an irrevocable crime and stains infected with offenses to their former state, and, while sin itself dies, gives life to the sinner. Behold, a person is immersed in the font, and by a secret gift only the person’s guilt is condemned. A criminal is dipped, and only the crime is extinguished. In this way that prophetic oracle is fulfilled: “And the water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained” (Ps. X). “One of them” signifies that one, first, original debt, which the water of the sacred font emptied. It destroyed the singular offense of the first parent.

Here [Col. 1048A] the magnificence of so great a gift displays the blessed presence of the Trinity. Behold, countless evils impressed by ancient and recent wounds, scarcely to be expiated by perpetual punishments in Gehenna, are cleansed by a threefold immersion. With God acting swiftly in a single moment, the fuel of flames is consumed amid the channels of the waters.

And therefore the blessed Apostle says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism into death.” Souls are submerged in the sacred whirlpool; they approach the boundaries of death and life. Those who had been subject to destruction at the rising of their first birth are reborn through a saving setting. They are stripped of the foulness of invisible old age and, of the deformity contracted through sins, clothed with the beauty of heavenly infancy.

We are sometimes astonished at the greatness of the new creation when we hear or read that the Lord Jesus Christ was born from a woman alone, without the union of a man [Col. 1048B]. Behold now, while the laws of nature make their way elsewhere, countless multitudes throughout the whole earth are begotten from the womb of the font alone, as though by a virgin birth. Let the Church of Christ rejoice, which, in the likeness of blessed Mary, is enriched through the working of the Holy Spirit and becomes the mother of divine offspring. Let the blind error of unbelievers cease to assert that a woman who could bear a son without a man could not remain a virgin.

Behold how many brothers, and brothers of how many, the fruitful Church—mother and bride—has brought forth for us in a single night from the womb of her integrity. A short while ago you marveled at a human being born in incorruption; marvel now that he is reborn, which is no less new. If it pleases us, let us compare these two mothers, and the generation of each will strengthen our faith in the other [Col. 1048C].

The overshadowing of the Holy Spirit filled Mary through a secret descent, and the infusion of the Holy Spirit espoused the Church in the blessed font. Mary bore a son without sin, and the Church, in those whom she has begotten, consumed sins. Through Mary was born what was in the beginning; through the Church was reborn what had perished in the beginning. The former brought forth for many; the latter brought forth peoples. The former, as we know, remaining a virgin, bore a son once; the latter, a virgin, always bears the Bridegroom. Therefore, what you thought was a unique miracle throughout the ages, now recognize as an annual gift.

If you doubt that you will rise again, marvel at the offspring within you whom shortly before you knew to be an heir of death. Where are those who say that there is some genesis or fate by which part of humanity is compelled by violent necessity to pass into sin? Where [Col. 1048D] are those who say that there are souls which, born under condemnation, are dragged to death by the predetermined condition of an evil nature?

First, if this is so, why does both human and divine law condemn the wicked, unless it is because the fault of the will is culpable? Justice does not punish what nature compels. But let it be so: someone may have been assigned to destruction, born under a predetermined lot. Behold, he descends into the font as into a tomb. Even if his nature had been stained, it would certainly have vanished into nothing. A worse origin would have received its end, because a better life was taking its beginning.

Here we now see how our God redeems us from the hand of the enemy. The whole person is washed away, absolved, renewed. When the devil comes, he no longer recognizes as his own the one whom nature, emptied and laid bare, has emancipated into the adoption of Christ and transferred into the bosom of the Father from the jurisdiction of the evil persuader [Col. 1049A].

Without doubt, the grace of rebirth has taken away the former bondage and bestowed freedom. Those born through a second birth can no longer be bound to their first origin. “Why now, whoever you are, do you thrust Adam’s natural bond upon me, when you recognize that I have been reborn in Christ? Why,” I say, “do you charge me with another’s sin, when you admit that my own has been forgiven? Why do you charge me with the debt of the old bond, when you see that it has been canceled by a new security?”

For in baptism we made a security and covenant with Christ: that the human being should preserve innocence for him, and that he should restore glory to the human being; that the servant should offer service, and that the Lord should prepare a kingdom. What can the persuader of another’s household do amid these things? He sees those who were once his slaves, unjustly seized by him, handed over to freedom through the recognition of Christ. He sees that he has fallen through the prior judgment of the case and that he has incurred the danger of making an excessive claim.

How has he incurred the danger of making an excessive claim? How did he make an excessive claim? Because, although the human being was owed to him through obedience to sin, he sought to seize God, deceived by the appearance of a human being, and dared to lay murderous hands upon the Lord of heaven. And suddenly, through so great a crime, he also incurred the charge of treason against majesty; thus, proscribed, he lost the human being whom he had violently held. Proscribed, I say: for immediately, in the very human being whom redemption restored to his origin, Christ affixed his titles.

This is that cross which we carry marked upon our foreheads, like the sign marked on the royal doorposts (Exod. XII), and which the Lord, the chief and legitimate emperor, most justly impressed as received into his possession [Col. 1049C], so that we may truly be called the house of God.

For God speaks through his Apostle to the human being: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (I Cor. III).

For these reasons the exceedingly powerful and proud one deserved to be proscribed, because, as has been said, he was now guilty of treason against majesty. Once dear to his maker in the heights, he then desired a share in the maker’s divinity, forgetful of his status as a creature; now, through his habitual impiety, he has extended bloody hands against the author of all things. Thus the just condemnation of the robber became the captive’s free manumission.

And therefore he now groans, envies, and prowls about, in the hope that he may somehow steal from us the instrument of that manumission and the tablet of the freedom we have obtained. With all his strength he strives to strip the human being of the privilege granted to him and, through the operation of sin, to prejudice him as an ungrateful freedman [Col. 1049D].

Our tablets, dearly beloved, are our faith, inscribed upon the pages of the heart. Our freedom is the grace of God and our way of life. Our freedom, I say, is the practice of religion, righteousness in action, and purity of chastity. Let us defend this with every vigilance of mind against the devil, for he is all the more eager to assault the treasure of the soul the more he knows it to be precious.

And because, as an exile from heaven, he remembers what is done in heaven and what great reward is being prepared for trembling humanity by the words of God, the magnitude of his zeal reveals this. He betrays glory while exercising envy. He is an enemy of the blessings of the one who promises that the human being taken from earth will reign with him in heaven, so that the blessedness of faithful mortals may become the confusion of the rebellious angels [Col. 1050A].

## HOMILY IV. On Easter.

Appropriately and suitably, on this day of the present distinguished solemnity, we rise into a voice of exultation and say with the Apostle: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI).

Today, when the Egyptians have been slain, the people of God are freed from mud and straw—that is, from works that are most worthless and empty (Exod. XII). Today that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world is offered for the redemption of human salvation, when we are commanded to inscribe the doorposts of our houses with his blood: that is, to paint our foreheads with the title of the cross, so that the destroying angel may find no place [Col. 1050B].

At this time Pharaoh and his army are hurled into the Red Sea. As sins perish in the sacred font, the Egyptians are plunged, as it were, into red waves—red, that is, consecrated by the blood of Christ.

At this time, for the return of the younger son who had perished and was found, for the salvation of the Gentiles, that fattened calf was sacrificed (Luke XII). The younger son, however, are we, who, while our older brother—that is, the Jews—delay and refuse to enter, return to our Creator in repentance for our sins.

For we had overturned and betrayed the substance received from God the Father. Let us see what substance this was: the goods of universal nature. Everything by which we live, understand, and think belongs to God: understanding and reason for distinguishing good and evil. The freedom of choice that we had received also belongs to God’s substance, whether for turning aside the allurements of sin, or for stirring the affection of a free will toward obedience to the author, or for preserving the image and likeness of God.

These riches, then, given to us and implanted within us by the Creator, we transferred to private uses and consumed in the practices of vices, abandoning the fountain of virtues and traveling abroad, very far from the father (ibid.)—not departing from him in places and regions, but in hearts and deeds. For whoever follows his own pleasures and is carried away by his passions becomes an exile from God.

When we return to him after acknowledging our sins—and indeed return not by bodily steps but by the affection of the mind—he comes to meet us with immense mercy, ineffable joy, and consolation amid the celebrations of the feast; he arranges dances and symphonies [Col. 1050D], that is, the rejoicings of heavenly joys with which the angels rejoice in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke XV). When we return, therefore, for amendment of life, this feast is celebrated every day.

Every day the Father receives the Son. Christ is always sacrificed for believers. This, then, is the fattened calf whom we are taught to offer in the Old Testament (Num. XXIX). The calf, descended from cattle—that is, from the patriarchs, the prophets, and the offspring of Abraham—is a spotless male.

A male, that is, one robust and strong against every sin. For it is characteristic of a masculine and manly spirit to reject the allure of sin, just as it is the cowardice of feminine weakness to accept the wantonness of vice. Hence Pharaoh, who bears the type of the devil [Col. 1051A], pressing down the people of God, hostile to the spirit and friendly to the flesh, was strangling their strengths and overturning their desires (Exod. I).

Christ, therefore, died on account of our iniquities; and as a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. This is the lamb whom the law commands us to eat in one house, with our loins girded (Exod. XII). We must eat it with its feet as well.

What does “in one house” mean? It means that we are commanded to partake of his flesh in the unity of the Church. Therefore the Arians and the various perversions of heretics do not eat him in one house. Just as in the Flood no one was saved except the one who was found within Noah’s ark, so people of differing faiths who do not have the Lamb, who is Christ, within the house of the Church cannot be saved [Col. 1051B].

As for the fact that Scripture recalls that we ought to eat the head of this lamb together with its feet, this means that we are to venerate God and man with an equal confession. Let us understand the head from what blessed John says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I). Let us understand the feet from what the Apostle writes: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II); and, “born of a woman, born under the law” (Gal. IV).

Therefore we must feed on the flesh of this lamb of ours with our loins girded—that is, with our carnal passions put to death—and with the utmost purity of heart and body. The head together with the feet means that we must believe that he was begotten from God and born from a human being.

When I said that he was begotten from God, perhaps some among the less educated may say in their hearts [Col. 1051C]: “How did God beget the Son?” Let us think of nothing bodily here. For what is “God begot God” other than that fire appeared from fire, light proceeded from light?

Therefore, for the sake of those who are slow to understand, let us now take some image or comparison from earthly and visible things. For example: if one lamp is lit from another, if one is illuminated from another, does it not seem to you that, in some manner, a flame gives birth to a flame and that splendor has begotten splendor? Does it not seem to you that, by an immeasurable mode, light has been born from light?

When this is transferred from one lamp to another, although two lamps are burning, the very same fire that shone in the first is certainly in the second. Was that fire made from nothing, or from some new beginning? Rather, it was poured forth from the nature of its own splendor [Col. 1051D].

Therefore the illumination that appears to have been kindled from the first lamp did not begin to exist in the second as though from nothing; it proceeded from a related splendor that already remained in the source of the first light. And although in both lamps a genuine and twofold flame appears to shine, both are nevertheless one substance.

So too with the only-begotten Son of God: although the form of the person is distinct, the nature of the kind is shared—not beginning from the Father, but subsisting from the Father with the Father. All things were created from nothing; he alone is God from God.

When he was therefore in the form of God, he assumed the form of a servant for the salvation of servants; and, though he was the tree of life, he was hung upon the wood of the cross, as though weighing himself out as the price of the lost. He was struck with blows; he was crowned with thorns [Col. 1052A].

As for his being clothed in a scarlet cloak, Christ’s garments are the merits of the saints. Even then, therefore, he is drenched in that scarlet color with the blood of martyrs. As for the Jews’ adoring him, clothed in a purple cloak, with a bent knee, whether they wished it or not, they confess him to be that king and Lord.

When he said on the cross, “I thirst” (John XIX), he was seeking faith in his own people. But because he came to his own, and his own did not receive him (John I), they offered him faithlessness in place of the sweetness of faith. The vinegar of malice is extended to him, because through sinning they had lost the wine of wisdom that they had received from Christ. He drinks the bitterness of our evils, in order to give the sweetness of his good things.

Even now, every day, whenever he is saddened and embittered by sins, a drink of vinegar and food of gall are, in a manner, administered to him [Col. 1052B].

The veil of the temple is torn (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV). The veil is an ornament of the tabernacle. Therefore, as grace flashes forth, the Church is built and the Synagogue is destroyed. The temple is stripped of the honor of the veil, the veil of the letter being removed through Christ’s coming, so that, with Paul (I Cor. III), the inner things of the law may be disclosed with unveiled face.

The saints rise with Christ, their place in Tartarus having been released; and those whom the heavens do not receive recognize in the underworld that he is God. Therefore, recognizing toward us the profound mysteries of the divine benefits, let us respond to the Redeemer’s mercy as we are able.

Let us give him, in place of his thorns, compunction through the amendment of our sins. Let us offer him, in place of his nails, a heart pierced with fear of him. Let us return to him, in place of his blows, the palm of perseverance.

## HOMILY V. On Easter.

[Col. 1052C]

The greatness of heavenly benefits exceeds the narrow capacity of the human mind. Therefore divine providence arranged matters so that what the reason, overcome by the magnitude of reality, could not contain within us, devoted faith might conceive, and steadfast belief might nourish understanding. Since, then, through Adam’s first transgression we were held liable to our origin and to death, God, looking down from above and discerning the condition in which we were debtors to life, repaired the circumstances of our captivity by the gift of redemption: that is, so that in place of the death that was owed he might offer a death that was not owed. And because we neither had the means by which we might live, nor did he have the means by which he might die, he took material from our mortality, so that, with his immortality placed within it, Life might die for the dead.

[Col. 1052D] Therefore, since he was about to remove from our eyes the body he had assumed and carry it up to the stars, it was necessary that on this day he consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood, so that what had once been offered as the price might continually be honored through the mystery; so that, because redemption for the salvation of human beings was proceeding daily and without weariness, the offering of redemption might also be perpetual; so that the enduring victim might live in memory, remain always present in grace, and be regarded as the one and perfect sacrifice by faith, not by outward appearance, nor judged by external sight, but by inward vision.

Hence the heavenly authority rightly confirms that “my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Let every uncertainty of unbelief, therefore, depart, since the one who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness to its truth. For the invisible priest, by the hidden power of his word, transforms visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.” And, repeating the consecration: “Take and drink; this is my blood.” Thus, at the command of the Lord who ordered it, the heights of the heavens, the depths of the waves, and the vast expanses of the earth suddenly came into existence from nothing. With equal power, in spiritual sacraments the force of the word commands, and the effect serves the reality.

What great benefits, then, the divine power of blessing accomplishes—ask yourself how this ought not to seem new and impossible: that earthly and mortal things are changed into the substance of Christ. You yourself, who have now been reborn in Christ, should question yourself. A short while ago you were alien to life, a stranger [Col. 1053B] to mercy, inwardly exiled from the life of salvation. Suddenly initiated into Christ’s laws and renewed through saving mysteries, you passed into the body of the Church—not by seeing, but by believing—and, from being a child of perdition, you merited through hidden purity to become an adopted child of God.

Remaining within visible measure, you became greater than yourself invisibly, without any increase of size. Although you yourself were the same person, you came to be something altogether different through the progress of faith. Nothing was added outwardly, yet everything was changed inwardly. Thus the human being became a child of Christ, and Christ was formed in the human mind.

Therefore, just as, without bodily perception, after laying aside your former condition for the sake of the benefit set before you, you suddenly put on a new dignity; and just as what God healed in you—the wounded, the infected, the stained—was entrusted not to your eyes but to your senses, so, when you approach the reverend altar to be satisfied with food, look upon the sacred body and blood of your God with faith, marvel at it with honor, touch it with your mind, receive it with the hand of your heart, and above all take it in through an inward draught.

If that manna of the Law, of which it is written, “He rained manna upon them, that they might eat” (Deut. 8; Ps. LXXVII), tasted to each person according to the desire he longed for, then what was taken was one thing and what was seen another: that taste was formed invisibly in the senses of each individual. Yet that manna of the Law, falling from heaven, surpassed the natural quality and character of its kind through its manifold sweetness. And although the providence of the giver seasoned his creature with varied diversity, taste supplied what sight did not know. According to the desire of the one receiving it, the novelty and dignity of that food came into being.

[Col. 1053D] That honey-sweet gift of rain restored each person with different and unfamiliar flavors, and the varied service of the dry rain. Since this is so, let what appetite accomplished there be accomplished here by faith. If food gives flavor to the body, let God advance in the heart through belief, as we read: “Let a person approach the deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Ps. LXIII). Therefore, just as delight prevailed there in the throat, so here let blessing work in the senses.

To know and receive the sacrifice of the true body, may he himself strengthen you and invite you through the power of the one who consecrates. May the one who was then hidden, prefigured in the manna, now be manifested to you in grace. That he was marked out beforehand in the form of that manna, the prophet also clearly shows, saying: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXVII). And what is the bread of angels except Christ, who satisfies them with the food of his love and the light of his splendor?

This bread, when the prophet says, “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much, but on the Sabbath you shall not gather” (Exod. XVI), since it is granted in the Law from the first day—that is, from the Lord’s Day—and denied only on the Sabbath, already then reveals that Christ is to be received by the Church, for which the resurrection consecrated the Lord’s body, and is to be denied to the synagogue, to which Sabbath observance belonged, since that day—that is, the seventh day—is deprived of the heavenly bread through this fraud.

Concerning this bread, the ancient narrative relates that neither did the one who had gathered more have more, nor did the one who had prepared less find less, because the sacred reception of the Eucharist consists not in quantity [Col. 1054B] but in power. The body, when dispensed by the priest, is as much in the small portion as it is known to be in the whole. When the Church of the faithful receives it, it is shown to be as full in all as it is entire in each individual. Concerning this meaning the apostolic judgment teaches, saying: “The one who had much did not have more, and the one who had little did not have less” (II Cor. VIII).

If we were to set out a loaf of bread for hungry people to eat, it would not reach each person in its entirety, because each would take his portion piece by piece and crumb by crumb. But when this bread is received, individuals have no less than the whole community. One receives the whole, two receive the whole, and many receive the whole without diminution, because the blessing of this sacrament knows how to be distributed but does not know how to be consumed by distribution.

We also find the form of this sacrament expressed in the pages of the Jews. For in Genesis we read about Melchizedek: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine, and blessed Abraham” (Gen. XIV). Melchizedek was a priest of the Most High God. While the one who was to be circumcised was blessed by an uncircumcised man—that is, a Gentile—the glory of the Church was proclaimed, and the people acquired from the Gentiles were set above the unbelieving synagogue.

Thus, in Melchizedek, whose genealogy or origin remained unknown to the knowledge of that time, this sacrifice of Christ was prefigured through the offering of bread and wine. Concerning him the prophet declares: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). For blessed Moses, too, speaking of that mystery, signifies wine and blood under one designation in the blessing of the patriarch, displaying the Lord’s Passion long beforehand, when he says: “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX).

Observe how clearly the creature wine is now designated by the name of Christ’s blood. To learn what more you should inquire concerning this twofold form, hear the Lord himself testify: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI). This testimony is most clear and powerful against the blasphemies of Pelagius, who, having seized upon impiety, presumes to assert that baptism should be conferred on little children not for life, but for the kingdom of heaven.

Under these words of the Lord, in which the evangelist declares, “You will not have life in yourselves,” it must plainly be understood that every soul deprived of the gift of baptism lacks not only glory but also life.

[Col. 1055A] The Lord showed not only by tradition but also by the very manner of his Passion that this wine of the Lord’s blood must be mixed with water: from his sacred side blood and water flowed when it was struck by the spear, just as the prophet had long before foretold, saying: “He struck the rock, and waters flowed” (Ps. LXXV). And the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X). “They drank,” he says, “from the rock that followed them.” You see that whoever drinks from Christ’s grace is followed by Christ’s mercy.

But in Solomon we read that the Lord himself was foretold: “Wisdom,” he says, “built herself a house” (Prov. IX)—that is, he assumed a human body in which the fullness of divinity dwelt. And he added seven pillars, because the blessing of the Holy Spirit filled him with its sevenfold grace. “She slaughtered her victims, mixed her wine in the bowl, and prepared her table.” And afterward: “Come, eat of my breads, and drink the wine that I have mixed for you.”

Since we read that wine was mixed with water, let us now inquire why the Lord wished both to be mixed. When, at the Jewish wedding feast, the nuptial wine—that is, faith in them—was failing, it was said, “The wine was failing” (John II), because the vineyard refused its fruit; concerning it Scripture says: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isa. V). Hence he also placed a crown of thorns on the Redeemer’s head.

When, at the time of the wedding—that is, when the Bridegroom was to be joined to his Church in paschal rejoicing—the Lord changed water into wine, he was plainly prefiguring that multitudes of the Gentiles would come through the grace of his blood. For sacred writings disclose that peoples are signified by waters, as we read: “The waters that you saw are peoples, nations, and tongues” (Rev. XVII).

We recognize that in the waters the figure of the nations is displayed, while in the wine the blood of the Lord’s Passion is shown. Thus, while water is mixed with wine in the sacraments, the people faithful to Christ are incorporated into him and joined to him, and are united to him by a bond of perfect love, so that they may say with the Apostle: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or persecution?” (Rom. VIII), and so forth.

God is also mixed with the human being through sanctification, when faith is poured into the breast itself through devotion to righteousness, mercy, and piety.

Moreover, in this very fact—that we know the bread is made from innumerable grains of wheat—we recognize that the unity of peoples is signified. Thus the grain, prepared with the customary care of the purifier, is brought by the labor of the millstones into a white form and, through water and fire, gathered into the substance of one bread.

So diverse peoples and different nations, coming together in one faith, become from themselves one body of Christ. The Christian people, like innumerable grains of wheat, is distinguished from sacrilegious nations by faith that purifies and sifts it, and is gathered into one, as the weeds of unbelief pass away. It shines with the instruction of the two Testaments, like a garment prepared by the double work of the millstones, and is changed by its native whiteness into the dignity of its first origin. Through the water of baptism or through the fire of the Holy Spirit, it becomes the body of that eternal bread.

[Col. 1056A] Therefore, just as the grains (genera [grana]) cannot be separated from the union of the bread that has been prepared, and just as water, once mixed into wine, cannot return to its own substance, so all the faithful and wise, who recognize that they have been redeemed by Christ’s blood and Passion, ought to be joined to their head as inseparable members through steadfastness and ardent devotion. They should be so united that they cannot be separated from him by will or necessity, by any ambition for earthly things, or finally even by death itself.

Let no one doubt that the primary elements can pass, by the command of power and the presence of majesty, into the nature of the Lord’s body, when he sees that the human being himself has been made the body of Christ through the work of heavenly mercy.

Just as anyone who comes to faith remains, before the words of baptism, still bound by the debt of the past, but, once these words have been spoken, is immediately stripped of all the dregs of sin, so, when creatures to be blessed by heavenly words are placed upon the sacred altars, before they are consecrated by the invocation of the holy name, the substance there is bread and wine; but after Christ’s words, it is Christ’s body and Christ’s blood.

What wonder is it, then, if the things he could create by a word he can transform by a word once created? Indeed, it seems a lesser miracle if he is able to change for the better what he is known to have established from nothing. Ask what can be difficult for the one who easily brought forth visible and invisible things by the command of his will; for whom it was easy to clothe the human being, fashioned from the material of clay, in the image of his divinity; for whom it is readily possible to call him back from the underworld, restore him from destruction, repair him from dust, raise him from earth to heaven, make an angel from a human being, make the human body conform to the body of his glory, and exalt his creation into fellowship with his kingdom—so that the one who assumed the body of our frailty might assume us into the body of his immortality.

May he deign to prepare us by righteous works for that glorious resurrection, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY VI

Just as the Lord demands from us the duty of speaking, according to the necessity of the office we have undertaken, so from you, dearest ones, he requires a disposition to listen. Thus, I say, it is beneficial for your love to obey what we say for your salvation, just as it is incumbent upon us not to remain silent. For if we fear offense because of silence, how much more ought you to fear it because of contempt? If, I say, it is a great danger for us not to reprove the sins of others, how much more dangerous is it to refuse to correct our own?

Blessed Paul says in one place: “Consider your calling, brothers” (I Cor. II). Therefore, beloved, let us also consider our calling. It is not enough that we have sought this place if we are such as we could have been in the world. For if we look carefully, not only does this concern compel us toward perfection, but the very multitude of our congregation also binds us.

Just as it is precious and extraordinary to act well while placed among many and to stir many toward progress in good works, so it is dangerous and destructive to break the faith of many and corrupt the souls of many by acting carelessly. As it is fruitful to live honorably while placed among many, so it is dangerous to have done anything destructive.

Why do I say this? Because we more easily find what is worse, and pursue things that are more depraved rather than those that are better. Human weakness is inclined to imitate evil. Therefore, let us not think it sufficient that we see ourselves gathered on this island [in this school], because the perfection we have professed condemns our negligences more forcefully than the perfection we have not undertaken.

For according to the testimony of Scripture, from those to whom much has been entrusted, much must necessarily be required. Oh, for how many people the convenience of this place and the opportunity of a suitable dwelling will be beneficial—and, on the contrary, for how many harmful!

It is not praiseworthy merely to have spoken well in this place, but to have acted well in this place. Consider again: does the seclusion of this dwelling benefit us when wickedness reigns in us with tyrannical domination? When anger rides above us? When the human eye induces greater fear in us than the divine eye? When we believe ourselves to be outside the world by a praiseworthy life, while through the vices of various passions we keep the world enclosed within us?

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “When those praiseworthy hermits whom we believe to be outside the world [m. n. e.], through …”]

Thus, although we thought that by our prayers we ourselves were coming to the aid of the world, it is almost necessary that we recognize that we need the world’s intercessions more. There is no doubt that the soul which becomes the possession of worldly conduct through desire for worldly pleasures cannot become the kingdom of divinity.

Therefore, brothers, consider your calling. To come to the desert is indeed the highest perfection, but not to live perfectly in the desert is the highest condemnation. What does it profit if a quiet place is occupied only bodily, while unrest is preserved [or: circulates] in the heart? What, I ask, does it profit if there is silence in the dwelling, while in its inhabitants there is the tumult and conflict of vices? If outwardly our surroundings are calm, but inwardly there is a storm?

We have not come together in this place so that the world might serve us, or so that we might abound in all things and enjoy complete ease. We have certainly not come here for rest or security, but for battle; we have advanced to the contest; we have hastened here to wage war against our vices, so that we may blunt the swords of our tongues; so that we may not only refrain from inflicting injuries upon one another, but may not even feel those inflicted by others.

More particularly, this belongs to our profession: to seek no consolation in this life, no rest; not to wish to receive good things during one’s lifetime; to flee honors; to rejoice in submission and abasement; to seek the pursuit of poverty; and to eradicate from our hearts not only possessions but even desires themselves.

Sometimes possessing nothing is a matter of necessity; desiring nothing through avarice is a virtue. Therefore a religious person must establish this rule for himself in particular: to have only as much as necessity demands, not as much as desire craves. For the love of possessing, unless cut away completely, burns more fiercely in small things, and people are more tormented over trifles.

And unless you are poor with your whole heart and in your whole disposition, poverty itself must be judged not a virtue but a misery. Know, then, brothers, that it does no good if we afflict [or: mortify] our flesh with fasts and vigils but do not amend our mind, or do not care for what is inward.

What does bodily affliction profit if we pollute our tongue with wickedness and slander? Are not all our labors reduced to nothing? Does not all our work vanish like smoke and shadow, and like the ash of straw become nothing?

Oh, how many and how long-lasting our labors suddenly perish; how many good things, frequently already acquired and stored up, are snatched from our hand when we neglect to seek, increase, or guard what we had striven to obtain!

Therefore we flatter ourselves in vain about the cross of the body and the affliction of the breast if our outward person is exercised by holy labors while the inward person is not cared for amid its passions. It is like someone making a statue golden on the outside, or like a house built with magnificent skill and painted on the outside in the most beautiful colors, while inside it is full of serpents and scorpions.

What does it profit that you afflict your body when your heart makes no progress? It is a very harsh and deeply lamentable condition to devote oneself wholly to labor and receive no fruit after the labor.

To fast and keep vigil without correcting one’s ways is like someone clearing or cultivating land outside a vineyard while leaving the vineyard itself deserted and untilled, so that it produces thorns and thistles, though, if the cultivator attended to it, it could produce the most delightful fruits.

Recognize, therefore, dearest brothers, that bodily abstinence alone is not sufficient for attaining everlasting salvation unless the soul’s fast is also joined to it through abstinence from vices.

What does it help if someone is chaste in body but polluted in mind; if malice corrupts him; if the fury of anger torments him with its torches; if pride strips him of every grace of God; if his tongue stains him with lies or curses? Does he not deceive himself, mock himself, and cheat himself if he believes that he can be sanctified by his fasts and vigils without the remaining virtues?

Therefore, beloved, let us exercise the body with fasts in such a way that we cleanse the mind from vices. Let us think constantly of the coming of that judge—may he find us prepared in the way no one can doubt that he will come!

If you ask how he will come: he will come in that very body which was assumed for our salvation, born [or: condemned] for our absolution, and pierced by spear and nails for the healing of our wounds. For the first unbearable sentence against the guilty will be the presence of the revered scars.

What, then, shall we do at that time, when, against the bruises of that crucified Lord, the marks of our sins and the stains of our lusts will be brought forth? Or with what expression, do you think, will our redemption look upon our destruction? Human offenses will be all the more serious insofar as divine benefits reveal themselves to be greater.

We must fear that, in his judgment, he will also bring forth to the vessels of iniquity that voice of the precious resurrection, proclaiming the marks of the cross: “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side” (John XXI); and recognize what divine compassion endured for you, an impious person.

Those marks of the nails are salutary to the good and terrifying to the wicked; they will not be erased until the day of judgment.

And what follows after this except that vast, terrifying chaos and separation placed between the living and the dead: the outer darkness, excluded from the nature of the living [or: exclusion from the nature of the living]; harsh separation [Col. 1059B] from the sweet sight of the saints and from the fellowship of the blessed; and, on the other hand, to go amid the tearful groans and wailings of mourners and the sad company of the miserable, and before the blessed homeland to undergo forever the exile of most dreadful death?

How mournful it will be for a person to see the Lord and lose him, and to perish before the sight of his Creator! Therefore, dearest brothers, while there is time, thinking on these things and recalling the benefits of our Redeemer, let us labor with God’s help in tireless devotion, so that what he offered [or: bestowed upon] us when he was judged, Jesus Christ our Lord may find whole within us when he comes to judge—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY VII

[Col. 1059C] Hurrying to this place, dearest ones, we have come together not for rest, not for security, but for battle and combat. We have advanced here to the contest, and have come together [or: contended] to wage war against our vices.

Our vices are our enemies, concerning whom Scripture declares: “Take care never to make a covenant with them” (Deut. VII). Vigilant care and tireless watchfulness are necessary for us, brothers, because this conflict is without end and this enemy without peace; he can be defeated, but cannot be received into friendship.

Therefore the battle we have undertaken is sufficiently broad and sufficiently dangerous, because it is waged within the human being, and does not end except with the human being himself. For this reason we have withdrawn to these tranquil retreats and spiritual camps, so that every day we may fight against our passions in an untiring struggle; every day submit our wills to our elders as to servants; circumcise the wickedness of the heart, or sheath the swords of the tongue [or: blunt the sword of the tongue]; so that we may not only refrain from inflicting injuries upon one another, but may not even feel those inflicted by others.

For this especially belongs to our profession: to seek no consolation in this life, to desire no honor, to flee the comforts of present things, to prepare the mind for the promises of eternal reward, to rejoice in submission and abasement, to seek the pursuit of poverty [or: to seek poverty with zeal], and to eradicate from our hearts not only possessions but even the desires to possess.

For sometimes having nothing is a matter of necessity; desiring nothing, however, is a virtue.

You must also know that those who have resolved to live among you do so either with great profit or with great danger, whether they are diligent or negligent. Hence blessed is that soul which, when it conducts itself well in the congregation, becomes the joy of many; and from which very many are either built up or enlightened. Its good qualities, when shared with many, increase.

The saying of that very wise man also applies here: “My son, if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbors.” Therefore, if someone placed in the congregation patiently [or: in patience] presents himself to humility, to the extent that he lends goodness from himself to his neighbors, to that extent he turns the gains of others into his own.

But if, on the contrary, through disobedience or pride you pursue what is worse—for this is usually found more easily—and draw others to the evil example of your wickedness, you incur the danger of condemnation for the many whom you have destroyed. To as many as you were a detriment, from so many you have incurred losses; and the sin that once departed from him flowed back upon him many times over.

Therefore, just as the person whose good course is the progress of many is greatly to be admired and praised, so the one whose evil life is the ruin of many is rightly to be mourned.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us strive to do what pertains to edification while placed among others: so that our life [or: our vices] may not harm the virtues of others; so that our lukewarmness may not weaken the fervor of others; so that our anger may not violate the patience of others; so that our pride may not corrupt the humility of others; so that our weakness may not corrupt the health of others; so that our ugliness may not stain the beauty of others; and so that we may not extinguish the burning lamps of others if we cannot light our own.

Those foolish virgins, indeed, however foolish they were, desired not so much to extinguish the lamps of others as to light their own (Matt. XXV). Therefore, following their likeness [Note: [Col. 1059D] “We resort to the comparison, so that if anyone …”], if anyone among us lacks the richest grace of humility, the fire of faith, the flame of fervor, the oil of love, or the light of discernment, let him go to those whom he sees to possess these things more abundantly. Let him transfer that grace into himself not by taking it away from his neighbor but by imitating him; and let him seize the good belonging to another without harm, indeed with profit to its possessor.

Nothing that another gains from you (alter [alteri]) is ever lacking to you. A lamp never feels the loss of its light when many are kindled from it, nor does the multitude of those who gaze upon it diminish the sun’s light. To as many as look toward it, it lends its gifts, yet itself remains whole.

Blessed by God is that soul whose humility confounds another’s pride; whose patience extinguishes the anger of a neighbor; whose obedience silently reproves another’s laziness; whose fervor arouses the inertness of someone else’s lukewarmness.

The person who illumines, through the grace of consolation and edification, the troubled eye of his neighbor’s heart, inflamed by anger, is better than the one who does not lift up a brother briefly saddened by someone, extending his hand in comfort, but instead, like a leaning wall, helps him fall under the force of slander; and, though he has been healthfully corrected according to the requirements of discipline, urges him on with sinister counsels so that he strikes him down, arms him so that he destroys him.

Therefore, brothers, if a person’s own evils are not enough for him, let him act in such a way that he does not also incur judgment for another’s destruction.

We are certain, dearest ones, that unless we take care, unless we cut away and circumcise our passions daily, we shall become much worse than we were while living in the world, so that “our last state becomes worse than the first” (Luke XI).

Indeed, beloved, as long as we belonged to the world and served those activities and occupations of which we are now ashamed, our adversary did not oppose us; rather, he even consented, because concerning our miserable and ruined life he found no occasion on which to exercise his envy. Our deeds pleased him; our crimes and sins were sufficient for him in themselves. For who would undertake war against his own soldier? Who would wish to attack his own subject?

Yet above every misery was the life of the one whom the enemy did not consider worthy of harming. But now, after we have renounced his desires [or: pleasures], he sees his worshipers returned to the former service of their creator; he sees in us, in a certain sense, his idols changed into temples of God. Gnashing his teeth and roaring like a lion, he explores every means of doing harm as a watchful ambusher.

The Apostle testifies concerning this lion: “Be vigilant, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V).

Blessed, therefore, are those whom this lion judges worthy of seeking and pursuing [or: worthy to be pursued], namely, by the traces of their virtues and the fragrance of their merits. For he seeks only the good, since the wicked thrust themselves upon him. He runs violently after the former, while he encounters the latter even negligently.

Blessed, therefore, are those whom this lion is compelled by envy to seek, but whom his malice is not permitted to find.

It certainly sounds terrifying in our ears when we hear: “Like a roaring lion.” But since it is said, “His food is the elect” (esca ejus electi [electae]), what he seeks belongs to election, while the fact that he roars belongs to despair. As we read elsewhere: “He will gnash with his teeth and waste away” [or: “He gnashes with his teeth and wastes away”] (Ps. CXI), so in this passage divine speech joins consolation to terror. That he gnashes is the sign of one tortured; that he wastes away, of one defeated.

Amid these things, even the envy of the enemy reveals how great are the things prepared by God for the human being.

Therefore, dearest ones, thinking on these things and laboring in this contest, let us remember that we are both disciples and sons of our glorious and illustrious Father. Let each of us seize what he can from the goods of a father who has died intestate (bonis intestati [bonis tanti] parentis): let one take from his inheritance the all-silk garment of faith [the printed variant reads: “the breastplate of faith”], and the precious variety of his deeds; let another claim the talent of gentleness and simplicity; let another take for himself the necklace of the heart’s beauty, benevolence, and wisdom; let another seize the pearl of compunction and the treasure of chastity.

Although that most wealthy friend of God carried away with him intact whatever he possessed, nevertheless, if we wish, he left everything to us. Let us therefore act by following his good qualities, so that he who is believed to be raised to eternal glory at the end of the ages may now rise again in the Church through the renewed merits of his children.

With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY VIII
We know indeed that a great reward is laid up in the future for the spiritual warfare to which we have devoted ourselves; but if we look carefully, we already possess, in a certain manner, a portion of the reward in the very work that we are undertaking, even in the present age. It is plainly a great fruit of life to have been able to despise the world and begin to serve God; to have escaped the most wretched domination of vices and fled the foulest slavery of gluttony and lust.

What then? Is it not already a great part of the reward to have nothing in common with the world; not to be tormented by desires for vain things; not to become involved in crimes; to pass the day in innocence; to devote oneself to blessed chastity; and to possess, with fear of the Lord, the sufficiency of glorious poverty?
