Concerning this Wisdom says: “Better is a small portion with the fear of the Lord than great treasures without his fear” (Prov. XIII).

Let us therefore understand how much the Lord has bestowed upon us through his gracious calling. Let us count, if we can, from the time when we seem to have begun living here, how many sins we have incurred, and from how many frauds, adulteries, robberies, perjuries, and sacrileges the Lord has delivered us; and then we shall see how much we also owe the Lord for his present benefits.

If we were now in the world [Col. 1062C], what else would we be doing than wallowing in our evils and defiling our souls with daily stains, piercing them with daily wounds, so that we could no longer even feel them? For sinful habit has this unhappy characteristic: the more someone sins, the less he understands the sins themselves; and the more he sins, the more he takes pleasure in it. Thus comes to pass what the prophet cries out to sinners: “There is no God before his eyes; your judgments are removed from his sight” (Ps. XIII). Indeed, when the delight of sinning steals upon someone, forgetfulness immediately hides the day of future judgment.

Conversely, the more concerned someone is about himself, the more he fears, as Scripture says: “The wise man, by fearing, turns away from evil.” The wise man, therefore, is always in remorse and always in fear; and just as he sighs over past [variant: “present”] evils, so he trembles over future dangers with vigilant concern.

He is anxious about the past and reflects and turns it over within himself, lest perhaps he has not sufficiently mourned his past sins; lest perhaps he has not yet made satisfaction for his innumerable debts; lest perhaps he has added new wounds to his former iniquities; lest he has impressed recent crimes upon the ancient stains of his conscience; and lest he has assumed the name of conversion for the purpose of sinning more gravely under a sacred profession.

We think it somewhat sufficient for us that we have done this, that we have climbed this, that we have changed our place and manner of life, that we have spent some time here, placing all our hope in the number of years [Col. 1063A] and thus deceiving ourselves with a ruinous persuasion. We think that our evils have vanished with the passage of time. And because we have forgotten them, we believe that they have slipped from the memory of divine severity. But it is not so. Everything has been stored up with him [variant: “gathered”] and sealed.

Let us hear what blessed Job says, he who fights hand to hand in single combat with the devil himself: “You have sealed up my sins as in a bag” (Job XIV). And the Lord says: “Are they not gathered up with me and sealed in my treasuries?” (Deut. XXXII).

Let us not suppose that crimes once committed and impressed by a deep wound into the inmost parts of the soul can be forgiven so easily. Much weeping is necessary, many sighs, and many acts of bodily contrition, to heal those very pains of the heart. The whole person must devote himself to spiritual remorse [Note: “Much weeping is necessary, many sighs, and much contrition for healing the pains of that very heart; the whole person must devote himself to spiritual remorse”], so that ancient evils may be torn from the innermost parts of the conscience like arrows.

It is not enough to say with merely the lips: “I have sinned; spare me and forgive me.” Saul also said, “I have sinned,” but he did not obtain the forgiveness that David earned by a single word of repentance (1 Sam. XV). And why? Because that bare confession expressed lamentation more in appearance than in truth; because the slight humility [perhaps: “the mild insolence”] of the suppliant was not proportionate to the magnitude of the crime.

One must not act with slight contrition when those debts are to be redeemed for which eternal death is owed; nor is passing satisfaction sufficient for those evils on account of which eternal fire has been prepared. If we wish to understand how gravely our Judge regards human sins, let us look to the punishments. For as patient as our God now is in bearing our offenses, so severe will he be in examining our deeds; and just as he has prepared immeasurable punishment for the wicked, so he will bestow unspeakable glory upon the just.

Let us therefore infer the severity of punishments, by contrast, from the greatness of rewards. For he who knows how to reward merits knows how to punish offenses.

The remembrance of future judgment and the recollection—or lamentation—of past sins are therefore most salutary and greatly necessary. But if there is anyone who flatters himself with the merits of an unblemished life in the past, and still thinks that he entered the Lord’s service innocent, and therefore believes himself secure, let such a person consider how uncertain and slippery are the ends of life. Concerning this it is said: “Do not praise anyone during his life” [Col. 1063D]; and when he has perceived that he has nothing from the past left to mourn, he still has something in the future to fear.

Let no one therefore be secure about the past. So many snares have been set before the feet of our soul; so countless are the enemies who watch and guard our path; so many sheer pits [variant: “and so many precipices”] lie between us and our end. The way itself, narrow and difficult by nature, is besieged by so many ambushes of spiritual robbers; we must cross so many reefs and so many waves that we do not know what may happen before we cast our anchor upon the desired shore.

And yet we think that we ought to be secure about the past and pass our day without daily care, without daily fear and trembling! Who, crossing the depth of some river over the narrow span of a very narrow bridge, even if he has traversed most of it with an uninjured foot, would think that he had escaped danger, when, in the final stretch of the bridge, if he stumbles even slightly, he may suffer the fall that he avoided in the middle of the crossing?

So also, even if a large part of this life seems to have been passed, let us not on that account presume confidence, since danger still threatens in its final part. Who, stationed in battle, lays down his arms before the end of the struggle or before victory is secure? Let no one therefore judge himself secure before he has reached the end by a blessed completion.

Nor should we think that this is sufficient for our complete salvation: that we are reckoned among God’s servants by our dwelling place or counted among them by name; that we are commanded to live in salvation and to sing psalms among the monks. For our Lord cries out to us: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII). And why is this? Because “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. II).

Therefore, even if we have lived well, we must commend our course by steadfastness and perseverance, remaining and bringing it to completion [perhaps: “making progress”] in the place of our calling. Truly I say: even if we had devoted twenty or thirty years here to the Lord—to whom, certainly, we know that we owe everything by which we live—and then lived merely one year in the world, immeasurable would be the extent to which we had defrauded ourselves of the joys of eternal life, because all our hope rests upon completion and the end.

What does it profit me if my green sown fields display the hope of a harvest, yet at the very time of the sickle a sudden change of weather or a flood of rains deceives me? What will it profit me if the vineyard promises every hope in its blossom, yet the invasion of wild beasts or the devastation of hail takes away every hope at the time of completion [variant: “in the completion”]? Therefore every prosperity and every success of one’s labors rests upon the end.

But if those who, after many rewards for their labors and after some progress through the years, are drawn away by certain desires must also grieve, what will become of those who think four or five years here a very long time and spend the entire remainder of their lives in the vanity of the world? Even one year in the world can consume the labors we acquired in the desert as a great sea might receive and swallow a tiny stream within itself, leaving it not even a name.

I do not know what gains we wish to pursue by living in the world. For while here it is considered a great loss not to acquire something every day, there the great profit must be considered not to lose what has been acquired. Here, I say, it is thought a serious disadvantage not to make daily progress; there, the highest virtue is not to perish.

Therefore, if we are still weak and poor, let us labor here to obtain something. But if we have obtained something, let us take care here to preserve it. This alone will be our expense [variant: “gain”] and joy: that you have lived for the Lord here. For as long as we remain here, it is within our power to turn toward the world whenever we wish. But once you have turned away, it will be difficult, almost impossible, to look back in thought toward this place.

If someone therefore thinks himself secure because he will one day be able to leave this place—because he has run well here and labored much here—such a person acts as though someone were to release a ship laden with merchandise from the harbor, hand it over to storms, and drive it toward reefs and rocks.

The more we labor, therefore, the more cautious we ought to be. For the enemy lies in wait for those who are making progress; and wherever he sees some hope or grace, there, like a roaring lion prowling about to attack its prey, he throws himself entirely upon it.

And because he cannot prevail against those who are stationed here, he wishes to lead some less cautious people away from this place through thoughts and various temptations, as though outside the camp, and to bring them down from a most lofty [variant: “an unconquerable”] fortress. Once he has brought them down, he fights them as if from a higher position, so that, even if he cannot sink the ship, he may at least carry off a most delightful prey from the losses and damages that abound in the world.

First he sends various impulses, indignations, and resentments, so that while a person strives to fulfill what he has once resolved and determined in anger, he does not consider his own loss or look toward his ruin. And once he has brought him down, remorse follows—though by then it will have accomplished nothing.

Here we are, and we are not safe. Either we are driven by various evil and dishonorable thoughts of the heart, or we are wounded by the poisoned swords of the tongue, scandalizing others over the smallest and most perverse matters [variant: “and being scandalized over trivial matters”].

Sometimes also, in a way unbecoming to a monk, we break out into quarrels and disputes and violate our profession by transgressing the rule. We dare to commit theft against our superiors—or rather against our own souls—under the eyes of God, not fearing that what we are ashamed to do in the presence of our superiors we ought not to commit under the eyes of God.

We are not content with what is necessary; instead, through the lukewarmness of our hearts, we again desire the abundance that we left behind in the world. Hence it is not enough that we have shaken off whatever possessions we had, when the desires themselves remain within us.

This is why we are sometimes stirred up over the most perverse [variant: “smallest”] matters and provoke the gravest contentions for the sake of desiring worthless things. Why is this? Because although we have left external goods behind, we still retain internal evils in our hearts.

And amid all this, how our adversary exults when he sees that we have despised great things for the purpose of being defeated more shamefully in the smallest! Therefore let us tear out by the roots those things which, though placed outside, have clung inwardly to the inmost parts of the soul.

Thus the Apostle did not say, “Gold or silver is the root of all evils,” but rather, “the desire for riches” (1 Tim. VI). And not only the rich, but also “those who desire to become rich fall into a snare and temptation.” The Apostle addresses not only those who possess, but also those who pursue [variant: “retain within themselves”] the very will to possess.

Therefore a person gains nothing by abandoning what he has outside himself if he retains vices within himself. Thus, as I said, brothers, we are here, and we are not safe. And if, placed within the walls, we scarcely resist, what will we do when exposed in the world? How will one who is in such grave peril in the harbor be able to stand amid the waves and the very violence of battling storms?

Therefore, insofar as we can, let us remain steadfast in this most tranquil haven [variant: “harbor”]. For however lukewarm someone may be, he does not run in vain if he reaches the palm of completion by persevering.

With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY IX

Dearest brothers, we have gathered in this place so that we may be free for our Lord, not for those things in which our enemy delights. For it is certain that whenever we speak of matters belonging to the world, or bite one another with wicked murmurings, he rejoices that our hours [variant: “our prayers”] are taken from God and acquired for himself.

What does it profit us to exhaust ourselves through precious vigils and labors while we do not possess those things that our God desires most in us? That is, a clean heart, free from these minor negligences—things which, when a person does not watch over them, cause him gradually to slip away and fall into greater ones (Eccli. XIX).

Let us therefore strive above all to possess what our God expects in us: namely, gentle and kind speech; a mind free from every curse and every malice; and, while avoiding those things by which the Holy Spirit is offended, a mind devoted to humility and quietness. These are the principal sacrifices; these are the rich burnt offerings that rise before the Lord as a pleasing fragrance.

Let us also strive especially to perform those things that we do in honor of our God with a cheerful spirit, with the joy of faith, and with the affection of a good and devoted will. Whatever we do unwillingly and under compulsion, let us understand that from it we gain not only no progress but the greatest loss.

Suppose that we were performing a service for some powerful man, such as persons of higher rank are accustomed to expect from their clients. If that man saw us rendering the service owed to him with an unwilling and forced spirit, and even with a certain disdain, would he not judge that an injury had been done to him, and declare that he had been dishonored rather than honored? Would he not think that such negligent and undevoted service deserved offense rather than gratitude?

If, then, the worship of a human name requires devotion, faith, and cheerfulness—indeed, sometimes the worshiper is better than the one worshiped, and the service itself achieves no fruit, and its only gain is to deserve to be called accepted—how much more ought we to be attentive in honoring our God, lest we be found undevoted, compelled, sad, ungrateful, unwilling, and unregarded in his service?

But God does not regard gifts brought with a negligent and contemptible spirit. Our faith ought to show—or to appear [variant: “ought to be seen”]—that it serves not a human being but him, and that it has devoted even its own soul to his service. It ought not to seem a small matter that even the angels in paradise acknowledge his service and benefits; to whom, finally, everything is owed, though nothing is ever paid to him as a gift.

For this miserable life, full of labors and sorrows, whose use is brief and whose very brevity is always uncertain, we strive to please human beings through our service. But for that life in which we will no longer labor, we do not strive now to offer devoted service to God. Even if devotion of will hesitates to offer that life to its author, the law of death will immediately exact it from us; and what is not given by vow is paid as a debt.

For this life, then, he will give that life which cannot be seen by the eyes or reached [variant: “grasped”] even by the silent thought of the mind; a life which is easier to attain than to describe; whose course will have no end, whose use will have no weariness, whose refreshment will require no food, whose assistance will have no failure, whose rest will have no night, whose leisure will have no old age [Note: “without the assistance of food, rest without night’s leisure, age without old age”]; an unfailing brightness beneath the face of God; an ever-new delight amid ancient and perpetual joys; and a happiness without any danger of losing it.

Let us therefore leave behind the sweetness of this life and, by thinking daily even now about the future ages [variant: “that future age”], strive to taste it in advance while still in this body. Let us drive the bitterness of worldly desires from our senses and draw into our hearts a certain sweet flavor of that blessedness. Having shaken off all sluggishness and all laziness, whose mother is unbelief, let us serve our Lord and God with that cheerfulness, that alacrity, and that joy with which we shall come, invited by joy, to his gifts.

May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this; he lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever [Note: “With his help may we come to his gifts; Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the eternal Father and the Spirit, throughout all ages of ages”]. Amen.

## HOMILY X

“Consider your calling,” dearest brothers. To come to the desert is indeed the highest perfection; but not to live perfectly in the desert is the highest condemnation. What does it profit if quietness is maintained in one’s dwelling while unrest dwells in the heart? If there is silence in the habitation, but tumult and the struggle of passions among its inhabitants? If outwardly our life is serene, but inwardly it is stormy?

We are accustomed to reckon our years and the stretches of time in which we now live. Whoever you are, do not let the number of days that you have spent here, having bodily left the world, deceive you. Count yourself to have lived only that day on which you denied your own wills, that day which you spent without any transgression of the rule.

Count yourself to have lived only that day on which you denied your own wills, resisted your desires, and passed without any transgression of the rule. Count yourself to have lived only that day which malice, envy, and pride did not stain; which the guilt of lying and perjury did not besprinkle.

Count yourself to have lived only that day which possessed the light of purity and holy meditation, which a dark way of life did not change into night. Add, I say, that day to your life, for its gain comes to your soul.

We are also accustomed to flatter ourselves about the constancy of our bodily vigils, though after the vigils—and perhaps because of the vigils themselves—we go out into slander, excessive talk, and murmurings. For the person who withdraws from the choir of those singing psalms to shameful feasts and secret drinking—not through a blameworthy transgression but through an abominable pursuit of advantage—would be doing something much less serious if, with sobriety [variant: “drunkenness”] prevailing, he were asleep.

And the person who, while fasting, carries a heavy and burdened breast enclosed in the constraint of anger or indignation—because he abstains from wine, while the poison of bitter discord is stirred up in his senses by an even more bitter intoxication—such a person, I say, afflicts himself through an outward and salutary moderation in drink, while his inward parts belch forth the deadly poison of hatred. Does he not understand that the prophetic words are directed against him, and that he is already condemned in the present life: “This is not the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord” (Isa. LVIII)?

Or consider this saying: “For their wine is from the vine of Sodom, and their vines are from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness in them” (Deut. XXXII).

Sometimes, when the devil perceives that a soul is empty of faith and stripped of the fear of God, he so intoxicates the mind with various passions that, when we curse, become angry, or slander—when we do such things—we think that we are harming others, not ourselves.

But it is not so. The evil of each vice returns upon its own author, as the divine word says: “My son, if you are wicked, you alone will bear your evils.” The foul-mouthed person stains his own tongue; the slanderer ulcerates his own heart; the angry person blinds the light of his own mind; the envious person corrupts his own soul like a moth.

And just as vipers are born from ulcerated parents—just as, I say, viperous offspring are said to be born by bursting through the entrails of their mother [variant: “mothers”]—so human hearts are first torn apart by the passions that they have conceived. Those very inward parts, from which the serpent-like generation of vices is brought forth, are themselves first violated by the monstrous fecundity of their offspring.

Of such a birth the divine word says: “Behold, he conceived injustice, was pregnant with sorrow, and gave birth to iniquity. His sorrow will return upon his head, and his iniquity will descend upon his crown” (Ps. VII).

Having said these things in advance out of the fervent charity that we bear toward you—a charity that had long been tortured with grief over the negligence of some—and having thereby relieved something of the heat within our breast, we command, admonish, and even beseech you on your own behalf—if you are not disdainful of hearing the affection of one who commands—that henceforth you correct your conduct and amend your negligences, lest we later come to you not with the rod of tongue and speech but with those lashes that hardened hearts demand.

Labor, dearest brothers, so that henceforth you may compete among yourselves in a praiseworthy contest and finally in a better rivalry. Let each of you strive to be more ready in God’s work, more frequent in prayer, more attentive in reading, purer in chastity, more sparing in sobriety, more lavish in the abundance of tears, more honorable in body, more sincere in heart, gentler in anger, more measured in meekness, rarer in laughter, more fervent in remorse, more firmly grounded in seriousness, and more joyful in charity.

Therefore let us discipline ourselves and daily examine our conduct with ourselves. Let each soul address itself in the secrecy of its heart and say:

“Let me see whether I have passed this day without sin, without envy, without slander and murmuring. Let me see whether today I have done anything that pertains to my own progress or to the edification of others.

“I think that today I foolishly destroyed that person; today I was disobedient to my elder; I lied; I committed perjury; I was overcome by anger or gluttony. Today I laughed more than I should have; I indulged more than I should have in food and drink, in leisure and sleep. I read less and prayed less than I ought. Who will return to me this day, which I lost in empty tales?”

And so, brothers, let us feel remorse for all our negligences in our chambers—that is, in our hearts. If you act in this way, we shall rejoice in your progress, while you will rejoice in the salvation you have gained. You will subject us to yourselves for the acquisition of your salvation [the Latin is uncertain].

But may the piety of the one who is powerful teach you to profit so greatly from our speech that you, in turn, may help us by your merits, and be for us both an ornament in the present world and a defense in the future.

With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XI

The fact that, at the supplication—and, in a certain sense, at the loving command—of your holy father [variant: “our holy father”] I offer your fraternity whatever sort of sermon this may be, I do not do out of any presumption but out of true and undivided charity.

And although, by God’s favor, you are so perfect that you scarcely need our admonition, nevertheless, under the command of charity, which does not know how to fear, we presume, with true humility and perfect charity, to suggest and admonish you concerning even those things that we know you fulfill exceedingly well—though not without embarrassment.

We know ourselves to be unfit disciples, yet we seem to rouse masters to holy work. Though we are lukewarm, we are compelled to admonish the fervent. Though we are sinners, we rebuke the just. Though we are ignorant, we instruct the learned. Though we are exhausted by the excessive waves of this world’s sea, we speak words of preaching to those who have already reached the harbor safely.

Nevertheless, brothers, ships that have overcome and conquered the waves of the sea often struggle even in the safest harbor and, unless there is great caution, are almost submerged. Therefore, with the greatest humility and profound reverence, we admonish you: since Christ has freed you from all capital crimes as from dangerous waves, now that you are established in the harbor of peaceful blessedness, hasten continually, with Christ’s help and with all vigilance, to drain away the small negligences and minor sins that flow into the soul as drops run through the tiniest cracks of a ship and collect in its interior [variant: “in its bilge”].

For just as a ship, after escaping the waves of the sea, is filled and sunk by the smallest drops if it is not prepared [variant: “its bilge is not pumped out”] in the harbor, so also a monk, after conquering and overcoming the storms of the world and the crimes of this world as dangerous waves, when he has come to the harbor of the monastery, incurs the danger of shipwreck in that very harbor if he neglects to pump out the creeping-in [variant: “sudden”], small, and daily sins from the bilge of his soul.

But someone may say: “How can a soul have its bilge pumped?” Certainly, by praying, fasting, keeping vigil, and showing true charity, true humility, and true obedience.

Attend, brothers, I beg you, to how a ship is pumped with a bucket: so the soul is freed from all evils by the Lord’s Prayer, if it says—and says truthfully: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI).

For whoever mercifully forgives all who sin against him will retain no trace of any sin, nor [variant: “in his own soul”] any stain. Attend, brothers; carefully consider what I have said: whoever forgives the person who sins against him. For he did not say that you must forgive someone who has sinned against the Lord [variant: “against God”], but that you must grant forgiveness to the one who has sinned against you.

What is worse, when someone sins against us, we sometimes grant forgiveness late or with difficulty. When someone sins against the Lord [variant: “against God”], we forgive quickly. But if we wish to act justly, we ought not to forgive entirely the person who has sinned against the Lord without the strictest discipline, lest, when forgiveness is granted to him through indiscriminate mercy, an example of destruction be offered to others.

Let each person therefore show himself merciful in matters concerning himself. For the Lord said: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive your sins” (Matt. VII and XVIII).

But when someone presumes to commit a sin against the Lord [variant: “against God”], he ought to undergo monastic discipline. This must be done with a good and pious intention, so that through spiritual correction he may be reformed in this world and not perish in the future. For every sin that is not corrected in this world will be punished in the age to come.

Thus Scripture speaks of a son or a servant: “You will strike him with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from hell” (Prov. XXIII).

Therefore, as I suggested above, let us beware not only of capital crimes but also daily reject perverse negligences as the poisons of the devil.

There are some who, after professing religion, because they seem to have gone out from the world, become relaxed through excessive security. In them is fulfilled that saying of the Lord: “Would that you were hot or cold! But now, because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III).

What does he mean by saying, “Would that you were hot or cold”? He means: “It would have been better for you either to have remained cold in the world or to be fervent in the monastery.” But now, because you have withdrawn from the world and yet, through negligence, have not wished to embrace spiritual fervor, having become lukewarm, you are vomited from the Lord’s mouth and will scarcely be received again.

Therefore, dearest brothers, with God’s help attend carefully to the sentence of divine Scripture, which says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV).

For just as we ought to rejoice over the person who, coming to the monastery, wishes to show himself meek and humble through gentleness, obedience, and patience, so, conversely, we ought to mourn over the person who appears to have left the world only in body, while in heart he is recognized either to have remained faithlessly in the world or unhappily to have returned to it; who offers pride instead of humility, anger instead of patience, contempt instead of obedience; who pours out the poison of malice instead of the medicine of charity.

To such people applies that true and greatly fearsome judgment of blessed Peter: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. II). And again: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud.”

But we must not despair even of such people, brothers, because God is powerful through your prayers to kindle the spark of remorse and consume every pleasure of the world like thorns and thistles of wickedness with a healing fire—the very fire of which the Lord said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII).

Pray, therefore, dearest brothers, not only that God may deign to grant us perseverance in ourselves, but also that he may command those who are negligent to be lifted from the pit and rescued from the snares.

For if, through your prayers and your charitable counsel, those who are lukewarm and negligent are corrected, the Lord will deign to repay you with a double reward: both for your own salvation and for their correction.

Neither should those who are good exalt themselves as though because of their own merits, nor should those who are negligent despair of God’s mercy. Let the former guard God’s gifts with humility, and let the latter hasten with great remorse to the remedies of repentance and correction. For if the good person begins to grow proud, he is quickly humbled; and if the proud person humbles himself, he is lifted up through God’s mercy.

Only let him not permit himself to be pressed any longer by the devil’s harshest yoke, nor, by excessive and dangerous dissimulation, remain longer hardened in sins. Let him flee to repentance so quickly that no trace of sin may remain in him.

A poultice or dressing is best applied to wounds while they are still hot, because if the intention of rising again is swift toward the heavenly physician, no trace of the fall can remain. Under the hand of the omnipotent physician, the disease quickly disappears and the sick person is speedily healed.

Again and again I ask and admonish you, brothers, to strive continually to show obedience, humility, and charity not only to your elders and equals but also to your juniors. For whatever good a servant of God may strive to possess, he will lose everything miserably if humility and charity are not found in him.

Do not murmur, because it is written (1 Cor. X) that those who murmured perished by serpents. Do not slander your brothers, because it is written: “The one who slanders his brother will be rooted out” (Prov. XIII). Do not harbor anger in your heart, because it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God.” Do not hate one another, because of what is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III [the supplied reference reads “Luke I”]).

But there is no need for us to teach your holy charity at greater length through words, since we know—and rejoice—that you fulfill it in deeds for the glory of Christ.

We ask only this especially: that the one who has deigned to place you in a place of quiet and tranquility, for our sake—whom the storms and countless waves of this world afflict—you may supplicate the Lord more abundantly, so that, if glory is not granted to us because we do not deserve it, at least, through your prayers, forgiveness of sins may be granted to us.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XII
If you attend carefully, dearly beloved brothers, or venerable sons, you clearly recognize that no human being lives for himself alone, and no one dies for himself alone. The Apostle Paul also confirms this in similar words, saying: “For no one lives for himself, and no one dies for himself.” Every person, therefore, however great an example of holy conduct he may have provided, will arrive at eternal rewards with as many others and on behalf of as many others. Conversely, whoever has displayed an example of evil life and corrupt conduct, and has provoked as many as possible to wicked deeds by his evil behavior, will endure everlasting punishments with as many others and on behalf of as many others.

Let us therefore not only refrain from providing others an example of evil living, but also continually urge them toward humility, charity, and obedience by holy and salutary admonition. Let us not be among those who, when any brothers or sisters are angry or raging, habitually provide fuel for pride through evil counsel, saying that they ought not to humble themselves and abase themselves for so long. Let us not be such people who, through their bitterest tongues, not only refuse to heal the wounded but even strive to wound those who are healthy; who, by murmuring, slander, disobedience, or anger, are accustomed not to serve Christ but to serve as soldiers of the devil.

For the crafty and cruel enemy, the devil, by the cunning of his ancient skill and his manifold ingenuity, compels the souls whom he has once made idle, lukewarm, or negligent through his most wicked persuasion to serve him also in the overthrow of others. Of such souls it is written: “Would that you were hot or cold; but because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III). The devil blinds such souls, prepared for disobedience or pride, to every light of truth and charity; and, like a most powerful hunter or a most cunning bird-catcher, he makes and prepares them as decoys for himself to capture, if possible, even holy souls.

Bird-catchers customarily do this: they first blind the pigeons they have caught and make them deaf, so that when the other pigeons gather around them, they may be caught in the nets that have been prepared. In the same way the ancient enemy habitually acts through lukewarm clerics, negligent monks, and sluggish virgins: when he has closed in them the eyes of patience, extinguished the fire of compunction and the flame of true charity, and persuaded them to glory in the mere habit of religion, as I have already said, he presents and prepares them as decoys, as an example for the destruction of others, so that when simple and less watchful people imitate them, they may be caught in various snares and nets.

Such people will have to render an account on the day of judgment not only for themselves but also for those whom, through the example of their evil conduct, they have recalled from the good of humility and obedience. For the ancient enemy, who has always been accustomed to envy the good, first persuades the servants or handmaids of God whom he has recognized as lukewarm and negligent to occupy themselves with idle stories, to provoke others to stubbornness by murmuring or slandering, and to become extremely slow in attending the reading. Once he has introduced into their hearts, as it were, a callus and, so to speak, a dross of lukewarmness, he prepares them for every evil deed and unhappily compels them to serve every vice and negligence, according to what the Truth said:

“Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin. And by whatever anyone is overcome, by that he is made a slave” (John V).

For just as holy and spiritual souls, kindled by the fervor of charity, are moved by the Holy Spirit and continually prepared for every good work, according to what the Apostle says: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. VIII), so, conversely, the negligent and lukewarm are possessed by that contrary spirit of which it is written:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through arid places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then, returning, it finds its house empty and swept clean, and it brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and the final condition of that person is worse than the first” (Luke XI).

Clerics, monks, virgins, the proud, the disobedient, and the lukewarm undoubtedly suffer these things. When, at the beginning of their religious life, they have abandoned worldly living and fled with fervent intention to the service of holy discipline, by the grace of God they are emptied of all evils. But afterward, through negligence and sloth, they fail to apply themselves so that, with God’s help, they may be filled with spiritual goods. Then the vices that had departed find them empty and return with a numerous [Perhaps “retinue” should be added], compelling them to return to their vomit. Just as a dog becomes disgusting when it returns to its vomit, so a sinner becomes disgusting when he returns to his sin.

The Apostle Peter cries out terrifyingly concerning such people:

“For if, after escaping the defilements of the world, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter condition has become worse than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them accords with the truth of the proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its vomit,’ and ‘the washed sow to wallowing in the mire’” (2 Pet. II).

This happens to those who, after abstinence, return to gluttony; after vigils, to sleepiness; after humility, to pride; after obedience, to stubbornness; and after patience, to anger—like a dog returning to its vomit and like swine returning to the wallowing-place of lust.

Therefore, whoever recognizes that he is such a person, while there is still time for correction, should strive to apply the medicine of humility to the wound of pride with groaning and lamentation, and should hasten to receive the remedy of obedience against the poison of murmuring or anger. Before his soul, burdened with many sins, departs from this light, let him acquire a remedy for himself on the day of necessity. Let him strive, while there is still time to gather and purchase it, to prepare for his lamp, extinguished by pride, the oil of humility and charity, so that among the holy virgins, with the lamp of virginity burning, the oil of charity may overflow in the vessel of his soul. For bodily virginity will be entirely useless if charity or humility has departed from the heart.

Holy souls observe these things, and those who wish to be like them do not cease to practice them. Others, however, who live not spiritually but carnally, submit their unhappy necks not to humility but to pride. They do not gather spiritual honey like bees; rather, like wasps, they spread cruel poisons. When they are disobedient to their elders, when they are set ablaze by the flames of anger, when they store hatred in their hearts, and when, through their murmurings, they cause both themselves and others—shaken by the wind of pride from the harbor of obedience and disturbed from the calm of patience—to suffer shipwreck.

Those who, at the beginning of their religious life, abandoned the storms of the world and fled to the quiet of the monastery are now shown to suffer shipwreck, through the excessive fury of pride, in the very harbor amid the storms of anger. Those who appear to serve the world are better than such people, because humble married life is far better than proud virginity. And more worthy of praise are those who, with God’s help, preserve themselves in the midst of the open sea than those who, through excessive negligence or security, are drowned in the harbor.

Happy, therefore, are those souls who strive, with Christ granting it, to fill their hearts with the various spices of the virtues, so that nothing but charity and humility, nothing but chastity, gentleness, and obedience, may ever proceed from their mouths; thus they provide both eternal rewards for themselves and examples of holy conduct for others.

Conversely, unhappy and wretched are those who deserve to be mourned with every fountain of tears, because they are so corrupted by evil conduct that from their mouths or thoughts proceed not Christ’s medicines but the devil’s poisons. Although outwardly they are covered with religious dress, as though with sheep’s skins, inwardly they are known to be ravenous wolves. Like serpents or vipers, they seem to display a feigned humility in their bodily appearance for as long as they are corrected by no rebuke. But when even a slight admonition appears, then, once their false humility has been removed, their concealed pride will become evident. Then it is truly recognized that one thing was uttered by the mouth and another hidden in the heart: false humility was feigned in the body, while the poison of pride was concealed in the mind.

Fearing all these things rather than suspecting anything unfavorable about you, we have offered them to your charity with complete humility and paternal concern. For this reason we wished to place before your eyes the negligences of the lukewarm, so that, spiritually rejoicing in the good things bestowed upon you by divine gift, you may give thanks to God; and so that you may continually implore God’s mercy for me and those like me, who are still weighed down by many negligences. Thus, when a crown is granted to you before the tribunal of Christ for perseverance in good works, forgiveness of sins may also be granted to us through your intercession, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XIII. On the Twelve Remissions of Sins

The first remission is the remission of sins by which we are baptized in water, according to what is written: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III).

The second remission is the affection of charity, as in the saying: “Her many sins are forgiven because she loved much” (Luke VII).

The third remission is the fruit of almsgiving, according to this saying: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sir. III).

The fourth remission is the outpouring of tears, with the Lord saying: “Because he wept in my sight and walked before me in sorrow, I will not bring evil in his days” (3 Kings).

The fifth remission is the confession of crimes, as the Psalmist bears witness: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. XXXI).

The sixth remission is affliction of heart and body, as the Apostle consoles us: “I handed such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. V).

The seventh remission is amendment of conduct, that is, renunciation of vices, as the Evangelist bears witness: “You have become well; do not sin any longer, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

The eighth remission is the intercession of the saints, as in the saying: “If anyone is sick, let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him. And the constant prayer of a righteous person is very powerful before the Lord” (James V).

The ninth remission is mercy, the merit of faith, according to this saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V).

The tenth remission is the salvation of others, as the Apostle James affirms: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James V).

The eleventh remission is forgiveness and our own remission, as the Truth permits [perhaps “promises”]: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI).

The twelfth remission is the suffering of martyrdom, with the hope of salvation and forgiveness alone, as the Lord replied to the bloodstained thief: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

## HOMILY XIV. On the Day of Judgment

*(Admonition 19 of Felicitarius [Note: [Col. 1075D] Here, through the error of scribes, the name Felicitarius has been inserted. The same should be understood concerning the name Augustine [Col. 1076D], which will be prefixed to the next three homilies. EDITOR], Bishop of Arles, in the Quintilianus manuscript.)*

We heard, when the Gospel was read, a terrifying and equally dreadful and desirable sentence of our Lord. It is terrifying because he says: “Depart from me, accursed ones”; desirable because he says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV). For who, having heard this voice, would not tremble and rejoice at the same time? Christ promises a kingdom to his servants and threatens sinners with eternal fire.

I ask you, dearest brothers, to hear this reading with attentive hearts and retain it in your memory. Whoever attends to this reading with a diligent mind, even if he scarcely understands the other Scriptures, can find this one reading sufficient for doing every good work and avoiding every evil work.

Pay attention, brothers, to what the Lord promised to say to those who will be on his right: “Come, blessed, because I was hungry and you gave me food.” But to those who will be on his left he will say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, because I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and so forth. He did not say: “Depart from me because you committed theft or murder” and other evils; rather, he said it because you did not give to the poor from your possessions.

Just as mercy alone will deliver those who will be on the right, so avarice alone will condemn those who are on the left. They will not hear “Come, blessed” because they did not sin, nor will he say to the others, “Depart from me, accursed ones,” because they sinned, but because they were unwilling to redeem their sins by almsgiving.

No one can be without sin, but every person, with God’s help, can redeem his sins by almsgiving. For the Lord says: “Whoever does not feed the hungry and clothe the naked will be sent into eternal fire.” And if the one who does not give to the poor is condemned with the devil, where will the one who takes what belongs to another be condemned? If the one who does not receive a stranger into his house is condemned in hell, where will the one who drives him out be condemned? If the one who does not clothe the naked is sent into the fire, where will the one who strips the clothed be condemned?

Hold fast, brothers, to almsgiving and mercy, because almsgiving does not allow its practitioner to go into darkness. As the prophet Daniel says: “My counsel, O king, is that you redeem your sins by almsgiving; and if you neglect this, you will knock at heaven without cause” (Dan. IV).

O soul, dwelling within walls of flesh and frailty, watch, pray, knock, and seek (Matt. XXIV). Watch by asking, pray by seeking, knock by giving. To you who watch and ask, the Lord says: “Behold, I am here”; and “If you pass through fire, I am with you, and the flame will not burn you.” If you seek him by praying, you will find him. When you knock by giving, Christ opens his doors to you, so that you may enter as the possessor of paradise.

And if you still think that the end of the world remains far off, consider your own end. Little by little, all the good things that existed are being taken away, and evils that did not exist are approaching. For it is written: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall go beneath the earth” (Job II).

Therefore, give alms while you have the price in your hands. Give yourself something from what is yours, because what you hold is fleeting and always belongs to someone else (ibid.). Consider your price; look upon your Lord. Consider what price he paid for you: he poured out his blood for you. He held you dear, since he redeemed you so dearly.

Flee the example of the rich man, whose dogs Lazarus fed with his wounds, and the rich man does not live. Though alike in the nature of the flesh, riches made them unlike; nevertheless, they died as equals, and their conditions were reversed in the underworld. Then the rich man said: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me.” Abraham said: “Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented” (Luke XVI).

O man, you hear the just comparison of the sentence: the one who did not give to the poor has no refreshment. My brothers, formed by the hand of God, hear the voice of the Lord and fulfill his desire, so that you may receive the inheritance in the kingdom of your Father.

You have been made a friend from a servant. Despise the fact that you were condemned; look upon the fact that you were reborn. In exchange for an earthly inheritance, make God your craftsman: God offers heaven. Then the Father, Lord, and friend will say to you, when you have made a heavenly exchange: “Amen, I say to you, what you did for one of these least ones, you did for me” (Matt. XXV).

“What I receive, I now return a hundredfold, indeed a thousandfold, and in the future eternal life,” as I promised through John; “a banquet of a thousand years,” and the kingdom at the Father’s right hand.

Therefore, I ask you, brothers, let each person, according to his means, extend something to a stranger with a good disposition. Hear the Lord saying in the Gospel (Luke XXI) concerning the widow who offered two coins: she put in more than all the others, because the rich had contributed from what they had in abundance, whereas she offered everything she possessed. Therefore she deserved that the Lord should praise her with his own mouth.

Let each person, therefore, do what he can. Except for reasonable food and clothing, let whatever remains be given joyfully and cheerfully to the poor. Why joyfully? Because he gives little and receives much. He extends a coin and purchases a kingdom. He gives a small sum of money and will receive eternal life. He gives temporal things so that he may merit eternal ones. He extends what is perishable and receives what will remain without end.

And if a faithful person were to say to you: “Give me one bronze coin, and I will return a hundred gold solidi to you,” would you not gladly give one in order to receive a hundred? How much more so because the Lord says to you: “Whoever gives to the poor lends to God” (Prov. XIX)!

Give to God on earth, therefore, so that you may receive in eternal life; so that, when you come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge in the presence of the angels, you may be able to say with a secure and free conscience: “Give, Lord, because I gave; show mercy, because I showed mercy. I fulfilled what you commanded; repay what you promised.”

And there may you deserve to hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XV. On Almsgiving

*(Admonition 20 of Felicitarius, Bishop of Arles, in the Quintilianus manuscript.)*

Tobias says: “Keep the Lord in mind throughout all the days of your life, and do not walk in the way of iniquity. From your substance give alms, and do not turn your face away from any poor person, lest God’s face be turned away from you. As you have means, so act. Even if it is little, share from that very little, and do not be afraid. When you give alms, you store up a good reward for yourself on the day of necessity, because almsgiving delivers from death and does not allow its practitioner to go into darkness. It is a good gift for everyone, for they offer it before the Most High God” (Tob. IV).

Solomon says: “Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God and will never be in want; but whoever turns his eye away from the poor will live in poverty” (Prov. XIX).

By almsgiving and faith sins are cleansed. For just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Prov. XV, XXVIII).

Tobias likewise says: “Son, when you have means, do good to yourself and offer offerings worthy of God; remember that death does not delay; enclose almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will free you from every evil” [Note: These are Ecclesiasticus XIV, 11–12, not from Tobit.].

The Psalm likewise says: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor.”

Again: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (Ps. XL).

The Lord says through the prophet: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. VI).

Likewise in the Gospel: “Store up for yourselves treasure in heaven. Where your treasure is, there also will your heart be.”

Again: “Whoever gives a cup of cold water in my name, his reward will not perish.”

Again: “He who made what is within also made what is without. Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Matt. IX).

The Apostle Paul says: “Let your abundance supply their need. Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. Whoever sows in blessing will reap from blessing.”

The Evangelist John says: “Whoever possesses the substance of the world and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John VII).

Again: “When you make a lunch or dinner, do not invite your friends or the rich, lest they perhaps invite you and repayment be made to you; but invite the beggars, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. It will be repaid to you in the resurrection of the righteous.”

The Apostle Paul says: “Even if almsgiving is small, the willing intention itself is sufficient if it is ready; according to what one has, it will be acceptable to the Lord” (2 Cor. VIII).

## HOMILY XVI. On Tithes

*(Admonition 21 of Felicitarius, Bishop of Arles, in the Quintilianus manuscript.)*

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Distribute all your tithes.”

He speaks through the prophet: “Bring every tithe into my storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me in this, says the Lord.”

The Apostle Paul said concerning the sons of Levi: “Those who receive the priesthood have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, from their brothers”; for “God loves a cheerful giver.”

Solomon said: “Some distribute their own possessions and become richer; others seize what is not theirs and are always in poverty” (Prov. XV).

Jesus son of Sirach said: “In every gift make your face cheerful, and sanctify your tithes with rejoicing. Give to the Most High according to what has been given, and make the work of your hands an offering with a good eye, for the Lord is one who repays, and he will return to you sevenfold.”

Augustine said: “Tithes are the taxes of needy souls” [Note: They are taxes for the redemption of souls.] [Col. 1079A]

If you give a tithe, you will receive not only an abundance of crops but also the health of your bodies. The Lord God is not in need, nor does he seek a reward, but honor. Our God, who has deigned to give everything, deigns to ask a tenth from us—not for himself, but for us, and undoubtedly for our benefit.

Therefore, through the prophet he said: “You shall not delay offering me the firstfruits of your threshing-floor and winepress. If you give late, it is sin; how much more is it not to have given at all?” (Exod. XXII).

Whether you live from business, craftsmanship, or any kind of work, return tithes. Since, by giving tithes, you can merit both earthly and heavenly gifts, why do you defraud yourself of a double blessing through avarice?

For this is the Lord’s most just custom: if you do not give him a tenth, you will be reduced to a tenth yourself. You will give to an impious soldier what you are unwilling to give to a priest.

God is always prepared to do good, but human wickedness prevents it. Tithes are demanded as a debt, and whoever is unwilling to give them has invaded another’s property. And for however many poor people in the places where he lives have died of hunger because he did not give tithes, he will appear guilty of that many murders before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, because he reserved for his own uses what had been entrusted by the Lord to the poor.

Whoever therefore desires either to gain a reward for himself or to merit forgiveness of sins should, after paying his tithes, also strive to give alms from the nine parts. Thus, from the nine parts, whatever remains after reasonable food and clothing should not be reserved for luxury or worldly profit, but should be stored in the heavenly treasuries through almsgiving.

Whatever God has given us beyond what is necessary, he gave not specially to us [perhaps “not for us”], but transmitted it through us to be distributed to others.

Hear these things willingly, brothers, according to your custom, and with Christ’s help strive to fulfill them.

## HOMILY XVII

Dearest brothers, let us recall to mind what is heard in your hearts through the sacred pages. Yet we must know and understand that before the coming of the Lord and Savior, the devil reigned in the world, and all peoples, sinners and righteous alike, went down into hell when they departed from the body, on account of the original sins that we drew from Adam, because the first man Adam transgressed God’s commandment in paradise.

But because God saw that the whole world had perished, he took pity on the human race and sent his Son, born of a woman and made subject to the law, to redeem those who were under the law. The Son of God deigned to descend from the seat of the Father—that is, the Word entered the womb of Saint Mary, ever-virgin.

He came in such great humility that, through humility, he might conquer the devil, the author of death, and free the human race through the cross of his Passion. In heaven he shone with the Father; on earth he lay wrapped in cloths in a manger. He was the one who fled into Egypt; the one circumcised in the body; the one baptized by John; the one who fasted for forty days and nights; and then he came to his Passion.

He endured insults for us, mockeries, spittle, scourges, blows, and a crown of thorns. He was hung upon the cross, given vinegar to drink, pierced with a lance; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit. Blood and water flowed from his side.

What is signified by the blood, if not our redemption? What by the water, if not the sacrament of baptism? Therefore the Apostle John said: “There are three who bear witness: blood and water and spirit” (John V). By the blood, the redemption of sins; by the water, the sacrament of baptism; by the spirit, our sanctification.

See, brothers, how dearly the Lord held us: not with gold, silver, or precious substances, but with his holy blood he redeemed us—sinners, so that they might descend into hell with the flesh; the righteous, so that they might receive the kingdom with the flesh.

For God’s judgment will be just: that flesh which sinned here and did not repent should itself, together with the soul, be tormented in the fire. Likewise, that flesh which is tormented here for Christ’s sake should itself, together with the soul, rejoice with Christ and all the saints in paradise.

The Lord will separate them for judgment, placing the righteous on the right and sinners on the left, and he will say to the sinners: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

O what a terrifying and dreadful voice! After this voice has been heard, no remedy of repentance will come to their aid. Always fear this voice, brothers; always place this voice before your eyes. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath” (Matt. XXIV). It is as if he openly said: “See that you do not seek [perhaps: begin] then to flee from sins, when it is no longer permitted to walk.”

Elsewhere the Truth itself says: “Bind the bundles of weeds to be burned.” The weeds will be sinful people. Hell burns sinful people; sinful people will be the wood of hell. “Bind the bundles to be burned”—that is, murderers with murderers, adulterers with adulterers, robbers with robbers. Those who were alike in guilt here will likewise be bound there in torments; and the greater their crimes, the more fiercely eternal fire will rage against them.

Let no one deceive himself, brothers: every person who, after baptism, commits mortal crimes—that is, murder, adultery, theft, false testimony, or other crimes for which he could have died under worldly law—if he does not repent and does not perform righteous almsgiving, will never have eternal life, but will descend with the devil into torments.

Therefore blessed Isidore says: “God will never spare the guilty, because he does not chastise sinners with temporal scourging for this reason: so that he may leave them to be punished in eternal judgment. Hence it is that the Lord will not spare the guilty.”

And blessed Augustine says: “God forgives no sins without punishment; that is, without vengeance. Either we take vengeance upon ourselves through repentance, or God will take vengeance through the severity of the judgment in which he will say: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire’” (Matt. XXV).

And believe this with complete certainty, brothers: every person, however sinful or criminal he may be, whatever evils he may have committed, if he repents and performs righteous almsgiving, will never descend into hell, but will be lifted by angels into heaven.

Therefore the Lord says: “A person is not judged twice for the same thing” [Note: Nahum I, 9, according to the Septuagint: οὐκ ἐκδικήσει δὶς ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό, “He will not take vengeance twice for the same thing.”].

The Apostle says: “If we judge ourselves, we are not judged by the Lord”; that is, whoever judges himself in the present life through repentance is not judged again for judgment, because the matter is ended here in the present life.

Dearest brothers, we must always attend to our end, and whatever we have done against God’s commandments, we must repair through weeping and lamentation. Therefore, after Adam’s sins, the Lord called him, [renewed him], saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. III). Here almighty God gives a sign that, after sin, he calls us all back to repentance; and just as the father was expelled through sin, so let the sons be recalled through repentance.

And blessed Gregory says: “If we perform perfect repentance, God not only forgives our faults, but after our faults he promises eternal rewards.”

And blessed Augustine says: “Dearest brothers, whatever we have done against God’s commandments, let us repair it through repentance and lamentation, because God will not ask what we once were, but what we ought to be at the end of the world.”

## HOMILY XVIII. On the Repentance That Must Be Undertaken

*(The following—whether homily, sermon, admonition, or something similar—has this title in the Quintilianus manuscript: “Augustine’s Exhortation to Repentance.”)*

Whoever has performed true repentance, and has been released from the bond by which he was bound and separated from Christ’s body, and has lived well after repentance—after reconciliation, when he has died, he goes to the Lord, he goes to rest, he will not be deprived of God’s kingdom, and he will be separated from the devil’s company.

Whoever performs repentance while he is healthy, and after being reconciled lives well, is secure. And what does it mean to live well after repentance? I tell you: if you wish, abstain from drunkenness and lust, from theft, evil speech, immoderate laughter, and idle words, concerning which people will have to render an account on the day of judgment.

Do you wish, brother, to be freed from hell and escape what is uncertain? Perform repentance while you are healthy. For if you have performed true repentance and the final day or sudden death finds you, you are secure. Go without delay to the priest, so that you may be reconciled. If you do this, you are secure, because you received repentance [variant: *egisti poenitens*, “you acted as a penitent”] at the same time when you were able to sin.

But if you wish to perform repentance only when you can no longer sin, your sins have abandoned you, not you them.

O repentance, which, by God’s mercy, forgives sins and reserves us for paradise! O repentance, what can I say about you? You soften every adversity; you heal every contrite heart.

O repentance, more radiant than gold, brighter than the sun, which sin does not conquer, decline does not overcome, and despair does not destroy! Repentance rejects avarice, shudders at rage, flees lust, strengthens love, tramples pride, restrains the tongue, orders one’s conduct, hates evils, excludes vices, is suppliant toward superiors, and subject toward inferiors.

In its heart there is contrition; in its mouth, confession; in its conduct, complete humility. This is perfect and fruitful repentance.

Thus God is present to the repentant: to the hungry he is a nourisher; to the thirsty, a giver of drink.

O repentance, mother of mercy and teacher of the virtues—great are your works! You raise up the fallen, restore the despairing; through you Christ shows that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near to us, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near.” Amen.

## HOMILY XIX. By the Same Holy Father Augustine, on Repentance

*(Also found in Ambrose.)*

[Col. 1082B]

I admonish you, brothers, in the presence of God, etc. But if he does penance with his whole heart—if indeed he performs true penance, as God saw David’s heart when, rebuked severely by the prophet and after God’s terrible threats, he cried out, saying, “I have sinned,” and immediately heard, “The Lord has taken away your sin” [Note: [Col. 1082D] The Lord heard him and took away his sin.]—how powerful are three syllables? For *peccavi* (“I have sinned”) consists of three syllables; yet in those three syllables the flame of the sacrifice of his heart rose to heaven.

Therefore, whoever has truly performed penance, and has been released from the bond by which he was bound and separated from the body of Christ, and has lived well after penance, when he dies after reconciliation, goes to the Lord, goes to rest; he will not be deprived of the kingdom of God, and he will be separated from the people of the devil. But whoever, placed in the final crisis of his illness, has received penance, and has immediately been reconciled and then departs—that is, leaves the body—I confess to you that we do not deny him what he asks, but neither do I presume that he leaves this life well. I do not presume, I do not promise, I do not say so; I do not deceive or mislead you, nor do I make you a promise. The faithful person who has lived well departs this life secure. Whoever performs penance while healthy, is reconciled, and afterward lives well, is secure.

“But,” you say, “what does it mean, ‘if he lives well’? Teach us this also, good priest, so that we may know.” You say that you do not know this: the one who, having received penance, has passed away at once—you say that you do not know whether his crimes will be forgiven on the day of judgment. In this matter you give us no security. What does it mean to live well after penance? Teach us.

I tell you: to abstain from drunkenness, from lust, from theft, from evil speech, from immoderate laughter itself, and from idle words, for which people will have to give an account on the day of judgment. See how trivial are the things I have mentioned—and yet all of them are serious and deadly. See, I say something else: a person must not only keep himself from these vices after penance, but also before penance, while he is healthy, because he does not know whether he will be able to receive that penance and confess his sins to God and to the priest. See why I said that it is better to do so even before penance.

But when someone performs penance at the very end and, after being reconciled, departs, whether he leaves this life secure, I am not secure. I can give penance; I cannot give security. Pay attention to what I say: I explain it more clearly, so that no one may misunderstand me . . . Am I saying that he will be condemned? No. But am I saying that he will be saved? I do not say so.

“And what do you say to me, holy bishop?”

I do not know what to say to you. I have said it: I do not presume; I do not promise; I simply do not know the will of God. Do you wish, brother, to be freed from doubt? Do you wish to escape what is uncertain? Perform penance while you are healthy. For if you perform true penance while healthy, and the final day finds you, hasten [or: run to meet it] so that you may be reconciled. If you act in this way, you are secure.

“Why are you secure? Shall I tell you? Because you performed penance at the time when you were able to sin.”

There: I have said why you are secure. But if you wish to perform that very penance only when you can no longer sin, your sins have left you, not you them.

“But how do you know,” you say, “whether God may perhaps have mercy on me and forgive me my sins?”

You speak truly, brother; you speak truly. How do I know? And for that very reason I give you penance, because I do not know.

But he says: “Then leave my case to God. Why do you trouble me with words and leave me to God as judge?”

I entrust you to the judgment of the one to whose judgment I commend myself. For if I knew that it would do you no good, I would not admonish you or terrify you. There are two possibilities: either you will be forgiven, or you will not be forgiven. Which of these will happen to you, I do not know. But I give this advice: leave the uncertain and hold fast to the certain. While you are alive, perform true penance, so that when you come before God’s judgment you may not be put to shame by him, but may be led by him into his kingdom. Amen.

## HOMILY XX. A Sermon of Saint Augustine.

[Col. 1083C]

We have often said that Christians suffer persecution. “This world is set in evil” (John V). Our adversary, the devil, reigns in the world, and we imagine that we do not suffer persecution. What is there that does not persecute the Christian? Do we wonder if others persecute us, if we wish to serve Christ, who is the life of all, when even our parents persecute us? Whoever is unlike us persecutes and hates us; and do we wonder if others persecute us, when our own body persecutes us?

If I eat a little and my small body becomes robust, the health of my body persecutes my soul. Wherever I turn, there is persecution for me. If I see a woman, my eye persecutes me; it desires to kill my soul. If I see riches, gold, silver, or possessions—whatever I see and desire, that persecutes my soul.

Let us not suppose that martyrdom consists only in the shedding of blood, for martyrdom is always present. If a young man is persecuted by the lust of the flesh, it wishes to kill and shed the blood of his soul. But when your soul is in danger and placed in great peril, then you must stand firmly in fasting and prayers before our Lord Jesus Christ, and must not consent to death.

If, therefore, there are martyrdoms in time of peace, there are also denials. Let no one say that this is not martyrdom: it is martyrdom, and it is denial. I, who today appear to be a monk—if I break my commitment, I have denied Christ. And if I deny Christ in time of peace, what would I do in persecution? If, while I am neither tortured nor burned, I deny him, what would I do if I were tortured and burned? What wound is there that ought to separate anyone from the love of Christ?

What is said to you amounts to this: “You were burning in fire, you were hanging on the rack, you were being tortured for my sake—and you say, ‘I could not endure the tortures’?” How did Peter endure them? How did Paul? How did the other martyrs endure them? They had bodies just as you do.

O monk, who flee fasting, do you think that you are fleeing fire? You who consent to drunkenness, do you believe that you will escape the brazen serpent? This, then, I say to you, brothers: there are martyrdoms at every time, and there are also transgressions.

Finally, what does the Apostle say concerning widows who have taken second husbands? What does he say? “They have condemnation, because they have made void their first faith” (1 Timothy VI).

What does he say to the widow? O widow, before you promised me that you were a widow, it was in your power to marry. From the time you confessed that you would remain mine, from that time you began to belong to me. If you wish to take a second husband, you have despised me. Likewise you, monk: before you promised me, it was in your power to do what you wished; your own voice bound you to me. Did I compel you? Did you do it under necessity? Were you not free? It was in your power to promise. You promised, and you began to be mine. I do not want you to leave what is mine; you do not have the freedom to leave, because you have a case against me. To promise was yours; to leave is not yours. If you leave, I no longer have you in the rank in which I previously had you.

At first you were free, belonging to your own household; you did not belong to my household. You were not before my eyes, nor were you among my ministers; yet you were of my household. You were not with me, but nevertheless you were my creature. From the time you began to serve as a soldier, if you withdraw, I no longer regard you as belonging to my household, but certainly as a fugitive and transgressor. For you will not find anywhere to which you can flee from me.

I say all this because it is in our power to make a promise to God, but it is not in our power to withdraw from it. You promised: you will have a reward. You denied it: you will have punishment [or: you will suffer punishment]. Both alternatives lead to shame. Again and again we say: Behold, before your eyes are the way of death and the way of life; choose whichever you wish.

I say all this, dearest brothers, so that none of you may think that he has free power to depart and descend with the devil into hell. Therefore I, who am a monk, who ceased to be a secular person and became a monk—either I will be saved as a monk, or I will not be saved at all.

The holy [blessed] Paul himself cried out daily, in the voice of the Holy Spirit: “Brothers, do not be deceived: God is not mocked; for whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. For the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Galatians VI). And again: “Do you not know, brothers, that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin leading to death, or of obedience leading to righteousness?” (Romans VI).

Thus the devil, and our flesh—which still retains the bonds of the world—suggest that we sin and depart. Let us therefore consider the days of old, and place the eternal years before our eyes (Psalm LXXVI). In penance let us call upon our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, and weep, saying:

“Lord God, who do not desire the death of sinners, but rather that they should turn and live” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII), look upon us, Lord, according to your mercy; and may the cords of our enemies be broken, so that we do not perish. Look, Lord, from your holy seat and from the assembly of your majesty, and drive the darkness from our hearts with the ray of your light. Protect us, Lord, with the shield of your truth and faith, so that the flaming darts of the devil may not pierce us; and whatever it is that our iniquity does not know how to ask of you, grant that, Lord, by your power, so that you may save our souls from death.”

Let us cry out these things, and let us not despair of God’s mercy, because despair is certain death.

If, then, you have sinned, monk, you are a wretched monk; nevertheless, you are a monk. It is in no way permitted us to change our commitment, but we must return to the place of penance. For in the monastery, whatever servants of God there may be, whatever they do—if, not for necessary use but for adornment or some kind of display, they act without the superior’s command—let them be corrected, because here too we see minds sick with vice: they wish to please people by their clothing or footwear, not for use but for display.

God has made this very clear: “Every tree is known by its fruit.” And again: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VII).

## SAINT CAESARIUS’S ADMONITION OR CORRECTION TO THOSE WHO, HAVING WIVES, ARE NOT ASHAMED TO COMMIT ADULTERY

He also censures those who, before or after taking wives, have wished to take concubines into an unhappy relationship.

I ask you, dearest brothers, to consider attentively the matter of our salvation, so that we may be able to escape all those evils that have been written concerning the future judgment, and may happily reach that blessedness which has been promised to us. With all the strength we possess, and with God’s help, let us strive with full devotion of mind to preserve charity, justice, mercy, and chastity together, so that by these things, as by a heavenly and spiritual four-horse chariot, we may be carried off to the principal homeland of paradise.

Let us go there meanwhile in our hearts, so that when the day of judgment arrives we may follow also in body; and let that be fulfilled in us which the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven”; and this also: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.”

Let us not love any of those four virtues less than is fitting. For what does it profit you if you appear to possess charity but are unwilling to possess justice? Or who will be able to help you if you say that you possess mercy, but by not possessing chastity you hate yourself, according to what is written: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul”?
