And because we know that very few wish to possess chastity, we now admonish your charity more attentively concerning it, on account of what is written: “Neither fornicators, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, will possess the kingdom of God”; and also: “Neither adulterers nor drunkards will possess the kingdom of God.”

But, to begin with, there are many who appear to have wives and who, persuaded by the devil, neglect to preserve chastity, yet, inflamed by the madness of lust, are not ashamed to commit adultery with their own or with other men’s female servants, fearing neither God nor reverencing human beings.

It would have been right, brothers, that among such people our frequent admonitions over so many years should have had some effect, so that they would neither make wounds for themselves from medicines nor kill themselves by means through which they could have been brought to life. For the priest’s correction will be to the glory of the obedient, but to the punishment of the disobedient.

And because, as I have already said, they neither reverence God nor fear human beings, you who, inspired by Christ, faithfully preserve both faith and chastity, whenever you learn that some are committing such sacrilegious sins, rebuke them once, twice, and three times. If they refuse to listen to you, neither converse with them nor invite them to your banquets, nor eat with them at other people’s tables, in accordance with what the Apostle says to such persons: not even to take food with people of this kind. In this way they may at least be ashamed when they see themselves denounced by honest people who fear God.

For if what I advise is not done, whoever knows that his brother or neighbor is committing adultery, and refuses to rebuke him, will be a partner in his sin, in accordance with what is written: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you made your portion with adulterers”; and with what the Apostle says: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who approve of those who do them.”

But those who themselves neither rebuke adulterers nor discreetly bring them to the priest’s attention give us reason to suspect that they do not rebuke them for this reason: that they themselves commit such sins.

For me it is enough that I cry out with great sorrow of soul and boundless groaning. But if you wish to be free both from your own sins and from those of others, do not spare such people. Or if they refuse to listen when you admonish them more privately and more frequently, see that the matter comes to the attention of our humility, in accordance with what the Lord said about sinners in the Gospels: “Rebuke him between yourself and him alone; if he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, tell it to the Church”—that is, bring it to the priest’s attention. “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.”

But what is worse is that those who commit so great an evil are not only not rebuked by some people, but are even flattered and received with expressions of affection. Thus those sacrilegious crimes are nourished and committed without any fear or shame.

We must fear what is written concerning Achan, who had stolen the golden bar from Jericho: when, on account of one person’s sin, the anger of God raged against all Israel, and God’s fury did not cease from the people until the one who had done the evil was crushed at the Lord’s command.

Since the men of whom we are speaking wish their wives to be chaste, with what conscience do they commit abominable adulteries? They say to themselves that what is entirely unlawful for them is permitted—as though God had given one set of commandments to men and another to women. Let whoever he may be say by what law permitting it he commits these crimes, when every adultery is punished by divine and human law.

This evil is not prohibited merely because many commit it; rather, the less it is distinguished by human beings, the more severely it will be punished by divine judgment. For what of those who rush into such shamelessness that they say these cruel evils are permitted to men but not to women? They do not consider that both man and woman have been redeemed by the blood of Christ, washed together in the sacred baptismal bath, and receive the Lord’s blood together; and that with God there is no distinction between male and female, nor is God a respecter of persons.

Therefore, what is not permitted to women has likewise never been permitted to men, nor can it ever be permitted. But an unhappy custom has been introduced: if a wife is found with a servant, she is punished; but if a husband wallows with many female servants in the sewer of lust, he is not only not punished but even praised by his companions. Speaking to one another, they confess with laughter and the most foolish guffaws which of them has done this more often.

But their laughter will be turned into mourning on the day of judgment, and their jokes will be turned into wounds. Such things are done by those who neither believe in the future judgment at all nor fear it.

For I cry out and testify alike with a clear conscience: whoever, while having a wife, commits adultery, unless lengthy penance and abundant almsgiving come to his aid, and unless he ceases from that sin itself, if he should happen to die suddenly, will perish eternally. The name “Christian” will not benefit him, because he not only failed to carry out what the Lord commanded, but also committed crimes against his commands.

Since even knowing one’s wife, except with the desire for children, is said to be a sin, what do such men think about themselves, or what hope can they promise themselves, when, though married, they prepare by adultery the means by which they will descend into the depths of hell? They are unwilling to listen to the Apostle saying: “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none”; and again: “Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passion of desire, like the nations that do not know God.”

Consider that those who use their wives except with the desire for children cannot be without sin if they do not give continual alms. If this is said even of legitimate marriage, what do you think will happen on the day of judgment to those who presume to commit public or secret adulteries without any consideration of divine fear? Of such people it is written: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers”; and the Apostle’s statement already cited: “Neither will adulterers possess the kingdom of God.”

What does it profit you, wretched man, whoever you are, that you are called a Christian, if through the sin of adultery you deserve to be excluded from the kingdom of God?

And this I ask, dearest brothers, and admonish your charity: whoever is going to take a wife should preserve virginity until marriage. For just as no one wishes to take a defiled bride, so no one ought to corrupt himself before marriage by adulterous intercourse.

But what is worse is that many take concubines for themselves before they take wives. And because the multitude is great, the bishop cannot excommunicate them all; instead, with groaning and many sighs, he endures them and waits to see whether the pious and merciful Lord may perhaps grant them fruitful penance, through which they may reach forgiveness.

And because this evil has become customary, so that it is thought not to be a sin, I declare before God and his saints that whoever takes a concubine for himself, whether before or after taking a wife, commits adultery—and this is the worse adultery, because, although it is unlawful in every respect, he commits it publicly and without any shame, as though by law.

Finally, we recognize from this also that the sin is not a light one: whatever children the concubines themselves conceive are born not free persons but slaves. For how is it that, after receiving their freedom, they are permitted by no law and no ordinance to possess their father’s inheritance? Consider also whether it can be without sin when the dignity of noble blood is so humiliated that slaves are born from the most noble people.

For it is such a grave sin that in the city of Rome, whoever wishes to take a wife, if he knows that he is not a virgin, does not dare come at all to receive the nuptial blessing. And now consider how harsh it is that he is not worthy to receive the blessing with the woman whom he desires to marry.

But when we offer these admonitions, I fear that some may wish to become angry with us rather than with themselves. Our sermon is set before your charity like a mirror. Therefore, just as a married woman, when she looks into a mirror, corrects in herself whatever she sees in its entirety rather than breaking the mirror, so each of you, whenever he recognizes his own foulness in some preaching, ought rightly to correct himself rather than become angry with the preaching as though with a mirror.

Likewise, those who receive wounds prefer to heal their wounds rather than reject the medicines. Therefore, so that no one may sin doubly by becoming angry with spiritual medicines, let him receive what is said not only patiently but willingly. For the one who willingly accepts salutary correction is already known to be turning away from evil in another respect. When a person is displeased with his own evils, may what is good also become pleasing to him; and thus, in proportion as he separates himself from vices, may he draw near to virtues. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXI. To Monks.

We know indeed that a great reward is laid up in the future for the spiritual warfare to which we have devoted ourselves. But if we look carefully at this very work that we undertake [Perhaps: *undertake*], in some way even at present we see a share of the reward after [text uncertain: *post idemus*], etc.

## HOMILY XXII. To Monks.

[Col. 1089A]

For this purpose, brothers, we have gathered in this place: so that we may be free for our Lord, and not for those things in which our enemy delights. It is certain that whenever we speak of matters belonging to the world, etc.

## HOMILY XXIII. To Monks.

“Consider your calling, dearest brothers” (1 Corinthians I, 26). To come to the desert is the highest perfection; to live imperfectly in the desert is the highest condemnation. What does it profit if quiet is maintained in a place while unrest is active in the heart? If there is silence in the dwelling, etc.

## HOMILY XXIV. To Monks.

The divine word says in a certain passage: “On the days of your solemnities, afflict your souls” (Leviticus XVI, 29; XXIII, 27). Why did he say this? Because fasts, vigils, and holy afflictions wear down humble [Alternative: *humbled*] bodies, but purify defiled hearts, etc.

You may see these homilies in volume L of the *Patrologia*, among the works of Saint Eucherius, to whom they are also attributed, columns 844, 848, 855, and 857.

# SECOND PART OF THE WORKS. SHORT TREATISES AND LETTERS.

[Col. 1089]

## ON THE OBSERVANCE OF THE CANONS

### CONSTITUTION OF THE HOLY BISHOPS WHO ASSEMBLED IN THE CITY OF ARLES

(C, S)

## TITLES OF THE CANONS

[Col. 1089B]

I. That a deacon is not to be ordained before the age of twenty-five, nor a priest before the age of thirty.

II. That a layman is not to be ordained before one year of conversion.

III. That penitents and those married twice are not to be ordained.

IV. That whoever receives another’s cleric is to be deprived of communion.

## OLDER TITLES

Or, the rulings of this Council from the ancient Lucensis Codex 490.

### From the Council of Arles

A deacon is not to be ordained before the age of twenty-five.

No bishop, priest, or deacon is to be ordained unless he has been converted for one year.

## PREFACE

[Col. 1089C]

Since the priests of the Lord had gathered in the city of Arles, by God’s will, for the dedication of the basilica of Saint Mary, it seemed fitting and reasonable to them that, first of all, after examining with the greatest care the observance of the canons and how the ecclesiastical rule should be maintained by them, they should establish this by a wholesome decision.

## CANONS

### I

Since it is known that, in the ordination of clerics, the statutes of the ancient Fathers have not been observed in their entirety, as they ought to be, lest perhaps the priests of the Lord be wearied by the importunate and disorderly petitions of certain persons and be compelled to transgress commands so often issued, they decree among themselves that the following must be observed:

No bishop shall presume to ordain a deacon before he has completed twenty-five years of age. No layman shall receive the honor of the episcopate or presbyterate before the conversion mentioned above, or before the age of thirty.

[Col. 1090B]

### II

Although the ancient Fathers prescribed longer periods to be observed in the case of laymen, nevertheless, because, as the number of churches increases, it is necessary for us to ordain more clerics, we agree among ourselves—without prejudice, however, to the ancient canons—that none of the metropolitans shall grant the dignity of the episcopate to any layman, nor shall the other bishops presume to confer the honor of the presbyterate or diaconate upon anyone unless his conversion has first preceded it by a full year.

### III

No one shall dare to ordain a penitent, anyone married twice, or a man married three times, to the offices mentioned above. Although nearly all the canons already contain these statutes, nevertheless, lest the importunity or wrongful persuasion of petitioners—as has already been said—steal upon any priest, it was necessary for the priests of the Lord now to impose a stricter rule upon themselves.

Therefore, whoever from this day onward presumes to ordain a cleric contrary to the provisions set out above shall, from the day on which this can be established against him, not presume to celebrate Mass for a full year. If anyone refuses to observe this, and, acting against the agreement of the brothers, presumes to celebrate Mass, let him know that he is excluded from the charity of all the brothers. For it is right that one who scorns to observe regulations beneficially instituted so many times by the holy Fathers should feel the severity of ecclesiastical discipline.

### IV

And if perhaps some cleric, evading the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, should wander away, whoever receives him and not only fails to reconcile him with his own bishop but even presumes to defend him shall be deprived of communion from the Church (21st Question, 5, “If perhaps someone”).

## [SHORT TREATISE]

[Col. 1091]

### PREFACE OF JOANNES CHRISTOPHORUS AMADUTIUS TO THE DISTINGUISHED MAN ANGELO M. BANDINI, CANON OF THE BASILICA OF SAN LORENZO IN FLORENCE AND PREFECT OF THE ROYAL MEDICEAN-LAURENTIAN LIBRARY, TO THE FOLLOWING SERMON
[Col. 1091B] I have always thought to myself, dearest and most learned Bandini, that the duties of gratitude are fitting for an honorable and upright man in such a way that, if anyone either knowingly neglects them or shrinks from them, he comes very close to being counted among the beasts of burden. Human society is sustained above all by mutual assistance, goodwill, and affection; if these are removed, humanity itself seems to me to be removed, and how proper these are to human beings is indicated even by the name itself. Let anyone who wishes hold to the principles of the opposing view, on which an entirely new and uncivilized philosophy, unworthy of a civilized person, is based. Surely you understand, best of friends, that I say this so that you, who have heaped upon me many benefits and expressions of affection, may recognize me as grateful also for your repeated services and generosity toward me, and may judge that I shall remain perpetually mindful of them all. Therefore, since I now have the opportunity to commit to print this discourse *On Maintaining Widowhood*, which I owe above all to you, to whom could these words that I ought now to preface it be more suitably dedicated than to you, so that at least some exchange of my devotion toward you may exist? I plainly see that my offering is small and unequal to your benefaction and merits; yet, since it proceeds from an upright heart eager to give greater things, may it be worthy for you to receive it favorably.

Once the author of the benefaction from which these things have flowed to us has become known to our readers, it is fitting that the remaining matters should also be disclosed—those more immediately relevant to the monument that is now appearing for the first time—and you, who know them very well, must now endure their repetition. The Medicean-Laurentian Library codex [Note: [Col. 1091D] Cod. XX, Plut. XVI.], over which you rightly preside, contains this discourse. You believe it to have been written in the eleventh century, and you have already described it in volume I of your *Catalogue of the Latin Manuscripts of the Laurentian Library* [Note: [Col. 1091D] Pages 261–265, no. 41, page 141.], whose appearance we await shortly. The celebrated codex contains various homilies of Saint Caesarius of Arles, among them this one, which nevertheless is attributed to Saint Augustine, Father of the Church, since at its end the following words are appended, though inelegantly: “Here ends Saint Augustine’s *On the Consolation of the Dead*.”

It is inscribed more clearly with Augustine’s name in another ninth-century codex, mutilated at the end, belonging to the Library of Saint Mark in Florence, which is held by the Friars Preachers. There, after several homilies of the same Caesarius of Arles, the codex contains three sermons. The first is by Saint Augustine, bishop, and begins, “Blessed is the man toward whom God will show mercy,” etc.; the second is likewise prefaced with his name and is *On Maintaining Widowhood*; and the third is assigned to Saint Ambrose and is *On Doing Penance*.

The very distinguished Francis Anthony Zaccherius describes this codex in his *Journey through Italy* [Note: [Col. 1092D] Part I, chapter 2, pages 49 and 50.] and lists each of its sections individually. The second sermon, *On Maintaining Widowhood*, copied from this codex, was communicated to us with the greatest kindness by the highly distinguished Philip Angelicus Becchetti, a member of the Dominican Order and most excellent continuator of the *Ursine Ecclesiastical History*; through his care, I also obtained a copy excerpted from the Laurentian codex, which you generously and courteously supplied.

The text I present is taken from the Laurentian codex. At the bottom of the page, however, I have supplied the variant readings found in the Saint Mark’s codex, which is two centuries older than the other. Its greater antiquity would indeed seem to require that its copy be presented in place of the text; [Col. 1092D] but when I discovered that, approximately halfway through the sermon, a fragment of another sermon *On Doing Penance* had been inserted into it—perhaps through the copyist’s carelessness—a fragment that has absolutely nothing in common with *Widowhood*, I feared that anyone might find it distressing to see something discordant with the original subject inserted into the text itself, even though the manuscript’s authority required this. I therefore decided that the Laurentian copy, although more recent, should now serve as the text, while this fragment itself should be appended among the other variant readings of the older codex.

Nor did it seem possible to omit the following point: despite the investigations I have undertaken, nowhere among the published sermons of Augustine, Ambrose, and Caesarius have I found this work. Zaccherius, in the passage cited, intimates that after the sermon *On Maintaining Widowhood* there follows another sermon by Saint Ambrose, *On Doing Penance*, or, as he calls it, Homily 44, which the printed books assign to Augustine. Accordingly, following his indication, I examined the cited number 44, assigned to this homily, in the works of Augustine and Ambrose, both in older and more recent editions—for Zaccherius does not clearly indicate which of the two Fathers he means there. I found that their homilies or sermons bearing this number, whether among their genuine works or among those considered spurious or doubtful, are entirely different and do not touch upon penance at all.

Augustine does indeed have two sermons *On the Benefit of Doing Penance* [Note: [Col. 1093D] Sermons 351 and 352, volume V of the Saint-Maur edition.], and several others on the same subject occur in the appendix [Note: [Col. 1093D] Sermons 254–262.], rejected by the highly learned Parisian monks of Saint-Maur; but in none of them did I find anything corresponding to the fragment just mentioned. The same should be understood of the Ambrosian and Caesarian sermons that I deliberately consulted.

But now I must state my opinion concerning the author of this [Col. 1093C] sermon, an opinion that I also wished to communicate to the distinguished Augustine Anthony George, procurator general of the Augustinian Hermits, a man exceedingly devoted to me, richly endowed with every kind of learning, and especially energetic and outstanding as a defender of Augustinian teaching. The style, if compared with the unquestionably golden and divine works of the most holy Father, will appear not merely unlike the style in which our sermon is composed but markedly different from it.

Moreover, the most holy Father adheres to the Greek text when citing Scriptural testimonies, as the Maurist monks also observed. In particular, the passage from the Apostle Paul to Timothy [Note: [Col. 1093D] 1 Timothy 5:5–6.], which first occurs in our sermon *On Maintaining Widowhood*, is quoted by Augustine in his little work *On the Good of Widowhood*. In the Vatican Palatine codex of the sixth or seventh century, numbered 210, that work is entitled: “The Book or Letter of Saint Augustine to Juliana on Preserving Widowhood.” It corresponds exactly to the Greek text, not to the Vulgate version. It reads as follows:

> “But she who is truly a widow and desolate has placed her hope in the Lord and persists in prayers night and day. But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives.”

Here, then, is the Greek text, so that you may easily compare it with both versions:

> Ἡ δὲ ὄντως χήρα, καὶ μεμονωμένη ἤλπικεν ἐπὶ τὸν Θεὸν καὶ προσμένει ταῖς δεήσεσι, καὶ ταῖς προσευχαῖς νῦκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας. Ἡ δὲ σπαταλῶσα, ζῶσα τέθνηκε.

> “But she who is truly a widow and alone has hoped in God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day. But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives.”

In our sermon, however, this passage is quoted in accordance with the Vulgate edition, although not entirely accurately, and differently from Augustine’s rendering. The same should be understood of the other passages from the New Testament cited here. In the work *On the Christian Life*, which the Maurist monks placed in the appendix to volume VI, this same Pauline passage is found quoted according to the Vulgate. Yet they deny that this work is by Augustine and attribute it instead to a certain Bishop Fastidius, a fellow countryman of Pelagius.

I therefore judge that this sermon should rather be attributed to Saint Caesarius of Arles, since it is found in codices containing his homilies and since several other sermons of his were formerly attributed to Augustine but were rejected by the highly learned monks of Saint-Maur in the appendix to volume V of the Augustinian works.

These are the matters, most learned Bandini, that I wished now to discuss with you, with whom I have almost seemed to engage in a learned conversation. You, who possess such great learning and who daily undertake greater projects for the benefit and advancement of the republic of letters, should not disdain these little learned addresses of mine or these small works. They are at least suited to your character and endeavor to approach the model of your works.

In any event, do not measure the extent of my gratitude and respect from this small service alone; expect from me each day even greater things, if I have the means, or indeed anything else whatsoever. Farewell meanwhile, most learned Bandini, and live in peaceful leisure for your country and the Muses.

[Col. 1094C] Given at Rome, on the Nones of January, in the year 1773 from the birth of Christ.

[Col. 1094]

# A Short Work: *On Maintaining Widowhood* (C, S)*

Listen, abandoned daughter, you who have lost the comfort of affection and from whose neck the yoke of a husband has been removed. Behold, you will be happier if you remain thus. Let no empty thought deceive you by saying, “Who will provide food for me at the proper time, or who will protect my orphans?” [Note: [Col. 1093D] The Saint Mark’s codex has “support.”] Rather, you ought now to rejoice more than when you were bound by the bond of a husband. Behold, you have been released from the law of the husband to which you were subject, so that you may be your own mistress.

Do not sigh because you have lost the hope of this world. Remember, daughter, that the Lord is the hope of all the ends of the earth. Do not be anxious because you have been left alone; remember the Lord, who receives the orphan and the widow. Pray to the Lord, as the Apostle says:

> “She who is truly a widow and desolate perseveres in prayers and supplications day and night; for she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives.”

If a widow has parents and grandchildren, let her first learn to manage her household well and to repay her parents with mutual service, for this is pleasing and acceptable before the Lord (1 Timothy 5:4–6).

Be humble, modest, and temperate in all things, lest you perhaps appear detestable [Note: [Col. 1094D] The Saint Mark’s codex has “to human beings.”]. Thus it is written: “Avoid younger widows, for when they have become wanton, they wish to marry in Christ,” [Col. 1095A] thereby incurring condemnation because they have broken their first pledge. They learn not only to be idle but also talkative and inquisitive, going around other people’s houses and saying things they ought not to say (1 Timothy 5:11–13).

Be assiduous in your house, praying with tears, so that he may grant you bodily chastity and continence. How unhappy and wretched you are, how evil a disgrace you bear, if you do not control yourself! What disorder is yours if you do not hold the reins of your flesh! Labor always in the work of God.

Behold the good widow: if she has been the wife of one husband, if she has raised children, shown hospitality, washed the feet of the saints, and supplied the needs of those suffering tribulation [Note: [Col. 1095B] The Apostle uses these words in the cited Epistle, verse 10.]. You will be blessed if you do all these things. For there are many widows who have had two or three husbands, but they have not received the command to be honored by all, as has she who had one husband.

There were many widows in the days of Elijah, but he was sent to none of them except to the widow at Zarephath of Sidon. See that none of them had merit except that one who offered hospitality in a time of need, when there was a severe famine, and, when holy Elijah arrived, prepared a table for him.

Likewise, that widow had nothing in her possessions except two coins; hoping with a pure heart that she would receive a hundredfold, she offered those very coins to the Lord. Likewise, there was the widow named Judith, who did not leave the upper rooms of her house but served the Lord day and night with fasts and prayers; the Lord guarded her from the hand of Holofernes, so that she would not be defiled by the work of sin.

Oh, how blessed is the widow who bestowed such joy [Note: [Col. 1095B] The Saint Mark’s codex additionally contains the following words, inserted through the copyist’s carelessness and apparently belonging to the other sermon *On Doing Penance*. They have been included here:]

> …Let her do what she so greatly desires to be done. When she has ended the day, life does not end but passes from life into life. Whether someone comes of his own will to baptism, or is baptized while in danger and departs, he goes to the Lord; he goes to rest. But if, after being baptized, he becomes a deserter and violator of the sacrament, he sins and drives the Lord away from himself.
>
> But if he does penance with his whole heart—let him truly do penance—where God sees, as he saw David’s heart, when, after being severely rebuked by the prophet and after the terrifying communications of God, he cried out, saying, “I have sinned”; and as soon as the Lord heard him, he took away his sin. How much three syllables can accomplish! “I have sinned” consists of three syllables, but in those three syllables the flame of the sacrifice of his heart rose to heaven.
>
> Therefore, whoever has done true penance, has been released from the bond by which he was bound and separated from the body of Christ, and has lived well after doing penance, when he dies after reconciliation goes to the Lord; he goes to rest; he will not be deprived of the kingdom of God and will be separated from the devil’s cup.
>
> But whoever, placed in the final crisis of illness, has received penance, and has immediately been reconciled, and then departs—that is, leaves the body—I confess to you that we do not deny him what he asks; but neither do I presume that he has departed this life well. I do not presume, I do not promise, I do not say, I do not deceive you, I do not mislead you, I do not promise you anything. The faithful person who lives well departs securely.
>
> Whoever does penance while healthy, and, after being reconciled, lives well, is secure. But you say, “What if he has lived well?” Either teach us this, good priest, or let us know it. You say that you do not know this: when someone receives penance for an hour and then departs, you say that you do not know whether his crimes will be forgiven on the day of judgment. Thus you give us no security at all. Teach us what it means to live after penance.
>
> I tell you: abstain from drunkenness, lust, theft, evil speech, even immoderate laughter, and idle words, concerning which people will have to give an account on the day of judgment. See how light the things I have mentioned are, and [Col. 1096B] I have omitted the grave and deadly ones.
>
> I say something else as well: a person must guard himself not only from these vices after penance, but before penance, while he is healthy, because he does not know [Col. 1096C] whether he will be able to receive that penance and confess his sins to God and the priest. See why I said that it is better to do so before penance.
>
> But if someone does penance at the very end and, after being reconciled, departs, whether he departs securely, I am not secure. I can give penance; I cannot give security.
>
> Pay attention to what I say. I explain it more plainly, so that no one may misunderstand me. Am I saying that he will be condemned? I am not saying that. I am saying that he will be freed.
>
> “And what do you say to me, holy bishop?”
>
> “I do not know what to say to you. I said that I do not presume and do not promise; I simply do not know God’s will.”
>
> “Do you wish, brother, to be freed from doubt? Do you wish to escape by what is certain? Do penance while you are healthy. For if you do true penance while you are healthy, and the final day finds you, you hasten to be reconciled; if you act in this way, you are secure.”
>
> “Why are you secure? Shall I tell you? Because you did penance at a time when you were also able to sin. Behold, I have told you why you are secure.”
>
> But if you wish to do that penance only when you are no longer able to sin, your sins have abandoned you, not you them.
>
> “But how do you know,” you will say, “whether perhaps God may have mercy on me and forgive my sins?” [Col. 1096D]
>
> “You speak truly, brother, truly you speak. How do I know? And for that reason I give you penance, because I do not know.”
>
> “Then leave my case to God.”
>
> “Why do you distress me with the fear of a word and leave me to God as judge?”
>
> “I commit you to the judgment of the one to whose judgment I commend myself. For if I knew that it would do you no good, I would not admonish you or frighten you.”
>
> There are two possibilities: either you will be forgiven or you will not be forgiven. Which of these will happen to you, I do not know. But I give this advice: leave the uncertain and hold fast to the certain. While you are alive, do true penance, so that when you come before God’s judgment you may not be put to shame by him, but may be led by him into the kingdom.]

This is what she did for her fellow citizens, and she deserved to acquire a good hope for herself, so that she might free her people from the mouth of the sword! Behold what the widow’s chastity accomplished: she became renowned throughout the whole earth, praiseworthy before the Lord, and illustrious in all things.

Oh, how blessed are you, widow whom the Lord remembers! Like that woman whose only son had died—how she obtained mercy from the Lord, so that he might be raised again [Note: [Col. 1096D] The Saint Mark’s codex has: “she obtained that he might be raised by the Lord.”]—so also that widow in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 9:36), named Dorcas, who performed many acts of charity. When Peter arrived, all the widows showed him the garments that Dorcas had made for them while she was alive. Peter saw the works of the widow, prayed, and raised her.

Likewise, there was the widow who came every day to the feet of a certain rich man, seeking justice against her adversary [Col. 1096B]. When the rich man saw her weeping, he said: “Although I do not fear God or respect human beings, nevertheless, because this widow is troublesome, I will give her justice.” Behold how the widow is vindicated if she possesses chastity and humility. I too have been commanded to visit her, as the Apostle says: “Visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27).

Oh, how blessed are you, widow who are commended in all things by the Lord! But whoever does not have mercy on you is judged by the Lord himself, who says [Note: [Col. 1096D] This passage is not found in Holy Scripture, although many testimonies concerning widows and orphans that point in this direction occur; perhaps one of them has here been adapted in sense, as is not unusual among sacred writers.]: “Since you do not judge the causes of widows and do not pity orphans, I will judge you, says the Lord.” [Col. 1097A]

Blessed are you, widow, because you have the Lord himself as judge and defender. Do not weep for anyone now, daughter, for you have become better than you were before. Formerly you hoped in a human being, but now in the Lord Jesus Christ; formerly you thought according to human standards, but now according to God; formerly you took pleasure in the desire of the flesh and in the danger of clothing, but now above all you think of the sweetness of the law and chastity; formerly you were the husband’s slave, but now you are free in Christ [Note: [Col. 1097B] The Saint Mark’s codex has “free in Christ.”].

How good it is for you to be secure rather than to endure a husband’s service [Note: [Col. 1097B] The Saint Mark’s codex has “servitude.”]! It is good to lie alone in bed and rise clean, rather than to lie there conscious of lust and the uncleanness of the flesh. Formerly you were bent down and were under the husband’s heavy yoke [Note: [Col. 1097B] The Saint Mark’s codex has “under the heavy yoke of the husband.”]; now you have been raised up from beneath Christ’s gentle yoke.

Rejoice, daughter, because you were sold to be a husband’s slave [Col. 1097B], but now you have earned freedom from the Lord. Remember, daughter, the Canaanite woman, who by her persistence deserved to obtain the favor of our Savior; and also the woman who watered the Lord’s feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair; or the woman who brought precious ointment and poured it over the reclining Lord [Note: [Col. 1098B] The Saint Mark’s codex has “and anointed the reclining Lord”]; or the woman who touched the Lord’s garments, and immediately the flow of her blood stopped; and the woman who sat at the Lord’s feet, listening so that she might learn how to escape the coming wrath.

Consider, daughter, by what path of humility these women walked and thereby obtained a good reward. Be like them in obedience, humility, almsgiving, hospitality toward strangers, vigils, fasts, and complete sobriety. These are the things that pleased Christ.

Labor, daughter, day and night in the work of the Lord, so that you who have been dismissed by a man may be gathered up by the Lord; so that you who were going to receive a thirtyfold [Note: [Col. 1098B] The Saint Mark’s codex has “thirtyfold.”] fruit may deserve to attain a sixtyfold one, through him who lives forever and ever. Amen.

Here ends [Note: [Col. 1098B] These words are absent from the Saint Mark’s codex.] Saint Augustine’s *On the Consolation of the Dead*.

[Col. 1097]

# Saint Caesarius’s Rule for Monks [Note: [Col. 1097C] Cointius describes this rule for monks of Saint Caesarius in his *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks* under the year 536, §124, volume I, pages 489ff., and begins a careful comparison of it with the Rule for Nuns, written by the same Caesarius and following below; he also provides notes illustrating both.]. (C)

## Testimonies of the Ancients Concerning Saint Caesarius and His Rule

[Col. 1097C] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 86:

> “Caesarius, bishop of the city of Arles, a man renowned for holiness and virtue, wrote excellent and highly esteemed short works, necessary for monks. He flourished while Anastasius was governing the empire.”

Cyprian, book I of *The Life of Saint Caesarius*, chapter 4:

> “Caesarius was first ordained deacon, then priest; nevertheless, he never abandoned the canonical monastic chant, nor the institutions of the brothers of Lérins. In rank and office he was a cleric; in humility, charity, obedience, and the cross he remained a monk.”

The same work, chapter 5:

> “When the abbot of an island in the suburbs of the city had died, Bishop Aeonius sent Caesarius there, so that, succeeding to the same authority of reverence, he himself might govern the monastery, which had been left without a superior, according to monastic discipline. Thus, willingly, he embraced in the suburban monastery the way of life that he had always pursued within the city through daily efforts and desired through perpetual vows. He instructed that monastery through such daily diligence and divine services that, by God’s favor, it may still be seen there today.”

Florianus, Letter 5 to Bishop Nicetius, volume I of the *Gallic Scriptures*, page 851:

> “And also your companion in the crown, the blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, whose memory is honored: he lived piously among barbarians, peacefully amid wars, a father to orphans and an outstanding shepherd. Though he distributed such great wealth, he lost nothing, demonstrating the rule of Catholic discipline by word and deed.”

## Critical Observation on the Following Rule

[Col. 1097D] All learned men acknowledge that Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, wrote two monastic rules: one for monks and the other for virgins. Holstenius inserted both into his edition; here he treats the first, the rule for monks.

After Saint Caesarius had been compelled to leave the monastery at Lérins because his health had deteriorated, he went to Arles, where Bishop Aeonius received him as a friend and formed such a close relationship with him that, once Caesarius had recovered, the bishop appointed him abbot of a monastery. After three years, namely in the year 502, he was chosen by unanimous vote to be bishop of the place.

Since, therefore, the most holy bishop had been educated from adolescence in the monastery at Lérins, we can readily suppose that he introduced no other monastic discipline into the monastery at Arles than that of Lérins. Thus this rule stands as a notable monument of the strict monastic discipline once practiced in the celebrated monastery at Lérins.

The rule consists of twenty-six articles, together with a brief but impassioned exhortation to the monks. It was written not only for the monastery at Arles but for every other cenobium governed by an abbot. Indeed, from the privilege of Pope Hormisdas sent to the holy virgins of Arles, it is entirely clear that after attaining the episcopate Saint Caesarius also founded other monasteries for clerics and monks within the city, in addition to the one founded by his predecessor on the suburban island, of which he himself had at one time been appointed abbot.

Moreover, at the beginning of this rule, Tetradius, Saint Caesarius’s nephew and perhaps the abbot of some monastery in Gaul, testifies that this rule was dictated before Caesarius assumed the episcopate, and therefore while Saint Caesarius was still abbot and priest of the monastery founded by Aeonius.

# Here Begins the Rule Sent by Saint Tetradius, Priest, Nephew of Blessed Memory Saint Caesarius, Bishop of Arles, and Abbot, at the Request of My Small Person; He Said That It Had Been Dictated by His Forementioned Lord Caesarius, Who Sent It to Various Monasteries While He Was Still a Priest

[Col. 1099]

[Col. 1099B] In the name of Christ, here begins the Rule concerning what the monastery ought to be like, wherever there is an abbot, whoever he may be.

## Chapter One

First of all, if anyone comes for conversion, he is to be received on the condition that he persevere there until his death. His secular clothing is not to be changed until he has first prepared deeds of sale for his possessions, as the Lord commanded, saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19).

Certainly, if he does not wish to sell, let him make deeds of gift either to his parents or to the monastery, provided that he is free and possesses nothing as his own. But if his father or mother is alive and he does not have the authority to do this, he must be compelled to do so when they have died.

Whatever he has brought with him, let him hand over to the abbot; let him reserve nothing for himself. If any of his relatives send him anything [Col. 1099C], let him offer it to the abbot. If he needs it, let him have it at the abbot’s command; if he does not need it, let it be placed in the common fund and given to whoever needs it.

## II

Let everything be common among you.

## III

No one is to have a private cell, a little cupboard, or any enclosed space; let everyone remain in one room.

## IV

They are not to swear, because the Lord said: “Do not swear at all, but let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no’” (Matthew 5).

## V

Whoever is found lying is to receive the proper discipline, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1), and “You will destroy those who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5).

## VI

They are not to curse, because it is written: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

## VII

They are not to perform whatever work each person may choose, but rather the work assigned to them.

## VIII

While we are chanting the psalms, no one should presume to speak.

## IX

While they are eating at table, no one is to speak; but one person is to read whatever book may be chosen, so that just as the body is restored by food, so the soul may be nourished by the word of God, as the Lord says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matthew 4). As earth without rain and flesh without food are, so is the soul if it is not nourished by the word of God.

## X

No one is to act as godparent at a baptism.

## XI

Women are never to enter the monastery. When the signal is given, no one who is in a remote place is to come late to any work of God. If he comes late, he is immediately to receive a stroke of the rod on his hands. When rebuked by the abbot, the provost, or any elder, he must not presume to answer at all.

[Note: [Col. 1099D] “Let them enter. Whoever is in a remote place.” In all printed editions this passage is corrupt and should be corrected as follows: “Let them enter. Except the one who…” Cointius, cited work, page 491.]

## XII

Do not have quarrels among yourselves, for the Apostle says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel but must be gentle” (2 Timothy 2). Certainly, if someone goes too far, as human weakness may cause, and they provoke one another with harsh words, “let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4).

[Col. 1100C] ## XIII

Nor should anyone presume to condemn the person who is angry. Rather, those who know that they have done what they ought not to have done should ask one another’s forgiveness, fulfilling that command of God in which he says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven. If you do not forgive, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6).

“The anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1). “If you offer your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5).

Be certain that while you are angry against another, your prayer is not accepted; nor is it permitted for an angry person to receive Communion. Therefore fulfill what the Lord says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14). “By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (ibid., 13).

John said further: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness. Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. God is love; whoever remains in love, God remains in him” (1 John 3). And since we are commanded to love our enemies and do good to them, with what face do we hate our brothers?

## XIV

At all times until the third hour, let them read; after the third hour, let each person perform the work assigned to him.

## XV

No one is secretly to receive anything; especially, no one is to receive or send letters without the abbot’s knowledge.

## XVI

The abbot is to provide food and clothing. Since it has been decreed that they are to possess nothing as their own, it is likewise just that they receive from the holy abbot everything they need.

## XVII

The sick are to be treated so that they may recover more quickly.

## XVIII

Perform every service willingly, so that you may fulfill the words: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Psalm 53). For the reward of the person who acts willingly will be sufficiently great—greater than that of the person who unwillingly does what is commanded.

## XIX

Strive to enter through the narrow gate, because the way that leads to life is narrow and difficult, while the way that leads to death is broad and spacious (Luke 13).

But just as you would be entering a contest if you were going into battle against some nation, so as not to meet death there, so much the more fight in this spiritual contest, so that the adversaries of your souls do not strike you.

Whatever vices you have, you will have an equal number of adversaries. Therefore fight like soldiers of Christ, so that you may reign with him in heaven. He said: “If anyone takes up his cross and follows me; if anyone leaves father, mother, wife, children, and possessions, he will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19).

Let this be your contest among yourselves: who will overcome another through humility and charity; who will be the lesser; who will be more vigilant in the work of God; who will possess greater patience; who will be silent, gentle, kind, and contrite. Thus God and his angels may rejoice over your holy way of life, while the devil, the ancient enemy, may be put to shame—he who always considers how to make wretched human beings act against God’s will, lest there be in them that for which he himself was cast down because of his presumption.

“Run in such a way that you may obtain the prize” (1 Corinthians 9), and be able to say: “I have run along the way of your commandments” (Psalm 118). See, brothers, how carefully you must walk, not as foolish people but redeeming the time, because the days are evil [Col. 1102A]. Therefore do not become thoughtless, but understand what the will of God is. And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and chanting in your hearts to the Father and to God, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ (Ephesians 5).

## XX

From October until Easter, let them perform two nocturns at the Vigils [Note: [Col. 1101C] “Vigils.” The vigil is the nocturnal office now called Matins. Cointius, cited work, page 492.] and three “masses” [Note: [Col. 1101C] “Masses.” Take care not to think that the term “masses” here signifies the most sacred sacrifice of the Mass. The word *masses* signifies readings taken both from the Old and New Testaments and from the passions of the martyrs. Caesarius uses the term in this sense shortly below, in chapter XXI: “Every Sunday perform six masses. At the first mass, let the Resurrection always be read.”

“Caesarius therefore prescribes three things in this regulation: that the reader, seated, should read; that for each reading he should read three pages; and that at the end of each reading the monks should pray for a short while, until the person presiding over the assembly, having given a signal, orders the reading to be performed again.” The same author, cited work, pages 493ff.]

For one mass, let a brother read three pages, and pray; let him read another three, and rise.

## XXI

Say an antiphon, a responsory, and another antiphon; the antiphons themselves are to be taken from the order of the Psalter. After this, let them say Matins [Note: [Col. 1101D] “Matins.” Today we call this Lauds. The same author, cited work, page 492.], directly [Note: [Col. 1101D] “Directly,” and so forth. Observe here two forms of psalmody: one *directanee*, or directly, and the other with an antiphon, or antiphonally. Psalms are said directly when they are recited without melody and uttered in an even tone of voice, without rising or falling. They are said with an antiphon, or antiphonally, when two choirs sing together alternately with melody, exchanging and alternating their melodic singing in turn. For ἀντιφωνεῖν means to sing opposite one another reciprocally and alternately. The same author, cited work, page 495.]:

> “I will exalt you, my God and my King.”

Then let the entire Matins service be said antiphonally. Every Sunday perform six masses. At the first mass, let the Resurrection always be read; no one is to sit.

When the masses are completed, say Matins directly:

> “I will exalt you, my God and my King.”

Then:

> “Give thanks to the Lord.”

Then:

> “Let us sing to the Lord.”

> “Praise the Lord, O my soul.”

> “The Blessing” [Note: [Col. 1101D] That is, the song of the Three Children: “Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord.” The same author, cited work, page 498.]

> “Praise the Lord from the heavens.”

> “We praise you, O God.”

> “Glory to God in the highest,”

and the little chapter [Note: [Col. 1102C] Or *capitulum*. Little chapters are short readings taken from Holy Scripture; they are called “collections” in chapter 30 of the Council of Agde, over which the same Saint Caesarius presided. The same author, cited work, page 499.].

Let it be said in this manner every Sunday.

## XXII

From holy Easter until the month of September, fasting is required only on Wednesdays and Fridays. From September until the Nativity of the Lord, fasting is required every day. Again, beginning two weeks before Lent, fasting is required every day, except on Sunday, when it is altogether forbidden to fast, because of the Lord’s resurrection. If anyone fasts on Sunday, he sins. From the Nativity of the Lord until two weeks before Lent, fasting is required on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; thereafter, until Easter, fasting is required every day except Sunday. Whoever fasts on Sunday sins.

“*Missus* indeed, three during the fast” [Note: In the *Library of the Fathers*, the reading is “three meals [*missas*] during the fast.” Holstenius, deleting *missas*, restored *missus*, most erroneously. For what sense can this wording have: “But three meals during the fast”? Saint Aurelian, who follows in the footsteps of Saint Caesarius, begins the arrangement of meals that he appended to the *Rule for Monks* as follows: “Three portions of food each day for the refreshment, two for dinner, and two for supper.” Saint Caesarius himself, in the appendix appended to the *Rule for Nuns*, likewise begins his arrangement of meals with provisions: “On all fasting days, three portions of food shall be prepared; at dinner only two.” From this we conclude that the beginning of the prescription whose corruption we are lamenting should be corrected as follows: “But during the fast, three portions of food,” and so forth. —The same, in the same work, pp. 500 ff.]

But during the fast three portions of food shall be prepared; at dinner [the text should read *prandio*] and supper, only two. At dinner they shall receive two drinks [Note: *Binas biberes*: Thus Holstenius, and correctly; for Saints Benedict, Aurelian, and Donatus use the same word in their rules, as does Evethelmus in the *Life of Saint Poppo* in the Bollandists, on 25 January. In Bollandus’s notes at this place and in Vossius’s *Errors of Speech*, *biberes* means “cups of wine”; but Holstenius, in his *Index*, more properly takes it to mean a draught or drink of any liquid. —The same, in the same work, p. 500.], and at supper; during the fast, three. No one shall presume to keep anything to eat or drink beside her bed.

## XXIII

Whoever has been excommunicated for some fault shall be confined in a single cell and shall read there with one of the elders until she is ordered to come for pardon.

## XXIV

When healthy, they shall never receive poultry or meat; for the sick, whatever is necessary shall be provided.

## XXV

Every Saturday and every Sunday, or on feast days, twelve psalms, three antiphons, and three readings shall be recited: one from the Prophets, another from the Apostle, and the third from the Gospel.

## XXVI

Although we are less capable warriors, we provide these spiritual weapons for you against the fiery darts of the devil.

Rejoice and exult in the Lord, venerable sons, and continually offer him abundant thanks, since in his goodness he has deigned to draw and summon you from the dark manner of life of this world to the harbor of rest and religion. Continually consider from where you have come and where you have deserved to arrive. You have faithfully abandoned the darkness of the world and have happily begun to see the light of Christ. You have despised the fire of lust and reached the refreshment of chastity; you have rejected gluttony and chosen abstinence; you have renounced greed and luxury and embraced charity and mercy.

And although battle will not be lacking for you until the end of life, nevertheless, with God’s help, we are confident of your victory. But I ask you, venerable sons, to be as concerned about the future as you are confident about the past. For all crimes and sins quickly return upon us if they are not daily defeated by good works.

Hear the Apostle Peter saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter V). As long as we live in this body, let us fight against the devil day and night, with Christ as our helper and guide.

For there are some—what is worse—who are negligent and lukewarm, who glory merely in the name of Christianity and think it is enough for them to have changed their clothing and merely assumed the habit of religion. They do not know the prophetic saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus II). Nor do they consider the Psalmist’s statement: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult paths” (Psalm XVI). And the Apostle said: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts XIV).

We can put off secular clothes and assume religious ones in the space of a single hour; but we must retain good morals continually and, with Christ’s help, labor throughout our lives against the evil and sweet pleasures of this world. For “not the one who begins, but the one who perseveres to the end, will be saved” (Mark XIII).

# THE RULE OF SAINT CAESARIUS FOR VIRGINS (C)

## TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING CAESARIUS AND HIS RULE

**Roman Martyrology, 25 August:** “At Arles, the deposition of Saint Caesarius, bishop, a man of extraordinary holiness and piety.”

**Cyprian, Book I of the Life of Saint Caesarius:**

“Meanwhile, he restored that principal monastery which he had begun to establish for his sister, making it like the former one. Like another Noah of our own time, because of the storms and tempests he built within the side of the Church of women a coenobium like an ark. He summoned from the monastery at Marseilles his venerable sister Caesaria, whom he had sent there for this very purpose, so that she might learn what she was to teach and might first be a disciple before becoming a teacher; and he introduced her, together with two or three companions, into the prepared dwelling. Many bands of virgins, renouncing their possessions and resources, and even their most beloved parents, flocked to her. They were so enclosed in that place that, until the final day of their lives, none of them was permitted to go beyond the monastery door.”

**The same, Book II, near the end:**

“Meanwhile Israel’s departure from the land of Egypt increases until its completion—that is, the migration of the holy soul from this world of bodily life. Therefore he ordered himself to be carried by the hands of attendants into the monastery of virgins that he himself had founded, as if to console the anxious women whose sleep had been taken away by the suspicion of his departure, and whose food had been taken away by forgetfulness. He addressed the venerable mother Caesaria, first among the two hundred girls, in accordance with her custom and gentleness; he consoled her, urged her to strive toward the palm of the heavenly calling, and admonished her to hold fast to the Rule that he had instituted several years before.”

**Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book IX, chapter 39; in the letter of Euphronius, Praetextatus, and the other bishops to Queen Radegund:**

“We specifically decree that if any woman from the places entrusted by God’s providence to our priestly governance should be received into your monastery in the city of Poitiers, then, according to the constitutions of the blessed lord Caesarius, bishop of Arles, she shall have no permission to depart any further [the manuscript reading is *ulterius*]. Since, as the Rule states, she appears to have entered by her own expressed will, let no one’s shameful disgrace bring into condemnation what shines forth honorably before all.”

**The same, chapter 40:**

“After this, when Radegund repeatedly sought the favor of her bishop but was unable to obtain it, moved by necessity she and the abbess whom she had appointed went to the city of Arles. There they received the Rule of Saint Caesarius and blessed Caesaria and fortified themselves under the protection of the king.”

**The same, chapter 42, in the letter of Blessed Radegund to the bishops:**

“Moreover, for the community that, by Christ’s favor, I had gathered through my efforts, I adopted the Rule under which Saint Caesaria lives—the Rule which the diligence of Blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, suitably compiled from the institutions of the holy Fathers.”

**Venantius, Book VIII, poem 1, on Saint Radegund:**

> The line of Caesarius’ Rule is known to you.

**The same, poem 4:**

> When Radegund embraces the faith of Christ in love,  
> Caesarius’ Rule embraces all that she possesses.

Saint Donatus the African also mentions this Rule in the preface to his *Collection*, as does Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, in his *Concordance of Rules*.

# CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

We have already treated Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, and his Rule for monks in its proper place. We must now discuss another Rule, given to holy virgins. The first and longer version contains forty-three chapters, besides the Recapitulation, which comprises twenty-one articles.

Saint Caesarius appears to have written this Rule after attaining the episcopate. It contains the complete discipline handed down to monks, adapted to holy virgins. Since, at the foundation of the new monastery, he was unable to set forth all the necessary precepts, he also wrote the Recapitulation, containing salutary admonitions proper to consecrated women, especially concerning food and clothing. Two final chapters were added to this Recapitulation long after Saint Caesarius’s death, having been taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict, as is noted in that place.

These remarks should be understood of the present Rule as edited by Holstenius. For Bollandus, in his *Acts of the Saints* on 12 January, presents a substantially different division of the same Rule, dividing it into twelve lengthy chapters and adding two fairly long chapters that are absent here: one containing the arrangement of the divine office, and the other concerning the regular fasts.

This different division of the chapters, however, should in no way impede the authenticity of this holy Rule, even though the two final chapters of the Recapitulation are not found in Bollandus. Holstenius recognizes that these too were taken from Saint Benedict, and both editions contain the same moral precepts and monastic admonitions, expressed in the same words and sentences. The only difference, therefore, lies in the varying division of chapters and articles.

The laws prescribed in this Rule are exceedingly beautiful and should frequently be proposed to all holy virgins of every order. They were embraced not only by Caesarius’s sister, the legislator, together with two hundred virgins, but also cultivated by other consecrated women of great renown in different places, especially Saint Radegund, who became a nun after having been queen and introduced this Rule of Saint Caesarius into her convent at Poitiers.

Holstenius also appended to this Rule an erudite sermon, as well as the letters of Saint Caesarius sent to holy virgins and the Testament of that most holy bishop. These monuments of venerable antiquity ought to be held in the highest esteem by all who cherish ecclesiastical and monastic discipline and diligently impressed upon the minds of religious persons of both sexes.

# PROLOGUE OF SAINT CAESARIUS TO THE VIRGINS

Caesarius, bishop, to the holy and most deeply venerable sisters established in the monastery which, under God’s inspiration and help, we founded.

Because the Lord, in his mercy, inspired us and deigned to help us establish a monastery for you, we have drawn up for you spiritual and holy instructions, according to the regulations of the ancient Fathers, concerning how you ought to live in that monastery, so that with God’s help you may keep them.

Residing continually in the little cell of the monastery, implore the visitation of the Son of God through constant prayers, so that afterward you may confidently say: “We have found him whom our soul sought” (Song of Songs III).

And therefore I ask you, holy virgins and souls dedicated to God, who await the Lord’s coming with burning lamps and a secure conscience: since you know that I have labored to establish a monastery for you, ask in your holy prayers that I may become the companion of your journey, so that when you happily enter the kingdom with the holy and wise virgins, your intercession may obtain that I not remain outside with the foolish. May your holiness pray for me, so that divine favor may cause me, shining among the most precious jewels of the Church, to be filled with present blessings and made worthy of eternal ones.

# CHAPTERS

1. First of all, it must be observed that no one is to leave the monastery until her death.  
2. They shall abstain from cursing and swearing.  
3. Concerning changing the habit and showing obedience.  
4. No one is to keep for herself anything she brought with her, nor give alms on her own.  
5. No little girl is to be received except from the age of six.  
6. Each one is to do not what she herself wishes, but what has been commanded her.  
7. No one is to have a private cell.  
8. No one is to speak while the psalms are being sung.  
9. No one is to take the daughter of anyone, whoever she may be, from the baptismal font.  
10. When the signal has been given, no one is to come late.  
11. What a handmaid of God ought to be when she is corrected.  
12. How the woman who has acted negligently in some matter ought to humble herself.  
13. During the vigils, care must be taken that no one sleeps.  
14. In the spinning work, each one is to receive her daily allotment of work.  
15. No one is to regard anything as her own.  
16. Obedience is to be given to the mother and superior; there is to be absolute silence at table.  
17. At all times they are to devote two hours to reading.  
18. While seated at their work, they are either to meditate on holy things or remain silent.  
19. Those who are noble are not to be puffed up by wealth or the nobility of their parents.  
20. While the psalms are being sung, what sounds on the lips is to be held in the heart.  
21. Concerning custody of the eyes.  
22. Another’s sin is not to be concealed.  
23. Nothing is to be received secretly.  
24. How those who have committed theft or laid hands upon one another are to be disciplined.  
25. Clothing is to be made under the care of the superior and distributed by the mother.  
26. The clothing of the holy nuns is to be stored in one cell.  
27. No one is to make anything privately for herself.  
28. What sort of cellarer is to be appointed and how.  
29. How they are to use the bath.  
30. What sort of superior there ought to be over the cell of the sick and how the sick are to have a separate storeroom.  
31. How she who has injured her sisters by insults, curses, or any accusations is to be disciplined.  
32. How the abbess ought to act.  
33. How the monastery’s administrators are to enter the monastery.  
34. Secular men or women are not to enter the monastery.  
35. How the abbess ought to proceed to the visitors’ room.  
36. No banquet is to be held for anyone in the monastery except for religious women arriving from other places or cities.  
37. How a handmaid of God ought to greet her parents.  
38. The abbess is never to eat outside the community except when illness requires it.  
39. Admonition or warning concerning how the abbess, the superior, or the cellarer ought to attend to the sick.  
40. The handmaids of God are not to accept anything sent by their parents without the abbess’s advice; whatever is more than necessary is to be given to those in need.  
41. How dyeing is to be done and what sort of bedding they are to have.  
42. Concerning embroidered hangings and the adornment of the monastery.  
43. Warning and recapitulation, so that nothing of the institution may be diminished.

# RULE OF SAINT CAESARIUS

[Note: The celebrated Cointius also illustrates this Rule of the nuns of Saint Caesarius with notes, in the cited work, pp. 472 ff.]

Since many regulations in monasteries of girls or of monks appear to differ, we have selected a few matters from among many, by which the elders may live regularly with the younger women and strive spiritually to fulfill whatever they have recognized as especially suited to their sex. These provisions are the first obligations appropriate to your holy souls.

## I

If any woman, having left her parents, wishes to renounce the world and enter the holy fold, so that with God’s help she may escape the jaws of spiritual wolves, she shall not leave the monastery until her death, nor even the basilica in which the door appears to be located.

## II

She shall strive to flee and avoid oaths and curses as the poison of the devil.

## III

A woman who is converted under God’s inspiration may not immediately assume the religious habit unless her will has first been tested and approved in many trials. Instead, entrusted to one of the elders, she shall remain for a full year in the habit in which she came.

As for changing that habit or having a bed in the school, the matter shall lie within the authority of the superior. According to the character and penitence that she observes, she shall strive to regulate the matter either more quickly or more slowly.

## IV

Widows, women who have left their husbands, or women who come to the monastery after changing their clothing are not to be received unless they have first made deeds, donations, or sales concerning all their property, as they choose, so that they retain nothing under their own control which they might appear to arrange or possess privately. This is in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess” (Matthew XIX), and: “If anyone does not leave everything and follow me, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV).

I say this, venerable daughters, because consecrated women who possess property cannot attain perfection. Those who are converted as virgins but refuse to fulfill this requirement are either not to be received or certainly not permitted to receive the religious clothing until they have freed themselves from all the impediments of this world.

Those, however, who cannot yet control their property because their parents are still alive, or who are still underage, shall be compelled to make deeds when they are able to control their parents’ property or have reached the lawful age.

We prescribe this to your holy souls because we fear the example of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts V), who, although they said that they had offered everything to the apostles, offered only part and unfaithfully kept part for themselves. Such conduct is neither fitting, lawful, nor expedient.

No one, not even the abbess, may keep a personal maid in her service. If she needs assistance, she may take one of the younger women for her support.

## V

If it can possibly be avoided, no little child is ever to be received into the monastery unless she is six or seven years old—already able both to learn letters and to obey. The daughters of nobles or of commoners are not to be received at all for upbringing or instruction.

## VI

No one is to choose for herself any task or craft to perform according to her own pleasure. It shall be at the superior’s discretion to command whatever she has recognized as useful.

## VII

No one may choose a separate dwelling, nor have a room, a little cupboard, or anything similar that can be locked privately. All are to remain in one cell, with their beds separated.

The old and infirm are to be accommodated and arranged in such a way that they do not each have separate cells, but are all received in one place, where they are also to remain.

## VIII

They shall never speak in a raised voice, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Let all shouting be removed from you” (Ephesians IV). Likewise, while the psalms are being sung, it is altogether forbidden to converse or work.

## IX

No one shall presume to take the daughter of anyone whatsoever, whether rich or poor, as a godchild at baptism.

## X

She who comes late, after the signal has been given, whether to the work of God [Note: “The work of God” means the canonical hours, or the divine office. It is called “the work of God” by excellence, to distinguish it from other activities that are simply called works. —Cointius, in the cited work, p. 475.] or to the work itself, shall be subject to a reprimand, as is fitting. If, after being admonished a second or third time, she refuses to correct herself, she shall be separated from communion or from the common meal.

## XI

When a woman is admonished, chastised, or rebuked for any fault, she must not presume to answer the one reproving her. Whoever refuses to fulfill any of the commands given shall, according to the seriousness of her fault, be separated from the communion of prayer or from the table [Note: “Or from the table,” according to the nature of the fault. These words clearly confirm that *vel* is to be taken disjunctively and show that two kinds of excommunication must be distinguished: one from prayer and the other from the table. —The same, in the same work.].

## XII

Those who cook are each to be given a *merus* for their labor [Note: *Meri*: *Merus* is a small vessel for wine and is frequently used in this sense in the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 27. In Stellartius, who published the same Rule at Douai in 1626, *merito* is printed erroneously for *meri*. —The same, in the cited work.].

In every bodily service—in the kitchen or in whatever the daily use of the monastery requires—they are to take turns among themselves, except for the mother and the superior.

## XIII

During the vigils, work is to be done so that no one, through idleness, becomes weighed down by sleep, and so that the mind is not withdrawn from hearing the reading. If anyone is overcome by sleep, she shall be ordered to stand while the others remain seated, so that she may drive away the torpor of sleep and not be found lukewarm or negligent in the work of God.

## XIV

In the spinning work itself, they are to receive their daily allotment with humility and strive to complete it with great diligence.

## XV

No one is to regard anything as her own, whether clothing or anything else.

## XVI

No one is to do anything with murmuring, lest she perish under the same judgment as the murmurers, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Do everything without murmuring” (Philippians II).

After God, all are to obey the mother and show deference to the superior. While seated at table, they are to remain silent and devote their minds to the reading. When the reading has ceased, holy meditation is not to cease in the heart.

If anything is needed, the woman presiding over the table shall take care of it, and what is necessary shall be requested more by a sign than by speech. Let your throats alone not take in food; let your ears also hear the word of God.

## XVII

All are to learn letters [Note: That is, they are to learn to read. —The same, in the same work, p. 477.]. At all times they are to devote two hours to reading—that is, from morning until the second hour.

## XVIII

During the rest of the day they are to perform their work and not occupy themselves with conversation, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Working in silence” (2 Thessalonians III), and: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs X).

Therefore, you are to speak only about what pertains to the edification or benefit of the soul. When the necessity of the work requires it, then let them speak. While the others are working together, one of the sisters shall read until the third hour; during the remaining time, meditation on the word of God and prayer shall not cease in the heart.

Let your soul and heart be one in the Lord, and let all things be common to you. For thus you read in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had all things in common, and each was given whatever she needed” (Acts IV).

## XIX

Those who possessed anything in the world when they entered the monastery shall humbly offer it to the mother, so that it may serve the common needs. Those who possessed nothing are not to seek in the monastery what they were unable to possess outside it.

Those who appeared to possess something in the world are not to despise their sisters who came to that holy fellowship from poverty. Nor are they to be proud of their wealth, which they offered to the monastery, as though they were enjoying it in the world.

What benefit is there in scattering one’s possessions and becoming poor by giving to the poor, if the wretched soul is puffed up by diabolical pride? Therefore, live together unanimously and harmoniously, and honor God in one another, whose temples you have deserved to become.

Devote yourselves continually to prayer, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Praying at all times, that you may be counted worthy” (Luke XXI), and the Apostle’s words: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians V).

## XX

When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let what is uttered by the voice be present in the heart. Whatever work you do, when no reading is being given, always meditate on something from the divine Scriptures.

The sick, however, are to be treated in such a way that they may recover more quickly. Once they have regained their former strength, they are to return to the happier custom of abstinence.

Your habit is not to be conspicuous; do not seek to please by your clothing, but by your conduct, as befits your profession.

## XXI

Let no desire for the eyes of any man arise among you at the devil’s instigation. Nor should you say that you possess modest minds if the eye is the messenger of an immodest heart.

A woman who turns her gaze upon a man in a way that is not simple must not think that others do not see her when she does this. She is seen precisely by those by whom she does not think herself seen. But even if she were hidden so that no human being could see her, what will she do about the heavenly observer from whom she cannot be hidden at all?

Therefore, let her fear displeasing God and take care not to please a man improperly. When you are standing together, if the monastery’s administrator or another man arrives with him, guard one another’s modesty. For God, who dwells within you, will guard you in this way also.

## XXII

If you see a woman behaving more freely than is proper, rebuke her privately as a sister. If she neglects to listen, bring the matter to the mother’s attention. Nor should they judge you malicious when you make this report with a holy intention. Rather, you are more culpable and make yourselves participants in her sin if you allow your sister, whom you could have corrected by chastising her, to perish through your silence.

If she had a wound on her body, had been bitten by a serpent, and wished to conceal it because she feared being cut, would it not be cruel to remain silent about it and merciful to disclose it? How much more, then, must you expose the devil’s counsels and his snares, lest the wound of sin grow worse in the heart and the evil of desire be nourished longer in the breast?

Do this with love for your sisters and hatred of vices.

## XXIII

If any woman—God forbid—has advanced so far in wickedness that she secretly receives letters, messages of any kind, or little gifts from someone, then, if she confesses this voluntarily, she is to deserve pardon and prayers are to be offered for her. But if she is exposed while concealing it or is convicted, she is to be corrected more severely according to the monastery’s regulations.
