She is likewise to be subject to strict discipline if she herself rashly and sacrilegiously presumes to send letters or little gifts to anyone. If, however, out of affection for her parents or in order to communicate with someone, she wishes to send some *eulogia*—a blessed gift of bread—she shall inform the mother. If the mother permits it, she may give it through the women assigned to the rear entrance [Note: We believe that this term designates the women in charge of the monastery gate. —Cointius, in the cited work, p. 478. See below, § XXVIII, where *posticium* occurs. On that passage, consult Du Cange, *Glossary of Medieval Latin*, s.v. *POSTICIUM* and *POSTICIARIA*.]. They themselves shall transmit it in her name to whomever she wishes. Without the superior or the gatekeeper, she must not presume either to give or to receive anything herself.

## XXIV

Although it ought not merely to be imagined but altogether believed that holy virgins do not wound one another with harsh words or insults, nevertheless, if by chance, as human frailty has it, some of the sisters should dare, at the devil’s instigation, to break out into such great wickedness as to commit theft or lay hands upon one another, it is just that they receive legitimate discipline, since they have violated the institutions of the Rule.

For it is necessary that the saying which the Holy Spirit spoke through Solomon concerning undisciplined children be fulfilled in them: “He who loves his son applies the rod to him continually” (Ecclesiasticus XXX); and again: “If you strike him with the rod, you will free his soul from hell” (Proverbs XXIII).

They are to receive this discipline in the presence of the community, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Rebuke sinners before all” (1 Timothy V).

## XXV

Since the mother of the monastery must be concerned for the salvation of souls, continually think about the monastery’s small resources and what is needed for bodily nourishment, show affection even to those who come to greet her, and answer the letters of all the faithful, all responsibility for spinning, from which clothing is supplied to the holy sisters, shall belong to the care of the superior or the woman in charge of the wool.

Through their diligence, all necessary clothing is to be prepared faithfully, with zeal and love of God, so that whenever the holy sisters need it, it may be distributed with holy discretion.

## XXVI

The clothing is nevertheless to be made in the monastery with such diligence that the abbess should never need to obtain it outside the monastery. It is not your concern what clothing is brought forth for you according to the season.

But if disputes and murmuring arise among you on this account, if some of you should receive something perhaps less worthy than what you had previously possessed, test yourselves by this: how much you lack in that inner, holy clothing of the heart, when you murmur about bodily clothing [Note: “When you murmur about clothing”: perhaps, “when you murmur about the clothing.”].

If your weakness is tolerated so that you have more than daily nourishment requires, nevertheless place whatever you possess in one location under a common custodian, and let your *registoria* keep the keys to your little chests or presses [Note: *Arcellis vel pressoriolis*: From *arca* come *arcula* and *arcella*. By *arcellas*, therefore, understand little boxes, cupboards, and similar storage places where food, books, clothing, and other such things are kept. —The same, in the cited work, p. 479. A *pressoriolum* means a pantry where food is stored—“where provisions are put away.” Hence perhaps its etymology: *serrer* also means “to press.” —Du Cange, cited entry, *PRESSORIOLUM*.], in your registers [Note: Bollandus, 12 January, p. 732, no. 28, reads *regestoraria*, perhaps more correctly. Du Cange explains this passage, cited entry, *REGISTORIA*: “It is an office among consecrated women to which the care of the registers, or of the monastic treasury, is entrusted.”].

## XXVII

No one is to make anything privately for herself unless the abbess has ordered or permitted it. Rather, let all your work be done in common, with the same holy zeal and ardent eagerness as if you were doing it for yourselves.

## XXVIII

For the cellar, the rear entrance, or the office of the wool, women of such a kind are to be selected by the superior that they consider, with fear of God, not the wishes of some sisters but the needs of all.

Therefore, no sister is to presume to keep or place beside her bed anything pertaining to eating or drinking. Whoever does so is to endure the severest discipline.

Above all, I adjure you before God and his angels: no sister is to buy wine secretly or receive it from any source. If wine is sent, the gatekeepers are to receive it in the presence of the abbess or superior and hand it over to the cellarers. Through the abbess’s administration, and according to the institution of the Rule, it is to be distributed to the woman to whom it was sent, in whatever manner is suitable to her illness.

Since it commonly happens that the monastery’s cellar does not always have good wine, it will be the abbess’s responsibility to provide such wine as may indulge the sick or those who have been more delicately nourished.

## XXIX

Baths are by no means to be denied to anyone whose illness requires them. They are to be taken without murmuring and on medical advice. Even if the sick woman does not wish to bathe, whatever is necessary for her health is to be done at the superior’s command.

If no illness compels it, however, her desire is not to be indulged.

## XXX

The care of the sick or of those suffering from any weakness is to be entrusted to one sufficiently faithful and penitent woman. She is to request from the cellar whatever she recognizes as necessary.

A woman is to be chosen who will both preserve the monastic discipline and serve the sick with compassion. If the needs of the sick require it, and the mother of the monastery considers it proper, the sick women may also have their own little storeroom and kitchen in common.

Those placed in charge of the cellar, wine store, clothing, books, rear entrance, or wool are to receive the keys upon the Gospel and serve the others without murmuring. If any of them should negligently use or guard clothing, footwear, utensils, or other supplies, they are to be corrected more severely as embezzlers of the monastery’s property.

XXXI. Have no quarrels, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “A servant of God ought not to quarrel” (II Tim. II); and: “Abstain from strife, and you will lessen sins” (Eccli. XXVIII). If quarrels do occur, let them be ended as quickly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred, the splinter into a beam, and the soul become murderous. For you read: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III); and: “Lifting up holy hands without anger or disputation” (I Tim. II).

Whoever has injured her sister by insult, curse, or even accusation of a crime must remember to cleanse her guilt by making satisfaction. If she presumes to repeat this fault, let her be struck with the most severe discipline until she merits being received again through satisfaction. Let the younger especially show deference to their elders.

If any sister is excommunicated for any reason, let her be removed from the congregation and reside in the place appointed by the abbess, together with one of the spiritually minded sisters, until she receives pardon through humble repentance. But if, as commonly happens, with the devil’s prompting, they injure one another, they must ask one another’s forgiveness and release one another from their obligations, for the sake of their prayers, which ought to be as much more frequent as they ought to be purer.

If the sister from whom forgiveness is sought is unwilling to forgive her sister, let her be removed from communion, and let her fear the saying: “If she does not forgive, neither will she be forgiven” (Matt. VI). A woman who never wishes to ask forgiveness, or who asks it insincerely, or one who, when forgiveness is sought from her, does not forgive, seems to be in the monastery without cause.

Therefore spare one another harsher words. If such words have been spoken, do not be reluctant to bring forth from the very mouth by which the wounds were made the remedies for them. When you who are appointed superiors are compelled by the needs of discipline to speak harsh words in order to correct bad conduct, if you should feel that even in those words you have perhaps exceeded the proper measure, you are not required to ask forgiveness; otherwise, among those who ought to be subject to you, excessive humility might weaken the authority of governance. Nevertheless, forgiveness must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with what benevolence you love even those whom you correct more severely than is just.

XXXII. Obey without murmuring the mother who cares for all of you, and the superior, lest charity in them be saddened. Those who preside over you should diligently maintain discipline and the rule with charity and true piety. In all things let them offer themselves as examples of good works (Tit. II): let them correct the restless, console the fainthearted, sustain the weak, often remembering that they will have to render an account to God for you. Thus, by obeying more holily, you will have pity not only on yourselves but also on them: for the higher they appear to be placed among you in rank, the greater is the danger in which they stand. For this reason obey with reverence and humility not only the mother but also the superior, the first-ranking or chief sister.

XXXIII. Above all, for the preservation of your reputation, let no man enter the secluded part of the monastery or the oratories, except bishops, the steward, and the priest, deacon, subdeacon, and one or two readers whose age and life commend them and who are to celebrate Mass from time to time.

When roofs need to be restored, doors or windows repaired, or anything of this kind put in order, only craftsmen and servants, if necessity requires it, may enter with the steward in order to carry out the work; but not even they without the knowledge or permission of the mother. The steward himself must never enter the inner part of the monastery except for the purposes mentioned above, and then either never, or only with difficulty, without the abbess or another most honorable witness, so that the holy women may preserve their privacy as is fitting and expedient.

XXXIV. Secular married women, girls, or other women, and men [Note: “[Col. 1113D] Or men.” These words seem intrusive. Indeed, they are absent from Bollandus, cited above, p. 733, no. 37.] who are still in lay clothing must likewise be forbidden to enter.

XXXV. Care must also be taken that the abbess does not go to those who come to greet her in the greeting room without the honor due to her—that is, without two or three sisters. Bishops, abbots, or other religious persons whose exemplary life commends them, if they request it, may enter the oratory for prayer. Care must also be taken that the monastery door be open at suitable hours for those who come to greet them.

XXXVI. You must never prepare a banquet, either in the monastery or outside it, for such persons as bishops, abbots, monks, clerics, secular men, women in secular clothing, the abbess’s relatives, or any nun whatsoever. Nor is a banquet to be provided for the bishop of this city or even for the steward of the monastery itself.

From the city, no religious woman is to be invited unless perhaps she is of exemplary conduct and one who greatly honors the monastery; and even this must happen very rarely. If, however, a woman from another city comes to seek her daughter or to visit the monastery, she should be invited to the banquet if she is religious and the abbess considers it appropriate. All others must never be invited, because holy virgins, devoted to God and more fully occupied with Christ, ought to pray for the whole people rather than prepare bodily banquets.

XXXVII. If anyone wishes to see his sister, daughter, or any relative or acquaintance, she must not be denied conversation with him in the presence of the housekeeper or any older sister.

XXXVIII. The abbess must not eat outside the community at all, unless compelled by some irregularity, illness, or duty.

XXXIX. Above all, I admonish and charge you, holy mother, and you, venerable superior, whoever you may be, and also whoever is entrusted with the care of the sick, including the first-ranking or housekeeper sister: consider most vigilantly whether there are any sisters who, because they have been more delicately raised or perhaps suffer stomach weakness more frequently, and whether there are others who cannot abstain or who fast only with great difficulty. If, because of modesty, they do not dare to ask, you must order that provisions be given to them from the storerooms, and direct them to receive them. Let them be completely confident that whatever they receive at any hour through the dispensation or command of an elder, they receive Christ in that refreshment.

Let the storekeeper and the woman who is to serve the sick be charged before God and his angels with the greatest concern and diligence for the sick. I also admonish you that, because of excessive disturbance, daily or continual almsgiving is not to be practiced at the monastery gate. Rather, whatever God has granted that can remain for the monastery’s needs, let the abbess arrange through the steward to be distributed to the poor.

XL. Above all, care must be taken that if anyone gives or sends clothing or anything else to her daughter or to someone related to her, it is not received secretly. For this reason I charge all who attend the back entrance, before God and his angels, not to permit anything to be given from the monastery or to allow anything from outside to be received into the monastery contrary to the abbess’s conscience or counsel.

If the abbess is occupied with visitors, as commonly happens, let the women in charge of the back entrance show the superior whatever has been brought. If they neglect to fulfill this duty, both those who permit such things and those who receive them will not only undergo the monastery’s most severe discipline; they must also know that, because of their transgression of the holy rule, they will have to answer with me before God.

If what has been sent is needed by the recipient for her own use, let her keep it. If she has no need of it, let it be brought into common use and given to the one who needs it, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Whoever has two tunics should give to one who has none” (Luke III). When they receive new clothing, if they have no need of the old clothing, let them return the old to the abbess, so that it may be distributed to the poor, beginners, or younger sisters.

All clothing must be of a simple and decent color: never black, never glossy, but only grayish or milk-colored [Note: “[Col. 1115D] Grayish or milk-colored.” “Grayish,” or “milk-colored,” opposed by Bollandus, cited above, to glossy, is the color of milk. Milk is white; white, however, is associated with pallor, while glossy or bright is associated with splendor. Cointet, cited above, p. 482.]. In the monastery they are to be made through the industry of the superior or the diligence of the wool-worker, and distributed by the mother of the monastery according to what is reasonably necessary for each person.

XLI. No dyeing is to be done in the monastery except, as stated above, grayish and milk-colored dyeing, because no other kind is suitable for the humility of virgins. The bed coverings themselves must be simple, for it is most unbecoming if secular blankets or painted carpets shine upon a religious bed. Do not have silver in your use, except for the service of the oratory.

XLII. Embroidery, needlework, every kind of multicolored fabric, blankets, and ornamentation must never be made in the monastery. The ornaments themselves must also be simple in the monastery, never embroidered, never silk; and nothing else is to be added to them except crosses, either black or milk-colored, made only in plain stitching from scraps of cloth or linen [Note: “[Col. 1115D] In plain stitching.” Plain stitching is so called from *sarsura*, and the word *sarsura*, used by Varro in *On Agriculture*, book III, chapter 9, derives from *sarcio*, “I mend”; for the ancients said *sartum* and *sarsum*. See Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XXIV, chapter 22. Plain stitching is therefore simple work containing nothing beyond the tailor’s hand. Id., cited above, p. 483.].

For no waxed curtains are to be hung, no painted panels attached, and no painting of any kind is to be made on the walls or ceilings, because the monastery ought to contain what pleases not merely human eyes but spiritual eyes. If any ornaments are contributed either by you or by another of the monastery’s faithful supporters, they are to be sold for the monastery’s needs, or, if necessary, assigned to the basilica of Saint Mary.

Needlework is never to be done except on small napkins and face-cloths [Note: “[Col. 1116D] On small napkins and face-cloths.” A *mappula* is a small napkin with which we wipe the nose. Cangius, *Glossary*, s.v. MAPPULA. Face-cloths are distinguished from napkins by their name, which derives from wiping the face. A *facitergium*, like a hand-towel, is so called from wiping the face or hands, says the author of the Arabic-Latin Glossary. Cointet, cited above, p. 483.], wherever the abbess has ordered it.

None of you may, without the abbess’s order, undertake to receive the clothing of clerics, laymen, relatives, or any men or women from outside, whether for washing, sewing, storing, or dyeing, lest through this careless familiarity, hostile to propriety, the reputation of the monastery be damaged. Whoever refuses to observe this must be disciplined by the monastery as though she had committed a crime.

XLIII. You, holy and venerable mother of the monastery, and you, superior of the holy community, I admonish and charge before God and his angels that no threats, slanders, or flatteries ever soften your resolve so that you lessen anything from the institution of the holy and spiritual rule. Yet I trust in God’s mercy that you may not incur guilt through any negligence, but may happily attain eternal blessedness through holy obedience pleasing to God.

## Recapitulation

[Col. 1115]

[Col. 1115D] When, with God’s favor, we made a rule for you at the beginning of the monastery’s establishment, we afterward added or removed something there on many occasions. For, examining and testing what you could fulfill, we have now defined what was consistent with reason, possibility, and holiness.

As far as we could determine through careful experience, the rule itself has been tempered by God’s inspiration so that, with God’s help, you may keep it in its entirety. Therefore we charge you before God and his angels that nothing in it be changed or diminished further.

For this reason, whatever earlier documents we may have made, we wish to be considered void. But this document, in which I have written the *Recapitulation* in my own hand, I ask and admonish you to fulfill faithfully and successfully, without any reduction, with God’s help. Continually implore God’s assistance, lest the ancient enemy hinder you by his poisonous counsel—the enemy who is accustomed to drag those who consent to him from the very summit of heaven down into the depths of hell.

Therefore, holy and venerable daughters, I admonish you to strive with every strength and the most vigilant concern to repel his suggestions. Run with God’s help in such a way that you may obtain the prize (II Cor. VI), because “it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end, who will be saved” (Matt. XXIV).

Although I believe that your holy devotion both remembers what has been written above and, with Christ’s help, strives to fulfill it not only faithfully but also successfully, nevertheless, so that what we have established may cling more firmly to your holy hearts, we wish this little *Recapitulation*, which I have written in my own hand, to be made. I ask that, with God’s inspiration, you willingly receive it and continually strive to keep it with God’s help.

I. This is what we particularly wish you to observe without any reduction: that none of you be permitted, or presume on her own, to leave the monastery until her death, or to leave the basilica itself in which you have your door.

II. No one is to have a private cell; no one is to maintain secret familiarity or any kind of association with either religious or lay people, whether men or women.

III. No one is to be permitted to speak alone with a man who is alone, even for a moment. Nor may she receive their clothing for washing, dyeing, safekeeping, or sewing. And, as we established in the rule itself, she must not dare secretly to send anything from inside to outside or receive anything from outside inside.

IV. No one is to possess anything of her own outside, have anything of her own inside, or reserve anything for her own disposal. Rather, as we said above, she must be freed from every impediment by making written dispositions to whomever she wishes. For the Lord says: “If anyone does not renounce all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). And: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. XVI).

If she has been commanded to deny herself, with what face does she presume to reserve for herself anything among the impediments of this world? Should she not rather tremble at what is written, that the impediments of the world have made us miserable? Attend carefully also to the Apostle’s saying: “I wish you to be without anxiety” (I Cor. VII). Observing these things faithfully, let her say with a clear conscience: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI). And: “I have counted everything as refuse, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. III).

V. No banquet is to be prepared for the bishop of this city, or of another city, or for any man, as we established in this rule.

VI. No letters from anyone, not even relatives, are to be received secretly, nor are letters of any kind to be sent to anyone without the abbess’s permission.

VII. I particularly admonish you that, as we have already said, you never use glossy or black clothing, or clothing with purple or beaver fur, but only grayish and milk-colored clothing. Never bind your heads higher than the measurement we made here with wax. Let them perform all work in common.

VIII. Whenever a woman comes for conversion, let the rule frequently be read to her in the greeting room. If she declares with a ready and free will that she will fulfill all the rule’s institutions, let her remain there as long as the abbess considers it just and reasonable. But if she says that she cannot fulfill the rule, let her not be received at all.

IX. The monastery door must never be made outside the basilica with your will or permission. It must never be open in the evening, at night, or at midday, although at those hours when food is taken the abbess is to keep the keys with her.

X. I charge before God the abbess herself of the holy community, who is permitted neither to possess anything nor to have anything personal, to provide, as far as possible, what is necessary for her sisters.

XI. Embroidery, ornamentation, purple clothing, and every kind of multicolored fabric must never be made in the monastery, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II).

XII. Whenever the holy abbess departs to God, let none of you, through carnal affection, consideration of birth, or family relationship, wish to make the choice less effective. Rather, with Christ’s inspiration, choose unanimously a holy woman; let none of you wish any woman to be made less effective through carnal affection, consideration of birth, or family relationship. Choose one who can effectively keep the monastery’s rule and can wisely give answers to visitors with edification, compunction, and holy affection. Thus all those who seek you with great faith and reverence for their own edification may bless God more abundantly and rejoice spiritually both in your election and in the conduct of the woman whom you elect.

XIII. Although, holy daughters, venerable to me in our one charity in Christ, I am confident in the obedience of your holy devotion, nevertheless, because of my paternal concern, since I desire you to be like the angels, I ask you again and again, and charge you by almighty God, not to permit anything to be diminished from the institution of the holy rule, but to labor with all your strength, with the Lord’s help, to preserve it.

Know that each person will receive her own reward according to her labor (I Cor. III). Above all I ask that your holiness not receive our admonition casually. We do not speak out of presumption, but, in accordance with what is read in the canonical Scriptures and is abundantly contained in the books of the ancient Fathers, we admonish you for your salvation with great affection and true charity.

You read that whoever neglects even one of the least commandments will be called least in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V). Do not despise the words of our humility as insignificant, because it is written: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X); and: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Eccli. XIX).

For just as in any carnal contest each person will be all the more humiliated the more a lesser and weaker person overcomes him, so in spiritual combat the saying that is written will be fulfilled in the one who is negligent in small matters: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James II).

Thinking of this with great fear and even trembling, while my heart is anxious lest any minor sins creep upon you, I not only admonish but also entreat and charge you. With great affection of charity I adjure you: may I deserve to see you all come without shame to that eternal blessedness, to the company of the angels and all the saints; may I see you happily receive crowns of glory with holy Mary and all the other virgins; and may I see you follow the heavenly Lamb. Therefore strive with all your heart and soul to fulfill the commands set out above, through which you may happily attain eternal rewards.

XIV. There is one further matter which I neither believe will happen nor believe that God in his mercy will permit. If at any time any abbess attempts to alter or relax anything in the institution of this rule, or wishes to maintain subjection or familiarity with the bishop of this city on account of family ties or any other circumstance, then, with God’s inspiration, resist her in this matter with reverence and seriousness by our permission, and do not permit this to be done for any reason. Rather, with the Lord’s help, strive in all things to fortify yourselves according to the sacred [ordinance or authority] of the most holy pope of the city of Rome.

Above all, however, I charge you concerning the *Recapitulation* written and subscribed by my own hand: let nothing whatsoever be diminished from it. Any abbess or superior who attempts to do anything contrary to the institution of the holy rule must know that she will have to answer with me before Christ’s tribunal.

If, God forbid, there should be among our daughters someone so stubborn in spirit that she scorns to fulfill this *Recapitulation* of the rule, written beneficially and according to the institution of the holy Fathers, remove her from the assembly of your holy community, inflamed with zeal for the Holy Spirit. Let her remain separated in the cell of the greeting room until, doing worthy penance, she humbly asks forgiveness. Let her not return inside until she has corrected herself according to the rule’s institutions.

We say this because we must fear that, while the negligence of one woman is tolerated and she is not corrected according to the rule, others who might have advanced will be corrupted. But we trust in God’s mercy that, while you conduct yourselves holily and correct those who are negligent with true charity, you may come together happily to eternal rewards, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

XV. From Pentecost until the Kalends of September, let the mother of the monastery regulate the fast according to the strength and ability she observes. From the Kalends of September until the Kalends of November, fasting is to be observed on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. From the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, fasting is required on every day except feast days and Saturday. Before Epiphany, there are to be seven days of fasting. From Epiphany until the week of Lent, fasting is to be observed on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. On the Nativity of the Lord and on Epiphany, there is to be a vigil from the third hour of the night until daylight.

XVI. We have also believed that the order of meals should be inserted into this rule. On all days of fasting, three foods are to be prepared; at midday, only two. On the greater feast days, additional dishes are to be added at midday and in the evening, and sweet foods are to be added for those leaving the meal.

On ordinary days, at midday in summer they are to receive two small kettles, and at midday in winter two small kettles; at the refreshment they are to receive three small kettles, while two small kettles suffice at the evening meal. The younger sisters are to receive two at midday, two in the evening, and two at the refreshment.

XVII. Chickens are to be provided only to the sick; they are never to be served in the community. No woman is ever to eat meat at all. If someone should happen to be in desperate illness, she may receive it at the command of the provident abbess.

XVIII. Finally, most pious sisters, I entreat and beseech you before the Lord God to repay this grace forever to my humility and to your holy mothers—that is, to the founders of the rule and the monastery—that the intercession of your charity may watch over us day and night. May the prayer of your holiness obtain, through public prayer, the daily solemnities, or the nocturnal vigils, that when your supplication ascends before the Lord, he may deem me worthy to be a bishop of his Church, and may deem and grant them worthy to be superiors in the service of holy virgins.

When we begin to render an account before his tribunal for the talents entrusted to us, if there are any faults or negligences—whether mine in caring for the Church or those of your mothers toward those entrusted to them—may the Lord, through your intercession, deign to forgive us and heal the wounds of our faults with the medicine of remission. For faults are not corrected unless he forgives them through the prayers of the saints, nor does he forgive them unless they have been corrected.

XIX. Because, for the protection of the monastery, I have closed and sealed certain doors, whether in the old baptistery, the school, the weaving room, or the tower beside the orchard, no one should ever presume to open them under any pretext of usefulness. Rather, it is permitted to the holy community to resist and not permit anything to be done that they recognize as unsuitable for their reputation or peace.

*(These last two chapters are not by Saint Caesarius, but appear to have been added later by someone else to the Recapitulation from the Rule of Saint Benedict.)*

[Col. 1121]

XX. Let the monastery’s storekeeper be chosen from the community: a wise woman, mature in conduct, sober, not excessively bold, not haughty, not turbulent, not abusive, not wasteful, but fearing God; and let her be like a mother to the entire community and care for everyone.

Let her do nothing without the abbess’s order; let her safeguard whatever is commanded to her; let her not sadden the sisters. If a sister happens to ask her for something unreasonable, let her not sadden her by rejecting her contemptuously, but let her reasonably and humbly refuse the improper request.

Let her guard her soul, always remembering the apostolic saying that whoever ministers well acquires for herself a good standing (I Tim. III). Let her care with every concern for the sick, children, guests, and poor, knowing without doubt that she will render an account for all these things on the day of judgment.

Let her regard all the monastery’s vessels and its entire property as though they were consecrated vessels of the altar. Let her consider nothing negligible. Let her neither pursue greed nor be wasteful, destroying the monastery’s property, but let her do everything in measured fashion and according to the abbess’s order. Above all, let her possess humility.

When there is no property to distribute, let her offer a good answer, as it is written: “A good word is better than the best gift” (Eccli. VIII). Let her keep under her care everything the abbess has entrusted to her; let her not presume to handle anything from which the abbess has forbidden her.

Let her offer the sisters their allotted ration without any word or delay, so that they may not be scandalized, remembering the divine saying concerning what is deserved by one who causes one of the little ones to stumble (Matt. VIII). If the community is larger, let assistants be given to her so that she may be helped, and let her herself fulfill the duty entrusted to her with an even spirit.

Let what is to be given be given at the proper hours, and let what is to be requested be requested at the proper hours, so that no one is disturbed or saddened in the house of God.

XXI. Let an elderly and wise sister be placed at the monastery gate, one who knows how to receive and give an answer, whose maturity will not permit her to wander about. The gatekeeper must have a cell beside the gate, so that those who come may always find her present and receive an answer from her.

As soon as someone knocks or a poor person calls out, let her answer, “Thanks be to God,” and bless with every gentleness born of fear, giving an answer promptly, with the speed and fervor of charity. If the gatekeeper needs assistance, let her take a younger sister.

Amen.

[Col. 1121D]

## SERMON OF SAINT CAESARIUS TO THE NUNS (C, S)

Rejoice and exult in the Lord, venerable daughters, and continually render abundant thanks to him who has deigned to draw and summon you from the darkness of this world’s way of life to the harbor of peace and religious devotion. Continually consider from where you have come and where you have deserved to arrive. You have faithfully abandoned the world’s darkness and have happily begun to behold the light of Christ. You have despised the fire of lust and have reached the refreshment of chastity. You have rejected gluttony and chosen abstinence. [Col. 1122A]

You have rejected avarice and luxury, and have maintained chastity and mercy. And although the struggle will not be absent from you until the end of life, nevertheless, with God granting it, we are confident of your victory.

But I beg you, venerable daughters: just as you are confident regarding the past, so be solicitous concerning the future. For all crimes and sins quickly return upon us if they are not daily conquered by good works. Hear the Apostle Peter saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking something to devour” (1 Peter 5). As long as we live in this body, let us fight against the devil day and night, with Christ as our helper and guide.

There are some—what is worse—who are negligent and lukewarm, who glory merely in the name of Christianity and think that it is enough for them to have changed their clothing and assumed only the habit of religious life. [Col. 1122B]

They do not know the prophetic saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2). Nor do they consider the Psalmist’s declaration: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult ways” (Psalm 16); or what the Apostle said: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14).

We can put off secular clothing and assume religious clothing in a single hour; but we must labor, with Christ as our helper, to retain good habits continually and to resist the evil and sweet pleasures of this world for as long as we live, because “not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24).

[Col. 1122C]

First, therefore, every soul that desires to preserve religious life should strive with the whole strength of faith to overcome the desire for gluttony and avoid drunkenness. Let her take care to maintain a measured meal and a moderate table, so that her flesh is neither weakened by excessive abstinence nor provoked to luxury by an abundance of delicacies.

Next, having cast away pride, which God resists, let her lay the foundation of profound humility. Let her detest and flee envy as viperous poison; let her restrain her tongue and reject detraction as poison. Let her neither utter idle words herself nor willingly admit into her ears words spoken by others.

Let her become accustomed to having clothing neither excessively poor nor conspicuously splendid or dangerously elegant. Let her either read frequently herself or receive the words of the reader with the full eagerness of her heart.

[Col. 1122D]

From the divine springs of the Scriptures let her continually draw the water of salvation—namely, that of which the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7). From the flowers of paradise—that is, from the meanings of the sacred Scriptures—let the holy soul continually strive to adorn herself; from them let her unceasingly hang precious pearls from her ears; from them let her fashion rings and bracelets for herself while she performs good works. There let her seek medicines for wounds, aromas of chastity, and holocausts of compunction.

[Col. 1123A]

But she who desires to preserve religious life with an undefiled heart and a pure body should either never go out in public or go out only for a grave and unavoidable necessity. Please, do not give anyone an opportunity or grant anyone familiarity. She who desires, with Christ’s help, to conquer lust must avoid familiarity; and she who does not reject unworthy familiarity will quickly destroy either herself or another.

But perhaps someone says: “I do not avoid familiarity because I want to have something to conquer, and I wish to hold my adversary captive.” See to it that the adversary does not begin to rebel against you; see to it that this captivity does not lead you away captive. Hear the Apostle saying: “Flee fornication” (1 John 6). Against the remaining vices we must resist with every strength; against lust, however, it is not expedient to fight, but to flee. Be, therefore, a fugitive from lust if you wish to be an outstanding fighter for chastity.

[Col. 1123B]

But attend carefully to what I have said. When some woman is alone and is stirred by the impulses of lust, with Christ’s help let her resist it as much as she can, since she has nowhere to flee. But when, through the companionship of another person, the devil supplies an opportunity for pleasure, let the holy soul, as much as she can, avoid that very familiarity, as we have said.

But so that we may be able to preserve all these things, let us maintain reasonable abstinence, for this is the true saying of that most holy man: “As you restrain your belly, so also restrain its poisonous movements.” Let us also preserve true humility as much as we can. For bodily integrity does not long remain where the mind is corrupted by the swelling of pride; especially if the flame of anger rises frequently, it quickly consumes the flowers of chastity and virginity.

[Col. 1123C]

A chaste soul devoted to God should not maintain familiarity not only with strangers but even with her own parents. If the vessels offered to the Church, to be placed upon the holy altars, are called holy by everyone, and if it is forbidden for them afterward to be taken back from the church into a lay household or adapted to human uses, consider what dignity before God belongs to the soul created in his image.

Therefore, just as holy vessels destined for human uses neither can nor should be taken back from the church, so it is not fitting, proper, or expedient for any religious woman to become entangled in many obligations to her parents or to be bound by the harmful familiarity of any outsiders.

[Col. 1123D]

Above all I admonish you to flee the evil of rivalry as viperous poison, and to preserve among yourselves the sweetness of charity in such a way that you may prepare spiritual medicines for one another through holy conversations. For there are some—what is worse—who, whenever they come together, inflict wounds upon one another by slandering each other or murmuring against their superiors, rather than preparing spiritual medicines.

But you, holy and venerable daughters: if you see someone fainthearted, offer her consolation; if you see someone becoming proud, apply the medicine of humility; if you see someone angry, administer the refreshment of patience. If you were born noble, rejoice more in the humility of religious life than in worldly dignity.

[Col. 1124A]

Hold your hands firmly to the plow, therefore, and do not look back (Luke 9). Remember Lot’s wife (Luke 17), who, looking back, was turned into a pillar of salt.

Never let an oath, never a curse, proceed from a virgin’s mouth. Guard not only your bodies but also your hearts with every care, because it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4); and because the Lord said in the Gospel: “For from the heart come evil thoughts” (Matthew 15). If nothing evil is conceived in the heart, whatever is holy is uttered from the mouth, because, as it is written: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matthew 12). The tongue is accustomed to utter what the conscience has supplied from the workshop of the heart. Therefore, if you wish to utter good things from your mouth, always think in your heart about what is holy.

[Col. 1124B]

You should devote yourselves to reading and prayer in such a way that, above all, you are also able to work with your hands, according to what the Apostle says: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3). Dedicate the better part of the day to holy work; become accustomed to giving time to reading.

Let your prayer proceed from the heart in silence, so that it is scarcely heard by the mouth. For whoever wishes to pray in a loud voice greatly harms both himself and another, since by his chatter he distracts another person’s mind from holy and secret prayer.

Despise and reject splendid garments, which serve not usefulness but vanity. For many display in their works what they love in their character: they prepare secular ornaments for themselves because they love the world and serve pleasure or luxury. Let nothing be shared between you and such people; rather, let all ornaments by which the flesh is arranged for luxury be rejected as hostile and contrary to your purpose.

[Col. 1124C]

There are some—what is worse—who, for the sake of this world’s vanity, take greater pains to pursue earthly desires than divine reading and righteousness. They wish to prepare beautiful coverings, decorated tapestries, embroidered hangings, and other things of this sort, with enormous expense and superfluous expenditure, to gratify the eyes. They do not know what the Lord cries out and says through the evangelist John: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the world” (2 John 2).

What does it profit a virgin to guard the integrity of her body if she is unwilling to avoid the desires of the eyes?

[Col. 1124D]

But you, holy souls worthy of God, do everything spiritually. Follow Christ, perseveringly holding to what you ardently desired. Again and again, holy souls devoted to God, I beg you and, with all humility, give you counsel for preserving the reward of virginity: strive with all your strength to drive inappropriate familiarity away from yourselves and from your souls.

For, in preserving the dignity of holy religious life, holy singleness is the most sacred witness. When anyone’s familiarity begins to become frequent, it sows nothing but corruption, makes vices sprout, conceives lust, gives birth to disgrace, rouses rage, feeds wantonness, nourishes insolence, exalts falls, builds ruins, purchases confusion, stores up reproach, magnifies accusation, inflames excuses, and heaps all these things together in a crowd and a single bundle.

[Col. 1125A]

For if a holy soul wishes to guard her secret and flees the evil of familiarity continually with the whole strength of her spirit, that holy singleness is for her an unconquerable defense of sanctity, a strong assault against infamy, an exercise of self-control, an emptying out of luxury, a secure peace of the virtues, and an unquiet attack upon battles; the summit of purity and the prison of lust; the harbor of honor and the shipwreck of disgrace; the mother of virginity and the enemy of uncleanness; the dignity of integrity and the rejection of fornication; the will to perform good works and the affliction of vices; the refreshment of modesty; the acquisition of triumphs and the loss of crimes; the rest of salvation and the exile of perdition; the life of the spirit and the death of the flesh.

[Col. 1125B]

All these evils will be strongly repelled, with God’s help, and those goods we have mentioned will happily be acquired if disordered familiarity is rejected by holy souls.

Pay attention, holy souls, because among all the struggles that Christian warfare always entails, the battles of chastity alone are harder: there the fight is daily and victory rare. The battles of chastity are hard, but its rewards are greater. No one safely receives the palm of chastity, for its outcomes are as difficult as its fruits are glorious.

Therefore, so that you may happily receive the rewards of chastity and the crown of virginity, with God as your rewarder, always exclude dangerous familiarity from yourselves. Run faithfully so that you may arrive happily, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Column 1125]

[LETTERS (C, S)]

THE FIRST LETTER OF SAINT CAESARIUS TO CAESARIA, ABBESS, AND HER COMMUNITY

[Column 1125C]

You compelled me, servant of God and venerable sister in Christ, and by frequent petitions you extorted from me—rather than asked—that I should write you some sort of exhortatory discourse. This is not because I can contribute anything to your knowledge or perfection, but because in it you may easily detect my foresight. I delayed doing what you asked for a long time and with great reluctance, fearing that I would incur the reproach both of boastfulness and of shamelessness, especially since I know that you devote yourself to the divine books in constant meditation and are entirely ignorant of nothing pertaining to your perfection.

[Col. 1125D]

But what am I to do? I dare not refuse what I cannot fulfill. Such faith and authority accompany your asking and commanding, and such perseverance in extorting this from me, that refusing you anything would seem irreligious. Nevertheless, if you promise that you will not read this to anyone else or publish it for others to read, I will do what you urge, insofar as God grants me strength.

You must pardon me if I cannot worthily fulfill the work imposed upon me; rather, the responsibility must be attributed to you, since you commanded me to undertake it. Let us therefore apply ourselves to the proposed work, removed from rashness and free from pride; nor let us despair because of the mediocrity of our talent, which we believe will be assisted through the merit of your prayer.

I want this, however, to be known: I have determined to write you nothing except what can instruct you in the standard of a perfect life and in the correction of conduct, [Column 1126A] which can place the world beneath the feet of the exposed blessedness of virginity [sic]. Let those who desire praise write such things at its feet; we must travel by a very different road.

Therefore, let your first study and first concern be to know the will of your Lord and to inquire carefully what pleases him and what displeases him, so that you may render God a reasonable service according to God. For it can happen that someone offends in his desire to serve because he has not first learned how he ought to serve.

Among all God’s commandments, the general command concerns justice, because no one is permitted to transgress what has been commanded to everyone. Concerning virginity it is said: “Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matthew 19:12). But “everyone who does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10). The Savior comprehended this fully, though briefly, in the Gospel, saying: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Luke 6:31).

[Col. 1126B]

Having therefore followed the counsel of perfection, take care not to look back, but save your soul on the mountain (Genesis 17). Since you desire to climb toward life, you must proceed along the narrow path of that way, abandoning the broad expanse and greatest pomp of the world. You who wish to display yourself as an apostolic virgin in body, prepare your lamp, lit with the oil of good works, to meet the bridegroom, always considering the things that belong to the Lord.

[Col. 1126C]

What must the perfection be whose beginning was such? Every work is carried out more easily when its beginning is continually renewed. Although every perfect person desires to depart and be with Christ, in this life it is necessary never to cease struggling against vices if one wishes to carry away a triumph over the enemy.

First, then, one must fight vigorously against the disease of pride, so that, once the root and head of the vices has been torn out, the other vices that arise from it may be more easily eradicated. For there is no easier fall toward ruin than that of which Scripture says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15). Rightly so, because just as it is the origin of all crimes, so it is the enemy of all virtues. In sin it is first, and in combat it is last. It either prostrates the mind through sin at the beginning, or finally casts it down from the virtues. Hence it is also the greatest of all sins, because through both virtues and vices it destroys the human mind.

[Col. 1126D]

Often, from the fault of pride, one proceeds to the abominable uncleanness of the flesh, because one thing depends upon the other. For just as through pride of mind one proceeds to the prostitution of lust, so through humility of mind the chastity of the flesh is preserved. But God sometimes casts down hidden pride of mind through an evident ruin of the flesh.

The devil chiefly exercises dominion over the human race through these two vices: pride of mind and luxury of the flesh. Therefore the Lord speaks about the devil to Job, saying: “He sleeps under the shade, in the secrecy of reeds and in damp places” (Job 40:16). By “reeds” empty pride is signified; by “damp places,” the luxury of the flesh. Through these two vices, as we have said, the devil possesses the human race, either lifting up the mind through pride or consuming the flesh through luxury.

[Col. 1127A]

One must fight against luxury with strong exertion, because the enemy is enclosed within. “All the devil’s strength against men is in the loins, and against women his power is in the navel of his belly,” as it is written (Job 40:11). Whoever does not restrain the pleasure of a lustful suggestion quickly passes to consent to lust. For the person who does not yield to tickling pleasure easily resists the act.

Although the intention of God’s saints remains unshaken in the love of God, they nevertheless endure many inward battles because of the flesh they carry outwardly. But God, who permits these things for testing, does not abandon his own when grace protects them. Therefore fornications must be removed from the heart, so that they do not burst forth into action.

[Col. 1127B]

Hence it is said through the prophet: “Gird your loins over your breasts” (Isaiah 32:12)—that is, cut away lusts in the heart. When, through the instigation of demons, the mind of each righteous person is obstructed, let the fear of divine judgment and eternal torments be placed before the eyes, because fear of the more severe punishment overcomes every other pain. For just as a nail drives out a nail, so remembrance of the fire of Gehenna excludes the heat of luxury.

Hear what the Lord acknowledges concerning the devil, saying: “He stiffens his tail like a cedar” (Job 40:12). His first suggestion is easily cut off like tender grass; but if he once fixes the tooth of pleasure, it hardens like a cedar.

[Col. 1127C]

Fleeing especially a feigned humility, pursue the humility that is true, which Christ taught and in which pride is not enclosed. Many pursue the shadow of this virtue, but few pursue its reality. True humility is shown by patience under injury.

Never let your soul be inflamed with anger, because “the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). If it inflames you even slightly, you must hasten to drive it out.

Let envy find no place in your soul. This is a very evil thing: when someone becomes worse because of another’s good, for from the very thing by which the good person advances, the envious person withers. It is difficult for anyone to receive medicine for this disease if she does not wish to reveal the fault. Confession of it is rare, because one thing is often said instead of another; and therefore one never reaches salvation. Concerning this the blessed Cyprian wrote to the people.

[Col. 1127D]

Place a sufficiently vigilant guard over your mouth. No one contracts the stain of sin more easily than through the tongue, as the Apostle James testifies: “No human being can tame the tongue” (James 3:8). Hence he piously admonishes, saying: “If anyone thinks he is religious but does not restrain his tongue, deceiving his own heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1:26).

According to the judgment of the wisest Solomon: “The one who releases water is the beginning of quarrels” (Proverbs 17:14), because whoever does not restrain the tongue destroys concord. Hence the Apostle declares that the one who does not offend in speech is perfect.

But many, while indiscriminately observing silence, withhold what could benefit their neighbors through speech. While they observe the vices of those whom they could correct through verbal admonition, while they fortify the barriers of their mouths, they abandon their neighbor in wickedness, so that they may be judged more severely; and to the extent that they could have benefited many through speech, to that same extent they are guilty through the fault of silence.

[Col. 1128A]

Prayer is hindered in two ways, so that it cannot obtain what is requested: either when someone is still committing evil, or when someone does not forgive an offense committed against her. Once a person has cleansed these two evils from herself, she immediately applies herself confidently to the practice of prayer and freely raises her mind toward what she desires to obtain through prayers.

As far as you are able, take care not to remember the face of a man except in pure prayer, lest through an impure desire you make an idol in your soul. A king’s wife does not turn toward servants, and Christ’s bride does not look upon mortals, because she loves the one who suffered for her and embraces him with her whole love.

[Col. 1128B]

Look upon the faces of priests and Levites with fear—namely, those who have been tested—knowing this: that the love of charity dwells in them. Let your soul not delight in the sweet voice of a reader through desire, lest your senses be corrupted and depart from chastity.

Perhaps you will say: “The labor is great.” But consider what has been promised. Consider, I beg you, the greatness of your reward, if it can be considered at all, and picture before your eyes the future recompense for your present hardship.

After the soul’s departure and the destruction of the flesh, you, virgin, are to be restored to a better state; your body, entrusted to the earth, is to be raised in heaven. After this you are to be granted the company of angels, to receive the kingdom of heaven, and to remain with Christ forever.

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME WOMEN

[Column 1128C]

Caesarius, bishop, the least servant of all the servants of God, sends eternal salvation in Christ to Caesaria, holy sister and abbess, and to her entire community.

I fear, venerable daughters in Christ, that, while I presume to offer you some advice in rustic and unlearned language for the preservation of tranquility or chastity, I may seem, among those who do not know how great is the power of true charity, to incur the charge of presumption. For although I am conscious of my sins and not unaware of your purity, I nevertheless presume, sluggish as I am, to admonish the fervent; slow and negligent, to urge on those who are running; weak, to give counsel to the healthy; and, remaining on the road, to summon you to desire the eternal homeland. And because I cannot visit you more frequently, as your holy vow requires, I have taken care, with devout humility, to send this little admonition in place of my presence. I have inserted in it a few chapters from the ancient Fathers and seasoned the barrenness of my understanding, as it were, with the pleasantness of strong men. But, as I said, charity itself imposes this presumption upon me, for it knows not how to fear. Therefore I beg you, venerable daughters, to forgive my boldness, receive patiently and kindly whatever I may suggest, and, out of consideration for my rusticity and modesty, read my exhortation in private, attributing it to no one else, lest the ears of some learned person be offended by the roughness of our most rustic speech.

For although, God being propitious, I entertain no unfavorable thought concerning your most holy way of life, nevertheless, because of the many snares of the enemy—of whom it is said, “He has a thousand names, a thousand arts of harming”—because, then, of his poisonous cunning and evil blandishments, we admonish your holy conscience with whatever words we can, even if they are lukewarm; and although we are poorly equipped soldiers, we provide you with spiritual weapons against the fiery arrows of the devil. [Col. 1128D]

Rejoice, therefore, and exult in Christ, venerable daughters, and continually give abundant thanks to him who has deigned to draw and summon you from the dark way of life of this age to the harbor of tranquility and religious devotion. Constantly consider from where you have come and where you have deserved to arrive. You have faithfully abandoned the darkness of the world and have happily begun to see the light of Christ. You have despised the fire of lust and reached the refreshment of chastity. You have rejected gluttony and chosen abstinence. You have repudiated avarice and luxury and held fast to charity and mercy.

And although the struggle will not be lacking for you until the end of life, nevertheless, with God’s gift, we are confident of your victory. But I beg you, venerable daughters, to be as concerned about the future as you are secure concerning the past. For all crimes and sins quickly return upon us if they are not daily conquered by good works.

Hear the apostle Peter saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5). As long as we live in this body, with Christ as helper and guide, let us fight against the devil day and night.

There are some—what is worse—who are negligent and lukewarm, who glory only in the name of Christianity and think it sufficient for them to have changed their clothing and merely assumed the habit of religion, not knowing the prophetic saying: “My son, if you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2:1). Nor do they consider the Psalmist’s statement: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult ways” (Psalm 16:4). Nor what the Apostle said: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14:22).

For we can put off secular clothing and assume religious clothing in an instant; but we must continually retain good habits and, with Christ’s help, labor throughout our lives against the seductive pleasures of this age. For “not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). [Col. 1129A]

First, therefore, let every soul that desires to preserve religion strive with the full strength of faith to conquer the desire for gluttony and avoid drunkenness, and let it weaken the banquet at table through the moderation of abstinence, so that it is not provoked to luxury by an abundance of delicacies.

Next, after casting aside pride, which God resists, let it lay the foundations of profound humility. Let it detest and flee envy as viperous poison; let it restrain the tongue; let it reject slander as poison; let it neither utter idle words nor willingly admit words uttered by another into its ears. Let it become accustomed to wearing clothing that is neither excessively mean nor excessively splendid or dangerously elegant.

Let it either read frequently itself, or receive the words of the reader with the full eagerness of its heart. Let it continually draw the water of salvation from the divine springs of Scripture—especially that of which the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

Let the holy soul continually strive to adorn itself with the flowers of paradise, that is, with the meanings of the holy Scriptures; let it unceasingly hang precious pearls from its ears; from them let it fashion rings and bracelets while it practices good works. There let it seek remedies for wounds, there the spices of chastity, there the burnt offerings of repentance.

Whoever desires to preserve religion with an unstained and pure heart should either never go out in public, or certainly do so only for a great and unavoidable necessity. Let such a person have dealings with men as rarely as possible; yet whenever necessity requires seeing or greeting men, let those be chosen whom age and holy life commend. Even with these, as I have said, contact should be rare, and conversation with them not prolonged throughout the day, but kept very brief. Young men should be seen either never or only with difficulty.

No layman or religious person should ever be admitted into constant familiarity. Both women in relation to men and men in relation to women should strive to observe this rule if they desire to preserve the wholeness of chastity.

Let no one say, “My conscience is sufficient for me.” Let each person say what he wishes to himself: this is a wretched excuse, quite hateful to God, arising more from shamelessness than from a good conscience. For when the first familiarity between a man and a woman, or between a woman and a man, begins, it is recognized as sufficiently modest and holy, because at first the devil conceals his devices. Then, as constant familiarity gradually increases, he nurtures a hostile friendship between the two. [Col. 1129B]

The cunning enemy makes them serve one another for a short time without any stimulation of lust and without any loss of chastity. Thus he surrounds them with a false security, leading them, as though in a soothing calm, like two little boats out into the deep. While they think themselves secure, they seek neither the assistance of fasts as oars nor the rudder of vigils. Once he has made them secure, he dashes them against one another, plunging them into a sudden storm, and, driving them onto destructive entanglements, kills them both with a single blow.

For a long time he conceals the smoldering fire without any flames, until, joining two torches, he sets them both alight at once. Thus the devil reveals what he had previously seemed to conceal; thus, as though from simple charity, he forges illicit love. At first he is content to yield, so that he may be able to seize more later.

Look: each person is secure concerning his own conscience, because, when he sees someone, he believes he cannot be scandalized by that person. But just as you know your own conscience, do you also see the other’s will? Look: your eye sees another simply, while perhaps that person cruelly desires you. You rejoice in your own chastity, but do you not fear the other’s ruin? For if you make yourself excessively familiar, you nourish another’s desire; even if you do not sin yourself, you nevertheless destroy another, and, even though you are without fault, another’s lust will be a cause for you to be defiled.

Please, do not—do not give anyone an occasion or grant anyone familiarity, lest perhaps someone’s desire, kindled wickedly against you, begin elsewhere to seek what it was unable to find in you. [Col. 1129C]

But perhaps some woman says, “I am secure in my conscience.” Heaven forbid that this should proceed from a religious mouth. For the one who trusts in his own virtue has already fallen. If, with Christ’s help, you desire to conquer lust, you must flee familiarity. Let it be known with absolute certainty that whoever has not rejected unworthy familiarity will quickly destroy either himself or another.

But perhaps someone says, “I do not flee familiarity because I want something to conquer; I desire to hold my adversary captive.” Take care lest your adversary begin to rebel against you; take care lest this captivity lead you into captivity. Hear the Apostle saying: “Flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 7:15, as cited). Against the remaining vices we must resist with every virtue; against lust, however, it is not useful for you to fight but to flee. Be, then, a fugitive from lust if you wish to be an excellent champion of chastity.

But attend carefully to what I have said. When someone is provoked by the goads of lust, let him, with Christ’s help, fight against himself as much as he can, because he has nowhere to flee. But whenever the devil supplies an opportunity for pleasure through the company of another, let the holy soul, as much as it can, flee that very familiarity, as I said above. And if someone is at any time tempted within himself, let him resist himself with God’s help; but when he is tickled even by a slight desire through someone’s company, let him flee it with all possible speed, as though it were a venomous serpent.

But so that we may be able to observe all these things, let us maintain reasonable abstinence, for true is the saying of that most holy man: “As you restrain the belly, so also [you restrain] its poisonous impulses.” Let us also preserve our humility as much as we can. For the integrity of the flesh is not long preserved where the mind is corrupted by the swelling of pride. Especially if the flame of anger also rises frequently, it quickly consumes the flowers of chastity and virginity.

For a chaste and God-devoted soul should not maintain constant familiarity even with its own parents, whether by having them come to it or by going itself to them, lest it hear what it ought not, say what is not expedient, or see what may be contrary to chastity. For if vessels that are offered to the Church and placed upon the sacred altar are called holy by everyone, and if it is unlawful for them afterward to be taken back from the church to a secular household or adapted to human uses, if vessels that can possess neither understanding nor sensation have such dignity, what dignity, do you think, do all things created in God’s image possess before God? [Col. 1129D]

Therefore, just as holy vessels intended for human use can neither be taken back from the church nor ought to be, so it is not proper, fitting, or expedient for any religious person to become entangled in numerous obligations to his or her parents or to be bound by the harmful familiarity of outsiders.

Above all I admonish you to flee the evil of rivalry as viperous poison, and to preserve among yourselves the sweetness of charity in such a way that you may prepare spiritual remedies for one another through holy conversations. For there are some—what is worse—who, when they come together, inflict wounds upon one another by slandering or murmuring against their superiors, rather than preparing spiritual remedies.

But you, holy and venerable daughters, if you see someone fainthearted, offer consolation; if you see someone becoming proud, apply the medicine of humility; if you see someone angry, provide the cooling remedy of patience.

If you were born noble, rejoice more in the humility of religion than in secular dignity. Dispense your earthly substance in such a way that, by giving well and promptly, you may acquire spiritual wings, rather than, by reserving something for yourselves or distributing it too slowly, possess carnal fetters. For earthly substance, if distributed too slowly, is known to bind the soul’s wings as though with birdlime, because true is what has been written: “The impediments of the world have made them miserable” [apparently an imperfect or corrupt quotation]. [Col. 1130A]

But if any woman was poor before she assumed holy religion, she ought to give thanks to God, who did not wish to bind her with the resources of this world. For many people—what is worse—their possessions hold them bound in such a way that they cannot return to the eternal homeland.

But you are already happy, even in this age, through Christ’s favor, since you have despised the possessions and pleasures of this age not only in your hearts but also in your bodies. Keep your hands to the plow, therefore, and do not look back. And because you have deserved to climb onto the roof of perfection, let not the pleasures of this age bring you down from it.

Remember Lot’s wife, who, looking back, was turned into a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:17). Never let an oath, never a curse, proceed from a virgin’s mouth.

Guard not only your bodies but also your hearts with every care, because it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23). And also what the Lord said in the Gospel: “For from the heart come evil thoughts” (Matthew 15:19). For if nothing evil is thought in the heart, whatever is holy is uttered by the mouth, because, as it is written: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matthew 12:34). The tongue is accustomed to bring forth what conscience has supplied from the workshop of the heart.

Therefore, if you wish to bring forth good things from your mouth, always think in your heart about what is holy. You should devote yourselves to reading and meditation in such a way that, above all, you may also be able to practice some work with your hands, according to what the Apostle says: “If anyone does not work, neither should he eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Above all, however, make a habit of devoting yourselves to reading until the third hour, and dedicate the better part of the day to holy work.

Let your prayer proceed from the heart in such silence that it is scarcely heard by the mouth. For whoever wishes to pray in a loud voice harms both himself and another, since through his chatter he interrupts another’s mind and draws it away from holy and sacred prayer. [Col. 1130B]

In the very works performed with the hands, despise and reject secular and ostentatious aids, which serve not usefulness but vanity, so that even in earthly matters you may practice whatever accords with sobriety and propriety.

For many people display in their works what they love in their morals. Those who love the world prepare secular ornaments for themselves and serve pleasure or luxury. But for you, to whom the world has been crucified, let there be nothing in common with such people. Let all ornaments by which the flesh is arranged for luxury be rejected from your way of life as hostile and contrary to it.

For there are some—what is worse—who, out of vanity toward this age, take greater pains to attend to earthly desires than to devote themselves to divine reading. They wish, at great cost and with excessive expenditure, to prepare beautiful coverlets, painted carpets, embroidered fabrics, and other things of this kind for the pleasure of the eyes, not knowing what the Lord cries out and says through the evangelist John: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (1 John 2:5, as cited).

What does it profit a virgin to preserve the integrity of her body if she is unwilling to avoid the desires of the eyes?

There are also some women who wish to give the greater part of their possessions to their parents—and perhaps to wealthy parents—rather than to the poor. They do not consider that, while giving their substance to those parents for luxury, they are consuming themselves in eternal poverty.

But someone says, “Then must I despise my parents?” Far be it from us to say that you ought not to honor your parents. How could we preach that parents should not be loved, when we say that enemies should be loved? Love your parents as much as you can; and, if they are chaste and honorable, always show them honor, and leave them some small gifts from your possessions as tokens of your remembrance.

But give everything that is greater and more useful, and that will be beneficial until the end of the age, to the poor, so that your alms may pass through the relief of the poor to the kingdoms of heaven on the day of judgment. [Col. 1130C]

What you give less to your parents, they may afterward provide for themselves; they may work. What you prepare less for yourself out of mercy, you will never be able to find in that age.

Nevertheless, if any parents are poor, so that they cannot adequately obtain food or clothing, you will have a reward before God if you give them what they can use for their support.

For we are going to come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge; and if we have acted well, we shall joyfully hear: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom, because I was hungry and thirsty” (Matthew 25:34). And shortly afterward: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these”—without doubt, to the poor—“you did it to me” (Matthew 5:40, as cited).

He did not say, “Come and receive the kingdom because you have added your parents’ wealth to your own wealth, because you left them what they could use for luxury in this age.” He certainly did not say this; rather, he said what the Gospel records and what he had earlier foretold through the Prophet: “He scattered; he gave to the poor” (Psalm 111:9).

Pay attention, I beg you: “He scattered,” he says, “he gave to the poor.” For that rich man also of whom we read in the Gospel, “who was clothed in purple and fine linen” (Luke 16:19), left his brothers rich; but afterward, burning in hell, he sought a drop of refreshment and could not find one.

But you, holy souls worthy of God, conduct everything spiritually, and offer—indeed, return—your substance to the one to whom you have consecrated your souls. It is fitting that the one who prepares eternal things should receive earthly things from you. Let the one who bestowed upon you the crown of virginity receive your earthly substance from you.

You are more deeply indebted to him because he granted you the ability to follow the immaculate Lamb wherever he goes. The rest of the multitude of the faithful also follows Christ, but not wherever he goes, only as far as they are able. Those who repent and those who are married can follow Christ by other paths of righteousness; but when he goes before them in the beauty of virginity, they have no means of becoming virgins.

But you, holy daughters, follow him by perseveringly holding fast to what you have fervently vowed.

Again and again, holy souls consecrated to God, I beg you, and with all humility I presume to offer counsel for preserving the rewards of virginity: strive with all your strength to drive unsuitable familiarity far away from yourselves and from your souls. Let that pest and plague which disordered familiarity hurls be very far, very far away.

There is no security in this association, which suffers collision as though from turbulent waves. In this familiarity friendly concord does not dwell; it creates only hostile discord. For preserving the dignity of holy religion, holy separation is a far more sacred witness than disordered familiarity.

Pay attention, holy soul, and understand carefully how many evils arise from disordered association. For when anyone’s familiarity begins to become frequent, it sows nothing but corruption, causes vices to sprout, desires desire, gives birth to disgrace, arouses rage, extends fury, feeds wantonness, nourishes insolence, heightens falls, builds ruins, raises banks, opens precipices, sails amid dangers, gives wind to shipwrecks, rejoices in destruction, fosters death, deserves confusion, stores up disgrace, magnifies accusations, inflames excuses, and heaps together, in a mass and in crowds, countless tracks of snares; through endless disgraces it will discover multiple deaths for the ruin of the lost. [Col. 1130D]

Such and so great are the evils of harmful familiarity. No one is overthrown except the one who has disdained to have, either with difficulty or at least rarely, the company from which he might be endangered.
