For if a holy soul wishes to guard its secret and flees with all the strength of its mind the evil of constant familiarity, that holy separation itself is an unconquerable defense of sanctity, a strong assault against infamy, the firmness of courage and the weakness of wantonness, the protection of uprightness and the destruction of wickedness, the victory of the soul and the plunder of the body, freedom from glory-seeking and captivity to crimes, the marriage attendant of holiness and the repudiation of disgrace, the indication of sincerity and the abolition of scandals, the exercise of conscience and the complete emptying of luxury, the secure peace of virtues and the restless defeat of battles, the summit of purity and the prison of lust, the harbor of propriety and the shipwrecking harbor of disgrace [thus printed; compare col. 1159, line 34], the mother of virginity and the enemy of uncleanness, the breastplate of modesty and the stripping away of disgrace, the wall of incorruption, the discernment of vulgarity, the dignity of integrity and the renunciation of fornication, the height of charity and the precipice of disgrace, the will toward good works and the affliction of vices, the refreshment of chastity and the punishment of insolence, the acquisition of triumphs and the losses caused by crimes, the rest of salvation and the exile of perdition, the life of the spirit and the death of the flesh, the condition of angelic quality and the funeral of human substance.

All these evils will be bravely rejected, with God’s help, and those goods we have mentioned will be happily acquired if disordered familiarity is rejected by holy souls.

Pay attention, I beg you, holy souls, because among all the struggles that Christian warfare always entails, the battles of chastity alone are harsher, where the struggle is daily and victory rare. Chastity has received a severe enemy, one who is conquered daily and yet never ceases to provoke; daily, I say, he is conquered, and he does not cease to provoke.

No one wins securely who fights with himself. Dangerous is the voyage where shipwreck occurs frequently, and through danger one passes across the waves where many have been drowned: the waves of lust. For desire, when conquered, does not end.

The battles of chastity are hard, but its rewards are greater. A flame that burns too fiercely soon turns to ashes; but when the body’s fire is indulged, it is kindled rather than extinguished. No one securely receives the palm of chastity; in proportion to the difficulty of its outcome are the glory of its fruits.

The one who takes up war against nature imposes upon himself a danger worthy of reward. The public enemy feeds by night; the robber’s ambushes operate only in darkness. But the desire of lust provokes by night and spares no one by day; it fears neither kings’ purple nor poor men’s rags.

Therefore, so that, with God as your rewarder, you may happily receive the rewards of chastity and the crown of virginity, always exclude dangerous familiarity from yourselves. Run faithfully, so that you may arrive happily. And remember me when immaculate virginity has been crowned in you.

This letter will make me excusable before the tribunal of Christ, because with true charity and perfect humility I have offered what I ought to say and you ought to hear. If anyone should neglect to obey—may God prevent it—it will stand as a testimony against that person; but for whoever willingly receives it, it will be turned into joy, not temporal but eternal.

May you flourish in Christ, holy and venerable women.

## The Exhortatory Letter of Saint Caesarius to a Virgin Dedicated to God
O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! And who has known his mind (Rom. 11:33)? For who could have supposed, in the days of your youth, O venerable lady—indeed my lady in integrity and merits, but my daughter in Christ by rank and degree—that, while you were gathered in the choir of holy virgins in the coenobium, devoted to the study and instruction of the divine Scriptures, you would then love me as though I were a part of your soul: a young man and a person of no great character, who was wandering through the precipices of pleasures and wantonness, and, through most grievous labyrinths, was hastening to plunge himself into a clandestine fall, for the sake, that is, of the joy of temporal prosperity? Moreover, you knew his name only by hearsay and were entirely unfamiliar with his face. Yet the dispensation of almighty God had predestined us for this service, namely, that he should entrust his household to our governance, in this particular order: that you should minister in the workshop of this Church, according to the oracle of the divine commandment. “If,” he says, “you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15:19).

You are like a most skillful money-changer among those who preserve within themselves the image of the eternal King, so that, because they stain his denarius against their conscience with a counterfeit key, you may separate them by a shrewd and discerning division. For you have not undertaken these sacred ministries as an inexperienced or newly converted woman; rather, from almost your very cradle, throughout the years of childhood and adolescence, and from youth onward, you have exercised your life in disciplined studies. In them you learned the rule of living and obtained an abundant store of instruction.

But I, who through sluggishness have not acquired the privilege of knowledge, and who see myself far removed from the abstinence which divine condescension has instilled in you, entangled as I am in earthly necessities, am rightly censured as a chatterer by the wise rather than as one who speaks anything correctly—as the unpolished material of my own speech also indicates. Yet although I am foolish and stained with the mud of earthly work, remembering our former affection, it cannot be believed, now that you have received the office which you presently hold, how great my concern and fear for you are.

Therefore, in proportion to the devotion I had that you should undertake that office in due order according to God and carry it without stain, fear all the more sharply lest either divine scrutiny or human opinion should reproach you for something open to reproach in your conduct. Let nothing be found in you by which those who wish to criticize may seem to tear you apart justly, or by which those who desire to imitate you may fall into wrongdoing. You will avoid this more nobly if you always place the heavenly judgment before the eyes of your heart.

Listen, therefore, to me, O sweetest virgin of Christ, sister and daughter. However much you may always desire to be occupied in spiritual studies, nevertheless, for the sake of your sisters, you will sometimes have to settle necessary external affairs. You must therefore take the greatest care to deal with temporal matters as matters of the moment, while always clinging more firmly to spiritual things through devotion and love, so that, when you have quickly administered spiritual matters, you may immediately return to prayer or reading as to your mother’s lap.

You ought to desire that, having cast off worldly anxiety, you may always think about the service of Christ, because of this saying: “No one serving as a soldier for God,” he says, “involves himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4). Think without interruption that you have been appointed the lamp of this Church, not to be hidden under a bushel, but placed upon a lampstand, so that you may impart the light of good works to all who inhabit this house by the examples of your life. For he says: “In all things show yourself an example of good works” (Tit. 2:7). Let your life, like a winged creature, always fly upward through desire; let it resound through speech and shine through example.

When you have resolved to announce the word of God to your sisters, or when necessity compels you to dispute for the benefit of souls and the preservation of the rule, first weigh the matter with cautious reflection, so that what you promise with your mouth you may fulfill in deeds, and what you preach to others you may demonstrate by your works. First feel upon your own shoulders and neck whether you are loading your sisters’ necks with heavy or light burdens—for example, if you decide to impose fasting beyond the daily fast, abstinence beyond the customary measure, or, as sometimes happens, the chanting of more psalms than usual in the synaxis.

Let yourself be found first in church and leave last; undertake the labors first and lay them down last. In the daily nourishment of the body and at the common meal, be equal to those with whom you sit at the same table, so that, since you sit at one table, one and the same food may refresh you all alike. Let you too take pleasure in the same flavors of dishes as your sisters; let common servers or cupbearers offer or pour out equal food and drink for all of you. And let your primacy at table be claimed first for the virtue of frugality, so that the abstinence which your tongue preaches may be felt by your neighboring throat and nearest stomach. Otherwise your subjects may say in silent thought: “How beautifully a full belly preaches abstinence to us, and commands us to be content with the cheapest foods and drinks, while a throat stuffed with carefully prepared and delightful foods is belching!” For the preaching of abstinence is acceptable when it is uttered by faces made pale by fasting.

In these matters and in all the rest, know that this is fitting for you: the narrow paths along which you admonish your companions to walk, you yourself should walk first; everything that ought to be done, you should first fulfill in deeds. Then, like a pliable trumpet brought to life by the blow, you may rightly break forth in speech, because of the Lord’s saying: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble” (Matt. 18:6), and what follows.

Among other things, you must guard with great care that you love equally all those in the monastery whose governance you have likewise taken upon your shoulders. Do not love one more and another less. Rather, arrange all matters, insofar as possibility permits, with equal moderation; administer them with equal restraint; bestow equal charity upon them; and do not distribute what is necessary according to private affection to particular persons, but to all according to the merits of each.

Do not prefer the one whose face and appearance please you, whom you have recognized as pleasing to your eye, or by whose more flattering service you have been won over. Prefer the one whom the love of Christ and the more religious life have shown to be worthy of preference. If the Lord should graciously grant some modest property to the monastery, let it be distributed with the strictest line of equity and an equal balance for all, according to each person’s need, while preserving reverence for the elders—those, namely, who have deserved to be pillars of the Church.

Do not be more splendidly dressed than the others. Display not what human malice [so], but what the devil can envy; let your adornment consist not in clothing but in conduct and character. Let divine reading season all these things.

For, as I fear, you must sometimes have a knife at your throat for the sake of certain women, carry a cautery on your tongue, and hold a rod and staff in your hand: with the knife, cut away vices; with the cautery, bring what has been cut back to health; with the discipline of the rod, correct; and with the staff, support those who have been disciplined.

If you impose penance upon anyone for her offenses, you must observe this: when you see her bending and stooping beneath the burden imposed by you, imitate the diligence of the ant, according to the command of the wisest Solomon, and place your shoulder beneath her spiritual burden, so that halfway along her journey you may meet her and lift up or support the one who is burdened. In this way admonish and instruct each one according to her particular negligence or fault, so that eternal glory from Christ the Lord may be credited to you for their salvation.

If at any time you are summoned to converse with secular persons and it is necessary for you to go, first arm your forehead with the trophy of the cross and impress Christ’s banner upon your breast, so that Christ may deign to accompany his little virgin. Yet remain always covered with virginal modesty, remembering blessed Mary, who spoke with the angel in very few words and afterward burst forth with Elizabeth into a song and praise of God.

When, after this, you come to them with such steadfast dignity, do not place even your speech before them, so that those who see you may give thanks to Christ the Lord, who has deigned to provide such a mother for his household. Your outward bearing should be no less rational than it is rare.

Your conversation with them should always be mingled with gravity and sweetness, specifically that which proceeds from holy and pure love. It should always be restrained and interwoven with modesty, as befits a virgin of Christ. Likewise, do not remain so completely silent that you incur the reputation either of pride or of stupidity; but speak only as the occasion of the matter and the time demands. When anyone departs, let that person desire you more than himself [*te quam se*, as printed], or desire to hear your speech—which is adorned by gravity of character, sweetness of affection, and brevity of speech.

If they ask you for something which you decide to grant, grant it with a cheerful face. If something ought not to be granted, at least soften their request by the courtesy of your speech. Let many know your name; let many, insofar as you are able, experience your benefactions; let few know your face.

If necessity for the monastery requires you to speak privately with its administrator, do so with two or at least three chosen sisters. Or, if a more secret matter arises, converse with the others at least watching in an open place. For the reputation of a good name, like the preservation of a perfect life, is necessary for you. Human detraction is to be despised only when Christ is at stake.

If something should occur which must be done in such a way that, constrained by uncertainty, whichever way you turn you proceed into the unknown, entangled as though in a syllogism, then, if you act, turn at last toward the lesser danger, which you can more easily direct toward the good by governing it. Let not only your doubtful matters, but your every action, be for God; your speech, about God; your thought, toward God. Except in the case of vices—which deserve not compassion but rectitude—I desire you to be compassionate toward all, agreeable to all, devout toward all, affectionate toward all, animated by goodwill toward everyone, just as Paul adorned the virgin of Christ: “that you may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34). May your bridegroom and Lord himself govern your mind and direct all your ways, he who, in perfect Trinity, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

**[NOTE.]**

(See the letters: of Ruricius to Caesarius, in *Patrologia*, vol. 58, cols. 108, 111; of Caesarius to Pope Symmachus and of the latter to Caesarius, vol. 62, cols. 53, 54; of Boniface II to Caesarius, vol. 65, col. 31; of Avitus of Vienne to Caesarius, vol. 59, col. 229; of John II to Caesarius, vol. 66, col. 25; and of Agapetus I to Caesarius, vol. 66, cols. 45, 46.)

# TESTAMENT OF BLESSED CAESARIUS, BISHOP OF THE HOLY CHURCH OF ARLES

[Note: This testament of St. Caesarius is found in Baronius, under the year 508, §§ 23 and following, and in Saxius’s *Pontificale Arelatense*, no. 30, as well as in Cointius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. 1, pp. 616 and following.] (C,S)

## PEACE TO THE CHURCH OF ARLES

Caesarius, bishop, to the priests and deacons; to the holy and venerable abbess Caesaria, whom the Lord has placed over our monastery through my humble instrumentality; and to the whole congregation whom the Lord, by his grace, has established there: eternal salvation in the Lord.

Since ecclesiastical piety ordinarily makes provision in accordance with its custom, namely, by extending the help of generosity to pilgrims and the destitute, how much more, when opportunity or necessity arises, ought it to enlarge the compassionate bowels of its mercy so as to bestow something upon the saints and those who fear God? And therefore, in accordance with this letter, which we have confirmed by the subscription of our hand and beneath which we have added the day and the consul, I have, by God’s dispensation, drawn up this testament of mine, subscribed it with my own hand, and confirmed it according to praetorian law or civil law, and in the manner of a codicil.

I, Caesarius the sinner, when I have paid the debt of human flesh, decree and order that the entire monastery of St. John, which I founded, shall canonically be under the authority of the bishop of Arles, and that I wish it to be and order it to be my heir; let all others, male and female, be disinherited. Whatever I have given, bequeathed, or ordered to be given to anyone through this testament of mine, let it be given and done. Moreover, I leave the bishop of Arles as co-heir with my monastery. Whomever I shall order to be free, male or female, let all be free.

Yet, since I possessed nothing from my parents’ property, I was ashamed to presume upon this testament of mine. Nevertheless, this consideration compelled me: that, moved by devotion, I should contribute something to my Church, for fear of the many terrifying words of the Savior which the wicked will hear him say: “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). And lest after my death some of my relatives should presume to trouble the Church over which I preside, except concerning those things which I shall give them as gifts [perhaps *eulogia*], I have therefore desired to set forth my intention more fully, so that none of my relatives may presume to demand anything from either the aforesaid monastery or the bishop of the Church of Arles beyond what I shall give or have given them.

To the holy lord and my archbishop who, though I am unworthy, shall worthily succeed me: although everything is in his power, nevertheless, if he wishes and considers it fitting, let all the Easter vestments which were given to me belong to him, together with the shaggy cloak and tunic, or *galnape*, whichever I leave in better condition. Let my remaining garments, except the woolen *birrus*, be divided among my clergy and laymen, with the grace or arrangement of the lord archbishop, at his own command—or rather, as his gift.

Those things which I previously transferred to the monastery by donation I now confirm; and if I have transferred anything to anyone by letter, writing tablet, or word, out of regard for piety, I wish it to remain valid.

I also earnestly ask that the lord archbishop deign perpetually to grant by right to the administrators of the monastery, for their secure protection, the cell which Augustus, the subdeacon of blessed memory, possessed in the atrium of St. Stephen, on the right-hand side for those entering, so that the administrators of the monastery may hold it as succeeding to them.

I specifically desire this, and so I ask you, lord archbishop: let the holy congregation have no one as administrator of the monastery or priest of the basilica of St. Mary except one whom it has itself chosen or requested to be ordained.

Although I presume upon your piety, lord archbishop, nevertheless, lest perhaps you should receive the importunate suggestions of some persons against our monastery, I adjure you by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and by the fearful day of judgment, never to allow the ancient enemy to prevail with you, so that you consent to grieve your servants or permit anything to be taken from what they possess and what we have bestowed upon them. For, by God’s favor, we have not sold Church property outright to secular persons without discrimination or justice, except only what is less useful and unproductive for the Church; and whatever we have given to holy souls devoted to God, with the consent or subscription of the holy brothers, let it remain theirs perpetually by right.

And you, our little daughters, I adjure by the undivided Holy Trinity and by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ: ask with all affection as your lord the bishop who, through God’s appointment, shall worthily succeed me, though I am unworthy; love him with a pure mind; and do not grieve him through your disobedience. For we trust in God’s mercy that he will bestow chaste love upon all priests who have received the charge of religion, so that he will not allow you to lack anything necessary to sustain your little bodies.

Again and again I ask you, excellent bishop, by divine grace appointed over the aforesaid monastery, to take the greatest care of it and diligently provide for their household with great compassion. If anyone should give you unjust counsel, I beg you to answer with authority; for what is done by the word of a bishop should not only not be taken away, but cannot be taken away at all.

This is especially so because the authority of the most holy Pope Urbicanus himself also advised this, so that I may believe this concerning my holy lord the bishop. [Note: Letters of Hormisdas, Roman pontiff, exist in Bollandus under January 12; they greatly reinforce the authority and credibility of Caesarius’s testament. Caesarius alludes to them when he mentions “the holy Pope Urbicanus,” that is, the Roman bishop. Cointius, cited work, p. 618. See these letters at the end of this volume. EDIT.]

For no such wicked suggestion will ever prevail with you that, against the just will of any bishop, the property which has greatly advanced through my efforts and has nearly doubled should benefit you.

To this is added the fact that merciful God, through my humble instrumentality, has also granted exemption from taxes, for the most part, both near the city and within it, as well as in the suburbs and villages.

Accordingly, from the Aucharian estate, from which we gave a small portion to the monastery, we retain much: for we have reserved approximately one hundred *aripennes* of vineyard and fields amounting to three hundred *modii*. Thus the aforesaid monastery has forty *modiates* of the land which I planted, while we transferred scarcely thirty *aripennes* from the old vineyard.

We have reserved for your holy Church, for the support of its women, the Gallicuman estate, the Mercloan estate, or the Gemellos estate, with its ponds and marshes, with all its rights and boundaries, and the pastures in the Stony Field, and whatever else there may be; also the field at Trifinitium above the fortified road, and all the rest of whatever exists; the Orvedus estate, the Martinatis estate, and the Silvanus estate, where the church of St. Mary of Ratis is situated; and the Missiamanus estate, with all its associated pastures and marshes, with all its rights and boundaries.

Therefore I adjure you, holy bishop, that if almighty God, through the hands of those who fear him, should bestow some greater benefit upon holy Mother Church or upon the monastery of holy virgins, your holy love should not separate one from the other. But if, God forbid, the congregation there has not been assembled, or if afterward, when it has been assembled, it should cease to exist—which may God forbid—let these things return to Mother Church.

I have written these matters to satisfy my fear. Far be it from me that you, most pious bishop, should be accused of ignorance, since, as I have already said above, divine mercy has granted that, through my humility, exemption from taxation should be given to the Church in so many respects. Whatever we have given to the monastery with the consent of the brothers, I confirm by this declaration of my will.

I wish the larger hempen cloak which our servant Caesaria the abbess made to be given to her. I wish the best cloak of all to be given to my lord Cyprian. Whatever I have bestowed upon my servant Bricianus, I now confirm by this testament of mine.

Let Agritia, my own girl, serve the monastery and the abbess Caesaria most willingly; and I confirm the little gifts [*gariolae*] which I gave to them or to their parents. I commend all my chamberlains to you, lord bishop, before God and his angels.

# SECOND COUNCIL OF ORANGE: ON GRACE AND FREE WILL

[Note: This holy gathering of bishops was held on account of certain writings of Faustus of Riez, who, around the year of Christ 472, succeeded St. Prosper in the bishopric of Riez [St. Prosper was not bishop of Riez]. For letters of Sidonius addressed to him as bishop of Riez at this period do exist. In that work, under an attractive title condemning Pelagius, Faustus in fact promotes Pelagianism. Since the work was sought out and circulated with great eagerness by readers not only in Gaul, as is clear from the testimony of Sidonius, book 9, letter 9, nor only in Italy, but also at Constantinople and in the African Church, Caesarius, bishop of Arles, not only wrote against him a treatise on grace and free will approved by the authority of Felix IV, but also summoned this council of bishops, so that by the common agreement of all the Fathers it might define what ought to be believed and held concerning this doctrine of the orthodox faith. No one in Gaul now dared openly attack the writings of St. Augustine against Pelagius. Since Pelagius had by then become nearly infamous, no one attempted to adhere to him without incurring infamy; but certain Gallic priests, together with Faustus, bishop of Riez, secretly sought to accomplish this through fraud and intrigue. Thus, at this gathering of bishops, twenty-five canons were established in defense of the Catholic faith and in support and defense of Augustine’s writings concerning grace and free will. Almost all of them, in both wording and sense, are the words of St. Augustine, taken from various writings, as we shall show below in the notes to the individual canons. Severus Binius.

In one of the three oldest manuscripts of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, the title is: “Here begin the canons of Orange of St. Caesarius on free will, or on the various conditions necessary concerning the matter itself,” etc. Sirmond first published them from the manuscripts of Lyon, Fossat, Tilianus, and others. Hardouin. The proceedings of this synod are carefully explained by Eminence Norisius in book 2, chapter 23 of his *History of Pelagianism*.

The Vatican manuscript gives this title: “Here begin the canons of Orange on free will, or on the various conditions necessary concerning the matter itself, to be sought through the eras without chapters.” Mansi.]

Celebrated at the dedication of the basilica built by the patrician Liberius, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the consulship of Decius the Younger, a man of senatorial rank—that is, in the year of Christ 529—and in the third year of Pope Felix IV, in the third year of King Athalaric of Italy.

[Note: There is no doubt that this is the year indicated by the consulship of Decius the Younger, which is recorded in Caesarius’s subscription. It was appropriate to assign to these later times this council which was formerly ascribed to the age of Pope Leo, because, during the intervening period, many men distinguished for learning and piety in Gaul appeared to favor the Semi-Pelagians, whose doctrines were finally wholly exploded and rejected in this synod, approved by the authority of the Apostolic See. Its simple title in the Lyon manuscript is: “Constitution of the bishops in the city of Orange concerning grace and free will.” Jacques Sirmond.

That this synod was held in the year of the Lord 529, under Pope Felix IV, is clearly shown: first, by the end of the acts of the council, where Caesarius is said to have reread and subscribed this constitution, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the consulship of Decius the Younger, a man of senatorial rank. These words undoubtedly refer to the consulship of Decius during which Caesarius governed the Church of Arles. Although the fasti record several years marked by the consulship of some Decius the Younger, this is the consulship assigned by Cassiodorus to the year of the Lord 529, when Felix IV administered the bishopric of Rome and Caesarius that of Arles. That Caesarius lived under Felix IV is shown by the letter written to him which we printed above from the Arles manuscript in this edition of the councils.

Second, the subscription of Liberius, patrician and prefect of Gaul, makes it clear that this synod was held at the time when that Liberius exercised the prefecture of Gaul granted him by Theodoric. Since this occurred at the end of Theodoric’s and the beginning of Athalaric’s reign, as may be gathered from the letters of those kings addressed to him, there can be no doubt that the acts of the council, dated by the consulship of Decius the Younger and approved by the subscription of the aforesaid patrician, were held in the said year of the Lord 529, under Felix IV.

The fact that many very learned men thought this Second Council of Orange had been held in the time of Pope St. Leo, when the First Council of Orange is certainly known to have been held, arose from the subscriptions of St. Prosper and St. Eucherius, the former of whom, as we shall say below, was wrongly believed to be the same Prosper who is certainly known to have lived in the time of Pope St. Leo. Who that Eucherius was who subscribed there, we have stated in the notes on the aforesaid First Council of Orange, where we also noted that the Caesarius whose name is found subscribed there was plainly someone other than this Caesarius of great renown, bishop of Arles; for at that time Hilary governed the bishopric of Arles, and Caesarius was not made bishop of Arles until after the deaths of three intervening bishops. See Baronius, year 463; also the appendix to year 729, vol. 10. Vasquius, vol. 1, disputation 91, nos. 76 ff., holds a different view. Severus Binius.]

(From volume 8 of Mansi’s *Councils.) (C,S)

## TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS

I. That through Adam’s sin not only the body but also the soul was injured.

II. That Adam’s sin harmed not Adam alone but also passed to his descendants.

III. That the grace of God is not given in response to invocation, but itself causes God to be invoked.

IV. That, in order to cleanse us from sin, God does not await our will but prepares it.

V. That the beginning of faith is not from us but from the grace of God.

VI. That without the grace of God mercy is not granted to those who believe and ask, since grace itself causes us to believe and ask.

VII. That by the powers of nature we cannot, without grace, think or choose anything good that pertains to salvation.

VIII. That no one can reach the grace of baptism through free will.

IX. On the assistance of God, through which we do good works.

X. On always imploring God’s assistance.

XI. On the obligation of vows.

XII. How God loves us.

XIII. On the restoration of free will.

XIV. That, in order to be freed from misery, we are preceded by the mercy of God.

XV. That through the grace of God the believer is changed for the better.

XVI. That one must not glory in what one possesses, since it comes from God.

XVII. On Christian fortitude.

XVIII. That grace is preceded by no merits.

XIX. That no one is saved except by God’s mercy.

XX. That a human being can do nothing good without God.

XXI. On nature and grace.

XXII. On those things which belong properly to human beings.

XXIII. On the will of God and of the human being.

XXIV. On the branches of the vine.

XXV. On the love by which we love God.

## PREFACE

[Note: “Here begin the decrees of the bishops in the city of Orange concerning grace and free will,” in the *v. c. cl.* Hardy, or Paris, manuscript. I compared it with Vatican manuscript 3827. Mansi.]

When, by God’s favor and at his invitation, we had assembled for the dedication of the basilica which our most illustrious prefect and patrician, our son Liberius, built in the most faithful city of Orange, and when a spiritual discussion had arisen among us concerning matters belonging to ecclesiastical discipline, word reached us that there were some who, through simplicity and insufficient caution, wished to hold opinions concerning grace and free will that were not in accordance with the rule of the Catholic faith.

[Note: From this passage it is evident that not four praetorian prefects, but only one—Liberius—attended this council, though he is recorded in the subscriptions under four names. On his account the kings of Italy, Theodoric and Athalaric, wrote the letters recounted by Cassiodorus. That Liberius of whom Theodoric writes to the senate and to whom Athalaric addressed a letter was one and the same person is shown by Liberius’s funerary inscription at Rimini, received from Peter Pithou and printed by Baronius under the year 529 in the appendix to vol. 10. It follows that the text of this council is corrupt in the subscriptions, where, contrary to the reading of the Vatican manuscript, four praetorian prefects are said to have attended and subscribed. Severus Binius.]

Therefore, in accordance with the admonition and authority of the Apostolic See, it seemed just and reasonable to us that we should present and subscribe with our own hands a few chapters transmitted to us by the Apostolic See, which had been collected by the ancient Fathers from the books of the holy Scriptures, especially with regard to this matter, so that all might observe them for the instruction of those who think otherwise than they ought.

[Note: What I stated above concerning the twenty-four chapters transmitted by the Apostolic See to Gaul, and concerning the constitutions of these Fathers, conformed and confirmed by the judgments of St. Augustine and the Roman pontiffs, is established and reinforced here. Severus Binius.]

[Note: It appears that the Fathers of Orange selected only the following eight chapters from the many transmitted from Rome. Consult note g, col. 1152. P. Labbe.]

After these had been read, whoever up to that point had not believed rightly concerning grace and free will should not delay to incline his mind toward the teachings consistent with the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTERS

[Note: As many chapters as this council contains, so many Catholic judgments of the Church are established here, from which no faithful person may depart without the guilt of transgression. They appear to have been taken almost word for word from various passages of St. Augustine, which we have noted below. St. Prosper included the same passages, extracted by him, in a book entitled *Sentences*. Only twenty-four canons were established in number, because the Roman pontiff had sent to Gaul an equal number of chapters concerning grace and free will—perhaps those contained in the letter attributed to Celestine, which you will find printed above, in volume 3 of the Councils, p. 473, together with my notes.

The following point must therefore be observed with the greatest care: these most holy and learned Fathers, preparing to fight against the enemies of God’s grace who attributed too much to free will, judged that this could be done in no more powerful way than by relying upon the authority of the sacred Apostolic See. They plainly considered it unlawful either to resist excessively the judgments of St. Augustine concerning grace and free will, which Pope Celestine had confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See in the letter cited above. Let innovation therefore claim nothing further for itself, and let human presumption presume nothing; rather, let it embrace and accept the approved definition of the ancient Fathers. Severus Binius.]

### I.

[Note: This chapter, together with almost all those following up to VIII, is found in the oldest Lucan manuscript 490.]

If anyone says that, through Adam’s transgression, the human being was not wholly changed for the worse—that is, in both body and soul—but believes that the freedom of the soul remained unharmed and that only the body was subject to corruption, deceived by the error of Pelagius, he contradicts the Scripture which says: “The soul that sins [variant: *peccaverit* / *peccat*] shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:20); and: “Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey?” (Rom. 6:16); and: “By whatever anyone is overcome, by that he is also enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:19).

[Note: See Augustine, book 2, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 34.]

### II.

If anyone asserts that Adam’s transgression harmed Adam alone and not his descendants, or testifies that only bodily death, which is the punishment of sin, and not also sin itself, which is the death of the soul, passed through one human being into the whole human race, he will attribute injustice to God, contradicting the Apostle, who says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death [variant note: *mors* is lacking] passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

[Note: This chapter appears to have been taken from chapter 4 of book 4 of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*. Severus Binius.]

### III.

If anyone says that the grace of God can be conferred in response to human invocation, but does not say that grace itself causes God to be invoked by us, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah—or the Apostle, who says the same thing: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I appeared openly to those who were not asking me” [variant: *interrogabant* / *interrogaverunt*] (Isa. 65:1; Rom. 10:20).

### IV.

If anyone maintains that God awaits our will in order that we may be cleansed from sin, and does not confess that, through the infusion and working of the Holy Spirit in us, we are also made willing to be cleansed [variant: *jam*, “already”], he resists the Holy Spirit himself, who speaks through Solomon [in the Lucan manuscript 490, “through Solomon” is lacking] [and the Apostle, who says]: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint); and the Apostle, preaching for our salvation, says [in the same manuscript and others, *the Apostle preaching for our salvation* is lacking]: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good will” (Phil. 2:13).

### V

If anyone says that, just as the increase of faith, so also the beginning of faith itself and the very inclination to believe by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly and arrive at the sacrament of holy baptism, is present in us naturally, and not through the gift of grace—that is, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit correcting our will from unbelief to faith and from ungodliness to godliness—he is shown to be an adversary of the apostolic teachings, since blessed Paul teaches: “We are confident that he who began a good work in us will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians I); and: “To you it has been granted for Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (ibid.); and: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; for it is the gift of God” (Ephesians II).

**Note:** [Col. 1146C] Codex Lucensis 490 reads: “the very [disposition] of belief, which, etc.”

For those who say that the faith by which we believe in God is natural define, in a certain sense, all those who are alien to the Church of Christ as believers.

**Note:** See Saint Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, through chapter 9. Severus Binius.

### VI

If anyone says that divine mercy is granted to us who believe, will, desire, strive, labor, [pray], keep watch, devote ourselves, ask, seek, and knock, without the grace of God, but does not confess that our believing, willing, and ability to do all these things as we ought comes about in us through the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit; and if he adds the help of grace to human humility or obedience, and does not agree that it is itself the gift of grace that we should be obedient and humble, he resists the Apostle, who says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians IV); and: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians XV).

**Note:** Codex Lucensis 490 and other manuscripts add “praying.”

**Note:** Thus far in Codex Lucensis.

### VII

If anyone affirms that, by the power of nature, he can think or choose anything good pertaining to the salvation of eternal life as is fitting, or assent to saving [or: “be saved”]—that is, to Gospel preaching—without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who grants everyone sweetness in consenting to and believing the truth, he is deceived by a heretical spirit, not understanding the voice of God saying in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV); and the Apostle’s words: “Not that we are competent to think anything by ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians III).

**Note:** Augustine says the same in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 26. Severus Binius.

### VIII

If anyone contends that some can come to the grace of baptism through mercy, but others through free will—which is acknowledged to be corrupted in all who are born from the transgression of the first man—he is proved to be alien to the right faith.

For he either asserts that everyone’s free will was weakened by the sin of the first man, or at least considers it to have been so injured that nevertheless some are able, without God’s revelation, by themselves to seek out the mystery of eternal salvation. How contrary this is, the Lord himself proves: he testifies that no one, not merely some, can come to him unless the Father has drawn him. Thus he also says to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven”; and the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus [Christ],’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians XII).

### IX

It is a divine gift when we think rightly and restrain our feet from falsehood and injustice. For whenever we do good things, God works in us and with us so that we may act.

**Note:** The same sentence occurs in Saint Prosper, no. 22, and under the verse “I considered my ways.” Severus Binius.

**Note:** The following statements seem to be not so much canons as sentences collected from Saint Augustine and other learned men in confirmation of the same faith. Mansi.

### X

God’s help must always be implored even by those who have been reborn and are holy, so that they may reach a good end or persevere in a good work.

**Note:** [Col. 1147D] Fossatensis likewise reads “reborn and holy”; the Lugdunensis and Rhemensis instead read “reborn and healed.” J. Sirmond.

### XI

No one can rightly make a vow to the Lord unless he has received from him what he is to vow, as it is written: “What we have received from your hand, we give to you” (1 Chronicles XX).

**Note:** The words “what he was to vow” are absent.

**Note:** Saint Augustine has the same in *The City of God*, book XVII, chapter 4; the sentence in Prosper is no. 54. Severus Binius.

### XII

God loves us as we shall be by his gift, not as we are by our merit.

**Note:** This sentence occurs in Prosper, no. 56. Severus Binius.

### XIII

The choice of the will [or: of freedom] in the first man, once weakened, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism. What was lost cannot be restored except by him by whom it was able to be given. Hence Truth itself says: “If the Son sets you free [will have set you free], then you will truly be free.”

**Note:** Tilianus, Fossatensis, and others read “freedom of choice”; in the Lugdunensis, “of the will.” J. Sirmond.

**Note:** Thus Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, book XIV, chapter 12. Severus Binius.

### XIV

No wretched person is freed from any [or: however great a] misery unless he is preceded by the mercy of God, as the Psalmist says: “May your mercy, O Lord, quickly go before us” [variant: “quickly went before us”] (Psalm LXXVIII); and: “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Psalm LVIII).

**Note:** This is sentence 211. Severus Binius.

### XV

Adam was changed from what God formed, but for the worse through [because of] his iniquity. The faithful person is changed from what iniquity produced, but for the better through the grace of God. That former change, therefore, belonged to the first transgressor; this one, according to the Psalmist, is: “The change is [the right hand, and ‘is’ is absent] of the Most High” (Psalm LXXVI).

**Note:** This is sentence 220. Severus Binius.

### XVI

Let no one glory in what he appears to possess, as though he had not received it; nor let him think that he received it because the letter appeared externally, either to be read or to sound so that it could be heard. For, as the Apostle says: “If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.” “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Galatians II; Psalm LXVII; Ephesians IV). From him derives whatever anyone has. But whoever denies that he has it from him either truly does not have it, or what he appears to possess [or: possesses] is taken away [or: will be taken away] from him.

**Note:** *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 28. Severus Binius.

### XVII

Worldly desire produces the strength of the Gentiles, but the strength of Christians is produced by the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts—not through the choice of the will that is in us [variant: “in us”], but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

**Note:** See sentence 295. Severus Binius.

### XVIII

With no merits preceding the grace [of God], a reward is owed to good works if they are performed; but grace, which is not owed, precedes them so that they may be performed.

**Note:** Prosper, sentence 297.

### XIX

Human nature, even if it had remained in that integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. Therefore, since without the grace of God it cannot preserve the salvation it received, how will it be able, without the grace of God, to restore what it lost?

**Note:** Prosper, sentence 108.

**Note:** See Saint Augustine, Letter 106. Severus Binius.

### XX

God does many good things in a human being that the human being does not do; but the human being does no good things which God does not enable him to do.

**Note:** See Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 8. Severus Binius.

### XXI

Just as the Apostle most truly says to those who wish to be justified by the law and have fallen away from grace: “If righteousness is by the law [from the law], then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians II), so it is most truly said to those who think that the grace which the faith of Christ commends and receives is nature: “If righteousness is by nature, then Christ died for nothing.”

For the law already existed here, and it did not justify; nature also already existed here, and it did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing, so that the law might be fulfilled through him who said: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matthew V); and so that nature, lost through Adam, might be restored through him who said that he had come to seek and save what had perished.

**Note:** The entire sentence from “For the law already existed” through “therefore” is absent.

**Note:** The whole passage beginning “so it is most truly said” and ending “Christ died for nothing” was absent from the common editions, but is found in all the ancient manuscripts, such as the Lugdunensis, Rhemensis, Fossatensis, Tilianus, Bellovacensis, and others. J. Sirmond.

**Note:** Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 13, has the same words and the same meaning. Severus Binius.

### XXII

No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin. Whatever truth and righteousness a human being has comes from that fountain for which we ought to thirst in this wilderness, so that, sprinkled by it as though by drops, we may not fail on the way.

**Note:** This is taken from Augustine’s fifth treatise on John; it is also sentence 325 in Prosper. Severus Binius.

### XXIII

People do their own will, not God’s, when they do what displeases God. But when they do [variant: “thus do”] what [variant: “thus”] they will in such a way that they serve the divine will, although they act willingly, it is nevertheless the will of him by whom what they will is both prepared and commanded.

**Note:** The text in Saint Augustine, *Treatise 19 on John*, reads: “They do what they do.” It is also sentence 336 in Prosper. Severus Binius.

### XXIV

The branches are in the vine (Prosper, *Sentences*, no. 364) in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine, but receive from it what enables them to live. For the vine is in the branches in such a way that it supplies them with vital nourishment rather than receiving it from them. Consequently, both having Christ abiding in them and abiding in Christ benefit the disciples in whatever way they do—not Christ.

**Note:** “Both,” a reading that seems entirely preferable to the Vulgate.

**Note:** “In Christ”; for when the branch has been cut off, both things benefit the disciples, not Christ.

For when a branch has been cut off, another can sprout from the living root. But the branch that has been cut off cannot live without the root.

**Note:** From Augustine, *On John*, treatise 81. Severus Binius.

### XXV

It is altogether the gift of God to love God (Prosper, *Sentences*, no. 368). He gave that he might be loved—he who loves though not loved. We were loved when we were displeasing, so that something might come about in us by which we could become pleasing. For the Spirit of the Father and the Son pours love into our hearts; with the Father and the Son we love that Spirit.

**Note:** Augustine, *Treatise 102 on John*, has the same thought in nearly the same words. Severus Binius.

And thus, according to the foregoing statements of the Holy Scriptures and the definitions of the ancient Fathers, we ought, with God’s favor, both to preach and to believe this: that through the sin of the first man free will was bent and weakened, so that afterward no one could love God as he ought, or believe in God, or do for God’s sake what is good, unless the grace of divine mercy had first preceded him.

Therefore we believe that the illustrious faith of righteous Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the whole multitude of the ancient Fathers—which the Apostle Paul praises in their honor (Hebrews XI)—was bestowed not through the good of nature, which had previously been given in Adam, but through the grace of God.

We both know and believe that, even after the Lord’s coming, this grace is bestowed through the generosity of Christ upon all who desire to be baptized, not possessed in free will, according to what has often already been said and what the Apostle Paul proclaims: “To you it has been granted for Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Philippians I); and: “God, who began a good work in you, will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., VI); and: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; for it is the gift of God” (Ephesians II).

And concerning himself the Apostle said: “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians VII). He did not say, “because I was faithful,” but “so that I might be faithful.” And: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (James I); and: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (John III); and: “No one has anything unless it has been given to him from above.”

**Note:** The following material is absent from manuscript C.H., but is present in our Paris manuscript. Hardouin.

There are innumerable testimonies of the Holy Scriptures that could be brought forward to prove grace; but they have been omitted for the sake of brevity, because in truth, for one whom a few do not suffice, more will be of no benefit.

We also believe according to the Catholic faith that, once the grace received through baptism has been accepted, all baptized persons, with Christ helping and cooperating, can and ought, if they are willing to labor faithfully, fulfill whatever pertains to the salvation of the soul.

**Note:** The Paris manuscript has “after receiving the grace of baptism”; the Lugdunensis reads “but having received the grace of baptism.” J. Sirmond.

We not only do not believe that some have been predestined by divine power to evil, but, if there are people who wish to believe so great an evil, we pronounce anathema upon them with complete abhorrence.

We also salutarily profess and believe this: that in every good work we do not begin first and then receive help through God’s mercy; rather, he himself, with no preceding good merits on our part, first inspires in us both faith and love of him, so that we may faithfully seek the sacraments of baptism and, after baptism, with his help, be able to fulfill what pleases him.

Hence it must be believed most clearly that the faith of the thief whom the Lord recalled to the homeland of paradise (Luke XXIII), of the centurion Cornelius to whom the angel of the Lord was sent (Acts XX), and of Zacchaeus, who was deemed worthy to receive the Lord himself (Luke X), that faith so remarkable was not from nature but was a gift of divine generosity.

**Note:** The Lugdunensis reads “but bestowed by the generosity of grace” [perhaps for “bestowed by grace,” Hardouin]. The Rhemensis and Bellovacensis read “but from the gift of divine generosity.” J. Sirmond.

And because we desire and wish that the definition of the ancient Fathers and our own definition, which has been subscribed below, should be a medicine not only for the religious but also for the laity, it was decided that the distinguished and magnificent men who had assembled with us for the aforementioned festival should also subscribe it with their own hands.

The conclusion is confirmed by what I said above under “Liberius Patricius.” Accordingly, the following appended reading is corrupt and depraved: “The most distinguished and illustrious men, prefects of the praetorium, agreeing, subscribed.” It should instead be corrected from the Vatican manuscript as follows: “Petrus Marcellinus Felix Liberius, a man of clarissimus rank and illustrious prefect of the praetorium of Gaul and patrician, agreeing, subscribed.” So Baronius in the previously cited place in the appendix. **Note:** That chapters concerning faith and morals were sometimes sent from the Apostolic See, and especially selected from the teaching of Saint Augustine, is demonstrated by many other things, and also by the preface of this synod, from which we cited earlier, column 1144. We noted that it could plausibly be inferred that the first eight canons of Orange were excerpted and abridged from some more extensive collection that the Roman pontiff had sent into Gaul.

But what if this is that very collection which the most learned and most beloved man to me, Reverend Father Alexander Wiltheimius of our society, sent here from a manuscript codex copied in the famous Benedictine abbey of Saint Maximinus at Trier, together with several other materials? Reader, accept it, weigh it yourself, and judge. P. Labbe.

## Appendix to the Works of Saint Caesarius (C, S)

### Exhortation of Saint Caesarius: On Holding or Preserving Love

*(From the library of Nicolas Fabri.)*

This admonition also shows that no one can ever excuse himself truthfully by claiming that he cannot possess true love. For we believe that some statements from Saint Augustine’s homily on love, insofar as they seemed useful to us, should be inserted into this sermon.

The chief reason, dearest brothers, why we so frequently impress upon you the good of true love is that it is the Lord’s primary and distinctive commandment, and there is nothing which can be possessed more sweetly or fulfilled more easily and happily with God’s help. The matter is transacted in our mind; if the will does not admit some evil into it, iniquity cannot find a place there. And where the desire for possessions, the root of all evils, is absent, the love that is the root of all good cannot be lacking.

The first and singular cause of divine mercy is that, through the Holy Spirit, love itself is poured into the hearts of all Christians in such a way that, if they wish, they can continually preserve it and continually savor its sweetness. Since opposites usually heal opposites, and nothing is so hostile or contrary to love, which is the foundation of all good, as desire for possessions, which is the root of all evil, these two can in no way exist together. Sweetness does not agree with bitterness, nor light with darkness, nor life with death.

Whoever recognizes that the root of desire for possessions dominates within him should implore God’s help so that he may uproot desire and plant love. Whoever faithfully does this will fulfill all God’s commandments with joy and rejoicing, because whenever some bitterness of the world comes upon him, the sweetness of love does not permit it to prevail in him. Thus true love makes him understand the sweetness of all heavenly goods and patiently endure the bitterness of earthly things.

The second reason is that the burden of love is so light that it does not press down but habitually lifts up. Whoever wishes to preserve it as he received it from Christ, with Christ’s help, will be able to labor without feeling weariness, whether running with his feet, working with his hands, or carrying heavy burdens upon his shoulders. For however long he exercises himself in difficult works for love’s sake, the sweetness of love itself will not allow him to grow weary, because whatever [variant: “anything whatever”] is burdensome to one who does not love is pleasant and light to one who does love.

Let each person, therefore, maintain good will, love all people as himself, and wish others to receive what he desires to be done to himself. Let him pray for the good, that they may be guarded by the Lord; for those of moderate character, that they may become better; and for the wicked, that they may quickly correct themselves. In all sinners, let him hate their vices rather than the people themselves, and, like a good physician, hate the disease, not the sick person.

For whoever hates his sinful people or any enemies more than their vices either desires that they be punished in the present or burned in eternal fire in the future. How detestable and abominable this is, your holy love clearly understands.

Good Christians, however, desire all their enemies to be corrected rather than perish. Because of their ineffable goodness, they strive neither to curse them nor anyone else, in accordance with what is written: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God.” They should never swear, because it is written: “A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the plague will not depart from his house.”

What it says about the plague not departing from his house is to be understood not of an earthly house but of the soul, which is the temple of God. Let him also strive never to lie, because it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul,” and: “You will destroy those who speak falsehood.” Let him strive to maintain justice, because of this saying: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice justice at all times.” Let him hasten to preserve love with his whole heart, because love makes angels [or: makes people like angels].

All these things which I have suggested are brief, so that they may be remembered by heart, and so pleasant and sweet that, with God’s help, they ought to be fulfilled in deeds. Behold, in all these works of true and perfect love, as has already been said, nothing is done by the hands or feet, so that no one may attempt to excuse himself on the ground of inability or weakness.

Since desire for possessions is more bitter than every bitterness and love sweeter than every sweetness, why do people wish to carry the harsh and rough yoke of greed with such dangers and labors, so that they may cast from their necks Christ’s sweet burden and his gentle yoke?

Against these things which I have suggested to your love, no one who wishes to do so can offer a similar excuse by saying that he cannot accomplish them. He is not told: “Fast more than you can; keep watch more than you are able.” Nor is he required to abstain from wine or meat if the weakness of his body cannot tolerate this. If perhaps he cannot be perfect, he is not compelled to sell all that he has and give it to the poor; and if he cannot be a virgin, he is not pressured to prevent himself from taking a wife.

In all these matters that concern bodily exertion, no Christian is compelled unwillingly. Let the one who can fulfill them give thanks to God; but let the one who cannot fulfill them hold fast to true love and have everything in it. For without the works mentioned above, love is sufficient for itself, whereas those good works without love can be of no benefit at all.

I say this again and again, dearest brothers, so that you may more fully understand that no one can excuse himself by claiming that he cannot fulfill God’s commandments. When he attempts to excuse himself from those matters in which the body labors, he cannot bring forward anything from those matters that consist in the virtue of the soul, and especially from love, in which all good things are contained, to show that he cannot accomplish them with God’s help.

Therefore, whoever does not wish to retain true love finds nothing which he can truthfully blame on others, but only something he must blame on himself.

Hold fast, then, dearest brothers, to the sweet and salutary bond of love, without which the rich person is poor, and with which the poor person is rich. If the rich person does not have love, what does he have? If the poor person has love, what does he not have?

And because, as the evangelist John says, “love is God,” what can the poor person lack if through love he has been deemed worthy to possess God? Conversely, what benefit will earthly wealth provide the rich person if he has not been deemed worthy to possess God?

Love and hold fast to love, therefore, dearest brothers, without which no one will ever see God. Do not reassure yourselves apart from love, even if you have performed the other good works. Rather, fear what is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all,” and what is this one thing except true and perfect love, concerning which the Apostle again said: “The whole law is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself”?

For the other works are so useless without love that the Apostle cries out with a free voice: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and give my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

Therefore, because that is true love which loves all people, whoever recognizes that he hates even one person should hasten to vomit out the bitterness of gall, so that he may deserve to receive within himself the sweetness of love. For without it neither fasts, nor vigils, nor prayers, nor almsgiving, nor faith, nor virginity can help anyone.

And because, admonishing us about love, the Apostle said: “Rooted and founded in love,” and because love is the root of all good things, it is abundantly clear that, just as any beautiful and pleasant tree, full of flowers and fruits, will wither in all its beauty if it does not possess a living root, so any Christian who shows that he possesses the other good works as though they were branches, yet presumes upon them without love and refuses to possess the root of love, will remain sterile and without any fruits.

True love endures in adversity, exercises restraint in prosperity, is strong amid harsh sufferings, cheerful in good works, safest in temptation, sweetest among true brothers, most patient among false ones, innocent amid snares, mourning amid iniquities, breathing freely in truth: chaste in Susanna toward her husband, in Anna after her husband, in Mary because of her husband; humble in Peter for obeying, free in Paul for reproving, huna [perhaps *humana*, “human”] in Christians for confessing, divine in Christ for forgiving.

For true love, dearest brothers, is the soul of all the Scriptures, the power of prophecy, the solidity of knowledge, the fruit of faith, the wealth of the poor, and the life of the dying. Hold fast to it faithfully, love it with your heart and with the whole power of your soul, and cling to it continually.

The Lord is sweet and sweeter than every sweetness; association with him has no bitterness, and conduct in his company has no deceit. If you wish to hold it with an undivided heart, it will make you fulfill God’s commandments with joy in this world and reach eternal rewards in the world to come. May he deign to grant this, he who reigns forever.

## Letter of Saint Caesarius to Certain Germans
I fear, venerable sons, that while I presume to offer you some advice, in a rustic and unskilled style, for the preservation of your peace and chastity, I may seem to incur the stigma of presumption among those who do not know how great is the power of charity. For although I am conscious of my sins and not unaware of your purity, I nevertheless, being lukewarm, presume to admonish the fervent; being slow, to urge on those who are running; being weak, to offer counsel to the healthy; and, remaining on the road, to summon you to desire the eternal homeland. And because, in accordance with your holy wish, I cannot visit you more frequently, I piously and humbly send this little admonition to your serenity in place of my presence. [Col. 1155A] Yet this presumption, as I said, is charity itself that urges it upon me, for charity knows no fear. Therefore I ask you, venerable sons, that, forgiving my boldness, you patiently and kindly receive whatever I suggest; and, making allowance for my rusticity or bashfulness, reread my exhortation in private, attributing it to no one else, lest the ears of any learned person be offended by the harshness of our speech.

For, by God’s favor, although we know nothing sinister about your most holy way of life, yet, because of the many snares of the enemy, of whom it is said, “He has a thousand names, a thousand arts of harming,” we admonish your holy conscience with whatever words we can, even if they are lukewarm, on account of his poisonous cunning and his evil, flattering desires. And although we are poorly equipped as warriors, we provide you with spiritual weapons against the fiery arrows of the devil.

Rejoice and exult in the Lord, venerable sons, and continually give him abundant [Col. 1155B] thanks, for he has deigned to draw and summon you from the darkness of this world’s way of life to the harbor of peace and religious devotion. Consider continually, brothers, from where you have come and where you have deserved to arrive. You have faithfully abandoned the darkness of the world and have happily begun to see the light of Christ; you have despised the fire of lust and reached the refreshment of chastity; you have rejected gluttony and chosen abstinence; you have rejected avarice and luxury and held fast to chastity and mercy.

But I ask you, venerable sons, that just as you are secure concerning the past, so you may be concerned about the future. For all crimes and sins quickly return to us if they are not conquered daily by good works. Hear the apostle Peter saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour.” As long as we live in this body, let us fight against the devil day and night, with Christ as our helper and guide.

There are some—and this is worse—who are [Col. 1155C] negligent and lukewarm, who glory only in the name of Christianity and think that it is sufficient for them to have changed their clothing and assumed the religious habit, not knowing the prophetic saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation”; nor considering the Psalmist’s statement: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways”; nor what the Apostle said: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven.”

We can put off secular clothing and put on religious clothing in a single day, or even in a single hour; but we must continually maintain good habits and labor, with Christ’s help, against the evil and alluring pleasures of this world for as long as we live, because “not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end, will be saved.”

Therefore, above all, let the soul that desires to preserve religion strive with the whole strength of faith to conquer gluttony and avoid drunkenness. Let it have a temperate meal and a moderate table, so that its [Col. 1155D] flesh is neither weakened by excessive abstinence nor provoked to luxury by an abundance of delicacies. Then let it lay a deep foundation of humility, restrain its tongue, flee detraction as poison, neither utter idle words itself nor willingly admit words uttered by another into its ears. Let it become accustomed to a manner of dress that is neither excessively shabby nor changeably ostentatious or dangerously elegant.

Let it frequently read, or receive the words of one who reads with the full eagerness of its heart. Let it continually draw the water of salvation from the divine springs of Scripture—indeed, that water of which the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” Let the holy soul continually strive to adorn itself with the flowers of paradise, that is, with the meanings of the holy Scriptures, and let it ceaselessly place those precious jewels in its ears; from them let it fashion rings and bracelets for itself while it performs good works. There let us seek the ornaments of chastity; there, the holocausts of compunction.

Whoever desires to preserve religion with an [Col. 1156A] immaculate heart and pure body should either never go out in public, or certainly do so only for a grave and unavoidable necessity [the manuscript has *evitabili*, “avoidable”; *inevitabili* is evidently intended]. Let no one say, “My conscience is sufficient for me.” Let each say whatever pleases him about himself: this excuse is wretched and very hateful to God, and proceeds more from immodesty than from a good conscience.

For when, at the beginning of an intimate relationship, either a man or a woman begins to associate with the other, the relationship is recognized as sufficiently modest and almost holy. But because at first the devil conceals his devices, until gradually, as constant familiarity increases between the two, they nourish hostility [the text has *nutriunt*, perhaps for *nutriat*, “nourishes”], the cunning enemy makes them serve one another for a short time, without any apparent reason of lust and without any loss of chastity. Thus he surrounds them with a false security, as though in a gentle calm, and like two little boats carries them out into the deep. While they think themselves safe and do not seek the aid of fasting, as though they were guilty, once he has made them secure, he suddenly dashes them upon themselves and sinks them in a storm; [Col. 1156B] driving them into wounded embraces, he kills them both with one blow.

For a long time he conceals sudden fires without any flames, until, joining the two torches together, he sets both alight at once [the manuscript reading *subito igne* is corrected in the apparatus to *subditos ignes*, “fires placed beneath”]. Thus the devil unfolds what he had previously seemed to provide; thus, as though from simple charity, he forges illicit love: when yielding has from the outset been despised, he is able to gain a stronger hold.

See how secure each person is about his own conscience: when he sees someone being scandalized by him, can he really be incapable of understanding it? Does he see another’s will in the same way that he knows his own conscience? Your eye sees simply, while perhaps the other person desires cruelly. You rejoice in your own capacity, yet do not fear the other’s ruin. For if you make yourself excessively familiar, you nourish another’s desire. Even if you yourself do not sin, you will nevertheless destroy another, and you will become a cause—even without a cause—for alien lust to stain you.

Do not, I beg you, do not give anyone an occasion [Col. 1156C] or grant excessive familiarity, lest perhaps someone’s desire, kindled wickedly against you, begin elsewhere to seek what it could not find in you. But perhaps someone says, “I am secure in my conscience.” Far be it that this should come from a religious mouth: the one who trusts in his virginity has already fallen. If he desires, with Christ’s help, to conquer lust, let him know with absolute certainty that whoever does not overthrow an unworthy familiarity will soon destroy either himself or another.

But perhaps someone says, “I do not flee familiarity because I want to have something to conquer; I desire to keep my adversary captive.” Beware lest the adversary begin to rebel against you. Beware lest that captivity lead you captive. Hear the Apostle saying: “Flee fornication.” Against the other vices we must resist with every strength; against lust, however, it is not fitting to fight, but to flee. Be, then, a fugitive from lust if you wish to be an outstanding fighter for chastity.

But attend carefully to what I said. When someone is alone and is stirred by the goads of lust, with Christ’s help let him resist himself as much as he can, because he has nowhere to flee. But when, through the companionship of another—though it may seem appropriate—the devil supplies an opportunity for pleasure, let the holy soul flee that very familiarity with all its strength, as I said above. Thus, when someone is tempted in himself, let him resist himself with God’s help; but when his conscience is even slightly titillated through another’s companionship, let him flee it with all possible speed, as he would a venomous serpent.

But so that we may be able to observe all these things, let us maintain [Col. 1156D] rational abstinence, for the saying of that most holy man is true: “As you restrain your belly, so also do you restrain its poisonous impulses.” Let us also preserve true humility as far as we can. For bodily integrity is not preserved when the mind is corrupted by the swelling of pride; especially when the flame of anger frequently rises, it quickly consumes the flowers of chastity and virginity [the text has *castitas et virginitas*; the apparatus suggests *virginitatis*, “of virginity”].

A soul devoted chastely to God should not maintain constant familiarity either with strangers or even with its parents—whether they come to it or it goes to them [Col. 1157A; the printed text has *non declinet*; the apparatus notes: “Perhaps read *debet*, as in column 1131, line 41”]—lest it say what it ought not or what is not beneficial, or see something that may be contrary to chastity.

If the vessels that are offered in the church or placed upon the most holy altar are called holy by everyone, and if it is not lawful afterward to take them from the church back into a secular household or adapt them to human uses, if vessels that can possess neither understanding nor sensation have such dignity, what dignity, do you think, does one have before God who was created in his image?

Therefore, just as [the text reads *Sunt*; the supplied correction is *sicut*, “just as”] holy vessels cannot and ought not to be withdrawn from the church to serve human uses, so it is not fitting, becoming, or beneficial for any religious person to be entangled in the obligations of parents or bound by the harmful familiarity of any strangers.

Above all I admonish you to flee the evil of envy as viperous poison, and to prepare spiritual medicines for one another through holy conversation. For there are some—and this is worse—who, when they join together, inflict greater wounds on one another by detraction or murmuring against their superior than they prepare spiritual medicines. [The apparatus adds *qui*, “who”; it also reads *magis* for *magna*, “more.”]

But you, holy and venerable sons, if you see someone [Col. 1157B] fainthearted, offer consolation; if someone is proud, apply the medicine of humility; if you see someone angry, supply the cooling remedy of patience.

If you were born noble, rejoice more in the humility of religion than in worldly dignity. Dispose of your earthly substance in such a way that, by giving it promptly and generously, you may acquire spiritual wings, rather than, by reserving something for yourselves or distributing it too slowly, acquire carnal chains. For if earthly substance is distributed too slowly, it is known to bind the soul’s wings, as though with glue or pitch [the text has *vi aut coactus*, “by force or compelled”; the apparatus suggests *quasi visco*, “as though with pitch”], because the saying written in Scripture is true: “The impediments of the world have made them wretched.”

But if someone was poor before assuming holy religion, he ought to give thanks to God, who did not wish to bind him with the resources of this world. For many people—and this is worse—their possessions hold them so tightly bound that they cannot return to their eternal homeland.

But you are already happy in this world, by Christ’s favor, [Col. 1157C] because you have despised the resources and pleasures of this world not only in heart but also in body. Put your hands to the plow, then, and do not look back; and because you have deserved to climb to the roof of perfection, do not let the pleasure of this world pull you down from it.

Remember Lot’s wife, who, or because she, looked back and was changed into a pillar of salt [the alternative *quae* is noted for *quia*].

Let no oath, let no curse, ever come from your mouth. Guard not only your bodies but also your hearts with every care, because it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance”; and the Lord says in the Gospel: “For evil thoughts come out of the heart.”

If nothing evil is thought in the heart, whatever is holy is brought forth from the mouth, because, as it is written, “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart.” The tongue is accustomed to bring forth whatever the conscience has supplied from the workshop of the heart. Therefore, if you wish to bring good things from your mouth, always think in your heart about what is holy.

You ought to devote yourselves to reading and prayer [Col. 1157D] in such a way that at times you can also work with your hands. Above all, however, accustom yourselves to devote yourselves to reading until the third hour, and dedicate the better part of the day to holy work.
