Let prayer itself proceed from the heart in silence, so that it is scarcely heard in the mouth. For whoever wishes to pray in a loud voice harms both himself and another, since through his chattering he distracts another person’s mind from holy and secret prayer.

And in the very works that you perform with your hands, despise and reject secular and ostentatious clothing, which serves not utility but vanity, so that even in earthly tasks you may be able to practice whatever is appropriate to sobriety and propriety. Many people display in their works what they love in their conduct. They prepare secular ornaments for themselves because they love the world and serve pleasure or luxury.

But for you, to whom the world has been crucified, let there be nothing in common [Col. 1158A] with such people. Clothing arranged for luxury, as though the flesh were an enemy and adversary, should be rejected by your superior [the preceding text is corrupt; the note reads: “It seems the reading should be *Quibus ad…*”].

For there are some—and this is worse—who, on account of the vanity of this world, take greater pains to pursue earthly desires than to devote themselves to divine reading. They want beautiful coverlets and decorated carpets, embroidered cloths and other similar things, at great cost and with extravagant expenditure, for the pleasure of the eyes, not knowing what the Lord cries out and says through the evangelist John: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the world” [the manuscript has *omnis quae*; the correction is *omne quod*, “everything that”].

What does it profit someone to guard virginity and bodily integrity if he is unwilling to avoid the desires of the eyes? There are also some who wish to give the greater part of their possessions to their parents—and perhaps to rich people—rather than to the poor. They do not consider that, by giving their substance to those people for luxury, they consume themselves in eternal poverty.

But someone will say: “Then [Col. 1158B] should I despise my parents?” Far be it that we should say that you ought not to honor your parents. How could we proclaim that parents should not be loved, when we say that enemies must be loved? Love your parents as much as you can, and if they are chaste and honorable, always show them respect; leave them some small gifts from your possessions. But give everything that is greater and more useful, everything that will benefit them until the end of the world, to the poor, so that your almsgiving may pass into the kingdom of heaven until the day of judgment for the refreshment of the poor [the apparatus adds *transeat*, “may pass”].

Whatever less you give, they will afterward be able to provide for themselves [the text adds: “who were unable to work”]. But whatever less you prepare for yourself through mercy, you will never be able to find in that world.

Nevertheless, if there are parents who lack food or clothing, we have a reward with God if you give them something from which they can be sustained. For we shall come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, and if we have acted well, we shall hear joyfully: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom, because I was hungry and thirsty, and so forth; whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me.”

He did not say: “Come, receive the kingdom of God, [Col. 1158C] because you increased your parents’ riches, because you left them provisions with which they might live luxuriously in this world.” He certainly did not say that, but rather what the Gospel records, which the prophet had previously foretold: “He scattered; he gave to the poor.” Pay attention: “He scattered; he gave to the poor.” He did not say “to rich people who live luxuriously,” or to those who love this world.

For that rich man whom we read about in the Gospel, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, left his brothers rich; but afterward, burning in hell, he sought a drop of refreshment and could not find it.

But you, holy souls worthy of God, do everything spiritually, and offer—or rather, return—your substance to the one to whom you have consecrated your souls. It is right that the one who prepares eternal things for you should receive earthly things from you; that the one who bestowed on you the crown of virginity should receive your earthly substance; for you are more deeply indebted to him because he granted you the ability to follow the immaculate Lamb wherever he goes.

The rest of the faithful multitude indeed follows Christ, [Col. 1158D] but not wherever he goes—only wherever they are able. Penitents and married people can follow Christ by other ways of righteousness, apart from the path on which he proceeds in the beauty of virginity. They do not possess what would make them virgins, since in them it has happened that they cannot be virgins.

But you, holy sons, follow him by perseveringly holding what you ardently vowed. Beware lest the good of virginity perish from you, since you can do nothing to make it return.

Again and again, holy souls consecrated to God, I ask you, and with all humility presume to offer counsel for preserving the reward of virginity: strive with all your strength to repel from yourselves and from your households all unsuitable familiarity.

Far away, far away be this plague [Col. 1159A] that disordered familiarity hurls forth. There is no security in a companionship that suffers collisions. In this familiarity, as though amid turbulent waves, friendly harmony does not dwell; it grows only through discordant hostility.

For preserving the dignity of holy religion, security is a far more sacred witness than disordered familiarity.

Pay attention, holy soul; understand carefully how many evils arise from disordered familiarity. Familiarity with any woman, if it begins to become frequent, sows nothing but corruption: it causes vices to sprout, conceives lust, prepares disgrace, extends fury, nourishes wantonness, feeds insolence, exalts falls, builds ruins, raises banks, opens precipices, is shipwrecked in dangers, makes shipwrecks contemptible, rejoices in destruction, sometimes cherishes [the text has *intertum*, uncertain], purchases confusion, stores up disgrace, magnifies accusations, inflames excuses; and in a crowd, all at once, numerous snares of entrapment are heaped together, and through endless disgraces it brings upon the lost the ruin of manifold death. [The text has *andagines*, perhaps *indagines*, “snares” or “traps.”]

No one overcomes all these and such great evils of harmful familiarity except one who strives to have little or, at any rate, only rarely, the companionship through which he might be endangered. [Col. 1159B] For the holy soul that wishes to guard its secret should flee the evil of constant association with all the strength of its mind.

That holy solitude is an invincible defense of sanctity, a strong assault against infamy, firmness of strength, weakness of wanton insolence, protection of one’s own integrity, destruction of weakness, victory of the soul, prey of the body, freedom of glories, captivity of crimes, bride of holiness, repudiation of shame, sign of sincerity, cleansing of scandals, exercise of self-restraint, total evacuation of luxury, secure peace of the virtues, restless attack upon quarrels, summit of purity, prison of lust, harbor of propriety and shipwreck-site of disgrace, place of virginity that cannot be wrecked, enemy of uncleanness, breastplate of modesty, spoil of [the text has *proprietatis*, “one’s ownness” or “property”; the sense is uncertain], wall of incorruption, restraint of vulgarity, dignity of integrity, overthrow of fornication, adherence to brightness, precipice of disgrace, will toward good works, affliction of vices, refreshment of chastity, punishment of insolence, acquisition of triumphs, loss of crimes, rest of salvation, exile of destruction, life of the spirit, death of the flesh, the state of angelic quality, and burial of human substance.

All these evils will be conquered bravely with God’s help, [Col. 1159C] and those good things we have mentioned will be acquired happily, if disordered familiarity is rejected by holy souls.

Pay attention, I beg you, holy souls, because among all the battles in which Christian warfare is continually engaged, the struggles of chastity alone are more severe: here the fight is daily and victory rare. Chastity has received a grave enemy, one who is conquered and feared every day. Every day, I say, he is conquered, yet he does not allow one to challenge him. No one wins securely when he fights against himself.

Dangerous [lacuna] glory in the Christian name.

For this reason those five foolish virgins and those five wise virgins are so called, because [Col. 1159D] all human beings are shown to possess five senses: sight, hearing [the text reads *anditus*, an OCR error for *auditus*], taste, smell, and touch. Through these senses, as through certain doors and windows, either life or death enters our soul. Concerning them the prophet also said: “Death entered through the windows.”

Therefore five virgins are called wise because they use these senses well, and five are called foolish because through these five senses they receive death rather than life.

Let us investigate more carefully how these five senses, like five virgins, either guard virginity or become subject to corruption.

If a man or woman sees his or her son or daughter, male servant or female servant, and looks attentively with desire, one virgin has been corrupted, because through the eyes—that is, through the windows of the body—the poison of death has entered the secret place of the heart.

But if anyone, whether religious or lay, willingly listens [Col. 1160A] to people who disparage others, or to those uttering idle words and luxurious or shameful songs, and receives them with pleasure through an indulgent hearing, another virgin has been corrupted.

If someone is not content with moderate food but seeks expensive delicacies, or if he is always eager to speak wickedly, the third virgin has been corrupted.

If he also carefully seeks foreign perfumes so that he may please people, the fourth virgin has been violated [the text has *Sed*, “But”; perhaps read *Si*, “If”].

But if he wishes, with pleasure and because of lust, to touch other people’s sons or daughters with his hands, and seeks excessively soft clothing with a voluptuous mind, then the fifth virgin too has been corrupted.

Because these five senses, arranged like five virgins, are corrupted in human beings, and conversely because holy souls restrain these five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—from everything illicit and release them soberly and chastely toward what is permitted (*licita*, evidently misread in the source as *ficita*) or lawful, therefore the five virgins signify all who are good, while the other five prefigure those who are evil.

And truly, dearest brothers, what does it profit a man or woman, a cleric or monk or [Col. 1160B] holy woman, if virginity is preserved in the body while the integrity of the heart is violated by evil desires? What does it profit to display chastity in one member while corruption dwells in all the senses?

For those virgins who follow the Lamb, if you pay careful attention, do not follow the Lamb because they preserved bodily virginity alone. Indeed, after saying, “These are they who have not defiled themselves with women,” Scripture immediately adds, “and no falsehood was found in their mouth. They are without blemish.”

Therefore, whoever glories in bodily virginity alone, pay close attention: if he loves falsehood, he will not be able to follow Christ with those holy virgins.

Let no virgin, then, presume on bodily virginity alone, because if she is disobedient or talkative, let her know that she will be excluded from the bridal chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom.

Although a virgin holds the hundredth degree and a married woman the thirtieth, a chaste woman is nevertheless better than a proud virgin. The married woman, serving her husband chastely and humbly, possesses the thirtieth degree; the proud virgin will retain not even one degree. In her is fulfilled what the Psalmist says: “You will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud.”

And because the blessed Apostle calls the whole Church a virgin, [Col. 1160C] considering in it not only bodily virgins but desiring the minds of all to be undefiled, he says: “I have betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” Therefore the soul not only of holy women but also of all men and women, if it wishes to preserve virginity with bodily chastity in those five senses mentioned above, should have no doubt that it is the bride of Christ.

For Christ must be understood as the Bridegroom not of bodies but of souls.

And therefore, dearest brothers, men and women alike, boys and girls alike, if they preserve virginity until marriage and, while using these five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—do not corrupt their souls, they will happily deserve to enter, when the doors are opened, the eternal bridal chamber of the Bridegroom on the day of judgment.

But those who [Col. 1160D] corrupt their bodies before marriage through adulterous union and afterward do not cease to violate their souls throughout their lives by living badly, seeing badly [the text has *vivendo*, “living”; perhaps *videndo*, “seeing”], hearing badly, and speaking badly—unless fruitful and fitting repentance comes to their aid—will cry out in vain when the doors are closed: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” And they will deserve to hear: “Truly I tell you, I do not know where you are from.”

Therefore, brothers, if clerics and monks, holy women [the text has *sanctimonialibus*; corrected to *sanctimoniales*], and those living in marriage faithfully and carefully attend to these things, and, with the Lord’s help, preserve the integrity of their hearts together with bodily chastity, we shall not be cast out with the foolish into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Rather, admitted with the wise to the spiritual wedding, we shall deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord.”

## Likewise: Saint Caesarius on the Ten Virgins.

In the Gospel reading that was recited to us concerning the ten virgins, dearly beloved brothers, it was said that all the virgins trimmed their lamps; but the foolish had no oil prepared for their lamps, whereas the prudent took oil in their vessels. When the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep. At midnight a cry was made: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.” Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. When the lamps of the foolish virgins were going out, they asked the others, in whose vessels there was oil, to give them some of their oil. They replied: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go rather to the sellers and buy some for yourselves.” While they were going to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready entered with him to the wedding, and the door was shut. Later the remaining virgins came, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” They were answered: “I do not know where you are from.”

When it says that, while the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep, that sleep signifies death. Accordingly, as the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep.” Midnight, when the cry was made, signifies the great day of judgment. It is called midnight because of ignorance, since no one knows when or at what hour the day of judgment will come.

That all the virgins trimmed their lamps, and that even the foolish had some oil, but only a little, so that it could not suffice for them at all, is shown by the fact that their lamps immediately began to go out. Therefore, as far as we can, with God’s help we must labor, dearest brothers, so that, since oil signifies mercy or charity, we may store in the vessels of our souls as much as will suffice for us eternally. A little is sufficient for no one, brothers dearly beloved, except perhaps one who, because of poverty, is unable to give more. The lamp of the soul must be full, so that through the oil of charity our light may shine eternally.

To the one to whom God has given greater possessions, let him open his hand as far as he can for almsgiving. Let him not believe that a little can suffice for him; rather, let each person consider, from the time when he began to have understanding, how much he ought to pay for what he has thought, spoken, or done wrongly. Let him take account of the multitude of his sins and carefully weigh the price of each one. Let him see what he owes for lies, oaths, perjuries, curses or slanders, drunkenness, gluttony and lust, filthy thoughts, and idle words.

Let each person consider all these things and others like them, which cannot even be counted. Then he will recognize how many alms he ought to give. Even if we were sold entirely [variant: “if we were all sold”], unless God’s mercy outweighed them, we could not redeem all our sins. Let us therefore do as much as we can with a humble and contrite heart—not for human praise, but because of God’s command [possibly: “for the sake of God’s commandment”] and in contemplation of eternal life.

As for what the foolish virgins said to the prudent—“Give us some of your oil”—and what the latter replied—“Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you”—I think this was said humbly, because such terror and such examination will take place on the day of judgment that even those who understand themselves to have prepared an abundance of the oil of mercy will fear that it may not suffice for redeeming all their sins.

What was said—“Go rather to the sellers and buy some for yourselves”—can be understood of the poor. They are the merchants who sell the oil necessary for the lamps of souls. Through them Christ is accustomed to conduct this commerce. In them he receives earthly things in order to repay eternal things. Thus he himself said: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.”

The lamps signify souls. The vessels in which the oil is stored signify good consciences. What does it mean to have oil in vessels except to store good works within the conscience? Since some perform good works out of love for God, while others do so out of desire for human praise, those virgins—both those who were virgins in body and those who exercised themselves in vigils, psalms, readings, or prayers—did all this for human praise, not for God [Col. 1162A] or for eternal blessedness. Therefore, when death intervened and human praise ceased for them, their oil also failed at the same time.

What was said to them—“Go rather to the sellers and buy some for yourselves”—may also be understood in this way: the sellers are those who praise the foolish virgins with flattering commendations. Thus it is understood that all who desire to receive human praise sell, through human flattery, what they appear to perform in God’s work, receiving empty praise and losing eternal rewards. But those virgins who had oil in their vessels placed every good work within their consciences, because they performed them not for praise but for divine mercy.

Therefore, faithfully considering these things, dearly beloved brothers, since this parable concerns the whole Church, let those who cannot preserve bodily virginity guard the integrity of their hearts. Thus, if they cannot attain the crown of martyrs or virgins, at least we may deserve to receive forgiveness for all sins.

But virgins who, with God’s help, preserve bodily integrity should strive with all their strength and with God’s assistance to avoid excessive talk; to reject slander and murmuring as the poisons of the devil; to fear the disease of envy and pride as one fears an enemy’s sword; to preserve obedience humbly; never to despise the commands of their superior; and to persist in reading and prayer. If illness does not prevent it, they should rise to the vigils with complete eagerness, whether in the oratory or in any other place. They should always strive to utter from their mouths what pertains to obedience and humility. If they see someone sad, let them console that person; if they recognize someone as disobedient, let them not cease to correct him.

And because in every calling both good and evil people are found, and in Christ’s Church there is not only wheat but also chaff, there are—what is worse—clerics, monks, and nuns so negligent and lukewarm that they do not, like spiritual bees, produce the sweet honey of souls; instead, like the most savage wasps, they strike the hearts of their brothers with the poisonous stings of their tongues. Such people are shown to be not Christ’s helpers but the devil’s defenders.

If they happen to see a brother or sister rising proudly against a superior, they do not merely strive to calm the person; rather, with malicious speech they try to inflame him or her still further, saying that this could and should no longer be tolerated. They even urge them to make the superiors regret it, because the latter wished to admonish or correct them with paternal kindness.

But because, as we have already said, in every way of life not only helpers or ministers of the devil kindle disobedience or pride through crafty whispering, Christ’s helpers also strive through gentle exhortation and holy, salutary counsel to recall people to humility and gentleness.

Those who, placed in the clergy or monastery, raise themselves and others to pride are like quivers full of the devil’s arrows: they strike the hearts of the simple and attempt to extinguish charity, humility, and gentleness in them. But because, by God’s favor, wheat is found in the midst of the chaff, holy souls, shown to be like Christ’s armories filled with spiritual antidotes, do not cease to heal with heavenly medicines whatever wounds those others have inflicted.

They say to every proud person: “Do not be proud, brother, for it is written: ‘God resists the proud.’ Do not be angry, for it is written: ‘Anger rests in the bosom of a fool’; and again: ‘The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God.’”

If they see someone disobedient, they say gently and humbly: “Do not be disobedient, brother, for it is written: ‘Obedience is better than sacrifice.’” And the Apostle cries out: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account.”

These souls, filled with God, if they see someone lukewarm and negligent, bring forth medicines from the spiritual armory—that is, from a good heart—and try to kindle him to repentance. If they see someone slandering and murmuring, they say to him that saying of the blessed Apostle: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer. Do not slander…”

[Here the supplied text contains a lacuna.]

Whoever recognizes himself, through his speech, as a helper and defender of justice should rejoice, give thanks to God, and, with God’s help, persevere to the end, because not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end, will be saved.

But whoever realizes that through pride, disobedience, or envy he is a helper or agent of the devil should grieve over the past, beware of the future, and by humility rebuild what he had destroyed through the tyranny of pride. Let gentleness calm what malice or disobedience had aggravated; let the sweetness of charity set things right. And while that darkened soul, which had been accustomed to serve the devil, is still held in this mortal body, let it acquire a remedy for itself on the day of necessity, so that, transferred from the left to the right among Christ’s sheep, it may deserve to hear: “Come, you blessed; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

And although these things are so, dearly beloved brothers, it is nevertheless necessary that the good not be exalted by their holy merits, nor those who have been evil be broken by excessive despair. Rather, let the former persevere humbly in good things, and let the latter quickly correct their evil, so that, when the day of judgment comes, life may be able to crown the good.

[The supplied text then contains a lacuna.]

# HOMILY: The Teaching of Abbot Macarius Concerning Those Who Are in Monasteries

First of all, when a person begins to recognize himself—why he was created—and seeks his Creator, God, then he will begin to repent of what he committed during the time of his negligence.

Then the good God, in his kindness, gives him sorrow for his sins. After this, again in his goodness, he gives him bodily affliction, fasts, vigils, persistence in prayer, and contempt for the world, so that he willingly bears the injuries inflicted upon him and comes to hate every bodily comfort [Col. 1163C], while loving mourning more than laughter.

After this, he grants him the desire for mourning and weeping, together with humility of heart, so that he may consider the beam in his own eye and not attempt to remove the speck from another’s. Let him always say: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 50).

Let him remember the end of his life and how he will meet God’s presence. Let him also describe before his mind the judgments and punishments, as well as the worthy honors given to the saints.

But if he sees that these things are pleasing to him, God tests him to see whether he renounces his own desires and resists the assaults of the prince of this world, who had previously bound him with food of varied delight that softens the heart, so that he might once again be able almost to conquer him.

The enemy also brings bodily weariness and prolonged desire, while his thoughts say to him: “For how long will you be able to endure this labor?” They say that it is arduous work for anyone to deserve to have God as an inhabitant, especially for you, who have committed many sins: how many sins can God forgive you?

But if he recognizes that his heart is firm in the fear of God and does not abandon its position, but strongly resists the thoughts, then thoughts come to him under the pretext of righteousness, saying: “You have sinned, certainly, but you have repented; now you are holy.” They make him remember the sins of certain people who did not repent, sowing empty glory in his heart.

Not only this, but they also cause certain people to praise him deceitfully and provoke him to works that he cannot bear. They cast into his soul thoughts of not eating or drinking, as well as of vigils, and many other things that it would take too long to mention. They grant him ease in accomplishing these things, if somehow they can entice him to them, although Scripture warns and says: “You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left, but walk on the straight path” (Deuteronomy 5 and 7).

But if the good God perceives that his heart has yielded to none of these things, as David says and indicates concerning such temptations: “You have tested my heart, and visited me by night; you have examined me with fire, and iniquity was not found in me” (Psalm 16).

It must be considered why he said “by night” and not “by day”: plainly, because the enemy’s ambushes are night, as the blessed Paul says that we are not children of darkness but of light, because the Son of God is day, whereas the devil is likened to night (1 Thessalonians 5).

But if the soul has overcome all these battles, then opposing thoughts begin to assault it: the desire for fornication and the unspeakable violation of boys. In all these things the soul grows weak and the heart wastes away, so that it believes the guarding of chastity to be impossible. They add, as I said, the length of time and the difficulty of the struggle, saying that their burden is great and unbearable. They also add bodily weakness and the frailty of nature.

But if he does not grow weary under these attacks, then the good and merciful God sends him holy strength, strengthens his heart, and gives him joy, refreshment, and ability, so that he is found stronger than his enemies and their assault against him does not prevail, because they fear the power dwelling in him.

As the holy Apostle says: “Strive, and you will receive strength.” This is the strength of which the blessed Peter says: “An incorruptible and undefiled inheritance, kept in heaven for you, who are guarded by the power of God through faith” (1 Peter 1).

Then the good and merciful God, if he sees that the man’s heart has been strengthened against his enemies, gradually withdraws the strength that was helping him and allows the enemies to attack him with various desires of the flesh, as well as with empty glory, greed, pride, and the other things that drag people toward destruction, so that he almost resembles a ship which, without a helmsman, strikes against the rocks here and there.

But when his heart has withered amid these things, so to speak, and has failed under each of the enemy’s temptations, then God, the lover of humanity, caring for his creature, sends him holy strength and strengthens him, subjecting his heart, soul, body, and all his inward parts to the yoke of the Paraclete, the Lord himself saying: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11).

Then at last that good God begins to open the eyes of his heart, so that he understands that God himself is the one who strengthens him. Then the man will truly begin to know how to honor God, with all humility and thanksgiving, as David says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Psalm 50), and gentleness is produced in hearts.

When he has been tested in all these things, then the Holy Spirit begins to reveal heavenly matters to him: namely, what is rightly and deservedly owed to the saints and to those who hope in God’s mercy.

Then the man says to himself that apostolic word: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8). And he recalls David’s saying: “For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Psalm 72). That is: “O Lord, how many things you had prepared for me in heaven—and what was I seeking from you in mortal life?”

Thus the torments that sinners will suffer are revealed to him, along with many other things that a holy man understands even without my speaking.

After all this, the Paraclete begins to make a covenant with the purity of his heart, the firmness of his soul, and the holiness of his body. Through the spirit of humility he makes him rise above every creature, so that his mouth does not speak the works of men; so that he sees rightly with his eyes; so that he sets a guard over his mouth; so that he makes his steps follow a straight path; and so that he possesses righteousness in his hands—that is, in his works—together with persistence in prayer, bodily affliction, and frequent vigils.

He arranges these things with him according to measure and discernment, not in turmoil but in tranquility.

But if his mind despises the arrangement of the Holy Spirit, then the strength that had been bestowed upon him departs. Thus the same battles and disturbances arise in his heart, and the passions of the body trouble him at every moment through the enemy’s assault.

But if his heart is converted and he obeys the commands of the Holy Spirit, the Lord’s protection will be cast over him. Then the man recognizes that it is good to cling to God without ceasing and that his life is in him, as David says: “I cried to you, and you healed me.” And again: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Psalm 35).

Therefore, according to my counsel, unless a person possesses great humility, which is the summit of all virtues; keeps watch over his mouth; places the fear of God in his heart; does not prefer himself to others in what he considers an achievement—as though he had done something good; bears the injuries inflicted upon him; offers the other cheek to the one who strikes him; rushes swiftly to every good work; carries his soul in his hand, as though he were dying every day; considers vain everything seen beneath this sun; and says, “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 2), and “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Galatians 6)—he will not be able to keep the commands of the Holy Spirit.

# In the Year of Our Lord 549. Rusticus, Deacon of the Holy Roman Church

[Col. 1165]

# NOTICE (from Gallandi)

## I

Few facts are available to be said about Rusticus, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, and they must be sought nowhere else than in the judgment pronounced by Pope Vigilius against that same Rusticus and his colleague Sebastianus, which is reported among the acts of the Fifth General Council and inserted into Collation 7 [Note: [Col. 1165D] Council, volume VI, page 183, first Venetian edition of Labbé]. The most learned men had already done this—Baronius [Note: [Col. 1165D] Baronius, under the year 550, §§ 15 ff.], Norisius [Note: [Col. 1165D] Norisius, Historical Dissertation on the Fifth Synod, chapter 4], and Pagius [Note: [Col. 1165D] Pagius, under the year 548, §§ 5 ff.]. Following them closely, we have accordingly composed the following account.

Vigilius, therefore, after holding a synod at Constantinople and being impatient of a prolonged stay in the imperial city, and also broken by the violence of the emperor Justinian, wrote a judgment in which he condemned the Three Chapters that he had previously defended, having later changed his position. He added this clause, however: “With the reverence of the Council of Chalcedon preserved in all respects.” This occurred in the course of the year 548.

At that time Rusticus and Sebastianus, very learned deacons of the Roman Church, were with Vigilius. The former, the pope’s nephew, after the judgment had been read, openly declared: “The judgment could not have been better made than it has been.” The latter said: “The judgment has been ordained from heaven.”

## II

But these same deacons, shortly before the great heralds of that judgment, were soon incited by the Africans to rebel against Vigilius himself. The chief instigator was Felix, abbot of the Gillitan monastery in Africa, who had come to Constantinople for this reason.

Although he had initially been rejected by the aforementioned deacons of Pope Vigilius because he avoided communion with the pontiff, Felix nevertheless overcame them by his deceit and persuasion. At the end of that same year, 548, they abandoned their former position and, with brazen insistence, separated themselves from Vigilius’s communion. They disseminated letters in every direction declaring that Vigilius had written something found to be contrary to the definition of the holy Council of Chalcedon, as Vigilius himself says in his writing against them.

As a result, letters full of complaints were written to that same pontiff from orthodox bishops everywhere, and a very great schism was brought about in the Church.

## III

Vigilius therefore understood that the unity of the whole Church would suffer grave harm if he delayed any longer in confronting such evils. Moved by a just indignation against those same deacons, who had increased the number of the enemies, and recognizing that they were unwilling to return to a better course, he struck both of them with anathema and removed them from their dignity and rank.

Baronius recounts the censure of Vigilius, which is mentioned in Justinian’s letter to the Fifth Synod [Note: [Col. 1165D] Baronius, under the year 550, § 16], and assigns it to the year 550. Pagius does likewise [Note: [Col. 1165D] Pagius, under the year 550, §§ 4 and 5]. Moreover, from Vigilius’s letter to Valentinian, bishop of Tomi, reported by Baronius [Note: [Col. 1166D] Baronius, under the year 550, § 2], he rightly argues that the same sentence of deposition was issued before 18 March of that year, 550. There he also argues against Garnier, who maintains that this occurred in the preceding year, 549 [Note: [Col. 1166D] Garnier, Dissertation on the Fifth Synod, chapter 5, § 9, and in the Supplement to Theodore, page 521, number 111].

Although Norisius declares that he does not oppose Baronius, he nevertheless appears to indicate a view less acceptable to himself [Note: [Col. 1166D] Norisius, cited work, volume I, page 598].

What happened to Rusticus afterward is reported by Sirmondus: he was deported into exile by order of Justinian, together with Felix the African, because they had disparaged the Fifth Synod in their writings [Note: [Col. 1166D] Sirmondus, notes on Facundus, Against Mocianus, at the beginning]. To this opinion he brings forward Victor of Tunnuna speaking as follows:

“Eighteen years after the consulship of Basil, a man of clarissimus rank—that is, in the year 557—Felix, abbot of the Gillitan monastery, died in exile at Sinope and departed this life to the Lord.”

But there is no mention here of Rusticus. Perhaps the very learned man was referring to what Victor had written shortly before, where he openly speaks of Rusticus’s exile with Felix the abbot and their companions.

For when Victor had related that the Fifth Synod was convened thirteen years after the consulship of Basil, he adds:

“There they subject the often-mentioned Three Chapters, together with their defenders, to condemnation … Rusticus, deacon of the Roman Church, and Felix, abbot of the Gillitan monastery in the African province, opposing their decrees in writing, are sent into exile in the Thebaid with their companions.”

Rusticus was therefore driven into exile in the year 553. At what time he died, however, is unknown.

## IV

The great Baronius calls Rusticus a most eloquent writer [Note: [Col. 1167C] Baronius, under the year 518, § 37]. Elsewhere he adds that this same deacon, in order to strengthen his position against Vigilius in defense of the Three Chapters, wrote a commentary in the form of a dialogue against the Acephali [Note: [Col. 1167C] The same, under the year 548, § 4].

We have brought forth this Disputation of his Against the Acephali, revised and restored in many places, from the Paris Library of the Fathers. It is clear that it did not reach us complete, but truncated at the end, at the point where the discussion concerned the Three Chapters.

For during the disputation, when the heretic was pressed by the orthodox interlocutor to anathematize Dioscorus, the heretic replied as follows [Note: [Col. 1167C] This passage appears below, col. 1232]:

“For the moment,” he said, “we are not discussing the causes of individual persons, but debating the faith universally. We will reserve this matter for the time when we shall discuss Diodore, Theodore, Ibas, and Theodoret, combining the case of persons with the question of faith.”

From this it is clear that the work is mutilated near the end, since the matters that the author had proposed to discuss are missing there. Perhaps someone cut them out for the reason that in those passages Rusticus criticized Vigilius more sharply than was appropriate.

Hence Baronius, speaking about this very Disputation of Rusticus, says [Note: [Col. 1167C] Baronius, under the year 548, § 5]:

“After the thorns with which that fertile field abounded had been removed from the book, and the brambles with which it had become overgrown in a corner had been cut away, what remains is indeed worthy of a learned man.”

## V

The same father of ecclesiastical annals believes [Note: [Col. 1168C] The same, in the same place, § 4] that Rusticus addressed that Disputation to the deacon Sebastianus, his colleague in the schism, whose name may for that reason have been removed.

He is led to this conjecture by these words placed in the preface of the work: “Remember,” he says, “that you are a Christian and a deacon of the supreme Church of the whole universal community, namely, the Roman Church.”

But Baluzius says [Note: [Col. 1168C] Baluzius, preface to volume I of the New Collection of Councils, § 25 and page 1228] that if anyone attends to Rusticus’s words, he will understand them to refer to Rusticus himself. For he pretends that he had resolved to remain silent, but reason suggested the contrary to him, so that he should not hide the talents entrusted to him.

Among these arguments, therefore, the reason that he introduces as speaking says: “Remember that you are a Christian and a deacon.”

But I am prevented from agreeing with Baluzius’s opinion by Rusticus’s own words in that same preface, where shortly beforehand he says: “All that remains for me is to hope for your prayers.” And again, after the passage quoted above: “It will henceforth be your prayer, if the speech of a man who scarcely presumes on the correctness of his faith alone is good.”

By these words it appears clear that Rusticus is addressing someone other than himself. For this reason, Baronius’s conjecture concerning the deacon Sebastianus also seems to me well founded.

For the rest, I agree with Baluzius in thinking that the Rusticus under discussion is one and the same person as the man who compared the earlier Latin translation of the Council of Chalcedon with ancient codices. Both are shown by the passages cited to have been enemies of the Acephali and defenders of the Three Chapters.

[Col. 1167]

# DISPUTATION OF RUSTICUS AGAINST THE ACEPHALI (C)

## PREFACE

[Col. 1167D] Knowing my sins, my needs, and my measure, I have often resolved to honor silence before dogmatic argument, especially since matters concerning Christians have never been so disturbed as in our own times.

First, no one emulates the zeal of the ancients; instead, people criticize their achievements. They do not acknowledge themselves to be children of those who long ago rested in the Lord, but appoint themselves their judges, adding to them as many accusations as cannot be counted.

Among the Acephali, as one must say, everyone behaves in this way. Among those who have recently arisen, however, it is chiefly the laypeople. Some of those who are called bishops, priests, and deacons, together with the rest of the clergy and the monks, act through error, some through greed, and others through ambition. More than that, all of them, through every kind of evil, have cast away Christian freedom, confidence, and sound zeal to such an extent that, as far as they are concerned, they have left no hope of correction.

With them all Christian virtue has departed, while no one truly cares for or considers worthy of speech what is common and belongs to the Lord Christ. Instead, everyone pursues his own interests more zealously than ever (Philippians 2:11), and places all hope in those through whom he hopes to enjoy these things abundantly.

That these things are true is demonstrated by the facts themselves. Every trace of virtue has disappeared, while every flood of wickedness has submerged the Roman commonwealth.

Considering these matters in my mind, I judged that I ought to abstain from such abominations, devote myself only to tears, and constantly await the divine judgment that has long and frequently struck many people powerfully from above.

But what shall I say? I desire with all my will to leave the world, yet I am exceedingly weak in virtue. All that remains for me is to hope for your prayers.

I shall therefore return to what I had proposed. While these and similar matters occupied my thoughts anxiously, zeal did not remain silent, but reason suggested the opposite:

“Why are you distressed, O man, and think that only despair is possible, looking solely at human impieties and forgetting the divine will? Consider the one who often raises up again those who were thought beyond hope, who so many times brought the dead to life as the Lord. For he who died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6) does not now despise the whole of creation.

“The world indeed betrays what belongs to it and, turning away from its own Creator, shows where it is tending. But the merciful Lord will not for that reason cease to display what belongs to him.

“Meanwhile, do not hide what has been entrusted to you, whether ten talents (Matthew 25:28) or one very small portion, lest he come afterward and demand interest on his own money.

“Moreover, how do you know whether many, or few, or no one will assent to what is said, either so as not to fall or so as to return to the faith of the Lord Christ? Even if what we suspect to be worst of all should occur, you have suffered no loss. Indeed, as though you had fulfilled everything, you will receive crowns. For the most upright, strongest, and rather the most merciful judge judges cases not by the outcome but by the will and intention.

“Since every excuse for remaining entirely silent has been closed to you, and an unfading reward has been set before you for refusing silence, if you remain silent you will hand yourself over completely to punishment.

“You must not fear the accusations of those who act unjustly. To the Lord they have been shown to be ministers of infinite blessedness. Nor should you fear the exiles, imprisonments, various afflictions, and diverse hardships inflicted upon you by those who forbid you to speak, for they are not comparable to the terror of Gehenna.

“Remember that you are a Christian and a deacon, and that you belong to the highest totality of the universal Church. If the burden of the order is unbearable, why did you undertake the dignity in any way? Once made a deacon, you were bound to God by its obligations. Otherwise, you ought to have refused beforehand and, concerning such a rank, kept peace with the adversary, investigating whether, with ten thousand, you could overcome twenty thousand adversaries (Luke 14:31).”

These and similar considerations compel me, as best I can, to write. The rest will depend on your prayer, if the utterance of a man who scarcely presumes upon the soundness of his faith alone proves good—not through ill will, God forbid, but because I am certainly conscious of my weakness.

My intention, therefore, is to collect what I have often read or heard in conversations, both at Constantinople and at Alexandria in Egypt, or at Antinoë in the Thebaid and in neighboring places, whether from myself or from others who defended the definition of the holy Council of Chalcedon. Against these I shall fit the questions of the adversaries that I have likewise encountered, adding only what is necessary for the completion, firmness, or adornment of the discourse.

To distinguish the questions and their solutions, the speaker is marked separately at each point before the words that have been spoken: in matters that are ours, “ORTHODOX”; in those belonging to the others, “HERETIC,” as the matters themselves require and as will be demonstrated in the course of the book.

A single convention is preserved here: not everything said by such people is of that character. Indeed, they often begin with things that we commonly confess and then attempt to demonstrate what belongs to them. To avoid confusing the speeches again through the same distinction, the opposing arguments have been divided between only two persons.

# DISPUTATION

[Col. 1169D] The silence of the place, the convenience of the time, the common agreement, and a holiday from other affairs that has meanwhile come upon us all, as I may say with God’s favor, have coincided together. Therefore, as you promised, ask appropriately whatever you wish about the matters on which we disagree, with every patience and good conscience preserved by us.

Remember for this purpose that we have met together without any contentiousness and, as far as possible, are expressing the matters themselves in words: I saying that one and the same Son of God, Son of man, our Lord Jesus Christ, is acknowledged in two natures; while you may speak as you please.

**The Heretic.** If you say that Christ is two natures and not one composite nature, and the most blessed Virgin gave birth to Christ, then she gave birth to two natures. Therefore, according to the natures that she gave birth to, she will be called Mother of God and mother of man.

This concerns the most impious Nestorius, who, because he thought the two names to be of equal force, preferred to call the Virgin by one name—“mother of Christ”—rather than by the two names “Mother of God” and “mother of man.” Moreover, using the divided terminology, Nestorius said “Mother of God” and “mother of man.” But Cyril, of holy memory, said only “Mother of God.”

Therefore, those who say that Christ has two natures are appropriately called Nestorians.

**Rusticus.** You consistently confuse yourselves in every respect by refusing to distinguish the natures of the Lord Christ. It is you, rather, who must say “Mother of God and mother of man,” without my meanwhile discussing the quality of your words.

For if Christ is one composite nature, and this nature was born from the Virgin, and this same nature is God and man, then the Virgin gave birth to God and man and is called both Mother of God and mother of man.

Therefore, if you call us Nestorians for this reason, you will not yourselves be free from that name. For we do not believe that you call this composite nature, as you say, God alone or certainly pure God. Indeed, you do not consider those who call Christ God in such a way that they do not confess him also as man to belong to your faith.

Nor do I think that you consider the nature of God to be composite.

**Heretic.** We call her only the Mother of God; for this reason especially the most blessed Cyril pressed Nestorius.

**Rusticus.** Why, then? Is the blessed Cyril shown to have used this expression in order to remove the designation “Mother of Man,” or for some other purpose? Say, then: to demonstrate one Son, the Lord Christ, one person, one substance.

**Heretic.** To demonstrate one Christ, Lord, Son, one person, one subsistence, one composite nature.

**Rusticus.** According to you, then, is this nature God alone, so that for this reason she is to be called only the Mother of God?

**Heretic.** Not God alone, but God incarnate.

**Rusticus.** Why, then, did the mother not receive her name from God and flesh—the mother who gave birth to this being?

**Heretic.** Because God is the cause of the flesh. When he wished to administer our salvation, he assumed it as he willed, and through it accomplished what he desired. Therefore both the birth, and the other miracles, and the words, and the suffering—in short, everything—are to be ascribed to God the Word through the flesh, who was incarnate for these very purposes.

**Rusticus.** Are they therefore to be ascribed to God in such a way that they are denied in every respect to the humanity, or are these things also to be said of the man or of the flesh?

**Heretic.** Everything is to be ascribed to God alone—not because these things accrued to one who was merely God, but to God himself incarnate.

**Rusticus.** Yet many of the holy Fathers have confessed that what belongs to the humanity, or to the flesh, ought not to be separated from it. So too did the most blessed Cyril in his synodical letters, and the holy Synod of Ephesus, in the testimonies of the Fathers, inserted this in its official acts as confirmation of its orthodox faith. It decreed that certain things belonging to the flesh are to be attributed, because of the union, to the person of God the Word, while nevertheless we acknowledge them to be proper to the flesh.

**Heretic.** Produce, if you can, testimonies agreeing with what you have just said—provided, of course, that you preserve, when the time demands it, the points we shall advance on behalf of our doctrine. Nevertheless, first, if you can, explain why everything administered through the flesh should not be attributed to God alone, as we demonstrated above.

**Rusticus.** Because it is neither true nor fitting; indeed, it is even harmful. It is not true, because you would not dare say that any of these things accrued to God who was not incarnate, or to him merely insofar as he is God. It is not fitting, moreover, to say that God was like flesh inferior to the Father, mortal, nonexistent before Mary, or that he received the beginning of his existence from her; nor that, through death, God was divided into two parts—that is, into the body and the soul separated from it.

For if we force upon the incarnate one everything that belongs to the flesh, whether by treating what is present as though it were so, or what is absent as though it were not absent, God the Word will be found, before the resurrection, to be neither equal, nor consubstantial, nor undifferentiated, nor coeternal with the Father, nor immutable. He will instead be from one substance and from the substance of the Virgin, which is different from the Father’s substance. He will also be found to be called man and flesh; and through this it follows that flesh was incarnate and that man was made human.

But if we likewise say that what belongs to the Word belongs alternately to the flesh, it follows that man is consubstantial with and equal to God and the Father, while God is inferior to the Father. From this it further follows that the flesh is better than the Word, and that the Word is inferior in comparison with his own flesh. The Father, therefore, is much greater than the Word, and still more so than the angels. I could say many similar things, but I leave it to your understanding rather than gather together an infinite multitude and magnitude of what is plainly incongruous—or rather, impious.

**Heretic.** Then nothing belonging to the flesh belongs to God, nor does anything belonging to God belong to the flesh! Where, then, have the statements of divine Scripture gone? Where are those of the holy Synod of Ephesus—or rather, of Nicaea? Where are all the writings of the illustrious Cyril?

**Rusticus.** Remember, my good man, that I did not say that we ought to say absolutely nothing belonging to the Word of the flesh, or conversely; I said that we ought not to say everything. Do not, then, bring accusations.

But let us return to the matter at hand. If, as is clear from these points, this indiscriminate manner of applying all names is useless and harmful, the matter nevertheless requires a treatment of its own. For if we are saved not only by believing but also by confessing—just as our faith is marked out in the heart or mind not by words but by realities and definitions—so it ought also to proceed from the lips. What is done otherwise is fraud and hypocrisy, and these are inevitably harmful.

If, then, the eternal Word is in every respect as the Father is, and the same divine Word is impassible and immutable as the Father is, let these things be said not merely with a similar expression but with the same expression and in reality. For “immutable” means that which cannot be otherwise.

But one for whom this is impossible neither changes, nor suffers, nor begins. The conclusion is unavoidable: mutable things change, and passible things suffer. Likewise, whatever suffers in any manner is passible in that respect; whatever is changed is mutable; whatever dies is mortal; whatever increases is capable of growth. None of these things, therefore, continues thereafter to preserve impassibility or immutability.

**Heretic.** Can you demonstrate these points for me from the confessions of the holy Fathers, and especially from the holy Synods—that is, from those which assembled at Nicaea and Ephesus—and from the writings of the illustrious Cyril?

**Rusticus.** Certainly, there are demonstrations of these matters. If you wish, this point too will be dealt with shortly; for the moment, a few things remain to be said concerning the first question.

If Adam, overcome by the devil, brought corruption upon our race, it was necessary for the devil to be overcome again by a man, so that we might be able to share in incorruption. But our nature, being weak and subject to slavery and corruption, could not accomplish this by itself; it was necessary that it be assumed by the Lord. Conversely, it was neither fitting nor God’s will that this should be done without our nature.

For God had not purposed to overcome the devil by violence—otherwise he, being pure, could have done this in every way—but wished to grant victory to the man who had been defeated. This could not have occurred more fittingly than through this most beautiful union, provided that in so great a mystery we believe that what was either possible only in this way, or could not have been accomplished more beautifully, was fulfilled.

What could not be accomplished without God ought likewise not to have been effected without man; nor did God will it, since he wills nothing except what ought to be. Therefore it is not permissible to say that all things of this kind belong to God alone, as though he himself had not also been man.

All such things, then, must be confessed as belonging to one and the same person, God and man; or certain things of this kind must be said to belong to God in such a way that we nevertheless do not remove them from being said also of man.

It is therefore not the blasphemy of Nestorius to call her the Mother of Christ, since to call her mother of Christ is the same as to call her mother of God and man. Rather, it is heretical to deny the Theotokos, since divinely inspired Scripture says—and says this repeatedly—“the mother of Jesus” (John 2:1; 19:25; Acts 1:14), and “from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:26).

Furthermore, if the one whom she bore is God, she is rightly called Theotokos; and because the one who was born is Christ, she is rightly called Christotokos. I think, moreover, that whatever reason is given for this name will either be the same as the reason for the other, or will apply even more strongly to it.

Further, if, while being the Mother of God, she is not the Mother of Christ, then Christ—God forbid—will not be God, by a reversal of the argument. For if one who confesses the Christotokos and denies the Theotokos does not call Christ God, then one who confesses the Mother of God and rejects the Mother of Christ likewise denies that Christ is God.

Indeed, it is so good to confess the Mother of Christ, while it is not pious to deny the Mother of God, that Nestorius himself, although he called her the Mother of Christ and denied her to be the Mother of God, was condemned not because he had said the former but because he had added the latter.

Moreover, not everything said by heretics is wicked. What was wicked in Nestorius is evident from the contradictions of the blessed Cyril contained in his letters to him—letters which the most holy Pope Celestine of great Rome also accepted as his own.

**Heretic.** Although I have much to say in response to what has been stated, I do not wish to prolong the discussion, since that might perhaps be both useless and laborious. I ask only that you briefly demonstrate from canonical testimonies whether what, as you say, happened to the flesh of God the Word ought to be said of his humanity, as was previously indicated.

**Rusticus.** You have asked well; for both the order of the discussion requires this, and it will therefore now be stated from a letter of the most holy Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, to John, archbishop of great Antioch, of holy memory, through which peace was established among all the holy Churches of God:

> “We therefore confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; before the ages, indeed, from the Father according to his divinity, but in the last days, for our salvation, born from the Virgin Mary according to his humanity; the same one consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and consubstantial with us according to his humanity. For a union of two natures has taken place; therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord.

> “With regard to the understanding of this unconfused union, we confess the holy Virgin to be the Mother of God, because God the Word was incarnate and made man, and from the very conception chose for himself the temple assumed from her.

> “We know that the evangelical and apostolic statements concerning the Lord are delivered by men who speak divinely, some making them common, as belonging to one person; others dividing them, as belonging to two natures; some attributing them, in a manner appropriate to God, according to the divinity of Christ; and others delivering them in a humble manner, according to his humanity.

> “When we approached these holy statements of yours, you find that we too think in this way—‘one Lord, one faith, one baptism’ (Ephesians 4:5). We glorified the Savior and God of all, rejoicing with one another that the Churches both among us and among you possess a faith agreeing with the divinely inspired Scriptures and the tradition of our holy Fathers.”

**Note:** [Col. 1173D] Greek, κοινοποιοῦντες, “making common.” Thus the edition of Cyril, *Works*, vol. V, part II, p. 106. The *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris, vol. IV, part I, p. 799, incorrectly reads *communicantes*.

**Note:** [Col. 1174D] More clearly from the Greek: “When, therefore, we had read these sacred statements of yours and had observed that we ourselves also held the same view … we glorified,” etc.

These same points are also stated in his letter to Nestorius. From that letter we shall later bring together, as testimony, those passages relevant to this matter and appropriate to the interpretations already given. For now, however, I shall bring the discussion to an end.

Since you accuse us of introducing a heretical doctrine by saying that our Lord Jesus Christ has two natures, and consequently introducing a Mother of God and a Mother of Man, I have been compelled to demonstrate that what follows from this is not heretical—a conclusion which, by divine grace, we have established appropriately.

**Heretic.** How many substances, then, belong to the one Christ?

**Rusticus.** Two.

**Heretic.** Why?

**Rusticus.** Because Christ is consubstantial with two complete—that is, perfect—natures.

**Heretic.** Then there are two Christs, or at any rate many Christs, or many persons, since Christ is consubstantial with many persons.

**Rusticus.** The number of natures that are consubstantial with one another always corresponds, answers, or is equivalent to the things that are consubstantial; but the number of persons does not correspond in the same way. God the Father, for example, is consubstantial with two persons, yet the Father is not two persons. The same applies to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Each one of us is one person, yet each is consubstantial with innumerable persons.

**Heretic.** Nor does it follow, merely because Christ is consubstantial with two natures, that there are two natures. For each thing is not necessarily as great in number as the things with which it is consubstantial. Otherwise, demonstrate something possessing as many natures as the things consubstantial with it possess. That is what is being asked.

**Rusticus.** I and you, or any human being, or any angel, are each of one nature and consubstantial with one nature; every individual living creature is likewise.

**Heretic.** You must demonstrate that one thing is consubstantial with many natures.

**Rusticus.** If any thing were consubstantial with two perfect natures, or with several existences, it would necessarily correspond in every respect to the number of its own natures that are consubstantial with it, since it is not one nature. Many things correspond to the number of many things.

From this it is clearly shown that Christ also corresponds, by the number of his natures, to the natures consubstantial with him. If each of the remaining things is consubstantial with one nature and each is of one nature, this in no way disproves my argument. Each thing nevertheless equals, by the number—or rather, the quantity—of its nature, the things consubstantial with it. For it does not have less than one in natural quantity than the number of things consubstantial with it; and this is not because nothing can be less than one in quantity.

Since Christ is consubstantial with those who are in two natures—that is, both with the Father and with us—and everything consubstantial equals the natural quantity of the things consubstantial with it, Christ therefore equals the natural quantity of the things consubstantial with him. But the things consubstantial with Christ are nevertheless two natures; therefore Christ’s natures, or substances, are likewise two.

This is also proved by the very term “substance.” Christ is said to be consubstantial both with the Father and with us; but he is not “copersonal” (*compersonalis*) with either him or us. Just as, if he were copersonal with the Father and the Holy Spirit as well as with us, he would not have merely one person but something more, so, because he is consubstantial both with them and with us, he does not have one nature but two—or rather, Christ is consubstantial with persons, not with natures.

Nevertheless, with them and with us he is confidently said to be not copersonal but consubstantial. And what is consubstantial except that which is wholly of the same nature? Therefore, whoever argues that things belonging to different natures are consubstantial not by nature but by person argues not with understanding but with bare words.

We therefore construct the argument as follows: if Christ is consubstantial with the persons of two natures—or, at any rate, if Christ is consubstantial with those persons who are in two natures—and everything consubstantial exists in as many natures as there are things consubstantial with it, Christ therefore exists in two natures. For there are two things that are consubstantial with him.

**Heretic.** The most holy and most blessed Father Cyril said “consubstantial with us according to his humanity” dispensationally and condescendingly, for the sake of peace, in his letter to John. Otherwise, if this is not true, produce other testimonies of his in which he says that Christ is by nature most like us in his humanity.

**Rusticus.** Then dispensation and hypocrisy differ in nothing, and the same thing will, in the same respect, be both good and evil at once.

**Heretic.** If they do differ, demonstrate it.

**Rusticus.** If one who merely condescends rejoices, what more could one rejoice who yields nothing and prevails? Read, I beg you, the very beginning of that letter, and cease resisting the truth; for it will immediately destroy your entire suspicion. Condescension does not bring perfect joy, since it is not done properly for the sake of that which is principally sought, but for the weakness of the infirm.

**Heretic.** We possess explanatory memoranda in letters from that most holy Father, in which he indicates that he wrote to the Easterners condescendingly, for the sake of peace.

**Rusticus.** First, there is considerable doubt whether these writings can be shown to be his. Even if they are his, what makes it clear that such passages have not been fabricated, since, when they were first produced by Eutyches, many accused them of being forged? And even if they are not fabricated, how is it certain that it was not rather what you cite that was said dispensationally and condescendingly—especially since he himself knew that the Church of God does not attend to private writings, whether memoranda or documents made for one person and for private purposes, but to those that are written concerning matters under dispute by synods or addressed to synods, dogmatically, publicly, and definitively?

This is clear from the fact that, when he sent these letters—his own and those of the Easterners—concerning the peace to the Roman Church, he took care to have them confirmed by the most holy Xystus. But he revealed nothing of what you cite to the chief apostolic see.

**Heretic.** Then Xystus confirmed the letters of union and their faith?

**Rusticus.** He not only confirmed them in writing, and with great joy, but added this in his reply to the holy Cyril:

> “Since our most holy brother John was never of the same mind as Nestorius, but was orthodox from the beginning, although formerly he suspended his judgment so that he would not condemn Nestorius together with us.”

He adds, saying:

> “We acted well in defining nothing premature against him; for the harvests of our joys are becoming clear.”

And much else of the same kind. If you wish, we shall also set down the very words.

**Heretic.** That too ought indeed to be done. Nevertheless, if you have a demonstration that he said something of this kind synodically in other writings, produce it; otherwise it is clear that he said it condescendingly, so as to win over the Easterners.

**Rusticus.** Without prejudice to the points already stated, let this too be established from the synod of the holy Fathers who assembled at Ephesus.

A testimony of Saint Anastasius:

> “Our salvation is not an illusion, nor is it the salvation of the body alone; rather, the salvation of the whole man has truly been accomplished. Therefore, that which came from Mary according to the divine Scriptures was human by nature and truly belonged to that Savior.”

From the same synod, a testimony of Saint Theophilus:

> “He did not come to us as one receiving a body from some precious heavenly material; rather, in clay he displayed the greatness of his craftsmanship. Correcting man, formed from clay, he himself came forth from a virgin as a man of new beauty. He changed the manner of generation, but in every respect indicated, without sin, a likeness to us that was not to be avoided.”

From the same synod, a testimony of Saint Ambrose:

> “Let empty disputes about words, therefore, be silent, since, as it is written, the kingdom of God is not in the persuasion of human speech but in the demonstration of power (1 Corinthians 2:4). Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh. The Son of God speaks as one in both, because both natures are in the same one. The same one speaks, but he does not always speak in the same manner.

> “Observe in him at one time the glory of God, at another the sufferings of man; for as God he teaches divine things, because he is the Word, but as man he teaches human things, because he was speaking in my substance.”

**Heretic.** If God and flesh are not one and the same nature according to the union, then one nature of Christ will be God and the other merely man. But that one nature, according to which he is God, is not consubstantial with us. God, therefore, is not consubstantial with us. If Christ is consubstantial with us, while God is not consubstantial with us, then Christ—God forbid—is not God.

**Rusticus.** In such a precipice, his deception always traps the man, so that he is caught in his own snares. For if Christ’s humanity is that according to which Christ is man, and this is not consubstantial with the Father, then man is not consubstantial with the Father. If Christ is consubstantial with the Father, while man is not consubstantial with the Father, then Christ is not man.

Furthermore, if this syllogism is valid, we shall likewise draw the same conclusion concerning God. If the substance of Christ’s divinity, according to which he is indeed God, is not consubstantial with us, then God is not consubstantial with us. If Christ is consubstantial with us, while God is not consubstantial with us, the absurd conclusion stated above follows: that Christ is not God.

Thus, according to your empty talk, either Christ’s divine nature will be consubstantial with us, or Christ—God forbid—will not be God; or, again, Christ’s humanity will be consubstantial with us, or Christ—God forbid—will not be man. Nothing, then, has been concluded in this manner.

**Heretic.** If Christ has two natures, each will be what it is and nothing else. Therefore humanity will be humanity alone and not also God, while God will be God alone and not man. Christ will consequently be pure God and pure man.

**Rusticus.** You slanderer, it is not the same thing to be “this alone” and to be “pure.” Your soul, for example, is soul alone and nothing else, yet it is incarnate and is not bare of a body; and your body is body alone, yet it is also animated.

If, then, humanity is not humanity alone but also divinity, and divinity is not divinity alone but also humanity, divinity and humanity have therefore been made human, and divinity and humanity have united divinity and humanity to themselves. Humanity, therefore, according to these things, has been made human and united to God as divinity.

**Heretic.** If one nature of Christ is God and the other man, and the one is not the same as the other, then God and man are not the same. How, then, according to you, is Christ one?

**Rusticus.** Your cleverness has been exposed. “The same” signifies either person or nature. We therefore say that Christ is the same God and man, but that he is not the same in nature. Christ is one, therefore, not one thing, as we say in a simple manner. “One,” however, means one person; it is not simply one thing. Thus he is one, but not one thing; different and different, but not a different person and a different person—God forbid.

**Heretic.** I cannot see how this can be. Everything that is different as a thing is also different as a person.

**Rusticus.** I am a different person from you, but not a different thing: for there is one thing according to which you are a man and according to which I am a man. My soul, however, is a different thing from your body, and your soul from my body; my soul in my body and your soul in yours are understood as something different, however these may be compared with one another.

“Different” (*alius*) is more properly applied to distinctions of persons, while “different thing” (*aliud et aliud*) applies to natures. For when your soul is compared with your body, it is not another man but another thing.

**Heretic.** On the contrary, “another person” is quite correctly said. Who is the outward man who is corrupted and the inward man who is renewed, according to the Apostle (2 Corinthians 4:16)? Everything that is another thing is therefore also another person; and, conversely, everything that is another person is another thing.

I am different from an angel, but I am also a different thing; and he is both a different person and a different thing from me. Thus anyone will find the same result by counting each item individually.

**Rusticus.** Let us inquire, if you agree, whether what you have said is true from things that stand in reciprocal relations. This one stands to that one as this other stands to that other—or to this other thing; and this one stands to this other as one thing stands to another.

If, then, “one thing” is not always the same as “one person,” “another thing” will not always be “another person.” Conversely, not every “one person” is “one thing,” nor is every “one thing” “one person.” The same follows concerning “another person” and “another thing.”

The Lord distinguished all these matters in the Gospel when he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), never saying, “We are one [person],” but rather, using the opposite form, “we are.” Again he said:

> “If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is not true. There is another who bears witness concerning me, and I know that the testimony which he bears concerning me is true” (John 5:31–32).

Afterward he added who this was:

> “The Father who sent me, he himself bears witness concerning me” (ibid., 37).

And concerning the Holy Spirit he said:

> “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever—the Spirit of truth” (John 14:15–17).

He did not say, “another consoling thing” or “another Spirit,” but “another Paraclete.”

**Heretic.** These statements concern only the fact that the Father and the Son are one, and that the Father is one person and the Son another, not the fact that they are not one person or that they are not different things. Since four propositions have been put forward, you have demonstrated only two: that the Father and the Son are one, and that the Father is another person from the Son and from the Holy Spirit.

It remains unproved that the Father and the Son are not different things, and that the Father himself is not the Son. These points you must establish by testimonies, especially since the Father and the Son are called one, for there is one God.

**Rusticus.** Even if the foregoing demonstrations have established what you seek—that what is one is not another thing, and that what is another is not one and the same—this too will nevertheless be demonstrated: namely, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are indeed the one God, but with the name “God” added.

If the name “God” is removed from the statements, it can no longer be said simply that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the same. For he says:

> “I have not spoken from myself, but the Father who sent me himself gave me a command—what I should say and what I should speak” (John 12:49).

There, then, the Father is not himself the Son; for if he were, the Son would speak from himself.

Earlier he said:

> “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me” (John 12:44).

And somewhat earlier still:

> “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God, and you have not known him; but I know him. And if I say that I do not know him, I shall be like you, a liar. But I know him and keep his word” (John 8:54–55).

And when the Pharisees said to him that his testimony was not true, since he was bearing witness about himself, he replied:

> “My judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me. In your law it is written that the testimony of two persons is true. I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (ibid., 16–18).

From these statements the point in question is also clear: the Father and the Son are not “one thing and another thing”—or, if “one thing and another thing” is said of person, there are two persons, but not “one thing and another thing” simply and absolutely. For, as has been shown, if “another” is not “one and the same,” and “another thing” is not “one and the same thing,” then conversely what is one is not another thing.

Since the Father and the Son are one, they are not another thing. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in that they have one nature, but they are not one person, because they are three persons.

Yet I again testify in a clear voice: “one” and “one thing,” and simply “one,” not one person but another; and simply “not one thing but another thing”—these are expressions for us when used absolutely. In combination, however, “another thing” can be said of person, and the Father God is not another God from the Son.

You therefore see that we have said that the Lord Christ, who graciously united to himself another nature besides the one common to him, is one because he is one person, but is not one thing because he is not one nature. Understand that this is how we speak whenever we say “one,” “one thing,” “another thing,” or “another person.”
