The Synod of Ephesus itself also set forth and established this point, together with readings from the holy Fathers, in condemnation of the blasphemies of Nestorius and in proof of its own faith. Indeed, it destroyed the contrary positions and confirmed its own doctrines, citing among the readings of the blessed Gregory of Nazianzus the following:

> “Different and different, from which the Savior consists: for the invisible is not the same as the visible, nor the timeless the same as that which is subject to time; yet not another and another person—God forbid. For both are one through the union: God made man and man made divine, or by whatever name one may call it. I say ‘different and different,’ in contrast to what occurs in the Trinity: there, there is another and another person, so that we do not confuse the subsistences; but not ‘different and different things.’ For the three are one and the same in divinity.”

Do not suppose that we have an abundance only of arguments by which we can overturn your contradictions. Rather, listen to those arguments by which the most certain truth itself habitually confirms our position.

Things whose genera and species are diverse are different in number. So too are things that have many features in common with many others, as do things whose genera and more specific classifications are diverse; likewise, the things called their species, substances, and natures are diverse in number.

But the simple and the composite, the eternal and the temporal, the changeable and the unchangeable, the mutable and the immutable, the passible and the impassible have different genera and species. Their substances or natures, therefore, are also different in number.

**Heretic.** This does not apply to the Lord Christ because of the union. Just as the genera and species of the rational soul and the body are indeed different, while the one living creature is man, with one substance and one nature, so in the Lord Christ the genera differ, but the natures do not.

**Rusticus.** What you have said is not true. Soul and body differ not so much according to genus as rather according to species. For the genus of both soul and body is substance capable of receiving contraries: the soul is capable of virtue and vice, and the body of health and sickness.

Nor does body differ from soul simply according to species. There is one species of humanity, though perhaps they differ according to the things intermediate between them. This is mortal, while that is immortal, and there are other differences of this kind. Therefore the proposition stated above is true.

**Heretic.** But once this principle has been granted, you immediately descend until you arrive at the conclusions of Nestorius. For things whose genera, species, substances, and natures are different have neither one individual, nor one subsistence, nor one person, but something more. If these two things you speak of are individuals, substances, essences, or rational subsistences, then they are in every respect two persons as well.

**Rusticus.** You have not drawn a necessary conclusion. Although the genera, species, substances, and natures of the world are diverse, the individual is not therefore diverse.

The world is one individual, even if different ages are spoken of; for ages arise from times, whereas the world consists of substances. Nor are those who imagine many worlds opposed to this argument. Even if there were another world, it would likewise contain within itself many natures and substances; yet each of those worlds would nevertheless be one.

Thus, if we were to say that two other individual substances subsist somewhere apart from the one Christ, we would necessarily and inevitably infer two or more persons. But if we say this of one and only one Christ, then, just as no rightly believing person has asserted that the constitution of all corporeal natures consists of two or more worlds, so neither do we assert two or more Christs.

Indeed, the comparison is not even adequate, but our case is much stronger: none of those things are united according to subsistence, as the natures of this Lord Christ are.

If the genera and species of divinity and humanity are not different, then Christ is not from different natures, nor is he from two natures. But if he is from two, then give their substantial differences; for you do not wish them to differ merely as individuals.

Furthermore, if he is truly man—that is, a rational terrestrial animal—and differs in no respect from God, then, which is most impious, neither are we consubstantial with him, nor is he consubstantial with us.

Further, if it is true that things whose genera are different are not the same, and that what is distinguished under different genera is likewise different—whether compared with other genera or with the things contained within them—then the things belonging to one genus, which the other does not possess, are shown to be even more different.

If divinity has neither a genus nor the species subordinate to a genus, while humanity is found to possess these, then it is demonstrated all the more strongly that the two cannot be united in one nature.

Let the earlier points, therefore, stand without prejudice: there we said that the genera and species of divinity and flesh are different.

**Heretic.** Divinity and humanity have one highest genus. Substance is the most general genus of divinity and humanity, which subsists through itself.

**Rusticus.** When “subsisting through itself” is said of God, it means that he depends on no other for his existence. When it is said of creatures, this is not so: they received their existence from the Creator, “for in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28).

But “substance”—that is, *οὐσία*—when said of God, is named from the fact that he always is, since *οὐσία* is that which always exists; in creatures, this is not so. Therefore, even though “substance” is one name, it does not designate one thing. Substance is not a common genus of divinity and flesh, but only a common name; and this is not a genus.

**Heretic.** But the soul, although it does not have the same genus as the body, completes one species with it.

Rust. They have, rather, one highest genus in common: for both are substance, both in name and in definition. If you still doubt that this is impossible in Christ with respect to divinity and humanity, it will be shown below. [Col. 1182A] Rational soul and human body therefore receive identity of nature in their union, inasmuch as they possess both one genus and the same species; yet they are also different natures, since they are sometimes placed under a different species and definition. But Christ’s divinity and humanity are not placed under one species.

Heret. Demonstration of uncertain things does not arise from uncertain premises, insofar as they are uncertain. If, then, you show that divinity and flesh do not fall under one definition, and that in one and the same human being the body and soul differ in definition, nature, and species, then perhaps what you have added will follow. Reserving these matters for a lower place, let us turn to other points, so that we do not extend the length of the discussion any further.

[Col. 1182B] Rust. You often declare the Lord Christ consubstantial both with the Father and with us, according to one and the same substance through the union, with nothing lost or confused. Yet it is impossible that this one substance, as you call it, should not contain certain things which, in comparison with one another, are rightly called different—such as flesh, soul, and the Word. For it is possible to identify many differences, which I leave as indications for your understanding. If, then, one thing and another are called substance and substance, one substance and another are rightly predicated. But if some of these is not a substance, how can certain things be consubstantial with it in this respect, since they are not consubstantial according to substance? How, moreover, will true divinity and perfect, individual humanity not be substance? If, then, divinity and flesh are one substance and another, why do you refuse to confess that they are two? But if you do confess that they are two, why do you depart from our position and communion?

Heret. By the same reasoning you could demonstrate two substances in any ordinary human being, and thus be compelled to posit three substances in Christ. For, according to the substance of the mind, a human being is consubstantial with angels; according to the body, with cattle and wild beasts alike. Again, according to the body we are consubstantial with the bodies of the dead, and according to the soul, with their souls—without even using only the example of angels, concerning which I admit that the question is uncertain to me.

Rust. All this is false. For consubstantiality according to a part, and not according to the entirety of the substance, is imperfect. The Son was called consubstantial with God the Father by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers for this reason: that we might understand that nothing belonging to the Father’s substance is lacking in him. Likewise, he was declared consubstantial with us by the holy Fathers who came later, so that we might believe that he possesses everything belonging to our substance. Therefore, whoever accepts consubstantiality in part uses the term through heretical deceit.

Whatever may be true concerning angels, a human being is not consubstantial with them; nor likewise with wild beasts, cattle, corpses, or souls. Further, a human being cannot properly be called consubstantial with rational beings simply according to any part. [Col. 1183A] For although the material from which the body is formed is one, the form of the body is nevertheless far superior. Hence it is not true that either part is consubstantial with part, or the whole with the whole—as though, because there is one material, we should be called consubstantial with snakes, bugs, fleas, flies, and all the things that arise from the evaporation of the human body.

Moreover, if everything that is consubstantial with a human being according to the body is plainly consubstantial with him, then Christ, in respect of this very feature, will also be consubstantial with those with whom a human being is consubstantial in this respect—God forbid!—and will be consubstantial according to the body with all the things mentioned above. For Christ is consubstantial with us in this respect. But even if someone, rejecting such blasphemies, grants these things as true, this nevertheless cannot be removed: such consubstantiality [Col. 1183B] is neither complete nor perfect. A human being, therefore, is not consubstantial with two perfect natures, as Christ is.

Further, if nature is more properly named from birth—if it is nature more in being generated than in being corrupted—a complete and perfect human being is born, whereas corruption separates body and soul from one another and makes two separate things, neither of which is a perfect nature. For if corruption perfects natures, and its effect is contrary in itself to the contrary, then generation destroys natures, which is utterly incongruous.

Indeed, at the time of Christ’s death, the nature of his humanity was separated into two and became two things, neither of which, however, was a perfect nature. Yet the resurrection is from two; still, the union of the most perfect natures in him is not of this kind, since each of the united natures subsists in the perfection of its species, without corruption and without diminution.

Moreover, if, as you say, two substances can be demonstrated in an ordinary human being, although neither of them is a perfect nature, they are not thereby not two because they are imperfect; therefore, since Christ’s natures are two perfect natures, how could they not all the more be two? If, then, no absurdity follows from those who say that a human being has two natures, what indecency will follow from confessing two natures in Jesus the Lord Christ?

But whoever says “three” counts imperfect things together with the perfect divinity. The unanimous voice of all the Fathers would then be superfluous when they say that Christ is consubstantial with us according to his humanity, thereby refuting those who say that the dispensation was without a soul or without a mind. If, however, things are called consubstantial in this way among human beings, it did no good for the Fathers to say that the Son is consubstantial with the Father. For some impious person could suspect that the Father bears the same relation to the Son as the rational bears to the soulless. Yet, in my judgment, there are many thousands of things more insane than this to say. But for the present, let this suffice.

Heret. If Christ is one substance and one thing, then Christ is one substantive, one substance through the union.

Rust. “Thing” signifies both person and nature. Christ is therefore both one thing and two; indeed, he himself is one thing, insofar as he is one person, but he is recognized in two natures.

Heret. Since for the moment you have not denied that Christ is one thing—for how could you not call Christ one, when you say that Christ is a thing?—and since this thing is substantive, Christ is therefore, as we said, one substance and consequently one nature. What does it matter to me whether there are also two things or not? For the moment, since he is one, you cannot contradict this.

Rust. It does not follow in every respect that one thing and one substantive thing are also one substance. Aaron’s rod, for example, which bore fruit (Num. XVII, 18), was indeed one substantive thing with its fruits, but it was not one substance with its fruits. Likewise, we call the tablets written by the finger of God (Exod. XXXI, 18) one thing, but not one substance.

Indeed, I think it can also appropriately be answered that Christ is neither a substantive nor an insubstantive thing, but a supersubstantive thing, since he consists of two most perfect substances or natures. For that bread which we ask for in the Lord’s Prayer is called “supersubstantial” (Matt. VI, 11). And I think that we ask for him in such a way that we seek Christ instead, until, as the Apostle says, Christ is formed in us (Gal. IV, 19).

Further, if a tree bearing grafted branches of both millet and pear is one tree and one thing, yet, because it also has its own branches, it is neither one substance nor one nature, then just as millet and pear are said to be two, while the tree is said to be one thing, what harms the unity of the person if we say that Christ is two things? Or what harms the duality of the natures if we confess that he exists as one thing? [Col. 1184C]

Moreover, even if we answer that Christ is substantive, he will not thereby be one substance. We call one person substantive, just as, if someone should say, for example, that this world is not insubstantive, he would not thereby be compelled to affirm that it has one substance. But if some utterly mad and contentious person says that the world has one substance, it follows that he cannot speak otherwise of any things whatsoever than by saying that they are one substance. For if all the diversities that exist in the world do not make substances plural in number, each thing, compared with another, will be one with it. Thus the substance of a human being, a stone, an elephant, an ant, heaven, and a mountain would be one substance.

[Col. 1184D] Heret. Such a union does not occur in this world, because there is not one son, one Christ, and one Lord. And although the world is simply one, there are thousands upon thousands who are called sons, persons, and substances. In Christ, however, an unshakable union has occurred.

Rust. Did I not say beforehand that the example is not inappropriate in every respect? Otherwise it would not be an example if it were identical in every respect. Since, then, you said that Christ is something substantive, I showed that something else may also be called substantive, yet not be of one substance but of many.

If I wish to speak of things made by art, it is possible to find many thousands of such things—for example, a ship, a house, a lamp burning, and [Col. 1185A] similar objects. All such things are indeed substances, but not of one substance.

Heret. Nature never contains less than a person; indeed, it is accustomed to contain more. I am speaking now of the natures of rational beings. For this reason we shrink from saying “two natures,” fearing that we will consequently have to say “two persons” as well.

Rust. This is an utterly insane fear. There are no two rational natures that do not contain thousands of persons; nor is there one that does not contain more than two persons. It would therefore follow that Christ also has not one nature, lest he have not merely two persons but more.

Moreover, according to our position Christ is not from two natures, lest he be said to have either more persons or sons, or more Christs or Lords. But if those who say that Christ is from two natures—or, like you, “from two”—are consequently said to have two or more persons, it does not follow that they must say that there are two Christs or sons. Nor will the same absurdities follow concerning those heretics who say that Christ has two persons. Much less, therefore, will they follow concerning the orthodox, who confess the Lord Christ in two natures: they will not thereby be compelled to say that there are two Lords, Christs, or sons.

Moreover, if you are afraid to say “two natures” for this reason—that perhaps, according to the customary inference, you will introduce two persons in the other respects—then you say that two natures are never less than two persons. You should therefore never confess this either: that the Lord Christ is perfect God and perfect man. For among all other rational beings it is impossible for perfect God and perfect man to be one and the same person. [Col. 1185C]

But if, since we are Christians, it is dangerous to doubt this most extraordinary miracle, because when God willed it, perfect God could be one person with perfect humanity, since nothing is impossible for him according to the Gospel (Luke I, 37), why do we doubt that this very person exists in two perfect natures, not to be separated but rather to be acknowledged? Thus, just as perfect God and perfect man are, beyond estimation, one single person, so the two perfect natures are wonderfully one Son.

And this, so to speak, is an unshakable rule in all other cases, but in Christ alone it has been dissolved. Therefore, because Nestorius makes bad use of the duality of substances, we must not on that account remain silent about there being two substances. Otherwise, because he makes bad use of perfect God and perfect man, the orthodox should not say this. To put it simply: if we must remain silent about, or altogether remove, everything that heretics misuse, then we have nothing to confess, and above all the Scriptures would have to be removed.

Heret. You force me to repeat the same question: when has divine nature contained less than a person? Or when has substance contained less than subsistence? Answer.

Rust. We have already answered this sufficiently. Nevertheless, I will add this appropriately: even here the two natures alone do not contain Christ’s person, although in him alone they are united according to subsistence. For his divine nature also contains the Father and the Holy Spirit, while his human substance contains the rest of human beings. But just as he subsists in the divine nature, as do the Father and the Holy Spirit, yet is not merely God, and in our nature, yet is not merely man, so, subsisting in two natures, he is not divided—for he does not have two persons.

I ask you, however, how you used the word “nature”: did you mean universal nature, or rather individual nature?

Heret. I take it without distinction. For what difference is there altogether, or what does it matter?

Rust. There is a great difference. If you mean universal or common nature, it is true that it contains no fewer persons—indeed, more and a greater number. But if you mean particular or individual nature, such as mine, yours, or that of another individual, shared with no one else—for I am not the same as you—then we find no example in Christ for the reason I stated. The only rational natures are God, the heavenly hosts, and humanity; yet never have two natures from among these been united to each other so as to make one and only one person, as occurred in the Lord Christ in the union of divinity and humanity.

For this is the most unexpected peculiarity of that union, an example of which cannot be found: never have two rational natures been inseparably united in one person. Moreover, there is no particular nature of God—that is, a nature belonging to no one other than one single person. Rather, the one and only divinity is, beyond all limitation, the nature of all three persons; for we truly confess one God.

Heret. If Christ is one and individual, and every individual has one species, while one species is one nature, then Christ has one nature.

Rust. There are many thousands of individuals that have neither one species nor one nature, but many species and natures—for example, cities, houses, ships, written documents, and the letters written in them.

Heret. But these arise from art, not from God or nature.

Rust. For the moment, if it followed by absolute necessity that, whenever there is one individual, there is also one nature, then one nature would certainly arise in all these cases as well. But if you say that every individual made by God has one species and one nature, that too is untrue. The world was made by God, yet it does not have one nature.

Heret. But I still wish to delimit the argument by adding a qualification, and I say: Every individual substantive thing made by God and inseparable has one species and one nature.

Rust. Again you seek something unremarkable in what is marvelous, a comparison in what is incomparable, and an example among things that cannot receive an example. But if you think this is the position of a rational person, I can bring you many such rules that you will be unable to explain throughout all the ages.

Tell me, then, when perfect divinity and perfect humanity became one nature and did not remain two; when Creator and creature became one substance through union; when two most perfect natures produced some other perfect thing; and not something even more perfect and better together; [Col. 1187A] when one species was, beyond all limitation, consubstantial with two perfect species.

Heret. Since no such thing has ever occurred, we too confess this. But from the time when one person was made through union, all these immeasurable and wondrous things occurred. Yet you accuse God’s mighty and immeasurable works of being incongruous. If, then, you think that from these things one Son, one Christ, and one Lord did not come into being, say so openly. But if you confess one person, according to the truth, then grant what necessarily follows from this.

Rust. Grant what follows from perfect divinity and perfect humanity. Grant what is proper to Wisdom, consubstantial with God the Father, and to flesh animated by a rational soul, consubstantial with us. Restore to things their proper number. Do not remove quantity if you pretend to confess perfection according to substance. For where there is perfection according to substance, there is also quantity of substances; where there is an unconfused union, there is also the number of the things united.

Every substance receives both being and being one at the same time. It is one in such a way that, when compared with one, the added union makes two complete, not that the number is destroyed. Otherwise, show me an unconfused union of perfect things that destroys only their number, while in no respect and according to no part destroys the being that each possesses, so that you may appear to say something not irrational.

I will add this as well. You said that every individual thing made by God, substantive and inseparable, is one species. If the incarnation has therefore come about in the manner of some other created thing, do you have anything to say? [Col. 1187C] I want you not to offer merely words, but the things themselves. Name one substantive individual made by God and inseparable, and one species, so that from this you may discover the truth.

Heret. We see that all such things are so. Nevertheless, I will mention one of them. Behold, each one of us is both an individual and one thing, substantive and made by God, and inseparable; yet each is one species, one nature, and one substance.

Rust. As usual, you have stated everything deceitfully. Since the example has made the matters discussed clearer, we too shall say that these things are not understood in the same way in the Lord Christ. You have treated as conceded the very matters under discussion. Christ is not an individual in the same way as the rest, or as we are. Each of us has an individual person, that is, one shared with no one else, and an individual substance of his own. In Christ, however, the person is indeed individual, for it belongs to him alone; but the nature is not individual in the same way, for it is common to all three persons, and it is impossible to find it except as common.

Again, “one” is not said of Christ in an unqualified sense, as though he were one thing, but more cautiously, because he is one person, as was shown above. The same has also been demonstrated concerning “substantive”: it is not only what subsists in one substance that is substantive, but also what subsists in several. And that something is “from God” is not said because it is one with God the maker, but because the thing made is one with its maker, as the soul is one with the body.

And we confess that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is undivided, and that his person is inseparable. But his natures are not one and inseparable; rather, they are two inseparable natures united. It is therefore clear that the same things have not come about in the Lord Christ as in other cases. It is insane, then, that you have deceitfully spun out words about such matters, when it would have been more appropriate to say that things are so among creatures, but not so in the case of the Creator who assumes a creature.

For it has never occurred in any other case that two most perfect natures should have pre-existed from the beginning in their own individual beings and afterward become one person from them.

Heret. What, I ask, do you say to this? Have not all the teachers of the Catholic Church used this example, saying, “Just as a human being is one, consisting of soul and body, so Christ is one, perfect God and perfect man”? Thus Christ too is an individual, one, substantive, and the rest, as I said.

Rust. I have already said this above: it is the most common rule among all rational beings that examples are taken from a part, not from the whole. The Fathers therefore used this example not to demonstrate the things you mentioned—which we showed long ago to be false—but to demonstrate one Son, one Christ, one Lord, and his one substantial person.

But so that you may not think that this example agrees in every respect, hear from us irrefutable arguments that overturn your falsehood. If you still hold the fables of the pagans and think that rational souls pre-existed their bodies, there will nevertheless be two most perfect substances and natures: God and mind. Moreover, there will be the persons of the Word of God and of the soul united to him, which, according to you, pre-existed from the beginning.

It is impossible for one person to arise from two pre-existing persons. Saint Cyril says in the letter confirmed both by the Apostolic See and by the holy synod of Ephesus:

> “Even if some should defame the union of persons, Scripture did not say that the Word united to himself the person of a human being, but that he became flesh.”

Behold how strongly he condemns those who say that a union of persons took place in Christ, so that he sets against them what is written: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14).

For the matter at hand, those who say that this union pre-existed, that the human being who was assumed pre-existed, and those who assert that Christ’s mind pre-existed do not differ. For the latter too wish those minds to have their own persons. They assert that they pre-existed as equal, similar, and in every respect naturally and substantially undifferentiated, though not indistinct with respect to the number of individuals.

For if this is not what they say, then there was originally one mind in every respect, which afterward became differentiated into several by merits. But how could a mind that was wholly one and did not differ from itself fail to be a mind of one and the same merit? If, then, that mind could begin to differ only because it was not identical with those things that subsisted through its differentiation, my mind too ought to be distinguished into as many individuals as there are merits.

But may such madness be far from every rational soul, that the number of sins should be blasphemously made the cause of multiplying souls. If, then, you embrace such doctrines, recognize that the example of soul and body does not agree in every respect. A human being does not arise from two most perfect persons, nor from pre-existing perfect natures, even though the body is formed from pre-existing matter.

Moreover, the human body itself was made for nothing other than to belong to this soul—as one might say, as its instrument. But the mind in those theories had a separate subsistence. The union that took place in Christ did not exist from the beginning. For if it had existed from the beginning, each mind would have been Christ—God forbid! They do not wish them to have been unlike one another in any respect from the beginning. Nor is Christ merely because of the body; otherwise only incarnation, and not inhumanation, would have occurred.

Likewise, if one mind was united to the Word, it was not inhumanation from the Virgin, because the entirety of our nature was not united from that moment; rather, what is much more substantial already subsisted beforehand. Indeed, what is more properly a human being—that is, the inner human being—would be inhumanation only of the one whose outward part was united.

But the holy Fathers did not understand matters in this way. With complete agreement they taught that our perfect nature was united to the Word, not merely the flesh formed in the Virgin from the time of conception. For the aforementioned letter also contains this:

> “The natures that came together for the true union are different; yet from both there is one Christ and Son—not as though the difference of the natures had been destroyed because of the union, but rather because, through the ineffable and indescribable coming together of divinity and humanity for the union, we complete one Lord, Christ, and Son.”

Behold, he said that the different natures were united in the Lord, and that this occurred in order to make Christ, so that you would not think it happened at some other time than when the body was conceived. And lest anyone think that only the flesh was then united to the Word, he added that divinity and humanity came together into unity.

Heret. We do not honor the doctrine mentioned above. For this is what is called Origen’s doctrine of pre-existence, which our holy Fathers and the archbishops of Alexandria condemned under anathema, especially Saint Theophilus, whom the most holy Cyril followed in every orthodox confession. You have therefore dissolved, to no purpose, doctrines that we do not honor. Since you once chose to accuse our doctrine and take the opposing side, you ought to speak about matters relevant to the issue.

Rust. Because some among you hold such opinions, and because it follows from your doctrine that you should say these things, as will be shown later, I was compelled to say this. But since you do not defend such views, I will turn to the remaining matters.

Since human souls do not pre-exist their bodies, it is clear that they are created by God for one another. The soul is created by nature to govern the body, while the body is created as that without which it is impossible for the soul’s activities to be carried out. For this reason an individual soul uses an individual body, and it is not naturally the governor of another body’s soul; each soul governs its own body, for this very purpose it also subsists.

But God the Word did not come into subsistence in order to become incarnate and inhumanated; he is eternal. Nor, therefore, did humanity come into subsistence in order to be united in this way; it has another reason for subsisting. And I am not speaking only of the individual humanity united to the Word, but of humanity in common. You therefore see how greatly the example of the union differs.

Heret. Although the example of God the Word and the soul differs—for God not only pre-existed the soul but pre-existed the human being infinitely, and because he himself is the creator both of all nature and of his own humanity—and although he not only moves his own humanity but also all things he wills, and in whatever way he wills, nevertheless, the point concerning humanity and flesh is defective in the text.

For just as human flesh was made for this purpose, that, governed by a rational—that is, human—soul, it might be useful for carrying out the soul’s activities, which could not otherwise be fulfilled, so the humanity of God the Word was made so that, while being moved by him, it might carry out his activities. Thus, through the union of the Word and his humanity, there is likewise one nature.

Rust. In no way is this so; rather, the opposite is true. For if the example is dissimilar and inappropriate in the greater respects mentioned, but similar and not discrepant in the lesser, then it is far more the case that God the Word and humanity are not one nature than that they are one. Since, then, it cannot both be and not be one and only one nature, it remains that, because of the similarity of the example, there is indeed one person, but, because of the much greater difference, not one nature.

If, then, one nature did not come into being, it is established that two remain. For you will not say conversely that God and humanity do not have one nature, while humanity and God do have one nature. Not only does this make no difference with respect to the matter, but I will immediately answer: Then there are two natures of the Word and humanity, even if humanity and the Word have not two but one nature. The incongruity will not arise from my proposition, but from yours.

Heret. I think no one who possesses a soul would refuse to confess this: if flesh and the Word have one nature, then the Word and flesh have one nature, even if there are two. The same thing is meant, however often someone reverses the words through verbosity.

But I ask this more particularly: if your reasoning is true, why should there be one nature and not one person in Christ, rather than one person but not one nature? How can Christ be one according to the example of a human being, when the example differs far more than it agrees? He ought much more not to be one than to be one Christ, Son, and Lord.

Rust. If the divine nature itself had been principally inhumanated—and that nature is certainly common to the Holy Trinity—the incarnation would have belonged to all three persons. For whatever belongs to the common nature principally and in itself is common to the Holy Trinity.

But since it was not the nature in itself that was incarnate, but one person—God the Word, the Son of God, alone was incarnate, and he is one person of that nature—the rational flesh united to him is therefore, without any intervening mediation, one person with him, and there is one Son, one Christ, and one Lord.

To be one person and one Son is not proper to the whole Trinity but to one single person alone. The nature of the Word is said to be incarnate through the Word and insofar as it belongs to the Word, rather than the Word being said to be incarnate through the nature and insofar as it is that nature; otherwise both the incarnation, the birth, and the passion would belong to the whole Trinity.

Thus the similarity in the example concerns one Son and one Christ; the difference concerns not several Christs or sons, but two natures. This is why I have gone through the whole matter: the examples of flesh and soul concern the difference, not the question of why in Christ the difference belongs to person rather than nature.

[Col. 1191B] Heret. I am not persuaded that this difference in the example is sufficient to prove that the Lord Christ has not one but two natures. If, then, you have other arguments, state them.

Rust. There are many others. The first is that the Word is distinguished from those consubstantial with him not by nature or substance, but by person alone. Each of us, however, in addition to what is common, has his own individual substance and nature; for this reason many human beings are named.

Again, the soul suffers with the body, but God the Word does not suffer at all. The soul has no principle of activity outside its body, whereas God the Word, while present in humanity, continued to perform his customary activities in heaven and everywhere, although he also performed certain immeasurable works through the body.

For what difference did it make to his activities, which existed from the beginning, whether he had or did not have humanity, since through humanity he did not cause rain, thunder, or move the stars—and, if one may put it simply, worked nothing more through it than those things newly accomplished for our salvation, for which he was also inhumanated? You regard these arguments as even less suitable, as though these things were insignificant and he had not also shared in works greater than or equal to them.

Rust. We did not introduce the preceding points for this purpose, but to show that the freedom of divinity is one thing, whether in the flesh or outside it, while the necessity of the soul is another: being bound to the body, the soul has, in this respect, the same power of moving a simple body. Nevertheless, let these points also be added—by way of concession—since the account of the nature and persons of the Trinity is sufficient.

[Col. 1191D] Heret. Is Christ’s subsistence one, or is it not one but rather two?

Rust. You ask this deceitfully as well. “Subsistence” is one name, but it signifies different things, to which one answer does not apply. Sometimes it signifies person, and sometimes substance.

In the holy synod of Ephesus both meanings are demonstrated. Saint Gregory the Theologian, among the other matters contained in the synodal records, is introduced as teaching the following, both as testimony to the most correct faith and for the destruction of Nestorius’s doctrines:

> “The Savior is of one thing and another; for the invisible is not the same as the visible, nor the timeless as the temporal. But there are not two different persons—God forbid! For both are one by their commingling: God inhumanated and man deified, or whatever name one may give it. But say ‘the one and the other’ in the reverse sense from that which obtains in the Trinity. For there there is one person and another, so that we do not confuse the subsistences; but there is not one thing and another, for the three are one and the same in divinity.”

Behold, the authority of the universal synod most clearly accepted and approved “subsistence” as referring to persons in the Holy Trinity.

Saint Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, in his third letter to Nestorius, asserting that the union in Christ occurred according to subsistence, again instructed that the expressions concerning him should not be divided between two subsistences, or rather between two persons. First he says:

> “We do not divide the expressions concerning our Savior that are found in the Gospel between two subsistences, or rather between two persons.”

Then:

> “If anyone assigns to two persons or subsistences either the expressions written in the Gospels and in the apostolic writings, or those spoken by the saints concerning Christ, or by Christ himself concerning himself…”

And elsewhere:

> “If anyone divides the subsistences after the union over the one Christ, joining them only by a conjunction according to dignity, authority, or power, and does not rather join them according to natural union, let him be anathema.”

By saying that it is abominable to divide the subsistences over the one Christ, and this after the union, and by likewise condemning those who join them according to this or that consideration rather than according to this union, he shows that they must be joined according to the latter. The subsistences in Christ, therefore, are not to be joined merely according to dignity or anything similar, but rather according to natural union.

Heret. I think that he spoke of the union in the Lord Christ as arising from two natures and likewise from two subsistences, as from two persons. For he would not have used this name, “subsistence,” so closely in such a different sense, especially when he says “after the union”—as though he were saying that before the union there were two natures and persons, but after the union there was one.

Rust. It is in no way true: for we have already demonstrated that he does not say “from two persons” concerning the Lord. For if he had wished to say this, just as, when saying that the Lord was made from two natures, he does not refuse to confess [Col. 1192D] that God the Word united our nature to himself, so he ought not to have refused to admit that he united the person of a man to himself. But now he approves the one and censures the other, saying in his second letter to Nestorius:

> “In no way does the right account of faith benefit if it is understood in this way, or certainly if some defame the uniting of persons. For Scripture did not say that the Word united the person of a man to himself, but that he became flesh.”

Behold, it is clear that he either puts it this way himself, or that, if one says what necessarily follows, to speak of the uniting of persons is to say that the Word united the person of a man to himself; and he set this down as contrary to divine Scripture, branding it with reproach, because it says that he became flesh. He is almost crying aloud that whoever speaks of the uniting of persons in Christ [Col. 1193A] removes from Holy Scripture what it says, namely, that the Word became flesh (John 1:14).

A little earlier he makes this clear, saying:

> “For the union of two natures has taken place; therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord. Clearly, then, the term ‘subsistence’ sometimes signifies person, but at other times nature; for it does not, as you assert, always signify both person and nature.”

And again, when he commands that the expressions spoken of Christ not be distributed between two persons or subsistences, he uses the term “subsistence” and “person” simply and indifferently, to such an extent that he himself later divided the expressions, speaking of two natures:

> “We know the evangelical and apostolic expressions concerning the Lord, spoken by men who speak of God. Some of them we make common, as concerning one person; others we divide, as concerning two natures.”

And after some intervening material:

> “We glorified the Lord, the Savior of all, because the churches both among us and among you possess a faith consistent with the divinely inspired Scriptures and the tradition of our holy fathers; these things have already been set out continuously and in order above.”

Behold, he confessed that the divine Scriptures and the Fathers preach in this way: that the expressions must be distributed between two natures. Since, therefore, he does not say things contrary to himself, it is evident that the expressions are to be distributed between natures, but in no way between persons, that is, subsistences. The term, then, is common to different realities: sometimes it signifies person, but at other times nature. We therefore speak of one subsistence of the Lord Christ, for his person is subsistent. Yet we do not shrink from speaking of two when someone wishes, with every precaution, to take the term piously as a designation of the natures; for two natures subsist.

Heretic. But behold, the Council of Chalcedon, which you venerate, speaks of one subsistence of the Lord Christ. Yet the most blessed Cyril says that one proceeds from two subsistences, and you said—or rather, you wished earlier to demonstrate—that he does not speak of two persons. Therefore he says that the Lord Christ is from two natures. And since the Father just mentioned immediately also speaks of one subsistence of him, he therefore recognizes one nature of the Lord Christ. For just as you do not refuse the expression “from two natures” and “from two subsistences,” so you will not be able to deny that he speaks of one nature when he proclaims that a union took place in one subsistence. For we are not now producing sayings of another Father, or sayings spoken by him in different works, but the same letter itself, and in passages not far removed from one another, displays both points there also. We hear him saying that the natures came together according to a natural, and not a personal, union—because there is not merely one person, but one nature from two.

Rust. What has been said is sufficient to resolve the points at issue. For just as we showed that in the same synod it was said that “subsistence” sometimes signifies person and sometimes nature, so in one and the same letter it can happen that different things are designated by one term—especially since, although it is one letter, the statements occur in different chapters. Moreover, you cannot deny that he used the term “subsistence” in different ways. For if you once concede that he did not say “from two persons” when he said “from two subsistences,” yet maintain that he said that one person and one subsistence were made through union for one nature, it is clear that he used the term in different ways: here he speaks of those subsistences which are not also persons, but only natures; there he speaks of that subsistence which, according to you as well, is a person. Thus what you had criticized as false when I said it, you too have confessed, although under a different term. It is therefore clear that, although you use the term closely related, you nevertheless use it in different ways. That he did not speak of one subsistence as one nature we shall show below.

Heretic. If he did not understand it in this way—that one nature had been made from two through union—why does he say, as I have already stated above, “according to a natural union”?

Rust. He says this to refute those who claim that it was not the very divine nature of the Word that was united to our nature, but merely something accidental belonging to the Word, such as dignity, authority, or power. He first says that the subsistences must not be joined according to dignity, authority, or power, and then adds only that they must be joined according to a natural union, that is, according to the natures themselves—as if someone were to say, “the angelic choir,” that is, “the choir of angels.”

It is also for this reason that a person was not united to a person, but that God the Word deigned to unite our nature to himself [Col. 1194C], not our person, lest the union be understood as neither real nor made into one person or one thing. The most holy Cyril himself, in his first exposition of these chapters, says that by “natural union” he meant “true union.” To confirm this, he adduces the Apostle’s testimony, saying: “You were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3). And he adds:

> “Just as he used the expression ‘by nature children of wrath’ for ‘truly children of wrath,’ so I used ‘natural union’ for ‘true union.’”

If, then, we understand “natural union” here as gathering the united things into one nature, it would also be necessary for a certain wrath to subsist according to nature there, whose offspring would by nature be evil—a conclusion appropriate to the utterly impious Manichaean. Moreover, if Cyril had wished to demonstrate that one nature had been made, it would have followed that he should have stated this more clearly in his exposition and added it against those who criticized the doctrine, saying:

> “It is true: this is what I said, and I said it rightly, for one nature has been made through union.”

Why, then, did he exchange “natural union” for the expression “true union”? No one, when explaining himself and wishing to make clear what he has said, substitutes a more uncertain term for a thoroughly precise one. We too speak of “true union,” and so do you; but you understand “natural union” as though it were a term belonging exclusively to your position. If, therefore, he had wished to say what you say, he could much more easily have said it, and he would not have changed the precise and clearer expression.

Heretic. Those to whom he was speaking were less capable, namely, the Easterners. For that reason he adapted his speech in this way, introducing the same point under another term—as if he had said: “Whoever speaks of true union speaks of natural union; and whoever denies natural union also rejects true union.” He yielded something of the exactness of his language for the sake of those who were not yet able to understand. If true union is not natural union, then show this more clearly.

Rust. No example is needed, since the matter itself resolves the question. You yourselves admit that you mean either a different union from ours or union in a different sense. But it is evident that we say that union was made into one person, one Christ, one Son, one Lord, and one substance; and it is clear that this union, which we believe, is true.

The holy Cyril, however, when he called the union “true” and “natural,” changing the term, as you say, for the sake of the weak, would hardly have fallen, in the interest of such an accommodation, into the enormity of attempting to prove from apostolic testimony that wrath subsists according to substance, and that those who are not at all [the text is defective] are its children—a consequence, we have shown, of your proposition. For if he called “natural” union here a union into one nature, and if there the children of wrath were called children of wrath by nature, then they would be of the same nature as wrath.

The aforementioned Father says in his exposition of the third chapter:

> “If we say ‘natural union,’ we mean ‘true union,’ since divinely inspired Scripture is accustomed to use this expression in this way. For the most holy Paul writes somewhere to certain people: ‘We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest’ [Note: [Col. 1195D] This passage is cited shortly before in this form, as in the Vulgate. The word *sicut* is absent in the printed editions.]. Let no one suppose that divine wrath subsists according to nature, so that those who sin are understood to be its offspring; otherwise we would agree in every way with those who are diseased with the madness of the Manichaeans. Rather, the word ‘nature’ that I used indicates what is according to truth.”

This passage overturns all your slanders against us—or rather, against holy Cyril.

Heretic. Do you say that Christ’s two natures are common, or that they are individual, as you call them? In either case, it necessarily follows that you also speak of two subsistences. For every substance and every individual nature is a subsistence. But if you call them general, universal, or at least common natures, they will never have fewer persons than there are of these natures. Therefore there will be two or more persons of the Lord Christ.

Rust. Here the words placed in response to the question are unnecessary; but in the conclusion there is an equivocation, which has already often been exposed. When we say that the Lord Christ has two natures, we call neither both of them common nor both of them individual. The divine nature is common, whereas the human nature is individual. Nor do we simply say that the Lord has two subsistences; we say that he has one subsistence, that is, truly one subsisting person. We do not shrink from speaking of two with an explanation, whenever the term is used for nature.

Heretic. Every individual nature is a person. If, therefore, Christ’s human nature is individual, the Word will be non-subsistent; and there are two natures. Therefore there are two persons of Christ.

Rust. There are many individual natures that are not also persons, such as those of inanimate and irrational things. A human being, although composed of soul and body, is nevertheless not said to consist of two persons, although it is confessed to consist of two individual natures. For if a human being consists of two persons, Christ will consist of three, and the Trinity of five persons. Yet we commonly call trees, branches, grasses, stones, and other inanimate things individual natures, but not persons.

Heretic. Much could indeed be said about this, although it would not properly address the point under discussion. I shall pass over the rest and define the proposition as follows: Every individual [Col. 1196B] rational nature is a person. For since three rational natures are confessed to exist—namely, God, the heavenly hosts, and humanity—each individual nature among them is a person. Since, therefore, you say that Christ has two rational natures, you inevitably introduce two persons as well. You therefore anathematize the name of Nestorius to no purpose, since you defend his doctrine; or, to put it more mildly, the error that necessarily follows from your doctrine accompanies it by strict reasoning.

Rust. I will not now inquire whether it is appropriate to call God “rational”; rather, I affirm this: in God there is an individual—that is, singular—nature, not a common nature but the nature of one and only one person. For the only common nature in God is the nature of the three persons. In the other case, however, person is not defined in this way. There is neither an individual nor a common nature there as a person, but an individual of the common nature.

Heretic. Therefore, as you say, there are rather two persons in the Lord Christ. For according to you, the proper account of person belongs to each nature: God the Word is an individual of the divine nature, while the humanity is an individual of a rational nature. These, then, are two natures; therefore there are also two persons. Nor can you say that things expressed equivocally, rather than univocally, are counted together, since by counting the common nature of the Trinity together with individual humanity you also admit two natures for this very reason.

Rust. Although in the other rational creatures an individual substance is a person, this is not so in the Lord Christ. For because you confess him to consist of two perfect [Col. 1196D] natures, it does not follow that, according to you, he consists of two persons. Otherwise it would no longer be incongruous to say that the Word united a person of a man to himself—something excluded at Ephesus by common agreement.

Since this has already been demonstrated, I shall add this as well: it is commonly confessed by us that the natures which came together for true union are indeed different, but that the persons which came together for true union are not therefore different. For if you too accept the letter of holy Cyril to which the Ephesian synod subscribed, you cannot refute this at all.

[Col. 1197A] Heretic. You will never be able to prove where that holy man ever wrote this.

Rust. The words of that most holy man himself will suffice. Testimony from St. Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius:

> “Uniting to himself, according to subsistence, flesh animated by a rational soul, the Word ineffably and incomprehensibly became man and was called Son of Man—not according to mere will or benevolence, nor as though by the assumption of a mere person. And although the natures brought together into true union are different, one Christ and Son is from both—not as though the difference of the natures had been abolished by the union, but rather as divinity and humanity make for us one Lord, Christ, and Son through an ineffable union [Col. 1197B] and an indescribable coming together.”

Therefore, although among other rational creatures an individual nature is a person, this rule is in no way true in Christ.

Heretic. What is said seems exceedingly irrational: that this rule is true in all things, but not at all true in Christ. For if he likewise shared blood and flesh with us and was made like us in all things except sin, why should what is true in all things not be true in him alone?

Rust. If this were the only extraordinary and unprecedented thing in Christ, even then it would have been fitting for you not to distrust his miracles. But if many things—indeed everything—in him are extraordinary, then it is all the more irrational that you should now at last reflect on this. You accept by faith so many wondrous and extraordinary things, yet you are doubtful about one of them.

For who, tell me, is like him besides this one? Therefore he was not made according to the law of customary things, since no one was made from himself as he was. He was made in a new manner, by a new union, according to a new, singular, and irregular law. Never before—for neither man, angel, nor any of the higher rational beings was God—was anyone united from another nature into one person with that God who is consubstantial with the Father. One Christ with the Word and God was made; no one was ever one Lord or one only-begotten Son of God, as we believe this one to have been made. For never, in truth, was one person made from two perfect rational natures, as it was made in the Lord Christ.

I shall say even more: not even among the substances of created things has anything of this sort ever taken place, that they should be united in the unity of one person. The Lord, therefore, is not subjected to the rule of other rational beings, for he was not made according to the law of the others. Just as we reject the syllogisms—or rather, the paralogisms, that is, false inferences—of Nestorius, so we reject those of others who likewise seek what is customary and extraordinary in things that cannot be evaluated, in things marvelous and surpassing the mind. From such arguments it cannot be inferred that the same one is perfect God and perfect man.

Thus, believing in God who governs all things and is almighty, we also resist you, who, by subjecting the union that shines above all things to comparisons, examples, laws, and rules, no longer believe it to be singular.

Heretic. I am a human being; I wish to be persuaded rationally. God created me rational.

Rust. Recall, I ask you, that you are also a participant in that divine baptism. Recall that the subject is that mystery to which nothing equal or similar has ever occurred, because the Lord of all himself accomplished it in himself. As he himself had said through the prophets:

> “I will do a new thing in the female, which all will marvel at” (Jeremiah 31:22).

But since you strongly compel me to undertake in words matters that surpass the soul, I shall first ask pardon from God and then, as best I can, begin to investigate the inscrutable matter.

I say, then, that if faith is to be accommodated to examples, Christ possesses everything belonging to our nature, but not everything belonging to a human person. For we see that each such subsistence possesses within itself everything that belongs to it, set apart from all others. My soul, for example, does not by itself govern another person’s body, either primarily or—even if we are said to govern children or servants—as an accidental relation.

But God never left that human nature bereft of his presence and governance, as though one might say that it exercised unrestrained free choice. Rather, for this very reason he created it—not that it might be its own, but his [perhaps read *sua*, “its own”]—and established it upon himself as upon a base or foundation, to speak truly, so that through it he might accomplish the most beautiful dispensation proposed by his immeasurable generosity.

Therefore, if every individual [Col. 1198C] nature is a person, this applies only to every nature that was not created for the purpose of remaining inseparably united to another. For the human body too is not a person distinct from its soul; otherwise, as I have already said, Christ would consist of three persons, and the holy Trinity of five.

Heretic. I must first accept what you said earlier, if you intend to proceed to the rest. For I wonder how you say that the Lord’s incarnation lacks an example, when many Fathers compare it to examples and liken it to them. The holy and universal Council of Ephesus itself, in explaining the mystery, also uses the example of a human being and teaches this fully from the readings of the ancients:

> “There are two natures, God and man, since there are also soul and body; but there are not two Sons or two Gods. For here too there are not two human beings, although Paul called what is within a human being and what is outside a human being by those names” (2 Corinthians 4:16). “And, if it is necessary to speak briefly, the things from which Christ consists are one thing and another.”

If, then, these most holy Fathers accept the example of a rational soul and a human body as an illustration of the Lord’s incarnation, and say that the natures in Christ are united just as the soul and body of a human being are united into one human nature, how do you prohibit us from holding this view concerning the incarnation, saying that the union is outside the example, when Fathers so great and so numerous offer this likeness?

[Col. 1199A] Rust. Then you say that the union celebrated in Christ differs in no respect from the union that constantly takes place throughout the world wherever a human being is composed.

Heretic. How could it not differ, since it took place once and only once, in divinity and flesh?

Rust. This created a difference not in the union itself, but only in the things that are united. For if, for example, it happened that a human being and an angel, or God and perhaps some rational heavenly power, were united, they would not differ from those things that were united by the union itself. It is one thing, therefore, for the things from which something is constituted to differ, and another for the mode of their union itself to differ.

Heretic. The union differs in some respect, but its result does not, [Col. 1199B] for they came together into one person.

Rust. But we are now arguing from the union to its result. Since we confess that Christ has one and only one person, we ask whether he also has one nature. But because every comparison or example must be neither entirely similar nor entirely dissimilar, we must consider several aspects in the example of a human being.

For from two natures there arise not only one human being, one person, and one subsistence, but also one species, one animal, and one substance or nature. It is evident from this that the holy Fathers do not take the example concerning the Lord as signifying one nature or substance merely because they accept the example. If the result were not only one person, one subsistence, and one individual, but also one species, substance, and nature, and if the number of the united things were in no way preserved, then it would no longer be an example.

But this was neither true nor intended by the writer. It was said only to demonstrate that, just as the things united there produced one and the same human being, so here they produce one Christ, one Son, one Lord, one person, and one subsistence. This can also be discerned from the very words.

For it was not said: “From two natures, God and man, as from soul and body; but the natures are no longer two, having become one through union.” Rather, after saying “two natures, God and man,” he added: “But not two Sons.” Why, then, do you distort what was said precisely so that it might be made clear that there is one Son and not two Gods; and so that no one might think that there are two Christs, an inner and an outer, as one thing and another? Rather, even if something of Christ is inward and something outward, according to the example given, and just as the Apostle speaks of a human being, there are nevertheless not two Christs, an inner and an outer.

Heretic. I understand what was said in another way. For when he said, “two natures, God and man, as soul and body; but not two Sons, nor Gods, for here too there are not two human beings, although Paul called what is within a human being and what is outside by those names,” it is as though someone were to say: “There are not two Christs, God and man, although the Apostle called the inner and outer parts, as it were, two human beings—that is, soul and body.”

Thus Gregory of holy memory applies a single designation to all the elements of the human being whom the Apostle divided, as it were, into two, lest, by comparing him with Christ, he appear to assert two Christs. Since, therefore, in the case of one and the same human being it is permissible, with reference to the Apostle, to speak of an inner human being and an outer human being, but in Christ it is not permissible, according to the holy Fathers who assembled at Ephesus, to speak of Christ who is within and Christ who is outside, lest we make two Christs, it is clear that there is a greater unity in Christ than the unity that occurred in a human being. Therefore, all the more, Christ is one nature through union.

Rust. I desire to hear more plainly what you said just now, for it is extremely obscure.

Heretic. The same point will be repeated briefly and plainly. The Apostle said somewhere: “As our outer human being is corrupted, so our inner human being is renewed” (2 Corinthians 4:16). As though he were speaking of another, he separated the one who is within from the one who is outside, so that they might be thought of as two human beings, one inner and one outer.

Gregory therefore says: “Christ is from two natures just as a human being is from body and soul.” Yet we are not permitted to say of Christ what we say of a human being. Just as the one who is within and the one who is outside are in some sense two human beings, so there would be two Sons. For we do not take the example to mean that one Son is interior and another exterior, but only that one Son is from both. He therefore took the example in part, not in its entirety.

Moreover, the Apostle seems to indicate not merely two, but even three human beings. For when he says, “our inner human being” and “our outer human being,” by saying “our” he indicates another human being to whom these two belong. For I am one person, and the one who is mine is another.

Rust. You speak most falsely and craftily. Neither did the Apostle write so incongruously, nor did that universal synod so lose its senses as to explain such an incongruity, as though in the person of holy Gregory, for the demonstration of its own faith. The expression “inner and outer human being” does not mean a complete human being in the simple sense, but an incomplete human being. Neither soul nor body is a complete human being.

Everything that is denied is expressed by adding a negative particle. For example: “A rational soul is not a human being.” The term “human being” is used, and it is said not to be that. Paul therefore describes a part of the human being, saying “outer human being,” that is, “not also inner,” and thus not the whole human being. Again, “the human being who is within” means “not also the one who is outside”; therefore, neither is a human being, but something belonging to a human being, and incomplete.

That the Father understood it in this way can be shown not only by the opposed incongruity but also by the consequence of the reasoning. He says:

> “If anyone introduces two Sons, one from God the Father and the other from Mary, and not one and the same, let him fall away from the adoption promised to those who believe rightly. There are two natures, God and man, as soul and body; but there are not two Sons or Gods. For these too are not two human beings, although Paul called what is within a human being and what is outside by those names. And, if it is necessary to speak briefly, the things from which the Savior consists are one thing and another. The visible is not the same as the invisible, nor the temporal as the timeless; yet they are not one person and another—far from it—for both are one by commixture: God is incarnate and man is deified, or however one may name it. I say ‘one thing and another’ in the opposite sense from what applies to the Trinity. There, it is ‘one person and another,’ so that we do not confuse the subsistences; it is not ‘one thing and another,’ for the three are one and the same in divinity.”

First, he did not say “Christ is from two natures,” but rather, “There are two natures, God and man,” that is, Christ. For if he were speaking of someone else, he would not have added, “But not two Sons.” There is no one who is both God and man as one Son except Christ.

Nor did he say that there had been two natures, but that there are two natures. For what is added immediately is not “there were,” but “there are.” He says, “as soul and body,” and adds, “but not two Sons or Gods”; he does not add “they are.” Therefore he did not add this for the purpose of implying that there are not two natures. Nor is the omission to be understood—far from it—as though there were two Sons; rather, it is a characteristic of the construction, leaving this part of the sentence to be supplied in the listener’s understanding.

If, then, there are two natures, God and man, which the Savior plainly confessed, how do you, through certain demonic subtleties, twist his words into the opposite? Tell me.

Heretic. For the moment, you must answer in order to what has been said, if indeed you have anything to say at all; then you may question me as to whether I have arguments in response. What, then, does he intend by saying, “although Paul called what is within a human being and what is outside by those names”?

[Col. 1201C] Rust. Listen patiently; this is what I shall do. After saying, “There are two natures, God and man, as soul and body; but not two Sons or Gods,” he added, “For here too there are not two human beings.”

It is not therefore permissible to say that there are two human beings in one and the same person. This would greatly damage the mystery of piety if we said that Christ is God and two human beings, or that the Word did not become man but that human beings were made. From this one could derive ten thousand conclusions at once incongruous and blasphemous.

Above all, you, while refusing to say that the Lord Christ has two natures, say that there are two human beings in him; and, while denying that there are two natures of God and man, you again insist, on the authority of the Apostle, that the one human being is two human beings, and that Gregory spoke contrary to the Apostle.

But, as we said earlier, the Apostle and the Fathers have stated that some things are said of one alone and not of two or more, while others are said similarly of one and not of one alone. Thus the Lord says of his body that it is a temple, when he foretold that the Jews would destroy it but that he himself would raise it; yet we too are called temples, either of the Son or of the Holy Spirit.

You see, then, that the same thing can be said both of one individual and of those who are not the same, but of different individuals. If, therefore, it is one thing to speak of two or more, and another to speak of one but in a similar manner as though of two, then in the latter case there is similarity of expressions, not identity of things. For the account concerning one is not without distinction from the account concerning many.

Gregory therefore says that although the Apostle used common and similar language concerning one human being as though concerning two, there are nevertheless not two human beings, the one within and the one outside. He did not state this without qualification, but as though with the sentence left suspended. For he did not say that the Apostle says this in every respect; he said:

> “If Paul called what is within a human being and what is outside by those names.”

Attention must also be paid to the word “called.” He did not say “confirmed,” nor “defined,” but “called.” Calling indicates similarity of expressions, not necessarily and inevitably identity of things. He therefore did not understand two human beings, although he called them, as it were, two.

Heretic. Why should we prolong the discussion? The reading does not say “in two natures,” but “from two”; for he added, “one thing and another, the things from which the Savior consists.”

Rust. For now, allow us to settle in order the matter that was formerly under discussion; we shall investigate this point afterward. In addition to what was said above, he also adds:

> “And, if it is necessary to speak briefly, the things from which the Savior consists are one thing and another, since the invisible is not the same as the visible, nor the timeless as that which is subject to time; yet they are not one and another—far from it.”

Here he represents what had been stated: Christ is from two substances, not from two persons. “One thing and another” is more properly characteristic of natures; “one person and another” of persons.

It must be noted that he did not say, “the Savior is from one thing and another,” but “one thing and another, the things from which the Savior consists,” lest one of you suppose that he is from two things but that there are no longer two natures. For he spoke in the plural: “the things from which the Savior consists.”

If the Savior is from two natures, and these are the very things from which the Savior consists, then there are two natures. It cannot be said here that he meant some other things from which he consists besides the two natures. For it is impossible to say that Christ is from anything else except from two existing natures. By “existing” I mean not pre-existing before the union—far from it—but continuing to exist even now.

I shall therefore repeat the point. This reading clearly intends the two things from which the Savior consists to be natures. How, then, do you attempt, unless by Satanic cunning, to turn into the opposite what has been correctly said? For you now say that the things from which the Savior consists are two natures, and that the Fathers called them two natures and “one thing and another.”

Just as he said here, “one thing and another, the things from which the Savior consists,” as though he were saying, “from which the Savior consists,” so above he said, “two natures, God and man,” as though he were saying, “there are two natures, God and man.” Pay attention also to the flow of this reading, for it proceeds in the same way through each expression.

Heretic. What is that to me? Let the two natures be spoken of only so that he is from them, but not so that Christ is in them, lest the one be divided into two.

Rust. However often you alter the words, we shall not grow weary of opposing truth to your falsehoods. It would truly be shameful and unbecoming for us to prove colder in defending the truth than you are in asserting perversities.

Listen, then, for the present, and allow me to persuade you still further from what follows:

> “For both of these are one by commixture: God is incarnate and man is deified, or however one may name it.”

Observe the reading, which speaks of “both,” whereas you do not wish two things to be named. Who could be so foolish—or rather, who so mad, impious, and godless—as not to say that “both” means two things?

At the same time, consider that, as we said above, “one” is more simply proper to nature than to person, just as “one person” is more proper to person than to nature. Yet such expressions are sometimes used without strict precision and interchangeably, while preserving a pious understanding. Thus the Apostle spoke of one human being as though of two, “the one who is within” and “the one who is outside.” So this writer speaks of two natures as though of one—not saying that Christ is one or that the person is one, but simply saying “one.” For he says, “Both of these are one by commixture.” Do not flatter yourself as though he thought he was speaking altogether of one nature. Otherwise I too will say that here “one” is not read without an added qualification, but is said to be one “by commixture,” that is, by union—not one by nature.

**Heretic.** I will say no more to you; behold, I shall overcome you with a single statement. Where will you flee from me hereafter? Where can you turn? For he not only said “one thing,” referring to both, but added “by commixture”: where there is commixture, there is altogether one nature arising from diverse things. Therefore one nature has been made from the two natures of the Lord Christ.

**Rusticus.** I glorify God, because, as though you had found an opportunity, you have most readily vomited forth all your poison. I ask—and hope—that, the more manifest your wound has become, the more quickly it may be healed. For the teaching of the saints did not say “mixture of natures”; it did not say “fermentation”; it did not say “confusion.” None of these preserves any longer the things that have been united. Therefore, if—God forbid—confusion has taken place, Christ is no longer God.

But he himself explained what he meant by “commixture,” when he added: “God having been made human, and man having been deified.” He did not say, “God having been confused, and man having been fermented.” There is, in fact—there truly is—a certain commixture that preserves the distinction of the things commingled. The holy Cyril long ago sufficiently explained this in the first volume Against the Blasphemies of Nestorius, saying:

> “Some of the holy Fathers also used the term ‘commixture.’ But since you say that you fear lest some sort of pouring together may perhaps be thought to have occurred, as happens with things that are mutually mingled in liquid form, I shall free you from such fears. For they understood the matter in this way; they never misused the term, but sought to indicate the complete union of the things that came together with one another. We say that they came together according to an indivisible union, with God the Word possessing immutably the properties of the flesh. We shall also find that the divinely inspired Scripture itself does not scrutinize this word too closely, but rather uses it, as it were, abusively and simply. Thus the most sacred Paul wrote concerning certain persons: ‘But the word they heard did not profit them, because those who heard were not united with faith’ (Heb. 4:2).  
>
> “Were those of whom he spoke, then, going to be mingled with one another in equal proportion, like wine with water, and to suffer some pouring together of their substances into one another?
