Or were they rather united in soul, according to what is written in the Acts of the holy Apostles: ‘The multitude of those who believed was of one heart and one soul’ (Acts 4:32)? I think the latter is truer than the former. Therefore, put aside your fears concerning these matters: the mind of the saints is exceedingly cautious.”

Behold: what had once been asked of Nestorius, holy Cyril has resolved.

**Heretic.** If you truly can, demonstrate something of this sort from his synodical writings. For the things said in struggle, contention, and contradiction were certainly not expressed with strict precision. I think that many things in such circumstances were said more in accordance with the economy. But the things belonging to the universal synod are the firmest of all, especially since one must first consider the common statements and then the writings proper to each person. I too have many such passages to produce from his writings.

**Rusticus.** If this Father’s authority concerning these matters is not enough to satisfy you, consider me to have said these things. Will you be unable to approve the Apostle’s words by which they have been demonstrated, or the sound interpretation of them? Nevertheless, I shall obey you even in this. For I hope in the name of the Lord that, if you are satisfied in every respect with everything you ask, you will also be corrected in every respect.

From the synodical and unitive letter of Cyril, of holy memory, to John, archbishop of Antioch, of holy remembrance, and to the synod under him:

> “But let your religiousness condemn those who say that confusion or fermentation occurred between God the Word and the flesh. For it is credible that some also boast such things about me, as though I had either held or uttered such an opinion. I, however, am so far from this view that I consider those who have in any way suspected that a momentary shadowing could occur around the divine nature of the Word to be insane. For what it is remains forever, and has not been changed; nor will it ever be changed or be subject to alteration. We all confess that God the Word is impassible in these respects.”

**Heretic.** We too do not mean the impious mixture that this teacher condemns, but the pious mixture that this very holy Cyril accepted in the words of St. Gregory, together with the entire universal synod of Ephesus. This pious mixture produced one nature of Christ.

**Rusticus.** Although what has been said should suffice, nevertheless, because of your obstinacy, and so that you may know that this is not the intention of the passage, let us examine the rest, which reads as follows:

> “For both are one by commixture: God having been made human, and man having been deified, or whatever one may call it. But I say that the relation here is otherwise than it is in the Trinity. For there, there is one and another, so that we do not confuse the hypostases; but not one thing and another, so that we do not divide the substance—for these three are one and the same in deity.”

In these words he clearly demolishes every genuine heresy, showing that “one thing and another” applies to Christ, whereas in the entire Trinity it does not at all; rather, there is “one and another.” You see, therefore, that “two natures” and “one thing and another” are said of the one and same Lord Christ, while “one and another,” where there are three persons, is not said because Christ is a fourth person—for without Christ there would no longer be three, but two persons or hypostases—but because, just as in the common teaching concerning the holy Trinity the distinction and number belong to the hypostases, not to the natures, so in Christ, who completes the Trinity, both the distinction and the number belong to the natures, not to the persons.

For if here the relation is otherwise than in the Trinity, what else does “otherwise” signify than this: just as there is not one person there, lest we confuse the substances, so here there is not one nature, lest we confuse the natures? Therefore, according to the judgment of the holy and universal synod, those introduce confusion in every possible way who say that one nature of the Lord Christ was made from divinity and humanity.

**Heretic.** He said “two natures” and “one thing and another,” from which the Savior exists—not “in which the Savior exists.” But you, like the Council of Chalcedon, say that he exists not from two natures, but in two natures.

**Rusticus.** He did not say that there had been two natures, but that there are two natures—not only because of what was said long ago, but also because of what has now been said. For he did not say that they had been so disposed in Christ, but that they remain so to the present. He says, “and otherwise than it is in the Trinity,” that is, up to the present; nor did he say, “There it was so disposed otherwise,” but, “In the Trinity it is so disposed.” Rather, after saying “otherwise,” he commonly adds “is.”

Therefore, just as the distinction of the hypostases remains there to the present, so does the distinction of the natures here. For how can “one thing and another” and “one and another” apply to things that once existed but no longer do, in contrast with things that always exist in this way? If this too is difficult for you, it has already been shown above that he used “God and man” as though he were saying, “There are two natures, God and man.”

**Heretic.** We do say that there are two natures even to the present, but in such a way that he exists from them, not in them. For to say that he exists in them is to divide him into two.

**Rusticus.** Then tell me: what are these two? It is plainly evident that they are his divinity and his humanity. Therefore, if Christ is in divinity and humanity, he is in two natures. For if Christ is not in the natures [perhaps: “from natures”], that is, if he is not from two natures—God forbid—then, since he is from divinity and humanity, he is either from some other divinity and humanity besides the two natures—God forbid—or he is not from divinity and humanity.

**Heretic.** And from where can you show me that Christ is in divinity and humanity?

**Rusticus.** For the moment, because he said not merely that the natures once existed alone, but also that they now exist, he demonstrates this as well when he says, “For both are one by commixture.” To say “these two” is the same as to say “both these.” Therefore, just as when he says “this one” we understand that he means not only that it once existed but that it exists now also, so when he says “both these,” we understand that he means not only that they once existed but that they exist now also. For if they are no longer “both these,” then this is no longer “one.”

Consequently—God forbid—it will no longer be said that Christ is one, nor, according to you, that his person is one. Moreover, the very demonstrative pronoun “these,” expressed in the plural, signifies not one nature but natures; and “both those,” that is, the two, are one. All these things are spoken of as one, as the reading of the passage demonstrates.

**Heretic.** Do not tell me many things. Prove only what I said: that Christ is in them.

**Rusticus.** I shall prove this to you in the same way from synodical passages.

**Heretic.** First let us investigate what remains of the testimony of St. Gregory, which, as I think, clearly declares one substance of the Lord Christ.

**Rusticus.** Let this statement also be preserved for you without prejudice. For now, while we still remember what has been said, receive a synodical passage showing that Christ is in divinity and humanity.

### Synodical Testimony of Ambrose, Most Holy Bishop of Milan

> “Let empty disputes about words therefore be silent, because, as it is written, the kingdom of God is not in persuasive human speech but in the demonstration of power (1 Cor. 2:4). Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh. The Son of God speaks as one in both, because each nature is in the same one; and, although it is the same one who speaks, he does not always speak in the same manner. Observe in him now the glory of God, now the sufferings of man: for as God he teaches divine things, because he is the Word; but as man he speaks human things, because he was speaking in my substance. You have heard: ‘Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh.’ The Son of God speaks as one in both, because in the same one there is both natures.”

Observe, I ask you, that in both of these expressions the Lord Christ is intended—that is, divinity and humanity—and that he says their distinction must be preserved. He adds that “in the same one there is both natures.” What, then, does “because” mean, unless it is as though he said: “For this reason he is in them, because these are in him”? If there are two natures in Christ, then Christ is in the two natures.

For this reason the same one does not always speak in the same way: because he is not one nature, but at one time he is as God and at another as man, “because he was speaking in my substance”—that is, “whoever”—or perhaps, according to the text, “he who was in my substance”—“was speaking.” The very distinction of times represents equally the glory of God, the suffering of man, and the distinction of the natures, when he says, “now this, now that.”

**Heretic.** You say these things; the synod did not say that Christ is in both natures, but that he himself speaks in both; “in him there is both nature.” It did not say “two,” but “both.” Yet “both” does not necessarily mean “two.”

**Rusticus.** How long, O man, will you distrust God, who spoke through the holy Fathers, and, sparing no shamelessness, overturn even the common conceptions of the mind through the blindness of despair? Who has ever said, or heard it said among human beings, that “both” does not mean two?

I convict you from your own conscience. Say, then, anathema to the one who does not believe that Christ is in both natures and that both natures are in Christ, so that we may believe you at least speak in good conscience. Why, then, do you seek occasions and variations in words? Say “anathema,” and then, as one who does not know, we shall reasonably persuade you.

But since you said, “he speaks in both,” and, “he was speaking in my substance,” he did not say, “because he is in this or in that,” but, “because he speaks in both.” One who is in both speaks. This construction is so placed that what follows is “the Son of God.” Restoring the order of the words, the meaning is easy, as though he had said: “The Son of God, who is in both natures, speaks.” He added, “speaks.”

Nevertheless, what follows from your words again indicates their incongruity. For if he is not in both, then he speaks where he is not. Moreover, if he is not in both natures, but both natures are in him, then the Son of God is not in those things that are in him.

In some matters such an arrangement is indeed true: I am in this world and in this place, but the world and the place are not also in me. But in matters pertaining to substance the relation is necessarily reciprocal. For if the Son is in the divine substance, then the divine substance is also in the Son; and if the nature of humanity is in him, then he is also in that nature; and if there are two natures in him, then he is in the two natures.

**Heretic.** I fear saying the same thing, as though in a confession of faith, that anyone could say while dividing and separating. For division is said to occur into two, or into three, or certainly into even more; and therefore I do not say “in two.”

**Rusticus.** Similarity of expressions does not make the same thing exist in reality. Otherwise, one could also bring the same accusation against the one who says that “in the same one there is both nature.” For, conversely, things that are confused are confused into one thing.

There is, however, the greatest—or rather, an absolute opposition—between saying that one and the same is in two natures and saying that he is divided into two or into two particular things. For whatever is divided, partitioned, or separated is not one in those things in which it is separated. It cannot be one and divided at the same time. After having once been one, it is no longer one after it has been separated.

This, then, is what impious division or separation signifies. But for one and the same to be in certain things is rather a more cautious and firmer affirmation of inseparable unity. For one who is in two and remains the same cannot merely be divided; he is also sufficient in himself to preserve united the things in which he exists according to hypostasis—that is, substantially—which are those things in which he participates without any intervening separation.

Therefore, with much greater caution and firmness, we do not say that the Son is merely one, as though ignoring the two natures; rather, knowing that he exists in two natures, we firmly and unchangeably recognize him as one. He is not, so to speak, to be bound by the duality of the natures in which he exists, as though he were divided into two; rather, in his own unbreakable union he prevails to preserve the very natures in which he exists.

**Heretic.** These words appear to me to be argumentation and, if I may say so, a subtlety of intellect. I shall turn instead to the most holy authority of the holy Fathers. From you, according to your promises, I shall demand that at last we review what remains of the reading of St. Gregory, which is as follows:

> “If anyone says that the Word operates, as in a prophet, according to grace, and was not joined and co-formed according to substance [the text reads *inoperatum*; shortly below, *operatum*], let him be empty of the better operation, or rather full of the contrary. If anyone does not adore this Crucified One, let him be anathema and be reckoned among the God-slayers. If anyone says that he was made perfect from works, or that after baptism or resurrection from the dead he was made worthy of assimilation, as the Gentiles introduce in their subscriptions, let him be anathema. For that which began, or progresses, or is perfected, is not God—or if it is said in this way in a manner of increase.”

Behold, those who say that God was not joined to the flesh according to substance, and was not co-formed with it, have unquestionably been anathematized. Therefore, if a union according to substance took place in Christ, it follows that it produced one substance. For the testimony did not say “joined according to substances,” but “according to substance.” Substance, however, is certainly one, not two substances, as you say.

I also remember that, when “natural union” was being discussed, you said that he had not at that point spoken of a union according to nature, but of a natural union. Here, then, he has expressly spoken not of a substantial union but of a joining according to substance—that is, a union. He added that God was co-formed with the flesh, and that the Jews were not merely man-slayers but God-slayers.

**Rusticus.** He is not now explaining how two natures came together with one another, but how one and only one divine nature came together with humanity—not also conversely. If you consider this implausible, let us attend to the beginning of the passage. For he says: “If anyone says that he worked as in a prophet according to grace.”

You see, then, the beginning of the proposition: it concerns how God was joined to the flesh, not how divinity and humanity were joined without union—that is, apart from one side of the union, so to speak. He therefore rules out the claim that God was simply joined according to grace, and according to that measure of grace by which he worked in the prophets. Instead, he proves that he was joined according to substance.

Nor did he say “united,” but “joined.” Joining is the relation of things that are not united without an intermediary. Let me try to state more clearly what I mean. God the Word is said to have been united to the flesh not through the divine nature, but the divine nature is said to have been united through the person of God the Word.

For if the whole Trinity had wished to become incarnate, then perhaps the nature itself would rightly have become incarnate through itself. For all the things that belong to that nature in itself and on account of itself are common to the Trinity, not proper to one single person.

The incarnation, however, is not common to the Trinity but proper only to the hypostasis of the Word. Therefore God the Word became incarnate, and so did his nature; but he did so through himself and according to what he himself is, whereas his nature did not do so in this way, but through the person.

Thus God the Word, according to himself, was united to the flesh: one person and one hypostasis was formed with the flesh. According to nature, however, he was joined rather than united, for the two natures remained. By comparison, the Word is more properly said to have been united to the flesh than his nature was; and for this reason the former is more properly called “union.”

The latter is more properly “joining,” although it too is a union; the former is more a union than a joining. For whenever “joining” is used, the number of the things joined—or even their quantity—is almost always preserved.

**Heretic.** This statement seems to me full of many incongruities. For there is no difference between saying how two natures came together with one another and saying how divinity was joined to humanity. If there is one nature, it does not differ from itself; therefore the Word was joined to the flesh in the same way as the flesh was joined to the Word.

Furthermore, what difference is there between the Word and his nature, so that he himself is said to have been united through himself, while his nature is said not to have been united through itself but rather to have been joined?

**Rusticus.** I ask you to listen to me more attentively than before, for the statement is subtler than can otherwise be understood. We say that God dwells in the flesh indivisibly and continually; but we do not say that the flesh dwells in God. The flesh is called the temple of God, but God is in no way called the temple of the flesh. God effected this kind of union, not the flesh; the flesh suffered and did not effect it.

“Suffering” is not said only of bodily, distressing, and evil things, but also of spiritual, pleasant, and good things, so that even the blessedness of creatures is called a passion.

The union is indeed one and the same, but the definition or account of the union is not one and the same. If, then, we must present by an image the distinction between divinity united to the flesh and flesh united to divinity, we may put it this way.

The accounts of one and the same road can be opposite. The ascent and the descent are the same road: from one starting point to another it is an ascent, while from the other to the first it is a descent; the subject, however, is the same. The place of the journey is the same, even if someone traverses it many times and thousands of times.

Thus, by way of example and for the sake of clarity, we may say that the union itself does not differ from divinity to humanity, but the account of the union differs in the reverse direction. There is, however, this further difference: the union of the two natures was effected not by both natures, but by divinity alone. For what could our nature in Christ, which received its beginning from the union itself, contribute toward the union?

Perhaps for this reason also the two substances are joined not “according to substances” but “according to substance,” because the union itself was a miracle not of two but of one alone. For it did not occur there as it does among the prophets or others, when divine grace extends a hand to us while we ourselves strive and in some manner cooperate in being united to God. It occurred in a wholly different and ineffable manner.

**Heretic.** Again I am compelled, in my uncertainty, to raise the question: what is the difference, or what lies between, the Word and his nature or substance, so that he himself is united to the flesh through himself, while his nature is united according to the person?

**Rusticus.** The reason you give for why the Father and the Holy Spirit were not made human, while the one nature of God the Word, which is common to the Trinity, became incarnate—that same reason we give for saying that God the Word became human through himself, while his nature did so according to the person.

Indeed, what we say appears much easier than what you say. For if humanity and divinity were united in such a way that one nature was made, and the Father and the Holy Spirit were not at all made human, although they are of the same nature and not of another, how can it be impossible that the Word became human in such a way that his nature did not become human through itself?

**Heretic.** Everything that the person possesses, nature also possesses without an intermediary; but it is not necessary that the things belonging to nature also belong to the person.

**Rusticus.** This statement, even before demonstration, seems utterly incongruous to everyone. Nevertheless, for the sake of the senseless, I shall answer as necessity requires.

You suggest that there is no difference and no intermediary between the person of the Word and his nature. Since nothing prevents this, the converse may also be said: there is no difference and no intermediary between the nature of the Word and his person.

Since the Father and the Holy Spirit are not different in the nature they share, when the Word and his nature became human, then, according to you, the Father and the Holy Spirit also became human. Therefore it is necessary, in view of your blasphemies, that the whole holy Trinity was begotten and suffered.

Moreover, according to you, the flesh will be three persons because of the Trinity—or the Trinity will be one person because of the flesh—or the flesh must have a nature but not a person.

Therefore, according to you, the one Christ, one Son, and one Lord does not exist from two natures. For among you these expressions signify one and only one composite person. Instead, as you say, only one nature was made.

Thus, from your argument, the unavoidable conclusion is either that there is one Christ, one Son, and one Lord, but not one nature of his made from two; or that there is one nature, but not one Christ, one Son, and one Lord.

Why, then, do you attribute your own crime to others, as though those who say there are two natures denied one Lord, one Christ, and one Son? We constantly confess these in words and in reality, while you alone constantly deny them by saying that there is one nature.

This too must be noted: earlier you denied that there is any difference between the Word and his nature, but now you have said that everything the person possesses, nature also possesses without an intermediary, whereas it is not necessary that what belongs to nature also belongs to the person.

**Heretic.** I confess that there is some difference. But this difference prevents certain things belonging to nature from also being common to the persons; it does not, however, prevent the things belonging to the person from also belonging to nature. Therefore the person became incarnate, and one nature was made. But once one nature was made, the Trinity did not become incarnate. For the things belonging to the person immediately also belong to nature, while the things belonging to nature do not immediately also belong to the persons.

**Rusticus.** If, then, as you say, the things belonging to the person immediately also belong to nature, since the two persons—the Father and the Holy Spirit—are other than the humanity of the Son, there is consequently another nature, according to you, namely that of the Father and the Spirit, besides the nature of humanity that is in Christ.

Therefore the nature of the Father and the nature of the flesh are two natures. Since the nature of the Father and the Holy Spirit is one, simple, and alone, and is also the nature of the Son insofar as he is God, there are consequently two natures of the Son.

**Heretic.** But in the Son alone it was made one with humanity; in the other persons there is one nature and another, and therefore two natures.

**Rusticus.** Therefore it was made one with respect to one of its own aspects, but not with respect to another. If this aspect is identical with the person of the Son, then you plainly confess with us that not one nature but one Son was made, and that his person is one.

But if it is not identical with the person, then, according to you, the divine substance will not be simple but composite: one part of it was made one nature with the flesh, while another part was not made one nature with the flesh.

Thus, while refusing to distinguish divinity and humanity from one another, you will distinguish the simple divinity itself—and this according to itself.

If you doubt that it is impious to distribute everything belonging to the Son of God among his divine nature, this will be demonstrated. For it is not permissible to call the sufferings of his flesh sufferings of the divine nature of the Son of God, nor to call the things proper to the Word—or, as I think, to the remaining hypostases—things belonging to that nature.

The reason is that the properties expressing the persons are distinct from one another, whereas the simple nature, insofar as it is simple, has nothing that differs within it. For the Father begot, but was not begotten; the Son was begotten, but did not beget; the Holy Spirit proceeds, and does not do the converse.

But the divine nature—that is, the nature common to the holy Trinity, which exists in three hypostases—neither begets, nor is begotten, nor proceeds. For if it did one of these things, it would also do the others: that is, if it begot, it would therefore also be begotten and proceed.

It is likewise impious to distribute everything belonging to the Son of God among his divine nature. Since it is proper to the Son of God neither to beget nor to proceed, these properties cannot now be referred to his nature as though it were the one that begets and proceeds. Indeed, if it is the Father’s begetting, which is not being begotten or proceeding, then for the Son this is … [A line was missing in the exemplar.]

**Heretic.** If the divine nature did not beget, how do the most holy Fathers at Nicaea say that the Son was begotten from the substance of the Father, saying, “begotten from the Father, the only-begotten, that is, from the substance of the Father”?

**Rusticus.** The creed does not contain that wording. Therefore those holy Fathers, the one hundred and fifty at Constantinople, did not say it either.

Nevertheless, even if someone grants that it is written in this form, it was said to mean that the Only-Begotten was begotten from the Father and exists of the same substance as the Father—not as though he were begotten from the substance itself. For the Son, God the Word, belongs not to the substance but to the hypostasis of the Father. The Father of the Word is not the nature common to the three hypostases, but the hypostasis of the Father alone.

**Heretic.** Then, according to you, the holy, great, and universal synod held at Ephesus corrupted what is true. For it inserted this wording in the creed, saying: “And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, the only-begotten from the Father, that is, from the substance of the Father, God from God, light from light,” and the rest.

**Rusticus.** When speaking of the Fathers, we ought not to use words so boldly. Otherwise I too might perhaps say: “Then, according to you, the holy and universal Council of Constantinople corrupted the creed of the Fathers.”

We ought instead to spare the holy Fathers and leave this point aside, saying only that, although the exposition differs in words, it does not differ in meaning. Therefore, when we say “begotten from the substance of the Father,” it is to be understood as we said above: that he is of the same substance; or the phrase should be divided as follows: “from the substance of the Father, God from God, and light from light.”

I also say this: in the one and same synod of Ephesus, where Charisius confessed his own faith, which the synod also approved, he did not state this passage of the creed in that form, but rather as follows: “And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, God from God,” and so forth.

I think this is the reason for the discrepancy: the wording was retained by many from memory, and, when some forgot certain parts, they substituted one expression for another.

**Heretic.** I would like to hear something more certain about this, for these matters are doubtful.

**Rusticus.** For the support of my exposition it is enough to undermine the sense of your reasoning—or rather, your suspicion or madness. For if everything belonging to each person, and especially to the Son, must be assigned to the common substance of the Trinity, then the suffering of the Son will also be suffering of the divine nature.

But if you say that only those things that belong to divinity are to be so assigned, then it is no longer one, as there is one person of God and man. For if, as you assert, everything belonging to the person of God the Word is assigned to the divine nature, the divine nature itself does not thereby become one person with the Word. How, then, can the humanity of that same Word, whose divine properties are not assigned to the divine nature, be one nature with it?

Even if we grant this as well—that everything belonging to the person must be assigned to the common substance of the persons, not because these things belong to that substance primarily and in itself—then, in itself, it both begot and did not beget; it was both begotten and not begotten; it both proceeded and did not proceed; it both became human and did not become human.

For the Father begot and was not begotten; the Son was begotten and did not beget; the Holy Spirit did none of these things, but only proceeds and does not do the converse.

There is no reason why, if the things belonging to each person are also properties of their natures, the things that are absent from each person should not also be absent from the nature itself. Consequently, true affirmations and negations would be made concerning the same thing, concerning one and the same simple substance—which is utterly incongruous.

Rather, these considerations demonstrate that the things proper to each person belong to that person in itself and through itself, because they are not opposites when predicated of the same person; but the things said of the common nature do not have this character.

Since incarnation is also a property of a person—I mean, of the Son—it was not the nature itself, primarily and through itself, that became incarnate. Thus all the demonstrations stated above remain valid for us.

I also say this: when I say simply “God,” I mean the whole Trinity; but when “God” has “Father” added to it, I no longer mean the Trinity but one person.

Thus, when I say “substance,” I signify what is common to the Trinity; but when I say, with the addition, “the substance of the Father,” I mean only the person possessing that substance.

**Heretic.** What, then, of the fact that the holy synod says that God was co-formed with the flesh, and that the Jews are God-slayers, as though not a man but God had been killed? How is God said to have been co-formed and killed, unless there is one nature? If there were two natures, while their number, distinctions, and properties remained intact, then, since these remained, it ought to have been said that the man was killed and that God was not killed with him; and that God was formed, but that he formed and raised up the temple—that is, the man.

**Rusticus.** You are paying even less attention to what has been said. For what we are saying always signifies either two things or more in number. If, therefore, God was co-formed with the flesh, then there are two things: God and humanity.

The most holy Cyril is my witness to this in his second letter to Nestorius, where he says:

> “We shall confess one Christ and Lord—not worshipping a man together with the Word, lest the appearance of division be introduced because of the expression ‘with,’ but worshipping him as one and the same. For his body is not alien to the Word, with whom it also sits together with the Father.”

In the third letter he says:

> “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be worshipped together with God the Word, glorified together with him, and called God together with him as one distinct from the other—for the expression ‘with,’ whenever it is added, always compels us to understand this—rather than honoring Emmanuel with one worship and assigning to him one glory, according to the fact that the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.”

**Heretic.** I am compelled to cry out the very same questions: How was God co-formed? How was he killed? And how does the holy Cyril, of blessed memory, not speak contradictions, when he fervently rejects from his own person the meaning conveyed by “with,” but elsewhere approves this same expression synodically? These are the matters that trouble and disturb me above all.

### Rust.

I suppose that we jointly confess that the Son of God, God the Word, being consubstantial with and by nature undifferentiated from his own Father, is likewise impassible as he is; nevertheless, for this reason the things that happened to his own flesh are not altogether alien to him. I am speaking about the union.

Since, then, the flesh was formed, while the eternal Deity of the Word remained unformed; and since God the Word was inseparably united to the flesh, making the things proper to the flesh his own, he is said, economically, to have been formed together with the flesh, signifying by this that the formation of his own flesh was impassible.

For just as, when his most holy flesh was generated from the Virgin, he himself is said to have been generated—the one who grants to all things their coming-to-be—so, when his flesh was formed, he himself is said to have been formed together with it. Thus, in what is said “together,” the account of the natures is preserved; but in what is said “formed”—although this properly belongs first to humanity, it is nevertheless also said of God the Word—the entirely inseparable unity of the union is preserved. If, therefore, he had wished to show us only the union, he could rightly and without fault have said, “The Only-Begotten was formed according to the flesh,” or “in the flesh,” that is, according to our nature. If he had wished to show only the difference, he would have said without ambiguity, “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. IX, 1), that is, the Word built flesh. But now, showing both things well and briefly, he introduced the expression “formed together,” not as though the formation occurred principally and without any intermediary, but in a speakable manner.

### Haeret.

There is something I do not know how you would explain. What, however, are you going to say about the Deicides—that is, the Jews?

### Rust.

I shall say the same thing to you again. If God once refers the things belonging to the flesh to himself, for our salvation, then not inconsequently, just as the one who formed his own flesh as God is said to have been formed together with the flesh, so those who killed his flesh are, I think, consequently called Deicides. This is not because they killed God pure and without flesh, but because that man whom they killed is God. For he was not a mere man, but the very same one, perfect both in Deity and in humanity.

If this does not seem convincing to you, accept another explanation. Before this judge, guilt is reckoned not from the punishment suffered but from the intention of the one acting. Since God is impassible by nature, consider what the Jews said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have the inheritance” (Matt. XXI, 38; Mark XII, 7; Luke XX, 14). In the Gospel they wished to destroy the Son of God in such a way that he would never rise again, and that his divinity would not exist at all, although no one could have extinguished him.

Those who nevertheless undertook with their own intention to do precisely what was impossible are rightly called Deicides—not on the basis of the outcome, for how could this happen when what they attempted was impossible?—but on the basis of the guilt of their very impulse and determination.

Perhaps it is also not inappropriate to say that a person kills God in himself when he does not reckon that he exists, or orders his own life as though he were not God. For he derives no benefit in the future life from his goodness, as though, so far as he is concerned, God did not exist. This concerns what is said: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. XIII, 1).

Thus the Apostle spoke of those who, after baptism, returned to Judaism as before: they “crucify again for themselves the Son of God” (Hebr. VI, 6), not simply, but for themselves. We also say that Sabellius and Paul of Samosata kill—that is, repudiate—the subsistences of the Holy Trinity; Arius kills consubstantiality; Nestorius, the union; and you, the difference. Perhaps this too may be said in such a way—not because they destroyed or killed God, but because they rejected him.

### Haeret.

If this is the meaning, why was this passage brought forward against Nestorius, when Nestorius certainly does not reject the things you mentioned a little earlier?

### Rust.

I already said above, at the beginning of the preceding discussion, what he entirely rejects: namely, that through the union the things belonging to the flesh are said of God the Word. In light, however, of what was said below, the discussion seems in some way not useless for overthrowing Nestorius’s doctrines.

For it shows the curse pronounced upon those who do not believe that the one who was crucified is to be worshiped. He is not a mere man, but God and man together. Nor is he co-worshiped as one person with another, but worshiped as one, because he is to be worshiped as one.

Perhaps, moreover, just as those who say that God is passible are called Deopassians—not because the impassible substance of Deity suffered, but on account of the blasphemy of those who think this way—so the Apollinarists may be called Deicides, because they think that God himself was changed into flesh and thus died.

And if what was said has this meaning, it amounts to the following: “If anyone does not worship him who was crucified, let him be anathema, and let him be enrolled with those blasphemers who say that God was killed in his own nature.”

It should also be noted that, where he said “to be joined” and “to be formed together,” he said neither “God,” nor “the Word,” nor “Christ,” nor “the Lord.” I think this was so that he might give the reader to understand that, according to person, he was formed as one; but according to nature, he was formed together as having another nature with which he was formed together.

### Haeret.

Having been led from the frequent use of the expression to another understanding, I understand “to be formed together” in this way: what did not previously exist is said to be formed only according to matter, as Adam was formed from clay. But what already existed previously and was already complete, when it is not made but united, is said to be formed together. This is like a house, in which some parts existed earlier while others are made at that very moment; or like a book, when gatherings that had previously been sewn together are taken up and someone says that they are being sewn together—while preserving, nevertheless, the pure rule of doctrine, which does not ordinarily fit all cases, as was formerly established between us.

### Rust.

That too is useful to me. For just as in that case “together” refers not to one thing but to several, so also here.

### Haeret.

How is it established that these things are so? Can you satisfy me from the very words, or from where are you deriving this interpretation?

### Rust.

Although what has already been said ought by itself to have completely satisfied you, nevertheless consider at least those things added at the end of the preceding statements. For he says:

> “For what has begun, or makes progress, or is perfected, is not God—or, if it is spoken in this way because of the increase that takes place gradually…”

What, then? Tell me: is not the difference between the natures evident? What began, made progress, and reached perfection is flesh; what always exists and is most perfect according to nature and substance is God.

Because, in their madness like Arius, they say of the crucified Lord that his Deity is not most perfect according to nature and substance, but received honor from the Father as a gift or reward—since it is changeable and mutable—the most holy Gregory opposed them, saying that if anyone were perfect through works…

The associates of Paul of Samosata, for their part, said that after his birth from the Virgin, and also after his baptism, and afterward still, after his resurrection from the dead, he progressed toward adoption. The former suspected that the Deity of the Son was broken and mutable; the latter regarded him as a mere man honored and deified by God because of the merit of his works, so that for this reason he might also be called God—not as one who existed before Mary and was made human.

Gregory crushed both groups together when he added:

> “For what has begun, or makes progress, or is perfected, is not God—or, if it is spoken in this way because of the increase that takes place gradually…”

That is: whatever has a beginning when it exists, and whatever is not perfect by nature but becomes perfect because of its works, is not God in the fullest sense; or else, if it receives perfection in a single moment, as soon as it is created by God the maker, or if it progresses gradually as some human beings do—

### Haeret.

Then, as you say, these words were spoken not against Nestorius, but against Apollinaris, Arius, and Paul of Samosata.

### Rust.

But because Nestorius’s doctrine has a certain kinship with Paul’s doctrine, the same arguments apply against both.

For in the synodical codex, among Nestorius’s other blasphemies, this passage also lies:

> “But just as we called God the creator of all things ‘God,’ and Moses ‘God’—for he says, ‘I have appointed you God to Pharaoh’ (Exod. VII, 1)—and Israel ‘the Son of God’—for he says, ‘Israel is my firstborn son’ (Exod. IV, 22)—and just as we called Saul ‘Christ’: ‘I will not lay my hand upon him, because he is the Lord’s anointed’ (1 Sam. XXIV, 7); and Cyrus likewise: ‘Thus says the Lord to his anointed, Cyrus’ (Isa. XLV, 1); and Babylon ‘holy’: ‘For I myself will command them; they are sanctified, and I will bring them’ [Note: [Col. 1215] Vulg., “I have commanded my sanctified ones, and I have summoned my mighty ones.”] (Isa. XIII, 3)—so the communion of names is similar, but the dignity is not the same.”

Behold: this impious man plainly says that, just as Moses was called god, Israel son, Saul and Cyrus anointed, and Babylon holy, so also the Lord himself is called God not according to nature but by name alone; not holy and Only-Begotten according to substance, but like the Babylonians and Israel. He does not want his difference from the others to be according to substance, but to concern dignity, since he does not understand God by nature.

### Haeret.

If the nature has not become one, how is God said to have been formed together with the flesh, as though there were no difference? But if, as you say, the things that happened concerning the flesh are called God’s, are they called so truthfully or falsely?

### Rust.

That the difference between the natures is preserved we heard long ago, when Cyril of holy memory said to Nestorius:

> “Since the natures that came together for a true union are diverse, but one Christ and Son arose from both—not as though the difference of the natures had been destroyed because of the union, but rather, through Deity and humanity effecting for us one Lord, Christ, and Son.”

Clearly, the difference between the natures has not been destroyed by the union to such an extent that he does not even use a singular participle for Deity and humanity effecting for us one Christ, but uses the plural: “effecting.”

If, therefore, the difference and number of Deity and humanity were not preserved at all, it would not have been appropriate to say, “as we establish this and that.” But things whose difference is preserved are not without union.

When, therefore, we look to their difference, we will not then attribute to the flesh the things proper to divinity. We do not call it co-eternal with God, nor do we say that it descended from heaven. Conversely, we do not refer to God the things proper to the flesh.

But when we look to their union, we say that the Son of Man descended from heaven, and that the eternal and Only-Begotten God was seen on earth and lived among human beings, according to the Scriptures (Baruch III, 38): “No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man, who descended from heaven” (John III, 13).

God the Word who descended from heaven is the Son of Man because of the union with what is ours. Otherwise, how is he called and how is he one Son, unless this is the meaning?

Again, the one who ascended from earth into heaven and changed place according to the body alone is himself the eternal Only-Begotten Son of the Father, the Word who became incarnate. For the one who was assumed was not a mere man.

Thus neither does the union destroy the difference, nor does the difference dissolve the union. If God had been formed according to his substance, he could not have been formed together with the flesh, but only formed. Since this is said of God not on account of his eternal nature but on account of the union, we speak truthfully: for the union is a true one.

### Haeret.

This does not mean that. It means that he was formed together like the soul with the body, so that no difference would remain which could produce the number or division of a duality.

### Rust.

Although I said earlier that the discourse was not simply about God, but expressed indeterminately—for above he spoke about the Crucified and later added “to be formed together”—still, so that you would not ask, “What was formed together, and with what?”, I added the expression “the Word with the flesh.”

But if, according to you, Deity and humanity were formed into one nature, then he did not rightly say “to be formed together.” For the expression “together” signifies either two formations or two things that have been formed together.

### Haeret.

But I shall say to you again, accepting the very point itself and once more accusing it: Cyril is inconsistent with himself.

### Rust.

That teacher is not inconsistent with himself. Rather, the expression “together,” and the expression “at the same time,” when said only of natures, piously signifies the difference of two natures. For this very reason, when it is said of persons or subsistences in Christ, it is impious: it immediately signifies two persons, two Sons, two Lords, and two Christs.

That he prohibited the use of the expression “together” in this way was clearly demonstrated above.

But because he again says that the Word sits with the flesh beside the Father, listen to the second letter of that same most holy Cyril to Nestorius, in which he says both things together:

> “If we confess one Christ and Lord, not as co-worshiping a man with the Word—so that the appearance of division may not be introduced on account of the expression ‘with’—but worshiping one and the same, because his body is not alien to the Word, with whom it also sits beside the Father, not as though two Sons were again sitting together, but as one, in the union with his own flesh.”

Behold: speaking also of the body, he says, “with which he sits beside the Father.” Pay attention to the expression “with which,” and again to “with his own flesh.” What he previously expressed by “with,” and what he expresses later by the prefixes *con-* and *co-*, are the same.

But whenever, as I said, the discourse concerns natures, divinity is said to be with humanity, and conversely. When, however, it concerns the Son, one may not say that the Son of Man is co-worshiped with the Son of God. For in the Holy Trinity only persons are co-worshiped.

Deity, just as it worked miracles through the flesh, is worshiped through the flesh. We all worship the cross, and through it the one whose cross it is. Yet we are not said to co-worship the cross with Christ, nor does this make the nature of the cross and of Christ one.

Similarly, we are not said to worship the Trinity together with the altar, but rather through the altar. Nor again is the Word through the flesh in the same way as the Father is through the Son. For Christ is not two persons. With the flesh—that is, through the flesh—as was said, he sits beside the Father and is co-worshiped.

### Haeret.

The most holy Cyril said that one Christ is worshiped and that he sits beside the Father with his own flesh. But how is this established? Is it because in Greek **σὺν** and **μετά** have the same meaning as what we call *cum* or *con-*?

### Rust.

That the most holy Cyril himself approved **σὺν**, that is, *cum*, is also clear from elsewhere. Not only in the universal synod, but everywhere outside it, against various opponents, the letter of the most holy Athanasius to Epictetus is approved in its entirety. Among other things, it contains this:

> “He said, ‘I gave my back to scourging, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting’ (Isa. IV, 6). For the things that the human aspect of the Word endured, the Word himself, who was with it, referred to himself, so that we might participate in the piety of the Word.”

You have heard that he referred to himself the sufferings belonging to humanity. Wherever there is being present together and referring, there is unquestionably a quantity according to nature.

### Haeret.

And where did the most holy Cyril approve this letter of Pope Athanasius?

### Rust.

He not only presented testimonies from it at the synod, but also in his letter to Saint John, in which he says:

> “Since we follow everywhere the decisions of the holy Fathers, and especially those of our blessed and entirely praiseworthy Father Athanasius, avoiding every kind of deviation from them, let your holiness believe this, and let none of the others doubt it.”

And again:

> “Since we have learned that certain persons, corrupting the letter to the blessed Epictetus of our entirely praiseworthy Father Athanasius, which was orthodox in its content, published it in such a form that many were harmed by it, for this reason, devising something useful and necessary for the brethren, we have sent copies to your holiness from the ancient exemplars that are with us and are free from error. Since we too possess copies of this edition, we have set it before you from those copies.”

Pay attention, then, that he called the Letter to Epictetus orthodox in its content, and that, devising something useful and necessary for the brethren, he sent a copy of it, praising its author as he deserved.

### Haeret.

If the nature of Deity and humanity has not become one, how could one person come to be, when certainly, whenever one person subsists from two natures, one nature also comes to be at the same time?

### Rust.

It is the height of senselessness and folly to ask of the Almighty, “How could he do it?” It is sufficient to answer: “As he willed,” because for God it is impossible that what he wills should not be present.

### Haeret.

And from where is it certain that God willed himself to be one person with the flesh, but did not will one nature to come to be, when the Apostle says: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. XI, 34).

Moreover, it follows that one nature comes to be whenever one person comes to be. And if we look to God’s omnipotence, God could, if he willed, have become one nature with the flesh. Since by a miracle of the omnipotent God one person came to be, why did not one nature also come to be by another miracle? Or why not by the same miracle—indeed, why not the very same thing?

Is it easy for God to do what appears impossible to human reasoning, namely, to make one person from Deity and humanity, but difficult for God to do what follows even from human reasoning, namely, that the one whose person it is should have one nature?

### Rust.

Great is the clemency of God, who, so that we might not err, not only deigned to become human but also showed us the principal reason for his becoming human. It was demonstrated above that he assumed everything belonging to us except sin.

He therefore assumed, together with the substance of our perfect nature, quantity as well. For this reason the Apostle often calls him one man (1 Cor. XV, 21; 1 Tim. XI, 5). This complete unity of our perfect nature, meeting the unity of perfect Deity, rationally completes the duality of the natures.

Moreover, God does not perform great works pointlessly, as though he did them merely for their own sake; rather, he weighs his intention appropriately with a view to our salvation. His purpose is not astonishment or empty glory, but our benefit.

Therefore it was necessary that he assume, like all the other things belonging to our nature and without sin, quantity as well—or rather, unity—as we demonstrated above.

For if the nature that was assumed is not one, then it is not one at all, and consequently is nothing. But if it is one, then just as it is impious to say that anything belonging to our substance is absent from it, so also it is impious to say that quantity is absent. That quantity therefore has this property as well: meeting the quantity of the divine substance, it completes the duality.

Moreover, our confession is found to be far superior even with regard to the miracle. Once the Word of God deigned to be one person with the flesh; thereafter, it would no longer be miraculous—for it would also be customary, as you see—to say that one nature had been formed. Nothing, however, is more miraculous, more beyond understanding, or more divine than what is unusual and incomparable.

What, indeed, is more extraordinary than that one person should subsist whose nature is not one? It is therefore clear that, in comparison of reason, miracle, and cause, we are found superior to you.

### Haeret.

Is it possible to state quantity in the words given without naming the things whose quantity it is? For example, if each of the human beings who is called one man is considered: may we then call him “one” after removing the name “man”?

For if we rightly say this also about the Holy Trinity, there will be two things, the Father and the Holy Spirit—for they are two persons—and there will also be two things in the case of the Son, for, according to you, there are two natures.

The Father, therefore, the Son, and the Holy Spirit will be four things. For you too argued a little earlier that the unity of the divine nature, together with the unity of the human nature, completes a duality of natures.

We therefore conclude according to your reasoning that two and two are four. Why, then, do you worship a quaternity instead of the Trinity? You are not orthodox.

Nor will you be able to maintain that the name of a number cannot be uttered without the name of the things themselves, since, while confessing Christ to be one of the Trinity and one from three, you cannot deny this.

But if you are asked, “One from which three?”, you will not find one common name that can be predicated plurally of the three. For it is not “from three Fathers,” nor “from three Sons,” nor “from three Spirits” or “holy Paracletes.”

### Rust.

You have set down ambiguous names in your customary manner, and instead of things you have spoken only a bare number. But when you say, “The Father and the Holy Spirit are two things,” say what two things they are; and, while we remain silent, you will convict yourself.

Likewise, when you say of the Son, “two things,” specify what those things are. You yourself will convict yourself of the falsity of your accusation while I remain silent.

For the first two things you mentioned you used for two persons, whereas the next two you used for the natures. But the Trinity is a Trinity of persons, not of natures. Again, the duality spoken of in the case of the Lord Jesus Christ is a duality not of persons but of natures.

If, therefore, while calling the Father and the Holy Spirit two persons, we likewise called the Son’s two natures persons—which would be blasphemous—or, conversely, while calling the Son’s two natures natures, we likewise called the Father’s and Holy Spirit’s two persons natures—which God forbid—then we would have given your calumnies some not wholly implausible occasion: two natures and again another two, or two persons and again another two, would be counted together in the Trinity.

But now, just as two persons and one person counted together make three, so it is necessary that one common nature of the Holy Trinity and another nature belonging to the Son alone—that is, to the one assumed—make two, and cannot be one.

Although, therefore, we believe that there are two natures in the Son, our confession does not consequently produce a quaternity. For apart from subsisting things we do not worship quantity alone, even if it were permissible to utter quantity alone.

Moreover, if the fact that we say there are two natures necessarily entails worshiping a quaternity instead of the Trinity, then you too must consequently worship a Trinity from a quaternity, because you say that Christ is from two natures.

### Haeret.

We do not say that the Trinity is from three persons; rather, we say that it is three persons. But we also say that unity exists both of the three persons and in the three persons.

### Rust.

But why should one Christ and two natures not be believed, if three persons are truly one God, just as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30)?

He said “one” and “we are”: “one” is assigned to nature, while “we are” refers to persons. If the Trinity of persons does not divide the simple nature, how does the duality of natures divide a person who, as you admit, is not simple but composite?

Moreover, “two,” “three,” and “four” are called things not with each one subsisting by itself, but when they are gathered and compared, or, so to speak, correlated—or rather, considered together. Nature is not counted together with the persons in the Trinity; otherwise, before the incarnation—God forbid—there would also have been a quaternity, since there are three persons and one nature, and the number does not advance to four.

### Haeret.

There, the reason is that unity is not external and the Trinity external; rather, the Trinity belongs to unity, and unity belongs to the Trinity.

### Rust.

If for this sole reason the divine nature is not counted together with the three persons—because the Trinity belongs to unity and unity belongs to the Trinity—then there is necessarily another unity in addition to the common unity, and it will be counted with the Trinity. [Note: [Col. 1221] The conjunction *et* (“and”) seems to need to be supplied before *connumerabitur* (“will be counted”), or the preceding substantive verb deleted.] But the flesh belongs to one of the three—that is, to the Lord Christ—not to the whole Trinity. For, according to you, the whole Trinity did not become incarnate.

There will therefore be a quaternity: the Trinity and the flesh.

Either show, then, that our nature—that is, the flesh—is not one; or accept that the divine nature is not excluded from being counted with the persons for the reason that the unity belongs to the Trinity and the Trinity to the unity. You are left to say with us that nature is not counted with persons.

### Haeret.

And why is nature not counted with persons? State the reason.

### Rust.

I am under no obligation to show why it is not counted with persons, since I have demonstrated my complete victory: namely, that what I proved is true. If, however, you wish to investigate the reason with us, let it be investigated without prejudice.

I think that things which are not contained altogether under one definition are not counted together. For example, if someone says, “You and I are one because I am a human being and you are a human being,” then we are two human beings; and we are one with angels because both we and they are rational beings.

Again, we are two natures because of difference; and we are also the same as the sky in this respect, because it too is a creature. Yet it is another thing in relation to us because of its substantial difference.

I think, therefore, that things which are counted together must have one common definition, as well as another definition which is not common but proper to each. Thus the two natures of the Lord Christ have in common that they are natures; their proper definitions are that one is Deity and the other humanity.

### Haeret.

If it has a definition, Deity is not incomprehensible. This also troubles me: how can the divine substance, common and undivided among the three persons, have one definition, and the nature of one and only one person—or, certainly, the substance of Christ’s flesh—have one definition? These things seem impossible.

### Rust.

It was not without reason, as it seems, that we formerly rejected the search for a cause which draws us into such long and difficult discussions. Therefore I ought not to add anything further of this kind, lest we be drawn unnecessarily into verbosity.

### Haeret.

Be patient, I ask, and proceed without prejudice. I wish to be satisfied about these matters; perhaps a suitable explanation can satisfy me in every respect.

### Rust.

I shall say what seems to me—perhaps not unreasonably—while preserving without prejudice what I have already said. I would not have added anything of this kind except under the condition now proposed.

Deity, then, is defined not according to what Deity is, but according to what nature is.

What do I mean by “not according to Deity, but according to nature”? It is one thing to ask what Deity is in itself, and another to ask how Deity itself relates to the three persons.

For example, it is one thing to ask what a human being is, and another to ask how human beings are—namely, whether all of us participate equally in the common substance or not; and again, according to proportion, whether we share a common humanity in the same way that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share one common Deity.

What we are asking in that case concerns proportion. But the one definition of the two natures is according to what they are as natures. For that which is participated in equally, similarly, and completely, so that each thing may exist, by the persons is substance; while those who participate in it are persons, differing from one another by their properties.

The common substance of Deity itself, which we contemplate in the individual Word, is nature. Likewise, the nature of the flesh is not individual, although we contemplate it in an individual.

Nature is never individual. For the definition is not the individual of which we say, “rational animal, subject to touch.”

Among physicians, however, human beings are said to differ by nature according to temperament—for example, one being hotter and another colder. We do not use “nature” in that way. Therefore, in this respect, the common definition of the two natures of the Lord Christ makes no difference.

Since each is similarly called a nature, and since again each does not have the same definition but differs according to its own definition, there are therefore two natures of the Lord Christ. Neither of them is counted with the Trinity so as to produce a quaternity, which God forbid.

### Haeret.

I think that the nature called common, or certainly the species of humanity, is nothing but a name. The existence of each one of us is in individual subsistences; but that common nature exists only in concepts, intellectual apprehensions, and the finest acts of contemplation—or rather, in imaginings of the mind. In reality it does not subsist.

In God, however, everything must subsist in the first place—that is, both nature and persons. Therefore, according to the common definition, there are not two natures.

### Rust.

I have no argument against this. It is sufficient for me that the substance of the assumed humanity is not counted with the subsistences of the Trinity so as to produce a quaternity from them. But why this is so, I do not know; I confess that I am ignorant of the reason.

### Haeret.

But why is the flesh counted with the nature of the Trinity, so that, as you say, two things are produced, while it is not counted with the persons of the Trinity? Then it is not counted with this nature either, and Christ’s natures are no longer two but one.

### Rust.

I think you do not wish the flesh to exist at all. For it must either be one, or not one. If it is not one, it is nothing; and if it is nothing, it does not exist.

In order that it not be counted with the three persons, we are driven to the conclusion that no quaternity is produced. Again, if it is not joined to the one nature of the Trinity, a complete denial of the flesh seems to follow. For if it is one, it is counted with the other one.

I affirm, however, that here a reason must necessarily be demanded of me. All the holy Fathers, and you yourselves, count the flesh with the nature of Deity, for you say that Christ is from two natures.

But if humanity is not counted with Deity, we ought not to say that it is merely in them, but also that it is from them. Therefore he is not from two natures.

Ambrose, according to you, also spoke wrongly when he said:

> “The Son of God speaks as one in both, because both natures are in him.”

And Gregory, when he said:

> “God and man are two natures, because there are both soul and body.”

And Cyril, when he said:

> “For a union of two natures has taken place; and because the natures that came together for the true union are diverse, but one Christ and Son arose from both—not as though the difference of the natures had been destroyed because of the union, but rather as we establish…”

The universal Council of Ephesus confirmed these statements, and the Roman popes Celestine and Xystus approved them. Likewise, they approved certain expressions concerning the Lord: that things be made common as though in one person, and divided as though in two natures.

### Haeret.

We know this. The natures are counted together so that he may be from them, not so that he may be in them. For even equivocal things, because they share only a name and not a definition, are counted in relation to one another—for example, a painted dog and a real dog. No one will call this dog and that one one thing; in every respect they are two.

### Rust.

Glory to the Lord Christ, because for the moment you have confessed that, in whatever manner, the natures nevertheless are counted together. That was the point at issue. Once this is conceded, it is no longer necessary to repeat the remaining demonstrations.

For it has already been shown together that there is a union of two natures; that the natures are diverse; that the difference of the natures has not been destroyed; that they produced [Sic]; that there is one in both, because both natures are in the same one; and that there are two natures, God and man.

I must also say this necessarily: if human nature is not counted with divine nature, then one nature of the Lord Christ was not made from two natures through the union. Rather, the one nature that has existed eternally remains by itself exactly as it was until now.

But if a composition, unfolding, or coming together has occurred, then the humanity is equally constitutive of the nature that, as you say, arose from the composition. Therefore it participates equally in the quantity of the divine nature.

If, then, the divine nature is one, the nature of the flesh is also one; if the former is half, the latter is also half; and if the former is nothing, the latter is nothing. Consequently, even what, according to you, was made from nothing cannot be something.

### Haeret.

Do you have grounds for showing that not only does the common nature of the Trinity differ from the nature of the flesh united to the Word, but that the Word himself also has some distinction in relation to the form of a servant?

### Rusticus

And this will be demonstrated as the discourse proceeds: our nature, which has been united to God the Word, is neither another person nor the person of another; nevertheless, the flesh is one thing apart from the Word, while the nature is another thing—not another person. For in Christ, the Fathers commonly speak of one thing and another not only with reference to the nature of the divinity, common to the remaining persons, and his own flesh, but also specifically with reference to God the Word and the assumed flesh, saying that one thing is one and another another.

Attend, I ask, carefully to the truth, lest the narrowness of the difficult path leading to life frighten you by its labor [Col. 1224D]. For we have not said that her person is one thing and the person of the flesh another; for both these belong to one and the same single person. Rather, apart from God the Word—who is one person of those ineffable persons—there is another thing, namely human nature, so that God the Word is indeed a perfect person from eternity, while the flesh, although a perfect nature, is by no means a person.

I say again: I did not say one person and then another person, but one substance and nature and another. For God the Word is clearly defined as one thing, and his humanity as another—not one person and then another, but he is one thing distinct from the flesh, while the flesh is another thing and not another person. We have also shown this from Gregory’s synodical reading, where he says: “Two natures, God and man,” because there are also soul and body [Col. 1225A]. You see, therefore, that he is speaking about this very person of the Lord Christ. For after saying, “two natures, God and man,” he added, “because there are soul and body”; yet these belong to one person. And again: “There are not two Sons.” You see that he did not speak of the whole Trinity, but called the Word alone “God.” And again, shortly afterward: “One thing and another, from which the Savior [is].” Do you see that he spoke of the Savior alone? And again: “For both are one”; and of one he says, “God indeed, made human.” The whole Trinity was not made human.

Then he added this as well: “I say one thing and another, in reverse of how it is in the Trinity. For there, indeed, there is one and another, so that we do not confuse the subsistences; but not one thing and another.” You see that the statement is not made generally about the whole Trinity, but specifically about the Son alone [Col. 1225B]. For speaking of the Trinity he said, “There is one and another”; but of the Son alone he said, “one thing and another, in reverse of how it is in the Trinity.” God the Word, therefore, is one thing apart from his own flesh.

Let the testimony mentioned above be set forth, and what has been said will become clear.

### Heretical interlocutor

If nature is not counted together with the persons, but pure number is nevertheless counted together with pure number, why are two and two four? For how otherwise is Christ said to be one of the Trinity—not existing simply and without flesh, but composed into one person—when, certainly, the two simple, fleshless, and uncompounded things are [according to the reading of the *Lectionary*: “two”]?

### Rusticus

The name “number” is uttered without the name of the things whenever some common likeness of the thing is attached to a number; for example, that each of the three is a person, although not the same person. For how would it be pious not to distinguish the subsistences in the Trinity? We have said this because, just as the Father is a person, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit. Here, then, there are three persons, three things of a kind.

Therefore, when we say, “these three,” if someone asks, “Which three?” we can answer, “persons.” But when we say, “those three,” and are asked, “Who are the three?” we hesitate to answer, “persons,” because of the awkward construction of the words, lest we seem to say “those persons” or “those three persons.” Since the things are present, but a noun common to those three has not meanwhile been supplied, it is permissible to say “these three,” even if, when asked “Who are the three?” we cannot immediately find an appropriate answer [Col. 1225C].

But when, speaking simply, we first say “these three” and are asked “Which three?”, we may at once appropriately add, “persons.”

In your quaternity, however, no common thing is found that can equally be fitted to the number four. And the impossibility follows not only in words but also in realities. Therefore it cannot even be a number, because no common thing underlies it.

This is also shown by the fact that in Latin *personae* is feminine—“these persons”—and not neuter—“these things”: that is, the expression is formed according to what grammarians call the feminine gender, not according to the neuter. *Paracletus* likewise is masculine, both in Latin and in Greek.

Concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, we do find the expression used in such a way that we can say “two”; and when asked which two, we can answer, “Paraclets.” But concerning the Father I do not yet dare to say this, since the expression is neither written nor expressly stated by any of the four synods that the Father is also called a Paraclete [Col. 1226A]. If this were granted, then, when asked “Who are the three?”, we could certainly answer, “Three Paracletes,” just as we say “three persons” and “three substances.”

### Heretical interlocutor

If he is called Paraclete because of consolation, and the Father is a Paraclete—for he consoles the souls of the righteous and soothes their pains, as it is written, “I remembered God, and I was comforted” (Psalm 76:4)—then the very statement of the Lord, “And I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17), shows that there are not merely two but three Paracletes. For “another” is said not of two but of three, while “the other” is said of two [Col. 1226B]. Therefore in the Trinity three Paracletes are spoken of.

### Rusticus

This exactness of expression is not observed at all in the divine Scriptures or by the holy Fathers, since it is not worthy of them but is an invention of human beings. I also showed that in the synod the expression occurs, “one thing and another, from which the Savior [is].” In speaking, therefore, of two, he said “one thing” and “another.”

Likewise, the testimony of Athanasius, of holy memory, which was approved there, said this:

> “Or how can those who say that the Word came upon a holy man as upon one of the prophets wish to be called Christians? They do not say that he himself became man, receiving a body from Mary, but that God the Word is another, existing before Mary and before the ages, the Son of the Father. Or how can those who say that there is one Son and another God the Word be Christians?”

Notice that above he used one expression without distinction, reproving those who say “another”; below, however, he reproved those who say “one and another” [Col. 1226C].

Most especially, Gregory’s testimony repeatedly uses this expression, saying:

> “There is not one and another—far be it! For both are one by mixture.”

Notice also that he said “both,” that is, not three, lest you suspect that he was speaking as though of three—of God, soul, and body—especially since what follows says:

> “In reverse of how it is in the Trinity: there indeed there is one and another, so that we do not confuse the subsistences; but not one thing and another, and so forth.”

Behold: of the Trinity he says “one and another,” but of Christ, “not one and another.” He does not say “not one and another” in the same form as the other expression. Moreover, the reading of Felix, of holy memory, is preserved as follows:

> “And not a man assumed by God, so that he should be another apart from him; for the Son of God did not assume a man, so that he should be another apart from him.”

Thus it has been shown that at the holy and universal Council of Ephesus the expressions “one thing and another” and, rather, “one and another” were used without distinction [Col. 1226D].

### Heretical interlocutor

For the moment, you too have confessed that if we demonstrate that there are three natures in the Trinity, it plainly follows that those who say there are two natures in Christ introduce a quaternity. If, therefore, we demonstrate three in the holy Trinity—for in every respect the Father and the Holy Spirit have two natures—and if, by adding two, we count them together with the natures of the Son, as you believe, around the unavoidable calculation of number, then we have shown that your confession results in the worship of a quaternity.

### Rusticus

This too is not necessary, as it has meanwhile been stated without prejudice [Col. 1227A], unless perhaps the Trinity has three natures in such a way that there is not one common nature. For if one nature is common, while three are proper, then “nature” is already being used equivocally. One nature is understood as that which is individually identical with each person; another is that which is not individually possessed by any one person but is common to the three. The former is one in three; the latter are contemplated as three in one.

If, then, by saying that Christ has two natures, we count the common nature of the Trinity together with our nature—that is, with the human substance that is in Christ—we introduce no quaternity whatsoever. We do not heap three upon that one and thereby make four; rather, by joining one and only one to one and only one, we make merely two.

Furthermore, even if the nature proper to the Word is such that it is identical with that person, and, joining it to the human nature, we say that they are two, quaternity still does not follow. For “nature” will be said in one way of that which is also a person—for it is identical with the person in every respect—and in another way of the flesh, which is nature alone and is not likewise both person and nature.

Nor, if this is so, will we add the nature that is also a person to the nature that is not also a person [Note: [Col. 1227D] We have added the negation that is absent from the printed editions; the context requires this addition]. Nor do we therefore call them two by way of addition. Rather, we fit together one nature that is also a person and another that is not also a person but is nature alone. That is, we designate [Note: [Col. 1228D] Paris edition: *condimus*.] a divine nature that is itself also a person, and a human nature that is nature alone and not also a person; thus we produce a duality of natures.

### Heretical interlocutor
