Then, according to you, there will be four—indeed, as you say, a quaternity—of the Trinity’s natures [Col. 1227C]. For you said that there are four things that are natures. This makes the difference of natures much greater. Not only is the nature of the Word one thing and the nature of man another, but the definition of nature is also different, and they are not the same in species. It is as though someone were to say that there is one genus or one thing. Therefore what differs in every respect contributes much more to making a fourth, if, as you maintain, difference also entails a corresponding difference in number.

The more widely the natures differ, the more they produce a number; and the more plainly a quaternity is introduced. Necessity therefore requires one of two things: either that the nature of humanity does not constitute a duality when joined to the nature of God the Word, or that it complete a quaternity by being counted together with the natures of the Trinity.

### Rusticus

But attend to this: however many the natures may be, the Trinity remains, for it is named from the three persons, not from the natures.

### Heretical interlocutor

It is called this neither from the natures alone nor from the persons alone, but rather from the number.

### Rusticus

But number is nothing when no thing underlies it.

### Heretical interlocutor

A thing does underlie it. For there are four natures, and your quaternity ought to be named from the number of the natures. Even if no common thing underlies the four natures, the name “nature” itself will suffice for me [Col. 1228A]. For equivocal terms are counted together, although counting equivocal terms or words with one name is one thing, and counting the things themselves is another—for example, a sea dog and a land dog are counted not as two dogs but as two equivocal terms.

### Rusticus

We grant everything you say. Let it therefore be as you say: let the Trinity be named equally from the number of natures and persons. Just as the Trinity is never called such unless three persons, of the same nature, subsist, so a quaternity is never called such unless four things exist that are not only natures but also persons. We, however, although we assert four natures, as you say, do not assert four persons but only three. We therefore do not introduce the worship of a quaternity.

### Heretical interlocutor

Rather, you contradict yourselves and worship both the Trinity and the quaternity. You worship the Trinity of persons and the quaternity of natures. For just as, if there were only three persons and likewise only three natures, there would still be a Trinity, and if there were four persons or four natures there would be a quaternity, so, even if there is a Trinity of persons but a quaternity of natures, there is simultaneously a Trinity and a quaternity.

### Rusticus

But even if—far be it from us—we were to confess three natures existing from eternity, we would worship and adore them not insofar as they are natures but insofar as they are persons.

### Heretical interlocutor

If there are three natures in the Trinity and another nature in the flesh, there are four. And even if you do not worship the quaternity, according to your confession a quaternity nevertheless exists, and that will be of no benefit to you. Indeed, choose whichever you wish: either there is a quaternity, and you do wrong by refusing to worship and adore in divine matters what you confess both to exist and to be; or there is no quaternity, and you act impiously by confessing and asserting the existence of what does not exist.

Further, if you assert that there are two natures in such a way that you count the common nature of the Trinity together with the proper nature of the flesh, or the latter together with the former, then you will worship a duality.

### Rusticus

It is clear that what was assumed became proper to the one who assumed it through the dispensation, but it is not common to the three. And even if it is something fourth, it is nevertheless neither coeternal, nor without beginning, nor uncreated, nor existing of itself or from its own substance. Rather, through the union it is what it is glorified as being.

Those three, however, are coeternal, consubstantial, without beginning, and uncreated [Col. 1228D]. Therefore, even if someone says that what is human is something fourth in order to exist as a fourth, it will not thereby be fourth in the same way for adoration, worship, or glorification.

For one thing is that which, as something other—inasmuch as it is created—adds to the uncreated things according to quantity, because it is not the same thing but something else; another thing is to co-adore, glorify, and worship something as consubstantial and coeternal.

Moreover, adoration and worship are not offered as though by number. There are not three acts of worship or three adorations of the Trinity. Therefore there are neither four nor two, even if, as I said, something else were proper to one or even to three.

For in ancient times the tabernacle in the wilderness, the ark, the temple, and the altars were not co-adored or co-worshiped with God; nor were they made one nature with God. He did not add them to the number of the Trinity, which is adorable and worthy of worship, because the Trinity is co-adored, whereas these creatures are not co-adored with the Trinity; rather, through them the Trinity is adored.

What then? Tell me: is it not written, “Adore his footstool” (Psalm 98:5)? This is the earth. The body that is from the earth is adored, not so that it should be adored as God in itself or for its own sake, but so that through the body and flesh, or humanity, God the Word who was made human may be co-adored [Col. 1229A].

Certainly he also worked through the fringe of the garments on the woman suffering from an issue of blood; yet no one says that the nature of the garments and the nature of the Word are one. He saved many by an act, and by sending forth a voice from his own mouth he raised Lazarus, who had been four days dead. Therefore, through whatever he works, while through it and in it he is adored and worshiped, he is pleasing to those who worship him.

Likewise, the nails with which he was fastened and the wood of the venerable cross are adored by the whole Church throughout the world without any contradiction. And not only are the two natures, God and the cross, involved; that holy iron also, apart from that venerable wood, is another nature, and the Lord’s flesh itself is again another nature.

And even if, as you say, there are three natures in the Trinity, while these have their own number, we nevertheless all adore all these things. No Christian has ever said that we worship a quaternity, quinity, or senary. For the things that are set apart and made proper to God, through which he is worshiped and adored, are like instruments and aids for our weakness in approaching God. As to their existence, they do not lose their distinctness according to quantity; but for worship, adoration, and veneration, created things are no longer counted together with the Creator. For it is one thing that the former is worshiped through the latter, and another that something should itself be worshiped according to nature, eternally, and in the fullest and proper sense.

### Heretical interlocutor

So then, is whatever must be confessed in the holy Trinity not in every respect to be adored, worshiped, or venerated?

### Rusticus

I have already said that it is not so in every respect and in every way alike. But I will add this: we neither confess nor worship a duality of natures in the Trinity. For the one nature of the flesh does not belong to the whole Trinity but to one person, God the Word.

In the Trinity, however, those things are counted together that belong similarly or equally to the three persons. If we worship a duality, then you also worship a composite Trinity—or a Trinity that is simultaneously composite and simple. For you call the natures or persons of the Father and the Holy Spirit simple, but Christ’s composite.

Moreover, one God in the Trinity and one Christ are worshiped. The three persons are one God; the two natures are of one Christ. But the four natures, since they are neither God nor Christ, how can they be worshiped, when among the three or among the two nothing is worshiped except either one thing or one person? [Col. 1230A]

But, so that the discussion may not be prolonged further, we demonstrate that the holy Trinity has one nature alone, not three, but only three persons or subsistences. For if there are both three natures and one nature, and nature and person are the same, then—far be it from us—there will also be one person of the Trinity. But if nature is both one and three, while person is not one but only three, then God will be one neither according to nature or substance nor according to person or subsistence. In what respect, then, is the Trinity one God?

### Heretical interlocutor

We speak of three substances and natures in the Trinity in such a way that their consubstantiality nevertheless remains intact. Thus there are both one and three substances and natures, and the one God is glorified not according to the three but according to the one substance and nature [Col. 1230B].

### Rusticus

Then, according to you, there is both one God and three gods. For if he is one because of the one substance and nature, then, because of the three substances or natures, there are, according to you, three gods.

Indeed, there will much more properly be three gods than one God. Properly speaking—far be it from us—there will be three gods; improperly, the Trinity will be one God, in accordance with the error of the pagans. For all the Fathers and teachers wrote that there is one God because his substance or nature is one and only one.

If, therefore, the Trinity has one substance and nature, while the three are not only persons but also natures and substances, then, since all three exist and none is undivided, there will much more be three gods [Col. 1230C].

### Heretical interlocutor

The Trinity has three natures to such an extent that we can show that each person has from eternity a proper nature that is not common to the other. This will be clearly proved if it is demonstrated of even one of them.

For if the three are equal and alike in every respect, whatever one person has, the other also has. If, then, we show that one of them has a proper nature in such a way that it is common to no other, you are likewise convicted concerning the others, without any possibility of contradiction.

The Fathers affirm that God the Word has a proper nature when they say, “We confess one incarnate nature of God the Word.” If, therefore, we believe that this one is rather the common nature, then this incarnate nature, which is common to the whole Trinity, necessarily introduces an incarnate Trinity. But since that is impious and contrary to the holy Scriptures and the teaching of the Fathers, it is clear that the one nature that was made human belongs to the Son alone.

You will not be able to deny the aforesaid statement of the Fathers. For Flavian, formerly bishop of Constantinople, whom you accept [Note: [Col. 1229D] Perhaps “whom you suspect”?], wrote as follows in the little book on his own faith that he sent to the emperor Theodosius and that was also accepted at the Council of Chalcedon.

### Rusticus

It is by no means necessary that those who confess “one incarnate nature of God the Word,” if this is said of the common nature of the holy Trinity, thereby introduce the incarnation of the holy Trinity—especially when, by explaining the expression, they add the very precise name “God the Word.”

For when the Fathers say that God the Word was made flesh and became human, although the common name “God” is predicated indiscriminately of the three persons [Note: [Col. 1231D] “Of the three persons” seems to be required. Immediately afterward, *eos dicere* or *dixisse* may perhaps need to be restored], it does not follow that the Trinity was made incarnate, even though the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. For this reason the one who was made incarnate is called God, one God, the only God, and God the Word.

Just as it is common to each person to be called God or one God, so, when we confess that God was made incarnate or that the Virgin is the Mother of God, it does not follow—far be it from us—that we should say that the Trinity was made human. Rather, it was one of those persons, that is, one of that Trinity which is God [Col. 1231B].

Likewise, when we say that one nature of God the Word was made incarnate, it does not follow that we should say that the Trinity was made incarnate together with its own nature. Rather, it was one of those persons who must be confessed as existing in that nature.

And just as, when we say that God was made incarnate, we do not, lest we appear to say that the Trinity was made incarnate, say three gods as a precaution, so neither, lest we appear to say that the Trinity was made incarnate when we say that one nature of God the Word was made incarnate, do we say three natures in the Trinity as a precaution.

For if God is said to have been made incarnate and again not to have been made incarnate—when the former is said of the Son and the latter of the Father and the Holy Spirit—and yet one God is neither separated, divided, nor distinguished into two gods, what incongruity follows if we say of the same God, that is, of one and the same nature, that it was made incarnate in the Son and was not made incarnate in the Father and the Holy Spirit?

You too, in saying that any nature or substance is common, will not be able to reject this consequence. You will neither be able to deny that substance to have been made incarnate in the Son nor affirm that it was made human in the Father and the Holy Spirit. There will therefore be one simple nature, both incarnate—as belonging to the Son—and not incarnate—as belonging to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

It is therefore not necessary, merely because one nature of God the Word is said to have been made incarnate, to say that it is the proper nature of the Son. Even if there were some nature that was not common, the same thing would nevertheless be said quite properly of that common nature [Col. 1231D].

It has therefore not been demonstrated that this is the proper nature of the Son alone, nor therefore that it is the proper nature of either of the other persons of the Trinity.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that you rather introduce a quaternity, since you cannot deny the council called the Second Council of Ephesus, because you do not wish to condemn Dioscorus.

For he, together with that entire wicked council, approved the statement of the heretic Eutyches, which was deposited there among the records:

> “I confess that there were two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature.”

If, therefore, before the incarnation there were two natures—one belonging to the Father and the other to the Holy Spirit, for otherwise the three natures could not be three—and if there were then also the two natures of Christ before the union, you introduce four natures according to your reasoning. Even if you do not say that they have continued to the present, you nevertheless assert that they existed before the union; and from a pre-existing quaternity you introduce the later formation of the holy Trinity.

Moreover, if you say that these natures existing before the union have continued to the present, then you worship a quaternity more truly and impiously than you accuse us of doing, since you yourselves cannot deny what follows from your statements.

But if the two specified natures have not continued until now, then your quaternity ceased to exist at some point. We have demonstrated that the Trinity does not have three natures and that, even if it did, our belief would not entail a quaternity [Col. 1232B].

But you, who posit this as a necessary consequence, will be defeated by your own madness. If that consequence displeases you, then first of all anathematize Dioscorus.

### Heretical interlocutor

For the present we are not discussing the causes of the individual persons, but are debating the faith universally. We will reserve this matter for the time when we discuss Diodore, Theodore, Ibas, and Theodoret, bringing the causes of persons into the question of the faith.

Thus, although we say that there are three natures in the most holy Trinity for the distinction of the persons, we nevertheless confess one common substance, according to which we call the Trinity consubstantial, and we are not willing even to hear of a quaternity.

### Rusticus

But the Fathers also call that common substance, without distinction, “nature.” It is common only to the three persons, and there is nothing else there besides it as something proper to each person.

Or, if it is called proper only in comparison with the natures of creatures, it is nevertheless itself said to be proper to each person, as when we say, along with the holy Fathers, that God the Word, the Son of God, did not bear an improper nature.

Furthermore, if nature and subsistence are the same [Note: [Col. 1232D] So the Lyon edition reads. The Paris edition has “substance”], you introduce four natures and substances. But if they are different, as both the reality and the name show, then the more they differ, the more, when counted together with the number of the persons, they result in four—unless perhaps you yield to our reasoning. For quaternity could exist if this nature of the flesh were not merely substance but also a person.

But now, since it is distinct upon mental examination precisely because it is not also a person, it is not counted together with that Trinity which the corresponding argument determines. For there are three persons there, whereas this is not a person but nature or substance alone [Col. 1232D].

### Heretical interlocutor

But this nature of the Trinity is present in those three natures. Therefore, even if it is another thing apart from them, it cannot be counted separately with each of them, because, existing in them and possessing all that they possess in itself, it is nothing apart from them. For the Trinity is unity, and unity is the Trinity.

### Rusticus

How, then, do you say that before the union the Son of God had two natures [Col. 1233A], if this common nature is counted together with what is proper to him? For what other nature did the Lord possess before his becoming human than the essence that existed before the ages, his own essence?

### Heretical interlocutor

We speak of the divinity and flesh of Christ. I say “two before the union” not as though I were joining the common nature of human beings to God. For if that were the case, how would there not also be two now, when every human being is nevertheless merely a human being, except for that one who was made human? Nor do I mean that the flesh first existed alone and was afterward united to the Word, for whoever says this is a heretic.

Rather, because by prior intellectual apprehension we recognize two natures and then bring the union upon them, we say that they immediately become one. Therefore, what we call “before the union” or “after the union” does not signify an order of time but an order of contemplation, since we cannot apprehend the understanding of these things simultaneously and instead contemplate the simple elements before the composition.

For it is impossible that the order of the natures in reality should be one thing and the order of contemplation concerning the understanding another, just as in speech the letters are naturally prior but were nevertheless devised later [Col. 1233B].

### Rusticus

If this contemplation, according to which you say that two natures are understood, is true even now, as resting upon existing realities, then there are truly two natures, which we perceive by a true understanding. But if you say that it is not true, then you ought not to confess two natures even before the union.

If, however, it was once true before the union but afterward became false, then the Lord’s flesh existed before the union—far be it from us. If it is believed to have been animated by a rational soul, then, according to you, a mere man pre-existed, and afterward he was united to the Word. You therefore blasphemously assert that from two persons, two Christs, and two sons, two Lords, there came to be one Christ.

These things must be rejected in every way. For a union according to subsistence cannot be made from persons that previously existed separately in themselves.

But if, even after the incarnation, two natures at some point subsisted, what other union do you say occurred by which they ceased to be two? Moreover, turn against yourselves everything you say against us, who say that the two natures exist even now. For you say that the same natures existed up to that point which we say remain forever [Col. 1233C].

### Heretical interlocutor

I think some of our people state the matter better: Christ’s individual humanity did not pre-exist the union; rather, the common human nature pre-existed, from which that flesh came.

### Rusticus

But this statement leads you to other inconsistencies. For even after the union, our common nature was not made one thing with God through union; rather, it was that individual nature which was assumed. The Fathers do not say this of the common nature but of this individual nature. Nor is it possible for a common nature ever to become a person by itself.

Moreover, it does not subsist in itself, but only in the rational conception formed from its individuals, from which it also receives its existence [Col. 1234A], just as those things called genera or species are understood by the wise men of this world.

For if there were a soul but it were not rational, it would not be the common nature of creatures, or what is called a genus and species.

Likewise, whoever says that there were two before the union but afterward no longer two, and instead wishes one thing to be completed from the very realities that had been two, must mean this; otherwise the expression “no longer” has no place.

But now you do not say that the common nature of all human beings was made one with the nature of the Word, lest all human beings appear to be identical with Christ in the common nature, or lest—far be it from us—the whole Trinity appear to have been made incarnate.

Rather, one individual thing—that is, one and only one flesh and one and only one soul—was united to God the Word in one person [Col. 1234B] and in one and only one subsistence.

### Heretical interlocutor

But the two natures must first be understood, and afterward the union must immediately be applied. Therefore Christ must not be said to be in two natures but to be from two natures.

### Rusticus

Then, according to you, the union is the destruction of the two united natures.

### Heretical interlocutor

The union is not the destruction of the natures but of the duality, so that they are no longer two but, according to the union, become one thing.

### Rusticus

If, as you say, the duality was destroyed, then it existed before its destruction and before the union. If I apply to the duality the same arguments that I applied to the two natures themselves, the inconsistencies mentioned above will again follow [Col. 1234C]. For nothing is destroyed unless it previously existed.

Therefore, if the duality was destroyed, it existed; and all the inconsistencies we have already stated come into view.

### Heretical interlocutor

The union prevented the duality from existing, so that it could not be present; and by “destroyed” I mean destroyed in potency, not in actuality. For the duality did not yet exist perfectly.

### Rusticus

Then it destroyed something that did not exist but was still in the future. Say, then, what made each nature imperfect, so that there would not be a duality.

I do not suppose that you claim a diminution of the divine nature and an immeasurable and ineffable advancement of the human nature. How, then, was the duality diminished, when something was added to the reality? How was the quantity of the substances blocked, when no defect of the substances occurred?

Moreover, if, as you say, equivocal things are counted together, how will the two natures of the Son, counted in potency with the two existing in actuality—namely, those of the Father and the Holy Spirit—not be four [Col. 1234D]? If the two natures, the divinity and humanity of Christ, have never failed to be two, how is he said to be from two natures, when his being from them is drawn from your confession?

### Heretical interlocutor

What then? Tell me: does the Lord not possess everything belonging to two perfect persons? Therefore, just as the union prevented there from being a duality of persons, so it also prevented a duality of substances.

### Rusticus

But our nature in Christ is not also a person. It does not possess its existence separately in itself and according to itself; rather, it subsists in the Word. Therefore he is not said to be from two persons as he is said to be from two natures, as though the Word had united to himself the person of a man. But he did unite human nature to himself, as both those at Ephesus and the other holy Fathers teach; and we have sufficiently demonstrated all this above [Col. 1235A].

### Heretical interlocutor

We do not deny that there are two natures, but neither do we affirm one because of the union. The former concerns nature; the latter concerns the union. Therefore there are two in contemplation, not according to reality.

### Rusticus

If this contemplation is true, there are two natures also in the reality itself. But if you say that it is not true, behold, you have denied that there are two natures.

### Heretical interlocutor

What, then, is the difference between those who bring forward impious doctrines and those who bring forward pious ones concerning the claim that there are two natures? For if there are two natures—for example, any ordinary man and God the Father—what difference is there between saying two natures in one way or in another, when you speak of Christ as you speak of an ordinary man and of God apart from humanity, simply because you say that there are two natures?

Rust. There are many things that at first sight we seem to confess in common with the impious; but by an addition they become determinate, and in themselves, even if they are suspicious, are not yet impious—nor, conversely, are those matters wholly beyond accusation. Apollinarius, then, says that Christ is one, that the Son is one, and that he has one person and subsistence; Nestorius also says that there are two natures. These statements do not yet reveal what sort of statements they are, but in the additions to the statements we recognize what they mean. Apollinarius says “one” as though the divinity were convertible and the humanity imperfect; Nestorius, however, while wrongly joining the two—through equivocation, namely, according to authority, according to juxtaposition, according to association—also wrongly divides and separates the natures into two subsistences and persons, and into sons and lords. Therefore, when we say “two natures,” if nothing precedes or follows that is sufficient to signify the union, your suspicion will have an opening; but if we say this both before saying “two natures” and afterward—namely, that there is one person of the two natures, one subsistence, inseparably, indivisibly, and without conversion—what further remains that those wishing to slander can suspect?

Heretic. This is what I criticize: you say “two natures” not after “two unions,” but after “union”; whereas you ought first to confess two natures, and afterward the union, and henceforth one nature. “From two” signifies that the union comes after these things; “in two” signifies that the two remain after the union.

Rust. If both two natures are to be confessed and the union removed, I do not see why we should not rightly say “from two” and “in two.” If you are so delighted with what is exact, say not “one Christ in two natures,” but “in two natures one Christ,” so that you do not first name Christ and afterward divide him, as you say, into two natures, but first say “two natures” and then name one Christ. Observe the same principle here also: do not say “one Christ from two natures,” but rather “from two natures one Christ.” Yet the Church of Christ has never devoted itself to such empty verbal distinctions. For although the divinity of the Son pre-existed from eternity, nevertheless it is sometimes named after the flesh. So completely does the order of the words prejudice no truth—especially here, where the two natures and the union are simultaneous.

Indeed, in the holy Council of Ephesus, among the other testimonies—and rather before the others—there is the testimony of Saint Peter, which reads as follows: “Hence the evangelist also truly says, ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14), namely, from the time when the angel greeted the Virgin, saying, ‘Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you’ (Luke 1:28). Behold: from the angel’s greeting, even now the union is celebrated.”

That the flesh is sometimes named first and the divinity afterward is shown by a passage of the most holy Gregory, which reads as follows: “Let people neither deceive nor be deceived themselves, believing the Lord’s man to be without a mind; rather, let them believe him to be our Lord and God. For we do not separate the man from the divinity.” Behold: at the beginning of the statement he plainly names the man first, and afterward the Lord and God; then again, the man and the divinity.

A little later he says again: “Passible in the flesh, impassible in divinity; circumscribed in body, uncircumscribed in spirit; the same one earthly and heavenly, visible and intelligible, originated and unoriginate, so that the whole man, who had fallen under sin, might be restored as the same whole man and God.” Behold how often, with the order changed, he first names him passible and then impassible; afterward circumscribed and then uncircumscribed; and after many similar expressions he adds: “as the whole man, the same one, and God.”

The Council of Chalcedon, after saying “in two natures,” added that he is to be acknowledged indivisibly, inseparably, and without conversion. It did not say “they are to be acknowledged,” as two, but “he is to be acknowledged” as one. It says again: “As our Lord Jesus Christ taught us, and as the creed of the Fathers handed down to us.”

But if, as you say, one nature has been made, then you ought to say not “from two,” but “from three natures,” since you also say that the union of the Word with humanity is of the same kind as the union of flesh with soul. For, by your concession, what has the soul closer to the flesh than this humanity has to the divinity, so that the Lord should be from two natures and not three?

Heretic. Answer us simply. Do you say that the two natures continued to subsist in order to produce one Christ, or that one Christ existed so that the two natures might subsist? But the two natures formerly subsisted in other subsistences. If, then, the two natures existed not in order that they themselves might subsist but in order that Christ might exist, the two natures no longer remain; only that for whose sake the two natures subsisted and were united remains—and that is one. Therefore Christ must not be confessed as two natures.

Rust. What astonishing madness: to suppose that the natures do not subsist because they subsisted for the purpose of converging in Christ, when nothing needs to subsist more than those things that subsisted for the purpose of bringing Christ into existence—and when, rather, we must confess that those things subsist united which existed in order to be united. Indeed, the divinity did not subsist in order to be united, for it is eternal; but the humanity, which was united at the very moment it began to exist, did so subsist. Therefore, according to you, Christ’s humanity is no longer humanity, since it subsisted in order to be united.

It is therefore manifest that two natures subsist united. Who, then, except one whose mind is captive, would say that things which subsisted for a certain purpose either no longer exist or are no longer two, while only that for whose sake they subsisted remains—although the union destroyed nothing of either, even though it immeasurably exalted one—and although each remains perfect according to the principle of its own nature?

This would be like someone saying that these letters were made for the sake of producing this sentence; therefore these letters no longer exist, but only the sentence exists. What could be more insane than that?

Heretic. Whatever else you may wish to say, let us return to the point. We cannot introduce a quaternity or worship a quaternity.

Rust. On the contrary, I have shown inevitably, from your own arguments, that you introduce a quaternity. Indeed, I should not have answered you, since you boast so disorderly about this matter. But lest those who rave as you do have occasion to say, “We have not been satisfied in every respect,” I shall add this: you say that the Holy Trinity has three natures. If they differ in no respect at all, how do you know that they are three, when you deny that the divinity and humanity, which differ so greatly, are two?

We confess that there are three subsistences because they are distinguished not in what each is according to nature, but in the manner in which each exists, by their properties. The Father has begotten and has not been begotten; he does not come from anything else, as the others come from him. The Son has been begotten and has begotten nothing coeternal. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, and nothing coeternal proceeds from him or is begotten by him.

[Note: It must simply be said that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son in the same manner, since both are one and the same utterly simple principle of the Holy Spirit. Conversely, it may be said of both that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father and the Son in the same manner, because the Father does not have the power to breathe forth the Holy Spirit from another, whereas the Son has it from the Father. Hence the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father through the Son. See Saint Thomas, *De potentia*, question 10, article 4, reply to objections 2; and *Summa theologiae* I, question 36, article 3.]

Some of the ancients added this also among the properties: just as the Spirit did not eternally beget the Son together with the Father, so the Spirit does not proceed from the Son as he proceeds from the Father. I confess that the Spirit did not eternally beget the Son—for we do not speak of two Fathers. Whether, however, the Spirit proceeds from the Son in the same manner as from the Father, I have not yet received a fully satisfactory answer. Since this has nothing to do with the question now before us, it should indeed be noted, but passed over.

Heretic. For the moment, I do not think it useful to speak of these matters themselves. I shall answer briefly your objection against us; indeed, I shall make you answer yourself. Those properties by which you say that the three are distinct, so that they are believed to be three persons, are the properties by which we say that the three are distinct, so that they are believed to be three natures.

Rust. But Christ’s natures, which you refuse to acknowledge as two, differ much more than the three persons, which you are willing to call three natures.

[Col. 1238A]

Heretic. Why, then, are there not also four persons, since the Son has altogether two persons?

Rust. Because the humanity of the Lord Christ is not a person, although it differs according to reason. As far as God the Word is concerned, it is nature alone. It is not, as someone might say, his own flesh, but the flesh of God the Word, as I have often said.

Heretic. What, then, does humanity lack in comparison with a person? Something belonging to the rational soul, or to flesh, or to quantity?

Rust. This is not your question against us, but the question of others against both us and you. We therefore have no need to overthrow this question while arguing against you—especially since it has already been shown above that God the Word united to himself not our person but our nature.

Nevertheless, in the treatise I composed against you and the Nestorians concerning definitions, it was demonstrated that nature represents the common species, as the expression ordinarily goes; whereas person is the concurrence of those things that describe a rational subsistence. An individual subsistence is, proportionally, like a foundation on which the other surrounding features rest, as the name itself indicates. It is also like the most proper cause in which all the things called accidents—such as color, character, condition, dispositions, and whatever resembles them—together with the properties, converge.

For when the first subject of the individual features that surround it has been destroyed, nothing further can exist. From the greatest cause by which each thing exists—that is, from that in which the entirety itself rests—it receives its name. In other words, from that subject which is like a foundation for the surrounding features, the whole consistency is called subsistence.

But since, according to the definition just given, the subsistences of irrational beings are also commonly so called, and even those of insensible and lifeless things, whereas these are not all properly called persons, I added that this subsistence is rational. Since some again wish to call the species and genera of substantial things “subsistences,” it was therefore added that this subsistence is rational and individual.

Heretic. What does this have to do with the question under discussion? I asked why a perfect man has an imperfect person, and I very much desire to hear this answered.

Rust. This too has already been stated. But since you paid no attention, listen to why the Lord’s humanity is indeed a perfect nature, but does not possess a person by itself; and why Christ has not two persons but one alone.

The reason is, as you yourself said at the beginning of your argument—although you were aiming at something else—that God the Word is the cause of the assumed flesh. The assumed nature, which is the form of a servant, rests as upon a foundation in him. It was assumed so that the Son of God, who is eternal God, might become man in the last days for our salvation.

A man could not have received his origin from a virgin unless God had been pleased ineffably to redeem us through him, united to himself according to subsistence. From the moment that any part of it began to subsist, it was united into one person and one subsistence, as we have often said.

Thus, even if, in the imagination or most refined contemplation of the mind, the humanity of the Lord Christ seems to be both substance and person—for it lacks nothing in comparison with other rational and individual subsistences—nevertheless, considered by itself, it seems to be this, but not as united to the Word. Therefore it is not the truth of the matter but a defect of the mind, as though it were forgetfulness of the union, that compels it to be thought so.

But when the mind recalls that what is human has been made proper to the subsistence of God the Word through the union—not as though it remained in itself—then it cannot accept it as a person. For it is not properly called a subsistence when another thing, namely the Word, is the eternal cause of its subsisting.

If the man were a subsistence, it would not have been necessary for God the Word alone to receive him into himself and, so to speak, establish what is ours within himself. Rather, either a pre-existing man would have made God the Word his own and would have established and founded within himself what belongs to God, or both would have pre-existed and come together with each other, so that there would be one Christ, one Son, one Lord, one person, and one subsistence, without each one remaining in its own prior existence.

But the opposite has happened. Therefore what is ours does not have a person.

Heretic. Therefore, if these had not been united, there could altogether have been two persons: God the Word lacks nothing of personhood—for just as God the Father is one person, so also God the Word is one person—and, on the other hand, perfect man lacks nothing of a complete person, consisting, as we do, of flesh consubstantial with us and a rational soul, and subsisting through their union.

Rust. Although every individual human being is a person, this is not the reason why that which makes him human also makes him a person. The reason he is a man is that he is a rational animal from the earth; the reason he is a person is that he is an individual rational subsistence.

But, as we have said, that humanity does not possess the reality of subsistence in the Word by itself. It was not created for the purpose of existing separately as its own, as we do, but in order to be united to the Word, to be his own precious garment and, so to speak, immeasurable instrument, and in order that God might be man, for the sake of our salvation. Therefore that cause is rather in the subject than the subject itself.

Thus, for example, in an ordinary man, the cause of the flesh’s subsisting is the immortal soul. When separated from it, the flesh does not remain in its own essence but continually moves toward non-being, since it must necessarily be wholly destroyed, however it may be corrupted.

Again, the souls of deceased human beings now exist without bodies, as the Lord says to the Sadducees: “God is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; he is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him” (Matthew 22:32). He did not say, “the God of this soul and of that soul,” but “the God of this one.” Nor did he say, “He is not the God of dead souls but of living souls”; he simply said that he is God, with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob existing perfectly. He added, “For all live to him” (Luke 20:33), and did not say, “For the souls of all live to him.”

Heretic. By this, he does not mean that the perfect soul is a person, as though Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were thereby each a complete man; rather, he means that God calls those things that are not as though they were (Romans 4:17), as it is written.

Rust. Do not interrupt the argument at an inconvenient point. Wherever resurrection is mentioned, the immortality of souls is necessarily represented—not as though they were things that do not exist but are called by God as though they existed, because God foreknows that things not yet existing will exist, but as things that do exist. No wise person will dare say that souls die together with their bodies, so that for this reason Abraham and the others do not exist except in God’s foreknowledge.

What I wished to say is this: just as, outside the body, although the soul is not a perfect animal according to nature, the rational soul is nevertheless a perfect person—and again, after receiving the body in the resurrection, it remains a perfect human person—so, in a certain manner, in Christ, before the incarnation, the person of God the Word was perfect; afterward, the person of Christ is perfect, and there is one person, God and man together.

The cause of that humanity’s existence is God the Word. In comparison with the Word, it is not a subject, but an accident—like an instrument through which our salvation was to be accomplished, and like that which rests upon it and uses it, as we have said.

Thus, when we say concerning the Apostle, “The head of the woman is man, the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3), we do not say that man has two heads, nor that woman has two or three heads—that is, man and Christ, or man, Christ, and God. For in relation to woman, man is head; in relation to Christ, he is no longer head but something else. Again, Christ in relation to man is head; in relation to God, he is not—neither is the Word the head of the Father, nor is the nature that comes from us the head of God.

So, insofar as it is possible to explain incomparable things by comparisons, the subject of humanity, in relation to those things that are specially accidental to it, displays the proportion of a subsistence; but when compared with God the Word, it is found not as a personal subsistence, but as one of the things belonging to a subsistence.

Just as there, although man is the head of woman and Christ is the head of man, in the order that follows it is man alone who is her head, while, by the excellence of glory, Christ alone is head—since he is God—so here also the humanity appears to be a subsistence in relation to the things that have accrued to our nature. According to the highest propriety of subsistence, however, it is the Word alone—from whom, thereafter, there is one and only one subsistence, and Christ is truly whole—or else it is what is in Christ that is named.

Whoever reads this should remember that we are comparing one proportion with another, insofar as possible, not comparing many persons with Christ’s one and only person. Otherwise, why would so much have been said?

Heretic. In truth, since these things are incomparable, it is difficult to apply even a slight resemblance.

Rust. I shall say something even greater. There, perhaps, someone—relying on impudence—might say that the woman has two or three heads, and perhaps not impiously, although incongruously. Here, however, it is impossible to find two persons.

For if there one were thought to have two heads in relation to one and the same thing, or in relation to different things, each thing would be the head of a different thing; the same will be the case here. For accidents are not compared to the flesh as they are compared to the Word in the same way: they are compared directly to the flesh, but not in the same manner to God, since he is not regarded as though he were unincarnate.

Yet God is the head of the woman even without mediation, for Christ is the head of the Church (Ephesians 5:23). Figuratively, the Church is the bride; and figuratively, man is the head of the woman.

To state the matter simply and briefly: I too confess that the example is not entirely suitable. I have adopted it not as a demonstration but as an explanation. If anyone finds a more suitable comparison, let him offer it; I shall readily, willingly, and gladly accept it.

Perhaps it is even better to say this: just as the entire world—that is, the whole earth—is often called “the world” even when it is considered alone, and again, together with the whole heaven and all the elements, it is called one and only one world, so let the same be said of that one and only person.

But if you believe that some people call Christ’s subsistences two—I mean, not as natures but as persons—because, in subtle contemplations and pure acts of understanding, Christ’s humanity considered by itself appears to them capable of being conceived as both a person and a subsistence in relation to its accidents, how can you yourselves deny that the Lord Christ has two natures? You cannot deny that the human nature in Christ not only can be understood in subtle acts of understanding or mental imagination, but also subsists in reality itself.

This is attested not only by what is ours, but also by what your Ephesian council teaches through the readings of the holy Fathers, and especially by the letters of the most blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

For what we say concerning person, you cannot object against us in reality concerning nature; its definition is far removed from the definition of person. Christ’s natures are, as was said above, the divinity common to the Holy Trinity and the humanity common to all of us, considered individually. The person and subsistence of the Lord Christ, however, was brought about by the union of these.

In these substances, we say that the whole is one and only one Son of God, our Lord Christ, whom we confess to exist in two natures.

It can also be gathered no less clearly from the synodical teachings of the holy Fathers that there are not three natures of the Holy Trinity, but one and only one. For if there were three natures of the Holy Trinity, then, as you yourself also said, the Son would have one divine nature, individual and distinct.

This nature would be identical in every respect with the person of God the Word and would in no way be distinguished from it. For it would contain nothing more or less, nothing in any way different or otherwise. Therefore, whatever we rightly say about the Son—that is, about God the Word, which is to speak about the person of Christ—whether before the incarnation or afterward, could also be said orthodoxly about his nature. And whatever ought to be avoided when said about the person of the Son, the Fathers would fear to say about the nature of that Son.

Thus, just as no Father anywhere ever said that the Son did not suffer in his own person, so none of them would endure saying that the Son did not suffer in his own nature. Yet the opposite is now done: they proclaim that the Son of God suffered in his own person, but these same holy Fathers deny that he suffered in his own nature.

From this it necessarily follows—and it has been demonstrated—that the nature of the Son is not the same as the person of the Son, although it belongs to the same Son. For if his nature were so proper to the Son alone that it were not common to the Father and the Holy Spirit, it would necessarily follow that his nature was identical with his person. Since this does not follow at all, it is clear that the nature is not proper to the Son alone in such a way that it is not also common to the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Trinity does not have three natures.

Heretic. From where will you produce demonstrations for me that the Son of God, God the Word, suffered in his own person—whatever he assumed of the things that befell the flesh—but did not endure them in his own nature?

Rust. Listen patiently, and this will immediately be shown. Let me simply bring the argument to an end. This demonstration benefits the true doctrine not only because it commends one and only one nature of the Holy Trinity, but also because it is itself a cause of victory, since it concludes that Christ’s nature must not be believed to be one, as will be explained below.

Now let testimonies be brought forward from the synodical book of the holy Fathers, and let the purpose of our present discussion be recognized directly.

A reading from the letter of Cyril of holy memory to Nestorius, which the holy and universal Council of Ephesus also confirmed through the interventions of all the bishops:

“We must follow these words and doctrines, understanding what it means for the Word who is from God to become incarnate and to become man. We do not say that the nature of the Word was transformed and became flesh, nor that it was wholly changed into the man consisting of soul and body. Rather, we say that the Word, uniting to himself according to subsistence flesh animated by a rational soul, became man ineffably and inexplicably, and was called the Son of Man—not according to mere will or good pleasure, nor merely by the assumption of a person.

“Although natures different from one another were brought together into a true union, one Christ and Son came from both—not as though the difference of the natures had been destroyed because of the union. Rather, while confessing one Lord, Christ, and Son, from divinity and humanity through the ineffable and indescribable concurrence into union, we say that he who existed in subsistence before the ages and was born from the Father was also born according to the flesh from a woman.

“We do not say this as though his own nature had received the beginning of its existence in the holy Virgin, nor as though he necessarily needed a second birth for his own sake after the birth from the Father. For it is both foolish and ignorant to say that he who subsists before every age and is coeternal with the Father needs a second beginning in order to exist.

“But because, for us and for our salvation, he united to himself according to subsistence what is human and came forth from a woman, he is for this very reason said to have been born according to the flesh. A common man was not first born from the holy Virgin, with the Word descending into him afterward; rather, united from the womb itself, he is said to have undergone a carnal birth, making the generation of his own flesh his own.

“In the same way we say that he suffered and rose again—not as though God the Word, in his own nature, endured either the piercing of nails or other wounds. This is impossible for what is divine, since it is incorporeal. But because the body that became his own endured these things, he himself is again said to have suffered them for us; for he was impassible in the suffering body.

“We understand the same principle in Moses. God the Word is immortal according to nature, incorruptible, life, and life-giving. But because his own body, by the grace of God, as Paul said, tasted death for everyone, he himself is said to have suffered death for us—not because he came into contact with death as far as his nature is concerned, for it is madness to say or think this, but because, as I recently said, his flesh tasted death. Likewise, when his flesh was raised, his resurrection is again attributed to him—not as though he had fallen into any corruption, God forbid.”

And a little later:

“This is asserted everywhere by the discourse of the most complete faith. We find the holy Fathers to have thought in this way; in this way they ventured to call the holy Virgin *Theotokos*—not because the nature or divinity of the Word received from the holy Virgin the beginning of its subsistence, but because the Word, united according to subsistence to the holy body born from her and rationally animated, is said to have been born according to the flesh.”

Heretic. If, in addition to all that you said earlier, you produce testimonies that support your doctrine, we too are prepared to bring forth and disseminate the testimonies of our glorious teachers, which have long been produced. We ought to follow those testimonies rather than pursue our own conclusions.

Rust. For the present, we have not yet produced any testimony from other books by which Christ’s existence in two natures is most clearly demonstrated, but only from the synodical writings, which you cannot refute. We have used them merely to demonstrate that the Holy Trinity has one and only one nature or substance.

Even if the Fathers call this nature proper to the Son of God, they do not mean that it excludes the Father and the Holy Spirit, but that it excludes all things that are creatures and created works; nevertheless, it also excludes the substance of the man whom he created and assumed at the same time.

They also show that this nature is not called proper to the Word in such a way that the Word was temporally born, suffered, endured blows, wounds from nails, or other injuries, or died and rose again according to his nature. Nevertheless, the Word, united from the womb itself, is said to have undergone a carnal birth, making the birth of his own flesh his own.

Likewise, the other human experiences are attributed to him because the body that became his own endured them. Again, he himself is said to suffer for us, for he was impassible in the suffering body.

Thus, beginning for the moment with the universal and commonly confessed synodical teachings, we have resolved the objections you raised and established what needed to be established. We have not yet touched upon other matters, lest by mixing together topics belonging to another work we create confusion. Nevertheless, the discussion of those readings may be reserved without prejudice for another conversation.

Heretic. I should also like to learn how you think this demonstration gives victory to those who hold your views, insofar as it proves that the Lord Christ’s nature must not be believed to be one through the union. You promised earlier that you would explain this.

Rust. You have rightly recalled it to my memory. I shall explain this also.

If one nature has been made through the union, then whatever is said about the Word, the Son, or Christ will also be said about this nature; and whatever is said about that nature, as you call it, will likewise be proclaimed of these names. This will hold in no other way.

Therefore, just as it is abominable to say that God the Word suffered in his own nature, so, if you dare to do so, avoid saying that he suffered in himself, or in his person, or in his subsistence. Or, as you say, “not coming into the experience of death as far as his nature is concerned,” so transfer this expression and say: “As far as his person and the Son himself are concerned, he did not die.”

But since it follows from your position that the nature and substance of the Word suffered, you must say that the subsistence of the Word, the person, the Son himself, the Only-Begotten, the same Lord, or Christ himself did not suffer. You cannot deny that those who say these things introduce two sons, since you know that Nestorius, who said such things, was accused of proclaiming two sons.

He said—for which reason he was also condemned—“I do not call this two-month-old or three-month-old child God.” Again: “The nourishment of milk must not be attributed to God.”

In his letter to the most holy Cyril, he called the holy Virgin the mother of Christ, not of God: “It is clear that David’s son was not God the Word.” Again he said: “It is good, and worthy of the evangelical traditions, to confess that the body is the temple of the Son’s divinity, and that the temple is united according to a certain supreme and divine conjunction, so that he might appropriate what belonged to it according to the divine nature.”

In what immediately follows, however, the same Nestorius denies what he has confessed here. He added these words:

“To assign to the name of appropriation the properties of the flesh—I mean birth and mortality—is the mark, brother, either of a mind in error concerning pagans or Gentiles, or of a mind diseased with the ravings of Apollinarius, Arius, or the other heresies; indeed, of something even more serious than theirs. For it is necessary, by the name of appropriation, to make God the Word, through appropriation, a participant in nourishment by milk, a sharer in the gradual growth that takes place little by little, and a participant, at the time of suffering, in the terror that arose and in the need for angelic assistance.”

Heretic. What, then, do you chiefly condemn in these statements, you who have maintained until now that the properties of the natures, and the duality itself, remain intact? For if these statements are true, God must not be said to be three months old, nourished with milk, recently born from the Virgin, the son of David, or to have suffered and died in the flesh, to have grown gradually, or to have taken upon himself in other ways the properties of the flesh through dispensational appropriation.

Rusticus. I say what we condemn—not we first, but together with the holy Fathers. First, as it were in passing, I say that he spoke most wickedly because he makes the things belonging to the temple proper to the nature of divinity. For it is not the nature of the Trinity, but one person existing in that nature, who makes the things belonging to the flesh his own. Secondly, because he indicates, in some fashion, that God the Word makes the things belonging to the flesh his own; yet, though he ought to have explained this, he subsequently denied that very point still more emphatically in what he said. For if, as he says, God makes the things belonging to the flesh his own through dispensational appropriation, it is even more necessary to attribute to the term “appropriation” the properties of the flesh—I mean generation, passion, death, and the rest. But he now approves this in no way; indeed, contradicting himself, he accuses it as heretical and pagan, and as something even worse.

Why, then, did God, who was made man, make the things belonging to his own temple his own, if they may not also be said of him, to the admiration of his love toward us? For what is greater: that these things become proper to the Word, or that they be said of him? While we confess that the properties of the natures remain intact, we likewise affirm that their duality nevertheless remains, because, just as their distinction is preserved, so too is their union. Accordingly, those things that are not proper to the Word according to nature are his in relation to the union, even if the impious man has refused this many thousands of times. For the properties are indeed preserved, but they converge in one person and subsistence.

Therefore Valerianus censures Nestorius not only as impious but also as self-contradictory, saying in the synod: “The contradiction of the revered Nestorius is evident to all—not only does he dissent from the faith of the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea and from the letter of the most God-loving and holy archbishop Cyril, but he is not even consistent with himself.”

Likewise the most holy pope Celestine wrote to that same Nestorius, saying: “We therefore read the tenor of the letters and the books that we received when the illustrious man, my son Antiochus, delivered them to us. In them we found, detected, and caught you slipping in a certain loquacity, while you conceal the truth beneath obscurities, again confusing both things together—either confessing what you had denied or striving to deny what you had confessed.”

Heretic. What you have said about appropriation and union is truly orthodox, and directly opposed, as though face-to-face, to the verbosity of Nestorius. In the remaining matters, however, I think you have put forward the same things as the man whom you have so severely accused.

Rusticus. Far be it from me, you who are skilled in slander! For, pressing the argument already stated, we shall overthrow your position still further and demonstrate the rectitude of our faith. If the man who says that it was not God the Word himself—who is consubstantial with the Father, the Only-Begotten, and incomparable with the things made through him—who was begotten according to the flesh, made man from the Virgin, nourished with milk, grew, became two or three months old, suffered, died, and rose again—if, I say, the man who says these things produces two sons and two Christs, then the man who says that the same Lord did not have, according to his divinity, his origin from the Virgin; that he was not suckled according to his own nature; that he did not grow; that he did not become two or three months old; that he did not suffer, die, or rise again, nor do the other things—adding, of course, “according to his own nature”—introduces two natures in every respect.

Therefore, just as we rightly abhor the things mentioned above, so we appropriately embrace the things now stated, because just as the former overthrow the boundaries established by the Fathers, so the latter accept them. Thus you are condemned by your own judgment. For in that you abhor and persecute those who say, or who are thought to say, that God the Word is one and the man assumed by him is another—the man born of the Virgin, formed in the Virgin, one of us, united to God the Word from the very conception in some complete and ineffable conjunction—in that, then, you rise up fervently against those who say such things and, as though barking, anathematize them without ceasing, so that, if anyone appears willing to favor such men, no punishment is thought unworthy of him, as though he were saying that Christ was merely a man or introducing two sons.

Yet you yourselves, and those who communicate with you, say that Christ’s human nature is one and his divine nature another; and although you hear that this was confessed by the Fathers whom you claim to follow, you abhor confessing two natures in the Lord Christ after the union. It seems to me, therefore, that you will be condemned on the day of judgment by the condemnation of Nestorius himself. For if you rightly hate Nestorius because by such words he introduced two sons, why, when you say these same things about the natures, do you not admit that you are proclaiming two natures? Indeed, you do not merely say these things about the natures, but you frequently name them in the plural and even acknowledge as equals those who named them in this way—something that Nestorius is not reported to have done with the name of Christ, Son, or Lord.

How, then, when you say these things about the natures, are you so blinded that you do not say what you confess? And how do you curse Nestorius as one who introduced two Christs because he proclaimed such things about God the Word and the man? In short, this argument against you proves insuperable, whichever part of it we examine.

Nestorius is therefore justly condemned by us, but unjustly by you, since your own position has been condemned along with him. Consequently, whenever we condemn Nestorius, we pronounce an anathema against you; and whenever you yourselves condemn him, it rebounds upon you. When you hurl this charge against us as against Nestorians, you do so as slanderers and as men who hate us utterly; and whenever such a judgment proceeds from us against your heresiarchs—I mean Apollinarius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus—you repeatedly and incontrovertibly fall under the same judgment.

Heretic. I cannot communicate with that synod which says that the Lord’s incarnation is something outside the Trinity. For in what is called the Definition, concerning the creed of the 150 Fathers, it teaches the complete doctrine concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and then presents the Lord’s incarnation to those who faithfully receive it. Certainly, if it teaches the complete doctrine concerning the Son, it presents his incarnation there—not outside and beyond the Trinity, as though concerning some fourth entity, but within it. Yet after speaking of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they then introduced another Lord and his incarnation.

Rusticus. It has already been demonstrated that it is in no way possible to introduce a fourth entity outside the Trinity and to speak separately both of the consubstantiality of the holy Trinity and of the incarnation of the Word of God. But you paid no attention at all to what had been established. The synod of Ephesus said:

“For the situation in the Savior is the reverse of that in the Trinity. There one is one and another another, so that we do not confuse the subsistences; but not one thing and another thing—God forbid. For in the divinity there is one, three, and the same; but in the Lord there is one thing and another, from which Christ consists, since this is not identical with that.”

You are therefore greatly blinded to the truth and refuse to accept what the Ephesian synod approved more clearly than the Council of Chalcedon. For it is one thing to speak of the common substance of the Trinity and another to speak of the properties of one person; and this concerns the form of a servant, which there is not consubstantial.

Heretic. Who can accept a synod that approves the Tome of Leo, which says the following about the Word and the flesh: “One of these shines with miracles, the other submits to insults”? What, then? Tell me: was God not insulted in the flesh? Did not the Word perform miracles through the flesh? What does this separation mean, when it says, “This one” does this and “that one” does that?

Rusticus. We do not deny that God the Word was insulted in the flesh. But he did not submit to insults—that is, he was not inferior to insults and sufferings, but superior to them. His flesh was not merely insulted; it also succumbed to affronts and suffered. For, existing as a passible nature, it died, and death—which serves God—had dominion over it.

But God the Word, having been made man, is said to have suffered on account of the union, making proper to himself the things belonging to the passible nature through dispensational appropriation [suification], as I have already said. He did not, however, suffer in the same manner as the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] The Word in Christ suffered not simply, but by making divine and appropriating to himself the things belonging to humanity. Scholastic theologians call this the communication of properties. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa theologiae*, Part III, Question 2, Article 6, in the body of the article.]

For if the absolutely impassible one suffered, then he is impassible to no purpose. For what other purpose does impassibility serve than to ensure that what is impassible does not suffer at all? If, then, nothing in God is superfluous or useless, but everything is perfect, fitting, and beautiful, it is plainly evident that his impassibility too is not useless. Therefore he did not suffer.

Heretic. But in mercy he endured—he whose proper nature did not suffer. Therefore, in this respect, he also submitted to insults according to what he suffered. How, then, do you say with Leo that “one shines with miracles, while the other submits to insults”?

Rusticus. The most holy Leo says that one shines with miracles with reference to the proper nature of God the Word, and he says what remains with reference to the flesh. You have now confessed that God the Word did not endure in his proper nature. Why, then, do you confess the same thing and at the same time accuse it? For he did not say, “This one shines with miracles, while that one submits to insults,” so as to suggest that he was speaking of two persons, but as speaking of two natures. For the things from which the Savior consists are one thing and another, since what is timeless is not identical with what exists in time.

Heretic. He speaks not only of the proper nature of God the Word but also of the Word himself, and he does so frequently, saying that he did not suffer. Yet to say that the nature of the Word did not suffer is the same as saying that the Word did not suffer; for, so to speak, the nature of the Word is no more impassible than the one whose nature it is. Therefore the same nature, remaining impassible, suffered out of compassion for us.

Rusticus. There is nothing contrary to God’s goodness; therefore compassion [perhaps “mercy”] does not dissolve his impassibility. But if God the Word, eternally impassible and never having suffered, recently endured suffering for the sake of mercy, as you say, he has been damaged by something far greater—indeed infinitely greater—than what he gained. For he gained us, his creature, and lost the impassibility of his own substance?

You therefore err greatly, praising something in God in such a way that you again blaspheme something else. God does not need your praise, so that you may cunningly exalt his mercy to the prejudice of his impassibility. We rightly exalt his mercy while preserving his immutability.

For the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes those who say that the Son of God is changeable or mutable, as the Council of Nicaea defined. Indeed, it would be an addition to his immutability—and, God forbid, to his power—if God could not save his creature in any other way than by the Creator’s losing his own property. Or it would be a reproach to his counsel if he could have preserved the one and saved the other, yet, while able to choose what was better, chose what was worse.

Let us therefore praise in God those things that benefit us, without attributing to him what is unworthy. This idea has come to you from kinship with the Manichaeans. For it belongs to them to imagine God as passible, and to say that every good nature belongs to the good God alone; and because God, foreseeing [perhaps “preceding”], would be endangered by what was to come, and his own kingdom would be at risk if the prince of darkness first attacked him, for this reason he sent something from his own substance, mixing it with that wicked substance in order to fortify his own kingdom. They blasphemously say that the world was made from a mixture of good and evil powers.

In the same way you say that God could not otherwise have saved us unless he himself became passible on our behalf.

Heretic. I remember that you said that the humanity, when compared with God, is more like an accident than a subsistent substance. How, then, can there now be two substances of Christ, when an accidental addition does not become substance but quantity?

Rusticus. I said this not of substance but of subsistence. When compared with the divine substance or nature, however, the flesh is nevertheless substance and nature. For it has been demonstrated that the Fathers who say “two natures, God and man,” and speak of each nature and of both, would not say these things unless they compared them with one another.

You yourselves do the same, making Christ from two substances and natures; and, in addition, you say that Christ exists from two subsistences. As for your attempt to blame the most holy Leo for saying, “This one is one thing, that one another,” receive the passage from the synod of Ephesus that was added by the representatives of the most holy Roman pope Celestine after they had arrived. From it they demonstrate how the creed of the 318 holy Fathers ought to be explained, on the testimony of Atticus of holy memory:

“And it receives all these things—not the nature of divinity, but the assumption of flesh: the one remaining in the inviolability of its own impassibility, while the other suffers and endures all things.”

There it is. Speaking of the divine nature, it says “the one”; speaking of the assumed body, it says “the other,” by which the Son of God endured, just as the same Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). And again: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41).

Heretic. What can you say to this: that the union of God with humanity is greater than the union of flesh with soul in any ordinary human being? For through death the soul is separated from the body, whereas God is inseparable forever from that soul and that undefiled body. If, then, from a lesser union one nature results, much more from a greater union there is one nature; and if a human being has one nature, much more there is one nature of divinity and humanity.

Rusticus. Before the demonstration, you have cause to be astonished. In wonder I agree with you that the union in the Lord Christ is greater and has produced something far greater; yet it has not made one nature. For the union of divinity and humanity accomplished in the Lord Christ, and the result of that union, surpasses what occurs in a human being by as much as it unites things that are much farther apart. Indeed, it surpasses by far—beyond what can be expressed—the possibility that divinity and humanity should be only one person, compared with the possibility that soul and flesh should be not only one person but also one nature.

For God infinitely surpasses the creature, beyond what can be expressed; and the ineffable union conquered that distance so as to make one person from natures separated by such a great distance in their boundaries or principles. The soul, however, surpasses the flesh only slightly; both are creatures and were made from nothing by the Creator.

If God’s power were not infinite, he would not have made so great a thing from nothing, for everything that exists is infinitely distant from what in no way exists. If, then, God’s power is infinite, while our substance is finite, that great and exceedingly radiant union was able to make one person from things so greatly disparate.

For just as the power of one who suspended a mountain in heaven and joined it to heaven—if such a thing could happen—would surpass that of one who joined a clod to a mountain, so the union accomplished in Christ surpasses the union that takes place individually in ordinary human beings.

Yet I also say this: it is not necessary that a greater union produce something greater. Otherwise, the more things are united, the more powerfully they would be united. Things that are confused are united more than things that are not confused, as liquids are. Again, because the soul is not mingled with the body, the union of things that are mingled is nonetheless not greater than the union of rational souls with their proper bodies. For God alone produces the latter union, whereas the former are subject even to us.

In addition to these points, the greater union has been assumed without definition. The answer will suffice even if the claim is stated definitively, as when someone says something more unexpected: it is more marvelous for one person and one nature to come into being in this manner than for one person and one nature to come into being in that manner.

[Note: [Col. 1249D] Some material appears to be missing here.]

[Col. 1250D]

Heretic. Tell me briefly: is the human nature in Christ the Son of God according to substance, or is it not? And is God the Word the Son of the Mother of God according to nature, or is he not? If it is according to nature, it is clear that both are one nature. But if it is not according to nature, then they will be sons by grace alone, separately: God the Word being by nature the Son of the Father and by grace the son of his mother, while the man is by nature the son of his mother but by grace the son of the Father. And just as the one is not the son of the other, so neither is this one the son of the other.

Rusticus. If there were only the two alternatives you have proposed, I would not even then have granted you simply what you have argued. But I say this: according to person and subsistence, the Son of God, God the Word, is the Son of the Mother of God; and likewise—and indeed saying the same thing—according to subsistence, and not according to substance or nature, the form of a servant is the Son of God.

And just as, if there were one nature, as you said earlier, so now there is one subsistence, and there is one and only one Son.

Heretic. Since this long discussion has brought us not only labor and exhaustion but also weariness, and since it greatly confuses the understanding, let us, if you agree, reserve the rest of our conversation for another day, should God will it. Let us nevertheless turn these matters over in our minds. For much examination conducted in silence within oneself will provide memory, understanding, instruction, and progress.

[Col. 1251B]

Rusticus. Please do not delay the time of turning to God. The end of human life is uncertain, especially in our days, when relentless destruction rages everywhere and the fire of Gehenna is impassable.
