Do not fear human friendships, so that you may not incur the hostility of the heavenly powers; do not fear the multitude of relatives, so that you may be numbered among all the saints from the beginning of the age; do not fear this garment, so that you may put on Christ; do not fear these flowers of temporal things, so that you may shine like the sun in the kingdom of God; do not fear the riches of this world, so that you may receive eternal life as your inheritance in perpetual and indescribable joy; do not fear the enjoyments of the age, and the manna of the Holy Spirit will be your food; do not fear transient dignities, so that you may reign with Christ.

By raising up your understanding, become a participant in higher things. Suspend yourself from worldly concerns, and then you will comprehend their worthlessness. Taste the sweetness of God, and you will perceive the bitterness of the world. Draw near, and see the spiritual light; then you will be rescued from the darkness of carnal confusion. Awaken yourself and leap toward the purity of higher things; then you will discern the abominations of worldly filth.

Break the bonds of Satanic captivity, lest you lose the freedom acquired through baptism. Flee participation in the most polluted demon, so that you may renew within yourself the adoption of God. Resist the devil, who desires to destroy you, and obey God, who desires to save you.

Consider the love of God; consider the enjoyment of the kingdom of heaven; consider the exceedingly terrible day of the future judgment; consider the judgment of the Lord Christ himself, which cannot be diverted from what is right; consider the unbearable torments of Gehenna; consider the worms that never sleep; consider the impassable and infinite flame; consider the useless repentance there, the fruitless laments, the unheard wailings, and the unprofitable showers of tears.

While you can, turn irrevocably and diligently to the truth. You will have neither excuse nor satisfaction before God if you persist in evil, especially since all the objections raised by you have been refuted.

A single authority of the universal synod would be sufficient for you—a synod that surpasses all others in number and has been confirmed so many times by the harmonious judgment of all the churches, both through the encyclical letters issued during the reign of Leo and through the memoranda of perhaps two thousand five hundred priests, under the emperor Justin, after the schism of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius of Constantinople.

Do not let the disturbance that has recently arisen in the universal Church trouble you; rather, let it strengthen you in the faith. For if our faith were not right, it could have advanced in those times rather than being thrown into confusion. Read the divine Scriptures, and you will find that the present time is one of unbelief and apostasy from the faith. Therefore you ought to hasten all the more toward conversion and correction, so that, having been made worthy to be rescued from present and future evils, you may enjoy the infinite blessings of God in the kingdom of heaven.

May we attain this through the grace and generosity of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Heretic. If you are willing to examine more subtly what I have said, you will certainly find that I did not demonstrate that you introduce two sons according to the one person and subsistence that you profess, but according to the fact that you also say there are two natures of Christ after the union. Consequently, unless you unravel my questions, however much you proclaim one Son, you nevertheless introduce two.

Rusticus. If the father of any physical person is also his bishop and teacher, he is his father not only according to the flesh but also according to the spirit. Although he is father in one way with respect to one thing and in another way with respect to another, he is not therefore said to be the father of two sons in relation to one person.

You yourselves, although you say that the nature of divinity and flesh is one through the union, do not say that they coincide in relation to its one and the same Father, so that the nature which is the Son of God is naturally the son of man. Nor will you now be able to speak of the simple nature of the complete Christ as you did before the incarnation, unless perhaps you mean divinity alone, since you say that he exists from two unconfused natures.

Either, then, your objection will be equally opposed to us and to you, and it cannot bring victory against us when it does not even prevail against those who introduce two sons; or, if you desire to overcome them together with us, give them the same answer that you hear from us. Thus conquer in order to conquer twice: both the falsehood that is in you and the falsehood that is in them. Otherwise, if it follows that we introduce two sons, it will also follow that you introduce one from two sons. But it is impossible for one son to be made from two sons.

Heretic. I wish to hear more clearly what you are saying.

Rusticus. Answer, if you can: in what respect is God the Word the Son of God? Is it according to the simple substance of divinity, which existed infinitely before the incarnation, or, as you say, according to the composite nature of divinity and humanity?

Heretic. According to the simple substance of divinity.

Rusticus. What about the man, or humanity, or flesh: according to the simple nature of divinity, or, as you say, according to the composite nature, is he the son of that same Father?

Heretic. Not according to the simple nature, but according to the composite nature.

Rusticus. How, then, in accordance with your delirious notions, are there not two sons, God and man, if God is the Son of God not according to the composite but according to the simple nature, while man is the Son of God not according to the simple but according to the composite nature? Behold, you have been caught in your own knots.

Heretic. But the simple and composite nature are one and the same.

[Col. 1254A]

Rusticus. Even if that were so, a difference would still remain, because the simple and the composite are not simply identical; nor is that which comes from one perfect nature simply the same as that which comes from two natures and is itself perfect.

[ADDENDA TO CAESARIUS.]

[Col. 1253]

OMITTED PROLEGOMENON, WHICH OUGHT TO HAVE OCCUPIED A PLACE BEFORE THE LIFE OF SAINT CAESARIUS, or A PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY ON SAINT CAESARIUS OF ARLES. (From the Bollandists.)

§ I. The writers of the Life; his cult; eulogies.

[Col. 1253B]

1. Saint Caesarius, formerly a monk and abbot and later bishop of Arles, shone forth in Gaul in the fifth century through the wondrous holiness of his life and the glory of his miracles. Mabillon published his Life, faithfully written by his disciples, in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, first century, where, on page 658, he introduces it as follows:

“We present here the Life of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, which had until now appeared interpolated in many places, in a sincere and complete form, from the manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Montmajour of Arles, divided into two books. Cyprian wrote the first, as is clear from section 30; the second was written by the presbyter Messianus and the deacon Stephanus, as is evident from the end of Book I and the beginning of Book II. That Cyprian is not different from Cyprian, bishop of Toulon, a disciple of Saint Caesarius, is shown by the fact that Caesarius left him a cloak in his testament.”

The most recent editors of *Gallia Christiana*, volume I, column 741, agree with Mabillon’s view, where they briefly explain the acts of Saint Cyprian of Toulon. Nor does the matter seem doubtful, since the Life makes clear, in section 46, that Cyprian of Toulon was a disciple of Saint Caesarius.

2. “It does not matter,” says Mabillon, “that the writer of the first book speaks modestly and humbly of himself . . . but magnificently of Cyprian, bishop of Toulon. For Cyprian did not write this about himself, but those who composed the first part of this Life together with him did so. Although Cyprian was the principal author, he was not alone in writing it; Firminus and Viventius also contributed their work with him.”

This is proved from the beginning of Book II, where Firminus and Viventius are expressly said, together with Cyprian, to be authors of the first part. Mabillon adds the inscription of the Life prefixed in the manuscript of Montmajour, which reads as follows:

“Here begins the prologue and Life of Caesarius, which the lord Cyprian, the most blessed Firminus, Saint Viventius the bishop [Mabillon says that *episcopi*, ‘bishops,’ should be read], the presbyter Messianus, and the deacon Stephanus wrote.”

That the first book had several authors is also demonstrated by these words in section 39: “One of our number, who wrote these things.” Hence the illustrious Mabillon concludes:

“That eulogy, therefore, which you read about Cyprian of Toulon in section 33 (in our edition, section 46), should be attributed to Firminus and Viventius, the authors. Just as, when at the beginning of Book II (in our edition, section 7) Messianus is called ‘the venerable man,’ everyone will concede that this was written by the deacon Stephanus, not by Messianus himself.”

3. There is no doubt that Firminus and Viventius, equally with Cyprian, were disciples of Saint Caesarius and were bishops; for they are called co-bishops at the beginning of the second part. Moreover, Viventius is named bishop in the title of a letter sent to him by Messianus, which we shall quote below.

Nevertheless, it has so far remained unclear over which churches they presided. Mabillon indeed says, “Firminus was bishop of Uzes,” and Baillet agrees with him in the Life of Saint Caesarius for 27 August, as do the authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, volume III, page 197. But the most recent editors of *Gallia Christiana*, volume VI, columns 611–612, where they discuss Saint Firminus of Uzes, speak as follows:

“In the acts of our Firminus there is nothing that supports this opinion.”

Nor have I been able to find anything in our manuscripts concerning Saint Firminus of Uzes by which I could establish that he was a disciple of Saint Caesarius or, together with the others, a writer of the Life. I am therefore compelled to leave the matter uncertain until 11 October, when Saint Firminus of Uzes will be discussed more fully.

“But who Viventius was is not yet established,” says Mabillon.

The Life composed by the five authors mentioned above was dedicated to the virgin Caesaria, at whose request it had been written. On 12 January we discussed Saint Caesaria, the sister of Caesarius, whom her holy brother established as the first abbess of the monastery at Arles. But she died before Caesarius, as is clear from his Life, section 44; consequently, this Life was not dedicated to her, as some have mistakenly written.

The Life itself testifies in the same place that another Caesaria succeeded that holy woman, and it is to this second Caesaria that the Life of Saint Caesarius is said to be dedicated. The writers of *Gallia Christiana*, volume I, column 619, honor her with the title “saint,” but so far we have no reliable information concerning her cult.

4. The aforementioned Life of Saint Caesarius had been published by Surius under 27 August and by Vincentius Baralli in *Chronologia Sanctorum Lerinensium*, pages 229 and following. Mabillon’s edition is preferable, however, since the style was altered in the others and Surius omitted not a few passages from the first book.

In addition, we possess the first part of this Life in a manuscript obtained through the work of the most learned Sirmond “from an old parchment manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in Paris, of the Cluniac Order,” as is noted in our copy. I compared this manuscript with Mabillon’s edition; it differs from it only in a few and relatively minor matters.

Nevertheless, so that the edition may be made more exact and the differences between the two witnesses may become apparent, I shall publish this part from the aforementioned manuscript and shall note wherever anything occurs that differs from the edition mentioned. I shall append the second part, which we do not possess in manuscript, from Mabillon.

In addition to these commonly known acts of Saint Caesarius, our fellow Chiffletius once transmitted to us another Life of the same saint from a very ancient manuscript of the church of Saint John at Besançon, much shorter than the preceding one. Either it was abridged from that Life, or it is itself the Life that one of the five authors composed at the beginning without the supplementation of the others.

Certainly it adds nothing to the preceding Life and contains no event that is not read there; rather, the same events are found there partly in nearly the same words and partly omitted. I therefore judged that this Life would serve no other purpose than comparison with the Life to be published, with its places noted whenever any events are expressed more clearly in it.

5. Although the acts of Saint Caesarius were written by those authors with such sincerity that they seem to require no confirmation, and although they teach such numerous and great things that scarcely anything could be added to the saint’s praise, I nevertheless wish to add from elsewhere several testimonies of outstanding men, so that from them too it may become clear how highly the holy bishop was esteemed.

Saint Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, whom we discussed under 17 July, celebrates his praises in these words in a letter to Caesarius, published by Sirmond in *Opera varia*, volume I, column 957:

“You, my lord, divine law brought forth into the already Christian world and nourished with the milk of the apostolic breast. You surpass the others as the sun’s greatness surpasses the lesser stars. Whoever has looked upon you with the eyes of the inner man has been instructed. For even while your very countenance fosters purity, you chastise sinners with a striking utterance. Wherever you go, the good find in your conduct examples to imitate; the wicked are shown things from which they must flee.

Blessed are you, to whom God has granted that you teach both by admonitions and by examples; you, who, always going before as a guide on the straight path of the devout life, have invited others to follow. Who would not wish, while you speak, to know more rather than read? By your account you reconcile genius with books and instruct teachers. Every great writer owes it to you that you enlarge him through the gift of eloquence. In you the light of speech and conduct meet.”

More may be seen there, or in the works of others who published the same letter.

6. Florianus, a monk and disciple of Saint Caesarius, also provides a notable testimony concerning him in a letter to Saint Nicetius, bishop of Trier, published by Chesnius in volume I of the *Scriptores of France*, page 851, in these words:

“And also the lord Caesarius, bishop of Arles, of blessed memory, a companion of your crown: he lived piously among barbarians, peacefully amid wars, a father to orphans, a shepherd to the needy; although he distributed so great a wealth, he lost nothing, demonstrating by word and deed the rule of catholic discipline. He himself taught me the alphabet in Latin letters; and I trust that I may obtain this man as his servant and disciple.”

Venantius Fortunatus, who mentions Caesarius and his rule in various places, touches briefly upon his virtues in Book V, poem 2, in this eulogy:

> He who was bishop of Arles, from the lineage of Lerins,  
> And remained a monk, the glory of the episcopate.

By saying that he remained a monk, he suggests that he retained the same austerity of life, constancy in prayer, humility, and other virtues in which he had flourished as a monk.

### 7.

The highly esteemed Sirmond, vol. II, col. 29, reproduces a letter of Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, to Caesarius, in which he commends to him Bishop Maximian, who was suffering from an eye ailment. In this letter the saint’s virtues are not indeed recounted, except for his mercy toward the afflicted, which is indicated in these words: “Since your piety, which everywhere seeks opportunities for mercy, is not unaware of where there is a place for misery.” Yet the fame of his miracles is discreetly suggested. For Maximian appears to have visited the saint for no other reason than to obtain through him a remedy for his blindness. Thus, I think, Avitus’s following words should be understood: “Yet, as far as he himself deigns to assert, his principal reason for coming is to seek out wherever he can a more skilled physician, who may assist the weakness of bodily sight by the art of whatever remedy may be available.” I think these words should be understood in this way, especially since he adds the example of Tobias, who was not healed by human art.

Hear the words of the letter: “As for the hope of recovering his sight, I think he also seeks it from the example—namely, that our Tobias . . . [lacuna] the medicine hidden in an angel restored, through the collyrium of gall, to the sweetness of health.” Avitus then adds: “Therefore receive your brother with your customary sincerity and with fitting respect; and, if any consolation is owed to a holy man, bestow it. The common desire will be fulfilled if a remedy is also provided for whatever illness he may have.” By these words he plainly urges Caesarius to restore Maximian’s sight. Nor will anyone who has read the miracles recorded in the Acts be surprised that the fame of his miracles was so widely spread that a bishop came to him from distant regions in order to recover his sight.

### 8.

We can also establish the renown of Saint Caesarius from the visits of illustrious men who sought his advice or admonitions. In our March volume, p. 352, the Acts of Saint Leobinus, bishop of Chartres, contain the following passage relevant to our purpose:

“Not long afterward, the blessed Aetherius, bishop of Chartres, imposed upon him—Leobinus, then a priest—the duty of seeking out and fearlessly visiting Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, in order to advance toward what was better. When Saint Leobinus had reached him, together with the blessed Albinus, who had been his companion on the journey, the blessed Caesarius asked him why he had undertaken the labor of so long a journey. Blessed Albinus replied that he had come solely because of his own desire; but that blessed Leobinus, having left the brothers over whom he had been placed, was hastening to Lerins, where he desired to be subject to all the brothers.”

Moreover, Saint Albinus, bishop of Angers, consulted Saint Caesarius about a very serious matter, as is recorded in his Acts, in our March volume, p. 60. It is uncertain, however, whether this occurred when he traveled to him with Saint Leobinus or whether he visited him again later. From these facts it is perfectly clear that the name of Saint Caesarius was held in the highest honor throughout Gaul, since holy men living at such a great distance from him traveled to him as to an oracle, seeking counsel and guidance for progress in virtue.

Saint Caesarius, for his part, ordered Saint Leobinus to return to govern the monks over whom he presided; and Leobinus did so, as is reported there at greater length. This is sufficient to demonstrate how greatly Caesarius flourished in the fame of his name and how universally his holiness and wisdom were esteemed.

### 9.

His memory is recorded in the sacred calendars on 27 August, on which day his feast is celebrated in the diocese of Arles. Hear, as representative of the others, Ado:

“In Gaul, in the city of Arles, Saint Caesarius, bishop and confessor, a man of extraordinary holiness, piety, and zeal.”

Nearly all the others agree with this, and it would be superfluous to quote their words. Trithemius, in *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book III, chapter 84, counts Caesarius among the Benedictine monks. Baronius, however, thoroughly refuted that error in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 27 August. Trithemius’s error arose from an anachronism: he thought that Caesarius flourished much later than he actually did.

From this, Andreas Saussayus fell into another error. Besides our Caesarius, he announces a second Caesarius, bishop of Arles, as a Caesarius of that name who was second. He may be seen in the appendix to the *Gallican Martyrology*, p. 1220, where he attributes certain deeds belonging to Saint Caesarius to that second and fictitious Caesarius. Since this error has no foundation whatever, it does not deserve a lengthy refutation, especially since it has already been rejected by learned men generally, as was observed in the case of Saint Veredemius, volume IV for August, p. 638. I therefore proceed to construct the chronology of his life.

## § II. The principal events of his life arranged chronologically up to the time when the monastery for holy virgins was founded, with an account of the two Rules written by the saint

### 10.

Some writers greatly erred concerning the period in which Saint Caesarius flourished—namely, Vincent of Beauvais, Sigebert, Trithemius, and Peter Suffridus. Their words may be found quoted in Vincent Barralis, *Chronology of the Saints of the Abbey of Lerins*, p. 259 and following. I shall not linger over refuting them, since those errors have already been corrected by various writers, and their opinion must collapse of its own accord from the sequence that we shall establish.

Baronius, too, deviated considerably from the correct path in assigning Caesarius’s age, in volume VI of the *Annals*, for the year 453, no. 41; but he corrected that error to some extent in the additions appended to volume X, p. 959. Subsequently, scholars came to know the age of this most distinguished man more precisely, and they now agree substantially about his chronology, apart from a difference of a few years regarding certain events of his life, whose chronology could not be established with complete certainty.

### 11.

According to the *Life*, book II, no. 33, the saint died in the seventy-third year of his age. Many believe that his death occurred on 27 August 542, and we shall prove this below. He must therefore have been born around the year 470—namely, after the middle of 469, if nearly the whole seventy-third year of his life had been completed, or otherwise in the year 470 itself.

According to our manuscript from Besançon and Mabillon’s Arles manuscript, he received the clerical tonsure in the eighteenth year of his age, which must have occurred around the year 487. After spending two years among the clergy, as the *Life*, no. 4, relates, he withdrew to Lerins and there began the monastic life around the year 489, at the age of twenty.

After spending several years in the monastery of Lerins, he fell ill through excessive bodily mortification and was sent to Arles for the sake of recovering his health. There his virtues became known to Saint Aeonius, archbishop of Arles, by whom he was ordained deacon and priest toward the end of the fifth century. Around the year 499 he became abbot—not at Lerins, as Trithemius incorrectly wrote in *On the Illustrious Men*, book II, chapter 16, but on an island in the Rhône near Arles—and governed the monks for more than three years, as is recorded in the *Life*, no. 11.

### 12.

From being abbot he was appointed bishop of the church of Arles after Saint Aeonius, who had desired him as his successor, as the *Life*, nos. 12 and 13, attests. The diptychs of the Church of Arles, published in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, should not obstruct this succession, since they possess little authority, as scholars have already observed.

Hear the editors of the revised *Gallia Christiana*, volume I, col. 534:

“In the diptychs, John is read after Aeonius, but he is mentioned nowhere else. There are, however, many considerations that diminish the authority of those diptychs. Elsewhere, on the contrary, we read that Caesarius succeeded Aeonius in the episcopate.”

Baronius, too, in the additions to volume VI of the *Annals*, printed in volume X, p. 960, arranged the succession of the bishops of Arles differently, writing that Caesarius succeeded Leontius and that Leontius succeeded Aeonius. But that error is sufficiently refuted by the succession assigned in the cited *Gallia Christiana*, which leaves no doubt that Aeonius came after Leontius.

Writers do not entirely agree about the year in which Caesarius began his episcopate. Dionysius Sammarthanus, in the *Gallia Christiana*, col. 535, assigns the year 501 or 502. Norisius, *Pelagian History*, book II, chapter 22, argues that he became bishop in the year 503. Fleury, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, book XXXI, chapter 2, places the beginning of his episcopate in the year 501. Finally, Pagius, in his *Critique* for the year 502, no. 8, and Longuevallius, in the *History of the Gallican Church*, volume II, book V, p. 267, believe that Caesarius succeeded Aeonius in the year 502. I shall briefly confirm their opinion as the more accurate of the alternatives.

### 13.

Aeonius died on 16 August, as we shall prove in his Acts for 23 August. It is therefore certain that he did not die before the year 502, because Pope Symmachus, in a letter to Avitus of Vienne “given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Avienus and Pompeius”—that is, in the year 501 of Christ—mentions him as still living. That letter may be seen in Labbe, volume IV of the Councils, cols. 1311–1312.

Now it is shown from the duration of Caesarius’s episcopate, when compared with the year of his death, that he did not become bishop after the year 502. For Caesarius died on 27 August 542, as I shall demonstrate below. He was near death, as the *Life*, book II, no. 33, testifies, “when the cycle of forty years in the episcopate was turning.” It necessarily follows that he was ordained bishop in the year 502, since the *Life*, no. 12, suggests that he succeeded Aeonius not long after the latter’s death. This perhaps occurred in September, so that he completed nearly forty years.

The aforementioned Norisius and Saxius, in their *Pontifical Register of Arles*, assign the beginning of his episcopate to the year 503 for no other reason than that they believe Caesarius died in the year 543.

### 14.

Most of the notable events of his episcopate are recounted in the *Life*, but not all of them. I shall therefore add, in chronological order, whatever else from other sources is worthy of reporting; and I shall continue to restore the events narrated in the *Life* to their chronological order.

In the year 506 Caesarius summoned to a council the bishops subject to Alaric, king of the Visigoths, having received permission from him, as is stated in the preface to the council. This council was held at Agatha, called Agde by the Gauls, in Occitania, “on the third day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of Messala, a most illustrious man”—that is, in the year 506 of Christ, the twenty-second year of Alaric’s reign as king of the Goths in Gaul, and the eighth year of Pope Symmachus. Thirty-five bishops attended.

This is how the title appears in Labbe, volume IV, col. 1381, although only thirty-four signatories are read there, some being bishops and some priests sent in place of bishops. Labbe gives seventy-one canons; but in the same work, col. 1397, Sirmond observes that only forty-seven are found in various manuscript codices, while the remainder appear to have been added from other councils. All of them were enacted for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline in Gaul.

Caesarius signed first in these words:

“I, Caesarius, bishop of Arles, in the name of Christ, in accordance with what pleased all my holy fellow bishops who have signed with me, following the statutes of the Fathers, have subscribed to these decrees, and so forth.”

### 15.

Bishop Ruricius of Limoges had been invited to the Council of Agatha. But he neither came in person nor sent anyone in his place; he had nevertheless written an apologetic letter to Caesarius, which had not yet been delivered. Caesarius therefore sent him a letter through the priest Capillutus, partly reproving him and partly excusing him, in these words:

“Although you sent your holy and desirable letter, nevertheless, as you yourself know very well, it would have been most fitting for you to send someone who could sign in your place, so that what your holy brothers had decided might be confirmed in your person. But because I know with what holy, earnest, and pious desire you wished to attend, I explained your wish and holy intention to all your brothers. For this reason we could neither nor ought to attribute any blame to your piety.”

The entire letter is found in Labbe, volume IV, col. 1399. Ruricius’s reply is also appended there, containing these words:

“As for your writing to ask why I did not come to the synod . . . [lacuna], it was illness, not unwillingness, that caused this.”

He then adds that Caesarius’s letter had been delivered to him late; nor does he allege any other reason for his absence. Consequently, what Jacobus Basnage wrote about the cause of this absence in his notes on these letters, in the reprinted volume I of Canisius’s *Thesaurus of Monuments*, p. 397, is fabricated: namely, that Ruricius had been unwilling to come because Caesarius was improperly claiming primacy and the authority to summon synods.

### 16.

Moreover, from the aforementioned letter of Caesarius to Ruricius we learn that this man, deeply devoted to ecclesiastical discipline, attempted in the following year to assemble a fuller synod from Gaul and Spain. Hear the words of the letter:

“I also inform your piety that your son Eudomius, if he is able to bring this about, desires that, with the coming year, we should have a synod at Toulouse, Christ being favorable, where he also wishes, if possible, to bring together the bishops of Spain. Therefore I ask you to pray that the Lord may grant effect to so holy a desire.”

I suspect that this council could not be convened because of the war between Alaric and Clovis, king of the Franks, who in the following year killed Alaric with his own hand in battle, as the Gallic historians commonly relate.

From the date of Alaric’s death we can to some extent determine the year of the first exile inflicted on the saint by that same Alaric, as the *Life*, no. 17, testifies. This appears to have occurred around the year 505. Some have placed it after the Council of Agatha; but I have scarcely any doubt that it must be placed before the council, since between that council and Alaric’s death there is scarcely sufficient time for the saint first to have been accused, then taken to Bordeaux, to have halted a fire there, and afterward to have been recalled honorably by Alaric—unless we imagine that all these events followed one another within a very short interval, which is hardly plausible.

I therefore prefer to believe that he was sent into exile in the year 505 and recalled at the beginning of the following year, and that on this occasion he obtained from Alaric permission to convene a synod.

### 17.

Around the year 507 he began to build a monastery for holy virgins. The buildings that had been begun, however, were destroyed during the siege of the city. Pagius, for the year 508, no. 7, and the Gallic historians write that the siege was begun by the Franks and Burgundians in that year.

Pagius adds that Arles was not freed from danger until the year 510, when the Franks were defeated by an army sent by Theodoric, king of the Goths in Italy, and that thereafter it remained under Theodoric’s authority. Cointius agrees about the time when the siege was lifted, under the year 510, no. 2, citing a letter of Theodoric in which he temporarily exempted the people of Arles from taxes because they had defended themselves splendidly and had suffered much during the prolonged assault on their city.

From this we infer that Saint Caesarius was imprisoned around the year 509 because of the slander reported in the *Life*, no. 21, by which he was attacked especially by the Jews during the siege. This was the second accusation of treason, followed later by a third, as we shall see; yet the saint always emerged from all of them with greater glory.

In the year 510, after the siege had been lifted, Caesarius’s immense charity shone forth in the redemption of captives, as the *Life*, no. 23, testifies.

### 18.

At the same time he again undertook the construction of the monastery that had previously been begun, and he brought it to completion two years later. It is not plausible that it was completed sooner. The *Life* also suggests, in no. 25, that it had been completed in that year before the saint was taken to Italy, which occurred in the following year.

Moreover, the *Life*, book II, no. 34, states: “The establishment of that monastery at the time” when the saint died “had stood for thirty full years.” Since the saint died in the year 542, the monastery was completed in the year 512.

The *Life* further states that he died on 27 August, after the day on which his monastery was dedicated:

“Therefore,” says Pagius under the year 453, no. 17, “that dedication took place on the seventh day before the Kalends of September in the year of Christ 512, when 26 August fell on a Sunday.”

### 19.

He instructed the virgins of that monastery by written laws and placed his sister, Saint Caesaria, over them, as the *Life*, no. 25, relates. Fortunatus, Saint Gregory of Tours, and, in Gregory’s work, Saint Radegund, who followed the Rule of Caesarius, mention in various places the Rule that Caesarius wrote for these virgins. Bollandus has already quoted their words in volume for January, pp. 729–730, where he also discussed the first abbesses of this monastery.

He then appended the Rule itself, divided into twelve sections, so that it is unnecessary to reproduce it here again [see above, col. 1107]. In its preface he addresses the virgins as follows:

“To the holy and most greatly venerated sisters in Christ who have been established in the monastery which, with God inspiring and helping us, we founded: Caesarius, bishop.

“Because the Lord, in his mercy, has deigned to inspire and help us to establish a monastery for you, we have composed for you spiritual and holy instructions concerning how you ought to live in that monastery, according to the institutions of the ancient Fathers. In order that, with God’s help, you may be able to observe them, remain continually in the little cell of the monastery and implore the coming of the Son of God through constant prayers, so that afterward you may confidently say: ‘We have found him whom our soul sought.’”

He then asks for their prayers and appends his regulations. Saint Caesarius’s prudence and wisdom shine remarkably through these laws. Cointius explained them at length in his *Annals of the Franks*, under the year 536, no. 47 and following.

### 20.

Nor was it enough for the saint to prescribe these constitutions for the virgins. He also took care that whatever he had done for the benefit of the virgins should be ratified by the supreme pontiff and that the monastery itself should be exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop, except for visitation.

We have this in a letter of Saint Hormisdas, the pontiff, appended to the Rule in our work. After praising Saint Caesarius’s zeal for promoting divine things in an outstanding eulogy, he continues on p. 737 as follows [see below, col. 1285]:

“This is why, since you have informed us by letter that in the Church of Arles, in addition to the customary vigils of clerics and monks, you have also newly established choirs of maidens dedicated to God, you ask that in the aforesaid monastery of maidens, recently founded by you, your successors should never at any time be permitted to exercise any authority whatsoever, so that the virgins consecrated to God, freed from every disturbance or annoyance, may continually serve almighty God with minds at liberty.”

### 21.

“It is a worthy priestly undertaking to bend hearts toward the singing of God’s praise and to offer to sacred worship, from those mystical seeds, the fruit of virginity. The Apostle declared that this was his supreme desire in those sacred writings when he said: ‘I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.’

“Therefore, gladly assenting to your fraternal petitions, we confirm and decree by apostolic authority that no bishop, including any of your successors, shall dare claim any authority whatsoever for himself in the aforesaid monastery, except that, out of regard for God, exercising pastoral care, he should endeavor in good faith, at suitable times and in the manner appropriate, to visit with his clergy the household of Christ the Lord established there.

“Furthermore, it is just that both sexes, with equal devotion, standing in places appropriate to them, should sing the glory of God, just as both await the hope of redemption with steadfast and complete faith.”

He then confirms the donations and sales made to the monastery. Caesarius himself mentions this confirmation by the Roman pontiff in his testament, which will be quoted below.

Dionysius Sammarthanus lists the abbesses of this monastery—which was first called Saint John’s and now bears the name of Saint Caesarius and still follows the Rule of Saint Benedict—in the *Gallia Christiana*, volume I, col. 619 and following.

### 22.

Saint Caesarius composed a monastic rule not only for women but also for men, although the writers of his life do not mention the Rule given to men. Hear Cointius under the year 535, no. 123:

“Besides the Rule . . . which Caesarius, bishop of Arles, gave to the nuns for observance, there also exists a Rule of monks whose author is the same Caesarius, as will be clear from its title below. This Rule was in force among most of the monks in that part of Narbonese Gaul which the Ostrogoths ceded to the Franks in this year.

“It has been published several times in the *Library of the Fathers*, as well as by Prosper Stellartius among the Rules of monastic and military orders, and by Luke Holstenius in the *Code of Rules* that the holy Fathers prescribed for monks and religious virgins to observe.

“Two titles are placed at the beginning of the work [see above, col. 1101]. One reads as follows:

“‘Here begins the Rule transmitted, at the request of my humble person, by Saint Tetradius, priest and nephew of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, of blessed memory, to an abbot. Tetradius himself said that it had been dictated by his above-mentioned lord Caesarius, who, while he was a priest, personally transmitted it to various monasteries.’

“The other reads:

“‘In the name of Christ, here begins the Rule concerning what ought to be observed in a monastery where there is an abbot, whoever he may be.’

“Such is the Holstenian edition, which, being the latest, is also the best of all.”

After a short interval Cointius appends the Rule itself, compares it with the Rule for nuns, and elucidates it with notes, so that it is unnecessary to print or explain it here again.

In the epilogue Saint Caesarius urges the monks, in most forceful words, to practice virtues worthy of a monk, and he concludes everything in these words:

“For we can lay aside secular garments and put on religious ones in a single hour. But we must continually retain good morals and labor, with Christ’s help, against the sweet but evil pleasures of this world for as long as we live, because it is not the one who begins but the one who perseveres to the end who will be saved.”

This is sufficient concerning the Rules written by the saint.

## § III. The chronology of his life extended to the year 514, with various matters omitted in the Acts supplied

### 23.

The two slanders already mentioned, by which the saint’s glory had been increased, did not prevent his Arian rivals from bringing a third accusation against him before Theodoric, the Arian king of Italy. The *Life*, no. 26, testifies that Caesarius was summoned before Theodoric and taken to Ravenna; but the outcome was ultimately such that the holiness of the man never shone more brightly in any matter, nor did his glory ever shine more clearly.

Sigonius, in book XVI of *The Western Empire*, assigns this event to the consulship of Boethius, that is, to the year 510. Pagius, under the year 508, no. 10, believes that this second exile of the saint occurred after the year 512, once the monastery had been dedicated. Muratorius, in his notes on the reprinted Sigonius, assigns this exile to the year 512, and Longuevallius, in volume II of his *History of the Gallican Church*, p. 326, likewise connects it with that year.

The *Life* lends some support to this view, since it first relates the construction of the monastery and then soon afterward reports this second exile. But the sequence of events that must be supplied persuades me that the matter did not occur before the year 513. I therefore believe that the saint was taken to Italy a considerable time after the dedication of the monastery, namely in the year 513, since in November of that same year he dealt with the supreme pontiff at Rome, as we shall see below.

### 24.

After remaining for some time at Ravenna, where he became renowned after raising a dead man and expelling a demon, he went to Rome to Pope Symmachus, by whom he was honorably received, as the *Life*, no. 30, relates.

The principal reason why the saint traveled to Rome was to have the rights of his church explained and confirmed. For a long-standing controversy existed between the bishop of Arles and the bishop of Vienne concerning metropolitan jurisdiction, or primacy, in Gaul; at one time the bishop of Arles and at another the bishop of Vienne had prevailed, as may be seen in Thomassinus, *On the Ancient and Modern Discipline of the Church*, part I, book I, chapter 30.

At the Council of Turin, which Pagius believes was held in the year 401, under that year, no. 30, the controversy had been settled as follows by canon 2:

“Furthermore, concerning the matter between the bishops of the cities of Arles and Vienne, who were contending among us for the honor of primacy, the holy synod decreed that whichever of them should prove that his city was the metropolis should possess the honor of primacy over the entire province and, in accordance with the command of the canons, should have authority over ordinations.

“Certainly, for the preservation of the bond of peace, it was decreed by this more useful arrangement that, if it pleased the bishops of the aforementioned cities, each should claim for itself those cities within the province that were nearer to it and should visit those churches that proved to be closer to its own towns, so that, mindful of unanimity and concord, neither might disturb the other by usurping for itself what was closer to the other.”

So it appears in Labbe, volume II, col. 1156.

### 25.

After this arrangement, by which their rights seemed to have been equalized, the bishop of Arles and then the bishop of Vienne again obtained the greater authority. Saint Leo, in letter 109, in Labbe, volume III, col. 1444, assigned to each the churches over which it should have jurisdiction: to the bishop of Vienne, namely, Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Grenoble; all the rest he subjected to the bishop of Arles.

Nevertheless, “that dispute was revived under Pope Anastasius, and again the case of Vienne was the stronger,” says the aforementioned Thomassinus, no. 7. But when Saint Caesarius acted before Symmachus, Symmachus confirmed Leo’s division in this letter addressed to the bishops of Gaul, found in Labbe, col. 1309:

“The institutions of the apostolic see demand that they be proclaimed, so that we may attend with vigilant care to the concord of the universal Church, which is spread throughout the whole world. That concord grows especially and more effectively when a later generation reverently observes what the Fathers established.

“Thus our brother and fellow bishop Caesarius, bishop of the metropolitan city of Arles, having been presented at the threshold of the church of blessed Peter the Apostle, has asked that what was formerly established concerning the privileges of the churches be renewed by our words.”

### 26.

“Therefore, everything that our predecessor, Pope Leo of blessed memory, arranged between the Churches of Arles and Vienne in this matter is declared by the faithful instruction of the Roman Church. And so, lest forgetfulness, which is always the rival of truth, should be able to claim anything for itself, and lest the force of the earlier decree should grow old through the passage of time, we have considered it necessary to bring what was once promulgated back into the light through our utterances.

“Accordingly, just as our predecessor Pope Leo determined long ago after hearing the arguments of the parties, we too decree that the number and extent of the parishes to be assigned to the bishops of Arles and Vienne must not be exceeded through anyone’s usurpation. Rather, as we stated above, by the indulgence of the aforesaid pontiff, the bishop of Vienne shall claim Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Grenoble as his rightful towns, and he shall presume nothing further beyond what was once granted to him by the apostolic see.

“As for all the other parishes or dioceses, the bishop of Arles shall defend them in the continuation of time with their privilege and honor. For neither the observance nor the reverence due to antiquity is preserved if the priestly dignity is raised still higher through humility.”

He then concludes the letter, after exhorting them to preserve the foregoing provisions, in these words:

“Given on the Ides of November, in the consulship of Probus, a most illustrious man.”

This date indicates the year 513, in which Probus was consul in the West, not the year 502, in which a certain Probus was indeed consul but in the East. For when only one consul was named in letters written in the empire of the West, the western consul was intended, as Pagius correctly observes under the year 502, no. 10.

### 27.

Symmachus also honored the Church of Arles with other privileges for the sake of Saint Caesarius, as the *Life*, no. 30, testifies. It says that the pallium was granted to him and that the deacons of the Church of Arles were permitted to use dalmatics, as was done in the Roman Church.

Thomassinus, part I, book II, chapter 54, no. 1, observes that Caesarius appears to have been the first person in the West to whom the honor of the pallium was granted. He then proves that the duties of a representative of the apostolic see in Gaul were also entrusted to him, and that both of these favors, which the *Life* says were conferred on Caesarius because of his outstanding merits, were transmitted for a long time to his successors.

Regarding the privilege of the deacons of Arles to use dalmatics, Mabillon observes in his notes, on the basis of Saint Gregory, that the use of dalmatics was not even common among bishops at that time, since Gregory granted the use of dalmatics to Aregius, bishop of Gap, and to Valatonius, his archdeacon, in letter 107, book IX of the new edition.

Baronius discusses the dalmatics at greater length in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 21 May. A considerable amount is also observed in the notes on the cited letter of Gregory, where certain errors of Baronius are said by Ferrarius to have been corrected in book IX of *On the Art of Clothing*, chapter 9.

### 28.

At the same time Saint Caesarius endeavored to abolish various abuses through the authority of the Roman pontiff. He therefore presented Symmachus with a petition in which he explained those abuses and requested their prohibition. I append the petition itself, from Labbe, volume IV of the Councils, col. 1294, so that the saint’s zeal may be evident:

“Just as the episcopate takes its beginning from the person of blessed Peter the Apostle, so your holiness must necessarily show clearly to each church, through appropriate regulations, what it ought to observe.

“For in the province of Gaul, ecclesiastical estates are being alienated by certain persons under various pretexts. Thus it happens that, according to his own arbitrary will, someone diminishes the resources assigned by devout minds to the needs of the poor and needy. We ask that the authority of the apostolic see prohibit this, unless perhaps something is to be granted to monasteries out of consideration for piety.

“We also request with equal supplication that no cleric or bishop be ordained from a secular way of life merely because he has served in the offices of judges or has governed provinces under some authority, unless he has long beforehand undertaken a legitimate way of life and his conduct has been examined.”

### 29.

“We also request that widows who have long since adopted religious dress, and religious women who have already spent a long time in monasteries, should not be left open to anyone’s freedom to join himself to them in marriage against their will or to carry them off unwillingly.

“We also humbly suggest that no one be permitted to approach the episcopate through canvassing, nor that powerful men be employed as supporters through the payment of money. And so that these matters may more easily be observed, let clerics or citizens not presume to make or subscribe to any decree without the knowledge or consent of the metropolitan.

“Prohibit all these things through the punishment imposed by your severity, so that in your own Church and in the aforesaid province discipline, friendly to good works, may be preserved.”

Caesarius presented this petition in person, as can be sufficiently inferred from its very form. Symmachus approved the holy man’s zeal and prohibited everything whose prohibition he requested in this petition, by a letter given on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Probus, a most illustrious man—that is, in the year 513. These letters may be seen in Labbe, where they are printed after Caesarius’s petition.

### 30.

When Caesarius returned to Arles, he did not immediately find all the bishops obedient to him, although, according to Saint Leo’s division confirmed by Symmachus, they were required to be subject to him as primate. Certainly the bishop of Aix showed himself less compliant.

Saint Caesarius therefore sent the following year Abbot Aegidius and the notary Messianus to Rome, so that they might present another supplicatory petition to Symmachus. It will be useful to append it from Labbe, col. 1310, where it reads as follows:

“As much as the apostolic see claims for itself primacy among all the bishops of the churches spread throughout the world, and as much as its authority surpasses all others in firmness through synodal decrees, so much ought it, through its provident care, to preserve unshaken what it once granted of its own accord, so that the Church of Arles may enjoy its privileges.

“Through the bishop Caesarius it now sets forth the substance of its petition and asks that the authority which it has hitherto possessed be confirmed by your authority, so that what the venerable see once ordered to be preserved by perpetual sanction, and what was specifically decreed in pragmatic constitutions, may now also be confirmed by the commands of your blessedness.

“Command also that the bishop of the city of Aix be admonished by your holiness concerning these decrees, so that, whenever he has been summoned by the metropolitan bishop of the Church of Arles to a synodal council, or whenever divine religion requires him for some matter of ordination, he may not at all refuse to come. Thus what the authority of the ancients established over many ages may remain inviolate through you bishops for the present and future generations.

“Given by Aegidius, abbot, and Messianus, notary.”

### 31

Symmachus replied by letter, inserted here from Labbe, in these words:

> “He who safeguards the venerable decrees of the Fathers shows himself a friend of unblemished religion; and he who takes care that no opportunity for excesses remains demonstrates that he is concerned for the good of grace. It is reasonable that the holy Church of Arles should enjoy its proper privileges; and what antiquity granted, and the authority of the Fathers strengthened, new presumption ought not to violate. Yet this must be done in such a way that the privileges acquired over time by the other Churches do not waver, since what touches the injury of the whole cannot be secure in only one part.
>
> “Since those provisions remain which the decrees of the Fathers granted to individual Churches, we decree that, concerning matters which may arise either in the provinces of Gaul or of Spain in relation to religion, the diligence of your fraternity shall keep watch. And if reason should require the presence of priests, then, preserving custom, each person summoned by the authority of your affection shall assemble when admonished. And if, with God’s help, the controversy that has arisen can be cut off, let us attribute this to his merits; otherwise, let the nature of the matter at issue reach the apostolic see through your report, so that, when everything has been conducted in its proper order, the enemy of goodness may find no place in which to flatter himself.
>
> “Therefore, as we said above, the privileges long preserved in each Church are to be maintained. And if the bishop of Aix, or anyone else, summoned by the metropolitan bishop in accordance with the definition of the canons, should refuse to obey, let him know that he will be subjected—which we do not wish—to ecclesiastical discipline.”

### 32

> “In this matter also we especially wish you to be vigilant: if anyone from the regions of Gaul or Spain, compelled by ecclesiastical rank and office, should have to come to us, let him undertake the journey of his pilgrimage with the knowledge of your fraternity. Thus neither will his honor suffer any insult through ignorance, nor, once uncertainty has been removed, will he be able to be admitted by us into the grace of communion with a confident mind. May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother. Given on the third day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Flavius, a man of illustrious rank”—that is, in the year 514.

From this we understand that at that time not only was the bishop of Aix compelled to be subject to the bishop of Arles, but that the functions of the Roman pontiff had been entrusted to Caesarius not in Gaul alone, but in Spain as well. Moreover, that primacy of the Church of Arles, extended throughout Gaul, was passed on to several successors of Caesarius, to whom the pontiffs for a long time entrusted their functions and transmitted the pallium. But it is not the place here to pursue that matter at greater length. I therefore proceed to other deeds of the Saint.

## § IV. Continuation of the same chronology up to the year 530, in which various councils and the deeds of the Saint against the Semipelagians are set forth

### 33

In the year 515, Pope Hormisdas wrote to Caesarius concerning the bishops of Dardania and Illyricum who had returned to communion with the apostolic see, after the Eutychian heresy had divided them. In this letter the pontiff declares the holy man’s zeal for the good of the Church in these words:

> “For these matters your fraternity has very often grieved with us, mindful of the apostolic reading in which it is shown: ‘If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.’”

Labbe presents the entire letter in volume IV, column 1474 and following. In the year 524, during the consulship of Opilio in the West, Saint Caesarius, on the occasion of the dedication of the church of Saint Mary, summoned the bishops to the Fourth Council of Arles, which some have called the Third.

Some have thought that Caesarius’s monastery church was then dedicated, but they were plainly mistaken, since that church was dedicated on 26 August, whereas the council was held in June. More correctly, therefore, Saxius writes in his *Pontifical of Arles*, under Caesarius:

> “In this provincial council the basilica of blessed Mary was dedicated, which the populace calls the Virgin of the Greater [Church]; today it is a college of canons.”

Five canons are recorded as having been enacted at that council, chiefly concerning the ordination of clerics. Caesarius presided and subscribed first; after him came sixteen men, partly bishops and partly presbyters serving as the bishops’ legates. Consult Labbe, volume IV, column 1622 and following, where you will find further observations concerning this council.

Among other matters, canon 2 decreed that no layman could be promoted to the diaconate, priesthood, or episcopate “unless conversion has first been undertaken by him for an entire year.” Concerning this matter, in the year 528 Pope Felix IV wrote to Caesarius, strongly insisting that this law be observed and that hands be laid upon no one hastily.

When first published, that letter was marked “after the consulship of Boethius,” and was therefore attributed to Felix III and dated to the year 488, when Caesarius was not yet a bishop. But Sirmondus detected the error from an Arles manuscript, in which “after the consulship of Mavortius” was correctly read; this corresponds to the year 528. The letter, together with Sirmondus’s note, may be seen in Labbe, column 1657 and following.

### 34

Before Felix’s letter came the Council of Carpentoractum, held in the year 527 by sixteen bishops, again under the presidency of Caesarius. Only one canon is recorded as having been decreed there. Yet, together with the other bishops, Caesarius showed how carefully he observed the statutes of the Council of Arles.

It was ordained there, in canon 3, that a person who ordained a cleric contrary to the decrees of the council “might not celebrate Masses for an entire year.” Agraecius, bishop of Antipolis, had violated the statutes of Arles by an unlawful ordination, although he himself had subscribed to them through a legate.

Therefore Caesarius, together with the Fathers of the Council of Carpentoractum, imposed the aforesaid penalty upon Agraecius by letter [see below]. The letter was published together with the council in Labbe, column 1663 and following. From this it is clear that the Saint was not only diligent in enacting laws, but equally firm and constant in enforcing their observance.

The councils convened by Saint Caesarius up to this point concerned only ecclesiastical discipline. It must now be examined what this same holy man did to eradicate the remnants of the Pelagian heresy in Gaul.

### 35

There is no doubt that around this time he wrote on grace and free will and refuted the errors of the Semipelagians. This is attested by the anonymous author who interpolated Gennadius’s catalogue *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*. Hear the author’s own words from chapter 86 of that catalogue:

> “Caesarius, bishop of the city of Arles, a man renowned for holiness and virtue, wrote excellent and highly esteemed little works, necessary for monks. He also published testimonies concerning grace and free will, supported by the judgments of divine Scripture and the holy Fathers, in which he teaches that a human being can do nothing good from his own resources unless divine grace has first gone before him. Pope Felix also strengthened this work by his letter and made it more widely known. He flourished at the time when Faustus also flourished, while Anastasius was governing the empire.”

Formerly Baronius thought in his notes on the Martyrology that these words belonged to Gennadius himself. But later writers proved clearly enough that they belonged to another person who interpolated Gennadius’s catalogue.

The lifespans of the two men are sufficient to demonstrate this. Hear Gennadius himself, in chapter 91, concerning Theodulus:

> “This writer,” he says, “died three years ago, while Zeno was reigning.”

Pagius therefore rightly concludes, under the year 490, that Gennadius wrote at the beginning of Anastasius’s reign and no later than the year 494, since Zeno died in 491.

But Caesarius lived until the year 542, as we shall prove, and the interpolator speaks of him as though he were already dead. Gennadius therefore could not have written these words while publishing his catalogue, nor could he have added them later, since it is in no way plausible that he lived so long. And even if he had prolonged his life that far, he could not have fallen into the errors committed by the author of this eulogy.

For the author of the eulogy first erred when he said that Caesarius’s work had been confirmed by Pope Felix; as we shall see, this was done by Boniface II. He erred again when he represented Caesarius as entirely contemporary with Faustus. For even if the year of Faustus’s death is uncertain, it is nevertheless unlikely that he lived into the sixth century, so that he appears to have died when Caesarius was still a young man, or perhaps even an adolescent. See *Gallia Christiana*, volume I, columns 392–393.

### 36

More recent writers commonly assert two things here: namely, that Caesarius wrote a book on Grace and Free Will, and that this book of Caesarius was expressly composed against Faustus of Riez.

I greatly doubt that anyone will ever produce an ancient and adequate witness for these assertions. I am therefore astonished that learned men have written them with such unanimity, as though they were unquestionable and certain. Perhaps they were led to this opinion by the eulogy just quoted.

Yet neither conclusion follows from it except by an entirely weak and ambiguous conjecture, drawn from the title prefixed to a certain book of Faustus. Hear Norisius, book II of his *Pelagian History*, chapter 22:

> “Caesarius . . . published a book on Grace and Free Will, under precisely the same title that Faustus had given his own work, so that by this most effective antidote he might drive out the poisons of the bishop of Riez; in that volume he most solidly defended the teaching of Saint Augustine against Faustus’s attacks. Hence that very celebrated man, Ennodius of Pavia, says to Caesarius in a letter: ‘Whatever great author he may be, he owes it to you that you magnify him with the gift of eloquence.’”

Baronius adds a notable marginal note under the year 508:

> “Namely, Saint Augustine, whom he defended against Faustus, who was attacking him.”

Thus Norisius writes magnificently, but with greater grandeur than solidity.

### 37

For just as we cannot doubt that Caesarius refuted the errors of the Semipelagians in writings on Grace and Free Will, among whom Faustus is numbered, so it cannot be proved—neither from the eulogy in Gennadius and the similarity of the titles, nor from the *Life of Caesarius*, where the matter is discussed in section 40, nor from any other source—that those writings expressly refuted Faustus, since no one mentions Faustus.

Moreover, what Norisius, following Baronius, draws here from Saint Ennodius’s letter cannot refer to these writings of Caesarius unless we overturn the entire chronological order. Ennodius’s letter was written around the year 513, since in it Ennodius congratulates Caesarius on the things that happened to him with Theodoric, king of the Goths, in the year 513. But the writings of Caesarius mentioned above are many years later, as will become clear. Ennodius is therefore speaking of Caesarius’s homilies, not of writings on Grace and Free Will.

Nor is Norisius’s further assertion any stronger, namely that Caesarius defended Saint Augustine. For although Caesarius was a lover of Augustine and of his doctrine, none of the ancients asserted that he took up his pen in Augustine’s defense.

Whether what Norisius adds in these words concerning a lost book is more certain than the other claims—“But this book too, to the great detriment of the Augustinian school, did not reach the hands of posterity”—I shall discuss below, when I examine whether these writings of Caesarius are different from the chapters of the Council of Orange.

### 38

The holy man, in order to strike the Semipelagians more forcefully from a higher authority, appealed to the Roman Church. After receiving from there articles of faith concerning grace and free will, he convened a council at Orange, at which the errors of the Semipelagians were condemned and the Catholic faith triumphed.

That council, which was the Second Council of Orange, was held “on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the consulship of Decius the Younger, a man of illustrious rank—that is, in the year of Christ 529, the third year of Pope Felix IV and the third year of Athalaric, king of Italy,” as stated in the heading in Labbe, volume IV, column 1666.

Caesarius presided and subscribed first. After him came twelve other bishops, and finally eight illustrious men, among whom the first was Liberius, prefect of the Gauls and patrician.

Thus the council was most celebrated, not because of the number of its participants, but because the Pelagian and Semipelagian heresies were utterly crushed and because the supreme pontiff subsequently confirmed its decisions.

### 39

The Fathers themselves explain the occasion of this council in its preface, and at the same time indicate that the doctrinal articles proposed there for the faithful to believe had been sent from the apostolic see. Hear the preface itself:

> “When, with God’s favor and at his invitation, we had assembled for the dedication of the basilica which our most illustrious son, the prefect and patrician Liberius, built in the city of Orange with the utmost devotion, and when a spiritual discussion had arisen among us concerning matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline, it came to our attention that there were some who, through simplicity, wished to hold less cautiously and not according to the rule of the Catholic faith concerning grace and free will.
>
> “Therefore, in accordance with the admonition and authority of the apostolic see, it seemed right and reasonable to us that we should set forth for observance by all, and sign with our own hands, a few chapters sent to us by the apostolic see, which had been collected especially for this matter by the ancient Fathers from the books of sacred Scripture, in order to instruct those who think otherwise than they ought.
>
> “When these have been read, let anyone who until now has not believed concerning grace and free will as he ought not delay to incline his mind toward those things which accord with the Catholic faith.”

Twenty-five chapters opposed to the Semipelagian heresy follow these words. They may be seen there together with the subscriptions, as may various annotations by different writers on them.

### 40

The Benedictines mentioned above, in volume III of their *Literary History of France*, page 225, think that the interpolator of Gennadius is referring to these chapters of Orange in the words already quoted:

> “He also published testimonies concerning grace and free will, supported by the judgments of divine Scripture and the holy Fathers, in which he teaches that a human being can do nothing good from his own resources unless divine grace has first gone before him.”

It follows from this that Caesarius wrote no book on Grace and Free Will apart from these chapters of the Council of Orange, which oppose the errors of the Semipelagians—and therefore those of Faustus as well—and which were drawn almost entirely from the books of Saint Augustine.

I admit that this opinion conflicts with most recent writers, who, following Baronius and Norisius, assert that Caesarius composed an additional book in defense of Augustine’s doctrine against Faustus. Nevertheless, I can scarcely doubt that the former opinion is true and that the aforesaid chapters of the Council of Orange are precisely the writings of Caesarius mentioned in Gennadius’s catalogue.

Let the diligent reader attend only to the words, and he will easily discover this with me.

### 41

That author says:

> “He published testimonies concerning grace and free will, supported by the judgments of divine Scripture and the holy Fathers, etc.”

What, I ask, are the chapters of Orange if not testimonies concerning grace and free will, strengthened by the authority of sacred Scripture and the ancient Fathers? Hear the words appended to the final chapter in Labbe, column 1671:

> “And so, according to the sentences of the holy Scriptures written above and the definitions of the ancient Fathers, we ought, with God’s favor, both to preach and to believe that through the sin of the first man free will was so inclined and weakened that thereafter no one could either love God as he ought, or believe in God, or do what is good for God, unless the grace of divine mercy had first gone before him.”

Thus, whether we consider the subject treated in the chapters, the form of the chapters themselves, or the doctrine defined in them, everything persuades us that these are the very writings of Caesarius of which the interpolator of Gennadius speaks.

We shall therefore search in vain for another volume of Caesarius on Grace and Free Will, since that work never appears to have existed.

### 42

In the same year Saint Caesarius held the Council of Vaison, as had been decreed the previous year at the Council of Carpentoractum. Five canons were enacted there, establishing various points of ecclesiastical discipline. The diligent reader will find them in Labbe, column 1679 and following.

Having briefly discussed this council in chronological order—it was the last council at which the holy man is recorded to have taken part—let us return to his deeds against the Semipelagians.

When the errors to which many had hitherto firmly adhered had been condemned at the Council of Orange, some did not fail to murmur strongly against Saint Caesarius. They were aware that through his efforts and authority the council had been held and that its statutes had been enacted.

The *Life*, section 46, bears witness to this, recording the following:

> “Many rivals indeed arose who resisted his teaching concerning grace . . . For through the whispers and malicious interpretation of certain people, a sinister suspicion—entirely without foundation—arose in the regions of Gaul against the preaching of the man of God.”

### 43

> “For this reason the bishops of Christ residing beyond the Isère, gathered together by love of charity, assembled in the city of Valence. The blessed Caesarius too, however, was unable to hasten there as he had arranged, because of his customary illness.”

Cointius, under the year 536, section 9, thought that the author of the *Life* had suffered a lapse of memory here and that the Council of Orange should be substituted for the Synod of Valence.

But I am astonished that such a thought could have occurred to a learned man. It is clear that another synod is designated, distinct from the Council of Orange.

First, Caesarius took part in the Council of Orange; he could not attend this one because illness prevented him. Moreover, the bishops residing beyond the Isère were bishops of the province of Vienne. They did not attend the Council of Orange, but they did attend this Council of Valence.

Therefore, what Cointius objects concerning the councils of Valence, which he notes as having been held long before or afterward, cannot at all invalidate this identification, since those councils were different from the present one, whose acts have perished.

This Council of Valence appears to have been held toward the end of the year 529 or at the beginning of the following year. For the *Life* indicates that it intervened between the Council of Orange, against which some had protested, and the confirmation of that same Council of Orange, in these words:

> “For Boniface, too, of blessed memory, trampling down the purpose of the quarrelers, confirmed the petition of Saint Caesarius by apostolic authority.”

It appears from the *Life* just cited that at first not all those bishops of the province of Vienne favored Caesarius and the statutes of Orange. This, I think, was the reason for their assembly.

Nevertheless, the better party prevailed, chiefly through the efforts of Cyprian, bishop of Toulon and a disciple of Caesarius himself, who acted on behalf of the good cause.

### 44

Finally, the confirmation of the supreme pontiff, sought and obtained by Caesarius in January of the year 530, contributed greatly to achieving complete victory over the Semipelagians.

To obtain this confirmation, the Saint had written to Boniface II, whom he still thought was a cardinal and his friend, asking him to act with Felix IV for the confirmation of the council.

But Felix died in the meantime, and Boniface himself was raised to the pontificate. He confirmed the Council of Orange by sending a letter to Caesarius, which is marked in Labbe, column 1689, “on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, men of illustrious rank”—that is, in the year 530.

I insert the beginning of the letter, which confirms the matters just mentioned:

> “Through our son Armenius, a presbyter and abbot, we received a letter from your fraternity, which, as appears, you had sent to us while still unaware of the priesthood entrusted to me, in the charity by which we are bound in God. In it you had thought that you should request that what you had asked of my predecessor, Pope Felix of blessed memory, for the strengthening of the Catholic faith, should be expressed through my intervention.
>
> “But since the will of heaven arranged that what you had hoped to obtain from him through us you should instead obtain from us directly, we have not delayed giving a Catholic response to your request, which you conceived with such praiseworthy concern.”

### 45

He then explains what Caesarius had requested, in these words:

> “For you indicate that certain bishops of Gaul, although they already acknowledge that all other good things proceed from God’s grace, wish faith alone, by which we believe in Christ, to belong to nature and not to grace; and that faith has remained to human beings from Adam—in free will, which it is impious to say—and is not even now bestowed upon each individual by the generosity of divine mercy.
>
> “You ask us, in order to remove ambiguity, to confirm by the authority of the apostolic see your confession, in which you define, contrary to these views, that right faith in Christ and the beginning of every good will, according to Catholic truth, are inspired in the minds of individuals through the prevenient grace of God.”

After inserting a few remarks to prove that faith comes to us from divine grace, he continues:

> “We rejoice that your fraternity, after discussion with certain priests of Gaul, has likewise understood this according to the Catholic faith.”

After adding other arguments against the Semipelagians, he confirms the definition of the Council of Orange in these words:

> “Therefore, after careful deliberation in a fitting spirit, we approve the confession written above as consonant with the Catholic rules of the Fathers.”

### 46

Later the pontiff also indicates that not a few people had resisted Caesarius, though he hopes that they will finally yield to the truth. He writes:

> “After briefly setting these matters forth, we have not thought it necessary to respond to the remaining absurdities of the Pelagian error, which that letter appears to contain—the letter which you informed us had been sent to you by a certain priest. For we hope that, by divine mercy, he will work through the ministry and teaching of your fraternity in the hearts of all those whom you reported to dissent, so that they may believe that every good will proceeds not from themselves but from divine grace, when they find themselves already wishing to defend what they had stubbornly endeavored to oppose.”

The pontiff prophesied truly. For, as the *Life* records:

> “With Christ granting it, little by little the bishops of the Churches accepted what the devil had wished them to abandon in a sudden outburst of anger.”

This is certainly a great glory of Saint Caesarius:

> “Thus I would dare to affirm concerning him that although other Fathers fought more extensively against heretics in their writings, none fought with greater prudence, a more successful outcome, or, finally, a fuller victory than he himself achieved in his struggle against the Semipelagians.”

## § V. Final part of the chronology up to the Saint’s death; the date of his death examined

### 47

After the victory over the Semipelagians just described, the Saint, who held purity of conduct no less dear than purity of faith, entered upon another struggle.

Contumeliosus, bishop of Riez, who had taken part in most of the councils held by Caesarius, had stained the holiness of his profession with various crimes. Against him the holy man proceeded with the Gallic bishops according to the canons, and sent the proceedings to the Roman pontiff, so that Contumeliosus might be removed from the episcopate as unworthy of that rank.

Accordingly, in the year 534, John II, who then presided over Peter’s chair, sent Caesarius a letter of this kind:

> “We willingly received the letter of your charity, in which, pleading bodily necessities, you also reported what that sacred man who has fallen had done. We grieve over the loss of a bishop, yet it is necessary to preserve the rigor of the canons. Therefore our authority has suspended the aforesaid man from the episcopal order. For it is not lawful that one polluted by crimes should serve in the sacred ministries.
>
> “But, under your direction, let him be sent to a monastery, where, mindful of his offenses, he should not cease to pour out tears in penitence, so that he may obtain mercy from our Lord Jesus Christ, who has mercy on all. In his place appoint a visitor until the Church, which has been deprived of his priesthood, may deserve to have a proper priest.”

This letter was published in Labbe, volume IV, columns 1756–1757, where the remainder may be seen.

Two other letters of the same pontiff precede it: one to the bishops of Gaul and another to the priests and deacons of Bishop Contumeliosus. In them the same judgment against Contumeliosus is expressed. In the latter, the pontiff adds that responsibility for the matter had been entrusted to Caesarius.

### 48

Contumeliosus appealed from the first judgment to Agapetus, the successor of Pope John. But it appears uncertain whether Agapetus was already pontiff before the sentence was executed. Indeed, since John’s letters were dated April 534, more than an entire year before Agapetus’s pontificate, it is scarcely likely that execution was delayed so long that Contumeliosus could appeal to Agapetus before it took place.

This point should have been observed because Contumeliosus complained to Agapetus that Caesarius had not granted his appeal but had executed the sentence despite it. Hear Agapetus’s letter, to be assigned shortly:
