> “Your fraternity would have acted better,” says the pontiff, “if, after he had lodged an appeal to the apostolic see and requested a hearing, you had allowed nothing concerning his person to be diminished from the time of the sentence, so that the matter under inquiry after the appeal might remain intact.”

The reason why Caesarius had not omitted anything in the execution of the sentence on account of the appeal can easily be inferred from these words: namely, that Contumeliosus was appealing to John, by whom he had already been condemned and who had entrusted Caesarius with the entire responsibility for executing the sentence.

If we accept this conjecture—and the sequence of events persuades us that we should—there was certainly nothing in Caesarius’s conduct for Agapetus to criticize or disapprove. Yet it is probable that Agapetus did not know that the sentence had been either issued or confirmed by his predecessor. This explains why he admitted the appeal and wrote to Caesarius that he would have acted better if, after the appeal, he had not proceeded with the execution.

### 49

Whatever the reason may have been for Agapetus’s admission of the appeal, it is certain that he admitted it. For he sent Caesarius a letter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, which begins as follows in Labbe, column 1798:

> “We had wished, dearest brother, that, while the reputation of Bishop Contumeliosus remained unimpaired, neither would you have been compelled to undertake a trial nor would there have been cause for us to pass judgment . . .
>
> “Therefore, since he wished to flee to the aid of an appeal, as he asserts, relying on the presumption of his innocence, let us strive [perhaps: endeavor] by constant prayers that the benefit of a renewed examination may restore him acquitted to the joy of all.
>
> “For, with the help of our God, we are going to delegate the hearing, so that, according to the provisions of the venerable canons and under the consideration of justice, everything that has been done or conducted concerning such a matter before your fraternity may be demanded by the most diligent investigation.”

### 50

Then, after attempting to prove that it was equitable for the defendant to be heard again, he adds:

> “We now wish Bishop Contumeliosus, his own property having been restored to him, to remain suspended from the administration of the ecclesiastical patrimony and from the celebration of Masses. For if truth supports him, he will receive by judgment, more honorably, what he seemed to have lost by judgment than he would have seized by usurpation.”

The remainder may be seen there.

It is not at all established, however, whether the pontiff actually sent judges to Gaul, much less whether anything was changed in the sentence pronounced against Contumeliosus.

Nevertheless, I scarcely doubt that Caesarius gave Agapetus a more accurate account of everything and explained that he had acted entirely according to the judgment of Pope John.

Moreover, when Pope John had sent Caesarius the canons according to which he was to proceed in the case of Contumeliosus, Caesarius composed from them a written treatise, furnished with considerable force of language and argument, in which he proves that a cleric convicted of adultery must never be restored to his former rank.

That writing, together with the aforesaid canons, appears in Labbe, column 1757 and following.

> **Note:** In our edition, volume LXVI, chapter 28 and following. Through a typographical error, that treatise, together with the appended canons, was not placed after John’s letter to Caesarius, which is printed in the same volume, column 25. At the head of the canons it would also be better to read “Canons sent by John to Caesarius” than “Canons attributed to John.” —Editor.

Scholars generally think that this work is Caesarius’s, since his zeal and style shine through it. There also seems to be no doubt that it was composed against Contumeliosus.

It is not equally certain, however, whether it was sent to Rome to the pontiff or recited to judges delegated by him.

Baillet, who discusses this event under 27 August in his entry on Caesarius, column 425, sets out the order confusedly. He reports that the first sentence was executed after the judges delegated by Agapetus had arrived, and then tries to infer from this event that the bishops of Gaul executed sentences despite an appeal to the pontiff.

But that does not follow from this history as we have truly related it. Baillet could never have proved that Caesarius continued the execution after Agapetus had admitted the appeal, although he narrates the matter confidently.

### 51

On the same day Caesarius received other replies from Agapetus, from which the Saint’s immense mercy toward the poor again becomes known.

He had not spared even the sacred ornaments of his Church in order to assist those in need. He had now consulted the pontiff about whether it was permissible to sell ecclesiastical estates for the same purpose.

The pontiff replied that this was entirely forbidden by the canons. His letter is preserved in the Labbe cited above, volume IV, column 1798. I insert its beginning:

> “So great, by God’s favor, is our devotion toward your fraternity, and toward those things which most willingly ought to be granted for the support of the poor, that we do not consider it burdensome at all when you ask what your desires require.
>
> “But the most venerable and unmistakable decrees of the Fathers hold us back. By them we are forbidden, under any title, to transfer estates belonging by right to the Church over which the almighty Lord has appointed us to preside into the rights of others.
>
> “In this matter, too, we believe that your wisdom will be most grateful that we do not presume, for any reason or out of regard for any person, to act in any way against the provisions or rules of the ancient definition.”

There is also preserved in Labbe, volume V, columns 293 and 314, a letter of Vigilius to Caesarius, dated 6 March of the year 538, at a time when Vigilius was not yet the legitimate pontiff. In it the Saint is entrusted with the responsibility of imposing penance upon a certain man polluted by an incestuous marriage.

From this, however, it does not follow that our Saint actually did anything in the matter, nor even that he consulted the apostolic see concerning it. Perhaps Vigilius attempted in this way to win Caesarius over to his side, while Caesarius took care not to acknowledge Vigilius’s pontificate by accepting the case.

### 52

Before beginning to discuss the date of his blessed death, it will be useful to insert here the apparition granted to the Saint and the temple built and dedicated on that account to Saint Hermes the martyr.

Messianus the presbyter, one of the authors of the *Life* and an eyewitness of these events, relates the whole matter in a letter to Bishop Viventius, which Mabillon published from an Arles manuscript in volume I of his *Annals*, page 683.

Here is the letter itself:

> “To my lord Viventius, bishop: Messianus, most humble in every respect—by name, though not in office—a presbyter, wishes you to prosper in the things entrusted to you.
>
> “Dearest brother, after reading your affectionate letter, I cannot explain in writing to you how sweet and pleasant the desert has been. You yourself know better than I how, under God’s direction, our journey was both happy and prosperous.
>
> “But we do not wish you to remain unaware of what happened after you departed from us, when we obeyed the words of our master—or rather, the apostolic leader—and how honorable it is to praise the mighty works of God.
>
> “For on the seventh day after we left you, when we had come to a certain place where there were very pleasant and delightful meadows, with a stream from a spring flowing below, we solemnly celebrated the rites of Mass there. It was the day on which the feast of the outstanding teacher, the most blessed Augustine, was being observed; by his admonitions and examples our devout master regularly instructs us in the schools of righteousness.

### 53

> “When we spent the night there, around the middle hour of the night the Lord appeared, bringing with him Peter the devout fisherman, Paul the outstanding teacher, Hermes the most glorious martyr, and Augustine the eminent preacher.

> “At their arrival I, a wretched and unhappy sinner, was awakened by a marvelous fragrance and incomparable light—not because my merits demanded it, but so that I might become a witness to the truth.

> “Then the Lord called our master by name, saying: ‘Caesarius, cultivate the vineyard entrusted to you; cut off what must be cut off and nourish what must be nourished, because the coin of your reward is not delayed. And do penance, because you have carelessly consigned to oblivion the memory of the martyr Hermes, which you presently possess amid the sacred mysteries of the Mass, whose feast is today venerated and celebrated by the faithful.’

> “After saying these things, he departed from us, blessed in every respect.

> “When morning came, we rose and devoted ourselves to the divine work. Before the divine office had yet been completed, he had disclosed to us more and more than usual. Finally, after the Gospel admonition, drawing long sighs from the depths of his breast, he began in this way:

> “‘Woe to me, wretched man, because for three years I have unhappily consigned the memory of the martyr Hermes to oblivion, occupied with various empty tales. His memory shall not be abandoned forever.’

> “Bringing his words to an end, he turned toward the altar and set about completing what he had begun. Unable to bear this, I proclaimed everything aloud before all, in the proper order, just as I had seen and heard it.”

### 54.

“Having completed the divine office, he raised a stone with us at the place where the Lord had appeared to him, and upon it fixed the banner of the Lord’s cross. Then, after arranging and appointing everything, as we were leaving, the priest Ursus, from the church of Catorro, came to meet us. From him we were kindly received that day and night. His boy—who, while you were present, slipped through the church railings and was suddenly seized by a demon—was delivered by our lord, the master of pious instruction; he still lives and serves you.

“On the following day we reached Arles, where we were received with great honor and glory by everyone, both clergy and people. To them he gave a blessing and the kiss of peace, and read aloud letters of greeting composed by the Apostolic See. After this he returned with the necessary equipment to the place mentioned above, where he built a church in honor of the blessed martyr Hermes, which he assigned in perpetual right to the See of Arles. At its consecration we wish and ask you to be present on the octave of Easter; then we shall speak more fully about these and other matters. Pray for me to the Lord, dearest father.”

It is indeed remarkable that nothing about this apparition is reported in the Saint’s Life, since Messianus is one of the authors of the Life. Nevertheless, we do not have sufficient grounds on that account for rejecting the letter’s authenticity: Messianus may deliberately have omitted this episode for reasons known to him. The letter’s credibility is confirmed by Life II.16, where the healing of the boy of the priest Ursus is discussed.

Moreover, it is not improbable that the vision occurred when the Saint was returning from Rome to Arles at the beginning of the year 514; the letters of greeting composed by the Apostolic See, which he is said to have brought to Arles, suggest this. The foundation of the church of Saint Hermes and its dedication, however, took place later, though at a time not sufficiently known to us. [Col. 1278A] I therefore proceed to examine the year of his death.

### 55.

I shall not linger over refuting the errors of those who thought that Caesarius lived in the seventh century, since others have already refuted them adequately, and their error is abundantly clear throughout this entire commentary. I shall therefore prove only that he died in the year 542, and briefly answer an opinion differing little from this.

The Saint died, as the Life states in II.34, on 27 August, a full thirty years after the foundation of his monastery and one day after its dedication. Since that dedication took place on 26 August, it seems that it could have occurred in no other year than 512. In that year 26 August fell on a Sunday, as is clear from the dominical letter, which was then G. Moreover, the dedication could not have taken place in 513, the year in which, according to the opinion of others, it would have had to occur, since in August of that year Caesarius was in Italy, as may easily be inferred from the events involving King Theodoric and Pope Symmachus reported in § III. Nor could it have occurred in 511: it is in no way likely that the monastery had already been completed then, since the city was not freed from siege until 510, after which the monastery began to be rebuilt.

This, then, was the first argument which was sufficient by itself for Pagi, at the year 544, no. 8, to declare this date absolutely certain.

### 56.

A second argument for this date was advanced by Bollandus in the commentary on Saint Caesaria for 12 January, no. 6, and is drawn from the time of the succession of Auxanius.

For there exists a letter of Pope Vigilius to Auxanius, the successor of Caesarius, dated 18 October, “again after the consulship of Basil, the most illustrious man,” that is, in the year 543. In it he writes that he had received letters concerning Auxanius’s ordination, as well as the pallium and other things requested by him, and that these had been brought by John the priest and Teredius the deacon.

Now it is not probable that, between 27 August and 18 October, so many and such varied events were completed: namely, the election and ordination of a metropolitan bishop; the dispatch of envoys with letters to the pope; their journey from Arles to Rome; their audience with Vigilius; and his reply—for all these matters are ordinarily conducted slowly and with mature deliberation.

Norisius denies this inference in *Pelagian History* II.22, arguing that everything was accomplished within fifty-two days, and consequently that Caesarius died only in the year 543. But this is scarcely plausible, even if every other argument were lacking, as will readily be apparent to anyone who considers how much had to be accomplished within that short interval.

The year of the death of Saint Caesarius was therefore 542, the year to which scholars today generally agree. The Saint’s actions during his final illness, his death itself, and his burial are discussed at the end of the Life.

## § VI. The Saint’s Testament; Writings Left to Posterity; Disciples; Epitaph

### 57.

Baronius published the testament of Saint Caesarius in volume VI of the *Annals*, under the year 508. He says there, no. 27: “We received a copy taken from the archive of the Church of Arles, transcribed by Claudius Saxi, notary, from the archdeacon of the Church of Arles, Franciscus Claretus, while he was in Rome.” He further notes in the same place that it “has been abridged at least in the date, the consul, and the subscription of Caesarius himself and of the witnesses.” Before no. 23 he had said that it was “somewhat corrupt and eaten away by age.”

The same testament was subsequently published by Saxius in *The Arles Pontificate*, under Caesarius; by Vincentius Barralis in the *Lérins Chronology*, p. 268 onward; by Holstenius in part III of the *Code of Rules*, p. 52 onward; and by Cointius in the *Annals of the Franks*, under the year 542, no. 23.

It is certainly worthy of being read here as well. I therefore append it from Baronius’s edition.

**Peace to the Church of Arles.**

### 58.

“Caesarius, bishop, to the priests and deacons; to the holy and venerable Caesaria, abbess, whom the Lord through my insignificance placed over our monastery; and to the entire congregation which the Lord in his grace has established there: eternal salvation in the Lord.

“Since ecclesiastical piety, in accordance with its customary practice, properly orders that assistance be given through generosity to pilgrims and the destitute, how much more, when opportunity or necessity arises, ought it to enlarge the pious bowels of its mercy in order to give something to the saints and to those who fear God?

“And therefore, in accordance with this letter, which we have confirmed by the subscription of our hand and beneath which we have added the date and consul, I, by God’s dispensation, have drawn up this testament of mine, or subscribed it with my own hand, and have confirmed it according to praetorian or civil law, and by a codicil in place of those [legal forms].

“I, Caesarius the sinner, when I have paid the debt owed by human flesh, decree and order that the entire monastery of Saint John at Arles, which I founded, shall canonically remain under the authority of the bishop of Arles, and I wish and command it to be my heir. Let all other men and women be disinherited. Let everything that I have given, bequeathed, or ordered to be given to anyone through this testament of mine be given and completed. Moreover, I leave the bishop of Arles as co-heir with my monastery. Those whom I order to be free, male or female, shall all be free.”

### 59.

“Although I possessed nothing from the property of my parents, I was ashamed to presume to make this testament. Yet a certain thought compelled me: that I should, out of pious affection, contribute something to my Church for the sake of the many fearful words of the Savior which the wicked will hear him speak: ‘Go into eternal fire.’

“And lest, after my death, some of my relatives should presume to trouble the Church over which I preside, except regarding those things which I shall give them as gifts of affection, I have therefore wished to set out my intention more fully: namely, that my relatives should not presume to demand anything from the aforesaid monastery or from the bishop of the Church of Arles beyond what I have given or shall give them.

“To the holy lord and my master, the archbishop who shall worthily succeed me, although everything is in his power, I nevertheless decree that, if he wishes and considers it fitting, all the Easter vestments given to me shall serve him, together with the shaggy chasuble and the tunic, or *galnape*, which I shall leave in the better condition.

“My remaining garments, except for the amictory *birrus*, let both my clerics and laymen divide among themselves, with the grace or authorization of the lord archbishop, at his command—or rather, at his gift. The things which I previously transferred to the monastery by donation I now confirm; and if I have given anything to anyone out of consideration for piety, whether by letter, by a written note, or orally, I wish it to remain valid.”

### 60.

“I also customarily ask that the cell which the subdeacon Augustine of blessed memory possessed in the atrium of Saint Stephen, on the right-hand side for those entering, may the lord archbishop perpetually deign to grant by right to the monastery’s administrators for their secure guardianship. Thus let the administrators of the monastery hold it in succession for themselves.

“And this in particular I wish, and so I ask you, lord archbishop: let the holy congregation have no administrator for the monastery or priest for the basilica of Saint Mary except one whom it itself has chosen or requested to be ordained.

“And although I presume upon your piety, lord archbishop, nevertheless, lest you perhaps receive troublesome suggestions from anyone against our monastery, I adjure you by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the dreadful day of judgment, never to allow the ancient enemy to prevail with you, nor consent to let your handmaids be saddened, nor permit anything to be taken from what they possess or what we have given them.

“For, by God’s favor, we have sold the Church’s property by direct legal right to no secular person without discernment or justice, except only what is less useful and unproductive for the Church. Whatever we have granted to holy souls devoted to God, with the consent or subscription of the holy brothers, shall remain theirs in perpetuity.”

### 61.

“But you, dear little daughters, I adjure by the inseparable Holy Trinity and by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ to beg the bishop who, by God’s appointment, shall worthily succeed me, with all affection, as your lord, and to love him with a pure mind, and not to grieve him by your disobedience.

“For we trust in God’s mercy that he will inspire all priests entrusted with religious communities with such chaste love that they will not permit you to lack anything necessary for the support of your little bodies.

“Again and again I ask you, excellent bishop, by the divine grace of the aforesaid monastery, to take the greatest care and to see diligently, with great piety, that their reputation is protected.

“If anyone gives you unjust advice, I beg you to answer with authority: for what is done by a bishop’s word ought not merely not to be taken away; indeed, it cannot be taken away at all. This is especially so because the authority of the holy Pope Urban himself urged this, so that I may believe this of you, my holy lord and bishop.

“Never will such an unjust suggestion prevail with you that, contrary to the just will of any bishop, the property which through my diligence has increased greatly for you and has almost doubled should be [affected—reading syntactically uncertain].

“Furthermore, the merciful God, through my insignificance, has granted exemption from taxes over a large part of the lands, both near the city and within it, as well as in the suburbs and villages.”

### 62.

“Accordingly, of the Ancharian estate, from which we gave a small portion to the monastery, we retain much: approximately one hundred *aripennes* of vineyards, more or less, and fields amounting to three hundred *modii*. Thus the aforesaid monastery possesses forty *modiates* of the land which I planted; and of the old vineyard we transferred scarcely thirty *aripennes*.

“We have reserved for your holy church, as their provision, the Gallicuman estate, the Mercloan estate, or the Gemellos estate, with its ponds and marshes, with all its rights and boundaries; also pasture in the Stone Field; and, if there are any others, the field at Trifinitium above the fortified road, and all the remaining properties; the Orvedan estate, the Martinatian estate, and the Silvan estate, in which the church of Saint Mary of Ratis is situated; and the Missiaman estate, with all its associated pastures and marshes, with all its rights and boundaries.

“Therefore, holy bishop, I adjure you: if almighty God, through the hands of those who fear him, grants some greater good to holy Mother Church, do not let your holy affection separate one from the other. But if—God forbid—the congregation there has not been assembled, or if afterward, when it has been assembled, it should cease to exist, let the property return to Mother Church.”

### 63.

“I have written these things to satisfy my fear. Far be it from me that you, most pious bishop, should be accused of ignorance; for, as I have already said above, divine piety has granted that, through my humility, exemption from taxes should be given to the Church in so many respects.

“What we have given to the monastery with the consent of the brothers, I confirm through this disposition of mine.

“To our handmaid Caesaria, the abbess, I wish the larger cloak which she herself made from hemp to be given. To my lord Leo the priest I wish a towel to be given. To my lord Cyprian the bishop I wish a cloak and the best of everything to be given. Whatever I have given to my servant Bricianus, I now confirm through this testament of mine.

“Let Agritia, my own girl, serve most willingly in the monastery of Saint Caesaria the abbess; and I confirm the *gariolae* which I gave to them or to their parents.

“I commend all my chamberlains to you, lord bishop, before God and his angels.”

### 64.

Cointius, under the year 542, no. 24, regards the word *archbishop*, which appears in the testament, as suspect and thinks that *bishop* should more correctly be read. This seems not improbable, since Caesarius himself calls himself a bishop in this way.

Dionysius Sammarthanus confirms this correction in volume II of *Gallia Christiana*, documents, col. 501, where he states that in the manuscript copy sent to him *bishop* is always read.

Here also is an explanation of certain barbarous words. In no. 59, the successor of the bishop is given “a shaggy chasuble and a tunic or *galnape*.”

The word *chasuble* (*casula*) has various meanings. When it designates a garment, however, it generally signifies an outer garment. Today it usually means the outer vestment of a priest celebrating Mass; but at the time when this was written it more frequently designated the ankle-length garment worn by bishops, clerics, and monks outside the sacrifice and other sacred offices. I think the word should be understood here in this sense. Consult Du Cange’s *Glossary* under *CASULA*.

The added word *shaggy* (*villosa*) signifies the type of silk cloth which the French call *velours*.

Cangius says in his *Glossary*: “The tunic is the priestly vestment which bishops put on beneath the chasuble, as in Amalarius,” and so forth.

The same author discusses various matters under *GALNAPE* and generally explains it as a coverlet; but that meaning does not suit this passage, since the word seems to designate the tunic itself by another name. Perhaps *galnape* is corruptly written for *galbana*, and the tunic was so called from its pale, whitish, yellowish color, the color of *galbanus*.

Certainly *galbana* is the name of a garment in Juvenal, in the following verse:

> Wearing a blue, striped garment and a smooth *galbana*.

### 65.

It is likewise obscure what garment the Saint means there by the *amictory birrus*, for this word underwent many changes of meaning, as may be seen in Cangius’s *Glossary*.

Baronius discusses the *birrus* at length under the year 261, and says in no. 44 that it covered only the shoulders and arms. But the word can scarcely be understood here in that sense, since in Life II.10 it is related that Caesarius’s *birrus* was seized by the wounded Liberius and placed upon his wound; this cannot be understood of a garment so short.

I would therefore prefer to understand *birrus* here as a linen garment commonly called a *rochet*, from the Italian word *rocchetto*.

A little farther below, *pitacium* should be understood as a sheet of paper or a small written note: both the sense indicates this, and Cangius, often cited above, shows that the word is frequently used in this way.

*Mantus*, or *mantum*, which recurs in no. 63, means a cloak. Mabillonius, in volume II of the *Annals*, p. 273, interprets *mantos* as chasubles, and, in my opinion, not incorrectly. Cangius observes under the same word that the *mantum* was the principal ornament of bishops.

A *manutergium* is a linen cloth for wiping the hands during sacred offices.

Finally, I do not understand what is meant below by *gariolae*. Perhaps the word is corrupt, or perhaps one word has been divided into two, so that *veregariolas* could be read, if that word yielded a better sense.

### 66.

Quite a few writings of Saint Caesarius survive, but it is not my purpose to enumerate them all. We have already discussed both of his Rules and his writings against the Semi-Pelagians.

The other works that have come down to us are mostly homilies, or sermons by which the careful shepherd splendidly nourished and instructed the flock entrusted to him.

Casimirus Oudinus, in volume I of *On Writers*, col. 1345 and following, lists 158 sermons or homilies, to which he adds four letters. Yet these little works of Caesarius have nowhere so far been collected into one body; they are scattered in various places.

The learned Benedictines, in volume III of the *Literary History of France*, p. 197 onward, discuss at length the writings of Saint Caesarius, list their various editors, and attempt to show which are certainly his homilies and which are doubtful or spurious.

More than one hundred of them are printed in the appendix to volume V of the latest Paris edition of the works of Saint Augustine. Many are also found in the *Library of the Fathers*, but not all those attributed there to Caesarius are really his. Some were published by Vincentius Barralis, others by Baluzius and others.

Reader, consult the aforementioned *Literary History of France* if you wish.

### 67.

Saint Caesarius left us excellent admonitions in his writings. As an example, I wish to quote what he wrote to the abbess Oratoria, especially because in these admonitions he portrays himself beautifully.

Holstenius published them in part III of the *Code of Rules*, p. 19 onward, as follows:

“Listen to me, therefore, dearest sister and daughter. However much you may always desire to be occupied in spiritual pursuits, nevertheless, for the sake of the sisters, you will sometimes have to settle external affairs as well.

“You must therefore take the greatest care to handle temporal matters as though only for the moment, while always clinging more firmly to spiritual devotion and love, so that, once you have administered temporal affairs quickly, you may immediately return to prayer or reading as to your mother’s bosom.

“You ought to desire that, having cast aside worldly anxiety, you may always think about the service of Christ, because it is said: ‘No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs,’ and so forth.”

### 68.

“In everything, according to the Apostle, present yourself as an example of good works. Let your life, like a winged creature, always fly upward through desire; let it resound through speech and shine through example.

“When you have applied yourself to announcing the word of God to the sisters, or when necessity has compelled you to dispute for the benefit of souls and for establishing the tenor of the Rule, first weigh the matter with careful consideration, so that what you promise with your mouth you may fulfill in your deeds, and what you preach to others you may display in your works.

“Thus, first feel upon your own shoulders and necks whether you are loading the sisters’ necks with burdens heavy or light. For example, if you decide upon fasting beyond the daily practice, or abstinence beyond custom, or, as is usual, singing more psalms than normal in the assembly, you should be found first in the church and leave last.

“Undertake the labor first and lay it down last. In the daily nourishment of the body and in the common meal, be equal to those with whom you sit equally at table. Finally, take delight in the same flavors of dishes as the sisters, and let the servers or cupbearers offer you equal foods and common drinks.

“Let your primacy, which you hold at table, be the first thing you claim for the virtue of moderation, so that the throat nearest you and the stomach closest to you may feel the abstinence which your tongue preaches. Otherwise your subjects may perhaps say in silent thoughts: ‘How beautifully a full belly preaches abstinence to us and orders us to be content with the cheapest foods and drinks, while a throat filled with carefully prepared foods and drinks belches!’

“For the preaching of abstinence is acceptable when it is sung by faces made pale through fasting.”

### 69.

“In all these matters you should know that the following is appropriate: you yourself should first walk along the narrow paths by which you admonish your companions to proceed; you should fulfill all that must be done beforehand by your actions, so that afterward, like a pliable trumpet brought to sound by being struck, you may more rightly break forth into speech, because of the Lord’s saying: ‘Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,’ and so forth.

“Do not be more splendidly dressed than the others, but be more splendid in character.

“Among other things, you must guard with great care that you love equally all those in the monastery whose reins you have imposed equally upon your necks. Do not love one more or less, but arrange and administer everything, insofar as possibility allows, with equal judgment and equal moderation, and show them equal affection.

“Do not distribute what is necessary to particular individuals according to private affection, but to all according to the merits of each.”

### 70.

“Do not give precedence to the one who pleases you by her face and appearance, whom you know to be pleasing to your eye, or by whose more flattering service you have been charmed. Give precedence instead to the one whom the love of Christ and a more religious life have shown to be worthy.

“For you must sometimes have a knife at your throat for certain persons, carry a cautery on your tongue, and bear a rod and staff in your hand: with the knife, cut away vices; with the cautery, bring what has been cut back to health; by the discipline of the rod, correct; and with the staff, support the one who has been disciplined.

“When you are summoned to converse with secular persons, first arm your forehead with the trophy of the cross and mark your breast with Christ’s banner, so that Christ may deign to accompany you with his little virgin.

“Let your conversation always be mixed with seriousness and sweetness, and speak only as the matter and the time require.

“If they ask something which you have decided to grant, grant it with a cheerful expression. If something ought not to be granted, at least soften their request by the courtesy of your speech.”

### 71.

“Let many know your name; let many, insofar as you are able, experience your benefits; let few see your face.

“If it is necessary to converse separately for the sake of the monastery, do so with two, or certainly three, chosen sisters, because a good reputation, as well as the protection of a perfect life, is necessary for you. Human detraction is to be disregarded only when Christ is at issue.

“Let every action of yours always be for God, your speech about God, and your thought directed toward God.

“Except in the case of vices, which call not for compassion but for rectitude, I wish you to be compassionate toward everyone, pleasing to everyone, and a pious superior to everyone.

“Thus, according to Paul, may you be holy in body and spirit, while your mind is governed by the Lord, your bridegroom, and he directs your holy ways—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

It is sufficient to have brought forward these passages from the admonitions of Saint Caesarius as a specimen.

### 72.

Finally, I wish to conclude this commentary with the Saint’s epitaph. Mabillonius, in volume I of the *Annals*, p. 99, reports the following:

“After his tomb had been destroyed by the Saracens, his epitaph was written by Paulus Illustris in the year of the Lord 873, in the fifteenth indiction, under Ranigaudus the master, as is read after the epitaph in an old Arles manuscript, under the title *Restoration of the Tomb of Saint Caesarius*. Beneath that title the epitaph follows, much more accurately corrected than in Saxius and others, in this form:

> Here is seen a roof renewed with varied marble  
>   
> For Father Caesarius, the holy bishop,  
>   
> Which the accursed host destroyed in savage fury.  
>   
> By God’s power the sea swallowed it.  
>   
> When Rostagnus occupied this See of Arles as bishop,  
>   
> Paul, bowing down, diligently restored the work.  
>   
> May Christ grant him the rewards of heavenly life,  
>   
> And has joyfully joined him to the angelic choirs.  
>   
> And have mercy on us in prayer, venerable Father,  
>   
> So that our God may wash away all our sins.”

# OMITTED WORKS

## First Little Work, or Letter of Pope Hormisdas

In which that supreme pontiff confirms various regulations established by Caesarius and grants his requests.

*(From the Bollandists.) (C, S)*

### Paulinus [Hormisdas], to his most beloved brother Caesarius.

I rejoice in the Lord, dearest brother, and I rejoice without ceasing that in you the zeal for religious reverence burns so strongly that, through the uninterrupted continuation of tireless concern, you keep watch so that whatever pertains to the worship of God in the Church may be increased by new advances, and so that you do not consider anything sufficient for your duty unless you have always added something further.

You have a special and faithful care firmly implanted as your purpose. Hence the prophet, beloved by God, when he said, “I have always hoped in you, Lord,” did not believe that this devotion was sufficient for him, but added: “And I shall add to all your praise.”

True love is not accustomed to be content with services; charity considers itself deficient unless the fervor of affection boils over.

God, who examines and knows secret things, may indeed see the faith that clings to your heart; nevertheless, he does not permit his dispensation to remain hidden or his treasure to be concealed without increase. He commands his worshipers to bring hidden reverence into the open and to sing his praise with resounding rejoicing.

I say this because, as you have indicated in letters sent to us, you have recently established in the Church of Arles, in addition to the customary vigils of clerics and monks, choirs of maidens dedicated to God. You ask that in the monastery of these maidens, recently founded by you, your successors should never be permitted to exercise any authority whatsoever, so that the virgins consecrated to God, freed from every disturbance and annoyance, may continually serve almighty God with free minds.

It is worthy of priestly foresight to pierce hearts with the praise of chastity offered to God and to present to sacred worship, from those mystical seeds, the fruit of virginity. The Apostle declared this to be his highest desire in the sacred writings, saying: “I have betrothed you to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ.”

Therefore, gladly granting the requests of your fraternity, we confirm and decree by apostolic authority that none of your episcopal successors shall dare to claim for himself any authority whatsoever in the aforesaid monastery, except that, out of regard for God, while exercising pastoral concern, he should sincerely endeavor at appropriate times, as is fitting, to visit with his clerics the household of Christ the Lord established there.

Moreover, it is fitting that each sex, established in places suitable to it, should sing the glory of God with equal devotion, just as each awaits the hope of redemption with firm and complete faith.

You also ask that the sale and donation previously made to the monastery of those maidens of God be confirmed by our authority, hoping that the alienation of ecclesiastical estates may thereafter be prohibited by our decrees. We approve your purpose and acknowledge your desire to be so praiseworthy that we rejoice that such things are not permitted to you either.

Yet what reason demanded should be granted from the Church’s property for the support of those who were to serve the Church ought not to have been alienated by sale. The fruit of a good work ought to be free; the reward of upright devotion should be awaited rather than sought, lest the remuneration of charity be diminished by the profit of a sale.

Nevertheless, we confirm what has been sold or donated by you around the monastery of the virgins, and through these present decrees we likewise establish the alienation of ecclesiastical estates. Have this carried out by all priests belonging to the diocese of your charity, under your direction; for it is right that matters beneficially ordered in general should be obeyed in general.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

# Second Little Work, or Council

[Note: From the acts of this council, the only matter found here is the decree enacted concerning how much, and in what manner, the bishop is thought to be allowed to take from goods bestowed upon a parish church. That Bishop Agroecius was suspended by the authority of this council from celebrating the sacred Masses because he had ordained improperly and, when summoned to the council, had stubbornly remained away, is clear below from the synodal letter written to him. Baron., year 463, no. 13. The precise year and day on which this synod was held are unknown. We can nevertheless easily conjecture that it was held around the period in question, since nearly all the same bishops are found to have attended and subscribed to it who subscribed to the two following councils, the Second Council of Orange and the Third Council of Vaison. I have therefore thought it appropriate to place this assembly before those councils with which it deserved to share the presence and subscriptions of the same bishops. Carpentoractum is a city of Narbonnese Gaul, mentioned by Pliny, book III, chapter 4. Severinus Binius.]

## The Carpentoractan Council Held under the Presidency of Caesarius

### Constitution of the Holy Bishops

Of the Council of Carpentoractum, on 6 November, in the consulship of Mavortius, a man of illustrious rank.

[Note: Although the chronological indicators of this council seem to present nothing doubtful, I nevertheless suspect that perhaps the writers have led us into error. I am uncertain whether what everyone accepts is true—namely, that this council should be assigned to the year 527, marked by the consulship of Mavortius.

I infer this from the Third Council of Vaison, which was held in the year 529, marked by the consulship of Decius the Younger, on 5 November. For this Council of Vaison was convoked at the Council of Carpentoractum for the following year, in these words: “It was also decided that this should be observed: in the following year a council must be assembled in the village of Vaison on 6 November.”

Since, therefore, the Council of Valence met in 529, the Carpentoractan Council must have been held in the immediately preceding year, namely 528. This is also indicated by the day on which this Carpentoractan Council was held, namely 6 November, which fell on a Monday—the day on which councils customarily began—only in the year 528.

If we accept this, then instead of “in the consulship of Mavortius, V. C.,” we should read “after the consulship of Mavortius, V. C.” Mansi.]

That is, in the year of Christ 527; in the second year of Pope Felix IV; in the second year of Athalaric, king of Italy; during the prefecture of Liberius.

[Note: This year was established by the consulship of Mavortius, which is supplied in the subscription of Caesarius, bishop, by the only but by far the best manuscript of the Church of Lyons. To it we also owe the indication of the day and month, which was mutilated in the other copies. Jacques Sirmond.]

### Sole Canon

[Note: Vatican Codex: “Here begin the chapters: the constitution of the holy bishops at Carpentoractum in the time of Pope Liberius, concerning how much and in what manner the bishop may presume upon what has been contributed to the Christian parishioners. The chapter ends. The constitution of the holy bishops in the city of the Carpentoractans. Although, etc.”]

Concerning what has been contributed by Christians to the parishes, and how much or in what manner the bishop may presume upon it.

[Col. 1287A]

Although everything which ecclesiastical discipline has commanded to be observed is contained in many canons, nevertheless cases arise which require the priests of the Lord to arrange what pertains to justice according to ecclesiastical discipline.

And therefore, since, when we were assembled at Carpentoractum, a complaint of this kind reached us—that what is contributed to the parishes by any of the faithful is seized by certain bishops in such a way that little or almost nothing is left to the churches for which it was contributed—we have judged it just and reasonable that, if the church of the city over which the bishop presides is sufficiently well provided that, by Christ’s favor, it lacks nothing, whatever has been left to the parishes should be reasonably distributed to the clerics who serve those parishes or to the repair of the churches.

[Note: Vatican Codex: *are known*.]

But if it is established that the bishop has many expenses and fewer resources, then, in parishes to which a more generous contribution has been made, only what is reasonably sufficient for the clerics or for repairs to the roofs should be reserved; whatever is beyond that, the bishop ought to reclaim for himself because of his greater expenses.

[Note: Lyons manuscript reads the same, and the Anian manuscript has “of the basilicas.” Jacques Sirmond.]

Nevertheless, he must have no authority to diminish anything from that small property itself or from the ministry of the clerics of that place.

[Note: Thus explicitly read the four books used here: the Lyons, Anian, Rheims, and Beauvais manuscripts. The common reading, however, is not irrelevant: it referred these words to the bishop—“that he should have no authority to diminish anything from the ministries of the clerics of that place.” Jacques Sirmond.]

[Note: The following words through the subscriptions are missing and have been taken from the Lyons manuscript.]

It was also decided that this should be observed: in the following year a council must be assembled in the village of Vaison on 6 November.

### Subscriptions of the Bishops
## Subscriptions of the Bishops

Caesarius, bishop, in the name of Christ: I have reread and subscribed to our constitution. Noted on 6 November, in the consulship of Mavortius, a man of consular rank.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “I noted below on 7 November”; nothing else is added, but the names of the subscribers follow immediately. In these, however, the title “sinner” is consistently absent. After the subscriptions appears: “Here ends.” Then a letter is added, in which those words—*quam ut eorum* (“than that of them”)—are read just as they appear in the ancient manuscripts. Sirmondus found this objectionable.]

Contumeliosus: I consented and subscribed. Eucherius, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Lupercianus, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Constantius, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Alethius, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Julianus: I consented and subscribed.

[Note: In the Paris manuscript of the Society of Jesus College, one of the two most ancient manuscripts, this man subscribes in the Greek manner as *Joulianos*. Julianus Amartolus, who subscribed at the Second Council of Orange, likewise subscribes in Greek. The other bishops subscribe in Latin as here, though not in the same order. Hardouin.]

Prosper, sinner: I consented and subscribed.

[Note: Prosper, who attended this synod among the other holy bishops, was not Prosper of Riez—as Binius mistakenly says—but the bishop of Orléans. A letter of Sidonius to him is extant in Book VII, Chapter 15. The public records of the churches testify that he was renowned for holiness; from these his praise is sung in the church every year on 28 July. It is clear from the Council of Epaon that Julianus was bishop of Carpentras, for he is found subscribed there. We shall discuss elsewhere below the other more prominent bishops subscribed here. Severinus Binius.]

Vindemialis: I consented and subscribed. Porcianus, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Heraclius, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Philagrius, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Uranius, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Cyprianus, sinner: I consented and subscribed. Principius, sinner: I consented and subscribed.

# Letter of the Synod of Carpentras to Agroecius, Bishop of Antibes

[Note: This letter indicates that Agroecius himself was suspended for a year from the celebration of the sacred Masses by the judgment of the Fathers, on account of an ordination improperly performed by him, and because, when summoned to the synod to give an account, he neither came himself nor sent anyone else in his place. We think that this is the same man who is mentioned in the Third Council of Arles and to whom letters of Sidonius are extant. It is probable that in the headings of many letters in Sidonius, “Greek bishop” (*Graecus episcopus*) is corruptly read in place of “Bishop Agroecius” (*Agraecius episcopus*). See Baronius, year 463, no. 13. Severinus Binius.]

### A bishop who had performed an ordination contrary to the canons is suspended for a period of one year from celebrating the Masses.

To our holy and venerable brother Agroecius, bishop: Caesarius, bishop, and the other bishops assembled in the Synod of Carpentras.

Although you ought to have been present at the synod, either in person or through a representative, so that at the synodal assembly you might give an account of the ordination which you are said to have performed, and so that, if you had acted rightly, you might return acquitted, with charity and God’s favor; but if it should certainly appear that you were a transgressor of the canons, you might learn the sentence pronounced by this present notification, so that the judgment issued in God’s presence might either strike the guilty man or absolve the suppliant—for although priests may not be ignorant of the canons, nevertheless your fault would have been almost less serious had you sinned through ignorance than if you had shown yourself a transgressor of the canons to which you or your representative had subscribed with your hand.

But now you are held bound by a twofold charge, since you are clearly shown to have acted rashly not only against the venerable Fathers but also against your own decrees. Therefore, by this common deliberation in Christ, we have decreed that, since our son Protadius is bound by the statutes inserted in the canons through you, and you likewise are bound by a similar sentence, you must not presume to celebrate the Masses until a year has elapsed.

[Note: The Lyons manuscript reads: “Within the sentence established by the canons, you are inserted and bound until the year has elapsed,” and so forth.]

[Note: This penalty had been established by canon 3 of the Council of Arles against those who ordained anyone contrary to the canonical statutes. It is therefore probable that Agroecius’s case concerns this matter, as I have said. Jacob Sirmondus.]

For it is just that what is established among bishops in God’s presence should, by God’s favor, be preserved inviolate. For what reverence for observance will later generations display if the law is first violated by those by whom it was established?

Caesarius, bishop: I subscribed. Cyprianus, bishop: I subscribed. Constantinus, bishop: I subscribed. Porcianus, bishop: I subscribed. Gallicanus, bishop: I subscribed. Alethius, bishop: I subscribed. Heraclius, bishop: I subscribed. Principius, bishop: I subscribed. Contumeliosus, bishop: I subscribed. Julianus, bishop: I subscribed. Philagrius, bishop: I subscribed. Eucherius [manuscript: *Euchirius*], bishop: I subscribed. Prosper, bishop: I subscribed. Uranius [manuscript: *Oranius*], bishop: I subscribed. Luperianus, bishop: I subscribed. Vindemialis [manuscript: *Vindimius*], bishop: I subscribed.

# Twelve Books in Defense of the Three Chapters

## Book One

Same place.

### Chapter One

That Justinian, in his confession of faith, rightly professed that one of the Trinity was crucified, that blessed Mary was truly and properly the Mother of God, and that Christ has two natures. Same place.

That the Eutychians fraudulently attack the Council of Chalcedon under the name of the Three Chapters; before answering them, he sets forth his confession of faith. 532.

That “one of the Trinity suffered” is more suitably said against the Nestorians than “one person of the Trinity.” The name “persons” began to be used in the Trinity because of Sabellius; and concerning baptism in the name of the Lord Jesus. 534.

### Chapter One

That it is not ignorance but obstinate defense of falsehood that makes a person a heretic; and that those who have erred in certain matters should not immediately be judged heretics. Same place.

### Chapter Two

That what has once been established in a synod ought not to be reconsidered. 833.

### Chapter Three

That rulers ought to show obedience in matters of faith, not usurp for themselves what belongs properly to priests; he teaches this by the example of the emperors Marcian and Leo. 838.

### Chapter Four

That the emperor Zeno, presuming to decide matters of faith, disturbed the Church with a long and serious schism. 845.

### Chapter Five

Conclusion of the entire work, with an exhortation to Justinian to acknowledge his error after the example of Theodosius. 849.

A chronological synopsis arranging and illustrating the principal events that occurred in the case of the Three Chapters. 851.

*Book Against Mocianus*. 853.

*Letter of the Catholic Faith* in defense of the Three Chapters. 867.
